## Part One: Basics

### 2.3.1 What Is Subjective Expectation?

The subjective expectation we discuss refers to the judgment the nervous system forms about impending events, based on all past and current information it can receive. Reading this sentence alone may suggest a clear, logical mental process, making subjective expectation seem highly rational. It must be emphasized that the term “expectation” here does not refer to a logically derived forecast such as the answer to “If it rains, what tool should one carry when going out?” On the contrary, most people describe this cognitive activity with the word “feeling,” and it typically occurs without deliberate “thinking.”

“Feeling” is in fact a rapid cognitive assessment and judgment formed by the neural centers when multiple strands of logical inference intermingle and influence one another. Its chief characteristic is that the individual does not know how the judgment was reached; the actor cannot clearly articulate the cognitive process.

For example, upon arriving at the office one morning, you notice more than one colleague glancing at you with flickering eyes; the moment they realize you are looking back, they all avert their gaze. Normally your assistant brings your favorite tea to your desk within three minutes, yet today the assistant seems to skirt around you—still busy with tasks, but noticeably odd. Someone is seated in the boss’s office with their back to you, identity unclear; when the boss sees you, they deliberately walk over and close the blinds. Even the ever-diplomatic Old Liu merely offers an awkward smile, bends slightly, then turns and retreats while walking backward.

Anyone placed in this situation would form a judgment of danger. Yet in the process of “sensing that something is wrong,” no “because… therefore…” reasoning occurs. Instead, like an animal, one applies the most primitive criterion—“how things ought to be at their best or most normal”—to perceive the surroundings. These are the expectations we refer to. More often than not, subjective expectation runs counter to rational thought, yet it is not easily noticed or brought into awareness.

Humans are an evolved animal species whose primary needs, like those of other animals, are survival and reproduction. To survive and reproduce, humans instinctively generate numerous expectations based on prior conditions. The following examples illustrate this seemingly abstruse concept.

1. **Subjective expectation in a dark environment**  
   Entering a pitch-dark space where one cannot see one’s own hand immediately slows and cautions every movement; this is an evolved instinctive reaction. The subjective expectation at that moment is that objects (people, animals, or otherwise) capable of causing harm may be present; even in their absence, collision with any object could cause injury. No one regards a dark environment as safe and warm, so the body naturally contracts while the limbs cautiously explore the surroundings. No one strides briskly or swings the limbs freely. In short, everything must be done with care.

   Some attribute this to fear of the unknown, because nothing can be seen. This explanation equates the root of fear with the unknown (invisibility). Yet why should the unknown necessarily produce fear, and why does this inevitable link exist? Continuing along this line of thought yields the answer: because the unknown (invisibility) implies possible danger. That is subjective expectation.

   Does the unknown therefore preclude any expectation of beneficial objects? Sometimes it can, but only when prior information has prepared the ground—for instance, secretive behavior by others on one’s birthday may suggest a surprise celebration. Such a situation is not truly unknown. Absent preparatory information and without any relevant signs, entry into an unknown situation triggers the survival instinct to generate a negative expectation at once; thoughts turn to self-preservation rather than to good fortune. For a living organism, seeking survival is the norm; expecting good fortune is not.

   A blind person remains unable to see yet does not remain perpetually fearful, because familiarity with dark environments and a distinctive mode of acquiring information render their subjective expectation of such settings safer than that of sighted individuals; darkness is ordinary for them. Certain psychiatric patients facing unknown dangers—for example, threatening gestures of anger from others—may likewise feel no fear, because they cannot cognize the stimulus and therefore form no subjective expectation. Thus the unknown is not the root of fear; the expectation that harm may occur is the root of fear.

2. **Subjective expectation in a bright environment**  
   Conversely, if no prior information suggests otherwise, pushing open a door and entering a brightly lit room where every corner is clearly visible usually produces no vigilance; one feels relaxed and at ease. In such an environment everything lies in plain sight, so the subjective expectation is that no negative stimuli will appear.

3. **Subjective expectation in a tense event**  
   The boss enters the open-plan office and loudly announces that year-end financial difficulties require laying off two-fifths of the staff. Tension instantly fills the room. Colleagues exchange glances; everyone fears for their own position. At this moment the subjective expectation of the great majority is that they themselves face dismissal. Even when rational analysis concludes that one does not belong to the group to be cut, few can fully trust that rational conclusion and remain entirely untroubled.

   Only when the final outcome is confirmed—including confirmation for those actually dismissed—can everyone truly exhale. Subsequent reactions differ: those retained feel relief; those dismissed feel dejected or argue their case; yet the preceding worry has certainly vanished. Estimating one’s score after the college entrance examination, however high, still leaves one unable to relax completely until the admission result arrives. The two situations are identical. Until a confirmed result is known, the inner expectation remains that an unfavorable outcome is possible.

4. **Subjective expectation in a relaxed event**  
   The most typical relaxed event is the collective, slightly foolish countdown of ten seconds at New Year’s to welcome the new year. The expectation discussed here is not the new hopes for the coming year—that is aspirational. We refer only to people’s subjective expectation of what will occur after those ten seconds. What is it? Cheering and leaping; every face around one beaming with joy; perhaps some tears as well, yet the atmosphere is certainly one of excitement and positivity enveloping everyone.

   This expectation requires no clear analysis or judgment, no deliberate thought—correct?

Dark environments and tense events share the same nature: both generate negative subjective expectations. Although the complexity of the triggers differs, the result is highly similar—fear of harm. Bright environments and relaxed events likewise share a nature: because one perceives a relatively strong sense of control and safety (for example, the setting or event is simple, or one’s command of the situation is strong), they produce a calm or positive subjective expectation. A positive subjective expectation, however, requires more auxiliary information to arise spontaneously. More often, when people feel strong control they generate only a calm subjective expectation.

Consequently, the human mental state tends more frequently toward the negative; yet this is not a misfortune, for the existence of these negative subjective expectations enables safer survival while simultaneously fostering a longing for happiness and hope. Once a happy fact arrives, the feeling of happiness becomes all the more precious, so that everyone pursues joy as a lifelong goal.

If happiness were the norm, normal human psychology could not sustain it. Deprived of the pressures of survival and reproduction, people would chase illusory spiritual pleasures such as drug use.

Those possessing genuine insight strive to maintain a balance—not quantitative, but qualitative—between pressure (negative subjective expectation) and joy.

A common saying holds that nine out of ten things in life fail to go as one wishes. The “wishes” in this phrase are not the expectations we discuss; they are the “intentions” formed after rational deliberation and may be rendered as “purposes” or “hopes.” Such considered aspirations are usually far more complex and ambitious than expectations generated by the survival instinct. Precisely for that reason, nine out of ten of them remain unfulfilled.

**Summary:**  
If the “subjective expectation” described above must be rendered in plain language, the closest equivalent is “a vague sense that … is possible,” yet it differs from a “premonition,” because a premonition is still something thought out and usually passes through conscious reasoning. With expectation, by contrast, one is often entirely unaware that such a judgment has already been formed.

### Emotion ABC Theory: Irrational Beliefs Deceived You

Activating event A is merely the indirect cause of emotional and behavioral consequence C; the direct cause of C is the belief B produced by the individual’s cognition and evaluation of activating event A.

Emotion ABC theory was originally proposed by the American psychologist Ellis. He maintained that activating event A is merely the indirect cause of emotional and behavioral consequence C, while the direct cause of C is the belief B generated by the individual’s cognition and evaluation of activating event A. In other words, a person’s negative emotions and behavioral disturbances (C) are not directly triggered by an activating event; they are directly caused by the erroneous beliefs (B) that arise when the person who experiences the event forms an incorrect cognition and evaluation of it<|eos|>

### 2.2 The Role of Emotions

According to the second explanation, the generation of emotions requires “situationality,” “objects that can satisfy a certain human need,” and “the opposite” (objects that cannot satisfy a certain human need) can trigger emotions of different natures. However, the dictionary’s standard definitions alone do not make clear exactly how emotions are stimulated.

People often say that reason is above emotion.

If we look at what people do in social life, it is true that rational thinking makes more decisions. Yet an important precondition is often overlooked at such times: everyone’s social activities follow the same or similar norms, and those norms themselves were defined by countless people using reason.

In the micro-reaction (微反应) research system, we hold that emotion is above reason.

Whether in social life or purely physiological activities (such as outdoor pursuits, sports, or eating), the first neural response to a stimulus is usually emotion; only afterward does thinking replace emotion as the dominant force. If the stimulus is too strong, thinking yields its dominant position and emotion takes over the body’s operations. Laughing at the wrong moment during an important performance, or impulsively harming someone despite knowing the serious legal consequences, are both decisions made by emotion.

Do not conclude that reason ranks above emotion simply because the quantity of decisions made by reason far exceeds those made by emotion. The human mind is actually quite fragile and easily drawn into emotional impulses; most major mistakes are driven by emotion, so the quality of emotion-driven decisions is closer to humanity’s animal nature. Moreover, most memorable events are the product of rational thought (because memory and thinking belong to the same type of cerebral-cortex function), whereas emotional impulses are not primarily based in the cerebral cortex and are therefore difficult to remember.

Emotions can be clearly perceived by others and exert an influence on the body. Some manifestations are obvious and may even produce serious consequences; others are harder to observe, such as changes in breathing or heartbeat. One thing is certain, however: wherever there is emotion, the body undergoes change. Even minute internal changes are still changes and can be captured by appropriate methods. This is the principle behind the development of the polygraph (formally called a “multichannel psychological recorder”).

Both emotion and reason are functions the nervous system uses to process external information. Reason is suited to relatively rational situations, while emotion is closer to animal instinct and better suited to handling intense stimuli.

Emotion is an evolved survival mechanism. From a Darwinian perspective, emotion better ensures survival (safety) and reproduction (love). All emotions operate on a single-layer logic: if something benefits me, respond positively; if it harms me, first compare and judge, then choose among rejection, confrontation, avoidance, or abandonment. These evaluative criteria are free of social standards and rest solely on the organism’s subjective feelings; therefore emotion can directly reflect the subject’s cognition and experience. This is also why analyzing emotion can reveal a person’s true thoughts.

In coping with complex environments, emotion can mobilize bodily energy and direct certain movements to maintain internal balance, especially the balance and stability of the nervous and circulatory systems. These tasks are too difficult for rational thought. No matter how intelligent a person may be, he or she is still an animal.

### 2. The Diversity of Expectation Mismatches

(1) A normal American driver in the United States

A normal American driver operating a vehicle in the environment described above forms expectations based on traffic laws and common sense, proceeding through intersections according to the rules. If another vehicle violates those rules, other drivers generally do not take excessive offense, though contempt is certainly present; a driver with a short temper may even become angry.

(2) A normal American driver newly arrived in China

A normal American driver who has just begun driving in China, besides learning the traffic regulations, does not know that China lacks the “unwritten rule” of taking turns at intersections. He therefore waits for vehicles from other directions to proceed in order. When he realizes that others are not waiting and that this does not violate any traffic rule, his long-standing habitual expectation is contradicted by the unfamiliar driving reality. Surprise, contempt, anger, and helplessness appear in succession, and he may eventually conform.

(3) An experienced Chinese driver in China

Chinese road conditions and driving habits constitute a self-contained system in the minds of most experienced Chinese drivers. In addition to obeying traffic regulations, actual road behavior includes many “flexible arrangements” that everyone tacitly understands. Consequently, ordinary Chinese drivers rarely encounter the kind of expectation mismatch an American driver experiences upon first driving in China. Although negative emotions may still arise when encountering particularly unreasonable vehicles, the subjective expectations of ordinary Chinese drivers generally align with actual road conditions, so normal Chinese traffic does not provoke excessive emotional fluctuations in experienced drivers.

(4) A “mature” Chinese driver in the United States

A driver familiar with Chinese road conditions and habits—for example, myself—encounters many expectation mismatches when first driving in the United States; in plain terms, he receives many stimuli.

The first time I queued at an intersection without traffic lights, I felt surprise mixed with confusion! Why had everyone stopped? There was no red light!

When my turn came to be first in line, I had not yet noticed the “unwritten rule” of alternating passage. I drove straight across the stop line and simultaneously saw the car on the left also beginning to move—fear! Wasn’t there going to be a collision?

My speed was faster; I did not see the reaction of the vehicle on the left, but I did see the driver opposite staring with wide eyes, then frowning in puzzlement, upper lip slightly raised and nostrils flared, expressing mild disgust. My confusion deepened! What was going on? There was still no red light!

Only after a companion later explained American driving habits did I understand the source of the disgust I had witnessed.

This example, presented solely to examine the origins of emotion, illustrates how different environments and different people produce different expectation mismatches and ultimately different emotions and reactions. Because of this diversity, special attention must be paid to the individual characteristics of the test subject and the testing situation when designing micro-expression testing protocols and analyzing results.

### 2.1 The Concept of Emotions

The Xinhua Dictionary gives two definitions for the word “emotion” (情绪):

1. Mood; state of mind; in low spirits; waking up in a bad mood.
2. The experience arising from a person’s attitude toward something. Often used interchangeably with “feeling” (情感), yet distinct. Emotion is linked to natural human needs and is situational, transient, and has obvious external manifestations; feeling is linked to social human needs and is stable, enduring, and not necessarily accompanied by obvious external manifestations. The emergence of feeling is accompanied by emotional reactions, while changes in emotion are also controlled by feeling. Ordinarily, an object that satisfies a certain human need elicits a positive emotional experience such as satisfaction, joy, or pleasure; the opposite elicits a negative emotional experience such as dissatisfaction, sorrow, or fear.

From an ordinary person’s perspective, the two definitions show no obvious distinction. If you wish to understand this book, however, you must read and reflect carefully on them, especially the second.

In the first definition, “mood” and “state of mind” commonly appear in phrases such as “in low spirits” or “in high spirits,” describing an overall bodily affective state. This kind of “emotion” lasts relatively long—hours or days, but also possibly only minutes. It corresponds closely to the English word mood.

The second definition contains two excellent points that require special attention: first, it is “situational, transient, and has obvious external manifestations”; second, what satisfies a need produces positive emotion, while the opposite produces negative emotion. The typical feature of this sense of “emotion” is that it requires a concrete situation to be triggered; different situations trigger different emotions, and the resulting emotions are short-lived. This sense corresponds to the English word emotion.

In the study of micro-reactions, the “emotion” we focus on and employ is limited to the second definition.

Because this type of emotion more accurately reflects the true inner state of the person involved. The first type of emotion can serve as a reference for overall judgment but cannot be used to determine truth.

The emotions examined and discussed in this book are generally very brief. The shortest lasts no more than one second (surprise); other emotions are measured in seconds and are extremely fleeting. Only one emotion—sadness—can last as long as several days, and the reason for this exception is explained in Chapter 8. It is precisely because emotion is both brief and authentic that the expressions it produces are genuine and reliable.

### 4. How to Manage Your Own Emotions

Emotion can constrain a person, can fulfill a person, and can also harm a person. Therefore we must manage our emotions well. To manage one’s emotions, one must understand a single point: emotion management is the adjustment of emotion, not the suppression of emotion. Emotion itself is neither good nor bad; what matters is the manner of its expression. What, then, is the healthy way to manage emotion? It is to express the appropriate emotion, in the appropriate manner, in the appropriate situation.

How, then, do we manage our own emotions?

First, we must observe our own emotions. Learning to observe one’s emotions is the first step in emotion management. We can frequently remind ourselves to pay attention to our emotions and ask inwardly, “How am I feeling right now?” For example, when a friend arrives late to a meeting, you can ask yourself, “What am I feeling? Am I angry?” Once you recognize that you are angry, you can adjust your emotion in time and remain its master.

Second, express your emotions appropriately. What constitutes an appropriate expression of emotion, and what constitutes an inappropriate one? Returning to the example of a late friend, consider the distinction. You might say tactfully, “The agreed time has passed and you still haven’t arrived; I was really worried something had happened to you on the way—you scared me!” By conveying the feeling “I was very worried about you,” your friend understands the effect his lateness has had on you. This is an appropriate way to express emotion. Conversely, if you accuse your friend, he will naturally focus on defending himself against the attack rather than considering the matter from your standpoint. That is an inappropriate way to express emotion.

Finally, release emotion in an appropriate manner. Releasing emotion means giving yourself an opportunity to clarify your thoughts and organize your feelings. What, then, counts as an appropriate method of release? We can measure it by asking several questions: How can I act so as not to repeat the mistake? Will this action cause greater harm? How can I reduce the unpleasant feeling? After asking these questions, you will understand that confiding in a friend, listening to music, traveling, or having a good cry are appropriate ways to release emotion, while drinking, speeding, or committing suicide are inappropriate ways.

### 4. Expectation Mismatches in Relaxed Events

At New Year’s, a large crowd foolishly counts down the final ten seconds to welcome the new year. Our expectation is that everyone will cheer and leap together at the last moment, surrounded by an excited, positive atmosphere.

- **Stimulus one**: At the instant the New Year bell rings, everyone around remains eerily silent instead of cheering and leaping as imagined. You feel extremely strange and may even sense that something bad has happened (promptly revising your expectation).
- **Stimulus two**: At the instant the New Year bell rings, in addition to the expected cheering and leaping, candy rains from the sky. You feel delighted—surprised and even happier!

If, having read this far, you still do not understand what we mean by subjective expectation, we must resort to our trump-card example.

The claim “I had no expectation” actually means you did not realize you held a certain expectation. Such subjective expectations usually concern matters one does not consider worth conscious attention. A simple illustration: you are using a computer to surf the internet, enthusiastically playing an online game or busily sending and receiving work emails. In this ordinary situation, do you have an expectation? What might it be?

Suddenly the network disconnects; web pages will not load; the game freezes. You can only stare helplessly. What is your reaction? You curse! If you determine that the disconnection was caused by human factors (the network administrator’s negligent inaction or malicious sabotage), you may feel contempt (for incompetence) or anger (for malice). If the other party then behaves arrogantly and self-righteously, your anger may trigger a fighting response. This occurs because your subjective expectation at that moment is “the network will remain connected and I will be able to continue what I am doing.”

Subjective expectation is therefore a trend judgment—“how things ought to be at their best or most normal.” Not only humans but animals possess it as well. If this important neural-response mechanism were lost and everything depended on rational thought to maintain external responses, animals lacking complex cognition could not survive, nor could humans.

It is upon encountering expectation mismatches that emotion is first directly produced.

### 3.1 Must Inner Emotions Always Have External Expressions?

Inner emotions always have external expressions, because these internal states of the nervous system and their external manifestations both carry important physiological significance; unlike thought, they cannot be retained purely in the brain without leaving any trace.

Every movement of the body’s muscles serves a physiological purpose, and the muscles of the face are no exception. Frowning, for example, besides signaling anger, doubt, or pain, can also indirectly close the upper and lower eyelids, thereby affecting the way the visual system receives information. Pressing the lips together, besides indicating displeasure, can prevent the instinctive urge to spit out bitter medicine. In other words, the facial expressions we take for granted not only convey meaning but also possess direct or indirect physiological functions.

Some of these physiological functions remain effective today; others have become evolutionary instincts that were once adaptive in ancient times.

Consider a threatening expression. Raising the upper lip to expose the canine teeth is not unique to humans; many wild animals open their mouths and bare sharp teeth before a fight. Such facial actions are essentially what we call expressions.

Human expressions, of course, can convey richer meanings. Before a friendly discussion, people smile at each other; when arguing a point, furrowed brows are common; upon hearing that a model couple has suddenly divorced, eyes widen in disbelief (“How is that possible?”); when someone self-importantly holds forth, a slight one-sided smirk (technically, unilateral upward pull of the corner of the mouth) may appear as a sign of contempt; in conflict, people glare or even curse; while watching a horror film, one gasps and the eyes widen as a chill runs down the spine; when bidding farewell to the deceased, the bereaved may have dull, lusterless eyes, yet the brows involuntarily lift in an effort to remain composed.

We must therefore clarify two points here:

### Psychology Mini-Class

Cognitive therapy emerged in the United States in the 1960s and 1970s. Its principle is to influence a person’s emotions and behavior according to their cognitive processes, thereby changing maladaptive cognitions.

Because people differ in cultural level, knowledge hierarchy, and environment, different individuals often hold different cognitions of the same issue. For example: in the same hospital, a child, based on their own cognition and experience, may regard it as a frightening place; an adult, based on their cognition and experience, may regard it as a place that saves lives and relieves suffering. Thus the key lies not in what the hospital objectively is, but in the different emotions different people develop toward the hospital because of differing cognitions, which then affect their behavioral responses.

For instance, a person with low self-esteem constantly feels they have not performed well enough, that those around them dislike them, and even their parents dislike them; consequently they remain gloomy and unwilling to interact with others. The strategy of cognitive therapy is to help them dismantle old erroneous cognitions, reconstruct their cognitive structure, form a correct self-evaluation, and thereby regain confidence.

Cognitive therapy master Ellis held that an individual’s interpretation and evaluation of an event they experience, together with their cognition and beliefs about it, are the root of the emotions and behaviors that follow. Therefore, when irrational cognitions and beliefs produce maladaptive emotional and behavioral responses, only by guiding and debating to change and rebuild those irrational cognitions and beliefs can the therapeutic goal be reached.

Cognitive therapy is mainly used to treat various illnesses and psychological disorders and has shown notable efficacy in treating emotional depression. It is especially effective as a short-term treatment for adult patients with unipolar depression. Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania found that three months of cognitive therapy produced significant improvement in 80 percent of patients with unipolar depression.

### Pendulum Effect: Emotions Also Have Cycles

Emotions function like a barometer and follow fixed cycles. In addition, male and female emotional cycles differ markedly. Only by accurately grasping the cycle of emotions can one reasonably control them.

Have you ever experienced this: after a promotion or raise your mood is ecstatic and euphoric, yet a few days later you suddenly feel there is nothing to be happy about and begin to feel irritated by interpersonal relationships or other matters.

Just as the sea has tides and the moon waxes and wanes, human emotions also have cycles. Like a pendulum swinging between high and low, emotions alternate between elation and dejection. In the course of psychological activity under specific conditions, the higher the intensity of feeling, the steeper the psychological slope, making it easy to shift toward the opposite emotional state. In other words, if you feel extremely happy at one moment, the next moment is very likely to bring sadness.

Scientific research indicates that, under normal circumstances, the human emotional cycle lasts 28 days, cycling repeatedly from peak through critical point to trough. When a person’s emotions are at the peak of the cycle, they typically feel refreshed and cheerful, display strong vitality, show rich feelings, and are amiable toward others; when emotions are at the trough, the person often feels lonely and isolated, becomes irritable, easily develops rebellious feelings, and may even display unpredictable mood swings.

The emotional cycle acts as a barometer of our feelings; we can use it to arrange work and life rationally. When emotions are high, schedule more difficult or tedious tasks and do things one would rather avoid; when emotions are low, go out for a walk, arrange recreational activities, chat with family and friends, and seek psychological support from others so as to pass safely through the low period.

Then what are the differences between male and female emotional cycles? Let us examine them below.

### Chapter 3 The Natural Combination of Emotion and Expression

There are six universal emotions in the world: surprise, disgust, anger, fear, sadness, and happiness. Each emotion possesses specific micro-expression morphological features; from these micro-expressions the corresponding emotion can be accurately inferred.

Is there truly a necessary connection between emotion and expression?

The first step is to clarify the meaning of the term “expression” as used in this book.

According to the Xinhua Dictionary, “expression” refers to the external manifestation of emotion and is divided into facial expression, verbal expression, and postural expression. Facial expression is the manifestation of emotion on the face and is the primary form of emotional expression; verbal expression is the manifestation of emotion through tone, rhythm, and speed of speech; postural expression is the manifestation of emotion through body posture and movement.

Under this definition, expression is an integral part of emotion, just as vocalization is an integral part of language; the two are inseparable. Neuropsychological research also supports this view, holding that after the nervous system analyzes and judges information from a stimulus source, it produces a state of excitation or inhibition that directs the body to act; this complete “internal + external” process is called emotion.

However, the dictionary definition of expression encompasses facial, postural, and verbal aspects, corresponding fully to all meanings of the English word “expression,” for which “expression” is the more appropriate translation. Native Chinese speakers share an implicit habit: when they say “expression,” they naturally mean facial expression in particular, so the standard definition does not fully align with common usage. For reasons of convenience, rigor, and respect for habit, we limit the “expression” or “micro-expression” discussed in this book to facial expression only. This limitation will not be repeated hereafter.

### Diversity of Expectation Mismatch

- **Normal American driver in the United States**: A normal American driver operating a vehicle in the above environment follows laws and common sense as expectations and proceeds according to rules at intersections. If another vehicle violates these rules, other drivers generally do not take it too seriously, though contempt is certainly present; if the driver has a bad temper, anger may also arise.
- **Normal American driver newly arrived in China**: A normal American driver who has just begun driving in China, besides learning the traffic regulations, does not know the Chinese “unwritten rule” of sequential passage at intersections, so they wait for vehicles from other directions to proceed in order. After waiting, they discover that others do not wait, yet this does not violate traffic rules. Long-standing habitual expectations are contradicted by unfamiliar road conditions, producing surprise, contempt, anger, and helplessness in turn; ultimately the driver may become assimilated.
- **Experienced Chinese driver in China**

Chinese road conditions and driving habits, however, form a self-contained system in the minds of most experienced Chinese drivers. In addition to obeying traffic regulations, actual road driving involves many “flexible adaptations” that everyone tacitly understands. Therefore, when ordinary Chinese drivers encounter complex situations on the road, they are less likely to experience the kind of expectation mismatch an American driver newly arrived in China would feel. Although negative emotions may still arise when encountering particularly unreasonable vehicles, on the whole the subjective expectations of ordinary Chinese drivers largely match actual road conditions, so normal Chinese traffic does not provoke excessive emotional fluctuations in experienced drivers.

### 2.3.3 Differences in Expectation—Using Driving as an Example

Expectation is subjective and therefore varies greatly across different situations.

Anyone who has driven or ridden in a car knows that the driver’s seat easily generates various negative emotions. Except when traffic suddenly clears after severe congestion—producing positive emotion—contempt, helplessness, impatience, fear, and anger almost always appear. We call these “driving’s bad emotions.”

The reason is that driving has clear rules. These rules include not only officially issued laws and regulations but also the driver’s subjective expectations—other vehicles driving reasonably, safely, and smoothly.

When you are rear-ended for no reason, your mental expectations of reasonable and safe driving by others are contradicted by the accident; your first instinctive reaction is anger. When someone drives unreasonably—making an abrupt U-turn, changing lanes, cutting in, or driving slowly for no reason when nothing is ahead, or braking repeatedly without cause—these situations violate your expectations of reasonable driving and smooth flow; your first instinctive reaction is contempt and anger. When roads are congested and vehicles crawl forward, the slow speed contradicts your expectation of smooth flow; your first reaction is anger, which turns to helplessness once you acknowledge you cannot change the situation.

Subjective expectation is complex, however; different people in different situations form different expectations and therefore experience diverse emotions.

### 3. Expectation Mismatch in Stressful Events

The boss enters the open-plan office and announces loudly that year-end financial difficulties require laying off one-fifth of the employees. Tension instantly fills the room; everyone looks at one another, each fearing for their own position. At this moment your subjective expectation is: I might be the unlucky one.

**Stimulus 1:** Your name is not on the layoff list. You will? Breathe a sigh of relief and even feel a bit of happiness.

**Stimulus 2:** Your name is on the layoff list, but the name of someone worse than you is not. You will? Feel dejected and angry. Dejection comes from being eliminated; anger comes from the unfairness of the elimination.

**Stimulus 3:** A few days later another notice arrives: no layoffs after all, and because new financing has come through everyone will receive a raise. You will? Of course feel happy.

Hence the joke: Leader A enters the office: “This year’s performance is poor; each person gets a 100-yuan year-end bonus.” Everyone is indignant. Leader B enters the office: “This year’s performance is poor; the boss says we have to lay people off.” Everyone falls silent and looks at one another. Leader B continues: “However, after I argued forcefully, our department will not have layoffs, and each person will still receive a 100-yuan year-end bonus.” Everyone cheers.

The joke illustrates how to be a leader—essentially, how to set subjective expectations. The greater the gap one can create between subjective expectation and reality, the stronger the stimulus to the person.

### 2.4 The Core Value Like a Treasure Trove—Studying the Role of Expectation Mismatch

If you have patiently read this far, congratulations: you have obtained a very important treasure!

Why devote an entire chapter to explaining the “expectation mismatch” principle of emotion generation? Because this principle plays a decisive role in psychological testing.

Only by designing effective stimuli can one elicit genuine emotions from the person being tested; only then is it possible to capture the subtle changes that appear on the face and ultimately determine lies and truth.

To deliver effective stimuli—especially directional effective stimuli—one must first analyze the subjective expectations of the person being tested. Once those expectations can be hypothesized, expectation mismatch can be manufactured to stimulate the other party. The direction of the mismatch (that is, the emotional direction) remains under the tester’s control: information above expectation (evaluation) guides positive emotion; information below expectation produces negative emotion, and the specific type of negative emotion varies with the nature of the evaluation.

Usually we employ role substitution and decision-simulation restoration methods to analyze the subjective expectations of the person being tested.

This method is discussed in a separate paper. Stimulus sources also take many forms; besides the most common verbal questions, they can include visual stimuli, actions and performances, and situational shaping. (See the discussion of stimulus sources in Micro-reaction (微反应).)

### (4) A “Mature” Chinese Driver in the United States

A driver familiar with Chinese road conditions and driving habits—for example, myself—encounters many expectation-mismatch situations when driving in the United States for the first time; in plain terms, they receive many stimuli.

The first time stopping in line at an intersection without traffic lights produces surprise plus confusion! Why has everyone stopped? There is no red light.

When I reach the front of the line, I still have not noticed the “unwritten rule” of alternating passage and drive straight across the stop line; at the same time I see the car on the left also starting to move—fear! Isn’t there going to be a collision?

My speed is faster; I do not see the reaction of the vehicle on the left, but I do see the driver in the oncoming car staring with wide eyes in surprise, then frowning in puzzlement, upper lip raised and nostrils slightly flared sideways, expressing mild disgust. Confusion deepens! What’s going on? There is still no red light!

Only after a colleague later explained American driving habits did I finally understand the source of the disgust I had witnessed<|eos|>

### 1. Male Emotional Cycles

Some people think men have few emotions, but this is a misunderstanding of men. In fact, it is because male emotions are relatively hidden. If you observe the men around you carefully, you will certainly find that they also have times when they feel irritable and periods of emotional lows. For example, he may be cheerful every day, greet acquaintances proactively, and be the "life of the party" in the office, yet one day he suddenly stops wanting to talk and sits alone. That is likely when his emotions are in a low period.

Some women do not understand this characteristic of men. They notice their husband suddenly distancing himself, acting cold, and hiding away playing games or watching television. When they try to approach him, his reaction is hard to accept. Women who do not know the truth often misunderstand and think it is because their husband no longer loves them, but that is not the case. Everyone has a certain emotional cycle; it is just that some people show it clearly while others do not. Most people experience an emotional low about once a month, so feeling irritable or getting angry for no reason during this period is completely normal. At such times, a wife should not complain or doubt but should understand her husband and help him with psychological guidance.

### 1. American Highway Rules

During my time in the United States, I drove in the three cities of Washington, Denver, and Los Angeles. I do not know whether the entire country follows the same traffic laws, but at least in the places I visited, saw, and drove, not every intersection has traffic lights. Most intersections, however, have a "STOP" sign. In the absence of traffic-light constraints, traffic-police direction, or camera surveillance, every American driver I observed followed a shared consensus rule: vehicles stop at the intersection in the order they arrive, and one car from each direction proceeds in turn. See Figure 2-1.

By regulation, a driver who sees a "STOP" sign must bring the vehicle to a complete halt (speed zero), regardless of actual road conditions. This is a strict standard for obtaining a U.S. driver’s license. The consensus rule of queuing and taking turns (whether or not it is explicitly written into U.S. traffic statutes) has also become an ordinary subjective expectation among American drivers. Everyone considers this the proper way to proceed; they know it, and they know others know it.

### Chapter 2 Emotional Triggers

Emotion is the first neural response when a person encounters an effective stimulus; it cannot be deliberately "faked." Therefore, purposefully designing stimuli to elicit genuine emotions in others is the key step in tearing away their false front and striking directly at inner truth.

This chapter examines, in order, the following questions: what we mean by emotion, the important role of emotion, the process by which emotion arises, and the important role of emotion in micro-expression analysis. The opening text is relatively rigorous; readers should be mentally prepared.

If you are already convinced that micro-expressions can reveal a person’s psychological state and wish to proceed directly to the various micro-expression features of the face, you may skip this chapter for now and begin reading at Chapter 4. However, if you still have doubts, question the reliability and scientific basis of micro-expressions, or are very interested in micro-expressions and need foundational knowledge to strengthen your analytical ability, please read this chapter through patiently.

After finishing it, you will discover a small treasure at the end of the chapter—one that can raise your micro-expression analysis skills to a professional level.

### Psychology Mini-Lesson

One day the famous German chemist Ostwald was suffering from a severe toothache and was in a terrible mood. He took out a manuscript sent by an unknown young man, glanced at it hastily, found it full of strange statements, and tossed it into the wastebasket. A few days later his toothache eased and his mood improved. Remembering those strange statements, he decided he should read the manuscript again. He quickly retrieved it from the wastebasket and examined it carefully. The paper turned out to have great scientific value.

He recommended the paper to a scientific journal. After publication it quickly caused a sensation in academic circles, and its author later received the Nobel Prize.

Imagine what would have happened if Ostwald’s mood had not improved.

When people are in a positive emotional state, they easily perform at their best; judgment and analytical abilities function normally. Conversely, when people are in a negative emotional state, reason is affected, self-control declines, judgment and analytical abilities drop, and they may even act in ways they themselves find unbelievable.

### 3. Cognitive Appraisal Theory

In addition to evolutionary theory and bodily-perception theory, there is another view called cognitive-appraisal theory. This view holds that an emotional response arises only after a prior condition—the appraisal of the event. In fact, as early as ancient Greece, the philosopher Aristotle proposed a similar idea: that human emotions come from our view of the world and our relationships with those around us. Anger, for example, arises because we feel others are slighting us.

Following Aristotle, researchers represented by Arnold argued that emotion stems from the evaluation of an event’s meaning and importance. In other words, the importance we assign to an encountered event directly determines the type of emotion we experience. Lazarus held the same view, stating that “emotion is the physiological and psychological organization of responses to good and bad information in the ongoing environment; it depends on short-term or continuous appraisal.”

This position regards cognitive appraisal as the core of emotional response and better explains the differences among various emotions. For instance, in the same environment and under identical stimuli, different people may experience different emotions.

### 2. Bodily-Perception Theory

Another line of research holds that emotion arises from the perception of bodily changes. The older view was that we first experience the feeling of emotion and only afterward experience a series of bodily changes. For example, we first feel fear and only then experience a racing heart or sweaty palms.

Early on, however, William James, the father of American psychology, proposed the opposite view: “Emotion is the bodily change that arises directly with the perception of the stimulus, together with our feeling of that bodily change. We usually think we feel sad because we have failed and then weep; we feel afraid because we meet a bear, tremble, and then run. Yet the actual sequence is the reverse: we feel sad because we weep; we feel afraid because we run.”

Following James, the Danish psychologist Lange put forward a similar view, arguing that emotion is the result of visceral activity and emphasizing the relationship between emotion and vascular change. Thus James and Lange agreed on the origin of emotion: the sequence is that an emotional stimulus first produces a physiological change in the body, and that physiological change then gives rise to the emotional experience.

### 3. The Influence of Emotion on Life

Many people strive and struggle in career, wealth, health, marriage, and interpersonal relationships yet ultimately achieve nothing and even become depressed or develop various psychological disorders. They do not realize that the root of the problem lies in living inside a program written by their own past experiences.

The emotions generated by our life experiences affect our present life at every moment. Although time, place, and events differ, the same emotions keep arising, the same outcomes keep repeating, and similar troubles and sufferings keep recurring. The psychologist Freud discovered and confirmed that human behavior is constantly governed by the unconscious—that is, by the influence of the mind—and that the mind is largely formed by the emotions stored from past life experiences.

Human emotions continuously evolve and develop with life. Past emotions are stored in the mind like seeds, becoming life programs that influence a person’s present and future. If they are not resolved in time, these emotional seeds will continue to act on our lives as time passes and will shape our destiny.

### Context

Context is a general term that mainly includes three factors.

1. **Test background information** (English: WHAT): What happened before the lie-detection questioning? What results will follow once the lie-detection conclusion is reached (whether correct or incorrect)? Who ultimately stands to gain? Who ultimately stands to lose?
2. **Who is being tested** (English: WHO): The specific circumstances of the person undergoing the lie-detection test, including personality, behavioral habits, upbringing and educational background, representative past actions, position within the overall matter (location within the relationship network), and so on. Later chapters will convince you that different people lie in different ways.
3. **Testing environment**: The layout, lighting, objects, personnel, and other factors inside the testing space that may affect the person being tested.

The same stimulus source may elicit different reactions in different contexts. The same stress micro-expression may also carry different meanings in different contexts.

### 1. Evolutionary Theory

In the study of emotion, one line of research holds that emotion is the product of evolution. This view regards emotion as an adaptation to the environment, gradually formed by human ancestors in the process of adapting to the natural world; it mobilizes multiple different components simultaneously to cope with and solve various problems encountered. Tomkins, for example, stated: “Emotion is the basic motive of the organism, a set of organized responses that, once activated, can simultaneously cause many bodily organs to produce corresponding response patterns.”

Following Tomkins, Izard also held the same view, emphasizing the adaptive nature of emotion. He pointed out that emotion is a motive closely linked with perception, cognition, and motor responses. From a functionalist standpoint he stressed the importance of emotion’s external behavior—expression—linking emotion’s innateness and social learnedness, its adaptability and communicative function through expression. He also maintained that emotion comprises three aspects: physiological arousal, subjective experience, and external expression.

### 1. Expectancy Discrepancy in a Dark Environment

If the light is turned on and a group of friends stands in the room holding flowers, what is your reaction? Not only does the tension immediately relax, but a strong feeling of pleasure also arises. Because the contrast is so great, the stimulus produces an enormous surprise!

If you slowly move toward the light switch, encounter familiar furniture such as sofas and tables along the way, then successfully turn on the light and find nothing unusual in the room, what is your reaction? Besides bodily relaxation, there should be no other reaction, because in this process neither a negative stimulus nor a positive stimulus occurred.

If you suddenly hear a sinister laugh and feel a breeze brush past your ear, what is your reaction? Fear instantly intensifies—greater than the fear caused by darkness alone and greater than the fear caused by the sinister laugh and breeze alone.

In this situation, the expectancy discrepancy that triggers fear is the sum of the absolute value of the negative expectation and the absolute value of the stimulus from the fear source.

### 1. Definition of Emotion

When discussing emotion, one must give it a definition, yet this seems an impossible task. Like the concepts of “time” and “consciousness,” we encounter and use them constantly in daily life, yet it is difficult to give them an accurate definition. In fact, psychologists and philosophers have debated the definition of emotion for more than a hundred years without reaching a consensus. One statistical survey showed that the psychological community has produced at least ninety definitions of emotion.

In emotion research, different investigators focus on different points and attempt to define emotion from their own research perspectives, resulting in the lack of uniformity mentioned above. Here, from the standpoint of ordinary public understanding, we offer the following definition: emotion is a collective term for a series of subjective cognitive experiences; it is a mental and physiological state produced by the integration of multiple sensations, thoughts, and behaviors.

### Psychology Mini-Lesson

Ellis studied human nature and identified several patterns, summarized as follows:

1. People can be rational and reasonable or irrational and unreasonable. If one thinks and acts rationally, one will be very happy, competitive, and effective.
2. Emotion arises from people’s thinking, so psychological distress often stems from irrational, illogical thinking.
3. People possess both sociological and biological tendencies—toward rational, reasonable thinking and toward irrational, unreasonable thinking. In other words, every individual inevitably harbors varying degrees of irrational thoughts and beliefs.
4. Humans are language-using animals; thinking proceeds through language. Continuously repeating an irrational belief in internalized language inevitably leads to irresolvable emotional distress.

### 2. Expectancy Discrepancy in a Bright Environment

Conversely, when entering a brightly lit room where every corner is clearly visible, a person can walk and move about with relative ease. In such an environment everything is in plain sight, so the subjective expectation is that no negative stimulus will occur.

**Stimulus 1:** If nothing happens, how do you react? No particular reaction.

**Stimulus 2:** If friends are already standing in the brightly lit room holding flowers, how do you react? There is surprise, but the degree of surprise is certainly not as intense as in the identical situation in a dark environment.

**Stimulus 3:** You turn around and suddenly find someone pressing a sharp pair of scissors against your abdomen while covering your mouth. How do you react? Intense fear. The prior expectation of safety clashes with the fact of fear, again producing an absolute-value summation.

### 2. Does the Presence of an Expression Necessarily Indicate the Presence of Emotion?

The answer to this question is: not necessarily.

From birth onward, years of accumulation enable people to produce various common expressions at will; this is even easier for actors. A good actor can even precisely control a single eye to shed a tear within two seconds.

Therefore, merely observing an expression does not confirm that the person has genuinely experienced the corresponding emotion.

In psychological testing, to maximize the chance of confirming inner states by observing subtle changes in expression, one necessary step must be added—effective stimulation. Effective stimulation means designing a stimulus source according to the specific circumstances of the person being tested so as to elicit genuine emotion. Once genuine emotion arises, it will be expressed through facial expressions; what we must do is filter out the false and capture the true.

### 2.3.2 What Is Meant by Expectancy Discrepancy

Simply put, it means that the way events unfold next does not match your subjective expectation. Expectancy discrepancy can be qualitative or quantitative. When expectancy discrepancy appears, emotion arises spontaneously. When events exceed (surpass, improve upon) expectation, people experience pleasant, positive feelings and thus positive emotion; when events fall short of expectation, people experience dissatisfaction and negative feelings and thus negative emotion.

1. **Expectancy Discrepancy in a Dark Environment**  
   If you enter a pitch-dark environment where you cannot see your hand in front of your face, your nervous system naturally assumes that objects capable of harming you may be present. Consequently you instinctively contract your body and send your limbs slowly exploring in all directions. You instinctively tell yourself: be careful.
