#### 4. Scenario Construction

Sometimes, to achieve more complex objectives, auditory, visual, behavioral, and performative factors are combined to design a scenario in which the target is placed without their knowledge, eliciting various reactions.

A film once depicted this method in detail; its English title is *The Truman Show*. The protagonist has been placed since childhood inside a scene constructed for a television program. Every street, house, object, neighbor, and person around him was arranged by the program; even the sky and ocean are virtual. Over the decades of his growth, every event and even every line of dialogue was scripted, yet he himself remained unaware. At the end of the film, the male lead walks out of this virtual world at all costs.

In criminal investigation and criminal psychology research, scenario-construction stimuli are also frequently employed. For example, investigators and relevant witnesses are positioned in the original crime scene; based on physical evidence, logical inference, witness statements, and other information, the suspect is required to reenact the crime process in order to help the suspect recall more details or verify whether prior statements hold. When the suspect is unknown, investigators may reenact the scenario in the suspect’s role to help identify more psychological and behavioral characteristics of the perpetrator and narrow the scope of the investigation.

Many real-world scams employ the same technique. In 2014, fraudsters rented space in an industrial park, disguised themselves as stationed military personnel, and posted “soldiers” in camouflage at the entrance to prevent outsiders from entering. They also spent heavily to install slogans such as “Listen to the Party’s commands, build the maritime frontier” on the roof of the rented office building. Even police attempting to enter for investigation were refused by the “soldiers” on guard, who cited the area as a military restricted zone closed to unauthorized persons.

The fraudsters created a highly realistic environment and claimed externally that a large infrastructure project was open for bidding, tricking bidding companies into paying various fees. After the case was cracked, prosecutors verified that the amount involved exceeded tens of millions of yuan.

Regardless of the stimulus method used, once the stimulus source takes effect, the target produces a large number of related reactions. The next task is to screen these reactions. The target’s responses may include social behaviors, emotional behaviors, and physiological behaviors appearing in combination. Based on the characteristics of the different behaviors, once emotional and physiological behaviors are identified, psychological analysis of the target can proceed.

This final step of psychological analysis is essentially an attempt to establish a causal link between the stress response and the stimulus source.

For example, if the suspect across from you is suspected of serial murder, then the following set of stimulus sources and responses may hold major investigative value.

Investigators show the suspect crime-scene and autopsy photographs from several recent murder cases and say: “The killing methods in these recent cases, although still using knives, seem much cruder than in the earlier ones!”

The suspect at this moment interlaces his ten fingers, stretches his body, leans his torso against the chair back, crosses and slightly extends his legs, and displays a trace of contempt on his face—short of disgust.

Although the suspect does not speak, analysis of his micro-reactions (微反应 (micro-reaction)) reveals the following responses:

- Interlaced fingers indicate a high level of self-control posture;
- Stretching the body and leaning the torso back are external signs of a relaxed mindset;
- Crossed and swinging legs are external signs of a dominant psychological state;
- The contempt expression maps an inner sense of superiority and negative evaluation;
- Not speaking is a social response that clearly expresses the suspect’s decision not to respond.

This entire series of responses stems from the crime-scene photographs and the investigator’s comment.

What kind of person, after such a stimulus source, would exhibit relaxed, superior, and negative subjective cognition? One logical explanation fits: these cases do not increase his culpability, hence the relaxation; the methods and results fall short of the level he believes himself capable of, hence the contempt. If this causal link holds, the suspect’s degree of suspicion rises substantially. Although he did not respond verbally and engaged in self-suppression, the emotional reactions that leaked out still provided major investigative clues. These two emotional reactions would not simultaneously emanate from an innocent person.

#### Greeting Your Own Expressions

Try doing this: stand in front of a mirror that shows your entire face, smile, frown, and pout. You will notice that as these facial expressions appear one after another, no corresponding emotions arise. In other words, smiling does not mean you are happy, frowning does not mean you are angry or worried, and pouting does not bring feelings of rejection or disdain. You can fully control the movement of your facial muscles.

Yet if you conclude from this that emotions and expressions have no necessary connection, you would be gravely mistaken.

You can certainly say that the presence of an expression does not necessarily indicate the corresponding emotion. However, when a genuine emotion exists, you must acknowledge that an expression will appear. But why do some people display one thing on their face while feeling something else inside, without others noticing? It is because most people cannot distinguish genuine expressions from fake ones.

Under the pressure of a series of social norms, everyone lives wearing a mask. For example, when meeting someone you dislike but cannot afford to offend due to various pressures, you will still smile despite inner disgust. Or when extremely angry yet unable to vent in public, you pretend to remain calm. Beyond social norms, some wear masks to conceal lies. Regardless of the reason, facial expressions convey only two messages: what one wants others to know and what one does not want others to know.

So what are genuine expressions? What are fake expressions?

Simply put, genuine expressions are unconscious reactions—for instance, the joy that lights up the face upon hearing good news—uncontrolled and without deliberate thought. Fake expressions are deliberately disguised ones, conscious reactions, such as a child showing a smile to parents while craving a toy.

Whether genuine or fake, the basic emotions remain the same: happiness, anger, sadness, disgust, surprise, fear, contempt, and so on. Frequently these emotions do not appear in isolation; anger and disgust may occur together, or surprise and fear together. This produces diversity and complexity in facial expressions. In addition, the escalation or de-escalation of emotional intensity produces different expressions, such as shifting from happiness to sadness or from impatience to rage.

The greatest difference between fake and genuine expressions lies in the mismatch between emotion and expression. For example, when you are happy but hear a friend’s complaint, you must adopt an expression of regret that matches your friend’s mood. The ability to consciously control one’s expressions is not learned only in adulthood. As young children, we often hear parental instructions such as “When someone greets you, smile back—that is polite,” “When someone gives you something, show happiness,” and “Don’t keep a straight face all the time; it makes people uncomfortable.” Over time, learning to control expressions and conceal true emotions becomes a habit and a principle of conduct, known as display rules (表现准则).

Setting aside the complexity that display rules introduce, expressions themselves number in the thousands, some lacking any corresponding descriptive word. Differences in intensity, simultaneous occurrences, timing, and duration further complicate the task of distinguishing genuine from fake expressions.

This does not mean we are helpless. Through extensive experimental research and practical experience, psychologist Paul Ekman summarized a set of “most seductive facial cues,” namely micro-expressions (微表情). Through micro-expressions, people can read the authenticity of expressions with greater subtlety. This analysis technique was adopted by the FBI in the early 1990s and remains in use today.

#### Observing a Series of Body Movements

Every posture a person adopts is like a word in language. To understand a language, we must combine words into sentences or paragraphs; only then can complete thoughts be expressed. Therefore, determining whether a group of gestures aligns with spoken language requires time. Likewise, identifying inconsistent movements to negate everything you hear demands repeated practice.

When observing someone, first consider all their words and gestures, then extract the main information, form complete sentences and paragraphs, and finally reach a conclusion. Do not focus solely on one sentence or one visible action. To ensure accuracy, observe the full sequence of behaviors. This is analogous to listening to someone speak: you must hear the entire statement, not merely a word or sentence, to grasp the intended meaning.

For example, while conversing with someone who appears highly capable, confident, and knowledgeable, you suddenly notice an extremely incongruent laugh. This single action largely overturns your initial impression. Moreover, tension appears in the arms and legs, and the body keeps shifting as if avoiding an unpleasant situation. You conclude that the person is not the capable, confident, and knowledgeable individual you first perceived. Yet you must also consider whether something you just said or did made the person uncomfortable or nervous. Therefore, when observing others, remain aware of how your own words or actions are being perceived so you can interpret the other person’s overall behavior more completely.

When observing a specific posture, note any other simultaneous behaviors that convey a similar meaning and use them for mutual confirmation. For instance, a salesperson’s coordinated set of movements (posture cluster) might look like this: while enthusiastically pitching a product, the person sits on the edge of the chair, feet apart with toes pointing forward, hands on the table, and torso leaning forward. In this book you will learn the meanings of these various postures, but the key is to consider them together to form a complete impression.

Understanding postural consistency functions like a monitoring device through which you can discern the meaning of a person’s attitudes and behaviors. This awareness prompts further observation and prevents premature conclusions based on superficial glances. In other words, it exerts a degree of control over your own conduct.

At first, interpreting body language may seem interesting and easy. Soon, however, you will discover that one posture can quickly be countered, reinforced, or confused by another. People untrained in “nonverbal behavior” often overlook postural consistency and reach one-sided conclusions. Our experience shows this has caused them considerable harm; many failures have arisen in exactly this way.

We have also found that the number of meanings a single behavior can carry depends on how many people interpret it. Therefore, remember that one posture represents only a single nonverbal cue; the information conveyed by the entire body is what matters. Shifting focus from individual postures to posture clusters reveals that they are inseparable, and body movements and postures become far easier to understand. This greatly aids recognition of the full meaning of human posture.

#### What Can Micro-reactions Be Used For?

Uncovering the “real thoughts” that a person intentionally or unintentionally conceals.

This description easily evokes thoughts of lie detection. Indeed, in popular culture and television dramas, the technique is often marketed as a mind-reading skill for exposing lies.

In reality, lie detection is one of the cutting-edge applications of micro-reactions (微反应), but relatively complete conditions are required to reach a true/false judgment. If the stimulus is inadequate, the subject maintains good control, and no obvious external reaction appears, micro-reactions cannot yield a judgment; the task must be handed to a polygraph. The polygraph measures indicators that are purely controlled by the autonomic nervous system—physiological signals entirely beyond the subject’s conscious will. Thus, even with no movement or expression and with heartbeat and breathing deliberately steadied, the polygraph’s sensitivity cannot be evaded.

Micro-reactions are not limited to lie detection. They apply to all interpersonal scenarios.

Whenever people interact, the technique can be used:

- Does the stranger you just met harbor malice or schemes?
- The blind date looks promising—should you invest real effort?
- What lies behind your boyfriend’s hesitation?
- Can the outwardly loyal subordinate be trusted?
- What is the true attitude of the deeply reserved boss?
- Why does the colleague’s polite and proper manner feel slightly off?
- Who in the team is secretly disloyal?
- Is the important client, whose face reveals nothing, satisfied or not?
- What does the other party’s silent smile mean at the critical moment of negotiation?
- Where is the fluent suspect lying…

The more complex social rules become, the more people must think and the more intricate their displayed behavior grows. Many harbor no malice and do not intend to do wrong or lie; they simply must act in accordance with social rules, sometimes without even realizing it. Many misunderstandings arise from this.

People’s genuine feelings and desires remain deeply hidden inside these “shells”; this is what we call “civilization.”

Obeying only the law of the jungle—communicating solely through body, teeth, and strength—belongs to a state millions of years in the past. If humans could always act like machines, making the most rational decisions and displays according to input rules, they would be “gods.” Unfortunately, no matter how complex social rules become and no matter how advanced the education of the person you are dealing with, that person remains human—a protein-based organism governed by the nervous system—whose every behavior is firmly constrained by the two fundamental drives of survival and reproduction. Precisely for this reason, feelings and desires closer to the animal core frequently leak through the “shell” in small traces that are difficult to suppress; most people are not even aware they should suppress them. These traces are micro-reactions and can be used to analyze and judge the person’s real thoughts.

Because behaviors triggered by physiological needs and emotional impulses are closer to humanity’s animal instinctual logic—a simple logic of “take the good, reject the bad”—these drives are powerful enough to have preserved humans on Earth through millions of years of evolution. A mere ten thousand years of civilization history cannot erase their influence.

Therefore, micro-reactions study and analyze human physiological and emotional behavior, not the readily observable words and actions.

#### 1. Micro-expressions

Micro-expressions (微表情) are a term that has attracted increasing attention. The so-called micro-expression is a psychological term referring to a complete emotional expression whose normal duration has been greatly compressed. Between different expressions, facial micro-expressions inadvertently reveal a person’s true inner state. In the United States, micro-expression research has been applied in national security, the judicial system, clinical medicine, and political elections.

Although micro-expressions appear fully on the face, they last only briefly before being masked by other or false expressions. Hence the defining feature of micro-expressions is their “micro” quality. Jiang Zhenyu notes: “The key point of ‘micro’ is the transition from emergence to disappearance; a micro-expression flashes by in less than 1/4 of a second.” Consequently, micro-expressions are generally difficult to capture, few people notice them, and research indicates that only 10 percent of people can detect micro-expression changes.

Precisely because micro-expressions are small and rapid, they reflect inner feelings and motives more truthfully than the other, consciously produced expressions people normally display.

Changes in facial expressions such as smiling, frowning, or showing anger quickly provide useful information about psychological and emotional shifts. By observing these changes, one can infer a person’s current intentions and motives.

People are often reluctant to voice their inner concerns, yet a sullen mood is written plainly on the face. Therefore, in daily communication we should obtain as much verbal and nonverbal information as possible through facial expressions. At the same time, understanding micro-expressions allows us to manage our own emotions so others do not read our thoughts.

A simple handshake, a glance, or a faint smile can convey significant diplomatic information. Accurately grasping the emotional meaning of these micro-expressions in everyday interactions, the workplace, or business negotiations can help capture opportunities for success.

In social interactions we deal with all kinds of people—some of good character, some not; some broad-minded, some petty; some reserved, some outgoing and warm. Misjudging people is one of the easiest mistakes to make, so reading people through micro-expressions is a profound art. How, then, can we accurately use micro-expressions to see into others’ hearts? This requires cultivating a discerning eye for observing micro-expressions.

Current micro-expression research remains at an early stage, focused on constructing effective measurement tools and equipment. Significant progress occurred in 2002 when Paul Ekman successfully developed the Micro-expression Training Tool (METT), which includes five parts: pretest, training, practice, review, and posttest. According to Ekman, training with this equipment enables people to quickly detect the presence of micro-expressions and improve their recognition ability.

#### 1. The Nature of Emotion

The nature of emotion is a survival mechanism that animals evolved and that has been continuously reinforced through evolution. Emotion supplies simple solutions to problems ancient humans frequently faced, such as generating fear and deciding to flee or generating anger and deciding to fight. The emotion mechanism is the behavioral drive produced after an animal cognitively appraises an external stimulus. It follows the simplest logic, like the most straightforward blunt person: whatever it thinks, it does, without hesitation.

Thus each emotion has a specific function—note, a specific function for the “primitive state” of humans. For people living under complex social rules, the function often lacks positive value, because the essence of social rules is constraint. By understanding the mechanism of emotion, we can work backward to infer the cognitive appraisal and feelings of the actor.

- Surprise is unexpected concern and prompts increased information gathering.
- When facing negative stimuli, first assess relative strength.
- If the stimulus is weaker, respond with disgust and move away or drive it off.
- If the stimulus is roughly equal in strength, respond with anger and attack to protect one’s interests.
- If the stimulus is stronger, respond with fear and flee or hide.
- If the stimulus has already caused irrecoverable loss, abandon effort.
- If facing a positive stimulus, feel pleasure or even excitement.

This simple mechanism evolved by animals ensures they adapt to the environment and survive and reproduce. Humans retain a powerful emotion mechanism; once an emotion arises, it can generate strong behavioral drive, including interference with social behavior. Therefore, when you see a certain emotion (micro-)expression on a person’s face, it indicates that the corresponding emotion has been generated. In a lie model, the cognitive appraisal and feeling represented by the emotion constitute the “reason for lying.”

A common dialogue illustrates this:

> “Why have you been avoiding me lately?”  
> “I haven’t! You’re the boss’s right-hand person now, busy every day until you’re exhausted—I wouldn’t dare disturb you.”

To aid understanding, the dialogue above has been made more direct, yet even from the words one can already form a rough judgment. In real life such exchanges are often more veiled, and the text alone does not reveal truth or falsehood. At this point, if the other person displays a disgust-type expression, it indicates unwillingness to meet you because of “looking down on you.” If an anger-type expression appears, the reason is “interests threatened” and hostility. If a fear-type expression appears, the reason is “power disparity” and reluctance to provoke you. If a sadness-type expression appears—helplessness or dejection—it indicates the person has already lost heart about the current situation. If a pleasure-type expression appears, the person is considering your welfare, does not want to add trouble for you, and hopes you will fare even better.

The same words, paired with different emotional drives, can mean entirely different things.

Therefore, we must identify the cause by recognizing the actor’s expression rather than listening only to the words spoken.

#### 1. The Nature of Emotions

The essence of emotion is a survival mechanism that animals evolved, continuously accumulated and reinforced through the process of evolution. Emotions provide simple solutions to problems that ancient humans frequently faced, such as generating fear and deciding to flee, or generating anger and deciding to fight. The emotion mechanism is the behavioral drive produced after an animal cognitively processes and evaluates external stimuli. It follows the simplest logic, like the most straightforward brute: it does whatever it thinks, without any reservations.

Therefore, each emotion has a specific function—note, a specific function for a person’s “primitive state.” For decision-making by people living under complex social rules, emotions often lack positive significance, because the essence of social rules is constraint. By understanding the mechanisms of emotion, we can reverse-engineer a person’s cognitive evaluations and feelings.

- Surprise is unexpected concern and prompts heightened information gathering.
- When facing negative stimuli, first assess the relative strength.
- If the stimulus source is weaker, respond with disgust by distancing or driving it away.
- If the stimulus source is roughly equal in strength, respond with anger by attacking to protect one’s interests.
- If the stimulus source is stronger, respond with fear by fleeing or hiding.
- If the stimulus source has already caused irrecoverable loss, abandon effort.
- When facing positive stimuli, feel pleasure or even excitement.

This simple mechanism evolved by animals ensures they adapt to their environment, survive, and reproduce. Humans retain a powerful emotion mechanism; once an emotion arises, it can generate strong behavioral drives, including interference with social behavior. Therefore, on the level of facial expression, if you observe a certain emotional (micro) expression on a person’s face, it indicates that the corresponding emotion has been triggered. In the lie-detection model, the cognitive evaluation and feeling represented by the emotion constitute the “reason for lying.”

For example, here is a common exchange:

“Why have you been avoiding me lately?”

“No way! You’re the boss’s right-hand person now, busy every day until you’re exhausted. I just don’t dare disturb you.”

To help readers understand, the dialogue has been made more direct, yet even the language already reveals the general picture. In real life such exchanges are often more veiled, making it impossible to judge truthfulness from the words alone. At that point, if the other person shows a disgust-type expression, it means he does not want to see you because he “looks down on” you; if an anger-type expression appears, it means he feels his interests are threatened and is therefore hostile; if a fear-type expression appears, it means he dares not provoke you because of the power gap; if a sadness-type expression appears—helplessness or dejection—it means he has already given up on the situation; if a pleasure-type expression appears, it means he is considering your welfare, does not want to cause you trouble, and hopes you will do better and better.

The same words, powered by different emotional drives, can mean entirely different things.

Therefore, we must identify the cause by reading the person’s expressions rather than by listening only to what is said.

#### The Meaning of Micro-expressions

To understand a person’s true thoughts and read another’s inner state, we must grasp the meanings of “micro-expressions”:

- **Raising the right eyebrow**: When a person’s right eyebrow rises, it indicates a question—either about what someone else has said or about something the person has done in the past.
- **Eyebrows pulled upward and tensed**: When a person’s eyebrows are pulled upward and tensed, the person feels intense fear. We produce this expression unconsciously while watching a horror film.
- **Staring into the other person’s eyes**: Sometimes a person maintains eye contact while speaking; this often indicates lying. The speaker is checking whether the deception is succeeding or has been detected. When someone speaks while staring into your eyes, pay attention.
- **Breaking eye contact**: When two people are engaged in eye contact and one suddenly breaks it, this does not necessarily mean lying; the person may simply be recalling something.
- **Eyes glancing left or right**: During conversation, eyes may drift left or right unconsciously, revealing inner processes. Glancing left usually signals recall; glancing right more often signals the construction of a lie.
- **Sudden pupil dilation**: This common expression conveys several states—fear, anger, or sexual arousal. Context and setting distinguish among them.
- **Flared nostrils and tightly pressed lips**: This expression indicates that the person is angry.
- **Left corner of the mouth raised**: When a person smiles with the left corner of the mouth raised, the smile is likely false. Roughly 74 percent of genuine facial feeling is expressed on the right side of the face.
- **Lip compression**: A classic ambiguous gesture frequently made by women. The person performing it is internally choosing or struggling.
- **Chin raised**: A sudden chin raise signals that the current topic is embarrassing; change the subject. If the corners of the mouth turn downward at the same time, the person is feeling self-reproach.
- **Prolonged surprise**: If a surprised expression lasts longer than one minute, it is feigned.

Many additional micro-expressions exist. Recognizing them helps us discern others’ true intentions in daily life. Once you understand micro-expressions, fleeting facial signals become sources of valuable information.

#### Question 2: Does Foreign Research Exist on Micro-reactions?

If we seek a foreign lexical counterpart for “微反应,” the original English term is “Micro-expressions.”

Many people know the striking term “micro-expression,” which corresponds to “Micro-expressions.” The term is not an invention of television drama; in its original literature, context shows it refers to facial micro-expressions—expressions of very brief duration or incomplete movement. Professor Paul Ekman is the leading figure in this research. He and his team have worked to apply micro-expressions to the judgment of genuine emotion in test subjects and have specifically examined their validity for lie detection, although the data have not been especially strong.

However, the Chinese meaning of “expression” is broader than facial display; it encompasses expression, manifestation, phrasing, and more. The standard translation is “mode of expression.” Facial displays, gestures, speech, and writing can all be “expression.” For instance, after a boyfriend says “I love you to death,” no woman takes the word “death” literally, because it is merely an “expression.”

The proper English term for “facial expression” is “facial-expressions.” Analyzing a person’s true psychological state should not be limited to facial expressions; one must observe and interpret the subject’s full range of expressions, body movements, and verbal content. In applied settings, judging intent solely from micro-expressions yields low success rates and efficiency.

Consequently, the literal translation of “micro-expressions” should not be confined to facial micro-expressions; “micro-display” would be more appropriate. Yet in everyday Chinese usage, “表现” usually implies deliberate display. If the object of analysis is deliberate behavior, one cannot reliably infer genuine psychological states, let alone use the data for lie detection.

When a stimulus is effective, a subject’s initial instantaneous reactions are overwhelmingly beyond conscious control and are therefore authentic. These reactions are quickly suppressed and masked, and their amplitude is small. For this reason we focus on “Micro-expressions,” where “Micro” means “minute.”

Because research on effective stimuli is as important as research on minute displays, we ultimately chose the word “reaction” to cover the complete stimulus–display process and distilled the entire subject into the single Chinese term “微反应” to correspond to the English “Micro-expressions.”

**Note**  
The most prominent scholar is the American psychologist Professor Paul Ekman. The term first appears in his works, such as *Emotions Revealed* and *Telling Lies*.

#### 3.4 Do Different People Show the Same Micro-expressions?

This is the final foundational question that must be addressed. When different people experience happiness, anger, or other emotions, are their facial expressions identical? Do identical expressions on different faces represent identical psychological states?

Humans can produce an enormous number of expressions. If one merely counts the combinatorial possibilities of the facial muscles involved, the theoretical number of distinct facial configurations far exceeds imagination—even before accounting for variations in contraction intensity.

Not every configuration qualifies as an expression, yet the richness of possible expressions is evident. People living in different societies may possess certain unique facial expressions for communication; many of these are learned. Nevertheless, from Darwin to Professor Paul Ekman, earlier scholars have scientifically demonstrated several basic expressions shared by all humans. Darwin clarified the evolutionary basis for such universal expressions; Professor Ekman traveled to primitive tribes in New Guinea to observe indigenous facial behavior among people who had never encountered so-called civilized society and therefore had no opportunity to imitate learned expressions. These respected studies confirm that the following emotions produce universally shared facial features in humans:

- Pleasure
- Sadness
- Surprise
- Disgust
- Anger
- Fear

Only these six basic emotions with universal expressions are noted here; further variations are discussed in later chapters.

In addition, expressions triggered by bodily stimuli—pain, drowsiness, and exertion—also exhibit cross-regional and cross-cultural universality and will be examined in the book.

Which emotions fall outside the scope of study?

Everyday language contains many additional terms for describing mood and state: awe, greed, suspicion, paranoia, jealousy, stupidity, pity, disappointment, expectation, regret, complacency, frivolity, and so on. Strictly speaking, these words do not denote human emotions; they describe external manifestations and often carry subjective evaluations.

We conducted a small experiment: the word “disappointment” was given to twenty different people, who were asked to imagine and describe the outward appearance of a disappointed person. The returned descriptions varied widely. Some described silence and departure; others described stamping and loud scolding; still others described a forced smile or a sigh.

Consequently, terms that carry evaluative connotations and do not directly name emotions (they should be neutral nouns) lie outside the scope of this book.

**Footnote**

[1] Of the facial muscles that construct expressions, twenty-two groups can be independently controlled. The combinatorial calculation of twenty-two yields approximately forty million possibilities. This calculation is merely a numerical exercise and has little relation to actual expressions.

#### Is This Too Dark?

In some situations an adversary wishes to conceal true intent; applying micro-reactions to adversaries can improve countermeasure efficiency. More often, friends cannot clearly express themselves through etiquette and language; applying micro-reactions to friends can improve communication efficiency. Just as knowing only Chinese limits one to a dubbed or subtitled version that may contain alterations or distortions, while learning English permits direct access to the original meaning, micro-reaction is a tool for understanding others.

What ordinary people observe is social behavior—performances staged for them.

“Ordinary people” here includes various professionals: police officers, soldiers, physicians, psychological counselors, leaders at every level, matchmakers, professional ideological workers, and so on. Most behavioral analysis rests on observed “performances” and draws inferences accordingly. When fortunate, the subject offers no concealment, and all words, actions, and micro-reactions are candid. Once the subject deliberately masks behavior, however, every word and action becomes potentially deceptive and cannot serve as a reliable basis for judgment.

Example:

A psychologist friend of mine, emphasizing his professional identity, discussed academic points with me. He argued that, based on the cases he had seen, clients seeking psychological counseling display extremely complex behavior that cannot be interpreted within a micro-reaction framework.

I showed him a recording. In the recording a suspect described his secret crush on a schoolgirl and his frequent fantasies of intimacy with her. Whenever such scenes arose in his mind, he felt intense shame, could not concentrate on his studies, and watched his grades plummet, becoming increasingly self-destructive.

After pausing the recording, I asked what he had observed.

My friend replied that he had seen the suspect’s tear-streaked face and anguished expression and had read pain, panic, helplessness, sadness, self-disgust, anger, and a young man’s self-reproach.

I told him I saw excitement. Clenched fists, a slightly hunched torso, gaze fixed on the words, rising volume, accelerating speech, and heavier breathing—all these signs of excitement occurred while the suspect described the girl and his infatuation. The nonverbal behavior contradicted the verbal content of guilt and remorse; it was not the behavior of contrition.

The recording was from an early interrogation in a rape-and-murder case. Several hours later, confronted with evidence, the suspect confessed.

I acknowledged frankly: “Yes, micro-reaction cannot interpret the ‘performances’ you observed. Social behavior is influenced by too many factors; its meanings cannot be exhaustively listed; theoretically it cannot be analyzed for truthfulness. In short, everything the person does and says is deliberately crafted for you to see. If you simply accept it and begin analysis, you are essentially jumping into the hole the other person has dug and helping to bury yourself. We look only at the minute reactions that could not be masked.”

#### Question 9: Can Micro-reactions Be Controlled?

You may think that, after rigorous training, you can control your own micro-reactions—immediately suppressing any outward sign once a stimulus is felt.

Controlling one’s body has two meanings:

- One is muscular control: the ability to execute movements precisely, skillfully, and with fluid start and stop. From this perspective, dancers—especially classical dancers—and athletes in disciplines that demand refined movement, such as martial arts or gymnastics, possess good bodily control.
- This ability, however, is entirely different from the control required for micro-reactions. It is control for performance.

The second meaning of bodily control is the capacity to manage responses so that the nervous system remains unperturbed by stimuli. Three types of people can truly remain “unmoved”:

1. The highest type transcends gain and loss. They feel no joy in gain and no regret in loss—even of life itself. This approaches a divine state.
2. The intermediate type possesses rich experience, deep reserves, and strong self-confidence. Anyone who reaches this level is no longer ordinary.
3. The lowest type practices self-hypnosis, forcing belief in something that is not true. This may be even harder; only certain individuals with mental disorders can fully achieve it.

These three types are also the most difficult to read when one is observing another’s inner state. Formidable politicians belong to the second type, accomplished actors to the third; the first type remains rare.

Yet none of these individuals can completely control their micro-reactions. Leaving aside physiological indicators governed by the autonomic nervous system—pupil size, heart rate, circulation, sweat secretion—which cannot be voluntarily controlled, even emotional motor actions executed by skeletal muscles are almost impossible to suppress.

Suppressing genuine reactions is a complex and demanding process:

1. First, one must not be surprised. One must anticipate the stimulus and decide in advance to control oneself.
2. Next, one must not care. Regardless of the stimulus, one must accept it and rapidly analyze its nature (benefit or harm) and intensity.
3. Then, one must not react. Through perception and thought, every possible bodily response must be identified and halted—perhaps with some missed.
4. Finally, one must double-check for any overlooked leakage and correct it.

Once everything is supposedly under control, are you satisfied? Listen: your rigid posture and wooden expression already indicate that something is abnormal and that you are hiding information you prefer others not know. That you show no reaction to such a gratifying (or horrifying) event is itself a tell. The inevitable existence of such tells is the very foundation on which the observation of micro-reactions rests.

#### What Are “Micro-expressions”

“Micro-expressions” are an involuntary revelation and concealment of inner feelings, a term from psychology. Sometimes people convey their inner feelings through facial expressions. Between or during these expressions, the face may briefly display a micro-expression that unconsciously “leaks” additional information. A micro-expression is an instantaneous expression, typically lasting 1/4 second and as short as 1/25 second. Through micro-expressions, we can determine whether we truly like someone.

Although this subconscious expression lasts only a moment, the trait readily reveals our underlying emotions. For example, during an interview a natural action can expose inner states: fiddling with one’s tie or jewelry indicates restlessness; tightly pursing the lips signals embarrassment; biting fingernails reveals a lack of security. Therefore, when others point out a small secret you harbor, do not be surprised—scratching the head, touching the nose, biting a finger, or blinking are all micro-expressions that can reveal psychological conditions. Sometimes a micro-expression conveys an emotion opposite to the one consciously felt.

Compared with deliberately produced expressions, micro-expressions more accurately reflect genuine feelings and motives. For instance, a fleeting contempt may appear within someone’s smile, or a stern face in a parking lot may suddenly flash fear.

Although we sometimes overlook micro-expressions, the brain is still affected by them and revises its interpretation of others’ expressions. Thus, when someone displays a natural “happy” expression containing no micro-expression, we can conclude the happiness is genuine. If, however, the “happy” face is accompanied by fleeting micro-expressions of “mockery” or “contempt,” we tend to perceive the face as “sly” or “untrustworthy” even without consciously noticing the micro-expressions.

In the popular American drama *Lie to Me*, the protagonist Cal Lightman is a micro-expression master who solves numerous major cases by reading these fleeting expressions lasting less than 1/5 second. When a person inadvertently shrugs, rubs the hands, or raises the lower lip, Lightman knows they are lying. By analyzing facial expressions he can read emotions—from hidden hatred to sexual impulse to jealousy. In short, micro-expressions betray a person’s true inner state.

#### 3.3 The Concept of Micro-expressions

In modern social life, controlled and disguised expressions far outnumber those that genuinely convey emotion. Although some authentic expressions flash by and are then suppressed or replaced by performance, careful observation can still reveal the inner state behind these brief, subtle changes. Such expressions may last only an instant and involve only slight muscle movement, yet even minute changes such as a slight eye movement carry meaning (provided an emotion is present).

We call expressions that are not under conscious control, may be triggered by emotion or by habit, last only briefly, or involve incomplete muscle contraction “micro-expressions.”

Each emotion possesses specific morphological features in its micro-expressions.

The word “or” connects “last only briefly” and “involve incomplete muscle contraction” because not every micro-expression is short-lived. A micro-expression may satisfy both conditions simultaneously (brief duration usually implies incomplete contraction), yet some expressions meet only the “incomplete contraction” condition while lasting longer. For example, a face that retains most features of a smile may also show a slight raising of the eyebrows that persists for a long time. The slight brow raise results from incomplete contraction of the medial frontalis. A full brow raise is a typical feature of sadness. Therefore the slight sadness marker mixed into the smile also falls within the scope of “micro-expressions” we study.

**Notes**:

1. Strictly speaking, habitual expressions are not genuine emotion-driven expressions and do not represent true inner states. Because habits, like emotions, are not under conscious control and produce unfeigned reactions, they serve as important benchmarks for judging changes in psychological state. Habitual expressions are usually treated as the subject’s baseline; they are important for analyzing the real psychological state behind expression changes and are therefore included in the concept of micro-expressions. For instance, a person who habitually blinks rapidly will continue to do so when not tense, so blinking cannot be taken as evidence of inner tension.
2. In *Telling Lies*, Ekman notes that as a clue to deception, micro-expressions “can fully display the concealed emotion yet flash by so quickly they are often overlooked. From appearance to disappearance, a micro-expression lasts less than 1/4 second.” Ekman further subdivides subtle expressions into micro-expressions, micro-momentary expressions, and other categories.

#### Faces Come and Go in a Flash

Under normal circumstances, the various reactions people display when expressing inner emotions occur naturally and instantaneously; any attempt to fake them appears stiff and deliberate. In most cases, if we do not pay attention to facial observation, we will not notice changes in the other person’s expression, because psychological states are reflected on the face in an instant—expressions come and go so quickly that missing them naturally prevents us from perceiving the other person’s emotional shifts.

The earliest research on micro-expressions took place in the United States. During the war on terror, the U.S. government sought greater advantage and therefore organized a large team of experienced psychologists to study lie-detection techniques in hopes of obtaining more information about terrorist organizations. Most current methods of detecting lies rely on instruments such as polygraphs. A polygraph works by registering physiological changes—elevated blood pressure, altered respiration, or changes in skin conductance—when the subject lies. In reality, a polygraph alone cannot conclusively determine that someone is lying, because it detects anxiety and other physiological reactions caused by lying, not the lie itself. Paul Ekman, professor at the University of California, San Francisco and one of the most distinguished psychologists of the twentieth century, evaluated the polygraph as follows: “It may miss the most dangerous liars—those who do not care whether they lie, those who do not know they are lying, or those who have been trained to lie.” Clearly, polygraphs are not reliable for exposing lies.

In his book *Telling Lies*, Paul Ekman introduces the Facial Action Coding System (FACS), the key to his research on identifying deceivers. During his studies Ekman discovered that the human face contains 43 action units, each formed by the movement of one or more muscles. These units can combine freely, producing the rich variety of facial expressions. Of the expressions formed, 3,000 carry emotional significance.

In China, research on micro-expressions and related topics remains in its early stages. The first scholar to explore the field is Professor Jiang Zhenyu, who studies psychological-stress micro-reaction testing. He states: “Many lies are accompanied by incongruent facial expressions that allow others to detect the deception. Even well-trained liars cannot always control the outlets of their true emotions; those fleeting facial expressions reveal the mismatch between words and emotion.”

#### Reactions to Nonverbal Information

Austrian psychoanalyst Sigmund Freud once said: “One person’s unconscious can unconsciously influence another person’s unconscious.” This means you may evaluate others on the basis of your own judgments and intuitions rather than facts—in other words, on the basis of a person’s body language.

A study by Harvard experimental psychology professor Robert Rosenthal and Nalini Ambady confirmed the power of nonverbal information. The researchers showed a group of undergraduates 32 video clips of different teachers lecturing and asked the students to evaluate the teachers. Because the audio had been scrambled or removed, the students could judge only by body language. The evaluations matched those given by students who had attended the full lectures and completed end-of-semester assessments. Although the latter attributed their ratings to friendliness or clarity of presentation, the study showed that most evaluations were formed on the basis of nonverbal communication.

By applying logical reasoning and deliberate assessment, you can avoid reacting solely to body movements. Without considering possible causes of those movements, you may be misled by body language. For example, a judge we know suffered a stroke during a trial; facial muscles twitched and the corner of the mouth drooped, making the defense attorney visibly uneasy. Had the attorney known the movements were involuntary, the unease would not have occurred.

To avoid misunderstanding, you must remember how your own expressions and gestures are perceived by others. At all times, be aware of the nonverbal messages you are sending. Are your arms crossed? Is your body leaning? If you adopt an open posture, others may be more receptive to your views.

You should also observe the other person’s body language. If you sense defensiveness, you can adjust your conversational style to make the person more receptive. Speakers call this “audience awareness”; they detect it readily. When they observe negative nonverbal cues from an audience member, they quickly change topic, tell a joke, or offer a humorous remark to elicit laughter and relaxation.

#### Experimental Case: Can Acting Counter Micro-reactions

We conducted an experiment in which subjects, while remaining naturally relaxed and in full control, were asked to repeat a performance three times to see whether rational control could produce identical repetitions. Cameras recorded each performance for later comparison.

During the experiment, three photographs were shown one at a time. After seeing the first photograph, subjects were instructed to devise a performance plan expressing the simple message “This girl is beautiful!” No restriction was placed on performance style; subjects were encouraged to use whatever style they controlled best—exaggerated or restrained—as long as all three performances were identical.

If subjects succeeded, the theory that micro-reactions can be suppressed by acting would be supported. If subjects could not succeed despite thorough mental preparation and a performance plan, the hypothesis—that acting cannot override psychological-stress micro-reactions (微反应 (micro-reaction))—would be confirmed.

The first two photographs were nearly identical images of a beautiful young woman; the third photograph differed markedly—an ugly animal, a disgusting face, a painful scene, etc.

The results were telling: none of the 87 subjects produced three identical performances, even though they had only one sentence to deliver. Even subjects with excellent control showed obvious reaction delays, prolonged gaze, stiffened and less mobile facial muscles, and increased respiratory control after the third photograph appeared.

The experiment demonstrates that changes in the stimulus source strongly affect response patterns; the greater the difference in the stimulus, the more it disrupts any performance plan the subject attempts to maintain.

In summary, when facing a highly skilled performer we hold two sharp swords. The first is control of the stimulus source: by presenting stimuli from multiple angles and at varying rhythms we can disrupt performance plans and leave the person little room or time to react. The second sword is baseline characteristics. Through successive layers of stimuli we obtain the person’s behavioral baseline—their genuine emotional and social behavioral features. Under these conditions, even if the person’s mind is highly developed and controls every coping behavior, they cannot restore the baseline features governed by real emotion. In simple terms, the performance no longer matches reality. This is why even excellent actors cannot use acting skill to counter micro-reactions.

#### Facial Asymmetry

Facial asymmetry refers to the situation in which one side of the face moves more than the other, indicating that the displayed emotion may not be genuine. As noted earlier, an asymmetrical smile is one clue that a person is lying.

Take smiling as an example. Smiling is one of the most common expressions in daily life. American psychiatrist Dr. William Fry emphasizes that life cannot do without laughter; without laughter people become prone to illness, including serious illness. Although laughter brings many benefits, in conversation we must recognize that not every smile is genuine; many people fake smiles every day. How can we distinguish them? It is not difficult.

When a person smiles genuinely, both corners of the mouth rise simultaneously and the eyes narrow. The zygomaticus major and the orbicularis oculi contract together. Because a genuine smile arises spontaneously and is not under conscious control, the emotional centers of the brain automatically tighten the orbicularis oculi in addition to reflexively lifting the corners of the mouth, causing the eyes to narrow, crow’s feet to appear, and the brows to tilt slightly.

In contrast, a fake smile involves only the corners of the mouth rising. A posed smile is produced by consciously contracting facial muscles, stretching the mouth, and lifting the corners. Unlike a genuine smile, the orbicularis oculi does not contract because the eye muscles are not under voluntary control and change only when emotion is truly felt. Sometimes fake smiles appear exaggerated, with strong muscle contraction that seems to bunch the entire face, creating the illusion of narrowed eyes. On closer inspection, however, the crow’s feet and tilted brows of the fake smiler cannot be faked. In other words, if we cover all but the brows and eyes of both genuine and fake smilers, the genuine smile is still recognizable, whereas the fake smile shows only lifeless eyes.

Therefore, to determine whether a smile is genuine or false, observe the eyes and brows—the most important clues. Even an expert in expression will show subtle differences between genuine and posed expressions. By paying attention we can detect those subtle differences.

#### Language Exchange from “One Glance”

In a vacuum, verbal communication is impossible. More precisely, people, speech, and body movements form a composite process. When communicating, we must combine these factors to follow and develop.

We are born with the ability to infer what someone is thinking from an expression. For example, we often notice that a person’s words do not match their body language. Intuition tells us something is wrong, but we often choose to ignore it or disbelieve its existence. Now is the time to trust intuition.

When verbal and nonverbal information conflict, nonverbal information proves more authentic. Therefore, in communication, it is crucial for posture and speech to remain consistent. The key to a politician’s electoral success lies in maintaining this consistency.

Of course, most candidates have received professional training to ensure their verbal information aligns with nonverbal behavior. Unfortunately, we can still see many senior politicians using body movements inconsistent with their words during speeches.

For example, when saying “I am very happy to have sincere exchanges with teenagers,” their fingers wave around, pointing and scolding them in public; or, trying to convince the audience they are enthusiastic, friendly, and concerned about people’s hardships, they repeatedly chop the podium with empty hands to emphasize their points. These are inappropriate body movements.

In the writing process, maintaining consistency between verbal and nonverbal information is also very important. This has been recognized by many famous writers. Especially in detective novels, key scenes often involve someone trying to cover up the truth, only for their behavior to betray them. World-renowned detectives like Sherlock Holmes and Miss Marple often use the subject’s body language to solve cases.

When studying an individual’s posture, we must make a series of related observations from various aspects, not relying on a single posture. This is what we call a “posture cluster”—a group of “nonverbal behaviors” combined from various forms. Posture clusters may involve many actions occurring simultaneously or one after another, such as arms crossed, ankles overlapped, and fists clenched, and so on.

#### Social Behavior

The most typical feature of social behavior is that the action is accountable to others; although ultimately for oneself, the direct connection is always something done for others. For example:

- Morning greetings must be heard or seen by others;
- Work presentations must be understood or approved by others;
- Polite gestures must convey goodwill to others;
- Party conversations must win others’ approval or even liking;
- Shopping requires handing money to others to receive goods;
- Job interviews, oath-taking, heartfelt talks, angry outbursts, chasing buses, queuing, seeking medical care, studying for exams, training for competitions, music and films, love and marriage, negotiations and competition, investigations and litigation—all are actions performed for others.

These matters follow different social rules; the specific steps and expressions may be simple or complex, and people must learn to master their performance in the process. The other side of the same matter is that mastery also means, in theory, complete control over how to perform.

Take language, a classic social behavior, as an example.

Language is an indispensable communication tool in modern civilized society, including both spoken words and written text. Language must be learned before it can be used; its function is to tell others one’s thoughts, which may be true or false. With practice, language can be mastered fluently; in face-to-face speech, one can achieve logical completeness and self-consistency, with steady and fluent pronunciation, whether the speaker is sincere or insincere. In fact, many true statements appear hurried, anxious, agitated, or indifferent precisely because the control is less refined.

From the perspective of cognitive psychology, the brain center controlling language is located in the cortex. Damage to specific cortical areas can severely impair or destroy language function. The human cortex is responsible for “thinking,” the highest cognitive center capable of logical and abstract thought and controlled behavior. For this reason, the proportion of the cortex in the human brain is far higher than in any other species on Earth.

In other words, every word you read and every utterance you hear is, in theory, 100 percent a deliberate product intended for you to read or hear. Given that, can what you hear or see be taken as “truth”?

The same logic applies to other social behaviors and will not be repeated.

#### Question 10: Can Performance Suppress Micro-reactions?

After repeatedly reading this book and memorizing *Microexpressions*, if one performs according to the rules for analyzing people, does that make lying invincible? Impossible.

Even the finest actors perform according to a script; even the most cunning swindlers execute fraud according to their own plan, yet they are more alert than actors because their opponents are living people, not scripted characters; even the most calculating corrupt officials rely on lines polished through countless prior corrupt acts, and once confronted with evidence they can no longer maintain consistency.

As noted earlier, without stimulus interference even a primary-school student can recite an essay vividly. To counter behavioral analysis with performance, one must know every possible stimulus that may arise during the performance, the most reasonable response to each stimulus, and then master every breath, every eye movement, every muscle relaxation, every postural shift, every expression, and every word through powerful memory and countless rehearsals.

You will find that an actor’s script essentially tells the actor which stimuli (plot points) will be encountered and how best to respond. Outstanding, emotionally invested actors therefore deliver lifelike performances. Their infectious realism stems from the fact that most professional actors adopt and practice the Stanislavski system—immersing themselves in the role, cultivating the required emotions, and performing from the inside out rather than mechanically. The performance feels authentic because genuine emotion is present; all expressions, movements, and vocal tones flow naturally under the appropriate emotion, which the actor has pre-generated in the mind through empathy or imagined situations. Thus they are not rationally controlling their actions and expressions; in fact, no one can.

In real life, even the finest actors, once deprived of a script and burdened with personal stakes, see every rehearsed plan collapse. Of course, actors who merely “show face” may engage in rational performance daily and feel they succeed, surrounded by fans; such cases fall outside our discussion.

#### First-Rate Operators Are Especially Sensitive to “Microexpressions”

As mentioned earlier, top-performing salespeople, interviewers who accurately judge whether candidates are lying, and management-consulting firms that revive multiple enterprises share the ability to perceive and interpret microexpressions at a high level.

Several individuals with superior judgment excel at distinguishing various forms of microexpressions; their abilities, both in experimental results and real situations, merit study. We therefore arranged interviews to learn from them.

One operator displayed remarkable sincerity; I wish to share an especially memorable segment of that interview.

The gentleman is referred to below as Mr. S. He has served as head of several enterprises, repeatedly turning near-bankrupt companies around. A management expert and first-rate operator, he remains a director of several well-known firms and chairman of his own company, a widely recognized figure.

Mr. S meets many people daily and communicates under varied circumstances. Especially during meetings, he can always identify “who does not fully agree with the content,” “who wants to raise a question but remains silent,” “who is interested,” “who supports his view,” and “who is skeptical”… When asked how, he simply replies, “No particular reason; I just sense it.”

I once attended a meeting with him and witnessed him correctly naming participants who wished to speak before they raised their hands, allowing the meeting to proceed smoothly.

Subordinates also recounted an impressive exchange. After a subordinate delivered an important briefing, Mr. S remarked only, “The briefing itself was fine, but your mood is off.” The subordinate had indeed been “in a poor mood”; he had quarreled with his wife that morning before entering the office.

These anecdotes illustrate how Mr. S routinely notices subtle changes or emotional fluctuations in his subordinates.

#### An Efficient Method of “Reprimand”

Consider the situation from the perspective of a team leader or supervisor. When a subordinate makes a work error, how should one reprimand? How can the same mistake be prevented?

Imagine this: a subordinate loses a major client’s lease renewal. When asked why the contract was not renewed, the subordinate accepts full responsibility, suggesting the explanation was insufficient and the client was displeased.

At that moment, what is the subordinate’s expression? Some show obvious remorse. Others merely feign remorse or even justify themselves righteously. Even if the surface expression appears remorseful or earnest, closer observation may reveal microexpressions that betray the true thought.

What microexpressions might appear? Try to picture them.

Expressions of “regret,” “shame,” “embarrassment,” or “guilt” indicate the subordinate is genuinely reflecting on the mistake and will accept advice or encouragement. After an error, such feelings activate a mechanism to avoid repeating it.

Conversely, if “contempt,” “disgust,” “anger,” or “fear” microexpressions appear while you are speaking or offering suggestions, attention is required.

A “contempt” microexpression suggests the subordinate likely dismisses your words. An “disgust” microexpression suggests the content will probably not be accepted. An “anger” microexpression suggests the subordinate feels your remarks are unfair. A “fear” microexpression suggests the error may have destroyed the subordinate’s willingness to try again.

Therefore, when reprimanding a subordinate or offering improvement suggestions, inferring emotional shifts from microexpressions enables appropriate responses and further guidance. The above examples illustrate how microexpressions can reveal emotions, guide success, and serve as a powerful support for team building and management.

#### Section 2: Are Microexpressions the Same as Expressions?

The German philosopher Nietzsche once said, “The mouth may lie, but the face reveals.” This indirectly shows that many lies are accompanied by facial expressions carrying special meaning, and these tiny facial movements can expose the shadow of a lie.

In real life, no matter how skilled a liar, someone can always expose the deception, because during the act the liar’s true feelings, though not expressed verbally, are fully revealed through tiny facial expressions, unnatural body movements, and hesitant or tense speech. Anyone familiar with microexpressions can quickly identify the liar. The renowned psychologist Freud noted that when conversing with a stranger, concentrated attention easily reveals whether the other is preparing to deceive. He added that during the act, a liar’s lips may tighten from tension and guilt, fingertips may “speak,” and every pore may betray the person—consistent with Nietzsche’s observation that the face reveals the truth.

Although people can identify liars through expressions and movements, most lack the ability to observe strangers’ microexpressions; they overlook important microexpression cues, allowing deceivers to succeed repeatedly. Jiang Zhenyu, director of the China Legal Information Center at China University of Political Science and Law, has stated: “In fact, most people cannot identify liars well; only a very small number are born with precise detection ability. The majority, even trained judges and customs officers, perform no better than a coin toss.” Thus, identifying liars through facial expressions is not easy. It requires both the awareness to read others’ psychology during conversation with strangers and mastery of certain microexpression-reading techniques.

To recognize microexpressions and thereby gain insight into an interlocutor’s mental state and obtain more advantages, let us now examine these remarkable microexpressions together.

#### Microexpressions: The Most Revealing Facial Clues

A microexpression (micro-expression) lasts only 1/25 of a second. It disrupts the integrity of an emotion and briefly replaces it with another expression. Because the duration is so short, it is difficult to capture with the naked eye, yet it is the facial clue most likely to betray emotion. Tracing the discovery of microexpressions inevitably leads to Paul Ekman’s experiments.

In the late 1980s, Paul followed a female psychiatric patient. Shortly after admission she applied for discharge, claiming she had emerged from her emotional gloom and longed to return to family life. Paul interviewed her and recorded the session on video.

Afterward, reviewing the tape in the observation room, Paul noticed, besides a few slight body movements, a fleeting expression. Slowing the footage, he clearly saw an extremely brief expression of melancholy quickly covered by a smile. The expression lasted roughly 1/25 of a second. Freezing the frame and comparing it with the subsequent smile, Paul realized the patient was lying; she had deliberately produced a radiant smile to convince the doctor she had recovered. In reality her depressive symptoms remained obvious. The patient later admitted she had indeed intended to deceive the medical staff so she could leave and attempt suicide.

Thereafter, Paul Ekman added a pause button to every playback of interview recordings so he could capture fleeting microexpressions at any moment.

Anyone can become skilled at detecting microexpressions through continuous practice. The practice is not merely memorizing expression features—although that is a basic exercise—but repeatedly viewing expression photographs. Research shows that after viewing several hundred faces, practitioners can usually capture microexpressions and distinguish genuine from false expressions.

#### Question 4: Why “One-Way Expression Is Not Analyzed”? (9787554606841)

If a person is autonomously outputting information from beginning to end (one-way output), none of the information expressed—including language, body movements, expressions, and even minute actions such as fist clenching, breathing changes, or torso leaning—can serve as a basis for micro-reaction analysis.

Large movements cannot be analyzed, nor can small movements. Why?

Because even the tiniest details are not reactions; they may be pre-prepared “expression schemes.” History contains countless real cases of this kind. Attempting to derive conclusions close to the truth from them is simply foolishly helping to bury the evidence.

A single extreme counter-example suffices.

A film contains a long, uncut take performed by a leading actor or actress. Every tiny eye flicker, inadvertent finger tremor, barely visible smile or pout—every detail on screen is moving. What does it prove? That the actor’s performed plot and emotions are his or her own real experiences and feelings? Of course not.

Whenever expression is one-way—whether by actor, politician, or schoolchild, whether recorded or live—full preparation is possible, employing every means to achieve the goal. Certain professions even require professional training before speaking to perfect the delivery.

Therefore, one-way expression is not analyzed, because it may in theory be 100 percent “performance”!

We analyze only “reactions,” which presupposes that we first apply a stimulus and then observe the subject’s instantaneous response to the stimulus information.

The more a stimulus breaches the subject’s psychological preparation, the more effectively it elicits a reaction; we call such stimuli “effective stimuli.”

Because these stimuli do not exist in the subject’s performance plan, the subject must temporarily engage the cognitive system for assessment and decision-making, thereby generating physiological, emotional, and social behaviors and, consequently, “micro-reactions.”

#### Question 4: Why “One-Way Expression Is Not Analyzed”? (9787554606841)

Actually, one-way expression can be analyzed

#### Stimulus Source

Genuine expressions must be triggered by authentic emotions. Therefore, to observe micro-expressions, appropriate stimuli are required to elicit the subject’s real emotions.

The most common method is to ask questions. Other frequent approaches include displaying images or videos, playing sounds, or delivering a message. In extreme cases, a person can appear suddenly after applying makeup. All methods capable of inducing emotional change in the subject are collectively termed stimulus sources in this book.

When analyzing authentic psychology through micro-expressions, it is especially important to note the logical relationship between the stimulus source and the subject’s micro-expressions.

For example, when a negative stimulus (such as a derogatory stimulus source) is applied, the subject is almost never expected to display positive emotions such as satisfaction or happiness. This logical relationship can both predict the direction of the subject’s micro-expression response to some extent and, when the nature of the micro-expression violates the logical relationship, support a judgment of deception in context. This serves as a key logical criterion for verifying truth or falsehood in psychological testing.

After enduring rigorous theoretical research, we finally begin examining the subtleties of each micro-expression.

Micro-expressions and standard expressions share the same lineage, originating from their common physiological mechanism—emotion. To master the morphological features of micro-expressions for each emotion, one must start with the fullest expressions, then progressively reduce certain local morphological features on the face and the amplitude of muscle movements until only the micro-expression features remain. Beginning with surprise, the morphological features of micro-expressions for disgust, anger, fear, sadness, and smiling are all studied according to this logic.

We start with the simplest: surprise!

> Note: The phrase “almost never” is used first to maintain rigor; second, in extremely rare cases, being belittled may elicit pleasure in the subject. For instance, if the subject intends to “play the pig to eat the tiger” (concealing strength while deliberately allowing the other party to underestimate them), they may briefly display a deceptive sense of satisfaction when belittled (as expected).

#### 3. Social Expressions

Social expressions are deliberately produced under the control of will, with the purpose of assisting verbal content so that the other party understands or trusts the speaker’s intent. Therefore, social expressions can convey only social intent and cannot be used to judge authentic cognition or feelings.

Through observation and imitation in various social situations from childhood, combined with many expressions that evolved from emotional prototypes into conventional forms, people employ numerous social expressions to aid communication.

Social expressions have two major characteristics:

- They lack a stimulus source as a prerequisite; the actor produces them voluntarily, and their meaning matches the semantics.
- They typically involve movement of a single organ or combinations of multiple organs, yet the movements are asynchronous and mismatched in amplitude.

In simple terms, social expressions are deliberately produced nonstandard emotional expressions. Because they are intentional imitations without underlying emotion, they cannot achieve the precision of genuine emotional expressions.

Examples include deliberately raised eyebrows, winking with one eye, smiling with lips pressed together or pursed while the eyes remain still, or a single lip-curl movement.

Social expressions vary widely and are always intentional; they cannot serve as evidence for analyzing authentic emotions. The most exaggerated social expressions can be described as “making faces.” Imagine someone conveying “sincerity” while making faces—would you apply serious attention and meticulous technique to analyze that expression?

Unfortunately, not all researchers worldwide can distinguish social expressions from the other two types. Much research focuses precisely on the recognition and analysis of social expressions, and interview expression-recognition software can identify only deliberately performed expressions. It struggles to detect single subtle expressions and is even less capable with composite subtle-expression combinations. This situation fails basic logical self-consistency and is regrettable.

#### 2. The Limbic System: The Emotional Center

The brain structure closest to the cortex is the limbic lobe, also known as the limbic system. The limbic system governs emotion; controls behaviors related to species survival, such as fight, flight, and sex; participates in regulating certain autonomic functions, such as hunger, sweat secretion, and heartbeat; and is involved in motivation, learning, and memory.

The limbic system is a collective term for several brain structures defined by their similar primary functions. These functions share the characteristic that they cannot, or can only minimally, be controlled by subjective will. Rational decisions from the cortex can at most intervene but cannot exert decisive control.

All human brain activity operates as an integrated whole rather than through independent parts, so information transfer and mutual influence necessarily occur between regions. Nevertheless, a region with clearly defined characteristics such as the limbic system can explain why a large portion of human behavior is not governed by will. Even highly capable individuals can at most indirectly interfere through “thoughts” and cannot exercise direct behavioral control—for example, over emotional behavior. This is an objective law determined by physiological structure and constitutes the scientific theoretical basis for using emotional behavior to interpret a person’s authentic feelings with high accuracy.

Positioned between the “rational brain” (cortex) and the “biological brain” (cerebellum and brainstem), the limbic system parallels how emotional behavior lies between social behavior and physiological behavior: it is close to biological instinct yet requires cortical cognition and reasoning for judgment.

Behavior controlled by the emotional center may be masked by social behavior, so methods are needed to filter it.

What method can filter it? The use of appropriate stimulus sources to force subjects back into an animal-like primitive self-preservation state, which reflects authentic psychological reactions. Such behavior receives the highest priority in observational credibility.

#### 3. Social Expressions

Social expressions are deliberately produced under the control of will, with the purpose of assisting verbal content so that the other party understands or trusts the speaker’s intent. Therefore, social expressions can convey only social intent and cannot be used to judge authentic cognition or feelings.

Social expressions have two major characteristics: they lack a stimulus source as a prerequisite; the actor produces them voluntarily, and their meaning matches the semantics; they typically involve movement of a single organ or combinations of multiple organs, yet the movements are asynchronous and mismatched in amplitude. Because they are intentional imitations without underlying emotion, they cannot achieve the precision of genuine emotional expressions.

Social expressions vary widely and are always intentional; they cannot serve as evidence for analyzing authentic emotions.
