#### Actually, One-Way Expression Can Also Be Analyzed

Actually, one-way expression can also be analyzed. This is not a contradiction but an emphasis on a basic principle.

If the goal is to obtain the other party’s authentic cognition (for example, whether they are lying) by analyzing their behavior, one must first establish a strict analytical rule—do not analyze one-way expression. The principle, already detailed earlier, is that one-way expression is easily faked and can become a tool of deception.

However, the vast majority of people in the world cannot control their behavior with such precision. It is extremely difficult to rehearse and control every movement, word, glance, and eyebrow. Consequently, even in undisturbed one-way expression, most individuals can control only the primary intended meaning, while the majority of subtle physiological and emotional behaviors remain.

The strict research principle of “do not analyze one-way expression” is adopted to ensure that scientific conclusions minimize interference from possible deception, so that the meaning of each micro-reaction (微反应) points cleanly and clearly to the actor’s authentic cognition and feelings. In practical application, it suffices to remember that social behavior carries the possibility of performative deception; one need not cynically assume every social behavior is a disguise.

Moreover, even the analysis of intentionally produced behavior alone can yield highly valuable information. This set of information is called “the actor’s intent.” Hairstyle, clothing, accessories, scripts, slides, fluent speech, etiquette, consumer goods, and so on, all plainly indicate what information the actor wishes to convey. Such information does not equate to objective fact, yet it accurately reflects the actor’s intent. Often this information is also very important: it forms the basis for building good social relationships and can be used to design partial response strategies toward the actor.

#### Muscles You Cannot Control

Once micro-expressions appear, another issue must be confronted: some expressions are simply beyond voluntary control. In other words, certain facial muscles possess strong autonomy and are difficult to govern by conscious will.

A 1982 report on the meeting between the Pope and Polish leader Jaruzelski described the Pope maintaining a smile and shaking hands with Jaruzelski with a “determined expression.” This conveyed an important message: the Pope had acknowledged Jaruzelski’s rule in Poland.

The event traces back to the strike at the Gdańsk Shipyard in Poland. Workers launched a major strike to secure a more relaxed political and living environment. The Soviet Union conducted months of military exercises along the Polish border to intimidate Poland. Many feared that if strike leader Wałęsa proved too radical, the Soviets would become dissatisfied and send troops to suppress the strike. After multiple rounds of confrontation, Wałęsa ultimately compromised. With Soviet support, the Polish army took charge, and military leader Jaruzelski became the nation’s top leader. A year and a half later, Pope John Paul II visited Poland. His arrival rendered the situation delicate; people speculated whether the Pope had come to support the strike or to support Jaruzelski. When the two men met, without a word spoken, everyone read the answer from the Pope’s expression—the Pope supported Jaruzelski.

Everyone knows the Pope was a master at controlling expressions. He could use his expressions to convey clear political signals, even if not always sincerely. Yet few people in the world could control their expressions as freely as John Paul II.

Some facial muscles can be controlled at will; others are difficult to control. We now clarify the most critical expressive muscles of the human face.

#### 3.2 Whether Expressions Are Honest

As illustrated by the images listed in Chapter 1, full and common expressions are quickly recognized by most people, who then judge the expresser’s state of mind. Historical records exist of individuals with brain-function damage who could not recognize expressions; infants under three years of age also cannot recognize all basic expressions. However, mentally normal adolescents and older individuals have no difficulty recognizing common expressions encountered in daily life.

Nevertheless, many obstacles arise in the process of interpreting expression meaning. These difficulties fall into two categories:

- The first concerns determining the meaning of complex expressions. As shown in the final set of images in Chapter 1, such expressions look familiar, yet ordinary people cannot accurately judge the expresser’s state of mind; they have a feeling but lack clarity and certainty.
- The second concerns expressions displayed by psychological experts with strong self-control. Whether a blank face or a convincing performance, these expressions are highly deceptive and difficult to interpret.

Overcoming the first category requires the ability to deconstruct complex expression features. Overcoming the second requires, in addition to deconstructing and knowing the subtle facial changes that belong to each expression feature, one further step: distinguishing genuine from false. In a single sentence, expressions triggered by emotion are genuine; expressions controlled by thought are false.

Expressions dominated by emotion are genuine expressions. The fuller the emotion, the more pronounced the resulting changes usually are, and the easier the meaning is to confirm. To determine whether an expression reflects authentic inner feelings, special attention must be paid to these genuine expressions triggered by emotion.

**Summary**: Where there is emotion, there is always an expression; yet an expression does not necessarily have a corresponding emotion as its support. Therefore, the generation of emotion is the foundation of the entire research system, and distinguishing genuine from false expressions is the core value of the entire research system.

#### Physiological Behavior

The most typical feature of physiological behavior is that it is directed solely at oneself. While objective outcomes may involve others, the direct associations are actions performed for oneself. Examples include:

- Eating, which resolves hunger and supplies the body with energy and nutrients;
- Drinking, which resolves thirst and supplies the body with water;
- Defecating, the final stage of food metabolism that expels unnecessary waste residue;
- Urinating, the final stage of water metabolism that expels excess water from the body to keep bodily fluids renewed;
- Sleeping, the rest process for the nervous system and body that relieves tension, enhances anabolism (production of cellular structures), and reduces catabolism (breakdown of cellular structures), among other functions.

These self-directed actions are necessary for individual survival. Except in extreme circumstances, no one can exercise complete control over them. On the contrary, these physiological internal needs exert powerful driving force on behavior and can even cause loss of reason and dignity.

In fact, among the eight major human physiological systems—including the respiratory, circulatory, digestive, nervous, endocrine, urinary, reproductive, and motor systems—only the motor system and the diaphragm plus related accessory muscles responsible for breathing can be regulated by cortical logical-thinking will[1]. Even the diaphragm’s routine movement does not require will; it is managed entirely by the autonomic nervous system under the joint control of the brainstem, medulla oblongata, and pons[2].

Thus, physiological reactions can map changes in the actor’s nervous system with high accuracy. The polygraph operates on this principle: it measures the subject’s skin conductance, heartbeat, respiration, blood volume, and other physiological indicators, then judges abnormal psychological activity (lying) according to the correspondence between anomalous indicator changes and the questions posed.

#### Keywords of This Book: Micro-expressions (Micro-expression)

You are probably already familiar with this term. Literally, “micro” means subtle, and “expression” refers to changes in facial or postural features that convey inner thoughts and feelings. It must be emphasized that expressions are not limited to facial expressions alone; that would be far too narrow.

Micro-expressions are inherited through long-term human evolution and are not subject to conscious control, so they most accurately reflect a person’s true inner world. In other words, micro-expressions are determined by the subconscious and represent an unmaskable truth of thought. They are often hidden beneath other expressions and vanish in an instant; only 10 percent of people can capture them. They can last as briefly as 0.04 seconds, yet that fleeting 0.04 seconds may betray you.

In the United States, research findings on micro-expressions are widely applied in national security, the judicial system, clinical medicine, and political elections. Many well-trained terrorists can easily pass polygraph tests, but micro-expressions shatter their false masks.

There is no doubt that micro-expressions constitute an advanced and discreet branch of psychology. Grounded in rigorous professional psychology, the authors of this book reveal without reservation how to simplify this difficult “professional technique” and apply it skillfully to everyday life and work.

If you are a manager, read this book carefully; it will show you how to lead a team more effectively. If you are an ordinary employee, be sure to master the “techniques” in this book; they will become your secret weapon for success. If you are a negotiator, do not overlook any detail; you will certainly need them. You do not have to predict the future with precision, but you must grasp the correct principles of analysis and maintain a broad perspective and vision.

Pick up this book. Until you see results, it will be your reliable assistant.

#### Common Facial Expressions

French physiologist Duchenne de Boulogne wrote in his book *The Mechanism of Human Facial Expression*:

We encounter many unfamiliar faces; these faces reflect people’s inner states. As age advances, the reflection becomes clearer. The face is a display screen that reveals all our inner activities—emotions, desires, expectations, and more.

The “face” we speak of includes not only static physical appearance but also dynamic facial expressions. A person’s forehead, eyebrows, eyes, nose, mouth, and other physical features, together with the movements of these parts, constitute what we call “facial expressions.” A normal person has 44 facial muscles that interact with blood vessels, nerves, and smooth, taut skin wrapped around cartilage and bone, enabling more than 5,000 distinct expressions. Each expression corresponds to a different psychological state. The ability to perceive these states has profound implications for success and happiness.

Psychologists have identified six basic emotions—happiness, sadness, surprise, fear, anger, and disgust—that are expressed relatively directly through facial musculature. The correspondences are summarized in the following table:

| Emotion | Forehead | Eyebrows/Eyes | Cheeks | Mouth |
|---------|----------|---------------|--------|-------|
| Happiness | Smooth | Lower eyelids slightly raised; crow’s feet appear at the outer corners | Cheeks bulge, sometimes narrowing the eyes | Corners of the mouth lift and the mouth lengthens; lips may part to reveal teeth; laugh lines appear outside the corners of the mouth |
| Sadness | Wrinkled | Eyebrows shortened and raised; a triangle forms between the brows, nasal root, and eyes | Muscles slack and dull |  |

#### Leading People Requires Leading Their Hearts—Start by Observing Subordinates’ Expressions

Many well-known companies with operations in Europe and the United States provide micro-expression training for their management teams. They understand that the ability to detect and interpret micro-expressions is highly useful for team building and management.

The essential elements of team building and management are “people, materials, and money.” Numerous solutions and countermeasures exist for issues arising from materials and money. But what about the human element? An organization is an aggregation of people, each with distinct emotions and values. The organization maintains the delicate bonds and distances among individuals. Yet if any one person’s emotions become entangled or collapse, the entire group suffers adverse effects.

In other words, when even one member of a team experiences poor emotional states, the impact is not confined to that individual or a few others; the overall team atmosphere deteriorates and everyone’s work efficiency declines rapidly. If early signs of deteriorating relationships or emotional friction among colleagues can be detected, timely repair becomes possible.

Team leaders who supervise many subordinates must monitor their team members’ emotional states to raise overall productivity. They must pay special attention to how subordinates are faring at work and whether their psychological condition is affecting performance.

Communication style with subordinates also cannot be ignored. Are you issuing instructions by email when a direct conversation would be possible? Do you assign tasks without making eye contact? Do you criticize subordinates’ mistakes solely from your own viewpoint?

Executives at well-known Western companies generally agree on the need to understand how to handle subordinates’ emotions. One method that has attracted attention is micro-expression analysis.

#### Observing Words and Expressions

People who study body language sometimes complain that their minds go blank and they fail to register information conveyed through others’ nonverbal behavior. You may encounter the same difficulty while learning, but take courage: fully mastering the techniques of nonverbal communication is a learning process, as difficult as acquiring fluency in a foreign language.

Most foreign-language teachers strongly recommend that students spend more time listening and watching fluent speakers’ pronunciation—that is, “immersive learning.” The same principle applies here: once you grasp the meaning of the body movements you observe, repeated practice will suffice.

As mentioned earlier, any gathering of people is an excellent observation site—airports, parks, shopping centers, and so on. Social gatherings and business meetings that permit free expression of emotion and attitude are especially suitable for thorough study, because participants are highly engaged and openly voice their views.

Another effective way to hone people-reading skills is to watch documentary reports, panel discussions, debates, or even fictional crime dramas on television. In simulated performances, actors display a wide range of emotions and intentions. Interview programs are also worth watching; during interviews you will unconsciously observe how the subject responds to questions through body movements.

While watching these programs, first try to follow the narrative from the visuals alone and note each person’s facial expressions, gestures, and postures. Then, every five minutes, turn on the sound and compare the verbal content with the conclusions you drew from the expressions and postures. Pay attention to the harmony and consistency of the expressions and postures.

#### Chapter 3 The Natural Combination of Emotion and Expression

Six universal emotions exist in the world: surprise, disgust, anger, fear, sadness, and happiness. Each emotion possesses specific micro-expression morphological features that allow accurate inference of the corresponding emotion.

Is there truly a necessary connection between emotion and expression?

The first step is to clarify the meaning of the term “expression” as used in this book.

According to the *Xinhua Dictionary*, “expression” refers to the external manifestation of emotion and is divided into facial expression, verbal expression, and postural expression. Facial expression is the manifestation of emotion on the face and is the primary form of emotional expression; verbal expression is the manifestation of emotion through tone, rhythm, and speed of speech; postural expression is the manifestation of emotion through body posture and movement.

Under this definition, expression is an integral part of emotion, just as vocalization is an integral part of language; the two are inseparable. Neuropsychological research supports this view, holding that after the nervous system analyzes and evaluates stimulus information, it produces excitation or inhibition that directs the body to act. This complete “internal + external” process is called emotion.

However, the dictionary definition encompasses facial, postural, and verbal aspects, corresponding fully to all meanings of the English word “expression,” which is better rendered as “expression” in the broad sense. Native Chinese speakers habitually understand “表情” to mean facial expression specifically, so the standard definition and common usage do not perfectly align. For convenience, rigor, and respect for usage, the “expressions” or “micro-expressions” discussed in this book are limited to facial expressions. This limitation will not be restated hereafter.

#### 2. Emotional Behavior

The central control of emotional behavior lies in the limbic lobe, positioned and functioning between the physiological and rational centers. Consequently, emotional behavior is guided by cortical judgment while simultaneously triggering physiological changes and muscle movements that are not easily constrained by the cortex. Once an emotion arises, basic physiological activities such as heartbeat, blood pressure, respiration, pupil dilation, perspiration, and gastrointestinal motility are affected, as are behaviors such as eye movement, muscle tension or relaxation, facial expression, and trunk posture. These behaviors may later be controlled by the cortex to achieve self-inhibition or concealment, yet they cannot be entirely prevented.

This is the origin of micro-reactions (微反应).

Behind every emotional behavior lies the simplest decision logic of the human organism as a biological individual, carrying the most direct physiological significance for safeguarding individual survival—identical to the emotional responses of animals.

For example:

- When surprised, one looks, listens, and senses more in order to judge whether the stimulus source is beneficial or harmful.
- When disgusted, one withdraws or rejects in order to reduce or block the continuing impact of a negative stimulus, without deeming it worth fighting.
- When angry, one mobilizes physical and mental resources to struggle, eliminating or reducing the threat the stimulus poses to one’s interests.
- When afraid, one hides or flees to ensure survival when victory is judged impossible.
- When sad, one accepts the outcome, ceases wasting physical energy on futile recovery, and relinquishes the attempt to reverse the result.
- When happy, one expends considerable energy laughing and becoming excited in order to quickly moderate the high neural excitation produced by a positive stimulus.

It is precisely for this reason that we can interpret emotional reactions to deduce a person’s true feelings and cognitions.

#### Training “Emotional Perception,” Starting with Reading the Other Person’s Expressions

Mr. S wanted to solve the mystery of “being able to tell what the other person is thinking or feeling.” It is undeniable that before acquiring mind-reading ability, Mr. S had conversed with all kinds of people and thereby gained intuitive and spiritual experience. Through countless social interactions and frontline management experience accumulated over many years, these encounters became spiritual gains.

Yet Mr. S’s wish was to “technologize experience.” Within the realm of experience, these abilities belong to rules of thumb that are difficult to convey clearly to others. Mr. S possessed the management skills required of an operator, most of which depended on his own level of competence.

When Mr. S learned of the existence of micro-expressions, he thought: “Perhaps it is because I can perceive micro-expressions. Micro-expressions are scientific; they can turn rules of thumb into techniques. Once techniques are created, they can be taught to others.”

For Mr. S, the phrase “balance of reason and emotion” was important.

Regarding this phrase, Mr. S said: “Acting reasonably earns others’ recognition while also understanding their emotions. Mastering the balance between ‘reason’ and ‘emotion’ sets an example for the new generation of leaders.”

In the terminology of emotional psychology, a rational mind riding the track of emotion constitutes the judgment, leadership, insight, and affinity that operators, supervisors, and managers must possess. The key to further strengthening “emotional perception” lies in the ability to detect and interpret micro-expressions.

#### Chapter 1 Without Micro-expressions, You Are “Out”

Is “micro-expression mind reading” truly so magical that a single, almost imperceptible micro-expression can reveal a person’s innermost thoughts? Although micro-expressions are remarkable, once you learn to observe and understand what they signify, they cease to be unfathomable.

After the American television series *Lie to Me* aired, it became hugely popular across the United States, especially among younger viewers, who began paying attention to micro-expressions and micro-reactions in daily life and social interactions. When the series, centered on micro-expression lie detection, was introduced to China, it rapidly captured Chinese audiences and sparked a wave of interest in lie detection. Subsequently, in 2010, Hong Kong’s Television Broadcasts Limited produced *The Mind Reader*, a drama strikingly similar to *Lie to Me*; its subject matter likewise involved solving criminal cases through expression observation. Although the actors’ expressions were somewhat exaggerated and stiff, this did not diminish public enthusiasm for “lie-detection techniques” and “mind-reading techniques.”

In *Lie to Me*, the male lead, Cal Lightman, states: “An ordinary person tells an average of three lies every ten minutes during conversation.” Have people really become so untrustworthy? Is “micro-expression mind reading” truly so magical that a single, almost imperceptible micro-expression can reveal a person’s innermost thoughts? Although micro-expressions are remarkable, once you learn to observe and understand what they signify, they cease to be unfathomable. This chapter will guide you into the world of human “micro-expressions” and explore their mysterious origins.

#### 1. Basic Physiological Activities

Basic physiological activities controlled by the autonomic nervous system proceed automatically without any cortical thought or command and continue even in the absence of any stimulus; examples include breathing, heartbeat, blood circulation, sweat secretion, food digestion, endocrine function, and pupil constriction or dilation.

In simple terms, these activities do not require “thought” to direct them. Their normal maintenance usually does not involve the first three processes—that is, they are managed directly by the autonomic nervous system without engaging the brain’s thinking and judgment.

However, cortical cognition, evaluation, and judgment can influence the state of these basic physiological activities.

When an abnormal situation arises—for instance, fright or joy—the brain receives stimulus information from the sensory organs, performs evaluation and judgment, and may also generate volitional behavioral decisions and overt actions. Yet the judgment produced by cortical rational cognition and evaluation also affects the autonomic nervous system and thereby influences basic physiological indicators.

For students, examination results are a highly significant stimulus, often carrying major implications for gain or loss. When a student sees his or her report card, the cortex applies highly complex rules of judgment that may include numerical scores, ranking percentages, scholarship or advancement prospects, parental reactions, peer evaluations, rewards or punishments, and so on. These purely social-rule judgments can cause pupils to dilate and blood pressure to rise in happy students, sudden cold sweats in fearful students, and listlessness in sad students.

Thus, the daily maintenance of basic physiological activities does not require volitional participation, yet the results of rational evaluation and judgment can significantly affect changes in their indicators.

#### Step Two: Sternly Tell Them—Don’t Think You Are So Impressive; in Fact You Understand Nothing!

When a hopeful person is completely rejected, his or her emotions fluctuate markedly and the mouth changes accordingly. You can first eliminate two types of people:

- People whose mouth corners turn downward: rigid, stubborn, strong self-esteem; they tend to withdraw when struck.
- People who purse their lips tightly: solid workers, but suspicious and prone to closing themselves off.

Therefore, focus next on the following types:

1. **People whose lips form a straight line**: strong character; they do not withdraw immediately when frustrated and can complete ordinary tasks well.
2. **People whose mouth corners turn slightly upward**: flexible minds, relatively open-minded; they do not become pessimistic when criticized harshly and maintain good interpersonal relationships.
3. **People whose lower lip protrudes forward**: strong self-esteem, adventurous spirit; even if you are the interviewer, they will show disagreement or even refute you if they believe you are wrong.
4. **People whose upper and lower lips both protrude forward**: calm and rational; they mentally raise defenses when they sense a situation unfavorable to themselves.
5. **People who bite their lips**: strong analytical ability; they may be listening attentively or analyzing your words against their own experience. Regardless of whether you are right or wrong, they will form their own judgment internally and, once decided, will carry it through to the end.

Believe me, once you combine these observations with the specific content and characteristics of the project, you will certainly be able to select the most suitable candidate from the five types above!

#### 1. Cortex: Rational Center

The first center is the perception and thinking center, served by the cortex. The cortex includes the frontal lobe, parietal lobe, occipital lobe, and temporal lobe, among others. Specifically:

- The frontal lobe is responsible for controlling somatic movement, integrating sensory information, and higher-order thinking and decision-making;
- The parietal lobe handles somatic sensation and constructs cognition of the world, such as spatial awareness and sense of direction;
- The occipital lobe primarily processes visual information;
- The temporal lobe manages auditory information, semantic and episodic memory, and the processing and control of auditory-related language.

The language functions unique to humans are all managed by centers located in the cortex. The auditory language center resides in the temporal lobe, the visual language center (for reading) is in the parietal lobe, with its visual input coming from the occipital lobe. The motor language centers for speaking and writing are located in the frontal lobe. Referring again to the earlier figure and annotations, one primary function of the frontal lobe is “higher-order thinking and decision-making,” which explains why, in the micro-reaction (micro-reaction) framework, verbal expression is classified as classic social display—the form most subject to voluntary control. In addition, the frontal lobe serves as the motor center, governing all deliberate somatic movements.

In the simplest terms, the cortex’s role is: “Figure it out, carry it out, say it out.”

Behaviors controlled by the cortex are the easiest to falsify and the least reliable when observing for deception.

Every skeletal muscle movement throughout the body can be precisely controlled by the cortex; the content one thinks before speaking and the vibration of the vocal cords during speech can also be cortex-controlled. This is why the micro-reaction framework follows the principle “do not analyze unidirectional expression.”

#### 2. Emotional Expressions

Each emotional expression possesses a unique combination of organ morphology features. Micro-expressions conform to these same features, differing only in that their amplitude and duration are smaller and thus easily overlooked.

Humans possess six basic emotions. Extensive scientific evidence shows that emotional expressions are consistent across geography, race, society, education, age, and gender. They are: **surprise, disgust, anger, fear, sadness, and happiness**.

These six basic emotions have many milder variants, listed below:

- Surprise has few variants;
- Variants of disgust may include revulsion, aversion, dislike, contempt, distaste, scorn, and dismissiveness;
- Variants of anger may include irritation, irritation, irascibility, temper outbursts, displeasure, seriousness, and sternness;
- Variants of fear may include apprehension, worry, anxiety, unease, dread, embarrassment, concern, and taboo avoidance;
- Variants of sadness may include sorrow, dejection, low mood, loss, guilt, regret, helplessness, grievance, and gloom;
- Variants of happiness may include satisfaction, smugness, joy, delight, and excitement.

The specific morphologies of these emotional expressions constitute the core of this book and will be examined in detail in the corresponding later chapters. Once the morphological features are mastered, the emotional category can be accurately inferred.

Emotional category is crucial for determining lies and the subject’s true cognition and feelings.

#### 3. Actions and Performances

Examiners can achieve strong stimulative effects by performing certain actions or staging performances.

For example, while serving tea or water, one may control interpersonal distance and torso posture, the placement and force with which a cup is set down; while conversing, one may regulate speech rate and gaze; upon meeting, one may control handshake style and duration or the intensity of an embrace; while walking together, one may adjust position, speed, and whether physical contact occurs. These subtle everyday behaviors exert a cumulative, subliminal stimulative effect.

If a stronger stimulus is deliberately required, “improper” behavior readily produces it. Examples include straightening a stranger’s collar, tie, or shirt buttons on first meeting; touching or stroking the other person’s body (arm, back, waist, or hip); or insisting on lighting a cigarette for a nonsmoker and placing it in their mouth.

Beyond interactive contact, performances can also be designed to generate intense stimulation. Examples include repeatedly digging one’s nose in front of a fastidious person; behaving with abandon—eating, drinking, and speaking without restraint—in the presence of a dignified individual; displaying murderous intent before someone already panicked; stammering before a person in deep grief; or feigning shock before someone who is self-satisfied. Such stylistic behaviors elicit strong reactions from different subjects and trigger numerous valid responses.

#### Summary

In summary, when humans face threats to survival or reproduction, their response mechanisms revert to an animal level.

At such times, animalistic reactions override rational “posturing” and assume control, revealing inner emotions and thoughts through myriad subtle responses.

**Other Limbic System Structures**

The following structures are also regarded in some literature as part of the limbic system:

- **Mammillary body**: Important for memory formation.
- **Pituitary gland**: Secretes hormones and regulates homeostasis.
- **Dentate gyrus**: Considered a factor in constructing new memories and modulating pleasure.
- **Entorhinal and piriform cortices**: Receive olfactory input within the olfactory system.
- **Fornicate gyrus**: The region surrounding the cingulate gyrus, hippocampus, and parahippocampal gyrus.
- **Olfactory bulb**: Handles olfactory sensory input.
- **Nucleus accumbens**: Mediates reward, pleasure, and addiction.
- **Ventral prefrontal area**: Essential for decision-making.

**Cranial Nerves**

These ten pairs include the oculomotor, trochlear, trigeminal, abducens, facial, vestibulocochlear, glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory, and hypoglossal nerves.

#### True and False Expressions: Human Expressions Are Best at Concealment and Disguise

Micro-expression keyword: Can expressions also be false? Indeed, apart from fleeting micro-expressions, the brain can direct the production of various expressions that accompany lies. Deliberately produced expressions either fail to synchronize with bodily movements or appear overly intentional, inevitably revealing small flaws. Careful observation can always expose aspects of a person’s inner state and remove their mask of pretense.

In daily life, when someone says “I love you,” do you privately wonder whether they are lying—whether the sentiment is genuine or feigned? When a new acquaintance treats you with elaborate courtesy, you may think, “Actually, he is not pleased to see me.” We routinely attempt to read others’ inner states through their expressions, yet how many can confidently claim to “see through” another person?

Our surroundings are not short of individuals whose outward appearance contradicts their inner nature and who excel at disguise, using a glittering exterior to conceal inner malice. When dealing with such people, one cannot rely solely on surface impressions; one must penetrate the appearance to discern their true thoughts, especially their ever-changing expressions. Distinguishing genuine from false expressions enables us to identify their inner reality.

Research has identified three cues that reveal an expression as false: facial asymmetry during conversation, temporal factors, and relative sequencing.

#### 3. Emotion–Expression Causal Logic

A complete logical link exists between the generation of emotion and the stimulus source; that link is the subject’s cognitive appraisal of the stimulus.

First, we observe muscle movements and changes in facial organ morphology. These movements and morphological changes follow universal patterns, allowing inference of the emotion category and intensity. The judgment that stress-induced emotional expressions are accurate rests on the fact that each muscle movement and morphology possesses an original physiological meaning shaped by evolutionary survival needs.

Next, each emotion corresponds to a category of cognitive appraisal and feeling—that is, the subject’s internal subjective judgment of the stimulus source.

Therefore, regardless of what the subject expresses verbally or through other social behaviors, the stress response contains critical information. The micro-expressions map the subject’s true cognition and feelings, enabling the most accurate assessment. Combined with the causal link to the stimulus source, this information can unlock many “secrets the subject cannot or will not state.”

**Figure 2-3** Psychological Analysis via Expression

#### Context

Context is a collective term encompassing three factors:

- **Test background information**: In English, WHAT. More precisely, what has occurred before the polygraph questions are asked? What outcomes (correct or incorrect) will follow the polygraph conclusion? Who ultimately stands to gain or lose?
- **Who is tested**: In English, WHO. Here WHO does not refer to narrowing the suspect pool but to the specific profile of the person undergoing the lie test—personality, behavioral habits, upbringing and education, representative past actions, and position within the overall event (location in the relational network). Later chapters will confirm that different individuals lie in different ways.
- **Test environment**: This cannot be rendered simply as WHERE in English. The environment here primarily denotes the spatial layout, lighting, objects, and personnel that may influence the subject during testing.

The same stimulus source may elicit different responses in different contexts. The same stress micro-expression may likewise carry different meanings in different contexts.

#### Temporal Factors

Temporal factors also permit differentiation of genuine from false expressions. These include the duration of a facial expression and the speed of its onset and offset, supplying additional cues about the speaker’s expression.

Generally, expressions that persist for a long time are almost always false; genuine, heartfelt expressions are brief unless the emotion reaches an extreme, as with Fan Jin’s expression in “Fan Jin Passes the Exam”—ecstatic or furious. Even in such extremes, facial expressions rarely last long.

No rigid rule governs onset and offset speed as a deception cue, except for surprise. When a person displays a surprised expression, its onset, duration, and offset are extremely brief—less than one second. If the expression lasts longer, it is usually either playful or declarative and can be judged as feigned. Once an unexpected event is clarified, a person quickly recovers composure. Although anyone can produce a surprised expression, few truly understand that genuine surprise appears and disappears rapidly.

#### 6. Orbicularis Oris Muscle

Among the fifteen groups of facial muscles, the orbicularis oris is the only one that does not appear in symmetrical pairs, although its internal structure is symmetrical.

Its name closely resembles that of the orbicularis oculi, differing by only one character. The nomenclature originated from the mistaken assumption that the mouth, like the eye, is encircled by a ring of striated muscle functioning as a sphincter. In reality, the orbicularis oris comprises four parts—marginal and peripheral portions—whose junction corresponds externally to the vermilion border. The peripheral portion connects in all directions to other major facial muscles of the lower face: levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, levator labii superioris, zygomaticus major, platysma, depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris, and mentalis.

Contraction of the orbicularis oris purses or protrudes the lips, while surrounding muscles may exert opposing forces, pulling portions of the orbicularis oris in different directions to produce actions such as raising the upper lip, elevating the mouth corners, stretching the lips, lowering the mouth corners, or parting the lower lip.

Consequently, the mouth is the second critical site, after the eyes, for capturing and analyzing expression changes.

#### 3.5.2 Decoding “Why Lie” via Micro-Expressions

In summary, dynamic facial expressions fall into three categories, as shown in Figure 2-2.

Whenever physiological, emotional, and social expressions contradict one another, or when physiological and emotional expressions contradict the subject’s verbal statements, the subject is likely concealing their true thoughts.

Knowing whether someone is lying, however, is not the most important goal. Knowing why they are lying is the far more significant analytical objective.

The final chapter of *Micro-Reactions* explores in detail why psychological stress micro-reactions can detect deception. The first question to resolve is: What constitutes a lie?

A lie is defined as “cognition differing from expression.” To establish that an utterance is a lie, one must identify and demonstrate that the subject’s subjective cognition differs from the expressed content; this is the internal logic of lie detection. Both “cognition” and “expression” are indispensable, and a contradiction between them must exist for a lie to be present.

Identifying a contradiction between cognition and expression identifies the lie.

#### Your Observation Record Sheet

While learning to read people as one reads a book, you must attend to many details. Only then can you accurately describe a person’s thoughts or feelings. Pay attention to the following:

- Facial expressions, including forehead, eyebrows, eyes, nose, mouth, and chin.
- Head position.
- Back and shoulder position.
- Shoulder and hand movements.
- Leg and foot movements, including gait.
- Pitch and other vocal changes, such as throat clearing.
- The interactions among all the above changes.

When these nonverbal cues are linked, they form highly instructive information. During interactions, this information helps determine the next step. Whether the encounter is casual and private or formal and professional, the information can, in certain situations, assist you—at minimum by maintaining harmony and reaching consensus.

#### Consider “Other Possibilities”

Observing others’ postures is simple; accurately interpreting their meaning is exceptionally difficult. For instance, when someone suddenly covers their mouth while speaking, this usually indicates uncertainty about the truth of their statement. If you encounter this gesture, do you conclude the person is lying? Human nature being what it is, we rarely consider alternative explanations instinctively. Most people automatically interpret the gesture as lying, uncertainty, or an attempt to hide something.

The facts may indeed be so, yet before concluding, recall whether the person has performed this gesture previously and under what circumstances. If not, consider whether they may have undergone recent dental work or been told they have bad breath and have just become aware of it during the conversation. In short, always entertain other possibilities.

#### 3. Cerebellum and Brainstem: Animal Center (or Physiological Center)

The brain structures that maintain basic physiological functions are the cerebellum and brainstem; the brainstem comprises the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata.

The cerebellum governs movement and balance. Complex limb movements—gymnastics, martial arts, square dancing—can be executed without consciously directing each muscle. Although cortical oversight remains available during competition or conflict, most everyday actions occur without “thinking” involvement.

The brainstem regulates complex reflex activities, including respiration, heartbeat, and blood pressure, all essential for sustaining life. Of the twelve pairs of cranial nerves, ten (excluding the olfactory and optic nerves) have their nuclei in the brainstem. Medicine therefore often uses “brainstem death” as the criterion for loss of human life. All basic physiological activities that require no conscious attention are managed continuously here.

#### Step ❸｜Design Dialogue That Supports Emotion

After interpreting micro-expressions, one can identify the suppressed emotion and its underlying cause, then craft questions that resonate with that emotion, allowing the conversation to proceed more smoothly. This is not merely a psychological insight; it is an essential skill whenever one must initiate interaction with colleagues or clients in professional settings. Greater experience facilitates smoother integration with Steps ❶ and ❷.

At this point, although concrete application methods have not yet been addressed, you may still find the three steps unclear. Rest assured—more explicit guidance follows. Once a micro-expression is detected, one can infer that the other person harbors an additional story beneath their surface words. In other words, the instant a micro-expression appears is the moment to pose a question and the focal point for uncovering the relevant topic.

#### Relative Sequencing

Relative sequencing refers to the precise temporal alignment of an expression with speech, voice, and bodily behavior. For example, if a person is angry, the facial expression of anger should appear simultaneously with the words “I’m furious.” If the expression appears only after the words are spoken, it can be judged as feigned. If the expression precedes speech, its authenticity cannot be determined without additional methods.

Any facial expression that fails to synchronize with bodily movements is likely feigned. Mastery of the techniques for distinguishing genuine from false expressions makes one a mind-reading expert; anyone in your presence will have their mask removed.

#### Corporate Executive Suppressed by the Board of Directors

We tested a corporate executive. She was a highly successful woman in every respect, with outstanding psychological resilience and personal cultivation. Yet when asked about differences in investment strategy with the board, she displayed several small signs of irritation, including changes in facial expression and shifts in body and leg posture. The most noticeable was that, while describing her own views and the current situation, she lit and smoked two cigarettes in succession. Although all outward manner and speech remained perfectly composed, we concluded that the matter was extremely difficult for her and that her mood was correspondingly poor.

After the test she confirmed our inference: she had indeed been suppressed by the board on investment strategy and felt quite depressed.

#### 2. Visual Stimuli

In scientific experiments, visual stimulation is a very common method. Different images or videos are displayed on a screen and subjects are asked to respond to the visual information. Eye-trackers are typical devices of this kind; some micro-expression experiments also employ them. Abroad, researchers have used the speed at which subjects like photographs of Black and White people to gauge the degree of racial bias. Tests for homosexual tendencies, advertising effectiveness, and product popularity are further examples too numerous to list.

In criminal investigation, photographs, slides, documentary evidence, and witness statements are likewise used to present visual stimuli that elicit relevant reactions from suspects.

#### 12. Platysma

The platysma originates from the upper chest and inserts, after passing over the mandible, into the orbicularis oris at the corner of the mouth; it is paired. In this book the term refers only to the facial portion of the platysma, because these fibers can pull the corners of the mouth and thereby form important facial expressions. Near the mouth angle the fibers lie between the depressor anguli oris and the depressor labii inferioris, on the same plane as the latter; at their margins the three muscles fuse and all attach to the lower lip.

The action of the platysma is similar to that of the zygomaticus major—stretching the corners of the mouth laterally—yet the direction is entirely different. The zygomaticus major pulls the corners toward the ears; the platysma pulls them laterally and downward (in concert with the depressor anguli oris). It typically appears in expressions of crying with an open mouth or of pouting and conveys negative emotion.

#### 3.6 Muscles That Produce Facial Expressions and Micro-expressions

Fifteen groups of muscles initiate and form facial expressions; additional craniofacial muscles also participate. For ease of study and memorization we divide the dominant muscles into upper and lower groups and illustrate them schematically. Muscles 1–5, centered on the orbicularis oculi (No. 5), constitute the upper-face expression group (abbreviated “upper face” from Chapter 4 onward). Muscles 6–15, centered on the orbicularis oris (No. 11), constitute the lower-face expression group (abbreviated “lower face” from Chapter 4 onward). Note that many other muscles exist on the face—temporalis, masticatory muscles, etc.—and actual anatomical diagrams are far more complex. The muscles shown are the principal bundles that dominate expression formation.

#### Reference Note

The levator palpebrae superioris is a thin triangular muscle arising from the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone immediately above the optic canal, separated from the attachment of the superior rectus. At its posterior attachment it is a slender narrow tendon that gradually broadens; as it passes forward above the eyeball it widens markedly and ends anteriorly as a broad aponeurosis. Some tendinous fibers run straight forward into the upper eyelid and attach to the anterior surface of the tarsal plate. The remaining fibers radiate through the orbicularis oculi to insert into the skin of the upper lid.

(Gray’s Anatomy, 39th ed., Susan Standring, trans. Xu Qunyuan, p. 776. Peking University Medical Press, 1st ed., January 2008.)

#### Micro-expressions Are Unconscious and Difficult Even for the Person to Control

The face contains thirty to sixty muscles known as “muscles of expression.” By controlling these muscles, a variety of expressions are formed on the face. Some of these muscles are difficult to move by conscious will; a person cannot arbitrarily control every expression. These hard-to-control muscles readily reveal micro-expressions in an instant.

We now turn to the psychology behind the appearance of micro-expressions in order to understand further what causes them to surface unconsciously.

A micro-expression is a suppressed emotion that appears unconsciously on the face for an instant and then vanishes immediately. It is not a deliberately feigned expression. Two situations may be considered:

#### 3.5 The Principle of Micro-expression Lie Detection

Once a genuine emotion arises it must be expressed, though not necessarily only through facial changes. It can also be judged and analyzed through body movements, posture (see the book Micro-reactions (微反应)), and language, ultimately approaching the truth.

First, do not attempt to analyze everything. The expressions you see on another person’s face may well be deliberately disguised or well-trained “shells.” Analyzing such expressions only causes you to “throw yourself headlong into a pit someone else has dug.”

What we must analyze are only the physiological and emotional expressions triggered after an effective stimulus. Social expressions must never be analyzed.

#### Question 3: What Does the “Micro” in Micro-reaction Mean and Where Does It Come From?

Human behavior can be divided into three categories: physiological behavior, emotional behavior, and social behavior.

After receiving an effective stimulus, humans produce physiological and emotional behaviors that reflect their true cognition and feelings. Yet they are unwilling to be seen through, so they attempt to suppress and disguise these behaviors with socially controlled behavior. As a result, the physiological and emotional behaviors shrink in amplitude or disappear, shorten in duration or cease, and become hard to detect—hence the word “micro.” Nevertheless these behaviors still exist and can still break through the inhibition and disguise of social behavior. Even when small in amplitude and brief in duration, they continue to convey large amounts of valuable and valid information.

#### Learning How to Read People

Learning comes from gaining insight through reading books, yet among all the knowledge in the world the most necessary is learning how to perceive others and studying all kinds of people with care.

—Lord Chesterfield

To learn to read people as one reads books, the first requirement is that you must become a keen observer. You can begin now by going to crowded places and observing everyone’s postures, expressions, movements, and interactions. This chapter provides a platform for cultivating sharp observational skills—the airport, an ideal setting for honing your powers of observation.

#### 1. Questioning

The most common form of stimulus is to ask a question and require the person to answer. Questions may be posed verbally or in writing; the latter is less common. In daily life and in criminal investigation, the great majority of exchanges consist of verbal question-and-answer sequences. The questioner can further modify the emphasis of the stimulus by varying volume, rhythm, stress, repetition, tone, and other paralinguistic features.

Besides questioning, many other forms can also serve as excellent stimuli.

#### Conclusion

This chapter prepares you for the careful observation that follows. Yet you cannot know whether your people-reading efforts will succeed until you act on your own intuition. It is the same principle as with a new car: it must pass tests before it reaches the showroom, but only real-world use can truly evaluate it.

Before you begin actual testing, however, you still need to learn a great deal. In the chapters ahead we will discuss in detail the meanings of people’s various expressions, gestures, and postures.

#### Micro-expression Keywords

When we observe others, the first thing we see is the head. It moves almost constantly. Through head movements we can analyze another person’s inner thoughts: approval or disapproval, friendliness or hostility, interest or boredom, and so on.

When using movement to read people, we begin with the head. This is not only because the head is at the top of the body and most conspicuous, but also because head movements convey a great deal of information. Below we list several examples at random.

#### 15. Mentalis

The mentalis originates from the inferior border of the orbicularis oris (below the lower lip) and inserts into the skin of the chin; it is paired.

When the mentalis contracts it produces two effects: it bulges on the chin, creating an uneven skin surface, and simultaneously pushes the central part of the lower lip upward. This important morphological feature appears chiefly in expressions of sadness. The action can also be performed voluntarily to express deliberate sorrow, contempt, or other negative meanings.

#### Step ❶｜Understanding the Relationship Between Muscles of Expression and Emotion

First, understand the relationship between muscles of expression and emotion. For example, movements such as “both eyebrows drawing toward the center” or “lower lip rising” are related to emotion. “Both eyebrows drawing toward the center” is associated with “anger,” while “lower lip rising” is associated with “sadness.”

Next, understand the causes of these emotions. For instance, “anger” arises when a desired goal is obstructed. Understanding the functions of expressions and emotions is very important.

#### 16. Buccinator

After the cheeks are puffed out, the buccinator can expel air between the lips—an important action when playing wind instruments, which is also the origin of the muscle’s name (Latin buccinator = trumpeter). Its main contribution to expression is “puffing the cheeks,” yet this artificial expression has no close relationship with emotion and at most signals relief from pressure. It is therefore marked “A” and is not explained in detail in this book, nor included among the principal muscle groups.

#### Head Tilted Backward

This movement indicates pride or confidence. Usually, however, it leaves a negative impression. In television dramas, for example, snobbish characters often tilt their heads back with nostrils pointing upward when facing someone they consider inferior. In life, when a person tilts the head backward, the emotional progression is roughly from smugness to self-importance to a sense of superiority. Basically, the movement makes others feel you are being provocative, so it should be used sparingly.

Psychological-stress micro-reaction analysis does not examine a person’s unidirectional expression, because it is impossible to determine which parts are controlled social behavior and which are inadvertent genuine disclosures; theoretically, unidirectional expression can be 100 % controlled.

Psychological-stress micro-reaction analysis examines only stress responses—reactions that occur after a stimulus. Therefore a stimulus source must first be present before analysis can begin.

Detecting and interpreting micro-expressions allows us to capture another person’s unconscious emotions. How, then, do we capture these unconscious emotions?

The following outline introduces the steps; detailed content and practical methods will be explained in this and the next chapter. Applying the ability to read micro-expressions in communication involves three steps, categorized as “understanding,” “interpretation,” and “support”:

#### Chapter 2 Eyebrow and Eye Corners Conceal Intentions; Voice, Expression, and Smile Reveal Mysteries

Micro-expressions are revelations of inner truth. When people express a thought or feeling, a fleeting expression may cross their face—this is a micro-expression on display and in communication. The information these micro-expressions convey constitutes the most accurate clues to another person’s inner intentions. People can be judged by their appearance; through careful observation and analysis of micro-expressions we can discern a person’s spiritual life and inner mysteries.

#### 7. Levator Labii Superioris Alaeque Nasi

The middle portion of the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi attaches to the major alar cartilage and the overlying skin; the lateral portion extends into the lateral upper lip (toward the mouth corner) and there fuses with the levator labii superioris and the orbicularis oris; it is paired.

Contraction produces two effects: the middle portion dilates the nostril; the lateral portion elevates and everts the upper lip, raising, deepening, and increasing the curvature of the top of the nasolabial fold.

#### Chapter 1 Observing People in the Subtle, Discerning People in the Invisible

Reading words and expressions is the fundamental skill for handling all human relations with ease. Without it, one is like someone turning a rudder without knowing the wind direction. In real life we must deal with all kinds of people and face extremely complex crowds; we must therefore train a pair of discerning eyes capable of accurately reading others’ inner thoughts. #### Question 5: What Can Micro-reactions Be Used For?

Interpersonal behavior is highly complex; the performance presented onstage and the motives backstage are usually processed multiple times before finally appearing before you. Do not readily believe the performance you can directly observe; instead, look through the performance for the “uncontrolled” micro-reactions of the parties involved. #### Head Lowered

This head movement signifies negation. For example, if your superior lowers the head halfway through your work report, it almost certainly means dissatisfaction with the work and unwillingness to continue listening. At that point you should tactfully stop and offer to improve the work. People also lower the head unconsciously when receiving criticism, thereby expressing remorse.

#### 14. Depressor Labii Inferioris

The depressor labii inferioris lies below the orbicularis oris, fuses with its inferior circumference, and is paired.

As the name indicates, this muscle pulls the lower lip downward and slightly laterally and can also help evert the lower lip. It participates in angry shouting, biting, fear, and sadness. To expose the lower teeth, the depressor labii inferioris must be engaged.

#### 13. Depressor Anguli Oris

The depressor anguli oris arises by a long attachment from the mental tubercle of the mandible and the continuous oblique line below the origin of the depressor labii inferioris; it is paired.

**Action**: When the mouth opens or when sorrow or distress is expressed, the depressor anguli oris pulls the mouth corner downward and laterally. When the mouth opens, the mentolabial sulcus becomes more horizontal, its middle portion level.

#### Head Suddenly Dropped

This can hide the face and indicates that the person is being humble or shy. In a competitive setting, however, lowering the head signals that the person can no longer bear the pressure and hopes the argument will end soon.

The head is the body’s “command center” and is the first to convey another person’s inner language; it truly cannot be ignored.

#### Head Held Straight

In ancient Chinese philosophy the phrase “neither偏nor倚 is called the mean” appears. It means that if the head posture remains in a normal position, the person neither approves nor disapproves of your viewpoint and maintains a neutral stance. Such individuals may be deeply calculating and extremely reserved; to persuade them you must present terms advantageous to them.

#### 11. Risorius

The fibers of the risorius interweave at the mouth corner with the zygomaticus major, depressor anguli oris, and orbicularis oris; some superficial fibers attach beneath the dermis of the nasolabial fold; it is paired.

The risorius assists the zygomaticus major in elevating the mouth corner during smiling and indirectly alters the shape and depth of the nasolabial fold.

#### Head Tilted to One Side

Generally, when we are interested in something or someone, or when we agree with a viewpoint, we perform this movement, often accompanied by repeated nodding. Therefore, when someone is speaking to you, simply tilting your head, nodding, and smiling will make the other person feel warmth and encourage continued conversation.

#### Micro-expressions: Only the Fleeting Expressions Are Authentic and Credible

**Micro-expression Keywords**  
People display inner feelings through expressions. Some expressions are not controlled by the brain; they are subconscious and often flash by in an instant. We call them “micro-expressions.” Only these very brief expressions reveal people’s true inner state.

#### Head Suddenly Raised

With an unfamiliar person, raising the head indicates surprise. In a familiar setting it indicates sudden realization or sudden understanding. In business interactions such movements generally leave an impression of instability and unreliability. This body language is also highly unwelcome.

#### 10. Zygomaticus Major

The zygomaticus major originates from the zygomatic bone and, at the mouth corner, fuses with the risorius, orbicularis oris, and depressor anguli oris to form a deeper muscle bundle; it is paired.

Although the zygomaticus major and zygomaticus minor have similar names, their actions are completely different. For expression, the zygomaticus major has only one function: pulling the mouth corner upward and laterally to produce a smile.

#### Section 1 The Secret Weapon for Seeing Through People's Hearts: Expressions

#### 8. Levator Labii Superioris

The levator labii superioris originates from the inferior orbital margin. Its muscle fibers, together with the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi and the zygomaticus minor, converge on the lateral side of the upper lip (near the corner of the mouth), symmetrically on both sides.

Contraction of the levator labii superioris raises and everts the upper lip, and together with other muscles, alters the shape of the nasolabial fold.

#### 9. Zygomaticus Minor

The zygomaticus minor originates from the lateral surface of the zygomatic bone and inserts on the lateral side of the upper lip (near the corner of the mouth), symmetrically on both sides.

Contraction of the zygomaticus minor raises the upper lip, exposes the upper maxillary teeth, helps deepen and lift the nasolabial fold, and primarily participates in expressing emotions of disgust and sadness.

#### What Is the 0.2-Second "Micro-Expression" Message

##### Seeing Through the Other Party's "Hidden Emotions" While Adjusting the Direction of Conversation

Understanding how to interpret the micro-expressions that appear on the other person's face can provide the following practical benefits:

1. In business negotiations, receptions, and similar situations, understanding the emotions the other party wants to hide allows you to adjust the focus and direction of the conversation

   When negotiating business, you can find points of interest from the client's "surprise" micro-expression, or in negotiations, understand the limits of acceptable conditions from the "disgust" micro-expression. If you can see "anger" and a polite smile from the client's micro-expressions, you can understand their true intentions and propose appropriate responses in a timely manner. Even during a presentation, you can clearly see if the listener is smiling but actually feels "contempt" toward the content.

2. Building good interpersonal relationships outside of managing organizations or teams

   A subordinate's smile may briefly reveal a "sadness" micro-expression, which could be a sign of a change in psychological state. When a supervisor offers advice to a subordinate, the "disgust" micro-expression can show that the advice is not genuinely accepted. Even in meetings, it is possible to anticipate who understands the content and who wants to raise questions.

3. Identifying suitable talent during recruitment interviews

   In recruitment interviews, the "fear" micro-expression can be used to determine whether the candidate is lying. By focusing on the points revealed through micro-expressions, timely questions can be posed to uncover aspects of the candidate not shown on the résumé.

4. Detecting "danger signals" hidden in emotions during arguments with a partner

   Micro-expressions of "contempt" or "disgust" during an argument are warning signs of an impending breakup. Early detection of signs that the other person's feelings have faded still leaves an opportunity to repair the relationship through effort.

Different situations produce different micro-expressions. Correctly perceiving and interpreting them allows the direction of communication to be adjusted appropriately.

Up to this point, how have you viewed micro-expressions? Does the world of micro-expressions and the extent of their usefulness seem interesting? Next, the profound world of micro-expressions will be presented step by step on each page. Follow along and enter the world of micro-expressions!

##### Identifying Moments When Emotions Fluctuate

From the above, seven micro-expressions are universal across countries, and eleven are generally common. In addition, other distinct expressions and facial movements appear on the face in an instant, especially around the eyebrows or corners of the mouth. Most of these expressions arise as reactions when emotions are suppressed.

For example, a typical "anger" expression is generally formed by four parts: the eyebrows, eyes, lower eyelids, and lips. However, when a micro-expression of "anger" appears, usually only one or two parts are visible, and occasionally all four appear simultaneously. This indicates that combinations of "anger" micro-expressions are far more numerous than ordinary "anger" expressions. No one knows exactly how many micro-expressions exist, but it is certain that micro-expressions are richer than ordinary expressions.

As mentioned earlier, micro-expressions reveal suppressed emotions. When emotions are suppressed, feelings and psychology manifest at the moment of oscillation.

Consider whether you have ever encountered such a situation. At what moments do micro-expressions appear instantly?

- When winning against an opponent in teasing or a game—"happiness"
- When finding someone else's presentation or opinion childish—"contempt"
- When unable to accept the other party's suggestion—"disgust"
- When treated unreasonably or when one's own ideas are not understood—"anger"
- When actually feeling sad but pretending to be energetic—"sadness"
- When worrying that a lie has been discovered and breaking into a cold sweat—"fear"
- When unexpectedly learning a fact but not wanting the other party to know—"surprise"

From these examples, it is clear that everyone at times deliberately suppresses emotions to prevent them from showing on the face. Therefore, possessing the skill to perceive and interpret micro-expressions should be very helpful in both work and life!

##### What Is the 0.2-Second "Micro-Expression" Message?

What exactly is a "micro-expression"? In simple terms, it is "a suppressed emotion that suddenly flashes across the face like lightning in an instant and then disappears immediately—a subtle change in facial expression."

How long does a micro-expression appear on the face? Research shows it lasts less than 0.2 seconds. Sometimes it is only about 0.1 seconds, or even just 0.05 seconds. Because it is so rapid, such subtle movements are mostly overlooked and go unnoticed in ordinary communication unless one has learned methods to perceive and interpret them.

There is no strict data on exactly how many micro-expressions exist. First, consider the broad category of "expressions." The expressions mentioned here refer to ordinary expressions that are normally visible. In terms of duration, they typically appear on the face for about 0.5 to 4 seconds.

Scientific research has found that people have at least more than ten thousand different expressions. In particular, the seven expressions "happiness," "contempt," "disgust," "anger," "sadness," "fear," and "surprise" are universal across cultures, ethnicities, genders, ages, eras, and even among people who are blind from birth.

These seven expressions are communication signals that people possess from birth, mechanisms already encoded in DNA. In recent years, eleven additional expressions—"shame," "humiliation," "guilt," "apprehension," "boasting," "joy," "pleasure," "excitement," "happiness," "reassurance," and "satisfaction"—have also been found to be common, and scientists continue to study them.

#### Two Scenarios of Micro-expressions

##### Conditions for Micro-expression Presentation and Cultural Differences

An expression of “disgust” should appear, yet a smile shows instead—why? Have you also accepted the argument that expressions are universal?

Now we return to the question raised at the beginning of the previous section: are micro-expressions truly universal? As noted earlier, the seven universal micro-expressions flash across the face in an instant of 0.2 seconds.

Micro-expressions usually occur when a person tries to suppress an emotion. Therefore, the degree of emotional suppression ability and the necessity of suppressing emotion both affect how micro-expressions manifest. In other words, depending on the individual’s level of expression control, a suppressed emotion may appear on the face as a micro-expression or may surface as a normal expression.

Yet “Americans and Japanese clearly express emotions differently!” The following experiment clarifies this point. One group of Americans and one group of Japanese participants were asked to watch a film that elicits disgust while alone in a laboratory; their expressions were recorded with a hidden camera. Analysis showed that both groups displayed an expression of “disgust” toward the footage.

Next, participants from the first group were joined by an observer in the laboratory, while a second group underwent the same experiment. An interesting result emerged. Compared with the first experiment, the Americans in the second group again displayed “disgust” directly, but the Japanese participants smiled instead.

This smile is understandable. Japanese people generally maintain harmony within a group and therefore rarely display personal negative emotions openly—an outcome closely tied to cultural norms. Consequently, the Japanese participants, who should have shown “disgust,” smiled instead, indicating that the emotion of “disgust” had been suppressed. In contrast, Americans do not mind displaying negative emotions openly in front of others and therefore express their feelings directly through facial expressions.

The difference in emotional expression between Americans and Japanese arises because individuals regulate their expressions according to the immediate context. At such moments the emotion may surface as a micro-expression or as an ordinary expression. Without the skill to detect and interpret micro-expressions, their presence remains unnoticed.

The conditions under which micro-expressions appear are influenced by culture or personal circumstances. Various studies show that whenever emotion is suppressed, micro-expressions appear on anyone’s face regardless of setting; interpretation must therefore take these conditions into account.

##### No Expression Does Not Mean No Emotion

When one person harbors feelings of disgust or unease toward another yet does not wish the other to know, the face becomes expressionless.

In daily life we sometimes encounter people who remain expressionless no matter what others say or do. Many find such individuals difficult to deal with. In reality, the absence of expression does not equal the absence of emotion. If inner activity fails to register on the facial muscles, the result appears unnatural; the more expressionless the face, the more intense the underlying emotion is likely to be.

For example, an employee who resents a supervisor’s words or actions but dares not voice the anger may deliberately adopt a blank expression. No matter how thoroughly the anger is suppressed, the inner dissatisfaction remains strong; close observation of the face will reveal that something is amiss.

People often describe such a wooden face as a “dead person’s” face—expressionless and indifferent. The “dead person’s” face itself constitutes an unnatural display.

Moreover, although such individuals strive to keep joy or anger from showing, when inner emotional intensity rises their eyes may suddenly widen, wrinkles may appear around the nostrils, or twitching may occur on the face. Thus, a sudden facial twitch indicates that the person is experiencing intense emotional conflict at a deep level of awareness.

When dealing with such a person, it is best not to reprimand directly or cause embarrassment on the spot. Upon noticing a subordinate’s pale complexion or facial twitching, a supervisor might say, “Have you been feeling unwell lately? If something is bothering you, feel free to talk about it,” thereby soothing the suppressed emotion.

A rigid or twitching expression at least signals that the relationship between superior and subordinate has reached a low point; both parties should then exchange views openly to clear up misunderstandings and improve relations.

A completely expressionless face can sometimes also signal goodwill or affection. Women in particular may feel that openly displaying affection violates social expectations and therefore show the opposite expression, appearing indifferent when they are in fact deeply concerned.

##### ❶ Unconsciously Suppressing Emotion

A person whose face displays a micro-expression is unaware that the emotion has affected the visible expression; neither the micro-expression on the face nor the suppressed emotion itself registers consciously. When micro-expressions were first discussed in the 1960s, American psychologists E. A. Haggard and K. S. Isaacs conducted a series of studies on their origins. They recorded therapy sessions, catalogued facial expressions and body-language features segment by segment, and discovered brief intervals in which patients displayed expressions of distress lasting only seconds. The patients themselves reported neither noticing the distressed expressions nor feeling the corresponding emotion.

##### ❷ Deliberately Suppressing Emotion

The opposite situation occurs when emotion is suppressed consciously. In such cases the individual is aware of suppressing the emotion at the moment the micro-expression flashes across the face, yet the facial muscles still produce the micro-expression involuntarily. For people who must wear a mask every day, the deliberate control of emotion probably feels more familiar than unconscious suppression.
