#### Eyebrow Main Movements

##### Eyebrow Raising

If a person raises only the left or right eyebrow, it usually indicates a lack of understanding or doubt about what the other person has said or done, as if asking: “Really? Are you sure that’s what you mean?”

If both eyebrows are raised, it signals great delight or extreme surprise and is sometimes used to indicate that a question is about to be asked.

George arrived at the director’s office as scheduled. Ordinary agents like George rarely had the chance to discuss work face-to-face with the director; only the extreme urgency of the situation had prompted him to bring his plan directly to the director.

The matter began when one of George’s informants told him that two terrorists might be arriving the next day at a New York airport carrying important documents on a very special flight. After investigating the flight, George discovered that it was the same one carrying a high-ranking U.S. official returning home. The intelligence struck George as bizarre, yet the informant had always been reliable, and George did not want to miss an opportunity to eliminate the terrorists. When George reported his idea to his supervisor, the supervisor rejected the plan for lack of sufficient evidence. Frustrated, George decided to take the plan straight to the director.

The moment George entered the office, the director, seated behind a large desk, looked him over from head to toe several times and showed little friendliness toward his arrival.

Sure enough, after only a few exchanges the director began to pick apart George’s plan, raising a long list of objections to both the overall scheme and its specific execution, and finally attempting to dismiss the operation outright as completely unfeasible. George had to keep stressing the plan’s importance, but the director merely grunted and, without realizing it, raised his left eyebrow while twitching the corner of his mouth, displaying an expression of complete disbelief.

Sensing the director’s rejection, George borrowed a sheet of paper, took out a pen, and wrote out every step and timing detail of the plan. He also listed, one by one, the losses that abandoning the operation would entail. Only then did the director lower his raised eyebrow, smile, and nod repeatedly, clearly accepting the plan.

Through the director’s alternating eyebrow movements, George had keenly detected an opening within the signals of rejection. Later George explained: “One eyebrow raised while the other remains lowered is a sign of ‘doubt’; when a person is both surprised and doubtful, one eyebrow rises; when both eyebrows rise, it indicates great surprise. At the time only one of the director’s eyebrows was raised, so I judged that he was both surprised and doubtful about my plan. I therefore explained the plan in greater detail and, during the explanation, drew out the reason for his surprise. Once the director’s surprise and doubt were resolved, he was certain to approve the plan.”

When someone says “Really? So that’s how it is!” while raising one eyebrow or repeatedly touching the eyebrow or eyelid, it shows that the person does not fully believe you. At such moments we must probe further for the reason behind the disbelief or produce stronger evidence. Only by eliminating the other person’s doubts can we earn greater trust.

If, after you say “Let’s have a drink sometime,” the other person’s eyebrows rise, it means the invitation is being taken as mere diplomatic language. If you then confirm the time and place of the gathering, the other person will surely feel grateful and trust you far more.

Under normal circumstances people rarely raise a single eyebrow, so whenever the movement appears it should never be dismissed as accidental; it must be taken seriously and its cause identified. In any interaction, lingering doubts on either side will sever the thread of communication. When we see an eyebrow rise, we must reason patiently, appeal emotionally, and supply enough evidence to prove our point, thereby removing any negative notions. We must not simply continue along the originally planned line of conversation, or the exchange will end fruitlessly.

##### 7. Eyebrow Shrug

Raising the eyebrows, holding them briefly, then lowering them is called an eyebrow shrug. It is often accompanied by a quick, brief downward twitch of the corners of the mouth and is most common during conversation. When people are engaged in heated discussion they tend to repeat small movements to emphasize their words, especially at key points; habitual complainers do the same. The gesture expresses an unpleasant surprise or a sense of helplessness.

Eyebrow movements are highly varied, each dynamic reflecting a different psychological shift. In general, displeasure or confusion can be shown by knitting the brows; jealousy or distrust by raising the brows; one brow raised and the other lowered by the classic signal of suspicion; both brows raised together by surprise; both brows lowered by dejection or sorrow; thick brows drawn sharply upward by anger; brows drawn together in a cold stare by contempt; winking and nudging by joking; lowered brows and downcast eyes by submission; raised brows by a sense of relief and satisfaction; and dancing brows by excitement.

##### 1. Knitting the Brows

Knitting the brows means contracting the eyebrows toward the bridge of the nose and narrowing the eye sockets. There are two types: protective and aggressive. The former protects the eyes from external harm; during the movement the cheeks beneath the eyes are also lifted while the eyes remain open. This occurs when facing an attack, sudden strong light, or intense emotional reaction. The latter is a defensive reaction and is essentially self-protective.

Knitting the brows can convey many moods: hope, astonishment, arrogance, ignorance, thoughtfulness, worry, displeasure, or difficulty. Common expressions such as “brows knit in deep concern” or “brows knit and a plan forms” are directly related to this movement.

##### 4. Raising or Lowering the Brows

A sudden raising of the eyebrows signals surprise; a full raising indicates that something or some news is hard to believe. Observing people around you, you will often see this movement when they first encounter something incredible. A sudden lowering of the eyebrows shows disapproval of what you have said. A half-lowering indicates incomprehension and lingering doubt. A complete lowering signals that the other person is angry and on the verge of explosion; at that point it is best to drop the sensitive topic or find an excuse to withdraw.

##### Deep Knitting of the Brows

Knitting the brows falls into two categories: protective and aggressive.

The purpose of protective knitting is to shield the eyes from external harm; the cheeks beneath the eyes are also lifted while the eyes remain open. This withdrawal reaction typically appears when a person faces an attack, sudden strong light, or intense emotional stimulus.

Aggressive knitting is still rooted in defense; it reflects concern that one’s own aggressive emotions might provoke a counter-reaction and is therefore linked to self-protection.

The most common deep knitting of the brows occurs in situations of annoyance, anxiety, dejection, or indecision.

##### Brows Relaxed

The opposite of knitted brows, this expression appears when a person feels cheerful and at ease, usually after encountering something pleasant or solving a difficult problem. It is an especially good moment to make a request; once the brows have relaxed, the person is more likely than usual to agree.

Although the eyebrows are merely accessories to the eyes and in some people their changes are not very obvious, they play as important a role as the eyes themselves. Their every stillness and movement subtly reveals the speaker’s state of mind. When observed together with the eyes, they allow a more accurate reading of another person’s mood.

##### 6. Lowering the Brows

Lowering the brows is a reaction to aggression. Protective lowering shields the eyes from external harm; when danger appears, the cheeks beneath the eyes are also lifted while the eyes remain open and attentive to the surroundings. This up-and-down compression is a typical withdrawal response to external stimuli—for example, the same reaction occurs when the eyes are suddenly exposed to strong light. It can also appear when emotions surge dramatically, such as during loud crying or laughing or extreme nausea.

##### Raising the Brows

The idiom “raising the brows and exhaling” describes the release of long-suppressed feelings and the joy of victory. In general, raised brows indicate emotions such as satisfaction or happiness.

However, if a person frequently raises a single brow, it suggests an arrogant character and indifference toward others. In states of extreme surprise or delight, both brows may also rise high along with widened eyes.

##### Eyebrow Shrug

This expression consists of raising the brows, holding them briefly, then lowering them, often accompanied by a downward twitch of the mouth corners. It conveys displeasure mixed with helplessness. For instance, when someone keeps bothering you and refuses to listen to any explanation, you may produce this movement to express dissatisfaction and resignation.

In addition, the movement often appears when the other person is emphasizing a point and wants you to agree.

##### Eyebrow Flash

An eyebrow flash occurs when the brows are raised and then instantly lowered, like a meteor streaking across the sky—quick and agile. It is a universal human signal of welcome and a friendly gesture.

The flash is usually accompanied by a head lift and a smile, though it can occur on its own. It generally appears in conversation to add emphasis. Whenever a speaker wishes to stress a particular word, the brows flash, as if to say, “What I’m saying is really astonishing!”

##### Knitted Brows

Ancient poems often used “knitted moth brows” to describe a woman’s sorrow. In real life, when a person is deeply distressed and cannot find an outlet, a worried expression with tightly knitted brows commonly appears. The same movement occurs when someone is extremely anxious or indecisive. At such times the person greatly needs comfort; offering concern can be like sending charcoal in snowy weather and may win lasting friendship.

##### 2. Eyebrow Shrug

When the other person feels unhappy or helpless, an eyebrow shrug often appears: the brows are raised, held briefly, then lowered, accompanied by a quick downward twitch of the mouth corners while the rest of the face shows little change. The movement also tends to occur when the person is emphasizing a viewpoint, usually to gain your agreement.

##### 5. Eyebrow Flash

At the moment of meeting, if the other person’s brows suddenly rise and then instantly return to their original position—like a meteor streaking across the sky—we call it an eyebrow flash. It is a universal signal of warm welcome and a friendly gesture. When the brows flash repeatedly, it indicates particular delight at the visitor’s arrival. This expression is common between old friends who have not seen each other for a long time and is usually accompanied by a head tilt and a smile.

##### Knitting the Brows

People generally knit their brows in two situations. First, when suddenly exposed to strong light or facing an external attack, they instinctively knit the brows to protect the eyes and resist the assault. Second, when confronted with a problem and unable to find an immediate solution, they may knit their brows involuntarily.

Usually, knitting the brows expresses emotions such as annoyance, dislike, disagreement, or defensiveness.

##### 5. Winking

Winking means suddenly closing the eyelids; the movement resembles a blink but carries a different meaning. Winking is often paired with nudging and is mainly used to signal the other person to act according to one’s intention, to convey affection, or to stop the other person. This expression most often occurs between couples or people who know each other well and usually requires mutual understanding and tacit cooperation.

##### Single Brow Raised

A single brow raised while the other is lowered resembles a large question mark. It is the characteristic expression of doubt, indicating disbelief in what the other person has said. If the doubt is not promptly addressed and dispelled, continued mistrust may damage the relationship or cause a plan to fail.

##### Eyebrow Shrug

Raising the brows, holding them briefly, then lowering them constitutes an eyebrow shrug. It is frequently accompanied by a quick, brief downward twitch of the mouth corners. The gesture expresses displeasure or helplessness. During heated discussion, a person may also shrug the brows repeatedly to emphasize important points.

##### 3. Raising the Brows

The idiom “raising the brows and exhaling” is often used to describe the satisfied expression that appears once long-suppressed emotions have been released. When a person’s brows rise, it indicates great delight or surprise. At such moments the other person’s emotions are highly agitated; if you have something to say, it is best to wait until the mood has calmed.

##### 1. Knitting the Brows

When facing difficulty, danger, or something unpleasant, people instinctively knit their brows, drawing them slightly inward and shortening the distance between them. Knitting the brows is an extremely common expression that can represent many emotions, such as happiness, doubt, astonishment, arrogance, confusion, fear, or denial.

##### Single Brow Raised

A single brow raised while the other is lowered resembles a question mark and reflects the raised-brow person’s doubt and incomprehension. This silent language is frequently seen on the faces of adult men.

##### Brows Knotted

Brows knotted means both brows are raised and drawn toward each other. When people encounter trouble or feel extremely depressed, they usually display this expression, resulting in a mournful face and “unfurrowed brows laden with worry.” Some patients with chronic pain also show it.

##### Brows Drawn Inward or Outward

If a person’s brows move toward the center, you know the person is thinking, as the saying goes: “brows knit and a plan forms.” If both brows flare outward, the person is clearly in high spirits—an expression called “dancing brows and radiant face.”

##### 4. Vertical Brows

Vertical brows—brows standing upright—can indicate fright, excitement, or agitation. In daily life, when a person receives an unexpected stimulus such as a scare, involuntary trembling and vertical brows may occur, even causing the hair to stand on end.

##### Brows Bristling

Bristling the brows usually shows that anger has reached its peak and an explosive outburst may follow. People who are already angry also often raise their brows.

##### 7. Eyebrow Arrangement: Neat or Disordered

People whose eyebrows are neatly arranged and lustrous tend to be honest in character and fortunate; those whose eyebrows are disordered and grow in inconsistent directions are often inconsistent in word and deed and are mostly hypocrites.

##### 2. Brows Spread

Brows spread means the eyebrows expand outward. The main meaning is relief and a pleasant, relaxed mood. The common saying “brows spread and eyes smiling” captures this sense.

##### 3. Horizontal Brows

Horizontal brows means the eyebrows form a straight line. Meeting someone with horizontal brows signifies hatred or anger toward that person.

#### Eyebrows Among the Seven Emotions

##### 1. Knowing Temperament from Eyebrows

Eyebrows form an important part of the face beyond the five sensory organs. From the perspective of traditional Chinese medicine, a person’s eyebrows reflect the condition of the endocrine system as well as the liver and kidneys. Because the liver and endocrine functions strongly influence temperament, eyebrow shape can reveal character. Ancient texts describe them this way: “Eyebrows are the graceful cover of the eyes and the standard of the face; they embody the essence of the eyes and distinguish the wise from the foolish. Sparse, fine, level, broad, elegant, and long eyebrows indicate an intelligent nature, while coarse, thick, unruly, chaotic, short, and furrowed eyebrows indicate a fierce and stubborn nature.”

1. **Eyebrows Have Thickness and Thinness**  
   Just as eyes vary in size, eyebrows vary in thickness, and this variation correlates with temperament. Thick eyebrows generally belong to more masculine, active, and impulsive individuals who often receive protection from their parents. Thin eyebrows belong to more feminine, passive, and indecisive individuals. The same eyebrow shape can produce very different effects on different people. For example, crescent-shaped eyebrows look attractive, yet a man with such eyebrows tends to have a weak character.

2. **People Whose Eyebrow Tails Point Upward or Downward**  
   Eyebrow tails that point upward usually belong to people with strong self-esteem and personality. They rarely compromise, lack coordination, and make decisions decisively; as a result, they often earn others’ respect. Eyebrow tails that point downward are commonly called “eight-twenty” eyebrows. People with downward-pointing tails are compassionate and typical “nice guys.” They enjoy helping others and often respond to teasing with a smile rather than retaliation.

3. **Eyebrow Tails Extending Beyond the Outer Eye Corner**  
   Such individuals possess generosity and excel at perspective-taking, allowing them to empathize with others; they also tend to enjoy financial comfort. From an emotional standpoint, people with short eyebrows have shallow marital affinity. Those with long, thick eyebrow tails enjoy good fortune and remain active in any situation. Excessive thickness, however, can incline toward arrogance and cunning, potentially fostering self-centeredness. People whose eyebrow tails are long yet sparse tend to be steady in temperament; they possess rich knowledge but lack initiative and leadership. Note that sparse eyebrows caused by alopecia areata can improve with attention.

4. **Willow-Leaf Eyebrows and Straight Eyebrows**  
   Willow-leaf eyebrows belong to gentle, intelligent, and meticulous individuals who value human relationships and therefore honor their parents and maintain harmony with siblings. Straight eyebrows belong to persevering, action-oriented individuals. Wide straight eyebrows indicate boldness, while narrow straight eyebrows indicate stubbornness and lack of endurance; such people can also be devious and may become high-intelligence offenders.

5. **Close-Set and Wide-Set Eyebrows**  
   The ideal distance between eyebrow and eye equals the width of one finger laid horizontally. People whose eyebrows press low over the eyes find it difficult to remain calm; they tend to be devious, suffer poor luck, and experience frequent family turmoil. They often lack vision, focus on immediate gains, and neglect the future. People whose eyebrows sit farther from the eyes usually have mild temperaments and an imposing presence, a sign of longevity.

6. **Wide and Narrow Eyebrow Spacing**

People with wide spacing between the eyebrows mature early, act steadily, and enjoy longevity. They possess broad-mindedness, wide perspectives, and an easygoing nature that avoids excessive concern over trifles. People with narrow spacing between the eyebrows are the opposite: narrow-minded and prone to serious illness in middle age.

##### Women Observing Men

- Men whose eyebrows are thick, close to the eyes, and whose gaze flickers should be approached with caution. Such men are naturally deceitful and may resort to any means for personal gain, including covert attacks. Having committed many unethical acts, they find it hard to trust anyone, including their girlfriends.
- Men with level, straight eyebrows are fair-minded and principled. They give an impression of safety and reliability, making them popular with women. They resist temptation and make ideal marriage partners, though they also hold their partners to high standards.
- Men whose eyebrows are fine, clearly defined, and grow smoothly along the brow bone often receive help from benefactors and enjoy good career luck.
- Men whose eyebrows extend straight and long past the eyes possess ambition and can advance rapidly in their careers.
- Men with high eyebrows and narrow noses tend to be knowledgeable, attuned to trends, refined in taste, and handsome; their standout qualities naturally draw attention.
- Men with messy eyebrows are usually highly opportunistic and lack a practical approach, so most achieve little.
- Men whose eyebrows press low over the eyes (the distance between brow and eye ideally accommodating one finger) are narrow-minded, timid, impatient, and profit-driven; most ultimately fail.
- Men whose eyebrows carry an “arrow” shape at the inner end love to stir trouble, criticize others while excusing themselves, and find harmonious relationships difficult.

##### Men Identifying Women

- Women with longer eyebrows are generally cautious and far-sighted. They approach marriage with great seriousness, love deeply once committed, and remain devoted.
- Women with shorter eyebrows are highly dependent, lack independence, and hold romantic fantasies while possessing rich and delicate emotions.
- Women with thick eyebrows are often careless and willful. They act decisively, refuse to accept defeat, and dislike a mundane housewife’s life. When given scope in the workplace they can become capable assistants to their husbands. In love they take the initiative, love and hate openly, and embrace new experiences.
- Women with fine eyebrows tend to be vain, status-conscious, and emotionally detached. They are emotional, intuitive, and inconsistent, making them unreliable.
- Women with narrow spacing between the eyebrows enjoy good interpersonal relationships and popularity; conversely, women with wide spacing are self-important, outgoing, and leadership-oriented.
- Women born with eyebrows set close together act impulsively and possess narrow minds.
- Women born with eyebrows set farther apart readily trust others, are easily deceived, and often waver in decisions.

##### Eyebrows That Are Soft and Well-Groomed

Eyebrows that are soft, extend gradually outward on both sides, and curve slightly indicate a cultivated person with a clear mind. Conversely, eyebrows that are stiff, upright, and sparse belong to people who lack cultivation, act carelessly, aim too high, and fail to stay grounded. If the eyebrows are also short, the person may shortchange friends because excessive self-protection and constant focus on personal gain create an impression of selfishness.

In addition, eyebrows that droop or hang low over the eyes indicate strong comprehension and keen observation. Level eyebrows indicate practicality. Curved eyebrows indicate sensitivity and love of beauty. Eyebrows whose tails point upward indicate a bold and strong character. Eyebrows whose tails point downward indicate a weak and pessimistic character. Spiral or whorled eyebrows indicate intelligence mixed with suspicion, strong vanity, and a tendency to encounter setbacks midway. “Eight-character” eyebrows indicate a tendency toward pessimism and inconstancy in love.

Of course, friends should remember that although “reading eyebrows reveals character” exists as a saying, truly understanding a person still requires comprehensive analysis and observation. Because people are the hardest to know, the saying “one may know a face but not the heart” remains true.

##### The Density of Eyebrows Reflects the Depth of Emotion

Thick eyebrows accompany deep emotions, while sparse eyebrows accompany shallow emotions. Beyond density, examine whether the eyebrows are thick yet soft and orderly, with clear upper and lower layers. If so, the person treats friends especially well, maintains sincere and lasting affection, and would go to any length for a friend.

Physiognomy generally holds that people with sparse, light eyebrows fundamentally disregard emotion, brotherhood, friendship, and marital bonds; they tend to “set morality aside and place profit in the center.” In daily life, those who abandon wives or sell out friends are mostly people with sparse, light eyebrows.

Each individual eyebrow hair represents care and feeling toward others. Especially under today’s market economy, such sparse-eyebrowed people will “step on friends’ heads” to pursue wealth for their own benefit and survival; once successful, they keep friends at a distance and prefer to enjoy their gains alone.

##### Which Eyebrow Shape Indicates Wealth Luck

The preceding discussion concerns eyebrows in motion. Even when eyebrows are still, their surface shape alone can reveal character traits.

Chinese folk wisdom also states: “Whether a person has money can be seen from the nose tip; whether a person can save money can be seen from the nostrils; but whether a person knows how to spend and earn money, or shares benefits with friends so that everyone profits together, must be judged from the eyebrows.”

##### Scattered and Fragmented Eyebrow Tails Symbolize Dispersal of Wealth

Eyebrow tails that are sparse, scattered, and broken—also called “broom eyebrows”—symbolize the dispersal of wealth. Such people often act without thorough consideration, lack planning, and easily act on impulse, so they frequently suffer unnecessary financial losses and scatter the money they have worked hard to earn. This shape shows the least sign of accumulating wealth. In addition, people with these eyebrows feel restless and worry excessively, making them even more prone to losing money.

##### People with Narrow Eyebrow Spacing Are Penny-Pinching

People with narrow spacing between the eyebrows are small-minded, fond of haggling over trifles, and petty; they find it hard to get along or cooperate with others. The reason is simple: whenever such a person encounters something disagreeable, they furrow their brows, and over time the muscles at the center of the brow atrophy, narrowing the space. Correspondingly, people with wide spacing between the eyebrows also have wide hearts.

##### People with Scattered Eyebrow Tails Feel Restless

The saying “when wealth disperses, people find no joy” fits these individuals perfectly. Because scattered eyebrows also represent scattered wealth, many financial problems arise and produce restlessness. If the eyelids are also puffy and press on the eyes, the person is even more likely to be a hot-tempered, selfish individual.

### Eyes

#### (1) Complete Closure

Eyelid closure is a voluntary movement that any normal person can perform at will. The content we examine focuses solely on instinctive reactions triggered by stimuli, excluding habitual eye closure (common among the elderly) and habitual blinking. These two behaviors lack a necessary stimulus source and therefore hold no value for psychological analysis. They can, however, serve as the subject’s **baseline reaction** for comparison. Deliberate closures or blinks are likewise excluded from consideration.

Stimuli capable of producing visual blocking fall into two broad categories: positive ones, such as music worth savoring, delicious food, or problems requiring concentrated thought; and negative ones, such as terrifying images or threatening questions. Both categories elicit the same cerebral response—“I don’t want to see it.”

**① Positive Stimulus Sources**

Positive stimuli prompt the brain to close the eyes in order to concentrate and prevent visual processing from diverting limited neural resources. Closing the eyes while listening to music heightens auditory perception; closing them while tasting food heightens gustatory perception; closing them while sniffing appears to sharpen the detection of subtle odors; and closing them while thinking allows mental energy to focus on finding a solution. More often than not, people do not close their eyes intentionally for these benefits; the action is an instinctive response to the stimulus itself, because visual processing consumes substantial neural capacity and closure conserves effort. As shown in Figure 10-11.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图10-11]*

Although precise data are unavailable, everyday observation and personal experience suggest—albeit “unscientifically”—that vision accounts for a very large share of human information intake. Reducing the neural load devoted to vision logically frees resources for other activities.

**② Negative Stimulus Sources**

Negative stimuli signal potential harm and generate unpleasant emotions such as sadness, worry (fear accompanied by thought), disgust, or fear (without thought). To reduce or avoid these stimuli, the nervous system orders the eyelids to close, cutting off visual input and thereby limiting damage.

A simple experiment illustrates the point: pick up a small object and make a sudden throwing motion toward a trusted companion (without actually releasing it). Even without prior warning, the person will almost invariably close the eyes reflexively. Long-term evolution has instilled an automatic self-protection mechanism that activates whenever harm is perceived, regardless of conscious trust.

Closure remains under voluntary control, yet sudden stimuli override conscious intention and are governed by evolved instinct.

Additional examples confirm that negative stimuli produce complete eyelid closure: after seeing a horrifying image, when feeling disgusted yet powerless, or when saddened and unwilling to look. As shown in Figure 10-12.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图10-12]*

High-frequency blinking in the absence of physical irritants (wind, particles) also constitutes visual blocking. The difference is that high-frequency blinking usually mixes instinctive closure with rational decision-making: the person both wants to block the image and strives to keep the eyes open to maintain rational engagement with the situation.

The clearest illustration occurs when people confront difficult decisions; blink rate rises noticeably.

“Difficult” here refers not to logical or computational problems—which typically produce frowning and a fixed stare—but to dilemmas involving choice: what to say, how to say it, or how to balance self-interest against risk. In actual testing, many effective stimuli have produced precisely this pattern: subjects unwilling to disclose the truth yet striving to appear forthcoming, resulting in rapid blinking.

**Test Case**

**What situations increase blink rate**

We tested a computer programmer whose résumé claimed years of experience and proficiency in multiple languages. When asked for algorithmic details of one language listed, his blink rate increased sharply for three to four seconds; he then admitted limited familiarity with that language.

**Principle:**

When facts must be concealed or details fabricated, intense cognitive effort is required. Prolonged closure or staring would be too obvious a tell, so the subject avoids them. The negative stimulus of the question, combined with the added load of concealment, produces elevated blink frequency even when the questioner is not visually aversive.

Note that this section addresses high-frequency blinking alone; in practice, increased blinking usually occurs together with gaze aversion, a topic examined separately below.

#### Interpreting Emotions Through Eye Expressions

The Indian poet Tagore observed: “Once anyone masters the language of the eyes, the variations of expression become endless.” Beyond their role as visual organs, the eyes convey a person’s genuine emotions.

Whenever circumstances permit, look directly into the other person’s eyes; doing so signals respect, sincerity, and a willingness to connect. Pay attention, however, to the duration of eye contact.

In *The Psychology of Interpersonal Behaviour*, Michael Argyle notes that mutual gaze typically occupies 30–60 percent of interaction time. When the proportion exceeds 60 percent, the parties are likely either mutually attracted or preparing to fight; further observation of accompanying behaviors is needed to distinguish the two.

What matters is not eye shape or size but the expression within the eyes. As Mencius wrote in “Li Lou I”: “Nothing about a person is better than the pupils. The pupils cannot conceal evil. When the heart is upright, the pupils are clear; when the heart is not upright, the pupils are clouded.” A person’s moral character is plainly visible in the eyes.

Thoughts and intentions frequently appear in the eyes; reading them reveals inner states. The following observations, drawn from classical and practical sources, illustrate how to discern intent from gaze during conversation:

- Steady, calm eyes indicate that the person already has a well-formed plan for the matter troubling you. If unwilling to state it openly, the reason is likely confidentiality; wait quietly for instructions.
- Scattered, unfocused eyes indicate helplessness. Anxiety or further questions are pointless; compose yourself and devise your own response.
- Eyes that dart sideways with a sharp quality signal marked coldness. Postpone any request and withdraw promptly; later analyze the cause and seek to restore rapport.
- Dark, sullen eyes are a warning of malice. Proceed with caution; the person may be preparing to strike from behind. Unless you intend confrontation, disengage.
- Restless, unusually mobile eyes suggest hidden schemes. Advance carefully; traps may lie on every side. Discount flattering words—they are bait.
- Dull, lifeless eyes accompanied by pale lips reveal extreme anxiety despite verbal reassurances. The person is still searching for a solution but has found none. Withdraw and formulate your own plan; if you have one, present it with an estimate of its chances.
- Eyes that seem to blaze indicate rising anger. Offer conciliation if you wish to avoid rupture; otherwise, further pressure will provoke open conflict.
- Serene eyes and a slight smile show genuine satisfaction. Compliments or requests are likely to be well received.
- Wandering, inattentive eyes indicate boredom; end the topic or change it.
- Steady, fixed eyes indicate that your remarks are considered worth hearing; continue as planned.
- Downcast eyes and lowered head signal heavy distress. Avoid cheerful or sympathetic topics; offer brief comfort and withdraw.
- Upward-rolling eyes indicate disdain; stop and seek another approach.

In short, eyes may be scattered or concentrated, mobile or still, flowing or fixed, sullen or dull, lowered or raised. Careful attention to these variations reveals character and intention with clarity.

#### Remember to Look at the Other Person One More Time

When two people meet each other’s gaze, both immediately sense a contradiction: they want eye contact yet also want to avoid it. This oscillation produces the complex patterns of human eye movement.

—Desmond Morris

We consciously regulate our actions to appear proper, yet our eyes often betray inner secrets. Others, like attentive hounds, watch those eyes for advantage. FBI experts, for example, detected panic in Saddam Hussein’s eyes—an observation that contributed to the decision to invade Iraq. Interrogators routinely mine fleeting glances for leverage.

Trust in conversation rests largely on eye contact. If a speaker’s eyes continually drift away, or if blink rate rises markedly above baseline, credibility suffers.

FBI agent Joe, acting on a tip, went to a suspect’s girlfriend’s apartment. She denied the suspect was present. During repeated questioning her blink rate rose noticeably while she remained outwardly calm. Joe concluded the suspect was inside and, after obtaining consent to search, found him in a wardrobe.

Joe’s detection of elevated blinking revealed the girlfriend’s concealed anxiety despite her composed demeanor.

Leonardo da Vinci remarked that “the eyes are the mirror of the soul.” Joe Navarro adds that sustained eye contact helps build rapport during interviews; when shaking hands or speaking, allow the gaze to linger before slowly shifting it to either side.

In daily interaction, eyes signal interest or aversion, maintain conversational control, and convey emotions words cannot express. They can foster warmth and openness or, conversely, tension.

During greetings, dominant individuals tend to maintain longer eye contact; more deferential individuals maintain shorter contact. Between men, prolonged same-sex eye contact can be misinterpreted; brevity is advisable.

To keep an interaction comfortable, break eye contact roughly every five seconds rather than staring continuously. Avoid looking down, which signals a desire to end the exchange. Instead, glance upward or sideways as if thinking; the other person will interpret the movement as cognitive effort and remain engaged. While listening, cycle attention between one eye, the other eye, and the mouth; the speaker will sense genuine interest.

In argument, steady, resolute eye contact can exert pressure without words. Maintain the gaze while the other speaks, observing tone and expression. Silence combined with unwavering attention is often sufficient to prevail.

#### Why Do the Eyeballs Keep Moving

In everyday conversation and communication, we can easily notice that a speaker’s eyeballs are not fixed on a single point. They sometimes move left, sometimes right, sometimes up, sometimes down. Most people overlook this, yet in micro-expression research, eyeball movement occupies a crucial position.

The first to discover that eyeball movement relates to a person’s thoughts were Richard Bandler and John Grinder, who together created NLP (Neuro-Linguistic Programming), which includes EAC (Eye Accessing Cues). They proposed that eyeball activity falls into the following categories:

- Eyes looking up and to the left indicate people are recalling images; eyes looking up and to the right indicate people are constructing images. These belong to visual memory and visual construction.
- Eyes looking horizontally to the left indicate people are recalling sounds; eyes looking horizontally to the right indicate people are constructing sounds. These belong to auditory memory and auditory construction.
- Eyes looking down and to the left indicate people are thinking to themselves, known as “internal dialogue”; eyes looking down and to the right indicate people are feeling, including emotional sensations and physical touch sensations, which belong to kinesthetic memory. Research shows that habitually looking down and to the right over long periods can make a person prone to depression.

Suppose you ask a friend whether they went to the beach on vacation. If their eyes first look up and to the left, then down and to the right, it shows they began by recalling the beach scene and then recalled the associated feelings, confirming the certainty of the trip. This proves they really went. If, upon hearing the question, they quickly glance up and to the right, it indicates they are searching their mind for previously seen beach photos or footage and using those memories to fabricate a beach experience. This is enough to prove they did not go but are trying to describe a beach convincingly.

Now let’s conduct an interesting experiment to demonstrate the relationship between eyeball movement and sensory memory.

Look up and to the left and picture the appearance of a friend you have not seen for several years. Although many details may be unclear, their overall look will still appear in your mind. Give yourself half a minute to recall, without rushing, and try to retrieve some details. After half a minute, look straight ahead and clear the image from your mind. Then look down and to the right and try to recall the friend’s appearance again. You will find that the earlier recall was smooth, but now it comes in fragments and your attention is hard to sustain. This shows that looking down and to the right does not aid visual recall.

However, this eye-accessing-cue pattern does not apply to everyone. Some people’s sensory memory and eyeball movement are reversed, although such individuals are rare. In those cases we cannot rely entirely on the pattern and must first determine the relationship between the person’s sensory memory and their eyeball movement. There is a very simple test.

You can ask them some straightforward questions:

- What color are the walls in your room? If their eyes look up and to the left before answering, it shows their visual memory follows the eye-accessing-cue pattern. If you are still unsure, continue with more questions, such as asking them to describe their mother’s appearance, until you are certain their visual memory matches the pattern.
- Next is visual construction. Try asking: Imagine what a person of the opposite sex would look like wearing your clothes. How would the wallpaper at home look if changed to a floral pattern? If their eyes look up and to the right, you can then judge the truthfulness of their statements using the eye-accessing-cue pattern.
- Then come auditory memory and auditory construction. For auditory memory you can ask: How does the chorus of your favorite song go? What does your favorite person of the opposite sex sound like? For auditory construction you can ask: What would music sound like if it could play underwater? Imagine the sound of ice cracking. If their eyes move left during recall and right during construction, they fit the eye-accessing-cue pattern.
- Finally, kinesthetic memory. You can ask them what moldy bread tastes like, or to imagine hugging their favorite person, or biting into a sour orange. If their eyes look down and to the right, it proves they fit the eye-accessing-cue pattern. If you wish to continue, you can ask what encouraging words they would say to themselves if they failed. If their eyes look down and to the left, it shows they are engaged in “internal dialogue.”

#### (2) The Erroneous Application of Cross-Control of Left and Right Brain Movement

If an improper summary of brain-function lateralization is still excusable, then deriving from that mistaken summary a link between eye-movement direction and left-right brain division is an even more ignorant display.

The basis for this derivation is presumably the principle of crossed control between the two hemispheres. Crossed control means the left hemisphere controls movement of the right-side limbs and the right hemisphere controls movement of the left-side limbs. This is a scientific conclusion.

What is hard to understand is that, if the crossed-control rule is followed, the left hemisphere should control the right eye and the right hemisphere the left eye. If recall or fabrication engaged only one hemisphere according to its specialized functions (which in fact does not occur), the result should be movement in one eye rather than both eyes moving together. Moreover, according to crossed control, if the right hemisphere governs left-hand movement, does that mean the left hand can only move leftward? If leftward movement is managed by the right hemisphere, then when both hands move leftward together, which hemisphere should control them?

Therefore, the direction of eye movement has no relation whatsoever to functional differences between the left and right hemispheres.

The original source of this fallacy may lie in NLP’s six-direction eye-movement theory.

In this well-known speculative model, the “NLP school” claims that when a person’s eyes turn up and to the left, they are recalling visual information, such as “What color are your curtains?” When the eyes turn up and to the right, they are constructing visual information, such as “What color is a purple zebra’s tail?” When the eyes turn horizontally to the left, they are recalling auditory information, such as the melody of a famous piece of music; when the eyes turn horizontally to the right, they are constructing auditory information, such as composing an original melody. When the eyes turn down and to the left, the person is talking to themselves; when the eyes turn down and to the right, they are perceiving kinesthetic and sensory information.

To prevent their speculation from being falsified, NLP also added a left-handed reversal supplement: if the person is left-handed, all directions are reversed. This still relies on the theory of crossed hemispheric control of the limbs.

In reality, to provide coherent visual information, eye movements must occur simultaneously and in the same direction; otherwise visual confusion results. Every nerve that controls the extraocular muscles receives input from corticobulbar fibers of both hemispheres.

In other words, each eye is simultaneously controlled by both sides of the brain.

Thus normal eye movements are conjugate; they do not allow the independent, asynchronous movements possible with the limbs.

Of course, with training some people can deliberately perform disconjugate movements, because during convergence both medial rectus muscles contract simultaneously, the lens thickens, and the pupils constrict, enabling near fine work. By contrast, the lateral rectus muscles responsible for divergence are not controlled by the oculomotor nucleus but by the abducens nucleus; therefore the two eyes cannot diverge without passing through the oculomotor nucleus, whereas the medial rectus muscles are directly controlled by the oculomotor nucleus, allowing crossed eyes.

The neurophysiological principles are presented to demonstrate that eye-movement direction is entirely different from the crossed-control mechanism of the limbs and cannot be arbitrarily applied by imagination.

This set of conjectures, published in 1979, has no data support and cannot withstand verification.

We conducted a small experiment: 200 participants each answered six questions while their eye movements were recorded on video and later analyzed.

The statistical results showed that some criteria had a mismatch rate above 70 percent, others close to 50 percent; the average falsification rate for the six rules was 63 percent. In other words, using six-direction eye movement to analyze another person’s thoughts carries nearly a two-thirds chance of being wrong—less reliable than a 50-50 guess. The probability that any one person fully conforms to the six-direction pattern is 37 percent, roughly three per thousand (2.6‰), an appallingly low figure.

Therefore this judgment criterion can produce erroneous conclusions and wrongfully implicate others.

At this point we can safely discard this “pseudoscience.” If interested, you may also carefully examine the similar rumor that “right-handed people are more rational (rigorous, conservative, etc.) while left-handed people are more artistic (innovative, emotional, etc.)” and identify where it goes wrong.

#### Those Who Look Away First Lack Confidence

The popularity of the American drama *Lie to Me* sparked a wave of “micro-expression research” in society. As one parent whose son is still in elementary school described: “My son is in elementary school. Because I didn’t want him watching television too late and affecting his studies, I told him the television might have a problem.” The son immediately replied with great certainty: “Don’t lie to me. You touched your forehead while speaking, which shows you weren’t confident when you said that, so you were lying. I know exactly what you’re thinking…”

In truth, the flamboyant Dr. Lightman on the show is no match for real FBI agents who must judge expressions daily.

The FBI possesses a videotape recording the entire exchange between agents and a person of interest in one case. The interviewee, Carter—a murder suspect—had every detail of his responses captured. After the agents posed a highly provocative question, Carter leaned forward slightly and gave a very mild reply. In those few seconds, most people would miss anything unusual and might even believe Carter’s gentle answer proved his innocence. Yet the experienced agents’ eyes did not miss it.

After the first interview, the agents reviewed the tape and noticed a subtle detail. They rewound and played it at one-quarter speed. In a segment lasting less than one second, Carter’s expression completely distorted: his nose wrinkled, facial muscles contorted, teeth bared, and eyebrows lowered—an unmistakable expression of anger and disgust. After finishing his answer he also stole two glances at the agents. Clearly Carter had very little confidence in his own reply.

Some human micro-expressions last only 1/25 of a second and are hard for ordinary people to detect, yet they accurately reflect the person’s true emotional changes. If, after we ask a question and receive a very affirmative answer, the speaker raises their head or shifts their gaze upward to observe our expression just as they finish, we can be certain they lack confidence in their answer. Because they lack confidence, they care greatly about others’ opinions and therefore secretly observe us. Such signals usually last only about 0.5 seconds. Spotting this expression near the end of a conversation allows us to grasp the other person’s inner world; we must not let the moment pass but should press for more time to uncover the truth.

In Carter’s case, after reviewing the tape the agents used the tactic of denying his answers and obtained the truth. Thus, during information-gathering conversations, accurately judging whether the other party’s expression conveys confidence is extremely important.

We also often hear statements such as “That price is already the lowest; I can’t go any lower” or “I’ve told you I don’t know, because I wasn’t even at the scene.” If the speaker delivers these firm words yet steals a glance at us at the critical final moment, we can conclude the firmness is feigned.

If we continue to maintain eye contact, the other person will often look away and lower their head, fearing their true thoughts will be exposed. To conceal this, they must lower their head. This further confirms their answer is not confident or that room for negotiation remains. We therefore have no need to compromise and can adopt an equally firm stance to counterattack. Faced with false firmness, greater firmness on our part will only increase their tension, forcing them to retract their earlier statements and ultimately reveal their bottom line.

Conversely, if we wish to feign firmness ourselves, we must not voluntarily look away during the exchange, as doing so would give the opponent an opening to probe our own bottom line.

#### The Eyes Are the Windows to the Soul

Every part of the human brain, like other parts of the body, develops with greater use and atrophies or loses function with disuse. Consequently, the language centers of talkative people are highly developed. This theory was first discovered in 1861 by the famous French surgeon and neuropathologist Paul Broca. At the time Broca was director of a Paris insane asylum. After some patients with aphasia died, he dissected their brains and found that a specific region in each case either contained a tumor or had been destroyed. This gray area lies just behind and above the eyeball; the medical community named it “Broca’s area” and the resulting aphasia “Broca’s aphasia,” or “motor aphasia.”

Under normal conditions, blood flow to this region increases when a person speaks compared with when they are silent. Therefore the more one talks, the more developed the area becomes, causing the eyeballs to protrude slightly downward and outward. In other words, of two otherwise similar people standing before you, the one whose eyeballs protrude slightly is usually the more talkative. Once they start speaking they become voluble, sometimes even gesticulating. You can take advantage of this by extracting useful information from their torrent of words.

Of course your counterpart may be taciturn, in which case you cannot obtain much useful information from their mouth, yet you can still capture through their eyes certain “truths” of which they themselves may be unaware.

For example, while you are earnestly presenting your proposal, if the other person’s gaze drifts elsewhere, they are probably uninterested in what you are saying or are thinking about something else. At such moments you need to change the topic or strategy promptly, or cooperation will be difficult. Likewise, when a person’s emotions change, their pupils change accordingly—an alteration they cannot see but you can observe clearly. Many expert card players win repeatedly because they are skilled at reading opponents’ pupil changes to infer whether their hands are strong or weak. When a person is excited, their pupils can dilate four- or fivefold; when calm, they constrict sharply. Similarly, salespeople can gauge whether a customer is interested in their product, and negotiators can sense whether the other side is satisfied with the terms.

The eyes easily betray a person’s inner state. If someone’s eyelids are half-closed, their eyeballs darting left and right, and they avoid direct eye contact, it is basically safe to conclude they have something to hide. By contrast, an honest person will look at you calmly and steadily—an expression that cannot be faked. Some cunning individuals deliberately feign honesty, appearing calm and composed, yet to mask the lack of confidence in their gaze they often overdo it by staring fixedly.

In addition, blink rate can reveal clues. Blinking is a subconscious behavior that is difficult to control without special training. Psychological research has found that when psychological pressure suddenly increases, blink rate rises. For instance, when a non-professional liar tells a lie, their psychological pressure surges and their blink rate can more than double compared with normal.

Some people also unconsciously glance sideways at you, sometimes briefly, sometimes for longer. Generally, a sideways glance carries three possible meanings:

- Interest in you, though the glance is usually furtive and not meant to be noticed;
- Inner hesitation;
- Dismissiveness toward what you are saying—this being the most common meaning of a sideways glance.

Of course we cannot stare at an opponent indefinitely; doing so makes people uncomfortable. Psychologists suggest that during conversation it is appropriate for one’s gaze to rest on the other person’s face 30–60 percent of the time; when managed well, this can effectively produce positive outcomes. Therefore correct gazing is very important in communication.

In daily life, three gazing styles are most commonly used.

#### Visual, Auditory, or Kinesthetic

Have you ever watched a skilled locksmith at work? It is almost like watching magic.

He handles a lock and hears sounds you cannot hear, sees things you cannot see, and senses conditions you cannot feel. In moments he understands the entire structure of the lock and repairs it.

An excellent communicator works the same way. He can discern anyone’s inner combination (also called strategy)—thinking and reflecting like a locksmith to map out another person’s internal structure.

The key to understanding someone’s strategy is to notice their words and actions. People transmit every signal you need about their strategy, sometimes through language, sometimes through behavior, and sometimes even through their eyes.

You can learn to read a person as skillfully as you read a book or a map. Remember, a strategy is simply an imagined combination that produces a specific result. Your task is to prompt people to experience their strategies while you observe their distinctive reactions.

People generally fall into three types: visual, auditory, and kinesthetic.

- **Visual**: People who primarily use the visual system tend to view the world in images. They obtain their greatest sensory power through the visual portion of the brain. Because their language tries to keep pace with the changing images in their minds, they often speak quickly. Because they simply want to describe the images in their heads, they pay less attention to phrasing and prefer visual language, describing how things look, what shapes they take, and whether they are bright or dark.
- **Auditory**: People with strong auditory senses speak more slowly, with fuller voices and measured rhythm. Because words carry great weight for them, they choose what to say with care. They often express themselves with auditory language, such as “That sounds right to me,” “I can hear what you’re saying,” or “Everything sounds fine.”
- **Kinesthetic**: People with strong kinesthetic senses speak even more slowly. They respond mainly to touch, their voices are deep, and each sentence seems squeezed out one word at a time. They frequently use kinesthetic language, always trying to “grasp” the “concrete form” of something—whether it feels “heavy” or needs to be “touched.” They commonly say, “I’ve found the answer, but I haven’t quite gotten hold of it yet.”

Everyone possesses all three systems, yet most people are dominated by only one. When you are learning someone’s strategy and decision-making process, first identify which sensory system is primary so you can tailor your message accordingly.

By watching and listening while paying close attention to a person’s eyes, you can immediately recognize which system they are using.

Consider this question: What color were the candles on your twelfth birthday cake? When answering, 90 percent of people raise their heads and look to the left; this is how right-handed people, and even some left-handers, recall visual images.

Now answer the next question: What would Mickey Mouse look like with a mustache? Take a few minutes to describe it. This time the eyes may rise and move to the right—the place where the eyes construct images.

Thus, simply by watching people’s eyes you can understand their strategies.

A person’s voice also carries meaning. Visual people speak quickly and sharply, often with a nasal tone and wide pitch variation. Kinesthetic people speak slowly and in a deep register. Auditory people maintain an even tone and articulate clearly.

Therefore, even limited interaction can reveal a person’s mental processes clearly and accurately. The best way to learn strategies, however, is not observation but practice. Apply these exercises to as many people as possible.

#### Understanding People’s Feelings Through Eye Expressions

Psychologists tell us that a person’s hidden thoughts and conflicts always surface unconsciously through changes in the eyes. FBI agents have long noted this and focus on suspects’ eyes during interviews.

How, then, can we read someone’s true thoughts from their eyes during conversation? The following points are offered for reference.

- When the eyes are calm and steady, the person already has a clear plan and is confident of success regarding the matter that concerns you. If you ask for advice and the person does not state it plainly, it is usually because the matter is confidential. Do not press; simply wait for their decision.
- When the eyes appear scattered and unfocused, the person also has no solution. Becoming anxious is useless, and asking for guidance is equally pointless. Stay calm, think of your own approach, and stop asking; further questions will only increase their confusion. This is your moment to show ability—devise a plan yourself.
- When the eyes shoot sideways with a sharp look, the person is unusually cold. If you have a request, do not present it; find an excuse to leave at once. Even staying a moment longer is inappropriate. Afterward, examine why they are distant and seek ways to restore rapport.
- When the eyes look dark and gloomy, recognize it as a signal of ruthlessness. Negotiate with caution. A dangerous hand may be poised behind you. Unless you are prepared for confrontation, withdraw quickly.
- When the eyes move in ways unlike their usual pattern, the person harbors a scheme and intends to make things difficult. Proceed carefully; do not approach lightly. Traps may lie on every side. Do not trust sweet words; they are bait on a hook or sugar coating on poison.
- When the eyes look dull and the lips pale, the person is extremely anxious about the current problem. Although they say it is nothing and are still trying to find a way, they cannot. Stop asking; withdraw and consider your own response. If you already have a plan, present it and state your level of confidence.
- When the eyes seem to blaze, the person is burning with anger. If you do not intend to break with them, signal compromise and seek a way out. Otherwise, further pressure will trigger open conflict.
- When the eyes are tranquil and a smile appears, the person is very pleased about something. To win favor, offer a few compliments. If you have a request, this is a good moment; they are more likely than usual to agree.
- When the eyes dart about and the person seems distracted, they have grown tired of what you are saying and further talk will be pointless. End the conversation, take your leave, or introduce a new topic they prefer.
- When the eyes fix steadily on you, the person believes your words are worth hearing. Present your case as planned. If your reasoning is sound and your proposal feasible, they will accept it.
- When the eyes lower and the head tilts downward, the person carries a heavy burden of worry or pain. Do not speak of happy matters, which would only deepen their distress, nor of painful ones, which would intensify shared suffering. Offer a few words of comfort and leave promptly; further talk is pointless.
- When the eyes turn upward, the person is unwilling to listen. No matter how strong your arguments or how skillful your delivery, the outcome will not be pleasant. Stop at once and seek another approach later.

In short, eyes may scatter or focus, move or stay still, flow or fix, appear dark or dull, lower or rise. Careful observation will reveal people’s feelings completely.

#### Eye Contact

When you listen intently to someone, have you noticed their eyes drifting to other objects? When you are halfway through a story, have you noticed the listener watching you closely the whole time? People generally seek stronger eye contact while listening than while speaking.

When we listen carefully, we usually look at the speaker, especially the eyes. This helps us understand what is said and provides clear feedback. When we speak, however, we tend to look around or fix on other objects to organize our thoughts.

If someone avoids your eyes during conversation, they are either not listening or hiding something.

In *The Psychology of Interpersonal Behaviour*, Michael Argyle notes that mutual gaze typically occupies 30–60 percent of interaction time. When gaze exceeds 60 percent, the individuals are likely either attracted to each other or preparing to fight; further behavioral cues are needed to determine which.

Cultural background and location determine whether eye contact is appropriate. In North America, people generally favor eye contact; elsewhere it may be viewed as an attempt to dominate and considered rude.

In some places, eye contact between a woman and an unrelated man is regarded as improper. In others, a woman’s use of eye contact signals that she is a prostitute.

Before interpreting someone’s eye contact negatively, consider their cultural background and the reasons they may avoid it.

Another factor is personality. Extroverts usually have no difficulty with eye contact, while shy people may engage in less. When a normally shy person suddenly makes more eye contact than usual, it may indicate they are pretending or lying. Do not overlook this basic point.

When asked a question that makes them uncomfortable or unsure how to answer, people often try to change the subject and adopt a defensive posture, producing more eye contact than usual.

In a state of staring or gazing, the eyes remain fixed on a particular object. Upon entering a room we instinctively scan it quickly and register our surroundings—an automatic action of which we are barely aware. If our eyes linger longer than usual on an object or person, it signals interest.

When observing someone who is staring or gazing, note whether the eyes are focused or vacant. Focused eyes indicate active thinking or analysis. Vacant eyes suggest daydreaming and lack of awareness of the object in view.

#### Reading Inner States from Eye Expressions

Micro-expression keywords: Many liars avoid eye contact; people expressing affection gaze deeply into each other’s eyes. A person’s inner secrets are written in the eyes. To read others, one must interpret their gaze.

The ancients spoke of observing a person’s “spirit,” which refers to the eyes. Successful social interaction depends on reading expressions; at every moment one must adjust approach according to facial changes. The most characteristic facial change is in the eyes. Therefore, recognizing others’ thoughts requires skill in reading their eyes.

When a person’s eyes are calm and steady, they already have a clear plan and are confident of success. For some reason they cannot state it plainly. Do not press; simply wait for their action.

When the eyes appear scattered, the person has no solution. Asking for advice is useless; stay calm and devise your own approach.

When the eyes shoot sideways with a sharp look, the attitude is unusually cold. If you have a request, set it aside for now, examine the reason for the coldness, repair the relationship, and then seek help.

When the eyes look dark and gloomy, the person is ruthless. Deal with such an individual with extreme caution. Unless necessary, keep your distance for safety.

When the eyes move frequently in unusual ways, the person harbors schemes and is deeply calculating. Do not trust their words, especially pleasant ones; they may be bait on a hook. Proceed with great care.

When the eyes look dull, the person is slow-witted, timid, and slow-thinking. Do not consult them about problems. A timely hint may earn their lasting gratitude.

When the eyes appear exceptionally sharp, the person is angry and emotions are running high. The slightest spark may trigger an outburst. Do not confront; compromise appropriately and seek an exit.

When the eyes are tranquil and a smile appears, the person is especially pleased with something or someone. To win favor, offer compliments. If you have a request, this is a good opening.

When the eyes wander restlessly, the person has grown impatient. Further talk will only increase annoyance. Stop at once, take your leave, or introduce a topic they enjoy.

When the eyes fix steadily on you, the person is keenly interested and eager to hear more. Whatever you say will be well received.

When the eyes lower, a painful memory has been touched. Stop immediately.

When the eyes turn upward, the person is unwilling to listen. No amount of reasoning or skill will persuade them; they have already seen through your intent and will only become more dismissive. Stop at once and seek another opportunity later.

In short, eyes may be dull or lively, dark or clear, sharp or gentle. Careful observation will reveal a person’s true inner state.

#### 1. Eyelids

For practical purposes, the eyelids may be understood as the common term “eye skin,” yet they are more than a simple layer of skin. Inside the eyelids lie glands and muscles. The glands secrete fluid that lubricates the eyeball, while closure of the eyelids is controlled by the orbicularis oculi muscle. When this muscle contracts, the upper and lower eyelids close, protecting the eyeball. In addition, inside the upper eyelid is the levator palpebrae superioris muscle, which raises the upper eyelid—commonly called opening the eyes. Both muscles are largely under voluntary motor control and can be moved at will; in academic terms this is called “voluntary movement.” The upper eyelid also contains smooth-muscle components controlled solely by the autonomic nervous system and cannot be moved at will.

From this we may draw an important conclusion: all eyelid-closure movements are executed under neural command. Sometimes closure occurs because one “wants” to close the eyes; a normal person can perform this action voluntarily at any time. At other times closure occurs without conscious intent, driven instead by emotion, instinct, or habit and without passing through deliberate thought. Two simple examples illustrate this:

1. Stand face-to-face with a good friend. Tell them “Don’t be afraid,” but do not instruct them “Don’t blink.” Suddenly make a threatening motion toward their eyes without actually striking them. Observe the reaction. They know you are a friend and will not harm them, yet the eyelids still close involuntarily to protect the eyes—an evolved instinctive response. Only if you specifically instruct them beforehand “Do not blink” might they be able to suppress it.
2. Place something foul-smelling (such as stinky tofu) or visually repulsive in a cup. Ask your best friend to smell or look at it, warning them that it is unpleasant but urging them to try. Despite the trusted instruction and mental preparation, they will still involuntarily furrow the brow and narrow the eyes (eyelid closure).

**Summary**: When confronted with disliked, difficult, or distressing negative stimuli, the eyelids close involuntarily in an attempt to reduce the impact of the stimulus. Although the action is involuntary in the sense that it is not directed by conscious thought, it remains under neural control. The anatomical structure of the upper eyelid is shown in Figure 10-7.

Inside the eyelid there is also a muscle called Müller’s muscle (Müller肌), which differs in that it is smooth muscle. Smooth muscle is governed by the autonomic nervous system and cannot be controlled by “wanting” to move it; its action is an involuntary neural response, academically termed “involuntary movement.” When the sympathetic nervous system is excited by negative stimuli such as fright, anger, or pain, contraction of these muscles increases the degree to which the eyes open. Consequently, effective stimulation produces involuntary reactions, and these “involuntary movements” are highly valuable for analyzing a person’s true psychological state.

#### 1. Eyelids

Loosely speaking, the eyelid can be understood as the commonly referred to eyelid skin, but unlike its colloquial name suggests, it is not merely a layer of skin. Inside the eyelid there are also glands and muscles. The fluid secreted by the glands lubricates the eyeball, while closure of the eyelid is controlled by the orbicularis oculi muscle. When the orbicularis oculi contracts, the upper and lower eyelids close, protecting the eyeball. In addition, inside the upper eyelid there is a “levator palpebrae superioris” muscle whose sole function is to lift the upper eyelid upward, commonly known as opening the eyes. Most of these two muscles are under somatic-nerve control and can be consciously directed—an action academically termed “voluntary movement.” The upper eyelid also contains a smooth-muscle component governed solely by the autonomic nervous system; it cannot be controlled by “thinking.”

From this we can derive an important conclusion: every eyelid-closure movement is executed under neural-system command. Sometimes the person “wants” to close the eyes and a normal individual can do so at will; at other times the closure occurs without conscious intent, driven instead by emotion, instinct, or habit and bypassing deliberate thought. The two simplest examples are:

1. Stand face-to-face with a good friend, tell him or her “don’t be afraid,” but do not add “don’t blink,” then suddenly make a threatening gesture toward the friend’s eyes—without actually striking. Observe the reaction. The friend knows you are a good friend and will not cause harm, yet the eyelids still close involuntarily to protect the eyes; this is an evolved instinctive response. Of course, if you had specifically instructed the friend beforehand “don’t blink,” he or she might have been able to suppress it.
2. Fill a cup with something foul-smelling (for example, stinky tofu) or visually repulsive, then ask your best friend to smell or look at it, stressing that the contents are unpleasant but urging the friend to try anyway. Despite the trusted request and mental preparation, the friend will still involuntarily furrow the brows and squint (eyelid closure).

**Summary**: When confronted with disliked, difficult, or distressing negative stimuli, the eyelids close involuntarily in an attempt to reduce the impact of the stimulus. Although the movement is involuntary in the sense that it is not directed by conscious thought, it is still executed under neural-system command. The anatomical structure of the upper eyelid is shown in Figure 10-7.
