Inside the eyelid there is also a set of muscles called Müller’s muscle (Müller muscle); these are smooth muscle and therefore governed by the autonomic nervous system. Their movement cannot be controlled by “thinking”; it is an automatic neural behavior, academically termed “involuntary movement.” When the sympathetic nerves are excited by negative stimuli such as fright, anger, or pain, contraction of these muscles increases the degree to which the eyes are open. Consequently, when a person receives an effective stimulus, involuntary reactions appear, and these “involuntary movements” are highly valuable for analyzing a person’s true psychological state.

#### Clue Four: Blinking and Eye Closure

The eye closure and blinking discussed here refer to reactions that occur after the eyes receive external stimuli. Because both types of facial change can be consciously controlled, deliberate or habitual blinking and closure fall outside the present discussion.

We can begin with a pleasant visualization:

Walking barefoot on a warm evening beach, sunlight spreading across the sea, a scene of molten-gold sunset. Beautiful music and the sound of waves reach the ears, prompting spontaneous dancing. From not far away your dream lover approaches; hand in hand you dance together.

Do you find yourself unconsciously closing your eyes while mentally picturing this romantic scene, even the appearance of the dream lover? This eye closure is triggered by positive stimuli; you are entranced and enjoying the moment, mentally filling in details. Clearly, the primary function of such closure is to heighten a particular sensory experience. Standing among flowers and closing the eyes to inhale deeply intensifies smell; tasting fine wine or food with eyes closed intensifies taste; listening to music with eyes closed intensifies hearing. In short, eye closure under positive stimulation serves to concentrate attention. Just as you mentally reconstruct the scene above, a high degree of focused attention is required.

From the standpoint of expression, eye closure under positive stimulation conveys relaxation and pleasure. The corners of the mouth lift slightly, the brows remain relatively level, and changes are minimal.

In addition to positive stimuli, many negative stimuli also cause us to close our eyes—for example, witnessing a bloody surgical procedure, a frightening scene in a horror film, coercion, grief-driven avoidance, something repulsive, or the helplessness of disappointment.

Under negative stimulation, eye closure serves to block unpleasant visual information and is often an unconscious reaction. When sudden negative stimuli arrive, the eyes close instinctively to protect the self before conscious thought can intervene.

From the standpoint of expression, eye closure under negative stimulation conveys discomfort and aversion. The chin shows uneven folds, the mouth corners turn downward, the brows furrow, and transverse wrinkles appear across the bridge of the nose. Multiple muscles—the frontalis, corrugator supercilii, orbicularis oculi, depressor labii inferioris, and orbicularis oris—are involved, making the movement difficult to fake.

Like eye closure, blinking can also be voluntarily controlled, yet rapid blinking belongs to instinctive closure. This commonly occurs when people encounter a thorny problem. We have all experienced situations in which an interviewer asks about a subject we are not good at. You may not notice it, but if recorded, you would see that within four seconds of facing the difficult question you blink several times. This results from simultaneously trying, by instinct, to close the eyes and escape the problem while striving to keep them open and solve it.

The “problem” here is not a mathematical or logical calculation; it refers to the need to decide what to do next, how to resolve the issue quickly, or what to say. When facing the former type of problem we usually furrow our brows; when facing the latter we blink rapidly. At the same time the direction of gaze also shifts.

#### People Whose Eyes Habitually Turn Rightward Are Impatient and Irritable

During conversation the eyes often move in different directions. Therefore, simply noticing which way a person’s eyes turn while thinking can reveal aspects of that person’s character without either party realizing it.

The “prisoner-abuse scandal” prompted outside scrutiny of U.S. prison management. The authorities assigned the FBI to investigate; the warden named Bert received the most accusations from inmates, so agents decided to interview him. The interview took place in Bert’s office.

The office was simply yet elegantly furnished, indicating that its occupant was a highly cultivated person. When the agents met Bert they found it hard to connect him with the inmates’ description of a “prison demon.” Bert’s attire, background, speech, and manner toward the agents all conveyed courtesy. Once everyone was seated the interview began.

Throughout the agents’ pointed questioning Bert maintained a mild demeanor and gave reasoned answers, reinforcing the agents’ belief that he bore no resemblance to the “irascible and brutal” figure described by the inmates. During the entire interview the only notable behavior was that Bert’s eyes repeatedly turned rightward when he answered questions; otherwise everything appeared smooth. Precisely because of this eye-turning habit, one astute senior agent began to doubt Bert’s true character.

Earlier, professors at Stanford University had conducted specialized research on the relationship between eye movement and personality. They invited several men and, for thirty seconds, continuously asked them various questions while recording the direction of eye movement. The subjects were then divided into two groups: Group A consisted of those whose eyes turned left while answering; Group B consisted of those whose eyes turned right while answering.

Analysis of the two groups’ personalities revealed that members of Group B were more impatient and aggressive; they found it difficult to suppress feelings of restlessness for long or to conceal them completely and would eventually seek an outlet. Members of Group A displayed the opposite traits; they tended to internalize displeasure and did not exhibit aggression.

From the eye-movement evidence the agents concluded that Warden Bert was in fact an irascible person whose mild façade was a disguise. In a second interview they deliberately provoked him with rude language, exploiting his character weakness to elicit the truth. Bert fell into the trap and revealed his irritable, violent nature.

People who are easily angered are usually poor at managing interpersonal relationships. Because such a temperament is not formed overnight, changing it is no easy task. Consequently, when interacting with others, if you notice that a person habitually turns the eyes rightward, you can infer that the individual is highly aggressive and difficult to handle. Only by making full use of this trait during conversation can you better accomplish your objective.

#### Reading Emotion from the Eyes

Modern cosmetic techniques can alter the eye socket, canthi, eye corners, eyelids, and even eyelashes, yet they cannot change a person’s gaze. No matter how advanced the techniques, makeup or surgery cannot mask the eyes. Therefore, rather than listening to eloquent speech, observe the eyes carefully.

On television we often see gamblers wear sunglasses while placing bets to shield their gaze and prevent opponents from reading their emotions. This demonstrates the close relationship between changes in the eyes and psychological activity.

In today’s society we inevitably encounter all kinds of people. To interact more effectively, one must be able to read emotion through another person’s eyes. Most people believe that only the eyes do not lie; if you wish to glimpse someone’s inner world, begin with the eyes.

What emotional changes, then, can be discerned from a person’s eyes?

1. Eyes bright, slightly sinister  
   If the other person’s eyes are bright and slightly sinister, it indicates distrust. During an argument, if one party displays this look, hostility is present. When a friend or colleague misunderstands you and you attempt to explain, the other person will often show this expression.

2. Lifeless eyes  
   Some believe that lifeless eyes appear only when a person harbors no dissatisfaction. This view is mistaken. For example, when you run into a former girlfriend and say, “I happened to be passing by and didn’t expect to see you—would you like to have coffee?” if she merely smiles briefly on her face and quickly returns to a lifeless gaze, it usually signals inner unease and dissatisfaction with the present situation.

3. Focused gaze  
   If the other person’s eyes remain focused while you speak, it means he or she is listening attentively. This can be interpreted in two ways: either the topic genuinely interests the listener, who is happy to hear you talk; or the listener finds your words of little use yet maintains politeness and respect by not interrupting rudely.

4. Shifting gaze  
   A shifting gaze is often a sign of inner unease. A special group merits attention here: individuals medically termed “gaze-phobia patients.” After their eyes meet another person’s, they immediately look away and then glance about involuntarily, feeling extremely uncomfortable.

5. Upward or downward gaze  
   An upward gaze signals respect and admiration; conversely, a downward gaze indicates an intention to preserve one’s dignity or a slight sense of emptiness.

6. Sharp, stern gaze  
   A sharp, stern gaze usually constitutes a warning not to cross the person’s底线.

#### (1) Absence of [I want to tell you]

The true psychological state is [I do not want to tell you]. Because the speaker does not wish to continue yet is compelled by the situation to say something, gaze aversion occurs and eye contact is broken.

Several behaviors may accompany the gaze shift:

- The speaker tells the truth but treats the act of speaking as a mere task, unconcerned whether the listener actually hears it.
- The underlying reluctance produces hesitant speech (pauses, stuttering, repetition, etc.) together with reduced volume and tone.
- Certain information is deliberately withheld.
- Fabricated information is supplied merely to manage the immediate conversational context.

**Specific Cases**

**Case One**: As a doctor, when a patient is gravely ill you are reluctant to deliver the bad news to the family for fear of causing distress, yet you must do so. At that moment you actively avoid eye contact, unable to bear watching the family’s reaction. Your inner wish at that instant is essentially “I hope you didn’t hear it, I hope you don’t know.” This subjective desire carries a strong emotional component; sentimentally you do not want the other party to suffer negative impact. Nevertheless, rational consideration leads you to deliver the message.

Imagine, by contrast, that examination confirms the patient has recovered. When you report the good news to the family, you will look the listener in the eye, eager to witness the relieved, positive reaction.

**Case Two**: As a subordinate, after mishandling a project you dread reporting the failure to your boss for fear of an outburst and subsequent repercussions, yet you cannot conceal or avoid the truth. Again you will actively avoid eye contact, afraid to see the boss’s reaction. Your inner wish at that instant is likewise “I don’t want to say it; I hope you don’t hear it, I hope you don’t know.”

Conversely, after extraordinary effort the project succeeds. When you report to the boss you will look him or her in the eye with enthusiasm, anticipating affirmation and encouragement in return.

**Case Three**: When a girl feels shy she often cannot look the other person in the eye and her voice becomes soft, almost inaudible. Rationally she wants the other person to hear her sincere confession, yet shyness creates an additional subconscious wish: “As a girl, how can I take the initiative to say something like ‘I like you’?” Social etiquette has taught her true inner awareness: she does not want to say it, she does not want to say it.

However, if the girl truly cares about the other person and faces a potential emotional threat from a third party, she will look the young man sincerely in the eye (anger, too, is sincere) and express her affection.

#### Section 1 The Eyes of the Mind

Confucius once said: Observe a person’s pupils, and nothing can be hidden! The meaning is that to understand someone, begin by looking into their eyes. As the saying goes, the eyes are the windows to the soul. Even a fleeting glance can reveal a surprising amount of information, express rich emotions, and even betray the deepest “secrets” of the heart. People are accustomed to using the eyes to explore and understand others. Upon first meeting, they typically look at the other person’s eyes before anything else.

In general, the first impression of a person comes largely from the information conveyed by the eyes. Eye contact can be said to be the primary element shaping that impression. Throughout history, countless descriptions of the eyes have allowed observers to gather extensive information. To a certain extent, a person’s eyes reflect their inner world. Depicting the eyes is therefore equivalent to describing someone’s inner landscape. This is evident in traditional Chinese opera face painting: positive characters are shown with thick eyebrows and large eyes or refined features, while villains appear with shifty or triangular eyes that look repulsive. Ancient people already knew how to read expressions and judge character by observing the eyes. Some individuals wear sunglasses even indoors or in shade and refuse to remove them, because they do not want others to discover their secrets through their eyes.

When we say the eyes can speak, we usually mean that eye movements convey a great deal of information. Level gaze, direct gaze, side glance, upward glance… each can reflect the relationship between people. When encountering someone they like, the eyes light up with special brilliance. An arrogant person’s eyes often dart about unconsciously. Someone with something to hide dares not meet another’s gaze. An upright and innocent person’s eyes are calm and convey sincere strength. Lovers’ glances carry a sweet quality… The rotation of the eyeballs, the opening and closing of the eyelids, the speed and direction of gaze shifts, and the coordination between eyes and head movements produce a complex and subtle language of the eyes that continuously transmits and exchanges information. Within these small eyes lies a vast world. So what specific information can human eyes convey, and how can we understand others? The most direct and effective method is to learn the meanings most people’s eye movements typically express, so that “your eyes betray you.”

#### Winking

Winking means using one eye to signal the other person. It indicates a tacit understanding between the two: “This matter stays between us.” If a third party is present, the wink can make that person feel excluded or isolated. When such an exchange occurs between two strangers, it shows they share the same view on something and signals strong mutual recognition.

People generally believe eye details reflect inner states:

1. Eyes sparkling indicate abundant energy and strong interest in the conversation.
2. Dull, lifeless eyes suggest a person lacking drive or confidence who finds everything uninteresting.
3. Shifting, unsteady gaze indicates indecision, distraction, or a state of tension and unease.
4. Eyes that brighten and dim suggest a calculating mind; during conversation, they show the person has grown impatient and wants the talk to end soon.
5. Bright, piercing eyes indicate integrity, courage, decisiveness, and trustworthiness.
6. Initiating eye contact shows an open heart and a straightforward character.
7. Avoiding or evading another’s gaze indicates inner tension, insincerity, or something being concealed.
8. Calm, steady eyes reflect inner composure and clear judgment.
9. Sharp, penetrating eyes indicate ambition, competitiveness, hidden aggression, and outward boldness—a person of courage and insight.
10. Restless, wandering eyes usually belong to deceitful individuals who should be avoided.
11. Clear, limpid eyes indicate simplicity, openness, and broad-mindedness—a person worth knowing.
12. Muddy, dim eyes suggest a crude, foolish, petty, or vulgar character.
13. Half-closed eyes, as if half-asleep, represent a calculating expression that reveals deep scheming, a preference for clever maneuvers, and fear of others seeing the true inner self.

In interpersonal interactions, therefore, we must understand not only spoken words but also the “language” of the eyes if we wish to maintain an active and advantageous position.

#### Chapter Summary

Different eyebrow shapes can express different mental states. Slight movements of the eyeballs produce subtle changes in gaze. These changes occur under explicit instructions from the nervous system, whether the action is deliberate or involuntary, and can therefore map to certain psychological states.

This chapter attempts to summarize the meanings behind subtle changes in eyebrows and eyes, but it is offered only as a reference direction for analysis rather than a set of rigid rules.

The main conclusions are as follows:

- Five micro-expression forms of the eyebrows and their meanings: neutral; lowered to show attention; raised to show confidence or rapport; “8:20” shape to show sadness; “10:10” shape to show anger.
- Mutual gaze expresses three elements: speak properly, listen properly, and show that one is listening properly. Interruption of mutual gaze therefore signals the absence of one of these factors.
- Pupil changes cannot be consciously controlled and directly map subjective likes and dislikes. Pupils dilate under positive emotions and constrict under negative emotions.
- Eyelid closure and widening can be voluntarily controlled. When stimulation is effective, however, many such movements are instinctive reactions beyond conscious control and can map inner changes. In general, widening indicates a desire to receive more information and commonly appears in surprise, anger, or fear; closure indicates refusal to receive more information and commonly appears in sadness or disgust.
- Two exceptions should be noted: first, during laughter the eyes close for physiological reasons; second, when concentration is required (whether handling negative stimuli or enjoying positive ones), the eyes may close to conserve neural energy and improve information-processing efficiency.
- Eyeball rotation can be controlled; different directions correspond to different inner states. Upward rotation often signals complacency, avoidance, or innocence; downward rotation indicates bearing pressure; leftward or rightward rotation requires comparison against an individual’s baseline and cannot be interpreted uniformly.

#### Test Case: The Elegant Woman Who Lied

We have tested many individuals whose gaze-shift baselines differ. Currently, the most common indicator of deception is movement that violates the personal baseline.

One test subject was a very elegant woman who answered questions calmly throughout the session. Later analysis confirmed that most of her statements were truthful. When faced with stressful questions (those requiring choice or recall), her habitual baseline was to shift her gaze to the right. Whether the task involved complex calculations (left-brain), visual-spatial puzzles (right-brain), or recounting how she had accumulated wealth through shrewd investments, her gaze moved right whenever she needed to formulate an appropriate response.

Only one question elicited a lie.

When asked whether she strongly disliked a particular female friend, her eyes rapidly shifted left by approximately three-quarters of an iris diameter, after which she calmly denied any dislike. No other obvious indicators appeared.

Because this gaze shift deviated from her baseline, we added two follow-up tests.

- Image test: We prepared ten images, including neutral landscapes (cell towers, normal traffic aerial views, regional maps), a positive stimulus (a photograph of a male singer she liked), graphic autopsy images of real corpses, and a photograph of the female friend. Her pupils dilated when she saw the singer’s photo. After neutral images, the sudden appearance of the friend’s photo caused her pupils to constrict.
- We then asked her to describe and evaluate a specific incident involving the friend. During the description and evaluation, a micro-expression of contempt (a derivative of disgust) appeared on her face.

These two results indicated that she harbored feelings of disgust toward the person. Consequently, the cognitive pressure of denying that disgust produced the anomalous gaze shift. It could be confirmed that she had lied on this question.

#### How to Tell Who Likes You

Once you read the following, you will know how to determine whether someone likes you.

- **Cannot meet your eyes**: Their gaze avoids yours. When your eyes happen to meet, they become flustered and blush, looking embarrassed. When you look at them, they look away or lower their head. While together they keep watching you, but the moment you turn to look at them they shift their gaze; when you look elsewhere again they resume watching. If you turn back, they smile and look away once more.
- **Nervously explains to you**: When you speak with someone of the opposite sex, they stare at that person. If they are seen speaking with someone of the opposite sex, they become nervous and offer explanations to you.
- **Creates opportunities to meet**: They find excuses to give you something or borrow something from you simply to arrange a meeting.
- **You are the constant topic**: When chatting with others, they repeatedly bring you up and always want to see your reaction to any event.
- **Concerned about everything about you**: They feel sad when you cry and care deeply about all aspects of your life. They think of many ways to show concern yet hesitate to act; if you face difficulties, they become more anxious than you are.
- **Shows off in front of you**: They seize chances to display humor, talent, capability, or depth in your presence, listen to music you like, and wear clothes in colors you prefer.
- **Appears awkward in your presence**: They never initiate conversation and sometimes blush. When they see you, their speech becomes disjointed. Passing you, they pretend not to notice. When alone together they feel embarrassed and unconsciously fidget with objects or jewelry.

#### Pupils Reveal Your Most Authentic Feelings

Scientists have found that pupils do not “lie.” They are sensitive indicators of vital functions, extensions of the brain, and markers of central-nervous-system activity; they most truthfully reflect a person’s inner feelings.

Pupils respond to interest with astonishing sensitivity. At a national conference of the American Society of Medical Hypnosis, Dr. Edward Hess presented clinical findings: “When the eyes encounter something sufficiently pleasurable or stimulating, the pupils dilate rapidly and unconsciously.” (See Figure 1.1)

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图1.1　瞳孔扩大的眼睛]*

People have long known how to read inner states through changes in pupil size. Ancient Persian jewel merchants, for example, reportedly set prices according to how much a customer’s pupils dilated when viewing jewelry. If a diamond’s brilliance caused dilation, the merchant would quote a higher price.

During courtship the eyes are the most effective organ for transmitting emotion. When a man encounters a woman he admires, his pupils involuntarily dilate under the strong stimulus of desire; the woman intuitively reads the signal. Especially in dim light, the pupils dilate quickly, increasing mutual attraction and fostering romantic connection.

Pupils also dilate under terror, tension, excitement, anger, or pain, while they constrict to a pinpoint—“laser-like gaze”—under disgust, fatigue, or annoyance (see Figure 1.2). If the pupils show no change, the person feels indifferent or bored.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图1.2　瞳孔缩小的眼睛]*

#### 1. Pupil Contact in Nonverbal Communication

When two people look into each other’s pupils, they instinctively feel they should say something or listen to the other; this situation is discussed in detail in the next section.

Summarizing participants’ subjective reports from the latter part of the experiments, we found that during prolonged mutual gaze without speech, both parties attempt to use eye contact to discern the other’s inner meaning. If the gaze continues even longer, they can no longer extract useful information; although their eyes remain fixed on the other’s pupils, their minds have already wandered.

When a stranger on the street stares directly into your eyes (and you simultaneously notice you are looking into theirs—this is pupil contact), one of the two usually breaks the gaze to avoid further interaction. If no conversation or directions are needed, continued pupil contact makes both parties feel awkward: “Why is this person looking at me?” If the other person is irritable, in a bad mood, or a street tough who feels challenged, the mutual scrutiny may be interpreted as provocation and lead to unnecessary physical conflict. The most common line in such situations is “What are you looking at?!”

Without anything to express, a few seconds of pupil contact cause loss of thinking ability and entry into a state of forced mental numbness. Staring at a single static object without receiving new information produces the same blankness as gazing at anything for too long; the mind has already drifted elsewhere.

Long-term evolution has tuned the human visual system and brain to prioritize dynamic information, because movement in the environment affects survival (predators) and reproduction (where one’s partner is). After a period, the brain therefore ignores static, unchanging sources of information.

#### Eyes That Can “Speak”

Although the eyes are a small organ, they are the most acute of the five senses, accounting for nearly 70 percent of sensory input and playing a major role. They not only display emotion but also reveal the code of a person’s mood.

Mencius said: “Nothing is better for observing a person than the pupils. The pupils cannot conceal inner ugliness. If the heart is upright, the pupils are clear; if the heart is not upright, the pupils are clouded. Listen to a person’s words and observe the pupils—how can that person’s true nature be hidden?” In other words, nothing surpasses the eyes for judging character. The eyes cannot mask inner flaws. An upright heart produces clear, bright pupils; a crooked heart produces dull, clouded pupils. By listening to speech and watching the eyes, one can determine whether a person is good or bad.

The eyes are the windows of the soul; they convey our emotions. It is no exaggeration to say that eye expressions are the most complex, subtle, and expressive component of facial expression. Almost never looking at the other person’s eyes while listening is an attempt to conceal the truth.

Customs officers, for example, often ask an extra question while examining a completed declaration form: “Is there anything else to declare?” At that moment their eyes are fixed not on the form but on the traveler’s eyes. If the traveler cannot meet the officer’s gaze steadily, it usually indicates something to hide.

Physiologically, the eyes are the brain’s extension into the eye sockets. The speed and direction of eyeball movement, changes in pupil size, and the opening and closing of the eyelids—all directly governed by cranial nerves—together with the coordination of eyes and head movements, allow the eyes to reflect a person’s emotions naturally.

What emotions, then, do the various changes in the eyes express?

#### The Key to Interpersonal Interaction Lies in Eye Contact

From childhood, teachers have taught us to look at others when speaking; this is the most basic social courtesy. If someone does not look at us during a conversation, it indicates either that they are not listening or that they are hiding something. Therefore, whenever and wherever we interact with anyone, we must look into the other person’s eyes. Mutual eye contact conveys respect, appreciation, and a deeper spiritual connection, yet the duration of that contact must be carefully managed.

In the book *The Psychology of Interpersonal Behaviour*, author Michael Argyle notes that people typically spend 30–60 percent of their total interaction time gazing at each other. When mutual gaze exceeds 60 percent, the individuals are likely either mutually attracted or preparing to fight. Determining which outcome will occur requires close observation of their subsequent behaviors.

An extroverted person generally has no difficulty with eye contact, whereas a shy person may engage in far less. Conversely, when a normally shy individual suddenly maintains unusually prolonged eye contact, it often signals that they are either acting or lying. One should never overlook this basic principle.

When observing someone who is staring or gazing, pay attention to whether their eyes are focused or appear vacant. Focused eyes indicate active thinking or analysis of the object in view. Vacant eyes, by contrast, suggest the person is daydreaming and unaware of the object before them.

#### (2) Incomplete Closure

The orbicularis oculi muscle contracts, moving the upper and lower eyelids toward closure without completing it; the eyes remain slightly more open than in a fully closed state. The internal state represented by incomplete eyelid closure is somewhat more complex.

**① “Passive” Closure**

One form is “passive” partial closure, triggered by the demands of other facial expressions. Examples include the eye narrowing that accompanies hearty laughter or sorrowful crying; in both cases the emphasis lies on emotional release rather than on the exchange of visual information. During genuine laughter the pleasurable stimulus has already been fully received, so further visual input is unnecessary. During genuine crying the painful stimulus has already registered, and the priority is emotional catharsis rather than visual exchange. In these expressions the eyelids close primarily for physiological reasons.

Consider laughter. Laughing and sneezing both involve rapid, forceful exhalation. This breathing pattern raises capillary pressure in the eyes and increases intraorbital pressure; eyelid closure forms a protective barrier that prevents the sudden pressure surge from injuring the eyeball.

Crying adds the factor of tears. The lacrimal glands produce abundant tears that well up between the eyelids. To channel the tears and fulfill the eyelids’ role of moistening the cornea during blinking, the eyelids automatically perform a closing motion.

#### (3) Controlling Gaze

In formal or serious settings, controlling gaze is common—for instance, between superiors and subordinates, teachers and students, or competing opponents. The focus rests on the triangular area at the center of the other person’s forehead, accompanied by a tense, serious atmosphere. The primary effect of this gaze is to exert psychological intimidation. Research shows that winners in sumo, boxing, and similar contests often prevail not solely through superior technique but because their gaze secures a psychological advantage. The same principle applies in negotiation: fixing one’s gaze on this region allows one to seize the initiative.

Eye contact, as a form of silent “language,” can backfire if misused. Out of responsibility to the reader, several cautions are necessary:

1. Align your line of sight with the other person. If your eyes wander across their body or fix on something else, they will sense deliberate avoidance or rudeness, and the conversation may end unpleasantly.
2. Keep the focal point on the other person’s face. As noted earlier, directing gaze between the eyes and chin helps create a relaxed atmosphere.
3. Avoid prolonged staring at any single feature. Studies confirm that gaze exceeding ten seconds raises the likelihood of discomfort, especially during opposite-sex encounters.
4. Do not abruptly avert your eyes. In formal settings, quickly shifting your gaze when someone looks at you suggests evasion or concealment. Even if uninterested, withdraw your gaze calmly rather than fleeing.

#### The Psychological Mystery of Pupil-to-Pupil Eye Contact

To explore the psychological effects of sustained pupil-to-pupil contact, we conducted a small experiment with fifty university students randomly paired into twenty-five dyads. Participants were instructed to gaze directly into each other’s eyes for twenty seconds without speaking. Observers recorded reactions, and participants later described their experiences.

**Experimental results:**

- At the instant of eye contact, both parties simultaneously sensed that the other might speak or that they themselves should say something.
- After two seconds, constrained by the no-talking rule, most felt awkward (many wanted to laugh) and began using their eyes to seek additional information in order to complete the twenty-second interval.
- After five seconds, participants felt an urge to look away; a few dyads continued exchanging nonverbal information through their eyes, accompanied by occasional laughter.
- Upon completion of the twenty seconds, every participant reported relief and expressed a strong desire both to speak and to break eye contact; suppressing both impulses proved uncomfortable.

**Experimental conclusions:**

The experiment revealed two functions of pupil-to-pupil contact: first, to signal readiness for verbal exchange (“I have something to say + you may speak, I’m listening”); second, to gather nonverbal information when speech is unavailable.

Note that the situation discussed here is pure mutual gaze without interruption or redirection, distinct from covert signaling that uses eye movements to indicate direction.

#### Clue Six: Half-Closed Eyes

Half-closed eyes involve a reduced degree of eyelid opening, usually serving as an adjunct to emotion and appearing alongside other expressions such as sadness or joy, disgust or contempt. At such moments the eyes themselves are not the primary vehicle of expression; when a person is intensely happy or deeply distressed, attention focuses on the emotional stimulus rather than on visual intake or output. The partial closure is therefore a purely physiological action.

During hearty laughter, rapid air exchange increases capillary pressure in the eyes. Partial closure relieves this pressure and protects the eyes, much as the eyelids automatically close during a sneeze.

Similarly, during intense sorrow or pain, rapid breathing occurs and the eyes again rely on partial closure for self-protection. Tears provide an additional reason for closure: to channel them and maintain corneal moisture, the eyelids cooperate physiologically by narrowing.

Another context for half-closed eyes is the “come-hither” look. Extensive research shows that when people feel comfortable and pleased in another’s company, their eyes narrow slightly—an evolutionary pattern in which eyes close during states of intoxication or enjoyment, so that half-closure signals comfort and pleasure.

Nearsighted individuals may also squint when viewing distant objects, but this action uses the ciliary muscle to flatten the lens for sharper focus. The ciliary muscle operates outside conscious control and activates only when the autonomic nervous system deems it necessary. Such squinting carries no expressive meaning; it is purely physiological.

#### Business Negotiation—Timing Determines Success or Failure

In the course of our work we frequently discuss cooperation with large enterprises. A unique domestic distillery group spends hundreds of millions of yuan annually on anti-counterfeiting efforts. Our team was invited to design an online platform integrating anti-counterfeiting, evidence collection, and litigation support. When the distillery’s chairman came to Beijing for an annual forum, we brought our proposal and sought a meeting. Our side’s leader enjoyed a strong prior relationship with the chairman, and we hoped to finalize the project.

Throughout the conversation, however, once the discussion turned to the proposal, the chairman’s gaze drifted slightly; he merely nodded and repeated “Good, good.” This visual withdrawal did not stem from contempt or disrespect but from the absence of the factor “I want to listen carefully.” We therefore concluded that the timing was inappropriate: the chairman was preoccupied with forum preparations and guest reception and would not absorb the proposal’s details. The meeting would not yield the desired outcome, so we ended the discussion and left materials with the responsible staff member.

We also observed that his seated posture remained tense, torso leaning forward, hands braced on his knees—the classic “escape reaction” indicating readiness to stand and leave (see the book *Micro-reaction* (微反应)). As predicted, once we finished presenting the project, the chairman restored direct eye contact, expressed polite apologies, observed all necessary courtesies, then quickly rose and began greeting other guests.

#### 6. Rolling the Eyes

Rolling the eyes is a common ocular expression that involves both complex eyeball movement and a complex gaze-shift sequence.

The classic eye-roll typically signals contempt. Slow-motion analysis reveals several variants:

1. When the roll begins from direct eye contact, the sequence is: eyelid closure; reopening with upward gaze (partial sclera visible); gaze then shifting laterally away from the stimulus while the head turns; continued downward lateral shift; final eyelid closure, with gaze settling sideways, level or downward, or the head returning to face the stimulus.
2. When the roll begins from a side-facing orientation, the sequence is: brief glance toward the other person (without full eye contact); upward gaze accompanied by eyelid closure; reopening while gaze returns to the original or opposite direction.
3. When a girl rolls her eyes flirtatiously at her boyfriend (not in genuine anger) while saying something like “You’re annoying,” an additional step occurs: at the end the gaze returns to the boyfriend’s pupils, conveying sincerity (sometimes accompanied by a coy or mock-stern smile) and checking whether the playful message has been received.

#### Clue Three: Tears

Tears are an autonomic response triggered by emotional stimuli such as sadness, fear, worry, relief, or joy. Determining whether tears are genuinely prompted by the immediate emotion can be difficult. As noted earlier, the Stanislavski acting method trains performers to relive authentic emotions in order to produce the required display. One certainty remains: whether performed or spontaneous, the underlying emotion behind tears is always real.

Consider the case of an American mother who appeared daily before the media, weeping over the loss of her daughter. FBI investigators suspected she had murdered the child, yet her display of inconsolable grief seemed so convincing that few believed the accusation. In one recorded segment, however, investigators detected a fleeting expression of guilt while she cried. They concluded that her tears might stem not from grief but from remorse over the killing. Perpetrators commonly experience guilt, fear, disgust, or contempt afterward; skilled deceivers can suppress these emotions, yet genuine feelings still flash across the face—this is the power of micro-expressions. Although the case remains controversial, the investigators remained convinced of the mother’s guilt.

#### (2) Absence of “Please Listen Carefully”

The underlying thought is “You need not listen carefully.” Whether the listener pays close attention is unimportant; feedback is irrelevant, and the speaker simply finishes speaking. In such moments the speaker’s gaze also tends to drift. Linguistic features include: unemphasized volume and tone, possibly at normal levels or reduced energy; smooth, continuous, sometimes rapid delivery. In short: “This matter has nothing to do with you.”

**Specific Cases**

**Example 1:** This pattern frequently appears in meetings when participants know their views will be opposed yet feel compelled to state them anyway. Eye contact is avoided while the opinion is delivered; the internal stance is “I’ll say my piece; your disagreement is irrelevant and I don’t care about your opinion.”

Conversely, when a dominant party wishes to issue a warning or compel acknowledgment, sustained direct eye contact is used to convey: “Listen carefully—this is my position. Your opinion? It doesn’t matter; I won’t hear it anyway. Just agree.”

#### Squinting

If a person squints but not because of strong light stimulation, it indicates they may be preparing to say something or expressing uncertainty. If a person squints while smiling broadly, it shows they feel extremely happy.

In addition, the eyelids are considered the area that most reflects a person's sexual desire; the shape of the eyelids can reveal a person's psychological attitude toward love.

- People with single eyelids on both eyes: Their personality is mostly introverted, solitary, sensitive, strong self-esteem, determined, hardworking and practical. Their expression of emotions is reserved and restrained; even when standing in front of someone they usually admire or like, they will try their best to remain calm and show no trace. In the company they can advance rapidly through solid professional knowledge; in family matters they are relatively conservative, and once they have an affair, their tracks will immediately be exposed.
- People with double eyelids on both eyes: Outgoing and enthusiastic, emotionally rich; they are easily moved by others' caring gestures or inquiries about their well-being, especially from the opposite sex, and therefore often cannot resist the temptation of the opposite sex. Whether in work settings or other social gatherings, they are always the most popular. They belong to the honest and reliable type, with a happy and fulfilling family life.
- People with one single eyelid and one double eyelid: Such individuals usually do not easily reveal their true intentions; they often complain and grumble during work or interpersonal interactions. People with this eyelid type have low loyalty in love, like to pursue change or stimulation, possess a flirtatious nature, are relatively open in sexual matters, and frequently accept advances without refusal.

#### Blinking Frequency

Blinking is both a spontaneous behavior and a subconscious behavior. Regardless of whether a person's eyes appear dry or moist, paying attention to their blinking frequency is very important. Always observe the blinking frequency of the person you are talking to, noting whether it is normal, too fast, or too slow. Note that what you say and do will also affect the other person's blinking frequency. When judging a person's intentions, observe their blinking frequency and consider it together with other postures.

It is well known that if a person is lying, their blinking frequency will be much higher than usual. For example, U.S. customs inspectors usually inform travelers that if they have undeclared prohibited items, they will be sent back to their country. You may think this is a very redundant procedure because travelers have already filled out declaration forms. In fact, it is not; when the inspector makes this request, they carefully observe the traveler's eyes to see whether the blinking frequency is normal. If the traveler's blinking frequency is too high, the inspector will check the traveler's luggage.

In addition, law enforcement personnel usually record a suspect's blinking frequency to help them determine whether the person is guilty. A higher blinking frequency can reflect a person's sense of guilt, while a lower blinking frequency indicates that the person is preparing to confess something. It is precisely for this reason that the suspect has no energy left to pay attention to their own eyes. This is why it is necessary to note all of a person's expressions and gestures.

#### Clue Two: Pupil Dilation

The FBI once handled a murder case involving sexual harassment. After the suspect was arrested, he consistently denied having any sexual intentions toward the female victim and denied killing her because she resisted. At the time, no bodily fluids from the suspect were found in the victim's body, making it difficult to establish evidence. Later, while reviewing the suspect's interrogation video, investigators noticed a detail: whenever the suspect mentioned the female victim, his pupils would dilate. This crucial detail revealed the suspect's true thoughts. People's pupils dilate only when they see or think of something they like; the most typical example is sexual desire. Investigators seized on this detail and continued questioning until the suspect finally confessed.

The pupil is not an independent organ but a small opening in the middle of the iris. Light can only form an image on the retina by passing through the pupil. When light is too strong, the pupil constricts to protect the optic nerve from damage. When light weakens, the pupil dilates to absorb more light and see a clearer image. The pupil is controlled by smooth muscle, which obeys only the autonomic nervous system and not conscious will. In other words, pupil dilation or constriction is entirely a genuine reaction and cannot be faked.

When people see something they like, their pupils naturally dilate to capture a clearer image. When they see something they dislike, their pupils naturally constrict to reduce the discomfort caused by negative stimuli.

#### (1) Erroneous Summary of Left-Right Brain Division of Labor

Earlier research conclusions in cognitive psychology stated that the left brain is primarily responsible for functions such as speech, reading, writing, mathematical calculation, rote memory, logical reasoning, and symbolic thinking; the right brain is primarily responsible for image-thinking functions such as recognizing object size and shape, spatial cognition, map reading, face recognition, painting composition, music, structural assembly, and perceiving others' emotions.

More importantly, the vast majority of human work is completed through coordinated effort of both hemispheres rather than through separate responsibility. For example, memory is often said to belong to the left brain, so to whom does image memory belong? If image information is processed by the right brain, then drawing a picture from the mind must involve the addition of logical and temporal order, which is the responsibility of the left brain! Similarly, musical notes are mainly processed by the right brain, but composing and singing songs must be completed by both hemispheres simultaneously. According to the latest brain cognition research, previous conclusions about left-right brain division of labor have gradually been corrected by more experimental findings and are not as absolute as in older textbooks.

Those seeking theoretical support for fallacies made their first mistake—superficially summarizing brain cognition as “left brain responsible for memory, right brain responsible for fabrication.” Setting aside whether creation, construction, and fabrication have the same meaning, even this derivation process is absurd. Further questioning: What relationship exists between eye movement direction and the distinction of left-right brain division of labor?

#### 2. Eye Contact in Verbal Communication

If speech is possible, mutual pupil gaze becomes the start of effective communication; this is the consensus of both parties. It is called a consensus because both parties in mutual gaze can feel the meaning of the gaze and what it will trigger; it is called a beginning because mutual gaze is the initiation process for both parties to engage in “full-duplex” communication.

**What is “full-duplex” communication?**

Here a technical term from the communications field is borrowed, meaning that at the same time, both parties in the communication can send and receive information; a simpler explanation is shown in the figure below.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图10-10]*

When both parties in a dialogue discuss important information that concerns them both, at least at the beginning they must be looking directly into each other's eyes. In normal verbal communication, mutual gaze expresses three meanings:

1. [Speaker] I want to speak to you;
2. [Speaker] Please listen carefully;
3. [Listener] I am listening carefully.

Because communication is bidirectional, both parties are simultaneously speaker and listener and therefore hold all three expectations at once. If any one of these expectations is missing during the dialogue, it will cause an interruption of mutual pupil gaze.

#### 5. Not Looking at Someone Directly

Not looking at someone directly means looking at them sideways, except the face does not turn sideways with the eyeballs and remains facing the person being looked at. There are two reasons for discussing this deformed gaze here: first, in this gaze state the pupil is on one side rather than in the middle, resembling the appearance of left-right eye movement; second, this gaze state reflects an unwillingness to look, equally lacking “sincerity” as eye movement.

Whether hoping for sincere communication or looking up in search due to an unexpected stimulus (for example, someone calling you from the side), a head-turning movement will occur so that one's face faces the viewed object as directly as possible. Turning only the eyes without turning the head directly reflects a relatively negative mindset (equivalent to unwillingness to look). It should be specially noted that the “unwillingness” mentioned here includes not only the conventional meanings of aversion and negation but also other negative intentions such as fear (stealing a glance, afraid of being discovered) and disdain, collectively termed unwillingness.

Emotions and mindsets that may cause sideways glances mainly include:

- Smiling with pride (I am better/stronger/correcter/…… than you)
- Contempt (I am better/stronger/correcter/…… than you)
- Worry (cannot clearly express concern and anxiety toward the other)
- Disgust (directly negating the other)

#### 2. The Eyeball

The eyeball is the organ through which humans obtain visual information.

Luminous light sources such as television sets and computer screens can use their own energy to project light into the eyeball, while most objects in daily life cannot emit light themselves and instead reflect other light into the eyeball; this is also the most common source of visual information we see. Regardless of the light source, the eyeball is the organ that receives light and requires light to enter in order to “see” anything. As humans possessing this organ, what we do is choose the direction we wish to pay attention to and locate the source of incoming light.

Therefore, gaze—the term we are very familiar with—is not a line emitted by our eyes but the direction we choose so that external light can accurately enter the eyeball. We actively “look,” but “seeing” is the passive entry of light; if we do not wish to see, we can either change direction or cut off light entry into the eyeball.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图10-8]*

The anatomical structure of the eyeball is far more complex than that of the eyelids, with many more individual components; this book will not introduce them one by one, as shown in Figure 10-8. Most of these are optical organs.

#### Summary

The various cases above confirm two points:

- First, if both parties need to conduct effective communication, they will spontaneously engage in mutual pupil gaze. We believe mutual pupil gaze is a necessary constituent condition and startup procedure for effective communication—that is, the full expression of both parties being ready with [I want to speak to you], [Please listen carefully], and [I am listening carefully].
- Second, during dialogue, when both parties subjectively harbor more complex psychological states (such as fear, guilt, shyness, displeasure, contempt, disgust, embarrassment, and other negative emotions), they actively cancel mutual gaze and shift their line of sight away from the other’s pupils. Although the content of the communication may still be serious and both parties at the rational level still hope the other can effectively express and receive information, emotion may override reason in decision-making, presupposing, defaulting to, or even hoping that the communication between the two at that instant will not be so effective, stopping mutual pupil gaze.

Therefore, working backward from this logical relationship, we arrive at a somewhat startling conjectural conclusion: stopping mutual pupil gaze (including gaze-blocking reactions and gaze-shifting reactions) must correspond to the absence of certain elements among the three. Research on gaze-blocking reactions and gaze-shifting reactions will be elaborated in 10.2.3 and 10.2.4 respectively.

#### Eyelids

In discussions of eye contact, the importance of the eyelids is usually overlooked. In reality, even a very small matter, such as how much sclera a person shows, can convey a great deal of information.

It is well known that drooping eyelids represent many meanings, so please judge accurately according to the specific scene whether a person feels tired, bored, depressed, listless, or is flirting.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.4　眼皮低垂]*

Straining to keep the eyes wide open usually indicates that a person is very interested in something. If the eyes are opened too wide, it means they may be very surprised or frightened.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.5　努力睁大双眼]*

If a person squints but not because of strong light stimulation, it indicates they may be preparing to say something or expressing uncertainty. If a person squints while smiling broadly, it shows they feel extremely happy.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.6　斜视]*

#### Blinking Frequency Reveals Lies

Blinking is both a spontaneous behavior and a subconscious behavior. Regardless of whether a person's eyes appear dry or moist, paying attention to their blinking frequency is very important. Always observe the blinking frequency of the person you are talking to, noting whether it is normal, too fast, or too slow. Note that what you say and do will also affect the other person's blinking frequency. When judging a person's intentions, observe their blinking frequency and consider it together with other postures.

It is well known that if a person is lying, their blinking frequency will be much higher than usual. For example, U.S. customs inspectors usually inform travelers that if they have undeclared prohibited items, they will be sent back to their country. You may think this is a very foolish procedure because travelers have already filled out declaration forms. In fact, it is not; when the inspector makes this request, they carefully observe the traveler's eyes to see whether the blinking frequency is normal. If the traveler's blinking frequency is too high, the inspector will check the traveler's luggage.

FBI agents usually also record a suspect's blinking frequency to help them determine whether the person is guilty. A higher blinking frequency can reflect a person's sense of guilt, while a lower blinking frequency indicates that the person is preparing to confess something.

#### ② Iris

The iris controls the amount of light admitted. People generally believe the pupil controls the amount of light admitted; both statements are correct, because the iris and the pupil are essentially the same thing.

The iris is ring-shaped, and its central part is the pupil; that is, the pupil really is a hole! The iris is composed of multi-unit smooth muscle. The portion near the center (that is, the edge of the pupil) is the circular muscle layer, innervated by parasympathetic fibers of the oculomotor nerve (the parasympathetic nerves are not controlled by thought); when it contracts, the pupil constricts, hence it is also called the sphincter pupillae. The peripheral portion of the iris consists of radiating muscle fibers, innervated by sympathetic fibers ascending from the neck (the sympathetic nerves are also not controlled by thought); when it contracts, the pupil dilates, hence it is also called the dilator pupillae.

Special attention should be paid to the fact that the sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves together are called the autonomic nervous system and cannot be controlled by “thinking.” Smooth muscle also exists in internal organs such as the stomach, intestines, and bladder; humans likewise cannot control the movement of these internal organs by “thinking.” These are “involuntary movements.” Therefore, if you find the preceding knowledge too complex, simply remember one sentence: iris movement cannot be commanded by “thinking” and can genuinely reflect the psychological state of the person involved.

#### ② Iris

The iris controls the amount of light that enters. It is commonly believed that the pupil controls the amount of light entering, which is correct; both statements are true because the iris and the pupil are essentially the same thing.

The iris is ring-shaped, with the pupil at its center, meaning the pupil is truly a hole! The iris is composed of multiple units of smooth muscle. The part near the center (the edge of the pupil) is the circular muscle layer, innervated by parasympathetic nerve fibers in the oculomotor nerve (parasympathetic nerves are not under voluntary control). When it contracts, it constricts the pupil, hence also called the sphincter pupillae. The peripheral part of the iris consists of radiating muscle fibers, innervated by sympathetic nerve fibers ascending from the neck (sympathetic nerves are also not under voluntary control). When they contract, they dilate the pupil, hence also called the dilator pupillae.

Special attention: The sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves together are called the autonomic nervous system and cannot be controlled by "thinking." Smooth muscle also exists in internal organs like the stomach, intestines, and bladder, which humans similarly cannot control through "thinking." These are "involuntary movements." So, if the previous knowledge seems too complex, just remember this: The movement of the iris cannot be commanded by "thinking" and can truly reflect the psychological state of the person involved.



#### 3. Rotation of the Eyeball

Rotation of the eyeball maximizes the visual field while also controlling the direction of gaze. Unlike control of pupil dilation and constriction, eyeball movement is governed by six muscles known as the extraocular muscles. These muscles attach to the exterior of the eyeball; each eye has six: the medial rectus, lateral rectus, superior rectus, inferior rectus, superior oblique, and inferior oblique. All six extraocular muscles are skeletal muscles and can be controlled by conscious intent. Therefore, under conditions of clear consciousness, the direction of eye movement is always "intentional." This point is important!

Each movement of the eyeball results from coordinated action among the muscles, and the movements of both eyes are normally coordinated. Abnormal insertion points of the extraocular muscles, underdevelopment of a muscle, or paralysis of the nerve supplying a muscle can produce strabismus and other disorders.

This establishes a very important fact, one of great significance for micro-expression research: why the eyes look straight at another person or why they shift away can both be confirmed as results of conscious control—though not solely of cognitive consciousness. So why do you shift your gaze direction during a conversation?

What we seek to explore is precisely this "why."

#### 2. Changes in the Pupil

As previously noted, the pupil is an opening in the center of the iris rather than an independent organ. The pupil permits light to enter the eyeball and form an image on the retina. When light intensifies, the pupil constricts to prevent excessive stimulation of the optic nerve; when light dims, the pupil dilates to admit as much light as possible for a clearer image. All these actions are performed by the smooth muscle that controls the iris. Smooth muscle is governed solely by the autonomic nervous system; no amount of effort allows direct control through cognitive commands. See Figure 10-15.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图10-15]*

Interestingly, as evolution progressed, human pupillary responses became more complex and sophisticated. Experiments show that when people see something they like, their pupils dilate (for example, when a man sees an attractive woman or a gambler sees a strong hand), ensuring they take in more of the pleasing sight; when they see something they dislike, the pupils constrict (for example, during a graphic surgical dissection), minimizing exposure to negative stimuli. This is the pattern of the pupil's stress response.



#### How to Use Eye Contact to Elicit the Truth

So how, in different settings and circumstances, should one employ eye contact to put the other person at ease and thereby gather more truthful information?

During a two-person exchange, sustained eye contact is generally positive, yet staring fixedly can make the other person uncomfortable and eager to end the conversation. To avoid this awkwardness, one may interrupt eye contact every five seconds. Remember not to look downward, as that signals the end of the talk. Instead, try looking upward or to the side, as though thinking.

In an argument, the power of eye contact should not be underestimated if one wishes to maintain an advantageous position. Used well, it can compel the other person to yield even without words; used poorly, one has already lost half the battle. Maintain steady eye contact with a firm gaze. Continue watching while the other speaks, observing tone and expression through that contact. Silence combined with steady gaze is the most effective way to prevail without speaking.



#### Remember to Glance at the Other Person One More Time

When two people look at each other, they immediately sense an internal conflict: they want eye contact yet also want to avoid it. This back-and-forth has evolved into a complex set of human gaze-shift patterns.

> —Desmond Morris

We use reason to govern every bodily movement, striving to keep them proper, yet our eyes can betray inner secrets. Others watch our eyes like keen hounds, treating us as quarry. For example, the sole reason President Bush decided to attack Iraq was that FBI experts detected panic in Saddam's eyes. For FBI agents, every interview can yield a breakthrough by reading an inadvertent glance.

In human interaction, the foundation of mutual trust is largely built through eye contact. If someone looks away while speaking with you, will you still believe what they say? If their blink rate rises noticeably above normal during conversation, will you still believe they are innocent?



#### a. Positive Expressive Half-Closure—Eyes Like Silk

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图10-13]*

Eyes like silk is a woman's way of conveying charm. See Figure 10-13. The word "silk" itself indicates that eyelid closure is nearly complete. Still, professional rigor requires us to dissect this appealing state and examine the underlying psychological reality.

The origin of eyes like silk is actually a variation of the "focused enjoyment" discussed earlier. The evolutionary process runs roughly as follows: focused enjoyment requires closing the eyes (already examined); over time this natural physiological response became a shared understanding that a closed-eye expression signals enjoyment; therefore people consciously half-close their eyes to display a pleasing expression that communicates "I am enjoying this (being with you) right now."

Thus, when applying makeup to appear alluring, draw the eyeliner finer and longer. To project a spirited look, avoid this style entirely; instead increase the distance between brow and eye so the eyelids appear more open.



#### Special Note

This conclusion applies only within rigorous psychological testing, where it may assist in judging the mental state of a subject while speaking, and must be combined with other factors for comprehensive analysis before any conclusion is drawn. The most critical step in every analysis is to determine the cause—that is, what stimulus prompted the eyeball movement or gaze shift.

If, after reading this section, you feel greatly inspired and proceed to apply this logic in isolation: the moment you observe the cessation of pupil-to-pupil contact, you immediately conclude the other person lacks sincerity in communicating and declare, "So your eyes moved away—you dare not tell me the truth (or you dare not listen properly)!" Such an approach is overly harsh and may produce erroneous conclusions and unnecessary trouble.

Therefore, if your purpose is simply normal daily life, never memorize these research conclusions by rote. Life should be enjoyed lightly; there is no need to haggle over every detail. Moreover, our research has already reached the level of "nitpicking." Such minute observations are useful only for uncovering the truth behind complex puzzles. Do not misuse them. Remember this well.

#### 3. The Eyes Light Up

Usually, when a person is happy—especially pleasantly surprised—the phenomenon of "eyes lighting up" occurs. The cause is not an illusion; the eyes genuinely become "brighter."

In moments of pleasant surprise the eyes widen, exposing a larger area of both the iris and the sclera (the white of the eye). On one hand, the overall reflective surface increases; on the other, the pupil dilation caused by positive stimuli, together with the pigmented iris, heightens the contrast between the dark region and the light sclera, making the eyes appear brighter. In addition, the increased blood circulation from excitement supplies the eyes with more energy, further contributing to the brightening effect.

Conversely, most sorrowful eyes (assuming no acute grief or indignation) appear dull simply because the above process is reversed: the exposed area of the eyeball decreases due to eyelid closure, contrast between light and dark regions weakens, and the absence of excitement-induced microcirculatory changes naturally produces a vacant look.



#### 10.2.2 Pupil-to-Pupil Contact

"Pupil-to-pupil contact" is an unusual phrase; ordinary people would not use it, yet micro-expressions must be examined at this level of detail to be valuable.

Pupil-to-pupil contact means two people are looking into each other's eyes—not merely gazing in the general direction, but precisely fixating on each other's pupils.

Gaze direction is extremely precise, and human detection of gaze information is likewise highly accurate. Experiments show that if your gaze shifts even slightly away from the other person's pupil, they will perceive that you have looked away. Sometimes, even within a 180-degree arc in front of you, you can sense whether someone is watching you or has shifted their gaze. See Figure 10-9.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图10-9]*

Of course,

certain works of art describe people sensing a gaze from behind; such perceptions are usually based on multiple auxiliary cues rather than any genuine physiological reception of attention.



#### 2. Downward Gaze Shift

In contrast to an upward gaze shift, a downward shift generally indicates that the person had already anticipated several possibilities in mind, one of which has now materialized in the situation at hand. We may broadly summarize a downward gaze shift as conveying a mindset of "endurance." Such shifts usually reflect relatively negative states, such as guilt (feeling one is not good enough, has made a mistake, or bears responsibility), disagreement (yet feeling powerless to change the situation), anger (yet suppressing it for the moment), or anxious thinking (searching for a way to respond to doubt). Unlike the escape impulse signaled by an upward shift, a downward shift typically shows that the person knows they cannot flee and must simply endure until the moment passes or they are defeated.

Even the downward gaze that appears in shyness carries the same psychological meaning. Shyness is actually fear of seeing the other person's reaction and learning of their disapproval (dislike), yet a strong desire for a positive outcome remains, so the person endures the pressure and persists.



#### 10.2.4 Gaze Shifts

After eye contact, a shift in gaze may indicate subtle psychological changes; the underlying reasons have already been analyzed. We now examine, one by one, the possible meanings of gaze shifts in different directions.

Before proceeding with this line of analysis, however, it is necessary to pour cold water on any would-be mind readers: determining the meaning of any individual's gaze shift requires first firmly recognizing that gaze shifts are highly individualized. Different people, through long-term environmental adaptation and learning, may develop distinct gaze-shift habits. Establishing a subject's baseline gaze-shift habits (called the baseline in psychological testing) is therefore the correct first step. Never mechanically apply the interpretations below.

Starting from pupil-to-pupil contact, gaze shifts occur in four basic directions: up, down, left, right, with combined variations then arising: upper-left, lower-left, upper-right, lower-right. Left and right, up and down, are all defined from the actor's perspective.



#### Pupil Dilation or Constriction

Pupil dilation or constriction is a physiological response beyond personal control. When one is in close proximity to another person, the process of dilation or constriction can be observed very clearly—especially in individuals with green, blue, or hazel eyes.

Of course, this physiological response normally occurs in reaction to light. The dimmer the light, the more the pupil dilates, and vice versa. Yet emotional changes can also cause pupil dilation or constriction. When a person is attracted to someone or something, the pupils dilate. When a person is very angry or indecisive, a "laser-like" gaze appears.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.2　瞳孔放大的眼睛]*

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.3　瞳孔收缩的眼睛]*



#### Psychology Mini-Lesson

Humans possess an innate talent for reading eyes, evident from infancy. A newborn can, within two to five days, judge whether another's gaze is directed at them. By four months they can distinguish between shifting and steady gaze. By nine to eighteen months they can interpret the deeper meanings conveyed by the eyes.

It is said that experienced police officers, amid a crowd, can identify a pickpocket who has not yet acted simply by reading the eyes. A pickpocket's gaze differs markedly from that of ordinary people. Regardless of circumstances, pickpockets continually watch pockets and handbags. Inside a store they neither shop nor examine merchandise; instead they watch where customers place their wallets while paying. Before acting they often look around to see whether anyone—especially police—is watching them. While committing the act they tend to hold their breath, appear tense, and stare blankly. Experienced officers can detect them through observation of the eyes.

#### Eye Contact in Daily Life

In daily life, people’s contact and communication always involve each other’s eyes. For example, eyes always let us see those we are close to or fond of, while we ignore or refuse a second glance at those we dislike; when we see the key point of something, we usually stare at it for a long time; in addition, we can use our gaze to convey a sense of strength and thereby control the entire conversation; when our emotions are affected, the eyes can express feelings that words struggle to convey. Therefore, what the eyes convey is not only secrets but also an atmosphere of pleasure and friendliness that exerts a more favorable influence on the conversation.

As mentioned above, during handshakes or greetings, people with stronger dominance tend to maintain eye contact longer, while those with milder personalities maintain it for a shorter time. For men, when greeting someone of the same sex, it is best to keep eye contact brief; otherwise, it can easily send the wrong signal and cause unnecessary trouble.

#### 10.2.3 Visual Blocking

When subjected to negative stimuli, the nervous system mobilizes every available bodily resource to prevent the increase of those stimuli. Retreating to control distance, contracting the limbs, or using hands or feet to create a barrier are all possible reactions. Visual blocking is one such reaction.

Visual blocking refers to the use of an obstacle to block one’s own line of sight. In more academic terms, it means using an obstacle to attempt to stop or partially stop light from entering the eyes, thereby refusing or reducing the reception of visual information. The obstacles mentioned here are generally other organs of one’s own body; the most common is the eyelid, followed by the arm or an object held in the hand.

Common actions such as closing the eyes and blinking (blinking being a high-frequency eye-closing action) achieve visual blocking through eyelid closure. In addition to eye closure, visual blocking also includes pupil constriction. Since micro-expressions focus on facial expressions, actions that use the hand or other objects for visual blocking are not discussed in this book; see the book Micro-reaction (微反应) for details.

#### ① “Black Eyeball”

A small piece of knowledge must be shared: the “black eyeball” is not an independent black sphere. As shown in Figure 10-8, the seemingly clearly demarcated “black eyeball” has the cornea on the outermost layer (readily associated with donation), accounting for about one-sixth of the eyeball’s area and completely transparent; this is the entry point for light. The colored part beneath the cornea, commonly called the “black eyeball” by Chinese people, is anatomically known as the **iris**.

Depending on the pigment contained in the iris, it displays different colors. Caucasians have less iris pigment and appear gray-blue; East Asians have more pigment and appear brownish-yellow; people of African descent have the most pigment and appear black.

The remaining outer shell of the eyeball is called the sclera. The sclera is hard, white, and opaque (the visible white of the eye is part of the sclera) and, together with the cornea, encloses the entire eyeball and protects its internal structures.

Among the numerous components of the eyeball, those directly relevant to micro-expression research are the iris and the pupil.

#### Psychology Mini-Class

Psychologists have found that the eyes convey spirit largely through the expansion and contraction of the pupil, the movement of the eyeball, and the degree of eyelid opening and closing.

A person’s emotions are closely related to changes in the pupil. Pleasurable stimuli cause the pupil to dilate, while aversive stimuli cause it to constrict. In addition, when a person is panicked or excited, the pupil can expand to four times its normal size; thus, some describe pupil changes as a marker of central nervous system activity.

Eyeball movement can also reveal emotion. For example, if the other person’s eyeballs are relatively stable and move little, it indicates sincerity; conversely, if the gaze wanders and flickers, it suggests a more calculating mind and insufficient sincerity.

The degree of eyelid opening and closing can likewise indicate emotion. If the other person’s eyelids droop, it signals dejection or annoyance; if the eyes are half-closed, it indicates arrogance and disregard for others.
