The colored part beneath the cornea, commonly called the “black eyeball” by Chinese people, is anatomically known as the “iris.” Depending on the pigment contained in the iris, it displays different colors. Caucasians have less iris pigment and appear gray-blue; East Asians have more pigment and appear brownish-yellow; people of African descent have the most pigment and appear black.

The remaining outer shell of the eyeball is called the sclera. The sclera is hard, white, and opaque (the visible white of the eye is part of the sclera) and, together with the cornea, encloses the entire eyeball and protects its internal structures.

Among the numerous components of the eyeball, those directly relevant to micro-expression research are the iris and the pupil.

#### Eye Baseline

The eye baseline refers to the position of the eyelids in a neutral static state; its indirect indicator is the size of the exposed iris region, which can be measured by vertical diameter.

Under normal conditions, what we commonly call large eyes means a greater vertical separation of the eyelids in the natural static state—that is, a larger exposed iris region; conversely, small eyes mean a smaller exposed iris region. For the expression models used in this book, the upper eyelid covers 19 % of the iris’s vertical diameter, the lower eyelid covers 9.5 %, and the exposed iris region accounts for 71.5 % of the entire iris’s vertical diameter.

With this set of baseline data, one will not misjudge whether a person is widening the eyes or closing the eyelids. From another angle, any slight increase or decrease in iris exposure can be immediately and sensitively detected against the baseline state, allowing inference as to whether the person is widening or narrowing the eyes.

#### 3. Scleral Show Indicating Depth of Character and Irritability

Scleral show refers to eyes in which the dark iris is displaced upward or downward so that the white of the eye is visible above or below the iris. People with scleral show are talented, mentally agile, deep in character, well-versed in strategy, and relatively likely to attain a certain status. Scleral show is further divided into upper scleral show and lower scleral show. Upper scleral show means white is visible above the iris. Such individuals are typically self-centered, highly neurotic, irritable and quick to anger, and prone to attacking others. They also harbor deep feelings of inferiority, are sensitive to criticism, tend to think the worst of situations, and exhibit a stronger criminal tendency. Lower scleral show means white is visible below the iris—that is, the eyes show white beneath a raised iris. These individuals are comparatively self-confident, strong-willed, bold, highly materialistic, and persevering once they have decided on something; however, they can also be willful and cold, inconsistent in word and deed, and occasionally disregard others’ feelings.

#### Orbicularis Oculi Muscle

The action of the levator palpebrae superioris is always closely linked to the orbicularis oculi; contraction and relaxation of the orbicularis oculi directly affect the tension and relaxation of the levator palpebrae superioris. The orbicularis oculi is distributed around the eyes and constitutes a crucial facial muscle region; it interacts with the frontalis, corrugator supercilii, depressor supercilii, levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, levator labii superioris, and zygomaticus minor, among others.

In our facial expressions, eye opening, eye closing, frowning, and eyeball movement all require the cooperation of the orbicularis oculi. Moreover, it indirectly influences the upward turn of the lips and the contraction of the cheek muscles—that is, smiling.

When observing expressions to judge inner thoughts, the eyes and their surrounding area are an important focal point. Every change in the eyes reflects, to varying degrees, the timely inner changes of the person involved. The orbicularis oculi is the key muscle that drives all of this.

#### c. Myopic Squint

Of course, there is an even more special case—myopia.

Myopia occurs because prolonged viewing of near objects keeps the lens in a tense, deformed state under the action of the ciliary muscle, making recovery difficult; as a result, distant objects cannot be focused on the retina, producing myopia.

Squinting the eyes uses the compression of the orbicularis oculi to slightly alter the anteroposterior circumference of the eyeball, thereby modestly improving image quality. Therefore, myopic students who are not wearing glasses will squint when they need to see something clearly, which can help to some extent. However, once the structure of the eyeball and the principles of image formation are understood, it becomes clear that only by using the ciliary muscle to flatten the lens can image quality truly be changed. Because the ciliary muscle is controlled by the autonomic nervous system and cannot be moved at will, squinting to compensate for myopia is of limited help.

#### 5. Protruding Eyes Indicating Optimism and Kindness

Physiologically, protruding eyeballs result from well-developed nerves behind the eyeball; consequently, people with protruding eyes are generally kind-hearted, optimistic, and cheerful. They are good at socializing, appear talkative in communication, work energetically and conscientiously, yet have a tendency to be forgetful; their thoughts can seem flighty and capricious. Their temperament leans toward impatience and a degree of neuroticism; they often torment themselves by creating unnecessary problems. Women with protruding eyes, especially young girls in love, tend to display a mixture of excited anticipation and anxious agitation. Boys may not understand why she rushes to a date, seems distracted and answers irrelevantly during the date, and then flees as if escaping at the end. In fact, not only boys fail to understand; the girl herself may not fully grasp her own emotions.

#### (3) Correct Analytical Approach to Lateral Gaze Shifts

The only certainty is that a lateral gaze shift indicates a nervous-system command, which may be intentional, habitual, or an instinctive unconscious command, but it necessarily interrupts the ongoing interaction; analysis can be performed by comparing each subject’s baseline.

Gaze shifting has no necessary connection to lying. Although it interrupts the current interaction, the reason may be to prepare for better communication, such as recalling facts, logical reasoning, or numerical calculation; it may also involve fabricating false information or concealing true information. In addition, lateral gaze shifts may simply be emotion-driven—for example, displeasure or disgust—with no complex thought involved, merely an unwillingness to continue the exchange.

#### Negative Emotions in the Gaze

Under normal circumstances, people turn their heads to face the other person’s eyes directly. If only the eyes turn without the head, a sidelong glance results, conveying negative emotions of disdain, contempt, disgust, or rejection.

This point is very important when establishing rapport with others. If your interlocutor begins by looking at you sideways, it shows he does not yet trust you and is unwilling to engage in the conversation. You need to establish rapport with him first; this will be discussed later. Observing whether he opens up to you, changes in gaze are a clear indicator. When he gradually faces you and begins to look at you directly, it proves your method is working and the other party is now willing to communicate further.

#### 1. Upward Gaze Shift

Based on our actual tests, we believe an upward gaze shift can map to three psychological characteristics: one is the implication of placing oneself in a higher status, often used to express disdain and frequently combined with the interjection “tch” to form a contemptuous expression; another is the implication of “this has nothing to do with me” or “I am staying out of it,” often appearing during feigned innocence; the third is the most common situation among subjects: the person had not anticipated being asked the question and begins to think on the spot, involuntarily rolling the eyes upward. Both recall and fabrication have been observed across different subjects; even during baseline-test medium-difficulty arithmetic questions, subjects have shown upward gaze shifts while performing mental calculations.

#### (II) Intimate Gaze

This gaze pattern is widely used between strangers meeting for the first time, friends of the opposite sex, family members, and close friends. Generally, it begins with both parties’ eyes, then moves to the chin and subsequently to various parts of the body.

For example, when someone approaches from a distance, you typically scan quickly from the face to the waist to determine gender. You then examine the person again to gauge their level of interest in you, focusing the gaze on the eyes, chin, and areas above the abdomen. If two people are relatively close, they focus the gaze on the region between the eyes and the chest. Young men and women often use this intimate gaze to convey affection.

#### 3. Lateral Gaze Shift (Debunking a Widely Circulated Fallacy)

A gaze shift to the left or right disrupts the most sincere pupil-to-pupil contact, yet no definitive mapping rules can be established for left versus right shifts because individual habits differ.

A so-called psychological claim states, “If recalling something, most people’s gaze shifts left; if fabricating, the gaze shifts right.” Those propagating this rule solemnly offer an explanation linking it to the crossed control of the brain’s hemispheres and the differing functional specializations of the left and right hemispheres: the left hemisphere handles memory, the right handles creation. Many treat this rule as a valuable lie-detection criterion; below we expose the fallacy.

#### ③ Pupil

Once the iris has been introduced, the pupil is essentially fully covered as well. The pupil is not an independent organ or component; it is simply the opening in the center of the iris through which all visual light enters. Therefore, regardless of ethnicity, the pupil always appears black—not because of pigment, but because of the darkness inside the body.

Thus, when light is too strong, the sphincter pupillae within the iris contracts automatically and the pupil constricts; when light weakens, the dilator pupillae contracts automatically and the pupil dilates. These adjustments are performed autonomously by smooth muscle under autonomic nervous system control and do not require separate instructions from the cerebral cortex (responsible for thought).

#### ③ Pupil

Once the iris has been introduced, the pupil is essentially fully covered as well. The pupil is not an independent organ or component; it is simply the opening in the center of the iris through which all visual light enters. Therefore, regardless of ethnicity, the pupil always appears black—not because of pigment, but because of the darkness inside the body.

Thus, when light is too strong, the sphincter pupillae within the iris contracts automatically and the pupil constricts; when light weakens, the dilator pupillae contracts automatically and the pupil dilates. These adjustments are performed autonomously by smooth muscle under autonomic nervous system control and do not require separate instructions from the cerebral cortex (responsible for thought).

#### (3) Absence of [I Am Listening Attentively]

When the true inner state is unwillingness to “listen attentively” to the other person, or when other factors such as embarrassment or awkwardness prevent attentive listening, the listener may also exhibit gaze shifting.

Imagine: if the other person is saying something you want to hear—for instance, information concerning your personal interests, the outcome of a punishment or appointment, or entertaining gossip that excites the nervous system—you will certainly look the speaker in the eye and listen carefully to every word.

However, when the content is uninteresting or unwelcome, the listener will choose to shift gaze while listening.

#### Gaze Direction as a Prelude to Communication

During conversation, the eyeballs often turn in different directions. Through these directions, one can glimpse a person’s inner activity.

When a person looks upward, it indicates they are likely thinking or trying to recall something. Perhaps they are a visual thinker attempting to form an image in the mind. If the eyes look downward, it may indicate submission or guilt about something. If a person’s eyes look to the side, note that they may be about to become angry. Of course, this can also be understood as an attempt to escape the conversation or a sign of distraction.

#### I. Eye Shape, the Color of the Mind

Eye size is not limited to length and width; it also includes the vertical opening when the eyes are open and the size of the pupils. Since ancient times, large eyes have been regarded as an important element of beauty and a synonym for purity and gentleness. People with large eyes have good expressive ability but also tend to be overly sensitive; their clear likes and dislikes may lead to communication difficulties with others. Women whose large eyes reveal spirit are especially prone to impulsive relationships, later regretting their rash actions. Therefore, when facing anyone or anything, avoid overly subjective assumptions and strive to remain prudent and objective.

#### Gaze Direction

During conversation, the eyeballs often turn in different directions. These directions can help you judge what a person is truly thinking.

When a person looks upward, she is likely thinking or trying to recall something. Perhaps she is a visual thinker attempting to form an image in the mind. If the eyes look downward, it may indicate submission or guilt about something. If a person’s eyes look to the side, note that she may be about to become angry. Of course, this can also be interpreted as an attempt to escape the conversation or a sign of distraction.

#### 1. Small Eyes Indicating Simplicity and Intelligence

People with small eyes are mostly honest, simple, and introverted; to outsiders they appear as mystics. They are all intelligent and strong-willed, yet sometimes overly fixated on minor matters and may lose the greater for the lesser. Such individuals are usually careful, patient, and good at persevering. Although many lack outstanding external features, their inner potential and strength often prove astonishing. Women with small eyes lead ordinary lives, dislike risk, and can be somewhat petty-minded; after marriage they become typical virtuous wives and mothers. In addition, people with small eyes whose gaze flickers constantly have great potential to become outstanding figures.

#### Micro-Expression Keywords

The eyes are the windows to the soul. A person’s psychological state and inner world can be conveyed through the eyes. Psychologists believe that to enter another person’s inner world, the first thing to look at is their eyes.

As the saying goes, the eyes are the windows to the soul and the most accurate expression of a person’s emotions and inner activities. A person’s moral character, behavior, and loyalty or treachery can all be reflected through the eyes. Therefore, psychologists believe that to enter another person’s inner world, the first thing to look at is their eyes.

#### Dilated Pupils Betray His "Love"

Indian poet Tagore put it well: "Once anyone learns the language of the eyes, the variations of expression become endless." Beyond serving as the body's visual organs, the eyes can also truthfully convey a person's various emotions. As the saying goes, "The eyes are the windows to the soul."

So how can one read a person's inner secrets or hidden matters from the eyes? FBI agents tell us that the answers lie in changes in pupil size, gaze direction, eye contact, and blink rate.



#### Clue One: Gaze Direction

**Emotional Changes and Gaze Direction**

Changes in emotion lead to changes in gaze direction: when depressed or sad, the gaze drops downward; when shy or guilty, the gaze moves downward or to the side; when rejecting or disgusted, the gaze turns away. Yet gaze is very easy to control and does not even require special training. Some people skilled at lying can keep their gaze fixed on you without you noticing a thing. Therefore, do not use the other person's seemingly sincere gaze as an excuse to convince yourself to believe them.



#### Clue Five: Rolling the Eyes Upward

Rolling the eyes upward is commonly understood to indicate contempt. Beyond that, it can also signal a desire for greater closeness, typically seen in the female partner within a romantic couple. This type of eye roll differs from contempt; the gaze usually returns to the male partner's pupils afterward, accompanied by a smile. The smile serves both to appear cute and sincere and to seek an affirming signal from the male partner. The male partner must distinguish this from eye rolls expressing contempt or disgust, or unnecessary misunderstandings and trouble may arise.



#### b. Half-Closed Eyes Indicating Negativity

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图10-14]*

Half-closed eyelids frequently appear in expressions of emotions such as disgust-related states (contempt, disdain) and sadness-related states (displeasure, crying), as shown in Figure 10-14. Note, however, that true anger and anger-related threats do not involve half-closed eyelids; the eyes widen instead. For detailed distinctions, see Chapter 6.



#### Eyes

People often say the eyes are the windows to the soul. If that is so, then the eyelids are the projections, and the eyebrows and forehead represent the window's decorations. These factors can help you build a complete picture of a person's psychological state.

In this section we will closely observe how the eyes "speak," including eye contact, pupil dilation or constriction, and blink rate. Later we will also learn how the eyebrows play a key role during eye communication.



#### Clue Seven: Looking at Someone Sideways

First, try a small experiment. Have a friend walk ahead of you at a distance of 15–20 meters, making sure your loud call can be heard. Do not tell the friend beforehand that you will call their name. When they are unprepared, suddenly call their name from behind. You will find that they will try to turn their head and even rotate their body to face you directly. Similarly, if you suddenly call a friend from beside them, they will turn to respond face-on as much as possible.



#### 4. The Eyes of Fear

When facing a fear stimulus, people often display a particular gaze shift—rapid multidirectional eye movement.

This action is difficult to fake; it is not impossible, but hard to do. Only the vigilance that accompanies fear causes high-frequency eye rotation to quickly notice every change nearby—an evolved instinct.

The value of this stress micro-expression lies in the fact that the frequency of changes in gaze direction is directly proportional to the degree of inner fear.



#### 4. Deep-Set Eyes Indicating Talent and Alertness

People with deep eye sockets and recessed eyeballs tend to be talented, possess strong comprehension, high alertness, and thorough thinking. They are rational individuals skilled at studying the essence beneath surface appearances. Such people are often calm and honest, finish what they start, tend to be silent and reserved, patient and responsible in their work, and are down-to-earth doers. However, they are not good at expressing themselves, act slowly, have somewhat short tempers, and focus more on their own and immediate interests.



#### 2. Narrow Eyes Indicating Kindness and Introversion

People with narrow eyes have meticulous minds, keen observation, orderly work habits, and highly detailed plans. Such individuals are usually kind and friendly, possess a spirit of dedication, yet are relatively introverted, lack decisiveness when facing issues, and often echo others. They can hold extreme views when assessing situations and frequently hesitate as a result, missing opportunities. In many cases, people with narrow eyes have fragile emotions, are somewhat neurotic, and tend to be suspicious.



#### Eyes: Windows for Peering into the Heart

"The human eye speaks as many words as the tongue and, without a dictionary, can reveal the entire world through the language of the eyes." This remark by American writer Ralph Waldo Emerson tells us that a person's eyes can reveal their inner thoughts, which is of great significance in deciding whether to advance or retreat, draw close or keep distance, in interactions with them.



#### 1. Eye Closure and Blinking

Full closure of the eyelids completely blocks light with imaging significance from entering the eyes (while still allowing light detection), meaning nothing is seen. Even high-frequency eyelid closures such as blinking severely affect visual imaging. At this point in the reading, try it yourself: fix your gaze on an object and deliberately blink rapidly three to four times. How does it feel?



#### (I) Social Gaze

When your gaze falls below the other person's eye level, it creates a typical social atmosphere. The focus of the gaze is between the other person's eyes and mouth, avoiding pressure and allowing the conversation to proceed in a warm, relaxed environment. Therefore, mastering social gaze is invaluable for business negotiations and commercial cooperation.



#### Eyes Wide Open

This indicates strong interest in what you are saying and attentive listening, with active thinking occurring. If the eyes are wide and the mouth is open, it shows that something you said surprised them and they can hardly believe it. At this point, you need to provide a clearer statement or further detailed explanation for the other person to accept it.



#### Sideways Glance

People who like to glance at others sideways are generally introverted and shy. If this behavior is accompanied by a smile, it tells the other person, "I am interested in you!" But if accompanied by a pout or lowered eyebrows, it signals doubt, contempt, hostility, or criticism.



#### Levator Palpebrae Superioris

The levator palpebrae superioris muscle lies within the upper eyelid, small in form yet crucial. When tense, it lifts the upper eyelid upward and opens the eyes. Every morning when we open our eyes, this muscle is at work. When the levator palpebrae superioris relaxes, the upper eyelid contracts, producing eye closure.



#### 6. Round Eyes Indicating Frankness and Affability

People with round eyes are naturally easygoing, cheerful, frank, consistent in word and deed, highly popular, quick to understand, and have wide interests and strong thinking ability. Such individuals work conscientiously and actively, are sensitive, and therefore easily influenced by external factors. They have strong self-esteem accompanied by a tendency toward self-righteousness.



#### Continuous Blinking

Blinking continuously while speaking indicates that the person is thinking about something else while talking. Blinking continuously while listening shows that they have no interest in what you are saying but find it hard to refuse, so they pretend to listen while their mind has already wandered far away.

Since the purpose of this book is not to treat eye diseases through surgery, it will not list every component of the eyes and their adnexa in exhaustive detail, covering only the parts related to the micro-expressions under study.

The case of "active" closure differs from the previously discussed maximum distinction in that the eyes are the primary initiator and executor of emotional and cognitive expression. Active half-closure, like full closure, also carries different shades of meaning.

#### Eyelids and Micro-movements

##### (1) Complete Closure

Eyelid closure is a movement that can be voluntarily controlled; a normal person can perform this action at any time. The content we will explore focuses solely on instinctive reactions triggered by stimuli, excluding habitual eye closure (common in older adults) and habitual blinking, as these lack a necessary stimulus source and hold no value for analyzing psychological states. However, these habitual actions can serve as the subject's **baseline reactions** for comparison. Of course, the research content does not include deliberately performed eye closures or blinks.

Stimuli that cause visual blockage generally fall into two categories: positive ones, such as music worth savoring, delicious food, or problems requiring focused thought; and negative ones, such as terrifying images or threatening questions. Both types elicit the same brain response—I do not want to see it.

**① Positive Stimuli**

Positive stimuli prompt the brain to order the eyes closed in order to concentrate and avoid letting visual processing divert limited neural resources. Closing the eyes while listening to music can intensify auditory sensation; closing the eyes while tasting food can intensify gustatory sensation; closing the eyes while carefully sniffing with the nose can seemingly detect subtler odors and intensify olfactory sensation; and closing the eyes while pondering a problem can concentrate mental energy to arrive at an answer. Note, however, that people more often close their eyes as an instinctive reaction to a stimulus rather than for any specific purpose, because processing visual information consumes excessive neural capacity and closing the eyes conserves considerable effort. See Figure 10-11.

Although we lack precise data on the percentage of external information humans obtain through vision, both inquiry and personal sensory experience allow an “unscientific” conclusion: the proportion is large. The logic holds that conserving neural resources otherwise spent on visual processing enhances the efficiency of other neural activities.

**② Negative Stimuli**

Negative stimuli make the nervous system perceive possible harm, generating various negative emotions such as sadness, worry (fear involving thought), disgust, and fear (fear without thought). To reduce or avoid negative stimuli, the nervous system commands the eyelids to close, cutting off visual input and thereby limiting harm.

A simple experiment illustrates this: pick up a small object and make a quick throwing motion toward someone you know well (without actually releasing it). Even if the person trusts you completely and has not been specifically instructed not to close their eyes, they will still involuntarily shut their eyes to avoid possible injury. Evolution has equipped the nervous system with an instinctive tendency to seek benefit and avoid harm; when harm is sensed, self-protection mechanisms activate automatically. Although the person knows you are reliable and would never harm them even at personal cost, such a prank still triggers a natural reaction.

Eye closure or non-closure can be consciously controlled. Yet under sudden stimulation, conscious thought exerts no control; the action is governed by instincts accumulated through evolution.

Additional examples confirm that negative stimuli produce eyelid closure. After seeing a terrifying image (note: afterward, not at the instant), when feeling disgusted yet helpless, or when saddened and unwilling to face something, a pronounced reaction—complete eyelid closure—occurs. See Figure 10-12.

In the absence of physical stimuli such as wind or airborne particles, high-frequency blinking is also essentially visual blockage. The difference is that high-frequency blinking usually mixes a large measure of rational decision-making into the instinctive impulse to close the eyes, resulting in simultaneous instinctive blockage of vision and determined attempts to keep the eyes open in order to maintain rational attention to the situation.

The clearest illustration occurs when facing a difficult decision: many people’s blink rate increases. A difficult decision here does not refer to logical deduction or computational problems; such pressure-free difficulties typically produce frowning and a fixed gaze—in other words, staring blankly—while visual input is effectively ignored. The decisions that raise blink rate involve choices about what to say, how to say it, or how to weigh options according to the principle of seeking benefit and avoiding harm. In actual tests we have conducted, many reactions to effective stimuli consisted of the subject desperately blinking because they did not wish to reveal the truth.

##### 5. Orbicularis Oculi Muscle

The orbicularis oculi is a broad, flat, elliptical muscle, symmetrical on both sides, encircling the orbit and extending inward to the eyelids.

The location of the orbicularis oculi carries significant strategic importance. Originating from the medial side near the nose, its fibers form a complete ellipse that links most of the muscles in the upper half of the face:

- Superiorly, some fibers merge with the frontalis and corrugator supercilii.
- Medially, some fibers reach the superolateral portion of the depressor supercilii.
- Inferiorly, some fibers variously cover or merge with adjacent muscles, including the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, levator labii superioris, and zygomaticus minor.

Consequently, the orbicularis oculi becomes the central connection point for the muscles of the upper face: above it influences the frontalis and corrugator supercilii that move the eyebrows; medially it connects to the depressor supercilii at the nasal root; below it influences and is influenced by the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, levator labii superioris, and zygomaticus minor. Any contraction of the orbicularis oculi necessarily draws these muscles into coordinated movement, while contraction of the surrounding muscles in turn stretches the orbicularis oculi, altering the morphology of the eye region.

Given this strategically vital position, the orbicularis oculi plays an important role in major facial expressions and various ocular reflexes.

The palpebral portion of the orbicularis oculi can readily draw the eyelids closed, as during sleep or in protective blinking triggered by light. Its most important function is to seal the eyes tightly or produce eyelid closure while simultaneously depressing and tightening the eyebrows, cooperatively reducing the amount of light entering the eyes. During full contraction of the orbicularis oculi, radial skin folds form at the lateral canthus; after middle age these folds often become permanent—the so-called crow’s feet.

In addition, contraction of the orbicularis oculi indirectly affects muscle bundles of the lower face, producing slight elevation of the upper lip and cheek prominence. These effects are indirect because the primary muscles responsible for upper-lip elevation and cheek prominence are not the orbicularis oculi; they will be described in detail later.

Thus the morphological changes of the eyes and their surroundings possess powerful expressive capacity precisely because of the strategic position of the orbicularis oculi.

Observing changes in the eyes and surrounding area is key to capturing shifts in expression.

##### Interpreting Your Love Life from Eyelid Shape

In discussions of the eyes, the importance of the eyelids is often overlooked. In fact, the degree of eyelid opening and closing can likewise reflect a person’s mental state.

- **Drooping eyelids**: Drooping eyelids carry many possible meanings, so judge according to context whether a person with lowered lids feels fatigue, boredom, dejection, laziness, or is flirting.
- **Effortfully raising the eyelids to widen the eyes**: Usually indicates strong interest in something. If the eyes open excessively wide, the person may be surprised or frightened.
- **Squinting**: If a person squints without being stimulated by bright light, they may be preparing to speak or expressing uncertainty. If the squint is accompanied by a broad smile, the person feels very happy.

Moreover, the eyelids are considered the part of the face most reflective of sexual desire; their shape can reveal a person’s psychological attitude toward love.

- **Both eyes single-fold**: Personality tends to be introverted, solitary, sensitive, strong-willed, determined, and diligent. Emotional expression is reserved and restrained; even when standing before someone admired or liked, the person strives to remain composed and show nothing. Professional expertise allows steady career advancement; in family life the person is conservative, yet any extramarital affair quickly becomes evident.
- **Both eyes double-fold**: Outgoing and warm, emotionally rich; small caring gestures or solicitous inquiries, especially from the opposite sex, easily move them, making resistance to opposite-sex attraction difficult. Whether at work or social gatherings they are invariably popular. They belong to the loyal and honest type whose family life is happy and fulfilling.
- **One single-fold, one double-fold**: Such individuals rarely reveal their true intentions and often complain or grumble in work and interpersonal settings. People with this eyelid configuration show low loyalty in love, enjoy change and stimulation, possess a tendency to philander, and are sexually open, seldom refusing advances.

##### ① “Passive” Closure

One form is “passive” partial closure caused by the requirements of other expressions. Examples include the eye closure that accompanies hearty laughter or sorrowful weeping; in both cases the emphasis lies elsewhere than on the transmission or reception of visual information.

During genuine hearty laughter the mind is in a state of great pleasure; the pleasurable information has already been received (the stimulus is complete—otherwise why laugh?), so there is no need to see anything or to signal that one is looking. Likewise, during genuine sorrowful weeping the mind is in acute pain; the saddening, aggrieved, or oppressive information has already exerted its stimulus, so there is no need—and no capacity—to see anything or convey anything with the eyes, because the priority is to release the emotion or else “internal injury” will result. In such expressions the eyes close more from physiological necessity.

- **Laughter**: Laughter operates on a principle similar to sneezing. Both involve rapid, voluminous exhalation; this respiratory pattern raises capillary pressure inside the eyeball and increases intraorbital pressure. Eyelid closure creates a barrier that protects the eyeball from sudden high internal pressure.
- **Crying**: In addition to the respiratory factor already mentioned (crying also involves spasmodic exhalation), there is the influence of tears. The lacrimal glands secrete abundant tears that well up within the eyelid structure; to direct the tears and fulfill their primary duty (one function of the eyelids is to moisten the cornea during blinking), the eyelids automatically close.

##### 4. Levator Palpebrae Superioris

Although small, the levator palpebrae superioris has a relatively complex anatomical structure[1] and lies mainly inside the upper eyelid, symmetrically on both sides.

Its function is to elevate the upper lid. Contraction of the levator palpebrae superioris raises the upper eyelid—the action of opening the eyes—while contraction of the orbicularis oculi and relaxation of the levator palpebrae superioris produces eye closure. The levator palpebrae superioris is also connected via check ligaments to the superior rectus, which moves the eyeball; when the eyeball performs an upward gaze, the upper lid automatically rises and the eyebrows are lifted by the frontalis.

Eyelid position depends on the coordinated action of the orbicularis oculi and levator palpebrae superioris together with the degree of eyeball protrusion. When the eyes are relaxed and open, the lower-lid margin normally passes at the level of the inferior limbus, while the upper lid covers the upper half of the iris width (one-quarter of its vertical diameter).

The levator palpebrae superioris contains smooth-muscle fibers (Müller’s muscle), which are controlled solely by the autonomic nervous system and therefore not subject to conscious volition. When a person is frightened or excited, sympathetic activation causes the smooth muscle within the tarsal plates to contract, widening the palpebral fissure. When sympathetic tone is inhibited (for example, during intoxication), the upper lid droops. Sympathetic overactivity can also produce conditions such as Horner syndrome.

##### a. Positive Expressive Partial Closure—Eyes Like Silk

Eyes like silk constitute a flirtatious expression in women. The word “silk” itself indicates that eyelid closure is nearly complete. Nevertheless, professional analysis requires us to dissect this appealing situation and examine the underlying psychological state.

The origin of eyes like silk is actually a variant of the “concentrated enjoyment” discussed earlier. The evolutionary process is roughly as follows: concentrated enjoyment requires eye closure (already examined); over time this natural physiological phenomenon became a shared understanding that a blissful expression with closed eyes signifies enjoyment; consequently people consciously half-close their eyes to display a pleasing expression that conveys “I am enjoying this (being with you) very much.”

Therefore, when applying makeup to appear seductive, the eyeliner should be drawn slender and elongated. To project a spirited, heroic air, such a line must never be used; instead the distance between brow and eye should be increased so the eyelids appear more widely open.

##### 10.2.3 Visual Blockage

When confronted with negative stimuli, the nervous system mobilizes every available bodily resource to prevent further increase in the stimulus. Retreating to control distance, contracting the limbs, or raising a hand or foot as a barrier are all possible reactions. Visual blockage is one such reaction.

Visual blockage refers to the use of an obstacle to obstruct one’s own line of sight. In more technical terms, it is the deployment of an obstacle intended to block or partially block light from entering the eyes, thereby refusing or reducing the reception of visual information. The obstacles in question are generally other parts of one’s own body—most commonly the eyelids, followed by the arms or objects held in the hands.

Ordinary eye closure and blinking (blinking being rapid, repeated closure) accomplish visual blockage through the eyelids. Besides closure, visual blockage also includes pupillary constriction. Because micro-expressions focus on facial expression, actions that use the hands or other objects for visual blockage are not discussed in this book; see the book *Micro-reaction* (微反应) for details.

##### 2. Blinking

If a person blinks several times within a single second, it indicates emotional arousal and strong interest in something; it can also be interpreted as timidity or shyness, an unwillingness to meet another’s gaze directly. Under normal conditions a person blinks five to eight times per minute, each blink lasting less than one second. A blink exceeding one second signals boredom, lack of interest, or even contempt and disdain. Continuous blinking indicates that the person is striving to suppress their feelings. Vigorous blinking often reveals tension.

##### Circumstances That Increase Blink Rate

We once tested a computer programmer whose résumé claimed years of experience and proficiency in multiple programming languages. When asked for algorithmic details of one language listed on the résumé, his blink rate rose sharply for three to four seconds, after which he admitted unfamiliarity with that language.

##### 4. Prolonged Eye Closure

Prolonged eye closure accompanied by exhalation indicates anxiety and high stress. It can also occur when a person is unwilling to face a situation or individual and wishes to escape. For example, while walking down the street and suddenly encountering someone one does not wish to meet, the person may close the eyes for an extended period out of fear of being noticed.

##### 1. Eye Closure and Blinking

Full eyelid closure completely prevents light capable of forming images from entering the eyes (though light detection remains), rendering objects invisible. Even the high-frequency closures of blinking severely disrupt visual imaging. At this point you may test the effect yourself: fixate on an object and deliberately blink rapidly three or four times; note the sensation.

##### 3. Squinting

During conversation, if the other person squints, frowns, and repeatedly scans you, it signals that they are filled with doubt and are searching you for clues to verify their judgment. This expression primarily conveys non-acceptance or uncertainty and frequently appears when someone feels unsure about a decision.

##### 11. Insecure and Low-Self-Esteem Blinking

Some people blink incessantly; such individuals often lack confidence and a sense of security. They may have received little affection in childhood and never stood out, resulting in low self-confidence. Because frequent blinking creates a poor impression, these people usually have few close friends and find it difficult to sustain relationships.

##### b. Negative Expressive Partial Closure

Partial eyelid closure frequently appears in expressions of disgust-related emotions (scorn, disdain) and sadness-related emotions (displeasure, weeping). Note, however, that genuine anger and anger-related threat never produce partial closure; the eyes widen instead. For detailed distinctions see Chapter 6.

##### (2) Incomplete Closure

Contraction of the orbicularis oculi produces eyelid closure that is not complete; the eyes remain slightly more open than in full closure yet less open than the normal resting state. The inner state represented by incomplete eyelid closure is somewhat more complex.

##### ② “Active” Closure

The chief distinction of “active” closure from the cases discussed earlier is that the eyes themselves are the primary initiators and executors of emotional and cognitive expression. Active partial closure, like complete closure, can carry different expressive meanings.

#### Pupil Dilation or Constriction

##### II. Your Pupils Betray You

The eyes are most critical at the pupils. To understand a person, try focusing on the other party’s pupils to help uncover the truth and judge whether their words are genuine, because pupil dilation and constriction are extremely difficult to control. Someone who has lied can spread their hands to show sincerity or wear an innocent expression to proclaim innocence, yet they cannot control the dilation of their pupils caused by excitement.

Long ago, people already knew how to use pupils to read others’ inner thoughts. When communicating or negotiating with others, watch their eyes carefully. We often see such scenes in novels or TV dramas: when the male lead is caught hiding something from the female lead, she presses for the reason and usually adds, “Look me in the eyes when you speak.” This is precisely about watching the other person’s pupils, because pupils expand and contract with the speaker’s emotional fluctuations. For example, at a critical moment in negotiations, the other party may claim the price has reached its lowest and cannot be discussed further, yet their pupils dilate—this indicates they are excited about an impending victory. The price they offered is definitely not the lowest; they are lying.

In addition, compared with dark-colored pupils, light-colored pupils are often more attractive because the dilation of light-colored pupils is more noticeable.

Pupil changes carry different meanings, and variations in size can also reflect certain psychological activities.

For instance, pupil dilation. When a person feels pleasure or excitement, or receives a certain stimulus, their pupils can dilate to four to five times their normal size. Pupils also expand rapidly when someone develops a strong interest in or motivation toward another person or thing. It is said that ancient Persian jewelers priced jewelry according to the size of the customer’s pupils. If a sparkling diamond ring caused the buyer’s pupils to dilate, the merchant would raise the price accordingly.

We often say or hear the phrase “You’re so happy your eyes are shining.” This expression is not without basis; people’s pupils may dilate from joy, appearing as if they are glowing. When people are in an excited state, their pupils likewise dilate. For example, when a girl watches a horror movie, she curls up while her pupils also dilate. This occurs because the terrifying stimulus excites her. Usually, a person appears more energetic when excited, precisely because pupil dilation during excitement makes them look more spirited.

Another example is pupil constriction. When a person is in a negative state such as anger, disgust, hatred, depression, or suspicion, their pupils contract to a very small size. For instance, after a couple quarrels, if the woman returns home angry, even if she tries hard to hide her emotions and appear nonchalant, someone nearby may still notice something is wrong and ask, “What happened?” This is not surprising. Once a person becomes angry or emotionally low, their pupils shrink, making the eyes look dull and lifeless. The same phenomenon occurs in business settings. If your client suddenly squints, it indicates they have doubts about something and are internally conflicted.

Yet another example is when pupils show no change. Sometimes, while discussing a topic with someone, you may find yourself speaking animatedly and growing hoarse, while the other person appears to be listening attentively with their head tilted, yet their pupils show little change. In such cases, it is advisable to stop the topic, because the other person is not interested or does not care. The absence of significant pupil change is a natural sign of inattention or indifference. Upon noticing such pupils, the initiating party should realize that the matter under discussion does not interest the other person.

##### 3.1.1 The Remarkable Pupil

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图3-1　瞳孔]*

In lie-detection (experiments), the pupil test can powerfully demonstrate this point. The pupil is an opening (literally a “hole”!) in the center of the iris (commonly called the black eyeball, though iris color varies across ethnic groups) that allows light to reach the retina. Its physiological function is that when light intensifies, the pupil constricts to prevent excessive light from stimulating the optic nerve; when light dims, the pupil dilates to admit as much light as possible onto the retina for clear imaging. These two changes occur constantly, yet humans cannot perceive them, because all dilation and constriction are performed by the smooth muscles controlling the iris, which are governed solely by the autonomic nervous system. No matter how hard you try, you cannot consciously control them. See Figure 3-1.

Interestingly, as evolution progressed, human pupil responses became more complex and advanced. Experiments show that when people see something they like, their pupils dilate—for example, when a lecherous man sees a seductive beauty or a gambler sees a strong hand—so they can take in more of the pleasing sight. When they see something they dislike, their pupils constrict—for example, when watching a bloody surgical dissection or filthy swill—to minimize exposure to negative stimuli.

A master of maintaining composure may exhibit only pupil changes while remaining otherwise impassive. Ordinary people, however, experience not only pupil changes but also more obvious accompanying behaviors; for instance, upon seeing a beautiful woman they are certain to widen their eyes and drool, while upon seeing a billowing white bedsheet they will have long since shut their eyes tightly and screamed.

This is one of the laws of visual stress responses.

##### 2. Changes in the Pupil

As previously introduced, the pupil is an opening in the center of the iris rather than an independent organ. The pupil permits light to enter the eyeball and form an image on the retina. When light intensifies, the pupil constricts to prevent excessive light from stimulating the optic nerve; when light dims, the pupil dilates to admit as much light as possible for the clearest possible imaging. All these actions are performed by the smooth muscles controlling the iris. Smooth muscles are governed solely by the autonomic nervous system; no matter how hard you try, you cannot directly control them through conscious commands.

Interestingly, as evolution progressed, human pupil responses became more complex and advanced. Experiments show that when people see something they like, their pupils dilate (for example, when a lecherous man sees a seductive beauty or a gambler sees a strong hand) so they can take in more of the pleasing sight; when they see something they dislike, their pupils constrict (for example, when watching a bloody surgical dissection) to minimize exposure to negative stimuli. This is the law of pupil stress responses.

##### 15. Small Pupils

Selfishness, strong self-awareness, and a lack of emotional sensitivity are characteristics displayed by people with smaller pupils. Such individuals are competitive and unwilling to admit defeat; they are better suited to acting independently. If people of this type are mature and socially adept, able to navigate relationships smoothly, they can achieve even greater success in their careers.

##### 14. Large Pupils

People with large pupils give the impression of bright, spirited eyes and are relatively attractive. They tend to have gentle temperaments, treat others with approachability, and lead simple lives. They are caring and considerate, perform well at work, enjoy excellent interpersonal relationships, and adapt readily, enabling them to seize opportunities effectively.

#### Gaze Types

##### III. Decoding "Eye Language"

In a dimly lit room, a woman sits at a table, head slightly lowered, eyes looking upward—this scene has captivated countless people. Raising the eyes upward while lowering the head conveys both submission and deference along with an ineffable charm. This posture, which makes a woman appear childlike, holds fatal attraction for men. A scene in the novel *Love in a Fallen City* depicts Bai Liusu doing exactly this upon meeting Fan Liuyuan: “That lowered head, so tender,” the coyness of words half-spoken inevitably stirs the heart. One wise woman in the world also won universal affection with this posture: the late Princess Diana of Britain. When her marriage was on the brink of collapse, she tucked her chin slightly inward, lifted her eyes upward, and revealed her slender, fair neck—an elegance unmatched, like a work of art. This childlike purity triggered affection in thousands, especially when people believed the royal family was attacking her.

Clearly, the eyes store and transmit vast amounts of information. Through the eyes one can glimpse a person’s innermost thoughts. Yet every eye movement carries rich inner meaning, and the same movement can convey very different meanings depending on the person using it. Consider the sidelong glance. The action carries different significance for men and women: if a woman uses it on a man during their first meeting, it indicates she rather likes him but feels too nervous to look directly, so she steals glances; the same action performed by a man carries a hint of contempt. A sidelong glance implies looking down on the other person. One must also integrate the accompanying eye expression for a full analysis.

Another common eye movement is the upward roll of the eyes. It produces an innocent expression used to signal that one has done nothing wrong or has been wronged. Whether the conveyed message is genuine still requires other factors for judgment, because this single expression can, like language, deceive the observer.

Then there is the wink. When people wish to signal mutual understanding, they often wink at each other; the expression says “only you and I know.” Outsiders see it as through a fog. Some people wink while making faces to heighten the realism of their performance; anyone who does so must hold a favorable impression and genuine liking. This occurs more frequently among children.

Additional movements include lowered eyes and shifting pupils. The former is an unfriendly gesture carrying contempt and also signals indifference or lack of concern. Its user is typically rational and calm, rarely impulsive, yet fundamentally self-centered and extremely willful, with views that are hard to change. As for the latter, rapid pupil movement usually indicates a sharp sixth sense, quick reactions, and the ability to read people swiftly; such individuals are also more emotional. When interacting with them, watch one’s words and actions, because they are easily influenced and may overreact. Conversely, people whose pupils move slowly tend to be less sensitive, experience smaller emotional swings, and are less easily swayed. Between romantic partners, a woman can glean information from the direction of her partner’s pupil movement: movement toward the upper left indicates recalling the past; toward the upper right indicates imagining something never seen before; toward the lower left indicates calculating something; toward the lower right indicates sensing one’s own body; and horizontal movement left or right indicates attentive listening and an effort to understand what is being said.

Different angles and directions of gaze convey different quantities of information. If someone looks up at you, the gaze expresses respect and admiration; conversely, looking down at you signals an intent to maintain personal dignity. If the other person pays no attention and continues working without shifting gaze, the behavior indicates indifference, neglect, and emotional distance. A serious, piercing gaze constitutes a warning that you may have unwittingly offended the person. A steady smile accompanied by a gentle, warm gaze shows respect and genuine interest in the topic.

“Eye language” is so important for an individual—especially for women—that skillful use becomes a powerful, invisible weapon that captivates. A charming smile and expressive eyes, every frown and smile filled with tender affection, eyes like autumn waters sparkling with light, convey infinite allure. Bai Juyi praised Yang Yuhuan in “Song of Everlasting Sorrow” with the lines: “One glance back, a hundred charms born; the six palaces’ powdered beauties lose all color.” Eye language thus serves not only as a tool for gathering information about others but also as a means of expressing one’s own emotions. Much can be mined from a person’s eyes; therefore, in social interaction the eyes must never be overlooked as a vital entry point.

##### (2) Erroneous Application of Cross-Control Movement Between the Left and Right Brain

If an improper summary of brain-function lateralization is still excusable, then deriving from that error a link between eye-movement direction and left-right brain division is an even more ignorant display.

The supposed basis is the principle of crossed control: the left hemisphere controls movement of the right-side limbs, and the right hemisphere controls the left-side limbs. This is a scientific conclusion.

Yet it is incomprehensible that, if crossed control is followed, the left brain should control the right eye and the right brain the left eye. If recollection or fabrication truly engaged only one hemisphere according to its specialization (which in fact never occurs), the result should be movement of a single eye, not both eyes moving together. Moreover, under crossed control, if the right brain governs left-hand movement, does that mean the left hand can move only leftward? If leftward movement is assigned to the right brain, then when both hands move leftward together, which hemisphere is in charge?

Therefore, eye-movement direction has no relation whatsoever to functional differences between the left and right brain.

The original source of this fallacy may lie in NLP’s six-direction eye-movement theory. Note that the following cited content is incorrect.

In this well-known speculative model, the “NLP school” claims that when a person’s eyes turn upper left, the individual is recalling visual imagery, as in “What color are your curtains?” When the eyes turn upper right, the person is constructing visual imagery, as in “What color is a purple zebra’s tail?” When the eyes turn horizontally left, the person is recalling auditory information, such as the melody of a famous piece; when turning horizontally right, the person is constructing auditory information, such as composing an original melody. When the eyes turn lower left, the person is talking to themselves; when turning lower right, the person is sensing kinesthetic or perceptual information.

To prevent falsification, NLP added a left-handed supplement: if the subject is left-handed, all directions are reversed. This still relies on the theory of crossed hemispheric control of limbs.

In reality, to provide coherent visual information, eye movements must remain simultaneous and in the same direction; otherwise visual confusion results. Every nerve controlling the extraocular muscles receives input from bilateral corticobulbar fibers. In other words, each eye is simultaneously governed by both hemispheres.

Normal eye movements are therefore conjugate; unlike the limbs, the eyes cannot move in opposite directions or at different times.

Of course, with training some people can deliberately cross their eyes, because during convergence both medial rectus muscles contract, the lens thickens, and the pupils constrict, enabling near work. In contrast, the lateral rectus muscles responsible for divergence are not controlled by the oculomotor nucleus but by the abducens nucleus; therefore the eyes cannot diverge independently. Because the medial rectus is directly controlled by the oculomotor nucleus, crossed eyes are possible.

The neuroanatomical principles are presented to demonstrate that eye-movement direction operates under an entirely different mechanism from limb crossed control and cannot be arbitrarily mapped by imagination.

This set of conjectures, published in 1979, lacks any supporting data and cannot withstand verification. We conducted a small experiment: 200 participants each answered six questions; their eye movements were videotaped and later statistically analyzed.

The results showed that some criteria failed to match more than 70 percent of the time, others approached 50 percent; the average falsification rate across the six rules was 63 percent. In other words, using six-direction eye movement to analyze another person’s thoughts yields an error probability approaching two-thirds—less reliable than a coin toss at 50 percent. The probability that any individual fully conforms to the six-direction pattern is 37 percent, roughly three per thousand (2.6‰), an abysmal figure.

Consequently, this criterion produces erroneous judgments and unjust accusations. We can therefore discard this “pseudoscience” with confidence. Interested readers may similarly examine the parallel rumor that “right-handed people are more rational (rigorous, conservative, etc.) while left-handed people are more artistic (innovative, emotional, etc.).”

##### Frequent Blinking as a Sign of Lying

Scientists have found that the pupil does not “lie”; it is a sensitive display of vital functions, an extension of the brain, and a marker of central-nervous-system activity that most faithfully reflects a person’s true inner feelings. When we interact closely with someone, we can clearly read minds and detect lies through pupillary recognition (a method of observing blink rate and pupil dilation or constriction).

Blinking is both a spontaneous and a subconscious behavior. Regardless of whether a person’s eyes appear dry or moist, monitoring blink frequency is crucial. One must continually note whether the interlocutor’s blink rate is normal, excessively high, or excessively low.

It is well known that when a person lies, the blink rate rises markedly above baseline. U.S. customs inspectors, for example, routinely inform travelers that failure to declare prohibited items will result in repatriation. One might consider this foolish, since travelers have already completed declaration forms. Yet when inspectors issue the reminder, they closely observe the traveler’s eyes for abnormal blink frequency. If the traveler blinks excessively, inspectors search the luggage.

Investigators likewise record a suspect’s blink rate to help determine guilt. Elevated blink rate can reflect guilt, while a lowered rate may indicate that the person is preparing to confess something. Precisely because of this, suspects lack the attention to monitor their own eyes. That is why every facial expression and gesture must be recorded.

Japanese management consultant Takeda Tetsuo has noted that blinking not only reveals the other person’s current state but often also displays personality. Generally, people who blink frequently are narrow-minded and less trustworthy. When negotiating or entrusting matters to such individuals, it is best to speak directly.

The pupil’s response to interest is astonishingly sensitive. Dr. Edward H. Hais presented clinical findings at the annual meeting of the American Society of Medical Hypnosis: “When the eyes encounter something sufficiently pleasurable or stimulating, the pupils dilate rapidly and unconsciously.”

People have long known how to interpret inner states through pupillary change. Ancient Persian jewel merchants reportedly priced gems according to the size of a customer’s pupils upon seeing the jewelry. If a diamond’s brilliance caused pupil dilation, the merchant would quote a higher price.

During courtship the eyes are the most eloquent organs of emotion. When a man encounters a woman he admires, his pupils dilate involuntarily under the strong stimulus of desire; the woman intuitively reads the signal. Especially in dim light, accelerated dilation heightens mutual attraction and fosters romantic love.

In states of terror, tension, excitement, anger, or pain the pupils dilate; in states of disgust, fatigue, or annoyance they constrict tightly, producing a “laser-like gaze.” Absence of change indicates indifference or boredom toward the person or object viewed<|eos|>

##### 6. Rolling the Eyes

Rolling the eyes is a fairly common eye expression. It involves complex eyeball movement and is in fact also a complex gaze-shift process.

The classic eye roll is often used to express contempt. If we slow-motion replay the action, several variations become visible:

1. When the eye roll begins from direct eye contact with the other person, the sequence is: eyelids close; then open while the gaze moves upward (partial sclera visible); the gaze then shifts from upward to the side away from the stimulus, accompanied by a head turn; next the gaze moves downward on that same side; eyelids close again; finally the gaze settles to the side, either level or downward, or the head may turn back to re-establish contact with the stimulus.
2. When the eye roll begins with the face already turned sideways toward the other person, the sequence is: first shift the gaze toward the other person’s side for a quick glance (without full eye contact); then move the gaze upward while closing the eyelids; then, as the eyelids reopen, shift the gaze again to the direction the face is already oriented toward, or even farther in the opposite direction.
3. When a girl rolls her eyes at her boyfriend in a coquettish rather than genuinely angry way, accompanied by lines such as “I hate you,” an extra step appears: at the end the gaze returns to the other person’s pupils, partly to convey sincerity (sometimes paired with a coy or domineering smile) and partly to check whether the playful message has been received.

For further reading, see http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuro-linguistic_programming.

##### (2) Missing [Please Listen Carefully]

The underlying thought is actually [You don’t need to listen carefully]. Whether the other person is “listening carefully” feels unimportant. The speaker does not care whether the listener hears or responds and simply finishes speaking. At such moments the speaker also shows gaze aversion. Typical speech features include: volume and tone lack emphasis and may stay at a normal level or drop in energy; delivery is smooth and may be rapid. In short: this has nothing to do with you.

**Specific examples:**

**Example 1:**  
This pattern is common in meetings when issues are discussed. Democratic decision-making invites differing opinions; it is normal for people to disagree on the same question, and everyone tries to seek common ground while reserving differences. When a speaker knows the listener will not accept the idea yet still insists on stating it, gaze aversion often occurs: the speaker finishes the point without looking directly at the listener. The real inner state is: I’ll say what I want; your disagreement is useless and I don’t care about your view.

However, in the same meeting, if the stronger party is making a show of force or pressuring the dissenting side to understand and respond, the speaker will stare directly into the listener’s eyes, conveying: Listen carefully—this is what I mean. What do you think? The subtext is: Don’t have an opinion; even if you do, I won’t listen; agreement is required immediately.

##### (1) Erroneous Summary of Left–Right Brain Division

Earlier cognitive-psychology research concluded that the left hemisphere mainly handles speech, reading, writing, mathematical calculation, rote memory, logical reasoning, and symbolic thinking, while the right hemisphere mainly handles recognition of object size and shape, spatial cognition, map reading, face recognition, drawing composition, music, structural assembly, and perception of others’ emotions.

More importantly, most human tasks are performed through coordinated activity of both hemispheres rather than exclusive control by one side. For instance, if memory is said to belong to the left hemisphere, to which side does visual memory belong? If visual information is processed by the right hemisphere, then drawing that mental image still requires logical and temporal sequencing—functions attributed to the left hemisphere. Likewise, musical notes are said to be processed mainly by the right hemisphere, yet composing and singing songs require simultaneous participation of both sides. Recent brain-imaging studies have also revised the earlier, overly absolute claims about hemispheric specialization found in older textbooks.

Those seeking theoretical support for a fallacy make a first mistake: they glibly reduce brain findings to “left brain handles memory, right brain handles fabrication.” Setting aside whether creation, construction, and fabrication are synonymous, the reasoning itself is flawed. Further questions follow: What does the direction of eye movement have to do with hemispheric specialization?

##### 5. Not Looking Directly at Someone

Not looking directly means glancing sideways while keeping the face oriented toward the person being observed. This distorted gaze is discussed here for two reasons: first, the pupil is positioned to one side rather than centered, resembling lateral gaze shifts; second, it signals an unwillingness to look, just as gaze aversion signals a lack of sincerity.

Whenever genuine communication is intended or an unexpected stimulus prompts a search (for example, someone calling from the side), the head turns so the face can face the target as squarely as possible. Moving only the eyes without turning the head directly maps a relatively negative attitude (equivalent to unwillingness to look). The “unwillingness” here includes not only the usual connotations of aversion and rejection but also fear (stealing a glance while afraid of being noticed), disdain, and other negative intentions—all grouped under unwillingness.

Emotions and attitudes that commonly produce sidelong glances include: smug laughter (I am better/stronger/correcter than you), contempt (same), anxiety (concern or worry cannot be expressed openly), and disgust (direct rejection of the other person).

##### 2. Eye Contact in Verbal Communication

When speech is possible, mutual pupil contact marks the start of effective exchange—an implicit agreement between both parties. It is an agreement because both participants sense the significance of the mutual gaze and what it will trigger; it is a beginning because mutual gaze initiates the “full-duplex” communication process.

**What is “full-duplex” communication?**

The term is borrowed from communications engineering. It means both parties can send and receive information simultaneously. A simpler explanation appears in Figure 10-10 below.

When two people discuss important information that matters to both, they begin with direct eye contact. In normal verbal exchange, mutual gaze conveys three messages:

1. [Speaker] I want to speak to you;
2. [Speaker] Please listen carefully;
3. [Listener] I am listening carefully.

Because communication is bidirectional, each person is simultaneously speaker and listener and therefore holds all three expectations. Interruption of mutual gaze occurs whenever any one of these expectations is missing.

##### 2. Downward Gaze Shift

In contrast to an upward gaze shift, a downward shift generally indicates that the person had already anticipated several possibilities and one of them has materialized. We can summarize the downward gaze shift as a mindset of endurance. It usually maps to relatively negative states such as guilt (feeling one is not good enough, has made a mistake, or bears responsibility), disagreement (combined with helplessness and inability to change the situation), anger (suppressed for the moment), or anxious thinking (searching for a way to answer a challenge).

Unlike the escape impulse signaled by an upward gaze, a downward gaze usually shows that the person knows escape is impossible and must simply endure until the moment passes or defeat occurs.

Even the downward glance that appears in shyness carries the same psychological mapping. Shyness is actually fear of seeing the other person’s reaction—fear of learning that one is disliked—yet a strong desire for a positive outcome remains, so the pressure is endured.

##### 10.2.4 Gaze Aversion

After mutual gaze, a shift in direction may signal subtle psychological change; the reasons have already been analyzed. We now examine the possible meanings of gaze shifts in each direction.

Before proceeding, however, a caution is necessary for those who would like to play God: any analysis of an individual’s gaze aversion must first establish that person’s habitual pattern (called the baseline in psychological testing). Different people, through long-term environmental adaptation and learning, develop different gaze-aversion habits. Therefore, determining the tested person’s baseline is the correct first step. The following observations should never be applied mechanically.

Starting from mutual pupil contact, gaze can shift in four basic directions—up, down, left, right—and then combine into diagonals: upper-left, lower-left, upper-right, lower-right. Left and right, up and down are defined from the actor’s perspective.

##### (3) Correct Analytical Approach to Lateral Gaze Shifts

The only certainty is that a lateral gaze shift indicates a neural command—whether deliberate, habitual, or instinctive—that interrupts the ongoing exchange. Analysis must compare the shift against each tested person’s baseline.

Gaze aversion has no necessary connection to lying. Although it interrupts the current exchange, the reason may be preparation for better communication—recalling facts, logical reasoning, or calculation—or it may be fabrication or concealment. Lateral shifts can also be purely emotional, such as displeasure or disgust, with no complex thought involved, simply an unwillingness to continue the exchange.

##### 1. Upward Gaze Shift

Based on actual testing, we find that an upward gaze shift can map to three psychological features:

- One is the signaling of elevated self-status, often used to express disdain and frequently paired with a “tsk” sound to form a contemptuous expression;
- Another is the signaling of “this has nothing to do with me” or “I am staying out of it,” commonly seen when feigning innocence;
- The third, and most frequent, occurs when the tested person did not anticipate the question and begins to think on the spot, involuntarily rolling the eyes upward.

Both recall and fabrication have been observed to accompany upward shifts; even moderately difficult arithmetic problems in baseline testing can elicit upward eye movement during mental calculation.

##### 3. Lateral Gaze Shift (Debunking a Widespread Myth)

A gaze shift to the left or right breaks the sincerity of direct pupil contact, yet no fixed mapping can be assigned to left versus right because individual habits differ.

A popular psychological claim states: “If someone is recalling an event, most people’s eyes move left; if fabricating, the eyes move right.” Proponents of this rule further explain it by reference to crossed hemispheric control and supposed functional specialization—left hemisphere for memory, right for creation. Many treat the rule as a valuable lie-detection tool. We now dismantle the myth.

##### (3) Missing [I Am Listening Carefully]

When the listener’s true state is unwillingness to “listen carefully” or inability to do so because of embarrassment or other reasons, gaze aversion also appears.

Imagine the opposite: if the speaker’s topic is something you want to hear—information affecting your personal interests, a disciplinary decision, a job appointment, or exciting gossip—you will maintain eye contact and listen to every word.

For uninteresting or unwelcome content, however, listeners choose to avert their gaze.

##### 5. Looking Elsewhere

When someone looks away during conversation, it often means lack of interest or unfavorable feelings toward the other person. Looking elsewhere can also indicate inferiority or shyness. The eyes are the window to the soul; prolonged eye contact can expose inner thoughts. Therefore, if the other person cannot meet your gaze and keeps looking away, it may be because they are trying to hide a secret and fear you will see through them.

##### 16. Strabismus

Strabismus has two causes: congenital or acquired. Congenital strabismus can sometimes be improved through eye-training exercises. Acquired strabismus, however, warrants extra caution in social interaction because most people who develop it are considered to have improper intentions, which also produce flickering or evasive glances. When a woman’s eyes show strabismus combined with a backward glance, she is said to be changeable and unpredictable, which is considered unfavorable for marriage.
