### Mouth

#### The Many Meanings of Sticking Out the Tongue

The tongue reveals a great deal through its movements. FBI agents remind us to observe changes in a person’s tongue during interactions.

Although the tongue is an internal organ, it can be exposed and thus serves as a medium for body language, conveying fear, desire, rejection, and aggression. All of these trace back to an infant’s instinctive feeding responses.

For example, many sensitive, fragile, and somewhat neurotic people frequently make “biting” motions. Tracing the origin, this reproduces the primitive instinct of an infant tightly gripping the mother’s nipple when hungry to feel secure.

Thus, “biting” is a form of “self-soothing.” It stems from habitual anxiety formed in infancy for unknown reasons. The infant’s thumb-sucking, the child’s nail-biting, and the adult’s chewing on ballpoint pens, cigarettes, or cigars differ in object, yet the underlying anxiety remains the same.

Among tongue movements, FBI agents consider the use of the tongue to express “rejection” the most noteworthy.

For instance, when people experience great fright, in addition to staring blankly, raising both hands with palms outward, they often extend the tongue fully. These gestures were once puzzling, but are now understood as exaggerated “rejection” actions. Raising the hands with palms outward represents an attempt to push away something frightening, while fully extending the tongue mirrors an infant pushing away unwanted food with the tongue—an expression of rejection, only more intense.

Because this gesture occurs when one is frightened, people sometimes direct it at others when aggressing: “doing unto others what one does not want done to oneself.” This is “aggressive tongue protrusion,” also called “sticking out the tongue and making a face.” Its purpose is to intimidate and rudely insult, yet its root remains “rejection,” which transforms into “contempt.”

When people encounter minor fright, tension, or embarrassment, they stick out the tongue briefly before retracting it. This form is commonly seen in kindergarten children and expresses the mildest degree of rejection. Lacking aggression and occurring mostly in young children, the gesture persists despite teachers’ corrections and has become a way to “act cute,” signaling minor tension, fright, or embarrassment.

Beyond rejection, tongue protrusion can also convey the feeling—shared by young and old, male and female alike—of having “narrowly escaped disaster.”

FBI agent Antonis wanted to buy a good car. He went to a dealership and told the salesperson, “I am willing to buy this car at this price.” After some bargaining, the salesperson used a familiar tactic: “All right, let me check with our manager.” He left to consult the manager, and Antonis stepped out of the office to browse.

A few minutes later, Antonis happened to glimpse the salesperson and the manager talking behind a glass door. Although he could not hear them, he could clearly see their movements. After speaking with the manager, the salesperson stuck out his tongue—briefly, but unmistakably.

Antonis returned to the salesperson’s office and waited. The salesperson soon came back and said, “Our manager believes the price I quoted is the best we can offer.”

Antonis replied, “You mean this is your lowest acceptable price?”

“Yes,” the salesperson answered.

“No room for further negotiation?” Antonis pressed.

“None,” the salesperson said, nodding. “This is our lowest price.”

“In that case, thank you,” Antonis said, rising and walking straight out of the office toward the exit without looking back. As he reached the door, he heard someone calling his name: “Wait! Wait!”

The salesperson brought Antonis back to the office and offered to lower the so-called lowest price by another 2,700 yuan—only 100 yuan above Antonis’s initial offer.

The key points of the story are: first, determine the true bottom-line price of the car; second, when you see the salesperson stick out his tongue, recognize that he is trying to get you to accept the supposed lowest price by luck.

Once you learn to observe this behavior, it proves highly useful in bargaining or intense competition.

#### Small Tongue, Big Secrets

Although the tongue is an internal organ, it can be exposed and thus serves as a medium for body language, conveying fear, desire, rejection, and aggression. All of these trace back to an infant’s instinctive feeding responses.

For example, many sensitive, fragile, and somewhat neurotic people frequently make “biting” motions. Tracing the origin, this reproduces the primitive instinct of an infant tightly gripping the mother’s nipple when hungry to feel secure. Thus, “biting” is a form of “self-soothing.” It stems from habitual anxiety formed in infancy for unknown reasons. The infant’s thumb-sucking, the child’s nail-biting, and the adult’s chewing on ballpoint pens, cigarettes, or cigars differ in object, yet the underlying anxiety remains the same.

Among tongue movements, the various ways the tongue expresses “rejection” are the most noteworthy.

For instance, when people experience great fright, in addition to staring blankly, raising both hands with palms outward, they often extend the tongue fully. These gestures were once puzzling, but are now understood as exaggerated “rejection” actions. Raising the hands with palms outward represents an attempt to push away something frightening, while fully extending the tongue mirrors an infant pushing away unwanted food with the tongue—an expression of rejection, only more intense.

Because this tongue-protrusion gesture occurs when one is frightened, people sometimes direct it at others when aggressing: “doing unto others what one does not want done to oneself.” This is “aggressive tongue protrusion,” also called “sticking out the tongue and making a face.” Its purpose is to intimidate and rudely insult, yet its root remains “rejection,” which transforms into “contempt.”

When people encounter minor fright, tension, or embarrassment, they stick out the tongue briefly before retracting it. This form is commonly seen in kindergarten children and expresses the mildest degree of rejection. Lacking aggression and occurring mostly in young children, the gesture persists despite teachers’ corrections and has become a way to “act cute,” signaling minor tension, fright, or embarrassment.

Beyond rejection, tongue protrusion can also convey the feeling—shared by young and old, male and female alike—of having “narrowly escaped disaster.”

Once you learn to observe this behavior, it proves highly useful in bargaining or intense competition.

Many years ago, I wanted to buy a good car. I went to a dealership and told the salesperson, “I am willing to buy this car at this price.” After some bargaining, the salesperson used a familiar tactic: “All right, let me check with our manager.” He left to consult the manager, and I stepped out of the office to browse.

A few minutes later, I happened to glimpse the salesperson and the manager talking behind a glass door. Although I could not hear them, I could clearly see their movements. After speaking with the manager, the salesperson stuck out his tongue—briefly, but unmistakably.

I returned to the salesperson’s office and waited. The salesperson soon came back and said, “Our manager believes the price I quoted is the best we can offer.”

I replied, “You mean this is your lowest acceptable price?”

“Yes,” he answered.

“No room for further negotiation?” I pressed.

“None,” the salesperson said, nodding. “This is our lowest price.”

“In that case, thank you,” I said, rising and walking straight out of the office toward the exit without looking back. As I reached the door, I heard someone calling my name: “Wait! Wait!”

The salesperson brought me back to the office and offered to lower the so-called lowest price by another 2,700 yuan—only 100 yuan above my initial offer.

The key points of the story are: first, determine the true bottom-line price of the car; second, when you see the salesperson stick out his tongue, recognize that he is trying to get you to accept the supposed lowest price by luck.

#### 2. Why Do People Bite Their Lips?

You often see people biting their lips and think little of it, yet this simple action reveals much about a person’s psychological state. The meaning of lip-biting varies by context.

Psychologists have suggested that lip-biting originates from the sucking reflex of infancy and serves to release tension and calm suppressed emotions.

The following outlines the psychological implications of lip-biting:

1. **Anger or irritation**  
   When angry, facial muscles produce slight twitching movements due to the emotion. In addition to flaring and wrinkling of the nose, the mouth stiffens and the person unconsciously bites the lips. Judging from the conversational context, if the other person bites their lips, consider whether you have said something offensive.

2. **Inner tension**  
   Many job candidates exhibit increased small movements and lightly bite their lower lip with their upper teeth while waiting for an interview. This lip-biting often stems from a lack of confidence and involuntary tension about the unknown interview situation; they hope to ease their psychological burden by biting their lips.  
   Research indicates that people bite their lips under tension because accelerated blood flow causes a slight swelling or itching sensation in the lips, prompting an unconscious light bite.

3. **Self-suggestion to relieve inner anxiety**  
   Anxiety also triggers lip-biting as a form of psychological self-suggestion aimed at easing the anxious feeling. During exams, test-takers may lightly bite their lips while pondering a difficult question to reduce the pressure of the temporary obstacle. It is said that former U.S. President George W. Bush made this gesture upon learning of the September 11 terrorist attacks in 2001.

4. **Manifestation of self-punishment**  
   Some people habitually bite their lips; this actually reflects self-compulsion and self-punishment. When facing failure, lightly biting the lips expresses both inner anxiety and self-blame for the mistake. This behavior appears more often in people with strong self-esteem and high personal standards.

5. **Concealing true inner emotions**  
   When facing accusations or misunderstandings, people may unconsciously bite their lips. When wronged yet unable to clarify or refute immediately, they feel strong dissatisfaction and resistance, which manifests in the lip-biting gesture. If you, as a supervisor, observe this during criticism of an employee, consider whether additional facts exist and offer the employee a chance to explain, thereby avoiding deeper rifts that could hinder work.

From the above, although lip-biting is subtle, it provides considerable information about psychological activity. A small micro-expression can betray one’s thoughts and reveal inner feelings. Generally, lip-biting conveys a lack of confidence and is not a favorable habit for job candidates or everyday social interactions, as it inadvertently signals negative emotions. Frequent lip-biting not only affects appearance and leaves a poor impression but also allows others to detect tension, anxiety, and fear. These effects hinder daily communication and business negotiations, so those with the habit should break it.

#### 1. Knowing What You Are Thinking Without You Opening Your Mouth

Inner emotions can be expressed not only through words but also through micro-expressions of the mouth; people often overlook these micro-expressions and thereby reveal subtle psychological shifts.

The mouth is closely linked to personality. Observing mouth shape allows a rough understanding of character traits. The following introduces mouth types:

1. **Optimistic and Cheerful Crescent Mouth**  
   Also called the upturned crescent, this mouth shape features corners that turn upward. The person’s personality matches the shape: lively, outgoing, emotionally rich, and mentally agile. They excel in adaptability and execution, often thriving in the workplace and earning leaders’ attention.

2. **Cautious and Stern Downturned Crescent**  
   The opposite of the upturned crescent, this shape has corners that turn downward. Such individuals are cautious in dealings, eccentric in temperament, and difficult to approach, giving an impression of aloofness; they often play the role of loners. Their sensitivity leads them to dwell on trifles and complain, yet they are considerate of others.

3. **Strong-Willed Straight Line**  
   A straight-line mouth, as the name suggests, forms a straight shape when the lips are closed. These people possess unmatched willpower and strong self-awareness, making them resistant to others’ opinions.

4. **Mild and Gentle Rectangular**  
   The rectangular mouth resembles the Chinese character “四.” Both upper and lower lips are full and plump. These individuals are mild-mannered, honest, and possess a strong sense of justice; they tend to succeed in work and life. Their distinctive personalities also help them make many friends.

5. **Selfish Protruding Lower Lip**  
   In this shape the lower lip protrudes as if ready to receive the upper lip. People with this mouth enjoy quibbling, are skilled at debate, and show strong endurance, yet they rarely receive important responsibilities from superiors.

6. **Justice-Oriented Protruding Upper Lip**  
   The opposite of the protruding-lower-lip shape, this mouth has the upper lip protruding to cover the lower lip. These individuals are reasonable, possess a strong sense of justice, and display a readiness to help when witnessing injustice. Their perfectionism is matched by a relatively perfect personal image.

7. **Sociable Elongated Mouth**  
   People with elongated mouths are generally mild. They offer more compliments than criticism, have good character, and know how to handle relationships, so others enjoy their company. They are meticulous, earn trust through reliability, and fully exercise their social and professional abilities in practice.

8. **Independent and Stubborn Odd-Shaped Mouth**  
   This mouth resembles the shape formed when blowing on a fire. People with this shape generally have independent personalities and distinctive traits, yet in interactions their stubbornness often makes others uncomfortable, creating a clear sense of compulsion.

Thus, even when the mouth remains silent, observing its movements reveals clues to a person’s psychological activity.

#### Mouth Micro-Movements Reveal Various Emotions

The mouth does not only display various emotions when speaking; even when silent, small mouth movements can reveal different emotions. In fact, the mouth is one of the most expressive parts of the face.

Among the organs on the human face, the mouth occupies a prominent position, is relatively large in target area, and can perform many actions. The orbicularis oris muscle around the teeth has been trained to be highly flexible through long-term speaking, so it often makes many movements subconsciously.

When observing a person’s facial expressions, one absolutely cannot overlook the small movements of the mouth, because changes in the mouth and surrounding muscles make these micro-movements a breakthrough point for seeing through the other person’s inner thoughts. Upward corners of the mouth indicate happiness, downward corners indicate pain, a wide-open mouth indicates surprise, tightly closed lips indicate anger… The muscles on the lips can exhibit subtle and complex changes, and even those hard-to-detect subtle emotional shifts will be expressed through the flexible orbicularis oris muscle.

The mouth holds an important position among the facial features; every action—opening and closing, moving forward or backward, upward or downward—is valuable information. It can be said that the mouth has rich forms of expression. So, how can one discern a person’s emotions through small mouth movements?

1. Lips pressed tightly together  
   When a person hides or tenses their lips, it often indicates they are facing pressure. As the pressure increases, the originally full lips gradually become flat and eventually turn into a straight line. At this point, it shows that their emotions have hit rock bottom. If a person presses their lips tightly together, it indicates they are anxious and under great pressure, because tightly pressed lips are a sign of self-suppression.

2. Lips pursed  
   During conversation, if the other person purses their lips, it means they are dissatisfied with what you are saying and hope you will stop or change the topic promptly. Lip pursing occurs in many situations. For example, when two lawyers debate, one lawyer states their view while the other often purses their lips to show disagreement. Another example: during police interrogation, if the information about a suspect contains errors, the suspect will purse their lips to indicate that the investigator’s statement is wrong.

3. Corners of the mouth turned up or down  
   Corners of the mouth turned up mean the other person feels cheerful and is also a sign of goodwill and politeness. Corners of the mouth turned down mean the other person’s mood is low, they are in sorrow or pain, and it is also an expression of helplessness.

4. Pouting  
   When a person is unhappy, they often extend the lower lip forward and turn the corners of the mouth downward; this action is called pouting. Pouting expresses a negative emotion and frequently appears in sadness, anger, despair, or contempt. During conversation, if the other person’s lower lip juts forward, it indicates they do not believe the external information received and hope for an affirmative reply.

5. Licking the lips with the tongue  
   A person frequently licks their lips because they feel dry-mouthed and hope to moisten the lips somewhat; this shows they are under great pressure. Research indicates that when a person feels uncomfortable or nervous, they repeatedly lick their lips with the tongue to comfort themselves and attempt to calm their inner state through this action.

#### Closed Lips

Although cultures around the world differ greatly, body language shows universality; people of different races and cultures maintain consistency in body language. Micro-expressions (微表情) belong to the category of nonverbal behavior. Within nonverbal behavior, the position occupied by the lips is not central; people pay more attention to information conveyed by limbs, torso, and facial expressions. Micro-expressions can transmit inner emotional changes more accurately and directly precisely because they are hard to detect, and the lips excel at this.

Besides producing smiles, people’s lips generally remain in a relaxed, pleasant state, yet at times people close their lips tightly, as if trying to hide them. This action occurs because the muscles around the lips tighten inward, causing the shape to contract. According to the principle that pleasant emotions cause the body to expand while negative emotions cause the body to contract, the tightening of the lip muscles also conveys a negative emotion. People who make this movement are generally in some kind of trouble; they may have detected an unsettling signal but are unwilling to express it immediately, so they use this action to control themselves. This movement is also called lip pressing, because it is like installing a lock on one’s lips to prevent them from making inappropriate sounds.

An American shipping company once reached an impasse during business negotiations, so they invited Nicholas Bartum, an FBI expert on nonverbal behavior, to assist the negotiation by observing the other party’s micro-expressions and help secure the deal.

At the negotiation table, Nicholas carefully observed every negotiator’s emotional changes, using their expressions, movements, and language to predict whether the negotiation would reach a mutually satisfactory result. When the shipping company’s CEO presented their contract terms, Nicholas suggested explaining each clause one by one and breaking the task into individual items so the other side could understand them in greater detail. This negotiation style gave Nicholas the opportunity to observe each person up close, and it proved very wise. When the other party heard one particular clause, Nicholas suddenly noticed a change in their nonverbal behavior: although their body movements remained unchanged, they locked their lips tightly shut. He quickly wrote a note and passed it to the shipping company’s CEO, informing him which clause the other side found extremely objectionable.

After receiving Nicholas’s information, the shipping company’s CEO immediately raised that key clause. Both sides held a highly productive discussion. Seeing the shipping company’s sincerity, the other side made certain concessions. The deadlock broke quickly once the key point was identified, and a negotiation that might have collapsed reached agreement; a contract worth tens of millions of dollars was perfectly resolved simply by detecting one instance of tightly closed lips.

#### Section Two “Big Mouth”

A folk saying goes: a man with a big mouth will eat from all directions, while a woman with a big mouth will impoverish her husband. To modern eyes this saying appears to lack scientific basis and is considered an undesirable notion. In addition, ancient physiognomy states that people with thin lips are relatively unfeeling, unrighteous, and stubborn; people with thick lips value emotions and are generous; people with cherry-small mouths are cautious in dealing with others and consider matters thoroughly from every angle. In general, the mouth is closely related to a person’s temperament.

The famous American actress Audrey Hepburn, once called a fallen angel, said: “For attractive lips, speak words of kindness.” In truth, an appealing mouth can not only voice praise for beautiful things but also reveal a person’s character and inner psychological activity; it can truly be called a “big mouth.”

The mouth, like the nose, is one of the five sensory organs. It is not only an important tool for communication with the outside world and for eating; some also call the mouth the “outlet officer.” Medically, mouth expressions are determined by the orbicularis oris, depressor anguli oris, and mentalis muscles.

In daily life, people use the mouth to express inner emotions, yet when the mouth produces speech it also transmits silent language information. Through the subtle expressive movements of the mouth we can glimpse a person’s psychological state, making the mind no longer unfathomable.

It is known that facial muscles change with inner emotions, with the muscles around the eyes and mouth showing the most obvious changes. People can recognize different inner states through the various movements the mouth displays. For example, when angry, a person not only flares the nostrils but also presses the lips together; when happy, a person smiles, causing the corners of the mouth to rise; when sorrowful, the corners of the mouth droop involuntarily; when surprised, people often open the mouth wide. In addition, people kiss those around them to express love, bite their lips to relieve inner repression, and pout to signal dissatisfaction. During conversation, if the other person’s lips move slightly backward at the corners, it shows they are listening attentively; if they occasionally bite their lips, it indicates they are thinking about what you said. All these subtle mouth movements provide us with valuable information.

Every opening and closing of the mouth reflects a person’s inner world; understanding mouth micro-expressions is highly useful in daily interactions.

#### “Rectangular Smile”

Decades ago, Professor Ewan Grant of the Psychology Department at the University of Birmingham proposed a professional term for expressions—the “rectangular smile.”

When people produce a “rectangular smile,” the lips pull away from the upper and lower teeth, forming a rectangle. In fact, the “rectangular smile” does not accompany a relaxed, happy mood and a genuine smile; it can even be considered an expression of pain.

When we are in low spirits, it is difficult to fake a genuine smile. A typical example: if you are unhappy, you cannot simultaneously engage both the zygomaticus major and orbicularis oculi muscles to display a radiant genuine smile, yet given the special circumstances you must politely force a smile, so a fake smile appears.

A fake smile does not come from the heart; it only engages the zygomaticus major that lifts the corners of the mouth—what Chinese call “smiling on the surface but not from the heart.”

University of Pittsburgh psychology professor Jeffrey Cohn is developing a machine to analyze facial muscle changes in suspects during interrogation. “We can state how many times each muscle moved, how long it stayed before changing, and whether the subject’s performance was genuine or feigned,” he explains.

Yet you do not need Cohn’s machine to detect a lying boyfriend or a guilty young woman, because a liar’s insincere smile can be exposed within seconds. “A genuine smile is even, symmetrical on both sides of the face; it comes quickly but fades slowly. It involves wrinkles from nose to mouth corners as well as crow’s feet around the eyes,” Cohn says. “A feigned smile comes more slowly and shows slight asymmetry; when one side is not quite real, the other side tries to respond positively. The eye muscles are not fully engaged—that is why the ‘villain’ in films has a cold, malicious smile that never reaches the eyes.”

After years of research, scientists have found that the key to a happier life lies in interpersonal relationships, and a sincere smile helps people get along better, so it is very important. For those who smile genuinely, happiness will not be far away.

#### The Mystery of Licking and Biting the Lips

When people find themselves in an unsettling environment, they often need to find an outlet to relieve negative emotions. Tense nerves not only make people irritable but also easily lead to mistakes, so seeking comfort is almost human instinct. Comforting actions are many and performed by different body parts; among micro-expressions there is also a comfort-related action—biting the lips.

Faced with pressure, people almost all show very similar reactions: stroking the forehead or neck, fiddling with clothes or hair—these are ways people relieve pressure. Women often play with clothing hems or hair because they feel nervous and their nervous system seeks comfort; they calm themselves this way. Men, due to social status and image requirements, cannot display too many comforting actions, yet they do not miss opportunities to soothe their tension through micro-expressions; lip-licking is an action that occurs in both men and women. When people encounter negative stimuli—sometimes a difficult question, sometimes hearing or seeing something oppressive—they lick their lips. The reflection of the limbic brain’s management system on the lips, though subtle, is real.

Similar to stroking oneself, people also scratch their heads; this action likewise reflects an extremely negative emotion, indicating the person is experiencing stronger tension, embarrassment, or unease. When lip-licking turns into lip-biting, the expression can be viewed as an escalation of anxiety. When a child faces a difficult problem or is caught doing something wrong by parents, they may lick their lips to comfort themselves and reduce worry. But when they have not reviewed before an exam or their father approaches, lip-biting appears, showing they sense the trouble has grown serious.

#### Mouth Features and Personality Analysis

The mouth reflects the condition of the stomach and digestive system. If a person has full lips, ruddy lip color, neat teeth, and healthy gums, then without doubt their stomach digestion and nutrient absorption function well; they are a vibrant person. Conversely, if a person has a small mouth, pale lips, and poor teeth and gum condition, it indicates weaker bodily resilience and the need for more rest.

Stanford University professor Jewell once conducted five brief conversations with 809 volunteers on the topics of family, career, friendships, future, and sex. Through comparative analysis he found:

- People with wide, thick lips become relatively excited when discussing sex-related topics.
- People with narrow, thin lips are relatively composed and possess stronger self-control.
- Among people whose lips appear relaxed, over 70 percent stated that their greatest career trouble is lack of resolve and difficulty persisting.
- People whose mouth corners turn downward become very dejected whenever setbacks are mentioned and feel pessimistic about the future.
- Among people whose mouth corners turn upward, over 90 percent are cheerful, full of confidence in family and career, and hopeful about the future, even though they have encountered many setbacks.

Another survey showed:

- Among people with short upper lips, over 85 percent like to hear praise; when harshly criticized they more easily lose morale and may even become decadent or self-abandoning.
- People with longer upper lips are the opposite; after being mocked or ridiculed, most of them reflect on the pain, draw lessons, and move forward courageously.

From a dynamic perspective, the mouth has four basic movement patterns: opening and closing, up and down, forward and back, loose and tight. Observing these movements together with the personality traits contained in the mouth’s static features allows us to form a rough judgment of a person met for the first time.

#### People Who Smile with Lips Pressed Together

Besides producing speech, the lips have another very important function: expressing emotion. A toothy smile can be considered its most charming moment. As one of the most common human expressions, a smile expresses inner pleasure and conveys positive, friendly information. Before people enter the world, they easily grin broadly over small gains, yet as age and experience increase, such pure, unrestrained laughter becomes rarer, while smiles achieved through mental control become more frequent. Often people part their lips to the sides to show great pleasure, yet they are not truly happy; it is merely a social requirement.

Fake smiling is one of the important features distinguishing humans from other creatures, because almost no animals except humans fake smiles. To cope with people or matters they dislike and to remain in uncomfortable, tense environments, people engage mouth muscles to produce a fake smile and handle awkwardness. This can also be counted as one of the fruits of human evolution: by issuing fake smiles, people can avoid much trouble, and it also supplies micro-expression observation with a severe yet interesting topic, attracting many experts and scholars to study the difference between genuine and fake smiles.

Distinguishing the meaning hidden in a smile is a very important lesson in micro-expressions. When a person parts their lips to reveal a charming and seemingly candid smile, how do you know whether they are truly happy or harbor ill intent? Besides rich social experience, we can also discover the truth by understanding how a fake smile is produced. Through long-term observation and analysis of smiles, the FBI found that fake smiles most easily appear when people smile with lips pressed together.

#### III. Disaster No Longer Comes from the Mouth

In daily life people inadvertently develop certain habitual actions of which they remain unaware; for example, small movements such as pouting reveal much information, and other mouth movements also “speak” one’s true inner feelings through nonverbal forms.

The information conveyed by habitual mouth movements is useful both in daily social interaction and in the workplace. If you can interpret the other person’s micro-expression information well, you can adjust the direction of conversation or action accordingly and help your life or work proceed more smoothly.

1. **Pressing the lips together: a sign of self-suppression**

   When a person suffers setbacks or failure, the lip-pressing action is common. Although small, if you observe carefully you will notice that the corners of the mouth of the person making this movement turn downward—the exact opposite of a smile’s upward corners. This shows that the person performing the lip press is in a state of emotional dejection and inferiority, truthfully reflecting their inner anxiety and distress.

   Lip pressing means applying pressure to both upper and lower lips to close the mouth tightly, as if conveying the message that nothing should enter the body. When people encounter trouble or pressure they unconsciously press their lips; at first they merely tense the lips, and as pressure grows the mouth becomes flat or forms a straight line—these changes occur in an instant.

   Generally, when people feel pressure and anxiety they try to use lip pressing to suppress their true inner emotions. Although it does not show on the face, this tiny, instantaneous mouth movement still reveals personal inner feelings without reservation.

#### Psychology Mini-Class

In business negotiations, what the other party says is often unreliable, but small movements of their mouth can reveal the truth. Body language experts have observed that subtle mouth movements frequently display a person's emotional shifts, causing lies to fall apart on their own.

1. Pressing the lips together  
   During negotiations, if you see the other party press their lips together, it indicates they have made up their mind, are fully prepared, and will not yield easily. If they press their lips together while avoiding eye contact, it suggests they harbor a secret they do not wish to reveal; the lip press occurs because they fear leaking information.

2. Biting the lips  
   During negotiations, if the other party frequently bites their lips, it shows they doubt their own abilities and lack sufficient confidence in the negotiation. Observing this movement during talks means the other side has begun to compromise and is about to concede.

3. Mouth opening unconsciously  
   During negotiations, if the other party's mouth opens unconsciously and they appear listless, it indicates they feel bored with their surroundings or do not understand the topic under discussion and lack the confidence to respond.

4. Lips pursed upward  
   Lips pursed upward means the other party has objections and is very dissatisfied with the terms you have offered. From a psychological perspective, this is the party's way of keeping their dissatisfaction "outside the door." In business negotiations, when the other side makes this movement, they typically will not agree to any conditions and are waiting for you to adjust your approach.

#### Smiling with Lips Pressed Together

Smiling with lips pressed together occurs when people stretch the muscles at the corners of their mouth while keeping the movement restrained, producing a controlled and polite expression on the face. This manner of expression often leaves the other person unable to read whether the attitude is positive or negative, yet whenever someone displays this expression, the meaning is usually one of refusal.

Failing to judge the other person's true thoughts through micro-expressions of the lips often leads people into misunderstandings and places them at a disadvantage in communication. Women frequently convey their emotions through micro-expressions of the lips. When they smile with lips pressed together, the corners of the mouth move slightly backward, producing a smile without warmth; this indicates that the attitude they are showing differs from their actual inner thoughts—they do not truly feel that way. When a woman praises a friend's unattractive dress or compliments a neighbor's child, she often smiles in this pressed-lip manner. In her heart, the dress does not merit praise; she offers it only for the sake of her friend's feelings. She also does not genuinely believe the neighbor's child is superior to her own; the compliment is given merely to meet social expectations.

The gap between true feelings and the demands of the situation prevents people from expressing emotions freely. When the lips cannot speak the heart directly, their micro-expressions become worth careful consideration.

#### Section 3 The "Dancing" Tongue

The recent CCTV documentary *A Bite of China* has sparked widespread interest. The tip of the tongue can taste the full range of flavors—sweet, sour, bitter, spicy, and salty—adding richness and color to daily life. Beyond taste, the usually hidden tongue also conveys psychological information; a simple tongue movement can reveal what someone is thinking.

Human emotions are subtle. Compared with foreigners, Chinese people tend to be more reserved when expressing genuine feelings, yet small tongue movements can still betray personal emotions. American basketball star Michael Jordan occasionally licks his lips while shooting on the court. Why? In general, people lick their lips with the tongue when they are under significant pressure; high pressure causes dry mouth, and licking the lips moistens them while also easing inner tension.

In addition, children often stick out their tongues when they misbehave or act mischievously. When adults make the same movement, it can signal shyness or an attempt to ease embarrassment. On the sports field, if a doubles partner misses a ball due to momentary carelessness, some players habitually stick out their tongue toward their teammate as an apology; the playful gesture also diffuses the awkwardness.

Clearly, the information revealed by the tongue tip should not be overlooked.

#### Pouting and Pursing Lips

Pouting is a deliberate forward thrust of the lower lip (see Figure 2.17) that can express various emotions such as sadness, disappointment, or dejection. People may pout when joking or when serious, but the expression generally signals a transitional reaction between dissatisfaction and anger. The look can also suggest immaturity, so it should be used with caution. Many people become irritated when they see someone pouting.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: Figure 2.17 Pouting]*

Pursing the lips generally indicates that a person is angry. In practice, two distinct pouting postures are recognized as "pursing the lips": one occurs when people suppress anger and press the upper and lower lips tightly together (see Figure 2.18); the other occurs when the lips are compressed from all directions, making the mouth appear small and tense. Either posture shows that the person is trying to restrain anger or avoid being judged by others.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: Figure 2.18 Pursing the lips]*

#### Licking or Biting the Lips

Licking the lips is usually viewed as a sexually suggestive signal (see Figure 2.19). If you are flirting with a man and he licks his lips, whether intentionally or not, it means he wants to kiss you.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: Figure 2.19 Licking the lips]*

Of course, licking the lips is not only a sexual cue. In daily life, people also lick their lips when their mouth feels dry in order to moisten it.

When a person bites their own lips, it usually indicates anxiety, discomfort, frustration, or embarrassment (see Figure 2.20). In addition, lip-biting can signal confusion.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: Figure 2.20 Biting the lips]*

Although lip-biting is regarded as a sign of restlessness (sometimes immaturity), many people have the habit and are often unaware of it.

#### 2. Pouting: An Expression of Dissatisfaction or Disagreement

Pouting, commonly called "pursing the mouth," is frequently seen on children's faces; they pout over minor matters to show inner discontent. Adults convey the same meaning when they pout. Because adults tend to feel self-conscious, their pout is usually less decisive than a child's and consists of a quick, slight forward thrust of the lips.

If you notice the other person thrusting their lips forward during conversation, you should consider whether they disagree with what you have said. Pouting appears often in meetings or at the negotiating table. When the other party disagrees with your statement but does not voice it, they may still reveal it through this movement. The stronger their inner resistance, the longer and more frequently they pout, often accompanied by crossed arms.

Some people also pout while thinking. Therefore, whether the movement expresses inner dissatisfaction or resistance must be judged according to the context and other body language; it cannot be interpreted in isolation.

#### 8.1.3 Grinding the Teeth

Similar to clenching the fists, when a stimulus provokes anger in the subject yet the subject remains silent, the most common reaction is to grind the teeth. Easily observed grinding includes changes in the contact points of the upper and lower teeth, such as rubbing the canines together or biting with the incisors ("gnashing"); another possibility is that the teeth remain in the same position but are pressed together forcefully, causing the masseter muscles on both sides of the face to contract and become visibly tense.

In actual investigative cases, some suspects manage to speak in a mild and reasonable tone while occasionally showing a brief contraction of the masseter muscles between sentences. This contradictory display—mild words paired with muscular tension—indicates that the suspect maintains good verbal control and conceals aggressive impulses, yet the behavior still reveals a flaw.

The inadvertent appearance of teeth-grinding during an interview is a classic sign that the subject feels threatened and under pressure; subconsciously, the subject hopes the teeth will "attack" and eliminate the negative stimulus.

#### 5. Covering the Mouth with the Hand: A Sign of Thinking or Shyness

In many situations we notice people covering their mouths with a hand. This movement suggests the person is rather shy and does not want others to see their less favorable side. In addition, some people unconsciously cover their mouths when deep in thought; the gesture helps them concentrate and solve problems.

Generally, people who frequently cover their mouths tend to be quiet around strangers and maintain stronger psychological defenses than others. You may also see someone quickly cover their mouth after blurting out the wrong words; the action is a response to realizing the mistake and expresses a sense of guilt.

People's true thoughts are not always spoken aloud; in many cases they prefer to keep them hidden. Yet everyday nonverbal behaviors such as lip-pressing lay a person's character bare. Understanding the various meanings of mouth movements therefore helps us control our own mouths so they no longer become "big mouths" that broadcast our psychological secrets.

#### Licking or Biting the Lips

Licking the lips is usually viewed as a sexually suggestive signal. If you are flirting with a man and he licks his lips, whether intentionally or not, it means he wants to kiss you. Of course, licking the lips is not only a sexual cue. If he feels his lips are dry, he may lick them to moisten them.

When a person bites their own lips, it usually indicates anxiety, discomfort, frustration, or embarrassment. In addition, lip-biting can signal confusion. Although lip-biting is regarded as a sign of restlessness (sometimes immaturity), many people have the habit and are often unaware of it.

Other common mouth movements are also easy to interpret. For example, a wide-open mouth indicates surprise, tightly closed lips indicate anger, upturned corners of the mouth indicate joy, and downturned corners indicate self-reproach. During conversation, never overlook the other person's mouth movements.

#### Teeth Reveal a Person's Emotional State

Micro-expression keywords: Are your teeth straight? Do not underestimate the teeth we keep hidden; besides helping us chew food, they can unintentionally reveal a person's emotions and character.

The portrait of Washington on the U.S. dollar appears to show a set of straight, healthy teeth. In reality, Washington suffered from periodontal disease and wore full dentures from an early age. The denture technology of the time was poor, and whenever he opened his mouth to smile the dentures risked falling out. The photographer solved the problem by having Washington remove the dentures and stuffing cotton into his mouth, finally capturing a natural-looking smile.

True or not, the story illustrates the importance of teeth. They affect not only health and appearance but can also, from a single tooth, allow us to infer personality and mood.

#### Pouting and Pursing Lips

Pouting is a deliberate forward thrust of the lower lip and can express various emotions such as sadness, disappointment, or dejection. People may also pout when joking or when serious, but the expression generally signals a transitional reaction between dissatisfaction and anger. The look can suggest immaturity, so it should be used with caution. Many people become irritated when they see someone pouting.

Pursing the lips generally indicates that a person is angry. In practice, two distinct pouting postures are recognized as "pursing the lips": one occurs when people suppress anger and press the upper and lower lips tightly together; the other occurs when the lips are compressed from all directions, making the mouth appear small and tense. Either posture shows that the person is trying to restrain anger or avoid being judged by others.

#### Mouth Movements Reflect Inner Activity

Micro-expression keywords: The mouth is an important channel for emotional release. Whether people are happy, angry, or melancholy, they vent through speech. If you observe their mouths carefully at such moments, you will notice that different moods produce different small movements.

The muscles around the mouth are exceptionally well developed, and the mouth is one of the most flexible parts of the body. We use it to eat, to speak, to laugh when happy, and to pout when angry. The mouth opens or closes, tightens or relaxes, forming a rich repertoire of movements that also convey a person's inner state at that moment.

#### Laughing in Short Bursts

People who laugh in short bursts are generally cold and indifferent by nature.

Yet laughter does not always symbolize kindness or goodwill. People often use fake smiles to hide feelings and mask expressions; without careful observation it is difficult to read them.

More than a century ago, scientists discovered that humans produce both genuine and fake smiles. When we do not feel truly close to those around us, we use fake smiles; genuine smiles are reserved for people and things we truly care about. In fact, infants only a few weeks old already know to save genuine smiles for their mothers and offer fake smiles to others.

#### Lips Also Undergo Seventy-Two Transformations

Although verbal expression plays a major role in daily life and the oral cavity together with the entire vocal apparatus carries out this task, people still attribute the credit to the lips. In people's eyes, two thin lips seem capable of withstanding a million troops; the power released when the lips meet is immeasurable. The muscular structure of the lips is extremely agile, the result of continuous evolution after humans learned to use language. Yet long experience has also shown that the more agile the lips, the more they can deceive; therefore, observing micro-expressions of the lips has become a key focus.

#### Overlapping Teeth

Overlapping teeth occur when two adjacent teeth cross, one in front of the other. People with this trait tend to be highly self-confident and capable; they handle work with ease and perform exceptionally well. Because of this, they can develop arrogance and strong jealousy, sometimes becoming willful and headstrong, which leaves them with few close friends. Women with overlapping teeth in particular tend to stir up trouble and are not suitable as friends.

Although teeth are small, their usefulness is great. Besides helping us chew food, they display a person's personality and emotions; we should not overlook them.

#### The Mouth

The mouth is the only body part that can communicate both verbally and nonverbally. It is well known that the verbal information a person emits may not reflect their true thoughts or feelings. However, the nonverbal information conveyed by the mouth is quite reliable and rarely misleads. For example, we can easily distinguish between a genuine smile, a nervous smile, and a fake smile. Next, let us examine what the mouth conveys when it is not speaking.

#### Licking the Lips Is Not Only a Sexual Signal

The mouth is the only body part that can communicate both verbally and nonverbally. We all know that the verbal information a person emits may not reflect their true thoughts or feelings. However, the nonverbal information conveyed by the mouth is quite reliable and rarely misleads.

Next, let us follow FBI agents in learning how the mouth conveys inner thoughts when it is not speaking.

#### Mouth Movements Expose Inner Feelings

The mouth is the only body part that can communicate both verbally and nonverbally. We all know that the verbal information a person emits may not reflect their true thoughts or feelings. However, the nonverbal information conveyed by the mouth is quite reliable and rarely misleads.

Next, let us examine what the mouth conveys when it is not speaking.

#### Laughing Out Loud with "Ha ha ha"

Hearty laughter usually appears when everyone is very happy. During such laughter the upper and lower incisors are exposed, and eye contact is usually avoided because the head is tilted backward.

People who laugh heartily are essentially lonely. They are informal, alternate between warmth and coldness, and act decisively without hesitation. When women frequently produce this kind of laugh, they are generally leadership types.

#### The Mouth: A Medium That Reflects the Mind

Chewing food and speaking both require the mouth. These frequent daily actions make the muscles around the mouth exceptionally developed and sensitive, turning mouth movements into a key that opens the inner world. Whether opening or closing, rising or falling, moving forward or backward, tightening or relaxing, these basic mouth movements form a rich variety of psychological cues.

#### People with Spaced Teeth

Although the teeth are spaced, overall health is good. Such people tend to be cheerful and optimistic, straightforward, and without guile. They are honest and treat others sincerely. Their shortcoming is that they cannot keep secrets; any small secret entrusted to them will not stay hidden and may be inadvertently revealed. Therefore, never tell them anything you do not want others to know.

#### Orbicularis Oris Muscle

The orbicularis oris muscle surrounds the mouth by 2–3 centimeters, forming a flat, round shape controlled by the facial nerve. Its functions include closing the lips, chewing, and producing speech. When the orbicularis oris muscle is tense, the lips perform actions such as tightly closing, pursing, corners turning upward or downward, or the lower lip parting. Like the eyes, the mouth is a key area for observing facial expressions.

#### Slight Smile with Mouth Slightly Open, Revealing Upper Incisors

When people smile lightly, their upper incisors become exposed, and they usually make eye contact with others. This smile often serves as a greeting among friends, family, and colleagues or business partners for whom one feels genuine regard. People who display this smile are typically imaginative, highly creative, full of vitality in their outlook on life, and possess a strong sense of humor.

#### 3. Pouting: Expression of Sadness and Contempt

Pouting appears more frequently on the faces of people who are habitually unhappy; their lower lip protrudes forward while the corners of the mouth droop. They use this movement to release inner displeasure. At the same time, a person who scoffs at something will also execute a quick pouting motion.

#### Small Teeth

People with small teeth have gentle, calm personalities and exceptional endurance. They are emotionally rich, enjoy helping others, and maintain good relationships. Their logical thinking is strong; they proceed methodically, work meticulously, and remain attentive to detail. However, they tend to be sensitive, even somewhat neurotic, and often fixate excessively on minor points.

#### Inward-Tilting Teeth

Both upper and lower rows of teeth tilt inward. Such individuals readily accept new things, frequently propose bold ideas and innovations, and prefer to stand out from the crowd, making them well suited for planning roles. They take pride in distinctive behavior. Their drawback is a strong tendency toward revenge.

#### Large Teeth

People with large teeth also possess good physical stamina, abundant energy, rugged personalities, and bold actions. Yet they lack sufficient care in their work and are prone to errors. They think deeply, act honestly, and love their jobs. In personality, they tend to be selfish and driven by strong desires.

#### Protruding Teeth

Most such people speak bluntly and without filter, often offending others. They are stubborn, self-centered, and may act outrageously to attract attention. Their obstinate nature also strains relationships with relatives and friends.

#### 4. Crooked Mouth: Extreme Inner Tension and Anxiety

When a person’s mouth appears stiff or skewed, it signals extreme inner unease so intense that the individual remains unaware the mouth has twisted. Sometimes, however, the crooked appearance simply reflects a habitual speaking manner.

#### Smile with Corners of the Mouth Turned Down, Mouth Barely Open

During this smile the lips remain tightly closed; it flashes briefly in familiar settings or when circumstances feel satisfactory. People who frequently display it are stubborn and ambitious, yet reluctant to reveal their inner emotions.

#### Levator Labii Superioris Muscle

The levator labii superioris muscle primarily raises and everts the upper lip while cooperating with other muscles to deepen and lift the nasolabial fold. It covers a broad area from the lower edge of the orbicularis oculi muscle to the outer side of the upper lip, with one muscle on each side.

#### Neatly Aligned Teeth

Teeth are evenly spaced and orderly. Such people are traditional, prefer routine, and resist change. They work conscientiously and steadily, shoulder responsibility, confront problems with courage and reason, and enjoy high esteem.

#### Laughter Has Not Only Sound but Also Shape

Laughter reflects mood, yet its forms differ widely. Drawing on research in nonverbal communication and psychology, FBI agents have concluded that observing how a person laughs reveals inner character and personality.

#### Usually Quiet, but Laughs Exaggeratedly

Such individuals seem reserved with strangers, yet once genuine bonds form they value friendship deeply and will go to great lengths for friends when needed.

#### Nervous Laugh

The laugh is hurried, stops abruptly, then resumes after checking others’ reactions. This signals inferiority and lack of confidence; the person fears even laughter may be inappropriate.

#### Zygomaticus Minor Muscle

The zygomaticus minor muscle lies outside the cheekbone and extends to the outer side of the upper lip. Its main action is to lift the upper lip and deepen the nasolabial fold.

#### Covering Mouth with Hand When Laughing

Most such people are introverted and gentle; they rarely disclose their true thoughts even to close friends.

#### Laughing Along When Seeing Others Laugh

Such people are optimistic, outgoing, emotionally responsive, compassionate, and maintain a positive outlook on life.

#### Depressor Labii Inferioris Muscle

The depressor labii inferioris muscle lies beneath the orbicularis oris muscle, adjacent to the depressor anguli oris and mentalis muscles; its primary function is to pull the lower lip downward.

#### Laughing with Whole Body Shaking

Such people are open-minded, straightforward, and sincere.

#### Mouth Muscles

##### 6. Orbicularis Oris

Orbicularis oris is the only muscle among the 15 groups of facial expression muscles that does not appear in symmetrical form, yet it is internally symmetrical as well.

The name of orbicularis oris closely resembles that of orbicularis oculi, differing by only a single character. This naming was in fact a misunderstanding; at the time of naming, the mouth was assumed to be encircled by a series of ring-shaped striated muscles functioning as a sphincter. In reality, orbicularis oris consists of four parts that together form the peripheral and marginal portions; the lips commonly referred to are the marginal portion. The line of junction between the peripheral and marginal portions corresponds on the external surface to the boundary between the red lip and the skin. The peripheral portion is open and connects in every direction to other important expression muscles of the lower face: levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, levator labii superioris, levator anguli oris, platysma, depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris, and mentalis.

Contraction of orbicularis oris produces tightening or pursing of the mouth, while the actions of surrounding muscles may exert opposing effects, pulling the respective portions of orbicularis oris in different directions and thereby producing actions such as raising the upper lip, elevating the corners of the mouth, stretching the lips, downturning the corners of the mouth, or parting the lower lip.

Consequently, after the eyes, the mouth is the second key site for capturing and analyzing changes in expression.

##### 12. Platysma

Platysma originates from the upper chest and ultimately terminates at the corner of the mouth on orbicularis oris after passing the mandible; it is bilaterally symmetrical. The platysma discussed in this book refers specifically to its facial portion, because it can form important expression configurations by pulling on the corners of the mouth. The fibers of platysma near the mouth angle lie between depressor anguli oris and depressor labii inferioris, occupying the same plane as depressor labii inferioris; at their margins the three muscles fuse and all attach to the lower lip.

The action of platysma resembles that of zygomaticus major—stretching the corners of the mouth laterally—yet the direction is entirely different. Zygomaticus major stretches the corners of the mouth toward the ears, whereas platysma stretches them laterally and downward (in coordination with depressor anguli oris). This movement typically appears in expressions of crying with the mouth open or pouting, conveying negative emotion.

##### 16. Buccinator

After the cheeks are puffed out, buccinator can expel air between the lips—an important action when playing wind instruments, which is also the origin of the muscle’s name (Latin buccinator = trumpeter). Buccinator’s primary contribution to expression is “puffing the cheeks,” yet this voluntary expression bears no close relationship to emotion and is used at most to indicate relief from pressure; it is therefore marked with an “A” and is neither explained in detail nor included among the principal muscle groups in this book.

##### 14. Depressor Labii Inferioris

Depressor labii inferioris lies inferior to orbicularis oris, fuses with the inferior peripheral portion of orbicularis oris, and is bilaterally symmetrical.

As its name indicates, this muscle pulls the lower lip downward and slightly stretches it laterally; it can also assist in everting the lower lip. It participates in actions during angry shouting, biting, fear, and sadness. Exposing the lower teeth necessarily requires the action of depressor labii inferioris.

##### 13. Depressor Anguli Oris

Depressor anguli oris arises via a long attachment band from the mental tubercle of the mandible and the continuous oblique line, situated inferior to the origin of depressor labii inferioris; it is bilaterally symmetrical.

**Action**: During mouth opening and expressions of grief or sorrow, depressor anguli oris pulls the corners of the mouth downward and laterally. When the mouth opens, the nasolabial folds become more horizontal, with their middle portions level.

##### 11. Levator Anguli Oris

The fibers of levator anguli oris interweave at the mouth angle of orbicularis oris with zygomaticus major, depressor anguli oris, and orbicularis oris; some superficial fibers attach beneath the dermis of the nasolabial fold; the muscle is bilaterally symmetrical.

During smiling, levator anguli oris assists zygomaticus major in elevating the corners of the mouth and indirectly alters the shape and depth of the nasolabial folds.

##### 10. Zygomaticus Major

Zygomaticus major originates from the zygomatic bone and fuses at the corners of the mouth with levator anguli oris and orbicularis oris to form a deeper muscular bundle; it is bilaterally symmetrical.

Although zygomaticus major and zygomaticus minor have similar names, their actions differ markedly. For expression, zygomaticus major has only one function: pulling the corners of the mouth upward and laterally to produce a smile.

##### 8. Levator Labii Superioris

Levator labii superioris originates from the inferior orbital margin; its fibers converge with those of levator labii superioris alaeque nasi and zygomaticus minor at the lateral portion of the upper lip (toward the corners of the mouth); it is bilaterally symmetrical.

Contraction of levator labii superioris elevates and everts the upper lip and, together with other muscles, alters the shape of the nasolabial folds.

##### 9. Zygomaticus Minor

Zygomaticus minor originates from the lateral surface of the zygomatic bone and terminates at the lateral portion of the upper lip (toward the corners of the mouth); it is bilaterally symmetrical.

Contraction of zygomaticus minor elevates the upper lip, exposes the maxillary teeth, and helps deepen and lift the nasolabial folds, participating chiefly in expressions of disgust and sadness.

#### Basic Mouth Movements

##### Licking or Biting the Lips

Usually, licking the lips is seen as a flirtatious sexual signal. If you're flirting with a man and he licks his lips, whether intentional or not, it means he wants to kiss you. Of course, licking the lips isn't just a sexual hint. If someone's lips feel dry, they'll lick them to moisten them.

When a person bites their own lips, it usually indicates anxiety, discomfort, frustration, or embarrassment. Additionally, lip-biting can also show confusion. Although lip-biting is considered a sign of restlessness (sometimes childish), many people have the habit of biting their lips and are often unaware of it.

Sometimes, smiling doesn't necessarily mean happiness

Smiling reflects a person's mood, but there are many variations in how people smile. Observing the way someone smiles can reveal their inner thoughts and personality.

##### Pouting and Pursing the Lips

Pouting is an action where the lower lip is deliberately protruded, which can express various emotions such as sadness, disappointment, or frustration. People may also pout when being playful or serious, but it generally leans toward a transitional reaction between dissatisfaction and anger. Moreover, this expression can evoke associations with childishness, so it should be used cautiously. When seeing a pouting action, many people tend to become annoyed.

Pursing the lips generally indicates that a person is angry. In fact, there are two different pouting postures considered "pursing the lips": one is when people press their upper and lower lips together while suppressing anger; the other is when the lips are squeezed from all directions, making the mouth look small and full of tension. Either posture indicates that the person is trying to suppress their anger or avoid being commented on by others.

##### Lips Pushed Forward

More protruding forward than the action of lips pushed aside, becoming pursed forward. This suggests that the person's mind may be in some defensive state and they are trying to speak. At this point, no matter what you say, they won't believe it; it's better to give them a chance to speak, and things might take a turn.

Usually, the inner messages conveyed by the mouth are relatively easy to observe and understand. However, observing the mouth alone may not be entirely accurate, and it needs to be combined with other facial movements for a final judgment.

##### Mouth Pressed into a Straight Line

A person making this gesture may be facing an urgent situation or needs to make a major life decision quickly. The lip-pressing action indicates they have already made a decision but feel great pressure, and they unconsciously do this to encourage themselves and build confidence. If someone frequently makes this gesture, it suggests they have a stubborn personality and won't back down when facing difficulties, so they have a high chance of success.

##### Smiling

The corners of the mouth turn upward, forming a slight arc. Generally, this action indicates mental pleasure; it is a natural expression of true feelings, conveying sincerity, conviction, friendliness, affection, joy, shyness, and other emotions. Both others and the person themselves will feel comfortable in body and mind. Smiling more, even if it's a forced smile, is a lubricant for interpersonal relationships and can promote harmony in relationships.

##### Mouth Forming an "O" Shape

The mouth opens into a circle, with accompanying expressions like eyes widening and eyebrows raising. This mouth movement may occur when encountering or hearing something unbelievable, feeling extremely shocked and surprised. For example, if a very unattractive person marries a beautiful bride, acquaintances hearing this would certainly open their mouths wide, as if asking, "Is this really true?"

##### Teeth Biting the Lips

During conversation, if the other person bites their upper lip with their lower teeth or their lower lip with their upper teeth, it indicates they are listening attentively to your conversation and carefully pondering the meaning of your words. If this happens at the negotiation table, it means they are very interested in your product or approve of the terms you've proposed. Next, you can persuade the other party quite easily without much effort.

##### Laughing Out Loud

The mouth opens wide, even without regard for appearance. Generally, this action represents extreme happiness and shows great trust in the other person, indicating a close relationship where they don't fear damaging their image. People rarely make this gesture in front of strangers. It usually occurs in front of acquaintances when emotions are extremely relaxed, leading to open-mouthed laughter.

##### Lips Twisted to One Side

This indicates inner anxiety and unease, possibly due to encountering significant trouble or being in a difficult situation. For example, this mouth shape can be seen on the face of a driver waiting for a traffic police officer to handle an issue.

Additionally, some mouth movements are very quick and small in amplitude, and if not careful, we might miss them.

##### Lips Pushed Slightly Forward

The lips protrude slightly forward, resembling a pout but with a small amplitude. This indicates a skeptical or uncertain attitude toward the received external information, hoping for confirmation or a more detailed explanation.

#### Mouth Shapes for Specific Emotions

In Hollywood’s golden age, male actors cast as despicable villains did not cover their mouths to imply the presence of a secret; instead, they lowered their voices and spoke with their mouths turned to one side.

This behavior typically leads us to associate the speaker with prisoners or people who have criminal records. In the past, prisons forbade inmates from conversing with one another. To avoid breaking the rules, prisoners spoke with their mouths turned to one side. Over time, the habit became deeply ingrained and continued even after release.

When people deliberately try to keep their conversation from being overheard, they often press a palm against their mouth while speaking. If a seated person rests both elbows on the table and clasps both hands over the mouth, the unspoken message is: “I don’t want you to hear what I’m saying” (see Figure 4.33). The same posture is held while listening to others and is released only when the speaker reaches a key point or an appropriate moment.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: Figure 4.33 Concealing One’s Conversation]*

Note that the gesture of covering the mouth should not be confused with the action of interrupting someone. Interrupting signals a desire to break into the conversation and offer one’s own suggestion (see “Can I interrupt?”).
