#### Anger

##### Lingering Anger

When people vent their anger, their body and mind achieve a certain degree of balance, but this does not mean the anger has completely disappeared. More often than not, after venting, the underlying problem still exists, so the intensity of the anger remains high. At this point, however, the facial expression of anger has changed completely: there are no longer movements in the lower half of the face, only changes around the eyes and brows—eyebrows lowered and furrowed, upper eyelids raised, lower eyelids tensed. If the eyes are covered, nothing can be discerned from the mouth alone.

From these analyses of anger types, it is clear that the most typical micro-expressions of anger are: eyebrows lowered and furrowed; upper eyelids raised, exposing part of the iris, with skin folds appearing on the upper eyelids due to the pressure from the brows; lower eyelids tensed. To determine whether someone is angry, one need only look at the eyes and eyebrows. The closer the distance between the upper eyelids and the eyebrows, the deeper the anger.

One case illustrates well how anger micro-expressions and triggers form.

A young man passionate about novel writing had been writing since graduating from university without taking any other job. Over five years he produced hundreds of thousands of words, yet no publisher accepted his work. He remained confident, believing his novels were unparalleled. His family urged him to find a job to support himself and write in his spare time, but he refused, insisting that publication had simply not yet come at the right time. His situation later became the subject of a reality television program.

On the show, a publishing expert bluntly told him that his novels had no publication value whatsoever and that he should seek other work. For the first ten minutes or so, he maintained a confident and composed demeanor, but at that moment he erupted, becoming highly aggressive. He began defending himself, accusing the expert of failing to recognize quality, and claiming that one person’s opinion did not represent all publishers. During his defense, his face displayed classic anger expressions while his mouth took on an expression of disgust.

Those five years had placed enormous pressure on him, yet he had continued to evade society and persist with writing. He was unwilling to admit this and did not want others to see through him. When someone opposed him, he inwardly rejected that person and felt disgust. The expert’s frank statement struck at his vulnerability, threatening what he saw as his survival interest (his belief that he could earn a living through novels) and thereby triggering anger. Disgust prompts a desire to escape, while anger prompts a desire to attack.

Sometimes anger mixes with disgust or fear, making it difficult to tell which dominates. Beyond micro-expressions, the presence or absence of an aggressive tendency reveals which emotion prevails. Another case: a mother witnessed her daughter being raped by a criminal. In desperation she attacked the criminal with a sharp object and killed him. Fear was present in her heart, yet the threat to her daughter ignited intense anger, producing an impulse to attack. Such anger micro-expressions prove useful in FBI investigations. After her arrest the mother initially denied the killing, claiming she had been panicked and helpless and that her daughter’s account matched. Yet when an investigator asked her to describe the scene, an angry expression appeared on her face. Although a single micro-expression cannot serve as courtroom evidence, it can assist investigators. Fear does not produce aggression; only anger drives a person to attack regardless of consequences.

##### “He’s No Good!”

This phrase denies another person’s ability in front of others. For the person being denied, it constitutes reputational damage and readily provokes anger. Reputation functions as a calling card in human society, recording much important information about an individual. People hope to use this card to build beneficial social networks that help them achieve various goals. Once erroneous information appears on the card, it directly threatens the person’s survival environment. A quick online search reveals many celebrities waging courtroom battles over reputation. Reputation is, to some extent, a bargaining chip for a better life; damage to it inevitably lowers future quality of life and triggers anger.

These are common triggers of anger. In various forms they threaten people’s survival and reproduction and therefore elicit anger.

It is now time to discuss the facial expressions of anger.

Every expression made after anger arises serves to attack or drive the other person away. Once the stimulus exceeds a threshold, it escalates into physical action and combat. Because the body rapidly mobilizes all available strength for attack, the force released in anger is astonishing and relatively brief.

The face likewise recruits every available muscle to produce a full anger expression. Consequently, a complete anger expression shows changes from the eyebrows down to the chin.

Let us begin with the eyebrows.

Lowered and furrowed brows constitute the typical expressive feature of anger. As noted in earlier chapters, brow lowering reduces intense light stimulation to the eyes. When people encounter difficulties or troubles, this brow shape appears in order to reduce glare and focus thought. Through evolution the action became habitual in times of trouble. When we fail to understand lecture content, our brows lower; when pondering solutions, our brows lower; when angry, our brows also lower. Regardless of the stimulus, lowered brows convey only one message: intense focus on the matter at hand.

Lowered brows alone cannot conclusively indicate anger, but when combined with raised upper eyelids and tensed lower eyelids, the expression is unmistakably one of anger. In anger the eyes widen while the brows press downward, creating a downward-closing tendency in the upper eyelids; the resulting compression produces a fold in the upper eyelid skin. What is commonly called “eyes wide with rage” describes this configuration.

In short, lowered brows combined with raised upper eyelids and tensed lower eyelids form the standard expressive signature of anger.

Next, the nose and cheeks.

Under the combined action of the levator labii superioris and the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, the upper lip rises, the nostrils flare, the nasal wings lift, the nasolabial folds deepen, and the cheek muscles bunch.

FBI investigators encounter anger expressions routinely. When suspects realize the truth has been uncovered, a fleeting anger expression often appears, indicating they feel threatened.

Finally, the mouth. In full-blown anger the mouth is generally not closed; it opens to varying degrees. When the stimulus exceeds the threshold and control is lost, the mouth opens maximally to permit roaring. This requires the joint action of the depressor labii inferioris, the platysma, and the mandible. The depressor labii inferioris pulls the lower lip downward, exposing the lower teeth; the platysma draws the corners of the mouth outward; the mandible opens the oral cavity.

##### “You’re No Good”

This is a negative attitude that intensifies with tone. Sometimes a single contemptuous glance suffices to provoke anger. Most people become angry, even furious, when faced with negation. This reaction occurs in all animals.

An animal psychologist once handled a case involving a two-year-old dog whose owner reported that after a trip the dog had become irritable and would bare its teeth at the owner. The psychologist asked for details of the trip. It sounded ordinary: the owner had taken the dog to stay at a friend’s estate for a while. The friend also kept several dogs, and the owner had expected his dog to enjoy the company. Instead, on the second day the dog became listless, avoided the other dogs, and hid in corners. After returning home it grew quick to anger.

The psychologist examined the dog and found nothing unusual except the colorful clothing it wore. He asked whether the owner had dressed the dog the same way during the estate visit. The owner confirmed that he had; at home the dog never wore clothes, but for the visit he felt the outfit would display his distinctive taste and prevent loss of face before his friend. The psychologist then asked whether the estate dogs were allowed to grow naturally without restraint or clothing. The owner said yes; those dogs were fierce, retained their natural instincts, and possessed beautiful coats.

After this exchange the psychologist identified the problem. He explained that the dog had been slighted by the estate dogs because of its clothing. To humans an animal’s coat is merely aesthetic, yet in the animal world a coat signals bloodline purity, breed quality, and social rank. Animals value natural form and freedom to run. Scent is also crucial for establishing friendly relations. A clothed dog resembles a stripped human—pitiful and alien among its kind. Deprived of the coat that symbolizes race, lineage, and status, and lacking the familiar scent of its peers, it naturally encounters contempt and exclusion.

Once slighted, an animal faces loss of authority and territory—matters that threaten its survival environment. The dog therefore became hostile, especially toward the human who had dressed it. Had the dog worn clothes from birth and lived among similarly attired peers, the outcome might have been different.

Even in developed civilization, being slighted or negated can threaten a human’s survival environment. Denied ability, one may be passed over for important roles or even fail to secure decent employment. This directly creates economic pressure and the pressure to form a family. Faced with such a threat, anger naturally erupts.

##### 1. Road Rage

Driving on the road readily generates anger, especially in heavy traffic. Anyone with driving experience can immediately recall situations that provoke anger. Minor cases include the car ahead failing to accelerate when it should, cutting in without queuing, refusing to yield when required, or changing lanes without signaling. More serious cases involve accidents such as being rear-ended or sideswiped without cause. In all these situations, violated expectations are obvious factors, and the indignant thought “Can’t you drive?” arises both mentally and verbally.

Some conclude from this that **unreasonableness** is the trigger for anger. They argue that if everyone drove reasonably, traffic would flow smoothly and such anger would not occur. Others maintain that unreasonable driving is something anyone might do and is not the key trigger; suffering a loss (harm to one’s interests) is the actual trigger.

When unreasonable driving amounts to arrogant self-importance or even malicious provocation, it does provoke anger—a natural response to a challenge to dignity, comparable to a stranger shoving you on the street. The connection to driving is incidental; the provocation simply occurs through driving. This negative stimulus to ability and dignity resembles an invasion of an animal’s territory and instinctively elicits anger.

When the behavior is not malicious provocation but merely a question of whether one suffers a loss, further analysis is warranted: what advantage does cutting in or overtaking actually confer?

The psychological process that truly triggers anger is not necessarily the direct obstruction, delay, or offense; it may lie deeper than the immediately apparent cause. Whether anger arises depends directly on the purpose of the trip.

Under normal circumstances, drivers care primarily about what they must do upon reaching their destination; the journey itself is merely a necessary process. If one is simply cruising aimlessly, ordinary unreasonable driving (non-malicious) and traffic jams rarely provoke anger. Being hit might still trigger anger, yet deeper reflection reveals that the anger stems from the ensuing complications—damage assessment, insurance claims, repairs, and wasted time—that disrupt subsequent plans. The car’s physical damage matters little provided no one is injured. Imagine driving an already damaged car for leisure; one more dent would hardly matter.

##### 6.1 The Roots of Anger

In the animal world, simple predator-prey dynamics produce hunger in the predator (its primary motive) and fear in the prey. Because the power imbalance is stark, the weaker party cannot eliminate the threat and can only flee (fear). If fortunate enough to run fast, it survives. The weaker party therefore does not feel anger. The stronger party, if it fails to catch the prey, likewise feels no anger; it merely conserves energy for the next attempt.

When the two sides are evenly matched, anger appears more readily. Territory represents a mutually recognized rule of interaction among animals that possess ruling power. Whether the challenge originates inside the territory or from an outside stranger, the territory holder feels anger, because the challenge implies two things:

- First, the challenger knows this is my domain yet dares to trespass—an enormous violation of expectations. How dare you show such disrespect!
- Second, if the challenger wins, the original holder loses everything—mate, offspring, quality of life, even life itself. This constitutes a massive threat encompassing both survival and reproduction. Such a threat must be eliminated! Anger arises, followed by physical combat.

In the human world, the stimuli that elicit anger are likewise **threats to interests**—threats that may harm survival and reproduction. This mechanism is essentially identical to that in animals.

Human anger, however, exhibits broader and more complex derivative forms. Civilization, education, and the fine-grained division of daily life cause anger to arise more often from various derived threats.

The threatening stimuli discussed here do not refer merely to overt threats such as verbal warnings or brandished weapons; they encompass a more abstract notion—the situations a person subjectively perceives as potentially harmful.

A person evaluates whether a stimulus constitutes a threat to interests. If the threat can be eliminated through personal effort, anger may arise; if no such confidence or intention exists, fear results; if the matter is dismissed entirely, disgust (commonly contempt) appears. Thus, whether an interest threat exists resides entirely in the mind of the individual and is strongly linked to self-perception.

##### Anger

Anger is a formidable negative emotion because of its destructive power. With disgust or fear one can simply walk away and ignore the source. Once anger arises, however, the person finds it difficult to discharge the emotion by leaving; instead, they tend to approach the other party, creating a sense of intimidation.

Countless events can provoke anger: failing to secure a seat, having a design stolen, a child’s disobedience, theft, a taxi driver ignoring a hail in cold wind, a computer freezing at a critical moment, unfair distribution of benefits, differing opinions…

Regardless of the variety, all such events share a single root: developments fall short of subjective expectations, generating a powerful sense of threat. A sense of threat can also produce fear or disgust. When one’s strength is far inferior to the opponent’s, fear arises; when one deems the opponent unworthy of engagement, disgust arises; when strength is comparable and a little effort could prevail, anger arises.

This anger response evolved from primitive society and has never been eliminated. In early human times, people shared land with wild beasts. Meat was the primary food source, so hunting was the original means of survival. When traps were set or beasts pursued and the prey escaped, anger arose. Without quarry, the group faced hunger. With the emergence and evolution of civilization, failure to secure prey came to signify incompetence and the threat of ridicule.

Beyond food, the most primitive anger also arose from territorial violation. Both animals and humans maintain defended territories that symbolize identity and status. Intrusion by an enemy naturally provokes anger. Two scenarios exist: when the defender is slightly stronger, the reaction is “You are weaker than I, yet you dare challenge me—clearly you do not respect me; you must be taught a lesson.” When the defender is slightly weaker, the reaction is “If I lose, my property, wife, children, and life will be endangered—how hateful! I must fight to the end and drive the intruder out.”

Today the triggers of anger extend far beyond contests over food and territory, as everyday life readily demonstrates.

##### Psychology Mini-Class

American psychologists conducted this experiment: they injected substances from the blood of angry people into mice and observed the mice’s reactions. At first, the mice appeared lethargic and lost their appetite completely. They stopped eating and drinking, and within just a few days they died.

American physiologist Elmer also performed a similar experiment. He collected “qi water” (breath condensate) from people under different conditions—anger, regret, grief, and calm—and compared them. The results confirmed that anger is extremely harmful to the human body. When he placed the “qi water” exhaled during calm into test water, it remained clear and colorless with no impurities. The “qi water” from regret left a protein-colored precipitate after settling; the one from grief left a white precipitate; and the one from anger left a purple precipitate. When the “anger water” was injected into white rats, the rats lost vital signs within minutes.

From these experiments, Elmer concluded that even ten minutes of anger consumes as much energy as running a 3,000-meter race. The physiological reactions during anger are intense, and the secretions produced are more complex and toxic than those from other emotions.

Therefore, people who anger easily find it difficult to stay healthy or live long. When a person flies into a rage or sulks, a series of physiological changes occur that damage various parts of the body and can even threaten life. For example, anger accelerates the heartbeat; the heart is invaded by rage, leading to palpitations, heartache, chest tightness, and lung distension, ultimately injuring the heart and lungs. Anger also produces extreme anxiety and a sensation of gastric fullness that suppresses appetite; over time this inevitably impairs gastrointestinal digestion and harms the spleen and stomach. Furthermore, during rage the mental state can become disordered, causing extreme emotional tension and mental confusion. Under such adverse psychological conditions and negative emotions, the “insular cortex” in the brain is stimulated and alters the brain’s control over the heart, impairing myocardial function, triggering sudden ventricular fibrillation, causing arrhythmia, and even stopping the heartbeat and resulting in death. Therefore, from the perspective of one’s own health, one should actively extinguish the anger within.

##### 4. Interest Conflicts

One of the most common forms of anger in human society occurs when others threaten one’s interests.

Two competing departments in a company ask the boss for budget. Regardless of the methods the department heads use or the final budget the boss grants, the competition is no longer benign and can already provoke anger and hostility between the two heads. Yet is the root of the anger truly the portion of the budget the boss approved or denied? One possibility is that the two are not merely concerned with the numerical amount of money but with the competitive outcome the numbers represent.

Whoever receives the larger budget approval will enjoy many derivative benefits; the approval may signify the leader’s recognition, “reputation in the arena,” and the loyalty of subordinates—all of which affect future survival and development. If the two departments receive equal budgets, or even if the side that receives more still feels threatened by the other’s aggressive competitive behavior, anger can arise.

Thus, much anger triggered by damaged interests has the interests themselves as only the surface phenomenon or trigger; the future threat represented by the damage is the core issue. If the damage to interests becomes an established trend—that is, if the competitor believes they will always lose to you—then their heart will fill with powerless fear or sorrow.

Many examples of the same nature exist: competing for people, money, or territory. Competition in romantic relationships is also a frequent context for anger. Driven by the pursuit of superior reproduction, any threat to one’s own love for another or to the loved one elicits a physiological impulse toward angry attack. But if true love has already passed, only tears of sorrow flow, not the hot blood of anger.

##### Suppressed Anger

Unlike inhibited anger, suppressed anger is sulking with no outlet. Anger must be vented to maintain mental balance and support healthy psychological development. Yet as civilization advances, people are constrained by countless external factors and cannot vent anger freely. Even as children we were told by parents not to lose our temper in public. A mere pout would draw a stern “Stop pouting—don’t be so childish.” Over time, holding anger in became associated with good upbringing.

After entering society, we experience more sulking than joy because we cannot vent anger at will and emotions cannot develop naturally. This is not only a matter of upbringing but also of survival. When negotiating with clients or communicating with a boss, any display of anger can jeopardize one’s future and livelihood. Anger must be forcibly suppressed, which in some ways is more frightening than shouting. Because one must exert effort to restrain and not shout, the muscles around the mouth tighten, forming tightly closed lips. Under the combined action of the levator labii superioris, levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, and mentalis muscles, the suppressed mouth shape curves downward overall—corners of the mouth droop, the nasolabial folds deepen, and the chin shows uneven wrinkles. The eyes display typical anger features: eyebrows lowered and furrowed, upper eyelids raised, lower eyelids tensed.

Note that without changes in the eyebrows and eyes, a pout alone cannot reliably indicate anger. Similar pouting appears in expressions of grievance or sadness. Therefore, to judge anger, one must also consider the shape of the eyes and eyebrows.

##### Restrained Behavioral Capacity

Anyone tied up with ropes becomes angry, yet in real life many invisible ropes bind us and continually provoke anger.

Parents want their children to be versatile; the more skills, the better—not only for cultivating temperament but also for securing a brighter future. So parents begin fostering artistic sensibilities: piano, violin, painting, calligraphy, dance, singing… After school or on weekends, children must spend one or two hours on artistic training after finishing homework. For children, constant movement better matches their natural inclinations—playing tag with friends, for example. Try picking up a toddler who has just learned to walk; the child will struggle to break free, and if unable to do so will flush, cry out, and breathe rapidly—an expression of anger. For a child who craves activity, sitting still to practice art is torment. They want to resist yet must yield to parental authority, creating a sense of restraint. The longer the restraint, the greater the negative emotion, until it becomes anger that erupts as shouting. Once the shouting draws parental rebuke, the anger turns into sadness and disgust.

The same dynamic exists between lovers or spouses. You may not want your partner to befriend members of the opposite sex or to dress revealingly. Early in the relationship such “don’ts” may be interpreted as love, but over time a strong sense of restraint fills the heart. One feels one’s behavioral freedom is controlled and constrained, and freedom is lost. At that point anger arises and leads to repeated arguments.

##### 3. Anxious Anger

Every parent has the same experience—coaxing a child to sleep, a sweet and loving moment. Can anger arise? Absolutely. The classic scenario is when the parent has an important commitment afterward (a conference call, for example).

If an important arrangement looms yet the child, as usual, demands another story or keeps wriggling and refusing to settle, occasionally speaking up just when you think they have fallen asleep, these originally endearing behaviors can ignite anxious anger. The inner script runs roughly: “Child, it’s time to sleep; it’s late. Daddy/Mommy has something important to do. Fall asleep quickly so I can get to it; if you stay awake this late you might ruin my plans.”

As time presses and anxiety accumulates, anger easily surfaces; one becomes irritable and may even scold the child. Yet if one truly has no choice but to wait until the child sleeps (for instance, when one is the sole caregiver), once the deadline for the important matter passes and the child is still awake, anger dissipates and calm returns—unless that matter matters more than the child’s distress.

Incidentally, this is also why especially busy parents tend to raise rebellious children: the child concludes that they matter less to the parents than earning money or attending a meeting. “Since I don’t matter, you might as well stop minding me.”

##### Anger Expressions

When anger has not reached its peak and one only wants to retort, the mouth closes less tightly. Because one still intends to vent anger through words—accusations or arguments—lower teeth are often visible, and sometimes upper teeth as well.

When freshly provoked and preparing to attack, the mouth closes a little more; the teeth meet. Yet the raising of the upper lip signals “Watch out, I’m angry.” At this degree of closure the upper teeth are definitely exposed, displaying a biting posture and strong aggression. The phrase “gnashing one’s teeth” accurately describes this state. Animals about to strike bare their canines to show ferocity, teeth closed and ready to tear. When humans prepare to attack, gnashing teeth both declares the resolve to bite through to the end and prepares to endure pain. Indeed, people also clench their teeth when bearing pain. Try the action: jaws tight, mouth stretched, both rows of teeth visible. In the mirror you look either ferocious or in agony.

Although the mouth shape of bearing pain resembles anger, the eyebrows and eyes differ markedly. In pain the brows rise at the inner ends and press down at the outer ends, the eyes close—signs of avoidance.

Having described the standard expression of full anger, we now turn to other types of anger expressions—namely, micro-expressions of anger.

##### 2. Restricted Freedom

Restricted freedom poses the greatest threat to survival. Without freedom of movement one is surrounded like prey with no escape and will surely die. Thus, in the instinctive awareness accumulated through human evolution, restricted freedom registers as an extremely serious threat.

When adults play with children they sometimes, out of affection, hold the little one to their chest and gently pin the arms and legs. Can you guess the child’s reaction?

Instantly the child’s face changes to anger, flushes bright red, holds a breath, and struggles to break free—an unmistakable anger response. The restraining force is not strong and does not hurt, and the preceding play atmosphere was pleasant; the mere act of restraint produces such a dramatic shift.

The child’s subjective expectation is free movement. Any behavior that restrains a child’s capacity to act creates a negative expectation violation. Even during play, sudden loss of freedom triggers instinctive discomfort and anger. After a brief moment and a feeble effort that fails to change the situation, the child opens the mouth wide and wails, expressing grievance (unwilling yet powerless to alter the situation) and bewilderment—this is the emotion of sadness.

##### 4. Sneer (Angry Smile)

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图11-27]*

1. Head slightly lowered, chin tucked (head-attack posture feature);
2. Eyebrows furrowed and lowered in a “10:10” shape, vertical glabellar lines present (anger feature);
3. Upper eyelids raised forcefully against the resistance of lowered brows, forming wrinkles on the eyelid skin (anger feature);
4. Lower eyelids tensed (anger feature);
5. Upper lip raised, exposing upper teeth; corners of the mouth pulled sideways and upward, lower lip relaxed (local smile feature);
6. Upper teeth show a tendency to bite the lower lip, indicating suppression.

**Summary**: Anger features are obvious, confirming it as the dominant emotion. Mouth features of a smile appear, yet the eyes do not participate, so the smile is not genuine and no pleasure is present. Combined with the lip-biting suppression action, the person can be judged to be suppressing anger (temporarily not attacking) while using the smile to convey a sense of control or low pressure. A smile issued under dominant anger can be called a sneer, expressing both offensive potential and inner satisfaction with the outcome of the fight.

##### Interest Competition

Anger arising in interest competition is common.

Two department heads compete for the design and execution rights of the same product. They submit the best designs screened by their departments to the client, who chooses which to use. In benign competition the probability of anger erupting is low. If one side uses improper means to win, the other side will certainly be furious. This is not merely about whether one’s own department’s design is adopted; it also concerns whether one will receive the boss’s favor, performance bonuses, and so on. Adoption signals recognized competence, spreads within the circle, motivates subordinates to work harder, and greatly increases promotion chances. Rejection, conversely, threatens promotion, public opinion, and finances.

Rivalry between romantic competitors follows the same pattern. As noted in the section on happiness, when choosing a mate people pursue superior reproductive genes. The appearance of a rival naturally threatens the loss of those genes, producing anger that is physiologically difficult to control and may escalate to physical fighting.

##### “Are You Up to It?”

This inner question typically arises during provocation. It conveys “I want to see whether you’re really up to it” or “Who’s better—you or me?” The provocateur usually hopes for an intense response and therefore uses this mindset and tone to enrage the other party.

Still, the provocative tone “Are you really up to it?” is relatively mild. Its implication—“I’m strong; let’s see how strong you are”—is gentler and more sincere. If the provoked person is steady, they will weigh whether to accept the challenge, sensing their own inferiority. Without outside instigation they may choose to retreat. But if the provocateur says “I can see you’re not up to it; even if we fight, you’ll lose,” the provoked person’s anger ignites easily. They will want to prove their strength and the other’s misjudgment. Precisely at such moments the provoked must stay clear-headed and control their anger, for this may be a “goading tactic.”

##### (1) Contempt

A common line of negation is “You’re no good!” Depending on tone, it can convey rich shades of meaning. Such contempt need not involve threatening actions; it may be only a sentence or a glance (expression). No one likes to be negated, especially when belittled (which amplifies the negation) or negated without factual basis (slander), both of which readily provoke anger.

When animals are regarded as inferior by their own kind during survival, they lose authority and control; their safety faces great risk—they may be preyed upon, defeated, lose mates or offspring, even life. In today’s highly civilized, specialized society, having one of one’s skills negated likewise means losing competitiveness and survival opportunities. This threat is the most direct stimulus for anger.

Even cultivated scholars will step forward to defend their reputation if baselessly slandered or belittled in their area of expertise. On the internet, minor differences of opinion routinely prompt opinion leaders to launch verbal and written attacks—fresh cases appear constantly.

##### (2) Provocation

Provocation usually precedes open struggle. The provoking party expresses a desire to fight and hopes the other will respond in kind, deliberately arousing anger by attacking whatever the other cares about most. Provocation is the behavior most likely to ignite anger. There are many forms; the key lies in the target’s personality and concerns. Broadly, one type says “Let’s fight and see,” the other “You have no skill; I disdain fighting you—if we did, I’d finish you easily.” The latter usually provokes more anger, because the former is often sincere, the speaker possesses real strength, and the target can more readily apply reason to consider the course of events and non-combat resolutions—unless bystander commentary interferes. The latter deliberately conveys a very low evaluation and uses disdain to intensify the expectation violation, making the target eager to disprove the assessment and teach the provocateur a lesson, since the evaluation is so low it seems easy to correct. Yet this is precisely a psychological trap.

##### Chapter 6 Micro-expressions of Anger

When the intensity of a negative stimulus escalates beyond the threshold of disgust and poses a threat to the individual, it triggers anger. Anger is characterized by an aggressive impulse aimed at driving away or eliminating the source of the negative stimulus.

The essence of disgust is a “top-down rejection” attitude toward the negative stimulus, involving attempts to exclude, avoid, or simply ignore it. At every level of disgust, there is no desire to change, attack, or eliminate the stimulus source; at most, one walks away. However, if the stimulus intensifies to the point of creating threat or harm, the individual’s emotion escalates to a new level—anger.

The essence of anger is the desire to attack and prevail—eliminating danger through aggression.

Events that provoke anger are richly varied in daily life. They range from a taxi driver ignoring a hail on the street to someone physically attacking you or your child. Therefore, readers should prepare for the first task: patiently sorting out the sources of anger.

##### Breach of Agreement

**Situation A**  
Woman: “Why are you so late? I’ve been waiting forever.”

Situation A

Man: “I’m sorry. Something came up at the last minute. I’m really sorry, darling.”

Woman: “I’m not eating.”

Situation B

Buyer: “You said you’d hold it for me. Why did you sell it to someone else?”

Seller: “They bought it on the spot. I couldn’t refuse. Next time—next time it arrives, I’ll notify you first.”

Buyer: “There won’t be a next time. No credibility.”

Both Situation A and Situation B produce anger from a breach of agreement. On the surface, what is lost is a date or an item; in substance, a threat has been perceived. When the man arrives late, the woman feels undervalued and threatened with possible abandonment. When the goods are sold to another buyer, two threat elements appear: a sense of disrespect and violated dignity, and the practical loss of the item, which may disrupt daily routines until a replacement is obtained.

##### 8.2.5 How to Distinguish Genuine from Feigned Anger?

Attack gestures can also be used to feign anger. A person who is actually worried (fearful or sad) may deliberately display aggressive movements to make others believe their words or to end an uncomfortable conversation. Such displays are not driven by genuine emotion.

The key question is how to judge the authenticity of these auxiliary movements.

When an action is genuinely driven by emotion, arm movements require no conscious thought; they match the force and rhythm of speech. Language and movement spring from the same source—anger. Anger concentrates force on the target, aligning gaze, weapon, and body posture in a single direction.

Feigned anger is constructed through deliberate thought control. Without direct emotional drive, the movements fail to synchronize fully in force or timing, revealing numerous tells.

##### Obstruction in the Process of Reaching a Goal

Anyone who has run a race understands the anger that arises when obstacles appear on the track. A better finish is lost because a stone trips the runner. In real life, much anger stems from blocked progress toward a goal; traffic jams are the classic example.

During a traffic jam people become irritable because the expected arrival time is delayed, potentially triggering a chain of negative consequences—late arrival at work and docked pay, a missed client meeting and an unsigned contract, or lost career and financial opportunities. These thoughts quickly turn irritation into anger. Conversely, if the day is free of obligations and no destination is urgent, a traffic jam does not provoke anger, because no goal exists to be obstructed.

##### Controlling Anger and Extinguishing Inner Rage

When inner rage burns fiercely, one must neither vent it without restraint—harming self and others—nor suppress it indefinitely and add to physical and mental strain. The skill is to extinguish the fire at the first spark.

Psychological research shows that frequent outbursts increase the risk factors for heart disease and other illnesses. People who rarely lose their temper experience significantly lower mortality and heart-disease recurrence rates. Therefore, effectively inhibiting anger helps maintain a calm state of mind.

Achieving this is not difficult; many methods exist for dousing inner fire. The practical question is how to cool the emotion.

##### Suppressed Anger

The foundation of suppressed anger is denial. In mild denial the orbicularis oris muscle relaxes while the mentalis and depressor anguli oris contract, producing a pout. This expression conveys “I don’t think so,” “This is awkward,” or “I’m a bit upset.” When the orbicularis oris also contracts, the denial deepens into displeasure. At a still greater intensity it becomes suppressed anger. Because reason demands that anger be forcibly contained, greater muscular effort is required. If this expression appears during conversation, the other person is already intensely angry yet is actively restraining it; changing the topic or pausing the exchange is advisable.

##### Disgust Escalating into Anger

Disgust can escalate into anger. The resulting expression shows anger in the brows and eyes while retaining disgust in the mouth and nose.

In the disgust expression the upper lip rises, forming the nasolabial fold. When combined with lowered and furrowed brows, raised upper eyelids, and tensed lower eyelids, the configuration indicates anger triggered by disgust. A slightly open mouth prepares for speech; lowered brows signal readiness to attack.

When one feels inner disgust toward another person, avoidance is the usual choice. When interaction is unavoidable, the disgust expression may appear unintentionally. If the other person then utters words that intensify negative emotion, disgust rapidly converts into anger.

##### Furrowed Brows and Biting Lips Both Signal Red Lights

The key facial markers of anger are “forceful eyebrows and lips.” The characteristic actions are “both eyebrows drawn toward the center,” “eyes widened,” “lower eyelids markedly tensed,” and “lips pressed tightly together or mouth open.” Anger encompasses irritation, annoyance, discord, defiance, and disagreement—feelings that arise when a personal goal is obstructed or when one rejects a current event or another’s statement. When anger occurs, muscles tense and heart rate rises. In evolutionary biology the anger expression serves to intimidate others and signal an impending attack.

##### 3. Jealousy Stems from the Monkey-King Mentality

Humans possess a strong innate “I alone am supreme” consciousness, often called the monkey-king mentality. Everyone wants to be the most important, the strongest, the undisputed number one. When others treat you as most important or when you regard yourself as the strongest, you feel happy and gratified. Conversely, when someone fails to treat you as most important or when you cannot accept being inferior, you feel inferior, hurt, anxious, and irritable. Once you recognize that you are not the strongest but the weakest and most pitiable, the monkey-king mentality collapses and jealousy arises.

##### Loss of Self-Control?

An extremely angry or frustrated person who cannot directly express feelings often scratches the head, strokes the neck, clenches fists, or grips arms or wrists in an attempt to maintain self-control.

If standing, the person may take a threatening step forward to close distance and display a “staring” expression. If the distance closes to within touching range yet self-control is still desired, anger may be redirected onto a substitute object—pounding a fist on a table, slamming a door, or kicking an item.

##### 2. Suppressing Rage and Responding Calmly

When someone shouts at you or attacks you verbally, how should you respond—ignore it or retaliate? Adjust your mindset and make no reply. The event has already occurred; you cannot change it or control the other person’s behavior. Retaliation only escalates conflict and worsens the situation. Non-response “removes the fuel from the fire,” making it difficult for the other person to continue the outburst.

##### 4. Facing the Root Cause

Virginia Williams once said, “The key is not to keep saying ‘I’m furious’ without taking action. You need to identify why you are angry and then move forward.” A simple request or action can produce results. Therefore, if your anger stems from your wife purchasing an expensive cosmetic without consulting you, confront the root cause by obtaining her commitment to seek your opinion before future large expenditures.

##### Signs of Anger or Resentment

- Cold attitude, silence
- Turning the head away
- Maintaining distance
- Lips pressed tight or pouting
- Arms or legs crossed
- Slamming the door in anger

Just as a child’s angry behavior should not be ignored, a partner’s signs of irritation or annoyance deserve attention. Interpreting the other person’s body language allows you to rebuild a good relationship in a timely and constructive manner.

##### 7. Shifting Your Attention

An enraged person can easily lose control and commit irreversible acts, so the emotion must be cooled. One effective method is to shift attention. For example, when someone provokes you and you feel the urge to strike, listen to soothing music, walk in a park, or stand by a lake in the breeze—any technique that redirects attention and extinguishes inner fire.

##### 5. Being Denied

Denial is a general term for a category of stimuli. As analyzed in the chapter on disgust, abhorrence, contempt, and disdain are all forms of denial. In concrete expression they subdivide into direct denial, belittlement (contempt and disdain), disgust, and, on the basis of belittlement, provocation and disrespect.

##### 3. Identifying the Cause of Your Anger

When the urge to become angry arises, wait until the emotion has cooled slightly, then identify the cause. Is it because friends repeatedly mock your figure and clothing? Because a supervisor constantly claims you are not working hard enough and you feel wronged? Because parents criticize you without reason and disregard your feelings?

##### 5. Avoid Coarse Language

Mutual understanding is the best way to extinguish inner fire, so practice empathy. Even when very angry, refrain from calling the other person a “fool,” an “idiot,” or worse; such language treats the other as an enemy and makes empathy impossible.

##### Signs of Anger

- Tears and rage
- Worried or irritable expression
- Turning the head away
- Slamming the door forcefully

#### Disgust

##### Disgust

When we see those nauseating foods, we squint our eyes, wrinkle our noses, pull the corners of our mouths back, and sometimes make a retching motion. This is the classic expression of disgust, originally triggered by spoiled, nauseating food. In times when humans had no concept of food hygiene, eating spoiled food could lead to vomiting, diarrhea, fever, and other illnesses, with severe cases possibly resulting in death. Therefore, disgust toward spoiled food became a survival skill.

With the development of civilization and technology today, humans rarely accidentally consume spoiled food, but the expression of disgust has remained, evolving into a reaction to undesirable phenomena, events, and people.

Compared to anger, sadness, and fear, the reaction of disgust is not as intense, and the facial changes are not as dramatic. This is because the stimulus from the trigger does not cause significant negative impact on oneself. The triggers for disgust vary with different stages of social development. For example, in feudal society, a man and a woman meeting alone would be considered disgusting, but today, it is not a trigger for disgust. In contemporary society, there are roughly two situations that can trigger disgust: negation of the stimulus; perceiving it as poor or despicable, yet not constituting a threat.

A volunteer (pseudonym H) participating in a psychology experiment recounted an incident from which we can analyze the formation of the emotion of disgust.

H is a beautiful girl who was pursued by many during her university years, but she focused entirely on her studies and did not date any boys until graduation. On graduation day, she suddenly received a letter that roughly said: H, I know you have had a crush on me for many years. Because of my busy studies, I have always pretended not to notice you. Today we have graduated, and the burden of study has been temporarily set aside. I hope to clarify this relationship with you and step into society together. It was signed by a boy named J. There were quite a few boys in H’s class, but only a few she interacted with regularly, and she did not recall any dealings with J.

At first, H suspected J had mistaken her for someone else, so she sought him out to talk. J was a self-important boy who, though neither handsome nor academically outstanding, always considered himself a heartthrob and would not easily glance at girls, carrying an air of a prince high above others.

H found him and asked if he had made a mistake. J insisted he had not and confidently claimed H had a crush on him. H asked on what basis he said that; over four years they had exchanged only a few words and had almost no intersection, so how could there be talk of a crush? J told H that at the opening ceremony she had deliberately stepped on his foot and smiled at him, and from that moment he had decided H had feelings for him; otherwise, why would she not date for four years when plenty of boys pursued her? It was obvious she was waiting for him.

H found this both amusing and exasperating. She said she had indeed stepped on him at the opening ceremony, but it was not intentional; smiling was basic courtesy, and not accepting others’ pursuits for four years was to focus more on her studies—she also planned to prepare for a master’s degree. If she were to date, it would be after entering a master’s program. Later J kept telling classmates that H had a crush on him, making H extremely embarrassed.

While discussing this matter, H displayed disgust once and anger once. Disgust appeared when mentioning J’s insistence that H had a crush on him; anger appeared when she spoke of J spreading the rumor to classmates. The psychologist asked why she felt disgusted by J, and she replied: “I hate boys with prince syndrome, so self-important. He is not handsome, his grades are poor, so on what grounds does he think I would like him? If I were to like someone, it would be tall, handsome, and at least cultured. In short, he makes me feel very low-grade.”

There is another similar case provided by a volunteer we will call M.

During his internship, M encountered a man who claimed to be a director and wanted to discover him as a talent. It is undeniable that M is tall, handsome, steady, kind, and knowledgeable, making him well-suited to be a high-quality idol. However, M still preferred the programming industry and had little interest in the entertainment industry. To persuade M to appear in his film, the director said he had collaborated with many famous directors and actors, naming several who had even won Oscars. M immediately grew suspicious: if he had worked with so many celebrities, why was he unknown? Out of politeness, M did not leave immediately but listened to what the man had to say.

While the director expounded on his artistic philosophy and current artistic trends, M found his ideas clichéd and somewhat vulgar, not what one would expect from a cultivated, knowledgeable person. The director told him that today’s films do not emphasize substance or culture but star power; as long as big names appear, the film will succeed. M asked: if you believe only big names should star, why must I appear in your film? The director said many big names had already signed on, but they were supporting roles; the male lead had not been found until he happened to see M and felt his temperament fit the role. M asked some professional questions about art, and the director stammered and evaded, nothing like someone with professional training.

Watching the boastful director, M felt disgust. He believed the director’s views were all incorrect; a good story is always the soul of a good film. Moreover, the director made M feel very low-grade.

From these two cases we can see that negation and low-grade quality are the triggers for disgust, making the person feel dislike, yet these do not affect them. One more point to note is the difference between disgust and anger. As in H’s case, her initial emotion was disgust, but when J spread the rumor that she had a crush on him, disgust turned into anger because it threatened her reputation and could affect her future romantic prospects.

Having understood the triggers of disgust, let us next examine the features of a full disgust expression.

##### The Man with Six Titles

A volunteer named Xiaoya who participated in our research recounted an encounter with a man of exceptional quality. During their first contact, the man first handed over his business card, which listed six different titles, from president of a certain company to advisor to a certain group, researcher at a certain research institute, and finally “class monitor of a certain university’s graduate course program.” After the surprise of this self-introduction, the two began exchanging views on the current state of the film industry in an attempt to find cooperation opportunities.

In this man’s view, making films in the industry required the “three bigs”—big investment, big stars, big publicity. Although he had so far only made two experimental music videos, he firmly believed that as long as someone invested enough money to hire big-name directors and stars and adapt a well-known historical story, a successful work would result. Then, from the start of shooting, hype and publicity would begin, even manufacturing gimmicks to attract attention, until the film finally entered theaters and achieved both fame and fortune.

When Xiaoya pointed out that film is an art form that tells stories through images and sound, so a good story should be the core element of a good film, the man strongly refuted her and repeatedly emphasized, “Who in China watches stories? As long as there are stars on screen, people get excited; the bigger the stars, the more people will watch, and the higher the box office!” While later describing his grand plans, his impassioned manner left no room for others to interject, and he frequently mentioned which entertainment stars he had attended events with, taken photos with, and whose phone numbers he had stored, looking completely self-satisfied.

Eventually Xiaoya had to end the meeting early, politely excusing herself with another appointment. We tried to point out the sources of her emotion at the time, and Xiaoya agreed with the two features we analyzed: “First, what this man said seemed wrong to me; second, he did not realize his views were wrong and still shamelessly boasted and promoted himself—this ignorance made me feel very low-grade.”

A similar real-world case involves an entertainment celebrity crossing over to act as an opinion leader. In March 2015, a well-known lawyer published on social media his critical opinions about traffic police conducting nighttime checks for drunk driving. This attention-seeking behavior drew widespread public criticism and questioning and became a laughingstock for a time.

After the entire incident, we analyzed the public’s disgust toward this lawyer and concluded it stemmed mainly from the fact that, in his capacity as a “legal professional,” he expressed views that showed ignorance of basic legal knowledge yet he considered them correct, criticizing the normal enforcement actions of traffic police. The public viewed his erroneous opinions as low-grade, and as a lawyer he should not have been so ignorant; this self-importance was deeply disgusting.

Of course, the public feedback also contained a large amount of abusive language. It should be noted that abuse is an aggressive act stemming from anger and has already exceeded the upper limit of disgust. A necessary feature of disgust is the absence of any desire to attack.

By discussing the two cases above, we can see that the triggers capable of arousing disgust in interpersonal communication share common patterns. For a person to feel disgust toward a stimulus, at least two necessary features must exist simultaneously: first, negation of the stimulus, specifically manifested as disagreement or non-acceptance; second, in addition to disagreement, the belief that the stimulus is low-grade, far below one’s subjective expectations of it.

Contempt very easily triggers anger. If A feels contempt for B and B refuses to accept it or even provokes, A very easily escalates to anger and attempts to “subdue” B, with lines roughly like: “You little punk, I’ll make you submit!” If B clearly knows A feels disgust toward him and must maintain a connection with A, B is very likely to feel anger to protect his dignity from infringement. We will explain anger in detail in the next chapter.

For example, two company executives engage in a reasonable debate, each supported by specific theoretical or factual evidence for their views. Although both may harbor negation, they will not necessarily feel disgust and may even appreciate each other. If a low-grade evaluation factor is added to this situation—for instance, the product manager believes the sales director’s proposed sales growth plan for the next year has no basis whatsoever, completely脱离s the company’s current objective conditions, and is all baseless talk—disgust will arise.

In some cases, the stimulus’s level may not objectively be low, but because its excessively high self-positioning exceeds reality, it can also produce a relatively low-grade evaluation. An arrogant senior colleague may indeed have ability, but because he cannot accept reasonable views from juniors and is blindly conceited, he can arouse disgust. Historically many famous ministers also aroused the emperor’s disgust because of such self-importance after great achievements. In *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, Wei Yan repeatedly caused Zhuge Liang’s disgust and vigilance for this reason (Zhuge Liang’s comment that Wei Yan had a rebellious bone at the back of his head is merely novelistic technique and will not be discussed). This subjective low-grade evaluation held by the actor is a relative effect caused by the stimulus’s excessively high self-perception; objective reality is made to appear low-grade by the stimulus’s arrogance.

If the objective situation is already low-grade and is paired with a blindly conceited display, the degree of disgust will be strongly increased.

##### 5.3.3 Features of the Disgusted Expression

When the intensity of the stimulus decreases, the degree of aversion also decreases. When our state of rejection is slightly weaker, the disgust dominated by the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi muscle is instead controlled by the levator labii superioris, resulting in an overall milder degree of facial deformation. As shown in Figure 5-11.

The disgusted expression shown in the figure can be analyzed with the following features:

① While the orbicularis oculi muscle contracts, it causes the eyebrows to press down slightly; the corrugator supercilii muscle also participates in contraction, forming slight frown lines;  
② Slight contraction of the orbicularis oculi muscle causes the eyelids to tense and close slightly;  
③ The levator labii superioris muscle dominates the contraction, lifting the upper lip upward;  
④ The alae of the nose are indirectly lifted upward and stretched to both sides, forming shallow grooves on both sides of the alae;  
⑤ The lower lip shows no obvious morphological change; the lips may remain closed or slightly parted.

It can be seen that when the overall movement of the facial muscles weakens, the most prominent feature is still the lifting of the upper lip and the alae of the nose, along with the resulting grooves on both sides of the alae; next, the morphological changes in the eyes and eyebrows are also quite prominent features.

Darwin, in his book *The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals*, also mentioned that disgust can sometimes be expressed without visible changes to the upper lip (for example, when obscured by a thick mustache), as long as the deep lines on both sides of the alae are observed, along with the eyes and eyebrows, it can be fully conveyed.

**Test Case**  
**Taking Risqué Photos to Seek Fame**  
Usually, when we talk about internet celebrities known for “aesthetic ugliness,” this expression appears involuntarily. If the visual stimulus is added, the effect becomes even more pronounced.

We tested a young girl who very much wanted to become famous. She had taken some rather risqué, ambiguous-style photos in an attempt to attract attention and establish herself in the entertainment industry for development. To determine her behavioral motives, we prepared photos of a famous internet celebrity “Sister X” and videos of TV programs she had participated in. When the girl saw her photos and videos, the expression in Figure 5-12 immediately appeared on her face.

By analyzing this natural facial reaction, we confirmed that she felt disgust toward “Sister X”’s appearance.

However, when several video clips of TV programs were subsequently played, the girl’s face showed great excitement and attention. Although “Sister X” performed and talked confidently and boldly in the programs, it did not increase the girl’s disgust. Through capturing and analyzing changes in the girl’s gaze direction, we noted that her increased excitement was directly related to the logos of major TV stations that kept appearing. Therefore, our analysis concluded that the girl very much hoped to achieve similar attention and fame, and participating in recordings on major TV stations was a stimulus that excited her. The feeling of disgust was limited only to aversion toward “Sister X”’s appearance; she had no objection to her method of becoming popular through “aesthetic ugliness.”

##### 5.3.2 Features of the Disgusted Expression

The physiological expression of disgust differs from vomiting in one obvious respect: because there is no need to create a passage for vomiting, the mouth does not open as widely as it does during the vomiting action. As shown in Figure 5-8.

This image shows the expression when tasting a very unpleasant flavor or odor. We make the same expression when we hear something disgusting or see a repulsive scene. Such an intense facial muscle configuration (which can be described as distorted) can convey an even stronger sense of disgust in real life than the vomiting expression. Because the mentalis muscle contracts and pushes the lower lip upward, pressing the lips tightly together, it visibly suppresses the vomiting action, in line with the rules of civilized society that prohibit vomiting at will. Compared with vomiting, this expression is more practical and less exaggerated. This mouth shape can be understood either as an effort to control oneself and not vomit in public (already at an extreme level of disgust) or as a primitive signal of refusing to accept any unpleasant taste.

The muscle movements and facial morphological features that constitute the disgusted expression are as follows:

① The corrugator supercilii muscle contracts, knitting the eyebrows tightly;  
② The orbicularis oculi muscle contracts strongly, closing the eyes tightly and simultaneously pressing the eyebrows downward;  
③ The levator labii superioris and levator labii superioris alaeque nasi muscles contract, lifting the upper lip while squeezing the sides of the alae to form the nasolabial folds;  
④ The mentalis muscle contracts, forcefully pushing the lower lip upward so that the lips are pressed tightly together; the chin simultaneously wrinkles upward, producing many folds on the surface skin; a deep groove forms between the lower lip and the raised muscle on the chin;  
⑤ The depressor anguli oris muscle contracts, pulling the corners of the mouth downward, counterbalancing the action of the levator labii superioris and forming bracket-shaped lines on both sides of the mouth.

Other disgusted expressions similar to this morphology differ mainly in the shape of the mouth. In some cases the lower lip is relaxed and the mouth opens slightly; apart from the upper lip, no other parts participate forcefully in forming the expression. As shown in Figure 5-9.

In other cases the corners of the mouth are pulled sharply sideways under the action of the platysma, flattening the lower lip, smoothing the surface skin, exposing part of the upper teeth while the lower teeth are partially covered by the upper teeth. As shown in Figure 5-10.

**Test Case**  
**Bloody Visual Stimuli**  
Producing such an intense disgusted expression requires a stimulus of very high intensity. Simple problem stimuli or verbal stimuli rarely achieve this effect. In the experiments we conducted, only the video *Forensic Autopsy Demonstration* and some bloody post-disaster corpse photographs elicited disgusted expressions approaching this degree in the subjects<|eos|>

##### 2. Disgust Expressions of Varying Intensity

If the stimulus is very strong, it produces intense disgust, that is, physiological disgust, prompting avoidance of any close contact or relationship with the stimulus source. If the stimulus intensity weakens to a moderate level, it produces revulsion; the rejection and disapproval represented by revulsion are also quite strong and can largely be triggered by psychological stimuli. As stimulus intensity decreases further, it produces contempt; contempt expresses a top-down sense of rejection on the part of the actor, yet the mindset remains light. If the stimulus intensity is very weak, it produces disdain; “not deigning to look” is the typical representative of this mindset.

Regardless of the degree of disgust, the common conclusion is this: the appearance of disgust signifies a top-down negation within the actor’s mind.

Full disgust triggers the action combination of brow furrowing + eyelid closure + upper-lip elevation. When social context imposes no restrictions, these features can be displayed without restraint. In important social situations, however, inner disgust often cannot be expressed freely, because doing so would be perceived as “very rude.” Therefore, once emotional expression is constrained, these full disgust expression forms cannot be displayed at maximum amplitude; the actor adopts the principle of reduced amplitude and reduced intensity to restrain emotional leakage, even though the actor remains unaware of the process.

Consequently, the micro-expression features of disgust concentrate on eyelid closure or upper-lip elevation. Slight eyelid closure replaces brow furrowing + eyelid closure, giving the appearance that the person is squinting at something; yet this isolated eyelid movement without accompanying brow action, when paired with steady gaze fixed on the stimulus source, can to some extent indicate the emergence of disgust. In certain social contexts the brows and eyes may remain still while the upper lip rises ever so slightly; this is the common “little contempt” expression.

##### Chapter Summary

The original stimulus sources for disgust-type emotions are pungent odors and rotten, nauseating food. Therefore, when disgust expressions are at their fullest, they consist of brow furrowing + tightly closed eyes + vigorous upper-lip elevation + lower lip pressing upward so that both lips are pressed tightly together. Translated, this means “do not look, do not smell, do not eat.” If the ears could move, “do not listen” might also appear. For example, during an argument a girl may cover her ears with her hands, tightly close her eyes, and shout loudly, “I don’t want to hear it, I don’t want to hear it!” The brow-furrowing action helps increase the force of eye closure; tightly pressing the lips together rejects taste and some gaseous stimuli. Yet what is the purpose of upper-lip elevation? Aquatic animals such as seals can actively close their nasal passages through muscle movement—an evolved function. Humans lack this ability; the human nasal passages cannot be moved voluntarily. However, when the upper lip is vigorously elevated, the levator labii superioris and levator labii superioris alaeque nasi objectively flatten the oval nasal passages, impeding free inhalation and exhalation and thereby reducing negative stimulation from pungent odors.

The essence of disgust-type emotions is negation; because these stimulus sources are not powerful enough to pose a harmful threat, the negation is usually top-down. An expression such as contempt is an extremely pronounced manifestation of this top-down negation. The emotion holder feels elevated above others (correct, rational, intelligent, excellent) while perceiving a vast gap between the stimulus source and themselves (wrong, reckless, foolish, inferior). Consequently, the contempt expression retains partial forms of the full disgust expression, typically including narrowed eyes, eyelid closure, and upper-lip elevation. In social situations where full contempt cannot be displayed, these standard expression forms often appear as unbalanced unilateral lip elevation and eyelid narrowing.

If the stimulus is very strong, it produces intense disgust, that is, physiological disgust, prompting avoidance of any close contact or relationship with the stimulus source. ##### The Slightly Overweight Person Sensitive About Body Shape

We once tested a slightly overweight young man. A core question during the session concerned whether he was sensitive about his body shape. Because he was studying criminal investigation, we began the conversation from the topic of “lie detection” technology.

- **Question**: How do you rate the effectiveness of traditional polygraph (lie detection) instruments?  
  **Answer**: They’re all right. In terms of sensitivity and objectivity, they are fairly accurate for excluding criminal suspects. Once the test is done, if the person did it and simply claims not to remember, saying they didn’t do it will definitely be captured.  
  【Expression: No obvious change; maintains baseline smiling appearance.】

- **Question**: How do you rate our micro-reaction (微反应) psychological testing technology for lie detection?  
  **Answer**: I’m not very familiar with it. From your introduction it seems it might work.  
  【Expression: Upper lip elevated, unilateral corner of the mouth raised, ipsilateral eye narrowed more tightly, forming a “disdainful smile.”】

- **Question**: So you don’t fully agree; you merely find the content we introduced reasonably logical, yet you do not accept the accuracy of the test—is that correct?  
  **Answer**: (Slight surprise and embarrassment, fleeting) Heh, I think this testing technology could be interfered with by the subject’s deliberate performance.

- **Question**: Do you feel your body shape is somewhat overweight?  
  **Answer**: A bit overweight.  
  【Expression: Returns to smiling appearance, appearing calm.】

- **Question**: Do you mind it yourself? Do you feel it is not attractive enough?  
  **Answer**: There’s nothing I can do about it; I’ll just let nature take its course.  
  【Expression: The unilateral corner-of-the-mouth raise and ipsilateral eye narrowing reappear, but this time the smile looks somewhat stiff.】

##### Test Case: Taking Provocative Photos to Seek Fame

Usually, when we discuss internet celebrities who have become known through “aesthetic ugliness,” this expression tends to appear involuntarily. Adding visual stimulation makes the effect even more pronounced.

We tested a young woman who very much wanted to become famous. She had taken a series of large-scale, suggestive photos in an attempt to attract attention, establish herself in the entertainment industry, and advance her career. To determine her behavioral motivation, we prepared photos and television program video clips of a well-known internet celebrity referred to as “Sister X.” When the young woman saw the photos and videos, the expression shown in Figure 5-12 immediately appeared on her face.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图5-12]*

By analyzing this natural facial response, we confirmed that she harbored disgust toward “Sister X”’s appearance.

However, when several subsequent television program video clips were played, the young woman’s face displayed great excitement and attention. Although “Sister X” performed and spoke confidently and boldly in the programs, this did not increase the young woman’s disgust. Through capture and analysis of changes in the young woman’s gaze direction, we noted that her increased excitement was directly related to the successive appearance of logos from major television stations. Therefore, our analytical conclusion was that the young woman very much wanted to be noticed and become famous in the same way; being able to participate in programs on major television stations was the stimulus source that excited her. The disgusted feeling of revulsion remained limited to disgust toward “Sister X”’s appearance; she had no objection to the “aesthetic ugliness” method of achieving fame.

##### 5.2.1 Extreme Disgust: Vomiting

The most fundamental feature of the disgust expression originates from a bodily action: vomiting, as shown in Figure 5-1.

To open the mouth to its maximum, in addition to lowering the jaw, a person instinctively elevates the upper lip (note the shape of the opened mouth in the figure, with both corners of the mouth lifted upward—this is an exaggerated expression of the upper lip being raised). Elevating the upper lip engages two muscle bundles: the levator labii superioris and the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, as shown in Figure 5-2. It should be noted that these two muscle bundles cannot be moved independently; they always contract simultaneously. The difference is that the levator labii superioris is more easily controlled voluntarily, whereas the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi located on either side of the nasal bridge is usually controlled spontaneously by strong emotion. Therefore, in particularly intense disgust expressions the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi plays the dominant role; in ordinary-intensity disgust expressions the levator labii superioris plays the dominant role.

As shown in Figure 5-2:

1. Orbicularis oris
2. Levator labii superioris
3. Levator labii superioris alaeque nasi

In addition to opening the mouth, the vomiting action also triggers an instinctive linked response—tightly closing the eyes and furrowing the brows. Tightly closing the eyes requires contraction of the orbicularis oculi, which, together with the raised cheeks, compresses the eyelids, producing a strong eye-closure movement (though usually not complete closure) and forming arc-shaped wrinkles beneath the lower eyelids. The contraction of the orbicularis oculi serves, on the one hand, to prevent increased internal pressure caused by vomiting from injuring the eyeball and, on the other hand, to reduce negative visual stimulation from the stimulus source to a certain extent. It should be noted, however, that contraction of the orbicularis oculi is not deliberate; it is a natural reaction to the vomiting action.

##### 5.1 Generation of Disgust Emotion

Among all emotions triggered by negative stimuli, disgust belongs to a relatively mild reaction type; anger, fear, and sadness all produce more severe reactions than disgust.

The effectiveness of specific disgust stimulus sources is greatly influenced by different social cultures and education. For example, an outgoing personality does not become a disgust stimulus source in a social atmosphere that advocates and encourages individuality, yet it can very easily provoke disgust in others when placed in a conservative, strictly hierarchical social atmosphere.

We have done our best to summarize the universal characteristics of stimulus sources that can trigger disgust emotion in human society, offering these observations for further discussion.

An actor makes two evaluations of a disgust stimulus source: first, negation; second, inferiority—here “inferiority” refers to a level that is detestable yet not threatening enough to harm the actor’s interests.

Two examples illustrate this point.

A “self-important” person is, in almost every society and culture, the stimulus source most likely to provoke disgust in others.

Self-importance is not the same as an outgoing personality; it is unfounded outgoingness. The inner meaning of the term is that the actor is in fact “not” something, yet believes themselves to be that thing. Here “is” can be translated as correct, successful, noble, perfect, or any other affirmative evaluation. In short, the mindset “I am good, you (all) are bad” is the mentality of a person who is actually not very good yet considers themselves important. Having an excessively high self-evaluation and then using it as a basis for showing off, arguing, or rejecting others’ correct opinions is the behavioral pattern most likely to provoke disgust.

##### 2. Displeased Disgust

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图11-34]*

**2. [Expression Description]**

① Obvious brow-furrowing action (brow wrinkles) together with twisting of the inner one-third of both brows, brows raised upward; combined with eyelid morphology this is judged not to be fear and constitutes a necessary feature of sadness emotion;

② Upper eyelids pressed downward under the action of the orbicularis oculi, almost covering the upper half of the iris and remaining above the pupil. Because this is not natural drooping but forced closure to this position, it is not vacant staring; combined with the downward pressure of the brows it is judged to be a typical form of disgust expression;

③ Orbicularis oris shows slight contraction; the lips are not completely relaxed but slightly pursed outward, to a very small degree, while the mentalis also shows a coordinating action, indicating self-restraint and refusal to express one’s own viewpoint.

**Summary:**  
The morphology of the brows and the forced closure of the eyelids express displeased (displeasure belongs to the sadness category) disgust, primarily unhappiness (denial), using an ignoring gaze (appearing vacant) to indicate unconcerned contempt (belonging to disgust), forming a contradiction with the tightened brows; the slight restraining morphology of the mouth expresses an inner state of bearing pressure, reinforcing the expression of disgust emotion through silence. This indicates that the inner disgust is very strong, yet cannot be fully expressed through obvious facial expressions. The absence of necessary anger features also means the absence of external manifestations of offensive desire, so this is not anger.

##### Interesting Case

**Returned Overseas Subordinate Sneering at Director’s Dialect Accent**

If you encounter an extremely foolish person (in your own estimation), and that person still overestimates their ability to challenge you, yet you believe you possess the instantaneous capacity to handle them, and because the disparity in strength between you is excessively large, you will display this disdainful expression. If the other party is serious and earnest, your expression may remain merely disdainful; yet if the other party attempts some clumsy and foolish action (movement or speech), you will involuntarily reveal a sneering expression.

Once, during a meeting with mid-level managers of an IT company, everyone was discussing improvement plans for an internet application product. Because the design plan involved a large number of English terms, everyone was mixing Chinese and English while speaking. When the technical director of the development department explained with a noticeable dialect accent, I noticed a very slight sneering expression flash across the face of one of his subordinates.

The director was recognized within the company as an expert in development experience and technical ability, so it could be judged that this sneer was certainly not directed at the modification plan. After the meeting I asked the director whether XXX had studied abroad; he gave an affirmative reply.

This confirmed that the previous judgment was correct: the subordinate’s disdainful smile had been triggered by the director’s non-standard English pronunciation. Because the subordinate was very pleased with their own English pronunciation, they involuntarily revealed their inner emotion.
