##### 5.3.5 Micro-Expression Morphological Features of Disgust

Disgust, contempt, disdain, and sneering all belong to disgust emotions of varying intensity. All facial expressions of disgust emotions share one identical characteristic morphology: elevation of the upper lip, with the alae nasi also elevated and grooves appearing on either side of the alae nasi. The differences lie in the degree of muscle movement and the degree of coordination with other facial organs.

The nose plays a less important role in other expressions, yet becomes a typical indicator when disgust emotion arises. When no other obvious changes occur on the face, simultaneous changes in nasal morphology and the appearance of grooves on either side of the alae nasi allow us to easily judge the presence of disgust through this feature, even if the upper-lip action is obscured. As shown in Figure 5-16.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图5-16]*

Therefore, **the micro-expression morphological feature of disgust**, that is, the necessary feature of the disgust expression, is the movement of the levator labii superioris and the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi.

Visually this appears as upper-lip elevation with nasolabial folds on either side of the alae nasi. Under effective stimulation, if such a feature appears on the tested person’s face, it can be concluded that disgust emotion has arisen within them. The fundamental meaning of disgust emotion is negation.

##### Chapter 5 Micro-expressions of Disgust

If the nature of the effective stimulus is negative, and after an instant of surprise the person develops ideas of rejection and withdrawal, disgust will arise. Contempt and disdain are also derivatives of disgust-type emotions.

When you see the word “disgust,” the classic expression immediately forms in your mind: eyes narrowed (signaling “don’t look”), nose wrinkled (signaling “don’t smell”), corners of the mouth pulled back, and possibly the tongue extended (signaling “don’t eat”). This is correct; the original source of disgust is rejection of spoiled food.

Because ancient ancestors who ate spoiled food suffered severe physical discomfort, vomiting, illness, or even death, they instinctively rejected such items upon seeing, smelling, or tasting them—an evolutionary survival skill.

Interestingly, although modern people have a strong understanding of food safety and rarely encounter actual spoiled food, they still produce the same expression when confronted with people or situations they find distasteful—for example, obsequious but incompetent officials or ignorant and arrogant playboys—as if those people or things carried the odor or taste of decay.

##### Disgust

Disgust is a common expression. When people encounter something inconsistent with their cultural or moral environment or receive negative news, they display a disgusted expression. This is the outward manifestation of an inner resistance to something they dislike.

When disgust intensifies to the point that the emotion cannot be resolved internally, it transforms into anger, and an angry expression appears on the face. Psychologically, anger arises from dissatisfaction caused by external obstacles, delays, offenses, or self-punishment, which then develops into anger. An angry person’s brows furrow, the nostrils flare, and the person may also clench the fists or display other body language.

##### Test Case: Gory Visual Stimuli

Producing such an intense disgust expression requires a stimulus of very high intensity. Simple question or verbal stimuli rarely achieve this effect. In our experiments, only the video *Forensic Autopsy Demonstration* and certain gory post-disaster corpse photographs elicited disgust expressions approaching this level in participants.

This expression closely resembles the pain expression. The subtle difference is that in disgust the upper lip is raised higher and the nasolabial folds on either side of the nose are deeper. This may occur because viewing such distressing visual information triggers an instinctive self-protective aversion rather than actual pain.

##### 5.2.2 Full Disgust Expression

The muscle movements recruited by the physiological need to vomit form the primitive shape of the disgust expression, as shown in Figure 5-3.

On the basis of the primitive vomiting expression, the extreme disgust expression adds tightly closed lips while the eyes and eyebrows remain essentially unchanged. The expression appears to be a reaction to a foul odor that is steadily approaching: eyes closed to avoid seeing, nose wrinkled to avoid smelling, lips sealed to avoid tasting—strictly preventing any offensive information from entering the body.

Common expressions of disgust, contempt, and disdain each contain one or more of these facial features, differing only in number and degree.

##### Fine Lines Around the Nose and the Expression of Sniffing “Something Smelly”

The key feature of the “disgust” expression lies in the “fine lines around the nose.” The face shows actions such as “wrinkling the nose” or “raising the upper lip,” or both features appear together. “Disgust” encompasses negative emotions such as aversion, rejection, and dislike. The pathway of the “disgust” expression can be described as the action of blocking an unpleasant smell (wrinkling the nose). However, “disgust” is not merely a physical phenomenon of shutting out an unpleasant odor; the same expression appears toward a disliked person or an unwelcome statement. In evolutionary biology, the “disgust” expression functions as a warning signal to nearby companions about the presence of spoiled food.

##### Disgust

Disgust is a negative emotion that is difficult to reverse, yet it is necessary to determine exactly what the other person finds disgusting. If the person is disgusted by you, your efforts may be wasted. You must find ways to reverse the disgust, first establishing rapport and then continuing the conversation. If the stimulus for the other person’s disgust is something or someone else, the situation is much easier to handle. You can ask whether they have encountered something unreasonable and, if appropriate, offer to listen. While they are speaking, do not interrupt; wait until they finish before offering your own views.

##### 3. Summary of the Meaning of Disgust Expressions

Whether it is profound disgust or rejecting contempt, the core is an attempt to expel something disliked. Therefore the actions center on the nose and mouth and are usually accompanied by brow furrowing, jointly expressing the instinctive desire not to see, smell, or taste.

Disdain, however, is slightly different. It merely conveys a sense of looking down on someone and a strong feeling of superiority, without any desire to reject. Because the mindset is relatively relaxed, disdain is often accompanied by an incomplete smile with one corner of the mouth raised.

##### Analysis

Based on the baseline state (smiling appearance) and the reaction to homogeneous questions in the micro-reaction (微反应) psychological test, the expression that appeared when the subject answered whether they minded their overweight figure indicates that they do mind. The reply “There’s nothing I can do about it” expresses both non-acceptance of their figure and a sense of helplessness, consistent with the expression. “Just let it be” continues the helpless message while adding a slight tendency toward “not minding much.”

The morphological features of disgust micro-expressions—that is, the necessary features of the disgust expression—are the actions of the levator labii superioris and the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi muscles. Visually, the upper lip is raised and the nasolabial folds appear on either side of the nose, as shown in Figure 5-17.

When an effective stimulus is present, if the subject displays these features, it can be concluded that disgust has arisen internally. The fundamental meaning of disgust is negation.

##### 5.3 Morphological Features of Disgust Micro-expressions

In everyday interpersonal communication, such exaggerated external displays are rare unless deliberately performed for others. Most disgust expressions triggered by genuine emotion retain only part of the structural morphology of the vomiting expression, yet are considerably milder than actual vomiting. Different degrees of disgust manifest in different expression morphologies.

##### 11.2.2 Disgust

After evaluating the stimulus source, the individual judges it to be negative, generating a feeling of annoyance and an impulse to withdraw, yet without any desire to change or eliminate the stimulus source. This emotion is expressed as a disgust expression.

The most primitive stimulus source for disgust is spoiled food.

##### 5.2 Full Disgust Expression

A classic line from a Stephen Chow film states: “Vomit, keep vomiting, and you’ll get used to it.” When a person feels extreme aversion toward someone or something, the body produces a reaction similar to vomiting, as though invaded by the smell or taste of decay.

#### Contempt

##### The Case of the Sneer

There is a particularly interesting case involving sneering. A university once conducted a survey asking whether respondents could accept having a boyfriend or girlfriend who was overweight. Some participants stated outright that they could not accept it, while others, out of politeness, said they could consider it. One student was especially typical: when asked if he would mind his girlfriend being overweight, he said he would not mind and displayed an expression resembling a smile. Many were deceived by his expression; it was not a smile at all but a sneer. His mouth showed clear left-right asymmetry, with slight fine lines on the lower eyelids. When he raised the corners of his mouth, it was accompanied by a quick exhalation, somewhat like a “humph.” This was a clear sneer, indicating that he fundamentally looked down on overweight people and would never choose an overweight girl as a girlfriend.

Here it is worth reminding those who feel insecure about certain aspects of themselves not to be deceived by others and not to belittle themselves unnecessarily. Recognizing both oneself and others is equally important. To change the status quo, one must work to improve oneself—at minimum by enriching one’s inner qualities and strengthening one’s advantages.

The micro-expressions of the seven basic emotions reach their conclusion here. The knowledge provided only teaches some basic skills and should not be relied upon completely. If you wish to become a true micro-expression researcher, much more knowledge must be acquired, many more books must be read, and—most importantly—extensive practice is required. Many experts in micro-expressions examine hundreds or thousands of photographs and video clips daily to capture more accurate expression signals. Never experiment widely after learning only the basics; the results may not be effective or accurate. Inaccurate results can lead to embarrassment and trouble. Therefore, use micro-expression knowledge with caution. Let it serve as a tool for self-protection rather than a weapon for attacking or harming others.

##### Facial Features of Contempt

- **Eyebrows**: Due to contraction of the corrugator supercilii, the eyebrows furrow and are pulled downward by the orbicularis oculi, just as in disgust.
- **Eyes**: The orbicularis oculi contracts, causing the eyes to close slightly.
- **Mouth**: Contraction of the levator labii superioris and levator labii superioris alaeque nasi raises the upper lip, forming the nasolabial fold. The lower lip shows no obvious change. The mouth in contempt may be closed or slightly open.

This expression is commonly seen when we observe comical figures, such as certain internet celebrities. We feel contempt not only for their appearance but also for their self-promotion tactics.

The expression of disdain is much milder than contempt. The eyebrows remain relaxed without furrowing or downward pull, and the eyes show little obvious change—only a clear nasolabial fold, a slightly raised upper lip, and partial exposure of the upper teeth. Because the person feels extreme disregard and a sense of superiority, a smile appears, causing the corners of the mouth to lift slightly. If the lift is more pronounced, it becomes a sneer. A clear feature of a sneer is the asymmetry of the mouth. However, the eyes do change: as the smile widens, the orbicularis oculi contracts, though only mildly, producing slight wrinkles on the lower eyelids.

##### Contempt

Many psychologists regard contempt as a derivative of disgust or as mild disgust. Contempt nevertheless merits separate discussion because it occurs more frequently than disgust.

Contempt is likewise triggered by negative stimuli, yet the intensity is low and poses no threat to the individual. The person considers the stimulus unworthy of expending energy to confront, because the other party is perceived as far inferior.

Mild contempt manifests as disdain. Disdain is complete disregard—a dismissal that places the other person on an entirely different, lower level, not even worth a glance. Because the other is wholly beneath notice, the mind treats them as insignificant, generating a sense of ease that produces a smile: a cold smile or a sneer.

For example, if you represent one of the world’s top one hundred companies and the opposing representative comes from a firm of only thirty employees, and both of you are competing for the same client, the disparity in strength leads you to look down on the opponent and disbelieve they could possibly win the client—hence the disdain. If the opponent refuses to yield and then embarrasses themselves, you may laugh: that is a sneer.

##### Contempt

If the other person directs contempt toward you, the best response is to withdraw, because this negative emotion is difficult to reverse. Once the person is fixed in this attitude, even the best suggestions will be futile and will not leave a deep impression. At such moments, it is advisable to avoid direct conversation and instead have someone else convey your suggestions and views; this is far more effective than speaking directly.

If the contempt concerns an unrelated matter, there is no need for concern; it will not affect the outcome of your exchange. If the person says, for instance, “That was really foolish of him,” they are seeking your agreement. You may offer a few words of concurrence to satisfy their psychological need; this will facilitate further communication.

##### Be Careful with the Unilaterally Upward-Curving Corner of the Mouth

The key feature of the “contempt” expression is the “unilateral upward lift of the mouth corner”; among the seven basic expressions, it is the only one that is not left-right symmetrical. “Contempt” encompasses negative emotions such as superiority, disdain, and a cold attitude (cold smile). It appears when one feels superior in experience or knowledge to others or observes another’s immoral behavior. Individuals who display the “contempt” micro-expression tend to criticize others in daily life and generally hold negative views of others. The “contempt” expression does not appear on infants’ faces; it emerges only when a person begins comparing themselves with others. “Contempt” is the expression signal that arises when one feels the need to evaluate or judge another.

1. One side of the upper lip is raised, exposing the upper teeth, with nasolabial folds forming on both sides of the nose (disgust feature);
2. One corner of the mouth is noticeably lifted, with one cheek raised (smile feature);
3. The eyelids are closed, yet the lower eyelids show no bulging or tightening, and no smile lines appear beneath them (denial of genuine smile feature).

#### Surprise

##### 4.2.1 Physiological Significance of the Surprise Expression

Why does the face make these specific muscle movements to express inner surprise at the very first instant of an unexpected stimulus? Breaking it down point by point makes the reason clear.

1. The frontalis muscle contracts fully, raising the eyebrows significantly;
2. The levator palpebrae superioris muscle contracts; together with the frontalis, it lifts the upper eyelid substantially, widening the eyes and exposing the sclera above the upper edge of the iris, as shown in Figure 4-3;

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4-3]*

The combined contraction of the frontalis and levator palpebrae superioris opens the eyes wide. “Eyes opened wide” literally refers to an increase in the gap between the eyelids (technically called the “palpebral fissure”), but it actually implies greater exposure of the eyeball. A full expression of surprise matches this implication, even revealing the sclera above the iris. When relaxed, a person’s upper eyelid normally covers about one-quarter of the upper edge of the iris.

Opening the eyes this wide is an instinctive response to admit more light. In darkness (or a low-light environment) before the eyes have adapted, a person naturally opens the eyes wide rather than squinting as they would in bright conditions.

Thus, widening the eyes serves to see more clearly and gather as much visual information as possible, helping the individual assess the nature and potential impact of the stimulus source. The raising of the eyebrows is a secondary result: the frontalis is recruited to help open the eyes maximally. Using only the levator palpebrae superioris to lift the upper lid is both strenuous and less effective. You can test this yourself: while keeping the eyebrows still, try to open your eyes as wide as possible; you will feel the urge to raise the brows. Coordinated contraction of the frontalis makes the action easier and more efficient.

3. The mouth opens involuntarily, accompanied by a quick inhalation; only the lower lip drops slightly under the pull of the jaw (mandible), without tightening the lip surface or stretching it sideways, as shown in Figure 4-4.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4-4]*

At the instant of an unexpected stimulus, a person cannot yet determine whether the source is benign or dangerous. Evolutionary experience dictates that the first step is to inhale and store energy. After the brief moment of surprise (the assessment phase), if the stimulus is negative, the person will flee or fight—actions that demand substantial physical energy. Even if outwardly still, the rapid mental processing belongs to the derived escape or combat response (figuring out how to cope). If the stimulus is positive, the person may calmly resume the prior state or rush forward with cheers and excitement, expressing delight (pleasant surprise).

The mouth movement exists solely to draw in more air, preparing the body for the energy required in the next action of fleeing or fighting.

Therefore, the mouth change does not involve stretching the lips or surrounding muscles; such effortful actions do not occur in surprise. Only the jaw drops downward intentionally (in the direction favored by gravity, which is economical), opening the mouth for a rapid inhalation.

Darwin explained why the mouth drops open in surprise. When we suddenly notice something, he wrote, “the other organs of the body (such as the muscles) are forgotten and neglected”; the weight of the jaw causes it to drop, opening the mouth. This also supplies air for the shock, preparing for “flight from danger.”

Although this conjecture can now be refuted—because the jaw does not automatically drop when a person is fully unconscious—the skeletal and muscular structure of the jaws shows that opening the mouth is certainly a voluntary movement. Nevertheless, Darwin’s line of reasoning remains highly illuminating, and his attention to such minute expressive details more than a century ago still commands admiration for his scientific acuity.

You can also test this yourself: inhale rapidly through the nose only. If you pay close attention, you will notice that rapid nasal inhalation without opening the mouth requires considerable contraction of muscles near the throat—an awkward action, as shown in Figure 4-5. Hence, breathing through the mouth during surprise is the least costly and most efficient way to store energy.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4-5]*

4. The rest of the body remains motionless;

One purpose of stillness is to avoid unnecessary energy expenditure; the second is to assess the situation before acting. Moving randomly while the facts are unclear can lead to serious errors and place oneself in danger. This too is an evolutionary adaptation paid for with blood and lives in the wild, where the strong prey on the weak.

5. The interval from the onset of facial muscle contraction to maximum contraction is very brief; the true inner moment of surprise lasts only about one-quarter of a second.

The reason surprise emotion and expression are so short-lived was already discussed when explaining the cause of the surprise emotion. For an unexpected stimulus, taking too long to judge its nature and impact (usually a threat) would miss the optimal response window; at best one is mocked for “still not figuring it out,” at worst one encounters danger or loses life. The exaggerated performances seen in Stephen Chow films are merely a way to signal to the audience that the character is surprised; they may also serve a comedic purpose.

##### 4.1 Generation of the Surprise Emotion (9787554606841)

For animals, when everything is normal they go about their business at leisure. But when they sense any disturbance, they immediately use their acute sensory organs to integrate sounds, sights, smells, and even air movements to assess possible dangers in the environment. They stop all activity at once, raise their heads (because most sensory organs are concentrated there), and use eyes, nose, ears, and every hair on the body to evaluate a large amount of information in an instant:

- What is happening? Is there danger?
- What is the source of the danger?
- How many are there?
- How fast are they moving?
- How far away are they?
- Can our group guarantee our safety?
- Should we flee or fight?
- Which direction offers escape?
- ……

All these questions must be answered in roughly one second; otherwise life may be lost. Why is the reaction window so brief? Because in one second a cheetah running at full speed can close 35 meters—longer than the entire length of a basketball court (28 meters). If surprise lasted longer, the outcome would be predictable.

Through generations of evolution, humans have retained this same instinctive response.

Upon sensing an unexpected stimulus, a person stops all activity, fully activates every sensory organ, and strives to gather as much information as possible to decide the next action.

Although the interval is short, it is critical. In addition to the facial expression, the entire body coordinates to maintain intense concentration and rapid mental processing. Because the task is demanding, that brief instant consumes the full resources of the nervous system. The high level of neural focus and expenditure causes other bodily movements to decrease sharply or cease. On one hand, the nervous system has no attention to spare (it issues no commands to move), and extra movement would add to its load; on the other hand, remaining still allows assessment before action—unnecessary movement could bring disaster while the situation is still unclear. (See the book *Micro-reactions* (微反应) for details.)

The stimulus that triggers surprise emotion is relatively simple: an unexpected change that matters to the individual.

“Unexpected” means the change was not anticipated, either by conscious thought or by unconscious expectations. The stimulus may suddenly appear or disappear, shift from stillness to motion, or change from noise to silence—any of these can be directly perceived.

However, stimuli that produce a clear expression are usually those the person cares about, so their impact is strong. A windfall and a sudden calamity both trigger the same initial surprise expression, which later develops into delight or terror respectively. If the unexpected event has no meaningful consequence—for example, an unrelated stranger rounding a street corner (literally an “unexpected” encounter)—it will not affect the person, who therefore will not care and will not experience surprise. Hence the key point:

A stimulus capable of eliciting surprise must be an unexpected change that matters to the person.

We now turn to the morphological features of the surprise micro-expression.

4.2 The Most Surprised Expression

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4-1]*

If you feel the image contains elements of fear, first note the eyebrows and mouth. The relaxed lip shape and natural (untwisted) eyebrows indicate she is not afraid (fear expressions are covered in Chapter 7). From here, focus solely on the features of surprise.

If the stimulus is strong enough, the fullest surprise expression appears as in Figure 4-2.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4-2]*

1. The frontalis muscle contracts fully, raising the eyebrows significantly; in older individuals horizontal wrinkles appear on the forehead, while younger people may show a smooth forehead without wrinkles;
2. The levator palpebrae superioris muscle contracts; together with the frontalis, it lifts the upper eyelid substantially, widening the eyes and exposing the sclera above the upper edge of the iris;
3. The mouth opens involuntarily, accompanied by a quick inhalation; only the lower lip drops slightly under the pull of the jaw (mandible), without tightening the lip surface or stretching it sideways;
4. The rest of the body remains motionless;
5. The interval from the onset of facial muscle contraction to maximum contraction is very brief; the true inner moment of surprise lasts only about one-quarter of a second. Once contraction reaches its peak and stops increasing, the genuine surprise emotion has already ended; any remaining facial expression is consciously produced to communicate surprise to others, usually as a context-appropriate feedback signal (“I’m letting you know I’m surprised”).

##### 4.1 The Generation of Surprise Emotion (9789620756689)

For animals, when everything is normal they go about their business in a leisurely manner. But the moment they sense any disturbance, they immediately use their acute sensory organs to integrate judgments based on sound, vision, smell, and even air movement, assessing possible dangers in the surrounding environment. They halt all actions at once, raise their heads (since most sensory organs are concentrated in the head), and use their eyes, noses, ears, and every hair on their bodies to instantly process vast amounts of information:

- What is happening? Is there danger?
- What is the source of the danger?
- How many are there?
- How fast are they moving?
- How far are they from me?
- Can our group ensure my safety?
- Should I flee or fight?
- Which direction offers an escape route?
- …

All these questions must be answered in roughly one second; otherwise, life may be lost. Why is the reaction window so brief? Because in one second a cheetah running at full speed can close a gap of 35 meters, while a standard basketball court is only 28 meters long. If surprise lasts too long, the outcome is predictable.

Through generations of evolution, humans have retained this same instinctive response.

When an unexpected stimulus is perceived, all actions cease and every sensory organ is fully activated to gather as much information as possible for deciding the next move.

Although the interval is short, it is critical. In addition to facial expressions, the entire body coordinates to maintain intense concentration and rapid processing. Because the task is demanding, the nervous system expends its full capacity in that instant. This high concentration and consumption cause other bodily movements to decrease sharply or stop altogether. On one hand, the nervous system has no spare capacity to issue movement commands, and excess motion would add to its load; on the other hand, the pause allows for deliberate action—unnecessary movements could prove disastrous while the nature of the change remains unclear.

The stimulus that triggers surprise is relatively simple: an unexpected change that matters to the individual.

“Unexpected” means the person had not anticipated it, whether through conscious thought or unconscious expectation. The stimulus may appear suddenly, disappear suddenly, shift from stillness to motion, or change from noise to silence—any of these can be directly perceived.

Yet stimuli that produce clear expressions are usually those the person cares about, so their impact is strong. A windfall and a sudden calamity both elicit the same initial expression of surprise, which then develops into delight or terror respectively. A trivial, inconsequential surprise—for example, encountering an unrelated stranger at a street corner—will not affect the person and therefore will not generate surprise. Hence the principle:

Any stimulus capable of eliciting surprise in a person must be an unexpected change that matters to that person.

We now turn to the morphological features of the micro-expression of surprise.

##### Chapter Summary

The essence of surprise is that something unexpected yet relevant has occurred. Surprise registers an unexpected piece of information that matters. In nature, any stimulus worthy of an animal’s surprise may bear on survival or reproduction.

Surprise is nevertheless a neutral emotion. It registers only that an unanticipated yet relevant stimulus has arrived; it has not yet evaluated the stimulus’s nature or intensity. Consequently, the duration of surprise is very brief—extremely brief. This is the source of the well-known line from *Lie to me*: “Surprise lasting more than one second is fake.” Note, however, that the original dialogue carries the adverbial qualifier “during interrogation.”

During this brief instant the organism’s sole task is to gather as much information as possible for the central nervous system to judge, assess, and decide. In the facial expression the eyes widen to increase light intake; humans also raise the eyebrows to help lift the eyelids. In the limbs a freeze response appears, reducing unnecessary small movements so the central nervous system can concentrate. Occasionally a quick inhalation occurs, stocking the body with oxygen for subsequent action.

1. The micro-expression feature of surprise is the raising of the upper eyelid, exposing more of the superior margin of the iris than usual. Once this subtle change appears on an otherwise neutral face, surprise can be identified. Of course, surprise vanishes almost instantly and the face soon returns to baseline.
2. The typical morphology of a full surprise expression is: both eyebrows raised high, eyelids open, eyes widened and attentive, lower jaw relaxed and dropped, mouth parted for a quick, slight inhalation.

After the expression of surprise, the emotion may shift into any of the primary emotions: surprise turning to joy, surprise turning to disgust, surprise turning to anger, surprise turning to fear, or surprise turning to sadness. Surprise is the first reaction upon encountering an effective stimulus.

3. In actual testing, because of resistance and concealment, most people respond to an effective stimulus only by widening the eyes slightly; the mouth may open (a quick inhalation) but no further overt display occurs. Therefore, observing the subsequent emotional reactions after surprise is the correct way to apply the principle of surprise in testing.

**Full surprise—eyebrows and eyes**  
**Moderate surprise—eyebrows and eyes**  
**Slight surprise—eyebrows and eyes**

In testing, the appearance of surprise is a valuable analytical clue, because it arises from an unexpected stimulus that matters to the subject. Hence **surprise = effective stimulus**.

When using the principle of surprise emotion and expression in psychological testing, the following points should be observed:

- Design questions in advance as stimuli. Based on topics the subject is likely to care about, prepare questions or related facts the subject does not know but the examiner does, and present them at unexpected moments.
- Once a surprise expression appears, the matter has analytical value; the fuller the expression, the greater the value of the stimulus.

If the stimulus is negative, what elicits disgust? Foul odors, ugliness, and anything the person rejects can produce disgust.

 covertly recorded 20 subjects under ordinary unexpected (non-threatening) stimuli using PAL video. The average duration of genuine surprise—defined as maximum muscle contraction and maximum change in facial features—was 6 frames; standard PAL video contains 25 frames per second.

##### Surprise

Consider the following exchange:

A: Someone in the department passed away.  
B: What? (head snaps up, eyes widen, mouth slightly open) Wasn’t he under thirty?

This is the emotion of surprise—the immediate reaction upon receiving unexpected information. It contains many rapid thoughts: Is it true? What happened? Illness or accident? What should I do? Will this affect my work? Will the company hire someone new? Surprise quickly evolves into other emotions—regret, worry, sadness.

The classic expression—head raised quickly, eyes widened, mouth slightly parted—is shared by humans and animals. Anyone who has observed a dog attentively will notice that at the slightest sound outside the door the dog lifts its head, pricks its ears, and turns them toward the source to determine whether the sound poses a threat to itself or its owner.

In nature, the first sign of danger causes animals to freeze, raise their heads, and mobilize every available sense—smell, sound, sight—to gather information. They stand and lift their heads because most sensory organs are located there, allowing them to see farther and hear more clearly. Is there danger? Where is it coming from? Are there many? How long until they reach here? Is this place safe? Where would be safer? Can we win a fight?

All this information must be processed within one second; hence surprise lasts only about one second. Any longer and escape might be impossible. To preserve life and territory, a response must be formed quickly.

Humans are no different. In primitive societies hunting was the primary means of survival; failure to react swiftly could mean becoming prey. Over time this became an instinctive response: when an abrupt stimulus arrives, all activity stops, the head lifts, attention turns to the source, and a coping strategy is rapidly formulated.

With social progress, full surprise has given rise to many variants. People can display surprise without raising the head or even while facing away from the stimulus, because the mortal threat once posed by wild beasts no longer exists. Danger has diminished and sensitivity to stimuli has correspondingly decreased.

Like animals, human surprise expressions are very brief—under one second. More precisely, a genuine surprise expression lasts only a quarter of a second. Anything longer indicates the person is deliberately allowing time for others to notice, yet even then the expression rarely exceeds one second. Because the interval is short and the information load heavy, all senses are mobilized to assist cognition. The sudden energy demand causes the nervous system to reduce other movements so that resources can be redirected to the brain. The freeze also buys a moment to assess whether the stimulus will affect the individual and what action should follow.

##### Variations in the Degree of Surprise

Full surprise is easy to recognize, yet in contemporary society—except in moments of great joy or grief—it is rarely seen. People habitually mask their true feelings, fearing that overt display will be read at once. Consequently, surprise expressions are often attenuated. Another important factor is the abundance of modern information; few events now produce genuine astonishment.

The surprise most commonly observed in daily life is slight or moderate.

During a tender meeting, the marketing directors of three companies were competing. The director from Company A took a call. After listening for only a few seconds his eyebrows lifted, eyes widened, and mouth closed—an expression that lasted one second. He then glanced at the director from Company B before returning to normal. This was a slight surprise expression, indicating he had heard startling news; the glance at Company B’s director showed the news concerned that company. Shortly after hanging up, Company A’s director requested the tender committee investigate Company B, citing a report that B had illegally obtained other companies’ bid prices. At that moment the tender-committee representatives and Company C’s director displayed raised eyebrows, widened eyes, and slightly parted mouths—moderate surprise.

In a public setting a full surprise expression would be inappropriate. Company A’s director kept his lips closed to avoid revealing emotion, yet the eyebrow lift and eye widening still occurred involuntarily, and he glanced at Company B’s director. The tender-committee representatives and Company C’s director showed moderate surprise because they had no need to conceal it. Their mouths, however, were only slightly open, indicating the stimulus was not especially strong; they were already somewhat inured to such matters. The degree of mouth opening is therefore proportional to the intensity of surprise. The same holds for changes in the eyebrows and eyes. In moderate surprise the raising of the brows and widening of the eyes remain noticeable. In slight surprise the brow change becomes subtle or invisible; only the upper eyelid lifts, producing a very small widening of the eyes. This expression shows the person is actively suppressing surprise or that the stimulus itself is weak.

From these observations we reach the following conclusion: the micro-expression feature of surprise is the raising of the upper eyelid. This change occurs across the entire spectrum from full to slight surprise and is the only consistent movement. During surprise the eyebrows may not rise and the mouth may not open, but the upper eyelid always lifts. At the same time inhalation occurs, though when the mouth remains closed the nose performs the quick intake. The amplitude may be small, yet an inhalation is always present.

##### 4.3.2 Morphological Features of Surprise Micro-expressions

After the progressive reductions described in the previous section, we can see that even without participation of mouth morphology, or even without participation of eyebrow morphology, an inner state of surprise can still be expressed through elevation of the upper eyelids. We therefore specifically propose the morphological features of surprise micro-expressions; the more formal term is the “necessary morphological features” of a surprise expression (this term will be used in later passages that require rigorous discussion).

Necessary morphological features refer to the facial morphological characteristics that must not be absent from an expression.

For example, among all facial morphologies of a surprise expression, the eyebrows may not rise, the mouth may not open, yet the eyelids must lift, and at the instant the eyelids open wide there must be a simultaneous whole-body stillness; the inhalation action is performed by the nose, its amplitude may be difficult to observe, yet an inhalation tendency is certainly present. These necessary morphological features that constitute a surprise expression are the micro-expression indicators for judging that a person has experienced surprise emotion.

This section is very important for micro-expression research. We summarize the necessary morphological features of a surprise expression as follows:

1. Contraction of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle, elevation of the upper eyelids, and exposure of a larger portion of the iris than in the normal state, as shown in Figure 4-12.
2. At the same time the upper eyelids are raised, the entire body performs no other movement and exhibits an instantaneous pause. Without this instantaneous pause, the expression cannot be identified as surprise; it may instead indicate an offensive tendency of anger or an avoidant tendency of fear.
3. Although difficult to observe, during surprise there is an inhalation action, or merely an inhalation tendency. Therefore, failure to detect an inhalation action does not negate the presence of surprise, because it may simply be unobservable; however, detection of the opposite action—exhalation—confirms that the expression is not surprise and is more likely anger.

**Calm face**  
**Necessary features of surprise (minimal features)**

Such minute changes are, on the whole, essentially impassive; if the stimulus source is not insufficient in intensity, one must admire the subject’s restraint and composure.

The last time I attended a friend’s wedding, several classmates sat around a table discussing the current situations of various prominent figures from our old class, everyone talking animatedly. During the conversation I noticed two situations that commonly elicit surprise micro-expressions: one is when an erstwhile romantic expert from those years has still not married; the other is when someone has unexpectedly divorced.

##### 4.3.1 Common Surprise Expressions in Daily Life

In real life, more surprise expressions involve only partial facial muscle morphology.

The first type is surprise without mouth involvement, as shown in Figure 4-6:

① The eyebrows are not raised as high, and the eyes are not opened as wide. Yet compared with the normal state, the eyebrows are indeed raised and the eyes are indeed opened wider, as shown in Figure 4-7;

Normal-state eyebrow-eye combination  
Medium-surprise eyebrow-eye combination

② Mouth movements may be very small (a very slight parting) or even absent. Yet if the lips do not part, they must coordinate with a nasal inhalation action; of course the inhalation force is insufficient to produce visible tension and contraction of the neck muscles, as shown in Figure 4-8.

Full-surprise mouth  
Medium-surprise mouth

The second type is surprise in which even eyebrow elevation is almost invisible, leaving only upper-eyelid elevation, as shown in Figure 4-9:

Relaxed face  
Slight-surprise face

① Only upper-eyelid elevation remains. Subjective control or insufficient stimulus intensity may cause the eyebrows to show no obvious elevation change, as shown in Figure 4-10;

##### 4.4.2 Surprise Turning into Disgust

As shown in Figure 4-14, careful observation of the upper-eyelid morphology reveals a clear break in the upper-eyelid line under the pressure of the eyebrows. Without this straight line the eyelids would rise high and expose much of the iris. This micro-expression morphological feature proves the presence of surprise.

The most direct scenario that could produce the expression in the figure is probably: hearing for the first time that a friend’s beloved dog has fallen ill and is covered in lice all over its body.

The typical features of disgust are furrowed brows plus a deepened nasolabial fold; once these morphological features are added to surprise, the expression in the figure appears. Of course, in actual life the transition from surprise to disgust is not as obvious as in Figure 4-14.

**Test Case**  
Successful but family-disliked paranoid woman

In one actual test the subject was a public-interest figure who had received social attention and many awards and accolades, yet maintained deep conflicts with her own family, including spouse, children, and elders; the family felt great worry and disgust toward her. Background analysis and investigation revealed that this pattern was related to her childhood experience of parental divorce and subsequent upbringing by her paternal grandparents. Her behavioral mode was extreme paranoia: whatever she decided to do, she would not listen to others’ opinions, and whoever offered an opinion became an enemy.

The subject had long been on guard or resistant toward possible negative evaluations from us. When we gradually brought the conversation to the relationship between her upbringing and her current problems, we posed the question: “Have your parents already divorced? How old were you then?”

From video playback we observed that the subject’s body paused very noticeably, yet her facial surprise expression was not full and was almost imperceptible to the naked eye, showing only a slight elevation of the upper eyelids. Immediately afterward she furrowed both brows tightly, her face became as still as water, and she displayed serious concern about the question; judging from the nostrils flared to the sides and the slight grooves beside the nasal wings, the emotion following surprise was disgust. We surmised that her inner script at that moment was “Hmm?!” (How do you know? Why ask this question?)

##### Eyes Wide Open—Does It Represent “Surprise” or “Concern”?

After discussing the “concentrated” face, we turn to the “information-gathering” face of conversational messages. Actions such as “both eyebrows raised,” “eyes wide open,” and “mouth open wide,” whether singly or in combination, express “surprise” in emotional display and “interest/concern” in conversational messages.

Both are mechanisms of information gathering triggered by events in one’s surroundings; I call this category of actions the “information-gathering” face.

Consider the situation in which you yourself display the “information-gathering” face: on a crowded train, swaying, you suddenly hear someone speaking loudly two or three meters ahead. At that moment you turn toward the sound source out of surprise, curious about what has happened, and continue to gaze in the direction of the voice. This is the transition from “surprise” to “interest/concern.”

In this situation the eyebrows first rise and the eyes widen because of “surprise”; then, when the emotion shifts from “surprise” to “concern,” the brain begins to work and converts the emotion into conversational information, so that wide-open eyes become the only remaining facial action.

Next, consider the situation when the conversational partner displays the “information-gathering” face: imagine a negotiation scene in which the other party hides points of interest. At such moments the other party, in order to convey “I’m very interested in this topic!” or “I’m listening to you!”, readily shows raised eyebrows.

This is conversational information. In addition, when you begin to speak on a topic, if the other party shows a momentary raising of the eyebrows, this can be judged as a “surprise” micro-expression. From this “surprise” micro-expression one can detect that the other party wishes to conceal a point of interest.

To distinguish “surprise” micro-expressions from “interest/concern” within conversational messages, duration of facial expression actions, as with the “concentrated” face, is an effective criterion. A “surprise” micro-expression appears only for an instant, whereas conversational messages remain clearly visible for a period of time.

##### 4.4.3 Surprise Turning into Anger

Looking at this figure, one can immediately recall the common line: “What did you say?!” Note her tightly furrowed brows and wide-open eyes (almost the entire iris exposed); these are the morphological features of a surprise micro-expression. Of course, the raised eyelids are blocked by the lowered brows, covering part of the iris and forming thick eyelid skin folds (the oblique line commonly called “triangular eyes”). The combination of furrowed brows and upper-eyelid elevation constitutes the morphological features of an anger micro-expression.

After a rapid surprise lasting less than one second, the stimulus source is recognized as negative and poses a great threat to the actor’s interests (the core stimulus source of anger; see the chapter on anger), instinctively generating an attack impulse—this is startled anger.

The common life situation that produces startled anger is when a person who possesses a sense of control is provoked, despised, or even threatened by someone under that control.

**Anecdotal Case**  
Startled-anger speaker at a high-level forum

In 2008 I attended a large high-level Sino-American forum. The main participants from both countries were expert-level figures and foreign-affairs officials with high achievements in their respective fields. The Chinese side sent a vice minister to deliver remarks. During the remarks, however, an unexpected situation occurred—the microphone produced feedback.

From start to finish the feedback lasted no more than six seconds, yet those brief six seconds allowed me to observe a clear sequence of changes on the speaker’s face. At the first instant the remarks were interrupted by feedback, the speaker’s face showed momentary surprise; apart from the mouth not opening noticeably, the eyebrow and eye movements were complete. Under the continued stimulus of the feedback (duration unmeasured but indeed short), the surprise then turned into furrowed-brow, glaring anger, and the originally relaxed lower face became a clenched, tense state—commonly described as an ashen face. After the feedback subsided, the speaker glanced at the person in charge of conference services, then the facial expression returned to normal and the speaker calmly completed the remarks.

##### Chapter 4 Micro-expressions of Surprise

When a person receives an unexpected stimulus, the first emotion produced is surprise. Surprise is fleeting and is quickly followed by a return to normal or conversion into another emotion; the fuller the surprise expression, the greater the intensity of the stimulus source.

Humans and animals share one identical expression—surprise. Upon encountering an unexpected stimulus, a person, in the very first instant—extremely short—of receiving the stimulus information, stops all activity, raises the head, opens the eyes wide, raises the eyebrows, and slightly opens the mouth. Unfortunately, human ears cannot swivel; otherwise we would certainly also observe the ear-raising and turning toward the stimulus source seen in cats, dogs, rabbits, and other animals, listening for every slight sound.

Of course, human intelligence and level of civilization produce many derivatives of the standard surprise expression described above. For example, the classic surprise expression always involves raising the head so as to see farther and more. Humans can produce a surprise expression while maintaining various head postures—lowering the head, tilting the head, or even not turning the head toward the stimulus source (for instance, with the back to the stimulus source). All these derivatives arise because humans can finely grade the risk level of an unexpected stimulus source. Surprise expressions triggered by low-risk unexpected stimuli are almost unrecognizable, yet when the risk level of an unexpected stimulus is assessed as high, the person still reverts to the animal state and produces a complete surprise expression.

Conversely, if surprise expression features are observed on a person’s face, one can conclude that the stimulus source was unanticipated, has attracted strong attention, and that the person wishes to gather more information for judgment.

Such a stimulus source is of significant meaning to the actor.

##### 4.2.2 Major Surprise in Life

Almost every year we conduct recruitment of new employees. Because formal positions in public institutions are very “precious,” résumé submissions have always been numerous. The résumés we receive reflect a full spectrum of introverted, extroverted, and even boastful types. We pay special attention to applicants whose résumés contain actual cases and descriptions of relevant abilities.

Last year we encountered a fresh female master’s graduate whose grades, works, and experience left a deep impression; merely reading the résumé already confirmed her excellence. During the interview, when we raised a discussion topic (not really a question) about a new animation technique used in one of her works, she immediately displayed a classic subtle surprise expression that then turned into a confident smile. This classic expression arose because she had not expected us to examine the résumé so closely (résumé screening is indeed not usually so detailed), to pose such a precise question, and to hit upon her specialty so exactly. After review by the higher department, when the employment notification call was connected, her tone alone made it clear how delighted she was, because a full second passed before she loudly confirmed and expressed thanks. Unfortunately, I was unable to see that instant of surprise expression; it must have been very full.

[1] We conducted covert filming of experimental subjects. Under ordinary unexpected stimuli (no harmful tendency), analysis of PAL-format video data showed that the true duration of surprise (maximum muscle contraction, maximum change in facial organs) for 20 subjects averaged 6 frames, while standard PAL-format video contains 25 frames per second.

##### Facial Expression Analysis

Eyebrows raised high and upper-eyelid elevation are features of a surprise expression; one second later, upon learning that the outcome far exceeds subjective expectations, the expression turns to joy. An open mouth, upturned corners of the mouth, and deepened nasolabial folds are all signs of a smile.

Spectators watching a ball game often display this expression. When the weaker team ultimately wins, the fans experience brief surprise followed by elation—this is what we commonly call pleasant surprise.

A person who earlier said they could not return for your birthday suddenly appears on your birthday—that is pleasant surprise; someone you thought disliked you suddenly confesses—that is pleasant surprise; receiving a long-desired gift from someone else—that is pleasant surprise; winning a big prize—that is pleasant surprise. Yet sometimes pleasant surprise is not so easy to produce and may backfire.

Still using the birthday example: you meticulously plan a birthday party for a friend and, in order to create a surprise, deliberately create various troubles on that day. Moderate trouble is acceptable, but once you create trouble the friend finds quite troublesome, the plan may fall through. For instance, you pretend to lose a document; you think it unimportant, yet to the friend it represents the fruit of hard work. When the fruit is destroyed, the first emotion produced is anger. Even if you later tell the friend that the document was not lost and that it was only a well-intentioned joke, the friend will probably not appreciate it. If pleasant surprise is mishandled, it can easily become fright without delight.

Therefore, if you wish to surprise someone, you must understand that person’s personality preferences, work style, and psychological needs; never make the self-righteous mistake that turns a pleasant surprise into a fright.

##### 4.4.4 Surprise Turning into Fear

After a rapid surprise lasting less than 1 second, discovering that the stimulus source poses an overwhelming threat that could directly cause significant harm to the actor's safety results in panic, as shown in Figure 4-16.

We have known since childhood that snakes are terrifying animals—sinister, vicious, and quick-moving, with snakebites being very serious. Therefore, upon suddenly spotting a thick, long snake on the beam or under the bed, one first stares intently (surprise), then quickly retreats and flees in panic (possibly knocking over several pieces of furniture), with the facial expression stemming from deep-seated fear.

In addition to facing stimuli that may cause natural harm, people also experience panic in another type of situation.

Having previously engaged in illegal or criminal acts or violated other social norms (morals), at the moment of exposure, when the actor confirms that their actions have been discovered by others and that severe punishment will inevitably follow, panic arises. Company financial personnel who violate company regulations and relevant laws by embezzling public funds to speculate in stocks or buy lottery tickets for personal gain are frequently reported in the news. Such matters are feared to be known by others; if the money can be replenished and no one insists on pursuing the matter, one might get away with it and quietly amass a fortune. But if losses occur or someone insists on auditing the accounts, at the moment when concealment fails, the individual will experience panic.

##### Test Case

A Paranoid Woman Who Achieved Career Success but Was Not Loved by Her Family

In one actual test, the subject was a public-interest figure who had received social attention and won many awards and accolades, yet deep conflicts existed between her and her family, including her spouse, children, and elders; her family members felt great concern and aversion toward her. Through background analysis and investigation, we found this related to her childhood experience of her parents' divorce and subsequent upbringing by her grandparents. Her behavioral pattern was one of extreme paranoia: whatever she decided to do, she would not listen to others' opinions, and anyone offering an opinion became an enemy.

The subject had long harbored defensiveness or resistance in her heart toward any negative evaluation we might make. As we gradually drew out the connection between her upbringing and her current problems, we posed the question: "Have your parents already divorced? How old were you at the time?"

From video playback, it could be observed that the subject's body froze very noticeably in her reaction, yet the surprised expression on her face was not sufficiently pronounced and was almost imperceptible to the naked eye, showing only a slight lift of the upper eyelids. This was followed by tightly furrowed brows and a somber, water-like expression indicating serious concern about the question. Judging from the nostrils pulled to the sides and the slight grooves on either side of the nasal wings, the emotion following surprise was disgust. We speculated that her inner monologue at that moment was "Huh?!" (How do you know this? Why ask this question?)

##### 4.2 The Most Surprised Expression

If you feel at this moment that this image contains elements of fear, first please note her eyebrows and mouth. Based on her relaxed lip shape and natural eyebrows (not twisted), it can be judged that she is not afraid (see Chapter 7 for the expression of fear). Therefore, next, simply focus fully on the characteristics of surprise.

If the stimulus source is sufficiently strong, the fullest surprised expression should appear as shown in Figure 4-2.

1. The frontalis muscle contracts fully, raising the eyebrows significantly; in older people, horizontal wrinkles appear on the forehead, while in younger people the forehead may remain flat without wrinkles;
2. The levator palpebrae superioris muscle contracts; together with the contraction of the frontalis, this raises the upper eyelids substantially, widening the eyes and exposing the sclera above the iris;

③ The mouth opens involuntarily in coordination with a rapid inhalation; only the lower lip, driven by the chin (mandible), opens naturally and slightly downward, with the skin on the lip surface remaining untightened and not stretched to the sides;
④ Other parts of the body remain motionless;
⑤ From the onset of facial muscle contraction to the point of maximum contraction, the duration is very short; the true moment of inner surprise lasts approximately 1/4 second[1]. Once contraction reaches maximum and ceases to increase further, it indicates that the genuine surprise emotion has already disappeared; the retained facial expression afterward is the actor consciously displaying surprise to the outside world, usually as a contextually appropriate feedback method (I am telling you, I am very surprised).

##### 4.2.2 Major Surprises in Life

We conduct recruitment of new employees almost every year. Because formal positions in public institutions are very "precious," applicants have always flocked to them in large numbers. The résumés submitted represent our first contact with candidates; they come in all varieties—introverted, extroverted, and even boastful. We pay special attention to those résumés that include actual cases and descriptions of relevant abilities.

Last year we encountered a fresh female master's graduate whose grades, works, and experience left a deep impression on us; merely reading the résumé was enough to confirm her excellence. During the interview, when we raised a discussion topic (not really a question) about a new animation technique used in her work, she immediately displayed the classic subtle surprised expression, which then turned into a confident smile. This classic expression arose because she had not expected us to examine her work so closely (résumé reviews generally are not this detailed) or to pose such a precise question that aligned so perfectly with her strengths. After review by the superior department, when the hiring notification call came through, her tone alone made it clear how delighted she was, as a full second passed before she loudly confirmed and expressed gratitude. Unfortunately, I was unable to see that instant of surprised expression, but it must have been very full.

##### Fun Case

An Angry Speaker at a High-End Forum

In 2008 I attended a large high-end Sino-American thematic forum. The main participants from both countries were expert-level figures and diplomatic officials with high achievements in their respective national fields. The Chinese side sent a vice minister to deliver remarks. However, during the remarks an unexpected situation occurred—the microphone produced feedback due to audio issues.

The feedback lasted no more than 6 seconds from start to finish, yet in those brief 6 seconds I observed a clear sequence of changes on the speaker's face. In the first instant the remarks were interrupted by feedback, the speaker displayed an instantaneous surprised expression; although the mouth did not open noticeably, the movements of the eyebrows and eyes were fully present. Under the continued stimulus of the feedback (duration not statistically measured, but indeed very short), the surprised state then turned into anger with furrowed brows and glaring eyes, and the originally relaxed lower face became a clenched, tense state—commonly described as a livid face. After the feedback diminished, the speaker glanced at the person in charge of conference affairs, then the expression returned to normal and the remarks were completed as if nothing had happened.

##### 4.4.1 Surprise Turning into Joy

The raising of the upper eyelids and the full exposure of the sclera above the iris prove the presence of the surprise emotion.

After a rapid surprise lasting less than 1 second, discovering that the stimulus source is positive and of great intensity, capable of producing strong satisfaction and pleasure, results in delight.

Winning a large lottery prize or achieving victory in a thrilling competition will produce the above expression. A common technique in film and television dramas for creating surprise is to first suppress before elevating. On the protagonist's birthday, relatives and friends deliberately create depressing situations—such as not mentioning birthday wishes or manufacturing scenarios that cause the protagonist to become busy, fail, embarrassed, or frustrated—then, when the protagonist is at an emotional low point, they resolve all misunderstandings and hold a grand birthday celebration. As long as the preceding negative stimuli are not excessive, this emotional-stimulation technique can achieve a universally satisfying outcome.

##### FBI Case

It is worth noting that if a person's surprised expression lasts longer than 1 second, it must be fake. In an American murder case, the suspect was a young man who disappeared after committing the crime. FBI agents located the suspect's father and asked whether he knew the suspect's whereabouts. The father insisted he had long since severed the father-son relationship and had not been in contact for several years. When the agents mentioned the fact of the suspect's murder, the father produced a classic surprised expression: he stopped what he was doing, turned to face the agent, slightly opened his mouth, widened his eyes, and raised his eyebrows. He intended this expression to tell the agent that he truly had not met the suspect and knew nothing about what the suspect had done. However, his surprised expression lasted far longer than 1 second. The FBI agents determined that the surprised expression was feigned, indicating he had already met the suspect and knew what the suspect had done. As expected, by following the father the agents ultimately located the suspect's hiding place.

##### Eyebrows Raised, Eyes Widened

Due to contraction of the frontalis muscle, the eyebrows are raised substantially while contraction of the levator palpebrae superioris raises the upper eyelids, widening both eyes and thereby completing the surprised expression in the upper half of the face.

Widening the eyes exposes more of the eyeball, allowing more light to enter so that the situation can be seen more clearly. In low-light environments, one must work hard to widen the eyes in order to see something clearly. When animals hear any rustling, they raise their heads and widen their eyes to see the stimulus source clearly and assess its potential impact. Humans are the same: widened eyes obtain more and clearer visual information, facilitating judgment and response. The upward raising of the eyebrows assists in widening the eyes, because the levator palpebrae superioris alone cannot open the eyes to the maximum. You can try it yourself: widen your eyes as much as possible without moving your eyebrows. You will find that once the eyes reach the desired degree of widening, the eyebrows must rise.

##### Surprise Turning into Disgust

The brows furrow under the action of the corrugator supercilii, and the nasolabial folds deepen—these are characteristics of the disgust expression. The upper eyelids are raised, yet because they encounter the furrowed, downward-pressing brows, slight creases appear on the upper eyelids; this nevertheless remains a characteristic of the surprise expression.

A well-regarded public figure was being interviewed. The reporter had previously asked only official questions, to which the subject responded fluently and with composure. But when the reporter asked, "Did you secretly divorce your wife last month?" the subject paused for less than 1 second; the upper eyelids lifted slightly while the eyebrows and mouth showed no change—this was mild surprise, with the subtext "How did this get out? How do you know?" Quickly the expression changed: the brows furrowed and a slight nasolabial fold appeared, typical of disgust, with the subtext at that moment being "Why ask such a question? I don't want to answer." From this it could be judged that the initial surprise had turned into disgust.

##### 4.4 Combinations of Surprise with Other Emotions

Relative to the other five universal expressions, surprise is the "smallest" expression. This smallness refers not only to its shortest duration but also to the fact that surprise itself is a "neutral" emotional response. Happiness is a positive emotional response, while disgust, anger, fear, and sadness are all negative emotional responses; only surprise is an instantaneous judgment process. Therefore, surprise is usually followed by a transition into another emotion. In that brief instant, a person has already determined the nature and intensity of the stimulus source and will immediately produce a corresponding subsequent reaction based on that determination: positive stimuli trigger positive emotions and reactions, negative stimuli trigger corresponding negative emotions and reactions, and the greater the intensity of the stimulus source, the greater the degree of reaction.

Usually, the emotions that immediately follow surprise are joy, disgust, anger, and fear, forming the composite expressions delight, disgust-surprise, anger-surprise, and panic, respectively.

##### Surprise

Covering the mouth with the hand while speaking is a behavior indicating surprise, doubt, tension, deception, or lack of confidence (see Figure 4.32). When a person feels sorry or regretful about what they are saying, they may also cover their mouth with a hand, as if trying to prevent their words from coming out. Law-enforcement officials typically view this gesture as an attempt to conceal the truth or fabricate a lie.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.32　以手捂嘴，表示惊讶]*

Many parents are very familiar with this action; when their child is trying to explain something and repeatedly covers their mouth with a hand, the parents intuitively know she is lying. This is because if the child were completely confident in what she was saying, her hands would not be near her mouth.

##### The Nature of Surprise

Surprise is the most easily overlooked of the seven major emotions, not only because it lasts a short time but also because it rarely exists in isolation and often appears only after transitioning into another emotion. It is a transitional emotion, also called a neutral emotion. Among the seven major emotions, anger, sadness, disgust, fear, and contempt are negative emotions, happiness is a positive emotion, and only surprise cannot be classified into any of those categories.

When good news is heard, surprise turns into delight; when bad news is heard, surprise turns into sadness or anger; when an annoying piece of news is heard, surprise turns into disgust or contempt; when threatened, surprise turns into fear.

In the space of one second the brain has already processed all the information, so the emotion then evolves into something else.

##### Surprise Turning into Anger

When surprise is followed by the discovery that the stimulus carries a threat, surprise turns into anger. At this point, although the upper eyelids attempt to rise, they encounter the downward-pressing brows, forming obvious creases; the entire eye appears triangular. The tightly furrowed brows indicate negative emotion toward the stimulus source. The combination of downward-pressing brows and raised upper eyelids forms the typical anger expression.

Surprise turning into anger usually occurs when loss of control has placed the person under threat.

This expression is commonly seen at large public events when a host or leader is speaking onstage and sudden discordant commotion arises from the audience. The person onstage will pause briefly; after about 1 second the brows press down and furrow. Although changes in the mouth may not be great, the anger following surprise is already very obvious.

##### The Expression of Surprise

Both eyes and mouth open wide in a startled expression.

The key features displayed by the "surprise" expression are "widened eyes and mouth"; when "both eyebrows raised upward" + "eyes widened" + "mouth opened" appear, "surprise" can be judged.

"Surprise" encompasses emotions such as astonishment, bewilderment, and being dumbfounded. "Surprise" indicates that something unexpected has occurred. The eyes widen in order to grasp the situation, and the mouth opens in order to breathe fully, thereby obtaining more information.

In evolutionary biology, the "surprise" expression signals to surrounding companions that an unanticipated event has occurred.

##### 4.4.5 Surprise Turning into Sadness

Accidentally causing trouble or receiving bad news is surprise turning into sadness.

At one time a member of our research group became obsessed with a certain smartphone and would play its curling game frantically whenever bored. One day, because of excessive force, the phone flew out of its old protective case at the moment the finger slid and struck, landing solidly on the floor; the originally smooth touchscreen developed artistically cracked glass patterns. The instantaneous change of expression in that moment was the classic process of surprise turning into sadness.

##### Mouth Opened Wide

The mouth opens wide in coordination with a rapid inhalation. Because it is impossible to judge whether the stimulus source will produce a positive effect, an inhalation occurs to store energy for response. Once it is determined that the effect is negative, the stored energy is used for fight or flight. If the effect is positive, the stored energy supports the person in jumping up or giving a hug.

Precisely because the mouth opens wide only for inhalation, very few muscles are involved; it is sufficient for the mandible simply to open naturally. On the other hand, air inhaled through an open mouth is far more abundant and carries far more energy than air inhaled only through the nose with the mouth closed; therefore, when suddenly stimulated, the mouth opens to allow a sufficient volume of air to enter the oral cavity.

##### Surprise Turning into Fear

When it is realized that the threat is sufficiently powerful to cause harm to oneself, surprise turns into fear.

Try to imagine: if you are playing in a zoo and suddenly discover a wild beast has escaped, you will first be stunned, pause for about 1 second, then immediately realize your life is under threat and turn to panic, with blood rushing to both legs in preparation for flight.

We also often see such scenes on television programs: after a criminal suspect is discovered by the police, the suspect may first stand still—sometimes for less than 1 second—then, upon realizing possible arrest, display a fearful expression and prepare to flee. Some economic criminals also display this expression when exposed.

##### The Triggering and Transformation of Surprise

The stimulus source capable of triggering surprise is an unexpected change in the matter the person cares about most. "Unexpected" means a possibility the person had not considered. "Cares about most" must be subjectively anticipated by the person. The greater the anticipation, the greater the stimulus the change produces for the person. For example, hearing long-awaited good news turns into delight; hearing the bad news of a relative's death turns into panic, which quickly turns into sadness.

As mentioned earlier, a full surprised expression features raised eyebrows, widened eyes, and an opened mouth. Here we need to analyze why these physiological reactions occur.

##### 1. Morphology of a Full Surprised Expression

The appearance of an unexpected stimulus source for the person produces a surprised expression.

The morphological characteristics of a full surprised expression are as follows:
- The frontalis muscle contracts fully, raising the eyebrows substantially;
- The levator palpebrae superioris muscle contracts; together with the contraction of the frontalis, this raises the upper eyelids substantially, widening the eyes and exposing the sclera above the iris;
- The mouth opens involuntarily in coordination with a rapid inhalation; only the lower lip, driven by the chin (mandible), opens naturally and slightly downward, with the skin on the lip surface remaining untightened and not stretched to the sides.

##### 4.3 Morphological Features of Surprised Micro-expressions

In real life, full surprised expressions are very rare. There are two reasons: first, people have seen a lot; even if they have not witnessed something in person, they have seen it across various public media, so stimuli capable of provoking great surprise are few; second, people have been heavily socialized not to display obvious expressions that would make them appear overly exposed. Individuals always attempt to mask and conceal their negative emotions, because an overly direct display of feeling produces the same effect as shouting one’s inner thoughts aloud for everyone nearby to hear.

##### 3. Morphological Features of Surprised Micro-expressions

Whether caused by subjective control and suppression or by insufficient intensity of the stimulus source, such subtle expressions may result.

The smallest surprised expression retains only the raising of the upper eyelids, while the eyebrows may show no obvious lifting.

**Summary**: The appearance of a surprised expression indicates the suddenness of the stimulus source—unexpected by the individual involved; such stimulus sources are usually effective ones.

##### 2. Common Morphological Features of Surprised Expressions

When the intensity of the stimulus source is reduced, the morphological features of surprised expressions more commonly seen in daily life are as follows:
- Eyebrows raised, upper eyelids lifted, exposing more of the upper margin of the iris than usual.
