##### The Psychological Defenses of a Braggart

The subject was a staff member at a public institution who, dissatisfied with a mundane and constrained daily life, invented a so-called folk science on a socially sensitive hot-button topic. Because the theme was sensitive, several mainstream media outlets embraced it enthusiastically. Television stations from central to local levels invited him to record programs; newspapers and magazines interviewed him repeatedly; for a time even overseas media took notice. The individual proudly publicized these “achievements” on his blog. Although mainstream outlets generally criticized the folk science he promoted, their coverage only amplified his visibility—an unintended outcome.

Previously, on a program aired by a top-tier national television channel, he had stumped a well-known psychologist. In his own words, “the expert was incompetent, which made me contemptuous.” Buoyed by that experience, he arrived to challenge another program that featured a different prominent expert. Commissioned by the production team, we conducted a psychological assessment of the man.

After examining the personal history he had published, we found numerous internal contradictions; virtually the entire promotional narrative appeared fabricated. Such an extreme case was rare in our prior experience. We therefore devised an enthusiastic testing plan: begin with minor details, use pointed questioning to dismantle his façade, first psychologically overwhelm his confidence and defenses, after which the core questions would become straightforward. Once lies are exposed several times in succession, most people can no longer perform or maintain the pretense smoothly.

Knowing he claimed to have been a soldier, received special training, and piloted aircraft, I chose the highly questionable claim of “having flown a plane” as the first point of attack.

**Question:** Have you ever piloted an aircraft?  
**Answer:** (He froze for a moment, then produced an awkward smile.) I can. I have flown, but I don’t fly every day.

[Analysis: The momentary freeze was a startle response; the slight surprised expression on his face likewise showed he had not expected the very first question to target this minor detail from his promotional narrative. The awkward smile already foreshadowed the direction of the test, because embarrassment is a derivative of fear, as noted earlier.]

**Question:** Have you ever taken off?  
**Answer:** Never taken off. I’ve only taxied on the runway.

[Analysis: The reply pattern—retreat one step, then advance half a step—is the mark of someone unwilling to concede. Yet the overall backward movement clearly indicated psychological disadvantage. Choosing the “never taken off” answer may have stemmed from his genuine inability to fabricate the sensory and technical details that would follow a takeoff.]

**Question:** What type of aircraft?  
**Answer:** (Slight hesitation) Fighter jet.

**Question:** Which specific model?  
**Answer:** J-6. (His nervous system was highly tense; he adopted a combat posture, head tilted forward, eyes alert.)

[Analysis: Once the first “type of aircraft” question was asked, he understood what we were probing. The slight hesitation was spent fabricating the specific model. The combat posture and alert state fully demonstrated that he perceived the threat posed by the question.]

**Question:** As far as I know, you never served in the air force. Would the military allow someone without flight experience to pilot an aircraft?  
**Answer:** Yes. It was a friend of mine, deputy commander of their flight regiment. (He maintained the combat posture, yet his gaze shifted slightly downward.)

[Analysis: The slight downward shift in gaze indicated mounting internal pressure. Continued maintenance of the combat posture showed he had not yet abandoned the attempt to lie.]

**Question:** When the aircraft taxied on the runway, how did you control acceleration and deceleration?  
**Answer:** Just like a car—don’t keep pressing the throttle all the way down and it will taxi without taking off. Step on the brakes and the plane slows down. (Gaze began to drift; eyebrows and eyes showed slight fear characteristics.)

[Analysis: Aircraft acceleration is achieved by advancing the throttle lever; ground deceleration normally involves main-wheel brakes, speed brakes, and reduced engine thrust. The answer revealed that the subject had never entered a cockpit to start and taxi an aircraft. Realizing he could no longer fabricate details, he also sensed the threat inherent in the meticulous detail-oriented questioning—exposure of his self-aggrandizement.]

**Question:** Does the J-6 have a throttle and brakes?  
**Answer:** No throttle; you press buttons. I only controlled the stick; another pilot set all the procedures. (After finishing, his face displayed the worried expression of tightly closed lips; he avoided eye contact and his gaze dropped completely downward.)

[Analysis: Unable to fabricate a plausible answer, he began shifting the fabrication. At this point he was grasping at straws; the newly invented information was even less credible.]

**Question:** Did that pilot allow you to operate the aircraft yourself?  
**Answer:** No. I sat in front, he sat behind; I operated the stick in front.

**Question:** How many seats does the J-6 have?  
**Answer:** … (Speechless, a guilty expression appeared.)

[Analysis: The J-6 cockpit has only one pilot seat. Unaware of this objective fact, the subject realized he could no longer maintain the pretense, abandoned resistance, and displayed a guilty expression. Guilt is a derivative of self-reproachful sadness and equates to an admission. Chapter 8 will explain this in detail.]

At this point, detail-oriented questioning had successfully dismantled a lie that was, for him, inconsequential. Throughout the process his emotions shifted from surprise to mild anger, then to mild worry; once he recognized he could no longer fabricate consistent details, his expression settled into the classic worried look of tightly closed lips. This classic micro-expression (微反应) revealed the fear inside him, indicating the questions had pushed him to a critical threshold and his psychological defenses would soon collapse.

After several similar questions, the subject’s defensive and resistant mindset vanished; he understood that lying was no longer easy. Consequently, when later questioned about fabricated supporting data for the folk science he had invented, the interrogation required far less effort.

##### 7.2 Full Fear Expressions

Only when facing a life-or-death crisis does a person rarely display a full fear expression, which comprises three basic typical features: eyebrows drawn together and raised, eyes widened, and mouth open, as shown in Figure 7-1.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图7-1]*

Viewing this full fear expression inevitably recalls the full anger expression discussed in the previous chapter; the two are highly similar—furrowed brows, widened eyes, open mouth. If summarized in words alone, the features appear identical. Therefore we compare them visually in Figure 7-2.

Full fear image  
Full anger image

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图7-2]*

We trust that any normal observer can instantly distinguish the two expressions. The challenge lies in articulating the precise differences; doing so requires comparatively professional observational skill. Figure 7-3 provides the analysis.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图7-3]*

① At first glance both images show lowered and tightly furrowed brows. Closer inspection reveals that in the fear image the brows are raised, whereas in the anger image they are drawn inward and downward. This is the difference between the so-called “8:20” brow shape and the “10:10” brow shape. Because fear raises the brows, an inverted “U”-shaped fine wrinkle forms in the middle of the forehead, as shown in Figure 7-4; such lines are deeper and more pronounced on Western faces.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图7-4]*

② Both expressions raise the upper eyelids to the maximum. When confronted with a threatening negative stimulus, whether the impulse is to fight (anger) or to flee (fear), the goal is to see the stimulus as clearly as possible. Yet the differing direction of brow muscle effort produces different angles of skin folds on the upper eyelids. Sometimes, especially on younger faces, the brow raise is not obvious and the brows appear merely horizontal; the upper-eyelid skin fold can then serve as an auxiliary indicator of brow elevation, as shown in Figure 7-5.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图7-5]*

③ Although both expressions open the mouth—sometimes even shouting—the width and height of the opening differ subtly. The mouth shape of fear cannot produce a sharp, threatening sound. The differing mouth shapes also produce completely different nasolabial folds, as shown in Figure 7-6.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图7-6]*

Thus, although the overall appearances are similar, the fine differences cause the two expressions to convey entirely distinct meanings. This is one method we use to study micro-expressions. By dissecting a facial expression, identifying its typical and necessary morphological features, one can move beyond ordinary experiential recognition and directly access the person’s true inner state.

We now dissect the full fear expression in detail, examining its muscle movements and morphological features, as shown in Figure 7-7.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图7-7]*

① Corrugator supercilii contracts, drawing the brows together and forming vertical wrinkles;  
② The medial fibers of the frontalis contract, raising the inner brows and creating an inverted-U wrinkle on the forehead;  
③ Levator palpebrae superioris contracts in an attempt to raise the upper eyelid, but because the opposing actions of the orbicularis oculi and corrugator supercilii are inhibited, a diagonal fold forms on the upper-eyelid skin. Without inhibition, the superior margin of the iris would be fully exposed (dashed line in Figure 7-7);  
④ Levator labii superioris and levator labii superioris alaeque nasi contract together, raising the upper lip and exposing the upper teeth;  
⑤ Platysma contracts, pulling the corners of the mouth laterally so that the horizontal width of the mouth exceeds its resting state;  
⑥ Depressor labii inferioris contracts, pulling the lower lip downward and exposing part of the lower teeth.

After studying the sadness expression in the next chapter, you will see that **the fear expression is a combination of surprise and sadness—essentially sadness that has been prepaid after surprise**. Fear arises when a stimulus exerts overwhelming intimidation; the person feels unable to resist (resistance would be anger) and believes a tragic outcome is imminent (though it has not yet occurred), so the only response is attempted flight or even surrender. Once the tragic outcome materializes, sadness follows. We therefore compare the fear expression with the surprise expression discussed earlier, given their natural connection, as shown in Figure 7-8.

##### 7.3.1 Different Degrees of Fear Emotions

Fear encompasses several derivative emotions of varying intensity. In ascending order of emotional fullness, they can be listed as four distinct states: **worry**, **anxiety**, **fear**, and **terror**. To clarify the distinctions among these four states, consider a threat event that harms one’s own interests as the stimulus source. The four states are differentiated as follows:

The **stimulus source** is a radio broadcast: reports indicate that a prison break has occurred, and a suspect in an intentional homicide has escaped custody. The individual may have entered the XX area. Local residents are advised to secure doors and windows at night and to remain vigilant when going out during the day.

- **Worry**: As a local resident, one feels worry internally. The psychological essence of worry is that the individual subjectively anticipates a low likelihood of an undesirable outcome (personal harm), yet the possibility still exists, preventing complete inner calm.
- **Anxiety**: As a local resident and the primary informant, the suspect knows the individual reported him. The informant’s inner state escalates to anxiety. The psychological essence of anxiety is that the individual subjectively anticipates an increased likelihood of an undesirable outcome. Although the outcome is recognized as probable, it remains uncertain (and undesired), leaving both facts and the mind in a borderline state.
- **Fear**: The suspect breaks in and explicitly states an intent to retaliate. The disadvantaged mindset before confronting an enemy is fear. The psychological essence of fear is that the individual subjectively anticipates a high likelihood of an undesirable outcome (injury or death) and wishes to escape or avoid it.
- **Terror**: After combat fails and a knife is held to the throat, with life or death depending on the knife-holder’s whim and uncertainty about whether the blow will fall, the inner sensation is terror. The psychological essence of terror is the belief that no means exist to avert the impending negative outcome, approaching a state of grief before the outcome occurs. If harm is confirmed at this point, the emotion shifts toward grief.

Building on these four levels of fear emotions, several complex sensations commonly encountered in daily life (not classified as emotions) also arise:

- **Concern**: Derived from worry, the added character implies repeated consideration of how to avert the “worried-about” matter.
- **Dilemma**: Also derived from worry. Unlike concern, a dilemma involves multiple matters, each with advantages and disadvantages; the difficulty stems from the challenge of choosing between them.
- **Embarrassment**: Derived from anxiety and more intense than anxiety, embarrassment typically arises when one has done something wrong that may lead to an undesirable outcome. One attempts to reverse the negative trajectory but lacks an effective means of recovery. For example, accidentally mentioning a former girlfriend one liked in front of a sensitive current girlfriend produces embarrassment afterward.

Because these sensations require a specific context and coherent action sequence to be fully expressed—unlike the relatively simple facial expressions triggered by emotions—they are classified in this book merely as derivative states of fear emotions. Their specific external manifestations are not examined in detail.

After the previous section covered the full fear expression, the three derivative expressions of fear are introduced in descending order of intensity.

##### 7.3.4 The Expression of Worry

When fear arises internally but remains mild and is deliberately suppressed, the classic facial features of fear disappear almost entirely. Slightly pursed lips combined with the typical fearful brow shape can reveal the emotion of worry. The pursed lips represent restraint, while the furrowed brow indicates inner pressure and focus. At this stage, the eyes do not need to widen in alertness, because no direct stimulus source is present and visual information does not need to be captured.

During the annual Spring Festival travel rush, people anxiously waiting in line at train-station ticket windows frequently display bitten or tightly pressed lips, as shown in Figure 7-14.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图7-14]*

In this face, eyelid expansion is further reduced and has largely returned to normal from the fearful state, yet a slight upward lift remains with no closing tendency. The most noticeable expression features appear at two points:

- ① The raised and twisted brow shape indicates pressure without indicating disgust or anger; the brow shapes of disgust and anger do not twist.
- ② The lips are tightly closed, the vermilion is hidden, and the orbicularis oris contracts to tense the lips. Contraction of the depressor anguli oris also produces a bulge at the corners of the mouth, confirming the presence of pressure.

Capturing this combination of brow morphology and lip tension during observation allows analysis of the subject’s neural state of “bearing pressure.”

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图7-15 没有嘴部形态的担忧表情]*

If the tense lip morphology disappears, the state of worry has lightened further, as shown in Figure 7-15. In this face, only the brows and eyes reveal worry. The brows show no large elevation; only the inner brow raise and the straight, twisted brow shape are observable. The eyelids appear natural overall, yet the upper eyelids remain slightly higher than normal, exposing a larger area of the iris. If the brow elevation and twisting intensify and the upper eyelids rise further, the expression may escalate to anxiety or even fear.

This expression is easily mistaken for sadness because the brow morphology closely resembles that of sadness. However, the eyes in sadness lack the expectant force seen here and usually appear dull. The micro-expression features of sadness are discussed in the next chapter.

At an airport, I once observed a girl standing on tiptoe, silently waving at a departure point with exactly this expression. She must have felt concern for the person about to travel far, and her heart surely also held the sadness of parting. Fear and sadness share an essential similarity in their emotional nature.

##### 7.1 The Generation of Fear Emotions

Fear is humanity’s most ancient emotion. In prehistoric times, humans lacked advantages in physical combat and occupied a lower position in the food chain. Encounters with predatory beasts therefore produced fear far more often than anger.

Fear is the emotion generated by the possibility of harm. Because the harm is only “possible,” it has not yet occurred; yet the stimulus source is so powerful that it exceeds the individual’s psychological tolerance, creating a sense of inability to eliminate the impending harm.

The manifestations dominated by fear are highly varied. Intense fear can trigger physiological changes such as altered heart rate, piloerection, and surface sweating. When the stimulus source is assessed as unbeatable, flight is the common response. When the stimulus source is assessed as overwhelming (so that even flight cannot eliminate the danger), the individual may fall into uncontrollable panic and freeze in place—the so-called “scared stiff” or “scared limp” reaction. In the most extreme cases, people may lose all energy, become extremely weak, or even die of fright.

In contemporary society, however, ordinary people rarely exhibit the pure fear described above. Only when facing direct weapon attacks or life-threatening situations such as shipwrecks or fires do most people display a fully saturated fear response. At other times, pure fear is seldom observed. Most fear arises from negative events that may cause loss.

Many situations can produce fear. Lower-level stimuli that cause physical harm, such as the pain of an injection, can elicit a fearful expression even on the face of a strong man. When a thief is exposed and draws a fruit knife to threaten others, only to see three or four plainclothes officers nearby, the face typically shows the classic transition from anger to fear.

In “higher-level” contexts far removed from life-and-death stakes—such as entering an unfamiliar environment, being criticized by a boss, facing creative failure, or risking stock-market losses—most fear-related expressions are consciously controlled and suppressed, revealing only partial features.

What interests us most is capturing facial micro-expressions that reveal leaked fear or anxiety. We learn the typical features from the fullest expressions, then identify the shared characteristics between the mildest worry and the most intense terror, thereby obtaining the micro-expression morphology of fear.

Mastering the micro-expressions of fear emotions allows one to determine whether others are “afraid.”

##### Chapter Summary (9787554606841)

The emotions of surprise, disgust, anger, and fear discussed in previous chapters share a common characteristic: they are all based on the emotion-holder’s subjective appraisal rather than on an established outcome. Sadness differs fundamentally from these four emotions because it is based on an established outcome—loss of interests—even if that outcome is only a misappraisal by the emotion-holder.

The stimulus source for sadness is “an irretrievable loss.” The emotion-holder appraises the situation and concludes that the loss has already occurred (including intangible losses such as reputation, status, social evaluation, or public perception), thereby triggering sadness. Sadness has a second characteristic: it is separated from fear by only a thin line. The two emotions are essentially identical; both involve a highly negative appraisal of the stimulus source, with the source’s force judged to far exceed one’s defensive capacity, producing either fear or sadness. The sole difference lies in whether the negative outcome has already occurred. Before occurrence it is fear; once the outcome is sealed it is sadness.

Consequently, their facial morphologies are also nearly identical. Both display the “囧”-shaped brow formed by furrowed and raised eyebrows. In fear, however, the eyes remain open to gather information and make judgments, so the eyelids are raised. In sadness, because the outcome has already occurred, no further information gathering is required, so the eyelids close. The mouth morphologies of fear and sadness also share features: both engage the depressor anguli oris, mentalis, and platysma. Contraction of the depressor anguli oris pulls the corners of the mouth downward; contraction of the mentalis raises the chin and pushes the middle of the lower lip upward; contraction of the platysma stretches the corners of the mouth laterally and downward, forming an inverted trapezoid with the lips wider at the top and narrower at the bottom. This shape frequently appears in fear as a stunned expression and in sadness as sobbing. Because fear is unstable and transitional, its mouth shape is less classic and stable than that of sadness and is often disrupted by screaming, breath-holding, or other needs. In sadness, the negative fact has already occurred, so fewer interfering factors exist and a relatively stable mouth morphology appears.

##### Chapter Summary (9787554606841)

Fear is an instantaneous emotion formed when the stimulus source is appraised as exceeding one’s defensive capacity.

During fear the brows furrow to indicate strong attention while the eyes widen and the eyelids rise to increase light intake. To gather information more effectively than anger allows, humans also recruit the central frontalis to lift the brows, further elevating the upper eyelids beyond the angry position. After all, humans fear death; when one feels outmatched, attention to the opponent’s every move naturally intensifies in the interest of survival.

Fear is an unstable emotion. The first instant after appraising the stimulus source as negative and more powerful than one’s defenses is the moment of fullest fear. No animal waits passively for death, however, so a dynamic secondary appraisal follows. If that appraisal widens the gap between stimulus force and defensive capacity, complete powerlessness produces freezing, fainting, or even death, abandoning instinctive escape behaviors. If the dynamic appraisal reveals a possibility of flight or counterattack, the next action may be taken—sometimes fighting more fiercely. Thus the classic fear expression, like surprise, lasts only a brief instant, though longer than surprise.

##### Chapter Summary (9787554606841)

The discussion of smiling is now complete. It is the most complex expression in this book. Because smiles are the most socially adaptable expressions, polite smiles can be produced even in the absence of the corresponding emotion. Capturing, filtering, and analyzing smiles is therefore the most difficult task.

Nevertheless, we still hope everyone can produce as many genuine smiles as possible, which requires remembering the micro-expression features of smiling. Although smiles are complex and variable, a pure smile is governed by only two muscles: the zygomaticus major and the orbicularis oculi. When genuine pleasure arises, these two muscle groups act in concert; the powerful emotional burst produces strong contraction that forms the full smile morphology.

##### 7.3.2 The Expression of Fear

In daily life, normal fear is rarely so saturated. Brow elevation is modest, eye opening is not exaggerated—only slightly larger than usual, or even normal—yet the expression of fear can still be readily identified.

Raised and twisted brows together with alert eyes are the typical features of fear.

The wider the eyes open, the greater the internal fear. In the full fear expression the eyelids attempt to expand maximally, sometimes exposing the sclera above the iris (though often obscured by the eyelid fold). Although the fear expression does not produce such extreme eyelid movement, observing eye shape remains key to determining the degree of fear.

Figure 7-11 shows a fear expression.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图7-11]*

- ① The twisted brow shape is produced by simultaneous contraction of the corrugator supercilii and the medial frontalis. The normal arched brow line (dashed) is disrupted; the inner brow rises and the overall brow twists upward in its medial third (arrow).
- ② The upper eyelid is raised, exposing more of the upper iris.
- ③ The levator labii superioris contracts slightly, lifting the upper lip and partially revealing the upper teeth.
- ④ The platysma contracts slightly, pulling the corners of the mouth laterally and increasing the horizontal width of the mouth beyond its usual relaxed state.

Compared with the brow and eye morphology, mouth shape is less important in the fear expression. In Figure 7-11 the woman’s mouth is generally relaxed, affected only by mandibular movement and platysma contraction; the corners are pulled slightly outward, exposing part of the lower teeth.

Although muscle contraction is greatly reduced relative to the full fear expression, such an expression in real life still signals a serious situation. For example, a playful university student who has already failed one course twice and, after a final effort, is summoned to the department office and learns of another failure—confirming that graduation is now impossible—will display exactly this expression.

##### 3. Differences in Mouth Shape

In the surprise expression the upper lip is not raised; the lower lip simply drops with the mandible to permit a quick, shallow inhalation. Surprise occurs before the nature of the stimulus source is determined and before any solution is chosen. Once the stimulus source is appraised as overwhelmingly harmful, the evolved instinct immediately initiates the escape response, opening the mouth to draw in the maximum volume of air for energy reserves. Consequently, in the fear expression the upper lip is raised, the corners of the mouth are pulled widely apart by the platysma, and the lower lip is not only dropped by mandibular relaxation but also lengthened and depressed by the depressor labii inferioris, exposing part of the lower teeth. This action, performed to store respiratory energy, is of the same nature as the全身 tension—trembling, skin tightening, altered circulation—that accompanies fear.

Finally, note that a full fear expression is usually accompanied by a deep inhalation. Observing the breathing pattern that accompanies the expression is also an important cue for emotion judgment.

One expression easily mistaken for fear must also be noted. In the instant of fear, because alertness toward the stimulus source is maintained and the tragic outcome remains uncertain, the eyes never narrow. The tightly closed eyes and screaming reaction often depicted in films actually reflect an acceptance that the worst outcome has already occurred and constitute a derivative of sadness. Screaming serves both as an instinctive release of inner pressure and as an evolutionarily conserved attack behavior—using high-frequency sound to drive the opponent away. Figure 7-10 illustrates this.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图7-10]*

*The Perfume of the Lady in Black*, Italy, 1977.

##### 2. Differences in Eyelid Morphology

The eyelids in surprise open naturally to their maximum, revealing the entire upper edge of the iris and sometimes even the sclera above. In fear the upper eyelids also attempt to open wide, yet the opposing pull of the orbicularis oculi and corrugator supercilii on the brows creates a fold that alters the overall eyelid shape; the natural degree of iris exposure nevertheless remains visible.

**Why Open the Eyes Wide?**  
The primitive motive for opening the eyes to their fullest is to gather visual information rapidly so as to determine whether one is safe.

When we are afraid, we become highly tense and acutely sensitive to our surroundings. The entire nervous system is primed for any imminent threat. This heightened vigilance is expressed by the widened eyes; when the stimulus is sufficiently terrifying, the eyes open to their limit in an instant.

The wider the eyes, the more fearful the expression appears. In this respect, **the ocular features of fear overlap with those of surprise and anger**. When fear is less intense—for example, in worry or unease—the eyes do not open dramatically and the sclera above the iris remains hidden.

Consequently, one way to observe fear is to cover all other parts of the face and examine only the eyes. Such close-ups are common in horror films. In the figure below, although the brow shape cannot be seen, the single eye alone suffices to show that the expression is not surprise, as illustrated in Figure 7-9.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图7-9]*

The left image clearly shows the eye of fear; the right image shows ordinary surprise without fear. The eyelid fold in the left image results from the distinctive brow configuration.

The eyes are opened more than in a neutral face but not dramatically; the upper lids are not lifted as high as in fear or fright, yet more of the upper iris is visible than in a fully relaxed face, as shown in Figure 7-13.

When family or friends who have not been seen for a long time are expected at the airport, and all passengers on the same flight have already emerged but the awaited person has not appeared and calls go unanswered, this anxious look surfaces involuntarily—because the mind is preoccupied with the possibility of a negative outcome.

##### 2. Typical Features of Fear Expressions

When fear is fully expressed, the brows assume a distinctly twisted configuration: they flatten overall, draw together, display vertical corrugator lines, yet the inner brows are raised by contraction of the medial frontalis, producing an upward slant at the inner third. Fine inverted-U wrinkles appear on the forehead.

The upper eyelids are markedly elevated, exposing more of the upper iris than in a neutral face. The degree of eyelid opening is proportional to the intensity of fear. In milder fear expressions the eyes open only slightly wider than usual, yet even this modest increase is significant. If the brows show any twisting (regardless of degree) and the eyes are opened sufficiently wide, the expression can be identified as belonging to the fear family even in the absence of other facial changes, allowing the inference that the subject is experiencing fear.

The mouth does not participate in every type of fear expression. In terror or fright the mouth may open; when the emotion is deliberately suppressed or only mildly felt—as in unease or worry—the lips may be pressed together or remain motionless. The extent of mouth movement reflects the strength of the fear.

##### 1. Differences in Brow Shape

The surprised brow is simply raised (frontalis contraction) and retains its natural arch. The fearful brow is knitted overall, with the inner ends lifted, producing a twisted shape together with visible corrugator lines and forehead wrinkles.

At the instant of surprise, no positive or negative judgment has yet been formed about the stimulus; the reaction may turn into delight, anger, or fear. Fear, by contrast, arises only when the stimulus is perceived as genuinely threatening and therefore demands concentrated attention. Consequently the raising of the brows (medial frontalis) is accompanied by involuntary corrugator activity that knits and depresses the inner brows. Remember: **knitting the brows signals intense focus**.

The fearful brow configuration is therefore more complex than the surprised one: the brows must simultaneously draw together to signal tension and pressure while being raised to help the eyes gather more visual information. As a result, the fearful brow lacks the free, sweeping lift seen in surprise.

A practice method: first raise both brows as high as possible, then knit and depress the inner brows.

##### Chapter 7 Micro-expressions of Fear

Fear arises once the threatening power of a negative stimulus exceeds a person’s psychological tolerance. Fright, unease, and worry are derivatives of fear, decreasing in intensity. The expression of fear is a composite of surprise and sadness—essentially the sadness that is anticipated after surprise.

Anger prompts resistance to a threat; although the stimulus is strong, the individual subjectively judges that fighting can alter or eliminate it. When the stimulus exceeds psychological tolerance, anger converts into fear. A stimulus capable of eliciting fear is one that threatens the individual’s interests and is so overwhelming that, after appraisal, the person no longer believes resistance is feasible. The primary behavioral option then becomes flight; under extreme pressure, despair may lead to complete surrender.

##### 1. Morphology of a Full Fear Expression

The morphological features of an extreme fear expression are as follows:
- Corrugator contraction draws the brows together, forming vertical corrugator lines;
- Medial frontalis contraction raises the inner brows, producing inverted-U wrinkles on the forehead;
- Levator palpebrae superioris contraction attempts to lift the upper lids, yet is opposed by the orbicularis oculi and corrugator, creating diagonal folds in the upper-lid skin; without opposition the entire upper iris would be exposed;
- Simultaneous contraction of levator labii superioris and levator labii superioris alaeque nasi raises the upper lip, exposing the upper teeth;
- Platysma contraction pulls the mouth corners laterally, increasing the horizontal width of the mouth beyond its resting state;
- Depressor labii inferioris contraction lowers the lower lip, exposing part of the lower teeth.

##### 3. Application of Fear Micro-expressions in Psychological Testing

A subject experiences fear only when confronted with a stimulus that threatens imminent exposure.

Because physical coercion is prohibited and the conclusions of psychological testing do not constitute physical evidence, no direct, severe threat is posed to the subject; consequently, expressions of fear or fright do not appear during testing. Moreover, because the purpose of testing is to uncover psychological inconsistencies rather than to pressure or harass, even anxious or uneasy expressions are rare; the most common micro-expression observed is worry.

##### (4) Morphology of Fear Micro-expressions

- The brows show no large-scale elevation; only a slight raising of the inner ends and a flattened, twisted configuration are observable;
- The eyelids remain largely natural, yet the upper lids are positioned slightly higher than normal, exposing a larger area of the iris.

**Summary**: These morphological features constitute the necessary characteristics of fear-family expressions. A subject experiences fear only when confronted with a stimulus that threatens imminent exposure.

##### 7.3.5 Morphological Features of Fear Micro-expressions

Summarizing the morphological features across varying intensities yields the micro-expression characteristics of fear-family emotions: **the inner brows are simultaneously knitted and raised, producing a twist at the inner third, while the upper eyelids remain elevated, exposing more of the iris**. Once this brow-eye combination appears—even at low intensity—it signals fear and is therefore the defining morphological feature of fear micro-expressions.

##### (1) Morphology of Fright

- Corrugator and medial frontalis contract together, destroying the normal arched brow shape; the inner brows rise and the brow twists upward at the inner third;
- Upper eyelids lift, exposing more of the upper iris;
- Levator labii superioris contracts slightly, raising the upper lip and partially exposing the upper teeth;
- Platysma contracts slightly, pulling the mouth corners laterally and widening the mouth beyond its relaxed resting width.

##### (2) Morphology of Unease

- The brows flatten overall yet retain their twisted shape; the inner brows are raised, though to a lesser degree;
- Corrugator produces slight vertical wrinkles;
- The eyes open more than usual but not dramatically; upper-lid elevation is less pronounced than in fear or fright, yet more of the upper iris is visible than in a fully relaxed face.

##### Expression of Fright

In evolutionary biology the expression of “fright” signals “I have no intention of attacking you” and “Please do not harm me”; it can also be used to assess whether the other party is non-aggressive or to indicate a desire to conserve energy for other purposes.

##### 1. Morphological Features of Fear Micro-expressions

The inner brows are simultaneously knitted and raised, the upper eyelids are elevated, and more of the upper iris is exposed. The fullness of the emotion is directly proportional to the degree of eyelid opening and to the degree of inner-brow elevation. This brow-eye combination is the necessary feature of fear-family expressions.

##### (3) Morphology of Worry

- The raised and twisted inner brows indicate psychological pressure without indicating disgust or anger;
- The lips are pressed together, concealing the vermilion border; orbicularis oris contraction tenses the lips, and contraction of depressor anguli oris produces a bulge at the mouth corners.

##### 2. Common Fear Expression Morphology

In daily life we readily recognize expressions arising from fear-family emotions. The raised and twisted brows together with the alert eyes are the typical features of fright.

##### 11.2.4 Fear

If the intensity of the negative stimulus continues to increase and overwhelms the individual’s psychological capacity to attack (resist), anger converts into fear.

#### The Micro-Expressions of "Anger" Are the Timing for Apology

##### Appendix: An Extra Piece on Anger Emotions

—— Paying Tribute to Professor Paul Ekman and Exploring

This is a purely academic discussion, a section paying tribute to the senior scholar along the way. If you are not interested in relatively pure academic theoretical issues, you can skip this section directly.

American scholar Professor Paul Ekman, who studies micro-expressions, believes that the emotion of anger can be divided into many different themes. In the examples mentioned by Paul Ekman, there are infants having their freedom restrained, being violated especially intentionally violated, being frustrated or feeling powerless, being insulted and slandered, being rejected by one's lover, others' anger, disappointment in others especially loved ones, behavior and beliefs being offended, and promoting behaviors and beliefs one opposes.

Paul Ekman once summarized, “We can consider frustration, others' anger, the threat of being harmed, and being rejected by others as variants of infringing on the subject. Even anger toward promoters of things we oppose can be seen as a variant.”

Based on these paragraphs, we believe that Professor Paul Ekman's description of the root causes of anger emotions in the book *Emotions Revealed* is somewhat loose, failing to clearly summarize the common characteristic of anger stimuli—threat. Whether being restrained, violated, disturbed, negated, or others' anger, they all ultimately point to a threat to one's own interests. We respectfully discuss with the senior scholar and readers whether this is appropriate.

Additionally, Paul Ekman specifically used the "Maxine Kenny case" to explain and illustrate anger. The case is very simple: a man named David Lynn Scott III raped and murdered Maxine Kenny's daughter. He was arrested a year later and convicted after another 4 years.

In the book, Paul Ekman uses a statement by Maxine on the day of the criminal's execution, a photo, and an attack on the criminal to attempt to explain the generation of anger emotions. However, the analysis of the direct stimuli for anger emotions is not detailed enough, which is also the reason why in his "Anger" chapter, the analysis of the origins of anger appears somewhat scattered. At least in this case, Paul Ekman did not mention the possibility of sadness existing, but in such a case, there would certainly be sadness.

We can speculate in chronological order about the emotional changes of the party involved, Maxine Kenny. Note that the following content is merely based on hypotheses, not a scientific research process using empirical methods, and cannot be used to draw conclusions.

1. If she was at the crime scene at the time and witnessed the criminal's violation of her daughter, she would certainly produce anger emotions. Although the criminal might be tall and burly and possibly holding a sharp knife, out of protection for her offspring, the party would certainly feel anger far greater than fear, and with the support of anger's power, she would fight the criminal to protect her daughter. Because the criminal's violation directly threatened her child's safety (a threat to reproduction), harmed the years of effort invested in raising the child, and threatened her future life state, especially her emotional state. Therefore, the anger at that time would certainly be extremely intense.

2. If the criminal had finished the crime, having raped her daughter and caused death, then her subsequent emotions would depend on the criminal's follow-up behavior. If the criminal then carried out a violent violation against the party Maxine Kenny, directly threatening the party's own life safety (a threat to survival), then with the support of self-preservation and anger over the daughter's victimization, the party would still bravely fight the criminal. If the outcome of the fight remains uncertain (win or lose), anger is the dominant emotion; but once the criminal gains an overwhelming advantage in the fight (being tangled together does not count as overwhelming, since one can still tear and twist forcefully), and the party is powerless to change the outcome (loss or even death), then fear and sadness may both become dominant emotions. Anger remains, but it no longer occupies the dominant position.

3. If the criminal finished the crime, killed the party's daughter, and then immediately left without further harming the party. Would the party pursue the criminal, or stay facing her daughter's body in inconsolable grief? An ordinary person without combat training or combat experience would certainly choose the latter. At this point, grief becomes the main emotion; the party focuses entirely on the daughter's life or death, and anger, having temporarily lost its stimulus source, recedes to secondary status or even becomes very slight. Before receiving confirmation of the daughter's death from credible personnel (such as a doctor or police), the party still has energy and believes there is still a chance for a turnaround in the situation, possibly maintaining a relatively excited neural state hoping the daughter can survive. At this time, the possibility of anger existing is extremely small, and even if present, it is far from the main emotion. But if the daughter is confirmed dead, then the party may be left with only sadness emotions, powerless to fight anything and having lost hope of salvaging anything.

4. We make some dramatic assumptions again. If we ignore the police and medical personnel at the scene and the criminal reappears, it is foreseeable that the situation of the second stage will inevitably occur—that is, the appearance of the stimulus source will trigger the party's intense anger emotions.

From 16:00 on February 5, 2011 to 16:00 on February 6, 2011, the research group initiated an online vote via Weibo, asking netizens to choose one of the following two options according to their own feelings: "When the party fights the criminal, what sentence might they mutter in their mouth or mind?"

- A. Why?! Why did you hurt her?!
- B. She's already dead! She's already dead!

The 24-hour voting results are as follows: Out of 931 votes, 72% chose option A, and 28% chose option B.

**Explanation of option A:**

In previous internal tests, all group members without exception chose this option. Because our theoretical research hypothesis is that anger is triggered by unexpected negative stimuli, and unexpected (unreasonable) violation behavior extremely easily causes the violated person to produce anger emotions. Moreover, unexpectedness is a very important factor, because if it is within expectations—that is, the party fully confirms that the harmful behavior is about to occur (such as criminal punishment)—then anger emotions are not easily produced, and fear is more often the replacement (with exceptions). The violated person completely did not expect and does not understand why the other party would violate their rights. This huge degree of mismatch with negative expectations (violation) will cause the party, while angrily counterattacking, to produce another non-rational desire—to "eliminate" the other party's unreasonable behavioral motive, attempting through "education" or "debate" to dissolve this threat and harm factor into nothingness. "Why did you hurt my daughter? She is innocent (she didn't hurt you), she is still so young, she is still in college, she has a bright future..." Perhaps there is another possibility: repeating these reasonable (should not be harmed) factors, contrasting with the unreasonable violation behavior, can enhance one's own anger emotions, thereby mobilizing more energy for counterattack.

It is worth special note that these desires are not the result of rational thinking, but merely a combination of habit and instinct. Therefore, the party is not trying to persuade the criminal to abandon the criminal intent; it is merely a primitive expectation. Of course, if it is a quarrel-type violation and counterattack, it requires substantial participation of rational thinking, but similar reactions will also occur: "Why did you cancel our plan? We stayed up for three days and nights for this plan; this plan is the heart and soul of the entire team. Did you read it carefully? On what basis do you negate our plan after just a cursory glance in less than a minute? This plan was drafted with reference to the XX classic case (or XX theory); it is absolutely correct!"

**Explanation of option B:**

The language in option B can also appear in actual situations, but the party's inner state is quite different. Loss is the source of sadness. If the daughter's death has no other factors interfering, then it will certainly only leave the party with sadness, with no strength to attend to other things. "She's already dead" may appear during frenzied fighting, but more often appears in the consciousness of sadness (true sadness is rarely spoken aloud); it is a reinforcement of loss.

**The party's unexpected, criminal's deliberate harmful behavior causing death will add a considerable degree of anger to the party's sadness emotions.** But the repetition of "She's already dead" is not a direct expression of anger, but an expression of sadness. The party uses this sad result to reinforce their expectation mismatch (healthy life versus unexpected victimization and death), thereby reinforcing the triggering of anger emotions and mobilizing energy for battle.

##### 6.3.2 A Variant of Anger One: Breath-Holding Lips (Breath-Holding Mouth)

Tightly closing both lips combined with the standard anger eyebrow-eye combination makes the face look exceptionally angry, as shown in Figure 6-12.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-12]*

This is a breath-holding expression. The energy provided by anger emotions infuses into the three bundles of muscles controlling the mouth, forming this special angry mouth morphology:

- Upper lip raised (action of levator labii superioris and levator labii superioris alaeque nasi), nasal wings raised, grooves appearing on both sides of the nasal wings
- Lower lip pushed up, tightly pressed together with the upper lip, lips thinned, stretched into a straight line, lower lip protruding
- Skin at the chin position raised and uneven (action of mentalis)
- Corners of the mouth severely downturned (action of depressor anguli oris), exactly opposite to when smiling with pressed lips

This morphology can be abbreviated as "breath-holding mouth," the typical form of genuine anger. Because it requires the coordinated action of three muscles, it is difficult to fake.

This breath-holding angry expression's muscle morphology features on the face are shown in Figure 6-13:

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-13]*

- Corrugator supercilii contracted, orbicularis oculi contracted, causing both eyebrows to furrow and press downward
- Levator palpebrae superioris contracted
- Contraction of orbicularis oculi also tightens the lower eyelids and slightly pulls them sideways
- Orbicularis oris contracted, causing both lips to close tightly together
- Depressor anguli oris contracted, causing both corners of the mouth to curve downward
- Mentalis contracted, forming muscle ridges on the chin with an uneven surface, while pushing the lower lip upward to keep both lips tightly closed

However, this mouth morphology cannot be used alone as a micro-expression morphological feature of anger. Although this "breath-holding mouth" morphology is a common component of angry expressions, it can also appear in other emotions, as shown in Figure 6-14.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-14]*

If we cover the upper half of this face or replace it with another eyebrow-eye morphology, we can see that the breath-holding mouth alone is still insufficient to confirm the true presence of anger. Because the raising of the upper lip and the changes it causes around the nasal wings are not as primary or obvious as in disgust, the breath-holding mouth can also appear as part of sadness, as shown in Figure 6-15.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-15]*

**Summary**: Tightly pursed lips can to some extent express anger, but they may also appear in other expressions. To confirm an anger expression, it must be paired with the standard anger eyebrow-eye morphology.

##### 6.3.5 Morphological Characteristics of Angry Micro-expressions (9789620756689)

Through the previous comparisons and analyses, we can deduce that the morphology of the eyebrows and eyes holds important significance for expressing anger: the eyebrows are strongly pressed downward, the muscles of the upper and lower eyelids contract and tense, and the gaze focuses intensely on the stimulus source. The more intense the anger, the shorter the distance between the eyebrows and the upper eyelid margin. As shown in Figure 6-19.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-19]*

When the intensity of anger decreases, the degree of muscular movement in the eyebrows and eyes lessens accordingly, forming a weakened version of the angry eyebrow-eye morphology. As shown in Figure 6-20.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-20]*

Both eyebrows press downward and tighten, the levator palpebrae superioris contracts, and its lifting force partially counters the downward pressure of the eyebrows, causing the eyes to open wider; however, they still encounter resistance from the pressed-down eyebrows, resulting in accumulated skin folds (thickening of the upper eyelid). When these two morphologies (lowered eyebrows + widened eyes) appear together, the expression can be called a glare.

Both eyebrows press downward, the upper eyelids lift, and the lower eyelids tense; a tightly closed mouth is a classic facial feature of an angry expression. If a person habitually (or physiologically) maintains any of these features over time (eyelids cannot remain lifted indefinitely), it can give others the impression of a bad temper, coldness, or extreme seriousness. As shown in Figure 6-21.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-21]*

In the comparison of Figure 6-22, merely observing the close-up of the eyes in the image below reveals the threat of anger. Due to changes in eyelid morphology, more of the upper and lower margins of the iris become visible, and the shape of the exposed sclera also differs from the norm. This sharply angled upper eyelid morphology, with the outer two-thirds nearly straight, results from the downward pressure of both eyebrows.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-22]*

It is evident that effective ways to intensify the expression of anger are the lifting of the upper eyelids and the tensing of the lower eyelids; the wider the eyes are opened, the stronger the conveyed meaning of anger. When criticizing someone, a piercing stare can induce fear. When a glare is combined with downward-pressed eyebrows and tightly closed lips, the expression of anger becomes very pronounced.

Depending on the specific context, if a person cannot or does not wish to express anger, their facial expression may show almost no change.

On an almost unchanged face, two features can still reveal the person’s inner anger:

- First, contraction of the orbicularis oculi muscle produces a highly forceful eyelid configuration, specifically manifested as lifting of the upper eyelid and tensing of the lower eyelid; at this point, even changes in the eyebrows may be difficult to observe;
- Second, intense visual focus; without gaze concentrated on the stimulus source, the angry expression is greatly diminished and becomes suppressed forbearance.

Therefore, in a restrained angry expression, although the entire face shows almost no change, the excessive effort to suppress the anger makes the tension and concentration in the eyes, along with stiffness in the rest of the face, clearly visible; it is by no means a relaxed state. During the process of maintaining a blank expression while restraining anger, the nostrils often flare and expel air forcefully.

Eye tension (lifting of the upper eyelid and tensing of the lower eyelid) combined with concentrated gaze, when the eyeballs and head remain completely still (unlike the slight backward movement in surprised wide-eyed expressions), creates a sense of powerful eye contact, forming a glare. Conversely, if the upper eyelid muscles cease contracting and return to normal, the lower eyelids relax, or the gaze shifts away from the stimulus source, then even if other angry features such as downward-pressed eyebrows and tightly closed lips remain, the original anger will completely disappear.

> carrying a weapon, searching everywhere for innocent, unarmed girls… You raped and murdered because you mistakenly believed that identity gave you such a right. You raped my daughter Gail, abused her, and brutally killed her—not once, but seven times. Her hands were covered with defensive wounds, yet you ignored her desperate struggle to survive. You do not deserve to live!

Yet the offender showed no remorse and faced the statement with a smile. The individual struck the offender’s head and was restrained by her husband and police officers.

This highly aggressive language fully illustrates the attack tendency and verbal manifestations of anger. However, using this case as explanatory support for the generation of anger is not entirely appropriate. The courtroom statement only demonstrates the individual’s expression of anger and does not clearly explain the root cause of that anger. The primary emotion from losing a daughter should be sadness; that should be the dominant emotion throughout the case from incident to trial. Anger exists only within a specific context—the absolute safety of the courtroom, the individual’s absolute dominance, and the offender’s absolute weakness. Without this context, the individual would not have possessed the force of anger to fully express inner resentment, let alone attack the offender; fear and sadness would have predominated.

A more accurate description of this mother’s feelings would be “hatred.” Hatred is a compound emotion: it expresses retrospective defiance, non-acceptance, and rejection of an already incurred loss through sadness, yet the person lacks the power to change the situation and therefore seeks psychological balance by harming the interests of the hated person, rather than altering the objective result of the loss. The party harboring hatred is usually the weaker party; although an offensive impulse of anger exists internally, the overall stance toward the hated person remains one of weakness. A person holding absolute advantage does not harbor “hatred” toward an opponent.

Therefore, using this case to illustrate anger easily leads readers to confuse the stimulus sources that trigger several primary emotions, which is inappropriate. Moreover, Paul Ekman himself added, “Anger rarely lasts long by itself. Fear often precedes or follows anger—fear that those who anger us may harm us, fear of one’s own anger, fear of losing control and harming others.” Such descriptions inevitably leave readers puzzled.

While respectfully debating with the predecessor, I also sincerely invite readers to share their insights.

##### 1. Anger While Driving

Driving on the road is a situation highly conducive to anger, especially when traffic conditions are poor. Anyone with driving experience can immediately think of potential triggers. Minor cases include the car ahead failing to accelerate when it should, cutting in line instead of queuing, failing to yield when required, or suddenly changing lanes without signaling. More serious cases involve accidents, such as being rear-ended or colliding without cause. In all these situations, a mismatch of expectations is an obvious factor, and both mind and mouth will angrily utter, “Can’t you drive?!”

Some people therefore conclude that **unreasonableness** is the stimulus for anger. They believe that if everyone drove reasonably, everything would proceed in an orderly and smooth manner, and such anger would not arise. Another view holds that anyone might drive unreasonably, so that is not the key stimulus; suffering a loss or feeling aggrieved (harm to one’s interests) is the true stimulus.

If unreasonable driving amounts to domineering self-importance or even malicious provocation, it can indeed trigger anger—this is a natural reaction to a challenge to one’s dignity, just like a stranger arrogantly shoving you on the street. It has no direct relation to driving per se; it is simply being provoked while driving. This negative stimulus to competence and dignity is equivalent to an infringement on an animal’s territory and instinctively provokes anger.

If the issue is not malicious provocation but merely whether one suffers a loss, we can probe deeper: what advantage does cutting in or overtaking by changing lanes actually confer?

In fact, the psychological process that truly triggers anger is not necessarily another person’s obstruction, delay, or offense; it may lie one layer deeper than the immediately apparent cause. Whether anger arises is directly related to the purpose of the drive.

Under normal circumstances, when driving, what one truly cares about is what needs to be done after reaching the destination; the journey itself is merely a necessary process. If one is aimlessly cruising with no destination, ordinary unreasonable driving (not malicious) and traffic jams will not easily provoke anger. Being hit might still trigger anger, but upon deeper reflection, the real cause is that the accident will entail insurance claims, repairs, and other troubles plus wasted time, directly affecting normal life arrangements afterward; the extent of damage to the car itself matters little (as long as no one is injured). Imagine driving an already damaged car that has not yet been sent for repair—if it sustains a little more damage while you are leisurely cruising, what difference does it make?

##### Interesting Case

**Angry Churchill**

Restrained mild anger can easily be mistaken for deep thought.

During World War II, Canadian photojournalist Yousef Karsh, attempting to capture Churchill in a state of deep contemplation while facing a major decision, risked snatching the cigar from his mouth as a provocation. The immediate reaction produced the now-famous photograph of Churchill with both eyebrows pressed down and lower lip jutting out, resembling a bulldog. The image made Karsh famous overnight.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-23]*

After so much study and research, we can use Figure 6-24 to test your ability to recognize angry expression features.

Please observe the image and determine whether it shows anger or grievance.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-24]*

**Answer**: It appears to be grievance but is actually anger.

The morphological feature most likely to be mistaken for grievance is the pouting of the mouth. Such a mouth shape does indeed appear in expressions of grievance. Because sustained lifting of the upper eyelids and maintenance of lower-eyelid tension are difficult, the glaring eye configuration does not last long. However, the morphologies of the eyebrows and mouth can persist more easily. Overall, the expression in the image looks more like grievance. Yet, for the following reasons, this image can be identified as an angry expression:

1. **Eyebrows**: The eyebrows are furrowed and pressed downward, indicating attention; judging by the force of the muscular movement, the level of attention is high;
2. **Eyes**: Superficially, the upper eyelids show no sign of lifting, and nearly half of the iris is covered by the upper eyelids. However, measuring the distance between the upper eyelid margin and the eyebrows reveals that the upper eyelids have been lifted with considerable effort. The downward pressure of the eyebrows was simply too strong, producing this morphology. In addition, the lower eyelids can be observed to be tense, positioned slightly higher and straighter than usual, with the gaze intensely focused on the photographer—precisely the morphological features of an angry micro-expression.
3. **Mouth**: The mentalis contracts and pushes the lower lip upward, creating an uneven ridge on the chin; both lips are tightly closed and thinned, protruding outward under the action of the orbicularis oris; the depressor anguli oris contracts and slightly pulls the corners of the mouth downward. This is the “breath-holding mouth” described earlier, a typical mouth morphology of anger.

##### The Mechanism of Anger Generation

In the animal world, if it is simply a matter of predator and prey, the predator feels hunger (the greatest driver of action), while the prey feels fear. Because the adversarial relationship between them is unbalanced, with dominance and weakness too pronounced, the weaker party lacks the power to eliminate the threat and can only flee quickly (this is fear). If lucky enough to run fast, it escapes. Therefore, it is certain that the weaker party will not feel anger, and if the stronger party fails to catch up, it will not curse inwardly either; it can only adjust its stamina in hopes of another attempt.

When the two sides are evenly matched, anger is more likely to appear. Territory is a rule of interaction that animals with ruling power mutually recognize. Whether the challenge originates from within the territory or comes from an unfamiliar force outside, it will arouse anger in the territory’s controller, because such challenging behavior implies two things:

- First, knowing full well that this is my domain yet daring to offend is a massive expectation violation; how can you show me so little respect?!
- Second, if the challenger wins, the original territory holder loses everything—mate, offspring, a good life, even life itself. This is an enormous threat, involving both survival and reproduction. Such a threat must be eliminated! Anger arises, followed by physical confrontation.

In the human world, the stimuli that trigger human anger are likewise **interest threats**—threats that may harm survival and reproduction. This is essentially identical to the mechanism that produces anger in animals.

Of course, the generation of human anger involves broader and more complex derivative variations. Civilization, education, and the detailed fragmentation of life cause anger to arise more often from various derived threats.

The threat stimuli discussed here do not refer merely to formal threats, such as verbal warnings or brandishing weapons, but to a more abstract concept: situations that the individual subjectively perceives as potentially harmful.

The individual assesses whether the stimulus constitutes an interest threat. If the threat is judged to be eliminable through one’s own efforts, anger may arise; if there is no thought or confidence in eliminating the threat, the response is fear; if the matter is dismissed entirely, the response is disgust (commonly expressed as contempt). Therefore, whether an interest threat exists lies solely in the mind of the individual and has a strong causal link to that person’s self-perception.

##### 2. Typical Features of Anger Expressions

The typical features of an anger expression are eyebrows pressed downward, closest to the upper eyelid edges; eyes glaring forcefully, upper eyelids raised, lower eyelids tensed, gaze locked intensely on the stimulus without shifting; mouth shapes in anger vary considerably, commonly showing bared teeth, roaring, or tightly closed lips.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-26]*

**Eyebrows**:  
Lowered eyebrows indicate intense focus. Because stimuli capable of eliciting anger carry threat-level intensity, they absolutely merit attention, so the natural expression shows the typical lowered-eyebrow configuration.

**Eyelids**:  
An anger expression must include raised upper eyelids (exposing more of the upper iris than usual) and tensed lower eyelids (slightly elevated, with the eyelid line straightened). The wider the eyes open, the deeper the anger. The glaring eyes combined with lowered eyebrows give the gaze strong penetrating power. When the brow-eye configuration is paired with the mouth shape of anger, the presence of anger is clearly conveyed.

**Mouth**:  
The mouth shape is the most variable element in anger.

factors. In roaring anger, the mouth shape is influenced by the content spoken. The upper lip is often raised; the lower lip varies more. It may form a bared-teeth biting shape, be pressed together and puffed by the mentalis and orbicularis oris, or remain in its usual relaxed state. When the degree of eyelid elevation is equal, a person with an open, roaring mouth appears angrier than one with a closed mouth.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-27]*

In modern social interactions, clear, full displays of anger on the face are rare. Noticing the momentary change in the glare allows observation of the person’s inner emotion.

Anger without focused gaze is a staged performance.

If the gaze wanders, lowered eyebrows and pressed lips alone cannot effectively express anger; the expression appears more like a response to pressure, commonly seen when someone is struggling to decide or thinking deeply. This is shown in Figure 6-27.

##### How to Distinguish Between “Deep Thinking” and “Anger” Expressions?

Regarding the interpretation of eyebrow shape or mouth shape in an “anger” expression, some may wonder: “Isn’t this the same as the expression when seriously thinking about something?” Exactly. When displaying an “anger” expression, the actions of “both eyebrows drawing toward the center” and “lips pressing together” coincide with the expression of serious thinking.

Facial movements fall into two categories: one expresses emotion, the other conveys conversational information about thinking. These conversational signals are facial movements produced while speaking to or listening to others and carry no emotion.

The meaning conveyed by “both eyebrows drawing toward the center” and “lips pressing together” is “concentration,” so I call this expression the “concentration” face.

The “concentration” face expresses “anger” in emotional display, yet expresses “deep thinking” in conversation. “Anger” arises when a desired goal is obstructed or an obstacle is encountered. When a goal is blocked, the aggressive emotion of “anger” appears. “Deep thinking” is the mechanism of concentrating to reorganize one’s own words or to understand another’s speech. For this reason, both the “anger” expression and the “deep thinking” expression are called the “concentration” face.

Next, let us observe whether the person before us is angry or seriously thinking, and how to tell the two apart.

Even when feeling “anger” in public, unless anger erupts irrationally and fully, the emotion is suppressed and therefore appears as the micro-expression form of “anger” (微反应 (micro-reaction)). In short, this display lasts only an instant and shows merely “both eyebrows drawing toward the center” or “lips pressing together.” That is, an expression that appears only momentarily has a high likelihood of representing the emotion “anger”; conversely, if the movement persists for a short while, it may represent “deep thinking.”

Some people around you may habitually maintain a frightening expression with lowered eyebrows and concentrated frown lines—supervisors, chairpersons, clients, and so on. They may not be irritable; they may simply be thinking seriously at that moment.

##### Test Case

**The “Inventor” Who Ignores the World**

Only when the test subject perceives a threat will anger be triggered.

In other words, once anger is observed on the test subject’s face, it can be concluded that the stimulus is a highly effective core issue—the matter the subject is most worried about and least willing to have exposed.

We once encountered an “extraordinary individual,” a person who did nothing except invent.

Xiao Lu was a well-known amateur inventor, famous for building an amphibious robot from scrap materials. Yet background checks revealed that, apart from tinkering with inventions at home, he did nothing: no job (no regular income), no friends, and even when his girlfriend became pregnant he still handled all household chores himself.

During our interaction, we deliberately asked how he viewed the “inventions” he had created. He began confidently, displaying unmistakable pride in his work. We hinted that everything he had made already existed in the world in earlier, more precise, more technologically advanced, and more practical industrial forms. He grasped the implication—“what you are doing and what you have produced have no meaning or value”—and flew into a rage. In addition to the classic anger expression on his face, micro-reactions in body language appeared during his subsequent rebuttals and self-justifications.

The reason was that all of Xiao Lu’s behavior stemmed from a single motive—hobby. Because the hobby was so consuming, it brought him attention while also imposing excessive pressure, forcing him to evade all real-life problems and bury himself in persistent action. This was the point he least wanted others to see through (though perceptive people could) and least wanted pointed out. Therefore, when his core interest (evaluation of his behavior pattern) was threatened (questioned), the test subject’s anger response was inevitably triggered.

##### Explanation of Option A

In previous internal tests, every team member chose this option. Our theoretical hypothesis was that anger is triggered by unexpected negative stimuli; unexpected (unreasonable) harmful acts readily produce anger in the harmed party. Unexpectedness is a crucial factor, because if the harm is anticipated—that is, the individual fully expects the injurious act to occur (such as criminal punishment)—anger is unlikely; fear is more common (with exceptions). The harmed party never anticipated or understood why the other would infringe on their rights; this massive negative expectation violation (the infringement) causes the individual, while angrily counterattacking, to generate an additional non-rational desire: to “cancel” the other’s unreasonable behavioral motive, attempting through “education” or “argument” to dissolve the threat and harm. “Why would you harm my daughter? She is innocent (she never harmed you), she is still so young, she is still in university, she has a bright future…” Perhaps repeating these reasonable (should-not-be-harmed) factors, contrasted with the unreasonable harmful act, can intensify one’s own anger and mobilize more energy for counterattack.

It is worth noting that these desires are not the result of rational thought but merely a combination of habit and instinct. Thus the individual is not trying to persuade the offender to abandon the criminal intent; it is simply a primitive expectation. Of course, when the infringement and counterattack take the form of an argument, rational thought participates heavily, yet a similar response still occurs: “Why did you cancel our plan? We stayed up three nights for this plan; it is the team’s entire effort. Did you even read it carefully? How can you reject it after a cursory glance in less than a minute? This plan was drafted with reference to the XX classic case (or XX theory) and is absolutely correct!”

##### 7. Threat or Destruction?

One view holds that anger arises from the destruction of interests. This view merits further examination. Destruction is an accomplished fact; threat is a negative stimulus whose outcome is uncertain—it may cause harm, yet it may also be eliminated through effort. Therefore, if negative harm has already damaged the interest the individual cares about most, is further struggle necessary? If struggle remains possible, the outcome is still undetermined and there is an opportunity to recover through action. Whether damage has already occurred depends mainly on whether the individual subjectively believes the most important outcome has been damaged; like threat, this is a subjective assessment.

Thus the stimulus for anger is indeed threat.

In real life, some people become angry when others touch their sore spots, even when the remarks are groundless slander; others can remain detached and dismiss such slander with a smile. The difference lies in the assessment of threat: those who perceive threat become angry; those who do not perceive threat remain calm. Threat is a subjective feeling.

Fear is the weaker mindset that follows assessment of a negative stimulus. If the stimulus threatens survival or reproduction, anger arises; if the negative stimulus is overwhelming, it is no longer literally a “threat.” Here, threat is a subjective feeling.

Of course, human intelligence can influence emotion in certain respects. When serious harm occurs—whether to oneself or to a loved one—memory and reason cause the person, beyond sadness, to dwell on the malignant effects produced by the stimulus; each recollection can trigger a degree of anger.

Having clarified that the source of anger is interest threat, we arrive at a formula:

When an anger expression is observed, the individual subjectively believes their interests are threatened, hopes to defend those interests through confrontation and struggle, and believes victory is possible.

##### 3. Differences in Mouth Shapes

In a surprise expression the upper lip is not raised; the lower lip opens naturally with the dropping jaw to allow quick, shallow inhalation. This occurs because, before surprise, the nature of the stimulus is still uncertain and no solution has been chosen. Once it is determined that the stimulus will cause overwhelming harm, the evolved human instinct immediately attempts to execute an escape plan, so the mouth opens to inhale the maximum volume of air for energy reserves. Therefore, in a fear expression the upper lip is raised, the corners of the mouth are pulled widely sideways by the platysma, and the lower lip not only opens with the dropping jaw but is also lengthened and lowered by the depressor labii inferioris, exposing part of the lower teeth. This action, performed to store respiratory energy, is of the same nature as the whole-body tension that occurs when we are afraid—trembling, skin tightening, altered blood circulation.

Finally, note that a full fear expression is usually accompanied by a deep inhalation. Observing the breathing movement that accompanies the expression is also an important indicator for judging emotion.

Finally, note one expression easily mistaken for fear.  
At the instant of fear, because vigilance toward the stimulus is still maintained and the tragic outcome remains uncertain, the eyes never narrow. The reaction seen in films—tightly closed eyes and a scream of terror—actually occurs because the individual has already resigned to the worst outcome; it is a derivative of sadness. The scream serves both as an instinctive behavior to relieve inner pressure and as an evolutionarily accumulated attack method—driving the opponent away with high-frequency sound. This is shown in Figure 7-10.
