##### 2. Differences in Eyelid Morphology

The eyelids in surprise open naturally to the maximum, exposing the entire upper edge of the iris and possibly even the sclera above. In fear the upper eyelids also attempt to open wide, but the opposing pull of the orbicularis oculi and corrugator supercilii on the eyebrows creates a fold that alters the overall eyelid shape, yet the natural degree of iris exposure remains visible.

**Why open the eyes wide?**  
The original motive for opening the eyes to the maximum is to receive more visual information quickly in order to judge whether one is safe.

When we are afraid, we become highly tense and extremely sensitive to our surroundings. The entire nervous system is responding to a threat that may appear at any moment. High attention can be expressed through the wide-open state of the eyes; when the stimulus is sufficiently terrifying, the eyes open to their limit in an instant.

The wider the eyes open, the more fearful the expression appears. In this respect, **the eye features of fear are the same as those of surprise and anger**. When fear is milder—for example, worry or unease—the eyes do not open especially wide and the sclera above the iris does not show.

Therefore, one special method for observing fear is to cover the rest of the face and look only at the eyes. Such close-ups are frequently used in horror films. In the figure below, although we cannot see whether the eyebrows are distorted, the single eye alone makes it easy to tell that this is not surprise. This is shown in Figure 7-9.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图7-9]*

It is clear that the left image shows fearful eyes while the right image shows ordinary surprise without fear. The eyelid-fold shape in the left image results from the special configuration of the eyebrow.

##### 2. Glaring: Upper Eyelid Elevation, Exposure of Upper Iris Margin, Lower Eyelid Tension (9789620756689)

Although the upper eyelid is closed downward by contraction of the orbicularis oculi while also meeting resistance from the downward pressure of the eyebrows, the levator palpebrae superioris still works in coordination to elevate the upper eyelid. Consequently, two opposing forces compress the skin of the upper eyelid, altering its shape and creating an overlapping fold.

Under normal conditions, the upper eyelid covers approximately one-quarter of the upper half of the iris. In an angry expression, however, the substantial elevation of the upper eyelid exposes a larger area of the upper iris margin. Although the upper eyelid crease is deformed by the overlapping fold, we can infer that, without the skin fold created by the downward pressure of the eyebrows, the upper eyelid line would cross the iris and leave the upper iris margin uncovered. While the upper eyelid is forcefully elevated, the lower eyelid is slightly raised, straightened, and tensed by contraction of the orbicularis oculi, making the glare appear more intense.

When the three factors—downward pressure of both eyebrows, tension in both upper and lower eyelids, and intense visual focus—occur simultaneously, the fire of anger erupts from the eyes.

Of course, the conditions discussed here represent the standard components of an anger expression; real expressions do not always conform exactly to every element. As shown in Figure 6-5, the shape of the eyebrows, the skin fold formed by the effortful elevation of the upper eyelid, the tensed lower eyelid, and the roaring mouth allow us to clearly determine that the woman is in an angry state, even though her eyes are not wide open and the iris is not greatly exposed.

Many factors can produce this phenomenon. For example, the image may capture a dynamic instant that is not the final state of anger, or the individual, though angry, may also feel slight fear and therefore lack a strong impulse to attack. What matters is not the size of the eyes or the degree of iris exposure, but attention to the combination of eyebrow and eyelid shapes.

##### 4. Interest Conflicts

One of the most common forms of anger in human society arises when others threaten one’s interests.

Two competing departments in a company request budget allocations from their boss. Regardless of the methods used by the department heads or the final budget outcome, any non-constructive competitive behavior can already provoke mutual anger and hostility between the two heads. Yet is the root of their anger truly the portion of the budget the boss ultimately approves or withholds? One possibility is that the two individuals are not merely concerned with the numerical amount of money but with the competitive outcome the numbers represent.

Whoever receives the larger budget approval gains numerous derivative advantages; the decision may signify the leader’s recognition, or it may imply enhanced “reputation within the field” and greater loyalty from subordinates, all of which affect future survival and development. Even if the two departments receive equal funding, or if the department that obtains more funding still feels threatened by the other’s unreasonable competitive tactics, anger can arise.

Therefore, in many cases of anger triggered by perceived loss of interests, the interests themselves are merely superficial or serve as a trigger; the core issue is the future threat implied by that loss. If the loss of interests becomes an established trend—meaning the competitor believes they will always be defeated—then their mind will be filled with powerless fear or sorrow.

Numerous examples of the same nature exist: competing for people, money, or territory. Competition in romantic relationships is likewise a frequent context for anger. Driven by the pursuit of optimal reproduction, any threat to one’s own ability to love another or to the loved one will generate a physiological impulse toward angry attack. Yet once true love has departed, only tears of sorrow flow, not the hot blood of anger.

##### (1) Mouth Shape Changes I: Angry Roaring and Biting

Angry roaring is also a common means of attacking an opponent and objectively requires the mouth to open. Biting serves to seize an opponent’s limb and therefore differs from chewing. Chewing involves the posterior teeth, whereas biting primarily uses the anterior canines and incisors; this likewise requires the mouth to open and the teeth to be exposed, engaging the mandible (to open the mouth), the levator labii superioris, the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi (to expose the upper teeth), and the depressor labii inferioris (to expose the lower teeth).

In addition to roaring, anger employs other mouth shapes to accompany the facial expression, conveying varying degrees of anger while also meeting the functional demands of different attack behaviors.

- **Left image**: The levator labii superioris and levator labii superioris alaeque nasi contract together, forcefully elevating the upper lip. This human anger expression closely resembles the warning posture animals adopt before attacking. The upper-lip elevation is similar to the shape seen in disgust but is executed with greater force, because instinctive awareness demands that the upper canines (located at the corners of the mouth) be fully exposed to convey the desire to attack.
- **Center image**: When language serves as the weapon of attack during argument or reprimand, movement of the lower lip exposes the lower teeth. One can imagine how angry the entire face containing this mouth must be; the phrase “gnashing of teeth” comes immediately to mind.
- **Right image**: The lower lip is stretched by the combined action of the depressor labii inferioris, the platysma, and the mandible. The mandible descends, opening the oral cavity. The platysma contracts, pulling the corners of the mouth sideways. The depressor labii inferioris draws the lower lip into a U shape, exposing the lower teeth and gums. The orbicularis oris contracts, straightening and tightening the lips—an important action during loud vocalization.

##### (2) Mouth Shape Changes II: Mouth Open, Teeth Clenched

In the absence of emotion, humans clench their teeth in two situations: pain and physical exertion. Both triggers commonly occur during combat—both parties exert effort to win and experience pain when injured. To achieve victory and endure pain, clenching the teeth is necessary. Moreover, for animals, teeth are an offensive weapon, and biting is a primary combat action.

Keeping the jaws tightly closed through teeth clenching is not a natural or comfortable posture; when relaxed, the teeth exert no mutual pressure. Exposing part of the teeth at the same time increases the difficulty, requiring more muscles to perform complex movements. One can test this by first clenching the teeth firmly and then stretching the lips to expose the teeth, as when enduring a headache or pulling hard in a tug-of-war. Unlike roaring anger, teeth clenching combined with an angry glare usually appears during effortful anger.

In Figure 6-9 the lower halves of the two faces are very similar. Both mouth shapes are formed by contraction of the levator labii superioris, levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, and zygomaticus minor, elevating the upper lip while the lower lip is stretched. Yet the overall facial expressions differ. If only the lower half of the face is considered, it is impossible to distinguish clearly between anger and pain. The eye configuration, however, identifies the left image as intense anger; the right image, with eyes closed, shows pain without anger.

##### 3. Anxious Anger

Anyone who has raised children shares the experience of coaxing a young child to sleep—an affectionate, loving moment. Can anger arise at such a time? It certainly can; the classic scenario occurs when parents have important plans (such as a conference call) after the child has gone to bed.

If important arrangements await, yet the child continues to request another story or repeatedly refuses to settle, occasionally speaking just when the parent believes sleep has finally arrived, these originally endearing behaviors can provoke anxious anger. The internal monologue might run: “Child, it’s time for you to sleep; it’s getting late. Daddy/Mommy still has important things to do. Go to sleep quickly so I can get on with my work; if you stay awake much longer, you may disrupt my plans.”

As time presses and anxiety accumulates, anger readily appears, manifesting as irritability or even scolding. Yet if the parent truly must wait until the child sleeps before attending to other matters (for example, being the sole caregiver), once the deadline for the important task passes without the child asleep, anger dissipates and calm returns—unless the task outweighs the child’s distress in importance.

As an aside, this also explains why particularly busy parents are more likely to raise rebellious children: the child concludes that they matter less to the parents than earning money or attending meetings. “Since I am unimportant,” the child reasons, “you might as well stop supervising me.”

##### 6. Unreasonableness

“It’s unreasonable!” represents another stimulus that provokes anger and another way of expressing it. Whether among collaborators on a shared front, rivals in competition, or strangers encountered while driving, unreasonable behavior can trigger intense anger.

Unreasonableness is, in effect, “inconsistent with the reasoning the individual accepts,” producing a mismatch with expectations. During a team discussion of solutions, after the leader has outlined a directional approach and members are anxiously refining it into an executable plan, someone who airily proposes an impractical idea may provoke anger (or possibly contempt). What results does unreasonableness produce? The individual believes that following their own expectations and logic will yield the best outcome—or, if the focus is on enjoying the process rather than the result, that this approach maximizes enjoyment. When others act “unreasonably” in the relevant process, the individual perceives a threat to the anticipated outcome (or process). The essence of obstructed action is obstructed freedom, identical in nature to the restraint an infant experiences when prevented from moving freely; combined with possible threats to interests, this naturally elicits anger.

Similar to unreasonableness is the frustration caused by non-human or unclear factors during an activity. Apart from the absence of a clearly identifiable “unreasonable” person, all other aspects parallel unreasonableness and likewise provoke anger.

##### 6.2.1 Morphological Features of the Anger Expression

As shown in Figure 6-1, the fullest anger expression includes five typical features:

1. Both eyebrows lowered and tightly knit;
2. Upper eyelid elevated, lower eyelid tensed, orbicularis oculi strongly contracted—commonly called a glare;
3. Mouth forcefully opened, upper lip stretched tight, teeth exposed as weapons of attack;
4. Chin lowered. This is important: genuine attack behavior does not involve a raised head or chin;
5. Nostrils flared, not only exposing the upper teeth in a threatening posture but also widening the nasal passages to maintain an unobstructed exhalation route.

Using the cues in Figure 6-2, the facial-muscle morphology of the anger expression can be analyzed as follows:

1. Strong contraction of the orbicularis oculi lowers both eyebrows; strong contraction of the corrugator supercilii knits the brows;
2. Strong contraction of the levator palpebrae superioris raises the upper eyelid to its maximum, attempting to expose the entire upper iris margin. However, the elevation of the upper eyelid combined with the downward pressure of the eyebrows produces a mutually compressing angry configuration, forming diagonal skin folds on the upper eyelid;
3. Lower eyelid tensed. The configuration of the upper eyelid together with the tensed lower eyelid is termed a glare;
4. Coordinated contraction of the levator labii superioris and levator labii superioris alaeque nasi elevates the nostrils while also raising the cheeks, creating deep grooves on either side of the nose;
5. Mandible opens downward; the lower lip is pulled down by the depressor labii inferioris, exposing part of the lower teeth, and is stretched sideways and thinned by contraction of the platysma, lying tightly against the mandible.

##### 6.3.4 Anger Variant III: Relaxed Lower Face

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-18]*

Examining only the lower half of the face in Figure 6-18—the area around the nose and mouth—makes it impossible to determine the subject’s expression or emotion. Because the upper lip shows no obvious elevation, the nostrils are not raised and no grooves are formed by compression between the nostrils and cheeks (the shading beside the nostrils results from crossed lighting during photography). Compared with an ordinary open-mouth posture, the main difference in the mouth shape is that the upper lip appears narrower and the orbicularis oris is only partially contracted. The mouth does not look particularly angry; if the upper half of the face were covered, the subject would appear to be speaking.

The actual situation is readily understandable. Once roaring subsides, the mouth relaxes, yet because the stimulus for anger remains unresolved, the eyes continue to express anger intensely. Overall, the facial expression still conveys a high degree of anger, produced entirely by the configuration of the eyes and eyebrows.

Thus, during anger the mouth does not always remain tense, nor does the upper lip necessarily elevate; even when the nose and mouth are relaxed, anger can still be expressed through a specific micro-expression configuration. That micro-expression configuration is the standard angry eyebrow-and-eye morphology.

##### (3) Damage to Reputation

Reputation is unique to human society; although animals may possess something analogous, this cannot be verified. Because of language and the complexity of evaluative systems, reputation functions like the scent-marking of territorial boundaries in animals, carrying a wealth of information about the individual. The communicative and consensual power of reputation far exceeds that of urine marks. Word-of-mouth transmission in human society imperceptibly creates a consensus force that shapes individual perception. Establishing and enhancing reputation strengthens and consolidates one’s own survival; this is also why celebrities enjoy higher income returns. Damage to reputation, conversely, can cause substantial loss to the individual in society and may even threaten continued survival.

Consequently, once reputation has been established, the individual will strive to perfect and defend this existing “territorial” marker, using reputation to build a platform for survival and reproduction while reducing costs. When reputation is attacked or threatened, the effect is equivalent to an incursion across a scent-marked boundary, endangering the individual’s survival and reproduction and readily arousing anger.

Those interested may search the internet for the number of celebrities who have responded to reputational attacks with angry lawsuits or public confrontations with their detractors. This book will not cite specific real-world cases of celebrities as supporting data.

##### 3. Nose and Cheek Morphology

Anger expressions engage the levator labii superioris and the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi. Although the direct action of these two muscles is to raise the upper lip, they also indirectly affect nose shape: the alae are lifted, the nostrils flare, and deep grooves form on either side of the alae. At the same time, the cheeks are indirectly affected and rise slightly.

In the opening scene of Season 1, Episode 1 of the American series *Lie to Me*, the tall, bald suspect displays a classic anger expression (eyebrows + nose forming an X shape) after hearing Lightman name the actual hiding place of the bomb. Lightman immediately realizes the bomb is hidden exactly where he had just asked about. The script, however, labels the expression “scorn” (accurately translated as “contempt”). This is one of the more obvious errors in *Lie to Me*. The raised upper lip and grooves beside the nose alone would indicate contempt, yet the eyebrow and eye configuration of the upper face cannot be ignored.

##### Chapter Summary

Anger is an aggressive emotion that arises when a person feels threatened or senses that their interests are about to be harmed. When angry, there is an impulse to act physically; in modern society this impulse may be channeled into debate, scolding, criticism, or other civilized forms. Regardless of the form, the essence of anger remains the same: the person believes they must interfere with or counter the stimulus through attack or retaliation. Failure to interfere risks harm; interference may change the threatened situation. The stimulus is usually assessed by the angry person as an equal opponent. Consequently, anger expressions share several consistent features: furrowed brows signal intense focus; the eyelids are raised forcefully to observe every movement of the stimulus; the opposing actions of the brows pressing down and the eyelids lifting create ridges on the upper eyelid skin. Another prominent feature is prolonged, steady gaze fixed on the stimulus—an exaggerated display of attention to an opponent—accompanied by bodily changes such as accelerated circulation, heavier breathing, muscle tension, and ample energy reserves, all preparing for imminent attack.

##### 2. Restriction of Freedom

Restriction of freedom poses one of the greatest threats to survival. Without freedom of movement, a person feels surrounded like prey with no escape and certain death. In the instinctive awareness accumulated through human evolution, restriction of freedom therefore registers as an extremely serious threat.

When adults play with children, they sometimes affectionately pin a child to their chest and gently restrain the arms and legs. Can you guess the child’s reaction?

The child’s face suddenly changes to anger, the body flushes bright red, breath is held, and the child struggles to break free—an unmistakable anger response. The restraint is not forceful enough to hurt, and the play atmosphere was pleasant until that moment; the change occurs solely because of the restraining action.

The child’s subjective expectation is free movement. Any behavior that limits a child’s ability to act creates a negative expectation violation. Even during play, sudden inability to move freely triggers instinctive discomfort and anger. After a brief, futile effort to change the situation, the child opens the mouth wide and cries loudly, expressing grievance (unwillingness coupled with inability to change) and bewilderment—this is the sadness emotion.

##### 6.3.1 Muscles That Tense the Lips

In the anger expression with tightly closed lips, mouth shape is determined directly by three muscles: the orbicularis oris, the depressor anguli oris, and the mentalis (see Figure 6-10). All three contract to press the lips together.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-10]*

The levator labii superioris and depressor labii inferioris open the lips and do not participate in closing them.

The pout that expresses denial (reluctance, difficulty, pathos) results from contraction of the mentalis and depressor anguli oris while the orbicularis oris remains relaxed. When the orbicularis oris also contracts, lip closure becomes firmer; mild contraction signals displeasure, while stronger contraction intensifies the denial into suppressed anger, indicating that hesitation has given way to the need for greater force to restrain the impulse to attack (see Figure 6-11).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-11]*

##### 1. Lowering of Both Eyebrows

Lowering of both eyebrows is a prominent feature of anger expressions and appears in the great majority of them. Darwin observed that brow lowering signals the encounter of trouble. He speculated that in primitive times the movement reduced glare when staring at a difficulty and later became a habitual response to any difficulty. Indeed, lowered brows frequently appear in expressions of disgust, confusion (commonly seen while lecturing students, disappearing once the point is clarified), difficulty, deep thought, and even physical exertion—all forms of trouble. Because “trouble” emphasizes the object, Darwin’s conclusion is updated from the subject’s perspective:

**Lowered brows indicate serious attention.**

Lowered brows alone do not confirm anger; the eyes must also be engaged in forceful looking. Forceful looking includes tension and contraction of the orbicularis oculi, producing characteristic changes in both upper and lower eyelids, as well as sustained, unwavering gaze. When lowered brows combine with a fixed stare, the result is a glare—the key morphological feature of anger expressions.

##### (1) Contempt

A common verbal expression of negation is “You’re no good!” Depending on tone, it can convey a wide range of meanings. Such contempt need not involve any threatening action; a single sentence or glance may suffice. No one likes to be negated by others, especially when the negation takes the form of contempt (which amplifies the effect) or lacks factual basis (slander), both of which readily provoke anger.

When animals are regarded as inferior by their own kind, they lose authority and control, placing their safety at great risk of predation, defeat, loss of mates or offspring, or death. In today’s highly developed civilization and division of labor, negation of a skill likewise threatens competitiveness and survival opportunities. This is one of the most direct triggers of anger.

Even cultivated scholars will often defend their reputation when their professional expertise is arbitrarily slandered or belittled. Countless examples appear online where opinion leaders launch verbal and written attacks over minor differences of view.

##### 1. Differences in Brow Shape

In surprise the brows are simply raised (frontalis contraction), preserving a natural shape. In fear the brows are knitted as a whole, the inner corners rise, the brows appear twisted, and clear vertical and horizontal furrows form.

At the instant of surprise, no positive or negative judgment has yet been formed about the stimulus; the next emotion could be delight, startled anger, or fear. Fear, however, necessarily arises because the stimulus is perceived as extremely dangerous and therefore requires concentrated attention. Consequently, the action of raising the brows (frontalis, medial fibers) is involuntarily accompanied by contraction of the corrugator supercilii, knitting and lowering the brows. Remember: **furrowed brows indicate intense attention**.

Fear therefore produces a more complex brow-eye configuration than surprise. The brows must knit inward to signal tension and pressure while also rising to help the eyes gather more visual information. As a result, the fear brow shape is less expansive than the surprise brow shape.

**Self-practice method**: First raise both brows as high as possible, then knit and lower them.

##### (2) Provocation

Provocation usually precedes open conflict. The provoking party expresses a desire to fight and hopes the target will respond in kind, deliberately arousing the target’s anger by attacking whatever matters most to them. Provocation is the behavior most likely to elicit anger. Its forms vary according to the target’s personality and concerns, but generally fall into two types: “Let’s fight and see” and “You’re worthless; I can’t be bothered to fight you—if we did, I’d finish you easily.” The second type usually provokes stronger anger because the first is often delivered seriously by someone of genuine capability, allowing the target to respond rationally and consider non-combat solutions unless bystander opinion interferes. The second type deliberately conveys a low evaluation and uses disdain to intensify the expectation violation, making the target eager to disprove the assessment and punish the provocateur. Because the evaluation is so low, correction seems easy—yet this is precisely the psychological trap.

##### Chapter 6 Micro-expressions of Anger

When the intensity of a negative stimulus exceeds the threshold of disgust and becomes threatening, anger is triggered. Anger is characterized by an attack tendency aimed at driving away or eliminating the negative stimulus.

The essence of disgust is a “top-down negation” attitude toward the negative stimulus—an attempt to reject, avoid, or simply ignore it. At no level of disgust does the person desire to alter, attack, or eliminate the stimulus; walking away is always an option. Once the stimulus intensifies to the point of threat or harm, the emotion escalates to anger.

The essence of anger is the desire to attack and prevail—eliminating danger through attack.

Events that provoke anger are richly varied in daily life, ranging from a taxi driver ignoring a hail on the street to a violent assault on oneself or one’s child. Readers should therefore prepare to examine the sources of anger systematically.

##### 6.3 Morphological Features of Anger Micro-expressions

Although a hysterical outburst and a cold stare appear vastly different, both can instill fear under certain conditions. This is because every anger expression shares one common feature: an attack tendency. Roaring attack, bared-teeth threat, tightly closed lips conveying severity, and piercing gaze all belong to different manifestations of anger.

Beginning with the fullest anger expression and working downward, the analysis focuses not on degree of emotion but on its morphological variations. Because anger is a dangerous, attack-oriented emotion and combat demands speed, expressions change dramatically within a short time; cold disgust can turn to fury in an instant.

Following common real-life anger expressions, the analysis proceeds from the lower face upward, examining changes in the mouth, nose, eyes, and brows to provide a comprehensive, systematic grasp of anger micro-expression and classic expression features.

##### Mouth

Mouth shape is the most variable element in anger expressions. In roaring anger the mouth shape is influenced by the words being spoken. The upper lip is usually raised; the lower lip varies. It may form a biting, teeth-bared shape, be pressed together and protruded by the mentalis and orbicularis oris, or remain in its usual relaxed state. With equal eyelid elevation, a person with an open, roaring mouth appears angrier than one with a closed mouth (see Figure 6-27).

In modern social interaction, fully displayed, unambiguous anger expressions are rare. Noticing the momentary eye-widening change can reveal the person’s inner emotion.

Anger without focused gaze is a staged performance.

Without concentrated gaze, lowered brows and pressed lips alone cannot effectively convey anger; the expression more closely resembles a response to pressure and is commonly seen when someone is reluctantly deciding or deep in thought (see Figure 6-27).

##### (4) Negation of One’s Group

Telling a capable university student “Your school is terrible!”—if the student rejects the evaluation—can provoke anger because the group to which the student belongs has been negated. The same applies to negation of a team, ethnicity, or nation. Although the negative evaluation targets an organization or group, or even other members of that group, a sense of belonging readily converts it into individual anger, sometimes of greater intensity.

Chinese people’s anger provides a typical example. For more than a century since the late Qing dynasty, China suffered invasion and humiliation by foreign powers; Japan’s eight-year invasion beginning in 1937 left later generations with enduring anger toward the former aggressor. People can reach a state of gnashing anger without needing further historical details.

##### Explanation of Option B

The language in option B can also occur in real situations, but the speaker’s inner state differs significantly. Loss is the source of sadness. If nothing else intervenes, a daughter’s death would produce only sadness, leaving no energy for other concerns. “She’s already dead” might appear during frantic struggle, yet more often it surfaces in a state of sadness (true sadness is rarely voiced) as a reinforcement of loss.

The unexpected, deliberate harm that caused the death adds a considerable degree of anger to the sadness. The repetition of “She’s already dead,” however, is not a direct expression of anger but of sadness. The speaker uses this sorrowful outcome to intensify the expectation violation (healthy life versus violent death) and thereby strengthen the anger that mobilizes energy for combat.

##### 1. Full Anger Expression Morphology

The morphological features of a full anger expression are as follows:
- Strong contraction of the orbicularis oculi lowers both brows; strong contraction of the corrugator supercilii knits the brows tightly.
- Strong contraction of the levator palpebrae superioris raises the upper eyelids to their maximum, attempting to expose the entire superior margin of the iris. The opposing actions of upper-eyelid elevation and brow depression create the characteristic anger configuration, forming diagonal skin folds on the upper eyelid.
- The lower eyelid tenses; the shape of the upper eyelid matches the tensed lower eyelid, producing a glare.
- Simultaneous contraction of the levator labii superioris and levator labii superioris alaeque nasi lifts the nasal alae, raises the cheeks, and creates deep grooves on either side of the nose.
- The mandible opens downward; the lower lip is pulled down by the depressor labii inferioris, exposing part of the lower teeth. Contraction of the platysma stretches the lower lip sideways and thins it, pressing it tightly against the mandible.

##### 2. Common Anger Expression Morphology

In everyday social interaction, ordinary people—except with close family or during actual combat—rarely open their mouths to roar even when angry. More often the lips are pressed tightly together while breath is held. Combined with the standard anger brow-eye configuration, the face appears extremely angry.

Morphological features:
- Contraction of the corrugator supercilii and orbicularis oculi knits and lowers both brows.
- Contraction of the levator palpebrae superioris.
- Contraction of the orbicularis oculi also tenses the lower eyelid and pulls it slightly sideways.
- Contraction of the orbicularis oris presses both lips tightly together.
- Contraction of the depressor anguli oris pulls both mouth corners downward.
- Contraction of the mentalis creates a muscular bulge on the chin with an uneven surface while pushing the lower lip upward to keep the lips closed.

##### 6.2 Full Anger Expression

Anger is a response to a threatening stimulus, mobilizing energy to attack, drive away, injure, or eliminate the opponent. Once a negative stimulus crosses the nervous system’s red line, anger suddenly replaces disgust. Because anger directly leads to attack—whether through verbal scolding or physical action—its roots trace back to ancient combat. These attacks require rapid expenditure of large amounts of energy, so genuine anger is difficult to sustain for long periods.

Other emotions lack such close coordination with physical action and, even at extreme intensity, do not carry an attack tendency.

##### 1. Morphological Features of Angry Micro-expressions

One thing you might not easily think of is that for an externalized emotion like anger, the core determining factor of the expression is actually a very small detail—the shape of the eyelids and the gaze. The intensity of the anger emotion has an instinctive direct correlation with the degree of upper eyelid lift and the tension in the lower eyelid; the higher the upper eyelid is lifted and the tighter the lower eyelid is tensed, the angrier the expression appears.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图6-25]*



##### Eyelids

An angry expression must include lifting of the upper eyelids (causing more of the top of the iris to be exposed than in a normal state) and tightening of the lower eyelids (position slightly raised, eyelid line straightened). The wider the eyes are opened, the deeper the anger. Eyes glaring in coordination with lowered brows give the gaze strong penetrating power.

When the shapes of the brows and eyes are combined with the mouth shape of anger, the presence of anger can be clearly expressed.



##### 1. Morphological Features of Angry Micro-expressions

One thing you might not easily think of is that for an externalized emotion like anger, the core determining factor of the expression is actually a very small detail—the shape of the eyelids and the gaze. The intensity of the anger emotion has an instinctive direct correlation with the degree of upper eyelid lift and the tension in the lower eyelid; the higher the upper eyelid is lifted and the tighter the lower eyelid is tensed, the angrier the expression appears. As shown in Figure 6-25.



##### Summary

In summary, the higher the level of civilization in human society, the more complex the various consensual rules become, and the more diverse and complicated the stimuli that can trigger anger become; in the analysis of specific issues, analysis must be conducted according to the specific situation and the individuals involved.

Overall, however, the stimuli for anger can be attributed to threats to matters of concern and can be traced back to threats to survival and reproduction in primitive times.



##### 3. Morphological Features of Angry Micro-expressions

In cases of extreme restraint, an angry expression usually retains only changes in the eyelids.

Morphological features:
- Contraction of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle, attempting to raise the upper eyelids (often meeting resistance from the brows being furrowed and pressed downward);
- Contraction of the orbicularis oculi muscle, tightening the lower eyelids and pressing them closer to the skull.

**Summary**: The characteristic of anger is an aggressive tendency, an attempt to drive away or eliminate the negative stimulus source.



##### 5. Being Denied

Denial is a general term for a category of stimuli; as analyzed in the chapter on disgust, the essence of loathing, contempt, and disdain is all denial, so in terms of specific manifestations, it can be subdivided into direct denial, belittlement (contempt and disdain), disgust, and various manifestations based on belittlement such as provocation and disrespect.



##### 2. Typical Features of Angry Expressions

The typical features of an angry expression are brows pressed downward, closest to the upper eyelid edges; eyes staring forcefully, upper eyelids lifted, lower eyelids tensed, gaze strongly focused on the stimulus source without leaving it; the mouth shape of anger is more variable, commonly including bared teeth, roaring, or tightly closed lips. As shown in Figure 6-26.



##### 4. Mouth Shape

In addition to the typical angry brow and eye shapes, a full angry expression also has several variations, mainly caused by different mouth shapes. The most fearsome angry expression is anger with the mouth open and shouting, which is a sign of emotional loss of control; with a bit more rationality, it turns into clenched teeth.



##### Summary

Therefore, the necessary features of an angry expression are tension in both the upper and lower eyelids plus strong concentration of gaze. If this necessary feature is missing, it can be determined that there is no anger emotion. This set of eye-shape features constitutes the morphological features of angry micro-expressions.



##### Eyebrows

Lowered brows indicate strong attention. Because stimuli capable of triggering anger possess threat-level intensity and are absolutely worth attending to, the typical lowered-brow shape appears in natural expressions.

#### Morphological Features of Sad Micro-expressions

##### 8.2.2 Adult Crying Expressions (9789620756689)

When adults cry due to sadness, the facial morphology is identical to that of infants. Sadness mobilizes energy that spontaneously triggers vigorous movement in the eye and mouth muscles to produce the crying expression, as shown in Figure 8-2.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-2]*

The morphological features of adult crying can be broken down as follows:

1. The orbicularis oculi and corrugator supercilii contract together, depressing the brows and creating vertical wrinkles between them. At the same time, the central frontalis contracts, slightly elevating the brows so that the overall brow shape flattens and twists upward in the medial third. Note that this twisted brow shape also appears in fear expressions, but the contraction of the orbicularis oculi in sadness produces a more pronounced twist than in fear.
2. Contraction of the orbicularis oculi forces the eyelids tightly shut, creating wrinkles at the inner eye corners and crow’s-feet at the outer corners (a single deep line is visible in the figure). The combined action of the orbicularis oculi and part of the corrugator supercilii produces tightly closed eyes. The physiological significance of this change was explained in the discussion of infant crying. The more intense the crying, the tighter the contraction around the eyeballs.
3. Contraction of the levator labii superioris raises the upper lip while, together with the orbicularis oculi, elevating the cheeks. The raised cheeks press against the lower eyelids, forming a depressed area beneath the lower lids and nasolabial folds on either side of the nose.
4. Contraction of the platysma pulls the mouth corners laterally, increasing the horizontal width of the mouth beyond its resting state; the stretched corners press against the cheeks to form marionette lines.
5. Contraction of the depressor anguli oris pulls the mouth corners downward while the depressor labii inferioris contracts, lowering the entire lower lip in an attempt to expose the lower teeth.
6. Simultaneous contraction of the mentalis pushes the middle of the lower lip upward, creating an uneven muscular bulge on the chin. This upward push conceals part of the lower teeth that would otherwise be visible, while the corners remain lowered, exposing the lower teeth only at the mouth corners. The lower lip forms a W-shaped curve. This mouth shape is unique to the crying expression, as shown in Figure 8-3.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-3]*

Note that the synergistic action of these muscles creates a sharp angle of inflection roughly one-quarter of the way from each mouth corner toward the center of the lower lip, giving the mouth an overall trapezoidal appearance. This shape is optimal for producing a sharp, well-supported sound. To verify, shout “wa” without any feeling of grief and observe whether the mouth shape closely resembles the crying shape.

The crying mouth is wider (horizontally) than the relaxed mouth because of platysma stretch. The trapezoidal lip shape results from elevation of the upper lip and lateral pull on the lower lip. The lip borders become taut and thin. Elevation of the upper lip also raises the cheeks; in addition to the nasolabial folds, the action of the depressor anguli oris beneath the mouth corners produces a vertical crease running from nose to chin, as shown in Figure 8-4.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-4]*

Given the complexity of the crying action, it is difficult to fake. In genuine sobbing, the lower lip forms a W shape through the coordinated action of the platysma, depressor labii inferioris, depressor anguli oris, and mentalis. A simulated cry rarely achieves this complex muscular pattern and therefore cannot reproduce the undulating contour; nor can the degree of eye closure be accurately imitated unless genuine sadness is aroused. In reality, the emotion supplies substantial energy to execute the normal crying movements, producing both the correct amplitude and force of the facial actions and their natural coordination—an internal consistency that is hard to counterfeit.

##### Chapter Summary

The emotions discussed in previous chapters—surprise, disgust, anger, and fear—share the common characteristic that they are all based on the emotion holder’s subjective appraisal rather than on an established outcome. Sadness differs fundamentally from these four emotions because it is based on an established outcome—loss of benefit—even when that outcome is merely the emotion holder’s misappraisal.

The stimulus for sadness is “an irrevocable loss.” Only after the emotion holder appraises the situation and concludes that the loss has already occurred (including intangible losses such as reputation, status, or public esteem) does sadness arise. A second characteristic of sadness is that it is separated from fear by only a thin boundary; the two are essentially the same in that both involve a highly negative appraisal of the stimulus, with the stimulus perceived as exceeding one’s defensive capacity. The sole difference is whether the negative outcome has already taken place. Before it occurs, the emotion is fear; once it is confirmed, the emotion is sadness.

Consequently, their facial morphologies are nearly identical: both display the furrowed-and-raised “囧”-shaped brows. In fear, however, the eyelids remain raised to gather information and make judgments, whereas in sadness the outcome has already occurred, so the eyelids close. The mouth shapes of fear and sadness also share features: both recruit the depressor anguli oris, mentalis, and platysma. Contraction of the depressor anguli oris pulls the mouth corners downward; contraction of the mentalis bulges the chin and pushes the middle of the lower lip upward; contraction of the platysma stretches the mouth corners laterally and downward, forming a trapezoid that is wider at the top and narrower at the bottom. In fear this shape often signals being stunned; in sadness it commonly appears during sobbing. It should be noted that fear’s emotional instability and transformability prevent the mouth shape from being as classic and stable as in sadness; screaming, breath-holding, or other needs frequently disrupt it. In sadness, by contrast, the negative fact is already established, so fewer interfering factors exist and a relatively stable mouth morphology appears.

1. **Morphological Features of Sad Micro-expressions**  
   The brows are raised while the overall brow remains depressed—a necessary feature of the sadness expression, as shown in Figure 8-19.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-19]*

2. **Typical Morphological Features of Sadness**  
   During weeping the brows are depressed overall (due to orbicularis oculi contraction). Although the eyes are usually tightly closed, social context makes wide-mouthed crying rare. The typical action is mouth closure: the taut lips experience upward pressure from below (mentalis) and lateral stretch (platysma). Crying itself is a spasmodic movement.

   As crying intensity decreases, the first muscles to relax are those around the eyes—the orbicularis oculi. After the orbicularis oculi relaxes, the medial frontalis contracts, raising the brows and producing forehead wrinkles; together with the corrugator supercilii this produces a slightly twisted brow shape.

   Next to relax is the platysma. Platysma contraction gives the mouth the appearance of being about to cry. Once sufficiently calm, the platysma relaxes and the mouth returns to its normal state.

**3. Derived Sad Micro-expressions**

When the elicited emotion belongs to other sadness-derived categories such as guilt, displeasure, bitterness, or reluctance, the typical morphology may be the “bitter pursed lips” of the mouth. This “bitter pursed lips” shape, produced by the coordinated action of the platysma, mentalis, depressor anguli oris, and depressor labii inferioris, is a clear feature of derived sadness expressions.

##### 8.2.1 Infant Crying Expressions

When very young children encounter negative stimuli (hunger, pain, fear, etc.), their instinctive response is to cry loudly, thereby attracting adult attention and protection. In infant crying, loudness is crucial; if the sound is insufficient, parents may overlook it.

Infant crying expressions are difficult to capture photographically, so a sketch is used to illustrate the morphological features, as shown in Figure 8-1.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-1]*  
Reproduced from *The Artist’s Complete Guide to Facial Expression* by Gary Faigin.

The morphological features of infant crying are as follows:

1. Contraction of the corrugator supercilii produces a strong furrowing of the brows.
2. Strong contraction of the orbicularis oculi tightly closes the upper and lower eyelids; the lids press against each other, creating wrinkles between the eyes.
3. Contraction of the levator labii superioris tenses the upper lip and raises the cheeks, forming nasolabial folds from the wings of the nose to the mouth corners.
4. The mouth corners are pulled laterally, stretching and thinning the lips.
5. Simultaneous contraction of the depressor anguli oris and depressor labii inferioris lowers the lower lip, producing an almost vertical drop near the mouth corners that approximates a square shape and exposes part of the lower teeth. This mouth shape facilitates vocalization.
6. Contraction of the mentalis pushes the middle of the lower lip upward, covering the central teeth.

The pure crying expression in the figure is organized around the need to produce sound; each organ’s shape serves a physiological purpose.

**1. Tightly Closed Eyes**  
During crying the eyes are always tightly shut. The orbicularis oculi and corrugator supercilii contract together, closing the eyes and depressing the brows. This innate linkage has a structural basis: the vigorous exhalation and circulatory changes during crying increase capillary pressure inside the orbit and intraocular pressure, objectively requiring orbicularis oculi contraction to tighten the periorbital skin and thereby relieve some pressure and protect the eyeball. The more intense the crying, the stronger the muscular contraction. The same muscular action occurs naturally in laughter, sneezing, and coughing, all of which also involve tightly closed eyes.

**2. Stretched Mouth**  
During crying the levator labii superioris contracts, raising the upper lip and elevating the cheeks, forming nasolabial folds on either side of the nose. Platysma contraction stretches the mouth corners laterally, widening the mouth. Depressor labii inferioris contraction lowers the lower lip. Mentalis contraction arches the chin muscles and pushes the middle of the lower lip upward. These four muscles together open the lips into an approximately square contour. Orbicularis oculi contraction also elevates the cheeks to some extent, reinforcing the cheek bulge and assisting the upper-lip elevation produced by the levator labii superioris.

This mouth shape is better suited than others for producing a penetrating sound that travels farthest and reaches maximum volume.

In addition, an interesting phenomenon occurs: during crying, breathing is not steady but spasmodic. Coordinating with this respiratory pattern, the mentalis and platysma jointly control frequent changes in mouth shape, producing spasmodic movement of the jaw and lower lip. When both muscles contract, the middle of the lower lip puckers and the corners are pulled straight; when both relax, the lower lip and corners relax. This is the first time the role of the mentalis has been emphasized, because the mentalis has an important function only in sadness expressions.

##### 8.3.1 Suppressing Crying with a Closed Mouth

In the crying expression, tightly closed eyes are a critical element, while the mouth may be open or closed but is always stretched. Whether the mouth is open or closed depends on the degree of distress and the degree of self-suppression. The stronger the closing action, the more intense the crying and the greater the suppression. Compared with standard crying, the most obvious difference besides the mouth is further contraction of the frontalis, which pulls the brows upward; corrugator supercilii contraction draws the brows together medially; and orbicularis oculi contraction depresses the brows and tightly closes the eyes, as shown in Figure 8-5.

No one can cry with eyes wide open; even excellent actors can only manage to shed silent tears with eyes open. Once breathing intensifies, tight eye closure inevitably accompanies the action.

The main difference between the crying shown in Figure 8-5 and full crying lies in mouth suppression. Closing the mouth during crying is intended to suppress vocalization and greatly reduce volume. An objective result is also to suppress energy expenditure, prolonging the sadness.

As shown in Figure 8-6, when the mouth is open during crying the upper lip is raised by the levator labii superioris. When the mouth is closed during crying, a subtle change occurs: the zygomaticus minor (1) takes over lip elevation with much gentler force, sharply reducing upper-lip lift; the platysma acts noticeably on the mouth corners, stretching the lips laterally (2); the groove lateral to the mouth corner is formed by the depressor anguli oris (3), but its downward pull is weaker than the lateral pull of the platysma; the mentalis raises the chin into a spherical, uneven bulge while pushing the lower lip upward into the closed position (4). Because of resistance from the upper lip, the lower lip remains largely straight and does not arch upward (as it can when the mouth is wide open during full crying), so part of the lower lip protrudes outward.

In suppressed sadness the emotion demands an open mouth to produce crying, yet conscious will requires the lips to remain tightly closed to stay silent. The result is highly tense lips with an inward pressure opposing the upward and outward forces. This state of equilibrium in the mouth continually switches, producing slight trembling.

##### Test Case: The False Promoter

We tested the case of the head of a commercial training school. This person promoted on some internet forums that his training content was the most professional and authentic, because he had once made a special trip abroad to study for a year under management guru Professor XX, and therefore had the most authority to speak on this training system. With such promotion, his training school indeed gained strong commercial benefits and reputation locally.

In fact, he is a very hardworking and intelligent person. To expand his business, he made this public claim to secure a higher starting point. Unfortunately, the doubts were numerous. After we asked two key questions, he knew defense was hopeless, froze for a moment, and his face showed sadness.

**Question:** In your promotional copy, you stated that you once went abroad to study with Professor XX for a full year. In which year did this occur?  
**Answer:** 2005–2006.

**Question:** Was it continuous study for one year?  
**Answer:** Yes, I only returned home once, for a vacation.

**Question:** Do you know what type of visa one should apply for in country X if one wishes to stay for a year?  
**Answer:** …This…  
【Expression: Eyebrows lowered and inner brows raised, eyelids widened, gaze flickering, showing an alert state—typical fear expression.】

**Question:** Did you actually apply for a visa and reside in country X for a year to study with Professor XX?  
**Answer:** No. I only visited the university where he works during a trip to country X and met him once.  
【Expression: Eyebrows relaxed but inner brows remained furrowed and raised, eyelids returned to normal, lips pursed—mild sadness expression.】

**Question:** Your promotional copy also mentioned that you would invite two renowned masters, A and B, from the club organized by Professor XX to lecture at your school. Do you know their appearance fees?  
**Answer:** …

In the end, when he realized he could not fabricate credible details, he bowed his head and admitted the false promotion, displaying a mild sadness expression: eyebrows slightly raised, gaze dimmed, mouth showing the “bitter pursed-lip” form.

##### 3. Sad Mouth Morphology (9787554606841)

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-10]*

Whether in loud sobbing or silent, slightly restrained grief, the sad mouth appears due to the action of the mentalis muscle. In the sad mouth morphology, the upper lip changes shape under the action of the zygomaticus minor (or levator labii superioris). Many sad faces also involve the mentalis and depressor anguli oris. The corners of the mouth still tend to pull sideways and stretch, yet the amplitude of change is minimal. In crying or near-crying faces, the platysma contracts. The platysma engages during intense sadness; as sadness lessens, the action weakens and then disappears. See Figure 8-10.

This mouth morphology is a typical feature of sadness expressions and appears across many degrees of sadness. Moreover, careful observation shows that the same mouth morphology occurs when swallowing very bitter medicine, so it can also be called the “bitter pursed-lip” form.

When the bitter pursed-lip appears alone without other morphological features, it can indicate mild emotions in the sadness category such as shame, reluctance, difficulty, or hardship.

We often see this typical chin morphology at formal award ceremonies. After lengthy leadership speeches, when outstanding employees are recognized one by one and their arduous achievements recounted, the honoree’s face frequently shows the mentalis contraction forming the “bitter pursed-lip.” This morphology usually appears together with a smile, signaling the person’s inner restraint of the smile and a reminder not to become overly proud or high-profile. Yet for those who have truly invested effort and cost, the “bitter pursed-lip” also serves as a self-assessment of the past—how difficult it was! See Figure 8-11.

##### 8.3.5 Derived Micro-expressions of Sadness

The essence of sadness is helplessness toward an (unwanted) outcome. Many emotional derivatives fit this mindset.

- **Shame**: Self-blame or regret for a negative outcome one has caused, after the outcome has occurred.
- **Displeasure**: Non-acceptance, non-approval, or dislike of the stimulus source, yet without feelings of rejection or distancing, thus differing from disgust (whose essence is also negation).
- **Bitterness**: A subjective evaluation of past facts; the matter has ended, yet a helpless sorrow wells up.
- **Reluctant or difficult decisions**: After a hard choice (during which fear-type emotions and expressions appear; see Chapter 7), the decision means losing some benefit (no alternative), so a sadness-type emotional response also occurs. See Figure 8-16.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-16]*

The classic mouth morphology can express the above sadness-category derivatives. When the brow and eye regions are viewed in isolation, no trace of sadness is visible. Further, even when the upper face is covered, the obvious “bitter pursed-lip” morphology alone allows easy judgment of the inner emotion. Of course, whether the feeling is guilt, displeasure, bitterness, or reluctance must be judged according to the specific context. See Figure 8-17.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-17]*

When the lips purse, the mentalis is the core driver. Contraction of the mentalis pushes the lower lip upward, straightening the middle of the upper lip, unnaturally lengthening the lip line, and forming an uneven raised surface beneath the lower lip. At the same time, the depressor anguli oris contracts, causing the corners of the mouth to droop. The orbicularis oris contracts, pressing the upper and lower lips together.

##### 1. Sad Eyebrow Morphology

Because the eyes must open, the complexity of eyebrow morphology increases. The eyebrows are pulled in opposite directions: first pressed downward, then raised mainly at the inner brows, with a noticeably greater lift than during eyes-closed sobbing. This is the most important distinction between weeping and loud crying; even after crying subsides, the sadness emotion keeps this complex eyebrow configuration in place. See Figure 8-8.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-8]*

When the intensity of sadness diminishes, the frontalis attempts to pull against the corrugator supercilii: the frontalis lifts while the corrugator pulls down. The frontalis can only show its action once the orbicularis oculi weakens. The downward press of the eyebrows is neutralized by contraction of the medial frontalis, lifting the inner brows. Relaxed eyebrows never display this state. Vertical wrinkles reveal that the corrugator supercilii remains contracted.

On some faces the corrugator supercilii dominates and the eyebrows stay level; on others the frontalis dominates and the eyebrows form an “8:20” shape. Yet on every face the eyebrows show some entanglement; the degree of twist at the inner third of the brow indicates the degree of inner conflict.

This eyebrow shape is one of the typical morphological features of sadness. Perhaps because it arises from the entanglement of sobbing and restraint, its twisted form carries strong expressive contagion.

The basic morphology of sad eyebrows appears not only in sobbing expressions but on any sad face, and occasionally on non-sad faces. On overcast winter days, harsh weather can also produce this eyebrow morphology. In that context, the shape seems to represent hardship more than sadness, because both harsh weather and sadness stimuli confront the person with a negative situation they cannot change, so the expression is the same.

##### 8.3 Micro-expression Morphological Features of Sadness (9787554606841)

Sobbing comprises two factors: muscle contraction and spasm that form the sobbing expression, and loud vocalization that accelerates energy expenditure, intensifies the person’s experience of sadness, and, if others are present, enhances expressive effectiveness.

Yet in adult society, most communicative content does not involve such intense emotion, and the communicative form is largely rational language, so adults rarely have the opportunity to sob like infants. For most people, this fullest sobbing occurs only at the moment a loved one passes. Therefore, sadness in real life takes many forms.

In all obvious crying expressions, the eyes, due to physiological structure, tend to close tightly, and the greater the force of closure, the more intense the crying. The mouth may be open or closed, but the corners are definitely pulled sideways. Whether the mouth opens or closes depends on the degree of distress and self-restraint. Deliberate eye-closing and mouth-stretching actions are never as forceful or natural as those during actual crying. This is because emotion mobilizes substantial energy for natural physiological responses; actions fabricated from experience cannot fully replicate them—only physical pain produces comparable intensity.

The strength of the stimulus and the person’s degree of restraint allow sadness to be divided into many grades: wailing, normal crying, sobbing, silent tears with mouth closed, grievance, melancholy, etc. In the fullest sobbing state the morphological features are clear and easy to recognize; in each weakened grade, even subtle morphological states of the eyebrows, eyes, and mouth can reveal sadness.

##### 8.2 The Most Intense Sadness Response — Crying

Crying is the most typical action response of sadness. Under what psychological state does a person cry?

I have specifically observed children under 3 years old. After they understand certain things, there is a period when they cry particularly often. Based on the recorded results, I found that all causes of crying stem from the children feeling that “there is no way out.” For a concrete example, a child has already eaten some snacks and agreed with the parents not to eat more, yet their actual desire is to eat a little more.

The child understands that the parents will definitely not allow further snacks. Knowing the matter is hopeless, the child begins to cry. Besides snacks, similar situations such as watching cartoons or buying toys produce the same result. A deeper look at the child’s psychology reveals that the failure to satisfy a simple need is a bad outcome, while the agreement reached with the parents and their supervision lie beyond the child’s ability to change the situation.

In simple terms, a bad outcome occurs and there is no way to alter it; the result is sadness expressed through crying.

The same principle applies to events that cause adults to feel sadness and cry.

Analysis of facial morphology features:

1. Furrowed brows and vertical frown lines indicate focused attention in response to pressure.
2. The eyelids show no obvious lift; the upper eyelid shape is entirely affected by the downward pressure of the brows, ruling out surprise, anger, or fear.
3. Gaze directed downward signals being under pressure; an energy-less gaze tends toward sadness (helplessness).

The expression conveys unwillingness to accept a negative outcome together with helplessness. Grievance is a derivative of sadness that combines unwillingness to accept criticism with helplessness.

##### 8.1 The Generation of Sadness

After worrying for a long time, the undesired outcome still occurs. Once a loss of interest is fixed, the instinctive drive to seek benefit and avoid harm means that failing to gain or suffering damage (loss) will trigger sadness.

Sadness originates from loss.

Examples include irreversible physical injury, the death of a close relative, the end of a cherished relationship, or the loss of important economic interests—all irreversible losses for the person involved. Facing an adverse outcome that cannot be reversed produces sadness. Sadness is the only emotion among all emotions that allows energy to dissipate; every other emotion mobilizes energy for physical expenditure.

The stimulus for sadness is “irrevocable loss.”

Sadness expressions are directly linked to crying. A person’s first expression after birth (more accurately, the first action) is loud crying. Of course, an infant’s cry does not express sadness alone; it can also convey anger, disgust, fear, and all other negative emotions. In the absence of negative emotions, the infant’s expression is quiet.

##### Close-up of the Mouth Suppressing Loud Crying

As shown in Figure 8-6, when the mouth opens to cry, the upper lip is lifted by the levator labii superioris. When crying with the mouth closed, a subtle change occurs: the levator labii superioris yields to the zygomaticus minor (1), whose force is much gentler, sharply reducing the lift of the upper lip; the platysma visibly pulls the corners of the mouth outward (2); the groove-shaped lines outside the corners are formed by the depressor anguli oris (3), yet its downward pull is weaker than the platysma’s lateral pull; the mentalis raises the chin into a bumpy ball while pushing the lower lip upward into the closed position (4). Because of resistance from the upper lip, the lower lip stays largely flat and does not arch upward (as it can when the mouth is open during loud crying), so part of the lower lip protrudes outward.

In suppressed sadness, the emotion requires the mouth to open for crying, yet conscious will demands that the lips remain tightly closed and silent. The result is highly tense lips under inward pressure that counters the upward and outward forces. This state of equilibrium in the mouth continually switches, producing slight trembling.

##### 2. Eye Morphology in Sadness

When sadness occurs with the eyes open, changes appear. The lift of the upper eyelid is restrained by the downward pressure of the brows, forming a fold on the skin, though less pronounced than in fear. This subtle difference is the key distinction between open-eyed sadness and fear, as shown in Figure 8-9.

**Sad eyes**  
**Fearful eyes**

The lower eyelid covers more of the eyeball than usual.

Partial contraction of the orbicularis oculi, mainly in its lower portion, straightens the lift of the lower eyelid. This subtle change plays a major role: the area of the iris that is covered increases, with more of both the upper and lower margins obscured. Consequently, the eye’s alert state disappears instantly; the gaze loses its luster and appears dim and weak. This results from reduced black-and-white contrast and a smaller reflective surface of the eyeball.

##### Morphology of the Crying Expression

Contraction of the upper lip muscles lifts the upper lip while, together with the orbicularis oculi, raises the cheeks; the raised cheeks press against the lower eyelids, forming the sunken area beneath the lower eyelids and the nasolabial folds on both sides of the nose wings;

④ Contraction of the platysma pulls the corners of the mouth outward, increasing the horizontal width of the mouth beyond normal; the stretched corners and cheeks create the nasolabial lines;

⑤ Contraction of the depressor anguli oris pulls the corners downward; simultaneous contraction of the depressor labii inferioris lowers the entire lower lip in an attempt to expose the lower teeth;

⑥ Simultaneous contraction of the mentalis pushes the middle of the lower lip upward and creates a bumpy muscular bulge on the chin. The upward push of the middle lower lip covers part of the lower teeth that could otherwise be exposed, while the corners remain lowered, allowing the lower teeth near the corners to show. The lower lip curve forms a W shape. This mouth shape is unique to the crying expression.

##### 8.3.4 Micro-expression Morphological Features of Sadness

From full crying to calm melancholy, through gradual attenuation, we observe that one micro-expression feature consistently appears across varying degrees of sadness expressions. On a calm face, simply adding the necessary brow morphology effectively conveys sadness, even without changes in the eyes or mouth.

Therefore, brows that are furrowed and depressed yet raised at the inner ends, with distortion in the inner one-third of the brow shape, constitute the micro-expression morphological feature of sadness.

The same brow morphology may also appear in fear expressions, but fear expressions must be accompanied by widened eyelids, whereas sad eyes show a closing action due to contraction of the orbicularis oculi. This is the greatest distinction between the two, as shown in Figure 8-15.

**Figure 8-15** The upper image shows sad brow-eye morphology; the lower image shows fearful brow-eye morphology

##### 8.3.3 Calm Sadness

Unlike crying, calm sadness can last a long time. Crying consumes large amounts of energy, whereas calm sadness merely allows the body’s energy to dissipate slowly. The saddening outcome has already occurred and cannot be reversed; nothing else matters, and only helplessness remains in the body, as shown in Figure 8-12.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-12]*

As crying subsides, the muscles on the sad face gradually relax. The platysma is the first to exit, followed by the orbicularis oculi. Finally the cheeks are no longer so puffed, and the lower eyelids loosen. What remains on the face are the sad brows and a slight pout. Even after the pout disappears, the troubled brows still convey the final message of sadness.

##### Chapter 8 Micro-expressions of Sadness

The most feared event has still occurred (the adverse outcome). This causes the original worry in the person’s heart to vanish completely and be replaced by helpless resignation; fear therefore transforms into sadness. Sadness originates from loss and is the only emotion that permits energy to dissipate, resulting in dull, unalert eyes.

The micro-expressions of fear discussed in the previous chapter actually combine morphological features of two micro-expressions—surprise and sadness. A sudden stimulus produces surprise; after evaluation, if the threat exceeds one’s coping capacity and cannot be eliminated through angry fighting, fear arises. Only a thin barrier separates fear from sadness—the question of whether the feared outcome occurs. Before the adverse outcome occurs, the emotion is fear; once it occurs, the emotion becomes sadness.

##### 2. Common Morphological Features of Sad Expressions

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图11-19 Morphology of closed-mouth crying expression]*

① Contraction of the orbicularis oculi and corrugator supercilii is reduced yet still depresses and furrows the brows; contraction of the central frontalis slightly raises the inner brows, producing an upward distortion so that the overall brow shape tends toward flatness;

② The eyelids are tense and tend toward closure;

③ Contraction of the levator labii superioris slightly lifts the upper lip, forming nasolabial folds beside the nose wings (shallower than in loud crying);

④ Contraction of the platysma pulls the corners of the mouth outward;

⑤ Contraction of the depressor anguli oris pulls the corners downward;

⑥ Contraction of the mentalis pushes the middle of the lower lip upward and creates a bumpy muscular bulge on the chin; the lip line is horizontal and the lips are pressed tightly together.

##### 2. Typical Morphological Features of Sadness

During crying the brows are depressed overall (due to contraction of the orbicularis oculi). Although the eyes are usually tightly closed, social context makes wide-open crying rare. The typical crying action is closure of the mouth; the tense lips experience upward squeezing force from below (mentalis) and lateral stretching force (platysma). Crying is in fact a spasmodic action<|eos|>

### Training and Practice

#### Even If You Can Grasp Emotions in an Instant, Decisions Must Still Be Made with Caution

When meeting someone for the first time and introducing myself as an expert in expression analysis, I am often asked, “Can you tell what other people are thinking?” or “What am I thinking right now?” Such reactions usually stem from the belief that “what is on a person’s mind shows on their face.” After reading this book, you should understand that this is a misunderstanding.

Let us now discuss what it actually means to be able to read expressions. If you can read a person’s expressions, you can “read their emotions.” According to the phenomenon of micro-expressions, you can interpret the emotions the other person is trying to suppress from an instantaneous facial expression. What is the difference between reading emotions and reading thoughts? For example, if the speaker wrinkles their nose for just an instant, this is the micro-expression of “disgust,” allowing you to confirm that the other person feels “disgust.”

However, we do not strictly know where this feeling of “disgust” originates. It may be that the person ate something too greasy at lunch and feels unwell, or the micro-expression of “disgust” simply appeared at that moment in the conversation. It is also possible that the speaker feels “disgust” toward their own words—that is, some sense of guilt hidden behind what they are saying makes “disgust with oneself” appear on their face. Or perhaps they disagree with what the other person has said and show the micro-expression of “disgust” because they do not approve.

Therefore, even if your ability to read micro-expressions improves, you may not necessarily grasp a person’s thoughts in an instant—why does this emotion exist? To read emotions from expressions and then understand thoughts from those emotions, you must establish this sequence before you can fully comprehend the other person’s true intentions. This is why the three techniques of “observing words and expressions” (察言觀色) from the previous chapter are so important.

Using the three methods described in the previous chapter allows you to analyze and infer the other person’s thoughts precisely. Even so, you still cannot reliably read their thoughts. Too many unpredictable variables and individual differences exist, along with many aspects that science cannot explain. The phenomena and methodologies introduced in this book are all grounded in scientific knowledge. So what should you do when the methodologies or scientific points in this book do not apply? You must rely on rules of thumb.

Set aside the idea of grasping someone’s heart through scientific knowledge. Put aside everything you have learned so far and listen to what your own heart tells you. Put yourself in the other person’s position and consider matters from their perspective rather than analyzing them. Observe the whole situation with empathy. Doing so may allow you to understand the other person’s thoughts.

Even then, you may not immediately perceive the other person’s thoughts. Whether you succeed or not, move day by day toward the ideal of understanding people’s hearts. Shift your posture from the suspicion of “peeking into someone else’s mind” to “caring about someone else’s mind,” and you will gradually develop a gentler heart.

#### Micro-expressions Are Limited to Those Directed at Yourself

Humans are interesting creatures. Sometimes, even while looking into another person’s eyes and listening to their words, they are actually lost in their own world. Their thoughts have entered a realm completely unrelated to the conversation, pondering matters unrelated to the dialogue. In such cases, even if a micro-expression appears on that person’s face, it is entirely unrelated to the day’s conversation. Therefore, when a micro-expression appears, it may seem caused by the person you are talking with, but it may actually stem from something completely unrelated. “Smiling because of a memory” is a typical example. While earnestly discussing a serious topic, a pleasant memory suddenly surfaces, producing an odd smile. The person tries to suppress the amusing emotion but cannot, so it appears as a micro-expression. Such a “smile from memory” has nothing to do with the content of the conversation or with the other person.

Moreover, even when a micro-expression arises in connection with the ongoing conversation, its cause is not necessarily the other person. For instance, during an exchange of opinions, your idea may give the other person a new thought. While that person appears to be listening, their mind is actually busy constructing a new idea. When they feel pleased with what they consider an innovative thought—“This is an idea that will impress everyone around!”—they may display the micro-expression of “contempt.”

Yet this micro-expression is not directed at you; it is an emotion shown toward a third party who is not present. Therefore, even when the person you are speaking with displays a micro-expression, it is not necessarily directed at you.

In most situations, people believe they themselves are the most worthy of love and respect. This is called self-esteem and is an indispensable psychological function. Everyone has self-esteem and feels they are most important. Because of this belief, people can overcome criticism, slander, and setbacks and keep moving forward.

When someone hears your words or suggestions, they may say aloud, “That suggestion is wonderful! Thank you!” yet display micro-expressions of “contempt” and “disgust” on their face. Even if the micro-expression indicates they do not truly wish to accept the suggestion, graciously accept their feelings and protect their self-esteem.

#### Example

Imagine two new colleagues conversing in the office on a weekend, discussing plans for tomorrow’s day off.

The company requires new hires to submit the results of their most recent English proficiency test after joining and to provide the relevant certificate by a set deadline. Because the deadline is approaching, Colleague B plans to take the TOEIC (an English proficiency test) at the company tomorrow.

- **A**: “Tomorrow is Saturday. Do you have any plans?”
- **B**: “I’ve already arranged to take the TOEIC tomorrow.”

During this exchange, a micro-expression of “disgust” appears on B’s face. The function of “disgust” is to “exclude unpleasant things or matters,” so we infer that the “unpleasant matter” is “having a day off taken up by an exam.” Based on this inference, find words that support the idea of “excluding the unpleasant matter” and say them to B.

For example:
- “You don’t have to take the test on Sunday. You can take it next Wednesday instead.”
- “If you have taken the TOEIC within the past two years, that score is acceptable in the HR department!”

If B replies, “Really? Then I won’t have to lose a day of vacation tomorrow! Thank you for telling me!” this reaction indicates that the earlier inference was correct and that the psychological inference proceeded smoothly.

However, if B says, “Oh, is that so?” the “unpleasant matter” is apparently not caused by “having a day off taken up by an exam” but by something else. To learn B’s true thoughts, other possibilities must be inferred and the conversation continued.

#### Idol Autograph Session Example

This example occurred at an idol’s autograph session.

- **Fan**: “I’ll support you! Keep it up!”
- **Idol**: (while shaking hands) “I’ll keep it up.”

Observing this scene, the analyst noticed that when the idol said the first word “I” of “I’ll keep it up,” a micro-expression of “disgust” appeared.
