This emotion was not a reaction to the fan’s shout of “Keep it up!” The key point is the micro-expression shown before the idol uttered “I’ll keep it up.”

Judging from the timing of the idol’s utterance, he was not reacting to the fan’s words but felt disgust toward his own statement. From these signs we infer that, although he was grateful for the fan’s support, he felt disgust at having to say “I’ll keep it up.” His gaze was directed at the fan, yet the target of the emotion was himself.

This situation requires attention to the “timing” and “discrepancy” between speech and expression. Expressions shown before or after speaking reflect emotions related to the content of the speech. Expressions that appear before the speaker begins to speak usually reveal the speaker’s true feelings, because the emotion arises first and then surfaces on the face.

In addition, when affirmative words appear together with negative expressions

#### Overly “Observing Words and Expressions” Can Become Annoying

When reading micro-expressions, even if you cannot immediately understand the other person’s thoughts, you can directly perceive their emotions. Be aware that this can sometimes cause distress to others.

This section offers advice, drawn from personal experience and arranged from easier to more difficult, on how to protect yourself by avoiding “overly observing words and expressions.” It is intended for those who can already use micro-expressions to read others’ thoughts, or as psychological preparation for those who interpret micro-expressions.

Once skill in reading micro-expressions reaches a certain level, you will automatically notice others’ micro-expressions even without concentrating on their faces. Given the number of people we meet and communicate with daily, the quantity of micro-expressions observed in a single day is considerable. Reacting sensitively to interpreted micro-expressions or pondering why they appeared can create significant mental stress. Here is a suggestion:

Plan in advance which micro-expressions you intend to notice, along with their possible causes and interpretations.

“Today I will pay attention to that salesperson’s micro-expressions,” “When speaking with that person, I will read their micro-expressions,” or “Regarding that particular topic, I will watch for micro-expressions.” It is advisable to decide beforehand which occasions or individuals warrant attention to micro-expressions and to maintain an on/off mechanism for whether to interpret the psychology involved.

#### Greater Ability Brings Greater Responsibility

One of my favorite sayings is “With great power comes great responsibility.” When you possess the ability to read micro-expressions that others lack, you hold considerable power. Yet if this ability is misused, it can generate distrust toward others or cause others to distrust you. The most typical example is using micro-expressions to detect lies. Once you master the methods of judging micro-expressions and asking questions, you can accurately spot lies.

However, whose lies should you expose? Sometimes lies are told to spare the other person pain. Exposing a lie not only destroys the liar’s consideration but also forces the truth into the open, leaving people unsettled. When, under what circumstances, and toward whom to apply this powerful micro-expression judgment ability constitutes a significant responsibility for the user.

Those who possess great power bear heavy obligations and must pass rigorous tests of reality before they can achieve greatness. If you agree with this and have the confidence to strive in that direction, continue honing your micro-expression reading skills and enjoy good communication in daily life.

#### How to Respond Most Appropriately According to the Other Person’s Emotions

| Emotion Type | Emotional Reaction | How to Interact When Seeing the Other Person’s Expression |
|--------------|--------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| Happiness | When one’s hopes are fulfilled… | Stimulate the other person’s expectations |
| Contempt | When one feels one’s experience or knowledge is superior to others, or when witnessing immoral behavior… | Support the other person’s sense of superiority |
| Disgust | Disliking people or things one finds unpleasant or unwilling to hear | Understand the cause of the unpleasantness |
| Anger | When one disagrees or one’s goals are obstructed | Remove the obstructing factor |
| Sadness | Feeling unhappy about lost people or things and seeking help | Extend a helping hand |
| Fear | When physical or mental safety is threatened… | Show empathy and reassure the person |
| Surprise | When something unexpected occurs and one wants to grasp the situation… | Provide relevant information |

#### The Second Step: Inferring Psychology

Using the interpreted micro-expressions and other information as a basis, infer the cause and target of the other person’s emotion.

Finally, we explain “taking appropriate action according to the situation and occasion.”

Communication requires correctly reading the other person’s verbal and nonverbal messages and then considering what action is appropriate based on that information. For example:

- When you know the other person is hiding impatience toward you, you can apologize first to ease their emotion.
- When the other person feels “sadness,” extend a helping hand.
- If you notice the other person feels disgust toward you because of a lie, you can urge them to reflect, perhaps helping them speak their true feelings.

This sequence of steps is called “observing words and expressions.” The most important and difficult part of the process is “correctly reading” within “inferring psychology.” In “observing words and expressions,” “inferring psychology” accounts for almost the entire weight. Therefore, “inferring psychology” can be said to be the key to “observing words and expressions.”

#### ❸ Consider Gaze Direction, Words, and Micro-expressions Together

Generally, the target of an emotion and the direction of gaze coincide. When the gaze is directed downward, the emotion is usually directed at oneself.

If a speaker displays a micro-expression of “contempt” while looking at everyone, the likelihood is high that the contempt is directed at everyone. If the gaze is directed downward, the speaker feels “contempt” toward themselves—that is, they feel “I am worthless” or “I have a sense of guilt.”

However, when someone wishes to hide their true intentions, they may also lower their gaze slightly, sometimes presenting a micro-expression in this manner. In such cases, even though the gaze is downward, the target of the emotion may not be themselves; caution is required during interpretation.

Conversely, even when the speaker’s gaze is directed at everyone, the emotion may still be directed at themselves; similar examples exist.

#### Three Techniques for “Observing Words and Expressions” Using Micro-expressions

When expressions appear, or conversely when negative words appear together with positive expressions, the more trustworthy element is the expression. Micro-expressions in particular cannot be freely controlled by conscious will; they usually reveal true feelings. When words and expressions differ, choose to believe the expression.

The three techniques for “observing words and expressions” using micro-expressions are therefore:

- Directly ask the other person about the emotion interpreted from the micro-expression
- Say something that supports the other person’s emotion
- Consider gaze direction, words, and micro-expressions together

You may use any one method alone or combine several. Practice a little each day, trying to make abstract expressions consciously “visible,” and you will glimpse the rich and varied world of emotions that you had never noticed before.

#### What Is “Observing Words and Expressions”?

What exactly is “observing words and expressions,” and how do you interpret it concretely?

To read hidden emotions from micro-expressions and find ways to touch the other person’s heart, we visualize the concrete process and define “observing words and expressions” as:

> “Correctly interpreting another person’s conscious or unconscious verbal or nonverbal messages and taking appropriate action according to the situation and occasion.”

“Another person’s conscious or unconscious verbal or nonverbal messages” refers to the fact that, whether conscious or unconscious, the other person’s words or body language come from the heart.

#### Verbal Example

With items scattered across a desk, a colleague says, “This desk is a bit dirty.” The intended meaning is “It should be tidied up,” expressed indirectly in the hope that the other person will understand. This is also called “reading between the lines.”

The English term for reading between the lines is *telepathy*. Such indirect metaphors are common in Japanese communication, but to Westerners they seem like a superpower.

#### Body Language

Body language consists of messages conveyed by expressions and bodily movements (nodding, shaking the head, touching the face, patting the chest, jiggling a leg, crossing arms or legs…), including posture and voice. Suppressed emotions therefore surface on the face in the form of “micro-expressions,” whether consciously or unconsciously. This bodily movement also has an advanced version that appears on the body as “micro-movements.”

#### ❶ Directly Ask the Other Person About the Emotion Interpreted from the Micro-expression

This is the simplest method. When the other person shows a micro-expression of “fear,” ask, “Is there something making you uneasy?” Directly inquire about the cause or reason for the emotion you have interpreted.

This method allows intuitive capture of micro-expressions and is easy to use. Because it directly touches the other person’s privacy, it must be used with caution.

#### The First Step: Reading Emotions

When reading emotions from the other person’s micro-expressions, this stage allows you to determine which specific emotion the person is suppressing—whether it is “happiness,” “contempt,” “disgust,” and so on. Even if you can infer the other person’s emotion, you still cannot know “why this emotion has arisen” or “who the target of this emotion is.”

#### ❷ Say Something That Supports the Other Person’s Own Emotion

Taking an action that supports the other person’s emotion makes it easier to hear their true feelings. This method was already mentioned in the exercises in Chapter 3. Infer the cause of the emotion from the other person’s facial reaction, then provide a stimulus that supports that inference or offer support for the emotion, and observe the other person’s subsequent reaction.

#### Correct Interpretation Is the Key

How do you “correctly interpret” these verbal and nonverbal messages? The most important thing is to base the interpretation on “observing words and expressions.”

“Correctly interpreting” means “inferring psychology from the other person’s emotions,” which can be divided into two steps.

#### Make Communication Easy! Three Tricks for "Reading People"

This section explores three techniques for "reading people" from micro-expressions and introduces methods for carrying them out. Before that, we first clearly define the matter of "reading people".



#### Three Techniques for "Inferring Psychology"

Now let's introduce the core of "reading people"— "inferring psychology". Its methods are roughly divided into three types.

#### Three Habits That Let You Understand Micro-expressions

##### ❶ Consciously Observe People’s Expressions

Pay attention to the expressions of people around you in daily life and observe them with interest; this is the starting point for understanding micro-expressions. If you want to detect subtle emotional changes on people’s faces, you must look at the other person’s eyes and face while conversing. Doing so through a computer or phone screen will not work.

Observing other people’s expressions with interest will reveal many facial movements that were previously overlooked, movements that actually contain a great deal of information. In addition to conversing with others, you can observe passersby’s faces while walking on the street or riding the subway.

What kind of expression do pedestrians on the street wear as they walk? What problems are they pondering, or what pleasant things are they thinking about? What expressions do people talking on the phone show? Are they discussing something complicated? Is the person on the other end a lover or a boss? What about the expressions of people reading email? Have they received a happy notification, or are they viewing something that makes them uneasy? What expressions do people reading books or newspapers show? What type of book or news content are they looking at? Conscious observation of this kind sharpens your sensitivity to changes in people’s expressions and teaches you how to respond.

##### ❷ Watch Programs with the Television on Mute

Turn the television volume to mute and carefully observe the micro-expressions of the people appearing on screen. News broadcasts are recommended for observation, because news anchors usually display only minimal changes in expression, which helps train the ability to read micro-expressions.

Observe the micro-expressions of news anchors to predict whether the next story will be good news or bad news. This method compensates for the shortcoming of method ❶. Although method ❶ improves your skill at observing and inferring expressions, you cannot confirm your inferences with the observed person, making it difficult to know whether your guesses are correct. Method ❷ lets you verify your inferences the moment the next news item airs, based on the anchor’s change in expression.

Another approach is to leave the sound on and infer emotions from micro-expressions. This is usually used while watching talk shows: observe the speaker’s micro-expressions to predict what the person will say next. Try to judge whether a participant agrees or disagrees with someone else’s opinion. Can you detect the moment an opinion shifts? Has the person been persuaded? While watching the various micro-expressions of the people on screen, attempt to forecast how the discussion will turn out.

##### ❸ Use Training Tools Designed for Micro-expressions

This is the most formal and reliable of the three methods. It involves self-study with specially made animated teaching materials that improve micro-expression judgment skills. Companies in the United States, Europe, and even many in Japan sell dedicated micro-expression training materials. These materials typically require viewers to watch characters in videos and judge what emotion each person is displaying. Judgments are usually made in multiple-choice format, and the correctness of each answer is revealed immediately.

Research on the learning effects of these micro-expression training tools shows that even a single hour of video training can raise micro-expression judgment ability. One learner’s pre-training accuracy rate was 40 percent; after one hour of training, the rate rose to 80 percent, and the effect lasted two to three weeks. The research indicates that using dedicated micro-expression judgment training materials for one hour every two to three weeks allows a person to retain micro-expression judgment skills indefinitely.

#### Three Habits That Let You Understand Micro-expressions

In this section, three techniques for learning to interpret micro-expressions (微表情) will be introduced. These range from the simplest methods to professional training; I will explain them in detail, so you can try the ones you like.

## Part Six: Deception

### Make an Appointment with Him in Haste to See If He Keeps It

**Micro-expression Keywords**

Whether in the East or the West, stories about keeping appointments are countless. Keeping an appointment is not only the basic etiquette of interpersonal interaction but also a way to judge a person’s character. Only someone who strictly honors commitments is honest and worthy of our trust and association. Therefore, it is worthwhile to make an appointment with him in haste and test his character.

Time is a non-renewable resource; once our time is exhausted, our life ceases to exist. Yet many people fail to truly recognize its importance and waste precious hours. Being late for appointments or work has become routine, always accompanied by various excuses.

Some may think, “What’s the big deal if I’m ten minutes late?” But failing to arrive at the agreed time forces others to wait, which is unfair and wastes their life. Such people neither respect others’ time nor keep their word. The way to identify them is to make an appointment in haste and observe whether they arrive on time.

American railroad magnate Vanderbilt regarded unpunctuality as an unforgivable sin. Once he arranged to meet a young man at his office at 10 a.m. to introduce him to a railroad superintendent for a position. The young man was delighted. Unfortunately, he arrived twenty minutes late. By then Vanderbilt had already left for another meeting.

Days later the young man finally met Vanderbilt, who asked why he had not kept the appointment. The young man replied, “Sir, I arrived at 10:20.” Vanderbilt immediately reminded him, “But I asked you to come at 10!”

“Yes, I know,” the young man stammered, “but twenty minutes shouldn’t make much difference, right?”

“No!” Vanderbilt said sternly. “Punctuality matters a great deal. Because you were not on time, you lost the position. That very day the railroad hired someone else. And let me tell you, young man, you have no right to undervalue my twenty minutes and leave me waiting while I had two important meetings to attend.”

We all prefer to deal with trustworthy people. Trustworthiness is like a person’s credit rating at a bank. To assess someone’s assets, check their bank records; to gauge their trustworthiness, simply set a time and see if they arrive punctually. Some lack a strong sense of time and think being a little late for a friend’s gathering is harmless. Yet others detect from this small detail a lack of respect and importance, which erodes trust.

Time is the best standard for testing truth. Those who do not keep time commitments can be judged as having low credibility. Only those who honor appointments on time earn others’ trust.

When PepsiCo president Carl Weilerup spoke at the University of Colorado, a merchant named Jack wanted to meet him. Carl agreed but could spare only fifteen minutes after the speech. Carl proceeded to the auditorium while Jack waited outside. As Carl spoke enthusiastically about his entrepreneurial journey and business success, he exceeded the agreed time and forgot the appointment. Suddenly a man entered from outside, walked straight to the stage, placed a business card down without a word, and left. Carl read the card: “You have an appointment with Jack at 2:30 p.m.” Realizing his mistake, Carl told the students, “Thank you for listening. I would like to continue, but I have an appointment and am already late. I cannot break it, so please excuse me and good luck to you all.”

Amid applause Carl hurried out, found Jack, apologized, and answered all his questions. Their fifteen-minute meeting stretched to thirty minutes.

Jack later became a successful merchant. He shared the story with friends, who grew to trust PepsiCo and decided to distribute and promote its products.

In real life, “trustworthiness” is often difficult to maintain. Some make promises to subordinates, colleagues, or friends only to forget them soon after. To know a person, first determine whether they possess “trustworthiness” and whether they are worthy of trust. When leaders assign tasks with tight deadlines, they are often testing whether subordinates can “keep their word and deliver results” and honor commitments.

Leaders can observe subordinates’ trustworthiness through two methods: “open” and “closed.” In the open method, a task is assigned with only a request to complete it as soon as possible, without a specific deadline. This reveals a person’s sense of responsibility and efficiency. Those with strong responsibility treat every assignment as a test and finish promptly; those lacking responsibility procrastinate. In the closed method, a firm deadline is set. Failure to meet the promised deadline indicates a lack of trustworthiness. Repeated occurrences show the person cannot be entrusted with important matters.

Key points must be observed:

1. Clearly state the exact time; avoid vague expressions such as “around two” or “three or four days.”
2. Confirm whether the other party can keep the appointment.
3. Ensure the matter lies within the other party’s capability.

However, do not take matters out of context. If an appointment is missed, determine whether the cause is objective or subjective and whether it is excusable. In any case, “testing through tasks” yields insights into character that other assessments rarely capture.

### Possess the Aura That Attracts Companions, and You Will Surely Succeed in Your Career

**Micro-expression Keywords**

In today’s society, a basic quality of successful people is the aura that attracts companions—that is, personal charisma. This refers to the moral character, personality, ability, and temperament that exert a powerful attractive force, making one popular and accepted. Such individuals are bound to succeed in their careers. When you encounter them, follow closely; you too can achieve success.

Few heroes succeed alone. Beside every successful person stand collaborators—Shi Yuzhu’s “Three Musketeers,” Jack Ma’s “Eighteen Arhats”—yet these partners do not appear by chance. They are drawn by the aura that attracts companions, which requires sufficient personal charisma. A person endowed with charisma will surely succeed.

Personal charisma is the attraction and infectiousness a person’s conduct exerts on others. In daily life we notice that some people seem luckier and achieve success more quickly. This is not because they possess greater wisdom but because they radiate an aura that draws companions. Their outstanding charisma makes more friends willing to help and more clients eager to cooperate. Personal charm is a magical resource that can elevate even an ordinary talent to enviable success.

A person may lack striking looks or substantial assets, yet if they possess the aura that attracts companions and boundless charisma, they will still become an object of admiration.

In the IT world, Jack Ma is an iconic figure. Under his leadership the “Eighteen Arhats” made Alibaba repeatedly ranked by Forbes as the world’s best B2B website. While passionate about his career, the now-famous Jack Ma has maintained a rare rationality that commands respect. In a Hong Kong Sun TV interview, after the host remarked that “some say Jack Ma is very smart,” he replied, “I don’t think I’m smart at all. Since childhood I’ve been worse at studying and games than other kids. When others treat you as a hero, never regard yourself as one—that can only bring trouble. Heroes are named by others; fame is given by others…”

Frankly, Jack Ma is no handsome man; some would even call him unattractive. Forbes once described this eccentric talent: “Deeply sunken cheeks, unruly hair, a mischievous toothy grin—a five-foot, one-hundred-pound urchin.” It added, “This oddly featured man has Napoleon’s stature and Napoleon-like ambition!” In his own words, “A man’s talent is often inversely proportional to his appearance.”

Although God did not grant Jack Ma handsome features, He gave him abundant talent. Starting with an initial investment of 500,000 yuan, Alibaba grew to a scale rivaling any major portal. His stake rose from 200,000 yuan to 500 million yuan in just five years.

Known as a “maverick genius,” Jack Ma is quick-witted. After being rejected three times, a single Harvard speech attracted dozens of outstanding graduates to join Alibaba. He also possesses remarkable charisma. During the early, difficult years of entrepreneurship, every friend stood as a steadfast supporter, offering the strongest backing and trust. He often received calls: “Hey, Jack Ma, how’s it going? No big deal—whatever happens, we’ve got your back!”

Jack Ma’s talent not only recruited excellent staff and accumulated friendships but also won him sincere love. He met his wife Zhang Ying in their freshman year; after graduation they quickly obtained their marriage certificate. Zhang Ying later recalled, “Jack Ma is not a handsome man. What I admired was his ability to do things handsome men could not: founding Hangzhou’s first English corner, guiding foreign tourists to earn foreign currency, taking on part-time teaching jobs, and becoming one of Hangzhou’s top ten outstanding young teachers…”

Personal charisma, like intelligence and education, is closely tied to one’s future. Napoleon Hill said, “Success is intimately related to personal charm; those who create wealth often possess a wealth-attracting personality. Good personal charm is a magical gift that can move even the coldest hearts.” Jack Ma’s success is inseparable from the aura that attracts companions—an aura forged by the charisma with which he conquered the Eighteen Arhats and built today’s Alibaba.

A person with charisma will be surrounded by those eager to collaborate. Even if they have nothing, others will believe in and help them. This charm is not merely handsome appearance, superior ability, or noble character; it is the integrated force of appearance, talent, personality, emotional intelligence, temperament, morality, and cultivation.

It can manifest as confidence, the internal drive that propels one forward and an essential psychological quality for success. With confidence, one maintains the certainty of victory amid hardship and faces unknown difficulties with composure that draws collaborators to follow wholeheartedly.

It can also appear as consistent integrity. In every setting they show their true selves, never altering their character to suit the occasion. Whether in intimate conversation, public speech, or job interviews, they remain consistent, free of affectation, revealing authentic personality. They communicate with their whole being; tone and posture harmonize with their words, everything natural and approachable.

In any case, those who possess the aura that attracts companions will achieve great things in their careers. Therefore, if you meet such a person, do not hesitate—follow them and you too can succeed. Just as the world remembers Bill Gates, the world’s richest man, it also remembers Paul Allen who stood behind him.

### People Who Can Convert Time into Money Are Those with Thorough Plans

Micro-expression keywords Many people complain that they are busy at work yet earn little money. In reality, they fail to convert time into money because they lack planning in their work, which leads to wasted time and futile efforts. A truly capable person always plans ahead and strives to exchange the shortest time for the greatest amount of money. Such individuals are ambitious, highly competent, and worthy of major responsibilities.

The *Book of Rites: Doctrine of the Mean* states: “Preparation ensures success; lack of preparation leads to failure.” This means that any undertaking succeeds with prior preparation and fails without it; here, preparation refers to planning. A person with thorough plans can convert time into money. Likewise, anyone who cherishes time and converts it into money is certainly someone with thorough plans.

People often say “time is money,” yet some endlessly waste time. They never make a plan and simply do whatever comes to mind, often squandering hours on trivial matters and delaying other tasks. They then complain about being too busy and having no time. The root cause is the absence of a thorough plan.

A certain leader frequently complained about his overwhelming workload and lack of breathing room, so he sought advice from a time-management expert. The expert asked, “What did you do this morning, and how much time did it take?” The leader replied, “Drafting a report took three hours.” The expert said, “Did you spend the entire three hours drafting the report?”

“Oh, not entirely. During that time I drank two cups of tea, smoked three cigarettes, took one break, chatted with a colleague, and answered several phone calls,” the leader said while thinking.

The expert then asked, “Can you calculate how much time all those activities consumed?”

After a moment the leader answered, “About an hour and a half.”

“Now you see: of those three hours, you actually spent only an hour and a half drafting the report. If you had used the remaining hour and a half productively, you would have felt you had far more time.”

The expert advised him to record everything he did each day along with the time spent, and to continue for half a month. He would then see exactly where his time went, how much was valuable, and how much was wasted. Targeted adjustments would reveal ways to improve efficiency.

The leader followed the advice and kept daily time records. He discovered he had wasted nearly one-third of his time chatting with colleagues, answering unimportant calls, and getting angry over excessive workload. He realized the problem was not insufficient time but poor utilization.

Thereafter, during work hours he stopped idle chatter and routed calls through his secretary, who transferred only important ones. By the end of each day his work was completed smoothly, and he no longer felt short of time.

Those who constantly claim to be busy do not actually have that many tasks; they simply waste too much time on individual activities. They understand the principle “an inch of time is an inch of gold” yet lack a thorough plan, so every action wastes time.

We constantly advocate saving and cherishing time, yet people sometimes fall into the misconception that merely avoiding waste brings one close to success. This is not the case. A successful person’s key lies in having a feasible plan and executing it consistently. Anyone who converts time into money necessarily maintains thorough plans, never wastes time needlessly, and follows those plans to turn time into substantial wealth.

In the spring of 1968, Dr. Robert Schuller resolved to build a crystal cathedral of glass in California. He shared his vision with renowned designer Philip Johnson: “I do not want an ordinary church; I want to create an Eden on earth.”

Realizing the dream proved difficult; the final budget reached seven million dollars—an astronomical sum far beyond Schuller’s means. Yet he did not consider it impossible and drew up a detailed plan:

1. Secure one donation of seven million dollars;
2. Secure seven donations of one million dollars each;
3. Secure fourteen donations of five hundred thousand dollars each;
4. Secure twenty-eight donations of two hundred fifty thousand dollars each;
5. Secure seventy donations of one hundred thousand dollars each;
6. Secure one hundred donations of seventy thousand dollars each;
7. Secure one hundred forty donations of fifty thousand dollars each;
8. Secure two hundred eighty donations of twenty-five thousand dollars each;
9. Secure seven hundred donations of ten thousand dollars each;
10. Sell ten thousand windows at seven hundred dollars each.

Sixty days later, the unique and beautiful model of the crystal cathedral persuaded wealthy merchant John Crean to donate the first one million dollars.

On the sixty-fifth day, a farming couple who had heard Schuller speak donated one thousand dollars.

On the ninetieth day, a stranger moved by Schuller’s perseverance mailed him a one-million-dollar bank check.

The following year, Schuller invited Americans to purchase windows for the crystal cathedral at five hundred dollars each, payable in ten monthly installments of fifty dollars. Within six months, more than ten thousand windows were sold.

In September 1980, after twelve years, the crystal cathedral—seating over ten thousand—opened as a marvel and classic of world architecture and a must-see destination for visitors to California.

A detailed, feasible plan combined with persistent action is the best shortcut to realizing a great dream. Dr. Schuller followed his plan, converted time into money, and fulfilled his grand aspiration.

Therefore, anyone who cherishes time and converts it into money necessarily operates with thorough plans. Such a person is absolutely worthy of major responsibilities, for in their eyes time is money, and they can transform it into wealth placed before us.

### People Who Can Gain from Losses Can Build Long-Term Relationships with Them

People often say “suffering a loss is a blessing,” yet in reality no one wants to keep losing. Those willing to accept losses make better friends than those who haggle over every penny, because cooperation with them frees us from fear of being cheated and lets us focus on the work itself. Hence, when choosing a partner, first check whether the person can accept losses.

In real-life interpersonal dealings, building long-term relationships is neither simple nor straightforward. The saying “suffering a loss is a blessing” is itself an equation of interest exchange. One should not assume that accepting a loss means suffering harm for nothing; certain losses must be taken, and taken skillfully, because a well-chosen loss can bring “blessings.” People who gain from losses trade short-term setbacks for long-term gains and are therefore worth long-term relationships.

Li Ka-shing said, “What appears to be a loss often turns out to be highly advantageous.” Those willing to accept losses view them as investments. They treat others generously, yield when possible, consider others first, forgo unnecessary disputes, help when they can, and therefore easily win support. Many friends gather around them because people want to build lasting relationships with them.

A reporter once asked Li Ka-shing’s son, Li Tzar-kuoi—known as the “Little Giant”—what success secrets his father had taught him. Li Tzar-kuoi replied, “My father taught me nothing about making money; he only taught me principles of conduct.” Li Ka-shing once told his son that when cooperating with others, if seven-tenths was fair and eight-tenths possible, he would settle for six-tenths.

This means Li Ka-shing is always ready to let the other party earn an extra two-tenths, selflessly ceding benefits he could have kept. Everyone knows that partnering with Li Ka-shing yields an advantage, so more people choose to work with him. Although he takes only six-tenths, with one hundred partners he earns far more overall than if he took eight-tenths and attracted only five partners.

Since “suffering a loss is a blessing” is commonly accepted, it contains truth. People generally dislike those who always grab small advantages; such behavior inflicts a greater loss on one’s character. These individuals never accept losses and fixate on tiny immediate gains. Others refuse long-term ties with them and remain guarded, knowing no lasting benefit can be obtained.

Throughout his life Li Ka-shing entered many short- and long-term partnerships. At parting he consistently yielded, taking a smaller share. Because of this willingness to accept losses, others gladly cooperated with him and his enterprises grew. Li Ka-shing is precisely someone who gains from losses, which is why countless people seek long-term relationships with him.

Thus only those who can and will accept losses become the first partners others seek. Such partners inspire confidence.

Song Chengrui, a Guangdong merchant, opened an electromechanical equipment company in Tongchuan, Shaanxi. Once an old client needed an electrical component, but Song searched his entire inventory without success. The client was anxious; without the part his factory faced shutdown, costing over fifty thousand yuan per day.

Seeing the client’s distress, Song reassured him and promised delivery within one day. After the client left, Song took a taxi straight to the supplier in Xi’an. Finding none there either, he flew overnight to Hangzhou and then traveled on to his hometown in Guangdong.

By the time he finished, it was four or five in the morning. Ignoring hunger and fatigue, Song contacted manufacturers across Guangdong and, after reaching more than ten factories, located the component. He then rushed to the airport without even visiting his parents.

The next day, when he handed over the part, the client was speechless with gratitude. The transaction was a “loss” for Song: the component cost three hundred yuan with a thirty-yuan profit, yet he spent over four thousand yuan on travel. Song voiced no complaint, for he valued more than the immediate numbers.

On the surface Song lost several thousand yuan, yet he gained the client’s trust. After receiving the part, the client’s company sent a large plaque with fanfare, brought media to interview Song, and publicized his client-first conduct. Word of Song’s willingness to “accept losses” spread throughout the industry; his business flourished, and the wealth he earned far exceeded the few thousand yuan sacrificed.

No loss is eaten in vain; every effort brings return. A person who yields on profit will receive compensation elsewhere. Conversely, excessive haggling over money leads to small gains and large losses. Those willing to accept losses harvest returns from them. Cooperating with such people removes any worry of being cheated, because they accept losses and gain from them. Therefore, when choosing a partner, first determine whether the other party can gain from losses. Only such a person merits a long-term relationship.

### People Who Value Knowledge and Skills Feel Proud of Their Profession

**Micro-expression keywords**: People who value knowledge and skills always find time to recharge their skills. They are ambitious and genuinely love their work. Skilled and knowledgeable, they take pride in their profession and devote all their energy to it. For any enterprise, such employees are rare and precious.

We often say “knowledge is power,” because knowledge provides substance and correctly guides people forward. A successful person must be knowledgeable. Gorky once said, “Knowledge is as precious as human blood; without blood the body weakens, without knowledge the mind withers.” These words underscore knowledge’s importance. Hence those who value knowledge and skills feel proud of their profession.

In today’s fiercely competitive society, anyone whose pockets are full but whose mind is empty will struggle to achieve anything. By contrast, those who value their own knowledge and skills become society’s favored ones. With solid skills and professional expertise, they feel proud of their work at any time, because the profession gives their knowledge and skills room to flourish.

National hero Xu Zhenchao was an ordinary quayside bridge-crane operator at Qingdao Port. Despite only a junior-high education, he mastered professional knowledge and skills to become a star in his field.

To others the bridge-crane job seemed to require little technique, yet Xu thought otherwise. Through diligent study and practice he mastered “silent operation,” lowering massive containers onto iron ships or trucks without a sound. This minimized wear on containers and vessels, reduced fault rates on crane spreaders, raised efficiency, and lowered costs for the company.

Once Qingdao’s old port area handled a shipment of highly toxic chemicals destined for Xinjiang via the Alashankou border crossing. The cargo could not tolerate even slight impacts. To prevent accidents, armed police and firefighters were stationed at the dock and railway spur. Officials from the Ministry of Railways, the ship owner, and the cargo owner all came to the pier. Unexpectedly, Xu Zhenchao and his team unloaded forty containers from the ship and loaded them onto the train in just ninety minutes, without a single sound. Everyone present was astonished and burst into cheers.

Xu also mastered “one-hook accuracy.” Each container has four locking holes; although large, they are hard to distinguish from dozens of meters above on the crane, let alone align a swinging spreader precisely. Yet Xu and his teammates achieved it. One apprentice said, “It took me a year of practice.”

Xu showed no pride, remarking, “I cannot become a scientist, but I can master a set of ‘unique skills.’ These skills allow me to become a master craftsman—the kind the times and the port need.”

As the enterprise restructured, many employees were laid off, including those with secondary- or tertiary-level diplomas. Xu Zhenchao, with only junior-high schooling, kept his job through his unique skills, became a model employee in a large enterprise, a “core figure,” and a national hero.

People who value knowledge and skills feel proud of their profession no matter their post. “Tsinghua’s steamed-bun god” Zhang Liyong achieved a TOEFL score of 650 because he valued knowledge. Many stop learning after entering the workforce, busy with socializing and neglecting professional knowledge and skills; when unhappy they want to change jobs. Having lost direction in their own field, they become bewildered and are eventually eliminated by society.

Anyone who constantly complains about work and feels bored with it must have outdated knowledge and skills that no longer match the times; unable to survive in the industry, they grow weary.

Meng Fanyu, a reporter for an agricultural magazine, spent every year writing the same seasonal stories: spring plowing, summer support for agriculture, autumn technology in greenhouses, winter leaders visiting workers and farmers. Repeating the cycle year after year, he grew deeply bored.

A friend advised him to skip some dinner parties in his spare time, read more, write articles in various genres, comment on interesting news, and submit essays to different magazines. By pursuing multiple outlets he would feel his learning was limited and would be too busy “recharging” to feel bored. Meng took the advice to heart and, putting it into practice, regained his drive.

Meng felt bored at first because he did not value his own knowledge and skills, was busy socializing, and did not actively learn. When professional knowledge is solid, ability strong, and skills proficient, one does not grow bored with the profession.

Thus those who value knowledge and skills feel proud of their profession, because their knowledge and skills let them lead their field. For business owners, such employees are invaluable; once acquired, they propel the enterprise’s competitiveness forward. If you are an employer, never let such an employee go.

### Entertain Him with Fine Wine and Observe His Behavior When Drunk

Micro-expression Keywords

Chinese wine culture has a long history. Today wine has become an indispensable part of social interaction. Before befriending someone, entertain the person with fine wine and observe his conduct once drunk; this reveals his true character.

As the saying goes, “wine loosens the tongue,” yet others claim “wine disorders the senses.” Therefore, in the art of judging character, “intoxicate him with wine to observe his nature” remains an effective method. China has long possessed a rich wine culture, and wine has become an essential medium of exchange between people. If we wish to get to know someone, entertaining him with fine wine and watching his behavior once drunk allows us to discern his true character.

Many believe that a person who grows irritable or argumentative after drinking must be even-tempered and agreeable when sober. In reality this view is absurd. History contains many heroic figures who enjoyed wine as well as many degenerate rulers who indulged in it, yet the rulers remained degenerate and the heroes remained heroic. Drinking is merely a form of enjoyment; wine does not invert human nature or manufacture emotions that did not already exist. It simply removes the sentry of reason, forcing us to display our various flaws.

Thus, after a few cups, a person’s every trait—irascibility, sentimentality, generosity, gentleness, greed—emerges with particular clarity. A true gentleman remains magnanimous even when drunk, as in Yue Fei’s “hair bristling in fury.” By contrast, a petty man wearing a mask, no matter how hard he tries to conceal his inner world, often exposes his base and shameless soul once intoxicated.

Zheng Ta, the general manager of a company, invited Liu Fei, who had served as acting manager of the enterprise-management department for just over a month, to dinner. During that period Liu Fei had been extremely attentive to Zheng Ta, even overlooking several instances when Zheng Ta arrived late. Zheng Ta therefore felt he should do something for Liu Fei.

After three rounds of wine and five courses, Liu Fei’s eyes were already glazed. Zheng Ta understood that the invitation itself had filled Liu Fei with pride and a sense of honor. Liu Fei raised his cup again:

“General Manager Zheng, you are the person I admire most in my life. Whatever you need, just say the word. As for the other directors, they are nothing in my eyes.” Zheng Ta was astonished; such insolence was completely unlike Liu Fei’s usual cautious demeanor. Normally Liu Fei was courteous to the directors and other mid-level leaders, yet Zheng Ta had sensed laxity in the enforcement of several regulations. Liu Fei’s words now clarified the reason: Liu Fei was responsible for that area and therefore had a direct connection to the problem.

Zheng Ta lifted his own cup. “Thank you. Let’s have another.”

Liu Fei pressed Zheng Ta’s hand. “General Manager Zheng, you are my superior at work and my elder brother in life. For a friend, I, Liu, will never be ambiguous…” Liu Fei was clearly drunk and began to speak from the heart. At last Zheng Ta understood why the two companies where Liu Fei had previously worked had performed so poorly.

It was evident that although Liu Fei concealed his nature well when sober, he lost control once drunk. Such a person becomes a liability in any enterprise, because his public face differs from his private one and may eventually lead the company to ruin.

Many individuals who appear upright in daily life ultimately display behavior we have never seen before; that behavior is their true character. Most of the time they are simply living behind masks, and we must not be deceived by appearances.

We can compare the following attitudes after intoxication:

- Some people like to sing when drunk. Such individuals generally lead orderly lives and are optimistic and enterprising; although their bodies may be intoxicated, their minds remain clear.
- Some people like to chat, argue, or even fight when drunk. Such individuals are emotionally unstable in daily life, possibly because of long-standing frustration or repeated setbacks; they are classic cases of unrecognized talent and may currently be at a low point in their fortunes.
- Some people fall asleep immediately when drunk. Such individuals are rational, practice self-discipline in ordinary circumstances, and rarely overstep bounds in word or deed.
- Some people boast and make reckless promises when drunk, freely issuing commitments at the table. Such individuals are representatives of the timid type: extremely vain and somewhat negative.
- Some people weep or seek someone to confide in when drunk. Such individuals have negative personalities and deep feelings of inferiority; they have usually suffered severe contempt or many grievances and frequently complain in daily life.
- Some people like to play finger-guessing games or other drinking games when drunk. These are lonely individuals who often feel emotionally isolated and use the physical activity of the games to dispel loneliness. They also tend to bury their troubles in busy work.
- Some people laugh a great deal when drunk. Such individuals are optimistic, easygoing, and informal in life; they also possess a strong sense of humor.

In his day Zhao Kuangyin staged the famous “Dismissal of the Generals over Wine” precisely because, once drunk, he could voice his true thoughts. Therefore, when we wish to understand someone, we may entertain him with fine wine; his behavior while intoxicated will lay everything bare.

### Inform Him of Confidential Matters and See Whether He Can Keep Them Secret

Micro-expression Keywords

In television dramas, admirable Communist Party members often treat “keeping secrets” as a principle and even sacrifice their lives for it; such people deserve respect and trust. The same holds true in real life. To determine whether someone is trustworthy, tell him something confidential and see whether he remains tight-lipped; only then is he truly worthy of confidence.

The ability to keep a secret is a matter of moral character. When we need to judge whether a person can be trusted, we may deliberately reveal a secret to him and observe whether he keeps it. We can also supply false information; if it leaks, we immediately know he cannot keep his mouth shut and is therefore unworthy of cooperation or trust. It is best to avoid such people.

In today’s fiercely competitive society, a single careless remark from someone who cannot keep a secret can cause irreparable damage to an enterprise. Managers must therefore pay close attention to this trait when selecting personnel.

Liu Jing worked as a receptionist at a consulting firm and therefore had access to very little confidential information. The most sensitive details she encountered were simply which colleagues had recently traveled where, which clients were visiting that day, and which hotels needed to be booked.

One day a friend invited Liu Jing to dinner and introduced her to another friend, a researcher at an institute. During the meal the researcher asked about Liu Jing’s work and casually inquired about her company. Eager to demonstrate her firm’s strength, Liu Jing mentioned several clients. The researcher took note, investigated the relationships, and succeeded in derailing a project Liu Jing’s company was about to sign, replacing it with his own institute.

The “cooked duck” flew away, and the manager was furious. Investigation traced the leak to Liu Jing. Considering that the disclosure had been unintentional, the company did not dismiss her but canceled her year-end bonus and promotion opportunity. Thereafter colleagues avoided casual conversation with Liu Jing for fear of being implicated, and the company quickly required all staff to sign confidentiality agreements.

Although Liu Jing’s incident was not catastrophic, such inadvertent leaks can still inflict major losses or even bankruptcy. Even if such people have no malicious intent, it is safer to keep certain secrets from them. As the saying goes, “Plans succeed through secrecy and fail through leakage.” The success or failure of any major undertaking depends heavily on the ability to keep secrets; we must not allow loose-lipped individuals to become the decisive factor in failure.

In social interactions many people reveal their secrets without reservation. Some feel uneasy unless they have told every detail of their troubles to anyone who asks, believing that withholding information would be insincere. Yet if the listener cannot keep a secret, the information quickly becomes public. Should a conflict of interest later arise, the other party may use the secret against us. People who injure others by disclosing secrets, amuse themselves with them, or treat secrets as leverage for advancement or blackmail are common in real life.

Wang Qiang, an employee at a public institution, worked diligently and earned his superior’s favor. To encourage better performance, the superior privately informed Wang Qiang of plans to promote him. Wang Qiang was delighted and decided to celebrate with his office friend Zhao Yong after work. Because the official document had not yet been issued, Wang Qiang asked Zhao Yong to keep the news confidential; Zhao Yong nodded.

Wang Qiang did not anticipate that Zhao Yong had long coveted the same position. Angered by the news, Zhao Yong went to the superior the next day and reported, “Wang Qiang has been openly boasting about his achievements, claiming the leadership has already decided he is the only candidate for promotion.”

The superior was enraged and concluded that Wang Qiang had become arrogant because of minor success and required further testing. Through this episode Wang Qiang also recognized Zhao Yong’s true character, but too late.

Wang Qiang was angry that Zhao Yong could not keep a secret, yet he himself had chosen to reveal it. Therefore we should not lightly entrust secrets to those who cannot keep them. We must use the method of “asking plainly to observe virtue” to test the other party; only when we know someone thoroughly should we consider entrusting him with confidential information.

People who can keep secrets earn widespread respect because their discretion makes every undertaking reliable. Conversely, those who cannot keep secrets are never worthy of trust. Recognizing their true nature protects us from harm.

### Let Him Handle Money and See Whether He Is Honest

Micro-expression Keywords

Human desire is boundless and difficult to satisfy. Many corrupt officials fall precisely because they cannot resist the lure of gain. To determine whether someone is reliable, let him handle money; if he withstands the temptation, he is dependable.

Once money enters the picture, whether in life or work, it becomes hard to disentangle ourselves. In the presence of money, inner desires are fully exposed. Therefore, to judge a person we can use financial interests as bait to reveal his inner good or evil. For example, in the workplace a manager’s greatest annoyance is an employee who deceives the company and lines his own pockets. In an era when kickbacks are common, if an employee accepts kickbacks and turns a blind eye to the quality of purchased materials, any resulting accident can cause irreparable damage—especially when the employee works in a critical department such as finance or procurement.

When selecting personnel for such positions we must therefore exercise strict scrutiny. Not everyone succumbs to money, so we can place a candidate in a profitable role, give him an opportunity to obtain funds, and let him handle money; his conduct will show whether he is honest and impartial.

Zhao Gang, general manager of a foreign-trade company, needed to hire a cashier because the previous one had been caught keeping gifts intended for clients. Zhao Gang was determined to assess the candidate’s character during recruitment.

A few days later the clever and attractive Liu Fang caught Zhao Gang’s eye. She was adept at reading people and her smile was genuinely pleasing, so she was selected as the company’s probationary cashier and warehouse keeper.

Intelligence and appearance alone did not guarantee suitability for the role, so Zhao Gang decided to test Liu Fang. He called her into his office and pointed to a batch of red porcelain cups a friend had just delivered. “Xiao Liu, take these cups to the warehouse; they will be given to clients soon.”

“All right, General Manager Zhao. How many cups are there?” Liu Fang asked.

“I didn’t count them. They were a gift; just move them over.”

Liu Fang said nothing more and picked up the cups. Zhao Gang added, “Xiao Liu, after you put the cups away, go to the office-supply wholesaler on West Eighth Road and buy one hundred archive folders like the one I’m holding.” He held up a sample.

“No problem!” Liu Fang smiled and headed for the warehouse. Zhao Gang watched her, hoping she would pass the test. He had already checked prices on West Eighth Road: retail folders cost 0.5 yuan each, while twenty or more cost only 0.3 yuan.

Liu Fang soon returned with the folders; the invoice showed 0.6 yuan each. Zhao Gang said nothing. A few days later he had several departments collect cups for clients. Liu Fang was told to record who took how many. Zhao Gang privately noted the quantities each colleague received. When he checked the final tally, three cups were missing.

Liu Fang failed the test. Such an employee is a cancer to the enterprise; if not removed promptly, she may cause serious consequences.

An enterprise’s survival and growth depend on sound financial management. If employees cannot resist the temptation of money, the enterprise cannot endure. The best way to judge an employee’s integrity is to observe him in practice. Let him handle funds and watch whether he shows any tendency toward embezzlement; even if none appears, check whether he accepts bribes. Financial matters often involve multiple parties, so bribery is always possible. Once bribed, an employee may violate company rules or favor one side; such risks must be guarded against.

In general, people display three types of behavior in the presence of money:

1. The first type shows no restraint; under the guidance of self-interest they openly and brazenly demand money. Once such people gain power, serious consequences inevitably follow.
2. The second type appears to reject money at a distance yet secretly tries to obtain as much as possible, easily creating a false impression; such people require special attention.
3. The third type maintains moral boundaries, remains upright whether observed or unobserved, and adheres to principle without taking anything improper. Such people are extremely rare and best suited for positions of great responsibility.

Human nature is complex. To see through it, use money as a probe. Faced with profit, anyone will shed the cloak of hypocrisy and reveal his most naked inner thoughts.

### Assign Him a Difficult Task to Gauge His Ability

Micro-expression keywords: It is often said that a diploma is a stepping stone, but does holding a graduation certificate from a prestigious university necessarily mean superior ability? Probably not. In fact, the simplest way to test someone’s ability is to assign them a difficult task and see whether they can complete it in a short time; the result is the best proof.

When we want to understand a person’s ability, the best method is to give them a difficult task. For example, increase their workload or assign a task that is hard to finish, or have them handle repetitive and tedious work. This approach accurately reveals a person’s overall quality, because those with special talent can always accomplish in the same amount of time what ordinary people cannot.

In today’s society, more and more people are good at boasting about their abilities, yet when it comes to real work they shrink like turtles pulling in their heads. Success does not depend on whether someone graduated from a top university or on how extravagantly they praise themselves; it depends on whether they possess real skill. As the saying goes, only true gold remains after the waves wash away the sand. When dealing with others, what you hear is not always fact; to tell whether it is a mule or a horse, take it out for a walk and the truth becomes clear at once.

During the Three Kingdoms period, when Shu chancellor Zhuge Liang launched his sixth northern expedition from Mount Qi, he assigned Li Yan the task of supplying grain and fodder to the rear. Li Yan regarded this as a misuse of his talent. Unable to withstand the test of such complex and arduous work, he not only failed to deliver supplies on time— forcing Zhuge Liang’s northern army to retreat—but also spread rumors before the Second Emperor Liu Shan. In the end, Zhuge Liang and the ministers had no choice but to petition the emperor to punish Li Yan severely, stripping him of office and title.

In sharp contrast to Li Yan’s failure, Xiao He, during the Chu-Han contention, helped Liu Bang “stabilize the state, pacify the people, and keep the supply lines open so that grain never ran out.” He ultimately secured victory in the war and was recognized by Emperor Gaozu of Han, who appointed him chancellor.

Whether a person has ability is not decided by what others say, nor by what they say about themselves; the outcome of their work is the best proof.

Ma Jiandong, from Weifang, Shandong, is 27 years old and a high-school graduate. He currently serves as sales director of an automobile company that has established more than 300 dealerships across over 200 cities nationwide, with total sales of 107,000 vehicles and net assets exceeding 100 million yuan; his annual salary is 600,000 yuan.

How did an ordinary high-school graduate reach the position of director and become a “gold-rush emperor”? After failing the college entrance exam, Ma Jiandong went to Beijing to work and found a job as a front-desk receptionist at an automobile sales company; later he was moved to clerical work in the office.

A year later, the company faced closure after media exposure of quality problems with a major brand it represented. At that time Ma Jiandong secretly applied to another automobile sales company, only to be told, “You haven’t even crossed the threshold of a university—why should we hire you?” and was turned away. That single remark spurred him to study automobile sales techniques and product knowledge with great determination. Through years of hands-on experience, Ma Jiandong accumulated rich expertise in automobile sales and set a record of selling 476 vehicles in five months, earning him promotion to supervisor. He was subsequently sent by the general manager to Peking University’s MBA program, dispatched to Germany to study automobile sales management, and eventually rose to sales director.

At any time, genuine knowledge and real ability are what convince people. Some carry an enviable diploma; others list attractive titles on their business cards. Truly wise individuals never judge ability by these things alone. Instead, they test a person’s competence through practice. A prestigious diploma may conceal an empty “straw sack,” and a title on a card may be nothing more than self-inflated vanity.

Everyone presumably remembers Zhuangzi’s essay “The Cook Carves the Ox.” The cook’s skill had reached such a sublime level that his technique appeared almost supernatural. With a touch of the hand, a lean of the shoulder, a press of the foot, and a nudge of the knee, his knife moved as if guided by a spirit; in a few swift strokes a massive carcass was cleanly separated—meat from meat, bone from bone, hide from hide. More remarkably, after nineteen years and thousands of oxen, the cook’s knife remained as sharp as if it had just been honed on a whetstone. If you wish to know whether someone truly possesses the ability they claim, or whether their ability matches the level they assert, simply assign them a task and observe the result.

### Touching the Cuffs Indicates the Other Party Is Beginning to Waver

What scheme is he plotting? What is she thinking? In an era when people’s hearts grow ever harder to read, let FBI agents tell you how to understand someone’s inner world through their words, actions, and movements.

A sexual scandal involving a well-known American figure drew intense media attention, and FBI agents played a crucial role in solving the case.

Agents obtained the perpetrator’s DNA sample from the assaulted hotel maid’s clothing. The next day, after confirming a match with the celebrity, they brought him to FBI headquarters. At first he was defiant, insisting the encounter had been consensual. As details emerged and witnesses appeared one after another, agents noticed that although he never verbally admitted to non-consensual acts, he began to waver internally. This convinced them that the maid’s account was not fabricated.

How did the agents detect this psychological shift?

World-renowned body-language expert and former FBI counterintelligence specialist Joe Navarro, with twenty-five years of experience, explains: “Approximately 60 to 80 percent of human communication occurs through nonverbal behavior. In this case, as evidence of sexual misconduct mounted, agents observed that during interviews the subject increasingly used one hand to adjust his cuff or fiddle with his watch—an unmistakable sign of internal wavering.”

Psychologists have confirmed through experiments that people instinctively play with cuffs, cuff buttons, or watches as a defensive gesture when feeling flustered. Women who repeatedly adjust the position of a handbag on their arm are likewise displaying signs of psychological unease.

Seasoned agents therefore used this cue as a breakthrough: whenever the subject adjusted his cuff or played with his watch, they pressed harder, extracting numerous facts and ultimately establishing his guilt of sexual assault.

Under normal circumstances, such cuff-fiddling behavior readily reveals inner instability and reduces others’ trust. Yet for eliciting information it is extremely useful, because the subject’s psychological defenses are then at their weakest.

In social settings, frequent cuff-fiddlers often give opponents an opening. In the workplace, those who repeatedly fiddle with their cuffs tend to remain at the bottom of the hierarchy, assigned trivial tasks because they betray inner anxiety. The same holds true in conversation: it is a game of strategy; whoever first exposes a weakness loses earliest.

Experts therefore advise that when trying to draw someone out, you may exploit another’s unease but should minimize similar gestures yourself. Especially when speaking with unfamiliar people or in public, avoid such behavior.

Control does not mean concealment. Placing your arms under the table is not foolproof; it too signals weakness. Unless absolutely necessary, keep your hands above the table. If you must adjust a cuff or watch below the table, return your hands to the tabletop immediately afterward. If you feel nervous and wish to hide it, adjust your breathing or take a sip of water instead.

Remember: never let the other person perceive you as lacking confidence or substance. Raise your own perceived value and maintain a superior posture that tells them, “I am the best.”

### Inability to Recount Events in Reverse Means Lying

A certain television drama contains an amusing scene: after waiting a long time, the protagonist finally finds a parking space, only to have another car speed in and steal it just as he begins to reverse. He confronts the driver: “Didn’t you see I had been waiting for this spot?” The driver nods, then shakes his head repeatedly, claiming innocently, “No, I was waiting too.” The protagonist replies seriously, “You’re lying—because before you shook your head you first nodded slightly…”

That single inadvertent nod betrayed the driver’s secret. Clearly, lies are not impregnable; careful observation easily reveals a person’s true thoughts through small, unintentional actions.

Everyone lies. A famous professor once noted that of every ten people we interact with daily, five are lying. Even the kindest person tells at least two lies per day on average. Most lies aim to conceal something or to prevent others from seeing one’s true thoughts. This tendency is especially evident during interrogations.

FBI agent Jack interviewed a suspect and asked, “What did you do on the day of the incident?” The suspect answered fluently: “At eight I went to the convenience store, at ten I was on my way to work, at twelve I was eating a working lunch…” The timeline seemed to prove he had not been at the crime scene. Jack then said, “Please repeat what you just told me, but in reverse chronological order.” After a long pause the suspect stammered, “At five in the afternoon I… I was…” He could not recount his activities backward. Jack therefore concluded he was lying.

People who prepare to lie can rehearse fluent answers in advance, but because they did not actually experience the events, those details never enter deep memory. Asking them to recount events in reverse exposes the fabrication. When facing a skilled liar, use this technique: pretend you did not hear clearly, pick out several time points from their account, and ask them to describe those moments again. If they cannot answer fluently, the lie becomes obvious.

The following signs during conversation also indicate lying:

- Speech is faster and smoother than usual, showing prior preparation.
- Answers are evasive and the mouth moves while the hands remain still.
- Long pauses, frequent hesitation, rigid posture, and minimal change in position.
- Eyes either avoid contact or pupils are larger than normal.
- Introverted individuals speak very haltingly when lying.

In short, no matter how sophisticated the technique, a liar always leaves traces. Even when words are seamless, body language betrays the truth. Detecting a lie grants a decisive psychological advantage; once you know the other person’s real thoughts, you are no longer at their mercy. In commercial negotiations especially, mastering these techniques allows you to seize the initiative.

### People Who Tug at Their Collar May Be Lying

In films we often see the male lead, upon discovering his beloved in another man’s arms, yank at his collar and undo the top button of his shirt. Even when wearing a tie he impatiently loosens it—gestures that perfectly convey agitation and unease. The actions stem from the heat of anger; he pulls the collar away from his neck to let cool air in.

More often, however, a man tugs at his collar for reasons other than mere irritation.

Jones had been troubled by questions about her new boyfriend. She wanted to know whether he had ever had a serious girlfriend before her. So she kept probing: “Was your ex-girlfriend pretty?” “Was she gentle?” Each time the topic arose, her boyfriend grew visibly agitated yet always replied cleverly, “Did I ever have a girlfriend? Of course not.” While speaking he would unconsciously tug at his collar. Seeing this, Jones realized he was lying; his evasive answers only confirmed his guilt. Instead of losing her temper, she smiled and said, “I hope we can be completely open with each other. You know I’m not a petty person…”

Research shows that when people lie, the sensitive nerves in the neck produce an itchy sensation, prompting an instinctive rubbing or scratching motion to relieve the discomfort.

Objectively, men tug at collars more often than women because men typically wear suits and shirts, whereas women’s clothing varies and some styles lack collars. When a woman lies, she is more likely to change the subject or turn her face away. For women who value poise, collar-tugging appears too masculine. Therefore, the gesture alone cannot confirm that someone is lying.

The accompanying facial expression is more telling. If the person is indeed lying, collar-tugging will coincide with subtle facial changes—such as averting direct eye contact. We usually determine deception by combining a shifting gaze with the instinctive collar tug.

Liars may also display an uncomfortable smile because their words do not match their feelings. A genuine smile is an unconscious facial movement beyond direct cortical control; it produces fine lines around the eyes. A false smile, directed by conscious thought, moves only the mouth muscles and looks unnatural, with fine lines appearing only around the mouth.

When uncertain whether a collar-tug stems from discomfort or from fear of exposure, follow Jones’s example: respond with a sincere smile and ask, “Is something bothering you? I hope we can be open with each other,” or “What did you just say? Could you repeat it?” This approach may elicit a more truthful response.

### Yu Pengnian: From Odd-Job Worker to Philanthropist

Yu Pengnian, originally named Peng Lishan, is currently chairman of Hong Kong Fude Development Co., Ltd. and president of the Hong Kong Yu’s Charity Foundation. Yu Pengnian is wealthy, yet he has directed all his money toward social welfare causes. He is passionate about supporting education and social welfare and is the first philanthropist in mainland China to establish a private charitable foundation exceeding one billion U.S. dollars.

On the subject of philanthropy, Yu Pengnian has many classic sayings: “If my son is weaker than I am, why leave him money? If my son is stronger than I am, why leave him money?” “Doing good is the way to nurture health; heaven knows when one does good.” It can be said that performing charitable acts has always been Yu Pengnian’s dream; he believes doing good brings him great happiness.

Yu Pengnian himself came from hardship. In 1958, at the age of thirty, he left his wife and children and traveled via Macau to Hong Kong. Starting as an odd-job worker, he advanced step by step to become a boss, mainly engaged in real estate, construction, and the hotel industry. After fifty years of struggle in Hong Kong and Taiwan, he became a wealthy industrialist with assets worth several billion. He operates hotels, office buildings, and real estate with holdings in Hong Kong, Taiwan, and overseas. Rising from odd-job worker to chairman of a five-star hotel and renowned philanthropist was no easy achievement.

Since 1981 he has donated more than 25 million yuan to his native Hunan province, building more than twenty social welfare projects. In 1995 he was elected a deputy to the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Congress. He invested 1.8 billion yuan to construct the fifty-seven-story five-star Pengnian Building in Shenzhen’s Luohu commercial district and pledged that the hotel’s net profits would be donated permanently and entirely to social welfare and education. As a member of the Standing Committee of the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Congress, he has proposed legislation stipulating that after his death the building’s ownership will neither be gifted nor inherited; a dedicated asset-management committee will operate it, and all profits will continue to be donated without compensation in perpetuity.

In 2003 Yu Pengnian signed a charitable-asset custody and supervision agreement with the Shenzhen branch of the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China. Under the agreement the bank would safely hold and oversee the use of his charitable assets. Yu Pengnian stated: “My money was not easily earned, but my personal wealth will not be left to my children or grandchildren.”

In May 2005, through the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, he disclosed an estimate of his assets, including the Pengnian Hotel building and his Hong Kong properties; total assets at that time did not exceed three billion yuan.

In 2007 Yu Pengnian was named one of the world’s fourteen greatest philanthropists by Time magazine. On 2 April 2008 the Hurun Philanthropy List announced in Shanghai that the eighty-six-year-old Yu Pengnian, called “the oldest philanthropist,” had again won the title of “China’s Most Generous Philanthropist” with donations totaling three billion yuan. This marked his third time topping the Hurun list.

Yu Pengnian was also the first person to make an actual “naked donation.” At a charity dinner on 29 September 2010 he announced on the spot that he was entrusting 9.3 billion Hong Kong dollars to HSBC for management, all to be used for charity after his death. The eighty-eight-year-old Yu Pengnian attended the “Barbie” charity dinner leaning on a cane and said: “My views are the same as those of Gates and Buffett. I am therefore very happy to accept their invitation.”

In daily life Yu Pengnian never lived luxuriously. He ate in the staff cafeteria; the Pengnian Hotel cafeteria reserved a seat for him, where he had three simple vegetarian meals and soup each day. On the cafeteria wall hangs his own calligraphy: “Oppose waste; better to serve one more helping.”

### Clinton’s Denial of an Affair with Lewinsky

Clinton’s lying-analysis case (denying an affair with Lewinsky) has appeared in many books on lie detection. Some psychologists have analyzed that when he denied improper sexual relations with Lewinsky, the direction of his eyes and speech differed from the direction pointed by his index finger, proving he was lying.

This analysis quickly became mainstream and remains so, accepted by countless people. It has also led to overuse: the public treats the subtle directional difference as a discovered treasure that can prove lying. Yet to date no one has demonstrated the deeper basis for this conclusion.

Does the claim hold water?

**Analysis begins:**

His script at the time was: “I did not have sexual relations with that woman, Miss Lewinsky. I never told anybody to lie, not a single time. Never. These allegations are false.” His tone was calm and his pace and pauses normal.

His action was to jab his right index finger forward and downward rapidly and repeatedly with force, while his eyes looked toward his own left front, as if speaking to another specific person.

The finger movement expressed inner anger.

The reason Clinton’s eyes and finger pointed in different directions while speaking was that, as president forced to explain the scandal to the media, his emotions were highly complex.

He must have felt intense anger—how could this matter have been exposed?—while also feeling fear about his future and negative public opinion. The clearly aggressive finger movement was meant to express that inner anger.

We have explained, however, that the offensive nature of anger causes the entire body to point uniformly at the stimulus source; an angry person’s eyes must be fixed on the opponent. If Clinton had been purely angry without any fear, his glaring eyes would have moved in sync with his finger, looking at the opponent while attacking. By shifting his more sensitive and critical line of sight, his eyes not looking toward the target of the finger attack, he revealed that his anger was mixed with another emotion—guilt that made the attack incomplete. Why would he feel guilty while denying the affair? There is only one answer.

At least the method of judging through emotional response has logic, unlike the blunt summary that “finger direction differing from eye direction equals lying.” Simply using mismatched eye and finger directions cannot be justified. Interested readers can search later Clinton videos and photos and will find numerous instances of mismatched eye and finger directions. Does that mean he was lying every time he spoke publicly?

Search other celebrities and observe how common the “eye and finger directions mismatch” phenomenon is; one will see that this formulaic conclusion is false.

### The Story of the Rural Old Lady and Bill Gates

A rural old lady left home for the first time to visit her nephew. When she pushed her large suitcase into the airport terminal, she found that the nephew who was supposed to meet her had not arrived on time. Unfamiliar with the surroundings, she had no choice but to sit and wait.

Having drunk a lot of water on the plane, she now urgently needed the restroom, yet she was carrying such a large suitcase. Although the contents were not valuable, they were gifts she had saved for relatives and friends. She could only endure, anxiously looking around in hopes that her nephew would appear soon.

A young man seated nearby noticed her anxiety and asked with a smile, “Ma’am, do you need help?”

“Oh, thank you, not for now.” The old lady glanced at the young man and inwardly blamed her nephew: “That unpunctual fellow; I’ll give him a good talking-to later.”

The young man then took a book from his pocket and began reading intently. After a while the nephew still had not come, and the old lady could no longer hold on.
