She pleaded with the reading young man: “I’m terribly sorry, but could you please watch my luggage while I go to the restroom? Would that be all right?”

The young man nodded readily.

The old lady returned quickly, thanked him gratefully, took a U.S. dollar from her pocket, handed it to him, and said, “Thank you, young man; this is your due reward.”

Seeing the old lady’s earnest expression, the young man accepted the money, replied “Thank you,” and put it in his pocket<|eos|>

### Yao Hai's Case

Yao Hai is the general manager of a planning company. Teachers' Day is approaching, and Yao Hai's company is preparing to organize a public welfare event involving teachers and students from several local universities. The success of this event affects the company's reputation and capabilities, so it cannot be neglected. Yao Hai therefore decides to check in briefly with Zhao Sicong, head of the public relations department and the person in charge of the event, to learn the details and see whether she has taken the matter to heart.

"Xiao Zhao, how will you ensure that the director of the education commission attends our event?" Yao Hai asks the moment Zhao Sicong enters the room.

"I'll tell the director that Deputy Mayor Li, who oversees education, will also attend. That way the director won't refuse!" Zhao Sicong replies confidently. Yao Hai nods and continues, "Then how can we guarantee that Deputy Mayor Li will definitely come? After all, this is only a public welfare event."

"I'll bring a student representative with me to meet Deputy Mayor Li and have the representative express how thousands of students are looking forward to his personal guidance at the event. Then I'll add details about the event's significance and scale, especially noting that all major news media are paying close attention and that twelve provincial media outlets will send reporters on-site." Zhao Sicong has clearly done her homework; she answers without hesitation, citing every detail.

"Then how will we ensure that the participating universities approach the event with a positive attitude while our company incurs no costs?" Yao Hai asks again.

Zhao Sicong smiles and says, "We'll simply tell them the truth. We'll say the education commission leaders hope every participating university will showcase its strength, and that many journalists will be present, so they should seize the chance to promote their institutions during interviews. I believe the universities will participate very enthusiastically!" Yao Hai nods with satisfaction.

As expected, on Teachers' Day the education commission director arrives with Deputy Mayor Li, the participating universities are well organized, and each brings its own distinctive features: some students wear matching school uniforms, others carry inspiring banners, and still others wave floral wreaths together. The event is a complete success, creates a major stir locally, and Yao Hai's company benefits greatly.

Naturally, Zhao Sicong, the chief contributor, is promoted to the substantive position of public relations department manager.

When an employee can answer every question with solid reasoning even without prior notice, every company values such a person. Only by asking sudden questions can we truly see whether an employee is devoted to the company and to their own work. This approach also reveals the employee's level of knowledge.

### Introducing People of Different Status to Observe Whether Someone Is Snobbish

Micro-expression keyword: To determine whether a person is snobbish, introduce them to several people of varying status. If their attitude clearly differs toward each, the person is snobbish; they will flatter you when you succeed and abandon you when you fail. Draw a clear line with such people and keep your distance. If their attitude remains consistent, the person is upright and worth knowing.

Many people in daily life are snobbish, favoring the rich over the poor, the beautiful over the plain, or foreigners over locals. Associating with such people often leads to eventual abandonment, because once you fall on hard times they will leave. The simplest way to identify them is to introduce friends of different status and watch whether their attitude changes.

For example, when attending a banquet or party with a friend, you may introduce several of your acquaintances and exchange business cards. If your friend glances at a card with obvious disdain, you have identified a snob.

Liu Yong once brought his friend Qiang Ning to a reception. Liu Yong spotted the president of a well-known company he knew from work, went over for a drink, and introduced Qiang Ning. After seeing the president's card, Qiang Ning's reaction astonished Liu Yong: her smile could melt ice cream, and she said in a honeyed voice, "President Liu, what good fortune from a past life brought me the chance to meet someone as accomplished as you!" She then launched into an eager conversation regardless of the other party's willingness.

Recognizing a rare opportunity to connect with someone of "status," Qiang Ning searched for topics, echoed every remark, and worked to create a pleasant atmosphere.

Seeing how animated Qiang Ning was, Liu Yong assumed she enjoyed meeting people and introduced another friend. Qiang Ning glanced at the new card, replied with a flat "Hello," and turned away to find food, showing no interest in further acquaintance.

Only then did Liu Yong realize Qiang Ning was an outright snob who would not even exchange basic courtesies with people of no use to her. From that day on, he gradually distanced himself.

Snobbish people fawn only over those in power and never spare a glance for those beneath them. You can never count on such a person for help; you should consider yourself fortunate if they do not ask you for favors.

### Song Gaozong's Test for Selecting a Crown Prince

During the Southern Song dynasty, Emperor Gaozong was aging and frail. Knowing that "a state cannot be without a ruler for a single day," he decided to appoint a crown prince while still clear-minded, to prevent chaos should he die suddenly.

Yet whom to choose? After consideration, two candidates came to mind: Zhao Ju, then Prince Enping, and Zhao Shen, later Emperor Xiaozong. Their strategic abilities were comparable, their qualifications adequate, and each had distinct strengths, leaving Gaozong undecided.

Zhao Ju was clever, calculating, and reserved; Empress Xian Sheng favored him and showered him with affection.

Zhao Shen, by contrast, was bold, wise, and upright; Gaozong liked him and was inclined to name him crown prince. When both the empress and Qin Hui urged Gaozong to appoint Prince Enping, the emperor paid no heed.

Gaozong ignored all advice. Neither candidate had yet demonstrated the qualities of an enlightened ruler capable of preserving the hard-won Song realm, so he resolved to test their character personally and choose the one of better moral fiber. He devised a method of observation.

One day Gaozong summoned both men and said, "I have been occupied with state affairs and have not looked after you adequately. I recently heard your palaces lack sufficient maids, so I am granting each of you ten palace maids. This will ease your burdens and spare you the need to recruit from among the common people."

Zhao Ju and Zhao Shen thanked the emperor, each received his ten maids, and returned to his palace.

A month later Gaozong suddenly recalled them and said, "The maids I granted you last time are needed elsewhere. Return all of them; not one may be missing."

After the maids were brought back, Gaozong ordered an inspection. All ten granted to Zhao Ju had been violated; the ten granted to Zhao Shen remained untouched. Shocked by the report, Gaozong drew a sharp breath. He had not imagined Prince Enping could be so dissolute. If such a man ascended the throne, he would spend his days lost in the pleasures of the harem and never attend to affairs of state.

Often people feign uprightness to achieve their ends. Without vigilance against such hypocrisy, one can fall into danger unaware. Probing character through human nature allows reliable judgment and underscores the value of personal integrity.

### Characteristics of "Snobbish" People

- **First, snobbish people overemphasize appearances.**  
  They often decide whether to befriend someone based on superficial markers: whether the person's employer is a well-known company, whether their title is senior, how much their clothing costs, or whether they pay with a gold or platinum card. If your "equipment" is not high-end, you may be classified as a low-priority contact even if you are wealthy.

- **Second, snobbish people treat others differently according to status.**  
  In *Soldiers Sortie*, Cheng Cai, newly arrived in the unit, exemplifies this behavior: he carries two packs of cigarettes, offering the good brand to leaders and the inferior brand to fellow soldiers. To identify a snob, simply ask how junior staff feel about the person; the answer will be reliable. In the workplace it is common for employees to show one face to the boss and another to colleagues. Snobs ingratiate themselves with the boss because they believe only the boss can grant favors. Yet if junior employees hold a poor impression, word eventually reaches the boss, who will see the true character. A clear-sighted leader must therefore learn to spot snobs.

- **Third, snobbish people rank their friends.**  
  The word "impartial" does not exist in their vocabulary. They not only treat people differently but also assign friends to tiers: the merely wealthy, powerful, or famous occupy the ordinary tier; those who are both wealthy and powerful occupy the middle tier; those who are wealthy, powerful, and famous are their "heavyweight" contacts. They adjust their flattery according to each tier, but the underlying attitude is always sycophantic; only the degree varies.

- **Fourth, snobbish people calculate how much benefit others can bring.**  
  They befriend someone only if that person can deliver tangible advantages or future help; otherwise they invest no effort. They never accept a loss. If an investment yields no return, they will find a way to recover the benefit.

A snobbish friend harms one's development. Identify such people by introducing them to friends of different status and observing whether their attitude changes. Once a snob is detected, draw a clear boundary, keep a safe distance, and avoid being used.

### Minor Questions Reveal Major Flaws

During an interrogation in a criminal case, investigators asked, "How did you find and hire the victim?"

The suspect replied, "I called a number from a domestic-service flyer posted on a utility pole."

Investigators followed up: "How much did you agree to pay?"

"Two hundred yuan per hour."

"Two hundred yuan per hour is expensive. What did you want her to do?"

"My wife had been away for a long time and I am lazy. The apartment had not been cleaned for half a year, so I asked her to do a thorough cleaning. The price was already discounted eight percent; a deep clean normally costs two hundred fifty yuan per hour. Later she agreed to the lower rate because we were from the same hometown and the job would take six hours."

The investigators exchanged glances, confirmed that local domestic-service rates matched the quoted figure, and moved on.

Seeing this, the suspect's lips curved in a faint smile. He leaned back, tapped the armrest with his right index and middle fingers, stretched his legs, and let his feet swing slightly.

This is a classic victory response, revealing the suspect's sense of triumph and accomplishment.

Interrogations often touch on basic local facts such as prices, culture, or common knowledge. When these questions have no direct link to the case, they are neutral; answering correctly should produce no smugness, and failing to answer should produce no discomfort or anxiety. The suspect's inappropriate emotional display therefore constituted a micro-reaction flaw.

Under sustained logical and detail-oriented questioning, supported by physical evidence, the suspect later confessed that he had impulsively attempted to molest the victim, causing her to fall and suffer a fatal skull fracture.

**Counter-conditioning therapy**: Replace an existing stimulus-response association with a new one. For example, if someone fears spiders, present a pleasant stimulus (such as food) whenever a spider appears, thereby converting the "spider-fear" link into a "spider-pleasure" link.

**Aversion therapy**: Also replaces an existing stimulus-response association, but substitutes an aversive stimulus for a pleasant one. In the boyfriend-and-gaming example, one would introduce unpleasant stimuli while the boyfriend plays games, gradually transforming the "gaming-pleasure" association.

### Case Analysis

Fang Ziheng is the general manager of a growing company. Overwhelmed by the expanding workload, he decides to hire an internal vice president who can handle major responsibilities independently. Because the candidate must possess genuine ability and genuine loyalty, Fang chooses to evaluate internal staff.

After reviewing eligible employees, he narrows the field to Hou Ming and Qin Kai, both of whom demonstrate strong capability. Fang decides to test their character using the "ask about right and wrong to observe their aspirations" method.

"I have a friend who is a business owner. One of his recruitment questions asks, 'What kind of person do you want to become?' One applicant's answer—'I want to become a successful boss'—greatly annoyed my friend. Isn't that ridiculous?" Fang raises the topic casually.

"Anyone who answers that way is unreliable and should never be promoted," Hou Ming says.

"I disagree," Qin Kai replies. "I think such a person is worth promoting. Only someone who aspires to be a boss or already possesses certain boss-like qualities will think from the boss's perspective and share the burden."

"Let's not argue about it," Fang says, steering the conversation elsewhere.

"Recently my friend has disappointed me. In the past he always took my calls personally; now his secretary answers, and several times she has said he is unavailable. Clearly he is avoiding me. Isn't that infuriating?"

Hou Ming responds quickly: "Anyone who becomes arrogant the moment they become a boss will soon have fewer and fewer friends." His remark is reasonable, yet Qin Kai's answer gives Fang pause: "A boss must be organized, and time management is part of that. Politely declining is more courteous than insincerely pretending to be available."

Unsurprisingly, Qin Kai is appointed vice president, while Hou Ming remains a conscientious and reliable office director.

### The Story of Chen Sheng Proclaiming Himself King

Sima Qian recorded in the *Records of the Grand Historian* the story of Chen Sheng killing his friends from his impoverished days after he proclaimed himself king.

When Chen Sheng was young, he was very poor and landless. He once worked as a hired hand for a wealthy family. One day, while resting on a field ridge, he grew indignant at the Qin dynasty’s reckless conscription of labor and its relentless oppression and exploitation of the common people. Determined to escape that oppression and change his own station, he told his fellow laborers, “If any of us ever becomes rich and noble, let us not forget one another.” The others replied, “You are only a hired hand—how could you ever rise to wealth and rank?”

Yet the world is unpredictable. A few years later Chen Sheng raised the banner of revolt at Dazexiang, became “King of Zhang Chu,” and truly attained wealth and rank.

His old companions were delighted and naturally made their way to Chen’s capital. Chen Sheng welcomed them warmly, brought them into the palace, showed them around with obvious pride, and treated them to fine meat and wine.

Gradually, however, the men grew presumptuous. They spoke to Chen as equals and repeatedly recounted his humble, inglorious past. Chen’s attendants warned him that such talk damaged his dignity. Newly enthroned and eager to assert authority, Chen Sheng found a pretext and had all his former companions killed.

Those who have long been rich speak fondly of the past when they fall into poverty; those who have long been poor speak of the past with aversion once they rise. Although reminiscing about shared hardship may seem friendly, to the newly rich it is a source of shame. More often they avoid their “poor brothers” altogether.

Thus wealth and rank reveal character most clearly. As the saying goes, “When the cunning hare is dead, the hunting dog is cooked; when the rival state is destroyed, the strategist is discarded.” In hardship people readily unite and become friends or partners, yet once that shared hardship ends they often betray one another to protect themselves. Therefore, whether choosing friends, partners, or talent, one must proceed with great care. Observing whom a person befriends after becoming wealthy is especially revealing.

### The Case of an Accidental Homicide

In an accidental homicide case, Party A led seven men in surrounding and beating Party B, who had taken refuge inside a car. During the melee one of Party A’s men was stabbed in the neck and killed. With no surveillance footage and extreme confusion at the scene, it was impossible to determine who had wielded the knife. Each of the seven participants claimed to have been unarmed, and the weapon was never recovered. All seven were therefore subjected to polygraph examinations. Before formal testing, each underwent a forty-minute to one-hour pre-test interview.

Most striking was Party B—the man who had been attacked. Throughout the interview his hands and feet remained completely motionless, as though frozen to the chair. His tone, facial expressions, and breathing, however, appeared natural: grief, anger, fear when recalling events, and aversion toward the assailants. When speaking of the deceased he displayed a fluid mix of contempt, anger, and a trace of sympathy—humanitarian concern for the man’s family and children. Yet the polygraph data clearly implicated him. During subsequent interrogation he admitted that, while defending himself, he had unintentionally stabbed the victim. Police later recovered the discarded knife at the location he indicated.

Re-examining the pre-test interview, the frozen posture of his hands and feet was plainly unnatural. If his emotions were genuine and he was the victim, there was no reason for his limbs to remain rigidly still while his face, breathing, and speech moved freely. That freeze response pointed to a psychologically induced state of constraint. What was he afraid of? He answered every question police posed with apparent naturalness and emotion; the only fear that could account for the immobility was fear of legal consequences for the unintended killing.

### Real-World Examples

In poverty everyone is alike and can readily “share hardship,” but once wealth arrives the situation changes. It is not uncommon for people who suddenly become rich to abandon their families and cut ties with former poor friends; such people are best avoided. Conversely, those who remain unconcerned about their impoverished friends after attaining wealth are worth knowing.

Jiang Tianyang and Peng Wu were close friends who worked together in a big city. When Jiang Tianyang went several days without finding work and could barely get by, Peng Wu supported him, buying food they ate together. Jiang Tianyang said gratefully, “Peng Wu, when I make it big I will treat you well.”

Fortune turned. A few years later Jiang Tianyang’s real-estate business flourished. Many people sought his company; he was constantly hosting dinners or sending holiday gifts. His old friend Peng Wu did not intrude—whether because Jiang was too busy or because Peng felt awkward about the changed circumstances. Jiang, however, had not forgotten his promise.

Hearing that Peng Wu had been laid off during an economic downturn, Jiang immediately sought him out, offered a sum of money, and said, “You helped me when I was down; now let me help you. Please don’t refuse.” Peng Wu was deeply moved. He had not expected the now-wealthy Jiang to remember his earlier pledge. He felt fortunate to have befriended the right person.

True friends never discard you after becoming rich; only the insincere do so in order to pursue equals or those even wealthier. Such behavior reveals a petty character. Therefore, to judge someone, observe whom he associates with after becoming wealthy before deciding whether the friendship is worthwhile.

### Lincoln’s Campaign against Douglas

Abraham Lincoln once competed against the wealthy Stephen Douglas for the U.S. presidency. Douglas traveled in grand style: at every stop cannons fired thirty-two times and a band played, creating an unprecedented spectacle. Douglas declared disdainfully, “I shall let that country bumpkin Lincoln smell my aristocratic scent.”

Lincoln remained calm and unperturbed. He bought ordinary train tickets and spoke across the country. At each stop he mounted a farm wagon friends had prepared and delivered his campaign speech:

> Many people have written asking how much property I own. I have only a wife and three sons, all priceless. I also rent an office containing one desk, three chairs, and a large bookcase whose books are worth reading. I am poor, thin, long-faced, and unlikely to grow stout. I have nothing to rely on except you, the people.

Douglas suffered a resounding defeat; Lincoln won. Lincoln’s modesty clearly worked to his advantage. Whether facing friends or opponents, humility enhances one’s image. Much of Lincoln’s victory can be credited to his modesty, which Douglas’s own arrogance only highlighted. The outcome was therefore unsurprising.

Confucius said, “The gentleman does not boast of his achievements nor grow arrogant in success.” When dealing with people of high status, the simplest way to gauge their character is to observe how they treat ordinary people.

### Micro-expression Keywords

It is often said that “even heroes find it hard to resist a beautiful woman.” Many heroes—Lü Bu, Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, among others—were undone by beauty. Those unmoved by beauty are worth befriending; those who become frivolous in its presence should be avoided.

The *Book of Songs* already contains the lines “Guan-guan cry the ospreys / On the islet in the river. / A modest, retiring, virtuous young lady / Is a good mate for our lord.” The love of beauty is universal, yet when a person cannot control that impulse and sinks into the “gentle trap,” the consequences can be disastrous.

In life one encounters many tests—power, wealth, and beauty among them. Passing them depends on character and conduct. People of high moral quality remain indifferent to such temptations; those of weak character and willpower rarely succeed.

Some appear upright and serious, yet beneath that façade lies a base heart. To expose such people, place a beautiful woman at their side and observe whether they remain unmoved. The hypocritical often change completely, becoming frivolous. Only those of genuine integrity stay composed, preserving dignity and principle even in the presence of beauty. Such people alone are fit for great responsibility.

### Micro-expression Keywords

The most important quality to discern in others is character. Whether someone is trustworthy or fit for great responsibility depends on character, values, and judgment on major issues. Before making friends or promoting subordinates, therefore, ask pointed questions about fundamental principles and analyze the answers.

Knowing others begins with knowing their character. Zhuge Liang, the foremost strategist of the Three Kingdoms period, excelled not only in planning but also in selecting and employing talent. In his “Seven Methods of Observing People,” “aspiration” ranks first. To understand someone, first examine his ambitions, attitudes, and values. Pose questions about fundamental issues and assess his judgment.

Character governs action; action reveals worldview and values. A person’s steadfastness of purpose, resistance to temptation, and conduct on matters of principle form the core of character and the basic criterion for judging others. When choosing a high military commander, for example, loyalty to the nation must come first; a commander who cannot distinguish friend from foe will bring disaster.

Thus, before entrusting someone with important responsibilities, examine his aspirations, values, and judgment. Only then can you decide whether he deserves the post.

### Suddenly Questioning Someone to Gauge His Knowledge

**Micro-expression Keywords**  
Examinations can test knowledge, yet if a person can answer fluently when questioned without warning, he demonstrates not only rich learning but also quick thinking and the ability to handle emergencies—true marks of talent.

To assess ability and wisdom, maintain timely communication. Use “sudden questioning” to evaluate knowledge reserves, especially when leaders wish to gauge subordinates. “Sudden questioning” need not be a surprise attack; it can also occur when an urgent situation arises and a leader needs immediate information or opinions. The capacity to respond to emergencies is an essential quality of talent.

Under sudden questioning, rapid reaction, verbal organization, and expressive ability are most clearly revealed. If subordinates are given advance notice and time to prepare reports, the information may be comprehensive, yet the test of their real-time ability and diligence is weaker than under sudden questioning.

### The Story of Marquis Wen of Wei Choosing a Chancellor

Marquis Wen of Wei needed to appoint a chancellor. Two candidates, Wei Cheng and Zhai Huang, were equally capable, leaving the marquis undecided. He consulted Li Ke, who said: “Zhai Huang recommended Wu Qi, Ximen Bao, and Yue Yang, all of whom became your officials; Wei Cheng recommended Bu Zixia, Tian Zifang, and Duan Ganmu, all of whom became your teachers. Officials are merely competent administrators; teachers must be ministers of both virtue and talent. Therefore Wei Cheng is superior.”

Many leaders today, when recommending talent, first ask whether the candidate is loyal to them personally, thereby burying many capable people—especially those who have disagreed with them or stood on a different side. Such leaders not only refuse to recommend but actively suppress these individuals. Association with them offers little chance of advancement.

A true leader never buries talent because of personal considerations. If someone is genuinely talented, the leader will recommend him regardless of whether that talent surpasses his own, because his concern is the realm, not personal position. Only with such leaders can one avoid worrying that one’s abilities will go undeveloped.

### How to Use “Sudden Questioning” in Talent Selection

Every enterprise needs personnel with strong knowledge reserves and strategic thinking. Genuine strategy differs fundamentally from petty cleverness. Useful strategy is the skillful application of management principles that safeguard and advance the enterprise’s interests, enabling calm response in emergencies.

Therefore, when selecting talent, employ “sudden questioning” to assess knowledge. The key is to pose concrete questions within the relevant domain rather than abstract ones. Questions such as “What are your views on financial management?” or “What are the duties of office staff?” elicit only abstract answers even from capable candidates.

- For financial talent, ask how to legally minimize tax or reduce expenditures to the greatest extent.
- For office staff, ask how to enforce attendance rules so that every employee feels the system’s authority and complies strictly.

Sudden questioning most clearly reveals a person’s actual knowledge level. Mastering this technique allows managers to select talent smoothly.

### Conclusion

*Forbes* reported that by 2007 China had sixty-six billionaires, ranking second only to the United States. That same year *Forbes* discontinued its China philanthropy list—the first time in eight years. Besides imperfections in China’s charitable system that discourage public donations, the chief reason was the weak philanthropic consciousness of Chinese billionaires and their conservative attitudes toward wealth. The cancellation of the list embarrassed China’s wealthy.

We often see people driving luxury cars and spending lavishly in nightclubs. Many rich individuals compete to display who spends most freely. Association with such people ultimately burdens one with money. For a wealthy person, the ability to control wealth is a sign of strength, yet how that wealth is used reveals character and taste. We should respect those who benefit the world and appreciate those who contribute to society directly or indirectly. For those who merely look after themselves, simply recognizing their true nature suffices.

A person in high office may not receive praise for competence, since the post itself demands it; yet the people he recommends clearly indicate whether he is wise or mediocre. This method reveals his true character.

### How He Spends His Money When Wealthy

Micro-expression keywords: Money is something everyone in society needs. It not only serves people’s basic needs for food, clothing, housing, and transportation but also has many other uses. Each person spends money differently—some on personal enjoyment, others on charity. In fact, the way people spend money reveals their true character.

Money is not everything, yet without it almost nothing is possible. Many people agree with this statement. But how one spends money is a personal choice. If we want to understand someone, observing where they direct their money when they have it is an effective way to judge character.

Some people, once wealthy, indulge in personal pleasures—eating, drinking, and living extravagantly, caring only for their own comfort. Others, even after gaining wealth, continue to aid the poor, distribute funds widely, and recruit talent. Some invest earnings in shops and factories, seeking appreciation at every turn. Some donate surplus wealth rather than leave it as a burden to descendants. Others quietly hoard it, spending more time counting than spending. In short, each person has their own way of managing wealth, and that way reflects a core aspect of their character.

### Historical Anecdotes

During the Northern and Southern Dynasties, Gao Huan, founder of the Northern Qi, wanted to test the ambitions and courage of his sons. He gave each a tangled skein of hemp and asked who could sort it fastest and best. While the others searched for ways to untangle the mess, his second son, Gao Yang, drew a sharp knife without hesitation, cut through the skein, and declared, “What is tangled should be cut.” The idiom “cut the Gordian knot” originates here. Gao Huan was impressed by the approach.

Gao Huan next assigned each son several soldiers and sent them in different directions. He then dispatched a general with troops to stage an attack. The other sons were at a loss, but Gao Yang rallied his men, surrounded the general, and—after the general removed his armor to reveal the ruse—still seized him and delivered him to Gao Huan. Gao Huan praised Gao Yang highly, saying, “Gao Yang’s insight and strategy surpass my own.” Gao Yang later inherited his father’s enterprise and became the first emperor of Northern Qi.

Clearly, those who remain calm in crisis and dare to resist can achieve great things. Therefore, before entrusting someone with responsibility, people often create an artificial setback to observe whether the person possesses the courage to overcome it.

### Lessons from Heroes Past and Present

Throughout history, countless “heroes” have fallen before beauty. Despite their literary or martial talents, they lost self-control in the presence of allure, behaved frivolously, and ruined their lives. Only those with strong willpower can shoulder heavy burdens.

Homer’s epics recount that after the Trojan War, the Greek hero Odysseus faced a deadly test of beauty on his return voyage: three bird-women sirens lived on a mysterious island. Though cannibals, their beauty and song were irresistible; almost no one could withstand them.

Odysseus knew that even his firmest resolve might fail against the sirens’ lure and that he risked becoming another set of bones on the island. He ordered his crew to plug their ears with wax and had himself lashed to the mast. Thanks to these precautions, the ship passed the danger safely.

A person’s conduct in the face of beauty reveals their truest character. Those who act frivolously will never achieve greatness. Only those who can look upon beauty without being moved earn our trust; recognizing this trait brings great benefit to our own lives.

### How He Recommends People When Holding High Office

**Micro-expression keywords**  
To understand someone in a position of authority, observe whom they recommend. A truly selfless leader who knows how to employ talent will promote the worthy. A hypocritical or selfish person will mostly advance personal cronies. Such a leader has a character flaw; following them risks burying our own abilities. We should choose carefully.

When someone holds high office, the talent they promote or appoint at least reflects their breadth of mind and leadership ability. If those they elevate or recommend are all personal associates or people who can deliver tangible benefits, their character is obvious.

Holding high office carries the duty to discover and employ talent. A leader must “know people and assign them appropriately.” If a leader can do neither, their leadership ability is seriously questionable. Only those who recommend capable people without regard for personal gain and who do not suppress someone more talented than themselves are truly wise leaders. The caliber of people a leader recommends represents one measure of the leader’s own capability.

### Summary

“Question them on right and wrong” means examining their judgment of right and wrong, their views on matters, and their aspirations. This shows that managers must consider the degree of aspiration when assessing talent. Throughout history, every successful person has been single-minded in purpose and firm in belief.

Those who remain ambiguous on major questions of principle, or who bend like “grass on the wall,” are usually adept at reading the room and currying favor. They lack clear standards of right and wrong and inner moral discipline; they merely trim their sails to the wind. Such people are most likely to harm the highest interests of the nation and people at critical moments. By contrast, those with lofty aspirations, firm positions, broad minds, and shared ideals will strive for a common cause. Such talent is worth seeking out.

A person’s nobility is not decided by eloquent speech. Therefore, when judging someone’s aspirations and values, we should ask them questions of major principle and assess their judgment from the answers.

### How He Behaves When Poor—Does He Accept Ill-Gotten Gains?

Micro-expression keywords: The saying “a gentleman loves wealth but acquires it properly” means there is nothing wrong with liking money, provided the means are legitimate. Ill-gotten gains should be refused. Someone willing to accept such gains will not have good character; associating with them risks eventual deception. It is best to keep distance.

“A gentleman loves wealth but acquires it properly.” The Confucian view of finance first emphasizes “the Way”—whether wealth is obtained in accordance with ritual, morality, and behavioral norms. Confucius said: “Wealth and rank are what everyone desires, yet a gentleman will not accept them if they are not obtained through the humane way; poverty and low status are what everyone detests, yet a gentleman will not escape them if it cannot be done through the humane way.” Therefore, to judge character, observe whether a person accepts ill-gotten gains when poor.

Those who refuse unjust wealth even in poverty can be trusted and relied upon. Otherwise, any amount of money remains merely “ill-gotten.”

### Liars Often Touch Themselves

When people lie, the more they try to hide their inner state, the more their changing body movements expose it. Psychologist O’Hair and colleagues conducted an experiment:

Subjects were instructed to answer an interviewer’s questions with lies while their nonverbal behavior was recorded in each time segment. Compared with truthful behavior, liars gave shorter answers and displayed subtle actions such as fiddling with their fingers or unconsciously touching parts of their body.

When lying, people often cover their mouths but feel this is inappropriate, so they usually end up touching their noses a few times to mask the gesture. Non-liars may also touch their noses while speaking, yet the action differs noticeably. Duration and pressure reveal the difference: truthful people touch longer and with greater pressure.

### What Kind of Friends Does He Make When Wealthy?

Once someone becomes rich, what sort of friends do they cultivate? Do they remember the “poor brothers” who struggled alongside them, or do they prefer fair-weather companions? People differ in their attitudes. Many can share hardship but not prosperity; once wealthy, they may not share their good fortune. This is a human weakness and an important means of judging character. The friends a person chooses after becoming wealthy reflect their character.

When someone attains wealth and status, many similarly wealthy people naturally appear around them. At that point their attitude toward former “poor brothers” may change. Many who become rich begin to fawn on others who are wealthy and powerful and sever ties with those who once shared their struggles, because those old companions now make them lose face or lower their status.

### How He Treats Others When Holding Status—Does He Observe Proper Etiquette?

Micro-expression keywords: A person’s cultivation shows in how they treat others. Cultivated people remain courteous to everyone, neither obsequious nor arrogant. Petty individuals fawn on those above them and lord it over those below. To see someone clearly, simply observe how they interact with ordinary people once they hold status.

A change in status often alters a person’s conduct. Some are mild and approachable—even somewhat deferential—while still commoners. Once their status rises, they receive office or rank, their tone changes, they speak from on high, and arrogance appears. They display the classic look of a petty person who has gained power.

Therefore, do not assume someone is refined merely because they are gentle in ordinary times. Observe whether they still observe the same courtesies after acquiring status.

### Tell Him Disaster Is Imminent—Does He Have the Courage to Resist?

Micro-expression keywords: In daily life, people’s abilities appear roughly equal. Yet at critical moments, especially when facing calamity, some reveal themselves by fighting difficulties to the end. Such people usually possess a sense of responsibility, courage, and boldness; they can be entrusted with important tasks.

A person’s true character emerges when facing major events. Therefore, to test someone’s courage and boldness, inform them of possible disaster or difficulty and observe whether they show the will to resist. Most people feel varying degrees of fear when told of difficulties; without sufficient courage they will not willingly shoulder responsibility. So deliberately describe a difficult situation. If they appear troubled or timid, they are not suited for great undertakings. Conversely, if they accept the challenge with genuine confidence, they can be given heavy responsibility.

### Chapter 7 Observe Carefully—the Answer Reveals Itself

Generally, a person’s character is discerned through ordinary interaction, not through deliberate testing. Everyday conduct proves what kind of person someone is, because character is not something that can be put on; it is an expression of inner quality. The Analects records Confucius’s famous words: “Observe what they do, note the means they employ, and examine what brings them contentment—how can anyone hide their true nature?” The idea is to watch why they act, how they act, and their state of mind while acting—whether at ease or uneasy. After such observation, where could that person hide?

Micro-expression keywords: The kind of friends someone makes after becoming wealthy reveals their character. Those who cut ties with former poor companions to befriend other wealthy people are hypocritical and base; they will achieve nothing great in the future. We should distance ourselves promptly.

### Is He Lying to Me?

In social interactions, the frequency with which people lie or are deceived by lies is astonishing. MIT psychologist Feldman’s research indicates that the average person tells at least twenty-five lies per day. Of course, lies vary in degree; some are well-intentioned and can be ignored. But when lies are meant to deceive or harm, how do we know whether we have been deceived?

A recent study from the University of California found that even habitual liars produce subconscious signals when their brains switch into pretense mode—signals ordinary people can detect, much like a lie detector, to catch the liar out.

Most liars fall into two categories: occasional liars and habitual liars.

### Liars Never Forget Any Detail

Try this with friends: ask what they did from leaving the office two evenings ago until bedtime. In their account they will almost certainly make a few mistakes.

Remembering every detail of a time period is difficult. People rarely recall everything that happened; they usually correct themselves repeatedly to get the sequence straight. They might say, “I went home and sat in front of the TV—oh, no, first I called my mother, then I sat in front of the TV.” Liars, however, make no such slips because they have already constructed the entire scenario in their minds. They will never say, “Wait, I got that wrong.” Their very reluctance to admit error during the account exposes them.

### Liars Blink or Rub Their Eyes

Some habitual liars have learned to stare directly at you to avoid detection. Because deceivers concentrate so intensely, their eyes dry out; they must blink or rub their eyes more often to relieve the discomfort, and this action leaks critical information.

Another reliable test is to watch the movement of the person’s eyes. Eye movement indicates the brain is working. When most people are “constructing” a sound or image, continued eye movement also suggests they are lying. This “eye movement” is a reflex that cannot be faked unless one has received rigorous training.

### After Being Asked the Same Question Repeatedly, Liars Become Angry

Ask a question and wait for the answer. Ask it a second time; the answer remains unchanged. Leave an interval between the second and third asking. During this pause their body calms down and they think, “I’ve gotten away with it.”

Once all physiological reactions subside and the body returns to a relaxed state, ask the question again unexpectedly. They are no longer in lying mode; they either become indignant or tend to confess. If someone says, “Haven’t I already told you about this?” and then erupts in anger, they are probably lying. They may also say, “All right, I’ll just tell you the truth.”

### Application in Business

Leaders in business can also use this method to judge people. Within companies there are many strategic thinkers and no shortage of courageous individuals. Yet some possess deep foresight but lack the courage to face difficulties and setbacks. Employees who combine courage and strategy are ideal, but in reality such people are rare. Leaders must therefore combine talent effectively and correctly identify who truly possesses courage.

For example, when a company encounters real setbacks, managers should deliberately inform employees of the misfortune and see who volunteers to help solve the problems. Only genuine talent will step forward to shoulder the burden at such times.

### Avoiding Eye Contact with Others

Everyone remembers their mother’s childhood rebuke: “You must be lying again—you won’t look me in the eye.” Some occasional liars touch their eyes while lying to avoid eye contact. Women generally touch below the eye lightly, to avoid seeming rude or smudging makeup; they may also look at the ceiling to escape the other person’s gaze. Men usually rub their eyes more forcefully and likewise look at the ceiling or elsewhere.

### Chapter 6 Skillful Testing—Practice Reveals True Quality

A common saying goes: “Whether it’s a mule or a horse, take it out for a walk.” The point is that testing shows who truly has ability; bluster and self-promotion are useless. Real skill is revealed by practice—the sole criterion of truth. “A long journey tests a horse’s strength; time reveals a person’s heart” is another method of testing through practice, yet more effective is the proactive design of scenarios for deliberate trials. This approach has a long history in traditional Chinese methods of judging character.

### Pulling at the Collar

The gesture of pulling at one’s collar seems ordinary; people usually adjust their collars for appearance. Psychophysiological research shows that lying creates psychological imbalance, triggering subtle changes in sympathetic nervous function that produce tingling sensations in the face and neck. The person then rubs, touches, or unconsciously tugs at the collar.

### Occasional Liars

Occasional liars usually lie to avoid an unpleasant situation or to cover up a mistake. Because they are not practiced at lying, they feel uneasy, and that unease shows in appearance, body language, and voice.

### Habitual Liars

Habitual liars, through practice, can control appearance, body language, and voice so convincingly that almost no trace remains—yet their lies are not without flaws.

### Sudden Changes in Volume or Pitch

If you ask your husband who just called and he suddenly starts chattering like a magpie, be alert. A sudden rise in pitch often indicates a liar trying to mask nervousness.

### Lie Detection Basics

#### Observe Whether He Stands Tall When His Status Is Low

Micro-expression keywords Most successful people have climbed up step by step from a lowly status. When a person is in a lowly position, whether he can still conduct himself with dignity to some extent reveals his character and foreshadows his future prospects. A person of humble status who lives with dignity and conscience will not fare too poorly in later development. At the same time, associating with such a gentleman will benefit us greatly.

The phrase “lowly status” here refers to how a person behaves when in difficulty. Does he adhere to his moral bottom line and continue to conduct himself with dignity as before, or does he give up, become despondent, even live in degradation and abandon his principles? Each person’s different responses reflect different personalities and qualities.

> Confucius said: “The orchid grows in the deep forest; it does not cease to be fragrant because no one is there to appreciate it. The gentleman cultivates the Way and establishes virtue; he does not alter his integrity because of poverty.”

This means that orchids and lingzhi grow in remote forests and do not stop emitting fragrance simply because no one sees them; the gentleman cultivates his moral character and does not change his aspirations because of hardship. Maintaining integrity in favorable circumstances is not difficult, but remaining upright even in lowly circumstances is truly admirable. Such a person demonstrates an extraordinary resilience of character; no matter how low his position, he will not compromise his principles. People of this kind are worth employing.

There was once a very talented young man skilled in music, chess, calligraphy, and painting, yet he remained unrecognized despite repeated examination failures. In the end he had no choice but to sell his calligraphy and paintings to make a living.

He set up a stall at his gate, writing and painting on the spot for customers in exchange for daily necessities. Because his work was beautiful, many people gathered to watch. He charged five wen for a couplet, ten wen for a plaque, and one tael of silver for a painting. When business was slow he played the qin to pass the time.

One day an official was drawn by the sound of the qin. Hearing the music, the official assumed it came from a scholarly household, but upon approaching he discovered only a poor young vendor of paintings. Still, the young man’s work was genuinely fine—elegant and free in style, unlike anything the official had seen before.

The official intended to buy several pieces to study at home and, feeling sympathy for the talent, purchased a few finished works and gave the young man five taels of silver, telling him to keep the change. To his surprise the young man refused the extra money and insisted on returning it. The official wondered how anyone could be so foolish as to reject money and suspected the young man might be putting on an act. He decided to test him, so he deliberately left his money pouch on the stall without the young man noticing and then walked away.

After only a few steps the official heard someone calling him. Turning around, he saw the poor vendor chasing after him with the pouch: “You dropped this.”

The official was immediately impressed by the young man’s integrity and talent, and resolved to help him. Back home he invited many prominent figures to view the paintings. They all praised them highly, assuming the official himself had painted them.

When the official revealed the truth, everyone was astonished. With the official’s vigorous promotion the young man met more distinguished people, his reputation grew, and he eventually became the foremost of the Four Great Talents of Jiangnan. He was Tang Bohu.

> Mencius said: “Wealth and rank cannot corrupt him; poverty and low status cannot sway him; force cannot bend him—this is what is meant by a great man.”

For a great man, neither high office nor poverty nor violence can alter his conduct. At all times, conducting himself with dignity remains his consistent standard. Such people earn respect no matter their circumstances or status.

Common people often say: “Conduct yourself with dignity; do your work steadily.” A person should live without bowing and scraping, without meekly agreeing to everything, standing tall with backbone. Only such people are worth knowing.

I once heard a story about a migrant worker:

A young man whose parents had died young carried the burden of supporting his younger brother through school. Alone in a strange city with no skills or higher education, he could only drift from one odd job to another. His greatest pleasure was visiting a bookstore to read. Each time he opened a book he felt renewed strength and forgot the fatigue of work. One day, while reading, he was startled by a commotion outside. A traffic accident had occurred at the bookstore entrance. After the dispute ended he realized he was still holding a book and hurried to return it. Suddenly the shop owner rushed out, slapped him without a word, and shouted: “It’s already bad enough that you read here—now you want to steal the book too? You ill-bred thing!”

The young man stood stunned for a moment, then quickly explained: “I’m not a thief! I want to buy this book!” The moment the words left his mouth he regretted them, because he had no money at all.

The owner seized the chance and sneered: “Fine! Pay first, then.”

“This…” the young man stammered.

“Go on, pay! You said you wanted to buy it. I’ve seen plenty like you—when you have no money you steal books. I caught one just the other day!”

The young man stopped arguing. He left his only valuable possession, a watch, as collateral and promised to return within a week with the money. Only then, he said, could he prove his innocence. He left.

A week passed, then another, and he did not appear. Instead his younger brother came, paid for the book, and retrieved the watch. The owner, puzzled, asked: “Why didn’t the young man come himself?”

“He… died. A crane collapsed at the construction site and crushed him. Inside his backpack I found this note: ‘I owe the bookstore for a book. I will repay it. I am not a thief!’”

The brother handed the note to the owner and said: “My brother was not the kind of person you think.”

Even in humble circumstances, dignity need not be humble. As the saying goes, “A scholar can be killed but not humiliated.” You may take such a person’s life, but you cannot insult him or wound his dignity. In daily life we encounter many such people. Although they hold no prominent positions and do humble work, they always act according to conscience and conduct themselves with dignity. At any time, these are the people worth knowing.

#### Making Suggestions in an Abstract Manner

If we could always express or receive conversational content accurately, communication would produce no ambiguity or misunderstanding. Unfortunately our exchanges are not always smooth. Some remarks sound one way at first but reveal another meaning upon reflection. Moreover, people like to use non-quantitative terms to express degree—words such as “not bad,” “okay,” “a little,” “very,” or “better”—which become even more ambiguous without a reference point for comparison.

You show a plan to your superior and the superior says “It’ll do.” What does “it’ll do” mean? If the other party does not state it plainly, you must guess: does it mean “not good enough” or simply “leave it at that”? So whenever you hear such phrasing you naturally want to press: “What exactly do you mean by ‘it’ll do’? Approved or not?”

Yet in many situations this vague, abstract style of communication is actually an effective way to offer suggestions. Because the concept is fuzzy, the other person must automatically fill in the missing information. An example will illustrate.

**A:** What do you think of the evening event?  
**B:** Not bad.  
**A:** Thanks so much for coming to support it.

The phrase “not bad” that B used is a fuzzy concept whose real meaning could be any of the following:

1. I didn’t pay much attention; a perfunctory reply will do.  
2. I watched; it wasn’t great but wasn’t the worst either.  
3. I couldn’t stand it, but I don’t want to hurt your pride, so I offered mild encouragement instead of saying it was excellent.  
4. Among events of similar scale, this one was quite good.

Whether A considers all these possibilities is A’s own affair. This method of offering suggestions carries the figurative explanation: “I didn’t actually say that.”

Sometimes, to deepen the impression a suggestion makes, we deliberately omit information so the other person senses it themselves; the effect is often better than stating it outright, at least because it respects the other person’s dignity. For instance:

**A:** What do you think of this plan?

A is stubborn and insecure; direct criticism would make him feel looked down upon. In such cases an abstract suggestion works best.

**B:** It’ll do.

This phrasing does not provoke resistance in A; it merely prompts him to wonder what “it’ll do” means.

**A:** Do you mean there’s still room for improvement?  
**B:** Yes, I think you could do better.

Allowing the other person to realize there is room for improvement is far more effective than stating it directly.

Although abstract suggestions are sometimes necessary to preserve another person’s dignity, the approach is not always recommended. It tends to create more misunderstanding than benefit, and sincere treatment remains the basic rule of human interaction.

Some abstract phrases cause considerable trouble. When we shop for groceries we often see food packages labeled “more delicious” or “tastes better.” At first glance there seems to be no problem; we buy the item happily, only to find upon tasting that it is ordinary or even inferior to other brands. The difficulty lies in the word “more.” “More delicious” or “tastes better” supplies no reference point. We do not know whether the product is better than the same brand’s previous version or better than a competing brand. If you confront the seller—“This isn’t better; it’s far worse than brand X”—the seller will reply: “We never said it was better than brand X; that was your own assumption.”

Abstract language allows different people to reach different understandings, and the understanding that arises in each mind is inevitably the one most convenient to that person. We believe our interpretation is correct, yet it often is not. During election campaigns, parties propose policies to win votes; some are pragmatic while others skillfully employ abstract concepts. In the area of medical welfare, one party once declared: “What kind of medical welfare system do you want? Exactly—that is what we will give you.” The statement sounds inspiring, suggesting a party deeply considerate of citizens. In reality the party has already prepared an escape hatch: if the system improves but falls short of expectations, the party can claim, “This is precisely what we promised; we did not lie.”

Therefore, whenever someone tells you “not bad” or “it’ll do,” observe the other person’s micro-expressions to determine whether the remark is affirmative or evasive.

In interrogations, however, an abstract style of questioning can be useful. For example: “We already know everything; you might as well confess.” Watch the suspect’s micro-expressions. If fear appears, it indicates the suspect did commit the crime.

The same technique works for drawing out information from others. When you say to a friend you suspect of hiding something, “I already know everything,” delivered with a confident expression, the friend will usually pause for a second. That pause signals surprise—the friend did not expect you to know. Once that expression appears, press further; the person is almost certainly concealing something. Follow up with “So you still won’t say it? How long do you plan to hide it?” This adds pressure few people can withstand unless they are exceptionally guarded.

Since the phrase “I already know everything” has been mentioned, the word “everything” itself deserves discussion. It is another fuzzy term, producing the same abstract effect as “always” or “never.” When someone says “I know everything,” does that mean all the facts or eighty percent? The distinction is hard to gauge. Likewise, after failing twice a person may claim “I always fail” or “I’ve never succeeded.” Teachers also favor such wording when evaluating students—“always late,” “never does homework,” “never studies properly”—even when the student was late only three times in a year, missed homework only a handful of times, and was merely occasionally distracted. People habitually exaggerate behaviors they dislike in order to elicit agreement and place reason on their side.

Some advertisements claim “everyone says it’s good.” How many people does “everyone” include—one hundred, two hundred, one thousand? The figure remains an ambiguous concept.

#### Opening: The Unfathomable Mind of the Big Boss

In this world, how many people will be completely honest with you?

Newspapers, television, and the internet hide writers behind their own industrial chains, producing content they want you to “believe is true” and then performing it for you.

You may spend every day switching between roles, yet still feel the helpless fog of uncertainty.

My goddess, I have poured every ounce of my best self into an hour-long torrent of conversation, yet you still show no sign of saying more. Why is it that every time I serve you food or pour you water, you smile politely, accept both, yet never let me touch your hand? Is it refined restraint, or simply no interest in me?

Any clear-headed, rational person can perform appropriate actions and conceal true intentions. Charging straight at a goddess’s wishes this way will cost you many opportunities.

Gaze, posture, and distance are all ways a goddess reveals her intentions. Study them carefully and you will capture valuable information.

The VIP across from me has heard our best product pitch, yet says nothing. What does that mean? His crossed leg sways slightly, his body leans back on the sofa, his eyes are half-closed in a smile, and he simply watches me in silence. Should I push harder now, or wait for him to speak first? Will speaking now backfire and make me look clumsy? Was he satisfied earlier?

Big clients are naturally stronger than you, at least on the surface, because they pay the bills. Professional credibility and respectful demeanor are basic skills every salesperson masters; these clients have seen them all. Shallow answers about interest or satisfaction will never come from their mouths.

The angle of the legs, the tension in the torso, and the amplitude and frequency of any swaying all carry special meaning.

I hear that another candidate for promotion has powerful connections and that the boss favors him. Yet the boss has always praised me, even patting my shoulder yesterday and saying I have great potential. Could the boss really “prefer” him? Watching him bow and scrape at yesterday’s meeting made me nauseous. Does the boss truly like that kind of sycophant?

The boss will not casually reveal preferences, especially during sensitive periods. Should one rely on the boss’s words or on rumors?

You can cut through the fog of language and judge closeness and interest through actual bodily reactions.

Of course, if the boss is the sort who practices nepotism, there is no need to invest effort in such a person or company.

After pitching an entrepreneurial plan to an investor, the other party seems to listen throughout yet never with full attention. Are they interested or convinced? The closing line “We’ll study it and get back to you” is the most torturous of all; the wait itself is agony. Will the plan now proceed smoothly?

People in urgent need usually overlook the listener’s reactions and simply recite what they prepared.

If, during communication, you can read the “patrons’” minds through small movements, you can seize the right timing and rhythm, deliver your pitch with precision, and greatly improve funding efficiency.

In short, when interests are at stake, no one will casually tell the truth. Language is the least reliable channel of communication. All real thoughts must be judged by oneself. Accurate judgment lets you seize the best opportunities ahead of everyone else. Unable to judge? Then leave it to fate.

Human behavior reveals many secrets. In social behavior we can clearly discern the motives behind these “made-up” actions; in emotional and physiological behavior we can, through the theoretical principles of micro-reaction (微反应), reverse-engineer psychological feelings and decision motives. When someone says “like,” “very good,” “support,” “believe me,” or “we’re like family,” do they truly mean it? Countless details across the entire body can reveal the truthfulness of their words.

At the company meeting, all senior executives listen with bated breath while stealing glances at the big boss’s every move.

The big boss is the boss’s boss. I am presenting; he is listening. If he is satisfied, the project becomes everyone’s gold mine.

Yet the big boss is British, the quintessential old-school gentleman, deep and impassive.

I possess one skill no one else knows: no tiny movement escapes my eyes, not even the slightest change in breathing.

I know he is listening attentively because his gaze follows the content. This matters greatly; if his eyes drift or lose focus, hope is already gone.

After listening, the big boss remains silent, his face expressionless.

A classic social display!

Seasoned veterans of the business world routinely wear this inscrutable look because they consciously hide their feelings. The British normally observe elaborate etiquette that puts people at ease. At a moment when everything feels life-or-death, however, that same restraint and self-control become a mask.

Still expressionless, the big boss glances at my boss as if seeking his opinion, then slowly shifts his gaze to my face. While calmly watching me, he taps the table lightly with his right pinky, ring finger, middle finger, and index finger in sequence. The motion is small and unhurried.

Seeing that finger-tapping, I relax considerably and quietly exhale. Only a positive, attentive state produces that rhythm and sequential finger movement.

A few seconds later he asks, “Young man, what do you think of your project plan?”

I smile inwardly. This is probably how senior leaders test people—by applying pressure to create deterrence. Most people cannot tell whether the pressure signals anger or appreciation, so anxiety rises. Having seen the “positive and attentive” attitude behind his restraint, I recognize the question as an expression of personal interest rather than doubt about the plan itself.

My own boss gives me an almost imperceptible nod.

Now it is my turn to take control of the room.

It's show time!

#### Othello Error

While detecting lies, people easily fall into the Brokaw trap and also commit the **Othello error**—mistaking truth for a lie. You may face this situation: someone leaks company secrets, senior leadership launches a full investigation, and everyone who had access is questioned, including you. Called into the office and facing several leaders and investigators, you feel nervous. Although you are telling the truth, fear of being wrongly accused makes you panic. If the investigators cannot distinguish whether your fear stems from lying or from worry about being framed, you may indeed be wrongly accused.

If you happen to have done something wrong earlier, the questioning naturally stirs up the guilt you already carry, which resembles the guilt of lying. Or, in your eagerness to defend yourself, you may become excited—an excitement that can be mistaken for the excitement of lying. Thus, whether telling the truth or lying, people experience many of the same emotions under suspicion and interrogation: disgust, surprise, fear, dejection, and so on.

The clearest illustration is *Othello*, which is why Ekman named this error the Othello error.

Othello suspects Desdemona of an affair with Cassio, questions her, and threatens to kill Cassio. Desdemona asks for Cassio to be summoned to confront the matter and clear her name, but Othello says he has already killed him. Having lost her only chance to defend herself, Desdemona feels fear, dejection, pain, and despair. Knowing she will not survive, she weeps and begs Othello not to kill her. Othello wrongly assumes her grief is over Cassio’s death and grows even angrier, more convinced of the affair.

Othello does not realize that an honest person facing sudden accusation can display the same fear, pain, and despair as a liar. Nor does he know that Desdemona weeps not for Cassio’s death but for her own mortal danger and for Othello’s distrust.

Othello mistakes truth for lies because he has already judged Desdemona guilty in his heart. Questioning with preconceptions means any reaction will be interpreted as concealment. Therefore, when detecting lies, one must discard preconceptions, avoid jumping to conclusions, and remain clear-headed and objective.

Even a person who is not naturally jealous or suspicious can commit the Othello error when confused; if others fan the flames, objectivity becomes even harder. We are told our partner had an intimate dinner with someone else. We already knew the two were close and worked well together. We then wonder why they were so in sync and conclude it must be because their relationship is improper. We answer our own question, treat it as evidence without verification, and become angry. Anger brings further emotions—disgust, sadness, despair—that block us from seeing the facts.

Another case: we already hold prejudice against someone because of past misconduct. When something bad happens, we automatically assume they did it. Such bias easily leads to the Othello error.

The best way to avoid the Othello error is to clarify the difference between the emotions of lying and the emotions of being suspected.

Distinguishing these emotions requires preparatory work: understand the person’s character so you know their usual manner and reduce bias; understand their emotional patterns so you can tell how they behave when lying versus when suspected. Emotional patterns are largely built on character.

Confident or arrogant people usually feel neither fear nor guilt when suspected. Timid people feel fear when suspected—the fear of being wrongly punished—but not anger or guilt. Someone who once did wrong and has long regretted it will, when suspected of something they did not do, feel the original guilt rekindled, yet not anger, fear, excitement, or pain. All these possibilities must be ruled out during lie detection.

Another crucial point: whether the person shows emotions similar to lying also depends on the relationship between the person and the lie detector. The following example illustrates this.

A father and son have an excellent relationship; the father has never wrongly accused or casually punished the son. The son therefore trusts his father deeply and knows he will not be framed. Consequently, when suspected, the son shows no fear, tension, or disappointment in front of his father because he believes his father will not wrong him.

If the father has wrongly accused the son more than once in the past, then even an honest son will feel fear when suspected—the fear of being unjustly punished again.

Another case: the son once made a mistake, lied, and destroyed his credibility with his father. Even if he did not commit the current act, he will still feel fear when suspected, afraid his father will no longer trust him.

If these emotions cannot be excluded, the lie detector easily produces miscarriages of justice.

Distinguishing the emotions of a liar from those of an honest person requires thorough investigation to learn how the person behaves when lying versus when suspected—a lengthy process. If the lie detector and the person enjoy a good relationship with no history of wrongful accusations, mutual trust runs deep. The detector will then know the person’s lying-emotion profile thoroughly, the person’s suspicion-emotion profile will be relatively pure, and the final judgment will be easier.

As the old saying goes, accurate lie-detection results require first understanding the person’s character, work style, and emotional patterns, eliminating bias, then combining four clues—micro-expressions, body language, slips of the tongue, and heated language—to reach a conclusion.

#### Keywords on Micro-expressions

Leaders are busy and cannot constantly watch employees to ensure they work diligently. How, then, can one tell whether a person is worth developing? A sudden test reveals who continues to work hard when the leader is absent and who remains loyal without supervision. Such a person is an ambitious, good employee worth cultivating.

In many companies, employees think the moment the boss leaves is the perfect time to relax. When the boss is present, they feel supervised; once the boss attends a meeting, travels abroad, or negotiates a deal, they treat it as the best chance to slack off. These employees work like schoolchildren who only study seriously when the teacher stands behind them and slack off the moment the teacher steps out. To truly know someone, remove the leader and supervision and observe whether they remain loyal to themselves.

In any boss’s eyes, loyalty matters even more than ability. Many bosses would rather have an employee of average talent who is highly loyal and trustworthy than a brilliant, capable person who constantly schemes for personal gain. Loyalty reflects noble character and basic professional ethics. An employee’s loyalty to the company shows most clearly when the boss is away.

A sales manager once recounted this incident:

He visited a client company to discuss the sale of a new mass-market printer model. The manufacturer planned large-scale advertising and offered generous margins to distributors. He decided to secure initial orders from reputable, well-connected dealers before the media campaign began.

When he arrived at a long-standing client, the boss happened to be out. When he mentioned the upcoming new model, the employee receiving him said coldly, “The boss isn’t here! We can’t decide anything.” He presented the promotional materials, explaining the product’s strong performance and quality plus the current discount for early orders. The employee refused to listen and simply repeated, “The boss isn’t here!”

He left, disappointed, and tried another company. The boss there was also absent, which discouraged him, yet he decided to try anyway. A newly hired female employee greeted him warmly. Instead of citing the boss’s absence, she offered to arrange delivery the next day and said the boss could finalize details upon return.

The outcome was clear. The first company’s employee lost an excellent opportunity because the boss was away; when they later requested stock, the discount had ended and profits shrank. After learning what happened, the boss fired the employee without hesitation. The second company, thanks to the female employee’s continued diligence in the boss’s absence, purchased the recommended product at the discounted price. Within a month they sold nearly 9,000 units and netted over 90,000 yuan. The female employee earned the boss’s recognition and was promoted to supervisor immediately upon joining the company.

In workplace rules, loyalty is indispensable. Albert Hubbard wrote in *A Message to Garcia*: “Strictly speaking, a little loyalty is worth a great deal of cleverness.” He even suggested that if you work for someone, do so in God’s name. Whether an employee treats their work loyally reflects their character.

An employee loyal to their work will strive regardless of whether the boss is present or whether anyone is watching. Employees who require the boss’s inspection and supervision always believe they work for the boss and shirk responsibility the moment the boss leaves. Such employees have low value to the company and are quickly eliminated by competition. They will never receive important assignments because they merely go through the motions rather than remain loyal to the work itself.

In *A Message to Garcia*, Lieutenant Rowan receives his superior’s order and carries it out with total commitment and no complaint. No one supervises him, yet he completes the task brilliantly. More than a hundred years later, people still remember him—not only because he executed the order without excuses but, more importantly, because of his loyalty to the mission.

Employees who remain loyal to their work whether the boss is present or absent are highly valued in any company. They are loyal to the enterprise, disregard personal gain, consider the bigger picture, fulfill their duties, and safeguard the company’s interests wholeheartedly. In contrast, employees who seize every chance to slack off or pursue personal gain ultimately face elimination.

If you are a boss and want to see your employees clearly, leave for a while and then return suddenly. Those who produce even better results in your absence deserve trust and promotion. Those who fail to complete their tasks deserve careful reconsideration; their presence hinders the company’s progress, and removing them early benefits the enterprise sooner.

#### Leaning the Body Backward Proves One Is Lying

Interpersonal relations researchers have observed that during face-to-face conversations, people establish different interaction distances based on their level of intimacy. With the closest individuals, the distance can shrink to 0.5 meters; between close friends, it is typically kept between 0.5 and 1.25 meters; and in public settings with strangers, people usually maintain a distance of 3 meters or more. This variation in spatial distance driven by psychological closeness is known in psychology as interpersonal distance.

If the other person wants to become better acquainted, their body will lean forward involuntarily to reduce the interpersonal distance; if they wish to keep their distance, they will lean backward to maintain a relatively greater separation. The size of the interpersonal distance reflects the closeness of the relationship.

A related phenomenon is personal space. Psychologists note that when people feel insecure, they instinctively create distance from others, carving out their own psychological territory.

FBI agent Grover observed during investigations of terrorists that the more vigilant the individual, the stronger the aversion to anyone entering their personal space. People often use objects to claim surrounding areas and build a protective barrier around themselves.

Many times you will notice that people prefer to sit alone in corners; if someone asks to sit beside you, you may feel uneasy. Leaning forward can be interpreted as opening up. The other person trusts you, so they expand their personal psychological space and shorten the distance between you. With someone they dislike, they will increase the distance and retreat as much as possible into their own “safe space.”

Grover tells us that if a person likes you, they are unlikely to deceive you. Whether the body leans forward or backward reveals the place you occupy in that person’s mind. Psychologists point out that when people express emotion through body language, they are often unaware of it. Body language is therefore one of the most authentic expressions of feeling and carries high credibility.

Psychologists have hypothesized that when people tell the truth, their bodies lean forward unconsciously in an attempt to draw closer, whereas when they lie, their bodies lean backward to maintain distance. Tests of this hypothesis showed that subjects adjusted their distance according to whether they were stating a lie or the truth. Those who knew they were recounting fabricated information leaned backward.

Experts have found that lying is accompanied by fear, prompting people to protect themselves unconsciously and avoid excessive closeness. Only by keeping greater distance can they remind their brains to construct a convincing falsehood.

Grover notes that people who like you are more willing to listen and lean forward to hear better. Therefore, when assessing familiarity between two people, first examine the spatial distance between them, then observe their listening posture.

We often notice that close individuals speak softly during conversation, sometimes so quietly that only the other person can hear. Someone friendly will move closer to catch your words; the simplest way to do so is to shift the body nearer. Conversely, someone who dislikes you will resist their words and may even wish to cover their ears to block the sound. Because such an exaggerated gesture is impractical, they settle for a slight backward tilt to create distance.

When a person shows liking, the underlying message is interest. People naturally draw closer to what interests them. Leaning forward signals that the individual has a certain interest in you.
