Researchers studying human behavior have found that infants’ bodies move toward objects that interest them. If a baby likes something, it will try every means to approach and obtain it; if it dislikes something, it will turn its head or cry in protest. From a very young age, our bodies react to what we like or dislike.

FBI agents observe that adults gradually become more polished and no longer display strong physical reactions to likes or dislikes. Instead they exercise reasonable control, leaving only subconscious movements such as leaning forward or backward or unconsciously averting the gaze.

#### People Who Cover Their Mouths While Speaking May Be Lying

Covering the mouth while speaking is a gesture that signals surprise, doubt, tension, deception, or lack of confidence. When someone feels regret or remorse for what they have said, they may also cover their mouth as if trying to stop the words from emerging. FBI experts generally interpret this gesture as an attempt to conceal the truth or fabricate a lie.

Today is the day Ruoer arrives at the FBI for an interview. Having passed the written test, he appears excited yet nervous. The interviewer notices on his résumé that he claims special-forces experience and asks what duties and training he handled. In reality Ruoer never served in special forces, but a friend who did frequently described his experiences and training to Ruoer and sometimes invited him to train together. Ruoer decided the experience would help his FBI application, so he included it.

Ruoer had prepared answers in advance, so when the question arose he recited them fluently. Nevertheless he was not hired. Although his verbal account was smooth, his body language showed anomalies that led the interviewer to suspect the special-forces claim was fabricated. Subsequent verification with the unit listed on the résumé confirmed that Ruoer had lied.

How did the interviewer detect the discrepancy in just over ten minutes?

Normally, people naturally add gestures to emphasize their words. We may tap a finger or hand on the table to stress a point, widen our eyes or raise our eyebrows to strengthen tone, or, when excited, rise onto tiptoes if standing or repeatedly lift and lower the knees or slap them if seated.

Liars, however, focus so intently on concealing the truth that their attempts to emphasize points appear unnatural or delayed. Another characteristic is that liars tend to stress trivial details rather than the main facts.

In the case above, Ruoer’s body language matched the normal pattern at the start of the interview, but changed noticeably when he discussed the “special forces” experience.

When asked whether he had served in special forces, Ruoer’s body language directly contradicted his words: although he answered “yes,” his head shook slightly, as if saying “I did not.” When pressed for details, he remained unnaturally calm, showing none of the excitement or animation that usually accompanies genuine recollection. His account stayed general and omitted many important particulars. Most telling, throughout the entire discussion he repeatedly covered his mouth with his hand—an action the interviewer recognized as an attempt to hide the lie or its traces.

Of course, real life is complex, and not every hand-to-mouth gesture signals lying. A “field manual” left by an American intelligence officer lists negotiation techniques, one of which advises covering the mouth during conversation to prevent lip-reading and protect sensitive information.

Similarly, people who wish to keep their conversation private often speak with a hand cupped over the mouth. If someone sits with elbows on the table and both hands clasped over the mouth, the unspoken message is “I do not want you to hear me.” The posture may persist while listening until the person decides it is safe to lower the hands.

Before drawing conclusions, therefore, consider whether the gesture has appeared before and under what circumstances. If it has not, consider other possibilities: recent dental work, a comment about bad breath, or simple self-consciousness. Always weigh alternative explanations.

#### The Story of Zhang Guoqiang

Zhang Guoqiang was the director of Taihang Chemical Fiber Materials Factory, a township enterprise producing industrial fiber. Outdated equipment, capital shortages, and outstanding debts had brought the factory to the brink of bankruptcy. Zhang was deeply troubled and unsure of the way forward.

One day he received a letter from a Shanghai chemical-fiber company proposing a joint venture to produce industrial fiber. The Shanghai side would invest two million yuan to build a production line, and profits would be shared according to the factory’s existing output.

Such good fortune? Zhang was delighted, yet he hesitated. With only a few old machines producing one or two hundred tons a year, he worried the profit split would be unfavorable. After much thought he decided to secure the large sum first and worry about the rest later.

The next day he wrote back, exaggerating that the factory employed more than two hundred workers and generated tens of millions in output value. He demanded the larger share of profits and operational control. A reply soon arrived agreeing in principle but stating that representatives would visit to inspect and negotiate.

Zhang devised a plan. He telephoned the municipal transport team and instructed the factory office director to borrow several old machines and dozens of workers from the municipal machinery plant. Preparations were quickly completed.

A few days later, engineer Xiao Wang from the Shanghai company arrived. Seeing that the visitor was a man in his twenties, Zhang relaxed.

The factory grounds looked clean, the workshops hummed with machinery, and trucks moved busily in and out. Zhang pointed to two trucks parked before the warehouse and said, “Those belong to out-of-town customers; some have been waiting several days.”

Xiao Wang nodded appreciatively and asked, “What is your annual output?”

“Around a thousand tons, but demand still exceeds supply. The only obstacle to expansion is lack of funds.” Zhang sighed and shook his head. “If your company could help, the prospects would be excellent.”

Xiao Wang nodded. “Funding can be discussed; cooperation should be mutually beneficial. But the figures you provide must be accurate.”

“Of course. Since we are partnering, credibility comes first.”

Chatting amiably, they drove toward the administrative offices. Suddenly Xiao Wang told the driver, “Excuse me, please stop. I need to use the restroom.”

Zhang saw that the nearest facility was a small toilet beside the boiler room and said dismissively, “That one is unsanitary. Let’s go farther ahead.”

“No need. I have a bit of stomach trouble and can’t wait. It will do; I’m not an honored guest.” Xiao Wang opened the door and stepped out.

Moments later he returned. As they reached the offices, Zhang handed over a report. “This is the first-half production statistic. At this rate we should exceed 1,200 tons this year.”

Xiao Wang took the report, tapped numbers into a calculator, then looked up. “Director Li, this cannot be right. I estimate your maximum annual output is 200 tons.”

Zhang was stunned. “Two hundred tons? On what basis?”

“On this basis.” Xiao Wang pointed to the calculator. “While I was at the restroom I measured your chimney. Its diameter is 1.5 meters, meaning the heat it generates daily can support only forty workers. Even at five tons per worker, that yields only 200 tons a year.”

Zhang looked embarrassed. He had not expected the young man to be so astute. Before he could respond, Xiao Wang stood and said gravely, “Supporting township enterprises is our company’s responsibility, but we will not cooperate with anyone who falsifies information. Goodbye.”

Xiao Wang walked out, leaving Zhang frozen in his chair, filled with regret. A person who resorts to deception will never earn others’ trust. Even if such a person succeeds temporarily in business, the eventual outcome is self-inflicted harm.

When a person is frustrated and unsuccessful, conscience reviews and directs their actions; afterward it evaluates the results, producing satisfaction or self-reproach, pleasure or shame. Only by upholding principles in adversity does one demonstrate a true moral底线. Such people deserve our respect.

#### Scratching the Neck Signals Duplicity

Micro-expression keywords: The distance between the neck and ears is short; scratching the ears indicates lying. Psychologists have found that scratching the neck likewise serves to relax emotions. In other words, when people unconsciously scratch their necks, they are very likely lying.

If, during bargaining, a shopkeeper says, “This is truly the lowest price; I cannot go lower,” while scratching the neck, do not believe the claim. The gesture has already revealed the lie. In fact, considerable profit remains, and you can press harder.

Psychologists have discovered that when lying, people feel tension and their brains unconsciously direct the hands to touch the body, providing self-protection and emotional relief. These movements include clenching the fists, touching the nose, touching the ears, and scratching the neck.

People usually scratch the side of the neck or the area below the earlobe with the index finger; women’s movements are smaller and typically involve covering the junction of neck and chest—an area anatomically called the “suprasternal notch.”

Former FBI counterintelligence agent Joe Navarro once interviewed the mother of an armed fugitive. Although visibly nervous, she answered questions smoothly.

“Is your son at home?” When Navarro asked this, she placed her hand on the suprasternal notch and replied, “No.” Navarro continued with other questions, then suddenly asked, “Is it possible he hid inside while you were out?” She again put her hand in the same place and said she did not know.

Recognizing the gesture, Navarro concluded she was lying. Before leaving he asked once more, “Are you certain he is not here?” She placed her hand on the notch a third time and again denied it. Navarro obtained a search warrant and found the son in a hidden room.

The mother lied three times and three times touched her neck; her body language betrayed her son’s presence.

When someone says “I completely understand how you feel” while scratching the neck with the index finger five or more times, we can conclude the statement is false.

After her colleague resigned, Liang Yajie had been doing two people’s work and was constantly exhausted. After two months she could bear it no longer and complained to her supervisor, requesting either a raise or a new hire. The supervisor appeared sympathetic, scratched his neck, and said, “The company sees everything you have done and acknowledges the volume of your work. I will discuss a solution with senior management.” Reassured, Liang continued working double duty.

Months passed without resolution. Liang felt frustrated that the supervisor had not kept his word. Had she understood what neck-scratching meant, she would not have trusted him so readily and would have pressed for action. The supervisor’s hand on his neck revealed his true position: “We understand your feelings, but the company has no current hiring plan.”

In daily life, if someone repeatedly scratches the neck while speaking, do not trust their words lightly. The sensible course is to avoid befriending such duplicitous individuals, for they will never deal with you sincerely.

#### Liars Make Extra Movements Unconsciously

Micro-expression keywords

The subconscious is not controlled by our conscious mind, yet its influence cannot be ignored. When people lie, the subconscious acts first, followed by conscious control. Consequently, even the most skilled liars produce superfluous small movements that give them away.

A highly skilled liar who manages to conceal every micro-movement might appear flawless. The answer is no.

Any individual, no matter how well trained, remains subject to subconscious impulses and will reveal themselves.

#### 11.5 How to Break a Well-Designed Lie?

Most premeditated offenders are deliberate actors. The more meticulous among them will, after committing the crime, eliminate evidence, coordinate with accomplices, and prepare every line of counter-investigation they can devise. Of course, these are only the “everything” they themselves believe they have covered.

Although objective perfection is impossible, such pre-planned countermeasures and preemptive moves do create substantial difficulties for investigators. Yet the alternating advance of law and crime remains the core driver that continually raises the level of civilization in human society.

Returning to the interrogation setting, let us examine the suspect’s lies.

If a suspect has already prepared a highly detailed strategy—both in words and in demeanor—is it still possible to expose the lie?

The answer is yes, for two strongly supportive reasons.

The first reason is that judicial investigation begins with the collection of partial evidence and leads. With evidence or leads already in hand, certain facts cannot be concealed by lies. Intelligent suspects will not attempt outright denial; their most common tactic is to rationalize, in logical terms, the facts that the evidence or leads point to.

The second reason is that, even for the most meticulous mind, rationalization cannot be supported by the same thorough, detailed information that would sustain a chain of true logic. As the saying goes, one lie requires a thousand more to maintain. Every piece of information in a case is connected to every other piece from multiple angles; altering any single element triggers a cascade of logical contradictions.

A everyday example may help illustrate the point.

Suppose someone says, “I love eating beef.”

We can test the statement by probing the logical chain that would normally follow:

- Question 1: “Why do you love eating beef?”
- Answer 1: “Because beef is high in protein.”
- Question 2: “Is beef higher in protein than chicken?”
- Answer 2: “That is what the sources I have read say.”
- Question 3: “Which sources?”
- Answer 3: “……”

Each additional layer of the logical chain increases the respondent’s cognitive load exponentially. Failure to answer any single layer does not by itself prove a lie—truthful people may also respond impatiently with “Mind your own business!” Yet the more effort a person invests in appearing truthful, the more complex the reactions become; this conclusion is backed by extensive evidence.

Therefore, in criminal investigation and interrogation, even when a suspect believes every preparation has been made, the preparation can never be objectively complete. Someone who can ready three layers of explanation in advance is already exceptionally shrewd; such individuals are rare. Most people prepare only a single layer of evasion.

The more elaborate the prepared responses, the greater the mental pressure during actual questioning. The following experiment demonstrates the effect.

**Experimental Case**

**Basic Model of Lying**

**Procedure**:

Participants perform two rounds of mental arithmetic, each consisting of ten addition problems using numbers no larger than ten. Each round is recorded separately for later comparison of reactions.

**Rules**:

In the first round, participants must give the correct answers.

In the second round, participants must give incorrect answers, subject to two constraints:

1. The answer must remain within the integer interval [1, 10]. For example, when asked “1 + 1,” the answer 2345 is invalid.
2. The answer may not reuse any number appearing in the problem itself. For example, when asked “2 + 3,” neither 2 nor 3 is acceptable.

A simple set of problems may be used, such as:

1+1=? 1+2=? 1+3=? 1+4=? 1+5=?  
1+6=? 1+7=? 1+8=? 1+9=? 2+2=?

The specific numbers and order may be randomized, provided the correct result falls within [1, 10].

#### 11.1 What Is Lying

One of the most striking applications of psychological-stress micro-reactions is lie detection.

Many young people develop a strong interest in “micro-expressions,” “behavioral science,” and “body language” because television dramas and programs portray these techniques as capable of exposing anyone’s lies. Viewers who do not reflect carefully often forget the analytical process and remember only a list of supposed rules, such as:

1. Eyes looking left indicate recall; eyes looking right indicate fabrication.
2. A man’s nose contains erectile tissue; touching the nose signals concealment.
3. Responding with contempt to a question means the question hit the mark.
4. Nodding first and then shaking the head is classic equivocation.
5. A single shoulder shrug signals insufficient confidence and therefore lying.
6. Botox-injected faces do not move, so micro-expressions cannot be analyzed.
7. Finger direction differing from eye direction indicates lying.
8. Folded arms indicate lying.
9. Two consecutive lip curls indicate lying.
10. A sudden increase in blinking indicates lying.

Unfortunately, these “standards” that so many enjoy are all incorrect.

Yes, all of them. I state this with full responsibility: they are wrong.

They are compilations made by viewers and netizens, often derived from Chinese subtitles of the American series *Lie to Me*. When Chinese dramas later adopted similar tropes, an uneven mixture of “miraculous techniques” appeared in books and online articles.

The more a book promises a single move that “defeats the enemy,” the more likely it is to be an irresponsible cut-and-paste job whose author never understood the material yet managed to produce hundreds of thousands of words through copying. Such books can be browsed, smiled at, and returned to the shelf.

“Can micro-reactions detect lies?”

“Yes.”

“Then why are everyone else’s methods wrong and only yours right?”

“Because those standards are mindless; using them leads to mistakes, and the mistakes harm the user.”

“Why are they mindless?”

“Do they have any mind? Let me ask: what is lying?”

Faced with this direct question, one-sentence formulas fall silent.

For example, why should “finger direction differing from eye direction” prove lying? Everyone knows the Clinton case—an apparently living example. Yet that single instance does not withstand scrutiny; there is also footage of Clinton himself displaying the same mismatch while telling the truth, as well as numerous other truthful speakers who exhibit the same behavior. How can one movement pattern be directly equated with lying?

Anyone willing to draw such a conclusion probably does not even know what the process of lying entails.

The most common definition of lying is “a deliberate act intended to mislead another, whose purpose has not been disclosed in advance and which the other party has not explicitly requested.”

Although this definition is clear, complete, and accurate, it remains somewhat abstract and invites both oversight and quibbling. Under this wording, a magic performance could count as lying, and so could the staged awkward situations in the “Mirror House” segment of a certain satellite-television variety show. The original scholars would likely be surprised by such extensions.

We therefore identify the core feature of lying as: expression contradicts cognition.

In plainer terms: if a person is thinking A but saying B, that person is lying.

Once this feature is clearly stated, it becomes obvious that determining whether someone is lying requires at least two pieces of information: what the person “thinks” and what the person “expresses” (usually says). The two must then be compared.

#### Sincerity or Courtesy: Look at His Expression

The American film *He’s Just Not That Into You* opens with an amusing scene: girls from every background—whether African villagers or New York professionals, whether middle-aged women or slender teenagers—ask their friends the same questions: “He said he would call; why hasn’t he?” “He said he would come see me; why hasn’t he?” Their friends reply with reassuring excuses: “He still likes you; he’s just busy right now.” “He’s very introverted.”

These girls prefer to invent kind explanations rather than analyze objectively whether the other person’s words are sincere or merely polite, and they repeatedly waste time and miss opportunities. The film’s ending reminds them that a man who truly wants to pursue a relationship will find a way to contact them—by phone, MSN, or any other means. Yet a girl need not remain passive; observing and eliciting more information is also legitimate.

FBI agents are experts at this task. During interviews they must accurately gauge the interviewee’s level of interest in order to control the pace of the conversation.

When an interviewee looks down, turns the face away, or presses the lips together, agents know interest has been lost and further talk will yield nothing useful. Turning the face signals a desire to leave; pressed lips signal unwillingness to speak.

A girl who sees these expressions in someone she likes should simply say goodbye, regardless of earlier enthusiastic promises to “definitely get in touch.” She should also note that if the person says “I’ll call you in a couple of days” while repeatedly rubbing the nose, the gesture clearly indicates inner rejection.

When an interviewee raises the chin, relaxes the mouth, and shows a hint of teeth, agents know the person is not entirely closed off and has accepted the topic to some degree.

A girl who observes these expressions should realize the conversation will be long; the slightly lifted chin shows the other person’s mind has opened. She should proceed gradually rather than rush, steering the talk toward the information she wants.

Eye contact also reveals acceptance. Mutual gaze lasting five seconds or longer indicates a receptive attitude. If the goal is to learn the other person’s real thoughts, this moment should not be missed.

Eye contact is not the only indicator. Additional signs include:

- Frequent incidental physical contact—light touches to the arm, back, or shoulder show the person regards you as a genuine friend.
- Head tilt—especially noticeable between romantic partners; a tender gaze naturally accompanied by a head inclined toward the other person is hard to resist.

In short, whether to take the initiative or wait depends less on words than on unconscious movements. Words can mislead; movements reliably indicate the correct response.

#### Touching the Ears Indicates Interest in the Topic

FBI agent Laura was assigned to investigate whether an insurance company had established a front operation abroad. Company policy required every probationary employee to sell a set amount of insurance within one month to become permanent.

One day a middle-aged couple visited. Laura greeted them warmly and presented policies suitable for their age group. The couple showed little interest, leading Laura to wonder whether they had come to buy insurance or merely to gather information. When she mentioned a family policy, however, one of them casually touched an ear. Laura concluded they were interested in family coverage.

To test the inference she asked, “Are you looking for family-combined insurance?” The couple looked surprised but answered seriously, “Yes, because we have children to consider.”

Laura then focused on family policies, explained the various family-based options in detail, and quickly found a product the couple liked. She completed the sale and secured her permanent position.

American marketing consultant Mike Stark once remarked, “If the other person touches an ear, it is a signal of interest.” When someone pulls an earlobe, touches an ear, or brushes the hair near the ear or the back of the head while you are speaking, the gesture shows interest in continuing the conversation. This matches the Japanese saying “pull the ears to hear better.”

The unconscious movement of touching the ears to signal a desire to keep listening is easy to notice. People who say “I’m very interested in this topic” or “Really? I’ve never heard that before” often accompany the words with an ear touch. Even someone who rarely voices opinions will reveal growing interest through this gesture.

Therefore, during conversation it is useful to identify the other person’s “sensitive words” and continue on those topics; both parties benefit. Normally, someone uninterested in the topic will not touch an ear.

Conversely, if the person folds the entire pinna forward to cover the ear canal, the gesture means “Stop talking; I’ve heard enough.” Children sometimes cover their ears with both hands when parents argue outside the room; adults do something similar when they no longer wish to listen. If a speaker is animated while the listener inserts a finger into the ear canal as if cleaning it, the listener is signaling disdain. When appropriate, politely ask whether the listener has any comment; otherwise, change the subject.

In any conversation, observe whether the other person is touching the ears or attempting to end the topic. When both hands hover around the ears, it is time to proceed with caution.

#### Pulling at the Collar May Indicate Irritation or Lying

In movies we often see this scene: when the male protagonist watches his beloved girl fall into another man’s arms, he tugs hard at his own collar and undoes the first button of his shirt. Even if wearing a tie, he impatiently loosens it. These gestures perfectly convey the protagonist’s agitation and unease. The actions arise mainly because irritation generates intense heat, prompting him to yank the collar away from his neck so cooler air can enter his clothes.

In reality, men tug at their collars for reasons beyond irritation.

Jones has been troubled by her new boyfriend. She wants to know whether he had a deeply loved girlfriend before her. So the petty-minded woman keeps trying to probe: “Was your ex pretty?” “Was she gentle?”…

Each time Jones raises these questions, her boyfriend grows visibly restless, yet he cleverly replies, “I had an ex-girlfriend? That’s impossible.” While saying this, he unconsciously tugs at his collar. Seeing the gesture, Jones realizes he is lying; the evasive words further reveal his guilt. Instead of losing her temper, she smiles and says, “I hope we can be open with each other. You know I’m not a petty person…”

Research shows that when people lie, the sensitive nerves in the neck produce an itchy sensation, so they unconsciously rub or scratch to relieve the discomfort.

Objectively, men tug at collars more often than women because men usually wear suits and shirts, while women’s clothing varies and some styles lack collars. When a woman lies, she is more likely to change the subject or turn her face away. For women who value poise, tugging at a collar appears too masculine. Therefore, the gesture alone cannot confirm that someone is lying.

The accompanying facial expressions are more important. If the person is truly lying, subtle facial changes will appear while tugging the collar—for example, avoiding direct eye contact. We usually determine whether someone is lying by noting both the evasive glance and the unconscious collar tug.

People who lie may also display an uneasy smile because their words do not match their feelings. A genuine smile is an unconscious facial movement not directly controlled by the brain; it results from the autonomous action of facial muscles and produces fine lines around the eyes. A false smile occurs when the brain issues a command to smile and consciously moves the facial muscles, making the expression look unnatural. An insincere smile lifts only the corners of the mouth, so fine lines appear only around the lips.

Therefore, when we cannot tell whether an answer is an unconscious reaction or mere irritation, we can do as Jones did. Unable to decide whether her boyfriend’s repeated collar tugs meant he feared his lie would be exposed, she asked with a sincere smile, “Is something bothering you? I hope we can be open with each other,” or “What did you just say? Could you repeat it?” to draw out his true thoughts.

#### People Who Repeatedly Adjust Their Cuffs Are Very Uneasy

A sexual scandal involving a U.S. celebrity drew intense media attention, and FBI agents played a key role in solving the case.

Agents obtained the perpetrator’s DNA from the assaulted hotel maid’s clothing. The next day, after learning that the DNA matched the celebrity, they brought him to the FBI. At first the celebrity assumed the agents had no evidence of forced sexual activity and insisted the encounter had been consensual. As case details emerged and witnesses appeared one after another, agents noticed that although he never admitted to coercion, he began to waver internally. This convinced them that the maid’s account was not fabricated.

How did the agents detect this psychological shift? World-renowned body-language expert Joe Navarro states, “Approximately 60 to 80 percent of human communication occurs through nonverbal behavior. Reading nonverbal cues is a core part of FBI interrogation work. In this case, as evidence of sexual assault mounted, agents observed that during interviews the celebrity adjusted his cuffs or fiddled with his watch with increasing frequency—an unmistakable sign of internal wavering.”

Psychologists have confirmed through experiments that fiddling with cuffs, cuff buttons, or a watch is an instinctive defensive gesture indicating extreme nervousness. Women who repeatedly reposition a handbag on their arm display a similar sign of unease.

Experienced agents used this cue as a breakthrough, pressing the celebrity each time he adjusted his cuffs or played with his watch, extracting numerous facts and ultimately establishing his guilt on the sexual-assault charge.

Under normal circumstances, cuff-fiddling reveals inner instability and reduces others’ trust. For information-gathering, however, the moment is highly advantageous because psychological defenses are most vulnerable then.

In social settings, habitual cuff-fiddlers often give opponents openings. In the workplace, such individuals remain at the bottom of the hierarchy, assigned trivial tasks because their unease leaks out. The same holds in conversation: it is a game of strategy; whoever first reveals a weakness loses earliest.

Experts therefore advise that while exploiting another person’s unease to extract information, one should minimize similar gestures oneself. Especially when speaking with unfamiliar people or in public, avoid the behavior.

Control does not mean concealment. Placing the arms under the table is not foolproof; it too signals weakness. Only when absolutely necessary should arms go under the table to adjust sleeves or handle a watch, and they should return to the tabletop immediately afterward. If tension arises and one wishes to hide it, adjust breathing or take a sip of water instead.

Remember: never let others perceive you as unconfident or insignificant. Raise your own value and maintain a superior posture that tells them, “I am the best.”

#### Recounting in Reverse Makes Lies Fall Apart

An American drama contains this amusing scene: after waiting a long time, the protagonist finally finds a parking spot. Just as he begins to back in, another car speeds up and steals the space. The protagonist confronts the driver: “Didn’t you see I’d been waiting for this spot?” The driver nods, then shakes his head repeatedly and says innocently, “No, I was waiting too.” The protagonist replies seriously, “You’re lying. You just performed a classic lying gesture—nodding slightly before shaking your head to say no.”

That single inadvertent nod exposed the driver’s secret. Lies are not impregnable; careful observation easily reveals a person’s true thoughts through small, unconscious movements.

Everyone lies daily. One noted professor has pointed out that of every ten people we interact with each day, five are lying. Even the kindest person lies at least twice a day on average. Most lies aim to hide something or prevent others from reading one’s mind, so people employ various cover-ups. This pattern is especially evident during interrogations.

FBI agent Jack questioned a suspect: “What were you doing on the day of the incident?” The suspect answered fluently: “At eight I went to the convenience store, at ten I was on my way to work, at twelve I was eating a work meal…” The timeline seemed to prove he had not been at the crime scene. Jack pressed on: “Could you repeat what you just said, but in reverse chronological order?” After a long pause the suspect stammered, “At five in the afternoon, I… I was…” Clearly the suspect could not recount his actions backward. Jack immediately recognized the lie.

People who plan to lie prepare fluent answers in advance, yet because they did not actually experience the events, those details never enter deep memory. Asking them to recount events in reverse order exposes the fabrication. The next time you face a skilled liar, pretend you did not catch part of the story, pick several time points, and ask for a fresh description. If the person cannot answer smoothly, the lie becomes obvious.

The following signs during conversation also indicate lying:
- Speech is faster and smoother than usual, showing prior preparation.
- Answers are evasive and the mouth moves while the hands remain still.
- Long pauses, frequent hesitation, rigid posture, and minimal body movement.
- Eyes either avoid contact or pupils are larger than usual.
- Introverted individuals produce markedly less fluent speech when lying.

In short, no matter how sophisticated the technique, lies leave traces. Even when words are seamless, body language betrays the truth. Once we see through a lie, we gain a decisive psychological advantage; knowing the other person’s real intentions frees us from being controlled. In business negotiations especially, mastering this skill allows us to “take the initiative.”

#### The Harm of Coveting Ill-Gotten Gains

Many people cannot endure poverty and, desperate to change their circumstances, take reckless risks for “unworthy gains.” They accept bribes to bend rules at work, pocket found items, or resort to theft, robbery, or fraud. Such individuals ultimately destroy themselves for the sake of ill-gotten wealth. They are unreliable; when faced with large temptations, self-interest overrides integrity and prompts further misconduct.

A website once carried this report:

A lottery-shop owner, tempted by a five-million-yuan winning ticket, lied to the ticket holder that it had not won, intending to claim the prize himself. He even enlisted a couple to help collect the jackpot.

The ticket holder, of course, remembered the numbers, and the winning information appeared in newspapers and on television. The owner’s scheme backfired. By fraudulently obtaining property of enormous value, he committed the crime of fraud and received a twelve-year prison sentence—an outcome entirely of his own making.

His accomplices were also convicted of concealing criminal proceeds and received corresponding penalties.

A person’s greed is terrifying. If such an individual is in our circle, we inhabit an unsafe environment. By observing how someone behaves when poor, we can gauge character and decide whether to entrust them with anything important.

The old saying warns, “Do not stretch out your hand; if you do, it will be caught.” Wealth exists in many forms, but it must be earned through honest labor; no dishonorable method can make it truly ours. Although we may be poor, our spirit need not be. We must firmly reject anything that does not belong to us. Even if a dishonest act succeeds temporarily, the gain will eventually be lost, and trust in that person will be permanently destroyed.

When choosing or entrusting someone, examine how they acted in poverty. Anyone who covets ill-gotten gains will become a “landmine” buried beside us; constant vigilance will be required, and an explosion may occur at any moment over “unworthy gains.”

In poverty everyone hopes for financial help and a comfortable life. Such hopes cannot be realized by grasping at ill-gotten gains; what is not ours cannot be forced. Some people, even when poor, disdain money that arrives unearned and uphold their integrity. As Tao Yuanming wrote, they “will not bend at the waist for five bushels of rice.” They rely solely on their own efforts. Only such people can truly achieve great things and are worthy of friendship and trust. With them, we can entrust anything at any time.

#### People Who Scratch Their Necks Are Saying One Thing and Meaning Another

Pete, a veteran employee at a company, had repeatedly asked his supervisor for a promotion and raise without success. One gloomy day he invited his FBI-agent friend Big to a bar. After a few drinks he recounted his frustrations.

Big laughed, clapped Pete on the shoulder, and said loudly, “Buddy, don’t worry. I had the same problem with the supervisor, and he gave me the same runaround. But a stubborn guy like me doesn’t let an old fox off that easily. Let me tell you what happened.”

“A few months ago I went to the supervisor and clearly raised the salary issue, because my experience and ability far exceed my current pay. The supervisor just smiled, scratched his neck, and brushed me off, saying the bureau had considered my compensation, valued my work, but believed I still had room to grow. Besides, I’d been there less time than many colleagues, so my salary was already reasonable.”

“As soon as I heard that, I knew he intended to reject me. So I proposed that he assign me the current ‘terrorist attack’ case that was troubling him. If I handled it well, I would get the raise; if not, my salary would stay the same. While I spoke, I noticed the supervisor’s hand move from his neck to his chin. I immediately realized he had agreed. As you know, that was the case for which I later received commendation.”

Pete could not help admiring his old friend, yet he asked, “How did you spot the supervisor’s intention so quickly and adjust your strategy?”

“Experts discovered long ago that when people feel uncertain or uneasy they unconsciously scratch their necks—usually with the index finger on the side of the neck or the area below the earlobe, roughly five times,” Big replied.

Big’s remark reminded Pete that his own supervisor had indeed scratched his neck during their conversations. At the time Pete had dismissed it as a habit; now he understood the gesture signaled reservation—hence the repeated requests that never received a positive answer.

Big continued, “Opposition during conversation is nothing to fear. When facing ‘doubtful looks’ and ‘duplicitous attitudes,’ the key is to respond actively. Once I identify these signs, I simply change my approach so that doubt and negation turn first into thought and then into agreement.”

These conversational techniques apply beyond promotions and raises. When offering suggestions to a leader, adding constructive ideas increases acceptance. When discussing an issue with colleagues, citing facts, figures, and authoritative reports strengthens one’s position. The most effective way to convert doubt into agreement, however, is to demonstrate courage and resolve through action.

#### Brokaw Trap

Tom Brokaw is a well-known anchor for NBC. He had excellent experience spotting lies on the program *Meet the Press*. He said, “Most of the clues I get are verbal rather than physical. When I look for signs of lying, I do not watch the other person’s face; instead I focus on answers that make no sense or on evasive remarks that sound plausible.” Paul Ekman endorsed this view, noting that Brokaw’s experience has a certain validity in the process of lie detection.

Liars often talk nonstop to cover up flaws and reduce loopholes, or they may stammer and deflect because of guilt. These behaviors can serve as clues. However, Paul Ekman points out that not everyone fits this pattern. Brokaw overlooked individual differences. Some people are articulate in private but become tongue-tied when facing an audience or a camera due to nervousness; someone who is already inarticulate will appear even more awkward in public. Ekman calls this situation the **Brokaw Trap**.

To avoid the trap, individual differences must be taken into account by observing a person’s usual behavioral habits. Comparing the person’s baseline state with their state after suspicion arises yields more accurate results. If someone normally displays few fidgety movements but shows an increase when suspected, this indicates inner tension and unease, suggesting they have not told the whole truth. Without prior knowledge of the individual, however, judging them as a liar solely on the basis of fidgety movements observed during a first meeting is arbitrary.

Consider the classic poker example. One player coughs loudly at critical moments. The other players, except his partner, believe they have discovered the signal and feel secretly pleased. At the final hand they raise the stakes, expecting a big win. The player coughs again at the decisive moment. Believing their chance has arrived, the others lose heavily. The player had been bluffing from the start to mislead opponents; the final cough was the real signal.

During a first meeting, take enough time to distinguish a “decoy cough” from a “real signal cough.” Never assume you have an opening the moment you hear a cough.

Everyone presents differently and feels differently during a first encounter. Some people become more reserved than usual in order to make a good impression, their every movement stiff and formal. Others appear nervous with strangers, stumbling over words, losing logical coherence, and fidgeting. In either case the person’s normal habits remain hidden, making comparison impossible and preventing any reliable judgment about whether they are lying.

Therefore, to detect lies it is best to arrange several meetings so the relationship becomes closer and the other person’s everyday behavioral and emotional patterns can be observed.

This is where micro-expressions (微反应) become especially important. Because certain expressions cannot be fully suppressed, they may leak out even on first meeting. Yet one issue cannot be ignored: the emotional source behind the micro-expression. Without identifying that source, the expression offers little help in exposing a lie. Combining micro-expressions with three additional lie clues—body language, slips of the tongue, and heated language—makes the judgment more precise.

#### 11.1.2 Determination of Lies

If the content expressed contradicts the person’s cognition, the individual can be judged to be lying.

Lying falls into two categories. One is the concealment of true information—“I don’t know” or “That is not the case”—or the refusal to respond at all through silence; this is academically termed “concealment lying.” The other is the fabrication of false information to replace true information, calling black white or calling black “a little black and a little white”; this is academically termed “fabrication lying.”

Content expressed through language, clearly meaningful gestures (such as nodding in affirmation), text, and so on is relatively easy to capture.

The difficulty in detecting lies lies in ascertaining the person’s subjective cognition.

Because it is subjective cognition, it cannot be taken at face value from the person’s own statements. Current scientific methods include many techniques that can obtain information from the human brain either directly or indirectly.

The most advanced is fMRI technology, which can already reconstruct scanned brain-image information into video form with considerable clarity. In one experiment, faces and movements reconstructed from fMRI closely resembled the faces and movements the subject had previously viewed.

A more traditional method is the polygraph, which measures changes in physiological indicators such as skin resistance, heart rate, respiration, and blood volume to determine which test questions have greater impact on the subject. When four of five options in a set produce no physiological change while one option consistently produces a similar change across multiple trials, that option contains the subject’s subjective cognitive information.

In a theft-case test, for example, questions may concern the amount stolen. Police might ask:

“The wallet contained 2,000 yuan?”  
Subject: “I don’t know.”

“The wallet contained 3,000 yuan?”  
Subject: “I don’t know.”

“The wallet contained 4,000 yuan?”  
Subject: “I don’t know.”

“The wallet contained 5,000 yuan?”  
Subject: “I don’t know.”

“The wallet contained 6,000 yuan?”  
Subject: “I don’t know.”

An innocent person does not know how much money was in someone else’s wallet, so all five options are equally non-stimulating. The thief, having counted the money, knows the exact amount. To avoid punishment the thief will also answer “I don’t know” to every question, yet when the remembered figure is mentioned the mismatch between the spoken answer and actual cognition produces an abnormal fluctuation in physiological indicators. If this fluctuation proves stable upon repeated verification, the subject is known to possess information about the stolen amount and is therefore lying.

The above method can reveal the subject’s subjective cognitive information.

[1] Paul Ekman, *Telling Lies: Clues to Deceit in the Marketplace, Politics, and Marriage*. SDX Joint Publishing, December 2008:10. ISBN 978-7-108-03004-7.

#### The Movie *Indecent Proposal*

Demi Moore once starred in the film *Indecent Proposal*, which tells the story of two people who cross a moral line for money.

David and Diana are newlyweds deeply in love but financially strained. During the Great Depression they cannot find suitable work. One day in a casino they meet billionaire John Gage. In casual conversation John says, “Money can buy anything.” David and Diana disagree; they believe money cannot buy everything—for example, it cannot buy love.

John then asks, “Would you let Diana spend one night with me for one million dollars?” One million dollars is an enormous temptation. The couple tosses and turns all night. In the end they cannot resist; Diana spends the night with John.

Although at the film’s conclusion John, seeing that the two young people truly love each other, cannot bear to keep them apart and voluntarily gives Diana up, this is merely the director’s concession to audience expectations. In reality such outcomes are rare.

In both work and career, setbacks occur; no one’s life is smooth sailing. Yet people respond differently to setbacks. Some who feel unappreciated at work blame others instead of examining themselves. They give up, stop trying, ignore assignments, and even leak company information to competitors. Such employees are detestable because they have abandoned their moral底线. The底线 becomes like the emperor’s new clothes—an excuse that comforts only themselves. Associating with such people risks contagion; one may become cynical and lose one’s own底线. Therefore we must draw a clear line with them.

Thomas Babington Macaulay said, “A person’s conduct when certain that no one will ever know reveals character.” In other words, whatever circumstances you face, your actions display your moral quality. Suppose a rival company offers you a high salary and a platform to use your talents on the condition that you bring your current employer’s technical data. Would you accept? This is a difficult choice. Those without a moral底线 will certainly go; morality cannot stop them and they are not worth retaining. Only those who can hold the line deserve promotion and trust.

An excellent person, even when career prospects are dim, still maintains a moral底线 and a clear conscience. Excellence is not an act but a habit. There is no such thing as an excellent act; only the habit of excellence is true excellence. A person may not excel in career, but must never lack a底线.

#### 11.4 Methods of Analyzing Lies with Micro-reactions

A simple case can illustrate the process of obtaining and judging information.

Suppose someone drops a rock on their foot and injures it.

They immediately show a pained expression and crouch to examine and relieve the pain. These are unguarded physiological reactions.

If asked, “Does it hurt?” they may, for various reasons, answer, “It’s fine, it doesn’t hurt.”

In that case they are lying.

Cognition = pain. Through expression and movement we can clearly see that the pain they feel is intense.

Expression = “It’s fine, it doesn’t hurt.” Because expression contradicts cognition, they are judged to be lying.

With micro-reactions the only difference from the above example is that the reactions we must observe are far less obvious. The person may exert great effort to suppress and disguise them, substantially reducing the visible physiological and emotional responses. Yet any leakage that escapes complete suppression follows regular patterns and can be used to judge the person’s subjective cognition, feelings, and even assessments and judgments.

These reactions can then be compared with the content the person explicitly expresses; the result is immediately apparent.

For example, if everything the person says is modest, low-key, and compliant, yet you notice them clenching their fists slightly while speaking, you can conclude that verbal expression and emotional reaction do not match. The language conveys weak submission while the small bodily movement betrays underlying anger. Thus the person’s language is a disguise.

At that point the credibility of their words drops, and more importantly their attitude is “lying.” In many criminal and anti-corruption cases, determining whether a suspect lies about minor details is not the primary task; accurately grasping the suspect’s attitude—i.e., subjective intent—is. Once a cunning suspect leads investigators by the nose with strategy and acting, opportunities may be lost and prior efforts wasted.

In short, a simple formula cannot determine whether someone is lying because the essence of lying is a contradiction between expression and cognition. To expose a lie one must know both the subjective cognition and the expression; neither suffices alone.

Judging a lie by formula alone is obviously naïve and fails under verification.

All the techniques presented in this book and in *Micro-expressions* aim to judge a person’s subjective cognition indirectly. Physiological and emotional reactions can map the person’s subjective state. When combined with information contained in the stimulus, a causal link can be established and the person’s subjective cognition becomes visible.

Exposing the lie then follows naturally.

More importantly, once the person’s subjective cognition is judged, appropriate strategies for dealing with them can be formulated.

In simple terms, learning to analyze micro-reactions teaches one how to interact with all kinds of people in all kinds of situations.

#### Use Negative Expressions and Words Cautiously

To gain acceptance for one’s ideas, minimize the use of negative expressions and words. As noted in the discussion of anger, a negative attitude most readily provokes anger. Whether one says “You can’t do it,” “Can you really do it?” or “He can’t do it,” the effect is to arouse anger to varying degrees. Anger triggers resistance, rejection, and even impulsive decisions. Therefore, to have one’s ideas accepted, first reduce negative attitudes so that negative expressions do not arise.

Imagine discussing a proposal with colleagues. Your idea is good, yet not everyone agrees. To win over the dissenters you use the wrong approach: “You say my idea is bad—do you think yours is any better? Look at your proposal; what is this?” Even if you do not voice the thought, if you hold it you will display a contemptuous expression. Never underestimate that expression. Even a faint one, or a quiet sneer, can drive the other person to fury. Once noticed, it generates anger. If the team has already been working overtime on the proposal and tempers are frayed, your expression becomes the spark that ignites an argument.

Therefore, avoid adopting a negative attitude or displaying negative expressions. Likewise, use negative words such as “no” and “don’t” sparingly.

Consider the sentence “Don’t think about that plan; concentrate.” You will first think about what the plan is; the moment you are told not to think about it, you already are. Parents frequently use “no” and “don’t” with children: “Don’t touch that, it’s dangerous,” “Don’t eat that, it’s spicy.” Children then do exactly the opposite, causing frustration. Negative words can, to some extent, emphasize the prohibited action and draw more attention to it. If someone says “Don’t think of the red monkey,” you will inevitably wonder what the red monkey looks like, how a red monkey could exist, whether it is a baboon or an orangutan—and your mind has already wandered to “thinking of the red monkey” rather than the preceding “don’t.”

A divorced man remained depressed, constantly thinking he was divorced. When his psychologist advised him to think instead that he had become single, his condition improved markedly and he met other accomplished women.

Living with a negative attitude is exhausting and dispiriting. If you wish to express yourself, avoid negative phrasing; offering suggestions directly is more effective. Instead of rejecting someone else’s proposal outright, describe the strengths of your own proposal. This gives everyone an objective view of your idea while preserving team harmony.

#### Building Rapport with Someone You Like

When you meet someone you like, how do you establish rapport?

The most charming expression is the smile. Few people can remain indifferent when smiled at; usually a smile is returned. You have probably experienced this: on a train, with passengers beside and opposite you, a young person roughly your age catches your eye. The journey is long and conversation would ease the tedium. You look at the person; they look at you. You smile; they smile back. The similar age already creates warmth, and the exchange of smiles deepens it. Soon the person initiates conversation.

The same approach works with someone of the opposite sex you find attractive. A smile is the first step in building rapport and the first step toward mutual understanding. If you see someone who moves you in a crowd, begin with a friendly smile to put them at ease.

Eye contact is another method. At a dinner you notice a stranger and feel an immediate liking. You can start with a smile, then maintain an open posture—uncross your arms, move glasses and cutlery aside—so the space between you feels clear and reduces distance. After chatting for a while, if you wish to test whether further development is possible, use eye contact. Look at the person for one or two seconds, then shift your gaze to the floor. Looking down signals invitation and conveys submission; the implied message is “You may come closer.” This cue is especially common in women.

When the other person feels noticed, they instinctively present their best self: a woman may adopt an elegant posture, touch up her makeup, or adjust her hair and clothing; a man may sit straighter and expand his chest to display strength. If the person is a woman, playing with her hair or earrings signals acceptance of the invitation. The key point is not the hair or earrings themselves but the display of the wrist. The person is usually unaware of the action; revealing the wrist or palm is an evolved signal that no weapon is held and friendly interaction is possible. The modern handshake originated from this gesture.

Next come postures that convey seduction, some of which are more common in women.

#### Imperfect Lies

Sheriff York recently took on a strange rape case. Based on his experience, he judged that something about the case was abnormal, yet he could not identify exactly what felt off. He therefore brought the victim’s statement and the evidence to the FBI and sought out his former colleague, now FBI agent Charlie, to help analyze the case.

The victim’s statement read as follows:

Last night after work, I was walking home when I suddenly sensed someone following me from behind. I became very frightened, so I turned around to see who it was. The person stayed hidden in the shadows, however, and I could not make out his face at all. My fear grew. Just ahead was a narrow alley; I quickly slipped into it, but the person followed. We kept walking forward. It grew darker and darker, and the person drew closer. He approached me, and despite my resistance we had sexual relations. At that moment I tore this chain from his neck.

York showed Charlie the chain mentioned in the statement. After examining it, Charlie asked for York’s assessment. York replied, “If we treat this as a rape case, I see several inconsistencies. We located the chain’s owner through it. Although the owner confessed to the rape, I still feel the incident cannot be classified as rape. I simply cannot pinpoint what is wrong, which is why I came to you for help.”

Charlie nodded. “I agree with your assessment. I noticed several suspicious details in the statement. For instance, the victim repeatedly used the word ‘we’ when describing the rape. That word usually signals familiarity between two people. The victim said ‘we kept walking forward’ and ‘we had sexual relations,’ which strongly suggests the two already knew each other. In addition, the chain shows no signs of damage. It was almost certainly not yanked off in haste; it was more likely picked up or deliberately removed. I recommend further investigation.”

York accepted the advice. Back at the station he re-interviewed both parties and checked their identities and recent circumstances. The investigation revealed that the victim and the defendant had been a couple who were in the process of breaking up. The victim wanted to end the relationship; the defendant, despondent, staged the opening scene.

#### Occasional Liars

People who lie only occasionally usually do so to avoid an unpleasant situation or to cover a mistake. They are not skilled at lying, so they feel uneasy while doing it. That unease shows in their appearance, body language, and voice.

- **Avoiding names of themselves and others involved**  
  University of Hertfordshire psychologist Wiseman notes, “Liars feel uncomfortable, so they instinctively remove themselves from the lie.” They often say “the car broke down” instead of “my car broke down.” Liars also rarely use the names of people they mention in the lie. A well-known example is President Bill Clinton, who, when addressing the nation, refused to say “Lewinsky” and instead declared, “I did not have sexual relations with that woman.”

- **Avoiding eye contact**  
  Occasional liars often touch their eyes to avoid eye contact. Women typically touch just below the eye or look at the ceiling; men rub their eyes more forcefully and also look away.

- **Sudden change in volume or pitch**  
  A sudden rise in pitch often betrays a liar trying to mask nervousness.

- **Genuine expressions flash for only an instant**  
  A normal expression lasts several seconds, but on a “masked face” a genuine emotion appears for only a fraction of a second.

- **The nose enlarges slightly**  
  Extra blood flows to the face during lying; some people blush, and the nose can swell a few millimeters. Liars feel discomfort in the nose and unconsciously touch it.

- **Liars touch themselves frequently**  
  The more liars try to hide their inner state, the more small movements betray them. People often start to cover their mouths, then, realizing it looks suspicious, touch their noses instead.

- **Pulling at the collar**  
  Psychological discomfort triggers subtle changes in the sympathetic nervous system, producing tingling in the face and neck. Liars therefore rub or tug at their collars.

#### Using Anchors to Influence Others

Anchors and micro-expressions appear unrelated, yet the correct use of anchors depends on micro-expression cues. You may recall a scene from *The Mentalist*: the inspector, wanting to confirm whether a thug had once been an undercover officer, arranged a meeting in a diner. The thug looked nervous. The inspector began asking questions he knew the man could not lie about, each time tapping the table twice.

“Are you called ×××?” Tap, tap.  
“Yes.”  
“Are you limping on one leg?” Tap, tap.  
“Yes.”

The inspector kept the tapping rhythm constant while accelerating the questions. All the questions were ones the man had to answer truthfully—until the final one.

“Have you ever worked undercover?” Tap, tap.  
“Yes,” the man answered without thinking, then froze. Surprise flashed across his face, followed instantly by fear. He had been embedded in a gang and could not let anyone know his true identity. Years earlier he had accidentally injured someone during a gang fight and served time. After release he had tried to sever all ties with his past, including his undercover work. If the gang discovered the truth, they would kill him. When he inadvertently told the truth, his first reaction was surprise—“How did I let that slip?”—then fear, because the secret now threatened his life. His answer and micro-expressions confirmed to the inspector that he had indeed been undercover.

This is how anchors and micro-expressions work together. Each time the inspector asked a question the man could not lie about, he tapped the table twice. After several truthful answers the man had formed the association “when I hear that sound I must tell the truth.” That association is the anchor.

The prototype of an anchor is classical conditioning. Pavlov rang a bell twice before feeding his dogs; eventually the bell alone made them salivate. An anchor is a conditioned-reflex technique aimed at humans; what is implanted is not saliva but an emotional state. Once mastered, the technique lets you influence others so that their emotions shift in the direction you choose.

#### Recreational Activities

Some people relax after work by listening to music or dancing. These are recreational activities, and we can learn about a person from the music or dance they prefer.

People who enjoy symphonies tend to be self-confident, eager to express themselves, and optimistic. They quickly connect with others, yet they can be overly trusting and impractical.

People who like rock music dislike solitude and seek out like-minded companions. They are energetic, enjoy sports, and often feel dissatisfied with society. They use rock music to vent emotions. They like to stand out but rarely leave a deep impression. They frequently feel lost and need someone to help them recover a sense of self.

People who prefer pop music are ordinary and go with the flow. They pursue a relatively simple, carefree lifestyle and use music to stay relaxed.

People who favor classical music are usually rational. They practice self-reflection and self-discipline, often appearing solitary because few people truly enter their inner world.

A person’s dancing style also reveals personality. Ballet lovers show great patience and perseverance. Tap dancers are energetic, attention-seeking, and punctual. Waltz enthusiasts are calm, affable, and project mature, refined charm.

#### Eating

This cue is common among women. Women may chew olives, gum, chocolate, or ice to draw attention to their lips, sometimes licking them. If you are already sharing a meal, however, the signal loses meaning.

You may meet a woman in a bar who wears revealing clothes, circles you, glances at you, and plays with her earrings or necklace—an obvious invitation meaning “I want to be approached.” Another woman, equally provocatively dressed, may sit with legs tightly crossed and hands on her lap, signaling rejection and conservatism.

*The Mentalist* featured such a case. A female entertainer accused a wealthy young man of rape; he insisted the encounter was consensual. Police reviewed two videotapes and concluded the woman was lying. The first tape showed the man approaching her in a karaoke room. She sat alone; he initiated contact and made suggestive gestures. The inspector noticed one detail: she had crossed her legs, slipped one shoe halfway off, and was dangling it from her toes—an unmistakable flirtatious signal. When a woman is interested, she often displays an erogenous zone; the ankle is one such area.

The second tape showed the man carrying the apparently intoxicated woman into a hotel. In a mirror the police saw her wearing a satisfied, knowing smile—proof she was not drunk and was pleased her plan was succeeding.

The tapes exonerated the young man.

These techniques alone cannot guarantee that someone will like you; they are merely initial tools for understanding. Whether the other person develops affection also depends on character, background, and many other factors.

#### The Secret of Anchors

Once something is labeled a “technique,” it can seem remote from daily life. In fact, anchors are already part of ordinary experience. Consider a simple example: you break up with a loved one on your birthday and afterward listen to the same song every day. Years later, each birthday brings sadness, and hearing that song revives the pain. The date and the song have become an anchor implanted in your mind.

We sometimes meet someone for the first time and instantly dislike them. Later we realize the person was wearing a purple fitted top—the same style once worn by someone who hurt us. The garment has become an unpleasant anchor.

Not all anchors are negative, though negative emotions tend to leave stronger impressions. Pleasant anchors also exist. University dormitory nights filled with gossip and laughter can create one. After graduation, simply sharing a room again with former roommates and chatting in the dark can instantly restore that happy feeling, even if the exact conversations are forgotten.

Music is a powerful anchor used by many therapists. Film scores become classics not only for their beauty but because they instantly evoke the emotions of a beloved scene. Horror-movie music, low and ominous, can still produce chills, rapid heartbeat, anxiety, and sweating long after the specific frightening images have faded.

By recognizing anchors we can read another person’s emotional state. If we are fortunate enough to discover a hidden anchor, we can use it to guide that person’s feelings. Most anchors, however, lie in the unconscious, unknown even to the individual. Creating new anchors therefore becomes essential.

#### 11.1.1 The Standard for Truth-Telling

If a person’s cognition and expression are consistent, the person is not lying.

Even if the expressed content does not match objective reality, the person is still not lying provided the expression matches their own cognition.

Imagine one hundred small balls of different colors arranged without obvious pattern. Subjects are asked to note each ball’s color, after which the sequence is hidden. They are then asked the color of a randomly chosen ball. Each subject answers according to memory. Even if the answer differs from the actual color, the subject is not considered to be lying, because the information matches the subject’s internal cognition.

Truthfulness is judged solely against the speaker’s subjective cognition, not against objective fact. This is why polygraph results are not admissible as evidence. No matter how accurate the instrument, it can only access subjective cognition. If that cognition itself is distorted, the technology cannot reach the earlier stage of objective reality. Although most people’s subjective perceptions align with objective facts, the method cannot verify physical evidence because it cannot trace the cognitive processing that intervenes between reality and perception.

By contrast, DNA, fingerprints, footprints, ballistics, and autopsies examine physical traces that can originate only from actual events and therefore possess full traceability and strong evidentiary value<|eos|>

#### Behavior

People dominated by visual senses are usually very quick in walking and speaking. They are also highly sensitive to color, structure, shape, and light. For them, everything visible is transient, so they must memorize rapidly; over time this becomes habit, making both walking and speaking very fast. Because their actions are swift, these individuals breathe rapidly when expressing themselves, with pronounced chest movement, and their gestures accompanying speech are frequent. When activating memory, visually dominant people look up and to the left.

People dominated by auditory senses speak and walk more slowly than the visually dominant. They are accustomed to thinking while answering, so their speech rate follows their thinking speed. Gestures that accompany speech are generally confined to the mid-body, serving as one of their ways to express and relax. Because their memory is primarily auditory, they are very sensitive to sound and are often distracted by noises. In addition, when listening to others, auditory-dominant people habitually tilt their heads; this posture enhances ear function and helps them hear more clearly. When speaking themselves, they pay close attention to tone and intonation, hoping to convey their message with a more pleasing voice.

People dominated by kinesthetic senses care deeply about anything they can touch—whether clothing feels comfortable, whether a seat is soft, whether the surroundings are elegant. When expressing themselves, their speech rate is moderate, gestures center mainly on the abdomen, and breathing is diaphragmatic. Compared with demands for sound or image, these individuals prefer to convey opinions through touch. You have certainly met people who, while talking, repeatedly touch objects, pat you, or nudge you with an elbow. They rely on kinesthetic memory; feeling matters more than anything else.

#### Timing for Anchoring

One point must be noted: the moment for setting an anchor should be chosen when a pleasant emotion is rising, not when it is about to fade or turn negative. In other words, anchoring is more effective when the other person is already happy.

If circumstances force you to implant a positive anchor quickly, you can only try to elicit the person’s happy emotion—for example, by helping them recall a past joyful event—and then set the anchor while the happiness is present. This approach yields twice the result with half the effort.

To know when the other person’s emotion has become happy, you must read micro-expressions.

Try this:

> “Do you remember what it felt like the first time one of your dreams came true? Do you remember the feeling when you finally obtained something after countless hardships? Yes, that feeling was wonderful. Do you remember it?”

When the other person shows a happy micro-expression, you can seize the moment to set the anchor you wish to create.

Practice several times and you will discover the benefits of anchoring. Remember two rules, however:

- First, do not overuse anchors; you cannot know what psychological shadow you might cast on the other person.
- Second, establish positive anchors, especially when you intend to influence someone.

Many parents like to frighten children. When a child enters a dark space, they say in an alarmed voice, “Come here, come here,” while making a turning-and-fleeing gesture. Their intention is to make the child obedient and keep the child from playing in dark rooms. Yet after several repetitions the child learns to fear darkness and wants to escape any dark environment. Therefore a positive anchor is important: even if its effect is not as obvious as hoped, at least it does not harm others.

#### Don't Let Him See That I Lied

Employee Xiao Wang wanted a quick look at the payroll sheet, so he slipped into the HR office when no one was around. Just as he finished and was about to leave, he ran into a colleague returning from an errand.

“What are you doing here? Need something?”  
Covering his mouth, Xiao Wang gave a light cough. “Ah, nothing. I came to see Xiao Li, but he’s not here.”

Psychologists tell us that when people suddenly cover their mouths during conversation, it is usually because they have just lied. They try to hide the lie or conceal its traces by covering their mouths. To appear more natural, some people, like Xiao Wang in the example, pretend to cough while covering their mouths.

In short, covering the mouth with a hand can indicate that a lie has been told and the speaker is trying to mask nervousness.

For instance, during a class meeting the room is quiet. After the teacher finishes, the class monitor is asked if there is anything to add. The monitor shakes his head and says “No,” yet unconsciously covers his mouth with his hand. He is probably lying, because he is hesitant about whether to raise a certain issue in front of the whole class.

Moreover, if you can see his mouth, it is likely pressed tightly shut or the upper lip is biting the lower lip. This shows inner conflict: “Should I speak or not?”

Covering the mouth is a self-warning that represents the thought “I must not put myself in danger” or “I must not offend anyone.” The implied subtext is “Don’t let him see that I’m lying” or “He must not learn this secret.”

#### Finding Flaws in Speech to Expose Liars

Micro-expression keywords

Even the most skilled liars cannot be completely watertight. Either an expression or a gesture gives them away. Although people deliberately monitor their words when lying, research shows that liars still reveal slips in speech. Careful observation will always uncover traces that leave the liar nowhere to hide.

American psychologist Feldman states that humans are boastful animals and lie more than they realize—on average at least twenty-five times a day.

Most lies, of course, do little harm. Feldman classifies lies into different levels and groups the motives into three categories:

- The first: to please others and make them feel better.
- The second: to boast about oneself or put on airs.
- The third: self-protection.

Feldman notes: “We lie to others unconsciously, sometimes without thinking, and even refuse to admit we are lying. Most lies are polite responses such as ‘You don’t look fat in that at all,’ ‘Let’s have tea sometime,’ ‘I can’t come today, I’m sick,’ ‘I called you but couldn’t get through,’ or ‘I had a great time tonight; let’s get together again soon.’”

Feldman explains: “Knowing when to lie or bend the truth is a social skill.”

Some lies, however, are highly damaging—those told deliberately to achieve a specific goal. When the other person’s speech shows the following features, you should pay close attention.

#### Experimental Requirements for Subjects

Subjects must control their performance as much as possible. If the two rounds of recording show consistent behavior with no obvious differences, the subject wins the trial.

In this experiment the first round requires the subject to tell the truth; the second round requires the subject to lie. Using “1 + 1 = ?” as an example, in the second round the subject first calculates the correct answer “2,” but the rules forbid saying “2.” This creates a conflict between the true cognition (“2”) and the required response, satisfying the definition of a lie.

Such simple lie material has two advantages: every adult can easily compute the correct answer to each question, and uttering these “lies” involves neither personal gain nor loss and therefore imposes no direct psychological burden (such as fear or guilt). It can thus be regarded as the most basic model of lying.

Comparison of the recordings shows that even in this pure lie model, subjects cannot keep their second-round reactions identical to the first. Time delays lengthen, eye movements increase, and inappropriate laughter and other anomalies appear repeatedly.

The reason is that processing a lie imposes a heavy cognitive load on the brain—at least several times the load required for telling the truth. The brain must first calculate the correct answer, then verify each step against complex rules to avoid it, and finally construct a coherent, self-consistent narrative of fabricated content. When this is compounded by emotions such as disgust, fear, guilt, or anger, plus the pressure of follow-up questions, the brain may bear a load dozens of times heavier than when telling the truth.

#### Poker Face

A poker face generally refers to a face showing no expression. It reveals neither happiness nor unhappiness nor neutrality. Successful poker players usually master control of their body language, especially facial expressions, so that their emotions remain hidden.

You will often see them wearing sunglasses to reduce the chance that their eyes betray emotion. Sometimes they also send false signals or strike poses to mislead other players. Such behavior is not criminal. Anyone can hide true intentions by displaying an opposing expression or maintaining a poker face.

If a person does not consciously control emotions and intentions, most expressions remain on the face for at least several seconds and can be detected. The micro-expressions discussed in this chapter occur largely without conscious awareness. They commonly appear when someone tries to conceal genuine feelings.

With advances in computer technology we can rapidly start and stop video clips to record and study the micro-expressions that arise during conversation or interrogation. If your goal is merely to train yourself to notice rather than deeply analyze these micro-expressions, a computer is unnecessary.

When studying facial expressions, if we wish to understand the other person’s meaning better, we must not overlook the fleeting, simplest emotional changes; they may be more important than any deliberately displayed emotion.

#### Exercise Preferences

In their leisure time many people choose to exercise and strengthen their bodies. Some also regard fitness, weight loss, entertainment, or relaxation as forms of exercise. Regardless of the hopes or ideas people attach to exercise, long-term, careful observation reveals that when individuals choose a particular activity they are satisfying needs of both body and mind; these needs, to varying degrees, also reveal different aspects of their personality.

Therefore, if we want to explain a stranger and gain deeper insight into personality traits, asking what sport the person enjoys in leisure time can be extremely helpful.

For example, people who habitually play basketball usually have high ideals and ambitious goals. They are often confident, hope to realize their aspirations, want to outperform others, and like to stay one step ahead. To achieve their objectives they are willing to make great sacrifices and exert great effort. People who habitually play soccer are passionate, hold a very positive attitude toward life, are always ready to fight, and brim with energy. People interested in walking maintain relative composure and steadiness toward matters that do not greatly interest them; they do what they should and can do. They trust their ability to handle every task and possess good patience. Most mountaineers who call themselves “children of the mountains” are introverted individuals who are also quite demanding of themselves.

#### Body Language Case Study

Consider body language. In an episode of the American series *Lie to Me*, a female teacher is murdered.
