The FBI suspects a male student who had long been infatuated with and spied on her, and immediately detains him. After analysis by Dr. Cal Lightman, however, the student is cleared: he had discovered a photograph. In the photo the murdered teacher stands at a car window, apparently talking to someone inside. Because of the angle, she blocks the driver’s face. Her body leans forward, left hand resting on the window frame, right hand hanging down with the palm raised at a 90-degree angle to the wrist. It is this right-hand gesture that gives Dr. Lightman a clue.

Reproducing the teacher’s movement with a raised arm yields a classic “stop” gesture. Traffic police use the same signal when directing vehicles to halt. In daily life the gesture means “Stop—don’t continue,” and is often seen in arguments. Dr. Lightman concludes that the teacher was arguing with the person inside the car. Following this lead, he locates the car’s owner and ultimately solves the case.

Still, the familiar caveat applies: body language alone cannot support a definitive conclusion; individual differences and conversational context must be taken into account. To avoid the Brokaw trap, it is best to analyze all four lie indicators—micro-expressions, body language, slips of the tongue, and heated language—together.

#### Applications of Anchoring

Before negotiating with a client, it is wise to learn the client’s preferences—favorite colors, foods, music, people, and so on. People feel happy when they encounter something they like; that is why catering to tastes works. If the client likes red, you can incorporate red into your clothing to activate the client’s happy anchor. If the client likes a particular piece of music, you can use it as background music for your presentation; this increases your chance of success, makes others like you more, and facilitates rapport.

Many parents frequently tell their children “You’re wonderful.” This too is a form of anchoring. When a child does something right, the parent immediately offers encouragement—“You’re wonderful”—and the child feels pride and confidence. Over time the phrase “You’re wonderful” becomes linked with pride and confidence. When the child later faces setbacks and feels low, the parent can say “Hey, you’re wonderful” to awaken that confidence and pride.

Similarly, if a leader wants subordinates to work hard, an anchor can be set. While praising an employee’s effort—emphasizing the word “effort”—the leader pats the employee’s shoulder. The word “effort” becomes an anchor inside the employee. Later, whenever the employee works, the memory of that day’s praise and the associated positive feeling surfaces, increasing diligence.

#### Habitual Liars

Habitual liars, through practice, can control appearance, body language, and voice so convincingly that few traces remain. Yet their lies are never flawless.

- **Blinking or rubbing the eyes while lying**  
  They have learned to do the opposite to avoid detection—staring fixedly at you. Because deceivers concentrate so intensely, their eyes become dry, forcing them to blink or rub their eyes more often to relieve the discomfort.

- **After being asked the same question repeatedly, the liar erupts in anger**  
  Ask a question and wait for the answer. Ask a second time; the answer remains unchanged. Leave an interval between the second and third questions. When you ask the same question again while the person is distracted, the reaction is either shame turning to rage or a tendency to confess. If someone says, “Haven’t I already told you this?” and then flies into a rage, deception is likely.

- **The liar never forgets any detail**  
  Remembering every detail of a time period is difficult. Liars make no mistakes in their statements because they have already constructed the entire scenario in their minds. They will never say, “Wait, I got that wrong.”

#### Liars Have Excellent Memory

A police officer is interrogating a suspect.

Officer: “Do you remember what you were doing at 10 p.m. on March 18?”

Suspect: “Oh, that night I finished dinner, lay on my bed at home, and watched TV. I remember it was Channel 5—my favorite soccer program.”

Officer: “What did you have for dinner?”

Suspect: “I had a cheese pizza and a glass of beer.”

Officer: “That was a month ago. Since you remember so clearly, tell me what you were wearing that day. Think carefully before answering—we have surveillance footage of you entering the apartment that night!”

“Um… I really don’t remember. I…” The suspect begins to sweat. The officer notices everything; after further questioning the suspect is revealed as the robber.

When asked for a specific piece of information, a liar will always attempt an answer rather than say “I don’t know,” because admitting ignorance risks arousing suspicion. In order to convince the police he had stayed home, the robber supplied details about the television program and the meal. Yet this person with such an excellent memory conveniently forgot what he was wearing. In reality, most people cannot recall what they did on a given day even a week earlier, let alone a month.

#### How to Respond to the Other Person's Micro-expressions

Once you have learned to recognize micro-expressions, the next important goal is knowing how to respond. We notice the other person’s micro-expression, yet we do not know whether that person wants us to be aware of the current emotional state. We must therefore determine whether the emotion is mild or intense and, if intense, whether the person is forcibly suppressing it. We can judge this from the content of the conversation. If micro-expressions appear at the very beginning of the talk, before the main topic is reached, several possibilities exist:

1. The person arrived with an emotion unrelated to the conversation.
2. The person does not want the conversation at all and is already resistant.
3. The person anticipates an unpleasant outcome and therefore begins with an emotional charge.

If micro-expressions appear during the conversation itself, they are most likely emotional responses to the discussion. In the following sections we will examine how to respond to each type of underlying emotion; doing so can noticeably improve your communication skills, or at least serve as a warning. Only sadness, anger, disgust, fear, and contempt will be discussed, because happiness and surprise generally require no special response skills.

#### Where His Moral Bottom Line Lies When He's Down on His Luck

Micro-expression keywords Everyone has times when they are down on their luck, yet people's mindsets and actions differ greatly. Some give up on themselves, abandon all restraint, or even discard their moral bottom line. Such people rarely achieve anything worthwhile, and we should keep our distance. Others reflect on themselves and hold fast to their moral bottom line; these are the people worth building relationships with.

What a person does when down on their luck reveals their moral baseline. Some actions earn genuine respect and admiration, while others provoke contempt, resentment, or ridicule. Behind these contrasting reactions lies an invisible yardstick: the moral bottom line.

When everything goes smoothly, almost everyone’s principles appear clear. But when circumstances turn unfavorable, how many can still uphold that bottom line? In society we often see people in straitened circumstances violate social ethics or cross their own moral line. Some sell out friends for money; others harm others for fame or profit. People who cannot maintain their bottom line when down on their luck cannot earn others’ trust.

#### How to Create a Positive Anchor

So how do you create a positive anchor? You can learn from the salesman Jerry.

When Jerry first entered sales, his performance was poor and his manager repeatedly pressured him to improve. One day he called on an elderly woman who looked despondent. She said her daughter had just suffered a miscarriage and had no interest in buying anything. After being turned away, Jerry thought that everyone carries some worry; if he could bring customers a bit of joy along with the product samples, it would be worthwhile. From then on, whenever he mailed trial products he tucked in a small note containing a joke or an amusing incident he had encountered.

A month later, surprisingly, Jerry’s sales rose sharply. Many customers were happy to buy from him because the sight of his product triggered a pleasant feeling. Without realizing it, Jerry had planted a positive anchor in his customers’ minds; the note with the joke was the anchor.

Remember, an anchor does not trigger an event but an emotion. It works because we habitually link our feelings to external cues. When you want to evoke positive emotions in others, create a positive anchor.

#### Spotting the Telltale Signs: Who Is Still Lying to You

**Micro-expression keywords**

Lies appear everywhere in daily life. We can overlook harmless white lies, but when deception is involved, how do we know we are being misled? It is simple: watch the other person’s hand gestures while speaking. These subtle movements reveal whether someone is lying and serve as a key to unlocking another person’s inner thoughts.

Many have seen the American series *Lie to Me*, based on a true story. Dr. Lightman is an expert at detecting deception; he reads facial expressions, body language, and tone of voice to determine whether someone is lying and why. Lies exist everywhere. A simple shrug, hand rub, or lip press can signal deception. Even skilled liars leak clues through minute physical movements. These subtle signals determine whether we control the interaction or are controlled by the other person.

Never ignore these faint bodily cues; they may become the key that opens another person’s heart. Below are the six most common lying gestures we encounter in everyday life.

#### Touching the Nose

In the fairy tale *Pinocchio*, the puppet’s nose grows when he lies. In real life, people touch their noses while speaking. The gesture consists of quickly rubbing the underside of the nose a few times, sometimes so lightly it is barely noticeable. Women perform the movement with even smaller amplitude than men.

Research shows that lying increases blood flow to the nose, causing slight swelling and an itchy sensation. People therefore rub their noses to relieve the itch. Note that nose-touching is a common everyday action; to judge whether someone is lying, combine this cue with other indicators of deception.

Genuine nasal itch differs from the lying version. A real itch requires firm rubbing or even digging to relieve it, unlike the light touch of the deceptive gesture. Purely physical itching also produces only repeated nose-rubbing, unrelated to the content, frequency, or rhythm of the conversation.

#### Kinesthetic Vocabulary

People whose dominant sense is kinesthetic experience the world primarily through touch or emotion. They recall events via tactile or emotional impressions and also favor taste and smell words. Common terms include: contact, touch, pain, cold, warmth, firm, soft, rough, slippery, light, heavy, sour, sweet, bitter, fragrant.

They often express themselves this way:

- You have to try it
- It smells really good
- I can feel it
- This thing is very solid
- She looks really sweet
- He is a soft, gentle person

When speaking with such individuals, emphasize how the matter will feel good to them. In real life, many conversations falter because the two parties use different dominant sensory vocabularies. A simple example:

A: You still don’t get what I mean?  
B: I heard you, but I don’t understand.

Rephrasing to match the other person’s visual vocabulary works better. If the other person is auditory, try:

A: Do you hear what I’m saying now?  
B: Yes, I hear you.

Identifying someone’s dominant sense requires effort. Here are several practical methods.

#### 3. Complex Lies

First question: Have you ever won a professional competition championship?

An answer of “no” is not necessarily truthful. Consider a contest open only to non-professional (amateur) entrants. All participants are nominally amateurs and compete at roughly the same level; the prize is substantial. Professional athletes may conceal their status, enter under false pretenses, and win. Motive: gain.

Second question: Have you ever secretly used company funds for personal expenses?

An answer of “yes” can also be a lie.

In reality, a friend (son, wife, girlfriend, or superior) took the money. The speaker is innocent but claims responsibility to protect the friend, who can deliver greater future benefits. This is the classic scenario in which a subordinate takes the fall for the boss. By quickly resolving the matter, the subordinate may later be promoted and the family well cared for (with settlement money); refusal could bring retaliation against both the individual and relatives. Under such complex rules, lying serves both gain and avoidance of harm.

#### Covering the Mouth with the Hand

Psychologists note that when someone suddenly covers their mouth during conversation, it usually means they have just lied and are trying to hide the falsehood. To appear natural, some accompany the gesture with a pretend cough.

In films and television, a thief or criminal passing a police officer often glances around, covers the mouth, coughs lightly, then lowers the hand and answers questions. Viewers sense the person is acting suspiciously or lying.

Covering the mouth is akin to the “shush” gesture of placing a finger to the lips: both signal a desire to withhold inner thoughts. If the other person unconsciously covers their mouth while you are talking, pay close attention to the deeper meaning. The gesture indicates concealment. You can then appear uninterested to put the person at ease; the conversation will usually proceed more smoothly afterward.

#### Volunteering Extra Information

In police interrogations, when asked what they were doing after dinner, robbery suspects sometimes reply that they were watching television and then spontaneously name the program. This is a classic sign of lying.

Liars feel insecure and fear detection. To appear credible they embellish their story with extra detail. Unlike earlier examples, they volunteer the information unprompted because they have already rehearsed it and can deliver it without hesitation.

Truthful people feel no need for such elaboration.

Example: A girlfriend calls her boyfriend; he answers after many rings. If he has nothing to hide he will simply say, “I was in the bathroom and didn’t hear the phone.” If he adds, “The water was running loudly, and the apartment has great soundproofing…” he is probably lying.

Whenever someone lies, certain words or speech patterns become overly deliberate. Careful observation reveals the inconsistencies.

#### Recreational Games

As times change, a person’s ability to keep pace with progress or adapt to new developments depends largely on openness to new experiences. Attitudes toward technology and games therefore reflect character and capability.

People who enjoy computer games tend to be introverted; they like order and excel at numbers and systems. Extroverts, by contrast, treat computers merely as electronic toys for killing time and avoid them for work whenever possible. More than 90 percent of those with a strong interest in computers are introverts.

Many other leisure activities—reading, playing chess, drinking—also reveal a person’s values and approach to life. Discovering how someone spends free time gives useful insight into their priorities.

#### 11.2 The Purpose of Lying—Gain and Avoidance of Harm

Lying takes many forms, yet its purpose is always the same: gain and avoidance of harm. A lie either escapes a negative consequence (criticism, loss, or punishment)—truth would bring trouble, falsehood offers a chance to dodge it—or secures a benefit (reward, profit, or affection)—truth would exclude the person, falsehood offers a chance to obtain it.

Both motives involve concealment and fabrication. Experiments show that fabrication occurs more often when seeking gain, especially when the liar invents facts to elevate their own status. When avoiding harm, denial predominates; unfavorable information is hidden or rejected. Fabrication still occurs, usually by inventing contradictory details or shifting blame to someone else. See Figure 11-1.

#### Standing Face-to-Face

Standing face-to-face exposes every vulnerable part of the body to the other person. When speaking with strangers or people we do not trust, we instinctively angle our bodies slightly, forming a 45-degree angle. Conversely, willingness to stand directly facing you signals that the other person does not reject greater closeness; mutual attraction and trust are present. Avoid approaching head-on at the first meeting, as it creates psychological pressure and defensiveness.

If the other person prefers to stand sideways, arms crossed, or touching the neck or collar, maintain distance. The same posture appears when the topic does not interest them; change the subject.

If the person is comfortable standing face-to-face, the position offers an excellent opportunity to build rapport and observe micro-expressions clearly. Use previously learned micro-expression techniques to gauge whether the other person wants to draw closer or feels positive toward you.

#### Fear

Real-life stimuli that produce full-blown fear are rare; more common is simple apprehension. Women may fear reptiles, children may fear needles, adults may fear horror films or bad news. When you detect fear, the best response is to create a sense of safety. If you must deliver bad news to an employee, you might say: “Your efforts have been obvious to everyone. You will not lose your job over this; we simply need to solve the problem together.” Remove the fear of unemployment first, then discuss the issue; results improve.

When someone close to you is afraid, a hug provides the best comfort. It evokes the security once felt inside the mother’s womb and reduces fear. As children, our first impulse when frightened was to run into a parent’s arms. With someone less close, ask why they are afraid while conveying that you can provide a safe environment.

#### Sadness

The best response to sadness is comfort, but first consider several factors: how close your relationship is, whether someone else might be better suited to offer comfort, and the history of your interactions. Not everyone welcomes comfort. Both children and adults often prefer private space to process negative emotions, especially sadness. In the presence of people who are not especially close, most suppress sadness out of politeness and to preserve personal space.

If your relationship is very close, a simple “What happened?” or “Are you all right?” is appropriate when you notice the sadness micro-expression. If the relationship is ordinary, locate someone closer to the person; that is more effective than direct inquiry. With family members, assure them that you will stay with them no matter what and that they will not face the situation alone.

#### See What He Pursues in His Leisure Time

Micro-expression keywords: In their free time, everyone chooses different ways to relax. Some prefer cultural activities, others sports, still others casual games. The chosen leisure activity reveals character and interpersonal style, offering valuable insight into the person.

A person’s hobbies function as a mirror of personality. Interests vary widely. To understand someone, observe what they pursue when idle. Some enjoy sports, others outdoor pursuits such as fishing; some play chess, others collect items. Leisure interests reflect aspirations and psychological state.

Therefore, the best way to identify a person is to start with their hobbies. This approach lets you see their true nature up close and devise targeted solutions. Leisure activities generally fall into the following categories:

#### Liars Often Omit “I”

Psychologist Richard Wiseman of the University of Hertfordshire observes that liars instinctively distance themselves from their falsehoods. When asked why they are late for work, someone who says “the car broke down” rather than “my car broke down” is probably lying; the real reason may be oversleeping. Repeated omission of “I” in answers therefore warrants suspicion.

Liars also rarely mention other people’s names. The most famous example is President Clinton’s denial during the Lewinsky scandal: he referred to “that woman” instead of naming Monica Lewinsky, stating, “I did not have sexual relations with that woman.” Pay attention to such small conversational details.

#### When Facial Expressions Lie

The face is a dual system that can both deliberately display expressions and spontaneously produce expressions without people realizing the information their facial expressions convey. The parts of the face that most reveal people’s true feelings (not necessarily the emotions they intend to convey) are the eyes, eyebrows, and mouth.

Blinking frequency reflects a person’s level of psychological comfort. The faster the blinking rate, the more it indicates that the person is lying, hesitating, or uncomfortable. Because there are differences between individuals, one should try to grasp each person’s normal blinking frequency.

During a conversation, we should also pay attention to how often the other person’s eyebrows raise when they say words like “how,” “when,” “why,” and “where.” This plays a key role in judging a person’s sincerity.

When others are listening to you speak, pay attention to the subtle movements of their lips and mouth. If the mouth twitches, tightens, or wrinkles, it means she is implying to you that she disagrees with what you said.

#### Nodding Subconsciously Before Shaking the Head

Boss Lin’s client owed a large sum for goods that had not been paid. Several subordinates went to the company to collect the payment but were told the person in charge was not there. This time, Boss Lin went himself. He asked the receptionist, “Excuse me, is your manager, Mr. Ma, in?” The receptionist hesitated briefly, then shook her head firmly and said, “No.”

Boss Lin stared at her and said, “You’re lying!” Then he walked straight to Manager Ma’s office and found him inside on the phone.

How did Boss Lin know the receptionist was lying? Because he noticed that after she hesitated, she made a very subtle nodding motion before shaking her head vigorously. This subconscious nod gave her away!

Researchers have found that many liars make a subconscious nod before shaking their head to deny something, indicating affirmation of the other person’s question. This quick nod is hard for the brain to control; it tells us that everything said after the head shake is a lie!

#### Rubbing the Eyes

Many of us have had the experience of rubbing our eyes when we do not want to see certain things or scenes. In fact, this happens because we are trying to stop our eyes from seeing something unpleasant, uncomfortable, or suspicious. It means: “I’m uneasy; I don’t want to look!”

In daily life, if you observe carefully, you will notice that a person rubs their eyes or smiles unnaturally while preparing a lie, while telling it, and after telling it. Men often rub their eyes vigorously when making this gesture; if they are trying to cover up a huge lie, they are likely to turn their face away. Women make the eye-rubbing gesture less often; they usually just gently touch below the eye.

Of course, nothing is absolute. We cannot assume someone is lying just because they rub their eyes. We must observe first, then judge, and only then draw a conclusion.

#### The Story of Zengzi

While living in the state of Lu, Zengzi was very poor and often tilled the fields in tattered clothes. When the ruler of Lu heard about Zengzi, he decided to grant him a small city. Unexpectedly, Zengzi firmly refused.

Someone asked in confusion, “This is a good thing. You didn’t ask the ruler for it yourself; the king offered it to you. Why turn it down?”

Zengzi replied, “If a person accepts favors from others, he will fear them, and the giver often feels superior. Even if the ruler does not become arrogant toward me, how could I not feel afraid?”

As the saying goes, “Poverty does not diminish ambition.” Although we may be poor, poverty should not rob us of our spirit. We should not accept rewards without merit, nor trade our dignity for wealth. Zengzi’s refusal embodied self-reliance; such a person is trustworthy and worth knowing.

#### The Small Action of Swallowing Saliva

Xiao Zhou arrived late again and was caught by the manager, who scolded him: “I hear you’ve gotten hooked on mahjong lately and stay up until two every night. How’s your luck—pretty good, I bet.”

Xiao Zhou’s Adam’s apple moved as he said quietly, “No, Manager. My wife hasn’t been feeling well these days, so I have to take care of her in the morning.”

The manager did not believe him, of course, because he heard Xiao Zhou swallow.

When a person wants to lie, inner tension creates a dry, itchy, or strange sensation in the throat, prompting them to swallow subconsciously to relieve it. So with this single action, we can tell whether the other person is telling the truth or lying.

Psychologists have found through extensive research and observation that people make many inadvertent movements when lying. The quick nod before shaking the head, eye squinting, and swallowing saliva mentioned above are all extra actions that, though brief, reveal the truth.

#### FBI Agent Case

FBI Agent Joe received a tip that a suspect was hiding at his girlfriend’s house, so he rushed over to make the arrest. When the suspect’s girlfriend opened the door, she claimed her boyfriend had not been there. Unsure whether to believe her, Joe questioned her further. During repeated questioning, although she remained calm, her blinking rate was noticeably higher than at the start. From this, Joe concluded the suspect was still inside. Ultimately, after Joe insisted, a search of the room turned up the suspect in the wardrobe.

In this case, Joe detected the frequent blinking in the suspect’s girlfriend’s eyes and realized she was feeling uneasy and tense. Despite her outward calm, her eyes betrayed her, allowing Joe to uncover more clues through conversation.

#### Pulling at the Collar

British zoologist and human behaviorist Desmond Morris observed that people feel an itch on the sensitive face and neck when lying, because once liars sense doubt from the listener, increased blood pressure causes the neck to sweat. They therefore subconsciously rub or scratch to relieve the discomfort. So if you see someone repeatedly pulling at their collar during a conversation, you can infer they are probably worried their lie will be exposed.

Of course, a person may also pull at their collar when angry or frustrated, so we must determine whether lying is involved. When you see someone make this gesture, you might say, “Could you repeat that, please?” or “Why don’t you just say what you mean?” This will prompt a response that reveals their true intent.

#### A Slip-of-the-Tongue Case

Here is a slip-of-the-tongue case for reference. It comes from Freud’s research and concerns a doctor describing someone else’s divorce proceedings. He said: “In a certain divorce case, a nurse and her husband were both listed as defendants. The case was originally brought by the wife against the husband, but she too became involved. In the end, ‘he’ was granted the divorce.” The doctor mistakenly said “he” instead of “she.” This was not a simple slip.

We must first understand the legal context of the time. Adultery was the only legal ground for divorce, and the suit was filed by the betrayed party. The outcome was usually victory for the plaintiff and a large alimony award. From the doctor’s slip, it is clear that the husband in the case was the doctor himself. Deep down, he wished he were the one filing for divorce and winning, and also receiving a substantial alimony payment.

Like micro-expressions, a slip of the tongue always carries meaning when it occurs.

#### Excessive Detail Raises Suspicion

When we ask someone about events from several nights earlier, it is hard for them to avoid mistakes while recounting, because remembering every detail from a period of time is difficult. They inevitably correct themselves and sort out their thoughts, so their speech becomes halting: “After work I took the bus home—oh, wait, after work I caught a ride with Xiao Wang…”

A liar, however, will never make such errors. Because they are recounting something fabricated, they have already planned everything in their mind’s hypothetical scenario, so their account will contain no “Wait, I said that wrong.” Yet this seamless narrative is precisely what exposes them.

#### Is He Lying to Me?

In social interactions, the frequency with which people lie or are deceived by lies is astonishing. MIT psychologist Feldman’s research indicates that the average person tells at least 25 lies per day. Of course, lies vary in degree; some are well-intentioned and can be ignored. But when a lie is meant to deceive or harm, how do we know whether we have been tricked?

A recent study from the University of California found that even habitual liars produce subconscious signals when their brain switches into pretense mode—signals an ordinary person can detect, much like a lie detector.

FBI facial-expression experts, drawing on years of research, generally divide liars into two types:

#### Anger

When you notice signs of anger in the other person’s expression, do not rush to respond. First clarify several points:

1. If anger appears only in the eyebrows and eyes, determine whether the person is simply thinking or is genuinely angry. Your conversation may have troubled them, and they are trying to figure out how to escape the difficulty.
2. If it is anger, identify the source of the anger—it may not be you.
3. Never blurt out, “What’s wrong? You look angry.” If you are certain the micro-expression is anger, the person is trying hard to suppress it and does not want you to notice. Your remark could undo all their effort and cause the anger to erupt twofold.

#### Liars Do Not Describe Events in Detail

A husband stayed out all night. The next day his wife asked, “Did you go gambling again last night?” The husband looked flustered and said, “No. I went drinking with friends.” The wife pressed, “Really? Which friends? Where did you drink?” The husband replied, “Just a few close friends, at the usual place.”

Clearly, the wife would not believe such a vague answer. When lying, a person feels guilty and fears that more information will create more holes. So when the wife asked for specific names, the husband dared not say more, afraid of being caught. A liar cannot withstand detailed questioning; if you are suspicious, a few extra questions will reveal the truth.

#### 2. Second Form of Lying

**Question**: Have you ever secretly misappropriated company funds for personal use? (Negative information)

**Lying response**: No.

Direct denial of negative information aims to avoid harm and escape possible punishment (loss of trust or material penalties such as dismissal).

If the answer is “Yes,” the likelihood of lying is lower. Admitting a mistake invites punishment or loss of opportunity, so there is no motive to lie.

The two examples above, however, are only first-level logical judgments. If the rules of the situation are complex or the subject has an elaborate deception plan, each case must be analyzed individually.

#### Sitting Face to Face

Standing for a while can cause fatigue, so you choose to sit and chat face to face. A table in front allows the other person to relax slightly, because vulnerable areas are shielded. If there is no table, remember not to cross your legs, as that creates a barrier; do not wear sunglasses, as they create a sense of insecurity<|eos|>

#### 1. Form of Lying One

**Question**: Have you ever won a championship in a professional competition? (Positive information)

**Lying answer**: Yes.

The response to this question constitutes fabrication, with the goal of seeking gain. The title of professional competition champion can bring additional benefits (spiritual admiration and affection, or material rewards).

If the answer is: No. Then the likelihood of lying is comparatively low. Denying possession of such a positive title brings neither gain nor avoidance of harm, and carries no motive for lying.



#### Micro-expression Five

Reporter: If you were to recommend a professional book to younger colleagues, which one would you recommend?

He abandons the answer, and his agent immediately indicates that time is up and the press conference is ending. At this moment, an expression of guilt appears on his face. Guilt is a derivative of sadness and represents complete abandonment of resistance, acknowledging that he has lied.

These small details may seem magical; with diligent practice, you too can discern who is telling the truth and who is lying. You will also learn how to guide a liar into admitting dishonesty.



#### Conversation Style Reveals the Secret of Lying

Micro-expression keywords: When people lie, they rely mainly on language. They are unwilling to let the other party detect flaws, so they prepare a set of statements in advance, believing this will conceal the truth. In reality, this makes the conversation style appear deliberate and inadvertently reveals the secret that they are lying.

When a person lies, they pay close attention during the conversation to avoid detection. Therefore, if you listen carefully, you will notice that their speaking pattern differs from that of ordinary people.



#### Micro-expression One

Reporter: In your book you mention using your spare time to supplement your professional knowledge. Which professional books have you read?

He pauses for about one second, indicating he did not anticipate such a detailed question. After an awkward smile, he replies: Not many, so I won’t mention them and make everyone laugh. Embarrassment is one of the emotions derived from fear, representing a loss of control over the development and pace of events and a sense that one’s reputation is threatened.



#### Ear Scratching

When people do not want to listen to others, they scratch their ears, indicating they do not wish to hear at that moment. For example, during a negotiation with a client, if you are expressing an opinion and the client suddenly tilts their head and rubs their ear with a finger, it means the client holds the opposite view of what you are saying and is formulating their own point. At this point, if you do not give the other party an opportunity to speak, the exchange is likely to be ineffective.



#### Micro-expression Analysis at a Celebrity Autobiography Press Conference

A certain celebrity published an autobiography that readers questioned as not written by the author. Because the celebrity’s educational level was not high, yet the entire book displayed solid literary skill in structure, logic, and wording, suspicion arose. To clarify the facts, the celebrity held a press conference to assure everyone that the book was indeed written by them. Most people found the celebrity very sincere, but in fact many micro-expressions betrayed them.



#### Micro-expression Two

Reporter: Which book are you reading recently?

Answer: A book by Stanislavski. While answering, a brief hesitation appears. The head tilts slightly forward, the chin retracts, and the upper eyelids lift. Although these changes are subtle, anyone who has undergone extensive micro-expression training can spot them at a glance. This is a fighting posture triggered by anger, representing the threat of the lie being exposed.



#### Micro-expression Four

Reporter: What help have those professional books given to your career?

Answer: Those pieces of knowledge filled the gap left by not having taken professional courses and brought me great improvement. They have been of tremendous help both professionally and in terms of professional dedication.

The answer is devoid of substantive meaning. At the same time, the gaze shifts downward, the lips press together, and an expression of unease appears.



#### Micro-expression Three

Reporter: In your book you quote Stanislavski’s most classic line, and I think it is used very well. Although everyone is already familiar with it, we still hope you can use it again to admonish younger colleagues.

Answer: I am still a newcomer myself; how can I admonish younger colleagues? At this moment the eyebrows lower, the inner brows raise, producing the typical facial features of fear. The gaze also wanders, indicating avoidance.

If you are deceived by one of them, your career may suffer a severe blow. What you must do is determine within five minutes whether the other party is telling the truth or lying!

##### 3. Emotional State Baseline

Behavioral characteristics dominated by genuine emotions. When unrestrained and emotionally heightened, individuals break through the self-imposed constraints of social behavioral rules and act without inhibition. The facial expressions, breathing, voice, body posture, and movement features displayed at such times also constitute a baseline; these behavioral characteristics revealed during genuine emotional expression can be called the “emotional state baseline.”

The emotional state baseline is harder to obtain than the calm state baseline, because the rules of civilized society in the modern world rarely permit actors to swing between great joy and great sorrow or great shock and great anger. This is unnecessary to mention when a person is alone; even when others are present, it is difficult to collect strong expressions of surprise, disgust, anger, fear, or sadness from the actor, and even hearty laughter is quite rare. However, these six basic emotions have many relatively weaker variants, listed as follows:

- Surprise is simply surprise; it has few variants and needs none.
- Variants of disgust can include nausea, aversion, dislike, contempt, distaste, scorn, and disregard, among others.
- Variants of anger can include losing one’s temper, irritation, irascibility, losing one’s cool, displeasure, seriousness, and sternness, among others.
- Variants of fear can include apprehension, worry, anxiety, unease, panic, embarrassment, concern, misgiving, and taboo, among others.
- Variants of sadness can include distress, dejection, low spirits, loss, guilt, regret, helplessness, grievance, and gloom, among others.
- Variants of pleasure can include satisfaction, smugness, happiness, joy, and excitement, among others.

Each of these emotional states may appear in relatively natural circumstances for any individual on any given day. Because there is no need for confrontation or disguise, these relatively “weaker” emotional states can serve as the actor’s emotional state baseline. Note, however, that because these states are not pure emotional states, they are very likely to be mixed with large amounts of unconscious interference, such as habit or etiquette and cultivation. When collecting emotional state baseline data, pay special attention to these interference patterns.

For example, if a person’s mouth corners are at unequal heights when genuinely smiling, that is a feature of his emotional state baseline; in future analysis it should not be identified as a smile carrying contempt.

Although collecting the emotional state baseline is relatively difficult, humans as a species have lived under highly civilized social rules for no more than 10,000 years. Millions of years of evolution have left humans, as a species, with a large number of animal habits, including common characteristics of emotional behavior. Emotion, as a single-layer logical survival strategy, drives various parts of the body to produce more primitive behaviors. These behaviors all carry physiological significance, so their patterns exhibit a high degree of stability and commonality.

Extensive scientific evidence shows that human emotional behavioral characteristics exist objectively across differences in region, race, society, education, age, and gender.

These valuable, physiologically significant characteristics are precisely the subject of this book and will be discussed chapter by chapter below.

Both the calm state baseline and the emotional state baseline can be observed and recorded from the following aspects:

- Facial features and positions of the five sense organs
- Breathing rate and amplitude
- Voice frequency and volume
- Spinal curvature morphology
- Head and chin angles
- Habitual hand positions and movements
- Standing and sitting postures
- Leg postures and angles
- Presence of prominent habitual movements, such as leg shaking or foot swinging

##### 4. Stable Social Behavioral Characteristics

Although social behavior cannot serve as an object of micro-reaction (微反应) analysis, and although countless decisions and motives lie behind social behavior, social behavior can still function as a very important behavioral baseline for analyzing abnormal reactions in an actor.

The social behavior an actor routinely displays can also be observed in the detailed aspects listed above. What distinguishes the recording of the social behavior baseline from the calm state baseline and the emotional state baseline is that the social behavior baseline records the characteristics the actor exhibits in specific social situations.

Examples include:

- The actor’s verbal and nonverbal features when speaking at a meeting
- The actor’s verbal and nonverbal features when meeting a superior
- The actor’s verbal and nonverbal features when meeting a subordinate
- The actor’s verbal and nonverbal features when reciting lines with emotion
- The actor’s verbal and nonverbal features when gossiping mysteriously
- The actor’s verbal and nonverbal features when earnestly expressing an opinion
- The actor’s verbal and nonverbal features when smugly criticizing or instructing
- The actor’s verbal and nonverbal features when defending under pressure

The behavioral characteristics the actor displays in these situations constitute the social behavior baseline. Data for the social behavior baseline are easy to obtain; once the actor produces an abnormal reaction that violates the baseline, it is relatively easy to detect. When an abnormality appears after a specific stimulus, we can quickly compare it with the calm state baseline and the emotional state baseline, search for matching characteristic clues, and then perform deduction and analysis.

Thus, when the young women mentioned earlier sense that their boyfriends are “acting strangely somewhere,” it is mostly because the boyfriends’ reactions have violated their own social behavior baselines. Those strange places are usually emotional behaviors governed by emotion; following the patterns, one can identify which emotional attribute is involved. Finally, linking the possible stimulus source may establish a clear causal connection.

Love requires honesty and a sense of harmony. Technical analysis carries risks; regardless of whether the analysis is right or wrong, merely entertaining the idea of analysis means you have already lost. However,

when encountering swindlers or scoundrels, one should certainly arm oneself with science to avoid being deceived.

These two lines of program language are entirely fabricated and do not necessarily conform to any programming syntax; they are intended only to express rigid judgment criteria.

##### An Elegant Woman Who Lied

We have tested many people whose baseline for left-right eye movement differs. Currently, the more common indicator of lying is movement that violates the personal baseline.

One test subject was a very elegant woman who answered questions calmly throughout the test; subsequent analysis confirmed that the vast majority of her statements were truthful. When faced with stressful questions (those requiring choice or recall), her habitual baseline for gaze shift was to the right. Whether the task involved complex calculations (left-brain), visual-spatial puzzles (right-brain), or recounting how she had accumulated wealth through shrewd investments, whenever she needed to think of an appropriate way to phrase her answer, her gaze moved right.

Yet on one question alone she lied.

When we asked whether she strongly disliked a certain female friend (a specific individual), her eyes rapidly shifted left by approximately three-quarters of an iris diameter, after which she calmly denied it; no other obvious indicators appeared.

Given this anomalous gaze shift (different from baseline), we temporarily added two test questions.

1. Picture test: We prepared ten image sets, including neutral landscape images (mobile communication base stations, overhead traffic shots of normal vehicles, regional maps), positive stimulus images (a male singer she liked), actual partial anatomical photographs of corpses, and a photograph of that female friend. When she saw the male singer’s photograph, her pupils dilated. After transition through neutral images, the sudden appearance of the female friend’s photograph caused her pupils to constrict.
2. We asked her to describe and evaluate a certain matter concerning that female friend in detail. During the description and evaluation, a micro-expression of contempt appeared on her face (contempt is a derivative emotion of disgust).

From these two results we inferred that she harbored feelings of disgust toward that person. Therefore, when she flatly denied her disgust, the cognitive pressure produced the anomalous gaze shift. It can be confirmed that she lied on this question.

##### Facial Expressions That Lag Half a Beat

Generally, when a person lies, they try to smile, nod, and blink in an attempt to conceal their inner activity. Psychological research shows, however, that facial features are difficult to control completely. When lying, the entire face briefly freezes; this process lasts roughly two to three seconds.

If you are observant, you will notice that many liars exhibit similar behavior.

Scene one: A comedian guest on a talk show tells a short joke on the spot. After listening, the host bursts out laughing and says, “That joke was really funny.”

Scene two: A comedian guest on a talk show tells a short joke on the spot. After listening, the host says, “That joke was really funny,” and then laughs.

Which scene, then, expresses the host’s true thoughts? The first one, of course. In the second scene the host is merely humoring the guest.

In other words, if an expression is not heartfelt, it often appears obviously belated and mechanical or stiff. For example, when a door-to-door salesman is asked, “Can you provide a one-year warranty?” if he nods first and then says “Yes,” he is telling the truth. If he first answers, “Um… yes, don’t worry,” and only afterward nods, you should doubt the truth of his words.

##### Question 8: What Is a Baseline?

Whether behavioral analysis possesses powerful efficacy depends on one very important precondition—whether performance behavior can be filtered.

Suppose an intelligent program could tell with 100 percent accuracy whether a person is performing. When interacting with others, wouldn’t it feel much easier if the program’s prompt came through your earpiece—“He is genuine” or “He is performing”—and you could feel as though you could see through every hypocrisy as if you were a god?

In any case, I would hope everyone would stop deceiving, would be straightforward, and would be candid with one another. That way, at least one would not have to guess back and forth only to guess wrong and suffer loss.

Yet in reality, even parents dealing with young children who do not yet understand will kindly try to make the “most reasonable” expression rather than say 100 percent of what they think, let alone two people who meet by chance in society.

As long as a person’s behavioral motivation contains a decision component of “this is the best way to act,” performance is inevitable, but performance does not always stem from malicious motives or produce malicious results.

The task of studying micro-reactions does not include judging good or bad; it only seeks to find the differences between expression and cognition and the patterns that exist within them. To accomplish this task, one must begin with a single step—finding the baseline—and this step cannot be bypassed.

Strictly speaking, any analysis without a baseline is mere grandstanding.

##### What Is a Baseline?

A simple example: suppose a person never blinks when telling the truth but always blinks rapidly ten times in succession when lying. These two fixed patterns would constitute the actor’s two baselines. When you see the person not blinking, you know they are telling the truth; when you see ten consecutive blinks, they are lying. If the number of blinks falls between one and nine, neither baseline is matched, so no judgment is made.

You may think such fixed baselines cannot possibly exist.

Indeed, for humans this is merely an impossible example; do not take it seriously, although many research institutions continue to search for formulas of the type [xx behavioral feature = lying]. Such stable judgment criteria can appear only in computer program responses, because programmers set rules such as:

```
if a=not blinking then print true;
if a=blinking 10 times then print false
```

Humans, however, do have baselines.

**Baseline** refers to the behavioral characteristics an actor possesses when not “acting,” and mainly includes the following aspects:

##### 2. Calm State Baseline

Behavioral characteristics in a calm state. When a person is neither flamboyant nor dejected, neither excited nor low-spirited—in other words, in a relaxed state—what their speech, manner, facial expressions, breathing, voice, and body movements look like can serve as a baseline and may be called the “calm state baseline.”

A completely relaxed state occurs in two situations: when alone or when in a safe and relaxed social environment. Behavioral characteristics when alone are difficult for outsiders to observe; unless secretly recorded, they remain unknown. In a safe and relaxed social environment, the actor will display the above baseline only when everyone present is someone the actor does not need to “worry about” and can fully trust.

Obtaining these baseline characteristics usually requires prolonged observation rather than a single session. Many young women have this feeling about their boyfriends—“I just feel something is off with him today; something must be up.” In professional terms, this “something is off” feeling is usually “capturing behavioral features that violate the baseline,” except that the young women have not studied micro-reactions and therefore cannot accurately and clearly enumerate these features.

##### Identifying the Other Party’s Lies Through Facial Expressions

Micro-expression keywords: Although liars can make their words seamless, that does not mean others will be deceived. The liar’s facial expressions will betray them; language can be controlled, but facial expressions are difficult to control. To determine whether someone is lying, simply look at their facial expressions.

Is the person lying? Often this cannot be discerned from words alone. People whose speech is more eloquent than singing are unreliable, and even those universally regarded as “honest” sometimes lie. So how does one judge whether someone is lying? The first thing to do is look at their facial expressions.

Liars deliberately control both their words and their facial expressions. Generally, these are the two aspects the conversational partners pay special attention to. Yet disguising words is easy—just prepare in advance—whereas concealing facial expressions is not easy.

##### Principle

When facts must be concealed or details fabricated, the person must think with all their might. At the same time, they cannot produce obvious reactions such as prolonged eye closure or staring blankly at one spot, because such reactions would be too conspicuous. At this moment the negative stimulus from the question is strong; even if the questioner is handsome, they become an unwelcome negative stimulus source. Combined with the brain’s need to laboriously conceal and fabricate, the result is an increase in blink rate.

Note that this section examines high-frequency blinking in isolation; in practice, increased blink rate is usually accompanied by simultaneous gaze shifts. Gaze-shift issues are discussed in a later dedicated section.

##### 1. Physical Examination Indicators

These are purely physiological baselines. Values within the normal range indicate health; values outside the normal reference range indicate pathology. If a person’s white blood cell count on a second physical examination is higher than on the first and exceeds the normal reference range, the person may be ill.
