### Eyes and Mouth in Deception

#### Can a Smile Hide a Lie

Micro-expression keywords: When lying, people feel guilty and will deliberately try to please you to lower your guard. A smile is a very good method. However, they do not know whether the smile comes from the heart or is an attempt to cover up a lie; some people can tell at a glance.

Generally, people think smiles show friendliness and happiness. Smiles are very common in life: you see colleagues smiling at work, waiters smiling while eating, and if lucky on the bus, the conductor smiling…

Have you ever wondered how many of these smiles come from the heart? Are all smiles sincere? The answer is: Not all smiles are sincere! Beneath a smiling face, lies may also be hidden!

Xiao Qing is a new employee with a strong sense of responsibility. Not long after joining the company, she discovered various problems in management. Xiao Qing mustered the courage to knock on her supervisor’s office door and offered many reasonable suggestions for improving the company’s internal situation. After she finished speaking in one breath, the supervisor smiled and told her: “Your suggestions are very good. I will discuss these issues with senior leadership.”

However, after a long time, the problems Xiao Qing raised were not improved. She could not figure out why the supervisor thought her opinions made sense but delayed giving feedback.

A study by French scientist Guillaume Duchenne de Boulogne might provide the answer.

Guillaume’s research found that human smiles are controlled by two sets of muscles. The first set is the muscles at the zygomatic bone, which can slightly part the mouth, pull the lips back to reveal teeth, lift the face, and then extend the smile to the corners of the eyes. We can freely control the zygomatic muscles to produce a false smile.

The second set of muscles is in the eye area, which can contract the muscles, making the eyes smaller and producing “crow’s feet” at the corners. These muscles are not under our conscious voluntary control. The smile they produce is generally a genuine one.

When Xiao Qing’s supervisor smiled, there were no crow’s feet at the corners of his eyes, meaning he did not agree with Xiao Qing’s suggestions. He said those words only to avoid discouraging her enthusiasm.

So, what kind of smile is sincere?

A few days later, employee Dong Wen also entered the supervisor’s office. He had prepared an excellent promotional plan for a new product.

Let’s look at the supervisor’s reaction:

While Dong Wen was demonstrating the promotional renderings, the supervisor nodded while watching. The smile spread from the corners of his mouth, and as the smile grew wider, the crow’s feet at the corners of his eyes accumulated more and more. Finally, after Dong Wen finished speaking, the supervisor laughed heartily, patted his shoulder, and said: “Well done, we’ll go with your plan!”

Which smile is more sincere? Clearly, the one for employee Dong Wen.

Comparing them, this smile showed crow’s feet. It indicates that both the mouth and eye muscles were engaged, especially the eye muscles, which are not under our conscious voluntary control. That is, only smiles with crow’s feet at the eyes are genuine, heartfelt smiles.

Now we should be clear. A smile cannot hide a lie. If the smile only involves the mouth muscles, then the smile is not genuine; the facial expression will look stiff. At this point, no matter what he says next, it is best to weigh whether it is true or false.

If, when smiling, not only does the mouth open, but the crow’s feet at the corners of the eyes are also squeezed out, the expression will look very natural. Such a smile must be genuine; he agrees with what you said, so he will inevitably tell you the truth.

#### Liars Often Touch Their Noses

**Micro-expression keywords** When people lie, they feel pressure. This causes cells inside the nasal cavity to swell and blood pressure to rise, creating an itchy sensation in the nose. As a result, people frequently touch their noses to relieve the symptom. Therefore, if you see someone touching their nose frequently while speaking, do not readily believe what they say.

In episode eleven of the American drama *Lie to Me*, a lying concealment gesture appears: rubbing a finger against the side of the nose.

After watching the show, a wife secretly observed and analyzed her husband’s tone, movements, and expressions when he spoke to her, trying to determine whether he was lying.

One Friday, her husband called to say he had to work overtime, but he hesitated while speaking. She knew he was lying but wanted to find out what he was hiding. She pretended to agree, then waited downstairs at his company and secretly followed him. As it turned out, after work her husband went to a gathering with a group of “questionable friends.”

When he returned home that evening, the wife pretended to know nothing. She took his hand and asked: “Was it very hard today? Did you finish your work?” Her husband touched his nose and said: “I work hard so you can have a better life; it’s not hard.”

People usually touch their noses when lying. Why? Scientists at the Smell & Taste Treatment and Research Foundation in Chicago may have the answer.

Their research found that when people lie, a chemical called catecholamine is released, causing cells inside the nasal cavity to swell. Using special imaging equipment that displays internal blood flow, the scientists also revealed that blood pressure rises due to lying. The technology showed that the nose enlarges during lying because of increased blood flow. The rise in blood pressure causes the nose to swell, triggering nerve endings in the nasal cavity to send out an itchy sensation. People then frequently touch their noses with their hands to soothe the itch.

This is the famous **Pinocchio Effect**.

Although people cannot see the nasal blood vessels swell, they can see the gesture of a liar touching the nose. It is easy to conclude that the person is lying.

Two well-known neurologists closely studied video footage of former U.S. President Bill Clinton testifying before a jury in the Lewinsky scandal. They found that Clinton rarely touched his nose when telling the truth, but whenever he lied, his brow would unconsciously furrow slightly before the lie left his mouth, and he touched his nose once every four minutes, reaching a total of 26 touches during the testimony! This strongly confirms the saying “liars touch their noses.”

When lying, the nose-touching gesture is usually a quick rub or two with the hand along the underside of the nose, sometimes so light it is almost imperceptible. Women perform this gesture with smaller movements than men.

Of course, not every nose-touching action means the person is lying. When someone is anxious or angry, the blood vessels in the nose can also swell and produce the same gesture. Sometimes people make the movement simply because of a cold, pollen allergy, or to wipe something off the nose.

Determining whether someone is lying also requires combining other lying indicators. For example, because lying requires improvising language, speech may become hesitant; some people pause or frown; others blush. As long as you observe carefully, these small details will not escape your eyes, and knowing whether someone is lying becomes much easier.

#### Frequent Blinking Indicates Lying

**Micro-expression keywords** Blinking effectively avoids direct eye contact with others. For a liar, this is the best way to conceal a lie. When you see someone blinking frequently, they are likely avoiding your gaze, meaning they are lying to you!

Before leaving work, the supervisor asked the secretary to write an important report. Because it was the secretary’s birthday and she had been celebrating with friends, she completely forgot the important task. The next day, when the supervisor asked for the report, the secretary rummaged through her bag and finally pretended to be anxious, saying: “Oh no, I forgot to bring the USB drive with the file.”

As soon as the supervisor heard this, he knew the secretary was lying with her eyes open. The secretary did not even own a USB drive; she had asked him a few days earlier to buy one. Moreover, he noticed that while speaking, the secretary kept blinking at a faster rate than usual.

Psychological research shows that a person’s normal blink rate is 30–50 times per minute. When under heavy pressure that feels unbearable, the blink rate increases noticeably. Because lying unconsciously increases psychological pressure, the blink frequency speeds up. From this, the supervisor confidently concluded that the secretary was lying.

Besides this reason, rapid blinking also helps avoid direct eye contact with the other person. When lying, people feel guilty and dare not look the other person in the eye, fearing their inner panic will be seen through. Yet if they turn their head away, the liar worries the movement is too obvious and will be detected. Rapid blinking allows them to avoid the other person’s gaze without drawing attention.

In movies or TV dramas, we often see scenes like this:

A judge sternly interrogates a prisoner: “What did you do last night?”

The prisoner lowers his head and says: “I didn’t go anywhere last night; I stayed home watching TV.”

This happens because when a person lies, they feel guilty and subconsciously avoid direct eye contact. This reduces pressure and allows the lie to be spoken. Conversely, if telling the truth, the person dares to look the other person straight in the eye, as if challenging: “I’m telling the truth; why should I fear you? If you don’t believe me, go investigate.”

In daily life, we also notice that when someone is preparing or delivering a lie, they often blink, lower their head, or make other unnatural movements. For example, when a teacher asks a student why homework is unfinished, the student may first lower their head to think, or blink a few times, then invent an excuse hoping to escape punishment.

This action signals guilt.

Often, like the secretary in the earlier example, many people will lie to your face with their eyes open. Detecting the lie is very easy because the eyes cannot deceive. A liar dares not look others in the eye, so they choose to blink rapidly or turn their head away, subconsciously hiding their gaze.

However, not all blinking means lying. If someone deliberately prolongs a blink in front of you, it simply means they are not interested in what you are saying and hope the conversation ends soon. If their eyes close for two or three seconds before reopening, it means they truly cannot tolerate the boring conversation and wish you would disappear from their sight immediately. At that point, you need to adjust your topic or simply walk away.

Only when the blink rate is faster than usual does it indicate the person is lying. Therefore, when observing, we must distinguish clearly and avoid wrongly accusing an innocent person.

#### The Glib Tongue

The tongue’s role in micro-expressions is not obvious. When nervous, lips become dry, and the tongue must lick the lips to relieve dryness while also soothing inner unease. Yet nervousness does not appear only when lying; it also arises when people feel suspected. Therefore, the tongue alone cannot determine whether someone is lying.

Still, when combined with other micro-expressions, changes in the tongue are worth noting. When a lie is exposed, a person feels enormous pressure, leading to sweating, flushed face, dry lips, and other signs; licking the lips becomes a remedy for relieving tension.

A man who claimed to have been a middle manager at a Fortune 500 company applied for a position at a medium-sized firm. When the interviewer asked why he left such a good job, he said the company’s philosophy did not align with his, so he decided to leave in search of a better platform. The interviewer then told him the company already knew some basic facts about him, including the real reason for his departure. At that moment he began to fidget and showed a fleeting expression of surprise. He quickly licked his lips and started defending himself. It turned out he had been fired for leaking company secrets to a competitor. The surprised expression showed he had not expected an interviewer at a medium-sized company to know these details; licking his lips indicated his inner tension and desire to quickly escape the awkward situation.

Of course, tongue changes alone do not prove lying. Consider this case:

Candidates facing a major exam are often mentally tense. When time is nearly up and some questions remain unanswered, they may sweat, feel cold hands, breathe rapidly, or even feel dizzy. At such moments the tongue tries to relieve tension in its small way by licking the lips.

Besides licking the lips, the tongue may occasionally expose its tip, which is what we commonly call sticking out the tongue. When we say the wrong thing in public, we may stick out our tongue; this not only relieves tension but also represents the brain’s attempt to expel the mistaken words. People sometimes show the tip of the tongue when surprised—for example, when unexpectedly winning an award. During live award-show broadcasts, we may see this: an actress who wins Best Actress opens her eyes wide in surprise and also gives a cute little tongue protrusion. Of course, this situation is uncommon. Not every tongue protrusion signals tension or excitement; children making faces stick out their tongues, and some people do it habitually. Certain athletes, such as basketball or soccer players, stick out their tongues after missing or scoring a goal; some do it as an expression of outgoing personality that becomes their signature move, while others do it because they are so focused they pay no attention to the tongue. Jordan would give a slight tongue protrusion when dunking; that was a sign of intense concentration.

Although the tongue, unlike other micro-expressions, cannot directly help expose lies, it at least reflects the person’s current mental state and provides auxiliary clues for other micro-expressions. However, interpreting what the tongue means requires considering the actual context, the individual’s personality, and behavioral habits. Judging solely by one facial detail always carries the possibility of error.

#### He Should Not Know This Secret

In the skit *The Policeman and the Thief* by Chen Peisi and Zhu Shimao, there is this scene:

Chen Peisi, playing the thief, is keeping watch at the alley entrance for his accomplice who is committing a crime when he happens to encounter Zhu Shimao, playing the policeman on patrol.

Zhu Shimao asks: “What are you doing here?”  
Chen Peisi replies: “I’m keeping watch.”  
Realizing he has let it slip, he immediately covers his mouth with his hand and corrects himself: “Ah, no, I’m just hanging around.”

Why did Chen Peisi instinctively cover his mouth? In his heart he was thinking: “He must not know this secret!”

When you are talking with someone, if the other person stops midway through speaking, or has only just begun, and then instinctively covers their mouth, it may mean they are unwilling to tell you this matter but have already blurted out half of it without thinking.

In such cases, do not believe what they say after covering their mouth; that is likely a lie they just made up. Only what they said before covering their mouth—the words that slipped out unintentionally—is credible.

Moreover, no matter what the other person says, and no matter how surprising the secret is, you must act uninterested. This will put the other person at ease, and the subsequent conversation will proceed more smoothly. Otherwise, they may dwell on the regret of having let the secret slip and will no longer engage seriously with you, rendering the conversation pointless.

#### How to Tell If He’s Lying During an Interview

The definition of micro-expression is “suppressed emotions, subtle facial movements that disappear in an instant like lightning.” When it comes to using micro-expressions, the first thing that comes to mind is “seeing through lies”! Because micro-expression detection techniques are related to lie detection techniques.

Simply put, people with higher skills in detecting micro-expressions also have high accuracy in seeing through lies. However, this does not mean that micro-expressions equal evidence of lying. What is going on here? Let’s explain step by step.

Research has found that liars tend to display more micro-expressions than truth-tellers. Among them, liars may experience emotions such as “guilt,” “distress,” “disgust,” “fear,” “secret delight,” and “contempt,” which may appear on the face as micro-expressions. Additionally, forceful movements of the upper and lower lips may also be an expression of lying. This reaction represents the message of “suppressing emotions” when about to lie and can also be thought of as a sign of feeling burdened by going against one’s true intentions.

In surveys on the frequency of micro-expressions, 51% of liars show them within 0.5 seconds, and 30% within 0.25 seconds.

#### Distinguishing Lies from Truth

How can we tell whether someone whose gaze appears steady is lying? We need to look further at their pupils! Psychological research has found that a person’s mental activity is closely related to changes in pupil size.

Teacher Zhang is an experienced homeroom teacher for ninth-grade students. Several mischievous students in the class dare not lie to Teacher Zhang because they are always found out. Teacher Zhang’s secret weapon is watching their pupils. Once, Wang Xiaomeng kicked a ball that hit another student’s eye but lied and said it was not him. Although he said this while staring straight at Teacher Zhang with righteous indignation, his pupils unconsciously dilated. Teacher Zhang naturally did not believe him; after questioning several classmates, it turned out he had not wrongly accused him.

When a person lies, they feel nervous. Stimulated by this nervousness, their pupils dilate, allowing us to conclude they are lying. Of course, not every instance of pupil dilation indicates lying; it can also occur in situations of terror, anger, or affection, so each case must be analyzed according to its specific circumstances.

#### Eyes That Convey Sincerity

When conversing with others, we need to look at them with steady eyes, but prolonged fixed staring may make the other person feel you are being overly artificial and untrustworthy. Therefore, to avoid misunderstandings, while maintaining steady eye contact, we should also coordinate with other body postures.

For example, while listening to someone speak, if you are interested in what they say, nod a few times to encourage them to continue; or offer a sincere smile; or interject some of your own thoughts. At such moments, the other person will sense your friendliness and respect.

If you are the one telling a story, to make your words more credible, begin with eye contact and then add gestures that convey confidence and affirmation. This will influence their emotions and make them firmly believe what you say.

In short, people with steady gazes may also be lying; check their pupils and other expressions to know. When communicating, avoid staring fixedly at the other person and instead coordinate with additional movements or words to express sincerity.

#### Liars Can Also Maintain Steady Eye Contact

Researchers once conducted an experiment: they gathered a group of people, divided them into two groups, and had them sit facing each other. One group was instructed to lie to the other. All expressions of the liars were recorded. The final results were surprising.

In the experiment, only about 30 percent of the liars looked away, while the other 70 percent maintained steady eye contact. They knew that shifting their gaze would reveal the lie, so they deliberately controlled their eyes and stared at the other person to avoid detection.

In reality, during or after lying, people’s gaze often drifts to the side; yet before lying, their gaze is usually very steady—partly to build their own confidence and partly to avoid arousing suspicion. Therefore, steady eye contact does not always indicate sincerity; sometimes it signals a lie.

#### What Does Scratching the Ears Mean?

Micro-expression keyword: In daily life, when we disagree with someone’s opinion, we habitually touch our ears with our hands. This is actually body language telling the other person our true inner thoughts. Therefore, adding this gesture while speaking is likely a sign that the speaker’s words do not match their true feelings.

Mother: “Xiao Ming, you’ve thrown your socks around again. Don’t you know to put them in the cabinet? Have you finished your homework? Stop watching TV—you only know how to play every day. No wonder you did so poorly on the last exam…”  
Hearing his mother’s nagging, Xiao Ming quickly covers his ears and puts on a pained expression: “Mom, please stop.”

Scenes like this are common in daily life. Covering the ears shows he does not want to hear your voice. In the adult world, people do not cover their ears but instead scratch different parts of the ear to express varying emotions and inner thoughts.

#### Eyes That Widen Then Shrink

Besides rapid blinking, the eyes have another movement that reveals the secret of lying.

Police showed a captured drug dealer a stack of photos and asked him to identify his accomplice. He looked through them one by one but refused to speak. Nevertheless, the observant officers had already noticed something in his eyes.

When he saw his accomplice’s photo, his eyes suddenly widened, then his pupils contracted rapidly and he slightly squinted. Later, during interrogation, it was confirmed that this person was also involved in drug trafficking.

Psychological principles explain that seeing his accomplice’s photo made him suddenly tense, causing his pupils to dilate involuntarily; fearing others would notice the change, he consciously squinted.

This reaction precisely revealed his inner thoughts.

#### Covering the Ear Hole with Hand or Ear

This carries the same meaning as a child covering their ears: they are directly blocking words they do not want to hear from entering. It expresses: “I don’t want to hear you continue!” At the same time, an impatient expression appears on the face.

For example, in a movie, the female lead is a chatterbox. While watching television, she often nags her husband about neighborhood gossip the moment he returns from work. The male lead has no choice but to cover his ear holes with his hands, so he sees only his wife’s mouth moving but hears no nagging.

Many people have the habit of scratching their ears, unaware that this gesture leaves an impression of tension and anxiety and may even cause the other person to misunderstand that you dislike listening or lack respect. Therefore, avoid scratching your ears unless absolutely necessary.

#### Continuously Scratching the Earlobe or Behind the Ear

This represents an anxious emotion, indicating the person is facing an unsolvable difficulty and needs help.

Xiaoyun is a very observant person who can always notice changes in people’s movements and interpret their meaning. Once, she saw her colleague Lu Chong repeatedly scratching behind his ear, so she walked over and asked if he needed assistance. It turned out Lu Chong was stuck on a programming issue and could not debug the desired result. Xiaoyun promptly helped solve the problem and earned Lu Chong’s deep gratitude.

When people feel anxious or worried, they release inner pressure by repeatedly scratching their ears. If you notice this sign and proactively offer help, you can greatly strengthen your connection with the other person.

#### Rubbing Behind the Ear

This indicates disagreement with the speaker’s viewpoint or a desire to express a different opinion. For instance, a salesperson keeps describing the benefits of a product. The customer glances at it once, then unconsciously touches behind the ear with a finger and soon says, “I’ll think about it.” This gesture means the customer dislikes the recommended item and does not want to hear more.

In everyday work and life, if you are expressing an opinion and the other person tilts their head while touching their ear, it signals that their view differs from yours and they are eager to speak. At that point, you should pause and listen to their opinion so the exchange can be productive.

#### Steady Eye Contact Does Not Necessarily Indicate Sincerity

Micro-expression keyword: When lying, do people look away? Researchers now tell us another fact: liars may also maintain steady eye contact with you! This is because they try the opposite approach to conceal their inner panic.

We all know that when lying, people instinctively look away to avoid eye contact. Does that mean steady eye contact always indicates sincerity? Probably not. Even if the other person stares fixedly at you, they may still be lying.

#### What Signal Does Covering the Mouth with the Hand Convey?

Micro-expression keyword: When people say something they should not have said, they instinctively cover their mouth to show regret or to stop themselves from continuing. This is a subconscious action that best expresses their true thoughts. Therefore, do not trust what they say afterward—it may well be a lie.

In ordinary conversation, we may notice that after finishing a sentence, the speaker suddenly covers their mouth. What does this reveal about their state of mind? Let us examine it together.

#### Detecting Signs of “Lying Micro-Expressions”

In business settings, all kinds of lies fly around. Detecting them gives one an advantage over competitors, clarifies the power structure within a company, and helps avoid falling into fraud or dubious investment pitches.

This section explains the relationship between micro-expressions and lying. Among various business lies, the most critical to a company’s survival is whether it can identify suitable talent during recruitment interviews and personnel evaluations.

#### Digging in the Ears with Fingertips

A common scene occurs when one person speaks at length while the listener appears distracted and keeps digging in their ears with a fingertip.

This gesture means the listener finds everything you say contemptible and also shows disrespect toward the speaker. At this point, stop speaking on your own and ask, “What are your insightful views on this matter?” If the other person is an elder, consider shifting to a topic that interests them.

See Part VI — Deception (p-deception).

See Part VIII — Applications (p-applications).

#### Avoiding Eye Contact

For a long time, the question of whether liars exhibit visual avoidance has also been a topic that psychologists have competed to verify. One American scholar even chose to convey the conclusions of his research through a television drama, arguing that “when people lie, they do not exhibit visual avoidance as the legend claims; instead, they tend to look at the other person more often in order to observe the other party’s reaction (whether the lie was believed).”

In reality, this question can never yield a single, uniform conclusion.

Human diversity ensures that the answer to the question above must also be diverse. When most people improvise a lie, they fear being seen through or exposed; under effective stimulation (such as interrogation), they will shift their gaze, consistent with the pattern we have summarized. See Figure 3-6.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图3-6　视线转移]*

But what if the person has come prepared? What if the lie has already been planned in advance?

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图3-7　视觉关注]*

Such a person will carry out the pre-formulated plan methodically, hoping to see what effect the lie may produce and to observe the questioner’s reaction so as to make the next deceptive move. Even after believing the deception has succeeded, the individual may take pleasure in watching the opponent’s interesting expression upon being duped. Even when faced with questions, this type of person feels no surprise; whether or not the questions were anticipated, they can respond calmly, think clearly, and gradually draw the questioner into the complex trap they have set, then watch with a smile as the opponent is brought under control. See Figure 3-7.

Do you suppose such people would seek comfort through visual avoidance?

The answer is no.

The reason these skilled liars display reactions that deviate from the visual-comfort pattern is not that they are extraordinary individuals, but simply that they experience no discomfort. This only indicates that the stimulus source is insufficiently effective.

If one can analyze the subject’s personality traits and behavioral patterns, anticipate possible countermeasures against testing, and deliver effective surprise stimuli during the examination, even the most skilled individual will still exhibit visual-comfort reactions—only the degree will vary (those with strong psychological control can quickly suppress or alter their responses).

At present, investigations and interrogations in anti-corruption and bribery cases confront such suspects every day. When confronted with sharp questions and solid evidence, suspects will still shift their gaze for self-comfort, just like ordinary people.

Of course, we must acknowledge that gaze shifting cannot serve as a necessary condition for determining deception. Many factors can cause gaze shifting—thinking, fatigue, or simply a purposeless movement. Gaze shifting is not the same as gaze avoidance; one may also look away briefly to rest the eyes on something pleasant. Even when gaze avoidance can be confirmed, one must still analyze what the stimulus source is and what type of person the subject is.

Gaze avoidance while watching a surgical procedure cannot be taken as a deceptive reaction, because the stimulus source has nothing to do with lying; moreover, most people would avert their eyes in that situation, yet surgeons would not, because those images are professional rather than frightening to them. This example shows that the absence of visual avoidance likewise cannot prove that the subject is not lying.

Therefore, when gaze shifting is observed, we must take a further step to determine whether it constitutes visual comfort. If analysis establishes that the gaze avoidance arises from seeking comfort after a negative stimulus, and that the negative stimulus source is related to content about which the subject may be lying (attempting to conceal or fabricate), then the clue is valuable and warrants deeper investigation.

See Part VI — Deception (p-deception).

See Part VI — Deception (p-deception).

#### Lip Comfort Reactions

##### The Outcome of Deliberately Lying to Counter the Test

We once tested a very interesting person. This person was interesting because, before the test, we had no information about the test subject, not even basic information like their name. This kind of test without any reason, purely for testing purposes, is technically called a “no-cause test.”

Before the test started, the test questions were designed on the spot. Because it was a no-cause test, the questions were all quite conventional, such as whether they smoke, drink, their romantic experiences and feelings, and so on. Unexpectedly, the test subject showed obvious reactions to almost every question, many of which were later proven to be deliberate performances intended to test our professional level.

Among them, three consecutive questions were designed regarding whether they drink alcohol.

The first question was, “Have you ever drunk beer?”

The other party answered, “I don’t drink.”

We followed up, “Not drinking isn’t a reasonable reason; describe it specifically.”

The other party pursed their lips and then answered, “I drank it when I was very young; it was too bitter, I didn’t like it, so I don’t drink.”

It should be noted that test subjects generally position themselves as disadvantaged. If telling the truth, they feel fulfilled and confident inside, with nothing to feel guilty about; if lying, they subconsciously fear being exposed, and when thinking about the question, they are easily guided by the tester.

In the previous example, if they had insisted on saying they “don’t drink,” there wouldn’t have been any obvious flaws. But when we gave them a guide, they started running in that direction themselves, and running like that makes it easy to trip.

Hearing them start running along the direction we guided, we knew that this question could be dug deeper.

So we continued, “Please list three differences between A beer and B beer.” A and B are both well-known domestic brands, common in northern regions.

The test subject thought laboriously for a few seconds and began to try saying, “I’m not very clear; the taste, price, and consumer groups are different, but they’re all bitter, for sure.”

Actually, how this question is answered isn’t important; what’s important is to put pressure on the other party and expose flaws.

Assuming you are the one taking this test, what would be your first reaction upon hearing this question?

1. If you are someone who drinks beer and knows these two brands, wouldn’t you have already started thinking about the differences between them?
2. If you really haven’t touched alcohol for most of your life, even if you drank a little when very young, wouldn’t you directly say “I don’t know”? I think so, because you really don’t know and don’t care about this question.
3. But if you are someone who drinks and are trying to lie to me that you don’t drink. In such a situation, what would you think upon hearing this question? Would you dare to directly say “I don’t know”? Especially after just changing your story?

So, seeing their response like that, the lying behavior was already quite obvious.

We waited for them to finish speaking and immediately followed up with the last question: “Explain the specific reasons for not drinking.”

The comfort reaction appeared at this moment.

This is a manifestation of increased psychological discomfort. The reason is that the intensity of the stimulus source increased, making it difficult for the actor: on one hand, they have to fabricate reasons, and on the other, they worry about the lie being exposed.

The test subject began to involuntarily scratch their face, of course lightly, but for a long time (several seconds). During this period, they had to think carefully again about how to fabricate a reasonable reason for not drinking.

This is quite a long story; the “face-scratching” reaction only appeared once, seemingly not the focus. However, the interlocking, layer-by-layer questioning made the intensity of the stimulus source continuously increase. When the test subject felt enormous pressure and discomfort, they would use such actions to comfort themselves and slightly relax their tense nerves. Although initially, they hoped to interfere with our test through deliberate confrontation.

##### 3.3.3 Swallowing Saliva

Swallowing food is even less likely to appear during lie detection than chewing, and if actual food is swallowed, the action has no analytical or evaluative value. However, saliva can be swallowed without food, and the act of swallowing saliva is more suspicious and carries greater analytical value. See Figures 3-15 and 3-16.

**Figures 3-15, 3-16 Swallowing Actions**

You can try it yourself: under normal circumstances, deliberately swallowing saliva once—especially when there is little or no saliva—remains a relatively complex and effortful action because it involves coordinated movement of the mouth, tongue, throat, and esophagus (which you cannot feel).

When receiving negative stimuli, a test subject may unconsciously perform this complex set of movements to obtain comfort. Yet the behavior may not be consciously perceived by the actor. The swallowing action signals the central nervous system: “I am eating; I have taken something in,” thereby attempting to ease the tense nervous system.

Standard lie-detection manuals often conclude that people who swallow saliva are mostly in a state of fear, and experimental data support this view. In reality, the emotions that can trigger swallowing are not limited to fear; they may also include sexual arousal or appetite. Therefore, the stimulus source that elicits the swallow must be considered when attributing the reaction.

When analyzing swallowing, pay special attention to three timings:

1. When the subject hears a key question—that is, the critical information from the stimulus source;
2. Before the subject prepares to answer;
3. After the subject answers.

Saliva accumulation in the mouth requires three conditions: a specific duration, abnormal saliva secretion, and deviation from the usual swallowing frequency (for example, being too busy to swallow). Consequently, saliva swallowing under the following three circumstances deserves particular attention and may hold significant value:

- The interval since the previous swallow is short, or swallows occur consecutively; this violates physiological norms and can be identified as a comfort reaction indicating tension.
- Increased saliva secretion is a prerequisite for swallowing. Increased secretion results from parasympathetic excitation, a phenomenon that occurs when a person is relaxed. If the actor has been displaying excitement, tension, effort, or agitation, a subsequent swallow may instead stem from thirst caused by reduced saliva, which can be suspected as a comfort reaction mapping to tension.
- Extended speaking leaves no opportunity for normal-frequency swallowing, so a swallow after finishing speech is normal. Conversely, if speech content is brief yet a swallow follows, the action can be suspected as a comfort reaction indicating tension. If a swallow is also observed before speech, it can be classified as a comfort reaction indicating tension.

##### 3.4 Skin Comfort

Among comfort reactions, visual, auditory, and lip-related comfort reactions are truly “micro” reactions (微反应). The most numerous and obvious behaviors are comfort actions directed at the skin. When these obvious macro reactions appear, the actor is unaware of them, giving them valuable interpretive significance.

Skin is the body’s largest organ, responsible for protecting the body from external invasion, receiving tactile information such as pressure, temperature, and friction, and expelling sweat. Appropriate temperature, humidity, pressure, and frequency produce sensations of comfort, warmth, and safety.

Many people do not realize that during embryonic development, neural tissue and skin tissue both originate from the ectoderm. Because of this natural “common origin,” clinical medicine has confirmed that mood affects skin health. Emotions such as tension and anxiety can trigger stress responses or endocrine dysfunction, prompting blood-vessel walls or tissue cells to release mediators such as bradykinin and histamine; these substances can induce or aggravate existing skin conditions. For example, competitive, high-desire, or overly conscientious individuals are prone to neurodermatitis; those under prolonged suppression or unfulfilled desires are prone to chronic urticaria.

Conversely, stimuli applied to the skin exert a very important influence on the nervous system and psychological state. Comfortable stimuli improve neural perception, while painful or thermal stimuli generate negative neural assessments.

Skin, densely populated with nerve endings and fibers, can transmit large amounts of stimulation back to the central nervous system. Comfortable stimuli (such as caresses) produce pleasure; negative stimuli (such as pain) produce alertness and prompt immediate adjustments to escape them. Because the central nervous system in turn acts on the skin (as noted earlier, via endocrine and microcirculatory effects) and because of long-term conditioned reflexes, the nervous system objectively creates “skin hunger.” These two mutually reinforcing interactions lead people to learn to relieve nervous tension and discomfort by comforting the skin.

In childhood, a mother’s caresses not only make a child feel comfortable and safe but also shape good character and psychology. In adulthood, skin contact with a partner expresses genuine affection. In old age, massage or washing by children or emotionally close individuals prevents eccentricity and promotes cheerfulness.

In daily work, life, and social interactions, people also unconsciously follow this pattern. During criminal investigations, when a test subject is being interrogated and receives negative stimuli, fear of losing benefits or punishment can produce worry, fear, anxiety, embarrassment, or anger. To mask these emotions, the subject often uses skin-directed comfort actions to alleviate them.

##### 3.3.2 Chewing and Its Variant Actions

Chewing and swallowing directly convey “eating” information to the central nervous system. Having something to eat is always good because it means survival without starvation. Long-term evolution has made the central nervous system consistently satisfied with—and pleased by—the act of eating. This is why overeating can improve mood to some extent when one feels down. The early film *Love on a Diet* starring Andy Lau and Sammi Cheng illustrates this “scientific” phenomenon.

During lie detection, actual eating rarely occurs. Some test protocols do arrange meals in advance to calm the subject and build a sense of security and rapport, but that belongs to test-protocol research and is outside the scope of this chapter.

In actual testing, what appears more often are variants of the “eating” action, mainly teeth grinding, chewing (usually gum), and swallowing saliva. When feasible, smoking and drinking water may also be permitted.

In tests we have conducted, subjects facing difficult questions (those requiring lies) sometimes exhibited teeth-grinding: opening the mouth and rubbing the upper and lower teeth together, usually the canines. See Figure 3-14.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: Figure 3-14 Teeth-grinding action]*

This action can make the facial expression appear threatening and can therefore also be interpreted from a micro-expression perspective. However, the friction between the canines sends the central nervous system the implicit message: “I am a predator tearing at prey (food); there is no need to worry—everything is under control and I am in a dominant position.” Consequently, the action substantially relieves nervous tension caused by negative stimuli and provides comfort.

If the subject is chewing gum or betel nut, observe the frequency and force of chewing. Upon an unexpected stimulus, chewing may pause—this is a typical freeze response. Upon a negative stimulus, the subject may feel restless or at a loss and intensify thinking and effort; during this process, chewing frequency and force may increase in an attempt to relieve nervous tension. The key is to observe change. If the subject has been chewing rapidly or forcefully all along, that may simply be personal habit (baseline) and cannot serve as a judgment criterion. Only changes triggered by stimuli constitute potentially valuable reaction cues.

##### 3.3.1 Lip Actions

When nervous, blood circulation accelerates in densely innervated areas to supply more energy, raising temperature and causing faster moisture loss from the skin surface.

Lips are such an organ.

When feeling uneasy, lips tend to become dry, prompting licking, pursing, or lightly biting the lips. Liars with weaker psychological resilience are prone to this sensation. Relieving lip discomfort and making this highly sensitive organ more comfortable correspondingly improves the overall state of the nervous system and yields substantial comfort. See Figures 3-10, 3-11, 3-12, and 3-13.

**Figures 3-10, 3-11, 3-12, 3-13 Lip Comfort Actions**

Although these small lip-related actions appear common and inadvertent, when they occur after a negative stimulus or after the actor has uttered a suspicious statement, they acquire value as suspicious cues.

Generally, self-comfort actions targeting the lips can be triggered by sexual impulses, appetite impulses, or basic physiological desires.

For example, light lip-licking reactions are frequently observed in the following question-and-answer scenarios.

When asking adolescents or post-adolescents, “What kind of person of the opposite sex do you like most?” or “What part of him/her (the idol) do you like most?”, subjects still sensitive to the opposite sex often exhibit lip-licking before answering.

Why do such questions count as negative stimuli that elicit comfort reactions?

Revealing one’s preferences regarding the opposite sex to the questioner means disclosing private information under non-injurious pressure. This privacy touches the root of one’s sexual impulses and, in modern society, is largely restricted by social norms and not to be discussed openly; hence it produces mild discomfort.

Another reason is that in the pairing of liking and being liked, the person who likes another is psychologically in a weaker position, and acknowledging that liking intensifies the sense of weakness.

##### 3.4.4 Derived Skin Comfort

The comfort reactions described above can also generate numerous variant forms, mostly reductions or deformations. Common examples include:

- Covering or grasping a necklace pendant
- Adjusting an earring (stud)
- Adjusting one’s collar (or tie)

More covert variant actions directed at chest and abdominal skin include grasping the collar or chest clothing and shaking it back and forth a few times to “ventilate.” This objectively induces microcirculation of the air surrounding the clothed body; sensitive skin registers the gentle airflow as comfortable, reducing tension while also lowering body temperature elevated by blood pooling.

Seemingly inadvertent actions that appear after a key question possess important investigative value. On one hand, they divert the person’s attention away from intense negative thoughts; on the other, they objectively soothe tense nerves.

Such reactions vary widely and are too numerous to list exhaustively. They share two uniform characteristics:

1. They are unrelated to the content being expressed and constitute “extra” actions.
2. They produce a physiological soothing effect.

Any small action possessing both characteristics is a comfort reaction. Its essence is the use of physiological comfort to regulate psychological discomfort in an attempt to reverse an unfavorable situation.

Note that not every test subject will frequently display such abrupt small actions. Professionally trained actors with performance experience produce no superfluous movements during performance; the audience sees only the role and the emotion. Performance training is a form of professional training. Ordinary people, when performing in front of an audience, frequently produce small actions involuntarily—that is, the micro-reactions (微反应) we discuss—which soothe their tense nerves and make them feel more at ease. Consequently, professionally trained individuals may exhibit very few small actions when tested.

##### 3.4.3 Torso-directed Comfort

Similar to facial comfort, when feeling discomfort, actors may also perform comfort actions on the torso and limbs—chest, abdomen, arms, thighs—such as lightly patting the chest, rubbing the abdomen, or rubbing the thighs, in an attempt to self-regulate, reverse the situation, and divert the other party’s attention.

Facial comfort reactions carry greater significance because, under normal circumstances, actors do not lose control to the point of touching and comforting the face; this usually indicates that the psychological stimulus is severe.

Although chest and abdominal skin is covered by clothing and less directly accessible to effective stimuli, its internal organs are vulnerable; evolutionary adaptation has rendered this skin region highly sensitive to better protect the fragile viscera. Consequently, actions applied to this skin area also produce good comfort effects<|eos|>

##### Chapter Summary

Comfort responses (安慰反应) have two essential characteristics: first, the actions are unrelated to verbal expression and serve no auxiliary semantic function; second, the actions allow the actor to feel comfortable.

In many speaking situations, hand, foot, and body postures can assist in conveying the speaker’s meaning, attitude, and stance—for example, indicating quantity, describing size or amount, sequencing items, pointing to locations, or vividly illustrating feelings (such as “my head is exploding”). These movements belong to social behavior and function as linguistic aids; they carry no evidential value.

However, when language and movement are unconnected, the actions merit attention. If the movements provide the actor with comfort relative to the prevailing emotion, they qualify as comfort responses.

Examples include:

- Rubbing the nose produces a physiologically comforting effect unrelated to expression and unrelated to any medical condition (such as rhinitis or nasal congestion from a cold), and therefore qualifies as a comfort response.
- Scratching the scalp produces a physiologically comforting effect unrelated to expression and unrelated to any medical condition (dirt, itching, headache, etc.), and therefore qualifies as a comfort response.
- When a person is emotionally distressed or agitated, slapping their own face can discharge emotion and shift pain, yielding a physiologically comforting effect unrelated to expression; it therefore qualifies as a comfort response even though the action would normally cause pain.

Kicking a wall corner, bumping the back, kneading the arms, smelling perfume, licking the lips, chewing gum, needing a drink, smoking, and similar actions meet both criteria and are comfort responses.

**Classic manifestations**: covering the mouth after a slip of the tongue, rubbing the nose while stammering, wringing the hands while nervously anticipating an outcome.

##### 3.4.5 Comfort Responses Targeting the Hands

The nerve endings in the hands are also highly developed. What makes analysis especially challenging is that many hand movements carry plausible everyday meanings, rendering hand-action analysis the most difficult.

Fingers are the most dexterous organs precisely because they can execute highly complex movement combinations. The skin on the backs of the hands is likewise extremely sensitive. Consequently, another typical comfort response that appears frequently under mental tension is the rubbing of one hand against the other. Common actions include:

- Wringing the hands, often seen in helplessness or anxiety
- Playing with the fingers—for instance, rubbing the thumbs together in circles while interlacing the remaining eight fingers—often seen in thoughtful anxiety or indecision
- Stroking the back of one hand with the fingers, often seen in fear or unease

In summary, if a subject exhibits any of the skin-directed comfort behaviors described above when confronted with a negative stimulus, that stimulus is especially significant and warrants further exploration and analysis; it may become a key clue to uncovering the truth.

It is important to note that the movements listed above cannot be treated as comfort responses—and therefore as signs of deception—in every situation. Do not memorize or mechanically apply the list; touching the face or wringing the hands does not automatically mean the person is lying. The individual may simply be following a personal habit or may consider straightening a tie to be a stylish gesture. To determine whether these actions constitute stress-induced micro-reactions (微反应), one must consider the entire testing context, especially whether the movements appear as changes after exposure to a negative stimulus (such as a pointed question) and whether those changes differ from the subject’s baseline behavior (habitual or non-stimulus movements). Only then can the actions be judged to have analytical value or interpretive significance.

##### 3.3.4 Comfort Through Taste

In addition to oral and lip comfort responses, another category involves attempts to soothe the central nervous system through gustatory stimulation.

One reason smokers find quitting difficult is the absence of substitutes that deliver equivalent taste stimulation. In many smoking-related experiments, participants expressed a strong desire for gustatory stimulation yet did not want to eat frequently, because doing so would burden the digestive system.

Smoking supplies both taste and olfactory stimulation and directly affects nervous-system state. The trace substances produced by burning tobacco suppress neural excitability and reduce blood oxygen levels. Whether the goal is sedation, stimulation, or anxiety relief, tobacco can indeed alter nervous-system activity and lower anxiety.

During testing we allow the subject to adopt a comfortable posture from the outset and, according to individual habit, provide water and an ashtray so that drinking or smoking remains possible. Once testing begins, every reaction can reflect the subject’s psychological response to the stimulus and manifest through micro-reactions. Observing the subject’s normal smoking pattern (to establish baseline) and noting any changes in smoking behavior when pressure questions arise permits a more comprehensive analysis of micro-reactions.

##### Digression

At this point it is necessary to describe the ideal conditions for micro-reaction psychological testing.

For micro-reaction testing to succeed, the fundamental requirement is the delivery of effective stimuli. Effective stimulus design depends on knowledge of the subject. The more thoroughly relevant information is gathered, the more clearly the subject’s personality traits, behavioral patterns, and concerns or aversions can be identified. Only then can a sound testing protocol be devised and possible stress responses anticipated, facilitating accurate judgments about truthfulness.

When nothing is known about the subject and the test has no specific purpose, the procedure is termed a “no-cause test.”

Media and enthusiasts often request such tests: “Come on, see if I’m lying! Can you tell what I’m thinking?” The request is usually accompanied by a slight expression of disbelief and schadenfreude—rather like fans spotting a famous comedian on the street and immediately shouting, “Hey, give us a routine!”

Recommendation: avoid no-cause tests whenever possible.

##### 3.4.2 Comfort Responses Targeting Facial Organs

A second category of skin-directed comfort responses centers on self-soothing through tactile contact with facial organs. Typical manifestations include:

- Lightly stroking the forehead or cheeks
- Rubbing the nose
- Touching the ears
- Stroking the beard
- Touching the mouth or chin
- Rubbing the neck

These actions originate in the early stages without cortical decision-making; they are controlled directly by relatively primitive limbic-system structures. Individuals without specialized training find them difficult to suppress.

The head, face, and neck lie closest to the brain’s central structures and are richly supplied with blood vessels and nerves (the neck is the obligatory pathway connecting the central nervous system to peripheral nerve nodes). Tactile comfort movements directed at this region can directly modulate nervous-system tension caused by negative stimuli; when performed with slightly greater pressure they can also reduce rising blood pressure, rapidly restoring calm after an overreaction. Unlike other comfort responses, the soothing effect here is not merely suggestive but rests on objective physiological improvement and is therefore especially noticeable.

##### 3.4.1 Comfort Responses for Hair and Scalp

Scratching the scalp when embarrassed is in fact a comfort response directed at the scalp.

Hairstyle adjustment is also frequently used as a camouflage or shield. During an interview or test, rising pressure may prompt both men and women to rearrange their hair as a self-soothing measure.

Women exhibit an additional distinctive comfort response: gathering the hair at the nape, sweeping it backward, or re-braiding it to relieve tension and self-soothe.

Although these movements appear to be routine grooming, they frequently occur when the hairstyle or makeup shows no visible disarray and may remain unchanged—making them noteworthy. When the adjustments recur frequently and consecutively, they more clearly exhibit the features of a comfort response and reflect an agitated mental state.

In addition, grooming or scalp-scratching movements can redirect attention so that the actor avoids becoming helplessly embarrassed, thereby aiding psychological recovery.

##### Practical Application

In actual use, first establish the subject’s smoking-habit baseline by recording smoking frequency, characteristic movements while smoking, and the manner of extinguishing cigarettes. Then watch for anomalous changes. If an anomalous reaction appears after a negative stimulus and the frequency or intensity of smoking behavior shifts noticeably, the subject’s psychological state has changed, indicating an attempt to relieve discomfort (fear, anxiety, embarrassment, or excitement) and obtain comfort through smoking.

##### 3.3 Oral and Lip Comfort

When under pressure, people employ various oral and lip behaviors for self-soothing—sucking fingers, biting nails, chewing on a pencil, eating candy, smoking, or swallowing saliva. These actions signal to the nervous system, “Don’t be afraid, everything’s fine, I’m eating.”

## Part Seven: Body Language

### Courtship Body Movements: Instinctive Physical Signals Emitted During Courtship Between Opposite Sexes

Micro-expression keywords Courtship between men and women relies primarily on the body. It is not only instinctive but also avoids much awkwardness because of shyness or uncertainty. Therefore, when members of the opposite sex court each other, they emit certain body-language signals while awaiting an unspoken response from the other party.

Many people have experienced this: when walking down the street and encountering an attractive man or woman approaching, we instinctively straighten our posture, pull in our abdomen, and radiate vitality. Even those with a “beer belly” will unconsciously tuck in their stomach and lift their head to appear taller and more imposing, while their stride becomes lighter. The purpose of all this is to present one’s best side to the opposite sex and win favor through personal charm.

Body language can be described as the most basic communication tool people use in the process of courting the opposite sex, because nearly all thoughts and emotions can be expressed through it. In this regard, women always hold the decisive power; in 90 percent of cases, it is the woman who initiates courtship. Typically, once a woman identifies a man she likes, she continuously sends subtle courtship signals via her eyes, body, or facial expressions until she believes he has noticed both her and the signals, and has responded in some way.

The courtship process also follows certain steps. For example, if a woman spots a highly attractive man, she will first gaze at him quietly until he notices her and eye contact occurs. Next, a fleeting smile appears on her face—an acquiescent signal women often use to hint that the man should take the next step. The third step is grooming, used to highlight her charm and attract his attention. The fourth step involves speaking and moving closer, attempting to close the distance through casual conversation. The fifth step is physical contact, when a woman may seize an opportunity to “accidentally” touch the man’s arm.

Although these five steps may seem insignificant, they exert a crucial influence on the beginning of a new relationship. Body language plays a decisive role throughout. For instance, the basic grooming actions of men and women are similar and include smoothing the hair, straightening clothing, placing one or both hands on the hips, and pointing the toes and body toward the person of interest. As long as one party has not received or given a clear signal, the other will try every means to court through body language.

Basically, women employ thirteen common body movements and signals when courting, through which they convey their single status.

1. Tilting the head back and playing with the hair—the two signals women use first upon noticing someone of interest.
2. Moist lips, pouting, and slightly parted lips.
3. Self-touching, which creates in the woman the illusion of being caressed by a man.
4. Displaying the soft inner wrist to signal gentleness and submissiveness in hopes of gaining the man’s attention. Men find women with soft wrists especially delicate and appealing.
5. Enthusiastically stroking cylindrical objects—playing with cigarettes, fingers, earrings, or any item resembling the male genitalia. This action is a subconscious externalization of inner thoughts.
6. Exposing the smooth, soft skin of the inner wrist to the man of interest; as interest grows, the frequency of wrist flashing increases.
7. Shoulders raised with a sidelong glance—the raised shoulders accentuate the woman’s characteristically rounded, graceful figure.
8. Swaying the hips, subtly highlighting the gender difference between men and women.
9. Twisting the pelvis—when standing, a woman’s pelvic twist often signals her reproductive capacity.
10. Placing a handbag near the man so he notices or touches it indicates strong interest and willingness to accept him.
11. A common posture in which one leg is bent and tucked under the other; the knee of the bent leg usually points toward the person of greatest interest.
12. Sliding a foot partially out of a shoe and dangling it by the toes is also a signal of relaxation.
13. Women often deliberately press their legs together to draw attention to them—the seated posture men find most captivating. In addition, slowly crossing and uncrossing the legs while lightly tapping the thighs with the fingers signals an inner desire to be touched.

Women’s courtship movements showcase their charm, whereas men’s essentially display power, wealth, and status. Men’s most common courtship body-language actions center on the crotch area.

For example, when facing a woman, the most direct way a man can highlight sexual difference is the aggressive thumbs-hooked-in-belt posture that makes the crotch more prominent. He will also gradually turn his body and toes toward the woman of interest, gazing at her with an ambiguous expression for a prolonged time to draw her attention. When seated, he may deliberately spread his legs to expose the crotch.

In public places, the most frequent courtship action men direct at women is crotch adjustment. Some women complain that men reach toward the crotch without apparent reason or warning. In reality, they simply do not understand the subtext: the area is so large that it becomes caught in the trousers, requiring constant repositioning.

It can be said that men and women often begin courting the opposite sex under the impetus of body language. Thus everyone has the opportunity to refine their appearance, enhance their attractiveness to the opposite sex, and gain more chances for contact. There are many courtship signals between the sexes; if the signals emitted are strong enough and penetrating enough, everything will fall into place naturally. Many people hesitate to confess directly because of shyness or lack of courage. If you also like the other person, respond clearly to these body signals.

### 6.2.1 Head Lowering + Spinal Curvature

Head lowering indicates a lowered self-positioning; trunk curvature indicates endurance and self-protection. These can be used to determine the emotion being expressed, its intensity, and its authenticity, as shown in Figures 6-7, 6-8, and 6-9.

When the head is lowered while the spine remains upright, the behavior usually expresses social submission.

Unless the person is a long-term member of a strictly disciplined force, the isolated head-lowering action together with verbal statements of agreement or obedience constitutes a “lie,” because it contradicts the person’s actual cognition.

When the head is lowered and the spine is moderately curved—yet lumbar curvature has not appeared—and no deliberate force or redundant expression is present elsewhere in the body, one can conclude that the individual harbors no confrontational mindset and is sincerely acknowledging the situation.

As shown in Figure 6-8. In modern society, if one party lowers the head while the spine curves during a standing conversation, it indicates that the person fully accepts the disparity between them or has abandoned resistance after being overwhelmed by the received information. For example, a student who feels guilty after making a mistake will display the reaction in Figure 6-8; if inwardly defiant, the student may adopt the posture in Figure 6-7 to signal internal resistance.

When the head is lowered and the lumbar spine simultaneously curves noticeably, producing substantial trunk curvature, the stimulus is extremely strong.

In moments of extreme fear, people adopt this pronounced trunk curvature for self-protection, always accompanied by flexion and enclosure of the limbs—the “curling” tendency discussed under the “freeze response.”

This action is easily faked.

When expressing flattery or humility, people frequently adopt such a posture, yet apart from the lowered head and pronounced spinal curvature, the rest of the body remains controlled. Combined with explicit verbal statements such as “It is my honor to have you guide our work,” “It is her good fortune that you regard her favorably,” or “Please do not take offense; calm your anger, calm your anger,” these are socially motivated expressions driven by self-interest and cannot be taken at face value, as they may conceal a highly complex inner state.

It is also important to note that head lowering plus lumbar curvature constitutes a widely recognized normative apology behavior.

We often see public figures apologize by bowing in addition to speaking, as illustrated in Figures 6-10, 6-11, and 6-12. Bowing is one of modern society’s etiquette rules and is used by everyone; to some extent it is a deliberately cultivated behavior. Especially when a public appearance and apology have been prepared at length, the degree of bowing cannot serve as a reliable indicator of psychological state.

What we must observe is the inadvertent postural change that occurs after an unexpected stimulus.

These apologies achieved relatively good public recognition and media acceptance because the posture involved lumbar curvature, fully conveying the individual’s remorse. Apologizing with an upright spine tends to invite widespread doubt and criticism.

You may ask: since the standard apology posture is a classic social behavior that can be learned or trained, how can it be cited as an example of emotional behavior?

If this question has occurred to you, congratulations! It shows that you have firmly internalized the distinction among “social behavior,” “physiological behavior,” and “emotional behavior,” and one foot is already in the professional domain.

In response to your question, I raise a deeper one: how did social etiquette become established by custom? Why, across all societies past and present, has this identical posture been adopted as a universal apology rule? Has anyone ever apologized with an upward gaze?

An apology delivered with an upward gaze, no matter how sincere and reasonable the words, will be perceived as arrogant and insincere, indicating an absence of genuine remorse. This is precisely why the upward-gaze response can be used to judge another person’s state of mind. Therefore, when an individual is in a position of psychological weakness, the posture adopted is invariably one of trunk curvature and lowered head.

Imagine walking along the street and accidentally jostling an elderly person so that they stumble. Your immediate reaction is a slight bow and lowered head to express apology while reaching out to steady them, accompanied by words of remorse such as “I’m sorry.”

Apology is certainly a social expression; public apologies delivered before audiences and media constitute typical “one-way expression.” We cannot judge the speaker’s true inner state from these displays. A carefully rehearsed apology performance may, after extensive preparation, convey remorse in an exhaustive manner, yet the goal may be to preserve public approval and related interests rather than to admit fault. At minimum, an opportunity for questions must exist, because only then can a stimulus be applied and a stress response observed.

Nevertheless, within the societal consensus on apology movements, every apology incorporates lowering the posture as a prescribed action. This is because, over time, the lowering posture has been the natural reaction of people who genuinely feel remorse; society has therefore extracted the pattern from these spontaneous phenomena, and the pattern necessarily aligns with human cognitive habits.

### 9.2.1 Body Drooping

Loss of energy produces noticeable changes in several areas: the eyes lose luster and become vacant; lacking energy, the body succumbs to gravity and exhibits an overall downward trend, ceasing all actions that resist gravity, including facial muscles, which assume a uniformly relaxed, drooping state (see the book *Micro-expressions*); the trunk can no longer remain upright and the head drops; in a standing posture, the center of gravity lowers, the legs naturally bend from loss of strength, and the person may squat or sit on the ground, the entire body contracting; breathing becomes shallow and reactions sluggish.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图9-11　失败的颓废]*

In short, the body of a defeated person conforms to the principle of gravity and lacks the strength to resist its pull. These reactions and their variants fully reveal the psychological state of the defeated: acceptance of loss and abandonment of resistance.

Therefore, if during testing one observes that after repeated stimulation the subject exhibits signs of energy and vitality depletion, it indicates that the subject’s psychological defenses are on the verge of collapse and the truth is about to be revealed.

Defeat and surrender represent psychological collapse—a state devoid of further expectation. The external manifestations of this mental state resemble those of sadness. The fundamental stimulus for sadness is the helpless loss of someone or something one cares about or loves, which to some extent also constitutes psychological surrender, such as the loss of a loved one or the failure to realize a goal after investing great effort. All such helpless losses can produce sadness. Consequently, the above reactions can also be used to infer sadness, with analysis adjusted according to the specific context and the nature of the stimulus.

Sadness and grief, however, arise from entirely different mental states. Sadness stems from “helpless loss,” whereas grief stems from non-acceptance, disbelief, and rejection of a negative outcome (for example, loss of someone or something one cares about or loves). Grief also involves regret, indignation, and a desire to change the situation, together with the energy to express these feelings. The classic expression of grief is therefore loud weeping, while sadness more often appears as a quiet, despondent state.

**Test Case**

The Unfortunate Marriage of a High-Quality Older Single Woman

During our testing applications, a classic sequence of grief followed by sadness was observed.

The subject was a high-quality older single woman who maintained strict standards for her life: regular routines, consistent exercise, careful diet, and cultural pursuits in which she had achieved a certain level of accomplishment. Her one possible fixation was the insistence on marrying only a man who was “accomplished in both the civil and martial arts.” Here the phrase did not mean both scholarly and combative, but rather possessing both literary achievement and substantial family wealth.

Such expectations were not excessive, given her own strong qualifications. The problem arose from prolonged selectivity and screening, which fostered a habit of suspicion. She felt compelled to investigate every candidate overtly and covertly before committing, hoping to ascertain the truth. This obsessive pattern of thought had reached an unacceptable level.

Eventually she found a man she liked and married him, yet her suspicious obsessiveness produced an unhappy marriage in which both parties suffered (whether the man also contributed factors remains unconfirmed).

When asked, “Do you unreservedly wish to continue this marriage?” the woman deliberated at length before answering “Yes.” The man, present at the scene, showed a slight smile. The testing team subsequently invalidated her answer, rendering all prior effort void. The man’s expression can be imagined.

The woman’s immediate reaction was grief. Clenching her fists, she wept and loudly denied and protested, her eyes brimming with tears and filled with anger.

After the room was cleared, staff explained the basis for the judgment: first, she had concealed her financial situation, a fact supported by evidence; second, during testing she had acknowledged that under certain circumstances she would protect her own interests by choosing divorce—an admission made in the course of the test. The woman’s body rapidly lost all energy; her gaze became lusterless. She collapsed backward onto the sofa, covered her face, and sobbed silently. This helpless sorrow constituted sadness.

### Test Cases

**The "Proud" Girl Who Corrected Her Boyfriend's Behavior**

While studying the relationship between emotions and reactions, we once conducted a type of experiment. The experiment was simple: volunteers were asked to recount, within a set time, the thing they were most proud of (and, of course, the saddest thing, the most contemptible thing, the happiest thing, the angriest thing, and so on). The sessions were recorded, and afterward the recordings were analyzed for synchronous matching among content, emotion, and micro-reaction (微反应).

Emotional changes do not arise or vanish abruptly. Our research shows that, except for surprise, most emotions accumulate gradually and then fade gradually. Disgust can sometimes be triggered suddenly by smell or visual stimuli, yet more often it too builds through repeated negative input. We call this pattern “the curvilinear nature of emotional change.” Accordingly, speakers in the experiment were asked to speak for five minutes. Those who achieved genuine emotional engagement and kept content, emotion, and micro-reaction synchronized received a material reward.

Although the data set was modest, every speaker describing a genuinely proud moment displayed the same outward signs: abundant energy and large or complex movements.

One girl recounted how she had “corrected” her boyfriend’s gaming addiction. She appeared to have studied psychology; she first cited Pavlov’s conditioned-reflex theory, then described a carrot-and-stick behavior-modification model (carrot for correct behavior as positive reinforcement; stick for mistakes as punitive stimulus). She concluded with evident satisfaction. When she reached the part she was proudest of, her expression brightened, her eyes shone, her hand gestures increased, her posture straightened and leaned forward, and her chin and face lifted slightly in concert with her assertive language.

When an experimenter interjected, “Have you studied counter-conditioning and aversion therapy? You treated your boyfriend like a lab rat, didn’t you?” the classic “head-shaking” reaction appeared. The girl had not expected her boyfriend-correction story to be compared with famous psychological research; the powerful sense of validation and achievement made her head shake four times within one second.

3. **Finger-drumming roll**  
   In offensive reactions we have already discussed desk-directed striking movements that reflect anger. Not every instance of finger-drumming, however, signals anger. One form expresses satisfaction or pride. When a person lets the four fingers (or all five, including the thumb) of one hand fall lightly onto the tabletop in sequence—“tap, tap, tap, tap”—and each finger pauses briefly in the air before the next descends, the action is called “leisurely fingers.” It is the characteristic drumming style of a self-satisfied state.

**Leisurely fingers**

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图9-10]*

**4. Straight-leg foot wag**

We have already examined leg-jiggling: baseline jiggling that stops, or baseline jiggling that begins, both map to negative emotion. When, however, a person extends both legs nearly straight, crosses the ankles, and rocks the feet from the ankles, the movement signals comfort and ease. In adversarial settings it can indicate a victory response—relaxed and self-satisfied—as shown in Figure 9-10.

By the same principle, rapid shoulder shrugs, small high-frequency torso sways, or rocking against an elastic chair back all express relaxation and pleasure.

### Female Car Model vs. Female Host

Two elegant women are conversing. The car model (hereafter “S”) maintains a professional posture throughout: smiling, hands folded on her lap, torso upright and never leaning back into the sofa, legs crossed in the classic “figure-four” position.

The host, however, asks pointed, impolite questions about private matters. A woman can remain outwardly graceful and smiling even when being rude, and both parties understand this.

S’s posture undergoes three subtle shifts that reveal three successive mental states during the recording.

At first the conversation stays light—fashion, modeling, clothing, food—and S’s crossed legs tilt slightly, indicating that, despite her professional bearing, she is relatively relaxed.

When the host deliberately moves to sensitive topics and grows increasingly sharp, S produces a series of reactions: several widened-eye “stares,” slight nostril flaring on exhalation (classic anger), and aborted arm-crossing gestures (checked by habit). A further subtle change occurs: her crossed lower leg rises from a tilted to an almost vertical angle. Although she keeps the figure-four posture, the shift itself constitutes a preparatory escape movement.

In the final stage the host’s aggression becomes so intense that S can no longer maintain a smile. After her agent quarrels with the director, S’s anger mounts; the woman who had preserved decorum for nearly half an hour now leans back against the sofa. Compared with her earlier posture, this is the clearest disgust-driven escape reaction—caused not by fatigue but by strong aversion. The interview soon ends acrimoniously.

Disgust-driven escape is therefore highly significant. Whether seated or standing, it maps directly to aversion. Its appearance is valuable because, translated into words, it says “go away,” “stay away from me,” “how tiresome,” “I no longer wish to talk.”

The state is dominant: it expresses refusal and marks the point at which communication difficulty peaks.
