If the negative stimulus continues or intensifies, aversion accumulates. Imagine an adolescent forced to listen to an incessant, unwelcome monologue; the feeling is unmistakable.

In commercial service, negotiation, or investigative interviewing, the appearance of this reaction is a critical juncture and must be handled in one of two ways.

First, if the topic under discussion is peripheral to core interests, the interviewee’s agreement or disagreement matters little. Once aversion appears, the best response is to change the subject unobtrusively; continued accumulation of aversion risks creating personal animosity that later blocks cooperation.

Second, if the topic is central to the case, the aversion must be dispelled. Allowing the person to refuse engagement through posture or words makes any later return to the same issue far more difficult. In criminal interrogation, for example, verbal pressure and physical instructions to abandon the escape posture can be used to compel renewed engagement.

### 5.2.2 Psychological Drivers of Approach Responses

An approach response occurs when two or more people move closer, enter, or remain within personal or intimate distance without rejection or withdrawal. The causes are as follows:

1. **Emotional closeness**  
   The embraces, leaning, and intimacy of lovers are classic expressions of this state.  
   Two old comrades-in-arms who once shielded each other from bullets will, on first sight after many years, perform the most intimate gesture—an embrace. The hug is not the polite pat of formal greeting; each man pulls the other tightly and draws him inward. This maximal closeness of action and distance maps the warmth of their friendship.

   An embrace is an expressive, warm form of approach etiquette.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图5-14　标准的拥抱]*

   A standard embrace has two necessary components: the fronts of the torsos (chest and abdomen) must touch, leaving no further space; and the arms must encircle the other person and pull inward, actively shortening the distance. See Figure 5-14.

   Precisely because of this bodily intimacy the gesture has become a universal signal of emotional closeness.

   Once the action becomes conventional etiquette, however, even people harboring reservations may use it insincerely in public settings to convey closeness to onlookers.

   Such insincere embraces still betray clear discrepancies with the two necessary components—torso distance and arm tension.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图5-15　违心的拥抱]*

   The first sign is control of torso-to-torso distance. The two people smile, open their arms, and appear welcoming, yet when they meet only the shoulders and heads touch; from the chest downward there is deliberate separation, and the torso and legs angle away (Figure 5-15). These movements expose genuine reserve or distance.

   The second sign is minimal arm effort. Politicians are often seen exchanging embraces in which torso alignment is correct but the arms merely brush the back without any genuine pull.

   In either case an insincere embrace need not be sinister; it may simply reflect unfamiliarity and the requirements of social ritual while the underlying relationship remains amicable.

   If two people consistently fail to close distance—either both maintaining it or one repeatedly withdrawing—the psychological state is one of rejection or aversion.

### 6.1.1 Arrogance

Arrogance is the attitude of regarding oneself as markedly superior (stronger, wealthier, nobler…) to another and therefore seeing no need to engage—the implicit message being “not worth my time.” The facts rarely match the self-assessment.

Beyond luxury cars, large houses, idle wealth, and ostentatious clothing, an arrogant person typically displays the following classic reactions: these external markers are insufficient; the person must also be physically higher. Instead of platform shoes, the individual lifts the chin above its normal angle, producing the sensation of greater height.

The head is the body’s commander; once the commander feels elevated, confidence follows.

Although humans are civilized, this evolutionary legacy is difficult to suppress consciously. One may maintain a cultivated appearance until emotion rises, at which point the primitive pattern reappears.

Arrogance and disdain are two outward expressions of the same emotion; their motor signatures are nearly identical: head tilted back, chin raised. The raised chin naturally directs the gaze downward, so the upper eyelids often cover half the eyes in a looking-down posture. Additional synchronous signs may include head-shaking or a half-bared canine-teeth expression of contempt.

Figure 6-4 shows Takayama Kiyoshi, second-in-command of Japan’s Yamaguchi-gumi syndicate, arrested at home on the morning of 18 November 2010. Although he denied the extortion charges, he offered no resistance and was described by the media as extremely arrogant.

In the photograph, neck fat obscures any obvious chin lift, yet the overall head posture is angled upward (judged by the angle between the vertical line through the ear and the horizontal). Another key feature is the open right eye (the closed left eye may be medical), half-lidded in the classic superior gaze that reveals inner arrogance.

Complete arrogance or disdain reactions are uncommon in daily life; milder versions predominate. During conversation, for example, one party may lift the chin slightly while politely stating, “Martial arts have no hierarchy; all serve health,” revealing an unspoken belief that his own views are superior.

When the face is not oriented directly toward the other person yet the chin still rises, the gesture adds an element of defiance. Combined with a provocative expression, it signals a dominant confrontational mindset—stronger than disgust-driven escape and indicative of impending opposition.

A subtler seated variant occurs when a person bends the torso yet keeps the head level, thereby widening the angle between torso and head while still conveying a trace of non-submission within an otherwise compliant posture.

### 4.2 Surprise: Unexpected and Attentive

The essence of surprise is that something is both unexpected and noteworthy.

“Unexpected” means the stimulus lies outside the subject’s anticipation; this is a necessary condition for the stimulus to register as effective. The immediate result is surprise, which may be followed by fear (preparation to flee), anger (preparation to fight), or joy.

Can you picture a surprised expression? That frozen look is already in your mind (Figure 4-1): eyebrows raised, eyes widened, mouth involuntarily open; in cartoons the jaw may even drop to the floor. For that instant the person is motionless.

In real life, however, few people produce such an obvious reaction. Most merely widen their eyes slightly and may part their lips (drawing a quick breath) without further display.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4-1　惊讶的样子]*

Moreover, if the subject has already formed defensive or resistant expectations, any genuine surprise reaction to a related negative stimulus will be brief and minute, almost imperceptible, and will quickly convert into a self-masking furrowed brow that signals serious concern.

The standard surprise subtext is “Huh?”; the masked version is “Hmm?” (internally: “How did he know?” or “Why is he asking that?”). The subsequent brow-furrow actually expresses displeasure or aversion following the surprise (Figure 4-2).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4-2　惊讶之后的厌恶]*

The instant of surprise is the nervous system’s emergency interval for processing complex information. An unexpected stimulus lies beyond conscious control; the subject cannot yet know its consequences. Long-term survival pressures have shaped an automatic response: the subject must rapidly assess the source’s nature and intensity and then select an appropriate countermeasure.

Imagine you have just accepted a “Hexi Express” delivery and are turning to open it when a knock sounds and a voice outside says, “Hexi Express!” You know you placed only one order and the voice differs from the earlier courier’s. Your first reaction is to freeze and evaluate, not to ignore the knock or open the door without hesitation.

Pleasant surprises can also produce freezing: when a revered mentor calls to say the student ahead of you has withdrawn and you may now prepare for graduate study, the initial response is not immediate thanks or elation; that would imply prior certainty. Only after the sub-second surprise do joy, excitement, and gratitude surge.

### 10.4 Weakened and Inhibited Breathing

When the human nervous and motor systems enter a depressed state, physiological activity decreases and objectively requires less oxygen consumption, so breathing shifts into gentle, low, shallow respiration. Typically, this state appears only after a complete state of sorrow, such as decadence, depression, or despondency.

If stimulation produces a stress response that simultaneously weakens both inhalation and exhalation, the result is respiratory inhibition. The person exhibiting this inhibition often remains unaware of it.

The instinctive reaction to surprise is to draw a quick breath and hold it in reserve. Yet when fear follows—especially when objective conditions prevent flight or resistance, such as modern social rules or etiquette—a freezing response appears in the form of breath-holding or reduced breathing.

This weakened-breathing reaction maps the person’s fear emotion and feeling.

A colleague once organized a conference and, amid the many details, forgot to send a car for an important leader. Fortunately the leader was magnanimous, raised no objection, and the meeting proceeded smoothly. Even so, the colleague’s own superior was furious. At the celebratory banquet that evening the colleague received a few mild criticisms. Although the words were light, the colleague felt ashamed, reined in his earlier high spirits, and listened attentively with lowered head. During the brief silences between sentences, everyone in the room unconsciously held their breath, fearing a sudden storm. The superior stopped at that point, called for more wine, and the frozen air dissolved back into noise.

Note why the air seemed to congeal: the sensation arises from everyone’s subtle breathing.

The ancient essence of this slight respiratory change is concealment—to avoid attracting a hunter’s attention. When hunted, the weaker party that cannot fight must flee; if escape is also impossible, it must hide. While hiding, any noticeable airflow or breathing sound reveals one’s location to the predator—an extremely dangerous outcome. Long evolutionary accumulation therefore produced the instinct that concealment involves weakening or stopping the breath. In modern society, visual concealment is rarely required except by soldiers, intelligence officers, and criminals; at most one feels the urge to “find a crack in the ground to crawl into” when embarrassed. Yet under negative pressure the psyche still seeks protection through concealment by actively weakening or suspending respiration in an attempt to reduce the other party’s attention.

Consequently, under normal conditions a person encountering negative stimuli involuntarily weakens or holds the breath. The same reduction occurs when someone tries to mask their true state—for example, while lying and remaining cautious.

From this conclusion it follows that if a subordinate’s breathing becomes markedly stronger while being scolded, the anomaly deserves attention; it often signals grievance, defiance, or resistance and warrants further inquiry.

The freezing response in breathing consists of holding the breath or reducing its amplitude and frequency—the state commonly described as “not daring to breathe heavily.”

### 5.2 Proximity Responses

We begin by taking the degree of intimacy and aversion between men and women in romantic contexts as two extreme reference points. Because these distances correspond to primitive and basic needs that everyone has experienced, the relationship between psychological and physical distance is relatively easy to grasp.

Lovers in the heat of passion feel the greatest closeness; the distance they maintain therefore serves as the positive extreme.

Before reaching this positive peak, two strangers first keep a normal polite distance while conversing; eye contact then lengthens, followed by physical contact beginning with hand-holding, until they enter a very close bodily range.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图5-12　恋人间脚的触碰]*

For adolescents experiencing first love, the nervous excitement of the first hand-holding lingers long in memory. Leg and foot contact represents a still more advanced form of intimacy than hand contact. When lovers lightly touch or rub legs or feet, the behavior can generally be taken as an indication that sexual desire has begun to stir, as in Figure 5-12. Men and women whose relationship has not reached a certain level of intimacy will not psychologically accept such contact. The final stage is complete intimacy in which two people function as one; only when one has fully accepted the other psychologically does this distance become permissible.

Conversely, if one person feels aversion toward another, close distance is never permitted. Imagine dodging a roadside beggar who pursues you, or recalling an unwelcome suitor who, in full public view beneath a dormitory, lights a heart-shaped candle array and dances naked in the snow: which scenario makes you more eager for the other person to vanish, and which makes you want to flee as far as possible?

Between individuals of the same or opposite sex who are not lovers, once mutual trust has been psychologically established, physical contact occurs naturally and the parties pay it little special attention. When the relationship remains distant, however, physical contact makes at least one party distinctly uncomfortable.

In social settings, therefore, two noteworthy phenomena can be observed.

If you are uncertain whether a man and a woman share an intimate relationship, watch for close-range contact between them. If neither shows any obvious reaction to the reduced distance or to bodily contact, the two evidently accept each other. One should not, of course, conclude that romantic love exists between them.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图5-13　对触碰厌恶]*

Another situation arises once you have already determined that the relationship is not romantic. If one party then initiates contact—perhaps a light touch on a less sensitive area such as the arm or back—and the other party displays a sensitive negative reaction, most often a slight withdrawal or else freezing in place, the initiator likely harbors improper intentions toward the other. In severe cases the behavior may constitute sexual harassment, as in Figure 5-13.

### 10.2 Whether Breathing Can Be Controlled

Can breathing be controlled by conscious will?

Many people, drawing on personal experience, conclude that it can: respiration can be deliberately strengthened, weakened, or even suspended for extended periods. This conclusion is correct, because most of the muscles responsible for breathing are skeletal muscles, whose movements are subject to voluntary control.

Under normal conditions the body relies primarily on contraction of the diaphragm to draw air in. When the diaphragm contracts, the ribs expand and the abdominal organs move downward, enlarging the thoracic cavity and creating negative pressure that pulls air into the lungs. When the diaphragm relaxes, elastic recoil of the lungs together with the combined action of the pleural membranes and abdominal muscles expels the air. During forceful breathing or respiratory failure, accessory respiratory muscles also assist. When forced exhalation is required, as when blowing out a candle, the abdominal muscles and internal intercostal muscles generate pressure in the abdomen and chest to expel air from the lungs.

Accessory respiratory muscles include the sternocleidomastoid, platysma, and scalene muscles of the neck; the latissimus dorsi and pectoral muscles also function as accessory muscles. All of these are skeletal muscles.

From this perspective, breathing movements can indeed be performed under voluntary control.

Yet who consciously directs every inhalation and exhalation at every moment? If respiration required constant control, a person would die rapidly during sleep or unconsciousness. Even in ordinary social interaction, coherent speech and thought would become impossible, because one would have to issue continuous commands: “Inhale now,” “Exhale now.”

In fact, breathing can proceed entirely without deliberate volitional control. Automatic respiration is governed by the autonomic nervous system, specifically by centers in the brainstem, medulla oblongata, and pons. These lower and middle brainstem regions form the respiratory control center; cells there regulate breathing movements independently of thought. The respiratory centers comprise the ventral respiratory group, dorsal respiratory group, apneustic center, and pneumotaxic center, all of which can operate without interference or direction from higher cognition.

In addition, when blood carbon-dioxide levels rise, peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies and central chemoreceptors in the medulla detect the increase and raise respiratory rate. Exercise, elevated body temperature, adrenaline release, and motor impulses from the brain also increase breathing frequency. These physiological demands automatically engage the respiratory centers, which then adjust respiration without requiring cortical involvement.

This theoretical foundation allows us to infer a person’s subjective cognition and feelings from changes in breathing.

[^1]: The diaphragm (English: Thoracic diaphragm) is a thin sheet of skeletal muscle extending across the base of the ribs. It separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity and performs an essential function in respiration.

### Criminal Case: Bribery Investigation

Investigators from the anti-corruption bureau of a district under a directly administered municipality examined a bribery case.

The suspect, a technical cadre highly proficient in computer systems and programming, had received numerous national awards. A tip alleged that he had altered technical specifications in bidding documents, improperly awarded the project to the briber’s company, and accepted cash in return.

Before formally filing the case, investigators conducted an initial contact interview. In a brief exchange the suspect displayed a repeated territory–freeze–territory–freeze pattern that aligned precisely with the stimuli presented. On the basis of his state, the command room immediately authorized formal interrogation, which ultimately yielded a confession and written statement.

Investigator: “Please describe your position and main work history.”

Suspect: “I graduated with a doctorate from University X in year Y, specializing in internet security. After joining the agency I served successively as section chief, deputy division director, and division director, and received several national awards during that period.”

While delivering this answer he exhibited a classic territorial response: torso erect, legs spread at nearly 90 degrees, hands braced on knees, forming an expansive upper-body silhouette; speech was fluent and his expression relaxed.

Investigator: “What was your role in Project Z?”

Suspect: “Our division prepared the entire project requirements document; I personally reviewed and approved the technical specifications.”

He maintained the previous posture, gaze fixed on the investigator to gauge reactions.

Investigator: “Did you ever modify the final technical standards? If so, why?”

At the question the suspect immediately drew his legs together into a crossed-leg posture, arms encircling his knees in a defensive, tense configuration. His entire body contracted—the hallmark of a freezing response.

Suspect: “Reviewing and amending bidding documents falls within my duties; I did indeed modify several clauses.”

Investigator: “Which clauses, and why?”

On this purely technical matter the suspect regained a sense of mastery; his legs again opened beyond 90 degrees, torso straightened and leaned forward, and he launched into a fluent, lengthy explanation of each standard’s meaning and the reasons for change—an unmistakable territorial display.

When professionals discuss their specialty they can always construct tighter logic than outsiders. Pursuing such points often impedes investigative progress and risks inflating the suspect’s sense of control and confidence, creating obstacles for later work.

The investigator interrupted: “Do you know Mr. A (general manager of the briber’s company)? Have you had any private financial dealings with him?”

The suspect again contracted into a freezing posture, this time with knees and ankles pressed together and torso bent forward—an expression of rapid internal shift to fear.

Subsequent confession statements and physical evidence confirmed that he had indeed accepted bribes and committed a crime.

### 6.1 Upward-Gaze Response

In human consciousness, anything perceived as larger than oneself elicits upward gaze and reverence.

In ancient times, large carnivores held an advantage in both hunting and combat; the same fangs and claws inflicted far greater injury or death when wielded by a massive opponent. Within early human groups, taller hunters more readily secured large prey to share with kin, thereby improving group survival. Towering ancient trees and sheer cliffs fashioned by nature further impressed primitive humans with overwhelming awe and a sense of mysterious, unreachable power.

Size therefore represented the unattainable and mysterious; size represented absolute superiority in struggle.

These generational memories of survival and death gradually became deeply imprinted in human consciousness. After the rise of civilization, building size corresponded to the owner’s status; imperial palaces of every era and culture were vast and imposing, and wealthy modern individuals share a common preference—ever-larger houses and longer, larger cars as visible proof of strength.

In cultural ideology, religious icons meant to be worshipped by the populace were likewise imagined and sculpted at enormous scale. The *Sutra on Contemplation of Amitayus* describes Amitayus Buddha as “having a body the color of the gold of the Jambudvipa river in the Yama heaven, measuring sixty trillion nayutas of yojanas in height, with a white tuft of hair between the eyebrows curling to the right like five Mount Sumerus, eyes pure as the clear waters of the four great oceans, and light emanating from every pore like Mount Sumeru.”

“Nayuta” denotes an Indian unit of ten billion or one trillion; “yojana” equals roughly thirty to forty Chinese li (approximately 16 km). Readers may calculate for themselves how immense the Indian imagination made the Buddha—essentially “inaccessibly tall.” The intent behind such iconography was to render the Buddha utterly unlike ordinary people through sheer height, thereby inspiring reverence.

The Leshan Giant Buddha, the colossal wooden Buddha at Beijing’s Yonghe Temple, and the Bamiyan Buddhas of Afghanistan (later destroyed by the Taliban) exemplify this tradition of gigantic statues. Standing before them, ordinary people must “look upward to see the full figure,” and a feeling of awe arises naturally.

Yet the *Diamond Sutra* records Shakyamuni’s own words: “All phenomena are illusory; to see phenomena as non-phenomena is to see the Tathagata.” In other words, one must disregard size and beauty alike. If accomplished Buddhist practitioners required height or weight to command upward gaze, something would be amiss.

Although thousands of years of civilization have witnessed countless instances of the weak prevailing over the strong and the small overcoming the large, these examples do not overturn the human tendency to look upward at height. On an individual level, however, ordinary people differ little in stature.

The subconscious principle that “taller is superior” therefore prompts people to present themselves as taller when competing.

### 4.1 The Mechanism of the Freezing Response

Carnivores must eat meat; the weak are eaten. One side must pursue and strike, the other must dodge and flee.

Both hunter and prey are acutely sensitive to moving objects—an ability honed through prolonged life-and-death struggles. Animals’ keen sensory organs integrate sound, sight, scent, and even air currents to detect motion. Only thus can predators locate escaping quarry and prey detect an approaching hunter.

Frogs represent an extreme of this evolutionary adaptation: their eyes can precisely calculate the trajectory of a flying or leaping insect and capture it, yet they ignore stationary insects; when surrounded by fresh dead flies they starve because they cannot eat motionless prey.

A gazelle grazing peacefully on a sun-baked savanna suddenly senses a subtle shift in air movement accompanied by the faint scent of a carnivore. It immediately halts all motion, raises its head (where most sensory organs are concentrated), and uses eyes, nose, ears, and every hair to assess:

- Is there danger?
- What kind of animal poses the threat?
- How many are there?
- How fast are they moving?
- How far away are they?
- Can the group ensure my safety?
- Must I flee or fight?
- Which escape route avoids ambush?

…

All these questions must be answered within roughly one second (animals rely less on conscious thought for such judgments), or the gazelle may end up in a predator’s stomach<|eos|>

### The Mouth Can Lie, But the Body Doesn't

Words are not humanity’s most basic form of expression and communication; body language is the most common and fundamental way humans express and communicate. To understand emotional displays beyond words, one must recognize non-verbal cues such as posture, movement, facial expression, clothing, and tone of voice, then interpret these non-verbal emotions to grasp others’ true intentions and communicate successfully.

When someone speaks in a cheerful tone yet shows no corresponding expression, their words contradict their real feelings. When someone struggles to articulate an idea but displays a sincere and credible look, the difficulty stems only from poor verbal skills. When someone has not yet spoken but already appears furious, they are genuinely angry. When someone speaks haltingly yet cannot hide their anger, they are enduring reluctantly.

These situations already reveal the speaker’s true state of mind, which cannot be concealed; even deliberate attempts at concealment are visible in their expression.

Experienced parents readily detect whether their children are lying; when a child labors to fabricate a story, their body and eyes have already betrayed them.

In daily life you have certainly encountered this: despite someone offering many reasons and arguments, you remain unconvinced. Someone pours out a litany of hardships to persuade you of their bitter and sorrowful circumstances—yet you do not believe them. Someone deliberately boasts in front of you about how well they are doing—yet you remain skeptical. Someone loudly declares how much they like and appreciate a gift you gave—yet you read a different message in their eyes.

Why is this? They have supplied so many reasons, yet you still do not believe them. The real cause is that their body is sending entirely different signals; through their body language you detect the lie.

In everyday interactions and information exchange, 80 percent of communication occurs through body language rather than words. Therefore, accurately reading body language is essential.

Familiarity with body language enables clearer expression of one’s own intentions. In interpersonal exchanges, one must both convey meaning through body language and accurately perceive and respond to the body-language signals of others.

Reading others’ body language is a key method and skill for discerning emotions. Mastery of this skill allows quick, accurate judgment of another person’s emotional state and provides material for analyzing one’s own past misjudgments, thereby accumulating rich life experience.

### 5.1.2 Disgust-Based Evasion

Unlike fear-based evasion, disgust-based evasion reflects the actor’s non-acceptance and rejection from a position of perceived superiority. Although the person may objectively be constrained and remain in a weaker position, their inner attitude is one of disgust—an evaluation of “top-down negation.”

Evasion movements prompted by disgust are typically slow and deliberate; the person dares to face the stimulus source directly with gaze, torso, and the angle of the legs. Fear-based evasion lacks this frontal courage.

The most classic fear-based evasion features are easy to spot: after an effective negative stimulus, the distance between the subject’s head and the stimulus increases while the body’s support points remain unchanged.

The first type is obvious: during conversation, when the exchange becomes disagreeable and further communication feels impossible, the body leans back indignantly (note: not necessarily driven by anger) against the chair back.

Many people cannot distinguish whether leaning back signals relaxation or disgust.

Leaning against the chair back in disgust differs clearly from leaning back in comfort and control: the difference lies in the degree of overall relaxation. When leaning back in disgust, even if the torso is not exerting force (unlike relaxation), other body parts (such as the legs) and especially the facial expression remain stiff and tense. This reaction indicates that the subject has received an effective negative stimulus and is experiencing reluctant anger, dissatisfaction, contempt, or disdain; the emotion drives them away from the stimulus to reduce psychological discomfort, much like moving away from an unpleasant odor.

The second type is less complete; the observable reaction may be only a slight backward lean of the torso while the head has already moved away from the stimulus, as shown in Figure 5-7.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图5-7　躯干后仰]*

This evasion reaction is interesting because the subject often tries to mask their true feelings—negation or disgust—by adding other expressions and lines, a classic pattern. For example, two people discussing a favorite idol: one says “I like XXX,” and the other may perform this slight evasion movement, leaning back slightly, eyes either meeting or avoiding the speaker’s gaze, while maintaining a smile and saying, “Oh, really? I think he/she is pretty good too.” The verbal appearance of agreement contradicts the bodily evasion reaction; this is a typical social lie that prevents the conversation from ending unpleasantly over a trivial matter.

Genuine agreement would look like the revolutionary-film scene: stepping forward, two hands clasping and shaking vigorously while exclaiming, “Finally found my people!” Younger people might lean their heads even closer, eyes sparkling with excitement, and begin discussing details about the idol.

### 7.4 Spatial Taboos

In many situations, a dominant individual within their own territory may approach anyone inside that territory at will, and the approached person, by virtue of subordinate status, will not or dare not object; this stems from the authority the dominant person holds inside the territory. Conversely, if someone approaches or intrudes upon the territory the occupant mentally claims, the act is perceived as a strong provocation that triggers displeasure or even retaliation.

The most extreme example involves China’s ancient imperial administrative system. The rules governing the emperor’s residence were extremely strict. The emperor could roam freely inside the palace, yet clear regulations dictated who could enter or leave and where each person was required to remain. The key point is that accidental violation of these rules could result in severe punishment. Unauthorized entry into the palace was said to carry grave consequences (the author is not a professional historian; this point awaits verification).

The other side of the same coin is that the emperor could grant “permission to ride horseback inside the Forbidden City” as a reward to ministers. Allowing a minister to walk, ride, or be carried in a sedan chair inside the emperor’s domain expressed closeness and trust.

As Reginald Johnston, tutor to the last Qing emperor Puyi, described in *Twilight in the Forbidden City*: “The side gate on the west was kept open daily for those permitted to enter at stated times—princes, imperial tutors, and ministers of the Imperial Household. All who entered the Forbidden City had to walk unless they had received the special grace of ‘riding horseback inside the Forbidden City’ or ‘being carried in a sedan chair inside the Forbidden City.’ Dr. R. K. Douglas remarked that within this sacred precinct the grant of ‘riding horseback inside the Forbidden City’ was the highest honor an emperor could bestow on a minister. Yet ‘being carried in a sedan chair inside the Forbidden City’ was an even greater honor. These privileges were sometimes awarded temporarily for major court ceremonies; those who enjoyed them permanently were more highly regarded. They hung wooden plaques bearing the imperial grant above their residence gates. Most princes and a few other imperial clansmen received the sedan-chair privilege; their sons and lower-ranking clansmen received the horseback privilege. Imperial tutors, holding high status, were frequently granted the sedan-chair privilege.”

This description illustrates, through the most extreme administrative system, how important the leader’s authority inside the territory remains. Inside a superior’s office, the superior may walk up to you or stand behind you without hesitation or concern; as a subordinate you must not move about freely, nor is it permissible to enter the office uninvited, let alone walk behind the superior’s desk or stand beside the superior—an act generally regarded as incomprehensible and reckless.

Therefore, one must sometimes refrain from crossing the red line in a leader’s mind; such details can determine one’s continued presence or even survival.

### 9.2.3 Long-Term Suppression

After defeat, individuals develop a lowered self-perception; the nervous system enters a suppressed yet hypersensitive state. Fearing further injury, they habitually maintain a subordinate and defensive posture for an extended period. The downward-gaze response discussed in Chapter 6, which signals respect and compliance, lacks this accumulated sensitivity and habitual quality that follows defeat.

**Test Case**

A category of seemingly successful individuals that requires careful handling in daily life

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图9-13　长期的压抑]*

Among the subjects we tested was a seemingly successful doctoral student enrolled at a top domestic research institution in a highly regarded specialty; only a dozen or so students nationwide pursued the same doctoral track (indicating the field’s elite status and future demand). The individual was also strict with himself, highly self-disciplined, passionate about various sports, and accustomed to pushing personal limits; he loved life, kept a packed schedule filled with meaningful activities, and was considered warm and reliable by friends.

The test topic was romantic psychology and behavioral patterns. Throughout the testing process this apparently high-quality subject maintained one consistent posture: chin slightly lowered, eyes slightly upturned when looking at others, as shown in Figure 9-13.

He also habitually kept a very slight forward hunch; when encountering negative stimuli he deliberately straightened his posture in an attempt to project strength. In our pre-test analysis we concluded that this was a person with deep-seated feelings of inferiority. His persistence and rigor in sports were attempts to compensate for inner insecurity by continually strengthening his physical condition—an approach bordering on obsession. If the stimulus proved effective, embarrassment, anger, or shame were highly likely to appear.

The test results fully confirmed our preliminary analysis. This doctoral student, outstanding in many respects, had experienced repeated romantic failures, each time ended by the woman. Long-term romantic setbacks had rendered him sensitive and self-deprecating; lacking proper channels to learn how to handle emotional communication barriers, he compensated through obsessive behavior in other areas.

Thus, prolonged feelings of failure can produce the following habitual posture: head slightly lowered (chin tucked), eyes slightly upturned when looking at others, body not erect, limbs tending to contract, movements rather constrained rather than natural.

Because such individuals are easily stimulated and tend to interpret neutral stimuli subjectively as negative, they should be handled with care in daily life.

### 3. Verbal Blocking

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-23　嘴唇的阻挡反应（偷乐）]*

Mouth-blocking reactions are mostly directed at one’s own speech. A common example is “covering the mouth while stealing a laugh,” as shown in Figure 8-23. Such an obvious display is a classic case of trying to hide what is already evident; everyone can see the person is laughing. What interests us more is the psychological motivation behind the reaction, which is quite intriguing.

The psychological sequence of this smile-blocking reaction is as follows:

① The person genuinely finds something funny at first;  
② Then realizes they should not laugh so openly—either to spare the target embarrassment, to avoid criticism for gloating, or because long-standing upbringing and etiquette prohibit excessive display;  
③ Finally covers the mouth with a hand to project restraint and composure.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-24　嘴唇的阻挡反应（捂嘴）]*

Covering the mouth while crying is also a blocking reaction; its psychological motivation is relatively simple: to prevent grief from overflowing, to restrain oneself, and to reduce the spread of a sorrowful atmosphere, as shown in Figure 8-24.

Although both reactions map to very straightforward meanings and require little interpretive effort, they are typical examples of social behavior suppressing emotional behavior and help us understand the analytical method for all micro-reactions (微反应).

Another mouth-blocking behavior is more valuable for lie detection: covering the mouth with a hand while speaking, as if to stop the words from continuing.

① If the movement occurs before speaking begins, the person is unwilling to say it;  
② If it occurs mid-sentence, with sudden cessation and hand over the mouth, it indicates a slip of the tongue or regret that the words “should not have been said”;  
③ If it occurs after finishing a statement and looks like wiping the mouth or accompanies a cough, it actually signals negation of one’s own words—the person is denying what they just said.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-25　挡嘴]*

This reaction has only two possible explanations: either the person accidentally let the truth slip out (usually accompanied by a startled breath hold, widened eyes, and a freeze response), or the person is unconsciously correcting a lie and usually pretends to remain calm, as shown in Figure 8-25.

### 3. Enhanced Exhalation as Relaxation

After experiencing intense pressure, if the person emerges unscathed or confirms that danger has passed, they relieve bodily and nervous tension through a pronounced exhalation, usually a voiced “whew” through the mouth.

We conducted an experiment with students. Ten playing cards—A, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, J, Q, K—each of a single random suit were used. Subjects drew one card at random and memorized it. Testers then asked rapid-fire questions in random order (“Is it the ace?” “Is it the king?” etc.). Micro-reactions were analyzed to determine which card had been drawn.

Although the experiment offered neither reward nor punishment, some students became highly nervous; when asked about the card they held, they displayed clear eye and mouth reactions that allowed testers to “guess” the card correctly. The experiment’s purpose was to test the sensitivity threshold of the interrogation method. Overall accuracy was admittedly not high, but this is normal for a no-pressure test.

Even this standard no-pressure test, however, produced one consistent reaction in most subjects: nearly everyone exhaled a long sigh of relief once the questioning ended, relaxing the nervous system that had been on guard. When the result was announced, those correctly identified reacted with widened eyes, open mouth, and an involuntary “Huh?!” (subtext: “No way?”). Those not identified smiled smugly.

The reason is that no one wants their reactions to betray their true thoughts inadvertently; hence the psychological pressure of being challenged during the test.

Note that, unlike other comfort behaviors, humming, whistling, or the accompanying breathing is not an avoidance tactic but a relaxation response that generally appears after the subject senses danger has passed.

When danger approaches, people inhale deeply to store energy for flight or fight; once danger recedes, they exhale fully to relax the nerves and prepare for rest. Therefore, during testing, several questions can be inserted that allow the subject to feel they have passed smoothly (for example, “We believe you had no opportunity to cheat at that time”). Observing the resulting reactions can reveal the stimuli that concern the subject and yield valuable clues.

### 6.2.2 Deformation of High-Low Positioning — Drinking Culture

In Chinese drinking culture, there is a very interesting phenomenon.

At the drinking table, especially when the people present differ in status, the person of lower status usually clinks glasses against the lower part of the higher-status person's cup. The higher-status person accepts this positioning gesture calmly and tacitly. The greater the difference between the two, the larger the vertical gap between the rims of the cups. If both parties are being especially polite, they may even compete to lower their glasses further, as though they will not clink until one has clearly gone lower than the other.

This is a deformed form of the high-low positioning described earlier and also an expression of the looking-up reaction.

**6.3 Different Meanings of Four Handshake Methods**

When the two parties are relatively equal in social attributes such as identity and status, the arrogant or submissive micro-reactions described in the previous two sections are less likely to appear. More common are reactions that express mutual respect and reciprocity.

Nodding is a common greeting gesture. Nodding is actually a reduced version of the bowing reaction that signals respect and obedience; both the duration and the amplitude of the movement are smaller. For this reason, the original meaning of nodding is to indicate recognition or respect for the other person, yet without a pronounced sense of hierarchy.

The origin of the handshake is even more interesting. The original handshake was not a gesture of courtesy but a way to prove that neither party was holding a weapon, allowing both sides to talk without fear of sudden violence.

This custom is unlikely to have originated in China's long feudal era. Feudal society had two major characteristics: first, a strict and explicit hierarchy meant that the two parties who needed to use etiquette almost always stood in a superior-inferior relationship, so the possibility of armed conflict was low; when violence did occur, it was between rulers and resisters, an adversarial relationship that did not require polite gestures. Second, etiquette was elaborate and thoroughly instilled through formal education; it was used to express absolute obedience and reverence from subordinates to superiors. A simple action would not have sufficed to convey one's intentions. Even between peers of the same class, people would ceremoniously perform a full bow (involving head, spine, and hands together) to express harmony. Therefore, the handshake more likely appeared in ancient Western societies that lacked such complex social stratification.

In real life, a handshake is a subtle matter. Especially between strangers, the first handshake can yield additional information.

### 4.4 Startled First, Then Afraid

Remaining still allows information to be gathered and reduces traces; contracting reduces injury.

When danger appears and the source or location of harm is still uncertain, the body's immediate reaction is not to flee but to freeze in place and adopt a contracted posture.

For example, when amateur players scramble for a rebound in basketball, if the ball suddenly threatens to hit someone, that person's instinctive reaction is not to run away—because there is no clear direction to run. Instead, the person lowers the head, hunches the back, and freezes, afraid to move. The worry is that any movement might expose a more vulnerable spot (such as the back of the head); it is safer to stay put and risk only the back or buttocks.

Many other bodily freeze reactions serve the same purpose of avoiding greater harm; this book will not list them all.

The same freeze reaction also occurs when the mind receives an unexpected stimulus, even in the absence of physical danger.

Rumors of layoffs had been intensifying, and there was even talk that an entire department would be eliminated because of a capital acquisition.

When the department head walked into the office with a grim expression, everyone held their breath and fixed their eyes on him.

He took out a list and slowly read several names.

The people whose names were called turned pale and froze in place, unable to move. Others sighed with relief or waited anxiously for more information.

The head continued: "You few, pack your things and report to the marketing department today. The rest of the colleagues, including myself, are all dismissed. Go to finance to collect n+4 compensation. I'm sorry, everyone—I did my best."

The situation reversed instantly. Everyone who had just relaxed, including the employees who had been reassigned, froze in place, unsure what to do next.

From this we propose an important hypothesis: the stronger the unexpected stimulus, the greater the amplitude and duration of the freeze reaction; the two are directly proportional.

However, stimuli of this magnitude do not occur every day in real life, so reactions of this obviousness are not the focus of this book—unless a test subject receives an extremely strong stimulus during testing and also has relatively poor psychological resilience.

The freeze reactions that truly matter during testing are almost always relatively subtle, localized freezes.

### 7.3 Flourish — My Territory, My Rules

To be a leader, one must have the ability to lead others toward happiness—whether by bringing in more prey or by accomplishing more tasks. Otherwise, why would anyone follow?

Stripping away all formalities and complex modern rules, achieving results simply requires strength (thinking power and action power).

Therefore, in a state of active control, the most common expression is flourish: issuing commands that are short and forceful. This includes language, actions, and even gaze. A person with a sense of control minimizes the time spent on command forms. On one hand, this leaves no room for questioning and demands 100 percent execution, smoothing the execution process and raising team efficiency. On the other hand, it reduces the leader's own energy expenditure, because internal friction is unnecessary when many external matters still require attention.

In language, the style is concise, favoring imperative sentences and often omitting the subject, beginning directly with the verb. Words that can be omitted are omitted; the omitted content is expected to be understood through tacit agreement.

**In actions**  
The amplitude is usually not large—quick, medium-to-small movements that are mostly unidirectional and pointing, such as chopping, slashing, slapping, pointing, or tapping. Unlike the fighting actions described in Chapter 9, these directional movements do not deliver force; they are relatively casual.

When the identity and status gap between the two parties is large, the leader may use small gestures to reinforce the difference—for example, pointing with only the index finger or using a slight movement of the chin to convey certain intentions.

The chin also has a pointing function, but this pointing is never used in relationships that should express respect, admiration, or obedience, because chin-pointing always carries a trace of contempt and self-satisfied arrogance.

Even in today's open society, its use is limited to interactions with very close friends, nodding acquaintances with no stake involved, or initial encounters where no interests are yet at stake. Of course, the top-down directive intent remains consistent, because such small movements allow the leader to avoid raising a hand, saving effort while still feeling a strong sense of control.

If used toward a superior, an elder, or anyone else who should be respected, pointing with a slightly raised chin will ultimately harm the person doing it.

### 5.2.1 Four Types of Psychological Distance

Emotional closeness is expressed through physical proximity.

This awareness is very similar to the territorial awareness of wild animals: people allow those they accept to approach, even actively moving closer themselves, while keeping those they dislike at a safe distance, as though sensing potential harm.

According to the research of American anthropologist Dr. Hall, the physical distance between people reflects their psychological distance and can be roughly divided into four categories:

1. **Public space**: This distance applies to people who do not know each other. Dr. Hall defined it as beyond 3.7 meters. The American style relies on large amounts of statistical data to demonstrate scientific rigor. However, this definition no longer fits an overcrowded planet. Strangers on the street may brush past you, not because you consciously accept them entering your public distance, but simply because the situation does not matter to you.
2. **Social distance**: This distance is widely used in formal social activities such as office work, meetings, and business interactions. Dr. Hall defined it as 1.2–3.7 meters.
3. **Personal distance**: This distance is common between friends, acquaintances, or relatives. Dr. Hall defined it as between 46 centimeters and 1.22 meters.
4. **Intimate distance**: This distance reflects very close relationships, ranging from no distance (0 centimeters) to 46 centimeters. People allow those with whom they have close relationships—spouses, lovers, owners and pets, or very close friends—into this range. The only situation in which a stranger may enter intimate distance is for professional health care or diagnosis.

The conclusions of this classification cannot be experimentally verified or falsified, but the underlying logic is worth adopting. In real life, people do in fact manage their interpersonal distances according to these categories, even if the exact numbers vary slightly.

### (1) Circulation and Energy Reserves

Fleeing requires a large expenditure of energy.

When a person runs, the entire body participates in movement, especially the legs. The muscle groups in the legs consume a great deal of energy. This energy comes from the oxidation of stored sugars and inhaled oxygen in the body (endurance energy also comes from the oxidation of fats and proteins). Therefore, to flee, at least two biologically necessary preparations must be made: breathing (see Chapter 10: Breathing Reactions) and blood circulation (to transport energy substances).

**① Facial color**

We often hear descriptions such as "his face turned white with fright." How does fear make the face pale?

This is a typical reaction during the preparation-to-flee stage. Once the subject receives a negative stimulus and experiences a high-intensity emotion such as fear, blood circulation automatically diverts more blood away from other parts of the body and toward the legs used for running. Facial skin is exposed and directly observable. When normal circulation changes (reduced blood flow), the reduction in blood color becomes clearly visible. This is the principle behind the common expression "scared pale." At the same time, the increased blood in the legs produces muscle tension and excitement, sometimes visible as slight trembling.

**② Body temperature and other effects**

Similarly, abnormal blood circulation not only reduces blood color but also triggers a chain of sensations: accelerated heartbeat (to speed blood transport), lowered surface temperature (due to blood being withdrawn), mental blankness and slowed reactions (reduced oxygen consumption by the central nervous system), and increased speech interruptions (also an oxygen-deprivation response).

**③ Practical application**

The reactions described above mainly map to the emotion of fear. When a person encounters a frightening negative stimulus, the nervous system generates fear. The primary function of fear is to adjust the body's energy distribution—including blood and breathing—to prepare to flee the stimulus source, as far as possible.

During testing, if the subject shows any of these reaction indicators, it can be judged that their psychological state toward the stimulus source is one of fear and a decision to escape. It can therefore be inferred that the stimulus source is effective for the subject and can serve as a clue for further extraction of valuable information.

### 8.4 Exceptions for Professionals

The attack and defense reactions described in this chapter apply to ordinary people; professionals are excluded.

People who have received systematic combat training and mastered fighting techniques possess extremely high control over their limbs, rich real combat experience, and psychological stability. They are unlikely to display fear or pre-fight agitation. Even when anger arises, they immediately enter a professional-level combat-ready state.

Earlier in this chapter we discussed how a person whose territory is invaded will straighten the body in a defensive display. This reaction occurs before combat and is intended to make the opponent back down. However, a professionally trained person, before initiating action (after the display phase), does not keep the torso fully upright for protection; instead, it is slightly curved, attempting to shield the chest and abdomen.

The ready stance of professional Sanda is described in textbooks as follows:

① Foot position: feet separated front and back, the distance between the front heel and the rear toe is one-and-a-half foot lengths; the lateral distance between the feet is slightly wider than shoulder width; the front toes turn slightly inward, the rear toes point diagonally forward, and the rear heel is slightly lifted (for stability and quick movement);

② Arm angles and positions: both arms naturally bent, the angle between left and right arms approximately 90 degrees; the left fist placed in front of the body slightly below eye level, knuckles facing diagonally forward, fist eye facing diagonally upward; the angle between the right arms should be less than 90 degrees, the right fist placed in front of the right ribs slightly above the lower jaw, elbow about one fist's distance from the body (can advance to attack or retreat to defend);

③ Torso posture: left shoulder and left abdomen side facing the opponent, chest slightly tucked, abdomen slightly drawn in, upper body leaning slightly forward, head slightly lowered, chin tucked, teeth clenched, lips closed, eyes looking forward. (Protects the vulnerable chest and abdomen from direct attack while maintaining high alertness.)

Of course, untrained people in combat will not necessarily be so precise; they easily make mistakes such as striking wherever they feel like, focusing only on offense, and lacking defensive awareness.

The points described in item 3 above are all combat reactions worth noting in micro-reaction research.

In addition, their striking movements display numerous professional characteristics, including energy allocation and limb coordination. Therefore, the standards described in this book cannot be applied wholesale when observing and testing them.

### 1. Visual Escape

Chapter 3 mentioned the visual comfort reaction: when the subject feels discomfort, the gaze shifts elsewhere to reduce intake of negative stimuli and obtain relief. In terms of gaze change alone, the visual comfort reaction and the visual escape reaction look very similar and are almost impossible to distinguish. Yet the underlying psychological states and motivations are completely different. The purpose of visual comfort is to reduce reception of negative stimuli so that nervous-system pressure stops increasing; it is relatively passive and can be expressed colloquially as "I don't want to look anymore." Visual escape, by contrast, is the worry that excessive visual contact will trigger new negative stimuli; it can be understood as "afraid of being seen through," a relatively active measure. See Figure 5-8.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图5-8　视觉逃离]*

The greatest difference between the two is that the visual comfort reaction always moves away from the negative stimulus source to seek positive visual information, such as a trusted person; the visual escape reaction does not necessarily move the gaze away from the negative stimulus source—often it is simply the subject's autonomous reaction of not wanting to be noticed or seen through. In appearance, visual escape more often manifests as "gaze drifting," which can generally be read as a sign of guilt.

One example:

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图5-9　视觉逃离]*

When a person who has completed a task by luck receives praise from a leader, they will usually look away from the leader's kind, caring gaze. It looks like modesty and composure, yet the heart is pounding and the person is inwardly thinking "I'm ashamed," as in Figure 5-9.

Imagine, however, that the task was completed only after immense hardship, even at the cost of health or life (a brother's). In that case, receiving praise from the leader is unlikely to produce gaze drift; instead, the person is more likely to stand tall with head raised, full of tragic, heroic resolve.

Therefore, the psychological state of visual escape is shame or guilt—an attempt to reduce attention to oneself by averting the gaze and thereby prevent any deeper probing that might follow.

### 2. Care and Concern

Dr. Hall has pointed out, “The only possible intimate distance between strangers occurs in the context of professional health care and diagnosis.” If an observer notes a very close distance between doctor and patient, or between teacher and student, it should not be interpreted as the result of emotional intimacy but rather as an expression of care arising from role or duty.

This principle can also be applied in reverse: by using caring behaviors and proximity-controlled responses, one can create a sense of being cared for and protected in the other party, thereby accelerating the building of trust.

Usually, most people try to convey their intentions through verbal expression and to signal “please trust me.” Yet everyone understands that language can conceal multiple motives, so verbal “declarations” are easiest for the speaker but hardest for the listener to accept.

At such moments, actions and distance control can serve as the primary means, supplemented by verbal expression, to speed the establishment of trust. For example, on a reasonable relational basis, one might take a small step forward when handing over documents or coffee; when walking alongside someone, move slightly closer so that shoulders occasionally touch or arms lightly brush, rather than trailing at an angle that creates a “being watched” feeling; when speaking, if conditions allow, bring mouth and head close to the other person’s ear for a low-volume statement, and so on. These seemingly casual approaches allow the other person to sense an increase in intimacy without realizing it; when the content of the exchange also aligns on benefits and risks, the building of intimacy is greatly enhanced.

Care must be taken, however, not to overuse the technique. Casually closing distance with a superior or with an unfamiliar person of the opposite sex can be perceived as presumptuous and may damage the relationship instead. Two prerequisites must be kept firmly in mind: first, all such attempts must occur “on a reasonable relational basis”; second, the situation or occasion must permit active trust-building. The methods may be used in contexts such as criminal interrogation, customer service, or negotiation and cooperation, but they must not be employed when strict protocol is required—hierarchical, solemn, or coldly formal settings—otherwise they may cause serious trouble.

### Test Case

Psychology Professional Challenges Micro-reaction Test (微反应测试)

During our early testing, one participant—a master’s graduate in psychology—agreed to take the test while holding a skeptical attitude toward our research and intending to use his professional knowledge to “crack” it. Consequently, when we met, although he voiced polite words, his chin remained slightly raised throughout, his handshake was perfunctory, and the moment he sat down he adopted a provocative posture with legs spread wide, torso relaxed against the chair in a classic posture of control.

Testing began with a baseline assessment consisting of questions we had designed around psychology research topics. Because the questions were highly specialized and referenced the views of earlier scholars with richness and accuracy, the participant involuntarily drew his legs back into a normal sitting posture and straightened his upper body to engage seriously with the examiners. The remainder of the test proceeded smoothly.

After reviewing the full test analysis report, he expressed approval of the research and a willingness to participate further.

The most relaxed appearance is one of complete unconcern, devoid of any social behavior.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: Figure 7-9　Buddha statue in serene form conveying superiority]*

Readers may examine various Buddha statues and observe that most display expressionless faces with eyes half-open (or half-closed), as in Figure 7-9. This is precisely the appearance appropriate to absolute superiority.

When a superior possesses absolute authority, issuing instructions or commands to subordinates rarely produces the arrogant reactions described earlier; instead, the superior more often exhibits calm and silent majesty. This is not mere self-importance but the genuine possession of life-and-death power. Such a person need not expend personal energy to push or urge subordinates; smooth operation relies entirely on institutional mechanisms or personal cult, so the face remains calm, largely expressionless, and the eyes are usually not fully open—the upper eyelids often cover part of the eyeballs.

### (2) Postural Adjustment for Escape

The escape-preparation reactions discussed earlier remain at the preparatory stage and are still far from actual escape movements, making them easy to overlook. By comparison, postural adjustment is a more noticeable form of escape preparation.

**① Sitting Posture Adjustment**

Crossing the legs is a relatively comfortable sitting posture (here we refer only to its comfort aspect; crossed legs may also indicate a defensive state, which must be judged in context—see Chapter 9, “Attack and Combat”). The posture of leaning far back in a chair with legs crossed is especially indicative of relaxation and a sense of control. Such a posture makes rising to flee difficult.

Using this posture as a starting point, if the subject encounters an effective negative stimulus, the crossed legs may immediately be uncrossed and the feet placed one in front of the other (not together) while the torso straightens, as though something has been noticed.

If the subject’s emotion at that moment is tension, fear, or embarrassment (note the absence of surprise or anger), the eyes will not fix on the stimulus source (surprise and anger would produce fixation); instead, the subject will quietly scan the entire testing environment in search of a possible escape route. If the subject lacks sufficient composure or if the stimulus is intense, the hands may also press down on the chair arms—or on the seat itself if there are no arms—as though fearing that leg power alone will not allow a fast enough escape, since pushing with the hands enables quicker rising.

**② Standing Posture Adjustment**

In a standing position, when a negative stimulus prompts preparation to flee, the legs assume a clear configuration: one foot placed forward and the other back, both oriented toward the stimulus source, rather than both feet facing it simultaneously. Geometrically, the plane defined by the two legs runs parallel to (or at a very small acute angle with) the plane formed by the subject and the stimulus source; the two planes never intersect at a right angle. This posture permits either advance or retreat and signals readiness to escape.

### 2. Obvious Escape

Once preparations are complete, actual flight follows.

Note that in real polygraph examinations and interrogations, escape-preparation reactions and escape reactions seldom appear in strict sequence; in the great majority of cases they occur separately (for example, only a deep inhalation without bodily movement).

In the course of survival, fleeing from danger is a common strategy. Over long periods of evolution, numerous instinctive leg and foot movements arising from anxiety (worry or fear) have accumulated. For instance, when my son was about two years old he would already stamp his feet and shout when he urgently wanted something; no one taught him this stamping behavior—it is purely innate—whereas the shout “Give it to me!” was something I consciously taught him so that he could express his needs in kindergarten. Adults, too, when worried, often pace back and forth unconsciously.

Legs and feet are farthest from the brain; apart from walking and running, ordinary people cannot finely control the use of leg power without specialized practice such as taekwondo kicking techniques. Consequently, actions performed by this less controllable part of the body are the most honest and credible reflections of psychological state.

After being startled, leaping backward is what we commonly call a “jump scare.” A jump scare never involves a vertical leap or a forward jump; retreat invariably increases distance from the stimulus.

All animals understand that only by increasing distance from the stimulus source can life be preserved. Animals that leapt forward when startled were long ago eliminated by predators and no longer exist on Earth. Humans retain this most primitive yet most rational mechanism, so the response occurs without any need for thought.

A relatively calm and subtle movement is controlled retreat. The subject appears composed while taking a few steps backward—usually half a step or one step—often still smiling; moving more than two steps generally constitutes a loss of composure.

### Speaker and Audience

Speaking before a large audience can indeed be daunting; if the audience shows no interest in what is being said, the situation can become awkward. It is no wonder some people experience stage fright or feel as though they are sitting on pins and needles. To capture the audience’s interest, a speaker must invest considerable time in preparation. Yet no matter how thorough the preparation, during the speech itself the speaker must pay close attention to audience reactions and adjust style as needed to maintain the topic’s appeal.

From the moment one steps onto the platform and begins speaking, one must closely monitor the audience’s “silent” feedback. If any negative behaviors appear, the speaker should insert a story or joke that is easy to follow and likely to draw participation. Audiences generally respond more favorably to a speaker who displays a sense of humor.

As a speaker, pay particular attention to critical gestures from the audience. Individuals making such gestures are usually waiting for something of value. If audience members tilt their heads, they are listening attentively and with interest; if their body language indicates that the explanation is unclear or the speech is dull, the speaker should promptly change approach—for example, by posing a question to the audience. Once those individuals are re-engaged, the speaker can return to the previously unfinished content.

Note that even when the topic is highly interesting, presenting too much information at once can produce a sense of “overload.” Audience members may therefore appear temporarily distracted because their brains cannot absorb additional information.

At such times one may observe their slightly forward-leaning torsos suddenly straighten, bodies shift restlessly, glances alternate between watches and the ceiling or between one another, and eyes finally fix on the exit. When the audience reaches this state, it is worth reflecting on the wisdom of the remark: “Why are you still speaking eloquently after all the audience has left?”

### 8.3.2 The Most Complete Defensive Posture

We conducted an experiment to verify human reaction patterns when facing extreme danger.

Before the experiment, all participants were instructed simply to remain still. Our experimenters then demonstrated the procedure by gently tossing a soccer ball at each participant so that it struck the body. The demonstration was performed in a mild, controlled manner.

Some participants requested a trial of the force; after the trial they stated they could remain motionless. The experiment included rewards and penalties: remaining still and absorbing the impact counted as success and earned the corresponding bonus; any movement counted as failure, and all recorded video and photographic materials were provided to us free of charge for use.

When the participants actually stood in position, however, the balls were thrown with full force and intimidating sound. Not a single participant remained motionless under these conditions.

The experiment was originally intended to demonstrate that even when one intends to stay still, movement occurs upon attack because physiological behavior takes precedence over social behavior. After easily confirming this conclusion, we reviewed the recordings and found that every participant’s dodging movement was nearly identical—bending and twisting the torso to create a barrier with the limbs, as shown in Figure 8-18.

More detailed elements included shrugging the shoulders while tucking the head downward, rotating and bending the torso to shield its anterior surface, and raising both hands and one leg to form a protective barrier in front of the torso.

This most complete defensive posture reflects a mindset that can be rendered as: “There is no way to dodge; I must take the hit. Taking a hit and dying (or being injured) is normal; I have no capacity to counterattack.”

Thus the most complete defensive posture maps onto the most powerless, non-resistant mentality. When this reaction pattern is observed in an opponent, it indicates that at that moment the person regards himself as the losing side and feels incapable of resistance.

### Anecdotal Case: How to Use Small Talk to Quickly Please the Other Person

Meeting a student one has not seen for a long time offers an opportunity to build a good social relationship through conversation.

Friend: “Long time no see!”

Me: “Indeed! You’ve put on quite a bit of weight since before.”

Friend: “Really?”

As he spoke, his eyes looked downward, he quickly pressed his lips together, lowered his head slightly, and spoke in a softer voice, though he soon regained composure.

Me: “Weight gain is actually a mark of successful people.”

Friend: “I really have gained weight.”

While saying this, his volume rose, his speech slowed, and his tone became gentle—a typical social reaction.

Me: “Still, I think you’ve matured a great deal since your school days. I hear you’re now handling things independently.”

Friend: “Of course. When you saw me back then, I was still a student.”

As he said this, his head-lift was pronounced enough to cause a slight backward lean of the torso; his face showed a full smile, his pitch rose suddenly, his speech quickened, and his tone became cheerful.

Although the exchange was simple small talk, the deliberate dip followed by elevation often produces a strong approach effect.

The lip-biting upon hearing the first remark is a classic self-soothing response; the gaze aversion and head-lowering reflect communication interruption triggered by negative emotion; the softer voice indicates a nervous system in a negative state with no resistive energy—signs of a guilty emotion.

In fact, I had no clear memory of whether he had gained weight; I merely noted that most people who maintain good living habits do not wish to become heavier, because weight gain usually signals problems with lifestyle or bodily function.

After I commented on his maturity, the head-lift, slight chin raise, and genuine smile showed that he was pleased with the assessment; his tone also conveyed happiness.

Although such conversational pleasantries do not involve real gains or losses and the stimulus is common and mild, the sequence of negative evaluation followed by praise still elicited clear reactions from the subject.

### 4.3 Fear: Kneeling and Kowtowing for Survival

Chinese ancient etiquette was intricate and complex; special institutions even provided training before an audience with the emperor, because errors in protocol could have grave consequences.

Among the many ancient rituals, the one most familiar to Chinese people is kneeling and kowtowing. Kowtowing, put simply, means kneeling and touching the forehead to the ground. This ritual was once condemned as a feudal remnant and, except for descendants paying respects to elders, has been removed from social etiquette.

In reality, kneeling and kowtowing were not invented as ritual actions; they are evolutionarily produced survival skills—instinctive self-protection movements.

Kneeling, with knees on the ground, lowers the center of gravity and prevents serious injury to the head and torso in the event of an accident, while also rendering escape or attack impossible, leaving only passive waiting. Kowtowing is even more effective: the head is placed directly on the ground (already at its lowest), and the hands are positioned behind the head (an action later possibly refined by ritual) to guard against unexpected danger. This single kneel and kowtow also perfectly conceals the chest, abdomen, and genitals—the most vulnerable areas—avoiding injury to the weakest parts. Such a perfect protective movement could never have been devised by conscious thought; the entire body assumes its maximum contracted posture.

Later, rulers adopted this survival movement and elevated it into ritual for good reason. After all, when a superior stands while a subordinate assumes this posture on the ground, both parties perceive an enormous disparity and accept it as natural. The greater the disparity, the more firmly the social hierarchy is anchored and the easier it is to rule.

One can imagine that when an emperor became angry, the minister being reprimanded would immediately and effortlessly perform the full set of kneeling and kowtowing movements without the emperor needing to utter a single coarse word. Although the action appears to be strict etiquette and utmost respect, it also carries an innate impetus.

### Chapter Summary

Offensive reactions within combat responses map onto the actor’s anger and desire to win—expressions of a dominant mentality; defensive reactions map onto avoidance and endurance—expressions of a subordinate mentality.

Combat responses proceed through three stages: combat preparation, combat execution, and defensive protection.

**Combat Preparation**  
The characteristic of combat-preparation reactions is that the actor exerts force in an inconspicuous manner, the target of the force being not an external object but “oneself against oneself.” Examples include clenching fists, gripping one’s own arms, pressing fingertips forcefully against each other, gritting teeth, tugging at one’s own clothing, stomping or grinding the foot, or forcefully squeezing a walnut in one’s hand.

**Combat Execution**  
The characteristic of combat-execution reactions is that the subject applies force—either overtly or covertly—to an external object, though the force is seldom aimed directly at the stimulus source. Examples include finger-pointing pokes, knocking on a table, slapping a table, flinging a book, slamming a cup, throwing a phone, or slamming a door. After transformation, these actions lose their obvious offensive meaning and become subtle, yet they still reveal the actor’s combative mentality and desire to prevail—an expression of a dominant mentality.

**Defensive Protection**  
The characteristic of defensive-protection reactions is curvature of the torso accompanied by the limbs forming a barrier; the torso also naturally rotates to prevent the stimulus source from directly striking the chest, abdomen, or genital surfaces.

Because a threat to interests is the root cause of anger and fighting spirit, the appearance of anger in a subject indicates that the stimulus source is perceived as threatening. In the specific context of testing, this stimulus source carries great significance and is very likely the very clue that everyone is concerned about and that the subject is desperately trying to conceal.

### III. Body Posture and Expressions

Human body posture and expressions are rich and varied. In general, when conveying complete information to the outside world, verbal expression accounts for only 7%, tone accounts for 38%, and the remaining 55% of the information must be conveyed through nonverbal body posture. This shows that body posture language plays a vital role in our daily conversations. It allows emotions to be expressed more directly and intuitively, and changes in posture language reflect fluctuations in a person’s inner emotions. It is no exaggeration to say that a single posture or movement can easily reveal the emotional state within.

Psychologists have cited a research finding: during conversation, if you are telling the truth, your body will involuntarily lean toward the other person, hoping they will better understand what you are saying; if you are lying, your body will maintain a certain distance from the other person, and the placement of your feet will also appear unnatural.

It is not difficult to notice that some people like to sit upright and proper. From this posture alone, you can roughly tell that the other person is in a state of deference or tension.
