U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation agents captured a high-level spy who had been operating undercover for years. To extract the names of higher-ranking spies from him, the agents subjected him to intense interrogation.

At first, the spy appeared cooperative and revealed several insignificant pieces of information, but whenever the questioning turned to his superiors, he fell silent and refused to speak.

The agents tried many approaches without success. Eventually, an experienced senior agent took over the case. He entered the interrogation room carrying a list of suspected spy leaders.

"I know why you are not talking," the senior agent said with a smile as he sat down in front of the spy. "Given your current situation, you are likely to be extradited back to your country. You must be waiting for that day, aren't you?"

The spy looked up at him briefly, then lowered his head again. No matter what the senior agent said, he showed no reaction.

Undeterred, the senior agent smiled slightly. "Your tight lips are admirable, but that approach is unwise here. We already have solid intelligence. The individuals on this list will soon be brought here to meet you. I believe you have met some of them. Let me read their names: Quinn Green, Nicole Carlins, Scock Hanks…"

After each name, the senior agent paused for a second to observe the spy's reaction. Although the spy's facial expression remained unchanged, when he heard the name "Rooney Smith," his index finger resting on the table twitched reflexively.

The senior agent caught this tiny movement and quickly concluded that Rooney Smith was the spy's superior. Sure enough, after a period of intensified surveillance on Smith, the FBI obtained evidence of his crimes and arrested him.

When communicating with others, we can often infer their thoughts from their words and attitudes. But what if the other person refuses to cooperate? They may not answer questions or even show the slightest expression. In such cases, are we powerless to judge their psychology?

In situations like this, we need the tools of behavioral psychology.

When people encounter external stimuli, their bodies produce various unique responses to adapt to the environment, such as muscle contractions, glandular secretions, or limb movements. These distinctive responses are what we call behavior, the primary subject of behavioral psychology. Drawing on Pavlovian conditioning, external stimuli can be paired with the body's unconditioned stimuli. An external stimulus can trigger bodily reactions that were originally elicited only by unconditioned stimuli, forming primary conditioned responses. When similar stimulating events recur or are presented verbally by others, the body produces corresponding unconscious reactions.

In other words, unconscious behaviors can be traced back to conditioned reflexes, and these reflexes reveal a person's true thoughts. Once you master behavioral psychology, even the most closely guarded secrets become visible.

Old Niu and Old Xu had been business partners for many years. Recently, a major deal came Old Niu's way, and his first instinct was to discuss it with Old Xu.

However, rumors had reached Old Niu suggesting that Old Xu had found new partners and was shifting investments overseas.

Should he tell Old Xu about the project? Old Niu was torn. Using the pretext of having tea, he invited Old Xu out to sound him out.

During their casual conversation, Old Niu repeatedly hinted at the matter indirectly, but Old Xu, a seasoned businessman, would not easily reveal his thoughts. After a long exchange, Old Niu gained nothing.

Growing frustrated, Old Niu casually placed his teacup right next to Old Xu's. Under normal circumstances this would not matter, and Old Xu would not have minded. This time, however, Old Xu frowned slightly and quietly lifted his own cup to take a sip.

Old Niu noticed the subtle movement and felt a sudden unease. He swallowed the words he had been about to say.

Sure enough, after watching for some time, Old Niu discovered that Old Xu had indeed shifted his investment direction and was gradually moving away from their partnership.

As a veteran in business, Old Xu could keep his words airtight, yet his small action betrayed his inner sense of distance from Old Niu. Had Old Niu not possessed some knowledge of behavioral psychology and recognized the hidden meaning behind that gesture, he might have continued treating Old Xu as before, only to face betrayal by his long-time partner and possibly even risk the major deal itself.

This shows how important it is in daily life to uncover the hidden meanings behind others' small actions. We usually study psychology books to judge others' mental states so that, knowing both ourselves and others, we can succeed in every endeavor. Learning psychology is like building a house: the height of the structure depends on the strength of the foundation. Techniques such as cold reading or psychological manipulation focus on skills and methods, whereas behavioral psychology addresses the root of judgment. Without accurately reading another's psychology, even extensive technique will yield half the results with twice the effort. With correct psychological insight, all techniques become twice as effective with half the effort.

#### Inferring the Other Person's True Psychological State from Behavior

**Micro-expression Keywords**

Psychologist Sigmund Freud once said: "Anyone with intact senses will eventually believe that no one can keep a secret. If his lips are sealed, his fingertips will speak, and every pore on his body will betray him." Our words may deceive, but behavior cannot lie.

As a child, I read the Sherlock Holmes detective stories and admired Holmes's seemingly supernatural deductive powers. After studying behavioral psychology, I realized that Holmes often judged whether someone was lying or hiding something by observing their behavior. These judgments, it turns out, were usually correct, and this intuitive approach aligns with the theoretical findings of behavioral psychology.

*The Silence of the Lambs*, *The Rock*, *The Rock* (alternate title), *True Lies*, *Die Hard*… These familiar film titles draw us into battles between justice and evil, filled with passion and intensity. At the same time, the weighty name FBI has entered the minds of most citizens.

FBI stands for Federal Bureau of Investigation, America's premier intelligence agency. Every FBI agent is among the elite of U.S. law enforcement. Only after multiple rounds of selection and three months of rigorous, fully enclosed training do candidates earn the right to serve as FBI agents. During this training, the most critical and important course is behavioral psychology.

Why must even FBI agents study behavioral psychology?

Dealing daily with terrorists and highly intelligent criminals, FBI agents need to determine immediately whether someone is lying to them or even what the person is thinking. Many criminals are skilled liars, so relying solely on verbal cues can easily miss the truth. Therefore, FBI agents primarily rely on behavioral analysis to understand a suspect's mental state.

Veteran agent Navarro, with more than twenty years at the FBI, once visited the mother of an armed fugitive during a pursuit. He and a colleague entered the elderly woman's home, showed their credentials, and began routine questioning. When Navarro asked, "Is your son at home?" he noticed the woman place her hand on her neck before answering, "No, he is not."

After several more questions, Navarro asked again, "Could your son sneak into your house while you are out?" Once more, the woman put her hand to her neck and replied, "No, I don't think so."

Navarro remained impassive and continued questioning until, just before leaving, he asked pointedly, "So, to summarize my notes, your son is definitely not in this house, correct?"

This time the woman again placed her hand on her neck and nodded.

Navarro was almost certain she was lying and that her son was hidden inside. After obtaining a search warrant, the agents found the fugitive in a concealed space beneath a stack of boxes.

In this real case, Navarro applied the principles of behavioral psychology. When people experience a negative reaction to something they have said or done—for example, lying—they unconsciously perform self-soothing gestures such as touching the neck or nose to mask or relieve inner discomfort. The elderly woman's repeated gestures allowed the experienced Navarro to see through her immediately.

In today's colorful society, lying has become commonplace for most people. Judging truthfulness from words alone is extremely difficult, especially with ruthless and cunning criminals who can lie without changing expression and argue calmly. Therefore, reading behavior to discern inner thoughts is the only reliable way to secure a confession.

Seated across the table, the suspect answered the FBI agent's questions with careful caution. His words were sincere, and he had solid evidence placing him elsewhere at the time of the crime. Still, the agent pressed on.

"If you were to kill someone, would you use a gun?"

The suspect shrugged, shook his head, and put on a helpless expression.

"Then, if you were to kill someone, would you use a knife?"

The suspect repeated the same gesture and shook his head.

"If you were to kill someone, would you use a hammer?"

"No." The suspect shook his head again.

"If you were to kill someone, would you use an ice pick?"

At this question, the suspect showed a slight change in expression. His eyelids visibly drooped, as if trying to hide something, but the movement vanished instantly.

The sharp-eyed FBI agent noticed it. The suspect became the prime suspect in the case. Further investigation confirmed he was the murderer.

A single blink lasting only 0.2 to 0.4 seconds revealed the suspect's flaw. The abnormal bodily reaction triggered by hearing the murder weapon he had actually used—an ice pick—gave the FBI the breakthrough they needed. It is precisely this sensitivity to physical actions that allows FBI agents to perceive psychological shifts at a glance, much like the superhuman figures in ordinary people's eyes.

It is no exaggeration to call behavioral psychology the FBI's ultimate secret for reading people. Senior FBI agents have stated: "In actual investigations, reading a person's inner world from their external body language is extremely helpful for solving difficult cases. That is why we make instruction on decoding internal information through body language a core part of FBI training."

After systematic training in behavioral psychology, FBI agents mentally "scan" every subtle movement of a suspect and analyze its precise meaning. Mastery of this skill enables them to seize critical details, solve extraordinary cases, and become the living legends among us.

#### Using the Subconscious to Help You Understand Others' Deepest Secrets

**Micro-expression Keywords**

In his work *Death in the Afternoon*, the renowned author Ernest Hemingway compared literary creation to an iceberg. In reality, human consciousness resembles an iceberg as well. Therefore, mastering 95 percent of another person’s subconscious through behavioral psychology proves far more useful than struggling to control the mere 5 percent of conscious awareness.

Anyone who has seen *Titanic* remembers the scene in which the liner strikes the iceberg. When the ship veered sharply to avoid an iceberg smaller than one-tenth its own size, many viewers held their breath. Yet how many have asked why the sight of such a modest iceberg caused panic among everyone aboard, why Captain Edward ordered an emergency turn, and why an iceberg of that volume could slice the supposedly unsinkable *Titanic* in two?

A detail in the film supplies the answer. As the hull advanced through the water, a massive dark shape scraped violently against the submerged portion of the ship, breaching the section hidden beneath the surface and allowing seawater to flood the engine room.

That dark shape was the part of the iceberg concealed below the waterline. It also illustrates the psychological principle we will discuss—the iceberg effect.

The iceberg effect, also known as iceberg theory, was proposed by the psychologist Sigmund Freud. He argued that personality resembles an iceberg floating in the sea: only the tip is visible above the surface, corresponding to the conscious level, while the far larger portion that remains hidden belongs to the subconscious, which to a great extent governs development and behavior.

The subconscious refers to a mysterious force buried beneath conscious awareness, sometimes called right-brain consciousness or cosmic consciousness. In daily life it is often described as “potential”—an undeveloped capacity that exists within the body.

In a report, Dr. Konstantin of the University of Vienna estimated that the human brain contains roughly 150 billion neurons. Each neuron connects with others to form neural circuits that process information. At least 95 percent of these neurons remain undeveloped; even a scientific giant such as Albert Einstein utilized only about 2 percent of his subconscious capacity.

This demonstrates the enormous influence the subconscious exerts. Although we cannot directly control it, our behavior, movements, expressions, and attitudes are shaped by it at every turn. Consequently, understanding another person’s subconscious offers invaluable assistance in approaching others and earning their trust without conscious effort.

Language and outward appearance reflect the conscious mind, which people can regulate, whereas the subconscious can be inferred only through observation of unconscious actions. The most rapid and reliable method for discerning another’s subconscious is therefore the behavioral psychology presented in this book.

Meihong, a graduate of a prestigious foreign university, secured an interview at a large company through a friend’s introduction.

The interviewer, a sharp and capable-looking female executive, displayed the polished demeanor expected of a mid-level leader in a major corporation. She invited Meihong to sit, reviewed her résumé, asked several professional questions, and inquired about Meihong’s impressions of the company.

Their exchange proceeded in a formal, measured manner, yet the observant Meihong noticed that the interviewer repeatedly glanced at her watch and kept her feet angled toward the door.

Once the standard questions ended, it was time for Meihong to speak freely. By then the company’s closing hour had already passed. Checking her own watch, Meihong made a decision that surprised the interviewer: “Manager Zhang, it is already quite late. Why don’t we continue while we walk? The time it takes to reach the parking lot should be enough for my self-introduction.”

“Er… all right.” Although surprised, Manager Zhang’s slightly furrowed brow relaxed.

On the way, Meihong delivered a concise self-introduction. Although incomplete because of time constraints, the interviewer’s attitude shifted from strictly businesslike to noticeably warmer and even slightly cordial.

The next morning Meihong received word that she had passed the interview and could begin work at the new company.

Most candidates would have tried to use every available minute to showcase their strengths. Why did Meihong’s seemingly “lazy” approach instead win the interviewer’s favor?

Attentive readers will recognize that Meihong succeeded by observing the interviewer’s behavior. As a mid-level manager, the interviewer felt obliged to maintain a professional image at all times. Even though she was eager to leave, she could not show it outwardly. Her actions, however, betrayed her: the unconscious glances at her watch and the feet pointing toward the door revealed an urgent desire to finish and go home.

These movements may have gone unnoticed by the interviewer herself, yet Meihong registered them. By responding to the unspoken cue, Meihong left a favorable impression on the interviewer’s subconscious. Combined with her own qualifications, the job offer followed naturally.

Judging another person’s subconscious thoughts through behavior is therefore far more practical than guessing conscious intentions from words or expressions alone. If human consciousness is likened to an iceberg, 95 percent of its volume lies hidden beneath the surface in the subconscious. Behavior, being directly linked to the subconscious, supplies the most important information available to us.

#### Hands Formed into a Steeple Shape, Indicating Confidence

FBI agents have observed that confident speakers rarely touch their mouths, noses, or hair. When watching a confident presenter, one notices that the speaker relies almost exclusively on hand gestures to emphasize words and avoids contact with the face or head.

Agents have also noted that confident individuals maintain an upright, proud posture, never slouching or shifting restlessly. They sustain eye contact longer than less confident people, who tend to do the opposite.

Confident people frequently form a steeple with their hands by pressing the fingertips of both hands together, creating the shape of a church steeple (see Figure 2.11). The gesture is sometimes interpreted as affected, arrogant, or proud.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.11　将手摆成尖塔状]*

In *The Art of Reading Minds in the White House*, author Henry H. Calero recounts an anecdote involving the steepled-hands gesture.

Steve McQueen, the American actor nicknamed “The King of Cool,” appeared in many popular films, including the classic *The Great Escape*.

During a flight, Calero found himself seated next to McQueen in first class. They began talking, and when the conversation turned to McQueen’s performance as a poker player in *The Cincinnati Kid*, Calero remarked that the portrayal was unconvincing.

McQueen folded his arms, fixed Calero with his piercing blue eyes, and asked sharply, “What do you mean?”

Calero explained that in a key scene McQueen’s character inadvertently revealed a winning hand by forming a steeple after placing a bet. McQueen nodded, and Calero continued: steady professional players never make that gesture unless they are bluffing, yet McQueen’s character clearly was not. The scene therefore contained a nonverbal error.

After hearing the explanation, McQueen dropped his arms, snapped his fingers, and told Calero that others had offered the same criticism but could not explain why—they simply “felt” something was wrong.

McQueen shook Calero’s hand warmly and thanked him. The remainder of the flight passed pleasantly.

People sometimes adopt the steepled-hands position while speaking or listening, though the hands may rest slightly higher or lower than shown in Figure 2.11.

Those who rarely use the gesture may raise their hands so high that they peer through the gaps between their fingers, an action that can make others uncomfortable. If you must continue a conversation with such a person, practice self-control. A lower steeple is most common among women (see Figure 2.12).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.12　双手位置较低的尖塔状手势]*

An elegant variation occurs when the hands are clasped with one hand gently enclosing the other, which is formed into a fist (see Figure 2.13).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.13　优雅的尖塔状手势]*

This refined steeple most often appears in business settings. Company employees, lawyers, doctors, and especially professors lecturing on favorite topics frequently adopt it, apparently signaling satisfaction with their current roles.

Most of the time the steepled-hands gesture is unconscious, yet some people deliberately employ it to project strong security and absolute confidence.

One piece of advice suggests that, after delivering a final offer in negotiations, a businessperson should lean back, smile, and form the steeple. The client, after studying the gesture for some time, may then declare, “Deal!” The movement seems to exert a quiet power that can sway the other party.

FBI agents have also observed that when the weaker party in a negotiation forms a steeple, the stronger party may conclude that the person is holding something back and knows more than has been said, prompting an immediate change of subject.

If your next argument lacks the persuasive force you hoped for, try forming a steeple, remain silent, and wait for the other person’s reaction.

#### Resting Chin on Hand: Contemplating or Bored

Success in business or social life depends on communication skills, so anyone who wants to know how well their message has been received must understand and evaluate feedback.

Several specific gestures indicate that a person is contemplating received verbal information. Without careful observation, however, these gestures can be difficult to detect. Consider a young teacher explaining a principle who notices a student staring fixedly, unblinking, sitting rigidly with almost no movement. The teacher may assume the student is fully attentive, yet that assumption would be mistaken. Some people can feign rapt attention when they are not truly engaged.

A genuinely attentive student sits on the edge of the chair, leans forward, tilts the head slightly to one side, and may rest the chin on a hand (see Figure 2.24). A tilted head usually signals that the listener is not only hearing the words but also reflecting on them.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.24　揣摩的姿势]*

As C. H. Woolbert wrote in *The Audience*: “When a student in class gradually becomes absorbed by the problem before him, he generally slumps his shoulders, spreads his feet, scratches his head, and performs many unconscious movements. Once the problem is solved, he sits up straight, straightens his clothes, and returns to his normal state.”

Auguste Rodin’s sculpture *The Thinker* exemplifies the language of posture. No one doubts that the figure is deeply pondering a difficult question and seeking its solution. In everyday life we often see “The Thinker” pose or similar postures, indicating that the person is reflecting on something puzzling or troublesome.

It is worth noting that contemplative gestures can easily be mistaken for signs of boredom. When someone loses interest, they may also rest their chin on a hand (see Figure 2.25), though in the latter case the eyelids droop and the gaze becomes vacant.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.25　表示厌烦的典型动作]*

Sometimes a person adopts a series of critical contemplative postures: placing one hand on the cheek, cupping the jaw, extending the index finger along the face while curling the remaining fingers beneath the mouth (see Figure 2.26). This posture shows that the individual is both weighing the speaker’s words and evaluating the ideas being presented.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.26　批判性的揣摩姿势]*

Another contemplative gesture involves stroking the chin or beard (for men with facial hair) (see Figure 2.27). This “let me think” posture typically appears when someone is about to make a decision. The accompanying facial expression often features slightly narrowed eyes, as if considering the matter from a long-term perspective to determine the best answer.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.27　抚摸下巴的揣摩姿势]*

Sliding glasses down the nose and peering over the rims at the speaker is another common contemplative gesture (see Figure 2.28). The person being observed may feel criticized or looked down upon. Anyone who habitually uses this posture should recognize its potentially negative effect; if you wish to avoid an unfavorable response, refrain from it.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.28　通过眼镜缝隙窥探]*

People who wear glasses sometimes remove them slowly and carefully clean the lenses—even when the lenses are already clean—to manage conflict or buy time for a decision. While performing this action they usually speak more slowly.

A similar time-buying gesture is to remove the glasses and place one temple arm between the teeth (see Figure 2.29). This posture indicates that the person is listening attentively and carefully considering what is being said.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.29　拖延时间，仔细思考]*

#### Section 2: Having a Pair of Confident Hands

Since ancient times, open palms have always been associated with truthfulness, honesty, and compliance. If you want to know whether someone is being candid, the most direct method is to observe their palm movements. Through long-term practice, gestures have acquired specific meanings and become a powerful means of expressing thoughts and feelings, holding a primary position in body language. Gestures assist speakers in conveying ideas and emotions through changes in the fingers, palms, and arms. Graceful and engaging gestures create a sense of pleasure, while gentle gestures evoke gratitude; negative and listless gestures produce feelings of depression and displeasure.

In interpersonal interactions, gestures form an important component. They reinforce the power of language and enrich its color through supplementation and clarification—thus enhancing emotional expressiveness while also describing objects more concretely. At times, gestures can even function as an independent and effective form of language, such as in situations where speaking is inconvenient. Moreover, gestures play a greater role for deaf and mute individuals than any other communication method.

Although gestures can assist speakers in expressing their intended content, improper use produces the opposite effect, as unnatural gestures become obstacles to interaction. When employing gesture language, observe the following points:

1. Apply gestures appropriately so they fulfill their function.
2. Gestures do not suit every occasion and every audience.
3. Using gestures to express meaning should occur unconsciously rather than through deliberate movements.
4. Gestures must coordinate with speech; avoid actions that directly contradict spoken words.

So, which gestures qualify as positive and convey constructive messages?

The most renowned is the “steeple” gesture. Psychologists Nivenber and Cabro conducted specialized research on the steeple gesture and found that professionals such as lawyers, accountants, and managers use it most frequently during interactions; when superiors address subordinates, the steeple gesture appears most often.

The steeple gesture has two forms: the “upright steeple” and the “inverted steeple.” Generally, the upright steeple indicates the person’s sense of confidence and superiority. When someone forms this gesture while also tilting their head upward, it shows they feel highly confident, even somewhat self-important, at that moment.

Note that, like spoken language, gestures require surrounding context for accurate interpretation. For example, a salesperson observes a customer leaning forward, palms open, smiling, and finally forming the upright steeple; this indicates the customer is satisfied with the products and signals the conversation is ending in preparation to place an order or make a purchase. However, if the upright steeple appears after a series of negative body-language signals—such as arms crossed over the chest, legs crossed, and gaze wandering—it shows the customer is dissatisfied and has no intention of buying. Many might view the second scenario as conveying negative information and conclude the upright steeple does not apply in all confident situations. In reality, for the customer the gesture expresses personal confidence in both cases: the first reflects firm intent to buy, the second firm intent not to buy. The difference lies only in the salesperson’s perspective—positive in the former, negative in the latter. Therefore, when encountering the upright steeple, always combine it with preceding body-language cues for a comprehensive judgment.

The inverted steeple commonly appears when listening to others’ opinions and occurs more frequently among women, suggesting a low-profile, slightly reserved stance. Like the upright steeple, an inverted steeple following positive body language indicates acceptance; conversely, following negative body language it signals rejection or negation.

Research shows that the higher a person’s confidence level, the higher the position of the steeple gesture—sometimes even level with the eyebrows, as if viewing others through the gaps between the fingers. Interestingly, negotiators sometimes unconsciously adopt this posture when at a disadvantage. The counterpart’s reaction is almost invariably the same: they assume the person displaying the gesture is concealing information and knows more than they reveal, prompting an immediate change of topic. In poker, if an opponent forms the steeple gesture, stop playing unless you hold a strong hand.

If you rarely use the steeple gesture yet wish to increase your own confidence, the following points may help:

#### Section 4: When Excited, Do Your Hands Sweat or Tremble?

Some people’s hands sweat or tremble when they feel nervous. Once the tension subsides, the sweating and trembling disappear automatically. What causes these reactions?

First, consider the causes of sweaty hands.

Under pressure, the body’s hormones trigger the release of stored energy to supply the brain and limbs for handling sudden events, rapidly raising body temperature. Yet organs function normally only at a constant temperature and cannot tolerate excessive heat. The body therefore secretes sweat to lower temperature and thereby relieve tension.

Sweating falls into three categories according to stimulus type: thermal sweating, emotional sweating, gustatory sweating, and exertional sweating. Thermal sweating results from elevated external temperature and generally affects all skin except the palms and soles. Emotional sweating arises from mental excitement or stimulation and occurs mainly on the palms, soles, and armpits. Gustatory sweating is a physiological response triggered by eating certain stimulating foods. Exertional sweating, as the name implies, occurs after physical activity.

Sweaty palms during tension, fear, or excitement constitute emotional sweating. Emotional sweating typically appears on the palms and sometimes on the backs of the hands, face, neck, forearms, and lower legs. Palmar sweating relates to physical constitution and endocrine factors. A healthy person’s palms remain dry even during profuse perspiration elsewhere. People who frequently experience sweaty palms often have dry skin elsewhere yet cold, clammy palms. In extreme cases of intense mental stress, some individuals sweat profusely over the entire body. Others progress to more severe symptoms: cold sweats accompanied by pallor, visual disturbances, limb weakness, collapse, or fainting. In such emergencies, first identify the cause. Under major shock, the body rapidly converts blood sugar and other nutrients into energy; this sudden surge can lower blood sugar and trigger the symptoms described. Pinching the philtrum (the point between the nose and upper lip) and the tiger’s mouth (the point at the base of the thumb) can alleviate symptoms. If sweating is accompanied by chills, cold extremities, irregular pulse, or shortness of breath, the issue may extend beyond emotional sweating and indicate a cardiac problem; seek an electrocardiogram at a proper hospital.

Next, examine the causes of hand trembling.

Hand tremors fall into two major categories: physiological and pathological. Physiological tremors are small in amplitude and rapid in speed, usually appearing at rest as fine, quick, irregular movements. They commonly occur under mental tension, fear, emotional agitation, severe pain, or extreme fatigue. Once the triggering factors are removed, the tremor disappears, so its impact on daily life remains limited. Pathological tremors involve involuntary shaking that is often permanent and subdivide into resting and action tremors. Resting tremor occurs when muscles are fully relaxed, i.e., in a quiet state; it disappears during sleep and follows a regular pattern, as seen in Parkinson’s syndrome. Action tremor appears only during movement and intensifies as the limb approaches a target. It is irregular, large in amplitude, and intensifies with emotion; it commonly results from lesions of the cranial or upper-limb nerves.

Trembling during emotional excitement belongs to physiological tremor. Although its daily-life impact is minor, it can still interfere in special situations such as interviews or speeches. The most effective way to address trembling is positive mental suggestion: first, reduce self-focus. Shift attention to the task at hand rather than monitoring personal sensations. Focusing on whether the hands are trembling activates the brain and reinforces the behavior, potentially worsening the condition. Therefore, decrease self-attention and concentrate on the actual situation—such as the interviewer, the examiner, or the environment. Second, abandon the intention to control. When people notice trembling, they often try to suppress it, yet the harder they try, the more ineffective the control becomes, increasing tension. Instead, relinquish the control impulse, ignore the tremor, and allow it to subside naturally once calm returns. Cultivating acceptance of the tremor and learning to coexist with it can also lead to eventual resolution.

#### Different Gestures Convey Different Emotions

In social interactions, many people possess several distinctive signature gestures. Through these gestures we can gain some understanding of a person’s psychological state and emotional changes.

Even before language emerged, humans had learned to express different meanings through various gestures. After language appeared, people continued to use gestures frequently in communication because many found that relying solely on the mouth often proved insufficient. Consequently, gestures have become an indispensable part of interpersonal communication. These gestures carry not only surface meanings but also numerous implied meanings.

During conversation, people habitually place their hands in front of the body, speaking while forming various gestures that serve as supplementary “language” rather than relying only on speech. It can be said that people unconsciously employ gestures to exchange ideas, express emotions, and convey feelings.

Various emotions manifest through different gestures. What emotions do specific gestures reflect?

1. **Palms facing upward**  
   In conversation, palms facing upward constitute a positive signal suggesting an open communicative attitude, indicating sufficient candor with nothing concealed and no malice. This gesture reflects the speaker’s desire for interaction and acceptance by the other party.

2. **Palms facing downward**  
   In conversation, palms facing downward represent a commanding signal denoting status, authority, or orders. For instance, when a couple holds hands, if the man’s palm faces down and the woman’s faces up, it indicates the man’s dominance. This gesture reflects the speaker’s wish to diminish the other person while elevating the self. Additionally, palms often face downward when refusing someone.

3. **Palms facing each other**  
   When the other person places palms facing each other with fingertips touching to form a steeple shape, it usually indicates a confident attitude. This common gesture has two variants: the lowered steeple, used when listening to others’ views; and the raised steeple, typically employed when expressing one’s own opinions or speaking.

4. **Extending the index and middle fingers**  
   With the palm outward, the gesture signifies “victory”; with the palm inward, it becomes an insulting expression.

5. **Fingers interlocked**  
   Many people enjoy forming the interlocked-fingers gesture, which relates closely to psychology. When someone interlocks their fingers, it signals confidence. Such individuals often smile, appear composed, and speak frankly. If they interlock their fingers on their thighs with thumbs touching, it means they feel uncertain and caught in a dilemma. If they interlock their fingers while staring at you, it indicates dissatisfaction and ongoing restraint.

6. **Clenching the fingers**  
   Clenching the fingers is commonly called making a fist. In combat, the fist embodies strength for both offense and defense. When used in daily life, the gesture communicates “I am full of power” and “You had better not provoke me.” It constitutes a provocative or demonstrative action.

7. **Hands clasped together**  
   Clasping the hands together expresses a sense of helplessness. Even when the person smiles, the inner feeling of loss and frustration remains visible. Typically, someone who feels their words lack persuasiveness or who perceives themselves in a passive position during conversation will clasp their hands. The clasped-hands posture has three variations: raising both hands to the face and clasping them tightly; resting elbows on the knees or table and clasping the hands; or standing with hands clasped in front of the lower abdomen. The height of the hands also reflects the intensity of the frustration. Hands held high in the middle of the body indicate a highly negative mindset and rejection of further interaction. Hands placed lower on the body signal milder frustration, making conversation relatively easier.

#### 2. Hands Restrained Behind the Body

Hands restrained behind the body also indicate endurance, yet without self-protective intent—an unyielding, head-on form of endurance.

Thus, when the spine is not fully erect, the torso leans slightly forward, the legs stand straight and together, the body remains still, and the hands are placed behind the back in restraint, this constitutes a freeze response. Because the person dares to face the stimulus source directly without defense, the posture carries a sense of “taking it head-on,” reflecting a stronger drive than hands restrained in front of the body.

When the hands are clasped behind the back with the torso erect and the head held high, the posture is often interpreted as a sign of maturity or control. See Figure 4-4.

Several subtler variations appear to have reasonable explanations for restraining the hands and may even seem stylish—for example, inserting both hands into trouser pockets. Similar adaptations include a novice host holding a microphone in one hand (thus occupying it and providing a plausible excuse) while placing the other hand in a pocket. See Figures 4-5 and 4-6. Such postures generally occur only in inexperienced young men (age extendable to 40), who also believe the stance looks dashing.

Less stylish examples include pulling the sleeves down to cover the hands, ostensibly because of cold weather, thereby concealing the restrained hands. See Figure 4-7. Unless the temperature is genuinely low, this posture represents a freeze response.

In essence, these postures use external means to restrain hand movement. In context, they can all be interpreted as freeze responses stemming from uncertainty, reflecting inner tension and anxiety. If this interpretation seems forced, consider a simple question: when have you seen national leaders place their hands in their pockets during formal occasions?

These hand-freeze responses follow an underlying psychological pattern. Expansive limb movements signify expansion and a positive mental state; varied limb movements indicate diversity and richness of mind; conversely, contractive limb movements represent concealment, self-diminishment, and a negative mental state. Whether the hands rest in front or behind the body, or inside pockets, the underlying psychology is to reduce the body’s visible surface area (military parade-rest posture excepted) or to decrease the variety of limb movements and the degree of attention received (less movement is wiser when unskilled), thereby minimizing exposure to harm such as criticism or rejection.

Conversely, individuals who feel strong control over a situation do not adopt these postures. In a popular television program, for instance, the host rarely places hands in pockets because reputation and experience grant command of the scene and a dominant mindset.

We can readily imagine that a boss feels similarly in control within their own domain. When reprimanding subordinates, the boss does not confine the hands to one location or posture. Trained professional actors, possessing command of the performance space, do not insert hands into pockets or adopt other restrained postures when taking the stage or speaking; instead, they naturally position the hands at the sides of the body, moving them appropriately with the action.

Even without a sense of control, mere situational security precludes hand-freeze responses. At a gathering of friends, genuinely happy people converse animatedly, raise glasses, and adopt relaxed, casual postures and movements rather than remaining restrained. Strangers, by contrast, often stay frozen in a corner, avoiding interaction. In such settings, anyone displaying a hand-freeze response stands out conspicuously—either from unfamiliarity or from low self-esteem—making the reaction easy to identify.

#### People Who Twirl Their Hands by Their Ears Are Giving Hints

FBI agent Laura received orders from the Federal Bureau of Investigation to enter a certain insurance company to investigate whether the company had established spy operations in other countries. However, there was an unwritten rule for entering this company: every employee on probation must sell a set amount of insurance within the one-month probationary period to become a permanent employee.

One day a middle-aged couple came to the insurance company, and Laura greeted them. Laura first welcomed them warmly, then introduced various insurance products suitable for their age group. The couple did not appear very interested, which made Laura wonder whether they had come to buy insurance or merely to gather information. Yet during the conversation, when Laura mentioned a family insurance policy, one of the couple casually touched an ear with a hand. Laura therefore concluded that they wanted to purchase a family combination policy.

To test her conclusion, Laura asked, “Are you interested in learning about family combination insurance?” The couple looked surprised but answered seriously: “Yes, because we have considered our children.”

Laura then focused on family insurance and explained in detail the various family-unit policies. Clearly she had found an effective entry point, and one of the products won the couple’s approval. In the end Laura met her sales target and became a permanent employee of the insurance company.

American marketing consultant Mike Stark once said, “If the other person touches an ear, they are signaling interest.” When we speak, if the listener pulls an earlobe, touches an ear, or rubs the temple or the back of the head near the ear, it means the listener is interested in the topic and wants to hear more. This matches the Japanese saying “Pull the ears open to hear good words.”

The subconscious act of touching the ear to signal a desire to keep listening is easy to notice. For example, when someone says “I’m very interested in this topic” or “Really? Why haven’t I heard of that before?” the words are often accompanied by an ear touch. The gesture shows that the listener has become engaged and wants the conversation to continue. We should therefore identify the other person’s “sensitive words” of interest and keep the discussion going; doing so helps both sides communicate effectively.

We should also note that if, during a conversation, the listener folds the entire auricle forward to cover the ear canal, the gesture is a signal to stop talking at once. The movement already conveys the message “I don’t want to hear any more; I’ve heard enough.” It is the same action children sometimes make when they cover their ears with both hands to shut out their parents’ arguing voices from another room.

Adults who do not wish to hear someone speak usually perform a similar gesture. While you are speaking enthusiastically, if the listener inserts a finger into the ear canal as though cleaning the ear, the action signals disdain for your topic. It is best to ask politely whether the listener has any comments or objections. If the person is not someone you can question directly, you should consider changing the subject.

Therefore, while conversing we must observe whether the other person is touching an ear or trying to shift the topic. In short, if the listener’s hands are twirling beside the ears, the gesture is telling us it is time to be on guard.

#### Interpreting Different Emotions from Ear Scratching

Ear scratching is a common action, and the precise spot being scratched reveals different emotions. When someone scratches an ear in front of you, the ear itself is “speaking.”

We often see children cover both ears with their hands when their parents scold them, signaling that they do not want to listen. Adults who do not want to hear someone speak will not cover their ears but will scratch them instead. Moreover, the part of the ear that is scratched carries a distinct meaning. What, then, do the different scratching locations signify? Let us examine them one by one.

1. **Using the fingertip to dig inside the ear**  
   If you are speaking enthusiastically and the listener, looking uninterested, inserts a fingertip into the ear canal and digs, the gesture expresses disdain. Many people find the action particularly offensive. When you see someone digging inside an ear with a fingertip, you can politely ask, “Do you have a different opinion? I’d like to hear it.” Giving the listener a chance to speak keeps the exchange going; otherwise the listener remains resistant and disengaged, rendering the conversation unproductive.

2. **Rubbing behind the auricle**  
   Suppose you are trying to persuade a customer. After speaking until your mouth is dry, you notice the customer unconsciously rub behind the auricle, then turn the head aside and say coolly, “I’ll think about it.” The gesture shows that the customer holds the opposite view and is preparing to state it. If you continue with the same sales pitch, the effort will most likely fail. Rubbing behind the auricle means the listener is trying to keep your words from entering the ear completely.

3. **Folding the entire auricle forward to cover the ear canal**  
   If, while talking, you see the listener fold the entire auricle forward to cover the ear canal, stop speaking immediately. The movement signals “I’m tired of listening and don’t want you to continue.” By covering the ear canal with the auricle, the listener physically blocks unwanted words and expresses impatience. In films we often see the female lead on a blind date with a man she finds unappealing; while she smiles politely, she folds the auricle forward to cover the ear canal. The gesture lets her see only the man’s moving mouth without hearing any sound. Although the scene adds an artistic touch, it vividly conveys the character’s inner feeling. When someone folds the auricle forward to cover the ear canal, remember to change the subject or end the conversation at once; otherwise you will only appear long-winded and make the listener dislike you even more.

4. **Repeatedly scratching the earlobe or the back of the ear**  
   If a person keeps scratching the earlobe or the back of the ear, the action indicates anxiety. Seeing someone scratch the back of the ear usually means the person is facing a problem. If you notice a colleague repeatedly scratching the back of the ear, you can approach and ask whether help is needed. The colleague may be experiencing work difficulties, and offering assistance will leave a favorable impression.

#### Confidence

Confident speakers rarely make small gestures such as covering the mouth, hiding the nose, or scratching the head. Watch any confident speaker and you will notice that the person uses the hands only to emphasize words and almost never touches the face or head.

You will also observe that confident people stand tall and proud, never slouching or shifting their weight from side to side. In addition, they maintain frequent eye contact and hold the other person’s gaze longer, whereas people lacking confidence do the opposite.

Confident people often form a steeple gesture with the hands—the same gesture discussed in Chapter 3—by bringing the fingertips of both hands together so they touch and form a “church steeple” shape (see Figure 4.22).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.22　尖塔状手势]*

People sometimes adopt this gesture while speaking or listening, though the hands may be positioned slightly higher or lower than shown. The lower steeple is most common among women (see Figure 4.23).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.23　双手位置较低的尖塔状手势]*

Another elegant version of the steeple occurs when the hands are clasped together and one hand wraps around the other, which is formed into a fist (see Figure 4.24).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.24　优雅的尖塔状手势]*

This elegant steeple, a sign of confidence, appears most often in business settings. Company employees, lawyers, doctors, and especially professors lecturing on a favorite subject frequently display it, as though expressing satisfaction with their current position.

People who seldom use the steeple sometimes raise it very high when they do use it, almost looking at others through the gaps between their fingers. The posture can make others feel uneasy. If you must continue a conversation with such a person, you will need to exercise self-control.

We have also found that most behavior is unconscious. In negotiations, a weaker party who makes this gesture may give the stronger party the impression that the gesturer is hiding something and knows more than is being said, prompting an immediate change of topic.

The suggestion, therefore, is that if your next negotiating position is not as persuasive as you would like, form the steeple gesture, remain silent, and wait for the other side’s reaction.

Another common sign of confidence is standing with the hands clasped behind the back and the body erect (see Figure 4.25). The posture conveys both confidence and authority. Law-enforcement officers around the world often adopt it. Anyone who has served in the military will immediately recognize it as the stance of a strict drill instructor. In short, the posture is an unmistakable display of power and dignity.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.25　权威的站姿]*

#### Readiness

Some people describe the “readiness” posture as aggressive. Here we retain the term “readiness” because a person with a clear goal and strong determination to achieve it is usually too busy gathering information and solving problems to behave in a hostile manner.

Such individuals resemble the people psychologist Abraham Harold Maslow described as operating at the self-actualization (自我实现 is the highest level need in Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. People with self-actualization needs seem to be doing their utmost to perfect themselves) level; they exhibit this trait to a greater or lesser degree. The following gestures, or any combination of them, are typical of such people.

One classic readiness posture that is easy to recognize is standing with the hands on the hips. A fully confident person who is ready to accept a task usually stands in this way (both men and women of all ages adopt it, though women tend to place one hand lower on the hip).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.16　表示准备就绪的站姿]*

In sports we often see athletes about to enter a game place their hands on their hips. In a business meeting, someone standing with feet apart and hands on hips is usually about to express a serious opinion. If the person is waiting patiently for objections from the group, the arms may also be folded.

Children challenging parental authority likewise place their hands on their hips. Some men, while standing with hands on hips, occasionally pull up their trouser legs.

When determined people stand with hands on hips, they usually place their feet farther apart than usual. The stance emphasizes their resolve and their commitment to their words or plans.

A similar but slightly different readiness posture is the seated version. Notice the consistent elements: (1) the body leans forward; (2) the bent arms and hands rest on the thighs; (3) the legs are apart, as though ready to stand and join the activity.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.17　表示准备就绪的坐姿]*

A person displaying a readiness posture—whether standing or sitting—is interested in what is about to be said or done. The interest does not necessarily mean a desire to participate; it may simply mean fascination with the speaker’s words. This is probably why the phrase “sitting on the edge of the chair” is used to describe someone who is keenly interested in a matter.

In business meetings, people sitting on the edge of their chairs are usually ready to compromise, cooperate, buy, accept, or make an offer. In other words, the posture signals that the person is about to take action.

Salespeople like to see this posture because it marks the moment they “close the deal.” However, if the posture appears together with other negative gestures, it may instead mean “stop,” indicating that the person is about to stand up, cancel the negotiation, or end the meeting.

#### Frustration

Postures that convey frustration are usually easy to detect. Watch a football game on television and you will see plenty of frustrated faces. For example, when a defensive back evades an opponent and passes the ball to a teammate who then fumbles it into the hands of an opposing player, the player who dropped the ball most often reacts by kicking the ground in anger and slapping the helmet.

If you are watching a baseball game and the batter strikes out, you will see the player angrily throw the bat, scratch the back of the neck, and kick up dirt (or anything else within reach) while walking dejectedly back to the dugout.

Non-baseball players may not throw bats to express frustration, but they perform similar actions: scratching the back of the neck and lowering the head (see Figure 4.20). Slamming a table, snapping a pencil, stamping a foot, and other behaviors carry the same meaning as kicking the ground or throwing a bat.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.20　沮丧地用手抓挠颈背]*

Another common frustration gesture is the “hot collar” (see Figure 4.12), in which a person tugs at the shirt collar. The next time you cut in front of another driver and then quickly change lanes, the driver you passed will often make this gesture.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.21　受挫后，用手扯衣领]*

Sometimes frustration is expressed not through body movement but through sound—deep sighs or rapid breathing. One colleague with a quick temper often struggles to control his emotions. When he feels he is approaching his “boiling point,” he begins to inhale forcefully. The sharp intake of breath shows he is trying to stay calm; otherwise he might lose control.

A rancher from Texas once told us that an angry bull snorts loudly through its nostrils before charging. It is a serious warning that must be taken seriously. Psychologists generally agree that when people are frustrated or angry, their breathing becomes rapid and deep, much like a bull panting. The sound is a warning.

Another sound worth noting is the “tsk-tsk.” It is commonly used to express disapproval or disgust and sometimes surprise or regret. We must therefore use all available cues to determine the precise meaning of the sound in any given situation (note: in Syrian, the “tsk-tsk” sound means “no” and is frequently heard in daily life).

If a person kicks the ground, the action indicates frustration. Be careful, however, not to confuse it with the slow, thoughtful walking of someone absorbed in a problem. A person may pause while thinking or deciding and kick the ground absentmindedly.

People sometimes misread frustration gestures, just as they misread other postures. The wise course is therefore to pay attention to what the other person says in order to judge their state of mind.

#### Hands on Hips Convey Hostility

Micro-expression keywords: When people argue or fight, they always place both hands on their hips so they can strike at any moment; such a posture is full of hostility. In daily life, some people unconsciously adopt this pose as well, which makes others feel uncomfortable. If you want to make friends, it is best to lower your hands first.

Friends who enjoy sports know that before certain major boxing matches, organizers often have the fighters strike provocative poses for promotional photos to build hype. We frequently see boxers standing with hands on hips, chins slightly raised, looking arrogant and fearless. In fact, if we observe carefully, the hands-on-hips posture appears not only in competitive settings but also often in ordinary life. In the classic work *Hometown*, Lu Xun depicts Yang Ersao with “thin lips…both hands resting on her hips,” portraying a woman of “sharp-tongued and mean” character. Clearly, hands on hips do not convey a friendly or approachable image.

The hands-on-hips gesture can be displayed by different people in different situations—for example, when children argue with parents, when athletes wait for a competition to begin, and so on. When a man’s territory is invaded by another male, he may also use this posture to issue a silent challenge to the intruder.

At a weekend work-summary meeting, colleagues Xiao Zhang and Xiao Wang disagreed over work responsibilities and progress, but thanks to other colleagues and leaders being present, their argument did not escalate. After work, Xiao Zhang went to the smoking area to relax his nerves and suddenly saw Xiao Wang there, hands on hips and a cigarette in his mouth, which instantly filled him with anger. In this scene, Xiao Zhang perceived Xiao Wang’s dissatisfaction with the earlier dispute and his unwillingness to let it go, so a new argument began.

Perhaps Xiao Wang had no aggressive intent, yet the posture conveyed an unfriendly attitude and caused misunderstanding.

According to foreign scientists’ research, the hands-on-hips posture produces subtle visual and emotional stimulation. With both hands on the hips, a person occupies more space; the elbows that jut outward resemble weapons and create an intimidating effect. This visual stimulus becomes even more pronounced when both parties already sense conflict, triggering psychological defensiveness.

This dominant posture is recognized worldwide; its signal is that the person is ready to attack at any moment. In countless American Western films, it became a classic cowboy pose: before a duel, cowboys always held a revolver in one hand and kept the other on the hip.

The posture makes others feel that the newcomer is ill-intentioned and determined to achieve the targeted goal. Even when conversation is casual and friendly, the hands-on-hips posture prevents a completely relaxed atmosphere unless the arms are lowered from the waist.

Therefore, when talking with others, avoid placing both hands on your hips, as it makes people feel threatened. Even during an argument, refrain from this gesture and instead seek a calm resolution; otherwise, the situation will only worsen.

#### 8.2.3 Pointing at the Target of Attack

A person’s offensive actions in combat include linear movements such as poking, slapping, or smashing with the hands—fast and forceful—as well as kicking or stomping with the feet, and even biting when enraged.

Similarly, in situations where direct attack is not permitted, although the individual restrains words and actions, once anger arises it is still vented toward the stimulus through various modified offensive gestures. Most of these movements point directly at the stimulus, mimicking real attacks to release inner rage—for instance, offensive hand movements.

The fingers most commonly used to convey meaning are the thumb and index finger.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-10　强势自我认同的手指指向]*

The thumb is naturally used to express praise or approval. Pointing the thumb at oneself while speaking—whether at the nose or the chest—is a very assertive form of self-affirmation whose subtext is “I’m impressive.” Raising the thumb toward someone else signals affirmation or encouragement of that person, as shown in Figure 8-10.

In some television dramas or films, pointing the thumb downward to express contempt is used to create a humorous or unexpected dramatic effect: first raising it to suggest approval, then lowering it to indicate disapproval doubles the gap between the two evaluations, making the negation far stronger than a single denial—hence the term “killing with praise,” as shown in Figure 8-11.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-11　蔑视的手指指向，有双倍的蔑视效果]*

The index finger is often used for pointing. In Asian cultural etiquette, pointing with the index finger alone is considered disrespectful, as shown in Figure 8-12. Subordinates, for example, normally do not point at superiors with the index finger because both parties recognize the contempt it conveys. Pointing or guiding with the entire palm is a sign of respect, as shown in Figure 8-13.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-12　不尊重的手指指向]*

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-13　体现尊重的手掌姿势]*

Besides fingers, fists and palms are also common weapons in attacks; offensive movements include chopping (horizontal swing), cleaving (vertical swing), slapping, and smashing. When these movements appear during speech, they reinforce the verbal message. A common positive context is expressing determination: clenching a fist or waving a hand can make others believe in one’s sincerity. Using similar gestures in an argument intensifies the anger being expressed. Issuing commands with such movements heightens the command’s appeal and impact while conveying the decision-maker’s firm resolve.

#### Interlaced Fingers, Clenched Fists, Clasped Hands

Imagine someone sitting in a conference room with both hands tightly clasped together while saying, “I have always maintained an open-minded attitude and sincerely hope we can solve the problem.” Everyone present would consciously or unconsciously notice the inconsistency between words and actions.

An open palm signals candor and sincerity, whereas a clenched fist signals the opposite. By attempting to deceive others in this way to obtain the desired result, the person is likely to achieve the opposite effect and provoke hostility or attack.

When facing pressure and feeling the need to defend, a person may interlace the fingers of both hands tightly (see Figure 3.8). Interlaced fingers usually indicate that the individual is trying to suppress strong emotions (often anger).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图3.8　十指交叉紧握]*

A clenched fist is sometimes used to emphasize an upcoming statement; this is common in passionate speeches. Some people raise a clenched fist and wave it in the air to indicate or express strong emotion, such as vehement opposition. Others hide a clenched fist under an armpit or in a pocket to conceal their feelings (see Figure 3.9).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图3.9　紧握成拳头且双臂交叉]*

In *The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals*, Charles Darwin notes that a clenched fist signifies determination or anger and is, in most cases, a hostile gesture. Darwin also observed that when one person clenches a fist, others tend to do the same, especially during a heated argument, which can easily escalate into actual physical combat.

When a person clasps both hands together (see Figure 3.10)—that is, tightly wrings the hands—it indicates anxiety. This gesture often accompanies clenched fists. When asked to answer serious questions or explain behavior, the person typically adopts this posture, revealing concern and tension.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图3.10　双手交握]*

If your conversation partner’s hands are tightly clasped or wrung together, you should try to put the person at ease. You will then notice the attitude soften, allowing you to maintain control of the situation.

#### Superiority

In every profession, countless nonverbal postures clearly define superior and subordinate status; this is especially common and obvious in the military. In most cases, the more aggressive the superior appears, the more frightened and insecure the subordinate feels and the quicker the response.

Anthropologists hold that men are naturally more “territorial” than women. Both men and women, however, can assert control through nonverbal body movements. One such posture is placing one foot on a table and silently displaying “superiority” (see Figure 4.26).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.26　脚置于桌上的姿势]*

In certain environments we also extend our control by placing personal items—books, papers, notebooks, wallets, etc.—on empty seats to prevent others from occupying that space.

For example, university students studying in a library often spread their books and notebooks across a table to discourage others from sitting nearby. This action clearly communicates “I want personal space.” British psychiatrist Humphrey Osmond termed this “sociofugal space.”

In fact, most of us unconsciously create sociofugal space every day. When watching a movie, we place a coat or scarf on the adjacent empty seat to stop others from sitting there. Upon entering an elevator, we immediately claim an unoccupied corner, just as professional boxers do upon entering the ring. All these behaviors stem from the same psychology.

Sometimes people create sociofugal space to keep out unnecessary individuals while awaiting more suitable ones. For instance, a passenger seated in the aisle may place a briefcase on the window seat until an attractive woman approaches, at which point the briefcase is removed to offer the seat.

When people stand face-to-face, an accepted sociofugal space is the appropriate interpersonal distance. This distance varies by regional culture and by the relationship between the two individuals. One stands closer to a spouse than to a stranger, for example.

If someone invades our space, we feel uncomfortable. Therefore, we must constantly monitor and maintain this distance to avoid making others uneasy.

#### Cooperation

Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius once said: “People are born to help one another, like hands, feet, and eyelids that depend on each other, or lips and teeth that cannot be separated!”

This is indeed the case. If the parts of our body cannot coordinate, trouble arises. Likewise, to achieve certain goals we must cooperate with others. If you wish to obtain help or form a cooperative group, it is essential to notice the following cooperative postures.

We have all experienced situations in which someone who was initially cooperative suddenly reverses attitude 180 degrees and the matter falls through, or someone who once affectionately used a nickname suddenly addresses you by full name in a formal manner while a relaxed smile turns into a frown. These changes indicate that the other party no longer wishes to cooperate.

Therefore, it is very important to observe team members’ behavior and find ways to secure their support and participation.

We (Henry Calero and Gerard Nierenberg) once attended a seminar discussing a new product of significant scientific value. Topics included patent rights, equity, royalties, research and development costs, and how to persuade the client company to manufacture and sell the product.

At the start of the discussion, one member of the opposing team adopted an eager posture: sitting forward on the edge of the chair, body leaning ahead, toes touching the floor like a sprinter awaiting the starting signal (see Figure 4.19).

Because this individual was a technical expert on the opposing team, his reaction directly affected our sales outcome. His “ready-to-spring” posture told us he was interested in what we were presenting. We therefore encouraged him to raise technical questions, which our researchers answered one by one.

In fact, we had deliberately chosen seats beside this key person at the outset so we could closely observe his every movement. Once we fully addressed his technical concerns and removed his doubts, his attitude became highly cooperative.

The key to the smooth negotiation was that we immediately recognized the cooperative posture displayed by this technical expert, made good use of it, and quickly concluded a win-win agreement.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.19　跃跃欲试的姿势]*

#### Is a Person Who Covers the Mouth While Speaking Necessarily Lying?

Observing and understanding others’ postures is quite simple, yet accurately interpreting their meaning is extremely difficult. For example, when someone suddenly covers the mouth while speaking, it usually indicates uncertainty about the truth of the statement. If you encounter this situation—someone covers the mouth while talking to you—do you assume the person is lying? Human nature being what it is, we rarely instinctively consider other possibilities. Most people automatically interpret the gesture as lying, uncertainty, or an attempt to hide something.

That may indeed be the case, but before drawing a conclusion, recall whether the person has made this gesture before and, if so, under what circumstances. If not, consider whether the person may have just had dental work, was told of bad breath, or suddenly became aware of it during the conversation. In short, always consider other possibilities.

Although objectively interpreting others’ postures is difficult at first, daily practice makes it easier. It is like learning a foreign language: once familiar, it can be used freely.

Most foreign-language teachers strongly recommend that students spend more time listening and watching fluent speakers’ pronunciation—that is, “immersion learning.” Similarly, once you grasp the meaning of the body movements you see, repeated practice will suffice.

Any gathering place is an excellent observation venue—airports, parks, shopping centers, and especially social gatherings and business meetings that permit free expression of emotion and attitude are ideal for thorough study. Participants at such events are highly engaged and express their views openly.

Another good way to hone people-reading skills is to watch documentary reports, panel discussions, debates, or even fictional crime dramas on television. In simulated performances, actors display a wide range of emotions and intentions. Interview programs are also worth watching because, during the interview, you unconsciously observe how the interviewee responds to questions through body movements.

When watching these programs, first try to follow the narrative from the visuals alone and note the person’s facial expressions, gestures, and postures. Then, every five minutes, turn on the sound and compare the verbal expression with the conclusions you drew from the expressions and postures, paying attention to consistency and coherence.

#### George's Case

George was a shareholder and manager at a listed company. He considered himself the most generous among all shareholders and never shortchanged his subordinates when it came to dividends or bonuses.

What annoyed George, however, was that in a recent leadership influence survey he had topped the list as the "stingiest leader."

Fuming, George returned to his office, complained to his secretary, and then sent her out for a cup of coffee. After she left, he casually picked up a chocolate from her desk, unwrapped it, and took a bite.

The moment he did so, George regretted it. Beneath the chocolate box lay a note: "Dear, this is my Valentine's gift for you…"

Having eaten someone else's Valentine's gift, what was he to do? George felt flustered but quickly calmed down. When the secretary returned, he would apologize and buy her two boxes of chocolate to make up for it.

Yet it was not merely a matter of a few boxes of chocolate; it was a token of affection from her boyfriend. A voice named conscience protested inside him.

After thinking it over, an idea suddenly struck George. He looked at the half-eaten chocolate still in his hand and reflected on his past behavior. He began to understand why he had been voted "stingiest leader."

He often sent his secretary to buy coffee, black tea, chewing gum, and similar items but never reimbursed her for these "small expenses." Moreover, whenever he felt hungry or thirsty and saw food or drink on someone's desk, he would simply take it. George had previously believed that the extra tens of thousands of dollars in annual bonuses he gave his staff meant no one would mind such trivial matters, but reality suggested otherwise…

Perhaps it was time to correct this habit, George thought.

Born into a wealthy family, George had always been accustomed to having everything handed to him. As a child, people constantly offered him all sorts of fine things to choose from. Although he later became a successful manager, the "little emperor" mindset formed in childhood remained deeply embedded in his behavior. Without recognizing this trait, George could never earn genuine respect from his subordinates no matter how hard he tried.

Through behavior we can uncover the hidden secrets in others' hearts. Likewise, through behavior we can discover another "self" within us that even we ourselves may not notice.

#### Whether the Other Person Is Sincere: Look at the Hands, Not the Face

How can one judge whether someone is sincere? FBI agents suggest looking at the hands rather than the face. If the other person places open palms in front of the chest with hands facing upward, it indicates an open and candid individual. Sometimes people accompany this gesture by saying, "I have nothing to hide." Actors frequently use this posture not only to convey emotion but also to project an open personality for the character.

When children feel proud of something they have accomplished, they openly show their hands. When they feel guilty or uncertain, they hide their hands in pockets or behind their backs.

Like other attitudes, an open demeanor encourages similar feelings in others. British biologist Charles Darwin observed that when animals express submission (a form of candor), they roll onto their backs with all four feet in the air, exposing their soft underbellies and throats. He noted that even highly hostile animals would not attack a submissive individual in such a posture.

Comparative psychologist Dr. Leon Smith, an expert in animal behavior and communication, once conducted an experiment with a wild wolf. As the fierce wolf snarled and bared its teeth, Smith lay on the ground and exposed his throat. The wolf gently nuzzled him, touching his throat lightly with its teeth but causing no harm.

In formal business meetings, participants seated at a large conference table usually keep their suit jackets on. Observing whether they button or unbutton their jackets reveals whether they feel open or defensive.

When a person feels friendly, relaxed, and comfortable, they unbutton their jacket. If someone says something they dislike, they are likely to button it again and cross their arms.

Those who keep their jackets unbuttoned tend to be active participants in the discussion. They usually lean forward and rest their arms and elbows on the table. Those who sit with jackets tightly buttoned, posture erect, and sometimes arms crossed are generally less engaged.

When participants begin discussing a topic of common interest and reach a basic agreement in principle, they remove their jackets. This signals that the negotiation is moving in a positive direction. Conversely, it indicates the meeting may face difficult issues.

#### Scratching the Back of the Neck Indicates Frustration

FBI experts note that gestures conveying frustration are usually easy to spot. If you doubt this, watch a football game on television; you will certainly see plenty of frustrated faces. For example, during a play the quarterback evades defenders and passes to a teammate, only for the teammate to fumble. The ball slips through the teammate's hands and lands at an opponent's feet. The player who missed the catch most often reacts by kicking the ground in anger and slapping his helmet to express regret.

If you are watching a baseball game and the batter strikes out, you will see him angrily throw his bat, scratch the back of his neck, then kick the dirt, pebbles, or anything else near his feet while hanging his head as he walks back to the dugout.

Non-baseball players may not throw bats to show annoyance or regret, but they perform similar actions such as scratching the back of the neck and lowering the head. Slamming a table, snapping a pencil, stamping a foot, and other behaviors carry the same meaning as kicking dirt or throwing a bat.

Another common gesture of frustration is the "collar feels hot" posture. Next time you drive, watch your rearview mirror; you may see someone tugging at their shirt collar. If you cut in front of another driver and quickly merge into their lane, the driver you passed may angrily perform this collar-tugging gesture.

Sometimes frustration is expressed not through body movements but through sounds, such as heavy sighs or rapid breathing. Another sound worth noting is the "tsk-tsk" noise. It is often used to express disapproval or disgust and sometimes surprise or regret. We must therefore use all contextual cues to determine its specific meaning. (Note: In Syrian language the "tsk-tsk" sound means "no" and is common in daily life.)

If a person kicks the ground with their foot, it indicates they are in a frustrated state. Be careful not to confuse this with someone walking slowly while deeply absorbed in thought. A person may pause and kick the ground while pondering a problem or making a decision.

People sometimes misread these frustration gestures just as they misinterpret other postures. Therefore, paying attention to what the other person says is the wise way to assess their mental state.

#### Asu's Case

Asu was a white-collar worker at a foreign company. His annual salary reached several hundred thousand yuan, placing him among the top performers in his field. Yet Asu had an embarrassing problem: he repeatedly could not control the urge to steal other people's wallets. Even when a wallet contained only a few dozen yuan, he derived pleasure from the act of theft.

The situation grew increasingly serious. Asu had to seek help from a psychologist to resolve the issue.

With the psychologist's assistance, Asu worked hard to recall childhood events and eventually remembered an incident from when he was eight.

It was New Year, and children loved buying firecrackers to set off. Because Asu's father had just gone bankrupt, Asu could only watch others play. One neighbor's child flaunted his firecrackers in front of Asu and called him a "poor ghost." Unwilling to accept the insult, Asu secretly ran home, took his mother's wallet, bought many firecrackers, and enjoyed setting them off.

When he returned home, his mother learned what had happened but did not scold him. After his father came back, however, the parents had a big argument.

Not long afterward the parents divorced. Although Asu's mistake played only a minor role in the divorce, in his childhood subconscious he believed the divorce resulted from his taking the wallet.
