#### Handshakes and First Impressions

Psychological research shows that in the workplace it is important to convey an impression of “competence” at first meeting, especially during interviews and negotiations; competent individuals tend to receive more opportunities. One detail that cannot be overlooked if you want to appear competent is the handshake.

A handshake is a conscious act. Even if your bones and muscles are soft and your personality is gentle, increasing the pressure during the handshake can still convey determination and sincerity. Conversely, a limp handshake may lead to rejection.

#### The Meaning of Hands on Hips

When you see someone with hands on hips, avoid overgeneralizing; analyze the specific situation so you can discern each possible emotion behind the gesture and reach an accurate judgment.

Hands on hips means the thumbs and remaining fingers are spread and pressed firmly against the sides of the waist. In daily life or at work, many people place their hands on their hips—perhaps while stretching after sitting for a long time, while speaking with acquaintances, or while walking. Men and women, however, convey different meanings with this posture. What, then, are men and women respectively “saying” when they place their hands on their hips?

#### Hand Movements That Indicate a Negative Attitude

Although the other person may feign interest on the surface, their hand movements can betray an inner negative attitude. The following hand movements often signal that the person is “unhappy,” “does not want to listen,” or “will not agree”:

- Clenching the fists
- Placing both hands on the thighs with thumbs pointing toward each other
- Crossing both hands behind the head
- Pressing a finger to the center of the forehead while toying with objects on the table during conversation
- Opening and closing a drawer as if searching for something
- Repeatedly tapping the table with a finger

#### (1) People Who Like Pocket Watches

Such individuals display three clear characteristics:

1. They manage time well; although busy all day, they are never slaves to the clock and know how to relax within limited time.
2. They are nostalgic, fond of old objects, and refined in speech and manner.
3. They are patient and steady in dealing with others, earning respect.

Of course, a small number of people carry a pocket watch merely to display status. These individuals are easy to recognize: those who hold a pocket watch with an air of importance and an arrogant gait belong to this group.

#### People Who Walk with Hands on Hips Are Impatient

Some people walk with hands on hips, resembling sprinters. They may be quick-tempered individuals who want to reach their destination by the shortest route and at the greatest speed. Such people possess strong explosive power and often adopt this posture when executing the next plan. The stance has become a signature of this type, much like using “V” to signify victory.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.40　奔向目的地的行人]*

#### (3) Steeple Gesture

In body language, understanding a posture generally requires combining it with other postures and the specific context; otherwise, misinterpretation is likely. One posture, however, is an exception—the steeple gesture.

The steeple gesture is formed when the fingertips of both hands touch each other while the palms remain apart, creating a shape resembling a church steeple. Its meaning is confidence.

Research indicates that confident high achievers in the workplace frequently use this gesture, especially among accountants, lawyers, and managers.

#### 1. Avoid Putting Hands in Pockets

When we feel nervous, we instinctively hide our hands, so a lack of confidence often leads us to slip our hands into our pockets without realizing it. Hands in pockets usually signal withdrawal and convey insufficient confidence along with a casual air. Keeping the hands outside the pockets, by contrast, projects confidence and transmits an open message. Experts also suggest that placing the hands at the sides of the hips or thighs can further boost confidence. The next time you feel insecure, try keeping your hands out of your pockets; the effect may surprise you.

#### Resting the Chin in a Dreamy Pose

At eight o’clock in the morning during English reading time, homeroom teacher Ms. Wang entered the classroom as usual. Looking around, she heard a chorus of reading voices and smiled with satisfaction. Suddenly she noticed that student A’s textbook in the farthest seat of the front row was standing upright on the desk, yet student A’s face was not visible. Ms. Wang walked over quietly, removed the textbook, and gently called, “Student A, Student A…” but received no reply. Student A was resting both hands on their chin, smiling, lost in pleasant reverie.

#### Frozen Hands

Research shows that compared with honest people, those who lie or lack confidence tend to minimize gestures and physical contact. Therefore, hand behavior is often more trustworthy than words and can reveal the speaker’s true thoughts. If a person lacks confidence, their hand movements appear stiff because they are unsure whether their lie will succeed. Consequently, when you observe someone’s hands freezing, it indicates that the person is experiencing extreme lack of confidence at that moment.

#### People Who Walk with Hands in Pockets Are Critical

People who habitually walk with hands in pockets, even in warm weather, tend to be highly critical and enjoy criticizing or belittling others. They often project an air of mystery, are skilled at concealing real emotions, and appear cynical. When interacting with such individuals, first overpower them with presence.

People who repeatedly pull their hands out of their pockets and then put them back in while walking are more cautious and deliberate, yet they easily become discouraged in adversity. Sometimes the behavior also signals nervousness.

#### Touching

Touching an object or another person expresses pride or ownership. It can also convey interest, concern, affection, understanding, sympathy, confidence, or comfort. In essence, romantic relationships are largely built on physical touch.

To determine the true meaning behind a person’s touch signals, remember that most information is conveyed through body language; observe the entire posture cluster the other person displays to interpret the touch more accurately.

#### The Nature Behind a Wristwatch

A truly successful person is someone who knows how to use time. In other words, your attitude toward time determines your probability of success. I am not about to repeat how precious time is; that is obvious. Since the first self-winding wristwatch appeared in 1926, both style and function have evolved. What I want to say is that a person’s treatment of time can be judged from the watch they wear.

#### 1. Purely Ritual Handshakes

A ritual handshake is formal and correct, typically occurring at a first meeting when the parties know little about each other. Its chief characteristics are brevity and light pressure; contact is minimal and quickly released. Between opposite sexes, the palms may not fully meet; only the fingers may touch briefly, especially when the woman initiates or holds the advantage. Such a handshake signals that both sides intend to remain completely independent for the time being and that further contact is required to deepen the relationship.

#### 2. Do Not Cross Your Arms

When we feel cold, dissatisfied, or tense, we generally cross our arms over the chest. This defensive posture transmits negative messages: emotional closure, low mood, unwillingness to communicate, or an attempt to mask discontent or anxiety. Who would want to befriend a pessimist? Therefore, in social settings we should relax appropriately and avoid crossing our arms, thereby appearing more open and confident.

#### 3. Avoid Biting Fingers

Finger biting is common among children and adolescents and usually appears after intense tension, reflecting depression, frustration, feelings of inferiority, or hostility. The root cause may be insufficient attention or lack of security. Many young people and adults substitute biting a pen or pencil for biting fingers. Finger biting signals not only insufficient confidence but also poses a health risk because fingernails harbor large numbers of harmful bacteria.

#### Section 3 Hands Can Also Be Unhappy

Hand gestures are external expressions of inner states and are determined entirely by mood, feeling, and interest. A gesture made in accordance with inner feeling can sometimes convey more information than a thousand words. The more genuine the emotion, the more natural the movement and posture appear. When we feel unhappy, our hands also appear unhappy, producing gestures of sadness, anger, or impatience; this is what is meant by the saying that the ten fingers are connected to the heart.

#### (2) People Who Wear Classical Gold Watches

They possess strong foresight and will not sacrifice long-term interests for short-term gains. Combined with strong willpower and meticulous thinking, they usually achieve success in their careers. Because of their maturity and tolerance, family and friends trust them deeply. If your opponent wears a classical gold watch, you will face a formidable challenge; if you also wear one, the contest will undoubtedly be intense and fascinating.

#### Fingers Interlaced and Clasped Tightly

When confronted with a major event or sudden change, many people habitually interlace and clasp their fingers tightly. This is an unconscious action performed under extreme lack of confidence or great pressure. As the gripping force increases, the color of the fingers may change; if you notice whitening in parts of the hands of someone whose fingers are interlaced, it suggests that the current situation may have become quite serious.

#### Hands

Hands are the most practical body parts humans possess. What a person does with their hands reveals considerable information about their thoughts and feelings. In sign language, the hands can convey endless information just like spoken words.

In this section we first describe the most common gesture used to express welcome—the handshake. We then continue with the meanings of other hand gestures.

#### Summary

When a person feels no sense of control, no security, worry (fear) of being rejected, or lack of confidence, a freezing response of the hands occurs. Once the subject exhibits this reaction, it indicates a shift toward psychological weakness; not only is there no offensive tendency, even defensive psychology is weak, placing the person in a state between caution and fear. At this point it is easy to increase the intensity of stimulation, and the effect of the stimulus will be relatively obvious.

#### Standing with Hands Behind the Back

Such individuals have conservative personalities; their most notable traits are respect for authority, adherence to conventional rules, and a strong sense of responsibility. Given sufficient time, however, they can also accept new ideas and viewpoints. In addition, their emotions are not very stable, so they often appear somewhat inscrutable. Their strengths include patience and perseverance; they do not fear trouble and can persist until the end no matter what difficulties arise.

#### 5. Resting the Chin

Resting the chin is an extremely common action; the gesture of propping up the chin in public is a negative social signal. When a person feels psychologically bored, they become listless and dejected; the head naturally drops, and the hand naturally props it up, producing the chin-resting gesture. Many students make this movement unconsciously when they find class content boring or the teacher’s lecture dull.

#### (1) People Who Carry Briefcases

In relatively formal settings, many people carry briefcases, mainly for work. If someone habitually uses a briefcase, they are likely a manager or higher-ranking executive in a company. They emphasize efficiency, are strict with subordinates, and set even higher standards for themselves. Women who like to carry briefcases are, nine times out of ten, assertive and strong-willed.

#### Hands on Hips

When a person places both hands on their hips, they project a surging presence. We often see this posture on police officers, soldiers, and leaders. It is actually a territorial-defense gesture frequently used to assert dominance or maintain authority. We can infer the other person’s identity from this posture, because apart from authority figures, ordinary people rarely place their hands on their hips.

Humans are like trees in nature: each tree has its own characteristics, yet commonalities exist. #### How Much Information Your Hands Can Reveal

Millions of years ago, our ancestors began using their hands to make weapons and employ tools. Scientific research shows that the hands contain a rich network of nerves and are among the body parts with the highest concentration of nerve endings. The color, structure, skin texture, flexibility, finger shape, and even the nails of the hands conceal a person’s temperament.

Overall, hands fall into six basic forms.

#### (II) The Hands of the Easygoing Type

Compared with the ideal type, these hands are slightly shorter and broader, with fingers that taper a little. Their owners are artistic, sensitive, impulsive, and delicate. Yet they prefer a life of ease and may even suppress their artistic talent for it. You can observe their thumbs further: whether they achieve anything depends on whether those thumbs are firm or weak.

#### Covering the Mouth with a Hand

This indicates that the person realizes a remark was inappropriate and quickly covers the mouth to conceal it. At such a moment, offering a few reassuring words will make the person deeply grateful to you.

We often say “the ten fingers are connected to the heart.” It is an undeniable fact that the hands can express a person’s inner voice. If we wish to understand someone’s inner thoughts, simply observing their hand gestures will suffice.

#### Tapping the Fingertips on the Table

When you are speaking to someone and they perform this action, they may be caught in a mental dilemma, considering how to solve a problem, or still hesitating over a decision. At this point you should tactfully stop; continuing may irritate the other person and make the situation worse.

#### (V) Hands on the Hips

This is a common posture that signals protest or aggression. Some observers call the gesture “ready for action,” yet its fundamental meaning is “challenge.” It is especially typical during arguments. Men adopt it to display bravery and strength, but when women do so it conveys a fierce impression.

#### III. Scratching the Neck

Scratching the neck is a bodily signal of inner melancholy and expresses anxiety and helplessness. When someone seeks a definite answer to a matter or question, they often scratch their neck while thinking. If you notice a friend making this gesture, you might ask what is troubling them and offer to share the worry or provide advice.

#### IV. Slapping the Table and Rising

When struck by an unexpected blow or gripped by extreme anger, a person is very likely to slap the table and stand up. The slapping action serves to defend one’s dignity and strongly condemns the other party’s words or deeds. When someone slaps the table and rises, it is best not to argue; otherwise the other person’s anger will intensify and irrational behavior may follow.

#### (II) People Who Prefer Square Handbags

The “square handbag” I refer to does not include the briefcases already mentioned; it means ordinary, mass-market bags. These bags are finely made, not very large in volume, yet roomy enough for daily essentials and money. People who like such bags generally fall into two groups: one consists of fashion leaders, the other of rather meticulous ordinary office workers.

#### Rubbing the Hands

When people are doubtful or under great pressure, they usually rub their hands involuntarily, especially when the situation is tense. The rubbing motion becomes more pronounced, revealing a lack of confidence, distress, irritability, and anxiety, along with uncertainty. Rubbing the hands serves to relieve tension and unease.

#### Chapter 3 Hands and Heart Are Linked—Body Movements Best Express Inner Feelings

American psychologist Albert Mehrabian once proposed the famous formula: “Total expression of information = 7 % tone + 38 % voice + 55 % body language.” The 55 % is enough to let someone skilled in “body-language mind reading” see through what another person truly wishes to express even when that person stops short or remains silent.

#### Handshake

##### Handshake

The handshake gesture evolved from an ancient hand signal in which people raised both hands upon meeting to show they carried no weapons. In the Roman Empire era, people did not shake hands but grasped the other person’s forearm as a greeting. In modern times, the handshake has become one of the world’s most representative greeting customs, signifying openness and unity.

A dry palm and firm grip usually indicate confidence and a tendency to take control. A weak handshake may be interpreted as a sign of weak character. Sweaty palms during a handshake can stem from nervousness, anxiety, or simply hot weather. All such interpretations, however, remain broad generalizations.

Some strong individuals avoid gripping tightly because they fear causing pain. Artists or surgeons who rely on their hands for work may also refrain from firm handshakes to protect themselves. Likewise, people with arthritis may prefer not to shake hands.

A standard or equal handshake occurs when both palms are vertical, the pressure is mutual, and the hands clasp rather than squeeze (see Figure 3.1). Eye contact during the handshake is limited to three glances, conveying confidence without arrogance. To further express friendliness and sincerity, maintain a smile while shaking hands.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图3.1　标准或平等的握手]*

In the politician-style handshake, the initiator typically uses both hands rather than one (see Figure 3.2). The right hand clasps the other person’s hand while the left hand rests lightly on top.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图3.2　政客式握手]*

Another common handshake involves the right hand shaking while the left hand grasps the other person’s forearm or shoulder. This style is acceptable between close old friends. After the handshake, the pair often immediately shares a warm “bear hug.” When used with someone who is not a close friend, however, most people feel uncomfortable, viewing the gesture as insincere or overly flattering. Whenever anyone greets us this way, we should treat it as a sincere expression.

In times of distress, people generally do not convey deep emotion through a handshake. Instead, they gently take both of the other person’s hands and communicate sympathy through facial expressions (see Figure 3.3), often adding an embrace. This gesture tells the person in need that you will remain by their side until the crisis passes.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图3.3　同情地紧握双手]*

Sometimes people unconsciously display superiority during an initial handshake by extending their hand palm-down, forcing the other person to respond with an upturned palm (see Figure 3.4).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图3.4　握手时伸出一只“带有优越感”的手]*

Conversely, some individuals instinctively extend an upturned palm, signaling inferiority and failing to align vertically with the other person’s hand (see Figure 3.5).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图3.5　握手时伸出一只“自卑”的手]*

In another variation, one person uses the transition of the handshake to flip the other’s hand underneath so that their own hand ends up on top. They extend their hand, grasp the other’s, then rotate it so the other person’s palm faces down. This conveys the simple nonverbal message: “I have the upper hand!” (see Figure 3.6).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图3.6　“自信VS自卑”的握手]*

Cultural differences also require attention. The French often shake hands when entering or leaving a room, while Germans shake hands only once. Learning appropriate greetings while traveling helps avoid unnecessary mistakes.

##### Hands Formed into a Steeple, Indicating Confidence

When the fingertips of both hands are brought together and touch correspondingly, they form a “church steeple” gesture. This is commonly used to express confidence, though it can also be viewed as affected, arrogant, or proud.

Most of the time, people form the steeple unconsciously. Some deliberately use the gesture to emphasize strong security and absolute self-confidence. One suggestion, for example, advises businesspeople to make this gesture after delivering a final offer during negotiations. The person leans back in the chair, smiles, and forms the steeple with their fingers. The client watches for a long time before firmly saying, “Deal!” During negotiations, the gesture seems to possess a certain magic that easily wins others over.

In *The Art of Reading Minds in the White House*, author Henry H. Calero recounts an anecdote about the steeple gesture.

Steve McQueen, the famous American film actor nicknamed “The King of Cool,” starred in many hit movies, including the classic *The Great Escape*.

Once, while seated in first class, Calero discovered that his neighbor was McQueen. They began talking. When the conversation turned to McQueen’s performance as a poker player in *The Cincinnati Kid*, Calero remarked that the acting was not outstanding.

“The King of Cool” crossed his arms, fixed Calero with his sharp blue eyes, and asked with slight irritation, “What do you mean?”

Calero explained that in one key scene, the poker player McQueen portrayed unconsciously revealed a winning gesture: after placing a bet, he formed a steeple with his hands.

McQueen nodded. Calero continued, noting that steady professional players never make this gesture unless bluffing, yet McQueen’s character clearly was not bluffing. Thus, it was a nonverbal error on McQueen’s part.

After hearing the explanation, McQueen quickly uncrossed his arms, snapped his fingers, and told Calero that others had given similar feedback about the role but could not explain why—they could only “feel” it.

McQueen shook Calero’s hand warmly and expressed deep gratitude. They spent the rest of the flight pleasantly.

People occasionally form this gesture while speaking or listening, sometimes with the hands positioned slightly higher or lower.

Those who rarely use the steeple gesture tend to raise their hands very high when they do, almost looking at others through the gaps between their fingers. This behavior often makes others feel uneasy. If you must continue a conversation with such a person, you need to exercise self-control. The lower steeple is most common among women.

There is also an elegant version of the steeple in which the hands are clasped together, one hand wrapping around the other, which is already formed into a fist.

This confident, elegant steeple is most frequently seen in business settings. Company employees, lawyers, doctors, and especially professors lecturing on favorite topics often adopt the posture, appearing highly satisfied with their current positions.

We also observe that most people’s behavior is unconscious. In some cases, the weaker party in a negotiation occasionally forms the steeple, giving the stronger party the impression that the person making the gesture is hiding something and knows more than they are saying, prompting an immediate change of topic.

The advice is: if your point in the next negotiation does not feel as persuasive as you imagined, try forming the steeple, remain silent, and wait for the other person’s reaction.

##### Handshake Reveals Inner Secrets

Micro-expression Keywords

Whether greeting an old friend not seen for a long time or a stranger just met, a handshake is essential. It is not only basic courtesy but also a way to sense the other person’s inner state and infer their character and behavioral tendencies through the handshake.

The handshake is one of the most common courtesies in interpersonal communication. It is also a form of communication that conveys respect, enthusiasm, encouragement, or indifference, flattery, and arrogance. Subconscious movements during a handshake reveal one party’s hidden inner secrets.

- **Habit of grasping the other person’s hand with both hands**  
  Such individuals are warm, gentle in character, kind-hearted, able to confide in friends, open with their emotions, and clear in their likes and dislikes.

- **Firm, strong grip during handshake**  
  This type of handshake feels like an arm-wrestling match and can cause pain. The person intends to convey sincerity but often leaves an impression of insincerity because the action is excessive. Many people, especially on first meeting, are unaccustomed to this style. In personality, these individuals are energetic and highly confident yet tend to be domineering and arrogant. They also exhibit strong organizational and leadership abilities.

- **Moderate pressure during handshake**  
  They shake hands with moderate pressure and steady movements while naturally looking at the other person. Such people are resolute, frank, responsible, and reliable. They think carefully, excel at reasoning, and frequently offer constructive suggestions. When others face difficulties, they quickly propose practical solutions, displaying the demeanor of a capable leader and earning trust. They possess leadership potential, so it is worthwhile to build connections; they may later become valuable allies.

- **Light touch during handshake**  
  This is a major taboo in social etiquette. A mere light touch without a firm grip creates an impression of perfunctoriness and disrespect. Generally, such people tend to be pessimistic, indifferent to most matters, and possess a carefree, worldly attitude. On the other hand, they are open-minded, modest, and easygoing.

- **Up-and-down shaking during handshake**  
  They grasp the other person’s hand tightly and shake it continuously. These individuals are extreme optimists, full of hope for the future, always energetic, and seemingly never seen worried. Their positive enthusiasm often makes them beloved and admired.

- **Holding on without releasing**  
  They often hold the other person’s hand until they finish speaking. Overall, such people are emotionally rich and enjoy making friends. When two men shake hands this way, the one who does not release may have a request and hopes the other will listen carefully and respond. When two women do so, the one holding on may be someone who enjoys gossip and discussing others behind their backs. When a man holds a woman’s hand this way, it indicates he has a favorable impression of her and hopes to convey it through this gesture.

- **Grasping only with fingers during handshake**  
  Such individuals are sensitive, emotionally unstable, and easily agitated. When interacting with them, one must be careful not to touch their sensitive spots, or one may end up embarrassed. In addition, they are kind-hearted and compassionate.

- **Unwilling to shake hands**  
  They do not initiate handshakes and appear reluctant when others extend a hand first. Most such people are introverted, shy, and conservative in character, yet sincere toward others.

Psychologists consider the best handshake method to be moderate pressure while looking directly into the other person’s eyes. Only then can one display confidence while conveying sincerity and goodwill. Through the handshake, a bridge of heartfelt communication is built between both parties.

##### Handshake Strength Correlates with Personality

A very firm handshake usually indicates that the person is confident and tends to control others. Excessive force, however, can appear rash rather than steady. It also suggests the shaker’s inner warmth, sincerity, or expectation. Such individuals are generally energetic, self-confident, frank, and strong-willed, yet inclined toward authoritarianism. They possess outstanding organizational and leadership abilities and are natural leaders.

A handshake with moderate pressure, steady movements, and direct eye contact indicates a resolute, responsible, and reliable personality. These people think carefully, excel at reasoning, and possess strong responsibility. When difficulties arise, they quickly offer constructive opinions and practical solutions, making them trustworthy.

A handshake that extends a lifeless, textureless, information-free “dead fish” palm that merely brushes the other person’s hand lightly—neither firm nor forceful—usually belongs to someone who is introverted, weak-willed, lacking drive, cold, indifferent, negative, arrogant, and without decisive or crisp energy.

##### Palm-Scratching Handshake

The specific form is: the hands clasp but do not release quickly; instead, they slide apart slowly, with the fingers lingering appropriately in the other person’s palm. Such individuals are emotionally rich and enjoy making friends. Once friendship is established, they remain loyal.

In addition, another common handshake involves the right hand shaking while the left hand grasps the other person’s forearm or shoulder. This style is acceptable between close old friends, and the pair often immediately shares a warm “bear hug” afterward. When used with someone who is not a close friend, however, most people feel uncomfortable, viewing the gesture as insincere or mistaken flattery.

##### Hand-Holding Handshake

The specific form is: one person gently takes both of the other person’s hands, usually with their own right hand taking the other’s left hand and their own left hand taking the other’s right hand. In times of distress, people generally do not convey deep emotion through a handshake. Instead, they gently take both of the other person’s hands and communicate sympathy through facial expressions, sometimes adding an embrace. This gesture tells the person in need that you will remain by their side until the crisis passes.

##### Flipping Handshake

The specific form is: one person uses the transition of the handshake to press the other’s hand underneath so that their own hand ends up on top. They extend their hand, grasp the other’s, then flip it over so the other person’s palm faces down. This handshake conveys the simple nonverbal message: “I have the upper hand!” It means the person has seized the initiative in the interaction.

##### Humble Handshake

Also known as the begging handshake or submissive handshake, its specific form is: extend the hand with the palm facing upward or upward to the left, without aligning with the other person's vertically extended palm. Some people, when shaking hands, to show respect or admiration for the other person, or to express their own humility and approachability, often subconsciously adopt this handshake method, implying that they are willing to be dominated by the other party.

##### Finger-grasp Handshake

Also known as the finger-pinching handshake, its specific form is: when shaking hands, intentionally or unintentionally grasp only a few of the other person's fingers or fingertips with the fingers, without the palm making contact with the other person. Most people who adopt this handshake style have a gentle and sensitive personality and are easily emotionally aroused. However, they are kind-hearted and extremely compassionate. Between opposite sexes it indicates reserve and composure; between same-sex individuals it indicates coldness, unfamiliarity, or high status.

#### Open Hands and Clenched Hands

##### Rubbing Both Hands Together Often Signals Expectation

Perhaps each of us has silently expressed expectation for something. For example, before participating in an activity, people rub their hands together as if washing them. Unless their hands are cold from the weather and they need friction to warm them, this is a nonverbal way of conveying strong interest in the activity. This may explain why gamblers always like to rub the dice between their hands before throwing them!

When a child sees the tour bus carrying their mother stop, they rub their hands together with delight, showing eager anticipation to see what “delicious” treats the travel bag holds. A company executive over sixty will make the same gesture upon learning the firm has just landed a major deal.

In many large cities, doormen, waiters, and other service-industry employees adopt expectant postures to signal their hope for a tip. They may jingle coins in their pockets or strike the pose of an “ancient Egyptian statue,” with palms held behind the back and facing upward.

Verbal pauses often form a crucial part of expectant postures. A waiter might say, “I hope you have a pleasant day and are satisfied with our service,” then pause to wait for a response. If the customer misses the hint, the waiter may add, “Sir, let me check whether a better table has been reserved for you.” Repeatedly ignoring such hints results in noticeably reduced service.

##### Open Palms Signal Openness and Sincerity

People often place open palms in front of the chest, facing upward, to indicate candor. Sometimes they accompany the gesture with the words “I have nothing to hide.” Actors frequently use this posture not only to convey emotion but also to reveal a character’s open nature.

When children feel proud of something they have done, they readily show their hands; when they feel guilty or uncertain, they hide their hands in pockets or behind their backs.

Like other attitudes, an open stance encourages similar feelings in others. British biologist Charles Darwin observed that when animals signal submission—an expression of openness—they roll onto their backs with all four feet in the air, exposing their soft underbelly and throat. He noted that even highly hostile animals will refrain from attacking a submissive individual in this position.

Comparative psychologist Dr. Leon Smith, an expert on animal behavior and communication, once tested this with a wild wolf. As the wolf snarled and bared its teeth, Smith lay on the ground and exposed his throat. The wolf gently nuzzled him, touching his throat with its teeth but causing no harm.

##### Clasped Hands Indicate Tension and Unease

When a person clasps their hands together—tightly wringing them—this usually signals anxiety.

The center of attention at a meeting often adopts this posture, especially when asked a series of difficult questions. During a California election, when the voting machine malfunctioned, the official explaining the failure to voters was photographed in exactly this clasped-hands posture.

If your conversation partner keeps their hands tightly clasped, they are tense and hard to approach; try to help them relax. One effective method is to lean slightly toward them.

For instance, during a conversation between a superior and a subordinate, the subordinate may feel uncertain about the superior’s attitude. If the superior remains seated behind a large desk and looks down over their glasses, the subordinate on the nearby sofa will likely keep their hands tightly clasped. Once the superior stands, moves closer, and sits near the subordinate while leaning forward to show trust, the subordinate’s hands will immediately separate and display a more confident posture.

##### Fingers Interlaced and Clasped Make a Person Hard to Believe

Imagine someone sitting upright at a conference table, arms resting on the surface, fingers interlaced and tightly clasped, while saying in a mild tone, “I have always been open-minded and sincerely hope we can solve the problem.” Everyone present will consciously or unconsciously notice the inconsistency between words and posture.

Open palms signal honesty and sincerity; clenched fists signal the opposite. Attempting to achieve a desired result through such deception is likely to backfire and provoke hostility or attack.

A person under pressure who feels the need to defend themselves may also interlace and clasp their fingers, indicating an attempt to suppress strong emotions—often dissatisfaction or anger.

##### Hands Placed on the Chest Signal Agreement

This is a common, emblematic gesture of approval, indicating agreement with what has been said or done.

For centuries, people have placed a hand on the chest to express loyalty, integrity, and honesty. Americans adopt a similar posture when pledging allegiance to the flag. The gesture actually dates back to ancient Rome, where soldiers saluted by placing one hand on the chest and extending the other toward the recipient.

Note that, except in formal settings, women rarely use this posture to express loyalty. When a woman places one or both hands on her chest, the gesture is usually protective or excited, signaling sudden fright or great surprise.

##### Open Palms

Open palms generally indicate openness and sincerity (see Figure 3.7). When children feel proud of something they have done, they open their palms. When people feel guilty or uncertain, the same gesture can help them find a way forward. An extended palm signals expectation—perhaps for money, an object, or even an idea.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图3.7　摊开双手，以示真诚]*

##### Hands Held Apart Can Also Reveal Inner Thoughts

The postures discussed above all involve the hands held together. When the hands are apart, however, different movements carry different meanings.

### Arms and Shoulders

#### Can You Take Off Your Jacket?

In formal business meetings, if someone is preparing to sit at a large conference table, they usually do not remove their suit jacket. However, observing whether they fasten or unfasten the jacket reveals whether they are open or defensive.

When a person feels friendly, relaxed, and comfortable, they unbutton their suit jacket. But if someone says something they dislike, they are very likely to button it again and cross their arms.

Those who keep their suit jackets unbuttoned tend to be active participants in the discussion. They usually lean forward and place their arms and elbows on the table. Those who sit with their jackets tightly buttoned, in a straight and upright posture, and sometimes with arms crossed, are usually less engaged.

When participants begin discussing a topic that everyone cares about and have essentially reached agreement in principle, they remove their jackets. This indicates that the negotiation is moving in a positive direction. Conversely, it suggests that the meeting may face some thorny issues.

The sculpture *The Thinker* by the famous French sculptor Auguste Rodin is a classic example of deep understanding of postural language. Who would doubt that the figure is pondering a problem and striving to find a solution? In real life, we often see “the thinker” posture or similar poses. This shows that the person is grappling with something difficult or puzzling.

Sometimes a person adopts a series of critical evaluation postures. For example, placing one hand on the cheek, gripping the jaw with the palm, extending the index finger along the face, and curling the other fingers beneath the mouth (see Figure 4.6). This posture indicates that she is not only evaluating what the other person is saying at that moment but also critiquing the ideas being presented.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.6　批判性的揣摩姿势]*

Another evaluation posture is stroking one’s chin or beard (in the case of some bearded men) (see Figure 4.7). This “let me think about it” gesture typically appears when a person is about to make a decision. The accompanying facial expression is often eyes slightly narrowed, as if considering the best long-term answer to the question.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.7　抚摸下巴的揣摩姿势]*

When a person stands up and paces back and forth in the room, it usually indicates they are pondering what someone has just said. Most people exhibit this behavior when solving difficult problems or making tough decisions, because standing helps them think more clearly. This is a positive posture.

Therefore, when you see someone pacing while deep in thought, remember to stay quiet, wait patiently for them to speak, and do not interrupt. Doing so would break their train of thought and prevent them from reaching a decision or offering a final offer. This explains why some negotiators fail to achieve their goals: they cannot remain calm.

Experienced salespeople are generally adept at reading this “pacing person” (see Figure 4.8). They know that when facing a pacing prospect, it is best to wait patiently, because the posture signals that the client is ready to decide.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.8　来回踱步的思考者]*

If a person pinches the bridge of their nose, it often indicates they are focusing on and reflecting upon a decision they must make. Similar gestures include lowering the head and pinching the bridge of the nose while experiencing intense inner conflict (see Figure 4.9), as if checking whether one is truly in a difficult situation or merely in a nightmare.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.9　捏鼻梁的姿势]*

In most cases, people close their eyes while pinching the bridge of their nose; this posture represents strong inner doubt. For example, a lawyer attending one of our seminars mentioned in a report that he knew a judge who frequently used this posture to express thoughts and feelings about a case. If the judge believed the defendant was guilty, the gesture would not appear; if the judge believed the defendant was innocent, the gesture would appear, sometimes with eyes closed for several minutes while internally struggling over how to determine the defendant’s guilt.

Sliding glasses down the nose and peering over the top at the speaker is another common evaluation posture (see Figure 4.10). Anyone seeing this posture feels they are being criticized and looked down upon.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.10　通过眼镜缝隙窥探]*

We emphasize that if this posture is one of your habits, you must recognize the negative effect it may have on others. If you do not want to elicit a negative response, it is best to avoid it.

Another posture glasses-wearers adopt when facing conflict or confrontation, or when buying time to decide, is to slowly remove the glasses and carefully wipe the lenses—even when the lenses are clean and do not need wiping. People usually speak more slowly while performing this action.

A similar time-buying posture is removing the glasses and placing one temple tip in the mouth (see Figure 4.11). This posture shows that the person is not only listening attentively but also carefully considering what the other person is saying.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.11　拖延时间，仔细思考]*

#### 9.1.1 Victory Posture

We often see winners of wars or competitions habitually perform actions such as raising both hands high or shouting loudly. These energy-intensive movements originally serve to attract more attention.

Victory brings joy. The person who achieves a competitive victory experiences positive emotions that mobilize energy reserves. Winning implies many subsequent benefits; these positive stimuli heighten the winner’s neural excitement. During combat, the body stores large amounts of energy for mental or physical confrontation. After the fight ends, excess energy must be released and tense nerves soothed so the body returns to its normal state; otherwise, prolonged excitement overloads the nervous and circulatory systems.

Many celebratory postures are anti-gravity movements.

Raising both hands high is a common victory gesture and one of the classic anti-gravity movements (see Figures 9-1 and 9-2).

- Figure 9-1　Hands raised high in victory response
- Figure 9-2　Phelps waving to the audience at the award ceremony

On the playing field, when an athlete scores a crucial goal, spectators frequently see various post-goal celebrations, one of which is raising both hands and leaping to chest-bump (see Figure 9-3).

- Figure 9-3　Chest-bump victory response, common in male sports settings

When two people celebrate together, they may also raise one hand each and perform a high-five (see Figure 9-4).

Jumping and cheering is essentially a fixed combination of actions after victory, captured in the idiom “jumping for joy” (see Figure 9-5).

- Figure 9-4　High-five victory response
- Figure 9-5　Jumping victory response

Some athletes perform a complex jump—a backflip—after victory to express inner joy and excitement (see Figure 9-6). Jumping is a classic anti-gravity movement, while cheering is a way to attract more attention through display; it also helps regulate breathing and expend energy.

- Figure 9-6　Backflip victory response

Another reaction equivalent to jumping is climbing to a high place after victory. It is common for winning athletes, in their excitement, to climb to an elevated spot or run around the field while raising one hand to salute the audience; the essence is display (see Figure 9-7). The increase in altitude and the greater area of visibility created by running attract more people to see and praise them.

- Figure 9-7　Arms raised in victory response
- Figure 9-8　Hands raised high in victory response

A more subtle “climbing high” reaction is stretching the body. Almost everyone has done this: after completing a worthwhile task (which, in a sense, counts as victory), they face the morning sun (or sunset, or city lights at night) and stretch fully. On one hand, this moves the cervical and lumbar spine and relaxes the nerves; on the other, it generates a sense of accomplishment and hopeful anticipation of a bright future (perhaps a greater challenge).

In fact, while raising both hands to express the joy of victory, the torso and legs naturally straighten, allowing the person to reach their natural maximum height. It is difficult to imagine someone hunching with bent knees raising both hands (except in cases of congenital disability) to display themselves (see Figure 9-8).

- Figure 9-9　Leg raised and fist clenched in victory response

Additional ways to express victory through sound include cheering, singing loudly, whistling, and roaring. These convert internal energy into sound waves while also attracting more attention through display; they involve substantial exhalation and reduced inhalation to lower energy reserves. In many high-stakes win-or-lose games, the winner often exhales deeply to relax.

Other ways to expend energy after victory include the common “Oh, yeah!” action (see Figure 9-9). Raising one leg, clenching both fists, and contracting the body’s muscles so the torso curves inward—sometimes to an exaggerated degree—mobilizes many muscles, consuming significant energy and neural excitement.

Of course, in the cautious setting of psychological testing, test subjects rarely perform such large-scale complex movements; they more often use refined, subtle, and complex actions to express joy and excitement, actions that also carry a performative quality.

#### 1. The Advance-or-Retreat Arm Barrier

The anterior chest and abdomen are protected only by the thoracic vertebrae, the thinner ends of the ribs, and the costal cartilages on the sides, while the entire abdomen lacks bony protection; the back, by contrast, is more thoroughly protected by the spinal column and the thicker proximal ends of the ribs. Consequently, the anterior chest and abdomen are areas to which the nervous system pays special attention—sensitive and relatively vulnerable. Over long-term evolution, humans have learned to use various movements and techniques to protect these vulnerable regions.

The front of the human body (including the anterior neck and the chest-abdomen area) contains most of the body’s sensitive and vulnerable organs, such as the throat, breasts, solar plexus (located below the thoracic vertebrae), and genitals; the nervous system therefore protects them with particular vigilance. When faced with negative stimuli (danger, discomfort, tension, provocation), humans instinctively create a barrier—sometimes merely conceptual—between the torso and the stimulus to protect themselves. This barrier may be as simple as crossing the arms or may involve objects such as books, cushions, or pillows.

Crossing the arms is an obvious defensive behavior, yet further analysis of accompanying body states can reveal different psychological conditions.

**(1) Maximum defensive state—ready to strike**

An active defensive state is a fight-ready defensive response, usually accompanied by an upright torso, head held high, chest thrust forward, and legs apart. This combination of movements generally arises under the dominance of anger, implying relative dominance and the possibility of counterattack (see Figure 8-15).

This combination can be interpreted as several psychological states:

- Arms crossed to increase torso protection; relatively slender individuals are more likely to adopt it for this purpose than those with stronger builds.
- If the legs are also spread, it reflects territorial awareness on one hand and, on the other, stabilizes the body to convey a non-retreating fighting mindset and strong territorial defense and counterattack readiness. (See Chapter 8 for details.)
- The posture makes the person appear more imposing and substantial, increasing pressure and deterrence.

**(2) Passive defensive arm crossing**

The passive defensive state is the opposite: the spine curves, the head lowers, the legs do not stand straight; if seated, the upper body may lean against the chair back and turn sideways toward the stimulus, resembling a reaction to cold (see Figure 8-16).

Such arm crossing stems purely from negative emotions such as fear or anxiety. Without body-temperature detection equipment, it is impossible to determine whether the person is cold or subconsciously afraid of attack. However, lowered body temperature and defensive reactions are not contradictory. The fight-or-flight preparation (emotion) redirects blood circulation, sending large amounts of blood to the limbs to store energy, which can indeed lower torso temperature and make the subject feel cold. Thus, passive arm-crossing can genuinely reflect the subject’s negative emotional state.

Interestingly, the arm-crossing posture can also be used without any psychological pressure, simply to appear weak through this self-protective gesture. Users are often female students who carry books, folders, or bags in front of their chests throughout campus. The action essentially makes them appear vulnerable in order to receive more care. Why do few boys use this posture? Because men are naturally combative and will not display weakness without reason; doing so not only fails to elicit care but may invite bullying or at least the perception that they are “acting cute.”

#### Explicit Resistance: Arms Crossed over the Chest

Our arms are highly expressive and can convey a great deal of information effectively. When interrogating a suspect, FBI agents can judge whether the person is in a natural state—and therefore whether their statements are true—simply by observing the amplitude of arm movements. The less natural the person appears, the smaller the amplitude of arm movements; the larger and more complex the amplitude, the more it indicates that the speaker is immersed in their account and is usually expressing something genuinely felt.

Among all human postural behaviors (including gestures, postures, and facial expressions), crossing the arms over the chest conveys the most easily recognized resistance and is the posture most likely to influence others’ behavior (see Figure 2.14). According to Darwin’s observations, this posture appears to represent resistance in cultures around the world.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.14　双臂交叉的男人]*

Because women’s upper-torso anatomy differs from men’s, women typically cross their arms lower than men do (see Figure 2.15). When a person crosses their arms while clenching their fists, the resistance is further intensified (see Figure 2.8).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.15　双臂交叉的女人]*

In negotiations, crossed arms are very common and indicate dissatisfaction with some aspect of the proceedings. It is important to identify this resistance immediately, locate its cause, and attempt to spread positive emotions. Unfortunately, most people fail to notice it, let alone act on it.

In failed negotiations, we often see that one party’s offers, questions, or demands go unmet precisely because the other party developed resistance that went unnoticed and was allowed to spread. Once a negotiator’s attitude shifts in this way, reaching agreement on contracts, treaties, or settlements becomes far more difficult.

Conducting a smooth negotiation is like steering a boat on a swift river: everyone must recognize the presence of turbulence and respond positively, or the boat will capsize. Therefore, when we notice the other party crossing their arms, it is time for self-examination—because they have clearly signaled their intention to end the conversation.

Baseball fans are familiar with the following scene: an umpire makes a call, and a coach disagrees. The coach runs onto the field, confronts the umpire, gestures angrily, and may even shake a fist.

The umpire stares hard at the furious coach and crosses both arms over the chest (except for football referees, who already wear chest protectors and cannot cross their arms; instead they place their hands on their hips and jut their chins toward the disputant). If the umpire feels they have heard enough, they turn their back on the coach to signal “you’ve said too much,” or simply walk away.

#### Social Centrifugal Space Invaders

Social centrifugal space is the private space a person imagines around themselves. As long as you remain outside another person’s mental comfort zone, the other party feels at ease. But if you intrude on the private space in their mind, they immediately feel anxious and unsettled.

Most people respect others’ social centrifugal space, yet some individuals, such as the so-called “intimate conversationalist” (see Figure 4.27), always try to invade that space. They tend to ignore the other person’s reactions and keep moving closer, shortening the distance, which forces the other person to step back repeatedly.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.27　亲密的谈话人]*

If the other person’s repeated concessions fail to stop the invasion of their mental private space, the best response is to end the conversation or frankly state that you need some breathing room.

Therefore, when you try to close the distance with others, pay close attention to their reactions and respond when necessary to maintain or restore mutual comfort.

Sitting with legs spread across a chair and using the chair back as a barrier is another posture that signals authority and dominance (see Figure 4.28). Salespeople never adopt this sitting position when visiting potential clients unless they have no intention of closing the deal.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.28　双腿分开跨在椅子上]*

Standing and looking down at a seated person also conveys arrogance through nonverbal body language. In general, raising one’s body above others demonstrates dominance. This is why thrones for kings and queens are placed on elevated platforms. Many common descriptive terms reflect this higher position, such as “Your Highness,” “high hall,” “reverence,” and “gaze up at.”

If you wish to convey dominance or control over someone, simply stand up while they remain seated or sit in a position higher than theirs. Exercise caution when making this move, as it can provoke resentment. If your goal is cooperation, eliminate this pretense of superiority and meet the other person on equal footing.

To convey equality through nonverbal body language, adopt the Lincoln-style sitting posture: legs apart on the chair, arms resting on the armrests, and jacket open (see Figure 4.29). This is an open, relaxed sitting position. When two people sit facing each other in the Lincoln posture, neither is signaling superiority.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.29　林肯式的姿势]*

#### Resistance

The opposite of gestures that express openness are those that signal readiness to defend against physical or emotional threat. Note that when openness is misunderstood or fails to resolve an issue, it can turn into offense.

Among all human postures (including gestures, body positions, and facial expressions), crossing the arms over the chest conveys resistance that is the easiest to recognize and the most likely to influence others’ behavior.

During negotiations, the crossed-arms posture (see Figure 4.2) is very common and indicates dissatisfaction with some aspect of the discussion. It is important to identify this resistance at the first moment, determine its cause, and then attempt to spread positive emotions.

**Figure 4.2**　Arms crossed, indicating resistance

In failed negotiations, we often see that a party’s offer, question, or request goes unmet because the other side developed resistance that went unnoticed and spread. When one party’s attitude shifts in this way, reaching agreement on contracts, treaties, or settlements becomes far more difficult. Conducting a smooth negotiation is like steering a boat on a swift river: everyone must recognize the presence of turbulence and respond actively, or the boat will capsize.

Another gesture that conveys resistance or lack of interest is draping one leg over the arm of the chair while crossing the other leg (see Figure 4.3). At first glance it may appear open and relaxed, yet we soon notice that the person adopting this posture is usually expressing hostility or disregard.

**Figure 4.3**　Casually draping one leg over the chair arm

Airline cabin crew generally regard passengers who rest a leg on the seat armrest as demanding and difficult to satisfy. Salespeople likewise find buyers seated in this posture hard to close. The behavior signals that the person is silently declaring dominance and strength in the transaction.

A very common posture expressing resistance is crossing the legs (see Figure 4.4). When negotiation participants are ready to raise and discuss issues, they generally do not cross their legs. If two or more people cross their legs together, it signals that a confrontation is about to begin.

**Figure 4.4**　Legs crossed, indicating resistance

When a negotiation is nearing agreement, participants almost never cross their legs. They lean forward, which both shortens the distance to the other party and reduces divergence in judgment.

#### Recognition

A common, emblematic gesture of recognition is placing both hands on the chest to signal agreement with what the other person has said or done (see Figure 4.40).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.40　双手放在胸前，表示认可]*

For centuries people have used this gesture to communicate loyalty, integrity, and devotion. Americans use a similar posture when pledging allegiance to the flag. In fact, the gesture dates back to ancient Rome, where Roman soldiers saluted to express loyalty and recognition by placing one hand on the chest and extending the other toward the recipient.

Recognition through touch is most often seen between acquaintances, friends, and family members (see Figure 4.41) and rarely occurs between strangers or casual acquaintances. People who communicate nonverbally through touch can readily express their emotions. The most common areas touched are the shoulders and arms.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.41　父子交流彼此的认可和爱意]*

Touch can also serve as a calming gesture. The person performing the action usually accompanies it with reassuring words such as “Don’t worry” or “Calm down.”

If someone slowly moves closer to you, steadily reducing the distance, it usually means they agree with your viewpoint, wish to share something privately, or both. Such displays of closeness can sometimes make you uncomfortable (see “Social Centrifugal Space Invaders”).

Interestingly, the distance between two communicating deaf individuals is generally greater than that between hearing people. This is because deaf people need sufficient space to clearly observe each other’s facial expressions and body movements. They focus most on the face (primarily the mouth), while hands and body movements are not the primary focus. Only when one person is signing does the other fully direct attention to the hands.

#### 2. The Innocent Shrug That Can Advance or Retreat — Shrugging Shoulders

A composite movement frequently observed, especially among Westerners, is raising both shoulders while turning the palms upward, usually accompanied by the lines “Nothing,” “Not my problem,” “I don’t know,” or “There’s nothing I can do.”

This shrug is also a classic defensive reaction, as shown in Figure 8-17.

Through long evolution, the same response can occur even without physical threat, simply when the nervous system receives negative stimulation and perceives a need for self-protection. The psychological state mapped by this reaction is a sense of needing protection—a posture of weakness. Thus the shrug with palms up can be interpreted as: “I am weak, I am afraid, I am powerless, and look, my hands are empty—I have no intention of attacking.” Paired with the lines listed earlier, the meaning is precise.

Building on this standard movement, foreign researchers have concluded that a quick, one-sided shoulder shrug while speaking indicates a lack of confidence and, by extension, that the speaker is not confident in what they are saying and may be lying. The reasoning is sound: an incomplete shrug is a weakened version of the full shrug, sharing the same root and belonging to the category of micro-reactions (微反应). However, in our actual testing, instances where this movement genuinely correlates with lying remain very few and require further verification.

Whether a shrug, like arm-crossing, expresses a dominant or submissive mindset depends entirely on the degree of torso curvature. With the arm posture of the shrug held constant, an upright torso conveys dominance and can be voiced as “Not my damn problem,” “I don’t care,” or “I’m indifferent,” depicting a cold, aloof interior. A curved torso, by contrast, conveys the submissive appeals “There’s nothing I can do,” “I don’t want it this way either,” “I don’t know,” or “Please let me off the hook.”

#### People Who Cross Their Arms Over Their Chest Have Strong Defenses

Micro-expression keyword: In daily life many people cross their arms over their chest. This is a gesture of defense, refusal, and negation. Especially during conversation, if the other person adopts this posture, they are likely in a defensive frame of mind. We must first find a way to reduce their defensiveness before the conversation can proceed smoothly.

When faced with danger, what is your first instinctive movement? Most people probably choose to wrap their arms around their body. This is a natural self-protection response.

In daily life we also frequently see people crossing their arms over their chest. The movement is an external manifestation of psychological defense. When we find ourselves in an unfamiliar environment, among strangers, or holding a rejecting attitude toward a certain viewpoint, we often unconsciously cross our arms over our chest.

It is a physical barrier we erect for ourselves; subconsciously it tells others not to cross that line, conveying a sense of defense, refusal, and negation. People who frequently adopt this posture have strong defenses.

An experiment was once conducted in which strangers who did not know one another were randomly divided into two groups and seated in circles. Members of the first group sat naturally relaxed. Members of the second group all tightly crossed their arms over their chests.

The first group quickly began chatting animatedly; by the end of the experiment they had become as familiar as friends. The second group remained subdued; no one initiated conversation, and at the end they were still strangers to one another.

The results demonstrate that crossing the arms over the chest projects an aloof, unapproachable impression, causing others to hesitate to approach. At the same time, it causes the person to miss many valuable social opportunities.

People who cross their arms over their chest essentially belong to the type with strong defenses. They trust no one, refuse to open their hearts, and keep others at a distance; naturally they do not have many friends.

#### 7.1.1 Establishing Territory: Hands and Arms

There are three common postures:

**Establishing territory with the hands**

The most obvious, and the one frequently used by celebrities or their security personnel, is a blocking movement. This includes human chains formed by linked hands or simply extending and waving an arm straight out—without offensive intent, merely to secure necessary space. This purely protective action uses the hands to create a barrier around the individual, ensuring they remain undisturbed.

**Establishing territory with the arms**

The second posture is to spread both arms slightly downward, usually accompanied by clenched fists, colloquially called “rolling up the sleeves.” Variations exist, but they require well-developed muscles: the arms do not spread widely, yet the shoulders widen through the extension of the back muscles. The person performing the action can feel the expansion and often adds a slight sway to enhance the effect.

The meaning of this reaction is complex. For the individual it serves both as a psychological cue for establishing territory and as a way to appear more imposing (the occupied area increases), thereby increasing deterrence to some degree. Even without developed muscles, the posture can still heighten deterrence.

**Establishing territory with the arms**

The third posture is crossing the arms over the chest. When performed by a powerfully built person with thick upper limbs, it usually stems not from a protective mindset but from a desire to intimidate. Because of skeletal structure, crossing the arms allows them to occupy more lateral space than arms hanging straight down; the contraction and overlap of muscles also make the upper body appear more imposing and substantial (more effective than rolling up the sleeves), increasing the sense of intimidation.

If any of the three reactions above appears, it indicates that the person being observed has a strong confrontational mindset. The situation you face is comparable to attempting to enter the territory of a wild animal.

#### Arms and Shoulders

Our arms are highly expressive and can convey a great deal of information effectively. In any setting, simply knowing the amplitude of a person’s arm movements allows us to judge whether they are in a natural state. The less natural speakers appear, the smaller their arm movements; the larger and more complex the arm movements, the more clearly they indicate that the speaker is immersed in their narrative.

Crossing the arms over the chest as a sign of resistance is very common worldwide (see Figure 3.12). Because of differences in upper-body structure, women generally cross their arms lower than men (see Figure 3.13). When a person crosses their arms while clenching both hands into fists, the gesture further intensifies their resistance (see Figure 3.9).

- Figure 3.12　Man with arms crossed
- Figure 3.13　Woman with arms crossed

Compared with the arms, shoulder movement has a more limited range. Yet careful observation can still yield information from shoulder movements.

For example, when the shoulders are held low, straight, and relaxed, the person is relaxed and confident (see Figure 3.14). If the shoulders slump forward and the head hangs, the person feels defeated, unhappy, or fatigued (see Figure 3.15). The typical shrug (raising then lowering) conveys “I don’t know” (see Figure 3.16). Sometimes a person also raises their eyebrows while shrugging.

- Figure 3.14　Shoulders held straight
- Figure 3.15　Shoulders slumped
- Figure 3.16　Shrugging movement

#### What Should We Do?

If the other person keeps their arms crossed over their chest throughout the conversation, it shows they are not listening to anything you say.

At a company seminar featuring a well-known expert, some attendees agreed with the speaker’s views while others opposed them. The boss observed that those who raised objections almost invariably crossed their arms over their chests while listening. Those who supported the speaker kept their arms resting naturally on the chair or their laps, displaying an accepting, open posture.

Therefore, if we can find a way to get the person to uncross their arms, we may lower their defensiveness and make them receptive to our ideas.

Several simple methods are worth trying:

1. Hand them a small object—a pen, a promotional flyer, or a notebook—so they must release their crossed arms.
2. Offer a chair with armrests so they can rest their hands on the armrests.
3. While speaking, use matching body language. Body language can be contagious and may prompt them to uncross their arms and imitate your posture.
4. Occasionally glance at their crossed arms during the conversation. Your gaze tells them “I don’t like that posture” and exerts pressure, encouraging them to lower their arms.

Crossing the arms over the chest indicates strong defenses; the person will not easily let you into their inner world. Try a few small techniques to get them to lower their arms. Only after they adopt an open physical posture will they begin to accept you.

#### Arms That Symbolize Territory: Arm Movements as Declarations of Power

Micro-expression keyword: People maintain a certain wariness toward those they do not know well. This is expressed in body language by instinctively crossing the arms over the chest in a posture of refusal or vigilance. Arms help people express feelings of defense, comfort, and acceptance. Therefore, by reading arm movements accurately we can understand others’ inner thoughts, respond correctly, and gain their goodwill.

Often, when people sense danger or encounter something they do not wish to face, they unconsciously cross their arms over their chest, erecting a physical barrier for themselves. This instinctive movement protects their territory. Clearly, arms are no less effective than other body parts at expressing comfort, confidence, and similar emotions.

When we encounter a threat, we find that the arms are always the first to react. If someone throws an object at us, our arms instinctively rise to block or catch it. Sometimes they even rise to protect us even when the action is illogical or based on a mistaken judgment—for instance, when a bullet is fired, we still raise our arms even though we know they cannot stop it.

Consequently, in many situations a person’s arm movements can reveal genuine feelings. Unlike expressions that are easy to fake, arm movements provide clear, authentic clues that allow us to understand others’ thoughts, feelings, or intentions accurately.

Below are several arm postures commonly seen in daily life:

#### Shoulder Contraction: Weakness, Insecurity, Low Mood

Some people slowly raise both shoulders to ear height during conversation, making it look as if their neck has disappeared. The focus of this movement is the gradual upward lift of the shoulders. Essentially, the purpose of this action is to pull the head back in, like a turtle. People who make this movement lack confidence and feel very uncomfortable. I have seen many people do this in meetings, especially when the boss walks in and says, “All right, I want to hear what everyone has been up to.” While others enthusiastically discuss their impressive achievements, those with mediocre results shrink lower and lower, their shoulders rising as if trying to hide their heads.

Because the torso houses all the body’s vital organs, which are fragile, the torso has developed strong vigilance over long-term evolution. It sensitively detects approaching danger and promptly produces various protective movements. In short, torso movements draw closer to what is beneficial—accepting or even liking people who benefit oneself—and move away from what is harmful—rejecting or even disliking people who harm oneself.

For example, when lovers share a close relationship and extremely high mutual trust, they instinctively want to approach, lean on, hug, or kiss each other. If two people are distant and lack sufficient trust, feelings of anger or disgust arise, along with strong defensiveness; physically, there is no desire for closeness, only an urge to stay as far away as possible. From torso movements, we can therefore easily discern the level of intimacy and trust between two people.

#### Hugging

The “hug” can be described as a behavior prevalent worldwide, conveying care and affection. Sometimes a well-intentioned hug may be taken as a gesture of goodwill. A person’s attitude toward hugging reveals whether that individual is polite or cold and difficult to deal with.

Although people can use words to conceal themselves, their arms cannot; arm movements expose all inner thoughts. If we understand these body-language signals, we can anticipate decisions that may work against us and gain time to reverse unfavorable situations. For instance, suppose you are a salesperson pitching a product. Near the end of the pitch, the client suddenly crosses both arms over the chest while keeping the thumbs raised and visible, accompanied by other affirmative gestures and expressions. You can confidently ask the client to sign a contract, because even though the client has not spoken, the purchase intention has already been clearly conveyed through body language.

Note that under the same circumstances, if the client adopts a clenched-fist arm-cross posture with a blank expression, any further request from you will meet resistance and yield no positive result. Thus, by reading arm body language we can perceive others’ thoughts and take better precautions.

#### 8.1.4 Hands on Hips

Both parties preparing for confrontation try to appear taller than the other; chest out and head up are essential. An erect spine and raised chin constitute one of the territorial-response features introduced in Chapter 7.

One interesting posture combines chest out and head up with both hands placed on the hips. Frequently seen in quarrel scenes, this pose is actually a contradictory combination. On one hand, the person tries to make their image appear extremely imposing; on the other hand, the hands are firmly restricted to the body, subconsciously reserved for display rather than attack. Experiments and real cases confirm this: when this posture appears, conflict usually remains at the stage of standoff or verbal sparring. A party truly intending physical attack will not adopt it.

However, although this posture indicates no physical attack will occur, the desire to attack has already formed and is very strong.

Please note that arm posture alone does not convey meaning. With the same hands-on-hips posture, if the person bends the torso while keeping the arms unchanged, an entirely different effect may result. In behavior driven by genuine emotion, anger never permits torso bending; bending can only stem from a sense of weakness, such as guilt or sadness.

#### Arms Spread, Hands Open on the Table, Indicating Anger

Whether seated or standing, a person making this gesture strongly communicates: “Listen! I have something to say!” Failure to recognize this posture and the hostile, resistant, or destructive emotions about to erupt can make the situation extremely awkward and may even trigger serious consequences.

Therefore, no matter who adopts this posture—your child, employee, boss, or customer—recognize it early, intervene promptly, or remain silent. Never add fuel to the fire or impulsively counterattack, pushing the other person into an emotional explosion. Unfortunately, many people do exactly that in real life.

Compared with the arms, shoulder movements are relatively limited. Yet careful observation can still yield useful information.

For example, when the shoulders are held low, straight, and relaxed, the person is relaxed and confident. Shoulders slumped forward with the head hanging indicate defeat, unhappiness, or fatigue.

The shrug (shoulders rising then falling) is usually accompanied by open hands with palms up, conveying a “What do you want me to do?” attitude. Sometimes a person also raises the eyebrows while shrugging.

#### Ventral Denial and Ventral Presentation

The former signals dislike of a person; the latter signals liking. Our ventral side gathers the eyes, mouth, chest, and genitals; it is sensitive to people or things we like or dislike. When encountering something good, the ventral side leans toward it; the same occurs with people we like. When we sense something is wrong—such as a change in relationship or an unwelcome topic—ventral-denial behavior appears: we shift posture or turn away. That is why, at a banquet, we instinctively rotate our bodies slightly when someone we dislike approaches.

The opposite of ventral denial is ventral display: we present our ventral side to people or things we like. When our child runs over to hug us, we move aside anything that might block the child, including our arms. We present the ventral side because it feels most warm and comfortable. Conversely, we express negative attitudes toward someone or something by turning away or ignoring them, because we always face what we like with our ventral side and turn our back on what we dislike.

#### Shoulder Movements

Compared with the arms, shoulder movements are relatively limited. Yet careful observation can still yield useful information.

For example, when the shoulders are held low, straight, and relaxed, the person is relaxed and confident (see Figure 2.16). Shoulders slumped forward with the head hanging indicate defeat, unhappiness, or fatigue (see Figure 2.17). The typical shrug (rising then falling) conveys “I don’t know” (see Figure 2.18). Sometimes a person also raises the eyebrows while shrugging.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: Figure 2.17 Shoulders slumped]*
