#### Touching the Neck

When a person touches the neck, they are telling us they lack confidence. For instance, when we ask someone for a favor, the other person may unconsciously touch their own neck, indicating they are not confident they can fulfill the request. At such moments it is best to prepare a backup plan.

When doing something or witnessing an event, we often hear people say they “broke into a sweat.” This means that although they appear outwardly calm, “hand expressions” are usually more truthful than facial expressions. Hand movements reveal inner emotions and thoughts; through these movements we can fully gauge a person’s level of confidence.

Therefore, learning to read hand body language not only boosts our own sense of achievement and helps us win more victories, but also allows us to understand others’ inner states. This way, we can interact with anyone with ease.

#### (7) Arm Folding

Folding the arms across the chest creates a protective barrier against threat. Thus, when a person feels nervous, negative, or hostile, they naturally fold their arms over the chest. This posture often appears among strangers, especially in unsafe settings such as elevators. During conversation, if the other person folds their arms, pay attention: they may disagree with your views even while verbally expressing agreement.

Of course, many other gestures exist—stroking the chin for thought, raising the thumb for approval, slapping the head for sudden realization, scratching the head for difficulty or confusion. These gestures seem simple yet play extremely important roles in daily life. Looking back, some of the knowledge you have learned may already feel fuzzy. That is all right; this “people-reading” knowledge is the summary of my twenty-five years of experience. Do not expect to master and apply it in just a few hours—that is unrealistic. I simply want to tell you: never rush for quick results. Reading people is a delicate skill that requires patience and care.

#### Defensive Torso: Torso Movements Reveal the Level of Trust Between Two Parties

Micro-reaction keywords: Human instinct—when sensing danger or discomfort, a person involuntarily uses the torso to protect themselves or adopts a challenging posture. Therefore, certain torso movements alone can indicate whether trust has already been established with the other person<|eos|>

#### 8.3.1 Establishing Barriers

The barrier-establishing response refers to the test subject attempting to use limbs or objects to create obstacles around the head or torso in order to hinder the advance of negative stimuli. A relatively classic defensive response is shown in Figure 8-14.

#### Arms Wrapped Around the Head

The action of wrapping both arms around the head indicates a sense of comfort and dominance. This is frequently observed in some business meetings, as if declaring to others: “This is my territory.”

See Hands (c-hands).

#### Arm Crossing Suggests Rejection

##### Arm Crossing Suggests Rejection

A person crossing their arms often indicates defense or rejection. However, arm crossing takes many forms, and the meaning of each must be analyzed according to the specific situation.

When we were children, whenever danger approached or a threatening person drew near, we instinctively hid behind our parents or under a table or behind a cabinet to signal rejection. As adults, we instinctively cross our arms in front of our chest when facing similar threats, creating a physical barrier that prevents others from crossing it.

Many people share the consensus that crossing the arms signals defense or rejection. We frequently observe strangers adopting this posture when they feel uncertain or unsafe. When two standing people converse and one makes this gesture, it generally suggests rejection; the likelihood is even higher when the individuals are meeting for the first time.

A reporter once attended a forum on energy conservation and emission reduction for small and medium-sized enterprises. The theme was “How SMEs Can Strengthen Energy Conservation and Emission Reduction During Development.”

The host speaker delivered an enthusiastic presentation, yet the reporter noticed that several rows of seated audience members had crossed their arms. For these SMEs, survival and growth issues had already exhausted them; energy conservation and emission reduction would only add pressure and make survival harder. Consequently, they viewed the speaker’s content with negation and doubt.

The organizers’ advocacy of energy conservation and emission reduction was not wrong, but they failed to consider the SMEs’ standpoint and therefore could not convey their message effectively. They did not promptly notice the crossed arms and could not sense the audience’s rejection, so they could not use the speech to overcome the opposition.

In public settings, many strangers habitually cross their arms, as if erecting a barrier between themselves and the outside world that separates them from disliked people and objects.

Arm crossing has three main manifestations:

1. Partial Arm Crossing  
   Because the full arm-crossing posture is too obvious, some people consciously adopt a subtler version—partial arm crossing. A common example is one arm reaching across the body to touch or grasp the other arm, forming a concealed barrier that provides a sense of security.

2. Disguised Arm Crossing  
   An even more sophisticated and concealed form is disguised arm crossing. One arm reaches across the body to touch a watch, bracelet, cuff, or jacket pocket, creating a barrier while appearing casual. If someone uses this method, stay alert; the disguise is effective and often goes unnoticed.

3. Reinforced Arm Crossing  
   A more overt form is reinforced arm crossing. When a person clearly senses imminent danger, they cross their arms while clenching their fists and occasionally gritting their teeth, signaling a defensive stance. If the emotion escalates out of control, an attack may follow. In such cases, maintain eye contact with a smile and open your palms to ease the tension in a friendly manner.

In summary, when conversing with someone, if you observe them crossing their arms, recognize their negative attitude and the possibility that you have voiced a disagreeable point. Even if they verbally agree, understand that they will not readily accept your view.

##### Arms Crossed in Front of the Chest Represents Defense

Baseball fans are familiar with the following scene: a referee issues a ruling, a coach disagrees, runs onto the field, gestures emphatically in protest, and may even raise a clenched fist.

The referee stares sternly at the furious coach and crosses his arms in front of his chest (football referees, already wearing chest protectors, cannot cross their arms and instead place their hands on their hips while jutting their chin toward the disputant), adopting a defensive posture. If the referee has heard enough, he turns his back to signal “you have said too much” or simply walks away.

Among all postural behaviors, arms crossed in front of the chest conveys the most easily recognizable resistance and is most likely to influence others’ actions. Darwin’s research indicates this posture represents resistance across cultures.

Women typically cross their arms slightly lower than men because of differences in upper-body structure. Middle-aged women adopt the posture more often than older women.

In negotiations, crossed arms are common and signal dissatisfaction with some aspect of the discussion. Identifying this defensive mindset promptly, locating its trigger, and attempting to introduce positive emotions is important. Unfortunately, most people neither notice nor act on it.

In failed negotiations, one side’s offers or requests often fail because the other side developed defensive psychology that went unnoticed and spread. Once a party’s attitude shifts this way, agreements, contracts, or settlements become harder to reach.

A smooth negotiation resembles steering a boat on turbulent water: everyone must recognize the currents and respond positively, or the vessel will capsize. Therefore, whenever the other party crosses their arms, it is time for self-reflection, because they have clearly signaled an intention to end the conversation.

##### Arm Crossing Affects Listening Effectiveness

Researchers divided volunteers into two groups to listen to a lecture and instructed each group to adopt a different posture. The first group was told to keep their arms in a natural, uncrossed position and listen in a relaxed, natural state. The second group listened at the same time and place but was required to cross their arms in front of their chest.

The researchers found that the first group raised fewer objections, while the second group was highly critical and frequently refuted the speaker’s points. After the lecture, retention testing showed that the first group remembered 38 percent more content than the second group, demonstrating that arm crossing seriously impairs listening effectiveness.

Therefore, when communicating with others, crossed arms indicate reduced listening effectiveness. You should find a way to get the person to uncross their arms. Rather than reacting after the posture appears, prevent it from occurring in the first place. For example, hand the person an object to hold so they must release their arms. Or, during the conversation, show materials that require a posture change to view, such as books or images placed on a table, to prompt a shift in position.

##### Psychology Mini-Class

American researchers examined the arm-crossing gesture and uncovered some concerning findings. The study indicates that arm crossing severely impairs listening effectiveness.

### Legs and Feet

#### Assessing His Willingness to Cooperate from Sitting Posture

Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius once said: “People are born to help and cooperate with one another, like hands, feet, or eyelids that depend on each other, or lips and teeth that cannot be separated!”

This is indeed the case. If the various parts of our body cannot coordinate and function together, trouble arises. By the same token, to achieve certain goals we also need to cooperate with others. If you are trying to obtain someone’s help or form a cooperative group, it is crucial to notice the following postures that signal cooperation.

Once, Gerard Nierenberg, the “father of negotiation training” whose ability to read people was no less than that of an FBI agent, attended a seminar discussing a new product of great scientific value. The topics included patent rights, equity stakes, royalties, research and development costs, and how to persuade the client company to manufacture and sell the product.

At the very start of the discussion, a key technical member of the other team adopted an eager posture: sitting forward on the edge of his chair, body leaning in, toes pointed as though a sprinter awaiting the starting gun (see Figure 2.37). Nierenberg immediately recognized that this “poised to launch” posture meant the man was interested in the subject under discussion. Nierenberg therefore guided him to raise several technical questions. Once those questions were answered, the man’s attitude became openly cooperative.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.37　跃跃欲试的姿势]*

In fact, Nierenberg had deliberately chosen to sit beside this important person from the outset so he could observe every movement. The negotiation proceeded smoothly precisely because Nierenberg spotted the cooperative signal at once and used it to secure a mutually beneficial agreement.

Thus, during a negotiation, if you notice the other party sitting on the front edge of the chair with toes lifted in an expectant posture, it indicates readiness to concede, cooperate, purchase, accept, or even outdo others. This is a positive emotion and a signal of willingness to cooperate; if leveraged well, it greatly increases the chance of reaching a mutually beneficial agreement.

We have all experienced situations in which someone who was initially cooperative suddenly reverses course 180 degrees and the matter collapses; or someone who once affectionately used your nickname abruptly switches to your full name in a formal tone, the relaxed smile replaced by a furrowed brow. These changes show the other party no longer wishes to cooperate.

During an interrogation, after FBI agent Jeff finished presenting the known facts, he waited for the suspect to provide further details. Although the suspect said sincerely, “I am cooperating with you in good faith; I have told you everything I know,” Jeff did not believe him.

Why? The suspect’s legs betrayed his true feelings. While speaking, he sat upright with his legs crossed (see Figure 2.38). This posture signals doubt and resistance, contradicting his claim of “good faith.”

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.38　双腿交叉，表示抵触]*

In negotiations, participants generally do not cross their legs when preparing to raise a question. Once a question is introduced or heated debate begins, one or both sides usually cross their legs. If both parties uncross their legs and lean forward, it signals that an agreement is about to be reached.

Some people cross their legs the moment they sit down. This indicates a guarded, competitive mindset, ambition, self-confidence, and a tendency to act decisively once a decision is made. This applies to men; women differ slightly.

A woman who boldly crosses her legs is usually confident in her appearance or attire and has a strong desire to be noticed. Such women tend to have high self-esteem, deliberately display charm, interact casually with the opposite sex, and aspire to be in charge; winning their affection or commitment is not easy.

Therefore, in negotiations, sales, or personal interactions, pay attention to anyone who crosses their legs. Once the other party crosses their legs, they are signaling competition or challenge. You must stay alert and focused to avoid costly oversights. Be even more cautious with someone who drapes one leg over the arm of the chair while lifting a foot (see Figure 2.39); such a posture often indicates a lack of cooperative intent, indifference to others’ needs, and even a degree of hostility.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.39　满不在乎地将一条腿搭在椅子扶手上]*

Flight attendants know that passengers who rest a leg on the armrest are usually demanding and hard to please. Salespeople likewise find buyers who sit this way difficult to close. The posture silently asserts dominance and control in the interaction or transaction.

#### Reading Superiority: Feet on the Desk

In every profession, countless nonverbal cues clearly define superior and subordinate status. This is especially evident in the military. In most cases, the more domineering the superior acts, the more fearful and insecure the subordinate feels, prompting an immediate response.

Anthropologists note that men are naturally more territorial than women. Both men and women, however, can assert control through nonverbal gestures. When an FBI agent interviews a suspect, if the suspect places one foot on the desk, he is silently displaying “superiority” (see Figure 2.33). Such individuals usually lack cooperative intent.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.33　脚置于桌上的姿势]*

In certain settings we also extend our control by placing personal items (books, papers, notebooks, wallets, etc.) on empty seats to prevent others from occupying the space.

For example, students in a library often spread their books and belongings across a table to discourage others from sitting nearby. This action clearly communicates “I want personal space.” British psychiatrist Humphrey Osmond called this “sociopetal space”—the imagined private zone surrounding an individual.

In fact, most of us unconsciously create sociopetal space every day. When watching a movie, we place a coat or scarf on the adjacent seat to stop others from sitting there. Upon entering an elevator, we immediately claim an unoccupied corner, much like a boxer entering the ring. All these behaviors stem from the same impulse.

Sometimes people create sociopetal space to keep unsuitable individuals away while awaiting more desirable company. A passenger seated in the aisle seat on a train may place a briefcase on the window seat until an attractive woman approaches, at which point the briefcase is removed to offer the seat.

When two people stand face to face, an accepted sociopetal distance also exists. This distance varies by culture and depends on the relationship between the individuals. You naturally stand closer to your spouse than to a stranger.

As long as we remain outside another person’s comfort zone, that person feels at ease. Once we intrude into their personal space, discomfort arises. We must therefore remain mindful of this distance to avoid making others uneasy.

FBI agents also note that straddling a chair with legs apart, using the chair back as a barrier, is another posture of authority and dominance (see Figure 2.34). A suspect adopting this posture may appear pleasant and friendly on the surface, yet the stance reveals a controlling and aggressive nature. A salesperson visiting a prospective client would never sit this way unless the deal is already off the table.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.34　双腿分开跨在椅子上]*

When a person feels satisfied, comfortable, and confident, they typically lean back, clasp their hands behind their head, and cross their legs in a “4” shape (see Figure 2.35). This posture conveys the impression that they are in control.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.35　“4”字形的坐姿]*

Standing while looking down at a seated person is another nonverbal way of expressing superiority. Elevating one’s body above others in their presence signals dominance. This is why thrones for kings and queens are placed on raised platforms. Many common honorifics—“Your Highness,” “highness,” “look up to,” “gaze upon”—reflect this association with height.

If you wish to project dominance over someone, simply stand while they remain seated or sit in a noticeably higher position. Exercise caution, however, as this action can provoke resentment. When seeking cooperation, it is better to eliminate any artificial elevation and meet the other person on equal terms.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.36　林肯式的姿势]*

To convey equality through nonverbal cues, adopt the Lincoln-style posture: legs apart, arms resting on the chair arms, jacket open (see Figure 2.36). This is an open, relaxed sitting position. When two people sit facing each other in this manner, neither is signaling superiority.

#### Different Walking Styles Reflect Different Moods

Walking appears ordinary, yet it most clearly reveals a person’s emotional state. Learning to read others’ walking postures therefore allows us to discern their changing moods.

Psychologists have found that the farther a body part is from the brain, the more trustworthy its signals. Areas closer to the brain’s central control are easier to disguise and therefore less reliable. In social interactions we habitually watch faces, yet the face produces the most deceptive information. The lower body, by contrast, concentrates the most authentic signals. Walking posture is difficult to fake or alter, so observing it quickly reveals personality and emotional state.

Walking speed and stride length are closely tied to mood. What moods do different walking styles express? The following detailed explanations address this question.

1. **Walking briskly**  
   Walking briskly with arms swinging naturally usually indicates inner excitement. People who walk this way are typically anticipating something pleasant or hopeful. They tend to be outgoing, lively, and sociable, approaching tasks with boldness and a spirit of adventure. Because they are impatient, however, they can become impulsive or even aggressive. They hurry even when there is no urgency, sometimes breaking into a trot. This gait signals impatience; such individuals are energetic yet often lack patience.

2. **Walking with the body leaning forward**  
   People who walk leaning forward, almost hunched, are generally modest, well-mannered, and emotionally sensitive. By keeping their heads down and shoulders rounded, they try to remain unobtrusive, as if saying, “Shh—don’t disturb others.” They are usually reserved, rarely confide in others, and tend to brood alone, making them prone to emotional hurt.

3. **Walking slowly and deliberately**  
   A slow, unhurried gait, regardless of others’ opinions, often reflects indecision. Such walkers avoid risk, prefer to think things through, and refuse to act impulsively. They wait until others have tested an idea and proven it safe before proceeding, frequently missing opportunities as a result.

4. **Walking with head held high and chest out**  
   Walking with head high and chest out expresses confidence and strong self-esteem, sometimes bordering on arrogance. People who walk this way are usually in good spirits. They trust only themselves, rely on subjective judgment, dismiss others’ advice, and center interactions on themselves, often appearing indifferent. Consequently they frequently operate alone.

5. **Walking with a steady, measured gait**  
   A steady, measured walk usually accompanies a pleasant, relaxed mood, because only emotional calm produces such even steps. These individuals are composed, seek stability in their actions, remain unflustered, and think before acting. Their deliberate approach allows them to advance steadily and succeed through calmness and courage in both career and life. They keep their word and treat others with integrity.

6. **Walking with a bounce or skip**  
   A bouncy or skipping walk typically signals that something joyful has occurred. Such people are usually open and sincere with friends, making interactions with them light and enjoyable. They tend to be optimistic, positive, and content with simple lives. Although occasionally careless, most are generous and kind.

In summary, walking postures vary widely and are closely linked to a person’s emotions and character. Walking style is not fixed, however. Someone who normally walks slowly may suddenly hurry because of an urgent matter; conversely, a normally brisk walker may slow down after a disheartening event. To interpret mood and personality from gait, always consider the immediate context.

#### People with Ankles Crossed Are Restraining Their Emotions

From childhood, parents and teachers taught us to learn self-control. “Just endure it for a while” was the phrase we heard most often. We also frequently use similar words to overcome emotions such as frustration and anxiety, the most important of which is suppressing anger. As we grow older, we gradually learn to use various postures to conceal our feelings and regulate our behavior.

When you see someone with both ankles crossed over each other, you should notice whether that person is restraining themselves. Because when people suppress strong sensations or emotions, they involuntarily press their ankles tightly together. Some people joke that this posture expresses a kind of “repression,” like “needing to use the restroom urgently but being unable to go.”

When negotiating with suspects, FBI agents often choose to have the other person sit while they stand. This is because people tend to produce more leg movements when seated, making it easier for their inner state to be revealed. For example, when a person is tense or fearful, they often adopt a posture with ankles crossed and both hands gripping the chair arms tightly (see Figures 2.30 and 2.31, noting the difference between how men and women cross their ankles).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.30　自我克制的男人]*

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.31　自我克制的女人]*

Flight attendants are highly skilled at reading passengers’ body language. They have a unique ability to identify passengers who truly need service but are too shy to ask. If a passenger repeatedly crosses and uncrosses their ankles after boarding—especially before takeoff—the attendants can determine that the person is very tense and uneasy. When the attendants bring coffee, tea, or milk, if the passenger’s ankles remain tightly crossed instead of separating and moving toward the edge of the seat, it indicates they may need something.

We have also observed that patients seated in a dentist’s chair and customers reclining in a barber’s chair for a shave both involuntarily press their ankles tightly together while gripping the chair arms with both hands. From this we can conclude that people in both situations are working hard to restrain unpleasant emotions.

Some may say that adopting this posture makes them feel comfortable. In reality, this is merely using comfort as an excuse to mask inner tension. When you lie down to rest, if you notice your ankles are crossed, uncross them and see whether doing so makes you feel more relaxed.

People also unconsciously cross their ankles when facing difficult problems at work or in daily life. Once the matter is resolved smoothly and everything proceeds well, they unconsciously separate their legs.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.32　自我克制的站姿]*

The self-restraining postures discussed above are those commonly seen while seated. When people are standing or walking, the most common self-control posture is clasping the hands behind the back, with one hand tightly gripping the wrist or arm of the other hand, which is already formed into a fist (see Figure 2.32). This posture clearly signals to everyone that the person is striving to control their emotions.

The act of gripping the wrist indicates that the individual is filled with frustration and is attempting to steady their emotions by holding their own wrist, keeping themselves calm and preventing an outburst. In addition, when a person feels frustrated, they involuntarily draw their chest inward in an effort to gain a sense of inner security.

This posture also reveals a sense of fear toward the situation at hand and a profound lack of self-confidence. Therefore, never adopt this posture during an interview; an experienced interviewer will immediately detect your inner tension and unease, and your lack of confidence will be unlikely to leave a favorable impression.

#### Walking Posture Is a Sketch of Personality

Micro-expression keywords

No two leaves in the world are identical, and no two people have exactly the same walking posture. This is due not only to physical differences but, more importantly, to differences in personality. Different ways of walking reflect each person’s unique character.

On the street, apart from soldiers marching in formation, everyone walks differently; no two gaits are exactly alike. Over time, you will notice that a person’s walking posture is closely related to their personality and psychology. In general, walking styles can be summarized into the following types:

- **Standard gait**  
  Back straight, abdomen and chest drawn in, springy steps, arms swinging naturally, eyes looking straight ahead. Such people are generally optimistic, confident, friendly, and forward-looking.

- **Hands in pockets while walking**  
  A person who keeps one hand in a pocket walks with a carefree air, places great importance on their image, values emotions highly, and understands feelings well. Someone who keeps both hands in their pockets is usually rather lazy and somewhat sentimental.

- **Arms swinging behind the back while walking**  
  Such people tend to be arrogant, dismissive of everything, and fearless. Their temperament is relatively overbearing, making verbal communication difficult. They enjoy championing justice, like to direct others, and dislike being directed. Nevertheless, they are mentally agile, methodical in their work, possess strong organizational skills, and have leadership potential.

- **Arms swinging in front of the body while walking**  
  Such people are often timid and cautious, overly compliant, listless, and frail. They cannot withstand even minor emotional shocks and their mood collapses easily. If the gait is deliberately adopted, however, it indicates the person is slippery and that others will find it hard to discern their true character or intentions.

- **Upper body leaning slightly forward while walking**  
  Most such people are introverted, modest, and reserved. When interacting with others they appear taciturn on the surface yet place great value on friendship. They seem calm outwardly but are actually quite proactive or impatient inside.

- **Very slow walking speed**  
  Walking at a calm, unhurried pace—half a beat slower than others—indicates a person who is strictly self-disciplined, cautious, methodical, and extremely tolerant toward everyone. They are shrewd yet steady, do not readily trust others’ words, value integrity, and keep their promises. Although they may appear somewhat weak, they are in fact thoughtful and independent-minded.

- **Very fast walking speed**  
  Most such people are intelligent and capable, energetic, courageous in facing life’s challenges, and highly adaptable. They work efficiently, never dawdle, and once they decide to accomplish something they pursue the goal with seriousness and determination—“a promise is a promise, and action follows through.”

- **Quick small steps**  
  Like ancient officials hurrying to an audience with their ruler, taking rapid little steps. Such people may have long been in subordinate or managed positions and have developed this habit, or they may be naturally impatient or currently in a hurry.

- **Large strides while walking**  
  Such people generally have a strong physique, high self-confidence, a stubborn and competitive personality, and work efficiently; they dislike others dragging their feet. They are kind-hearted and will do their utmost to help when asked.

- **Dragging feet while walking**  
  Such people do not lift their feet, causing their heels to rub heavily against the ground. They often feel fatigued, unhappy, and depressed. They lack initiative, prefer to stick to conventions, show no pioneering spirit, and possess no outstanding talents; they frequently encounter obstacles or setbacks in life.

In summary, the best way to walk is with head held high, chest out, eyes looking forward, and a steady, unhurried pace. Only then will you convey an impression of confidence and positivity and easily win others’ trust and goodwill.

#### Unconscious Leg Jiggling Is a Sign of Inner Tension

Micro-expression keywords: When encountering pressure or danger, people feel tense—a normal psychological response. When tense, individuals often unconsciously jiggle their legs or perform other small movements, which can hinder the expression of their true thoughts.

Everyone experiences tension at times. Especially in unfamiliar environments, when handling uncertain matters, or when feeling unpredictable worry and lack of control over external circumstances, a sense of tension arises psychologically.

To steady tense emotions, people usually make small, subtle movements—clenching fists, biting lips, or unconsciously jiggling their legs. With careful observation these are easy to catch.

Xiao Fei’s first blind date began with both parties sitting in awkward silence, each appearing slightly nervous. Under the table, both their legs were jiggling unconsciously.

“Would you like some water?” Xiao Fei stood to pour water for the young woman and accidentally knocked over the cup.

“Sorry, sorry…”

“It’s fine…” The young woman helped clear the table, and the atmosphere suddenly became lively.

As the conversation continued, both shifted to more comfortable postures and their legs stopped jiggling forcefully.

In daily life, careful observation reveals that people experience varying degrees of tension. Speakers at meetings, students in exam halls, and new graduates entering the workplace all share one common action—leg jiggling.

From a neuroanatomical perspective, when we feel tense, the cerebral cortex sends commands via the central nervous system to the limbs, which then unconsciously jiggle the legs to relieve neural tension. Similar actions include clenching fists, biting lips, and smoking.

Therefore, if someone’s face appears completely calm during a conversation yet their legs keep jiggling, their level of nervous tension must be high. We should then pay attention to what is causing such tension.

If the other person’s legs keep jiggling and tension is evident, we must take note. They may have been asked a sensitive question they do not wish to answer, they may lack confidence in what they are saying, or they may simply be lying.

In the first case, reflect on whether the question touched on personal privacy. Adjust the topic promptly, avoid pressing further, and casually change the subject.

If your statements are guiding the conversation and are factual, yet the other person begins jiggling their legs, this may indicate guilt. Boldly consider where their tension originates. They may be about to lie; in that case, ask several follow-up questions to truly understand their inner world.

For example, Xiao Zhang and Xiao Li are chatting. Xiao Zhang: “This month’s bonus is really generous. I got a full 2,000 yuan. How about you?” Xiao Li: “Ah? Really? I… I got the same as you.” At the same time, his legs begin to jiggle unnaturally. In fact, Xiao Li received 3,000 yuan, and he knows that most colleagues received 3,000 yuan as well.

He was afraid of discouraging Xiao Zhang and dared not tell the truth. The white lie also made him tense, causing the leg jiggle. Xiao Zhang noticed the movement but, to avoid embarrassment, skillfully changed the topic. Xiao Li relaxed considerably and his legs stopped jiggling.

In short, when interacting with others, gaining a better understanding requires more careful and detailed observation. Through a person’s small movements we can glimpse their vast inner world; through their inner thoughts we can truly understand their character, thereby securing greater advantages for our own lives.

#### Crossed Legs Symbolize Confidence and Comfort

Micro-expression keywords: When strangers converse, they often feel constrained and guarded, so most conversational postures involve sitting upright and proper. Among friends, people relax much more and adopt comfortable postures during conversation, such as crossing their legs. Therefore, when you see the other person adopt this posture, it indicates they already regard you as a friend.

In the high-end conference room of multinational company H, Xiao Li, Commercial Director Wang, and President Liu of H Company were discussing domestic agency rights for H Company’s products. The meeting proceeded smoothly and both sides were relatively relaxed. President Liu even stood up, brewed a cup of tea, leaned against the conference table, placed his left leg in front of his right, and sipped his tea. After further detailed negotiations, both parties happily signed the cooperation contract.

Afterward, Director Wang said confidently, “Actually, halfway through the meeting I could already predict that the contract was in the bag.”

Xiao Li was surprised: “Why? Could Director Wang really calculate everything in advance?”

Director Wang laughed and replied, “Small cues happen around you at every moment. You must have noticed how candid and natural President Liu of H Company appeared, without excessive formality or restraint, indicating he was quite satisfied with our communication.”

Xiao Li: “You mean he still had the mood to brew tea midway through the meeting?”

Director Wang: “That’s not the main point. Notice how he crossed his legs with an air of complete ease, as if victory were already assured—that already tells the story.”

Xiao Li: “Crossed legs can also indicate something?”

Millions of years ago, before humans developed language, legs and feet became the most effective tools for rapid and efficient communication because mutual understanding was impossible. In dangerous situations they enabled escape from wild beasts, disasters, and so on. During that period, crossing the legs could only be done when relaxed and at ease, because the posture made the body unstable and hindered quick reactions. Therefore, the appearance of this posture proves that both parties feel comfortable with each other and consider each other trustworthy.

Generally, in situations that feel constraining, people initially adopt a formal sitting posture—sitting upright and proper—because an invisible psychological constraint governs their behavior, making their performance appear more official. At the start of business exchanges, both parties exchange slight nods out of politeness; this is a defensive posture. Psychologically, the person’s mind is not calm and lacks confidence.

After a series of verbal and physical exchanges that foster greater understanding of the conversation partner, people gradually integrate into the group and their bodies shift from formal postures to the casual crossed-leg posture. They can now raise topics that were previously awkward to discuss openly. This intimate attitude shows they have gradually become good friends. Interestingly, people standing with crossed legs often appear relaxed, and the conversation seems quite casual.

Thus, the entire process of postural change during conversation actually reflects the psychological changes driving bodily expression. As a person’s mood moves from tension to relaxation, the body shifts from formal to casual posture.

Research shows that people lacking confidence frequently use formal sitting postures, while those who feel confident, comfortable, and in control often adopt crossed-leg postures. Therefore, to obtain more useful information during communication, you must make your counterpart feel comfortable and at ease, without psychological burden.

#### 7.2.4 Leg Jiggling

Many people believe that leg jiggling indicates the person is relaxed.

Indeed, many individuals unconsciously jiggle their legs when relaxed in order to enjoy inner ease and comfort.

However, when using micro-reaction (微反应) analysis, one must be cautious and identify the stimulus source, baseline, and response pattern before beginning analysis. Therefore, the meaning of leg jiggling is not so simple; one cannot conclude relaxation merely upon seeing the movement.

People newly interested in behavioral analysis often ask: “What does leg jiggling represent? Tension or relaxation?”

Before answering, set aside the pursuit of “what it represents.” Quiet down, adopt a neutral stance, and experience the jiggling action itself and its physiological effect.

Jiggling while standing is usually due to a physiological condition and will not be discussed here. While seated, whether the movement involves raising the toes and jiggling up and down or gently swinging the knees inward and outward, both count as leg jiggling. Quietly and calmly experience the action; you will find it produces a very obvious physiological pleasure—do not misinterpret this; it refers to relaxing the muscles of the buttocks and thighs, improving blood circulation, and sending a positive comfort signal to the brain via the nervous system.

In short, the leg-jiggling action is comfortable.

At this point, do not rush to conclude “leg jiggling means relaxation.”

When people jiggle their legs while singing in a KTV or drinking in a restaurant, they are simply enjoying themselves.

But what about high-pressure situations such as job interviews, business negotiations, or important meetings? Is there time to enjoy one’s own relaxation movement?

Remember this point:

People do everything to seek benefit and avoid harm. The leg jiggling you see in restaurants and KTVs represents “very relaxed, very comfortable”; the leg jiggling you see during negotiations and meetings precisely indicates that the other person is under pressure.

At this point, do not rush to conclude that “leg jiggling in formal, serious, or pressured situations always means the person is tense!”

Consider carefully whether the following two scenarios both indicate tension.

Scenario 1: A young troublemaker with a poor record is taken to the police station after a fight. During questioning he initially shakes his head, sways, and jiggles his legs with a distracted air. Later, realizing he is about to be detained, he freezes and stops jiggling. Does the transition from jiggling to stillness represent a shift from tension to lack of tension?

Scenario 2: A senior official, normally very reserved and proper, wastes no movement or glance. Under investigation for corruption, he initially maintains a dignified demeanor. When asked a key question, one leg begins to jiggle slightly—almost imperceptibly—while he continues to offer fluent explanations. Does the shift from complete control to the appearance of slight jiggling indicate an increase in tension?

To determine what leg jiggling means, first ask yourself several questions.

1. Who is jiggling? Do they usually jiggle? This is called the baseline.
2. When did the jiggling occur? If the person jiggles all the time, it may be a habit or performance and has no diagnostic value. If they do not usually jiggle but suddenly begin at a critical question, that jiggling has value.

#### Toes Reveal Your True Thoughts

Compared with hand movements, leg and foot movements are clearly fewer, so their expressions are much simpler than those of the hands. Moreover, when a person is emotionally agitated, foot movements become even more limited, which is why the emotional information conveyed by the feet is often overlooked.

Yet precisely because people always forget to pay attention to their own feet, the information they provide is instead more valuable and better reflects a person’s true inner state. As former FBI counterintelligence expert Joe Navarro, with twenty-five years of experience, put it: “Facial expressions can be faked, but few people know how to disguise the movements of their feet.”

For example, three men stand chatting with a beautiful woman nearby. On the surface, the three men appear absorbed in conversation and pay no attention to the woman beside them, but that is not actually the case, because each of them has one foot pointed toward her. In other words, all three men are noticing the beautiful woman; their apparent concentration is merely a mask concealing their true feelings.

You may have encountered a situation like this. While speaking with someone, the other person suddenly turns their body and points their feet toward the door instead of directly at you. This posture means they want to end the conversation, gathering, or other ongoing activity as soon as possible. Upon receiving this signal, you should sincerely say to the other person: “It’s getting late, and it’s been a pleasure talking with you—the time has flown by!”

In addition, the direction of the toes serves as a reliable gauge for estimating the closeness of relationships between people. For instance, if two people standing and talking have their toes pointed directly at each other with very little distance between them, it indicates an extremely close relationship. If their feet form a 90-degree or 60-degree angle, they are not particularly familiar and would allow a third party to join the conversation.

The physical distance between seats can indicate the degree to which one party subjectively intends to intrude upon the other’s personal space. For example, a couple deeply in love will sit as close as possible to each other even when plenty of space is available, reflecting their inseparable affection. Similarly, in a university classroom, students who wish to participate actively in discussion choose seats near the front, while those uninterested in the subject sit toward the back.

Seating arrangements are also quite revealing. People favored by or seeking to please a leader usually sit beside or near the leader to demonstrate loyalty and attentiveness. Those disliked by the leader or harboring resentment typically sit far away or in a corner. This shows that the psychological distance between them matches the physical distance between their seats.

Thus, by observing the direction of the toes and the physical distance between seats, we can infer people’s psychological states and related information, giving us a basis for any action we may take.

#### 4.5.2 The Freezing Response of the Feet

The most common freezing response of the feet in a standing posture is standing with legs together and straight, muscles tense. When escape is known to be impossible (if escape were possible, the ready-to-flee starting posture discussed in Chapter 5 would appear), such as during training or reprimand, the nervous system, after receiving negative stimulation, does not dare issue an order for the legs to stand in a wide, casual stance or a completely relaxed posture. Instead, it commands the legs to stand straight and tense, motionless, enduring the subsequent stimulation.

The most common freezing response of the legs and feet in a seated posture is constraining both legs into a state where they cannot move freely. The most frequent versions are keeping both feet together with knees and ankles simultaneously closed, or tucking the feet behind the chair legs, as shown in Figures 4-8 and 4-9.

If you deliberately perform these two actions while relaxed, you will find them rather strenuous. After some time they also cause fatigue and soreness in the legs. Yet when a person is afraid, they involuntarily adopt similar movements to restrain the feet, displaying a localized freezing response. As with the hands, contracted limbs mirror a contracted mindset; by controlling the feet through external force or one’s own effort, unnecessary movements are reduced, thereby lowering the likelihood of attack (criticism). This completely passive, receptive mindset expresses the actor’s inner sense of weakness.

We conducted a simple survey of more than 6,000 samples. When suddenly asked about their seated posture, none of the thousands of classroom participants kept both knees and ankles simultaneously closed. The “surprise attack” success rate was 100 percent. The reason for the “surprise” was to avoid triggering the listeners’ attention and defensive awareness. The underlying cause is simple: the audience’s mindset is relaxed and unthreatened.

A job interview is the best moment to observe the freezing response. Candidates generally fall into two categories: the majority who lack confidence, and the minority who feel confident. To feel confident, meeting the stated requirements is only the minimum; one must also have a grasp of the overall situation—such as the nature of the organization, the positioning of the role, and HR habits—and, of course, having connections counts as well.

Candidates who feel admiration and a sense of supplication invariably sit with hands and feet restrained and speak haltingly. Some have memorized their lines yet cannot converse normally. Confident individuals, by contrast, appear relaxed and natural, with no overall or localized tendency toward contraction.

Asking a nervous job seeker to stand with legs apart is tantamount to violating their fragile psyche; they will be extremely reluctant and unwilling to comply, believing it makes them seem overbearing and disrespectful and will harm their own interests.

Beyond sitting and standing postures, walking can also reveal a person’s state through leg and foot responses. A cautious, weak mindset causes the person to take small, infrequent steps and to move hesitantly.

#### Confidence or Not, Look at His Stance

We often describe a woman’s beauty as “gracefully upright” and praise a man’s heroic bearing as “tall and straight.” Standing like a pine tree reflects an upright spirit; standing crooked shows a lack of strength. A person of integrity can stand with sleeves carrying a pure breeze; a person with ill intentions will set traps even while standing.

Although elders constantly remind us to “sit properly and stand properly,” most people’s standing postures vary widely. Next, FBI agents will reveal the psychological secrets behind standing postures.

Standing with hands clasped behind the back, one hand gripping the back of the other, body erect, creates an aura of authority whether viewed from the front or the back. Such individuals are usually highly confident, like to control situations, or regard themselves as superior.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图2.45　权威的站姿]*

An official inspecting grassroots work walks through a production workshop where workers are focused on their tasks. Head held high, chest out, hands behind the back, spine straight, accompanied by local leaders, the official slowly paces from one end of the workshop to the other.

Besides this official, we encounter many others adopting this posture in daily life—senior officers reviewing troops, principals inspecting teaching, and so on. Generally, people in high positions habitually assume this posture when facing subordinates. The posture is unequivocally a symbol of power and dignity.

Can people stand confidently or stand uneasily? Of course they can.

Standing confidently is usually shown by both feet stably supporting the entire body, legs straight yet with relaxed leg muscles, knees not unnaturally locked as during roll call. The feet are not completely parallel; the toes point slightly outward.

In this state, people usually do not move about frequently or shift their body restlessly from side to side. Those with a confident stance tend to act decisively and with resolve. Moreover, they engage in frequent eye contact and maintain longer mutual gazes.

People lacking confidence stand in a bent, stooped posture, head lowered, shoulders hunched, gaze directed downward. Such individuals act timidly and avoid taking risks or responsibility.

An uneasy standing posture typically involves shifting body weight onto one supporting foot while extending the other foot, toes possibly pointing slightly inward. In this case, people usually do not stand still but keep walking around, trying to find a better spot.

#### Legs That Can Never Hide Tension

Which part of the body should we observe first for nonverbal signals? Which part best reveals a person’s true intentions? FBI veteran Joe Navarro tells us: “The legs and feet.”

FBI agent Jason was interrogating an informant connected to a terrorist incident. After several hours with no progress, the suspect had maintained an impeccable facade, offering Jason no meaningful signals. The only anomaly was the constant shaking of his legs. Yet this could have been a habitual movement and did not prove the suspect knew anything.

When Jason asked the key question—“Were you at the scene of this terrorist attack?”—the suspect’s legs underwent a striking change. Although he had not yet answered, his legs shifted from side-to-side rocking to up-and-down kicking. This single clue told Jason that the question had affected the suspect’s emotions. Jason used it as an opening, continuing with more intense verbal probing until the suspect finally spoke, confirming he had knowledge of the attack.

Drawing on years of intelligence experience, Joe Navarro tells us: “When a person’s foot movements change from gentle side-to-side rocking to up-and-down kicking, it indicates that the individual has seen or heard something negative or unpleasant. This change in body language is entirely unconscious on the part of the individual, yet many remain unaware of it.”

Why, then, can the legs or feet reflect our emotional and psychological changes so precisely?

Over millions of years of human evolution, our legs and feet have continuously responded to external threats through instinctive reactions that require no thought. When we sense danger, our legs and feet naturally enter a state of readiness and respond accordingly—stopping, fleeing, or kicking at an opponent.

We have long practiced “reading faces and expressions” to understand others, yet the cunning face has gradually learned to bluff or conceal true emotions. On reflection, such deception is understandable. From childhood we are taught that “such an expression is unattractive” or “why frown at such a young age?” Consequently we learn to hide, deceive, and lie.

Thus, in an era when “reading faces and expressions” has become difficult, we can readily master the rhythm of any conversation by observing the most honest part of body language—the legs and feet.

#### The Touch Effect

Do not underestimate the power of the “touch effect.” People have a tendency to relax their vigilance toward others because of physical contact, a phenomenon psychologists call the “touch effect.” Various studies have examined the psychological impact of physical contact with others.

Dr. Damien Els of the University of Brittany in France surveyed 40 male customers at a used-car dealership about the touch effect.

The salespeople greeting these male customers were also male. The doctor instructed the salespeople to accompany the phrase “Please be sure to look inside the car” with a one-second grasp of the wrist for half the customers, while making no physical contact with the other half.

Afterward, another staff member asked the customers to rate their satisfaction with the salesperson’s service.

The result was that customers who had been touched gave significantly higher ratings than those who had not. The specific scores were as follows:

| Item          | No Touch | With Touch |
|---------------|----------|------------|
| Friendly      | 5.20     | 6.65       |
| Honest        | 4.68     | 6.45       |
| Integrity     | 4.50     | 6.05       |
| Nice person   | 4.95     | 6.65       |
| Enthusiastic  | 5.25     | 6.65       |

(Out of 10)

When the touch is without motive and casual, no one questions it. Yet when touched, people often develop a favorable impression of the other person—an effect they themselves may not consciously notice. In other words, the touch reaches the heart. Many businesses’ “free trial” marketing strategies actually leverage the touch effect to gain customer approval.

The touch effect possesses the magic of opening people’s hearts. For example, when you want someone to buy something for you, offer advice, or work overtime, an appropriate physical contact combined with a sincere tone can make your request hard to refuse.

Psychologists have also found that intentional touch effectively reduces barriers and eases relationships. When couples or partners are in a “cold war” after an argument, a light pat on the shoulder, head, or forehead—or a big hug—works better than purely verbal reconciliation.

#### Walking

By observing a person’s leg and foot movements, we can obtain a great deal of information. In fact, the information conveyed by the legs is more reliable than that from any other part of the body, because when people try to conceal their emotions they usually do not consider their legs and feet.

In the next chapter we will learn how sitting and standing postures clearly convey a person’s thoughts and emotions. The remainder of this chapter focuses on the most important leg activity—walking.

Each person’s walking style is as unique as a fingerprint. Because everyone has a distinct gait, our friends can recognize us from a distance. However, a person’s walking style can change with mood and age.

Generally, people who walk quickly with arms swinging freely usually have firm goals and are prepared to pursue them actively. People who habitually walk with hands in their pockets—even in warm weather—are usually very picky, somewhat mysterious, and skilled at hiding their true emotions.

When depressed, a person often walks with head lowered, dragging their feet, hands in pockets, rarely looking up to see where they are going (see Figure 3.17). A person walking quickly with hands placed on the hips usually wants to reach their destination in the shortest possible time (see Figure 3.18).

- Figure 3.17　Depressed pedestrian
- Figure 3.18　Pedestrian heading for destination

Some people walk very slowly because they are making an important decision. They clasp their hands tightly behind their back and occasionally stop to think (see Figure 3.19). A self-satisfied or even arrogant person is likely to hold their head high, swing their arms exaggeratedly, and stride forward as if deliberately trying to make an impression (see Figure 3.20).

- Figure 3.19　Deeply focused pedestrian
- Figure 3.20　Striding pedestrian

“Setting the pace” means subordinates match the leader’s stride and follow behind. Following is a nonverbal signal representing the subordinate’s unwavering loyalty to the goals and principles set by the leader.

#### 2. Distance Between Feet in Standing Posture

In a standing posture, the feet are also used to establish one’s territory. The clues revealed by the state and changes of the feet are closer to human primal instincts and thus more accurate. The more limited the area in a confined space, the more obvious this pattern becomes.

In an elevator, observing the different standing postures of passengers can roughly determine the status differences and mindset differences among these people.

Generally, junior employees, due to long-term direction and even criticism, basically stand with their feet together, not daring to occupy too much space in the limited area. Higher-status managers or bosses naturally adopt a comfortable posture to stand, but in crowded situations they may spread their feet apart, instinctively occupying more territory, highlighting their dominance, and ensuring they are not overly disturbed (disturbance can be others’ smells, breathing, or the sticky touch in summer). Of course, it is also possible to appear indifferent, standing on one foot too casually while lifting the other, purely for comfort.

**Spreading Feet to Establish Territory**

Spreading the feet occurs in many situations and almost always reflects a dominant mindset (at least a desire to appear dominant), such as in soldiers or police officers. During confrontations, the dominant and aggressive party often makes this move, frequently combined with arm movements to occupy more territory with the upper body, appearing more imposing.

The spreading of the feet is an expression of power consciousness; it does not inherently carry a defensive meaning but subconsciously indicates that this is my territory. If there is an intrusion, other reactions will be taken to respond to the challenge. Usually, the purpose of spreading the feet is to express a dominant mindset.

In the process of establishing and expanding territory, a person will simultaneously exhibit the head-up and chest-out reaction of looking up, which is an inevitable manifestation of high self-perception. Therefore, an upright torso is also one of the typical characteristics.

#### Either End the Conversation and Leave, or Continue Talking for a While

Whether in a formal business meeting or in informal exchanges with friends, family, or strangers, if someone wants to end the meeting or conversation, you will see a clear action: turning the body toward the door or another exit.

This posture clearly tells you that the person wants to end the discussion and is ready to leave. If the person is seated, you will notice constant fidgeting, as if on pins and needles, indicating a strong desire to depart.

When you observe these postures in others, you can take one of the following two measures according to your own needs:

- If you do not want to end the conversation, it is best to change the topic and ask the other person some personal questions.
- If you also want to end the conversation, you can say, “I think that covers everything; I should get back to work.” You will then see the other person nod quickly and stand up to leave.

Among all body movements people display, the above postures are the easiest to overlook. Noticing these behaviors can prevent you from speaking to an “empty wall.”

Generally, during the final half-hour of a social visit, people’s bodies exhibit “ready to leave” postures. An observant and thoughtful host will notice these postures and end the visit with remarks such as “I’m glad you came over tonight.”

When someone wants to discuss a very important matter with you but hesitates because you are speaking on another topic, they will not turn the body toward an exit but will lean closer to you, as if preparing to whisper in your ear.

If you notice this behavior, you can say something to allow the other person to express their view comfortably. For example, “Is there something you want to say?” If your guess is correct, you will immediately see a relieved expression on the other person’s face, followed by an open sharing of their thoughts.

#### Tension That Is Hard to Conceal

After years of research, behaviorists have found that the human brain has two innate functions: first, directing the body to obtain what is needed for survival; second, commanding the body to quickly leave what is unwanted. The legs (and of course the feet) help the brain carry out these two functions.

Parts of the body closer to the brain are easier for the brain to control and therefore easier to disguise. The face is closest to the brain, so it has the lowest credibility; the legs and feet are farthest from the brain, making immediate disguise difficult. When danger approaches, the legs naturally enter a state of alert and produce involuntary movements. Therefore, observing a person’s legs and feet can sometimes help us understand their inner state.

Experienced operative Jack was interrogating a suspect in a terrorism incident. Other operatives told Jack that the suspect was extremely cunning; after several hours of questioning he had given no meaningful signals, and everyone was at a loss.

Jack sat down and glanced at the suspect. The man appeared neither nervous nor afraid, only constantly shaking his legs. Of course, this alone proved nothing; it could simply be a habitual movement.

“Were you at the scene of this terrorist attack?”

As soon as the question was asked, the suspect showed no reaction on his face, and his hands and body remained completely normal, yet the leg that had been swaying side to side suddenly jerked up and down for an instant before resuming its side-to-side motion. Jack calmly noted this fleeting change and used it as a breakthrough for skillful questioning and probing.

What I will share with you next are methods for judging a person’s inner thoughts from leg and foot postures. Of course, you may already be using some of these methods without having formalized them.

#### Psychology Mini-Lesson

A person’s walking style can reveal their emotions, personality, and character. So how can we read people through different walking styles?

1. **Swaying Type**  
   This style is usually seen in women. Their waists are supple and they walk with a graceful sway, but this should never be mistaken for wantonness. Many of them are honest, warm-hearted, and kind; they are easy to get along with, often the center of attention in social settings, and very popular.

2. **Gentle Type**  
   The so-called “gentle type” walks with feet placed flat, hands swinging naturally, without any affected manner. Such people are generally timid and conservative, yet calm and composed when facing situations and not easily angered.

3. **Pigeon-Toed or Splay-Footed Type**  
   The so-called “eight-character type” refers to feet turned inward or outward in an eight shape. The walk is forceful and impatient, yet the upper body does not sway left or right. These people are not good at socializing and prefer to do things quietly.

4. **Casual Type**  
   The so-called “casual type” walks with no fixed pattern. Sometimes both hands are in the trouser pockets with shoulders hunched; sometimes the hands are extended and the chest is thrust out. Such people are generally generous, loyal, and unconcerned with trifles; they have ambitions to build a career, though at times they can also be unyielding.

5. **Charging Type**  
   The so-called “charging type” walks rapidly without looking back, barging through whether in a crowded place or a quiet one. These people generally enjoy conversation, are open and upright, and will not do anything to betray friends. However, they can be somewhat impatient.

#### Shallow Sitting and Deep Sitting

For humans, the standing posture is the normal state most suited to activity, so when sitting people adopt a posture from which they can stand up immediately. Shallow sitting on a chair is one example.

Many people, out of nervousness, only dare to sit on the edge of the chair; they are often in an urgent state of readiness to act. In psychology this is called high “alertness.” Once they relax, their “alertness” drops; they settle fully into the chair, extend both feet, and appear at ease, indicating they will not stand up right away.

We can see this in lions and horses: lions are fierce and powerful, so they can sleep all day, seemingly representing confidence; because lions like to prey on horses, horses remain nervous all day, even sleeping standing up, yet they still cannot escape being hunted. 

Looking at humans, people who sit deeply hold a psychological advantage or deliberately assume a superior position; at the very least they wish to look down on others. People who sit shallowly often feel uneasy inside, displaying a subordinate state and subconsciously wishing to show respect and obedience.

In front of someone who sits shallowly, never be arrogant or appear too powerful, because they harbor strong inner resistance. If you show friendliness or concern, they will genuinely like you and be willing to approach you, laying the foundation for expanding your network later.

Remember that anyone can be useful. If most people are willing to draw close to you, you gain an invisible advantage; at least in interpersonal relations you have already won. Your work and studies will therefore move more easily toward success.

#### 8.3.3 Crossing the Legs

Another common barrier is crossing the legs, usually seen in seated postures. See Figure 8-19.

In Chapter 5 on escape reactions we discussed the comfortable crossed-leg sitting posture. If the observed person, while seated, leans back with the torso relaxed, this does not belong to the barrier reaction we are discussing now. Note that even when the torso rests against the chair back, it cannot be taken as proof of a relaxed state. Relaxation usually has two clear features: one is that the head also rests against the chair or sofa back and is tilted backward in the same direction as the torso; the other is that the lower leg of the crossed leg may swing comfortably at a natural, unhurried rhythm.

Conversely, a crossed-leg posture that can be judged as establishing a barrier may possess the following features:

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图8-19　作为屏障的二郎腿姿态]*

① The torso is upright and tense; the person may even clasp the knee with the hands, forcing themselves into an uncomfortable seated posture. This action reflects inner fear and worry.

② If the head remains alert and upright and eye attention has not diminished, then the backward lean of the torso belongs to an escape reaction and suggests dissatisfaction or displeasure.

③ The crossed leg shows no voluntary movement.

When the above features appear, crossing the legs is an intentional attempt to increase distance from the stimulus source, trying to build a barrier to protect oneself from negative stimuli.

#### Scenario Two: Senior Official

Usually deeply reserved and well-mannered, no movement or glance is wasted. Suspected of corruption and under investigation. At the start of the conversation the official maintains an upright and dignified demeanor. When asked a key question, one leg begins to tremble slightly, the movement barely visible, yet the mouth continues a fluent defense. Does this shift from total bodily control to a faint tremor indicate increased tension?

**Analysis:**  
A senior official never allows any meaningless movement; this is an efficiency habit cultivated over years in officialdom—too many resources and affairs to waste time on idle matters, too many watching eyes to move casually. This silent state is the baseline. Such a baseline shows that at the beginning of the conversation the psychological state was controlled.

However, when hearing a question that is disadvantageous or even dangerous, one leg breaks through both habitual and willful control and begins to tremble, proving that biological emotional will is stronger than social logical will. On the surface calm is maintained, yet inside there is great torment; therefore the biological emotional will demands active pursuit of physical comfort for self-soothing. This reaction is called a comfort response, using physical comfort to compensate for psychological discomfort. The person himself is unaware of it.

#### Seat Distance Can Reflect Psychological Distance

The physical distance between seats can indicate the degree to which one party subjectively wishes to encroach on the other party’s personal space. In other words, unrelated people who are seated too close will feel unpleasant or uneasy. Therefore, physical seat distance can be used to infer psychological distance.

For example, an affectionate couple will sit as close as possible even when plenty of space is available, reflecting their inseparable state. In a university classroom, students who want to participate actively in discussion choose seats near the front, while those uninterested in the subject choose seats at the back. By the same logic, among staff in a government office, those who actively communicate with leaders and those who hold negative feelings toward superiors will choose different seat distances from the leader.

Seating arrangements are also quite interesting. People favored by the leader or eager to please the leader

**Relationship Between Seat and Leader**

usually sit beside or near the leader to show loyalty and attentiveness; those the leader dislikes or who hold grievances usually sit far from the leader or in a corner. This shows that the psychological distance between the two is as great as the physical distance between their seats.

#### Reading People Through Their Shoes

More than ten years ago I took a friend to buy shoes. The owner of the shoe store happened to know me slightly, so we chatted for a while. Looking at my friend who was choosing shoes, the owner said, “He looks casual, but I know he should be a rather meticulous person, right?”

I was surprised and replied with a smile, “Oh, exactly right. I didn’t expect to meet a colleague here, haha!”

The owner shook his head and said, “No, no, I’m just a shoe seller; I don’t understand those complicated analytical methods.”

“Then how did you judge?”

“Shoes.”

“Shoes?”

“That’s right. From a person’s choice of shoes one can roughly judge their personality. Have you noticed that the several pairs your friend picked are all the same style as the pair he is wearing? People who consistently wear one particular style they like tend to be conscientious; that’s my experience selling shoes over the years.”

That conversation gave me great inspiration, and afterward I began to include shoes in my “people-reading techniques.” So specifically, what connection exists between shoes and a person’s inner state?

#### People Pacing Back and Forth Are Thinking

When a person stands up and paces back and forth in a room, it usually indicates they are pondering what someone has just said. When solving difficult problems or making tough decisions, most people exhibit this behavior because standing allows better thinking.

Therefore, when you see someone pacing and deep in thought, remember to stay quiet, wait patiently for them to speak, and do not interrupt. Doing so would break their train of thought and prevent them from reaching a decision or offering a final quote. This also explains why some negotiators fail to reach their goals: they cannot remain calm.

Experienced salespeople are very good at reading this “person pacing back and forth.” When encountering a potential customer who is pacing, they usually wait patiently, knowing the posture means the customer is ready to make a decision.

#### Psychology Mini-Lesson

During interrogations, police often read a suspect’s psychological state from leg movements. For example, when a suspect frequently shakes both legs, it usually indicates inner anxiety and unease.

In a major criminal case the police could not find a breakthrough and only located one eyewitness at the scene. During questioning the police obtained no valuable information, only noticing that the witness’s legs were shaking frequently. From this movement the police concluded that the witness must be lying. After further interrogation the witness told the truth, identified the perpetrator, and helped the police solve the case smoothly.

The reason the witness kept shaking both legs was inner fear and a desire to end the interrogation quickly. When a person pretends to be calm, facial expressions are hard to read, yet leg movements are easy to detect. Even if the other party tries hard to conceal their emotions, they may inadvertently reveal them through leg movements.

#### Scenario One: Young Thug

Usually unruly, brought to the police station after a fight. At the start of questioning he shook his head, nodded, and shook his legs, looking distracted. Later, upon learning he would be detained, he froze in place and stopped shaking his legs. Does this change from shaking to stillness represent a shift from tension to calm?

**Analysis:**  
The initial combination of head-shaking and leg-shaking stemmed from a lack of proper upbringing and the bad habits acquired in his social circle. Only this way could he appear cool and “in the scene” and maintain good relations with his peers. Therefore the leg-shaking belonged to the baseline, showing that the young thug, without realizing the depth of the situation, believed he had control—a relaxed expression of territorial reaction. Given this baseline, the leg-shaking itself carried no special meaning.

However, the instant he learned he would be detained, all bodily movement ceased and the legs stopped shaking. This reaction is highly meaningful; it is called a freeze response.

The above describes a cartoon. Clearly, the politician sitting in the “4” posture holds the upper hand. When a person casually places one leg over the other, it indicates inner defensiveness or negation.

In negotiations, if the other party maintains this posture for a long time, it signals that you have reached an impasse unless you are willing to concede. #### Self-Restraining Standing Posture

Hands placed behind the back, one hand tightly gripping the wrist of the other hand, which is clenched into a fist, similar to crossed ankles. This posture typically appears when a person is under extreme tension or great pressure.

The wrist-gripping action indicates inner frustration; the person hopes to steady their emotions by holding their own wrist, remaining calm without losing temper. Additionally, when facing frustration, a person instinctively contracts the chest to seek inner security.

This posture also reveals fear toward the situation at hand and extreme lack of confidence. Therefore, never adopt this posture during an interview, as an experienced interviewer will immediately detect your nervousness and insecurity, leaving a poor impression.

#### Seating Direction Reveals Two People’s Mindset

Sitting face-to-face or side-by-side reveals distinctly different personalities.

Sitting face-to-face creates a sense of distance; a table or other barrier between them makes it feel more comfortable. Sitting side-by-side, facing the same direction and observing the same object, easily fosters a sense of connection.

When two people sit face-to-face, both occupy optimal positions for observing the other, readily generating a confrontational feeling. Thus, choosing to sit directly opposite signals a desire for the other person to understand oneself better. This seating style is common during first meetings or business interactions. Choosing to sit side-by-side indicates an intent to gauge the other’s psychology. In hotel lounges, waitresses often sit beside guests for this reason.

#### How Walking Reveals Your Inner State

When someone is far away, although their physical features may be unclear, their walking posture can still convey information. In other words, gait reflects not only health but also character.

For example, people who walk with a steady, grounded step tend to be composed and methodical, remaining calm even in emergencies; those who walk with chin raised, arms swinging, and stiff legs often appear arrogant or self-important; people who walk briskly are usually straightforward, efficiency-oriented, and plan their work and life meticulously, making success more likely.

#### Authoritative Standing Posture

Hands clasped behind the back, one hand gripping the back of the other, body erect. Viewed from front or back, this posture projects authority and confidence.

An official inspecting grassroots work walks through a production workshop, head held high, chest out, hands behind his back, back perfectly straight, strolling slowly from one end to the other accompanied by local leaders.

Besides this official, many others adopt this posture in daily life, such as senior officers reviewing troops or principals inspecting teaching. Generally, those in high positions habitually assume this stance when facing subordinates. It is undeniably a symbol of power and dignity.

#### Confident and Unconfident Standing Postures

A confident stance features both feet stably supporting the body, legs straight yet relaxed, knees not unnaturally locked as in a roll call. Feet are not perfectly parallel; toes point slightly outward.

In this posture, people rarely pace or shift side to side. Those with confident posture tend to act decisively and boldly. They also maintain frequent eye contact, holding gazes longer, whereas those lacking confidence do the opposite.

People lacking confidence or feeling inferior stand hunched, head lowered, shoulders rounded, gaze directed downward. They hesitate to take risks or responsibility.

#### 1. Thigh Angle in Sitting Posture

While seated, pressing the thighs together requires effort; if the mindset weakens into fear, it becomes the freeze response discussed earlier. The most natural state is legs slightly apart at roughly a 30-degree acute angle, thigh muscles completely relaxed. This angle represents the natural resting position of the thigh muscles when seated without support, neither deliberately constrained inward nor exaggeratedly open, indicating a relaxed, natural mindset. An exaggeratedly wide angle between the thighs signals a dominant mindset, first establishing territory through bodily expansion (the span of the angle) and showing willingness to face all stimuli from that territory with chest, abdomen, and genitals.

When a person suddenly turns their toes inward or interlocks both feet, the signal is that they feel insecure, anxious, or threatened. This is the brain’s reaction upon encountering threat.

Legs slightly apart, crossed front to back, one foot bearing body weight while the other maintains balance.

#### 5. Leg Crossing
