#### Crossed Legs and the Figure-Four Position

##### Ankles Crossed, Indicating Someone Is Suppressing Strong Emotions

When you see someone with both ankles crossed over each other, you should note that the person may be restraining themselves. People instinctively press their ankles tightly together when suppressing intense sensations or emotions. Some jokingly describe the posture as looking like “someone who urgently needs the restroom but cannot go.”

In business negotiations or various social settings, a person under tension or fear often sits with ankles tightly crossed and hands gripping the chair arms.

Flight attendants are highly skilled at reading passengers’ body language. They have a unique ability to identify passengers who genuinely need service but are too shy to ask. If a passenger repeatedly crosses and uncrosses their ankles after boarding—especially before takeoff—the attendant can tell the person is very tense or uneasy. When the attendant offers coffee, tea, or milk, if the passenger’s ankles remain crossed and do not move toward the edge of the seat, it indicates they may want something.

Similarly, patients in a dentist’s chair and customers in a barber’s chair preparing for a shave often cross their ankles tightly while gripping the armrests. This tells us both are trying to control unpleasant feelings.

Renowned negotiation experts Gerard Nierenberg and Henry Calero observed that during negotiations, crossed ankles usually mean the person is hesitating to reveal an important concession.

People also unconsciously cross their ankles when facing difficult problems at work or in daily life. Once the issue is resolved and everything proceeds smoothly, they tend to uncross their legs without thinking.

Therefore, when you cannot read someone’s true intentions, it can be useful to observe their feet and interpret their “foot language.”

##### Sitting Upright with Legs Crossed, Indicating Doubt and Resistance

A businessman once noticed his counterpart looking displeased and reluctant to continue the discussion. Still hoping to close the deal, he said tactfully, “I sincerely want to make this transaction. I have laid all my cards on the table.” He expected his apparent sincerity to win agreement, yet the other party grew even more rigid. The counterpart had detected the inconsistency between words and body language and ultimately refused to sign.

The cause lay in the businessman’s legs. While speaking, he sat upright with his legs crossed—a posture that signals doubt and resistance, directly contradicting his claim of sincerity. The other party naturally declined the agreement.

During negotiations, participants rarely cross their legs when preparing to raise a question. Once discussion or heated debate begins, one or both sides typically cross their legs. When an agreement is near, if both parties uncross their legs and lean forward, the chance of reaching consensus rises sharply. Therefore, pay special attention to anyone sitting with legs crossed during talks.

Some people cross their legs the moment they sit down. This shows they are on guard, competitive, ambitious, confident, and ready to act once decided. This applies mainly to men; women differ slightly.

A woman who boldly crosses her legs in this manner demonstrates confidence in her appearance or clothing and a strong desire to be noticed. Such women tend to have high self-esteem, enjoy displaying charm, and are relatively casual with the opposite sex. They often aspire to leadership roles, yet winning their affection or commitment is not easy.

##### Satisfaction and Celebration

When someone feels highly satisfied, they typically lean back, clasp their hands behind their head, and cross their legs in the figure-four position (see Figure 4.30). The posture conveys the impression that they are in control.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.30　“4”字形的坐姿]*

Conversely, a person who feels deeply discouraged tends to hunch forward, letting their arms hang limply over their knees in a listless manner (see Figure 4.31).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.31　沮丧的坐姿]*

When feeling satisfied, comfortable, and confident, a person may emit a “cluck” sound. The tongue presses against the roof of the mouth and then relaxes quickly, allowing the tongue to drop. You may have heard the expression “She clucked like a proud hen,” indicating strong self-satisfaction.

People who make this sound often accompany it by snapping their fingers or clapping their hands as if striking a bottle cap with a bottle.

A common celebratory gesture for satisfaction and celebration (such as concluding an agreement) is raising a fist in the air and then pulling it back sharply a few inches, as if yanking the whistle cord on an old steam locomotive. This is sometimes viewed as a fist-pump.

Another familiar celebratory gesture is the thumbs-up: both hands formed into fists with only the thumbs extended upward.

##### The Figure-Four Sitting Posture and the Discouraged Sitting Posture

A cartoon shows two well-known politicians seated face-to-face discussing current affairs. One leans back with hands clasped behind his head and legs crossed in the figure-four position—one foot resting flat on the opposite thigh, ankle on the knee—looking thoroughly pleased with himself. The other slumps forward, shoulders hunched, arms dangling over his legs, appearing thoroughly dejected.

At a seminar organized by Gerard Nierenberg and Henry Calero, the instructors showed participants this cartoon and asked who was speaking and what was being said. Most participants said the man leaning back was speaking and appeared confident in his words; some even described him as arrogant and fond of showing off. The other politician was characterized as sullen, discouraged, and suspicious.

The figure-four posture is a typical American sitting style; many American women adopt it when wearing trousers. Female lawyers attending Nierenberg seminars have acknowledged that they unconsciously assume this posture while listening to a client’s complaints, noting that it helps them focus more intently on analyzing the client’s words.

##### One Leg Draped over the Arm of the Chair, Expressing Hostility or Disregard

Sitting with one leg casually thrown over the arm of the chair while the other foot remains on the floor may at first appear open and relaxed. Closer observation reveals that the person is usually signaling hostility or disregard.

Flight attendants note that passengers who rest a leg on the armrest tend to be demanding and difficult to please. Salespeople likewise find buyers seated in this posture hard to satisfy. The behavior silently asserts dominance and superior status in the interaction or transaction.

##### Legs Straddling the Chair, a Posture Indicating Authority and Dominant Advantage

Sitting astride a chair with legs spread and the chair back used as a barrier is a posture of authority and dominance. It conveys a meaning similar to placing one’s feet on a desk. Salespeople visiting prospective clients never adopt this posture unless they have no intention of closing the deal.

Therefore, in negotiations, sales, or social interactions, remain especially alert to anyone sitting backward on a chair. Such individuals often lack cooperative intent, show little regard for others’ needs, and may even harbor hostility.

##### The Lincoln Sitting Posture, an Open and Relaxed Position Conveying Candor

Placing feet on a desk or straddling a chair are nonverbal ways of displaying arrogance and authority. In contrast, the Lincoln sitting posture—sitting squarely with legs apart, arms resting on the chair arms, and jacket open—conveys equality through nonverbal means.

The Lincoln posture is candid and comfortable. When two people adopt this open stance, communication flows more easily, neither resists the other, and neither projects a sense of superiority.

##### Legs Crossed with One Foot Swinging Lightly, Indicating Boredom or Impatience

At times we become restless or lose interest in our surroundings. How can we tell when someone else is also bored?

A signature movement is crossing the legs and swinging one raised foot back and forth. People often perform this action while waiting—for example, before a plane departs or a meeting ends.

#### Direction and Orientation of the Feet

##### Where the Toes Point, the Heart Follows

In the human body, the farther a part is from the brain, the more trustworthy it tends to be. The face is closest to the brain yet least honest, which is why people often use smiles or frowns to conceal their true thoughts. The hands sit in the middle-lower region of the body and are only moderately reliable; people occasionally use them to lie as well. The feet, however, occupy the lowest position, farthest from brain control, and are therefore far more honest than the face or hands. They produce a distinctive form of psychological leakage known as foot language.

Compared with hand movements, leg and foot movements are noticeably fewer, so their expressions are simpler. When a person becomes emotionally agitated, foot movements actually become even more limited. As a result, the emotional information conveyed by the feet is often overlooked. Yet because people routinely forget to monitor their own feet, the signals they provide are especially valuable and more likely to reveal a person’s genuine inner state. As body-language expert Joe Navarro observed, “Facial expressions can be faked, but few people know how to disguise the movements of their feet.”

##### The Direction the Feet Face Usually Indicates What a Person Truly Cares About

For example, three men stand together chatting while a beautiful woman stands nearby. On the surface, the three men appear absorbed in conversation and pay no attention to her. In reality, each of them has one foot angled toward her. In other words, all three men are noticing the woman; their apparent focus on the conversation is merely a mask hiding their true interest.

Numerous studies of courtroom behavior have reached the same conclusion: when a judge dislikes a witness, the judge’s feet will point toward the courtroom door through which the judge entered earlier. Likewise, when you are speaking with someone whose feet are angled away from you rather than directly toward you, that person is signaling a desire to end the conversation as soon as possible.

##### Feet That Turn Away

When a suspect feels relaxed about the topic under discussion, both feet usually point toward the agent. If the feet point elsewhere, something in the exchange is likely making the suspect uneasy. For instance, when a suspect dislikes the agent conducting the interview, the suspect will turn one or both feet toward the nearest exit. Although the upper body may still appear to be listening attentively, the feet have already chosen to leave.

### Voice and Speaking

#### “May I Interrupt?”

A person who wants to become a good listener faces the greatest difficulty in overcoming the urge to interrupt others. Normally, during conversation, we can hear 650–700 words per minute, while even the fastest speaker can utter only 150–160 words per minute. This leaves us with 75 percent of our listening time to evaluate, accept, or reject the other person’s viewpoint.

We all remember from elementary school that raising a hand above the head was required before speaking. This habit is so ingrained that as adults, even without needing to raise our hands, we sometimes lift them partway (though not above the head) to signal that we have something to say or a question to ask.

Although raising a hand clearly signals an intention to speak, most adults prefer not to use it. They often start the motion and then withdraw it, substituting subtler gestures such as touching an earlobe or the lips before returning the hand to its original position.

When the hand rises only to ear-lobe height, it gently tugs the ear and returns (see Figure 4.34). When it reaches the mouth, the index finger lightly covers the lips as if trying to hold back words. If the finger remains on the lips for an extended period, the listener taps them lightly while continuing to attend.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.34　用手扯耳朵]*

Some people occasionally manage to suppress interruption gestures altogether. They raise a hand without touching the head, lift it a few inches, and return it to the lap or table. This motion may be repeated silently several times. Unfortunately, such subtle interruption signals are often overlooked.

When a speaker becomes animated, listeners may also wish to speak, requiring a role switch. On some occasions, however, the speaker does not want to yield and ignores the listener’s cues.

Skilled communicators do the opposite: they watch listeners’ body movements and facial expressions and pause when they detect a desire to speak.

A hand placed on the speaker’s arm or shoulder indicates a firmer intention to interrupt. To soften the gesture, the listener may add, “I’m sorry to interrupt, but…” or “I largely agree, but….”

Noticing these interruption signals and treating them as a listener’s wish to participate does not harm the speaker. The listener may simply want to express appreciation or to flag potential objections ahead.

Responding positively to such cues leads others to regard you as an excellent conversationalist, because you allow them to join the exchange. The Greek philosopher Zeno observed, “We have two ears but only one mouth, which shows we should listen more and speak less.”

When standing or walking, the most common self-control posture is hands clasped behind the back, one hand gripping the wrist or forearm of the other hand, which is clenched (see Figure 4.35). The posture clearly signals that the person is working to control emotion.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.35　站立时自我控制的姿势]*

When seated, the common self-control posture is ankles tightly crossed and hands gripping the chair arms (see Figures 4.36 and 4.37, noting the difference between men and women).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.36　坐着时自我控制的男人]*

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.37　坐着时自我控制的女人]*

Flight attendants are adept at reading passengers’ body language. They can identify travelers who need service yet hesitate to ask. If a passenger repeatedly crosses and uncrosses the ankles (especially before takeoff), attendants recognize acute nervousness. When coffee, tea, or milk is offered and the ankles remain tightly crossed rather than moving toward the seat edge, the passenger likely wants something.

Similarly, dental patients and customers in barber chairs awaiting a shave often cross their ankles tightly and grip the armrests, indicating they are suppressing discomfort.

People also cross their ankles unconsciously when facing difficult problems at work or in daily life. Once the issue is resolved, they tend to uncross their legs.

#### Section 3: Being Right Does Not Require Raising One’s Voice

A common saying advises, “Forgive others when possible.” Yielding even when in the right is a social virtue, because being right does not require raising one’s voice. Chinese tradition values harmony and tolerance, yet two regrettable patterns appear in daily life: the unreasonable party twists facts and wrongs the reasonable party, or the reasonable party presses so aggressively that the other is driven into a corner.

Why do these patterns occur?

Consider the first case. The unreasonable party has no valid argument yet overwhelms the reasonable party through glib speech for three reasons: first, to mask inner weakness—knowing they lack justification, they rely on forceful rhetoric to save face; second, to exploit the tendency to “avoid the strong and yield to the weak,” hoping an aggressive stance will prevail; third, because they genuinely fail to recognize their error and therefore keep arguing rather than concede.

When facing any of these three types, remain calm. Allowing oneself to be provoked only escalates the conflict and strengthens the other side. If patience is exhausted, respond without trading verbal blows. Silence, cool observation, and an occasional smile can suffice. A reasonable person will stop rather than continue a monologue; persistent ranting will only earn disapproval from bystanders. This “silent victory” may prove more effective than argument. Yet when someone is truly overbearing, endless tolerance invites further mistreatment. In such cases, stand firm, present evidence, and assert one’s position without descending to the same level of shouting. A wise person uses logic and irrefutable facts to deflate the opponent’s momentum.

Now consider the second case. The reasonable party refuses to yield and corners the other simply because they believe, “I am right, so why should I not claim my rights?” They are willing to fight to the end to protect those rights.

It is best not to become this kind of person. If one is right, why not explain calmly instead of raising one’s voice? News stories frequently show customers who discover a fly in a restaurant meal, confront the owner, and, knowing they hold the advantage, intimidate the owner into kneeling and begging forgiveness. While the owner’s lapse in hygiene is at fault, such escalation is unnecessary. Observers often view the customer as lacking basic decency for driving another person into a corner. The saying “Uphold principles in major matters and style in minor ones” suggests that small frictions can be handled peacefully. Most people respond to reason. When emotion overrides judgment and one scolds or resorts to extremes simply because one is right, the original advantage is lost. Therefore, avoid confrontational argumentation and seek calm resolution.

Both the overbearing unreasonable party and the unyielding reasonable party are, at root, weak. Spending precious time on verbal victory leaves little room for meaningful pursuits. Even if they “win,” the victory is hollow. Combative individuals accumulate enemies, damage relationships, and rarely succeed in their careers.

In short, being right does not require raising one’s voice; when right, one should still yield. If genuinely wronged, choose the appropriate person, occasion, and method to raise the issue. Resolve matters calmly to avoid hurtful words that may produce unintended consequences.

#### Boredom or Lack of Interest

At times we become restless or lose interest in our surroundings. Can we detect the same state in others? A signature movement is crossing the legs and swinging the raised foot back and forth (see Figure 4.38). People often display this gesture while waiting—for a plane to depart or a meeting to end, for example.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.38　厌倦或不耐烦]*

Another sign of boredom or disinterest is rhythmic tapping of fingers or a pencil on a table. The action may be unconscious or deliberate; either way, the repetitive sound eventually irritates.

Some mental-health professionals suggest that when bored, impatient, or anxious, people recreate a reassuring rhythm they experienced as fetuses—the steady beat of the mother’s heart. By producing repetitive sounds, they nonverbally express a need for comfort.

A colleague nicknamed a labor negotiator “the hammer” because he constantly tapped his fingers on any hard surface within reach. Observing the speed of the tapping revealed the negotiator’s state of mind: rapid tapping with all four fingers signaled boredom with the proceedings; slower, middle-finger tapping indicated he was weighing a final offer; complete cessation, accompanied by a glance at the ceiling and a deep breath, meant he was about to state his conclusion.

Years after the negotiator retired, an opponent revealed that he had “read him like a book” by interpreting these gestures.

When listening to a speaker or watching a presentation, a person who props their head on one hand with drooping eyelids is bored (see Figure 4.39). The posture makes no attempt to conceal disinterest; the open hand supports one side of the face in a visibly unhappy expression.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图4.39　表示厌烦的典型动作]*

A vacant stare is another indicator of boredom. The eyes appear fixed on the speaker yet register nothing. Initially one may assume the person is attentive, but soon it becomes clear the mind has wandered, as if asleep with eyes open. The most definitive sign of total disinterest is a blank, unblinking gaze.

Fidgeting or pained shifting also suggests extreme boredom, though other possibilities must be considered:

1. The person is tired and wants to rest.
2. Lunchtime is approaching or a restroom is needed.
3. The person feels physically unwell.
4. The person is preoccupied with other important matters.

Because multiple explanations exist, additional contextual cues should always be examined.

#### Verbal Tics Reveal Personality

Micro-expression keyword: A verbal tic (口头禅) is a habitual phrase that gradually forms and expresses inner feelings and expectations. It carries a distinct imprint of character and offers the most direct window into personality. Understanding someone’s verbal tics allows one to read the person.

Most people in social settings have one or more recurring verbal tics. These habits reflect clear personality traits. Examples include:

- Jay Chou’s tic “diao” conveys “cool,” “great,” “handsome,” or “good,” revealing a desire to appear more masculine and powerful while also expressing insecurity about being a “good boy” and a need for a stronger, more distinctive persona.
- Jolin Tsai’s tic “是哦” (“yes, oh”) shows caution and a slight tendency toward compromise and accommodation.

In everyday life, common verbal tics fall into several categories:

**“To be honest,” “frankly,” “indeed,” “I’m not lying”**  
These phrases are inserted to preempt doubt. The speaker tends to be impatient, harbors a sense of injustice, cares about others’ opinions, and wants to be trusted.

**“Maybe,” “perhaps,” “probably”**  
Such speakers are usually diplomatic, strongly self-protective, and reluctant to reveal their full thoughts. They remain composed in social situations and generally maintain good relationships. Many politicians favor these expressions.

**“I heard,” “it is said”**  
These phrases create room for retreat. The speaker is typically well-informed and smooth but often lacks decisiveness.

**“You should,” “you must,” “it is necessary”**  
These speakers possess strong self-confidence and a controlling streak; they expect unconditional compliance. People in leadership positions frequently use them.

**“Ah,” “ya,” “um,” “well”**  
Two types employ these fillers: those who are slow to respond or have limited vocabulary and use them to gather thoughts, and those who are cautious or calculating—often leaders—who pause to project authority and avoid mistakes.

**“Okay,” “right,” “that makes sense,” “exactly”**  
This signals compliance. The speaker is usually polished, even Machiavellian, appearing to agree in order to gain favor or encourage further disclosure, yet ready to turn hostile if interests are threatened and to weaponize the other person’s words.

**“But,” “however”**  
The speaker seems agreeable yet introduces a counterpoint to defend their own position. They are generally mild-mannered, avoid outright refusal, and speak gently. Public-relations professionals often use this tic.

**“In addition,” “also”**  
These speakers think quickly, display curiosity about many things, and enjoy involvement, yet they tend to lose interest after a short time and rarely see projects through. They are forward-thinking and innovative, frequently producing fresh ideas.

**“Actually,” “the thing is”**  
These individuals are usually stubborn and somewhat arrogant, holding firmly to their views and resisting persuasion. They also possess a strong need for attention.

Recognizing the information contained in verbal tics shows that even small habits can greatly aid in understanding another person’s character.

#### II. Tone

Tone is also an important link in revealing information. Tone refers to the attitude with which one speaks. Tone carries an individual's emotional coloring; by observing tone, one can discern a person's joy or anger. Different speaking tones produce different effects. For example, the sentence "You are really capable," when said in a cheerful tone, expresses great appreciation for the other person, while said in a flat tone, it indicates limited approval of the other person.

Tone can be divided into the following types, each representing people of different personalities:

1. **Tone mild and steady**  
   People with this speaking tone often possess the demeanor of elders, consider problems deeply, and have strong endurance. Once they set a goal, they advance toward it step by step and never give up until it is achieved; however, they proceed slowly and methodically. Interacting with such individuals may feel somewhat difficult at the outset, but the longer one knows them, the more one senses their loyalty and reliability.

2. **Tone solemn and profound**  
   People whose tone is solemn and profound generally have mature thinking and a strong sense of responsibility; they are trustworthy. Such individuals possess high learning and are skilled at grasping the ways of the world and human nature, yet their straightforward temperament often leaves their talents without outlet. In addition, they have strong self-respect, a touch of aloofness, and a love of competition; they never yield easily.

3. **Tone sharp and incisive**  
   People whose tone is sharp and incisive tend to be aggressive in conversation. Their thinking is distinctive, and they possess keen observational ability, allowing them to penetrate to the essence of matters. Such individuals are often candid and frequently point out others' shortcomings or mistakes without mercy; sometimes they embarrass others by failing to consider the occasion. In their careers, they tend to seek quick success, neglect fundamentals, overlook important matters, and thus fall into difficulties.

4. **Tone resolute and strong**  
   People whose tone is resolute and strong act openly and uprightly, distinguish clearly between right and wrong, and adhere to principles. Such individuals display strong organization and discipline, earn the support of the majority, and are suited to leadership roles. Yet they are inflexible, rather stubborn, and never leave room for discussion, so they may offend some people.

5. **Tone blunt**  
   People whose tone is blunt have strong personalities and relatively unstable emotions. Such individuals possess a strong sense of self and may tend toward authoritarianism; they always hope others will act according to their will.

6. **Tone tactful and gentle**  
   Such people are magnanimous and gentle at heart; their speech is mild as water, unhurried, and measured. They are kind-hearted, cheerful, open-minded, warm and sincere toward others, and possess sympathy and tolerance. Their ability to accept new things is not strong, yet they generally adopt an understanding attitude. In social interactions, they handle people and matters smoothly and rarely offend others.

7. **Tone restless**  
   People whose tone is restless are often irritable and quick to anger. They generally act rashly, lack thorough thinking and patience, pursue results without plans, and are easily swayed by emotion; thus they frequently create imbalances that bring unnecessary trouble upon themselves.

#### Those Who Speak Overly Deferentially Must Harbor Caution

Micro-expression Keywords  
Our country is one that values etiquette; moderate politeness is an important tool for maintaining good interpersonal relationships. Excessive deference, however, can also cause dislike.

Xiao Xin was hired by a chain enterprise and assigned to a store as a cashier. On her first day she reported to the store. The manager greeted her warmly. To show respect, Xiao Xin kept bowing to the manager and responded to everything the manager said with "Yes," "All right," or "No problem." The next day at work, her new colleagues pointed and laughed: "That's the one who kept bowing, right? She thinks she's Japanese." The manager, who had been warm the day before, now barely acknowledged her. Feeling insulted, Xiao Xin quit on her second day.

In fact, many people resemble Xiao Xin. When interacting with others, they habitually speak in a humble, deferential manner, always using respectful language and a flattering tone. At first contact the other party may feel embarrassed, yet may not develop dislike. As familiarity grows, however, the other party gradually senses that "this person is actually duplicitous and only outwardly respectful," concludes that the deference is in fact an insult, and becomes deeply annoyed. This explains why the manager's attitude changed.

People who overuse deferential language may have received overly strict upbringing, especially regarding etiquette. Consequently, desires that seem normal to most people are forbidden by their conscience, producing fear and unease; they become guarded toward others. As these desires and guard accumulate, they may one day erupt in powerful aggression. To conceal this, such individuals activate a reactive defense mechanism—growing ever more deferential toward others—creating a vicious cycle.

In other words, people who speak overly deferentially are not necessarily showing respect. On the contrary, they may harbor caution toward you, and their deferential words serve only as a cover. For example, when a woman uses excessive honorifics with a man, she is signaling: "I have no interest in you. You'd best stay away." She simply does not wish to continue the relationship.

Therefore, if an acquaintance suddenly addresses you with honorifics, you should reflect on whether some misunderstanding or barrier has arisen between you.

People who speak overly deferentially generally have poor interpersonal relations. Such deference easily makes others sense your caution and feel displeased. For instance, when a colleague brings you a meal, some people feel they owe a great favor, repeatedly say "Thank you," and promise to return the favor next time. A small matter is turned into a debt of gratitude; even if unintentional, the other person will think, "Does he not want to associate with me?" and feel unhappy, unwilling to continue the relationship.

In reality, with unimportant or very familiar people we have no need to use honorifics. Honorifics signal the closeness or distance of a relationship, status, and power; when used inappropriately or incorrectly, they disrupt the proper relationship. Being more relaxed makes it easier to connect with others.

#### Those Who Are Overly Deferential in Speech May Harbor Caution

Accurately determine a person's emotional fluctuations. For example, someone normally eloquent may suddenly stammer and be unable to complete a sentence; someone normally taciturn and introverted may suddenly speak fluently and eloquently, leaving others astonished. Upon encountering such a situation, one should heighten vigilance to guard against the unexpected, for a problem has certainly arisen.

Moderate politeness is one method of maintaining good interpersonal relationships. Excessive eagerness, however, and overly deferential speech, is actually a form of rudeness. When the other party is excessively deferential toward you, it often indicates that he harbors caution toward you.

A prerequisite for successful interpersonal interaction is the existence of an appropriate psychological distance between the parties. Language can narrow or widen that distance. To ensure smooth and satisfactory interactions, it is necessary to use appropriately deferential language. Such language must be employed at the right time and in the right setting, and applied in balanced measure; otherwise the result will be counterproductive.

Moderate politeness is one method of maintaining good interpersonal relationships. Excessive eagerness, however, and overly deferential speech, is actually a form of rudeness and easily causes dislike. As the French writer Rabelais said: "The outward forms of courtesy can be fully mastered with only a little knowledge; to display inner moral character, however, requires far more temperament." Thus, those who are always deferential in word and deed may be lacking in temperament.

When interacting with others, such people habitually humble themselves, use deferential language throughout, and lavish praise. At the beginning of contact their deferential attitude merely causes embarrassment rather than dislike. As the relationship deepens, however, this extreme deference provokes anger; such people are judged "duplicitous villains" or "hypocrites who only pretend respect."

When the other party uses excessively deferential language in interaction, the speech appears artificial and creates a sense of hypocrisy. In daily life, when we first meet someone we may use deferential expressions such as "you," "please take care of me," "please," "thank you very much," "excuse me," or "you've worked hard." Such deferential speech precisely indicates that the two parties do not yet know each other well, so they remain distant and speak with extreme caution, fearing to offend. Once further interaction makes the parties familiar, they no longer use such deference and instead communicate directly with everyday language. Thus, through dialogue one can accurately gauge the stage the relationship has reached. For example, a man and woman meeting for the first time often use honorifics; the man appears refined, the woman reserved. Once they have spent time together and confirmed a romantic relationship, they dispense with those honorifics and say whatever comes to mind.

#### Psychology Mini-Classroom

If the other party is excessively deferential toward you, it often indicates that he harbors caution toward you. What causes this situation?

1. A new barrier has arisen between you  
   Japanese semanticist Kashima Tadao states: "Honorifics signal the closeness or distance of interpersonal relations, status, and power; when used inappropriately or incorrectly, they disrupt the proper relationship." Therefore, when speaking with very familiar people we have no need to use honorifics. If a friend suddenly uses honorifics with you, you should heighten vigilance. Perhaps you should consider whether a new barrier has arisen between you, or whether you have unwittingly offended him without realizing it, causing him to feel distant and to use honorifics to keep you at arm's length.

2. Hostility toward you  
   During conversation, if the other party frequently uses honorifics unconsciously, it indicates a large psychological distance and a relatively distant relationship. If the other party uses honorifics excessively, it signals strong hostility, jealousy, and caution toward you. For example, when a woman uses many honorifics with a man, it does not express respect but hostility; what she actually means is "I have no feelings for you" or "I have no interest in talking with a man like you."  
   If you have known someone for a long time and understand each other deeply, yet he remains excessively polite, speaks with great caution, and even overuses honorifics, it is generally because he harbors hostility toward you. People who have grown accustomed to speaking deferentially and treating others with excessive deference often harbor strong aggressive impulses toward others.

3. Attempt to control you  
   When the other party deliberately uses humble and polite language in interaction, he may be attempting to breach your psychological defenses and enter your mind through this manner and attitude. In reality, the psychological motive behind such behavior is to control you and achieve the goal of communicating from a position of superiority.

4. Psychological defense  
   Many people are extremely deferential in both speech and behavior; this may stem from a certain lack of temperament. Perhaps they received strict parental upbringing in childhood, especially regarding etiquette. Consequently, behaviors that seem entirely normal to others appear to them as violations of conscience, producing unease, guilt, and fear. They therefore suppress all impulses, desires, and emotions that their conscience does not permit. Yet they are especially afraid that these impulses, desires, and emotions will accumulate until one day they erupt in powerful aggression. Hence they decide to mask them with deferential language and use this method for psychological defense.

#### Changes in Speaking Speed Can Reveal a Person's Psychological Secrets

Generally speaking, people who speak quickly tend to be extroverted, eloquent, and full of youthful vitality, giving others a sunny impression. Because of their speed, however, they can also create a sense of tension and pressure, as though something major or urgent has occurred, and may also seem anxious, disorganized, or somewhat rude.

People who speak slowly appear more taciturn than those who speak quickly, giving an impression of honesty, sincerity, thoughtfulness, or unfathomable depth; yet they may also seem indecisive, careless, deliberately mystifying, or even negative and pessimistic.

For the same individual, the situation must be judged differently. When speaking speed is slower than usual, it indicates dissatisfaction or hostility toward someone; conversely, when a person feels guilty or is lying, speaking speed naturally increases. Encountering such a situation, one must be especially careful; a problem has certainly arisen, and close observation is required.

If a man usually returns home on time after work, but one day colleagues keep him late to play poker in the office, upon arriving home he immediately explains to his wife that he worked overtime and, while speaking, curses the excessive workload. Careful listening will reveal that his speaking speed is faster than usual, because this helps relieve his underlying unease.

When harboring affection, unease, or fear, speaking speed also increases, because people generally use rapid speech to express inner affection or to dispel inner unease and fear.

When a person's speaking speed suddenly slows and he falls into thought, it indicates that he has already revealed a secret.

During the Second World War, Japan secretly decided to appoint Tōjō Hideki as prime minister. Reporters from various newspapers tried hard to discover the secret by interviewing ministers who had attended the meeting, but obtained nothing.

One reporter was particularly clever. He studied the ministers' psychological pattern: none would reveal who would become prime minister, yet if the question were posed cleverly, the other party would unconsciously reveal some clue, making it possible to uncover the secret. The reporter therefore asked a minister who had attended the meeting: "Is the person appointed prime minister bald?"

At the time, three candidates existed: one bald, one with a full head of white hair, and one half-bald. The half-bald candidate was Tōjō Hideki. The question appeared to be casual conversation; the minister did not realize it contained a trap. Upon hearing the question, his expression grew hesitant and he did not answer directly. In that instant the clever reporter deduced the final answer and obtained an exclusive story. Because the other party paused, he was certainly thinking: Does "half-bald" count as "bald"?

#### Distinguishing Emotions Through Voice

A speaker's voice is closely related to his state of mind and emotions; different emotions produce different vocal characteristics. Therefore, with only slight attention to his voice, one can determine his emotions and state of mind.

If you ask someone, "How have you been lately?" the reply may be "Quite well." You usually do not judge his emotions by the words alone but by the pitch and rhythm of his voice when he speaks. For example, if his pitch is low and rhythm slow, it indicates he has not been well lately; conversely, if his pitch is high and rhythm fast, it indicates he has indeed been well.

In daily life, without using our eyes, we can often recognize a person or even guess who he is simply by listening to his voice. The reason is simple: each person's voice is distinctive. Some voices are resonant, some hoarse, some shrill, some heavy, some thin like the sound of metal striking metal, some thick like the sound of a drum.

When facial expressions or body movements fail to reveal the other party's emotions, one can generally begin with the voice and carefully discern emotional changes. It is no exaggeration to say that voice is an important clue for understanding the human heart and seeing through emotional shifts.

The *Yizhoushu* · "Vision and Hearing" chapter also contains discussions on judging a person's inner world through voice: a sincere person is relatively calm, and his voice is clear and rhythmically distinct; a dishonest person, being uneasy, speaks haltingly; a magnanimous and gentle person speaks in a mild, gentle voice, flowing steadily like a gentle stream; a mean and perverse person, harboring ulterior motives, speaks in a strange, grating tone.

When a person encounters joyful events or becomes emotionally excited, volume increases unconsciously. When attempting to persuade others or overpower them with presence, volume also increases unconsciously. The speaker believes that sufficient volume conveys confidence and thereby persuades others. For example, in the workplace, when a leader assigns a task and a subordinate refuses, the leader often says, "No more discussion—do as I say!" At that moment the leader's volume is noticeably louder than usual.

Generally, when a person's mind is clear and open, the voice is bright; when calm, the voice is even; when lacking confidence, the voice is soft; when full of confidence, the voice is resonant; when nervous, the voice trembles. In short, changes in voice precisely reflect changes in emotion.

#### Learning to Hear the “Words Within Words”

Chinese speech tends to be indirect, avoiding blunt statements, so people often rely on implied meanings to convey their intent. If we fail to catch these “words within words,” it becomes difficult to grasp what the other person truly means.

An old Chinese saying reminds us: “Listen to the tone in speech, and the rhythm in drums.” It urges attention to what lies beneath the surface. In daily life many things cannot be stated outright and must be expressed through implication. For example, when you ask someone “How have you been lately?” and they reply “Fine” in a sarcastic tone, taking the word at face value would be a serious mistake.

“I’m really upset and need to talk about it,” “This job is driving me crazy,” “I need to vent to you”—such direct statements are probably heard most often in therapy rooms. In everyday interactions people play emotional hide-and-seek and speak in implications. Therefore, listening cannot stop at the literal words; one must learn to detect the deeper meaning hidden between the lines.

A small newspaper once visited a prestigious university to recruit editors. A journalism student sailed through the early rounds only to fail at the final interview.

The interviewer asked, “Your school is top-ranked and your major matches the job, yet we’re just a small paper. Don’t you think this would be a waste of your talent?” The student missed the implied question: “Are you planning to use us as a stepping-stone to a bigger publication?” He had no such intention, but because he failed to hear the “words within words,” he lost the opportunity.

“Words within words” appear everywhere. When someone says “It was only a joke,” the implication is often “How could you take that seriously?” When someone says “I’m just telling the truth,” the subtext may be “I’m honest; your inability to accept it shows your narrow-mindedness.” When someone says “What more do you want?” the hidden message is frequently “You’re too demanding and I’m getting tired of you.”

People’s spoken words and their real intentions often diverge. To catch the “words within words,” ask yourself: Why did they phrase it that way? Is there something they hesitated to say outright?

#### II. Vocal Tone and Expression

Facial expressions directly reflect inner emotions, and vocal tone and expression serve the same function. Language itself conveys complex feelings; in conversation we also modulate volume, speed, pitch, and melody to make emotions richer, more vivid, and more precise. Vocal tone and expression reveal a person’s cultural level, values, and personality.

By observing differences in vocal tone we can judge emotional state and character. When sad, people usually speak more slowly, in a lower pitch, with limited range—matching the heavy, stiff look on their face. When excited or agitated, the voice rises, becomes sharper, speeds up, and shows wide pitch variation, often with a tremor. Rapid speech with frequent slips is commonly associated with lower status or timidity. A loud but unhurried voice suggests higher status and composure. Stammering or disorganized speech often signals lack of confidence or insincerity. From a gender perspective, a breathy male voice is frequently read as youthful and artistic, while a breathy female voice is perceived as more feminine.

In daily interaction, understanding another person’s mood and intent requires attention not only to content but also to delivery—pitch, variation, rhythm, volume, range, inflection, and speed all betray concealed emotions. This is how one hears the “words within words.”

Verbal exchange reveals inner thoughts and fosters mutual understanding, while vocal tone adds emotional color. From vocal expression we can infer thoughts, feelings, and intentions. Language allows fluent expression of emotion beyond the limits of body language alone; combining vocal and physical cues lets us read people more accurately.

#### I. Volume

Volume refers to loudness and is closely tied to personality. People who speak loudly tend to be extroverted, dominant, and inclined to impose their will; they speak clearly so others will understand. People who speak softly are often introverted, suppress their feelings, and rarely reveal their full thoughts unless pressed. Thus volume offers a rough guide to character.

Volume is not fixed; adjusting it improves listener comfort and depends on setting, audience, and the privacy of the content.

At a noisy street-side food stall, a whisper will be drowned out by traffic, chatter, and cooking sounds. In an upscale Western restaurant, loud conversation draws disapproving glances for poor manners.

Volume should also suit the listener: speak softly to children to create closeness; speak louder to older adults who may have hearing loss. Privacy matters too—jokes or harmless topics can be loud, but personal or sensitive matters should be kept quiet and considered carefully before being shared.

Adjusting volume is a matter of upbringing. As Taiwanese writer Liu Yong observed: “The right volume depends on the environment. If you want charm and elegance, first check whether your volume is appropriate. Observe neighbors and friends, then compare yourself. If you realize you have been too loud in every setting, or that stress and fatigue make you speak faster and louder, correct it at once. Change speed first, then practice speaking softly to those nearby and more loudly to those farther away so your volume varies.”

#### Psychology Mini-Classroom

“Words within words” take several common forms.

1. **Compliment form**  
   A remark that sounds like praise may actually conceal criticism. “You really put a lot of thought into this” can become sarcastic when delivered with a particular rhythm and tone.

2. **Reproach form**  
   Phrases that include qualifiers of quantity often carry reproach: “You’re a bit careless,” “Your conduct falls a little short of normal standards.” The implication is dissatisfaction.

3. **Warning form**  
   Some implications issue warnings. Stressing “meaning” in “My meaning is…” signals that disagreement is acceptable; stressing “my” signals “Listen, but you have no choice but to agree.”

4. **Self-mockery form**  
   A friend you once teased about her weight may, upon meeting again, say first, “Have I gotten even fatter?” This preemptive self-mockery blocks further teasing and conveys, “We haven’t seen each other in a while; you’d probably tease me again, so I’ll do it myself.”

5. **Negation form**  
   This form subtly expresses disapproval. A visitor to a new apartment may say, “For someone so young, having a place like this is already quite good,” with emphasis on “like this” and “already.” The hidden message is that the apartment is mediocre but the owner is still young enough to buy something better.

#### Detecting Insincere Irony

Both saying the opposite of what one means and meaning the opposite of what one says fall under irony. The *Guiguzi* advises: “Those skilled at reverse listening change like spirits and gods to learn the truth… To hear the sound, first be silent; to expand, first contract; to rise, first descend; to take, first give.” In practice this means observing reactions by speaking in opposites.

People long to be understood yet often hide their true wishes and say the reverse: claiming to be satisfied when they are not, or claiming indifference when they actually desire something. During the Spring Festival parents may telephone and say, “If work is busy, don’t come home,” while hoping their children will return. If the children stay away, the parents feel deeply disappointed.

Irony is common among close relations, especially couples. A wife may say “You’re so annoying” when she means affection, or “Get lost!” when she means “Come here.” On an anniversary, a wife may scold her husband for buying flowers—“You’re so impractical!”—yet feel pleased. Failing to recognize the reversed meaning makes one seem insensitive; misreading it leads to unnecessary arguments.

#### Following the Voice into the Heart

A beautiful voice is an important aspect of human aesthetics. Sweet, rounded, or deep and resonant voices leave pleasant impressions. Many public figures have worked to improve their voices to gain favor.

Generally, loud speakers fall into two types: those whose roughness conceals refinement and who are trustworthy, and those who are impulsive and hot-tempered. Both tend to be frank and outgoing. Soft speakers are often introverted, sensitive, suspicious, and lacking courage; they vent through gossip.

Slow speakers are steady, good at concealing emotion, thorough, and persistent once committed. Fast speakers are quick-thinking, responsive, and expressive, though their haste can cause interruptions and trouble.

People who speak sparingly may seem impolite, yet their few words are usually sincere and reliable; they finish tasks quietly and can be trusted.

A normally loud person who suddenly lowers their voice is probably not gossiping—such people criticize openly—but may be reacting to a superior’s arrival. A normally soft speaker who suddenly raises volume may be trying to escape feeling ignored. Someone whose voice remains clear though not loud is usually deliberate and mentally stable, suited for important work.

A normally slow speaker who suddenly accelerates is likely agitated, making agreement difficult. The reverse—sudden slowing—suggests distraction or discomfort.

#### Psychology Mini-Classroom

The voice carries strong emotional coloring; its strength, speed, pitch, and clarity reveal complex feelings. As the *Lingshan Miyè* states: “Observe the breath and tone to gauge bearing; note the timbre to distinguish quality; listen to the force to assess power; examine the emotion to infer intent.” Volume (breath and tone) reveals bearing; duration and force reveal strength.

Joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure surface in the voice even when suppressed. Listening therefore reveals inner states and emotional shifts.

1. **Sharp and severe speakers**  
   They enjoy debate, seize verbal openings, and counterattack relentlessly. Their insight is keen, yet their focus on weaknesses can cause them to miss the bigger picture and descend into pointless argument.

2. **Grave and profound speakers**  
   Their words are measured and insightful; they understand human affairs accurately and act conscientiously. They dislike discord and manipulation. In complex environments they are often overlooked and find it hard to advance.

3. **Resolute and steadfast speakers**  
   They uphold principles, distinguish right from wrong, and earn respect for fairness. They judge others without personal bias, yet their rigidity can appear unfeeling.

#### III. Extremely Slow Speakers

Extremely slow speakers frustrate listeners with their tortoise-like pace. Their temperament is likewise unhurried, sometimes timid or introverted. Their strengths are attentive listening and honesty; their weaknesses are lack of confidence and an impression of dullness or poor social skills.

No universal standard defines ideal speed; norms vary by occasion and profession. CCTV news anchors average about 300 characters per minute, debaters 450–520, poetry reciters 70–90, and ordinary Mandarin speakers roughly 240.

Abnormal speed can hinder communication and employment, yet speed can be trained. Appropriate pacing, pauses, and intonation improve clarity and appeal. Practice by reading articles aloud, following television news subtitles, or recording and reviewing one’s own speech.

Most people speak at medium speed, so excessive worry is unnecessary. Speed offers clues to personality but does not fully reflect inner cultivation. Fast speakers may lack focus; slow speakers may be coherent and substantive. Regardless of natural speed, one must first enrich one’s knowledge; only then will speech be orderly and earn respect.

Speed is not fixed; it shifts with psychological state. Emotionally healthy, expressive people vary their pace according to circumstances, and such shifts are interpretable.

#### Anxiety

You might guess that the most obvious and accurate way to express anxiety is not through body movements. Indeed, the truly reliable and easily recognizable carrier of an anxious state is the voice.

A person clearing their throat before speaking or midway through a sentence indicates unease or anxiety. In fact, when someone must speak in front of a group, a tense feeling arises in the throat, followed by mucus that prevents sound from emerging. Therefore, the throat must be cleared before speaking to restore normal voice.

Sometimes, people unaccustomed to public speaking repeatedly clear their throats during a speech, with accompanying changes in pitch and tone, all signaling anxiety or tension. When children feel anxious, they typically do not clear their throats but instead stammer “uh” or habitually say “you know.”

We suggest that the next time you feel the urge to clear your throat before speaking, consider whether it stems from actual throat discomfort or from an unconscious anxious reaction.

Restlessness is often a sign of tension. During witness questioning, skilled defense attorneys pay close attention to questions that make the witness restless. They will repeatedly probe such questions to elicit clear answers.

A person slowly rubbing their hands on clothing or a handkerchief nonverbally signals anxiety, frustration, anger, tension, or doubt. In such cases, the palms are usually sweaty.

Generally, the above phenomenon occurs when people engage in stressful activities. We see these “sweaty palms” in witnesses testifying in court, first-time public speakers, or athletes at the starting line of a competition.

#### How Topics Reveal Inner Thoughts

I once surveyed 200 managers, more than 80 percent of whom attributed their success primarily to superior communication skills. Choosing the right topic is a prerequisite for smooth communication; in other words, in interpersonal interactions, finding the correct topic means you have already won half the battle.

Yet everyone’s interests differ, making it seem complicated to lock onto a topic. With someone you have just met, begin with neutral subjects such as the weather or work. As the conversation deepens, the other person will gradually disclose more information. Effectively integrating these fragments helps guide the topic in a direction favorable to you.

If the other person voluntarily raises personal topics, it indicates they are in a happy state. On this point, I once conducted a survey with 80 women. I divided them into two groups: one watched a comedy film, the other a tragedy. I then observed what they first discussed with friends or family afterward. The results showed that women whose mood improved after watching the comedy mostly talked about private matters such as money, health, or sex. Thus, when a person is happy, they tend not to put up defenses. If you seize the moment, success is near.

In addition, avoid two types of topics that can lead to failure:

- Subjects you yourself find uninteresting—how can you engage the other person if you lack interest?
- Subjects you only partially understand—if you speak vaguely or incorrectly, you will leave an impression of superficiality.

#### How to Read Others’ Inner Worlds from Their Speech Patterns

When conversational partners hold differing views, each may rebut the other to assert their own position, and people rebut in different ways. How, then, can we understand someone’s psychology from their style of rebuttal?

If the other person does not bother with tact and directly retorts “You’re wrong,” it shows they are self-centered, attach great importance to their own opinions, and will offend others rather than yield.

If the other person speaks tactfully, first expresses agreement, then states their own view with a rebuttal such as “That’s right, but…,” it indicates they are kindhearted and considerate. This approach is steady and sincere, far gentler and more indirect than a blunt “You’re wrong.”

If the other person rebuts with “So…” or “In that case, why…,” the implication is “We’ve already reached this point—why are you still not getting it?” Such rebuttals carry an undertone of blame. Rather than confident, this person is arrogant and headstrong, always believing their own mind works best.

In short, a person’s thoughts often surface unconsciously through their manner of speaking, and their emotions are likewise reflected in it. Therefore, careful observation will allow us to see through others’ inner worlds via their speech patterns.

#### People Who Like to Say “Right”

People who frequently say “right” lack strong self-awareness and generally maintain good interpersonal relationships, yet the phrase is not their genuine sentiment; it is merely a way of accommodating others while privately calculating their own interests.

In addition, those who repeatedly use “indeed” tend to be self-righteous and strongly self-centered; those who often say “actually” have a strong desire for self-expression and are somewhat conceited; those who habitually use “this…” “that…” “um…” are cautious, avoid trouble, and are generally agreeable; those who frequently say “in the end…” usually harbor unfulfilled desires; those who often say “exactly” are mostly shallow and ignorant yet self-important; those who repeatedly say “really” tend to lack confidence; those who frequently use “you should…” “you can’t…” “you must…” are authoritarian, stubborn, and domineering, with a strong desire to lead; those who often say “my personal thought is…” “isn’t it…” “couldn’t we…” are amiable, non-dictatorial, respectful of others, and in turn respected and liked; those who frequently use “I want…” “I think…” “I don’t know…” are mostly simple-minded, act on impulse, and have unstable emotions.

#### Chapter 5 The Mystery of Speaking Styles

Observing others’ speaking style, wording, speed, and accompanying gestures reveals their true inner thoughts. A pleasing speaking style easily earns favorable impressions, whereas poor speaking habits readily create negative ones.

From a physics perspective, the human voice is produced when airflow vibrates the vocal cords, which in turn vibrate the air. Pitch and volume are determined by the tension of the vocal cords and the amount of exhaled air. Voice is also closely linked to psychological activity. Hence different people have different voices and different speaking styles—this is the foundation for identifying character through voice.

Observing others’ speaking style, wording, speed, and accompanying gestures reveals their true inner thoughts. A pleasing speaking style easily earns favorable impressions, whereas poor speaking habits readily create negative ones. As the renowned Taiwanese success expert Lin Daoan said, “A person fails to speak well because they do not know what the other party wants to hear. If you can read the other person’s psychological activity like a scout, you will understand how powerful speech can be.”

As the saying goes, “One remark reveals the whole truth.” Which aspects, then, indicate whether your speech is good or bad? This chapter will uncover the answers one by one.

#### 2. Ways of Answering Questions

Often we are still enthusiastically talking while the other person has already disengaged. If we fail to notice and keep chattering, communication becomes ineffective. How, during a conversation, can we tell whether the other person is still willing to engage?

In a conversation, if you are doing most of the talking, pay attention to whether the other person is absorbed or merely hoping you will finish soon and fearing that any response will encourage further monologue. People usually respond actively only when they find the conversation interesting. The more responses your words elicit, the more it shows the other person enjoys talking with you. If you notice the other person suddenly become silent and stare blankly, it indicates they no longer wish to continue.

Sometimes, even when uninterested, people will ask simple, polite questions out of courtesy—“What time did you go?” “It was fun there, right?”—yet if genuinely interested they tend to ask more complex questions such as “What did you mean by ×× earlier?” “Could you explain exactly what happened?” or “How did you feel at the time?” This shows they are following your train of thought and are engaged with the topic.

#### 5. A Sweet and Sticky Tone

This is a feminine tone that makes the speaker seem like a hothouse flower.

Women with a slightly nasal, sticky tone usually crave public affection. Yet such people are often restless; their excessive desire to please can instead annoy others. Men with this tone are usually only children raised under excessive protection. They feel especially lonely when alone and become bewildered when forced to make independent judgments. They are very reserved toward women; in one-on-one conversations they often appear tense and will never take the initiative.

Humans have two kinds of expressions: one on the face, the other in the manner of speaking. Speed, volume, and tone of speech contain rich secondary information. Removing the surface veil reveals a person’s true inner thoughts. Speech can be said to be the outward manifestation of character and intellect. Therefore, before words leave the mouth, if you wish to avoid leaving a bad impression, carefully consider how to phrase each sentence appropriately and comfortably.

#### Psychology Mini-Class

Everyone has a different temperament, and different speaking styles reflect different temperaments. Below are several speaking styles and the temperaments they reveal.

1. **Gentle-speaking people**  
   Gentle speakers have soft personalities, dislike competition, and rarely offend others, yet they are weak-willed, lack confidence, and are timid. They often adopt an avoidant attitude toward people and situations.

2. **Even-paced speakers**  
   Even-paced speakers have elegant temperaments and treat others generously and kindly, but they react slowly, lack decisiveness, and tend to be conservative in thought.

3. **Righteous and stern speakers**  
   Righteous and stern speakers possess an indomitable spirit, act fairly and impartially, distinguish right from wrong, hold firm positions, and exhibit strong principles. However, they are inflexible and can seem stubborn.

4. **People who pepper speech with trendy words**  
   Such people readily accept new things and feel compelled to use newly learned buzzwords. Yet they lack independent judgment and tend to be weak.

Sarcasm takes two forms: saying the opposite of what is meant, or saying what is meant in an opposite tone.

For example, during a quarrel a husband asks, “How have I treated you all these years?” The wife angrily replies, “Great, really great—how could it be so great?” Here the wife is using sarcasm.

One point to note: judge whether a remark is sarcastic by the speaker’s tone. The same sentence can mean the exact opposite depending on tone. For instance, “How could you be so sensible?” might mean “You’re really not sensible” or “You’re truly so sensible.”

#### Reading the Other Person’s Mind from Intonation

Within speaking style, intonation itself is an important factor. Friendliness or hostility, calmness or agitation, sincerity or falseness, modesty or arrogance, sympathy or mockery—all can be conveyed through intonation.

Generally, a gentle tone indicates frankness and friendliness; a trembling tone indicates agitation; a low tone indicates sympathy; any statement delivered in a sarcastic tone appears mocking and insincere.

When facial expressions, gestures, and words fail to reveal another person’s state of mind, we can still infer their character from the rhythm of their speech.

Confident people speak in an affirmative rhythm; those lacking confidence or with weak personalities speak in an uncertain rhythm; dishonest people hem and haw—an outward sign of a guilty conscience; calm people speak calmly; kind and gentle people speak like a gentle stream—smooth, soft, and highly approachable; restless people talk endlessly; people whose minds are clear and orderly speak clearly and evenly.

#### 3. A Husky Tone

People with this tone expand their influence through personal strength, take the lead in guiding others within organizations, and possess the fighting spirit to bounce back from setbacks; many become politicians, writers, or commentators.

Women with a husky tone usually have strong personalities; even if they appear delicate outwardly, they possess inner resilience. They have refined tastes in clothing and art and often possess musical or painting talent. They are courteous yet do not easily reveal their true feelings, giving an elusive impression. Generally, they have poorer relationships with other women and are prone to disagreements or exclusion, yet they are popular with men. When dealing with such women, avoid forcing your own views, or they will become resistant. Men with a husky tone are usually highly enduring and action-oriented; they charge forward even when others hesitate. Their shortcoming is a tendency toward self-importance, which can appear arrogant, and they may be careless about seemingly minor matters.

#### 9.2.2 Helpless Sigh

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图9-12　捂脸]*

Failure reactions also appear in uncontrolled exhalation—commonly known as sighing. When expressing helplessness, a person uses a long exhalation to lower internal body pressure; it is also the nervous system’s attempt to reduce blood carbon dioxide levels and shift from a suppressed state to an excited one, although people themselves are unaware of this process. It may be accompanied by a restorative gesture of covering the entire face while wiping, as shown in Figure 9-12. Such sighs generally express helpless assessment and feeling; if expressed verbally, they appear as refusal to abandon or accept, such as “I can’t believe it,” “Oh my God!,” “How could this happen?!,” or “No way,” “Impossible.” Beyond surface disbelief and non-acceptance, the essence is helplessness together with regret and self-blame.

#### 1. Topic Preferences

A person’s inner world often reveals itself unconsciously through the topics they discuss. Therefore, to understand someone’s character, thoughts, or emotions, start with the topics they habitually raise.

If their topics center on themselves or family, it indicates strong self-awareness and a tendency to be self-centered. For example, some middle-aged women frequently talk about their children and dislike sudden topic shifts while doing so. In such cases, simply listen and hand the conversational floor to them.

Some young men like to discuss cars, often mentioning brands, specifications, appearance, and prices in front of others; this likely signals their future purchasing ability or shows off their extensive car knowledge. In such situations, listen attentively, occasionally ask questions about cars to satisfy their vanity, and avoid showing annoyance or impatience.

#### Why Do Women Love to Speak Ironically?

Why not just say what you mean? There is a common psychological motive: concealing inner shyness. For instance, when a man asks, “Do you miss me?” a woman replies, “No!” Some women worry, “If I say I miss you, you’ll look down on me,” while others simply feel too embarrassed to say it.

People speak ironically for four reasons:

1. To protect themselves, not wanting others to see through their thoughts and expose their inner world completely.
2. To spare others worry, out of kindness, yet this often becomes the chief culprit that hinders communication and creates unnecessary misunderstandings.
3. To project an image of magnanimity—harboring resentment yet appearing friendly and tolerant on the surface.
4. To satirize others, highlighting absurdity through contrast to achieve a strong ironic effect.

#### 7.2.5 Voice

Voice frequency is moderate and consistent with the individual’s normal baseline—neither excessively high (because high volume requires extra excitatory energy to intensify vocal-cord vibration) nor weak and listless. Speaking rate also matches the person’s habit; it may be slow but is unlikely to be fast, since rapid speech corresponds to rapid thinking and high-speed vocal-system movement, demanding high excitement and consuming considerable energy. Specific frequency varies by individual, so the tested person’s baseline must first be established for accurate comparison.

The states described above reflect a relaxed condition on one’s own territory with no concerns, indicating normality—neither negative emotion nor anything particularly joyful or exciting. For each different tested person, record their behavioral and nervous-system relaxation baselines according to the above framework; this is extremely important for later observing changes and analyzing micro-reactions.

In real life, such people are also common. Chinese people value face and are skilled at using polite remarks in conversation. For example, the greeting “Have you eaten?” is not a genuine invitation to a meal but a conventional polite remark. Many foreigners fail to understand this and create numerous awkward situations.

Therefore, we must learn to discern the other party’s true intentions from polite remarks in order to behave appropriately and graciously.

#### 5. Sudden Slowing of Speech Rate

If a person who normally speaks quickly suddenly slows down, one of the following four situations may be the cause:

- A shortcoming or weakness has been touched upon by the other party; lack of confidence or timidity has caused the speech rate to slow.
- Something is being concealed from the other party, so the speaker can only stall, reflecting a guilty state of mind.
- The speaker may also hope that the slower pace will draw attention and make listeners more convinced; this is a debate tactic of “blunting the opponent’s edge and boosting one’s own confidence.”
- The fourth situation occurs when reading beautiful, lyrical prose or poetry, or when recalling a pleasant memory; the relaxed pace simply expresses the speaker’s appreciation of beauty.

Speech rate and its changes can reflect a person’s psychological state. Much information can be gleaned from a person’s speech rate, so do not underestimate the role of speech rate in conversation!

#### Section 1 Information Revealed in Speech Rate

Human language is a complex system combining sound and meaning. Speaking, unlike an animal’s instinctive roar, serves to exchange ideas and simultaneously reveals psychological and emotional states. Among these, speech rate subtly reflects the speaker’s psychological condition.

Everyone has a fixed personal speech rate: some speak slowly, some quickly, and some at a moderate pace. Generally, fast speakers tend to be extroverted and youthful, yet they can also convey tension or urgency. Slow, deliberate speakers are often seen as sluggish, reacting half a beat behind others. At the same time, changes in speech rate reflect the speaker’s current psychological state. Speech rate is related to gender, personality, experience, age, and occupation. Based on long-formed personality traits, we can analyze different speech rates and the “secrets” behind changes in pace.

#### 8.2.1 Sparse and Monotonous Language

Because most blood is directed to the limbs for fighting, the energy available to the cerebral cortex (responsible for higher functions) decreases. Consequently, an angry person is more likely to lose rationality, with only one thought in mind—defeating the opponent—while judgment of the surroundings and situation declines. The same cause also weakens another higher function besides thinking: language.

Angry people often say little or nothing at all; their mouths are usually tightly closed. If fighting begins, any words spoken will be as simple and meaningless as possible—“Charge!” “Kill!”—or profanity (which explains why swearing is common in fights), because these utterances require no thought.

In a verbal confrontation such as a debate, language itself tends to be rapid and forceful.

#### Polite Remarks Spoken Excessively May Indicate a Request

In social interactions, if someone has a request, their speech will certainly contain many polite remarks.

A “guest” arrived at Director Qian’s home—Xiao Jin from the same company, carrying several expensive gifts. Director Qian asked what the matter was. Xiao Jin replied, “Nothing special. It’s the holidays, so coming to see the leader is only proper. The leader is usually very busy and works so hard. There are so many big and small matters in the company that require attention.” Director Qian was not so naïve and said, “I’m not a big leader; I’m not as busy as you say. Are you about to be made permanent?” Caught out, Xiao Jin nodded sheepishly and admitted he wanted Director Qian’s help.

When someone’s polite remarks seem excessive and insincere, it indicates they have a request. Do not rush to respond; wait patiently until they state their purpose.

#### Language Style Reflects Personal Cultivation

Language is the key that opens the door to communication and the most important tool in social interaction. Besides appearance, speaking style is an important indicator of a person’s cultivation. As the saying goes, “Words are the voice of the heart”; a person’s language style is the best certificate of their cultivation.

Language is an art. In social dealings we often judge whether another’s speech suits our taste. The main impetus for deciding whether to continue associating with someone is the most direct feeling their language produces in us.

In interacting with others, we tend to focus on whether their speech brings us pleasure and overlook observing their inner activity and character through their words. Only by deeply understanding a person’s character and inner needs can we cater to their preferences and gain the initiative in interpersonal relations.

#### 1. High, Sharp Tone

People with a high, sharp tone are generally neurotic, react strongly to their environment, possess creativity and imagination, have an aesthetic sense, refuse to admit defeat, dislike yielding to others, speak fluently, and enjoy imposing their views. When encountering such a person, it is best not to contradict them; showing a modest attitude will satisfy them.

Women with a high tone usually have fluctuating emotions, are easily hurt or enraged by trifles, and display clear likes and dislikes. Once fixated on something, they often neglect everything else and may make statements that completely contradict the past without learning from the experience. Men with this tone are usually passionate, easily excited yet easily fatigued, and prone to falling in love at first sight or blurting out their feelings, often startling the other person.

#### Recognizing the Other Party’s Humorous Motives

Shakespeare said, “Humor and wit are flashes of wisdom.” A person with a strong sense of humor can not only bring joy through wit, self-mockery, teasing, and playfulness but also help eliminate hostility, ease friction, prevent escalation of conflict, and allow you to achieve twice the result with half the effort on the road to success.

In fact, everyone possesses a stronger or weaker sense of humor, yet the ways of expressing it differ. Canadian psychology professor Rod Martin notes, “In social life, men and women also differ in their use of humor. Men prefer to use ‘malicious’ jokes to criticize one another and establish ‘superior’ status, while women use humor to maintain relationships and put each other at ease.”

When a person displays their sense of humor, their character is revealed.

#### The Psychology of Greetings

Greetings are a means of connecting emotionally, enhancing spiritual communication, and reducing distance. Whether between acquaintances or strangers, greetings are extremely common.

During my acting career I met far more people each day than I do now. Sometimes I would shake hands, sometimes simply wave and say “Hi,” and sometimes merely nod. Receiving a friendly response always made me happy. Of course, I also encountered rebuffs. When leaving, I never forgot to say goodbye. After more than twenty years of experience, I can responsibly tell you that a person’s character and mood can be read from the simple act of greeting. When you greet others, you generally encounter the following types of people:

#### Those Who Pad Their Answers

Such people possess life experience and know how to protect themselves wisely and safeguard their interests. They never speak first; they wait until the end, then repackage others’ already-stated views into something that sounds more incisive. In personality, they are mostly timid, even-tempered, and averse to argument. They prefer the status quo and lack the courage to change. They are harmless yet also lack significant ability.

In short, the more one tries to hide or cover what lies in the heart, the more it is exposed. Personality, for example, is revealed the moment one begins to answer, whether after careful deliberation or without thinking.

Body language is a subconscious action and the least deceptive, so it often betrays a person’s true thoughts.
