## Part Eight: Applications

### People Who Put Others First Can Be Trusted in Interactions

Micro-expression Keywords Living in society, everyone needs to interact with others. In this process, people who put others first are welcomed everywhere. Because, when with such a person, there is no need to worry about being betrayed or suffering losses in interests. When in difficulty, they will extend a helping hand. Such people are few, but if you meet one, be sure to make friends with them.

If a person can always put others first and consider others in every situation, then we can interact with such a person with confidence. When with them, we need not worry about being deceived or harmed, because in the face of interests or danger, they think of others first rather than themselves.

“Never benefit oneself at the expense of others, but always benefit others at the expense of oneself” is a noble sentiment, yet many find it hard to practice. It cannot be denied that some people in life follow the philosophy of “sweep the snow from one’s own doorstep and ignore the frost on others’ roofs.” Some even pursue personal gain at all costs, disregarding morality and law, and commit acts that harm others for their own benefit. In their view, their own interests come first. With such people, you may never know when you will become their scapegoat. Only those who put others first will think of others rather than themselves.

I once watched a television variety show in which the host asked the guests on stage: “When we ride an elevator, there is often a large mirror inside. What is that mirror for?”

The guests below began offering answers one after another:

- “It is used to check one’s appearance.”
- “It is used to expand visual space and create a sense of airiness.”
- “It makes the elevator look clean and bright.”

The guests gave many answers, none of them correct. After repeated prompts still failed to elicit the right answer, the host finally revealed a very simple reason: “It is so that people with limb disabilities in wheelchairs do not have to turn around to see the floor indicator lights.”

Once the answer was given, the guests looked embarrassed. One complained, “How could we have thought of that?”

Only a selfish person considers only their own interests, because in their eyes there is only themselves and no one else. Interacting with such a person means that when danger arrives they will abandon you, and when interests are at stake they will isolate you or even frame you.

In life, when facing a problem, if someone considers only their own gains and losses while ignoring others, that person is not worth getting to know. How many people live only for themselves? Their selfish nature prevents them from offering even the slightest convenience to others, let alone sacrificing any of their own interests. Others will certainly be unwilling to offer them any convenience in return.

A father once asked his son to hand him a pen. The son passed the pen over, but accidentally placed the tip in his father’s hand.

The father said to his son: “When you hand something to someone, you must first consider whether it will be convenient for them to receive it. By handing over the tip, they would have to turn it around; if there is no cap, they might get ink on their hand. This is especially true for knives and scissors—never point the blade or tip toward someone.”

This is an ordinary example Mr. Ye Shengtao used to teach his children to think of others.

A kind person can always put themselves in others’ shoes, feel compassion when seeing others in distress, sympathize with them, help them, and put others first. This is a noble quality, and such a person will surely be accepted by others. The Northern Song philosopher Cheng Yi once said, in essence: the willingness to consider others in all matters is the highest form of learning. This is a simple statement that not only expresses a profound truth in plain language but also identifies the foremost element of being human.

As the saying goes, “Those who plant trees enjoy the shade later,” reminding us to think of others. One cannot think only of oneself; one must also think of others. Those who consider others first will surely earn others’ appreciation.

The French banker Lafeist, before he made his fortune, was once unemployed and at home.

One day he summoned the courage to visit the chairman of a major bank to seek a job, only to be rejected upon meeting him. This was not his first such experience; it was already his fifty-second rejection. Lafeist left the bank dejected and accidentally stepped on a thumbtack on the ground.

“Everyone is against me!” he muttered angrily, about to walk away. But then he thought better of it: he could not let it prick anyone else, so he picked up the thumbtack.

The next day, to his surprise, Lafeist received a hiring notice from the bank. Excited yet puzzled—he had already been rejected—he learned that the thumbtack had “saved” him. The moment he bent down to pick it up, the bank chairman saw it. From this small act the chairman concluded that Lafeist was a careful, considerate person and changed his mind, hiring him.

From then on, Lafeist’s career began at that bank, and he later became a leading French banker.

Although Lafeist’s opportunity appeared to stem merely from picking up a small thumbtack—seemingly accidental—his ability to maintain good conduct even in disappointment and to think of others demonstrated his noble character. The chairman, who could discern spirit in small details, was an expert judge of people; he had spotted Lafeist as a “thoroughbred.” It can also be said that Lafeist’s success owed much to that chairman’s unique insight.

Thinking of others and putting them first is a virtue. Being kept in others’ hearts and receiving their help is a happiness. Everyone carries a scale in their heart: those who are cold and selfish toward others will eventually be shunned; conversely, those who always put others first and think of them will surely be welcomed. With such people we can interact with confidence.

### People Who Offer a “Choose One of Two” Option Are Setting a Trap for You

Micro-expression Keywords: When asked whether you want tea or plain boiled water, no one asks for a bowl of rice. This is a form of habitual thinking. People with ulterior motives exploit this psychology by setting traps for others to fall into. Therefore, when someone forces you to “choose one of two,” the best response is to choose neither.

In sales there is a “choose one of two” rule: salespeople can present price packages and appropriately pressure customers to decide between option 1 or 2. For example, a salesperson might ask a prospective customer, “Would you like the two-door or the one-door refrigerator?” or “Would you like delivery on Tuesday or Wednesday?” With such “choose one of two” questions, once the prospect selects one, the salesperson has essentially made the decision for them and prompted the purchase.

A boss once opened two identical congee shops on opposite sides of the same street. The number of customers each day was roughly the same, yet the left shop consistently earned nearly a hundred yuan more than the right one, almost every day. Puzzled, the boss sent someone to investigate the operations and service of both shops to solve the mystery of the differing revenue.

The investigator posed as an ordinary customer and first entered the right-hand shop. Seeing a guest arrive, the waitress greeted him with a beaming smile, served a bowl of steaming congee, and then asked warmly, “Sir, would you like to add an egg?” The investigator noticed that every customer received the same question: “Add an egg or not?” Roughly half the customers said yes and half said no.

He then entered the left-hand shop. The waitress likewise greeted him with a smile, served a bowl of hot congee, and asked amiably, “Sir, would you like one egg or two eggs?” Other customers received the same question. Usually those who liked eggs asked for two, those who did not asked for one, and only a few declined. By the end of the day the left shop had sold far more eggs than the right one. The different phrasing produced different revenues.

The question “Would you like one egg or two eggs?” traps customers inside the asker’s preset premise, prompting an involuntary choice.

This is a psychological tactic. The other party sets the answers in advance and gives you the power to choose. On the surface you have great autonomy; in reality it is a trap, because whichever answer you pick is the one they want—just as Sun Wukong could never escape the Buddha’s palm.

If you encounter a salesperson skilled at reading consumer psychology, maintain sufficient reason and clarity to avoid being misled. For instance, if you are sitting on a sofa, an ordinary salesperson might ask, “Do you need a sofa?” If your desire to buy is not strong, you will say, “I’m just looking” or “No.” Naturally you will not purchase a sofa that does not meet your wishes.

If you meet a more sophisticated salesperson, they will ask, “Would you like a leather sofa or a fabric one?” If you genuinely intend to buy a sofa, you will make a choice from their options.

Sometimes salespeople guide you toward the answer they want through their questions. For example: “Would it be convenient for delivery on December 1 or December 8?” “Would you like red sheets or white ones?” “Would you like to pay a 1,000-yuan or 1,500-yuan deposit?”

Many people find it hard to resist this “choose one of two” sales approach. In psychology this is called “false-premise suggestion.” From the salesperson’s standpoint, success comes as soon as the customer buys. They therefore assume a purchase premise, turning “buy or not buy” into “buy red or purple.” Although the customer chooses under a false premise, they believe the choice of color stems from their own will and end up buying as the salesperson intended.

If you are a consumer and truly have no intention of completing the transaction, the best method is to reject both answers. By refusing to choose, you largely dismantle the trap the other party has carefully laid.

If you genuinely need the product but are undecided about price, color, or style, you may consider the salesperson’s suggestions and choose what suits you. If you have no need at all and are merely browsing, or if nothing appeals, do not let the “choose one of two” sales pattern influence you. The best approach is to choose neither.

### People Who Constantly Complain About a Third Party May Be Indirectly Complaining About You

Micro-expression Keywords: There is an idiom “point at the mulberry while cursing the locust tree,” meaning to scold one thing while appearing to address another. Such people are common in life. They do not wish to confront others directly yet want to vent their dissatisfaction, so they pretend to grumble about someone else in front of you while actually complaining about you. At such moments you should carefully check whether you have offended them and correct the matter promptly.

Many people prefer not to voice complaints or criticisms directly because such remarks easily offend. Instead they choose a roundabout method, expressing dissatisfaction with you by complaining about a third party.

Mr. Ma lived in an apartment. Recently a new neighbor, a music lover, moved in upstairs. The neighbor played the piano every day, even late into the night. Mr. Ma endured it silently, but the constant disturbance eventually exhausted his patience.

Finally Mr. Ma met the neighbor on the staircase and said, “I can still hear your piano through the floorboards, which shows the floor has a problem—the soundproofing is too poor. The builders of this building are responsible; we should ask the original construction company to fix it.”

The music lover understood that his daily playing disturbed his neighbor. After returning home he placed soft padding under the piano for soundproofing and stopped playing late at night.

Mr. Ma had cleverly shifted the blame onto the building’s constructors while implicitly telling the music lover that the piano disturbed his life. The music lover fully grasped the intent and ceased playing at night.

We often use this speaking style ourselves. This indirect method of complaining can sometimes avoid direct confrontation. For example, when the neighbor’s child repeatedly invites her son—who is preparing for the college entrance exam—out to play, a mother might say to the neighbor’s wife, “Your son often comes looking for mine; I’m afraid it disturbs his studies. I feel very sorry.” The other party quickly realizes her own son’s behavior is inappropriate and that the mother is complaining about lax discipline.

If the mother had gone directly to the neighbor’s home and demanded, “You should discipline your son properly—he keeps coming to play with mine, and mine is preparing for the exam…” and the other side had retorted, a fierce argument would have been inevitable.

Because people dislike direct, face-to-face complaints, some express them indirectly to prompt reflection. Such people are clever and prefer to avoid open conflict. When a superior uses this method with subordinates, it indicates a relatively gentle personality that can earn more trust and affection than a blunt superior.

The general manager of a department store often inspected the sales floor to check employees’ work. One day, while touring the floor, he noticed a customer waiting at a counter while the sales assistant Xiaoqiao chatted and laughed with another assistant nearby.

The manager wanted to reprimand Xiaoqiao but realized that scolding an employee publicly in the store would look bad. Instead he walked to the counter and served the customer himself.

Xiaoqiao saw the manager, walked over awkwardly, expecting a scolding. The manager merely said calmly, “Oh, you were busy just now, so I happened to pass by. The previous assistant, Xiao Zhao, once left for something and received a customer complaint, resulting in a month’s bonus being deducted. That really wasn’t good—it wasted the customer’s time and harmed her own reputation. In the future, if you need to leave, just let me know so I can arrange for someone else to cover.”

Xiaoqiao replied, “It won’t happen again, Manager.” Indeed, for a long time afterward, whenever the manager inspected the floor he saw Xiaoqiao standing attentively behind her counter, never leaving her post even when no customers were present.

In interpersonal interactions, some people are straightforward and speak their minds openly. Although candid, they can easily offend others. Smarter individuals choose another approach: when they have a grievance they do not state it directly but pretend to complain about someone else in front of you, implicitly signaling that they hope you will improve.

Human relationships are subtle. Sometimes the other party does not express their meaning directly but takes a detour. If you do not react quickly enough to grasp the underlying message, you may be seen as slow-witted. Therefore, when someone complains in front of you, be alert: quietly examine whether you have done something wrong and correct it in time.

### People Who Ask for a Third Party’s Opinion Actually Want to Know Yours

Micro-expression keywords

As the saying goes, “Listen to what is said and what lies between the lines.” Skilled listeners discern the unspoken implications in others’ words. For instance, when someone asks you for a third party’s opinion, they are really seeking yours. In such cases, simply stating your own view will satisfy them.

Sometimes people are reluctant to voice their true thoughts directly, fearing they might say the wrong thing or face negative consequences. They therefore adopt a clever indirect approach: “How do his neighbors view him?” “What does his teacher say about him?” “How do his classmates describe him?” This removes the speaker’s inner reservations, because they can tell themselves, “After all, I am only reporting what the neighbors, teacher, or classmates think, not my own opinion, so I bear no responsibility.” As a result, they reveal their real views.

Many journalists skillfully use this third-party technique to draw out a subject’s genuine opinions, especially when covering life-and-death cases. Instead of asking “What is your impression of the deceased?” or “Did you notice anything unusual about the deceased recently?”—questions that often make people wary and evasive—reporters ask, “How did the deceased’s neighbors view him?” The interviewee then lowers their guard and expresses their own thoughts under the guise of reporting the neighbors’ views. *Dream of the Red Chamber* contains numerous examples of this technique.

In Chapter 6, “Granny Liu’s First Visit to the Rongguo Mansion,” Granny Liu and her grandson Ban’er kowtow to Xifeng. Xifeng says she is “too young to recognize the visitor and does not know the exact relationship, so she dares not address her properly.” Zhou Rui’s wife replies, “This is the granny I just mentioned.” Granny Liu then tries to bring Ban’er forward to bow, but the boy refuses out of shyness.

Xifeng smiles and says, “Relatives who seldom visit grow distant. Those who know us will say you disdain us and refuse to come often; those who do not know us will assume we look down on everyone.”

Xifeng’s final remarks are spoken through the mouths of imagined third parties, yet they express her own feelings. It is not really “those who know” who think “you disdain us,” nor “those who do not know” who think “we look down on everyone”; it is Xifeng herself who holds these views. A similar scene appears in Chapter 45:

When Ping’er brings tea, Granny Lai rises to accept it and says with a smile, “Miss, you need only have sent any child with it; there is no need to trouble yourself on my account.” While drinking, she continues, “The old lady does not realize that these young ones must be kept under strict control. Even so, they still find moments to stir up trouble and worry their elders. Those who understand will say the children are merely mischievous; those who do not will claim we rely on wealth and power to bully others, damaging even the masters’ reputation. It angers me so much that I often summon their fathers and scold them before things improve.”

Granny Lai is not reporting what “those who understand” or “those who do not” think; she is voicing her own opinion while shifting potential responsibility onto unnamed others.

When we wish to learn someone’s true thoughts but the person is unwilling to speak openly because of interests or other concerns—and especially when they hold opposing views—we can use the third-party technique. Ask what other people would most likely think about the matter. Because the speaker is ostensibly reporting others’ opinions, they feel no personal responsibility and will relax their guard, revealing their own views.

You may wonder whether they are truly describing someone else’s ideas. In the vast majority of cases, they are expressing their own real thoughts. Even if they claim to be citing others, those others rarely share a single opinion, so the speaker must choose the view they consider most plausible—thereby indicating their own preference. Moreover, they rarely repeat the supposed source verbatim; their own wording and framing make the statement essentially their personal opinion. Some people add a final disclaimer—“They think this way, but I do not”—to mask the fact that the view is their own. If you then ask, “Could you share your own thoughts?” they usually smile and remain silent, because they have already told you.

### Social Gatherings

In Chapter 1 we noted that airports offer the best panoramic view of human behavior. Social gatherings likewise provide an excellent setting both for observing others and for practicing the interpretation of body language. Let us now examine some of the gestures and postures commonly seen at such events.

We find that married women tend to cluster together at gatherings, as do married men, while single people gravitate toward other singles.

Couples on a date walk very close to each other and touch affectionately. Intimate married couples display similar gestures of affection. By observing these movements we can often identify which couple has been married the shortest time.

Newlyweds, for example, frequently walk with an arm around the partner’s waist or hand in hand. The gesture silently announces to everyone, “Hands off—she (he) is mine!” Touch thus signals both possession and a posture of protection and trust.

The two couples in Figure 5.1 are clearly enjoying each other’s affection. Notice that the woman on the left has her arm around her husband’s neck, while the man on the right has his arm around his wife’s neck—both gestures conveying deep warmth.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图5.1　表达爱意的两对夫妻]*

Some individuals are more openly expressive of emotion than others. At gatherings, one partner in a couple is often more inclined to display affection through physical contact.

If a couple argued before arriving and the tension has not eased, they are likely to appear stiff, their smiles forced and rectangular.

Regardless of marital status, couples who are not getting along well show almost no physical contact. If one touches the other, the touched person quickly withdraws the hand or shoulder. Even when seated on the same sofa, they deliberately maintain distance rather than sitting close (see Figure 5.2).

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图5.2　各怀心事的一对夫妻]*

At a large gathering, if you notice two people repeatedly closing the distance between them while talking, you may assume they are sharing a private matter. If you are nearby, you may also observe them shift from standing side by side to facing each other. The nonverbal message they send is: “This is private space—please do not disturb.”

Observing and correctly interpreting attendees’ body language can be as enjoyable as participating in the gathering itself. The key is to become an active “player,” accurately reading others’ nonverbal cues and responding appropriately so that the social event fulfills its purpose.

For example, if you attend a gathering alone and meet someone who attracts you, how can you tell whether they are open to meeting you? Here are some common gestures you may encounter:

### Schwab’s Path to Success

Charles Schwab, founder of the Bethlehem Steel Corporation in the United States, was born in a rural village and received only a brief formal education. At fifteen, with his family impoverished, he took a job as a stable hand in a mountain village.

Three years later he found work at a construction site owned by steel magnate Andrew Carnegie. From the moment he arrived, Schwab resolved to become the best worker on the site. While others complained about the hard labor and low pay and slacked off, Schwab quietly accumulated experience and taught himself construction knowledge.

In the evenings, while others chatted, Schwab sat in a corner reading. The manager glanced at the book in Schwab’s hands, flipped through his notebook, and left without a word. The next day the manager summoned Schwab to his office and asked, “What are you studying for?” Schwab replied, “Our company does not lack laborers; it lacks technicians and managers who possess both practical experience and professional knowledge, doesn’t it?” The manager nodded. Soon afterward Schwab was promoted to technician.

Many of his fellow workers mocked and ridiculed him, but Schwab remained unmoved. “I am working for myself,” he said, “and for my own company.” With this conviction he rose step by step to chief engineer. At twenty-five he became general manager of the construction company.

Even as general manager, Schwab did not relax his standards. While overseeing construction of the company’s largest plant, the Braddock Steel Works, he arrived at the site earlier than anyone else each day. When engineer Jones asked why he came so early, Schwab answered, “Only this way can I avoid delays if an emergency arises.” After the plant was completed, Jones recommended Schwab as his deputy to oversee all plant operations.

Two years later Jones died in an accident, and Schwab succeeded him as plant manager. Thanks to his exceptional managerial skill and work ethic, Carnegie appointed him chairman of the steel company a few years later. Schwab eventually founded the Bethlehem Steel Corporation and achieved remarkable success. Through persistent dreams and practice he rose from laborer to entrepreneur, while many of his former coworkers remained manual laborers all their lives, struggling daily for a living.

What employer would not value an employee like Schwab? The same service rendered with different attitudes produces different results. All new employees start on equal footing; their initial pay and performance differ little. The vast differences that later emerge stem from the attitudes they bring to their work.

Employees who see themselves merely as hired hands and regard “the company as the boss’s” never integrate fully and never become outstanding. Only those who treat the company as their own—caring for it as they would their home—stand out, earn the boss’s recognition, and become true stakeholders.

Only those who approach others’ affairs with the same care they give their own are worth partnering with. Therefore, when choosing collaborators, observe how they handle tasks assigned to them; their attitude toward such work reveals their attitude toward work in general.

### Saying “Welcome to Offer Opinions” While Not Wanting to Hear Your Criticism

Micro-expression keywords: Think about it—have you often met people who say “Welcome to offer opinions” yet become visibly displeased the moment you actually voice one? This is human nature; no one truly enjoys criticism, and verbal modesty does not equal genuine humility. So when someone utters such words, do not take them literally, or you may wound their self-esteem and cause offense.

No one likes feeling negated, yet some people adopt a magnanimous pose and declare, “Everyone is welcome to offer opinions.” Do not assume such individuals are different or genuinely open to dissent. The more someone claims to be indifferent to criticism, the more sensitive they actually are and the less they wish to hear it.

After graduating from a top university, Zhu Feng joined a private refrigeration-equipment company. The owner valued Zhu highly, promoting him to sales supervisor in his first year and then directly to assistant general manager because of outstanding performance. Their personal relationship was close; they often socialized, and the boss relied heavily on Zhu in business matters. Gradually Zhu came to feel he held a status equal to the owner’s within the company<|eos|>

### Zhang Fan's Story

Zhang Fan joined the office of a state-owned enterprise after graduating from university. Although young and inexperienced, she felt she had every advantage over the sluggish office director, Lao Guo, who was always nodding and bowing to leaders and responding with deferential murmurs. Despite being a newcomer, she showed no respect for her elder.

The most demanding part of office work was drafting various reports and speeches. Seeing Lao Guo struggle with them day after day, Zhang Fan volunteered to take on those tedious writing tasks. Lao Guo felt immense relief and thanked her repeatedly. Yet her offer was not motivated by a desire to serve others; she had her own agenda. She believed Lao Guo was too old to match her professionally trained abilities in speech or manner, so she intended to display her own competence and talent in order to replace him.

One day the general manager asked her to help complete an academic paper, and Zhang Fan finally saw her chance. Relying on the leader’s favor, she began to take charge, assigning tasks to Lao Guo and managing the office’s daily affairs. In the office she frequently flaunted her professional knowledge, boasting about how highly the general manager valued her, which drew murmurs of discontent from her colleagues. Lao Guo, however, remained unchanged, always wearing his trademark smile; even when Zhang Fan issued orders, he kept grinning. She completed the academic paper brilliantly, and the general manager was pleased.

The leader’s appreciation and attitude made Zhang Fan secretly smug and extremely arrogant. She began to run the office with a commanding air. Lao Guo’s authority at work was almost entirely supplanted by hers. Zhang Fan confidently assumed the directorship was hers and was merely waiting for the leader to announce it at the right moment.

Matters did not unfold as she expected. In the biennial leadership election, Lao Guo retained the directorship by a wide margin, while Zhang Fan received only verbal praise and encouragement. Unconvinced, she demanded an explanation. The general manager looked at her and said: “Ability alone is not enough to lead; experience and a character that commands respect are also required. You are still young—learn well. There is always someone better; keep striving.” His words reminded her of the respect and support other employees showed the “mediocre” Lao Guo, and she seemed to understand.

Zhang Fan’s work ability was indeed strong, yet she constantly showed off, considered herself exceptional, looked down on the director, and compared colleagues unfavorably with the leader’s regard for her. The result was colleagues’ dislike, a poor reputation, and the loss of a great opportunity. Had she modestly assisted Lao Guo, treated colleagues kindly, and sought advice humbly, the departmental directorship might well have been hers within a few years.

### The Art of Reading People: Observing Words and Expressions

A successful candidate for the imperial examinations finally obtained a county magistrate post in Shandong after arduous exams and further selection. On his second day in office he went to pay respects to his superior but could think of nothing to say. After a long silence he suddenly asked, “What is your honorable surname, sir?” The superior was astonished and reluctantly gave his surname.

The magistrate fell silent again, thought for a long while, and said, “Your surname does not appear in the Book of Hundred Surnames.” The superior grew more puzzled and replied, “Do you not know I am a bannerman?” The magistrate stood up again and asked, “Which banner do you belong to, sir?” The superior answered, “The Plain Red Banner.” The magistrate said, “The Plain Yellow Banner is the best; why are you not in that one?” The superior flew into a rage and roared, “Which province are you from?” The magistrate replied, “Guangxi.” The superior retorted, “Guangdong is best; why are you not from Guangdong?” Only then did the magistrate notice the superior’s face was flushed with anger and hastily withdrew. The next day the superior ordered him back to Guangxi to serve as a school instructor. The reason was simple: he lacked the skill of reading people and situations.

In social interactions, the ability to observe words and expressions and adapt accordingly is itself a valuable skill.

During a visit, if the host speaks with you while glancing elsewhere and someone nearby is whispering, it indicates your arrival has interrupted an important matter he must attend to. Although he is physically receiving you, his mind remains elsewhere. The wisest course is to stop and take your leave: “You must be busy. I will not disturb you further; I will return in a day or two to hear your reply.”

When you depart, the host will feel both gratitude and guilt—guilt for having been preoccupied with his own affairs. Consequently he will exert greater effort to fulfill your request as compensation.

If the host’s doorbell or telephone rings during conversation, you should pause and allow the host to attend to the visitor or call. Continuing to speak at length places the host in an awkward position.

When you later inquire whether the matter you entrusted has been completed, you may find that despite the host’s considerable effort the outcome is imperfect or progress is slow. You may feel impatient, yet you must restrain yourself. Turn the urge to urge into thanks, fully acknowledge the host’s efforts, then explain your current situation to seek understanding and sympathy. The host will then realize that although much time and energy have been spent, the issue remains unresolved, and will be determined to see it through to the end.

### The Art of Winning Hearts and Providing Incentives

We often say there is an art to winning hearts; in essence it means grasping the other party’s inner needs. Give meat to those who love meat and grass to those who love grass, and both will be sent away delighted.

Some people spend half the day anxious, unable to guess why the boss has summoned them; others pursue a deal for months yet dare not assume sincerity until the contract is signed; still others exhaust themselves pleading for help yet cannot discern whether the other party intends to assist. What these people lack is the ability to perceive and meet others’ needs. Those skilled at identifying needs are usually attentive and capable. When they become leaders, they can appropriately apply incentives to arouse subordinates’ enthusiasm.

A small mold-making company had cramped, cluttered workspaces, yet every employee worked with total concentration and no supervision. The owner explained: “The key is that detailed quotas and corresponding pay for each process are clearly defined. Workers know exactly how much more they earn for doing more or better work.” By aligning labor efficiency with income, the owner raised employee initiative.

Effective incentives meet actual needs. In modern enterprise management, the most important step in mobilizing staff is to analyze differing needs, set visible goals, and give employees a sense of purpose and drive. This demonstrates managerial skill.

No matter the position or industry, those who can promptly grasp others’ needs inspire confidence and achieve results. Such people inevitably accomplish great things. Therefore we should recognize individuals who understand others’ inner needs; such employees or partners bring lasting benefits. Under such managers we can fully exercise our abilities, because they provide the necessary stage.

In daily life we are constantly busy and often expend great effort on tasks that remain unfinished. Yet if we encounter someone who can instantly grasp another’s needs, every problem ceases to be a problem.

### Ms. Zhuo’s Experience

Ms. Zhuo was a highly regarded sales professional. She recently resigned to rest before deciding her next move. Many headhunters and companies pursued her; one offered an annual salary exceeding two million yuan, yet she remained unmoved—she was not short of money.

At a friend’s gathering she met a Mr. Chen. They conversed congenially, but he did not invite her to join his company that evening. Afterward he invited her to dinner and proposed she join him, but she declined. He did not press the matter and continued to stay in touch.

During one phone call he learned she would soon travel to Beijing and offered, “What a coincidence—I am also going to Beijing. Let me book your ticket.” Ms. Zhuo gave no clear reply, assuming he merely wished to ingratiate himself. On the flight they chatted about various topics, yet to her surprise he did not mention employment again.

Later Mr. Chen happened to return on the same flight, still without raising the subject. Some days afterward he invited her to visit a newly opened branch. Upon returning to the Shanghai headquarters he led her to an elegantly appointed office that matched her taste exactly.

He said sincerely, “This is the office we have prepared for you. Are you satisfied?” Shortly thereafter Ms. Zhuo became a partner in Mr. Chen’s company—an outcome that astonished the industry. Everyone had assumed her new employer would be either a leading firm or one offering lavish compensation; instead she chose a relatively modest company.

A major factor in her decision was Mr. Chen’s skill at creating seemingly coincidental encounters that demonstrated sincerity and regard. Although Ms. Zhuo had remained noncommittal about the deliberate same-flight arrangement, she felt inwardly warmed by it.

### Sales Case Analysis

In an automobile dealership a star salesperson consistently met or exceeded targets under any circumstances. He regarded selling as straightforward.

When colleagues lost confidence in an ordinary salaried couple and refused to pursue the sale, he took over and successfully sold them a car. Colleagues viewed the couple’s purchasing power as too low; buying a car would exhaust most of their savings, so the likelihood of a purchase seemed negligible.

The salesperson thought differently. He believed the couple genuinely needed a car; precisely because their means were limited, they would choose carefully to maximize value. They did not require a luxury vehicle to display status; they simply needed reliable transportation to and from work. He recommended a small-displacement model with low fuel consumption that met their needs at minimal cost. They purchased it without hesitation.

When colleagues dismissed a wealthy man who already owned several luxury cars, believing he would not buy another, the salesperson sold him one. Colleagues assumed the man had no need for an additional identical vehicle. The salesperson understood that the man bought cars to display status rather than for comfort. Accordingly he spent little time describing performance and instead emphasized the vehicle’s prestige. The wealthy man became deeply interested in the “high-status” car and bought it.

The salesperson succeeded by identifying each client’s true needs.

### Mei Ling’s Love Story

If someone were willing to contrive various coincidences to meet you, you would surely be moved. The same tactic is frequently used in romance. People tend to believe in fate; when a coincidence is added, they conclude heaven has destined the match and will strive to overcome every obstacle to love.

Mei Ling was exceptionally beautiful, yet her husband was of ordinary appearance and shorter than she. Whenever she recounted their meeting, courtship, marriage, and the birth of their child, her face glowed with happiness.

Mei Ling walked the single stop from the subway station to her office. One rainy day without an umbrella she took shelter under an eave, watching the downpour and worrying she would be late. An umbrella appeared above her head. The young man holding it asked, “Heading to work? Where is your company?”

She pointed to a nearby building. He said, “Let’s walk together; I work there too.” Mei Ling looked at him doubtfully; he gave her a reassuring nod. They walked side by side, exchanged a few words, and became acquainted. They did indeed work in the same building—she on the eighth floor, he on the tenth.

The next day they “happened” to meet again on the route from the subway to the building. Mei Ling learned he, like her, preferred walking from the station. From then on they “coincidentally” met every weekday, chatting as they walked; she alighted at the eighth floor, he at the tenth. As they grew closer they began dating.

Only later did Mei Ling discover he did not actually work in the same building; his office was two stops farther away. All their encounters had been deliberately staged so he could pursue her. Each day he accompanied her one stop, rode the elevator with her to the eighth floor, then descended from the tenth and hurried to his own workplace. Mei Ling was deeply moved; she knew marrying such a man would be the right choice.

### Carnegie’s Story

While teaching, the American Dale Carnegie received a visit from a company manager perpetually overwhelmed by endless work. The manager was astonished to find Carnegie’s desk neat and empty; he had expected it to be buried under papers like his own. He asked, “Mr. Carnegie, where do you keep the letters you have not yet handled?”

Carnegie replied, “I have finished all my correspondence.”

The manager, puzzled, continued, “Then to whom have you delegated today’s unfinished tasks?”

“I have completed everything,” Carnegie answered with a smile.

Seeing the manager’s confusion, Carnegie explained: “It is simple. I know there is much to do, yet my energy is limited. I can handle only one matter at a time. I therefore list tasks in order of importance and address them one by one. The result is that everything gets done.”

The manager suddenly understood. “Ah, I see. Thank you, Mr. Carnegie.” Several weeks later the manager invited Carnegie to his now spacious office and said gratefully, “Mr. Carnegie, thank you for teaching me how to manage work. Previously my large office was piled with documents and letters like small mountains; one desk was insufficient, so I used three. After adopting your method the situation improved dramatically—nothing remains unfinished.”

The manager not only escaped the backlog but years later became one of America’s most successful figures.

Those who work methodically, with clear priorities and goals, possess superior understanding and guidance. They analyze situations quickly and effectively, then proceed step by step. Such people are worthy of admiration both in life and at work.

### The Story of Three Workers

A psychologist once visited a church under construction and noticed three workers performing identical tasks yet displaying markedly different expressions. He approached each and asked the same question: “Who are you working for?”

- The first worker replied resentfully that he was smashing unbearably heavy stones with an impossibly heavy hammer—working merely for the sake of working.
- The second answered helplessly that he was smashing stones to feed his family—working for his wages.
- The third replied calmly that he was helping build a magnificent church and a modern city—working for the value of his life.

The same work, yet three different perspectives that produced three different feelings about the work and three different outcomes. The first two workers were merely enduring their jobs; only the third truly regarded his labor as serving others and himself.

Employers naturally prefer the third type of employee. The first two will only complain; the third works with genuine purpose. While an employer pays wages, the employee receives experience, training, the exercise of ability, and the tempering of character. An employee whose sole aim is to extract money from the employer will inevitably adopt a negative attitude; such a person will never be entrusted with important responsibilities.

Therefore the employees employers most need are those who abandon the notion of “working for the boss,” treat the company as their own, and regard themselves as partners. Such employees are worthy of being entrusted with significant duties.

### Couples

Due to certain reasons, most people find it difficult to correctly interpret their closest loved ones, even if they appear to be in harmony overall. People always take their intimate relationships for granted, thus neglecting those silent communications.

Here, we strongly recommend that no matter how well you think you know your spouse or partner, you must patiently listen to the other person finish speaking and carefully observe the body movements they display. Because body movements usually reveal true feelings more than words. Many marriage counselors have said that most marital problems stem from poor communication between the two parties. Therefore, patient listening and careful observation are very important for maintaining a long and happy marriage.

In the 1980s, Japanese women could not express their dissatisfaction with their husbands verbally, but they could show their emotions in other ways. After the husband returned home from work, he could infer his wife's mood by observing the placement of the flower bouquet at home and further consider how to respond.

Below we list some movements that lovers may use when expressing affection and anger. While interpreting these movements, please remember that some people may prefer to show their emotions, especially when others are present. When a person places an arm around his wife to express affection, the other party may adopt more subtle movements, such as leaning against him while he speaks.

In addition, people vary in the movements they use to express dissatisfaction and anger. You can draw on your knowledge of your loved one to help you correctly interpret their behavior.

### People Who Can Grasp the Other Party’s Needs in Real Time Are Capable at Handling Affairs

Micro-expression keywords: How to speak so as not to be rejected? How to speak so as to move the other person? It depends on what the other party needs most and on grasping the other party’s true needs. Of course, people generally do not state these needs outright, but as long as you carefully analyze their psychology, you can understand what they want. Focusing on this point can achieve twice the result with half the effort.

Being capable at handling affairs refers to a person who proceeds without dragging things out, can rapidly grasp others’ needs in real time, identify the key points, and thereby bring matters to a satisfactory conclusion. For example, when fishing, it is not a matter of simply setting the rod in place and waiting for a fish to bite; rather, you must judge from the circumstances what the fish like to eat and where they linger. Only then can you catch fish quickly and effectively.

Therefore, whether one can grasp the other party’s needs in real time is the key to success in handling affairs and also a manifestation of one’s capability. Needs are not always shown on the surface; they also have deeper layers. Just as we sometimes think a person needs only one car, yet some people insist on buying several. In these people’s eyes, a car is not merely a means of transportation but also a form of showing off; what it brings them is not only material satisfaction but, more importantly, spiritual satisfaction. Hence they are willing to purchase things they seemingly do not need. The same principle applies when handling affairs: only by identifying the other party’s true needs can one bring matters to a successful conclusion.

### Humble People Naturally Attract Many Helpers

Micro-expression keywords: A popular person is necessarily a humble person. Humble people consider others in every respect and know how to respect others’ feelings, so they win everyone’s affection and assistance. Therefore, to see whether a person is humble, one need only look at how many friends they have when facing difficulties.

Socrates once said: “Humility is the sweet root hidden in the soil from which all noble virtues sprout and grow.” Humility is a virtue and a noble human quality. In life there are always people who, once they accomplish something or achieve some credit, go around boasting, even treating the achievements of their ancestors as their own glory. Seniority naturally deserves respect, but constantly singing about it on one’s lips causes it to lose value. What is more lamentable is that boasting also incurs the envy and resentment of those around one, ultimately leaving one isolated.

Truly capable people do not need to proclaim their abilities themselves; only humility and courtesy can display one’s cultivation and virtue. Humble people are also more welcome. If a person only knows how to elevate themselves in front of others, they are invisibly belittling others; this is disrespectful and harms others’ self-esteem, inevitably leading to denial and contempt. Conversely, when a person shows deference in front of others, it is a sign of respect; once the other person’s heart is satisfied, they will repay with a higher evaluation. Therefore, humble people naturally have many helpers around them, because they can place themselves in a lower position and are not stingy about seeking advice from others.

### Parents and Children

During the first two years after birth, infants communicate with their parents mainly through sound. When hungry, wet, or uncomfortable, they cry or scream until the parents respond. As infants grow older, they begin to integrate into their surroundings and develop various body movements that express emotion.

Parents should understand their children’s gestures, expressions, and postures, because these movements are sometimes the only clue that a child is facing a problem. Below we introduce some body movements young children may use when communicating normal emotions such as anger, fear, or happiness.

It should be noted that some of the following postures can be seen in children of any age, while others appear only in adolescents or younger children. Generally, the younger the child, the more obvious the body movements used to express emotion. As they grow older and their minds mature, they tend to adopt more subtle postures.

It is also important to interpret a child’s behavior by combining your knowledge of the child with your understanding of their various actions. For example, slamming a door may indicate excitement about going out to play with friends, but it may also indicate anger and frustration.

### People Who Regard Serving Others as Their Own Duty Can Coexist and Prosper Together

**Micro-expression keywords**: Human nature is selfish, so people generally do not regard doing things for others as their own duty. In fact, they overlook the principle that hard work creates wealth for others while simultaneously enhancing one’s own value. Therefore, if someone regards serving others as their own duty, it shows that this person has strong ambition and is worth coexisting and prospering with.

Sometimes, to see a person clearly, we can assign them a task and observe their attitude toward it to discern their character. Only those who regard serving others as their own duty are worth coexisting and prospering with. In other words, only those who treat work assigned by others as their own work and devote themselves wholeheartedly to completing it are worth coexisting with.

For example, in the workplace many people view work as a simple employment relationship; whether they do more or less, well or poorly, makes little difference to them, because they always feel they are working for the boss. If a person holds this mentality, then no matter what work they do, they will merely go through the motions. With this attitude they will never grow or develop, will never have a chance to “get ahead,” and certainly cannot accomplish anything great.

### Bill Gates’s Humility

Bill Gates and his team led Microsoft to create one myth after another in the IT industry. Li Kaifu, Microsoft’s first Chinese vice president, admired not only Bill Gates’s business achievements but, above all, his humble character. A widely circulated story illustrates Bill Gates’s humility.

A staff member at Microsoft who was specially assigned to prepare Bill’s speeches said that before every speech Bill would carefully annotate the draft himself and prepare and practice earnestly. After every speech, Bill would come down and talk with him, asking, “Where did I speak well today, and where did I speak poorly?” He did not merely ask; he would also take a notebook and carefully record what he had done wrong so he could correct and improve it next time.

It is rare for someone who has achieved such success in his career to remain so dedicated, so humble, and so willing to learn, because many people become arrogant once they succeed. Yet, as the saying goes, “the tall tree catches the wind.” A person who is overly conspicuous will inevitably incur others’ envy and resentment and will be isolated; after all, no one wants to be with an arrogant person.

### People Who Handle Affairs in an Orderly Manner Possess Understanding and Guidance Ability

**Micro-expression keywords** There are two kinds of people in the workplace: one kind handles affairs with great efficiency and clear order; the other kind appears busy but never finishes work on time. Where does the difference lie? In fact, it comes down to personal understanding. A person with understanding will arrange work according to importance, set priorities, and then complete tasks one by one. Consequently, their work is not only orderly but also highly efficient.

We often say efficiency comes first, and rightly so; no matter what one does, efficiency is most important. For example, in the workplace, whoever can complete a task first is an outstanding worker; in studies, whoever can master the most knowledge in the shortest time will rank at the top. Therefore, improving efficiency has become everyone’s goal.

Efficiency in work reflects a person’s understanding and guidance ability. Someone who works methodically and in an orderly fashion necessarily possesses strong understanding and guidance abilities; conversely, those who work without order, without sequence, in a chaotic manner, and without distinguishing priorities may appear to be working hard on the surface, yet in reality they achieve little efficiency.

We cannot control our surroundings, but we can master our own behavior.

—Benjamin Disraeli

Whether you are facing your own children, loved ones, business partners, or strangers, clearly understanding the meanings of body language can help you better grasp the situation and effectively communicate your own emotions and thoughts. In this chapter we discuss non-verbal movements related to specific interpersonal relationships.

While reading the following content and suggestions, try to recall some non-verbal exchanges you have had with your own children, loved ones, business partners, and others. Consider what role your body language plays in these social relationships. Then think about what techniques you can use to improve your ability to handle interpersonal relationships.

### Deliberately Emphasizing “Coincidence” May Be Intentional

Micro-expression keywords: In television dramas, many plot points are too “coincidental”; this is indeed the screenwriters’ deliberate arrangement to advance the story. But in real life there are also many “coincidences,” especially when the other party deliberately emphasizes them; these may well be intentional acts designed to achieve a certain purpose.

“Wow, what a coincidence that you’re here too.” An accidental encounter always brings extra surprise. Because coincidence appears completely devoid of self-interest on the surface, it easily brings people closer. For example, if you happen to meet someone who moves you at a friend’s gathering, and the other person happens to feel the same, you may think it was arranged by heaven and you may quickly fall in love…

Accidental coincidences can rapidly dismantle the other party’s psychological defenses and generate trust in you. Therefore, many people carefully stage coincidences, exploiting people’s unconditional trust in them, in order to achieve their own ends.

### Signs That Others Are Willing to Talk

- More eye contact
- Clearing the throat, as if preparing to speak
- Maintaining a closer distance from you
- Facing you or leaning the body toward you
- Relaxed standing posture
- Arms or legs apart
- Open expression or a smiling face

Earlier we mentioned that when interpreting a person’s body language one must consider the person’s character traits as a whole, not merely individual postures. When observing a stranger’s posture and body movements, one should realize that one is not familiar with this person, so there is a high possibility of making an erroneous judgment.

For example, her posture may appear uninterested in you, yet in fact she may simply be shy; therefore do not retreat—step forward bravely and try to talk with her. If you appear relaxed and candid and can offer some good suggestions at any time, you will soon find that you have already entered a meaningful conversation.

### The Meaning of Coincidence and a Reminder

Coincidence, in interpersonal interaction, reflects the other party’s respect and regard for you. In romantic relationships, it reflects the other party’s deep affection for you. Both can make you accept and approve of the other party in a relatively short time. Of course, these deliberately arranged coincidences are well-intentioned; while feeling moved, we must also guard against “coincidences” created by people with ill intentions.

For example, some swindlers pop open a can of soda and exclaim, “Hey, I won a prize!” Then they offer various reasons to sell the prize at a low price, luring you to take out your wallet. This is now a well-known scam. Nowadays, prize-winning messages sent via mobile phones or QQ, as well as claims that your bank card was used for a certain amount of spending in a certain place and instructions to transfer money to a certain account, all exploit coincidence to defraud money; one must not fall for them easily.

### Conclusion

People react differently to arrogant and humble individuals because life has formed the view that proud, boastful people are ignorant and uncultured, while humble people are usually those with real talent and cultivation.

Therefore, only humble people win others’ goodwill and receive their help. Even if a person’s ability is truly lacking, they still do not want to see others placed above them; those who understand humility can place themselves lower everywhere, so they are bound to win everyone’s affection. Hence, to see whether a person is humble, one need only observe their attitude toward those around them and the attitude of those around them toward them; humble people will be surrounded by helpers.

### All True Greatness Is Humble

All truly great things are simple and humble. In this world, all those with real talent and learning, all true heroes and outstanding figures, are without exception open-minded and humble. Those who are overbearing, arrogant, and self-satisfied may be superior in one aspect or another, but more often than not they have no outstanding qualities and merely use bluster and mystification to conceal their limited ability.

In daily life, interpersonal interaction is unavoidable, yet the world is complex and human hearts are hard to fathom. Especially for young people just entering society, lack of experience in discerning others’ intentions often leads to failure. In fact, reading minds and understanding people is not difficult! As long as you can carefully explore the other party’s way of conducting themselves, you can adjust your own interaction style and easily handle complex human hearts!

### Chapter 4: Through the Other Party’s Words, Probing Inner Needs

A person’s speech, including tone and rhythm, is an expression of their inner voice. Learning to analyze the basic characteristics of voice and to interpret deeper meanings from simple words allows you, even with vague or obscure speech, to hear the speaker’s true thoughts and emotions, thereby gaining a deeper understanding of the other party and seeing through human hearts.

### Signs of Expressing Affection

- Standing or sitting beside you
- Moving closer when speaking with you
- Holding your hand
- Wrapping an arm around your shoulder
- Frequently touching your hand, arm, or shoulder
- Frequently making eye contact with you

### Signs That Others Are Unwilling to Talk

- Less eye contact
- Maintaining a certain distance from you
- Turning the head away from you
- Tense standing posture
- Arms or legs crossed
- Cold expression or an unhappy face

### Workplace and Professional Applications

#### Listen, Listen, and Listen Again

Listeners are irresistible because they are compassionate, willing to share people’s weaknesses, and ready to hear people express unpleasant emotions. If you want others to like the real you, become a listener and never shy away.

One day, American host Linkletter interviewed a young child. Linkletter asked, “What do you want to be when you grow up?” The child answered innocently, “I want to be a pilot!” Linkletter followed up: “If one day your plane flies over the Pacific and all engines fail, what would you do?” The child thought for a moment and said, “I would first tell everyone on the plane to fasten their seat belts, then I would put on my parachute and jump out.”

The audience laughed uproariously, yet Linkletter kept watching the child to see if he was being clever. Unexpectedly, tears streamed down the child’s face. Linkletter felt deeply moved by the child’s compassion. He asked, “Why would you do that?” The child’s answer revealed a child’s sincere empathy: “I’m going to get fuel, and I’ll come back! I’ll come back!”

When the child jumped out with the parachute without regard for others, who “heard” the child’s compassion? Writer Powell once said: We must listen to the meaning behind the words, not the words themselves. In sincere listening, we can penetrate the words and discover the other person’s inner world.

People like listeners, especially compassionate ones. They are as important as close friends, exerting a positive influence on individuals and groups alike, and they make people feel reliable, trustworthy, and loyal. Listeners consider others’ needs before their own, and they support and help others. Listeners enjoy entering other people’s hearts and minds and gladly share others’ deeper feelings. People tend to open up to listeners because they long to be cared for, and sincere listeners truly deliver that care.

Freud was arguably the greatest listening master of modern times. Someone who once met Freud described his attitude while listening to others.

“It was simply astonishing. I had never seen anyone so focused, with such a keen soul capable of insight and scrutiny.”

“His gaze was modest and gentle, his voice soft, his posture almost unchanging. Yet his attention to me, the way he showed he enjoyed my speaking—even when I did not speak well—you truly cannot imagine what it means for someone to listen to you like that.”

What is the most effective way to listen in order to understand the other person, communicate, and build rapport? Psychologists recommend “empathic listening.”

Empathic listening means listening with the heart to another person’s thoughts and feelings. It is a way of listening that puts oneself in the other’s place and tries to see the world through their eyes. Among all listening styles, it is the only one that truly reaches another person’s psyche and is a hallmark of high emotional intelligence.

While listening, listeners often put themselves in the speaker’s position and offer opinions or suggestions. Many listeners, driven by the other person’s emotions, believe they can solve the other person’s problems.

Suppose your friend has quarreled with his wife and tells you about it. You naturally react. You might comfort him like this:

- If I were in your place, I couldn’t stand it either.
- It’s unbelievable. I never thought your wife would act that way.
- This is just like last time; you two always argue about these things.
- You have to draw your own conclusions.
- Don’t take it too hard; everything will soon return to normal.

In reality, none of these reactions is what your friend expects, and none offers him substantial help. Some remarks may even make him angrier, while others are mostly empty words.

As a listener, you may not realize that you are not truly putting yourself in his place; your reactions may make him feel you are showing off rather than caring about him.

A listener should understand that the views you express cannot fully solve someone else’s problems. The only thing you can do for another person is to show understanding and consideration while listening attentively.

During listening, you can use appropriate exchanges and guidance to help the other person gain more insight into the issue they face and encourage them to find solutions through their own strength.

You can guide others toward solutions in two ways during conversation.

1. Restate in your own words what you heard, for example, “You think…” On one hand, this shows you listened carefully; on the other, it gives the speaker a chance to revise or add to what they said.
2. During the conversation, appropriately analyze the other person’s psychological state and evaluate their emotional state from your perspective. For example, “You are so angry about…” What you say may be something the other person has not yet recognized, allowing you to hit the core of the problem and help them see it clearly.

Listening to others’ disclosures is the best way to identify their inner emotions and the prerequisite for communication. Only by listening attentively can people engage appropriately in conversation.

The following principles deserve attention while listening:

- Maintain eye contact with the speaker throughout.
- Focus entirely on the other person.
- Show your interest.
- Do not let others distract you.
- Avoid distracting actions such as browsing a newspaper.
- Devote your full time.
- When someone cannot immediately reach the point, you share responsibility.
- Do not interrupt.
- Put yourself in the other person’s situation and imagine being in their place.
- Use body language to convey your signals, such as nodding to show agreement and interest.
- Do not remain completely silent, staring only at the other person’s eyes and nodding constantly.
- You may drink a cup of coffee while listening.

These so-called principles are merely reference points, not mandatory rules. Each conversation style requires different listening behaviors.

#### Choosing a Career That Suits You

In the opening section of this book, I already discussed the importance of knowing oneself. To make what follows more valuable, I feel it necessary to briefly explore the issue of career choice.

Recently I received a letter from Mr. Davord. He wrote: “Mr. Balken, you once said I am suited for independent work and suggested mechanical manufacturing. In fact, I worked as an accountant for six years. Later I quarreled with my boss, lost my job, and could not find satisfactory work. One day I remembered your advice and decided to sell things I made myself. Guess what happened? Ha-ha, my income more than doubled compared with my accounting days. Now I even employ two assistants. Of course, what pleases me most is no longer having to serve those unscrupulous bosses.”

I retrieved Mr. Davord’s personality analysis from old files. The data showed he had fair skin (willing to take on challenges), a large build (energetic and quick-tempered), and a sturdy frame (rough and straightforward). With even a little knowledge of personality analysis, one can easily see that the dull, meticulous work of an accountant did not suit him. Fortunately, he eventually found his place and stepped onto his own path to success.

To date I have provided career analysis for at least sixteen thousand people. From my experience, many people fail not because they lack ability, but because they apply their ability in the wrong place. To succeed and be happy, a person must have a clear understanding of themselves and their career.

Many young people tell me:

- “I want to change jobs.”
- “I plan to resign and open a restaurant with friends.”
- “I’m not going to be a salesperson anymore; I want to become a photographer.”

…

Changing jobs carries risk; switching fields is even riskier. For these young people I ask three questions: First, what aspects of your current job dissatisfy you? Second, have you assessed the risks of the new job? Third, if you fail, have you prepared a contingency plan?

I know a young woman who wanted to work in photography. Based on my analysis and understanding of her, photography was a good choice, yet I still asked her to consider the three questions. Ten minutes later she gave me her answers—

First, although her current job paid well, it was not what she liked, so she could never muster enthusiasm.

Second, although the new field was competitive, she had three advantages. First, she had done extensive research on children’s photography; second, she had rich personal networks and many friends; third, she enjoyed being with children and children liked her.

Third, she had decided that if the business failed, she would accept a friend’s invitation to join a magazine as a photographer.

Soon she opened a photo studio and announced it on cards sent to her married friends. She carefully recorded the birthdays of her friends’ children and, before each child’s birthday, sent the parents a sincere letter suggesting they take a commemorative photograph. Through her careful management, the studio’s business grew steadily.

Returning to the topic of young people changing jobs or fields: Further inquiry revealed that a large portion of these young people were overconfident and held excessively high expectations for the new work. Confidence itself is not wrong, but creating miracles requires two conditions: first, a deep understanding of one’s own potential abilities; second, the techniques to bring those potential abilities into play. The former comes from self-analysis; the latter comes from study, training, and experience. Without these two conditions, greater confidence only increases the likelihood of failure. Therefore, before changing jobs, carefully consider the three questions I raised—this is my advice.

Now that you have chosen a career, step together into the turbulent workplace. The following content will influence your career for better or worse.

#### Fill the Other Person’s Stomach First, Then Loosen Their Mouth

“Dining-table culture” (饭桌文化) not only enriches daily meals but also relates to people’s livelihood and safety. Looking around, many business deals are concluded at the table, many contracts are signed at the table, and many heartfelt words are spoken at the table… Clearly, the dining table is an important arena that cannot be ignored when extracting information.

During training, FBI headquarters arranged a special experiment for trainees to help them complete future tasks. The experiment was conducted by Dr. Bert of the New York Comprehensive Institute. The process was as follows:

Some trainees were sent onto the street to find two presumed target informants and invite each to a pre-designated room. The first informant was taken to a room filled with food; the second was invited to an empty room. The final interview results surprised the trainees: in the food-filled room, 56 percent agreed to help; in the empty room, only 20 percent agreed. The reasons for requesting help and the conversation content were identical; only the environment differed, yet the number of agreements and refusals differed by roughly twofold. This shows the power of food should not be underestimated.

Why does food exert such a strong influence on interview outcomes?

- First, after people eat and drink their fill, they become more talkative. If you doubt this, observe crowded restaurants at mealtimes and you will see people at the tables shedding their usual reserve; laughter rises and falls, and complaints and dissatisfaction increase noticeably. Therefore, extracting someone’s true thoughts at such moments is easy even without special techniques.
- Second, sharing a meal effectively demonstrates mutual closeness and helps promote and deepen friendly relations. FBI agents have a conversational technique called “Luncheon,” meaning lunch-table exchange. Its purpose is to strengthen closeness through shared meals. In Japan the technique is renamed “Dinner,” or evening meal, because Japanese hosts usually entertain guests in the evening. Japanese contains a term translated as “people who eat from the same pot,” used to describe friends who live together and implying psychological closeness that makes it easier to speak the truth.
- The final reason is that after eating, people become very tolerant. With a full stomach, they rarely feel hostility toward the other person. Discussing matters at this time can objectively restrain the other person from raising objections, no matter how difficult the request. Even if the other person wants to object, speaking with a mouth full of food is impolite. Therefore, one can try to state one’s request just as the other person puts food in their mouth; this is an extremely effective tactic for preventing objections.

Some say, “Meeting often is not as good as eating together occasionally, and eating occasionally is not as good as drinking heartily once.” This statement highlights the importance of meals and also mentions drinking. If the relationship has reached the point where drinking together is possible, the other person may reveal the truth even without deliberate prompting. However, if the drinking session has a purpose, one must never get drunk, or the result may be counterproductive.

#### How to Make the Chair Most Practical

When entering McDonald’s or KFC, one notices that most chairs are fixed. Consequently, when the restaurant is crowded, people often complain about having to sit with strangers. Yet few realize this is a merchant strategy to increase customer flow by preventing patrons from lingering.

Clearly, seat choice affects daily life. So what kind of seat should one choose to facilitate successful information extraction? The answer depends on the specific purpose of the conversation, the other party, and similar factors.

FBI agents can actively assign the interviewee’s seat, so they usually place the interviewee in a chair lower than their own. If two identical chairs are available, they add extra cushions to their own chair or place something underneath to ensure their seat is at least five centimeters higher.

Why do agents perform these small actions? The sole purpose is to raise their own line of sight. Looking down from above conveys more authority than looking straight ahead or upward and elicits more truthful information.

A psychologist at Washington University once showed photographs of two people conversing to more than one hundred students and asked them to judge which speaker appeared more dominant. The results showed that the person whose chair was slightly higher conveyed a stronger sense of power. Clearly, seat height exerts a direct influence on a person’s presence.

In daily life one can observe that leaders speaking, teachers lecturing, and even ancient emperors all chose elevated positions to display status and authority. When the two parties are equal in strength or one is slightly weaker, choosing a higher chair creates a psychological advantage whose effect often exceeds expectations.

If one does not wish to raise the seat yet still wants to strengthen one’s presence, what can be done? Visitors to FBI headquarters notice that interrogation rooms mostly contain chairs with wheels. One might assume this is for easy movement, but that is not the case. During interviews the roles between agent and interviewee constantly shift; when the interaction moves from confrontation to cooperation, wheeled chairs allow the agent to slide quickly beside the interviewee to offer encouragement.

Thus the main reason FBI places wheeled chairs in interrogation rooms is to let agents adjust distance according to the conversation’s dynamics, thereby controlling the interviewee’s psychological state to extract more information. This method achieves an effect similar to raising the seat.

One can also choose chairs with armrests, because such chairs make it inconvenient for the other person to use hand gestures or other body movements, naturally diminishing their presence. To further reduce the other person’s presence, one can even deliberately shorten one leg of the chair. Dr. Madairu once had students unknowingly sit on chairs whose legs had been shortened and made wobbly while performing attention-demanding proofreading work. Students working on the wobbly chairs made significantly more errors because the unstable chair seriously disrupted their concentration.

Of course, these techniques must be applied with moderation; overuse easily alerts the other person, and once suspicion arises the objective becomes difficult to achieve.

#### Nod Your Head, and the Other Person Will Say More

Many times we see people handing out flyers along cars after the red light comes on. Some of them bow to each driver in the hope that the driver will roll down the window and accept the flyer they push into the car. People sitting inside the car are moved by the bow and roll down the window. Lowering one’s posture is therefore the first step toward acceptance.

Jesse, an outstanding FBI negotiator, is called in whenever agents face a difficult suspect. For Jesse, the most common technique for getting a suspect to tell the truth is “nodding.” Every time he meets an interviewee, Jesse opens with three sentences: “You are Mr. XX, right?” “You are the subject of this interview, correct?” “You are very punctual today!” Each interviewee nods three times in response. These three nods should not be underestimated; they make the exchange smoother because they signal agreement and act like subconscious hypnosis.

During the conversation Jesse nods to show agreement with what the interviewee says. When someone is speaking freely and receives no sign of agreement, they gradually lose the desire to continue. Most people only nod slightly while saying “mm-hmm” or “uh-huh,” but the motion is too small to register. For interviewees who find it hard to open up, the low frequency of nodding is another reason they remain distrustful. Therefore Jesse listens with his whole body and nods noticeably. He often says, “If you want to pry open a suspect’s mouth, nodding is essential.”

American psychologist Dr. Matarazzo once conducted an experiment with police officers and firefighters. Twenty participants each spoke for about forty-five minutes on family background and educational experience, fifteen minutes per topic. In the first fifteen minutes the doctor listened normally; in the second he nodded vigorously; in the third he stopped nodding entirely. A recorder tracked how long each participant spoke.

The results showed that when the doctor nodded vigorously, seventeen of the twenty participants increased their speaking time. Nodding was perceived as a friendly act that satisfied the human need for social recognition.

The experiment also showed that slightly faster or more exaggerated nods worked better than ordinary ones. Checking one’s own nod in a mirror reveals that a normal nod is usually too small to be effective.

When we want the other person to continue a topic at a certain rhythm, we can nod at the right moment to signal agreement. The motion makes them feel our enthusiasm and speak without reservation. When they fall silent, we can nod exaggeratedly and say, “Yes, what you said makes sense; I think so too.” They will immediately feel favorably disposed and often resume the topic.

Communication between people is not complicated. As long as we keep nodding while listening attentively, the other person feels satisfied and keeps talking. If our nodding rate is twice the usual frequency, they sense twice the agreement and return it twofold.

#### Interrupt the Other Person’s Speech, but Don’t Let Your Own Be Interrupted

Zorro was one of the most difficult interviewees FBI agent James ever faced. A former high-ranking government official, Zorro dominated every session with lengthy monologues and gave James no chance to object.
