Because Zorro was widely read, James rarely found an opening, and the first two interviews ended in failure, derailing the entire interrogation plan. James had no choice but to bring in his experienced supervisor, Peter.

Once they were seated, Peter asked a question and Zorro launched into his usual performance, expanding one question into many anecdotes and citing similar cases from home and abroad. While impressed by Zorro’s knowledge, Peter refused to let the monologue derail his plan. He interrupted whenever Zorro was in full flow: “May I interrupt for a moment?” or “I’m not familiar with that incident—could you explain it?” At first Zorro stopped to explain once or twice, but as the interruptions increased he grew impatient. Unwilling to have his train of thought constantly broken, he said, “I haven’t finished yet. Explain after I’m done.” Peter did not yield. He replied firmly, “I really cannot follow what you are saying. If you do not clarify this part, I will understand even less of what follows.” Zorro was forced to stop repeatedly and explain the points Peter claimed not to understand, completely disrupting his own line of thought.

In the end, unable to deliver a long speech, Zorro had to cooperate and complete the interview.

Interrupting someone is normally considered rude. Anyone whose speech is cut off without reason feels displeased, and frequent interruptions can be especially humiliating for people with strong self-esteem. Yet as a conversational technique, interrupting can exert pressure during an exchange, signaling “I know at least as much as you” or “What you are saying is not important enough for me to let you finish.” The two most effective forms are asking the speaker to explain difficult terms or to illustrate abstract points with examples.

Interruption is used mainly in purposeful conversations such as business negotiations or interrogations. Dutch social psychologist Dr. Arco Kalma has said, “Keep interrupting the other person; that way you control the conversation and increase your own power.” In his view, commercial negotiation is less a refined activity than a fight to the death. Although many businesspeople objected, experimental data ultimately supported the technique’s effectiveness.

Dr. Kalma also noted that an interruption must succeed; failure carries serious consequences. If the attempt fails, the other person’s momentum grows while yours weakens. Therefore one must weigh this risk before interrupting—or, like Peter in the example, force the interruption.

#### No Matter Who You Meet, Consciously Open Your Eyes Wide

Helen of Greek myth summoned ships with her captivating gaze; national hero Davy Crockett drove off a bear with his eyes; lovers convey affection through their eyes… In many situations the eyes play a vital social role, and a well-judged glance can carry great impact.

A psychologist once showed participants two photographs of eyes—one wide open, the other slightly narrowed—and asked which they preferred. Most chose the wide-open pair.

People like wide eyes because the pupils dilate at the same time, making the eyes appear brighter and the person more energetic and lively. Wide eyes also send the message “I am very interested in you” or “I enjoy talking with you.” Recipients feel pleased and become more willing to engage.

Former FBI agent Charlie once gave a lecture at a university. Several hundred students filled the auditorium; Charlie was quickly drawn to one female student. Her appearance was unremarkable, yet he could not stop noticing her, as though the entire talk were addressed only to her.

The reason became clear when Charlie realized the student’s eyes were wide open and fixed on his face, as if eagerly absorbing every word. Her admiration energized him; he spoke fluently, adding many examples not in his notes, and the lecture ran long.

Afterward Charlie approached the student, hoping to discuss the talk. When he asked which part had impressed her most, she apologized and shook her head: “I’m sorry, I couldn’t hear you clearly. The student in front of me was wearing headphones, but the music was still loud. I had to read your lips and expressions instead.” Although her answer disappointed him, the impression of her wide-eyed attention remained vivid.

When people encounter something or someone they find interesting, their pupils dilate involuntarily. Observe men viewing photographs of women bathing: pupil dilation averages 11.3 percent; even with swimsuit photos the rate can reach 20 percent unconsciously. Therefore, whenever we meet anyone, consciously widening our eyes makes at least two to three times the impression we would make with normal eyes.

In daily interactions—with friends, clients, or superiors—avoid narrowing the eyes if you want to be liked. Narrowed eyes signal “Please stop,” “I dislike this topic,” or “I am not interested.” Instead, open your eyes wide; beautiful wide eyes open the other person’s heart and earn their trust.

#### Standing Conveys More Presence Than Sitting

Recently a young university lecturer was criticized by the academic affairs office for sitting while teaching. The teacher felt the school’s rule requiring lecturers to stand was unfair.

Throughout history, “teachers stand while teaching” has been standard professional practice. Many schools regard standing as a basic requirement. Standing, they argue, brings energy to the lesson; sitting drains that energy and reduces student interest. Young teachers likewise believe sitting makes them appear listless and fails to engage students. Education experts note that while the two postures are not fundamentally different, standing facilitates interaction and improves classroom results.

A professor at the University of Washington surveyed the different effects of standing versus sitting. Participants viewed one photograph of a seated person and one of a standing person and were asked which posture seemed more imposing. Fifty-nine percent found the standing figure more imposing; forty-one percent chose the seated figure.

FBI supervisor Matt, the youngest in his unit, always stands when addressing agents. Even meetings on complex cases that last three or four hours are conducted standing. When asked why, Matt replies, “I am the youngest supervisor here—an outsider, essentially. Although I graduated from a top university, my practical experience is less than that of the veteran agents. I know this clearly. If I sat down during meetings, my professionalism, enthusiasm, and authority would all diminish. My weaknesses would become psychological disadvantages and my presence would shrink.”

A seated posture suits people who want to relax, but once the lower back relaxes, the voice loses projection. Therefore sitting is not recommended during conversation. Standing, by contrast, silently conveys the message: “I am now in attack mode and ready to engage you at any moment.”

The higher the social status or power of the person you are addressing, the more important it is to stand, because the posture itself exerts a deterrent effect. Consider which feels more comfortable: looking down from above or looking up from below. The former, of course. When making a request—promotion, raise, leave—do so while the other person is seated and you are standing; success rates rise significantly.

The choice of posture must still suit the situation. If you wish to create a relaxed atmosphere, invite the other person to sit first, then sit yourself. Standing can heighten tension and turn light topics serious.

#### When Late for an Important Appointment, Don’t “Apologize”—Say “Thank You”

Although the words “I’m sorry” are easy to say, they must be used with care; apologizing is not always the right move. In certain situations an apology can give others leverage and exact an unforeseen cost.

“Thank you for waiting so long. Are you ready? Let’s begin…” FBI agent Charlie’s remark left Millie, who had waited fifteen minutes, with no further grounds to dwell on his lateness and no reason to refuse the interview.

You may wonder why Charlie did not apologize. Was he being rude? For Charlie the important interview had to reach its substance quickly; the case had already been delayed by Millie’s repeated postponements. A simple “thank you” expressed gratitude while minimizing the awkwardness caused by his lateness.

Among FBI conversational techniques, refusing to apologize and saying “thank you” instead is one of the most assertive ways to seize control and is used frequently during interviews.

Whether in interrogations or ordinary exchanges, every word FBI agents use is carefully chosen; even a slight misstep can alter the atmosphere and outcome. Below are simple examples illustrating the importance of precise wording.

- **The difference between “but” and “and”**: When agreeing with a friend’s view you might say, “That’s a good topic, but there are still many…” Your agreement is thereby discounted in the friend’s mind. An FBI agent would say, “That’s a good idea, and if we refine it a little it will be even better…”
- **The difference between “first” and “already”**: When reporting a newly assigned task to a boss, one might say, “Boss, first I need to familiarize myself with the situation…” The boss may infer that much work remains undone. An FBI agent would typically reply, “Boss, I have already familiarized myself with the situation here…” The tone conveys optimism rather than pessimism about future progress.
- **The difference between “around X o’clock” and “exactly X o’clock”**: When setting an interview time, FBI agents give a precise hour. They rarely say, “Are you free around nine on Wednesday? We’d like to talk.” Such phrasing suggests uncertainty and implies the matter is not important. Instead they say, “We would like to speak with you at nine o’clock Wednesday morning. Do you have time?”

#### II. The Eyes Reveal Your Soul

A smile is a weapon that displays friendliness outward, while the eyes are the window that reveals the mind. Gaze and eye contact are the most infectious forms of facial language. In interpersonal interactions, the eyes coordinate with spoken language to express countless variations of thought and emotion. The duration of eye contact, the degree to which the eyelids are open, the extent of pupil dilation, and other changes in the eyes all convey the subtlest information.

During an interview, an experienced interviewer obtains various information about you by observing your gaze. Of course, if you are familiar with reading the micro-expressions in the interviewer’s eyes, you can also gather useful intelligence from them.

When conversing with the interviewer, pay attention to the other person’s expressions:

- Gaze directed upward from below generally indicates inquiry and means “I am willing to listen to you.”
- Gaze directed downward from above generally means “I am paying attention to what you are saying.”
- Head slightly tilted with gaze fixed on you generally means “Oh, so that’s how it is.”
- Eyes showing brightness generally indicate interest.
- Glancing at the watch every few seconds signals urgency or impatience and means the speaker hopes the other person will end the conversation.

If a candidate understands the meaning of eye language, they can skillfully use it to support their speech during the interview. The requirements for using eye language in an interview are:

1. Look at the other person with a natural, gentle, friendly, and sincere gaze. Each type of eye contact carries a specific meaning: direct gaze conveys seriousness; sideways glance conveys contempt; upward glance conveys contemplation; downward glance conveys shyness, and so on.
2. In the interview, gazing attentively at the other person shows strong interest in what they are saying. To avoid making the interviewer uncomfortable with prolonged staring, use “soft scattered gaze” appropriately by placing your eyes on the upper triangular area from the eyes to the middle of the forehead.
3. Avoid staring fixedly at the other person’s eyes, as this will make them extremely uncomfortable. Also avoid letting your gaze dart up and down within a localized area, which will leave the other person baffled.
4. Do not look around or glance left and right, which appears distracted; do not hunch your chest and lower your head, which appears timid or uninterested; do not tilt your head high with eyes looking at the ceiling, which appears arrogant. All of these are signs of rudeness and lack of cultivation.
5. Note how often the other person blinks. Blinking 6–8 times per minute is normal. Excessive blinking indicates doubt about the truthfulness of what is being said, while a blink lasting more than one second becomes an eye closure, indicating disgust or disinterest.
6. When your eyes meet, maintain natural eye contact for 1–3 seconds before slowly looking away. This conveys openness and makes it easier to gain the other person’s trust. Someone who immediately averts their gaze upon meeting another’s eyes easily arouses suspicion or is seen as timid.

#### II. Through the Boss’s Eyes

The eyes are the window to the soul. A person’s words can lie, but the subtle differences reflected in the eyes are hard to hide. No matter what scheme a person has in mind, their eyes will immediately and faithfully reveal what they are thinking. When dealing with a boss, if you can carefully observe their eye movements and gaze, you can discern their inner world.

1. The boss does not look at you at all while speaking, or even raises their head. This often means they look down on you, consider your abilities insufficient, and think your suggestions unworthy of consideration.
2. The boss looks down at you from above, indicating a person who likes to dominate others. This gaze expresses a sense of superiority as well as arrogance and self-importance.
3. The boss stares at you for a long time while you report work or present a plan, showing they expect more detailed and comprehensive information; their impression of you may still be incomplete.
4. The boss always appears sharp-eyed, as if wielding two swords, and maintains the same expression. This is a display of cold indifference and superiority, while also implying: “I can see through your thoughts one hundred percent! Do not try to deceive me!”
5. The boss occasionally glances upward, meets your eyes, then looks down again, repeating this several times, indicating they have not fully trusted you and are still uncertain about you.
6. When the conversation reaches the main point, the boss sometimes shifts their gaze into the distance, showing they have no interest in what you are saying; however, if their eyes suddenly brighten, it means what you said has caught their attention and sparked interest.
7. A dull look in the boss’s eyes most likely means something unpleasant or unexpected has occurred.
8. A flickering gaze in the boss’s eyes most likely means they are worried about something but cannot truly speak openly about it, or do not want to reveal the actual situation.
9. Continuous blinking by the boss indicates they are trying hard to suppress their emotions; if the blink is slower and larger in amplitude, it means they cannot believe their own eyes, so they blink hard to clear them and confirm whether what they see is real.
10. The boss’s gaze shifts to the side with eyebrows slightly raised or a smile on the face, indicating interest; if the sideways glance is accompanied by lowered eyebrows, a furrowed brow, or downturned corners of the mouth, it signals suspicion, hostility, or a critical attitude.
11. The boss looks at subordinates in a friendly and candid manner, or sometimes winks at them: the subordinate is capable and likable, and even mistakes can be forgiven.
12. The boss gazes into the room while nodding slightly from time to time: this is a very bad signal, indicating the boss wants the subordinate to obey completely, regardless of what the subordinate says or thinks.

#### IV. Recognizing the “Expressions” of Closure—Leave in Time

You have paid attention to the interviewer’s micro-expressions and to your own speech and demeanor. A good beginning and process are important, yet many people overlook the ending.

University graduate Xiao Li once chatted confidently with an interviewer for more than two hours during an interview. Toward the end, the interviewer began checking the time frequently, though still remaining polite in speech. Xiao Li failed to notice the interviewer’s change and continued talking at length. Finally, when the interviewer’s colleague rushed in to announce a meeting, the interviewer had to stand up politely, apologize, suggest rescheduling, and then leave hurriedly. Xiao Li did not shake hands or say goodbye when the interviewer departed.

Xiao Li had believed the job was certain, yet never received any response from the interviewer.

Successful interviews have a set time limit. Too short a time prevents a full presentation of oneself; too long wastes both parties’ time. Within that period, the basic exchange of information is usually complete, so one can check whether the other party shows signs of wanting to end the interview.

If the interviewer keeps looking at the watch or changing posture, it means they want to conclude the interview. If you fail to notice and keep talking, the interviewer’s impression of you will drop sharply. At the end of the interview, no matter how pressed for time, always shake hands and say goodbye. If a candidate lacks even this perceptiveness and courtesy, job hunting will be difficult.

Usually, when an interviewer believes the interview should end, they send body-language signals indicating closure. You should recognize these cues.

There are three main signals:

1. The interviewer frequently checks the watch, meaning they are pressed for time or have grown impatient. The action often implies “You have already taken up a lot of my time,” “Can’t you see I dislike you?” or “We have said enough; it is time to go.”
2. If the interviewer frequently changes sitting posture, it means they feel they have been sitting too long and need to shift position, indicating they have other matters to attend to and want the interview to finish quickly.
3. If the interviewer obviously looks around, rarely maintains eye contact, shifts their gaze elsewhere, or appears restless and fidgety, these all indicate they want to end the conversation. You should stop your long speech and conclude the talk.

At this point, you must still close the interview with proper courtesy. If you made a strong impression at the beginning and became the interviewer’s preferred candidate, pay special attention to your final manners. Failing to observe small courtesies can still cost you the job you almost secured.

#### Interpreting the Boss’s Hand Gestures

1. The boss particularly likes to place both hands behind the back and clasp them while speaking, especially when inspecting work or facing subordinates. From any angle, this posture conveys authority, confidence, and strength.

   However, if one hand behind the back grasps the wrist of the other, it indicates the boss is filled with frustration or anger; the higher the grip, the stronger the frustration or anger. The gesture is an attempt to regain a sense of control.

2. The boss likes to rub the palms together while speaking, conveying a positive expectation and heartfelt joy. Another situation: if the boss is undecided about something, they will also rub their hands together.

3. The boss likes to rest one hand on the cheek while listening. This gesture often means the topic feels uninteresting, your remarks fail to engage them, or they are thinking about their own matters and wish you would listen to them.

4. The boss always gestures animatedly while speaking, even on the phone, indicating strong work ability and the capacity to convey intended words and actions smoothly and effortlessly. Such a person can mobilize others and themselves, excelling at enlivening the atmosphere and uniting everyone.

5. An open palm always represents truthfulness, honesty, loyalty, and compliance. When wanting to show frankness and sincerity, the boss will extend one or both palms toward the other person—an often subconscious action indicating complete openness. If both hands are pressed together and downward with the body maintaining balance, it signifies moderation and calmness.

6. Hands on hips with elbows pointing outward: this is a traditional body-language posture of someone accustomed to giving orders, usually adopted when facing a concrete power issue.

7. The boss leans back in the chair, places both hands behind the head, and spreads the elbows outward: this certainly shows relaxation at the moment, but it may also indicate arrogance.

8. The boss pats a subordinate on the shoulder—signaling recognition and appreciation—yet only a pat from the side truly conveys acknowledgment and appreciation. A pat from the front or above indicates looking down on the subordinate or displaying power.

9. Fingers together forming a pyramid shape with fingertips pointing forward: a signal that the other person’s suggestion will be rejected.

10. Clenching the hands into fists: not only to intimidate others but also to defend one’s own viewpoint; striking the table with a fist is simply an attempt to prevent others from speaking.

#### I. Through the Boss’s Head Movements

Liu, the company sales manager, once submitted a payment request to the company owner. He felt quite uneasy at first because he had no idea whether the owner would approve it. While reading the document, the owner asked questions, and Liu answered truthfully and logically. After finishing, the owner lowered his head, thought for a moment, finally said “good,” and offered some words of praise and support on the spot. Liu assumed the owner had agreed and felt relieved. He waited for the signed and stamped application to be issued, but one week passed, then two weeks, and the payment form remained untouched. When he finally asked a colleague in the owner’s office, he learned the owner had been dissatisfied with the request all along and had simply left it on his desk.

Liu could not understand why the owner had said “good” to his face yet immediately went back on his word and rejected the request. In fact, he had not noticed that while the owner was saying “good,” his head kept shaking slightly.

Head movements, also called cephalic language, are among the most common in interpersonal communication: nodding and shaking the head. The types are simple, yet because these movements are easier to overlook than body language or facial expressions and often occur unconsciously alongside speech, they are frequently missed.

Nodding generally expresses affirmation or approval. When the boss holds a positive or affirmative attitude, they will nod sincerely while speaking as a hint.

When the boss agrees with your viewpoint, observe their head movement. If accompanied by a slight nod, you can trust the answer. If the boss gives an affirmative reply without nodding, “lowers the head to think,” or even shows signs of shaking the head, you can basically conclude the words do not match the true intention; do not place high expectations on the answer.

Shaking the head usually expresses “no.” If the boss claims to agree with your opinion, check whether they make a slight head-shaking motion. If they offer various affirmations and promises while gently shaking the head, it reveals an underlying negative attitude.

If your boss tilts the head, leans forward, rests the chin on a hand, and appears thoughtful, it means your words carry considerable persuasive power and they are seriously considering your proposal. If your boss likes to tilt the head upward, you must not take it lightly. This signals an unequal dialogue and rejection of your proposal. You should proceed with caution.

#### Explanation

Did you notice Mr. Miyashita’s eyebrows drawing toward the center? Is this the micro-expression of “anger,” or the conversational signal of “deep thought”? To distinguish “anger” from “deep thought,” the key lies in the speed of the expression.

An instantaneous change with only slight alteration in complexion indicates the micro-expression of “anger”; if the change in complexion is obvious, it represents the conversational signal of “deep thought.”

If it is the micro-expression of “anger,” it can be understood as irritation caused by not understanding the clerk’s explanation: “How do I log into the official website?”, “What does this card mean?”, “Does ‘free’ mean the battery is free, or is the monthly three-hundred-yuan membership fee free?” It is not difficult to imagine several reasons why Mr. Miyashita might feel puzzled.

For the micro-expression of “anger” in this case, a careful and easily understood explanation is advisable. Avoid unclear wording or omitted subjects; it is absolutely necessary to demonstrate how to use the membership card for the customer.

If it is the conversational signal of “deep thought,” it means the clerk’s explanation was difficult to understand. The cause of the difficulty can be viewed as the same as in the “anger” situation. The response method can also follow the same approach used for “anger.”

However, if one wishes to advance a step further in customer service, the level of care and attentiveness toward Mr. Miyashita must be arranged differently according to whether the expression is “anger” or “deep thought.”

Compared with “deep thought,” “anger” is a more negative emotional state. Handling the micro-expression of “anger” requires finer attention. For example, adding words of apology, greeting the customer with a smile, and eliminating or confirming the causes of irritation and points of confusion one by one are all good ways to respond.

This case has a follow-up. Because Mr. Miyashita did not know how to log into the official website and three hundred yuan in membership fees were automatically deducted from his account each month, he angrily declared, “I will never buy anything from that store again! I had no idea what was going on, and three hundred yuan is still deducted every month. The explanation was far too sloppy!”

The possibility of losing a repeat customer because micro-expressions could not be read is the consequence this case illustrates.

#### Missing the Micro-expression of “Contempt” Dooms the Presentation

The micro-expressions that require special attention during a presentation are those already discussed earlier, including “anger,” “surprise,” “disgust,” “conversational signals,” and “contempt.” Among them, the micro-expression of “contempt” appears as “one corner of the mouth raised.” At first glance this micro-expression resembles a smile. If the micro-expression of “contempt” is masked by a smile, detecting it correctly is quite difficult; missing the micro-expression of “contempt” leads to disastrous consequences.

If the presenter sees the audience listening with a “smile” and feels reassured, they will assume the presentation was successful. Yet the expression taken for a smile may actually be “contempt.”

The listener may feel superior to you or look down on you. Mistaking the micro-expression of “contempt” for a smile becomes a major cause of presentation failure.

- A team member displays a “smile” while listening to the presentation but lacks motivation during execution.
- The general manager praises my proposal with a “smile,” yet the proposal is ultimately not adopted.
- The interview examiner speaks to me with a smiling face; why was I not hired?
- The client signs the contract with a “smile.” Could it be that I lowered the price too much?

Have you experienced anything of this sort? The reasons for these failures can of course be considered in various ways, but the possibility of mistaking the micro-expression of “contempt” for a smile is very high. Failing to perceive the true meaning of “contempt” is usually a major cause of presentation failure.

How can one notice the micro-expression of “contempt”? How should one respond once it is detected?

The key to noticing the micro-expression of “contempt” is to observe the other person’s expression carefully while presenting the content in which you feel most confident.

The moment you think “Great! I am speaking really well right now” is especially important. Your confidence may make the other person feel “This person is not saying anything important at all!” This emotion can flash across the face as the micro-expression of “contempt,” yet it is often masked by a “smile.”

#### "Changes in the Buyer's Facial Expressions" Are Important Clues for Observation in Sales Negotiations

In business negotiations or direct sales to consumers (clients) at retail locations, accurately assessing the other party's payment limit or sensing the depth of the client's pockets and appropriately suggesting an amount can facilitate a successful transaction.

On the other hand, when a contract is concluded, one may later regret that "it could have been sold at a higher price" or "there was still plenty of room in the other party's budget," or one may be overwhelmed by the client's momentum, resulting in poor sales performance and a selling price lower than the originally planned discount level. What causes these differences between successful and failed negotiations?

Success and failure in negotiation arise from a complex interplay of various factors, not from any single cause. However, performance achieved through negotiation is closely tied to the ability to read facial expressions, as confirmed by experiments conducted by Hillary Anger Elfenbein, professor of organizational behavior at Washington University.

These experiments established that sellers who achieve good results in negotiations possess a highly developed ability to accurately interpret facial expressions. In contrast, buyers' negotiation ability showed no correlation with their facial recognition skills.

Although the experiments did not clearly reveal how sellers effectively use buyers' facial information to close deals, inferences from other negotiation experiments and real-world negotiation experience suggest that the combination of "changes in the buyer's facial expressions" and "differences in how buyers and sellers perceive product information" plays an effective role. Generally, sellers possess more information about a product than buyers.

In other words, high-performing sellers can detect changes in the buyer's interest, preferences, or budget range and adjust the strength of their product pitch points, recommend suitable items, and skillfully leverage their product knowledge to make sales. Of course, the ability to interpret a buyer's psychological state from facial expressions and apply that information varies depending on the seller's choice of words and depth of product knowledge.

A seller's facial recognition ability can be considered a necessary condition for successful negotiation.

#### Find Your Own Position

The famous French fabulist La Fontaine[^1] once told a story about the stomach and the limbs—

The limbs no longer wanted to work for the stomach; they wished to live a leisurely, gentlemanly life. They said: "Without our hard labor, the stomach would have nothing but the northwest wind to drink. We toil like beasts every day, all for its sake. Yet while we sweat and suffer here, it sits there well fed and watered. Let's strike and make the stomach understand that we have been sustaining it all along."

So the hands stopped grasping, the legs rested, and everyone unanimously told the stomach to find its own food and drink.

Yet the poor limbs, deprived of nourishment and fresh blood, soon grew weak. They finally realized that although the stomach appeared idle every day, its contribution to the collective was no less than that of the limbs.

This story teaches us:

- In any collective, each person has their own division of labor and responsibilities. The "limbs" cannot demand that the "stomach" perform tasks outside its scope, and vice versa. Whether you are an ordinary employee or a manager, you must maintain a clear understanding of your role, neither neglecting your duties nor overstepping boundaries, and remain vigilant against role misalignment.
- Only when everyone fulfills their respective roles and responsibilities can the whole operate organically and protect the interests of each individual. Otherwise, not only does one suffer, but the collective is also harmed.

Upon entering the workplace, the first task is to clarify your identity, define your responsibilities, and establish a clear sense of your position. The Temple of Apollo at Delphi bears the ancient Greek maxim that has influenced humanity for millennia: Know thyself. If you aspire to become an excellent manager, you must first develop a clear and accurate understanding of yourself before becoming the boss. Only by recognizing your role in the workplace will you know how to manage and be managed, and what to say or not say. Conversely, if one's self-positioning deviates, not only will one fail to utilize one's talents and contributions effectively, but one will also hinder others' work and damage both personal reputation and company interests.

#### Techniques for Leading Negotiations

Next, let us examine how sellers, in negotiation scenarios, apply facial recognition skills in concrete situations. The procurement process is divided into several stages; here we focus on the final stage—"whether to confirm the purchase of the product." We consider the situation from the seller's perspective in business negotiations or retail sales.

You have already provided a detailed product explanation to the potential buyer and fully answered all questions. You have said nearly everything you can; your remaining cards are almost played out. The buyer's questions gradually decrease, and both you and the buyer fall into silence. The final moment of decision is approaching. Will they buy, or not? Before you and the other party are Product A and Product B displayed side by side. At this moment, the negotiating counterpart may be considering comparisons between the old and new products, between Product A and Product B, or between price and budget. Imagine the various possibilities.

Under these circumstances, various expressions or micro-expressions (微表情) appear on the buyer's face. Which expression or micro-expression indicates a willingness to purchase or sign a contract, so that one more push will result in a "deal"?

In conclusion, when a certain degree of emotion appears on the other party's face, that expression must be taken seriously; the display of emotion indicates that the buyer is using it to help confirm their decision, meaning they are considering whether to buy.

Whether the emotion appears as a regular expression or a micro-expression depends on the importance of the situation. Compared with purchasing a small item in a store, concluding a large contract in a business negotiation places heavy responsibility on the buyer, who must therefore conceal their true intentions, making micro-expressions more likely. Even in small purchases, if the client's budget is limited yet the item must be bought, the decision's importance increases and micro-expressions may appear.

#### II. The Pupils That See Straight into the Client's Heart

During a business meeting, junior salesperson Xiao Zeng accompanied Manager Liu to meet a client. The client nitpicked the samples relentlessly. Xiao Zeng grew restless while watching Manager Liu, who remained calm, held the price line, and eventually the meeting ended unhappily.

Curious, Xiao Zeng asked Manager Liu, who smiled confidently and replied, "They will call soon and accept all our terms." Xiao Zeng wondered whether Manager Liu had become overconfident.

A few days later, the client did call and accepted almost all of Manager Liu's conditions for the batch. Xiao Zeng was astonished. Manager Liu then revealed the key: although the client had expressed extreme dissatisfaction with the product, Manager Liu noticed that when the client's boss picked up the sample, his pupils immediately dilated, indicating that only this company's product met their requirements; the criticisms were merely bargaining tactics.

The human pupil is one of the most honest organs; it enlarges or shrinks according to psychological changes. When a person sees something they like, their pupils dilate even if their face remains expressionless. This dilation and constriction can accurately reveal a person's mental activity and its shifts.

If a client’s pupils dilate while examining materials you hand them, it indicates liking or excitement, and your work can proceed smoothly. Conversely, if the pupils constrict, the client is in a negative, guarded, or even angry state, and you must devise another approach.

Clients often criticize your product with various excuses. When facing such clients, always check their pupils first. If the pupils dilate, they are lying. Hold your ground. If necessary, add bargaining chips to the transaction and do not be misled by their words.

#### Section 5: Precautions for Recognizing Micro-Expressions

The preceding text introduced many workplace applications of micro-expressions. In practice, the most important factor is the accumulation of daily experience. Some widely circulated techniques for reading micro-expressions may reflect momentary subconscious reactions or habitual movements rather than fixed rules; one should not rigidly apply micro-expression doctrines such as "eyes looking left indicate recall, looking right indicate fabrication of lies," since habits differ between individuals and between Eastern and Western cultures. Colleagues should therefore maintain good daily interactions and familiarity so that micro-expression techniques can be applied while minimizing misreadings.

In many work situations—discussing progress, reporting status, or addressing responsibility issues—observing the other party's movements, demeanor, and micro-expressions to identify their bottom line protects oneself and provides the advantage of knowing both sides. In reality, both parties at the negotiating table usually possess some intuitive "people-reading" experience, even if it has not been systematized into academic "micro-expression" knowledge. Tension is typically higher in meetings and negotiations, so micro-expressions may appear more briefly and require sharper observation.

In the workplace, is there a way to correct one's own micro-expressions? Micro-expressions are often mistaken for habitual actions without awareness of the underlying emotions. One can adopt daily stress-release methods such as running or listening to music. Asking friends to observe your micro-expressions can also help identify and correct undesirable ones that appear under pressure.

Focusing excessive energy on "reading faces" is insufficient and may even invert priorities. Strengthening professional knowledge and continuously improving one's capabilities so that one's abilities truly match job requirements remains the fundamental way to prevail in competition.

#### Dangerous Signals That Destroy Relationships

Although views on maintaining marriage differ, the key to marital harmony lies in a balanced relationship of mutual respect together with care and tolerance—principles that should be universal. Love, in the end, is about learning to "accept."

Consider the act of kissing. If a stranger placed their tongue in one's mouth, the mere thought would evoke disgust; yet with one's lover it is acceptable. Love initially transforms rejection into acceptance. Once "disgust" (expressing a sense of rejection) arises, separation naturally follows.

Dr. Gottman has also studied couples' interactions. The logic of relationship breakdown is that the emotion of "contempt" destroys the balance of mutual respect, while the emotion of "disgust" converts tolerance (acceptance) into rejection, causing intimate relationships to collapse. This applies not only to spouses but also to romantic partners and other interpersonal relationships.

Observational evidence confirms that displays of "contempt" and "disgust" are dangerous signals of impending relationship destruction.

A group leader, speaking critically of a rival organization before a crowd, displayed a combination of "anger," "contempt," and "disgust" on their face, igniting riots or terrorist attacks. The precise mechanism by which such an expression combination incites violence remains unclear.

It is conceivable, however, that the messages conveyed by "anger," "contempt," and "disgust"—images of "aggression," "moral superiority," and "rejection"—become embedded in the crowd's subconscious, stirring thoughts that translate into direct action.

#### The Micro-Expression of "Anger" as a Moment to Apologize

Suppose you are a salesperson or receptionist. While explaining product features, a client suddenly displays a micro-expression of "anger." Why might the client feel angry? Various possibilities exist. Your explanation may be too slow, too complex, or too fragmented for the client to grasp the main points. Conversely, it may be too fast, too jumbled, or too abstract. Repeatedly explaining what the client already understands can also cause annoyance.

"Anger" is an emotion triggered by "obstacles to achieving a goal." The client's goal in listening to the product explanation is to decide whether to purchase. The obstacle can therefore be defined as whether they can efficiently obtain the information needed to decide.

How to remove this obstacle, and whether the client can obtain the necessary conditions, are important considerations. When a crisis arises and you detect the client's micro-expression of "anger," apologize immediately.

"I'm sorry my explanation was unclear! Please tell me what you most want to know." Responding appropriately in this manner can ease the client's "anger" and steer the conversation toward the client's needs.

How, then, should one handle a client whose face conveys a message of "deep thought" or puzzlement?

The "deep thought" situation is easier to understand than "anger." When a client shows "deep thought," they are usually puzzled by your explanation. The response is similar to handling "anger," but in most cases, providing a careful explanation, allowing time for reactions during the explanation, and appropriately asking for the client's thoughts prove more effective.

#### Do You Want to Know How Much Your Boss Trusts You?

The relationship between superior and subordinate is based purely on business. A superior selects you as a subordinate because of the company's operational needs, not for personal social or recreational reasons.

If a superior does not trust a subordinate, they generally will not assign important tasks. A calculating superior may put on a show of trust and utter inspiring words. If you believe those words literally, the blow will be exceptionally heavy when you later realize they were false. If you notice your superior unconsciously rubbing their eyes while talking with you, looking at the floor while raising their eyebrows, tilting their head slightly downward to one side, or pressing their lips together with a forced smile at the corners, these actions clearly indicate a negative attitude and show that their words are insincere.

If your superior's previously smiling face suddenly turns gloomy, their hands resting on the table are drawn back to their chest, their eyebrows knit together, and from then on they stop saying things like "Everything depends on you" or "I feel at ease with you handling it," while ignoring your suggestions or taking measures such as sidelining you or narrowing your scope of work, it means they have never truly trusted you.

Even if this is the case, do not develop feelings of inferiority, lose motivation, or discard what little confidence you have, nor should you reproach or despise your superior with thoughts of "So that's the kind of person they are." Recognize that this is simply a superior's standard method of motivating subordinates. What you should actually do is work harder to enrich and demonstrate yourself, gradually increasing your superior's trust in you.

#### II. Micro-Expressions During Colleague Collaboration

For colleagues to work in harmony, they must learn to read faces and understand each other's true thoughts. The following 11 common micro-expressions are provided for reference.

1. Speaking rapidly, holding an object in front of the chest as a barrier, and deliberately maintaining distance from the interlocutor indicate anxiety.
2. The corners of the mouth turning downward is a classic expression of having made a mistake.
3. When asking a question one already knows the answer to, the eyebrows rise slightly.
4. Facial features drawing toward the center of the face indicate hidden dislike.
5. Hands placed flat at the sides with a rigid posture is a "stop" gesture, indicating the person is in a state of irritation or anger.
6. Genuine versus feigned anger: suddenly speaking loudly accompanied by strong body language; if there is a time gap between the two, the anger is feigned.
7. When inquiring about something, if the other party's shoulder on one side twitches, it indicates lack of confidence in what they are saying.
8. Nostrils flaring outward with lips tightly closed indicates anger.
10. Hands clasped and rubbing together: a typical self-soothing posture, usually indicating that the person does not believe what they are saying and is trying to reassure themselves.
11. Touching the forehead or brow ridge as if wiping sweat indicates shame.

People who "get along well" in the workplace are simply those who say the right things and do the right things to the right people at the right times. In workplace interactions, one must always pay attention to the other party's state, emotions, and psychological needs.

In workplace interpersonal interactions, knowing how to "read faces" is extremely important. Whether requesting a raise from a superior or collaborating with colleagues, you need sharp observational skills to interpret others' thoughts. Correctly applying micro-expression techniques minimizes misunderstandings and helps build rapport with colleagues more quickly.

#### Before Divorce, There Are Precursors in Facial Expressions During Communication

**Case:**  
You are discussing your child's education with your wife. She wants the child to attend a private elementary school, but you believe a public school is sufficient. Opinions clash and an argument nearly breaks out.

Wife: "Honey, I want the child to go to a private elementary school. If accepted, it is basically a direct path to university, which will be very helpful for finding a job in the future."

You: "Public school is fine. Simply studying hard will not make the child a mature adult. Besides, how can we know they will easily find a good job in the future?"

Wife: "Is it not good to study well? And I am not saying it will be easy, I am saying it will be 'helpful.'"

**Question:**  
What action should you take in response to your wife's reaction?

**Explanation:**  
Your expression shows the left corner of your mouth raised. This is the micro-expression of "contempt." From your wife's expression when she speaks her second line, wrinkles appear around the nose and the nasolabial folds form a bell shape, with the upper lip pulled upward, indicating the micro-expression of "disgust." Both "contempt" and "disgust" carry rejection and can interrupt the ongoing communication.

Of course, a single instance of the "contempt" or "disgust" micro-expression will not seriously damage the relationship, but if such emotional states continue to appear, the couple may enter the countdown to divorce.

To maintain marital harmony, it is important to apologize to your wife, show that you are willing to lower your posture, and once again express respect for her. For example: "Sorry, sorry! Could you bring me the school information so we can discuss it together?" Keeping the conversation going is most important.

#### 1. Pay Attention to Your Gaze

You observe others through your gaze, and others observe you through your gaze. Using your gaze well leaves the best impression on colleagues, superiors, and clients. Below are three different methods of using gaze and their occasions.

1. **Staring**: When communicating and listening, staring is the most commonly used gaze. Focus your eyes on the other person. For business matters, limit the gaze to the forehead down to the eyes to convey sincerity and seriousness. For social situations, look at the triangular area from the eyes to the mouth.
2. **Scanning**: When you are seated with a group in a meeting room and they are listening to your speech, pay attention to scanning... During scanning, look forward and then sweep purposefully. The benefit is that everyone listening feels you are paying attention to them rather than communicating with any single individual, allowing you to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the audience's psychological reactions. You can also adjust the rhythm, content, and tone of your speech at any time based on the scan, maintaining control of the conversation. Make each person feel you are looking at them. The specific method is to focus primarily on the main target (the highest-ranking person present) and move your gaze from left to right, then right to left (or front to back, then back to front) to achieve simultaneous communication with everyone present, avoiding neglecting anyone and thereby gaining unanimous goodwill.
3. **Soft focus**: This is looking without truly focusing. Speeches require alternating between soft and focused gaze—"focused" on a portion of the audience, "soft" on everyone. A speech should achieve "no one in the eyes, yet everyone in the heart."

#### 4. Watch the Client's Micro-Expressions During Negotiations

During meetings and negotiations, micro-expressions can be used to determine whether the other party is deliberately provoking, shifting responsibility, or lying, achieving the goal of knowing both yourself and the opponent to win every battle.

1. Repeating the question stiffly when answering is a typical sign of lying.
2. Rubbing the nose is an attempt to hide the truth. (This has been explained earlier.)
3. Raising the chin and pursing the lips indicates embarrassment.
4. Chin raised and corners of the mouth turned down indicates self-blame.
5. If you make a mistake, the other party will show a slight upward curl of the mouth corners that quickly returns to normal.
6. Shrugging one shoulder or pressing the lower lip while speaking indicates extreme lack of confidence in what is being said.
7. Inconsistency between body and words indicates lying; facial expressions that are asymmetrical left to right are the same, and such emotions are likely fabricated. For example, before shaking the head to deny something while lying, there may be a momentary nod.
8. Left corner of the mouth raised with lips tightly closed indicates contempt.

Every change in the client's expression or demeanor may signal the end of further business discussion. Therefore, astute professionals must capture every subtle tremor and change in the client's expression and demeanor, promptly inferring the client's psychology from these changes and identifying the other party's bottom line. This protects oneself and provides a path to knowing both sides for victory in every battle. In fact, both parties at the negotiation table are usually more nervous than usual, so micro-expressions may appear for shorter durations than normal, requiring sharper observational skills.

#### Frequent Eye Contact Can Also Convey Affection

If one wishes to prevent relationship breakdowns such as divorce, breakup, or violence before they occur, what should be done? Relationship breakdown results from the interweaving of various complex factors and has no simple solution. However, from the perspective of expression studies, the following two methods are recommended.

The first method is to observe the other person's expressions regularly. This allows clear mastery of the other person's emotional changes and expression characteristics, enabling more sensitive detection when emotions shift. Once emotional changes are noticed, appropriate words or actions can be used to respond at any time. Furthermore, being frequently noticed by a loved one creates a sense of being acknowledged, which pleases the other person. Simply paying attention to the other person's expressions in daily life can maintain the relationship and reduce the likelihood of disputes.

The second method is to watch for "contempt" and "disgust" expressions on the other person's face during arguments. When these expressions appear, the person will not accept what is being said. Therefore, in such situations, regardless of how unreasonable the other person seems, one must temporarily accept their statements and apologize.

No matter how justified one's position, insisting on it at this moment will only sever communication between both parties. This damages the relationship and begins a downward spiral in the relationship.

Properly interpreting expressions and micro-expressions allows prediction of future interpersonal relationships and construction of a mutually desired future.

#### Are "Interest and Concern" Conversational Signals Faked?

How should one respond when a client displays conversational signals of "interest and concern"? The client may genuinely be interested, or may simply be matching your tone.

Some clients deliberately display "interest and concern" out of consideration for the salesperson. However, there are also cases where the expression is not deliberately faked but naturally emerges during the conversation. Upon seeing signals of interest, no immediate response is required.

When explaining a product, if the client raises both eyebrows for two to three seconds, displaying an "interest and concern" appearance, it may indicate continuous interest or a deliberate display of "surprise." When "interest and concern" reactions appear consecutively, even if not in deep thought, the client may have questions about your words, desire more information, or simply be interested.

The key to distinguishing genuine "interest and concern" from acting "surprise" is the presence of a smile. "Interest and concern" signals are usually accompanied by a slight smile. A faked "surprise" expression raises both eyebrows noticeably, opens the mouth wide, and gives an artificial impression. "Surprise" micro-expressions are harder to fake. However, interpreting a client's "surprise" micro-expression reveals what the client is truly interested in.

#### The Micro-expression of "Surprise" Is the Best Time for Explanation

If, under the same circumstances, the client’s face shows a “surprise” micro-expression, what does that mean? Compared with “anger,” surprise is a very brief emotion whose meaning is also quite limited. Therefore, the micro-expression of “surprise” is a critical focal point, indicating a high likelihood that the client is particularly interested in a specific part of the explanation. So when a client displays a “surprise” micro-expression, that point should be explained in greater detail.

Sometimes the selling points a salesperson or receptionist wants to emphasize differ from the points the client wants to hear. When the desire to close the deal is too strong, the salesperson may enthusiastically rattle off product features that have nothing to do with what the client actually wants to know. Like a double-edged sword, this approach has both advantages and disadvantages. There are certainly cases closed through enthusiasm and sincerity, yet there are also countless examples of deals that fall through.

Moreover, this nonstop “hawking” style suits extroverted, lively people with a natural sales personality. Adjusting the sales approach according to the client’s micro-expressions and conversational cues is less constrained by personal character or temperament; it is a method anyone can use to improve sales skills and raise the probability of a successful close.

#### Being Able to Speak Does Not Equal Successful Communication If You Cannot Read People

Many professional courses and books focus on “successful presentation techniques” or “precise speaking skills.” A presentation is the act of conveying key points and core messages to others. Therefore it is important to craft strong openings and closings and to learn appropriate vocabulary, tone of voice, body language, and conversational style.

“Conveying” is not merely a one-way transmission of information; it is a two-way process that requires observing the other person’s reactions. Learning how to convey a message means mastering not only speaking techniques but also the ability to interpret the listener’s responses.

Studying only the sending side is like learning only the speaking portion of English conversation.

No matter how fluently you speak English, if you cannot understand what the other person says, a conversation cannot take place. Likewise, no matter how skilled you are at speaking, if you cannot read the other person’s reactions during the exchange, you cannot know whether your message has been received correctly.

To optimize presentation skills, the following sections therefore focus on the micro-expressions that must be watched most carefully.

#### ❷ Precursors of “Disgust,” “Fear,” and “Sadness”

When a buyer shows a “disgust” expression, it indicates that although the person wants to buy, they cannot yet make the decision; some condition is causing hesitation. At this point, a compromise must be found.

When a buyer shows a “fear” expression or micro-expression, it means the buyer will be troubled if they do not purchase the item. A firm stance while waiting for a decision is one approach, but offering some concession will usually lead to a smoother transaction.

A “sadness” expression or micro-expression carries the same possibility as fear: it signals regret that the purchase may not happen and is a sign that a decision is imminent. If the seller wants the item purchased, it is necessary to explore how to reach agreement.

“Contemplation” conversational cues also frequently appear on a buyer’s face. The moment a buyer shows “contemplation,” the seller should seize the opportunity to emphasize selling points or restate key sales information to deepen the impression and give the wavering buyer a helpful nudge.

#### What to Do When You Detect a “Contempt” Micro-expression

When the emotion of “contempt” expresses a claim of superiority, the person displaying contempt feels superior to you and will seize any chance to demonstrate that superiority. Therefore, when a “contempt” micro-expression appears, the appropriate response is to “allow the other person to assert superiority.”

Using the earlier example, if the other party shows a “contempt” micro-expression toward your opinion, you can stimulate their sense of superiority with statements such as:

“What does Mr. ○○ think?” “My idea seems inadequate.” “If my suggestion needs improvement, how would you do it better?”

In contract negotiations, during the final price discussion, if the other party shows a “contempt” micro-expression, they are likely thinking, “I won this price negotiation!” In such cases, consider offering non-price concessions or added-value options.

#### “Anger” and “Surprise” Expressions That Salespeople Must Remember

The micro-expressions sales and reception staff most need to remember are “anger” and “surprise,” along with the corresponding conversational cues.

Ideally, one would master every type of micro-expression and respond appropriately. Yet if priorities must be set, the most important are the micro-expressions of “anger” and “surprise” and the conversational signals of the “concentration” face and the “information-gathering” face.

The reason is that the core task of sales or reception work is explaining products and services. When clients cannot understand the explanation, they display the “concentration” face in order to follow the content. When they are interested and want to learn more, they show the “information-gathering” face.

Accurately reading the customer’s state of mind, knowing when to add selling points and when to skip explanations, is a vital skill for sales and reception staff. Let us now examine concrete situations.

#### Section 1 Using Micro-expressions Appropriately in Interviews

The first threshold when moving from campus to society is the job interview. Even the calmest person feels nervous facing a stern interviewer; no matter how hard you try to stay composed, your micro-expressions may still betray you.

Many graduates are eliminated because their micro-expressions reveal them, with interviewers citing “poor psychological resilience.” How a candidate reacts under pressure is often something interviewers deliberately test. Sometimes they even pose pressure-inducing questions to observe the response.

The best way to eliminate unfavorable impressions and present your best self is to reduce your own stress. Chewing gum, listening to music, or focusing on deep breathing before the interview can all help. In addition, pay attention to the following points:

#### Section 6 Watching Your Partner’s Micro-expressions

When you begin a relationship, use micro-expressions to read the other person. After marriage, monitoring your spouse’s micro-expressions is also an important topic.

During dating, micro-expressions in the matchmaking phase often conceal personal shortcomings; in the cohabitation phase they more often hide mistakes. Once married, the relationship gradually settles into a stable state that involves mutual exposure and systematic desensitization. At this stage micro-expressions also help coordinate the couple’s relationship—for example, by pinpointing problems more accurately when repairing the bond. Given the average statistic that people lie three times in every ten minutes of conversation, it is necessary to stay alert to small cracks in the relationship, whether to prevent problems or to “stockpile grain.”

#### ❶ Pay Attention to the “Social Smile”

First, consider the situations in which a social smile appears. When a buyer displays a social smile, it can be viewed as a sign that further negotiation is desired or that the negotiation is about to collapse. A genuine smile indicates satisfaction with everything. If a buyer maintains a genuine smile throughout the purchasing process right up to the final moment, the buyer is likely to proceed directly to purchase. However, when a social smile appears, it suggests the buyer is trying to curry favor with the seller—perhaps a prelude to “Can you lower the price a bit more?”—or a sign that the buyer hopes the relationship will not deteriorate and wants to reset the negotiation to its original blank-slate state. Experience shows that a social smile surfacing at the final stage of negotiation often signals an impending breakdown, a tendency frequently observed among Japanese and other Asian negotiators.

#### (3) Recognizing Different Types of Colleagues

It can be said that the types of people you meet on the street are the same types you will meet as colleagues in the workplace.

Some people stay busy all day yet produce no results. Some work hard only when the boss is watching and become lazy the moment the boss leaves. Some remain silent but deliver impressive results. Some are passionate about work and warm toward others yet constantly make mistakes… Only by identifying each colleague’s type can you adopt the right approach and reduce friction and conflict. For example, with colleagues who habitually watch the boss’s face or those who stay silent, you must remain alert, because they often say one thing to your face and another behind your back. With outgoing, straightforward colleagues, careful attention can yield a great deal of useful information.

#### Reading the Other Party’s “Hidden Emotions” in Business Meetings and Negotiations

This chapter introduces micro-expressions that require special attention in common work and daily-life scenarios. What micro-expressions may be hidden during ordinary conversations without any particular purpose?

Business negotiations involve the exchange of various ideas and objectives. Some emotions are expressed directly; others remain hidden. When ideas or objectives must be concealed, there is usually a reason for doing so.

What causes these hidden emotions, and how should one respond? This section explains how to detect the other party’s true intentions in meetings and negotiations and how to adjust the direction and focus of the conversation accordingly.

#### Detecting “Danger Signals” Hidden in Emotions in Daily Life

Even with close people, etiquette must be observed. In other words, one should remain courteous toward those nearest to oneself—family members, romantic partners, good friends. No matter how well you know each other or how attuned your minds are, directly expressing inner feelings can still feel awkward.

Sometimes familiarity makes one even more reluctant to let the other person know one’s deepest thoughts. Yet in such cases the relationship may develop shadows precisely because genuine emotions are being hidden. How can one avoid invading the other person’s privacy while preserving important relationships?

This chapter introduces, from the world of micro-expressions, potential crisis situations between spouses, lovers, and parents and children, as well as techniques for maintaining interpersonal bonds.

#### Chapter 8 Micro-expressions, Great Success

Once you master the recognition of micro-expressions, you hold a window into the other person’s inner world. Applying this skill successfully in the workplace and in life gives you a powerful advantage, allowing you to interact with greater confidence and precision.

Usually, when people hear or see something they like or dislike, or feel uncomfortable with the person they are talking to, their body language changes. These changes require you to develop a keen “sense of smell” to read their “micro-expressions” and infer their psychology. In this way you can navigate smoothly both at work and in daily life.

#### ❸ Use Gaze as a Clue When a “Neutral” Expression Appears

If the buyer maintains a “neutral” expression until the end of the negotiation, their thoughts and intentions are difficult to read. However, one usable clue is the buyer’s gaze. Does the buyer’s gaze rest on the product? If it remains fixed on a particular point, it indicates interest in the item and that the buyer has reached the final consideration stage. People’s eyes naturally drift toward things that interest them. Likewise, when thinking, people’s eyes tend to fix on a single point. The appropriate response is the same as for “contemplation”: seize the moment to emphasize key selling points.

After purchasing a personal computer, Mr. Miyashita was persuaded by the salesperson to sign up for a membership card. The card costs three hundred yen per month; if the computer breaks, the card provides warranty coverage and priority service.

The salesperson explained:

Salesperson: “Please register on the official website. Whether it’s a battery replacement or any other part, with this card everything is free.”

Mr. Miyashita: “I see. Understood.”

After completing the purchase, Mr. Miyashita left the store.

#### (5) Knowing When to Yield

Colleagues are peers, and the relationship among them is the most delicate and difficult to harmonize within a company. Competing for limited opportunities, mutual wariness, exclusion, and suspicion are common. As a newcomer, to win colleagues’ goodwill you must know when to yield. Opportunities that will not significantly advance your career are better given generously to colleagues; there is no need to fight tooth and nail for them. Doing so not only earns goodwill but also allows you to observe the company environment more calmly and prepare for better opportunities.

In addition to your assigned duties, here is a small technique for gaining goodwill: perform “small favors.” For example, when fetching the newspaper, bring a colleague’s copy as well; when buying coffee, bring one for a colleague too.

#### Body Language Observation When Dealing with Superiors

##### Unable to Read the Boss, Busy to Death Without Favor

In the workplace, employees cannot help but guess their boss’s thoughts, and bosses also try to figure out what their employees are thinking. This creates a dual relationship of “seeing through” and “being seen through” between bosses and employees. As an ordinary employee, you do not need to like your boss or hate your boss, but you must understand him so that you can turn your boss into a “resource” for your success. It can be said that whether you can read your boss is the best test of a person’s level of “insight.”

Jesse passed the assessment last month and joined a large company as a manager’s assistant. On his first day, his direct supervisor told him: “You’re new and don’t understand the work yet. You can go around to the various departments first and familiarize yourself with the specific business and processes.” But two weeks later, the supervisor harshly criticized Jesse for being idle and lacking enthusiasm for work.

Now Jesse sits across from me, his two thick eyebrows almost knitted together: “Mr. Balkan, I can’t stand it! How can there be such a person? He told me to do that, and now he says if I keep this up I should quit.”

I reassured Jesse: “Don’t worry yet, Jesse. I want to know, what exactly have you been doing these past two weeks?”

“Following the manager’s instructions, learning about the work of several key departments such as the planning department, marketing department, and publicity department. Every day is the same. Actually I find it very boring, but since the boss instructed it, I had no choice but to comply.”

That is how I knew why Jesse had been criticized. He had not understood the “implied meaning” of his supervisor’s words—that a new employee should quickly familiarize himself with the environment and get involved in the work. Of course, Jesse’s oversight was not surprising. When I shook hands with him, I clearly sensed that his body structure was of the sturdy type, and his eyebrows, way of speaking, and movements all told me he was a straightforward young man, careless and not inclined to think deeply about things.

In the workplace, however, you need an extra eye and must think from another angle. Often a boss’s intentions are not expressed directly and require careful interpretation. Sometimes a boss says one thing but expects you not to do it; sometimes, because of his position, a boss cannot easily state his position but has already given a hint, so you must be “discerning” and never force the boss. If a boss praises you in private, it may not be genuine appreciation but a reminder that if you do not reflect on yourself, you may be in trouble. In short: if you cannot read your boss, being busy to death will not win favor.
