Through my analysis, Jesse finally recognized his own naivety and oversight. He began to calmly ask me how to read his boss’s mind. To understand a boss is to know his character, work style, and thinking habits. This returns us to the core of this book—“reading people”—which I have already covered in sufficient detail and need not repeat.

Every month I meet young people like Jesse. Through conversations with them, I have summarized several “workplace iron laws” that I believe will be helpful to you.

##### Body Language Observation When Dealing with Superiors

When interacting with a superior, observing the eyes and hands reveals the inner mind more clearly.

- The superior speaks without looking up or at anyone. This shows contempt for the subordinate, regarding the person as incompetent.
- The superior looks down at people. This conveys a sense of superiority—domineering, arrogant, and conceited.
- The superior stares at the subordinate for a long time. This indicates the impression of the subordinate is still incomplete—waiting for more information.
- The superior looks at the subordinate in a friendly and open manner, or occasionally winks. This is a good sign—the subordinate is capable, liked, and even mistakes may be forgiven.
- The superior’s gaze is sharp, expression unchanged, as if a sword were piercing through the subordinate. This expression displays power, cold indifference, and superiority, while also implying to the subordinate: do not try to deceive me; I can see through your thoughts.
- The superior occasionally glances upward, meets the subordinate’s eyes, then looks down again; if the superior does this repeatedly, it confirms uncertainty about the subordinate.
- The superior gazes into the room, nodding slightly from time to time. This is a very bad sign and may indicate that the subordinate must obey completely; no matter what the subordinates say or think, the superior pays no attention.
- During conversation the superior presses palms together from above, using the body for balance—this indicates relaxation and calm.
- During conversation the superior places hands on hips, elbows pointing outward; this is often the posture adopted when facing a concrete power issue.
- The superior sits in a chair, leans back, places both hands behind the head, elbows pointing outward; this posture shows relaxation at the moment but may also indicate conceit.
- During conversation the superior points an index finger at the other person—a naked display of superiority and combativeness.
- During conversation the superior clasps hands behind the back; this is also a sign of superiority.
- During conversation the superior pats the subordinate’s shoulder—this indicates recognition and appreciation; only a pat from the side truly signifies recognition and appreciation. A pat from the front or above signals looking down on the subordinate or displaying power.
- During conversation the superior brings fingertips together, forming a pyramid shape with both hands pointing forward—this is a signal that the other party’s suggestion must be rejected.
- During conversation the superior clenches fists; this posture indicates not only an attempt to intimidate but also a determination to defend one’s own views. If the fist strikes the table, it is simply an attempt to stop others from speaking.

##### Stress Signs Leaking from Subordinates’ Expressions

- A subordinate suddenly hands in a resignation letter!
- An outstanding subordinate suddenly says they want to change jobs!
- A subordinate who has always been serious, diligent, and proactive about every task suddenly develops emotional problems…

Whether for yourself or those around you, you have probably had such experiences: “suddenly” quitting a job, “suddenly” wanting to change jobs, “suddenly” being unable to continue working… In fact, none of these are truly “sudden.” They are the accumulation of depression or a state of ongoing dissatisfaction. Before the “sudden” event, the person has very likely already sent out several distress signals.

The precursor to these distress signals is discussion of anxieties and expectations regarding promotion and compensation, workplace interpersonal troubles, and so on. If good communication occurs in advance, the relationship between subordinate and superior deepens and management crises are more easily avoided. In reality, however, it is unlikely that either superior or subordinate will have sufficient time and energy to discuss and communicate everything.

From the subordinate’s standpoint, “Can I really consult the boss about this?” leads to hesitation, accumulating until something “sudden” happens. From the superior’s standpoint, the thought arises: “If only we had discussed it earlier, we would not have reached today’s situation.”

Both sides usually differ in their view of the “timing” of discussion. In other words, the balance point between “wanting to consult the superior” and “wanting to discuss with the subordinate” is misaligned.

How can the balance point of discussion be found? At this moment, the reading of micro-expressions (微表情) comes into play. Because micro-expressions are suppressed emotions that leak out, in certain situations the appearance of a micro-expression on a subordinate’s face indicates that the emotion can no longer be fully suppressed and psychological fluctuation has occurred.

This emotional fluctuation usually disappears automatically as the subordinate gradually becomes accustomed to the work and builds confidence, but some people are never able to resolve it and accumulate depressive emotions. In either case, if the subordinate’s micro-expressions can be detected and read, showing a little extra care at that moment can reduce the possibility of future escalation into a major problem.

##### Have “Sadness,” “Contempt,” and “Disgust” Been Overlooked?

People with suicidal intent who hide it may say with a smiling face, “I’m doing fine right now!” Although the smile conceals the distress, the distress that cannot be hidden reveals a micro-expression of “sadness.” When someone carrying a heavy burden who has hinted at wanting to commit suicide more than once suddenly appears full of energy, special attention is required! Although the words say “It’s already fine!” if a micro-expression of “sadness” is still visible, it means the distress has not actually been resolved.

In a hospital consultation room, psychiatric patients listening to a doctor’s suggestions sometimes display micro-expressions of “contempt” or “disgust.” It should be noted that the appearance of “contempt” or “disgust” micro-expressions does not necessarily mean mental illness; however, patients showing these emotions are less willing to follow the doctor’s instructions and suggestions compared with other patients, making recovery more difficult.

When a doctor offers various treatment suggestions or future treatment directions, patients unwilling to seriously accept the instructions tend to show “contempt,” while patients who do not want to accept them tend to show “disgust.” Patients displaying these expressions will not follow the doctor’s professional advice and will instead act in their own way. The result, of course, is that the mental condition will not be cured. When a suggestion is made to a subordinate regarding a certain issue and a micro-expression of “contempt” or “disgust” appears on the subordinate’s face, it indicates that the suggestion has not been taken to heart.

One final reminder: the “asymmetrical” expressions, “motionless above the nose” expressions, and micro-expressions of “sadness,” “contempt,” and “disgust” introduced so far should not be taken as immediate proof that a subordinate has a mental health problem. When these expressions are captured, please consider that they result from accumulated stress in the subordinate. The most appropriate action is to pay closer attention and observe the subordinate’s movements than usual.

##### Common Facial Features of Mental Health Problems

Here the key micro-expressions and facial points to watch for regarding “mental health problems” are explained. Detecting “mental health problems” from expressions has been identified through various studies. Research to date indicates that “asymmetrical” expressions, “motionless above the nose” expressions, and micro-expressions of “sadness,” “contempt,” and “disgust” are all associated with “mental health problems.”

However, observing these expressions does not allow an immediate conclusion of “mental health problems.” First, it is important to consider the expression together with the context. Next, we will examine the reasons for each expression one by one.

An “asymmetrical” expression appears when a person deliberately tries not to reveal their true intention on the face. In simple terms, it is the expression shown when trying to control emotions at that moment. The brain’s actual emotion interferes with the emotion-control mechanism, causing the facial muscles to move asymmetrically and forming an asymmetrical expression. The person may say “It’s fine!” or “Full of hope!” yet contradict their true intention.

A “motionless above the nose” expression means the will to send or receive messages is weak—in other words, an expression in which emotion has died. During conversation, our eyebrows usually move. Eyebrows raised emphasize words or phrases; eyebrows lowered indicate disagreement with the other person’s opinion. When sending or receiving messages, eyebrows always move unconsciously. If these movements are absent, it indicates a weak will to send or receive messages. In the worst case, emotion has already been wiped out. When a subordinate’s face shows no expression, especially when the mouth moves but the eyebrows do not, it is very possible that the subordinate’s mind is overshadowed by a great shadow.

##### Bosses and Employees

In common work relationships, a large amount of verbal or written language communication is usually involved, but people occasionally “converse” through body movements. The relationship between bosses and employees is no exception. Therefore, we must recognize and correctly interpret those different postures and make full use of them.

Of course, as an employee, learning to interpret the negative facial expressions shown by the boss is very important. For example, raised eyebrows, slight head turns, doubtful looks when rejecting a suggestion, or not looking the employee in the eye. If the employee does not realize the boss does not want to talk at the moment, the boss may enter the second stage—moving the body and looking at the watch on the wrist while sighing deeply (see Figure 5.3). The ability to interpret and accurately predict the boss’s attitude in a timely manner is a very valuable asset for your career.

##### (2) Do Not Get Too Close to Your Superior

A young man told me that he often drank and chatted with his superior, just like friends. Then one day he was suddenly informed that he was being transferred from the New York headquarters to the Texas branch. The young man ran to ask his superior in disbelief, but the superior shrugged and said, “There’s no way around it; this is the company’s decision.”

As a workplace professional, it is understandable to build a good relationship with your superior, but getting too close is very dangerous. Why? Because the more a leader is understood by a subordinate, the greater the sense of crisis; they will never keep danger by their side. Moreover, being close to the superior easily arouses resentment from colleagues and is not beneficial for handling interpersonal relationships. Therefore, between you and your superior, you must approach at the right time yet still maintain distance.

##### Observation Techniques for Solving “Interpersonal Relationship” Problems

In student days, we can avoid people whose personalities do not match our own in daily life. But after entering society, we can no longer do as we please; whether we get along or not, we must learn to interact with them. Especially for supervisors who lead subordinates and teams, regardless of personality compatibility, they must be able to manage people and organizations within interpersonal relationships.

Once you have subordinates, the superior bears additional responsibility and must also understand how to respond. In this scenario, let us glimpse the management method of “leading hearts” from the world of emotions.

##### Signs Indicating Boss or Employee Satisfaction

- Frequent eye contact with others
- Open expression or smiling face
- Casual standing posture, arms or legs apart
- Body continuously moving closer to others during conversation
- Hands placed in front of the chest
- Lincoln-style sitting posture

When you notice that your boss or colleague is dissatisfied and feels irritable or angry, never let the situation worsen. Based on your judgment of the other person’s body movements, you should find a way to solve the problem before it seriously damages your relationship or affects productivity.

##### (3) Make Yourself Indispensable to Your Superior

Every excellent leader has both a “think tank” and an “execution team” around them; the former helps with planning and advice, the latter helps implement and execute, and the two complement each other under the leader’s direction. If you are a rational person, use your intelligence and strive to become a core member of the “think tank”; if you are a practical person, use your execution ability and make the “execution team” your platform. In short, becoming someone the superior cannot do without will be the capital for your greater success.

##### (1) Always Remember You Are a Subordinate

Between superior and subordinate there is always a “leading” and “being led” relationship, so no matter how outstanding you are or how terrible you think your superior is, you must never openly “challenge” them.

#### Business and Negotiation

##### Clients and Professionals

The relationship between clients and professionals is one of the most sensitive interpersonal relationships. Successful lawyers, accountants, consultants, and others understand the importance of body language communication, while less successful professionals seem unable to send signals of wanting to build good relationships. In fact, the communication skills between professionals and clients can be improved. Below, we will discuss their relationship from the client's perspective.

If a client seeks help from a newly practicing professional, they are likely to doubt the other's ability but also hope for some advice. If the advice given is too simple or too general, the client may become full of doubts, because most of them firmly believe their situation is special, and the professional must come up with some fresh ideas. Even worse, some clients only listen to the advice they want to hear and are not prepared to accept other opinions from the other party. All these factors can make it difficult for the professional to convey conclusions to their client.

So, how can professionals avoid causing client concerns and build a constructive relationship with them?

One way for professionals to build trust with clients is to record what the client says, regardless of whether the client thinks it's important. This approach makes the client feel that the other party understands and notices their specific situation.

Another way to make the client feel attended to is for the professional to adopt the postures we discussed earlier for interpreting others' behavior. For example, tilting the head slightly to one side, supporting the head with one hand, etc. These postures not only indicate that the professional is interested in what the client is saying but also show that they are thinking of ways to help the client.

In the process of negotiating with clients, it is equally crucial for professionals to avoid negative body movements as it is to adopt positive ones. If the professional leans back in the chair with hands in a casual steeple shape, the client will see it as indifference to their problem.

If there is a large desk between you, the client will think: "He is not on my side; he doesn't care about my problem, only about making money." To solve this, more and more professionals are rearranging their offices, such as removing large desks, to reduce unnecessary hostility and promote communication with clients.

Additionally, professionals should not display a commanding or lecturing posture toward clients but should convey an approachable feeling. Avoid the hand-grabbing-collar gesture that indicates arrogance, as it will damage the relationship with the client.

Below, we briefly summarize some common negative and positive actions between clients and professionals.

##### Buyers and Sellers

Successful salespeople know that the ability to correctly identify and interpret buyers' body language and the skill to control their own body movements are key to whether a deal is reached. Buyers are also very aware that salespeople will make gestures or movements to make them feel relaxed or to draw them into the promoted product or service.

In many buying and selling transactions, both buyers and sellers evaluate various negative emotions shown by the other party with an "I must win, you must lose" attitude. For example, the buyer leans back in the chair, stares at the seller, crosses arms and legs, and asks in a skeptical tone: "What do you want to talk about?" Meanwhile, the seller may lean forward in a sprinter's eager posture while using fingers to indicate their intent.

If the buyer dislikes this hard-sell approach, they may lean back and adopt a defensive posture. If the seller becomes uneasy because the pitch failed, they too will adopt a defensive posture, such as fidgeting, crossing arms and legs, or even turning their head away from the buyer. The situation then deteriorates rapidly.

Experienced salespeople quickly infer the buyer's personality traits by observing their body movements—for instance, whether the buyer's sitting posture is casual and relaxed or formal and serious. Once the salesperson identifies the buyer's personality, they adjust their sales approach accordingly. If the buyer appears casual and has a sense of humor, opening with a joke will instantly liven up the atmosphere; if the buyer looks serious and formal, the salesperson should stick to conventional, structured opening lines.

Salespeople can also convey friendliness and sincerity through their own body movements to shorten the distance with the buyer. For example, some salespeople consciously mirror the buyer's posture, such as spreading their legs or tilting their head. This helps most people feel relaxed and sets the stage for the sales discussion.

Once the buyer shows interest, the salesperson can present the product according to the buyer's needs or move directly to the buyer's desk to introduce it. In this situation, the buyer will notice the salesperson's nonverbal actions and may signal that they do not welcome the close proximity. If the buyer leans back, moves away, or even shifts their chair aside, the salesperson should immediately return to the original position.

Below, we briefly summarize some negative and positive actions that may occur between buyers and sellers.

##### Answering Techniques

In negotiations, answering questions is unavoidable, and how you answer often determines your position. If you are inadvertently led into a trap, it means negotiation failure. Therefore, I believe it is necessary to teach novice negotiators several practical answering techniques.

- **Answer selectively**: Experienced negotiators know that not every question must be answered. For provocative questions that harm your side's image or boring questions about personal privacy, you can choose to say "no comment."
- **Avoid absolute answers**: Always leave yourself room when answering. Revealing your strength too early gives the other side an opening; stating things definitively almost guarantees the end of cooperation.
- **Do not rush to answer**: Before replying, analyze the substance of the question, clarify the other party's true intent, and then respond in a targeted way. If you sense a trap, use ambiguous phrasing to avoid being put on the defensive.
- **Go along with a misunderstanding**: Sometimes the other party may have misunderstood your meaning, but if the situation favors your side, going along with the misunderstanding can be a good choice.

##### Watch for Small Movements

Once negotiations enter the substantive phase, both sides usually discuss terms. When an immediate agreement cannot be reached, how should the conversation continue? Pay attention to the following small movements; they indicate the other party is likely about to take the next step.

- **Clearing the throat**: If the other party clears their throat during negotiations, it means they cannot accept the proposed terms and you need to prepare; if they clear their throat when talks are stalled, it shows they are about to speak and feel somewhat nervous.
- **Fingers spreading open**: Spreading the fingers releases tension and increases confidence. If the other party gradually opens their fingers, it indicates they are relaxed and ready to state their views.
- **Leaning forward with mouth slightly open**: When talks fall silent, if the other party leans toward the table with mouth slightly parted, it shows they have formulated terms and intend to continue the discussion.
- **Lightly clenching both hands**: If the opponent places lightly clenched hands in front of them, it means they are still thinking. You need to consider internally how to break the deadlock, because the other party usually will not speak first. They are cautious, planned, and will not decide easily.

##### Facial Expressions

During negotiations, the face is the part of a person that receives the most eye contact. Most people prefer a friendly, approachable face over a stern, rigid one. In other words, "cold faces," "bitter faces," and "angry faces" all detract from your position and are best avoided.

In daily life, we can easily read a person's inner thoughts through static features and dynamic changes in the forehead, eyebrows, eyes, and mouth corners. In professional negotiations, however, "disguise" is a common tactic. Therefore, you must be more cautious when interpreting facial expressions.

For example, a "smile" can indicate either agreement or disagreement. If one corner of the other party's mouth rises while their gaze shifts elsewhere, they likely have reservations about your proposal. At such times, you need to readjust your thinking.

Another example: throughout the negotiation the other party appears attentive and focused, yet at the end shows a hesitant expression. They are probably testing you to see if you will make further concessions.

##### Using Props

True negotiation experts rarely negotiate empty-handed because they understand the principle that seeing is believing. They often bring models, pictures, charts, reports, samples, and other visual items as props to strengthen their negotiating position. However, several points must be observed when using props: first, you must be very familiar with the props you bring; second, you must ensure their quality; third, you must time their use correctly during the negotiation—knowing when to deploy and when to put them away. I can tell you without exaggeration that the correct use of props can increase your negotiation success rate by more than 50 percent.

##### (1) Eye Contact

There is an invisible "weapon" in negotiations: presence. Whether a person's presence is strong or weak can easily be seen in their eyes. As I mentioned earlier, the eyes readily betray a person's inner state. You can tell at a glance whether the other party is sincere and confident or timid and hesitant. The other party can likewise read your thoughts from your gaze. Therefore, to close the deal, you must let the other party perceive your sincerity, and the most effective way is through eye contact. Remember the gazing technique I taught you? Used well, it doubles the results.

##### Positive Actions That Yield Significant Results for Professionals

- Lincoln-style sitting posture
- Taking notes
- Frequent eye contact
- Chin-supporting or chin-stroking interpretive postures

When professionals first meet a client, they must pay attention to the client's various body movements. If you sense the client harbors doubts or unease, you can pair your words with positive body movements to build trust. When you do so, you will soon see the client display a relaxed expression and quickly accept your professional advice.

##### Eyes

If the other party's eyes suddenly widen—even for just a second—they have likely heard or thought of key information; if their eyeballs move slightly, they are thinking about what you just said and you should press the advantage; if they avoid looking at you or glance away immediately, congratulations—you are in the dominant position; if they stare at you with a cold, hard gaze, they are clearly threatening you to accept their terms.

##### Positive Actions That Yield Significant Results for Sellers

- Casual body posture
- Sincere facial expression
- Mirroring the buyer's body movements
- Once the buyer shows interest, move closer and tailor the product introduction to their needs

Like other interactive relationships, buyers and sellers are engaged in a dance. The seller takes the lead but must keenly observe the buyer's reactions and then carefully choose their own movements. Only then will the buyer be successfully "drawn in" by the seller.

##### Signs That the Buyer Is Resistant or Uninterested

- Arms or legs crossed
- Angry, dissatisfied, or exclusive facial expression
- Critical interpretive posture, with index finger placed on one side of the face and other fingers curled below the mouth
- Head turned away from the seller while looking sideways
- Suspicious nose touch
- Suspicious ear-root rub
- Suspicious eye rub

##### Signs That the Client Is Doubtful or Worried

- Arms or legs crossed
- Hands tightly clasped
- Critical interpretive posture, with index finger placed on one side of the face and other fingers curled below the mouth
- Head turned away from the professional while looking sideways
- Suspicious nose touch
- Suspicious ear-root rub
- Suspicious eye rub

##### If You Cannot Handle the Opponent, What Proves Your Worth

To succeed and persuade the opponent, relying on words alone is not enough. Effectively using body language together with appropriate speaking strategies greatly increases the likelihood of negotiation success.

##### Signs That the Buyer Is Willing to Accept or Interested

- Arms or legs apart
- Sincere expression or smiling face
- Less frequent face-touching
- More frequent eye contact
- Chin-supporting interpretive posture

##### Negative Actions That Backfire for Sellers

- Arms or legs crossed
- Adopting a sprinter's eager posture before the buyer shows interest
- Quickly closing the distance with the buyer

##### Negative Actions That Backfire for Professionals

- Leaning back in the chair with an arrogant air
- Forming a steeple with the hands
- Placing feet on the desk
- Grabbing the collar with the hand

##### Signs That the Client Trusts and Is Satisfied

- Arms or legs apart
- Less frequent face-touching
- Interpretive postures

#### Interview and Lie Detection

##### Spotting Small Lies from Micro-expressions

**Case**:

When you, as the interviewer, ask the question “What do you think is the most important thing in work?” during a company recruitment of new graduates.

Applicant: “I think the most important thing in work is action. For example, I have a very smart friend, Mr. K. He has opinions on every matter regarding the goods displayed at our school festival booth, procurement, or how to make profits. Having opinions is a good thing, but the problem is that he doesn’t participate in any actions at all and only talks. Without actually taking action, you completely don’t know how difficult it is to concretize ideas.”

Interviewer: “Indeed, the action to concretize ideas is important. So, what do you think of Mr. K’s ideas? And have you taken any measures regarding Mr. K’s reactions?”

Applicant: “Mr. K, who takes no action at all, makes me very angry, so I demanded that he participate.”

**Question**: To know more deeply about this student’s action characteristics or personality, what kind of question should be asked?

**Explanation**: It can be seen that the applicant’s eyebrows are raised upward and drawn toward the center, with eyes wide open. The expression of wide eyes and wrinkles between the eyebrows easily shows that this is the micro-expression of “fear”.

This is inconsistent with the “anger” expression indicated by the applicant’s words “I feel very angry”. The moment the micro-expression is revealed is the timing for questioning, especially the moment when the micro-expression is inconsistent with the words, which is the key point that needs attention for questioning.

The ways of questioning include direct inquiry or indirect questioning that supports the emotion.

- The direct method is for the interviewer to use the interpreted emotion and directly ask: “Was there any feeling of unease at that time?”
- The indirect method to support the emotion is: “It takes courage to voice opinions to others or to prompt them to act! How did you encourage Mr. K to actively participate?”

The emotional function of “fear” is “ensuring physical and mental safety and avoiding crises”. The interviewer first expresses the emotion on behalf of the applicant with “It takes courage!”. This way, the applicant can feel supported and be more willing to express their true feelings.

Whether using the direct or indirect method, the fundamental principle is the same. In reality, one should feel angry rather than afraid and uneasy about Mr. K’s behavior, so it can perhaps be interpreted that the feeling of fear or unease was stronger than anger at the time, and from this, infer the applicant’s emotional tendency.

If continuing the conversation based on the literal meaning of the applicant’s words “makes me very angry”, it is very likely that the applicant’s emotional tendency cannot be correctly judged. If the “indirect questioning method” can be practiced, perhaps the applicant can also discover their true emotional tendency. Finally, infer personality from emotional tendency.

People who generate “anger” emotions toward similar events will proactively understand the “obstacles” of the problem, which can be inferred as having an inner strength to independently and proactively solve problems; while people who feel “fear” emotions will dread the threat of the problem, which can be inferred as trying to solve and handle it, but with less proactive action.

By listening to the applicant’s inner voice using different micro-expression detection techniques, the interviewer can more accurately infer personality, and even emotional tendencies or action tendencies that the applicant themselves have not noticed can emerge.

##### Scene Setting: Interview

You must prove to the interviewer: I am a capable person! Regardless of whether your personality is gentle and delicate or rough and unrestrained, slow and methodical or impatient and aggressive, once you decide to enter a certain industry or department, you must display the abilities most suitable for that industry or department.

1. Appear neatly and appropriately in front of the interviewer. You cannot change your body type, skin color, appearance, and other features, but you can choose clothing suitable for yourself. Based on industry characteristics, wearing appropriate clothing can reflect your qualities and abilities. If you are not good at grasping colors, then wear black; it can give you a sense of power and authority.
2. The handshake should have strength. If you have the opportunity to shake hands with the interviewer, remember to put in some force. As I analyzed earlier, through the handshake, you can very intuitively feel the other’s muscle tension and bone hardness or softness, and this is not only a means for you to understand the other but also a means to showcase yourself.
3. Timely make your gaze meet the other’s gaze. When the interviewer asks you a question, never lower your head and remain silent, nor look around. In the limited time, what best reflects your honesty and confidence is the eyes. Research shows that appropriate eye contact can increase favorability.
4. Maintain a smile, making people feel you are an outgoing person. No matter who it is, no one wants to be with a gloomy person, while outgoing people have an aura that makes people unconsciously generate trust. You can be introverted, but you must not be timid. When you smile while looking at the other person, it can make people feel you are relatively outgoing and effectively reduce inner tension, killing two birds with one stone.
5. Speak less and listen more. Time is limited; do not expect one interview to fully showcase yourself. The more you speak, the more emotions will inadvertently be revealed, and the greater the possibility of loopholes, which directly relates to whether you can pass the interview. So even if you are eloquent, temporarily put away your desire to perform and be a sincere listener.

##### Mastering Four Minutes to Win Over the Interviewer

I can confidently tell you: It only takes four minutes to read a person.

From the moment a person walks into my office to sitting down, just one minute, then opening pleasantries and self-introduction, at most three minutes. In these brief four minutes, I can basically figure out the other’s intentions. Perhaps you will question that I am talking nonsense, but language communication experts, through tracking analysis of thousands of business negotiations, finally concluded: Between two people who do not know each other, 60%~80% of the initial impression is formed within four minutes after the first meeting. — Completely consistent with the conclusion I reached through practice!

Never underestimate these four minutes, because your success or failure is very likely to depend on the impression left on the other within these four minutes, which is what we often call the “first impression”. From a psychological perspective, the first impression refers to the brain forming certain views and making certain judgments based on the other’s gender, age, clothing, posture, facial expressions, and other features. Generally speaking, the first impression is very stubborn. If a bad first impression is left, it often means the cooperation will end in failure; even if you luckily get the opportunity, you will have to spend more time and energy to reverse this impression. So if you can leave a good first impression, it means you are one step closer to success!

Next, I will use the knowledge in this book to tell you some basic techniques and simple methods to correctly and effectively master these critical four minutes, thereby winning the first “pass” in the workplace and business world.

##### Techniques for Accurately Distinguishing Lies

When using micro-expression detection techniques in recruitment interviews, how exactly should it be done? To see through others’ lies, in addition to micro-expressions, one must deploy all lie-judging techniques from non-verbal information such as body language and tone, verbal information such as wording or logic integration, and even questioning methods that can distinguish liars from honest people; otherwise, it is difficult to accurately distinguish lies.

Instead, make use of micro-expression information, explained as follows:

- Do not make people feel suspected
- Consider the questioning focus of micro-expressions

If the interviewer does not make the applicant feel suspected, and the aforementioned micro-expression occurs, then one must consider that besides the pressure given by the interviewer, there are other reasons causing the micro-expression.

But this cannot directly conclude that the applicant is lying, because the applicant may be unaccustomed to the interview atmosphere, causing emotional fluctuations. Therefore, at the beginning of the interview, it is necessary to ease the applicant’s tension. If the applicant shows micro-expressions on the face without being under additional pressure, it indicates that behind the applicant’s words, there may be other meanings.

That is to say, the interviewer should note that when a micro-expression appears, it is the time to question why the applicant’s face shows a micro-expression, and ask questions based on the micro-expression to guide them to explain, thereby understanding the true meaning.

##### Micro-expressions Also Shown by Honest People

From this, it can be known that if one can detect and interpret micro-expressions, of course one can see through the applicant’s lies. However, emotions generated when lying may also occur even without lying.

When the applicant is telling the truth, if the interviewer suspects it is a lie, the applicant will feel “guilt” toward themselves for being suspected of lying, and feel “distress” about such a scene, and perhaps also feel “disgust” or “contempt” toward the interviewer who suspects them.

In addition, the applicant may also feel “fear” about being wronged and unable to prove innocence! Being suspected of lying does not produce “secret delight”, but the seemingly “happy” smiling face on the surface is actually to encourage oneself in a difficult situation, or to leave a good impression on the interviewer.

Even without lying, when suspected of lying, one uses feigned calmness to suppress emotions. Emotions that cannot be completely suppressed will become micro-expressions and appear on the face.

How does that feel? Whether lying or not lying, the same emotions and same micro-expressions will be produced. Compared to truth-tellers, liars have a more obvious tendency to display micro-expressions. And what is produced from being suspected of lying is the micro-expression of honest people.

##### Lying Emotions in Recruitment Interviews

Next, let us imagine the emotional state of an applicant lying in a recruitment interview. People who want to enter the company through lying will, when facing themselves, feel “guilt”, “distress”, “(self-)disgust” due to conscience’s reproach, and additionally, will have a “fear” feeling worrying that the lie will be exposed.

Conversely, there may also be applicants who feel excited “happiness” about lying, and this emotion is called “secret delight”. “Contempt” is a sense of superiority relative to others; when one feels that one’s clever lie has been smoothly accepted and affirmed by the interviewer, one will feel “contempt”; of course, such applicants will not reveal the emotion on their expression, and if they accidentally show a flaw in front of the interviewer, the lie will be exposed. Therefore, they will deliberately suppress such emotions, and if they cannot suppress them, they will appear on the applicant’s face in the form of micro-expressions.

## Part Nine Psychological Testing

### 1.1 Recognition of Ordinary Expressions

This level of the test contains 6 images. After viewing each one, give an intuitive judgment. The reference answer is on the back of the image; you do not need to match the wording exactly. If your judgment is close in meaning to the reference answer, it counts as correct. Each correctly judged expression image earns 5 points.

**Beginner Test 1**  
Reference answer: A happy smile.

A hearty laugh represents the emotion that is the lifelong pursuit of every person—joy. A genuine smile is highly recognizable and contagious. Even from 100 meters away, a bright smiling face can be easily identified. If you judged correctly (which, presumably, you did not get wrong), flip back and observe at random: in a smiling face, what state are the various organs—from eyebrows to mouth—in?

**Beginner Test 2**  
Reference answer: Surprise.

When encountering or hearing something unexpected, a person instinctively produces this expression. The eyes widen to see clearly what is happening, and you may notice that opening the mouth is always accompanied by a quick intake of breath.

**Beginner Test 3**  
Reference answer: Disgust.

Whether in ancient times or today, encountering foul odors, spoiled food, or disliked people or things during the process of survival elicits this expression. The facial movements convey the attitude: do not look, do not smell, do not taste. If the ears could move, there might also be a refusal to listen. If you see this expression on someone else’s face, you can probably gauge your standing in that person’s mind.

**Beginner Test 4**  
Reference answer: Anger.

When provoked or even offended, anger is triggered. The direct manifestations of anger, beyond the angry face itself, include other aggressive actions such as roaring, shoving, kicking, or at least heavy breathing. The teeth bared in the image are essentially no different from those of an animal preparing to attack.

**Beginner Test 5**  
Reference answer: Fear.

When facing something terrifying, what is feared? It is the possibility of harm, coupled with the inability to eliminate, drive away, or remove the threat. Fear of that harmful outcome is fear itself. When confronted with an overwhelming threat and feeling powerless to resist or eliminate it, anger subsides and is replaced by fear. The most immediate response to fear is flight; under extreme pressure, it may lead to despairing surrender.

**Beginner Test 6**  
Reference answer: Sadness.

The death of a loved one, or expending great effort and cost only to fail, may trigger uncontrollable weeping.

### 1.4 Test Result Evaluation and Recommendations

- If your score falls between 0–50 points, you can identify relatively obvious expression meanings, but your recognition of complex micro-expressions (微表情) is not high. You need to meet more people and experience more events, building perceptual understanding through accumulation to improve your recognition ability.
- If your score falls between 50–60 points, you possess good intuitive sense and are quite sensitive to people’s expressions, yet you tend to doubt your own judgments when questioned or when self-doubting. You need to read this book carefully to master in detail the morphological features and judgment criteria of each type of micro-expression.
- If your score falls between 60–80 points, you have relatively high expression-interpretation ability, whether from extensive experience with people or from specialized study of human expressions. Building on this solid foundation by reading the entire book will give you a more systematic and comprehensive grasp of micro-expression morphological features, leading to greater accuracy.
- If your score exceeds 80 points, there is only one piece of advice—read this book thoroughly, for it belongs to you. Then, in actual events or cases, apply consistent standards for judgment, forging stable criteria and convictions so that this skill becomes a personal strength. Early on you may make more mistakes, but each error is worth ten correct judgments, and proficiency will grow rapidly. Afterward, we can enjoy practicing together.

After completing the above test, firmly remember your current feeling: are the faces before you clearly legible to your eyes? Do genuine and false expressions cause confusion or misunderstanding? Chapters 4 through 10 of this book dissect the necessary and typical features of various micro-expressions. Using these standards, you can retake the advanced test after finishing your study. At that point, recognition and analysis of these complex faces should become as clear and definite as consulting a dictionary.

Before that, however, we must first confirm a core question: is analyzing a person’s inner state through micro-expressions reliable after all? Myth or science? This requires you to exercise patience and read the next two chapters.

### 1.2 Recognition of Common Expressions

This level of the test also contains 6 images. After viewing each one, give an intuitive judgment. The reference answer is on the back of the image. If your judgment is close in meaning to the reference answer, it counts as correct. Each correctly judged expression image earns 5 points.

**Intermediate Test 1**  
Reference answer: Smile.

The key question is whether this smile is sincere. Such smiles are very common in daily life. Can the structural morphology of this face alone determine that the other person truly likes and is happy?

To judge whether a smile is fully sincere, two criteria must be observed: first, examine the morphology of the eyebrows, eyes, degree of cheek elevation, and mouth shape; second, examine the force-matching relationship among the four organs. Combining the above features shows that the smile is sincere, yet the mouth displays a deliberate suppression—the lips are pressed together, indicating the person intends to restrain the full expression of the smile.

**Intermediate Test 2**  
Reference answer: Surprise.

The degree of surprise in the image can be inferred to mean the unexpected stimulus was not very intense. However, can you determine whether fear is also present in this expression? The answer is no.

**Intermediate Test 3**  
Reference answer: Disdain.

Disdain belongs to the mild tier of disgust-related emotions. Its difference from intense avoidant disgust lies in the fact that disdain involves viewing the disliked matter with great contempt and deeming it unworthy of entanglement or attention. Disdain is a derivative of disgust; therefore its micro-expression morphology retains the muscular features of extreme disgust expressions.

**Intermediate Test 4**  
Reference answer: Mild anger.

Usually, when facing someone harboring dissatisfaction, one can often see this expression on the other person’s face. Beyond revealing the other party’s discontent, this expression also conveys an important piece of information—the other person is still holding back a surge of determination and, given the opportunity, may act according to their own wishes.

### Psychological Testing

Psychological testing is a broad concept that includes various tests conducted in psychology using scientific methods and techniques, and to a large extent even physiological indicator tests caused by psychological activity; it also encompasses numerous small games that analyze personality and emotional intelligence through means such as astrology or blood type.

In this book, the scope of psychological testing is limited to analyzing real emotional states, information cognition, and information expression through stress micro-expressions, with particular emphasis on filtering disguises and discerning lies. Therefore, if strict rigor is not required, it can be briefly called lie detection.

### Are Your Emotions Stable?

#### Chapter 1: Expression Recognition Ability Test

The first step is to understand; the second step is to control! Expressions are an important code in interpersonal communication and a key step in understanding others. Take the expression recognition ability test in this chapter to see how well you read faces.

This chapter contains three levels of expression tests, ranging from the simplest to the most complex, designed to test and differentiate readers’ ability to recognize expressions.

Real-life micro-expressions fall into two categories: one consists of subtle facial changes that leak out inadvertently under extreme suppression, when emotions cannot be freely expressed; the muscle movements are incomplete and brief, representing relatively pure micro-expressions. The other consists of compound expressions in which various complex emotions are blended onto a single face, often described as “conflicted” or “meaningful.” The latter type appears far more frequently. Unless people are under intense pressure, such as during a judicial investigation, they usually do not make every effort to suppress their emotional expressions.

With that in mind, let us proceed with an “easy-in, deep-out” expression recognition test.

#### Psychological Testing

Psychological testing is a broad concept that includes various assessments conducted with scientific tools and methods in psychology, as well as a large number of tests that measure physiological indicators caused by psychological activity. It also encompasses numerous small games that analyze personality and emotional intelligence through means such as astrology or blood type.

In this book, the scope of psychological testing is limited to analyzing real emotional states, information cognition, and information expression through stress micro-expressions, with special emphasis on filtering disguises and detecting lies. Therefore, if strict rigor is not required, it can be abbreviated as lie detection.

#### Beginner Test 1

**Reference Answer:** A happy smile.

A hearty laugh represents the emotion that is the lifelong pursuit of every person—joy. A genuine smile possesses extremely high recognizability and contagiousness. Even from 100 meters away, a bright smiling face can be easily identified. If you judged correctly (which, presumably, you did not get wrong), flip back and observe the smiling faces at random: what states are the various organs—from eyebrows to mouth—in?

There is no need to match the wording exactly; if your judgment is close in meaning to the reference answer, it counts as correct. Each correctly judged expression image earns 5 points.

## Part Ten: Peripheral Topics

### A Small Scenario

Woman: Let's break up.

Man: What did you say? (Surprise. He did not expect her to bring it up so directly.)

Woman: Yesterday I got a call from XX (note: ex-boyfriend's name). He said he can't forget me.

Man: Why is he still calling you now? (Disgust. He feels repelled by her ex-boyfriend.)

Woman: I think he's right. He understands me better than you do.

Man: What!! (Anger. He feels an urge to attack; if the other man were present, he would probably charge at him.)

Woman: Being with you is fun, but it's equally painful. We've argued so many times, yet you still can't fully understand who I am. He may not be romantic, but I feel more secure with him. I can't let him go. I've thought about it for a long time. For both our sakes, let's just be friends.

Man: I can change. I'll change anything for you. I can't live without you. (Fear. He knows the chance of reconciliation is slim.)

Woman: You deserve a better girl, and there are plenty of good ones around you. This reluctance is just habit. I know it's cruel, but I really don't want us to repeat the same arguments. Here's your phone back, and the house key. Goodbye. I'll always wish you well.

Man: … (Sadness. He knows it's irreversible.)

This is only one of many common scenes in life. Indifference simply means the heart no longer cares; as long as care remains, emotional reactions will occur.

Are humans rational, superior beings or slaves to emotion? Both claims are extreme. Adding a condition makes it more accurate: when not pressed, humans are masters of reason; when pressed, they become slaves to emotion. The “pressed” here refers to encountering an effective stimulus.

When we encounter an effective stimulus, the first reaction is surprise. Unexpected or uncertain sudden stimuli draw attention. If the event was already confirmed and anticipated, the worrying is already done and one simply waits calmly.

Simultaneously with surprise, a rapid judgment follows: is the stimulus source beneficial or harmful? If beneficial, the response is simple—great joy for major good news, quiet delight for smaller good news. If harmful, further intensity assessment is required.

Stimuli that are disliked, disapproved of, or unacceptable—such as an unpleasant smell or offensive words—but that carry no aggression or threat, elicit disgust. The immediate thought with disgust is to confirm that the source will not harm oneself; rejection suffices, so the impulse is merely to move away or ignore it. Contempt is the most common form of disgust: disapproval combined with a very low evaluation.

If the negative stimulus escalates to a threat—whether to physical safety, opinions, reputation, or even minor contradictions and obstacles—anger arises. Anger is characterized by an urge to attack, a desire to eliminate the threatening source through specific action.

However, if the negative pressure exceeds the person's capacity to bear—for instance, being unable to fight back, argue effectively, or reverse a decline—the individual loses confidence to attack (or resist) and to remove the threat. The only options left are flight or resignation. At this point the harmful outcome has not yet occurred, so the emotion is fear.

Once the outcome materializes and becomes an irreversible fact, fear ceases and is replaced by sadness. Any negative stimulus that produces a result entails loss of benefit, and sadness stems from that loss. All prior concern and effort were aimed at preventing the adverse outcome; once it occurs, the body goes limp and loses energy—the most typical outward sign of sadness.

*[Figure omitted from source conversion: 图1]*

In summary, the first reaction to an effective stimulus is surprise, after which two emotional directions emerge: the positive direction produces varying degrees of pleasure; the negative direction, depending on stimulus intensity, produces disgust, anger, fear, and sadness in ascending order. These six basic emotions encompass all possible emotional reactions when humans process external information. Common emotions such as contempt, irritation, apprehension, embarrassment, displeasure, and guilt can be classified as derivatives of these six at different intensities. See Figure 1.

Likewise, American micro-expression pioneer Paul Ekman holds that humans possess six universal emotions and expressions that transcend race, culture, and geography: surprise, disgust, anger, fear, sadness, and pleasure. To substantiate this crucial conclusion, the professor traveled to primitive tribes in New Guinea to study facial expressions among populations that had never had deep contact with the outside world. This single pioneering study alone commands the respect of later generations.

Emotions process different stimuli, while expressions constitute another human communication channel—more authentic and accurate than language. More importantly, these six emotions and the expressions they drive are naturally linked. By dissecting expressions and analyzing the emotions behind the face, one can, to some extent, discern others' true inner thoughts (see Chapters 2–3 for details).

Therefore, this book organizes its research and discussion of micro-expressions along the trajectory of these six emotions. In addition to the six basic emotions—surprise, disgust, anger, fear, sadness, and pleasure—it incorporates as many derivative emotions as possible, seeking the core essence of their subtle expressions to help readers improve their ability and efficiency in capturing micro-expressions. Surprise is a relatively pure emotion; only afterward do various judgments arise. If the judgment is negative, the following sequence appears according to stimulus intensity: disgust-type emotions (including disgust, contempt, disdain, and other derivatives), anger-type emotions (including anger, threat, irritation, and displeasure at varying intensities), fear-type emotions (including fear, apprehension, unease, worry, and other derivatives), and sadness-type emotions (including sadness, guilt, helplessness, and other derivatives). If the judgment is positive, pleasure arises and triggers a smile.

Each emotion possesses its own distinctive expression. No matter how complex, every expression has necessary and typical morphological features. These minute and subtle features are the so-called micro-expressions (微表情).

Whether dealing with pure “micro-expressions” or complex compound expressions, only one method exists for grasping their true meaning: capture every subtle change on the face, distinguish genuine from feigned elements, and finally confirm the inner thoughts they represent.

Next, test your current level of expression-recognition ability.

### What You Know and Don't Know About the Psychology of the Sexes

Men and women differ visibly in outward appearance. Overall, men have darker skin, coarser hair, and sturdier bones and muscles. Women, by contrast, have lighter skin, finer hair, and softer bones and muscles. These differences determine distinct social roles for men and women and shape perceptions of gender relations—namely, that men are dominant and women are merely appendages.

For a long historical period this traditional view of the sexes was widely accepted and is still staunchly defended by some today. Whether in ancient times or in the modern era, men have been natural warriors who contend with nature and enemies; they symbolize strength and pursue honor and admiration. Women's primary tasks have been household management and child-rearing, creating a sphere of tranquility. Although this clear-cut division of labor has undergone some changes today—women have become increasingly independent and work outside the home rather than relying on men—the psychological needs and characteristics of men and women have not changed substantially.

Men resemble fierce lions; aggression and dominance are instinctive. They are combative, highly possessive, and regard conquest as the highest glory. Once they identify “prey,” they usually strike directly and forcefully. Women resemble docile sheep, seeking stability and warmth—even outwardly capable career women remain inwardly delicate and yearn to be protected.

In relationships, men tend to be careless while women are sensitive and attentive; men are accustomed to taking the initiative, women to being passive—if reversed, the situation can become dangerous.

Men like to conquer; women like to be conquered. Men enjoy women's admiration; women long for a man they can admire.

For men, career is the highest goal; for women, family matters most. In other words, men strive for wealth, power, and women, while women seek beauty, tranquility, and happiness. An interesting phenomenon therefore arises: a strong man is taken for granted and wins women's favor, whereas a woman who is too strong often intimidates men.

I once conducted two surveys. One targeted successful career women; more than 75 percent reported unsatisfactory emotional lives. The other surveyed ordinary unmarried men; 90 percent said they preferred to be depended upon and did not want a future wife who was too formidable.

Under normal circumstances, the physical differences between men and women are absolute, yet psychological differences are relative.

No purely masculine man or purely feminine woman exists in the world. Many men display feminine traits such as sensitivity, delicacy, gentleness, and strong empathy; many women display masculine traits such as combativeness, toughness, carelessness, and strong ambition. When feminine traits predominate, the person tends to be gentle and compliant; when masculine traits predominate, the person tends to be brave and assertive.

Civilizational progress has made relations between the sexes increasingly harmonious. Compared with the savage primitive era, contemporary men clearly possess more feminine traits; they also value emotion, art, and family and understand gentleness, compassion, and compromise. Women, likewise, have gradually acquired certain masculine traits. They are no longer merely “cave-dwelling animals” responsible for childbearing; they have become confident, courageous, and proactive, and a minority have achieved remarkable success in politics, economics, and other fields alongside men.

For women, the ideal partner possesses both distinct masculine traits and a measure of feminine traits—ambitious and conquering yet considerate. For men, the purely submissive, unmotivated, and indecisive woman is not the most desirable partner either.

### Makeup “Reveals” a Woman's Inner World

Women are born lovers of beauty. Through their own methods they display attractiveness, intelligence, and taste to win the favor of the opposite sex. To understand the woman you meet, in addition to inherent physical features such as skin tone, figure, and face, makeup is another reference that cannot be ignored.

Many women enjoy following fashion trends and adopt currently popular makeup styles. These women are enthusiastic about new things and full of passion for life, yet they lack independent personality. Being with them feels exciting, but if marriage is the goal, further consideration is advisable; nine out of ten lack financial-planning habits and have no long-term plans.

Heavily made-up women possess a strong desire for attention and wield unique charm and control in attracting male gazes. Outwardly glamorous and warm, they are inwardly lonely because they frequently face attacks from conservatives. They are undoubtedly strong, independent, and contradictory. Yet if one day they willingly abandon vivid makeup for a plain style, they can become excellent companions and assistants.

Women who prefer light makeup are generally simple and traditional, not fond of drawing attention. When facing difficulties they may sometimes appear weak. They favor tangible things over avant-garde or dazzling ones. Consequently, most make good domestic partners; only a small portion, being overly sensitive, are prone to hysteria, depression, or autism.

Women who never initiate makeup can be roughly divided into three types. The first are coarse and practical women who are too busy surviving to care about appearance and care only about having enough to eat. The second are plain women who also love beauty and often envy attractive peers, yet due to upbringing they have never tried makeup and dare not, fearing they will make matters worse. The third are women who pursue natural beauty; they understand and appreciate beauty, possess refined artistic taste, and hold deep insights into many matters.

Women who spend a long time applying makeup are perfectionists and somewhat lacking in confidence. Women who pay special attention to one particular feature during makeup demonstrate clear self-awareness and know how to accentuate strengths and conceal weaknesses.

Lipstick color also reflects a woman's inner state. I can guarantee that at least half the women in the world use lipstick. Some feel as awkward without it as if they had not dressed properly.

Generally, bright red lipstick accentuates the lips and projects a sexy, passionate, outgoing personality; such women are socially adept and often work in public relations or sales. Women who use pink lipstick tend to be gentle, innocent, and caring, with lower psychological resilience; they are somewhat reserved in social interactions yet warm inside. Women who favor purple lipstick usually have a strong desire for attention and a sense of superiority; they pursue extraordinary lives and often captivate men.

Corresponding to their innate love of beauty, women also love compliments, yet complimenting women requires care. Using the same phrase for every woman will, I guarantee, make 80 percent of them dislike you.

When interacting with women, you must capture their individual characteristics at any moment, identify their strengths, and highlight them. For example, praise a young woman for her radiance and vitality; praise an attractive woman for her beauty and charm; praise a middle-aged woman for her maturity and grace; praise a woman who enjoys dressing up for her striking appearance; praise a woman who dislikes makeup for her natural beauty…

In short, a woman's beauty is brought out by praise. Even if you are not eloquent, do not stint on the well-chosen compliment.

### The Barnum Effect: Others Can Always Influence Your Emotions

In daily life and work it is unrealistic to engage in constant self-reflection, so many people rely on external information to understand themselves. Consequently, during the process of self-understanding people are easily swayed by outside information, lose direction under surrounding cues, and adopt others' words and actions as their standard.

The Barnum effect refers to the tendency for people to regard a vague, general personality description as accurately revealing their own traits. Even when the description is hollow, they still believe it reflects their personality, even if they are not that kind of person at all.

Einstein's father once told him this story:

“Your Uncle Jack and I went to clean a large chimney at the south factory. We had to climb the steel rungs inside to reach the top. Uncle Jack went first, I followed. We held the handrail and finally reached the top rung by rung. When we came down, Uncle Jack still went first and I followed behind. When we emerged from the chimney I noticed something strange: Uncle Jack's back and face were blackened by soot, yet I had not a speck on me.”

Einstein's father continued with a smile: “Seeing Uncle Jack's appearance, I assumed I must look just as clownish, so I washed again and again in a nearby stream. Uncle Jack, seeing me come out clean, naturally assumed he was clean too and merely rinsed his hands before striding off down the street. The people on the street laughed until their stomachs hurt, thinking Uncle Jack was mad.”

Einstein could not help laughing.

At that point his father said solemnly: “In reality, no one else can serve as your mirror; only you yourself are your own mirror. Using others as a mirror, even an idiot may see himself as a genius.”

In life people are constantly influenced by others. Seeing what others do, they subconsciously feel they should do the same, so they act without independent judgment and develop cognitive biases in everything, always unable to find the correct approach.

We are social beings and cannot survive apart from society. Therefore our emotions are inevitably affected by others' words and actions. We should view matters objectively, maintain our own values and judgment standards, so that we can control our emotions and prevent them from being easily swayed by others.

To avoid the Barnum effect, recognize oneself objectively and truthfully, and manage one's emotions, the following paths can be taken:

1. Learn to face yourself

Consider this scenario: a woman falls into the water, is rescued, and upon waking finds herself naked. What is her first reaction? The answer is a scream followed by covering her eyes with both hands. Why does she act this way? Psychologically, this is a classic case of unwillingness to face oneself. Because she perceives a flaw, she covers it in a manner she believes is correct. Therefore, to control one's emotions one must first have an accurate self-understanding and learn to face oneself.

2. Cultivate the ability to gather information and exercise keen judgment

No one is born with prudent judgment. Judgment is the capacity to make decisions on the basis of collected information; the supportive role of information must never be overlooked. Without sufficient information, wise decisions cannot be reached.

3. Stay calm

### Love Personality: Dangerous Traps in the Emotional World

When with someone of the opposite sex, we instinctively hide our character flaws and bad habits. While in Britain, the family I rented from had a daughter who was young and rather cold, even indifferent to her own parents. Yet the moment her boyfriend appeared at the door, the girl instantly became warm and lively, shedding her usual languor. He was a fine young man with a healthy complexion and a resolute face. From the way he greeted people and shook hands, he seemed well-mannered and, with a little polishing, destined for success.

No matter how cautious and shrewd a person usually is, once romance enters the picture, intelligence plummets—sometimes to zero. When two people enter the hall of marriage, they shift from lovers to family. In the grind of daily life, flaws and conflicts unnoticed during courtship surface. We often hear complaints such as “How did you become so slovenly?” or “Can’t you be as diligent as before?”

For example, the lady told me: “Reginald made me feel the thrill of romance. He was humorous and always made me laugh. At meals his manners were elegant, unlike my husband, who waves his hands about while eating.”

I understood her distress and hesitation. She believed she had found a better man than her husband and hoped to fly away with him, yet the decision felt like a gamble requiring courage and resolve; she needed someone to support her emotionally. As a counselor, I never give a direct answer in such cases. I simply asked: “On a scale of 100, what score would you give your husband before marriage, shortly after marriage, and in the past six months?”

She thought for a moment and replied seriously: “Before marriage, despite some bad habits, we got along pleasantly enough—90 points. After marriage I noticed he grew lazier; we argued occasionally, but I thought that normal—70 or 80 points. Now… oh, I really can’t stand it. He boasts, shows no gentlemanly manners, and dislikes brushing his teeth… even 60 points feels generous.”

“Indeed, madam. The longer one lives with someone, the more visible their shortcomings become. Have you considered that during your time with Mr. Reginald you have shown only your best side? You did not want him to see your shortcomings, correct? Mr. Reginald’s mindset is the same. If you had lived with him for seven or eight years, would your assessment of him really be higher than your current view of your husband? What do you think?”

She fell silent for a while, then said: “Perhaps I should think it over more carefully.”

In the emotional world, “love personality” is an extremely dangerous trap. Men and women in the throes of passion consciously conceal their flaws, creating an illusion of perfection. Once two people truly share daily life, shortcomings in character and habit gradually appear. Many couples end up unhappy in marriage precisely because they were blinded by “love personality.”

### Conclusion: Letting the Right Person Do the Right Thing

A couple I know forced their eleven-year-old son out of the house to play football with other children. They told me: “Mr. Balken, we only want him to become stronger and more energetic. But Bill does not understand our good intentions at all; he buries himself in books all day…”

I met the boy. He enjoys quiet and is interested only in books; he refuses all vigorous exercise, even though both parents are sports enthusiasts.

This reminds me of another case. Years ago, a young European man came to me for advice. He said that to survive he had become a tailor, yet he disliked the work. Unable to escape the “terrible” job, he felt miserable.

Compared with most Europeans, the young man was slight in build with small hands and feet, but he had a large head, a high broad forehead, and a prominent chin—if one applied the earlier analytical framework, this described an energetic, enterprising young man who liked to ask “why,” with strong logical thinking and observational skills.

Such an intellectual type is clearly unsuited to the monotonous, mechanical work of tailoring. I recommended he join an advertising agency; I later heard he was doing well.

The point of this example is that habits can be formed or changed, but innate nature cannot be altered. Like the boy mentioned earlier, he was born an intellectual type—diligent, studious, and thoughtful. Forcing him into an athletic mold would only distort both body and mind, ultimately producing neither a practical doer nor preserving a thinker. Therefore parents and teachers must first grasp a child’s physical and psychological characteristics, then provide purposeful, planned cultivation and training so the child can develop most fully.

Besides the intellectual type already mentioned, there are also the energetic type and the active type. The energetic type harbors great inner reserves of energy; the plump person described earlier is a typical example. The active type is outwardly lively, enjoys movement, and tends to be extroverted. In reality, most people are mixed types; purely intellectual, purely energetic, or purely active individuals are rare.

The intellectual-active mixed type combines thinker and doer; automobile magnate Henry Ford, Madame Curie, and General Pershing all belong to this group. The intellectual-energetic mixed type is generally plump and often plays key roles in education, finance, law, advertising, and the arts—for instance, Columbia University president Nicholas Murray Butler, scholar Hendrik Willem van Loon, and young director Orson Welles. The active-energetic mixed type is the active plump person whose domains include railways, construction, sports, manufacturing, and the military; they usually serve as managers—Italian dictator Mussolini, steel magnate Andrew Carnegie and his assistant Charles Schwab are famous representatives.

Once the characteristics and expressions of each type are understood, one can match the right person to the right task and the right task to the right person.

### Watches: Glimpsing Innate Nature Behind Time

Time is precious. A person’s attitude toward time is closely tied to character, and the influence time exerts is often conveyed through the watch one wears. The relationship between the two is intimate; a brief explanation follows.

One new type of electronic watch appears completely black at first glance, showing nothing, yet pressing a button reveals the time in red. People who like to wear such watches tend to be somewhat unusual. They possess strong independent awareness, dislike constraints, prefer a free and easy life, and do whatever they please. Others see them as mysterious, and they themselves wish to remain so, enjoying the speculation others direct at them.

People who favor liquid-crystal-display watches are usually frugal, straightforward in thinking, and fond of simple, convenient things.

Those who wear alarm-style watches can strictly discipline themselves and keep their nerves taut at all times. Although not especially traditional or conservative, they habitually follow rules when handling affairs. They are responsible and sometimes deliberately cultivate and train that sense of responsibility.

Wearers of multi-time-zone watches tend to be somewhat unrealistic. They possess a bit of cleverness, yet it remains confined to imagination and is never put into practice. Such people are often indecisive and, when responsibility is required, tend to evade it.

Wearers of classic gold watches have a long-term perspective and plan everything with the future in mind. They will not sacrifice the overall picture for minor gains and make good businesspeople. They are meticulous, flexible, and can often foresee developments.

Wearers of pocket watches manage time well, arrange every matter appropriately, and know how to balance work and rest.

Wearers of wind-up watches generally have strong independent awareness. They dislike receiving favors and prefer self-sufficiency; they insist on doing things themselves and value the sense of accomplishment that follows. They enjoy tackling tasks that involve a certain degree of difficulty; if something is accomplished too easily, they feel it lacks meaning or value.

People who wear watches without numerals hold strong abstract concepts; they like ambiguity and prefer that matters not be explained too thoroughly.

Those who wear watches specially designed for them by a designer care greatly about the image and status they project to others and may even change themselves for a particular matter or person. Some things become exaggerated in their telling so they can draw attention to themselves.

People who wear no watch at all are relatively independent and autonomous; others cannot easily control them. They like to do what they want and display strong adaptability wherever they are, quickly devising responses to thorny problems. They also enjoy making friends.

### Handbags: Revealing Character and Preferences

In daily life the handbag has become an inseparable assistant. Precisely for this reason, observing the handbag a person uses can help one understand its owner.

Handbag styles vary endlessly, and different personalities choose different styles.

- People who choose ordinary, mass-market styles usually lack a particularly distinctive character; they mostly follow the crowd and echo others.
- People whose handbags have striking features fall into two categories: first, those with strong individuality who hold unique thoughts and views on many matters—most of them possess artistic sensibility and enjoy novelty and risk; second, those who deliberately act for attention, whose desire for self-expression and vanity are especially strong.
- People who like casual-style handbags know how to enjoy life and are not overly strict with themselves.
- People who like briefcases are often company executives or employees of formal firms; they handle matters with care and caution.
- People who like small, decorative handbags have usually never faced hardship; they are emotionally fragile and easily abandon their ideals when setbacks occur.
- People who like medium-sized shoulder bags value independence yet remain conservative in character.
- People who like small, delicate but impractical handbags have limited worldly experience, little guile, and hold optimistic expectations for the future.
- People who like small handbags with strong ethnic or regional flavor often dress and think differently from most; at times they appear out of place, so their interpersonal relationships are not especially good.
- People who like oversized handbags enjoy freedom and lack of restraint; they easily form relationships but also easily break them, approach life with a casual attitude, and lack strong responsibility.
- People who like handbags with many pockets and keep everything neatly arranged lead orderly lives, keep a clear head, and rarely act foolishly.
- People who keep their handbags in disorder tend to be vague in their actions and unclear about goals, yet they are warm and approachable; getting to know and befriending them is relatively easy.
- People who like metal handbags are sensitive, keep pace with trends, and readily absorb new things.
- Women who like masculine leather bags are relatively strong, capable, and tend to be extroverted.
- People who like neutral-color handbags do not wish to create pressure for themselves; they avoid performing in public, dislike being noticed, do not want to offend others, and prefer to remain neutral.
- People who dislike carrying handbags fall into several groups: first, the lazy who find a bag too troublesome; second, the strongly autonomous who desire independence. Neither type possesses particularly strong responsibility.

### Money Follows the Heart: Payment Methods Hold Hidden Clues

Material life is determined by earning money, while spending money reflects spiritual life. The same expenditure can produce entirely different outcomes depending on whether the spender acts consciously or unconsciously.

People who often feel pain when spending money will never find their work easy; their methods and results are unlikely to satisfy bosses or colleagues.
