Generally, when speaking, their facial expressions are stiff, their tone distinctive, and their vocabulary unusual. They often leap from one topic to another that seems almost unrelated. This kind of idiosyncratic associative thinking is one diagnostic criterion for schizoid personality.

Beyond an exaggerated emphasis on their own unusual perceptual experiences, the chief difference between this subtype and the first is that these individuals are willing to interact with others, even if the interaction is often unsatisfying. Their emotional state is atypical; suspicion, paranoia, and anxiety dominate. Maintaining close relationships does not reduce their inner tension; instead, the difficulty of sustaining good relations increases their distress.

Psychologist Freud attributed both forms of schizoid personality to childhood trauma. Incorrect upbringing in early years or prolonged exposure to contradictory environments can, under environmental or other stressors, produce schizoid personality.

When interacting with the first subtype, one should show understanding, avoid discrimination or ridicule, and discuss topics in their areas of expertise. When interacting with the second subtype, one must not be dazzled by their mysterious behavior and speech into admiration, nor should one belittle them or make jokes at their expense. Although people with schizoid personality may not care much about mockery, thoughtless ridicule can still hurt them and may provoke anger, leading to unnecessary consequences.

#### Eight Physical Features for Judging People

We live in a complex society and interact daily with many different people, many of whom we have never met before. This requires us to remain cautious, employing every mental resource and method to discern, in the shortest possible time, another person’s character traits and psychological calculations. Only then can we gain the upper hand in subsequent encounters, seize the initiative, steer the psychological contest, and remain undefeated.

A geologist can read a rock and recount a vivid story of the earth; a botanist can examine a plant and produce an engaging botanical record; an astronomer, using a 100-foot telescope and spectroscope, observes a star millions of light-years away and, by calculating its size, speed, structure, and chemical composition, completes a scientific treatise. Reading people is like observing a rock, a plant, or a star: it requires theoretical guidance and practical verification.

The object of “reading people” is “people”; the key lies in “reading.” As parents and teachers, how do we discover a child’s potential and guide its proper development? As leaders, how do we identify subordinates’ strengths and channel them into productive work? As subordinates, how do we understand a superior’s intentions and complete tasks successfully? As negotiators, how do we probe an opponent’s psychology and enter the adversary’s mind? As business operators, how do we see through consumers’ inner desires and convert those desires into revenue?

You must first become a personality analyst—note the term: “personality analyst,” not “character analyst.” Although many call me a “character analyst,” you know my work involves more than analyzing “character.”

To many, “analyst” sounds professional, yet it simply means making judgments based on observation and then applying scientific knowledge and experimental data to analyze or predict. Believe me: once you know a few standards and master a little “technique,” anyone can become a personality analyst.

The first step in reading people is to form an intuitive judgment from external appearance. In general, human physique exhibits eight features. These obvious external traits encode a person’s inner character, lifestyle, thinking habits, strengths, and weaknesses. The eight physical features are as follows:

1. **Body color**, including the color of skin, hair, eyes, and beard. Some people have blond hair, blue eyes, and fair skin; others have black hair, black eyes, and yellow skin. Differences in color correspond to differences in personality, physique, and intelligence.
2. **Body type**. Some people are tall and robust; others are small and compact. Overall, Eastern and Western populations also show clear differences in stature.
3. **Hair, skin, and facial features**. Some people have soft hair and delicate skin; others have dry hair and rough skin. Both innate genetic factors and acquired environmental influences are at work, reflecting lifestyle habits, interests, and values.
4. **Body structure**. A person’s physical build is closely related to their way of life. Generally, the thinker type is intelligent, plans ahead, highly creative, and skilled at analysis and reasoning; the doer type tends to carry out the plans formulated by the thinker type; the manager type possesses drive and often assists and supervises the other two.
5. **Facial features**, including the forehead, eyes, nose, mouth, and chin. The shape and movement of these parts all hint at a person’s inner state.
6. **Muscle tone and bone flexibility**. This is easy to understand: whether a handshake is firm or limp, whether the body is supple or stiff, indicates what a person is suited for and enjoys doing.
7. **Proportions of body parts**. Studying these ratios yields many interesting discoveries.
8. **Movements and voice**. The most dynamic and textured elements of body language are a person’s movements and voice. Gait, posture, handshake style, and tone of voice all convey thoughts and desires. You must learn to distinguish what is deliberate from what is spontaneous, avoid the traps others set, and capture fleeting micro-changes; success will follow.

Everyone has a door that belongs to them alone. If you wish to enter another person’s inner world and see the truth of their thinking, the key is to find the right key. These eight “body languages” are the golden keys that open others’ hearts and also the golden keys that lead you to success and happiness.

#### The Inner Connection Between Skin Color and Personality

According to existing scientific data and theories, our ancestors originally lived in the tropical and subtropical regions near the equator. To resist intense ultraviolet radiation, nature endowed them with melanin, giving them brown skin and eyes. Later they discovered fire, achieving a great leap forward. Some began a journey of world conquest. They traveled from the warm south to the cold north, continually adapting to changing environments along the way. In the north, whether frozen or rainy and overcast, sunlight was markedly reduced compared with equatorial regions; consequently their melanin decreased and their skin and eye color gradually lightened.

To survive, the ancestors living in the cold northern regions had to struggle against a harsh environment, fighting other tribes for hunting and fishing grounds. Over time they developed strong competitive awareness, materialism, courage to challenge, and sharp vision. In contrast, the ancestors living in the south were more enduring and down-to-earth, and less combative.

Thus the inner connection between skin color and personality is the result of ancestors adapting to natural environments. In today’s modern world, people of different skin colors can appear in the same place, and the exchange of information and culture has long transcended geographical limits; yet this link, transmitted over hundreds of thousands or even millions of years, does not completely disappear.

According to Haeckel’s[^1] theory, human skin can be divided into two major categories: dark skin and light skin. In the West, both yellow and black races are considered dark-skinned. Further distinctions exist within both dark-skinned and light-skinned groups, and the theory mentioned above still applies.

[^1]: Haeckel (1834–1919), German biologist and naturalist, defender and popularizer of Darwin’s theory of evolution.

One winter five years ago, the owner of an automobile company brought a pair of young twin technicians to see me.

The owner said, “They are both people I deeply care about. I hope they will be positive and motivated. Frankly, I am not worried about the older brother, but the younger one truly gives me headaches. They grew up together, studied together, and are both intelligent. Why can’t the younger one stay in the workshop like his brother? Mr. Balkan, do you have any good suggestions?”

I called the brothers from the reception room into my office. They looked as though they had been cast from the same mold—golden hair, light-gray eyes, even similar eyebrows. Yet I could tell at a glance which was the older and which the younger, because their skin tones differed. I said to the young man with the slightly darker skin, “Young man, I can see you prefer outdoor activities and dislike machines, correct?”

The young man looked surprised, then shrugged. “Yes, sir. I hate staying in the assembly room all day doing the same thing. It’s driving me crazy!”

I turned to the young man with the slightly lighter skin. “And you? I don’t think you dislike the machines.”

“I find it quite interesting to try tightening screws faster and tighter, and I can share experiences with my colleagues.”

Afterward I told the owner, “My friend, both of your technicians are talented. With the right placement, guidance, and training, they will both achieve success. Since you are so concerned about the younger brother, why not give him a different position? Let him introduce new cars or serve as a field instructor. With his knowledge of cars he will certainly do well. For him, monotonous work is simply poison.”

Today one brother is director of the assembly department and the other is director of the sales department. This is a simple real-life application of “skin-color psychology.”

#### Judging a Child’s Personality from Reactions to Mistakes

A study examined the relationship between children’s personality and their facial expressions. In the study, children of different personalities faced an interviewer in a face-to-face oral test, and their expressions were analyzed. The subjects were seventy children aged twelve to thirteen. After each child answered a question, the interviewer immediately told the child whether the answer was correct or incorrect.

The focus was on the emotions the child felt when the answer was wrong and on the facial reactions that appeared. The results showed that a child’s reaction when corrected for an incorrect answer corresponded to the child’s individual personality.

Most ordinary children without personality deviations displayed an expression of “shame,” whereas children with tendencies toward inattention, hyperactivity, aggression, or antisocial behavior tended to show “anger.” In addition, children with excessive anxiety, fear, psychosomatic symptoms, or depressive traits tended to show “fear.”

What problems arise from reacting to mistakes with “anger” or “fear”? First, such reactions may create negative impressions in others and damage interpersonal relationships; second, the child loses the proper direction for solving the problem.

Imagine the impression given by a child who reacts to mistakes with “anger” or “fear.”

A person who shows “shame” when making a mistake elicits goodwill and sympathy from others and is more socially acceptable. Research indicates that people who do not display “shame” produce the opposite result.

The child mentioned earlier who reacted to mistakes with “anger” not only frequently forgot things and was inattentive in class but also displayed irritability. Such a child is likely to have tendencies toward inattention, hyperactivity, aggression, or antisocial behavior. Moreover, if a child continues to react to mistakes with “anger” and the personality does not improve, these traits persist and may eventually cause serious social problems.

A child’s loss of proper direction for solving problems is closely related to the function of emotions. Emotions serve as adaptive mechanisms that allow various feelings and situations to proceed smoothly.

For example, the function of the emotion “shame” is to apologize and repair one’s self-image. A person who feels “shame” signals an apologetic attitude, gets back on their feet after failure, and seeks goodwill. In the present case, a child who feels “shame” after giving a wrong answer will be more careful to avoid repeating the mistake. By contrast, the function of “anger” is to remove obstacles to a goal, and the function of “fear” is to avoid threats.

A child who feels “anger” at a wrong answer treats the mistake or the person correcting it as an “obstacle” to be eliminated. The child’s goal is to avoid being disturbed by anyone; when things seem to be going smoothly and an error is pointed out, that correction itself becomes an obstacle to be removed.

Most people grow from mistakes through correction and do not regard mistakes as obstacles; conversely, treating mistakes as obstacles causes one to miss opportunities for self-growth.

“Fear” is more complex than “anger.” It treats the mistake as a threat and seeks to avoid it. Facing mistakes with a positive attitude leads to solutions and preventive measures. Acting with a negative attitude leads only to simple avoidance without confronting the mistake itself. Experience suggests that children who feel “fear” about mistakes rarely act proactively without adult prompting. Therefore, when a child reacts to mistakes with expressions or emotions of “anger” or “fear,” the child easily loses opportunities for self-growth.

#### Characteristics of Antisocial Personality

The reason antisocial personality receives this name is inseparable from the behavioral code in their hearts that runs counter to society’s prevailing norms. When first encountering people of this type, they often appear enthusiastic and can create a very harmonious atmosphere. However, once contact deepens—especially when it comes to shouldering responsibility or paying the bill—they always smile and brush it off or simply flee. In their minds, the etiquette and morals we take for granted are nothing more than jokes written on paper.

Identifying someone with antisocial personality is not difficult at all. Psychologist Cleckley, in his book *The Mask of Sanity*, describes in detail the various behavioral characteristics of antisocial personality:

1. Appearance and intelligence show no problems; the first impression is usually favorable, with no signs of schizophrenia or anxiety found in other personality disorders.
2. They lack necessary responsibility and sense of duty, disregard social norms, morality, and law. In childhood they may already lie or steal; after adulthood they become even more unrestrained, possibly engaging in illegal transactions or even dangerous criminal activities.
3. They are extremely self-centered, using charisma and charm to manipulate and deceive others, remaining completely at ease about it and never believing they have harmed anyone. After satisfying their own desires, they refuse to give anything back to others.
4. They feel no remorse even when they know they are wrong and are very skilled at making excuses for themselves. They believe victims were fooled because of their own stupidity and fully deserved it; even if the antisocial person had not acted, the victims would have been deceived by someone else. They never reflect on their own actions.
5. Their emotions are cold and lack variation; they rarely display the joy, anger, sorrow, or happiness that normal people show when moved. They never pay attention to others yet strongly need others’ attention and trust. In interactions they focus only on self-gratification and never offer genuine feelings to the other person.
6. They act impulsively, without plans, often cramming at the last minute. Even acts that infringe on others’ interests usually stem from hidden impulses rather than clear motives or plans.
7. They are irritable and reckless, with poor tolerance, easily provoked into aggressive behavior, and completely unconcerned about their own or others’ safety. Many engage in binge eating, tattooing or piercing, speeding, or even drug use and self-harm. After drinking they also display crude and ugly behavior.
8. Their lives lack regularity; most people of this type have no steady job, and even if they do, they cannot hold it for long. They do everything possible to avoid work yet want more money. They often run up heavy debts but are always pressing others to repay what they owe.

These eight characteristics basically cover the behavioral manifestations of people with antisocial personality. Such individuals are not rare around us. People who slip away the moment the bill arrives, falsify accounts to satisfy private desires without any remorse, or slack off at work while brazenly offering improper excuses all carry traces of antisocial personality.

Most psychologists believe that only a small portion of antisocial personality arises from heredity or poor brain development; the majority stems from family and social environment. Faulty educational methods, childhood psychological trauma, and negative social environmental factors can all contribute to the formation of antisocial personality.

Given the lack of shame and responsibility that characterizes antisocial personality, the best approach when encountering such people is to keep a respectful distance. Once entangled with them, it is like being bitten by a leech: after sucking your blood they will still frown in disgust, complaining that your blood is not sweet enough.

#### Sheldon’s Theory: Research on the Relationship Between Body Type and Personality

| Body Type | Physical Characteristics | Personality Type |
|-----------|--------------------------|------------------|
| Endomorph | Soft, plump, well-developed digestive organs | Viscerotonic: leisurely, fond of food, slow-moving, sociable, generous; psychological traits include being calm and empathetic |
| Mesomorph | Muscular, strong and powerful | Somatotonic: confident, bold, robust, energetic, adventurous and impulsive; psychological traits include being willful and stubborn |
| Ectomorph | Slender, frail, sensitive nervous system | Cerebrotonic: introverted, reserved, not good at socializing, enthusiastic and responsible at work, loves art; psychological traits include being timid yet overly steady |

You may find the above theory overly specialized, yet it is not hard to understand when placed in daily life.

It is very difficult for a tall, large person to fully rouse body and mind and become truly angry, because it requires consuming a great deal of time and energy to change their heavy frame, let alone generate a highly tense state of anger in a short time. Therefore, people with large builds are mostly gentle, better able to control their emotions, and more stable. Dr. Paul of the University of California once tracked eighty people weighing over 200 pounds and found that sixty-eight preferred a comfortable, easy life while only four were willing to try a stimulating lifestyle. In contrast, people of small stature are easily impulsive and excitable, yet they also possess greater endurance and explosive power. Many world-renowned achievers are not large in build—for example, Napoleon. Who could imagine that a body of five feet two inches could unleash the astonishing energy that swept across Europe?

Therefore, if you are a leader, remember this: do not assign tasks requiring quick reactions and high dexterity to your large-built subordinates, because most of them will disappoint you; nor should you force your short, agile subordinates to perform slow work that demands patience, because they will likewise disappoint you.

In short, the body is a mirror of emotion, and a mirror with memory-storage function. Every instance of joy, anger, sorrow, or pleasure leaves subtle traces on various parts of the body. When you repeatedly experience a certain emotion, the traces belonging to that emotion deepen until they become your label. You will notice that people who often frown have narrower space between their eyebrows, people who frequently glare have protruding eyeballs, and people who laugh heartily have more developed muscles in their cheeks… Although everyone experiences multiple emotions, it is still possible to roughly classify personality according to the dominant emotion a person displays.

The research and development of “body-type theory” added a striking chapter to psychology. Despite certain drawbacks—for instance, body type can change with environment and age—it is undeniable that using body type as a “ruler” to measure the formless aspects of personality and psychology is indeed a way to simplify complexity. Moreover, a large body of evidence shows that people of certain body types do tend to develop certain personality qualities and characteristics. As long as the theory is not applied mechanically, using “body-type theory” for rough observation and preliminary judgment of psychology remains very effective.

#### Xiao Nan’s Encounter

“Good afternoon.”

Community volunteer Xiao Nan was sitting in the office sorting documents when a coquettish voice suddenly sounded outside the door. He looked up and saw a woman in her fifties, dressed in gaudy attire, walk in.

“Hel… hello.” To be honest, Xiao Nan was startled.

“Young man, you must be new here?” The woman blinked eyes painted with royal-blue eyeshadow. “I’ve never seen you before.”

“Yes.” Cold sweat broke out on Xiao Nan’s forehead. “Is there something I can help you with?”

“Ah, this time I really do have a bit of a headache, but can I talk to you about it?” The woman put on a mournful expression.

“Su… sure.” Xiao Nan nodded.

“See, a handsome young man like you should be trustworthy.”

Please… what does being handsome have to do with being trustworthy? Besides, this is just the community office. What kind of matter requires someone to be trustworthy before it can be discussed? Xiao Nan grumbled inwardly.

“Actually, it’s like this. My head has been hurting lately and I can’t sleep…”

“Then you should go to the community hospital. Turn left when you go out the door; it’s two hundred meters away.” Xiao Nan could hardly wait to send this plague god away.

“I’m not here because of physical discomfort.” The woman, speaking with a Taiwanese accent, stamped her foot and refused to leave.

“Please go ahead, please go ahead.” Xiao Nan raised both hands in surrender.

“Actually… it’s an emotional problem.” The woman’s next words left Xiao Nan stunned. “My husband and I have been in a cold war for several months, but I know he still loves me. Recently, however, another man has been pursuing me. I don’t know whether I love him or still love my husband… But when my husband heard about this, he became extremely jealous and we had a huge fight. I really don’t know what to do, so I came here for help. A handsome young man like you should be able to mediate for me, right?”

Watching the woman’s gaze gradually grow misty, Xiao Nan felt both amused and exasperated. “But… this is a community office, not a marriage agency or a counseling center…”

“If that man were as handsome as you, I would agree to him without hesitation.” The woman seemed not to have heard Xiao Nan and suddenly grasped his hand with deep emotion. “Handsome boy, even though I’m a bit older, women of any age still need the nourishment of love. You can understand that, right?”

“Yes, yes…” A wave of nausea swept over Xiao Nan as he desperately tried to pull his hand back.

“What, do you dislike me?” Sensing his resistance, the woman stared at him resentfully.

“No…” Even if he disliked her, he could not say so to her face. Xiao Nan was on the verge of tears.

“Then why are you rejecting me like this?”

The woman’s question left Xiao Nan speechless. Watching his “little hand” about to fall once more into the “devil’s claw,” Xiao Nan could no longer care that he was still on volunteer duty. He made up an excuse and fled the office at top speed.

If Xiao Nan’s experience were posted online, it would surely earn that woman the title of “Most Terrifying Auntie of the Year.” When we encounter such people in life, we are either left speechless or, like Xiao Nan, flee in panic.

These individuals always give an exaggerated, affected impression, yet they themselves do not feel anything strange about it. On the contrary, if they lose others’ attention they feel extremely uncomfortable. Therefore they constantly crave to be the center of everyone’s attention.

#### A Du and the “Old Ghost’s” Story

A Du was a newcomer at a multinational company. On his very first day he noticed many colleagues casting sympathetic glances his way.

“This newcomer is really unlucky, assigned to Old Ghost. He’s in for it.”  
“Yeah, no one has lasted more than three months under Old Ghost. This guy’s probation is going to be a problem…”

“Old Ghost” was the nickname of A Du’s immediate superior. Although the boss was a bit strict and rigid, it could not be that bad. At worst he would just be more careful. That was what A Du thought.

At first, because A Du was cautious and followed every rule, nothing major went wrong. After a few days he relaxed, and one careless moment produced a small error in the plan he submitted.

“What is this?” When Old Ghost called A Du into his office, A Du knew he was in trouble.

“I… I didn’t do it on purpose…”  
“Who knows whether you did it on purpose!” Old Ghost cut off A Du’s explanation. “This plan was going straight to the president. If I hadn’t glanced at it first, this mistake would have reached the president. You’re new, so the president won’t say anything to you. The responsibility this time will fall entirely on me!”

“I’m sorry, truly sorry.” A Du had not expected such serious consequences and stopped explaining, apologizing repeatedly.

Yet Old Ghost’s next words left him completely baffled: “Are you dissatisfied that I’m too strict with you? So you deliberately tried to make me look bad?”

“How could that be? You’re my superior…”  
“Exactly because you’re my superior, right? When have you ever shown me respect as your superior? You’ve only been here a few days, kid, and you already want to step on my head to climb above me?” Old Ghost’s questioning left A Du wanting to defend himself but not knowing where to begin.

After a storm of scolding, A Du was finally released from the office.

This time he learned his lesson. The next morning A Du arrived early, grabbed a broom, and cleaned both the office area and Old Ghost’s office.

A Du’s action delighted the cleaning auntie. She had also witnessed the miserable scene of A Du being scolded, so she put in a few good words for him in front of Old Ghost: “Manager Huai, this new young man is really good. Look how clean he made your office—cleaner than when I sweep it.”

“Hmph.” Old Ghost snorted coldly and shot A Du a sidelong glance. “Cleaning? Is that necessary? Does he think I would hold a grudge over that little matter? Am I that kind of person? The way he’s acting, he’s probably just putting on a show for others to see, isn’t he?”

A Du was completely dumbfounded.

A Du’s superior, Old Ghost, was narrow-minded, sinister, and suspicious. No matter what A Du said or did, Old Ghost could always find fault. In Old Ghost’s eyes, although A Du had just joined the company, he had already set his sights on Old Ghost’s position. The mistake A Du made was also intended to make Old Ghost lose credibility in front of the president. Even the cleaning auntie in the company was someone A Du wanted to impress with a false image of respect toward his superior. It was truly detestable.

Of course, all of this was Old Ghost’s own imagination. Having such a paranoid superior, A Du was truly unlucky.

#### Dr. Yang’s Encounter

Recently Dr. Yang had been thoroughly annoyed by a newly arrived patient. Dr. Yang was known for his good temper, and the new patient did not look like a vicious person either. When he first came for treatment he had acute gastritis, but because Dr. Yang was busy operating on a patient with acute appendicitis, it took nearly half an hour before he could see him.

The patient appeared very polite and readily accepted Dr. Yang’s apology. While chatting with Dr. Yang he first complained about society, then about his parents and wife, as if everything were at odds with him. Next he lavishly praised Dr. Yang, saying his medical skills were superb, his prescriptions accurate, and that he had promptly controlled the acute gastritis.

It should have been a win-win situation, yet in the following days Dr. Yang noticed that the number of patients in his clinic had dropped sharply. One day, when he stepped out to buy coffee, he happened to see the patient, wearing a hospital gown, sitting on a bench in the waiting area chatting with other patients.

“I heard the doctor named Yang in this department is quite good—experienced and skilled,” one patient said.

“His medical skills are all right, but the attitude of the medical staff here is really too negligent. I came for acute gastritis and was delayed for more than half an hour,” the patient replied.

“Really? Even for an acute condition?” The other patient’s eyes widened in surprise. “The medical ethics of the doctors here are really poor…”

“Who knows.” The patient waved his hand with a laugh.

When Dr. Yang discovered this he became very angry. He asked himself: he had been sweating on the operating table and had not even had time for a sip of water before immediately inquiring about the patient’s condition, yet the man was bad-mouthing him behind his back.

Unable to contain his anger, Dr. Yang went to confront the patient, but the man looked at him innocently and defended himself: “Doctor, you misunderstood. I wasn’t talking about you; I was talking about the nurses here. I was already feeling unwell, but their attitude toward me was cold and indifferent. It really made me angry.”

So that was it. Dr. Yang suddenly felt he had wrongly blamed a good person. But when he turned around and scolded the nurses in his department, they protested: “That patient was respectful enough to you, but he orders us around and yells at us over the slightest oversight. With so many patients every day, how can we revolve around him alone?”

What the patient said seemed reasonable, yet the nurses also had plenty of grievances. At this point Dr. Yang truly did not know what to do. He could only hope that the troublesome patient would be discharged soon so he would no longer sit idle in the clinic swatting at flies.

Dr. Yang’s experience is pitiable. That patient was like a soft pillow: when Dr. Yang directed anger at him, he found there was nowhere to apply force and even felt as though he were bullying a “pillow.”

Have you ever had this feeling?

#### Reading Preferences Reveal a Person's Work Attitude

Books are the items in the home that best reflect personality. If there are bookshelves or desks holding books and magazines in the room, observe them carefully. Identifying the types of books can yield surprisingly rich information.

For example, although the other person collects many books introducing health topics, they may not care much about health. Yet even a single book on a specific disease can indicate that the person or a relative or friend suffers from that condition. If a bookshelf is filled with unopened "deluxe editions of world classics," the person probably likes to put on airs.

Books and periodicals kept at the workplace reflect not only personal taste in reading but also one's attitude toward work. Romance novels or parenting magazines on the desk indicate that the person's mind is elsewhere.

The following book types reveal corresponding psychological traits and personalities.

- **People who like to read financial magazines**: These individuals are not content with the status quo, unwilling to remain subordinate, competitive, and eager to surpass others. They revere authority and crave honor; given a good opportunity, they can spot it in advance.
- **People who like to read fashion magazines**: These individuals pursue trends, spend generously, and devote time and energy to appearance while neglecting inner cultivation, making it difficult for them to achieve great things.
- **People who like to read martial-arts novels**: These individuals are imaginative and romantic, hoping one day to rise above others. They are emotionally rich, yet sometimes overly delicate, which can make them less appealing to the opposite sex.
- **People who like to read romance novels**: These individuals (mostly women) value emotions and share the joys and sorrows of the story's highlights. They possess strong insight, handle affairs with confidence, and remain open-minded.
- **People who like to read biographies**: These individuals are highly curious, cautious in their actions, skilled at overseeing the big picture, and adept at weighing pros and cons. They never fight a battle without certainty and will not overstep boundaries if conditions are not ripe.
- **People who like to read comic books**: These individuals enjoy games, retain a childlike heart, possess an outgoing personality, are easy to get along with, and dislike constraints. They do not guard against others and only realize their own naivety after being taken advantage of.
- **People who like to read detective novels**: These individuals enjoy challenging mental difficulties and possess rich imagination and creativity. They excel at solving problems and can analyze difficulties from multiple angles when they arise.
- **People who like to read horror novels**: These individuals enjoy complex lives and crave stimulation and adventure to activate their brain cells.
- **People who like to read science-fiction novels**: These individuals are imaginative and creative, deeply fascinated and attracted by science and technology. They like to plan for the future but lack persistence.

#### The Story of Old Wei and the Hong Kong Merchant

Old Wei had been hosting a Hong Kong merchant on behalf of his work unit for several days. The merchant looked distinguished, wore designer clothes, and projected an air of great wealth.

On the first day of the visit, Old Wei arranged for several subordinates to accompany the merchant to a three-star hotel in the city for dinner. The guests and hosts enjoyed themselves thoroughly. The merchant was quite forthright, repeatedly toasting Old Wei and his subordinates, and conveyed eagerness to cooperate. Seeing that the task showed promise, Old Wei grew cheerful and drank a little more. Halfway through the banquet, however, a phone call from his superior summoned him back to the unit for an urgent matter.

Still slightly tipsy, Old Wei hurried back, forgetting in his haste to leave money for his subordinates to settle the bill. After working at the unit for some time, Old Wei checked his phone and found more than a dozen missed calls, all from one of the subordinates who had accompanied the merchant.

Old Wei called back immediately. The subordinate said tearfully, "Section Chief Wei, please come settle the bill quickly. We don't have enough money, and the hotel staff are holding us here."

"What?" Old Wei was startled. "What about Mr. Tong?"

Mr. Tong was the Hong Kong merchant. Upon hearing the name, the subordinate gritted his teeth. "After he finished eating, he told the waiter that we would pay and left for the hotel you arranged, without waiting for us to speak."

Although he was a guest, covering a modest bill was hardly a big deal and the amount was small; how could he behave this way? Old Wei muttered inwardly and rushed to the hotel to "rescue" his subordinates.

"Section Chief Wei, that Mr. Tong was really dishonorable," subordinate Xiao Huang complained angrily. "After you left, he kept pouring drinks for us. At first we thought he was generous, but when it came time to pay, he saw you were gone and noticed our awkward expressions. Without giving us a chance to speak, he pretended to be drunk and slipped away!"

Xiao Huang vented at length, but Old Wei took note. Why would a Hong Kong merchant worth tens of millions quibble over such a small sum? Back at the unit, Old Wei immediately contacted relatives in Hong Kong to investigate Mr. Tong's background.

The results were startling. According to the relatives' investigation, Mr. Tong was indeed from Hong Kong, but he possessed no tens of millions in assets; instead, he was deeply in debt. His trip to the mainland posing as a wealthy man was purely an attempt to "scrape some benefits" before fleeing. With evidence in hand, Old Wei reported the matter to the police and prevented major losses for the unit.

The fake "Hong Kong merchant" Old Wei encountered was a typical antisocial personality. His habitual refusal to pay bills had given him away.

#### Definition and Characteristics of Dual Personality

Personality refers to an individual's unique and stable patterns of thinking and acting that distinguish them from others. Dual personality, taken literally, means that a person's mind contains two entirely different modes of thinking and acting. The coexistence of these two personalities makes dual-personality individuals more changeable and complex than ordinary people. Interacting with someone who has a dual personality feels like riding a roller coaster—constantly stimulating and thrilling.

The protagonist Travis in the American film *Taxi Driver* is a typical dual-personality individual. A Vietnam War veteran, he returns to New York and drives a night-shift taxi. Travis usually drifts along and enjoys watching erotic films, yet he also harbors a deep loathing for crime and depravity. On one hand, he pursues Betsy, an aide to a presidential candidate; on the other, he befriends the underage prostitute Iris in New York and tries to help her escape the grip of her criminal environment so she can return to school.

Reality, however, proves heartbreaking. Ultimately, after being rejected by Betsy and failing to help Iris, Travis launches a series of frenzied actions. He buys four handguns, attempts to assassinate another presidential candidate, then single-handedly storms the gang controlling Iris, fighting his way out with her in a bloodbath...

Clearly, Travis harbors two opposing personalities: the degenerate and the hero.

Dual personality is not an occasional flash of conscience or an outburst of anger; rather, it is a fundamental, subconscious psychological habit and imprint that does not change with status and does not recede simply because one personality dominates. These two personalities permeate the dual-personality individual's life at every moment and continue to manifest even when they affect daily living. In severe cases, external factors can cause the person to become someone else at any time, much like Travis, who, under environmental pressure, transforms from an ineffectual everyman into a tragic "hero."

Dual-personality individuals commonly experience poor social adaptation. Their dual nature can cause them internal confusion, yet many fail to recognize this confusion and instead extend it into a more subjective, self-centered mindset—what is commonly called self-righteousness.

Because of this mindset, dual-personality individuals are harder to persuade and more inclined to defend themselves than ordinary people. When faced with embarrassing situations, they do not admit fault frankly but instead offer various excuses and rationalizations.

#### Hobbies Reveal One's True Nature

Interests and preferences, over time, become a person's hobbies. Nothing reveals a person's essence more clearly than hobbies. Hobbies require no consideration of others' opinions and are free from external constraints; they are the direct expression of one's nature and therefore expose the deepest layers of the psyche.

- **People who like performing**: These individuals have delicate, sensitive emotions and rich imagination, though they can sometimes be unrealistic.
- **People who like fishing**: These individuals yearn for inner purity and seek a clear conscience. They value the process more than the result, hoping to experience joy and self-realization along the way.
- **People who like gardening**: These individuals willingly spend time, energy, and money on flowers and potted plants. They generally know how to enjoy life, possess strong sensitivity to things, and are warm and hospitable.
- **People who like cooking gourmet food**: These individuals have good creativity and imagination and often create pleasant surprises for family and friends. They set high goals and ideals and pursue them persistently.
- **People who like playing chess or cards**: These individuals often surpass others in intellect, possess strong logical thinking, and enjoy a higher likelihood of success.
- **People who like writing**: These individuals have strong analytical ability, seek unique insights on every matter, and enjoy putting their thoughts in writing.
- **People who like stamp collecting**: These individuals are skilled at self-regulation when emotionally unsettled and care greatly about face. Often, not knowing how to refuse others, they create unnecessary troubles for themselves.
- **People who like hunting**: These individuals are relatively rugged and forthright, value loyalty, avoid excessive quibbling, and possess courage and insight, daring to take responsibility for their actions.
- **People who like traveling**: These individuals are outgoing, curious, and restless; only varied and stimulating experiences satisfy them.
- **People who like high-risk activities**: These individuals are drawn to thrilling pursuits such as hang gliding, skydiving, and mountaineering. They are physically robust, meticulous, and always cautious, considering every possible problem before acting. They are resilient and stubborn; once they decide on something, they rarely change course even in the face of great difficulty. They possess boldness and drive, willing to challenge unknown fields.

#### Personality Traces on the Desk

The office is a workplace filled with work-related furnishings. Careful observation can reveal many secrets, because every item incorporates the employee's preferences. The appearance of the desk can display the person's character traits.

- **Desk surface and drawers both neat and orderly**: Such people have high work efficiency and are excellent employees. They are self-disciplined, lead regular lives, and plan tasks in advance. They treasure time and allocate it carefully for meaningful activities. Accustomed to following plans, they often feel at a loss when sudden changes occur.
- **Desk surface clean and tidy, but drawers in chaos**: Such people lack great wisdom, cannot work steadily, like to play petty tricks, and focus on appearances. They tend to be lazy and unreliable in dealings. Like their desks, their interpersonal relationships appear good on the surface but lack any truly intimate friends.
- **Both desk surface and drawers completely empty**: These individuals are usually impatient. To facilitate work and avoid searching for materials, they keep needed items within easy reach. They are highly ambitious and can generally become bosses.
- **Drawers and desk surface both messy**: Such people often lack planning, fail to consider matters thoroughly in advance, and frequently respond hastily with poor results. They pursue simplicity in life, disregard minor details, and lack long-term vision.
- **Desk contains mementos**: These individuals are relatively introverted, not good at socializing, and unwilling to have excessive contact with strangers. They often come and go alone. Although they have few friends, the few they have are very close. They value these relationships deeply. Emotionally rich yet psychologically fragile, they are easily hurt and often lack sufficient perseverance, retreating at the first sign of setbacks or difficulties.
- **Cash kept in the desk**: These individuals are highly suspicious. They do not fully trust banks and therefore do not deposit all their cash there; they also constantly worry about theft at home and choose to keep cash in the desk.

#### Personality Analysis of Fat and Thin People

The most typical hotel owner in British novelist Dickens's works is fat; Shakespeare once described a loud-voiced, heavy-drinking man popular with women who was also fat. Some cartoonists, when satirizing stock-market tycoons, often choose fat protagonists. If you observe carefully, you will find that fat people are not rare in finance and politics.

Generally speaking, we classify fat people as vitality types. The "vitality" referred to here means the latent capacity and recuperative power stored in the body; it is static and differs from the vitality displayed by athletic types. When with fat people, you rarely feel tense, because their large frames and calm dispositions give a sense of security.

Fat people are often labeled "pleasure-seeking," "lazy," or "gluttonous," yet their advantages are obvious: affability, kindness, humor, and so on. Most fat people are warm and lively, enjoy socializing, and are easily understood and accepted by those around them, making them popular. Fat people exercise good self-control in many areas but lose all resistance when faced with delicious food. Another annoying shortcoming is their aversion to exercise—or, more precisely, to moving at all. In addition, because they overestimate themselves and like to meddle, some people dislike them, yet this does not harm their good interpersonal relationships.

Many fat people are born with leadership ability. As noted earlier, large-framed people react more slowly, and precisely because of this they prefer not to handle everything themselves but to delegate. They are neither perpetually high-strung like intellectual types nor physically overtaxed like restless types, so they can become leaders. Many fat people are intellectually superior and morally upright, making them ideal notaries, commentators, or judges.

In contrast to fat people, thin people are sensitive, delicate, and alert. The thinner the person, the more tense and oppressive you feel in their company. Some thin people are introverted, quiet, sincere, and somewhat neurotic, making them harder to get along with. They are emotionally unstable and prone to anxiety, yet they possess the courage to shoulder everything. If your friend is thin, be sure to keep your promises; if your superior is thin, strive to complete tasks well. They have the personality of "if you do it, do it perfectly," pursuing excellence.

#### (II) The Slender Type

- **Facial features**: Soft contours, delicate skin, fine soft hair, gentle and pleasant voice.
- **Psychological features**: Delicate and refined.
- **Behavioral features**: Gentle.

Slender-type people love beauty greatly; exquisite, clever, and idealized things are what they pursue. Their income may only afford beer, yet they have the palate for champagne. They find it hard to discover joy in harsh environments, so you rarely see them in brick factories, iron mines, slaughterhouses, or steel mills.

They emphasize quality of life. Faced with a pair of eighty-dollar leather shoes and a pair of twenty-dollar shoes, most will choose the former even if their wallet is not full. Therefore, a clever salesperson need only say the following to win such customers: "Although the price is a bit high, this is absolutely genuine leather, and the sole design is extremely comfortable. Oh, these shoes look perfect on you. Trust me, you need them."

Observe and you will notice an interesting phenomenon: slender-type people often gather in refined settings such as symphony concerts, social dances, and opera performances. They enjoy associating with courteous and elegant people. Getting along with a slender-type person is like handling a delicate work of art: you must mobilize all your knowledge, humor, taste, and artistic sensibility; otherwise, it is difficult to please them. So if the girl you admire has delicate features, small hands and feet, and silky smooth hair, please note the following:

1. Do not shout at her;
2. Do not appear before her unkempt;
3. Compared with vulgar but amusing street art, she may prefer an elegant concert;
4. Take her to a restaurant with a good atmosphere, because she does not care whether the portions are large; she cares about soft lighting, graceful music, gleaming silverware, a white tablecloth, and your gentle words.

Note: The above points also apply to business negotiations, seeking cooperation, interpersonal interactions, enterprise management, and any occasion requiring contact with the outside world.

In summary, judging a person's character and divining their psychology from skin, hair, voice, and other bodily features is by no means nonsense. The key lies in whether you possess the devil's eye!

#### Case Two: Dr. Bai and the Patient's Conversation

Dr. Bai recently encountered a patient who gave him a great deal of trouble.

That was a woman in her thirties. After entering Dr. Bai's consultation room, she politely greeted him: "Hello, Doctor."

"Hello." Dr. Bai smiled and gestured to her. "Please have a seat. What's bothering you?"

"I've had some stomach pain recently," the patient replied.

"Stomach pain? You should see an internist for that, but this is the neurosurgery department." Dr. Bai was somewhat surprised.

"Well, I've had some stomach pain recently, maybe from eating something bad." With Dr. Bai's nod, the patient continued, "So I took some stomach medicine, like this bottle, roughly."

She picked up the medicine bottle on Dr. Bai's desk and gestured with it: "I probably took about a bottle's worth, but my stomach still feels uncomfortable."

"This is an antidepressant." Dr. Bai still didn't know what she was getting at.

"Ah, are you saying I need to take antidepressants? Do I have depression?"

"No, no, I didn't say you have depression. I was just saying that what's in this bottle is an antidepressant." Dr. Bai quickly clarified.

"Could it be that I took the wrong medicine?" The patient began pulling at her hair. "That can't be. I have a friend who ended up in the hospital after taking the wrong medicine and almost died."

"It shouldn't be that serious." Dr. Bai wiped the cold sweat from his forehead. "Didn't you say you took stomach medicine?"

"Okay, it should be stomach medicine. But the internist said this is neuralgia caused by too much stress, so I came to see you." The patient picked up the paperweight on Dr. Bai's desk again. "Sometimes when it hurts, it's like this thing is smashing my stomach."

"Then you should go see a psychiatrist," Dr. Bai suggested. "For neuralgia, they're more specialized."

"What? Shouldn't neuralgia be treated in neurosurgery? How are these two not the most relevant? Aren't you just trying to push me out?"

At this point, Dr. Bai had no idea how to respond.

Talking with this patient was more exhausting than dealing with three or four people at once. She kept veering off topic, creating trouble, and didn't listen to Dr. Bai's explanations at all. In the end, before any problem was resolved, the doctor was already exhausted.

#### Identifying Personality from How People Handle Documents

Americans have long been dedicated to studying the work environments in which people can achieve the highest productivity. During this research, an efficiency expert unexpectedly discovered that certain personality traits can be revealed by the way employees handle documents.

- **Documents scattered everywhere, piles here and there**: Such people handle tasks with a degree of aimlessness. They struggle to see things through from start to finish, have poor self-control, and cannot promptly adjust their emotions and habits, making it difficult for them to adapt quickly to new external environments.
- **Documents and materials in complete disarray, requiring a thorough search for each file**: These individuals have weaker work abilities and often achieve half the results with twice the effort. They lack organization and cannot proceed step by step. Their sense of responsibility is weak, and they lack persistent perseverance.
- **Habit of stuffing documents here and there**: Such people are often flashy but insubstantial. They like to play clever tricks, excel at maneuvering for advantage, and place great importance on appearances.
- **Documents on the desk and in drawers all neatly arranged, clearly layered and categorized**: These people handle tasks in an orderly manner, possess strong organizational and hands-on skills, work efficiently, and have a sense of responsibility. They approach everything with caution and diligence. However, they lack a pioneering spirit and have weaker innovative abilities.
- **Opening and reading mail immediately upon receipt and replying in the shortest possible time**: Such people have a strong sense of time. They want to complete everything as quickly as possible before moving on to other tasks.
- **Tossing letters aside without even looking at them**: If this person is not deliberately ignoring the letter, it indicates they are very busy at the moment, with their time tightly scheduled. Letters that are not particularly important to them will naturally be set aside for later processing. Of course, they may never find the time to handle them.
- **Having someone else read letters on their behalf**: Such people place great trust in others. They are not skilled at hiding themselves and can share many of their secrets with others.
- **Enjoying reading junk mail**: They have strong curiosity and can quickly absorb new things.
- **Deleting junk mail on sight**: They are quite cautious, with strong self-defense awareness, and do not easily trust another person.

#### Identifying People by Color Preferences

In daily life, we see the presence and application of various colors. For example, Coca-Cola's logo is red, and McDonald's brand identity is yellow... Some merchants have openly stated that the color of a logo, to some extent, represents the spirit of the enterprise. Everyone has their own favorite colors, so what meanings do these colors symbolize when applied to people?

FBI agent Henry Gies tells us that a person's preferred colors can reveal a great deal about their inner self. When negotiating with terrorists, FBI agents also use the colors of the other party's clothing to determine their personality. It can be said that there is a very close relationship between psychology and color.

When feeling restless, a visit to a park filled with green or a seaside full of blue can quickly restore calm. Yet in a bar where the sofas are all red, people often remain agitated and can only drown their sorrows in drink. Different colors evoke different feelings in us. In other words, people who like different colors also differ in their attitudes toward life and interactions with others.

Gies points out that human brainwaves respond to red with alertness and to blue and green with relaxation. In other words, blue and green have a spontaneous regulatory effect on tense and agitated states of mind; they are nature's best psychological sedatives for humans. Many experiments conducted by psychologists have confirmed this conclusion. They found that in a blue environment, people's emotions are relatively stable and their pulse rates are steadier. However, when people are in a red environment, their emotions tend to become excited, blood pressure rises, and pulse rates quicken.

A person's preferred color often represents their personality. Through monitoring terrorists' brainwaves, FBI agents have determined that brainwaves change with alterations in the colors within the visual field. This scientifically confirms the influence of color on the mind. Accordingly, they often provide terrorists with items of various colors and allow them to choose their favorite hues, with the goal of unlocking their "multicolored" psychological packaging through their color selections.

What personality traits do different colors reveal? Let us look at the conclusions drawn by FBI agents.

#### Story: The Conflict Between the Father and Tom

He could not understand why his son refused the ready-made department store and insisted on pursuing the unpromising field of fashion design.

Young Tom had inherited his father's stubbornness. He insisted on working at the department store while attending night school.

"Mr. Balkan, you must understand my intentions. I had high hopes for him. For three years he worked at the store during the day and attended that night school in the evening. Now he tells me he has found another job as a designer at some silk factory... Oh, heavens! I really don't know what he's thinking!"

I poured him a glass of water and asked, "So you've come today hoping I can tell you what he's thinking?"

"Yes. You know the economy is poor right now, and I need his help. The boy is capable, but I can't persuade him. So, Mr. Balkan, I can only ask for your assistance to see what this child is actually suited for. I'm worried he's just trapped in his own imagination and wasting his prime years." As he spoke, he handed me several photos of Tom. "I know you're always accurate at reading people."

From the photos, Tom appeared to be a very handsome young man. His skin was good, and his well-developed muscles wrapped around his bones, giving an impression of creativity. His forehead was flat, his brow high and broad, his nose straight and slightly pointed, conveying an artistic quality.

"He's a lively young fellow. Do you want him to take over the store?"

"Yes. This child has many ideas. He knows how to arrange items to better attract customers and has good judgment about wrapping paper. So if he were willing, he could certainly make my store thrive. But he says working in the store doesn't make him happy..."

That was the crux of the conflict: an idealistic child full of artistic creativity, and a father who, though aware of the child's talents, did not know in which area those talents lay.

If this conflict is not resolved well, two outcomes often result: first, the child's rebellion exceeds the parents' expectations, leading them to pursue their own path in lonely isolation; second, the child chooses to obey the parents and toils in another field that is entirely incompatible with their nature. Whichever outcome occurs, I believe, is not one you would wish to see.

#### Typical Case Analysis

In a psychological clinic in South Korea, a middle-aged woman dressed appropriately and with refined makeup was invited into the counselor's consultation room.

"Hello, Ms. Wen," the counselor said after greeting her, referring to the results of the psychological assessment. "Based on your assessment results, we believe you possess basic emotional intelligence and can maintain ordinary interpersonal relationships..."

"Mm." Ms. Wen nodded repeatedly, displaying a good attitude and composure.

"However, your depression is quite severe. You cannot regulate your temper well and often experience intermittent outbursts due to excessive stress..."

"Is that so?" Ms. Wen continued nodding but countered, "I'm not like that. I don't lose my temper much."

"All right. You may be resistant to this result, but please listen patiently until I finish..."

"From the very beginning it's wrong. I don't have depression at all!"

"Please let me finish." Sweat had already begun to appear on the counselor's forehead. "The assessment results indicate that you cannot properly recognize your own emotions, and as a result, certain problems have arisen in your relationships with others..."

"Is this result reliable?" Ms. Wen was still nodding, yet her words were filled with doubt. "I think I'm quite normal. There's nothing that strange about me, is there? But why does this assessment keep saying bad things about me?"

"When one's shortcomings are pointed out, people always deny them at the first moment."

"Is that so? But I'm not like that." Ms. Wen rebutted at the first moment.

A brief silence fell over the consultation room. Soon the counselor could not help laughing. Ms. Wen seemed somewhat embarrassed, lowered her head silently, and blushed.

This Ms. Wen was a typical case of someone with a dual personality. On one hand, she was a privileged middle-aged lady of refinement who possessed good manners and virtue; even when others pointed out her faults, she could refrain from anger or irritation and simply nod to show she was listening attentively. On the other hand, she also possessed an overbearing mindset that assumed she was always right and would not allow others to say anything negative about her. The combination of these two personalities produced the strange behavior described above.

#### Xiao Jiang's Blind Date Experience

Through a friend's introduction, Xiao Jiang went on a blind date with a man said to be very handsome.

The moment she saw him in the café, Xiao Jiang was indeed drawn to his appearance. The man had a rugged build and melancholic eyes; even the way he held his coffee cup appeared elegant and graceful.

Xiao Jiang's own appearance was only average. The man clearly did not take her seriously, yet he still chatted with her in a friendly manner.

Through conversation, Xiao Jiang learned that his family had once been prominent, though it had declined in recent generations. Even so, he knew many celebrities in the film and television circles and political circles. He had also studied in the United States and now worked as a white-collar professional at a multinational company...

His conditions were so favorable that Xiao Jiang felt somewhat ashamed of herself. She had assumed he would not want to see her a second time, but a few days later he actually called and asked her out again.

The conversation covered the same topics as before, yet Xiao Jiang now harbored a trace of doubt. After the date, she contacted the friend who had introduced them and inquired about the man's situation.

"Him? There's nothing special. His family background is ordinary. Right now he's working as a gas station attendant."

The friend's words left Xiao Jiang deeply puzzled. During their third date, she voiced her doubts to him.

"So you never believed me at all." The man's attitude shifted so abruptly that Xiao Jiang was startled. He shouted at her: "Yes, I was recently laid off and I'm working as a gas station attendant now, but so what? Don't successful people ever hit a low point?"

With red-rimmed eyes he stormed out, leaving Xiao Jiang uneasy yet somewhat guilty. Only after questioning her friend did she learn that everything the man had boasted about was a lie. He had never been abroad, had never worked at a multinational company, and the story about a prominent family was pure nonsense...

Just like the man Xiao Jiang met on her blind date, individuals with histrionic personality disorder are typically vain, superficial, and hypocritical, with extremely rapid emotional shifts. When others suit their tastes, they appear cordial and polite, but once exposed, they immediately become hysterical and storm off.

#### Ah Sang's Story

Ah Sang was regarded by everyone as a "strong woman." She was decisive and bold in her actions, with a strong drive to advance. In less than two years at the company, she rose from an ordinary employee to vice general manager.

On the day Ah Sang assumed the vice general manager position, every colleague who was on good terms with her was delighted and praised her for "achieving success in her career." Yet Ah Sang herself still wore a dejected expression.

"Don't tell me there's anything you're dissatisfied with after taking the vice general manager position?" the general manager, who greatly valued Ah Sang, asked her.

"It's not that, Mr. Yang." Ah Sang shook her head. "Of course I'm very happy to have been promoted to this position, but sometimes I wonder: I keep pursuing success nonstop, but what exactly is success to me?"

The reason Ah Sang felt this confusion was inseparable from her family environment during childhood. She was the eldest daughter and had a younger sister two years her junior.

The younger sister was small and exceptionally intelligent, so she was favored by their parents more than Ah Sang was. After every exam, their parents would lavish praise on the sister's test papers and offer verbal or material rewards. Because Ah Sang's academic performance was weaker, she was not favored by her parents and was always left aside and neglected.

Unwilling to accept this, Ah Sang worked exceptionally hard and her grades improved steadily. Yet no matter how diligently she studied, her parents remained indifferent to her achievements. Gradually, Ah Sang came to feel that her successes were not yet big enough or obvious enough, so she needed to achieve even greater successes to prove herself to her parents. After striving for so many years, however, Ah Sang grew increasingly confused, unsure what exactly she had been pursuing all these years.

Ah Sang's feeling stemmed from the "inner child" she had developed in childhood. Her inner child had such a strong need for success and attention. Yet after growing up, she clearly could no longer obtain the affirmation her parents had once given, and this produced confusion within her. At such times, if someone could provide her with a similar feeling, she would inevitably become devoted to that person.

#### Seeing Through Others' Past Through the Inner Child

**Micro-expression Keywords**

Do not underestimate the influence of the word "past" on a person. All our current behaviors reflect consciousness that remained unsatisfied in the past. By understanding our own inner child, we can understand ourselves and correct our shortcomings. Understanding others' inner children is even more helpful for reaching people's hearts and controlling them.

A young pony was tied to a wooden stake. It was still small and very mischievous, always wanting either to chase fluttering butterflies or to nibble on roadside grass. Yet with its strength, it could not budge the stake to which it was tied. Over time, whenever the young pony was tied to the stake, it would stay obediently and stop struggling.

Gradually the pony grew into a horse. Its strength multiplied, enabling it to pull carts weighing hundreds of pounds and to uproot that small wooden stake. Yet whenever the horse was tied to the stake, it would behave as obediently as it had in childhood, with no thought of moving the stake.

Habit is a terrifying force, especially when it is a deeply rooted habit formed in childhood. This terrifying force of habit is closely connected to the "inner child" we are about to discuss.

The neo-psychoanalytic school and modern object relations psychology hold that most modern people possess an internal relational pattern. This pattern determines how we interact with others, society, the world, and even ourselves. The pattern is usually established before the age of six and is referred to in behavioral psychology as the "inner child."

In simple terms, the inner child is a fixed pattern formed in a child's mind due to the ways, methods, and behaviors with which parents treated them during early childhood. In adulthood, individuals unconsciously apply this pattern to themselves and even to others. Based on this, we can work in the opposite direction: through the external manifestations of a person's "inner child," we can easily infer their past and personality, and through this, achieve the goal of controlling them.

#### Organizational Structure Psychology

Once there was a prince who wanted to marry a real princess. He traveled the world in search of one, but always encountered obstacles. There were plenty of princesses, yet the prince could never be sure whether they were truly real, for something about each of them seemed off. In the end he had to return home, deeply unhappy, for he longed so much for a genuine princess.

One night a terrible storm suddenly broke, with thunder and rain that struck fear into everyone. At that moment someone knocked on the door, and the old king went to open it.

The girl standing outside said she was a princess. But heavens! After the wind and rain she looked dreadful. Water streamed down her hair and clothes, into her shoes, and out again at the heels.

The old queen thought, “No matter, we shall know soon enough.” She went to the bedroom, removed all the bedding, and placed a single pea on the bed. She then laid twenty mattresses on top of the pea and twenty eiderdown quilts on top of the mattresses.

The princess slept on this arrangement that night.

In the morning everyone asked, “Dear princess, how did you sleep?”

“Ah, not at all comfortably!” the princess replied. “I hardly closed my eyes all night. Heaven knows what was pressing into me beneath the bed—something so hard, it was dreadful!”

Everyone then knew she was indeed a real princess. Only a true princess could feel a single pea through twenty layers of mattresses and twenty eiderdown quilts. No one else would have skin so delicate.

You are surely familiar with this fairy tale. I am no master of fairy tales; I recount it only to introduce the topic that follows—human body-structure psychology, or, in plain terms, reading a person by the thickness of hair, muscle, and skin. It may sound improbable. In brief, human body structure can be divided into two types: robust and slender.

#### Life Portraits and the Path to Success

Many years ago I hosted a small family gathering. Someone suggested a game: each person would sum up their life in a few sentences, as if for a gravestone. After everyone finished, we passed the papers around. One young man’s entry has stayed with me ever since. He wrote only three punctuation marks: a dash “—”, an exclamation point “!”, and a period “.” When I asked what it meant, he answered sadly, “A headlong rush, ending in sorrow and self-pity, then a quiet close.”

I would say this describes the life of most people.

Success and happiness require exploration, yet the real question is how much time and energy you devote to that exploration. We allow setbacks and failures, and we allow a certain amount of starting over. But if you still wish to reach the shores of success and happiness within your lifetime, you must shorten the period of exploration.

Winners win because they find the right path in the shortest time and then follow it unwaveringly to the end. This brings us to questions of personality analysis and career guidance, and back to the example of Tom I mentioned earlier.

I did not want to see a designer of exceptional talent buried under a noisy pile of money, so I told the father, “From your description and these photographs I see a spark of art. If you trust me, give Tom the confidence to walk his own path.”

Although the father had a rather hot temper, he listened and agreed to a deal with his son: if Tom achieved nothing in fashion design within two years, he would return to help in the store.

Tom was undoubtedly fortunate, though he had already walked many thorny roads before that fortune arrived. A month ago I met Tom again. He was now head of the design department at the silk factory, with five or six designers under him, and he also handled cooperation and negotiations with other companies. He had come specifically to ask me for advice on the skill of “reading people.”

#### Emotional Support Can Rescue a Child’s Future

Next we must address a deeper issue. This section has already discussed the expression of “shame” and “anger.” Some may ask, what about micro-expressions (微表情)?

In conclusion, the problem of micro-expressions is more profound than that of ordinary expressions. Children generally have less ability than adults to suppress emotion. When they feel negative emotions, whether they cannot suppress them or cannot suppress them completely, the expressions appear readily. A child’s facial changes are therefore easy to notice.

However, when a child expresses emotion through micro-expressions, it is possible that even the child has not registered the emotion. This means a child’s micro-expressions must be treated as danger signals and handled with care.

Finally, for children whose mistakes produce different emotional changes, we offer a solution: emotional support.

“Shame” is an important opportunity to revise one’s self-image. For example, explain an incorrect answer, help the child discover the cause of the mistake, and then present a similar problem for another attempt. Once the child answers correctly, offer appropriate praise—“Well done!”—to facilitate correction and reflection.

When a child feels “anger,” the impulse is to remove the obstacle. At that moment tell the child that the mistake itself is not an obstacle but an opportunity to grow. For the child to accept this idea, patient repetition is required.

If a “fear” response appears, the child will instinctively try to avoid the threat. Begin with simpler questions, guide the child step by step toward correct answers, and gradually bring the child to the point where the same level of problem can be handled without avoidance—learning instead to overcome it. This approach shows the child that, besides avoidance, more proactive methods exist for solving problems.

#### (7) Round Heads and Square Heads

In general terms, the former refers to a head shape close to spherical, while the latter refers to a head shape close to square.

Not long ago an engineering-company owner came to see me. He had a large manufacturing plant and wanted to know how to select an efficient crane operator from a large group of workers. It seemed a small matter, yet it had troubled him for a long time; every operator he had chosen had caused an accident through negligence. Following his usual standards of caution and steadiness, the owner hired two new workers, but accidents increased rather than decreased. In desperation he came to me for advice.

I visited the factory and met the two new workers—dark-skinned, with clearly angular occiputs when viewed from behind, both square-headed types.

I pointed to a fair-skinned, rough-featured, broad-built young man with a short, round head and said, “That fellow looks promising. Why not try him?”

“Mr. Balkan, you mean Michael? Oh, he won’t do. He’s too unsteady; I can’t take the risk.”

“Trust me. At least give him a trial.”

Events proved my judgment correct.

The owner later reported that in all his years of monitoring manufacturing operations he had “never seen anyone manage a crane as skillfully and safely as Michael.”

I had met the two new workers and Michael only once, with no physical contact or verbal exchange. I had simply analyzed their psychology from the shape of their heads. The new workers kept making mistakes because square-headed people tend to be excessively cautious in everything; by contrast, round-headed people, though prone to impulsiveness, are also adaptable, adventurous, and capable of being meticulous within their boldness.

#### Characteristics of Passive-Aggressive Personality

There are people who, when dissatisfied with you, never express it to your face. Sometimes they themselves do not realize how strong their dissatisfaction is. Instead they make inexplicable mistakes or behave in a negative, dilatory way that leaves you embarrassed and furious. Yet when you try to vent your anger, they always have a ready excuse or look at you with innocent eyes. In extreme cases the people around you may even turn hostile toward you because of this person, who stands aside smiling like the schemer in a film who sows discord among others.

Such individuals are truly troublesome, and in behavioral psychology they have a specific name: passive-aggressive personality.

The reason it is called passive-aggressive rather than active-aggressive is that their aggression is not active or spontaneous; it takes the form of negativity or error.

When dealing with others, such people are usually in a weaker position. Yet no matter how weak that position, when anger arises their first impulse is still to strike back. Because the power imbalance is severe, they cannot express anger or even refuse the stronger party’s demands, for fear of losing what they currently possess.

At the same time, the anger stored in their unconscious prevents them from maintaining an objective attitude. They frequently procrastinate, break promises, or bungle simple tasks. Although this behavior does not directly express anger, it has the same effect as active aggression: it leaves the stronger party anxious and enraged.

#### Typical Features of Paranoid Personality

People with paranoid personality are constantly suspicious of others and brood over injuries and insults they believe others have inflicted. They are like porcupines at every moment—either quarreling openly, publicly accusing others, or making sarcastic remarks behind their backs. Once they decide someone is making things difficult for them, they can see no virtues in that person; even sincere attempts at reconciliation are met with absolute distrust.

The Chinese Classification of Mental Disorders and Diagnostic Criteria once listed the common behavioral features of paranoid personality:

1. They interpret others’ unintentional or even friendly actions as malicious and, without sufficient evidence, believe others are exploiting, deceiving, or trying to harm them.
2. They are extremely conceited and self-important, always considering themselves correct and capable; if anything goes wrong they blame others. Even when the fault is clearly their own and evidence is presented, they refuse to admit it.
3. They easily develop pathological jealousy and never forgive others’ offenses, remembering them long afterward and interpreting every action through a suspicious lens, convinced that others are targeting them.
4. They connect unrelated events in their environment to themselves, feeling that everything is aimed at them; they may even identify with content in broadcasts or television and maintain intense vigilance and hostility toward supposed “conspiracies” from the outside world.
5. If married, they repeatedly suspect their spouse of infidelity and cannot tolerate even the slightest hint of disloyalty.

#### Case 1: Driver Old Zhang’s Conversation with the Girl

Driver Old Zhang picked up a young woman. After she got in, he asked politely, “Where to, miss?”

“Um, just drive ahead for now. I haven’t decided—probably somewhere south of the bridge,” she replied.

Old Zhang started the car. They had not gone far when the girl suddenly asked, “Master, the houses south of the bridge are expensive, right?”

“Huh?” The question caught Old Zhang off guard. After a moment he answered, “They really aren’t cheap. I live over there myself. Prices have risen sharply these past few years…”

“Is the scenery north of the bridge better?” the girl interrupted.

“North of the bridge?” Old Zhang thought again. “There are more universities over there…”

“Universities? Going to university must be really interesting.”

Old Zhang was baffled by the girl’s remark. He ventured, “Miss, are we heading south or north of the bridge? Are you going to look at houses?”

“Oh, no. I’m thinking of opening a milk-tea shop recently,” she said, shaking her head.

“A milk-tea shop?” Old Zhang was almost in tears. What did opening a milk-tea shop have to do with where they were driving right now? “Yes, it should be quite profitable.” “Never mind profit for the moment—where exactly are we going?” Old Zhang exploded.
