Many people cannot help smiling at the exchange between poor Old Zhang and the girl. Yet the girl had no intention of toying with him. The effect was produced entirely by her ADHD-type personality.

#### Main Behavioral Characteristics of ADHD-Type Personality

This is the most striking behavioral feature of ADHD-type personality. Generally, people with this personality do not pay attention when others speak. In other words, when listening they let words go in one ear and out the other; they may believe they are listening attentively, yet in reality they have no idea what was said.

Second, they tend to interrupt in order to voice their own thoughts. Their ideas flit about so rapidly that they fear forgetting them if they do not speak at once. Because of this they are often considered rude, although they themselves are unaware of it.

Finally, people with ADHD-type personality frequently suffer from restlessness and low self-confidence. Their character is rather scattered—in colloquial terms, a bit “off-kilter.” Their reactions are always half a beat slow, and they often fail to give others feedback. While performing an action or speaking a sentence, their thoughts may already have circled the universe, making it difficult for ordinary people to understand them; they are frequently judged as absent-minded and erratic.

Getting along with someone who has ADHD-type personality simply requires a little extra tolerance. They are not inherently difficult; their thoughts merely move too quickly. The important point is never to let their leaping thoughts lead the conversation, or you may spend a long time discussing something only to forget what you originally wanted to achieve. At that moment you will be like Dr. Bai or Old Zhang in the cases above—either flying into a rage or surrendering completely.

#### Xiao Bin’s Story

A-Sang may not have shown the pattern very clearly, but Xiao Bin, whom I know, is a very typical example.

Xiao Bin and Xiao Xu were colleagues in the same group. Although Xiao Bin was considerably more capable than Xiao Xu, he often did Xiao Xu’s work, and Xiao Xu took it for granted that he could order Xiao Bin around.

Many colleagues could not understand the relationship. In their view Xiao Bin had no need to depend on Xiao Xu; with his ability he could handle matters independently.

For Xiao Bin, however, the situation was different. Before he met Xiao Xu, he would hesitate over every task, worrying that he would not do it well enough, that others would outperform him, or that the boss would scold him. He always tried to make his work perfect, yet this very perfectionism caused delays that provoked the boss’s fury.

After “teaming up” with Xiao Xu, Xiao Xu’s daily task became to encourage and flatter Xiao Bin so that he could work without anxiety about the future.

There is no doubt that Xiao Xu had accurately identified Xiao Bin’s “inner child” and, by accommodating his temperament, created value for himself.

The influence of the inner child is profound. It does not grow naturally with age; on the contrary, it erupts powerfully when we fall into pain or difficulty. It is a force that binds us, yet if we recognize and break through it, it can greatly propel our growth.

#### Jenny’s Example

Jenny was always bustling about the office, yet no one liked her. The newcomer A-Dan felt some sympathy and grew closer to her.

“Please take care of the report,” A-Dan instructed during a joint project. “I’ll finish the contract.”

“No problem, leave it to me,” Jenny promised earnestly.

The next morning, just before the report to the manager, Jenny slapped her forehead and said, “Oh no, I forgot the report. I’m really sorry—I’ll do it right away.”

Although A-Dan had handled the contract successfully, Jenny’s lapse caused both of them to receive a scolding from the manager.

The same thing happened repeatedly. Gradually A-Dan saw Jenny’s true nature: her “forgetfulness” was not occasional, and it was precisely this trait that made colleagues avoid her at every turn<|eos|>

#### The Glib and Flattering Person

In real life, some people, in order to achieve a certain expected goal, or to broaden their career prospects, or to gain some business benefits, use sweet words to flatter and fawn, or do things that make you feel overly intimate, tricking you into being deceived. Others try to pull strings, get close by claiming relations, or drag you into kinship and friendship, and so on.

During the Three Kingdoms period, Xun You was one of Cao Cao’s strategists. When Xun You was thirteen, his grandfather passed away. While the family was still in mourning, Zhang Quan, a former subordinate of Xun You’s grandfather, came to pay his respects.

As soon as Zhang Quan reached the coffin, he began to wail loudly, as if he had lost his own parents. While weeping, he declared that he wished to guard the tomb of the late prefect in order to repay the deep kindness and great virtue of Xun You’s grandfather.

Zhang Quan’s display moved the Xun family deeply, and they prepared to grant his request with gratitude. At that moment, the ever-calm Xun You, after careful observation, sensed that the man’s behavior was highly unusual. Xun You recalled that his grandfather had never mentioned this person to the family, indicating that Zhang Quan had not been a close associate. Nor had anyone heard of any great favor the grandfather had shown him. Xun You reasoned that when someone offers excessive kindness, there must be an ulterior motive. Moreover, Zhang Quan’s request was overly insistent, his words evasive, and his face showed alarm and worry. Xun You concluded that the man was hiding something and was afraid.

After spotting these flaws, Xun You quickly shared his suspicions with his uncle. Sure enough, after the uncle questioned him, Zhang Quan confessed that he had killed someone and had hoped to use the pretext of guarding the tomb to escape legal punishment.

#### Like Signatures from Student Days

The handwriting of their signatures remains the same as it was in their student days. Although such people may appear quite mature on the surface, they are in fact immature. They cannot adapt to the adult world and may still be living with their parents even at age forty-five. They often harbor ideas that sound childish and unrealistic, yet they themselves fail to notice this.

Besides handwriting revealing character, spontaneous doodles can also expose psychological secrets.

When taking phone calls or attending meetings, if paper and pen are nearby, do you have the habit of doodling absentmindedly? When facing troubles at work or in life, or when feeling bored or distressed, do you scribble on paper without thinking, then toss the paper aside as if nothing happened?

Experts at Germany’s Bonn Institute of Psychology spent a year observing people’s superfluous movements during phone calls and meetings. They found that this unconscious doodling is closely linked to certain personality traits.

Renata Belkova, a researcher at Russia’s Human Development Center and a doctor of psychology, commented that abstract drawings can indeed reflect a person’s inner thoughts. Someone preoccupied with worries may show nothing on the surface, yet the “pictures” drawn subconsciously reveal their attitude toward those around them and the thoughts they are trying to conceal.

#### The Boastful Talker

Such people often speak with great fluency, covering broad and lofty topics yet remaining careless about details. They never concern themselves with trivial matters.

The Nagoya Chamber of Commerce and Industry urgently needed to hire a director. Nagao Yoshiro, president of Meitetsu Department Store, recommended one of his friends to Chairman Tsuchikawa Motoo.

After the interview, Nagao asked Tsuchikawa how his friend had performed. Tsuchikawa immediately replied, “Your friend is not the right talent; he will be hard to retain.”

Nagao was astonished and somewhat annoyed. “You only spoke with him for twenty minutes. How can you be sure he is not the right talent? Your judgment seems hasty and arbitrary.”

Tsuchikawa explained: “From the moment he met me, he talked nonstop and gave me no chance to speak. When I spoke, he looked around distractedly, half-listening and indifferent. That is the first reason I say he is not the right talent. Second, he loves to advertise his personal connections, mentioning high officials as close friends and celebrities as drinking buddies, all to show he is no ordinary person. Third, when I asked about his management methods, he could not provide any answers. Is this the kind of person who qualifies as talent?”

After hearing Tsuchikawa’s words, Nagao nodded repeatedly, acknowledging that they made perfect sense.

#### Body Type and Personality Psychology

A giant ocean liner crossing the Atlantic begins to move so slowly that the motion is barely perceptible. Gradually it accelerates. Once at full speed, no matter how skilled the helmsman, it cannot execute a sudden turn or stop, unlike the small tugboats alongside it. Similarly, once a train has gathered speed, stopping requires considerable braking time. Automobile advertisements often praise cars for being “nimble and responsive,” yet no one uses those words for a twelve-ton truck.

This is the simplest distinction between “large” and “small.”

You may wonder what this has to do with the subject of this book. Indeed, what follows is the psychology of personality as expressed through body type. The same “large” and “small” principle applies to people. In short, a large-bodied person tends to react more slowly, while a small-framed person tends to react more quickly.

The first to link body type with personality psychology was German psychiatrist Ernst Kretschmer. He identified four basic body types: pyknic, asthenic, athletic, and dysplastic.

Through extensive clinical research, Kretschmer showed that people of different body types also differ in personality and susceptibility to certain disorders, and he summarized these findings.

#### Dual Personality: “Two People” in One Body

Micro-expression keywords: Every one of us has multiple facets, yet not everyone possesses a dual personality. Only when personality has split to such an extent that one personality cannot be influenced or controlled by the other can it be called a true dual personality.

Many people born in the 1970s and 1980s are familiar with Akira Toriyama’s Dragon Ball, and many born in the 1990s know it as well. In Dragon Ball there is a girl named Launch who “transforms” whenever she sneezes.

Normally, Launch is a gentle girl with blue hair and a simple mind, skilled at housework and cooking. But once she sneezes, she becomes a blonde, hot-tempered, violent criminal who robs banks with machine guns and rocket launchers.

The character in the manga is fictional and exaggerated. In real life we do not encounter people who change into someone else after a sneeze. Yet around us there are indeed many individuals with dual personalities. When we first meet them, we may think they are affable gentlemen or refined ladies. After getting to know them better, however, we discover they are not as they first appeared; they possess another set of habits completely different from, and sometimes directly opposed to, their outward image, yet these two sets of habits coexist within the same person.

#### (I) The Robust Type

- **Facial and physical features**: Large build, coarse and stiff hair, deep and resonant voice.
- **Psychological traits**: Rough, bold, straightforward.
- **Behavioral traits**: Impulsive, physically strong and powerful.

Of course, they can also be intelligent, compassionate, and full of imagination. The great sculptor Rodin was a robust type; his masterpiece The Thinker expresses his powerful and vigorous nature.

Robust types pay little attention to details. Clothing, hairstyle, and fingernails are not their concern. They often ignore social settings, laughing heartily, speaking bluntly, or even telling crude jokes. They enjoy the company of other robust types and display leadership qualities. Former New York mayor Fiorello La Guardia was a representative figure; his image of clenched fists and fearless combativeness remains vivid. Lenin exemplified the people’s leader: sturdy in build and unconcerned with trifles. Peasants arriving from all over Russia would exclaim in surprise at first sight, “Why, he looks just like us!”

Do not ask a train driver to do embroidery, nor ask a poet to shovel coal. This is the art of recognizing talent that every leader must master. A leader’s true value and ability are proven by guiding subordinates to success.

#### Personality Projected in Head Shape

The shape of the skull bears certain natural connections to personality traits.

Consider animals: lions and tigers have broader skulls, while elk and giraffes have narrower ones; correspondingly, the former are fierce and the latter gentle. Broad-skulled eagles, hawks, and vultures are predators, while narrow-skulled doves and chickens are usually prey.

By the same logic, the shape of a person’s skull reflects, to some extent, their psychological characteristics. By studying skulls, anthropologists can determine a person’s race, sex, personality, and talents. They have also found that Greeks, Italians, and Germans tend to have longer skulls, Asians generally have broader skulls, Sicilians have smaller and narrower skulls, and Swedes and Scots often have square skulls. Of course, as ordinary people without special abilities, we cannot see another person’s skull directly, so we must rely on external indicators—namely, the shape of the head above the ears and eyebrows—to make judgments.

In daily life and work, the ability to discern someone’s psychology at first glance is key to success. At the end of this chapter, we will analyze in detail the relationship between head shape and psychological characteristics.

#### Wang Yaru in the TV Drama Yearning

In the television drama Yearning, the person considered the most lacking in human warmth and the most stubborn and headstrong is Huifang’s sister-in-law, the skilled physician Wang Yaru.

Wang Yaru is arrogant, aloof, eccentric, suspicious, and cold. Although she is an excellent doctor, she is poor at social interaction, rarely smiles, and does not get along with Xiaofang, Yuejuan, Aunt Liu, or Huifang. Even her only brother seldom sees her smile. Toward her former lover Luo Gang, who once wronged her, she behaves in an utterly unreasonable manner. Even her only close classmate, Tuan Li, cannot tolerate her rigid and peculiar temperament and nearly breaks with her several times.

Wang Yaru’s behavioral pattern exemplifies a very typical personality feature in behavioral psychology: the paranoid personality. The most prominent characteristic of such people is that they live in a state of constant suspicion and complaint. They act entirely according to their own will, disregarding others’ feelings and social consequences. They speak and act solely according to their own preferences. Even when they are wrong, they refuse to admit it, and thus they almost always hurt others, reaching the point where “everyone hates them.”

#### People Who Like to Expose Others’ Privacy

When four or five colleagues gather, conversation often revolves around someone’s private matters. Some play the role of revealing the secrets, while others play the role of listeners. What are the psychological motives of those who enjoy exposing others’ privacy to create topics, and of those who listen?

People who disclose others’ private information usually harbor hostility, envy, or inferiority toward that person. Listeners often share similar mindsets, which is why they pay attention.

- Desire to relieve psychological frustration from unmet needs: Such people usually have conflicts with the subject of the conversation and feel resentful, so they supply these privacy-revealing topics.
- Envy-based psychology: The targets of discussion are neither superiors nor subordinates but colleagues. By revealing such information, these people hope to gain favor with superiors and popularity with the opposite sex. The content usually concerns the target’s private life, with the aim of damaging their image. If listeners also dislike the target, the speaker’s goal is even easier to achieve.

#### Manifestations of Dual Personality in Daily Life

Dual-personality individuals are common in everyday life. Examples include:

- A normally quiet and shy girl who at home chatters incessantly and loses her temper without reason
- An easygoing optimist who sometimes “gazes at the sky at a 45-degree angle and sheds lonely tears”
- A worker who always shouts and curses loudly yet treats women with more courtesy and consideration than a gentleman

All of these are expressions of dual personality.

When dealing with dual-personality individuals, there is no need to become overly nervous. Generally, they will interact with you using the personality that met and knows you. You may ignore the other personality they occasionally display, provided it does not affect you. If it does interfere with communication, you must stay alert, try to adapt to the other personality, and turn a two-person conversation into a three-person one. As long as the dual personality has not reached a pathological level, interacting with such people is generally safe.

#### The Definition of Histrionic Personality

In behavioral psychology, such people are defined as “histrionic personalities.”

As the term suggests, individuals with this personality always behave in an extremely dramatic manner, as if performing in a poorly written, exaggerated television drama. They typically wear outlandish clothing or, in milder cases, dress in an overly ornate style in hopes of attracting attention. Their behavior is also flirtatious and seductive—not because they wish to flirt with or seduce the person in front of them, but because they seek permission, praise, and protection. To achieve this, they consider even age-inappropriate actions normal and interpret others’ strange looks as signs of attention.

Histrionic personalities crave attention so intensely that they frequently become overly emotional. Once they sense insufficient attention, they express their feelings in exaggerated ways, even reversing their attitude 180 degrees, bursting into tears at the slightest provocation and becoming quite annoying.

#### ADHD-Type Personality: The “Alien” with Leaping Thoughts

Micro-expression keywords: People with ADHD-type personality have difficulty maintaining attention; therefore, during interactions one must constantly bring them back to the topic. For most people this requires patience and strong self-control.

ADHD, known in psychology as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, was originally recognized as a common childhood mental disorder—commonly called childhood hyperactivity. With increased understanding of the condition, psychologists have recently discovered that the symptoms can also appear in adults and form a specific personality type known as ADHD-type personality<|eos|>

#### Other Characteristics of Histrionic Personality and Ways to Get Along

In addition to the above traits, people with histrionic personality are usually highly susceptible to suggestion. Both external environments and other people can easily influence them. In interpersonal relationships, they always overestimate the closeness of their bonds with others and place excessive trust in people. At first glance they may seem easygoing, yet actual interactions quickly reveal their various shortcomings.

Moreover, to achieve their own ends, people with histrionic personality can employ a variety of tactics—lying, deception, or obsequious flattery. For them these are merely performances that cause no psychological burden. When dealing with someone who has histrionic personality, playing along with their “act” is not the best approach. The optimal way to get along is to identify their personality type and show tolerance without indulgence.

#### Causes and Suggestions for Getting Along

The causes of paranoid personality are generally considered to be a lack of love in early years or setbacks experienced later in life. Being distrusted in childhood, or being unable to bear frustration, injustice, or failure in adulthood, can all lead to the development of paranoid personality. In addition, excessive self-demand may also contribute. For example, someone without formal education may feel inferior and therefore resent any mention of academic qualifications by others; a person with unattractive features may feel that others are constantly targeting their appearance.

When interacting with someone who has paranoid personality, remain tolerant and do not let their suspicions provoke your own anger. It is also essential to uphold principles and maintain a certain distance. When faced with their endless doubts, express resistance at the appropriate moment.

#### (5) Long-Shaped Head

Measured from the midpoint between the forehead and eyebrows over the top of the head to the back of the skull, the length is 7.6 inches or more.

If your child has a long-shaped head, I can guarantee they will always come up with peculiar questions that leave you dizzy. For instance, they like to ask, “Where will we go on vacation next summer?” or “What should I do when I grow up?”

Indeed, compared with the present, they prefer to focus on the distant future. In work, when negotiating with such a person, you must prepare a long-term plan and a precise budget; otherwise you cannot expect their support. In daily life they excel at socializing and enjoy group living, so they are very family-oriented.

A wise leader knows to place employees with long-shaped heads in social positions to fully utilize their sociable nature.

#### People Who Like to Keep Dogs Are Gentle

Such individuals are easygoing and docile, appearing very approachable. They are extroverted, dislike loneliness, laugh and joke all day, and quickly blend in with others. They are warm-hearted, sensitive, and candid; any genuine thought immediately shows on their face or in their words and actions, yet they also tend to follow the crowd.

Generally, people who keep dogs with unattractive appearances mostly lack in their own looks; those who keep poodles are lively and childlike; those who keep large dogs have strong vanity; those who keep pedigree dogs come from affluent families and enjoy smooth careers; those who keep only Oriental dogs tend to be dictatorial and suspicious; those who adopt stray dogs are compassionate.

#### (3) High-Shaped Head

Measured from the top of the ears to the crown, the height is 5.8 inches or more.

People with high heads also have high aspirations. They possess strong willpower, are upright and positive, yet they are also ambitious; their powerful self-esteem is their Achilles’ heel. Many educators, missionaries, social workers, politicians, and judges have high head shapes. To defeat such an opponent you must maintain an even higher state of mind and pursuit; if you cannot, simply smile and remain silent.

If you are a manager and encounter a subordinate with a high-shaped head, pay close attention to their development. The seeds of success are already within them; all they may need is your timely nurturing.

#### (6) Short-Shaped Head

Measured from the midpoint between the forehead and eyebrows over the top of the head to the back of the skull, the length is less than 7.6 inches.

People with short-shaped heads lack focus and dislike socializing; they are interested only in themselves. They often possess remarkable talents yet have no grand goals. If your competitor belongs to this type, you must stay calm and plan for the long term; otherwise you may well be defeated.

Viewed from behind, if a person’s head is short and round without angles, they are likely to enjoy cutting corners and are keen on gambling or risk-taking. If the back of the head is square, they are cautious—sometimes overly so, appearing weak.

#### (1) Wide-Shaped Head

Measured with a curved ruler at the top of the ears, the width is 6.5 inches or more.

If your opponent has a wide head shape, you must be fully alert, for they are a true warrior. They are energetic, aggressive, and every glance radiates powerful intensity. When facing such a person, never meet force with force; doing so will only leave you humiliated. The most effective way to defeat a wide-headed opponent is to yield in order to advance. Another fatal weakness is insatiable greed, so appropriate inducements can serve as another powerful weapon.

#### People Who Like White

White is a color that represents passivity. Those who choose white have strong self-protective instincts and a pronounced sense of shyness. They may sometimes appear aloof, yet at heart they are kind and soft-hearted. They rarely fight for greater benefits within their social circles and are somewhat sensitive to interpersonal communication.

Different colors represent different personalities; therefore we should learn to read the psychological code behind colors. Only then can we catch others off guard in communication. The other party will surely be surprised that you already understand their character and style before they have even spoken.

#### People Who Prefer to Sit in the Center Are Self-Centered

Such individuals have a strong desire for self-expression. Whenever they speak with others they center the conversation on themselves, repeatedly emphasizing their own words while ignoring others’ matters and opinions.

When a shop becomes crowded and customers are asked to push tables together, these people immediately display annoyance and dissatisfaction, even seizing on the shop’s mistake to lodge strong protests. They are by no means easygoing or communicative. If they order milk tea and the server mistakenly brings lemon black tea, they will be extremely displeased.

#### Chapter 11 Identifying Personality Types and Understanding Behavioral Patterns

Personality refers to the unique and stable patterns of thinking and acting that distinguish one person from another. If a person is likened to a computer’s main unit, personality is the operating program running on that unit. Different personalities produce different styles of conduct. Understanding someone’s personality type helps greatly in determining what “model” they are and which “program” to use when communicating with them. Identifying others’ behavioral traits and seeing through their psychological activities offers significant and far-reaching assistance in recognizing, observing, and employing people.

#### People Who Steer Conversations Far Off Topic

When talking with others, some people frequently steer the topic far away, making it impossible to grasp what they actually want to say, or they keep changing the subject, leaving listeners bewildered. Constantly shifting content can be positive, yet when the discussion becomes incoherent and pointless, listeners quickly lose interest. This behavior indicates a strong desire for control and self-expression. Such people rarely consider others; they prefer to act as they please and expect others to follow their lead.

#### People Who Steer Conversations Back to Themselves

In real life there are people who, regardless of the occasion, always redirect conversations to themselves, boasting about how they struggled in the past. They fear others may not know their glorious history, yet such talk rarely achieves the desired effect. Close observation reveals that these individuals are largely dissatisfied with reality. They fail to realize that self-aggrandizing remarks struggle to adapt to changing times. Perhaps they are genuine failures who rely entirely on nostalgia to get by.

#### Signature Slants Right While Other Characters Slant Left

People whose signature slants right while other characters slant left are social experts. They quickly become the center of attention through interpersonal skills as well as their cheerful, enthusiastic, witty, and humorous nature. Although their open personality makes them appear fully integrated with others and the setting, they often step outside the circle to observe everything as bystanders.

#### People Who Sleep in the Prone Position

Such individuals are confident and highly capable. They accurately recognize themselves, always know who they are and what they are doing. They pursue life goals persistently and possess both the confidence and ability to achieve them. In emergencies they make timely decisions, demonstrate strong adaptability, and know how to adjust themselves. They are also adept at concealing their true feelings so completely that others cannot detect any flaw.

#### People Who Seem to Know Everything

These individuals possess broad knowledge. They can cite examples from many fields during conversation and offer opinions on any topic, appearing erudite. Yet because they have accumulated too much information without sufficient system or depth of thought, they often miss the main point. They can produce dozens of ideas at once, none of which hit the mark. They are also not very modest; their knowledge, experience, and insight are wide but shallow—learned yet not refined.

#### (4) Low-Shaped Head

Measured from the top of the ears to the crown, the height is less than 5.8 inches.

People with low-shaped heads are pragmatists. They have ideals, yet these lean toward material concerns and tangible things. Spending time with them involves little pressure; defeating them requires no great wisdom or strategy—only realistic benefits. If you wish to befriend them, remember to give and take in moderation, for they tend to be selfish and your efforts may not be reciprocated.

#### People Who Like Red

Red symbolizes action. Those who choose red act immediately on any idea. They want to finish everything quickly, so they speak and act rapidly without much thought. They are usually energetic, vibrant, and driven by strong curiosity and desire, which they satisfy through action. They handle interpersonal relationships skillfully yet lack patience, easily becoming angry over trifles—though the anger passes quickly.

#### People Who Like Yellow

Yellow is associated with joy. Those who choose yellow love power and enjoy dominating others. They are intelligent, calm, and possess strong analytical and judgmental abilities, yet they tend to be self-centered. They have good business sense and often seek success through intellect. They are not very candid, especially under pressure, when they close themselves off and hide their true emotions while presenting a cheerful, positive image to outsiders.

Anyone who has watched *Slam Dunk* is familiar with the protagonist Sakuragi Hanamichi. He is a straightforward high-school student and a key player on the basketball team. Unlike the other members, Sakuragi is extremely narcissistic; every time he appears, he bursts into exaggerated laughter and boasts, “I’m a genius.”

Convinced he is a genius, Sakuragi refuses to take orders from anyone on the court except the coach and the captain. When his “rival” Rukawa Kaede shows disdain, Sakuragi interprets it as jealousy and sometimes ends up in a fight.

As a manga character, Sakuragi’s narcissism differs somewhat from the clinical narcissistic personality. Beyond narcissism, Sakuragi mainly displays a simple, straightforward nature. In real life, however, narcissistic individuals are rarely so endearing.

Xiao Chen, newly employed at a foreign-trade company, visited the notoriously difficult client Manager Li. After respectfully knocking and entering the office, Xiao Chen received only a sidelong glance: “Who are you? What do you want?”

“I’m a sales representative from xx Company…”

Before Xiao Chen could finish, Manager Li rudely interrupted: “Just a sales rep? Who sent you?”

“Our General Manager Yang asked me to discuss this deal…”

Xiao Chen had barely spoken when Manager Li cut in again: “Hmph, only a sales rep to talk business with me? Does your company have no one more suitable?”

Suppressing his anger, Xiao Chen explained, “Because I’ve been following this project, General Manager Yang thought I was the right person…”

“Suitable?” Manager Li gave him another sidelong look. “Sending a junior salesman to negotiate with a company manager—does that seem appropriate? If General Manager Yang looks down on me like this, I’ll have to revise the project. Your company’s quote must be 20 percent lower than the listed price!”

The demand was unreasonable, yet a 20 percent reduction still left the company with acceptable margins. Believing a deal remained possible, Xiao Chen nodded and said, “All right. I’ll go back and calculate whether we can offer you a satisfactory price.”

“Is the price something you can decide?” Manager Li snorted. “I’m not asking you; I’m asking General Manager Yang. Go run the errand and report back.”

Furious, Xiao Chen pulled out his phone and began dialing while saying, “Since you feel you can’t discuss details with me, you might as well speak directly with General Manager Yang.”

“What are you doing…” Manager Li tried to stop him, but the call connected and General Manager Yang’s voice came through: “Hello…”

“Ah, General Manager Yang, it’s me, Little Li.” Instantly dropping his earlier arrogance—even though General Manager Yang could not see him—Manager Li forced a smile. “Here’s the situation: one of your junior salesmen came to quote a price. I thought it was a bit high, so I wanted to ask if you could lower it.”

“We’ve worked together for years; that’s negotiable. Talk to Xiao Chen about it and have him report back to me,” General Manager Yang replied briskly. “I’m busy—got to go. Let’s have tea sometime.”

“Yes, yes, no problem.”

After hanging up, Manager Li’s face changed again. He tossed the phone back to Xiao Chen and said coldly, “What are you still standing there for? Your task is done—go report back.”

Business circles contain no shortage of people like Manager Li. Once they gain a little status, they become arrogant, refuse to deal with anyone they consider beneath them or useless, and treat even potentially useful people as inferior. Only those who flatter and obey them may win approval; any resistance or questioning triggers immediate contempt and dismissal.

Everyone harbors some narcissistic tendencies, but only when these tendencies are deeply rooted in one’s core thinking and exert a strong influence on personality can the condition be called narcissistic personality. Typical narcissistic individuals frequently exhibit the following behaviors:

1. They spend long periods lost in fantasies of unlimited power, success, brilliance, beauty, or perfect love, often becoming self-absorbed in these daydreams.
2. They place extreme value on themselves, possess intense self-confidence, expect to be treated as extraordinary successes, exaggerate their talents and achievements, and demand special favors and privileges.
3. They flatter and ingratiate themselves with those they perceive as stronger, yet secretly envy others’ accomplishments and possessions; toward those they view as weaker, they are arrogant and dismissive. When criticized, they immediately assume others are jealous or envious rather than reflect on their own faults.
4. They crave more admiration than most people and want everyone to worship and respect them. They frequently award themselves titles, emphasize their special privileges, and believe they are exempt from ordinary rules—even when they make mistakes.
5. In relationships they tend to take petty advantages and exploit others, stopping at nothing to achieve their goals.
6. They feel no empathy for anyone except themselves and have no interest in others’ feelings or needs, focusing only on how others’ shortcomings might cause them loss.

People with narcissistic personality usually developed greedy, selfish, and cold-blooded traits in childhood due to various negative influences. Most are intensely drawn to power and skilled at using others; they remember someone only while that person remains “useful,” and quickly discard “useless” friends as burdens.

One narcissistic individual asked a friend to help him find a job. On the day of the interview the friend fell ill and could not accompany him. Instead of considering how unwell his friend must have felt, the man blamed him for breaking the appointment and leaving him “feeling insecure”—a classic display of selfish behavior typical of narcissistic personality.

Dealing with someone who has narcissistic personality is exhausting. They may be capable leaders or successful professionals, yet they can never be caring, understanding friends. Therefore, when interacting with them, never endure humiliation or yield completely; doing so only encourages further exploitation. The correct approach is to remain neither obsequious nor arrogant, maintain an even demeanor, and let them sense that you are a cultivated and substantial person. They will then naturally refrain from treating you as beneath them.

#### Obsessive-Compulsive Personality: The "Workaholic" with Obsessive Tendencies

##### Obsessive-Compulsive Personality: The "Workaholic" with Obsessive Tendencies

Micro-expression keywords: People with obsessive-compulsive personality always force themselves to do this and that. Little do they know that this obsessive and anxious mindset may actually be the reason things go wrong.

During the Joseon Dynasty, there was a famous general named Yi Sun-sin. He came from a declining scholar-official family and grew up in poverty, yet he was ambitious and excelled in poetry, literature, riding, and archery. In his thirties he passed the military examination and devoted his entire career to the army.

Throughout his life Yi Sun-sin was deeply concerned for his country and people. His character was upright and uncompromising. While leading the Joseon navy against Japanese invaders, he achieved indelible accomplishments.

Yet this great figure recorded in Joseon history also possessed a personality trait that could be viewed as either a flaw or a virtue. Beyond striving for thorough preparation and meticulous planning during wartime, Yi Sun-sin remained constantly on guard even in peacetime, drilling his troops and preparing defenses. He made detailed plans for every matter and could not help but strongly oppose or condemn any behavior or opinion he found unacceptable. Even in battle he would never engage unless victory was certain.

Yi Sun-sin’s superiors considered him overly strict, his colleagues found him difficult, and his subordinates were annoyed by his numerous demands. It was precisely this character, however, that enabled his wartime achievements.

Individuals like General Yi Sun-sin, who are principled and demanding, are undoubtedly national treasures in wartime. In today’s society, however, they often become “problematic” figures who cause headaches for many. Their obsessive tendencies manifest not only in self-restraint but also extend to others; they frequently “show concern” in ways that feel intrusive.

Xiao Luo’s immediate superior, Director Ma, was an out-and-out workaholic. After more than twenty years at the office he remained diligent, handling more tasks and performing better than anyone else, often working unpaid overtime on weekends. Despite this dedication he was still only a minor director and had not been promoted in nearly a decade.

Xiao Luo found this puzzling and felt sympathy for Director Ma. One day, after everyone else had left, he saw Director Ma still busy and approached with concern: “Director Ma, it’s already this late—aren’t you going to eat?”

“I’ll go in a moment. I can’t rest easy until I finish these tasks,” Director Ma replied.

“Let me help you,” Xiao Luo offered kindly and stayed behind.

After more than an hour of work the official business was finally completed. Director Ma patted Xiao Luo on the shoulder and said, “Young man, you have real drive. Let’s go eat together.”

Pleased to have earned his superior’s approval, Xiao Luo soon found his satisfaction replaced by regret. At the table Director Ma talked nonstop, but every topic concerned the just-finished tasks; he worried that one thing had not been done properly and that another needed supplementation. Finally, setting down his chopsticks, Director Ma patted Xiao Luo again: “Come on, let’s go back and revise that plan.”

By now the lights were on outside. Xiao Luo wanted only to go home but could not refuse, because a large part of the plan Director Ma mentioned had been prepared with Xiao Luo’s help.

Thus the energetic Director Ma dragged the reluctant Xiao Luo back to the office for another night of overtime.

Anyone with a superior like Director Ma would surely complain. Such people are passionate about work, obsessed with scrutinizing details, and hold extremely strict standards for themselves and others, pursuing perfection to a pathological degree. People like Director Ma belong to the obsessive-compulsive personality type.

Of course, obsessive-compulsive personality does not manifest only at work. In every aspect of life, individuals with this personality exhibit compulsive behaviors—for example, having a cleanliness obsession, repeatedly checking whether doors are locked, or recalculating figures on a report multiple times without feeling reassured.

##### Behavioral Manifestations of Obsessive-Compulsive Personality

1. They possess strong moral and ethical values and a keen sense of responsibility. They show extraordinary focus on matters they deem important and always demand perfection from themselves with no room for error. They invest excessive time and energy in details such as lists, sequences, reports, and schedules, often neglecting the main objectives of the work.
2. They exercise excessive self-restraint, appear rigid and inflexible, and remain emotionally tense—in other words, they lack a sense of security. They are constantly preparing yet feel uncertain about what they have done; any questioning from others leaves them uneasy.
3. They have almost no hobbies or personal life and few friends. They are reluctant to delegate tasks; even when they do, they impose their own strict rules. If others fail to follow their methods, they become even more anxious and distrustful.
4. People with obsessive-compulsive personality are often stingy and stubborn. They handle matters in an orderly fashion but struggle to accept new things. They also tend to keep childhood belongings and refuse to discard them, even if the items are nothing more than useless scraps of paper.

Obsessive-compulsive personality usually forms in childhood. When parents are overly strict, children often develop cautious and restrained characters. Fear of punishment for mistakes leads them to deliberate repeatedly before acting, creating habitual tension and anxiety that eventually solidify into obsessive-compulsive personality. In addition, children who suffer severe setbacks or stimulation, or whose family members already exhibit compulsive habits, may also develop this personality.

In reality, mild obsessive-compulsive personality is not necessarily a bad thing. The renowned director Stanley Kubrick, for example, had obsessive-compulsive personality, and this trait drove him to make his films more perfect. In China, Stephen Chow also shows this tendency; actors who have worked with him commonly note that his requirements are extremely strict and that he insists others follow his exact specifications, becoming angry at the slightest deviation. Yet it is undeniable that Stephen Chow stands as a monumental figure in the history of Chinese comedic cinema.

Interacting with people who have obsessive-compulsive personality can be taxing, but unlike those with narcissistic personality, they still consider others’ feelings to some degree—though they may be unable to open up because of pride or other reasons. Therefore, when dealing with such individuals, it helps to guide them toward opening up or to deliver a blunt “wake-up call” when they become fixated, helping them recognize the flaws in their behavior. Generally, once mutual resonance is achieved, the interaction becomes far less troublesome than expected.

### Penetrating Psychological Weaknesses Through Defense Mechanisms

#### Compensation Mechanism: Those Who Vent Their Anger Must Have a Fragile Heart

**Micro-expression keywords**  
Compensation has two sides: one is “I cannot target you, so I target someone else”; the other is “I cannot obtain you, so what I have is not bad either.” This is a relatively reasonable way to relieve anxiety.

There is a joke about a father who doted excessively on his son. One day the little fellow mischievously provoked his grandfather, who flew into a rage and gave the boy a thorough beating. The father watched, heart aching, yet dared not intervene. Instead he began slapping his own face. The grandfather, distressed, asked why. The son replied, “You hit my son, so I have to hit your son.”

Many people know this joke, yet the term compensatory defense mechanism may be less familiar. The father in the story, seeing his child punished, felt unbearable distress and used self-punishment to shift his emotions while also arousing the grandfather’s sympathy.

Such incidents are common in daily life. Another online joke makes a similar point:

A company manager quarreled with his wife early in the morning, then hit traffic and was running late. He ran a red light and was stopped by a traffic officer who issued a ticket.  

When he finally reached the office, he saw yesterday’s documents still sitting on his desk. Furious, he summoned the secretary and berated her.  

The secretary, who had received clear instructions the previous evening, felt wronged but did not dare talk back. After the scolding she took the documents to the reception desk and blamed the receptionist for leaving too early the day before and failing to mail the package.  

The bewildered receptionist, seething with anger, spotted the cleaner who had not yet removed some trash and seized the opportunity to reprimand her sharply.  

The cleaner, unable to find anyone lower in rank, swallowed her anger and continued working. That evening she returned home, saw her son watching television instead of doing homework, and flew into a rage, scolding him severely.  

With no one else to vent on, the son noticed the family’s big yellow dog lying by the door and kicked it.

In this chain of bullying, the most pitiful victim was a dog that could not even speak.

Humans seem born to “bully the weak and fear the strong,” a habit rooted in our innate compensatory defense mechanism. The mechanism allows people to express rationally suppressed anxiety through a new channel similar to the one originally avoided, thereby restoring psychological balance. In the example above, the manager, secretary, receptionist, cleaner, and the cleaner’s son all first wanted to argue with the person who scolded them, yet reason told them the consequences would be severe. They therefore suppressed the impulse and waited for a suitable moment and target.

The “reverse-attitude mechanism” mentioned earlier represents reason’s total negation when anxiety arises: losing one’s temper in front of a superior is unacceptable, so one must grovel. Reason completely negates and controls the impulse to vent at the superior. Compensatory behavior, by contrast, is an incomplete negation: one cannot lose one’s temper at the superior, but one can still take it out on the child at home. Because reason’s suppression is incomplete, the compensator does not appear so “two-faced.” It can be described as a relatively safe way to transfer anxiety.

Compensatory behavior is equally common in emotional life.

Wu Lili, a freshman, and her classmate Sun Gang discovered on the first day of school that they were from the same hometown and were seated at the same desk. They began to interact more. At first Sun Gang often visited her dorm to chat, repeating seemingly profound yet empty remarks from magazines; these soon won Wu Lili’s heart. She fell madly in love with him but, out of shyness, could not speak. Sun Gang remained unaware and treated her with deepening friendship.

He grew increasingly candid with her, even boasting about having seduced the department beauty from another major. Wu Lili suffered in silence yet could not bring herself to cut ties. Eventually Sun Gang turned his attention to Wu Lili’s roommate and best friend.

Wu Lili wanted to intervene but found no grounds; as their mutual friend she should even help bring them together. The pain finally prompted her to fix her gaze on another classmate, an ordinary young man. She began to discover in him several traits that reminded her of Sun Gang: a love of rollerblading, tabletop games, medium-short hair, double eyelids, a preference for single-strap backpacks, a low growl when spitting, and an unconscious twirling of the index finger when hands were clasped.

Wu Lili spent day and night convincing herself that she loved this young man. She carved his name on her desk, painted it on walls, and wrote it in every textbook. Everyone around her said “Lili is deeply in love”…

“I refuse to be anyone’s substitute” was once a staple line in romantic soap operas, yet in real relationships it is hard to say that anyone is not someone else’s substitute. In the end Wu Lili herself came to believe she loved the young man, while only her unconscious—beyond rational awareness—retained the original impulse of love for Sun Gang.

This behavior of treating X as a substitute for XX is a typical compensatory act.

The idiom “point at the mulberry while cursing the locust tree” and the recently popular “venting centers” in big cities operate on the same principle.

Although compensatory defense mechanisms cannot fulfill the original wish, they produce effects sufficiently similar to the initial goal and quickly release anxiety; therefore they remain one of the defense mechanisms people frequently employ without realizing it.

When discussing compensation, one must mention a variant: the “sweet-lemon mechanism.”

A fox that cannot reach the grapes settles for lemons and declares the grapes sour and the lemons sweet. “Sour grapes” is itself a typical variant of compensatory behavior.

When an effective compensatory object is found, typical compensation occurs. When no suitable object appears, another, less typical form of compensation is required to dispel anxiety—the sweet-lemon mechanism.

- A young man with an overweight girlfriend says, “Being thin is useless; it feels bony.”
- A young woman with a poor boyfriend says, “Rich men are no good; they’re unfaithful.”
- Someone who cannot afford a large house says, “A big bedroom is empty and the acoustics are poor.”

…All such varied “sour-grapes” statements can be classified as compensatory behavior.

#### Lapse Mechanism: When Reason Fails to Restrain You…

Micro-expression keywords: When reason proves insufficient to suppress or relieve anxiety, the anxiety slips past rational defenses and manifests in a form contrary to reason, producing lapse behavior. Lapse behavior easily harms the individual and should be avoided whenever possible.

Famous CCTV football commentator Han Qiaosheng is known for his “lapses.” Consider some of his unintentionally comical remarks:

- “With the goalkeeper’s whistle, the match has ended.”
- “Dear viewers, the Mid-Autumn Festival has just passed; I wish you all a belated New Year.”
- “Players must strengthen physical fitness and confrontation training in daily practice so they can withstand the intensity of competition; otherwise they will topple like a roly-poly toy at the slightest touch.”
- “Foreign players are very professional—for example, Matthäus played a match only three months after his child was born.”
- “A few days ago Fan Zhiyi was running a high fever—36.8 °C; goalkeeper Ou Chuliang is 1.82 m tall and weighs 28 kg.”
- “Last week a wedding ceremony of a different kind was held.”
- “Some viewers may have just turned on the elevator; let us repeat the score…”
- “With pursuers behind and blockers ahead, Baggio dribbled into the penalty area.”
- “If this goal counts, it is invalid.”
- “Several clubs have expressed interest in buying Piero; Lazio offered 30 million USD, Manchester United a higher bid—28 million USD.”
- “Every blade of grass is fiercely contested.”
- “One defender has two legs, two defenders have four legs, three defenders have eight legs.”
- “Player XX shoots from 30 km away!”
- “With the speed of thunder that cannot cover the ears while stealing a bell.”
- “The ball was blocked by the goalkeeper’s back leg.”
- “The Brazilian defense is composed entirely of Brazilian players.”
- “Goalkeeper An Qi participated in this year’s World Table Tennis Championships held in Mexico.”

Mr. Han’s “lapses” have become a style and a trademark whose humorous effect keeps audiences entertained.

Beyond appreciating his humor, we may examine the cause of these lapses.

When objective circumstances produce imbalance, anxiety arises. Reason attempts to suppress it. Successful suppression yields the two-faced behavior of reverse attitude. When suppression is incomplete, lapses occur.

In *Xiang Xing Gu Jian* there is a short story titled “Yang the Evaluator Discerns the Boatman’s Crime.” Zhao San and Zhou Sheng, both from Huzhou, were close friends who planned to do business together in Nanjing.

At dawn Zhao San rose early, reached the river first, and woke boatman Zhang Chao. Because it was still early, Zhao San dozed in the cabin. Zhang Chao, seeing the large amount of silver Zhao San carried, was seized by greed. While Zhao San slept, Zhang Chao killed him and sank the body in the river.

At daybreak Zhou Sheng arrived at the river and, not seeing Zhao San, asked Zhang Chao to fetch him from home. Zhang Chao knocked on the door and called, “Madam Zhao San, open the door.”

Madam Zhao San opened the door, exchanged a few words with Zhang Chao, and remarked in surprise that her husband had already left and should be on the boat by now. Zhang Chao returned and told Zhou Sheng. The two, together with Madam Zhao San, searched everywhere but found no trace of Zhao San. They filed a complaint with the county office.

The county magistrate, knowing the couple had quarreled, suspected Madam Zhao San of murdering her husband but lacked evidence. The case reached the Ministry of Justice. Evaluator Yang of the Court of Judicial Review studied the dossier and declared: “Zhang Chao called for Madam Zhao San, not Zhao San himself, which proves he knew Zhao San was no longer in the house.”

On this single point Yang concluded that Zhang Chao was highly suspect. During interrogation Zhang Chao, conscience-stricken, confessed and revealed the details of his crime for money.

Evaluator Yang’s ability to read subtle clues commands admiration, while Zhang Chao’s “unintentional slip” exposed his guilt and brought him to ruin.

Was Zhang Chao’s mistake truly unintentional? More precisely, it should be called an “intentional slip.” He had killed Zhao San and knew he must conceal the fact, yet his unconscious had already accepted Zhao San’s death as settled; thus the truth leaked out in his later behavior without his awareness.

When reason’s “oversight” allows anxiety or unease to surface in an unexpected form, the phenomenon is called the lapse defense mechanism.

In the storytelling work *Northeast King Zhang Zuolin* there is the following episode:

One day Zhang Zuolin attended a gathering of social notables that included many prominent Japanese figures. Knowing Zhang had little education, they deliberately and warmly asked him to write a piece of calligraphy for them, hoping to embarrass him.

Zhang realized it was a trap but had no choice. He stepped to the table, dipped his brush, and wrote a large character “虚” (void). After inspecting it with feigned satisfaction he added his signature and seal.

Just as he was about to feel pleased with himself, his secretary noticed a glaring error: the signature should have read “Zhang Zuolin’s hand-brushed ink,” yet Zhang had mistakenly written “Zhang Zuolin’s hand-black.” The Japanese guests looked puzzled.

Realizing the blunder and unable to correct it, Zhang found himself in an awkward position. The interpreter quickly whispered, “Marshal, the signature reads ‘hand-black’ instead of ‘hand-brushed ink’; the character for ‘earth’ is missing.”

Zhang had a flash of inspiration. He slammed the table with his fist and pretended to scold the interpreter: “Damn it! Do you think I don’t know there’s an ‘earth’ under ‘ink’? But this piece was requested by the Japanese, so not an inch of earth will be yielded!”

The coarse remark drew thunderous applause from the Chinese guests present.

In terms of defense mechanisms, lapses and reverse attitudes are classic counter-examples. Reverse attitude arises when accumulated anxiety produces a resistant defense against reason; lapse occurs when anxiety, unease, or reluctance slips past reason’s guard and finds expression. People may be aware of their reverse-attitude defenses, yet before a lapse occurs they can take no preventive action.

Lapse defense mechanisms commonly appear as slips of the tongue or other errors. Saying “the meeting is over” when one meant “the meeting begins,” or leaving an unfinished report at home, are both manifestations of the lapse defense mechanism.

Individuals who frequently experience lapses generally suffer from poor concentration. The conflict between unconscious and conscious mind makes them more prone than others to escape reality and to rationalize their behavior. Analysis of lapse behavior readily reveals a person’s true inner thoughts; most often, the unintentional slip expresses what the person actually wanted to say.

#### Daydreaming: The Mental Sanctuary for Those with Unfulfilled Desires

Daydreaming is in fact a form of escape, and while this escape can provide significant relief from anxiety, when the relief becomes addictive, a person easily falls into inescapable erotic fantasy.

Xiao Hua was a quiet and somewhat introverted child. Recently, a group of delinquent youths several years older than him had moved into the alley near his home. Every day they blocked him at the alley entrance and “squeezed a little spending money” out of him.

Timid Xiao Hua, under coercion, dared not tell his parents or his teachers. He could only endure in silence, and when he cried alone he would fantasize that one day he suddenly gained superpowers. Then, when the youths bullied him, he would erupt and beat them until they were groveling on the ground…

In this way, although he continued to be bullied, Xiao Hua could find “self-consolation” in fantasy.

Situations like Xiao Hua’s are not uncommon. When people encounter something they cannot achieve or feel crushed by external pressure, in order to maintain a certain physiological and psychological balance, those intense, repressed instinctual desires are discharged in a manner detached from reality yet still controllable by consciousness. This is what we ordinarily call daydreaming.

Everyone has daydreamed, yet few realize that daydreaming is itself a defense mechanism—a defensive process in which unfulfilled desires from reality are consoled through fantasy, thereby restoring psychological equilibrium.

Daydreaming is based on fantasy and, to a certain extent, aligns closely with the needs of certain professions. The renowned psychologist Freud made an interesting claim: artistic creation is essentially an act of daydreaming. Ordinary people have a daydream and then move on, but artists differ in that they write their daydreams onto manuscript paper or paint them onto canvases, allowing those daydreams to circulate widely and be shared with all readers.

At this point we must mention the currently popular online “YY” novels. Although YY novels do not reach the level of art, they embody daydreaming even more explicitly than art does. “YY” is taken from the pinyin initials of “意淫” (yì yín), and conceptually “意淫” is indistinguishable from daydreaming.

Is this phenomenon unique to China? Of course not.

In the United States, young people are obsessed with superheroes. The two most famous teams are the Justice League—featuring Superman, Spider-Man, Batman, the Flash, and Green Lantern—and the Avengers—featuring Captain America, Iron Man, the Hulk, Hawkeye, Black Widow, and Thor.

These superheroes either possess superpowers or have developed a single outstanding talent to its utmost. Their moves and skills differ, and their personalities vary widely, yet they are all good people who perform morally upright deeds.

The true homeland of anime, however, is Japan. Japanese anime style is more distinctive and better suited to Eastern aesthetics; feminine beauty is exaggerated to the extreme. Most anime beauties, for example, have large eyes that occupy a quarter of the face and deep, attractive pupils even without colored contact lenses.

Combined with stirring, heartfelt plots and vivid character personalities, a large number of Japanese people have become hopelessly immersed in the world of manga. They even regard the real world as fake and believe true love exists only in the “2D realm.” “2D realm” is their term for the anime world, and such people call themselves otaku. The words “otaku male” and “otaku female” originated this way.

Lacking the strength to confront reality and unable to resolve anxiety through reason, people place themselves in an illusory world to alleviate anxiety and become addicted. This is why fantasy-oriented literary and artistic works have become so prevalent.

Occasionally daydreaming is harmless; it helps relax body and mind, relieves real-world pressure, and can expand imaginative capacity. Yet because the psychological satisfaction fantasy can provide is very limited, if a person relies excessively on the daydreaming defense mechanism and cannot convert it into reality, neural pathology or mental distortion and perversion may result.

In the mid-Qing dynasty, after Cao Xueqin wrote Dream of the Red Chamber, Gao E completed it and a major bookseller published the work, which quickly became popular throughout the empire. Many lovelorn men and women became obsessed. It is said that in the prosperous regions of Jiangnan, Red Chamber fans split into two factions—one favoring Lin Daiyu, the other Xue Baochai—and the two sides frequently clashed in street fights…

An even more curious anecdote occurred in the north. A young lady from an official family obtained a copy of Dream of the Red Chamber from a close friend. She opened the first page, began reading, and became enchanted. From then on her only pastime was staring into space. While other young ladies’ boudoirs contained needlework and rouge, hers was filled with every edition of the novel. Conservative estimates suggest that even the late Redology master Zhou Ruchang’s collection of Dream of the Red Chamber editions did not amount to half the number this young lady possessed.

In the blink of an eye, while daydreaming and lost in reverie, the young lady reached the age of twenty. “A twenty-year-old daughter still unmarried” was an unequivocal insult in ancient times, because women of that era typically gave birth for the first time between the ages of fifteen and sixteen. The young lady was now twenty and had never been touched by a man; all sorts of rumors began to circulate.

Yet the entire household understood that she was simply addicted to Dream of the Red Chamber, and the whole estate grew anxious. Her father tried every method, even summoning shamans and diviners, but nothing worked. Once he grasped the crux of the problem, he decided to administer a “strong medicine” to rescue his daughter.

One day he brought several servants, lured her to the front hall, had them search her boudoir for every copy of the novel, and piled them in the courtyard to be burned to ashes. The commotion naturally alarmed the young lady. She ran into the courtyard, saw her beloved books about to be incinerated, and tried to throw herself into the flames. Had the servants and maids not restrained her, it would have been a real-life case of the moth flying into the fire.

Watching the copies of Dream of the Red Chamber burn away, the young lady cried out in grief, “Why burn my Baoyu?” and fainted.

For the next several days she drifted between sleep and wakefulness, unable to eat or drink, growing thinner by the day. Her parents watched with aching hearts, yet they knew that emotional ailments require emotional remedies. They spared no effort to gather several editions of the novel for her. Only after reading them did her furrowed brows gradually relax and her health return.

#### Counter-Attitude Mechanism: The Two-Faced Person Bound by Rationality

Micro-expression keywords: Because the object of discharge in the counter-attitude mechanism is not the direct source of anxiety, counter-attitude often fails to vent anxiety completely. If one continues down this path, extreme, pathological, or perverse counter-attitude behavior may develop.

Xiao Wang, who had just obtained his driver’s license, took his friends for a drive in his new car, but was stopped by a traffic officer at an intersection.

“You violated traffic regulations. Please hand over your license,” the officer said politely, extending his hand.

“I just got my license. Please be lenient—don’t deduct any points,” Xiao Wang said with a smile, pulling several hundred yuan from his wallet instead of his license.

“Stop the nonsense. Give me the license.”

“There aren’t many officers as upright as you these days.” Seeing that bribery failed, Xiao Wang reluctantly produced his license. As he handed it over he flattered the officer: “It really wasn’t intentional. Please go easy on me. I’ll be more careful from now on…”

Taking back his license, Xiao Wang watched the officer walk away and spat heavily on the ground. “Pah! What a piece of work…”

Such scenes are commonplace. Drivers stopped by traffic police, subordinates dealing with nitpicking bosses, and criminals facing escorting officers all display outward compliance while harboring intense inner resentment. In the catalog of defense mechanisms, this behavior pattern has a specific name: “counter-attitude.”

When awake, people remain rational; reason suppresses anger so that, in threatening situations, one does not suddenly explode into attack or other destructive acts. Yet the repressed anxiety and anger remain “stored” in the brain. Through powerful mental investment they produce a reaction formation, causing one to exhibit behavior diametrically opposed to one’s true feelings. This is how the counter-attitude defense mechanism arises.

Old Lady Pang had six children. After she raised them with great effort, each started a family and began to neglect her. At first they visited infrequently; later they sent less and less living expenses. For several years the old lady voiced many complaints, yet she dared not fall out with her children because she would need their support in old age.

A few years later the children had offspring of their own but were too busy with work, so they entrusted the grandchildren to the old lady. Having toiled half her life, she had hoped to enjoy a quiet old age, but she could not refuse her children’s requests and reluctantly began caring for the grandchildren.

Thus the following scene emerged: when the children were absent, Old Lady Pang was neither indifferent nor particularly affectionate toward the grandchildren; she often treated them coldly. Yet the moment her children appeared, her attitude toward the grandchildren executed a 180-degree turn. She smiled benevolently, inquired after their well-being, and played the role of the kindly elder to perfection.

Children’s hearts are sensitive, however. After growing up, the grandchildren never developed deep affection for Old Lady Pang, even though she had raised them for several years.

As Old Lady Pang aged and became frail, she could no longer live independently and began rotating among her children’s homes. Each household had its own life; although they treated her decently, they could not devote excessive attention. The old lady harbored grievances about this attitude but dared not voice them.

She did, however, dare to criticize one child in front of the others, so that every child came to believe he or she was filial while the siblings were not. Over time the estrangement deepened until several violent confrontations occurred. After Old Lady Pang’s death the children never visited one another again; the family became complete strangers.

Old Lady Pang was dissatisfied with her children, yet reason told her that an open rupture would make her final years miserable. Therefore reason imposed a constraint: no matter how much she wished to complain, she must not do so in her children’s presence. When the children were absent, she was less kind to the grandchildren—sometimes even unkind—thereby compensating for the subservience she displayed before her children.

In the 1940s, China’s finest actor, the “King of Spoken Drama” Shi Hui, played the lead role in the celebrated film This Life of Mine—a humble patrolman in the old society.

In the film, his most brilliant extreme performances almost all embody “counter-attitude behavior”: in front of dignitaries, an exaggerated, false smile, bowing at the waist, ready at the slightest misstep to slap his own face; when the powerful walked, he would fussily sweep the dust from the ground before them. The instant the dignitaries left his sight, the patrolman’s expression changed instantly—he spat, cursed, and uttered every form of belittlement.

Shi Hui’s method of character portrayal was hailed as a classic.

This pattern of one face in front of people and another behind their backs is typical counter-attitude behavior. In this case, what merits attention is the patrolman’s dramatically exaggerated performance before the powerful.

Because the counter-attitude defense mechanism forces reason to suppress anxious emotions, individuals employing it often display obvious exaggeration and compulsiveness. They frequently speak glibly, repeatedly profess their sincerity in an inflated manner, and when smiling their facial muscles stiffen or tremble involuntarily, accompanied by blinking, nose wrinkling, and similar movements.

Thus, outward compliance does not necessarily indicate heartfelt conviction; it may stem from an inner counter-attitude defense mechanism driven by anger and resistance. In general, people who frequently exhibit the counter-attitude defense mechanism are also prone to lying, denial, and shifting responsibility in daily life. What we ordinarily call “one face in front, another behind” largely refers to this type.

#### Projection Mechanism: Criticizing Others Is Criticizing Yourself

Micro-expression keywords: People who habitually use the projection mechanism to displace anxiety may not be morally corrupt, but they can certainly be called unprincipled. Therefore, to avoid becoming a slave to the projection mechanism, recognizing one’s own desires is essential.

In a village beside the Yellow River lived two widows whose husbands had died in a natural disaster several years earlier. Both women were young and reasonably attractive, so their private lives gradually became less restrained.

The two widows did not live close to each other, so although they sometimes shared the same lovers, they managed to coexist without incident.

Then a university graduate arrived in the village. He had graduated from a prestigious teachers’ college and came to teach English at the town’s only middle school. Because the village was near the town and the English teacher preferred quiet, he moved into the village.

The teacher stood 184 centimeters tall, had fair skin, and a fine physique. Both widows immediately took notice and began courting him with attentiveness and flirtatious glances. In the end, Widow Zhang succeeded in luring the teacher into her bed.

Widow Li was furious when she learned of this and began spreading rumors about Widow Zhang throughout the village—claiming she was a husband-killer, that she was promiscuous, that she changed men every night…

When the teacher heard these rumors, he began to believe them and left Widow Zhang. Widow Zhang discovered the reason, became equally enraged, and started spreading similar gossip about Widow Li. As the two women slandered each other, their reputations deteriorated…

When people experience unfulfilled desires because of rational control, they adopt this defensive posture: they externalize anxiety in the form of deliberate emphasis, accusation, or slander and direct it at someone whose behavior resembles the action their own reason has forbidden.

The “chief culprit” behind the projection defense mechanism is usually a life impulse repressed in the unconscious. For example, a person may wish to curry favor with a superior but, lacking sufficient social skill or thick skin, bungles the attempt. Upon seeing colleagues who have won the superior’s favor, the person openly expresses disdain, calling them sycophants or flatterers, without realizing they have done the same thing themselves.

In other words, the projection defense mechanism uses criticism of others’ behavior to exonerate oneself and to dispel the anxiety and unease that cling to the unconscious in opposition to reason and moral sense. People who employ projection generally conceal or disguise their own private matters—the root of their anxiety—and present them from another person’s perspective, openly criticizing or expressing contempt in order to satisfy their unconscious sense of morality and justice.

In the Qing-dynasty scholar Yu Yue’s Miscellaneous Compilations from Yu Garden there is a short anecdote about a capital official about to be transferred to a provincial post. Before departing, he paid a special farewell visit to his teacher’s residence.

The teacher was delighted to see his prized student and asked, “What preparations have you made for this journey?”

The official replied, “I have prepared one hundred tall hats; whenever I encounter difficulty, I will present one to the person involved.”

The teacher was displeased and scolded him: “We are men of integrity; how can we engage in such crooked practices?”

The official remained calm and answered, “Teacher is correct, yet how many people in today’s world are as upright as you?”

Hearing this, the teacher’s anger turned to pleasure. “You are right; there are indeed few upright people under heaven.”

After leaving his teacher’s residence, the official laughed to his attendants: “Of the one hundred tall hats I originally prepared, only ninety-nine remain.”

Any discerning reader can see that the teacher in the anecdote was himself fond of wearing tall hats and hearing flattery. Yet his high position and role as a mentor prevented him from displaying this trait openly. He therefore employed the projection defense mechanism, declaring that he detested the crooked practices of other officials—only to reveal his true nature and give himself away.

The same holds true in daily life. Men who constantly proclaim they “defend women’s rights” are often the most chauvinistic; people who declare “I most hate those who speak ill of others behind their backs” are often the most fond of spreading gossip; those who claim “corrupt officials are the most detestable” may, once in office, prove even more rapacious than the officials they once despised. Such behaviors are frequently the work of the projection defense mechanism.

Although not every act of projection appears so despicable, in most cases projection is unprincipled and, within the framework of public morality, even pernicious.

During World War II, in order to sustain a massive three-front war and realize Hitler’s personal delusion of world domination, Germany requisitioned every available resource. Consequently, although Nazi Germany possessed the greatest controllable resources of any nation, its people still went hungry and threadbare because of the war.

To strengthen unity and requisition still more resources, Hitler and Goebbels promoted the notorious slogan “Tanks, not bread.” Countless Germans began to starve while producing weapons.

At the same time, the entire Nazi Party leadership set an example, with reports daily describing how high- and mid-level officials responded to the Führer’s call by practicing frugality. Many officials personally testified, denouncing those “heartless rich who refuse to economize.”

In reality, a considerable number of these ostensibly austere Nazi high officials were merely performing. They spent at least half of every year vacationing in villas along the Seine in France, surrounded by several beautiful women, drinking rare wines, and listening to French musicians—now reduced to slaves of a conquered nation—perform the Eroica Symphony…

#### Defense Mechanisms: The "Converter" of Emotional Stress

Micro-expression keywords: Defense mechanisms originate from people's self-protection mechanisms, avoiding excessive anxiety and repression in one's mind due to shocks. Understanding defense mechanisms is of extremely important significance for judging others' behaviors and even psychological activities.

In the Old Testament of the Bible, there is this legend:

To test the prophet Abraham's loyalty to him, God asked him to offer his only son Isaac as a sacrifice. When Abraham took Isaac to the altar and raised his knife to kill his son, God, moved by his loyalty, sent an angel to stop him. At that moment, a stray goat passed by on the roadside. Abraham led the goat over and offered it in place of Isaac.

This legend was passed down and inherited by ancient Judaism. During annual sacrifices, the high priest of ancient Judaism would bring a goat, place his hands on its head to signify entrusting the sins of the entire nation to the animal, then drive it into the wilderness to fend for itself, thereby cleansing the nation's sins.

Most people find this allusion familiar; it is what we commonly call a "scapegoat." In life, a scapegoat often refers to a pitiful, unfortunate person who suffers in another's place. In reality, however, our brains also possess this "scapegoat" mechanism.

This mechanism is called a defense mechanism, also known as a displacement mechanism.

When humans face setbacks, conflicts, or other tense situations, they experience negative emotions such as anxiety and distress. These negative emotions may be temporarily suppressed, yet until they are released, they continue to disturb the subconscious. To avoid this interference, people consciously or unconsciously tend to restore psychological balance and stability.

Defense mechanisms operate on this principle. To prevent excessive accumulation of anxious emotions from creating mental barriers between the subconscious and conscious mind, people transform repressed anxiety into another form and project it back into real life. In short, a defense mechanism is the body's "firewall" that displaces anxiety into other forms of release, preventing psychological problems.

Defense mechanisms appear everywhere in daily life. For example, a child breaks expensive dishes during the New Year. The parents feel distressed but, given the festive occasion, cannot scold the child outright, so they console themselves with "peace every year" (a pun on "broken every year").
