This is a typical defense mechanism.

Another example: a wife sees her mother-in-law soil the new bedsheets but cannot confront her directly, so she vents her anger on her husband for forgetting to change his slippers at the door. The husband cannot understand why an occasional occurrence provokes such fury today.

A few years ago, an astonishing scene unfolded in a building in Xidan, Beijing: a middle-aged man in a sweatshirt, dressed like a migrant worker, flung a thick stack of hundred-yuan notes at a sales clerk, then pulled out a large pair of scissors, cut a set of expensive Armani suits into strips, and strode away disdainfully.

Media outlets followed up on the incident. Investigations revealed that the man came from a rural area. Before reaching adulthood, he had joined a village construction crew to "make a living" in the big city, enduring hardships and the snobbery of others. Later, through skill and boldness, he rose to the position of "crew leader." He then connected with a major construction company and began trading building materials. Step by step, over decades, he became a multimillionaire. Yet the cold treatment and humiliation he suffered in his youth remained deeply rooted in his heart.

He often wore shabby clothes while browsing luxury malls. That day, at the Armani counter, the sales clerk sharply rebuked him: "Can you afford this? Don't touch it—you couldn't pay for the damage if you soiled it!"

What followed was the scene described above.

Some called the man a show-off; others said he was psychologically twisted. In truth, this was merely a common manifestation of a defense mechanism. Although wealthy, the man's mind remained filled with the shadows of his youth. These shadows prevented him from integrating into so-called "high society," so he devised this method to elicit others' astonished gazes, release his inner knots, and gain momentary satisfaction.

Defense mechanisms are a natural human response to self-protection; therefore, the vast majority are displayed unconsciously. This is precisely why we emphasize them in this book. The psychological activities we observe through conversation or other means may have been carefully disguised by others and are difficult to verify. Reactions produced by defense mechanisms, however, are unconscious actions. In other words, judging human psychology through defense mechanisms more easily reaches the root of the mind.

Because individuals differ in personality and habits, each person's defense mechanisms manifest differently. The following chapters will detail the ten common types of defense mechanisms to give readers a deeper understanding.

#### Sublimation Mechanism: Memoirs of the Bittersweet Past of Successful People

Micro-expression keywords: The sublimation mechanism not only benefits oneself but also benefits the entire society and even humanity. To become a better person, sublimate!

There is a fable about a man who, whenever he got angry, would run three laps around his house and land. After sweating profusely, his anger would subside.

Thanks to his good temper and exceptional mind, his land and house grew larger and larger, yet his habit of running three laps around his property when angry never changed, even into his eighties.

His grandson was puzzled and asked, "Grandfather, whenever you are unhappy, you run around the house and land. Is there a secret to this?"

"There is," the old man replied. "When I was young and quarreled or got angry, I would run around my house. As I ran, I would think: my land is still so small, my house so tiny—I have no time to be angry with others. It is better to use that energy for work and study."

"Then why do you still run around the land now that you are so wealthy?" the grandson asked, still confused.

The old man smiled. "Even in old age, one cannot avoid anger. As I run, I think: I already own such vast land and so many houses—why haggle with others? At that thought, my anger disappears."

The anxiety in this man's mind was clearly anger arising from conflict with others. He transformed that anger into a pursuit of success and wealth, using it as motivation to achieve goals others could not reach. This exemplifies the sublimation defense mechanism.

Many renowned writers and composers produced immortal works through the sublimation defense mechanism. Austrian composer Schubert suffered repeated heartbreak; emotional setbacks left him despondent yet also stimulated his creativity and imagination. During his fifteen-year creative career, Schubert wrote more than a thousand pieces. He himself said, "The works I wrote in the deepest pain are the ones most appreciated by the world."

French writer Romain Rolland, likewise tormented by lost love, swore "I shall create or die" to escape the pain and spent ten years writing the epic *Jean-Christophe*.

For these composers and literary giants, trauma was not a quagmire but a driving force. With the sublimation defense mechanism, every wound became a benchmark and footprint of progress and success.

Truly happy people do not generate sublimation defense mechanisms. Only those whose instinctive desires remain unsatisfied develop powerful inner drive from unfulfilled life impulses, achieving remarkable sublimated results.

There is a saying that anger produces poets, but I believe suffering produces poets.

Qu Yuan loved the state of Chu, yet corrupt officials and a foolish ruler held power. From this pain came the timeless *Li Sao*, *Nine Songs*, and China's first ultimate interrogation, *Heavenly Questions*.

Li Bai devoted his life to politics but was treated by Emperor Xuanzong merely as a favored courtier. His apparent glory masked deep frustration. Later he wandered destitute and nearly faced imprisonment. This suffering turned him into the brightest note in Tang poetry.

Ten years younger than Li Bai, Du Fu spent his life without a fixed home, which produced the accusatory "Three Officers" and "Three Partings."

Li Yu, the last ruler of Southern Tang, possessed outstanding talent while ruling Jiangnan and enjoying the company of the two Zhou sisters, yet his early ci poems rarely moved readers. Only after Zhao Guangyi captured him and repeatedly humiliated his wife did intense suffering produce the line: "How much sorrow can one man bear? It is like a river of spring water flowing east."

Foreign poets followed the same pattern.

T. S. Eliot could not escape self-doubt and spent his life casting himself into this abyss, writing "We are the hollow men."

W. B. Yeats's lifelong love regarded him only as a friend; he wrote plaintively that others loved her for her charming demeanor, youthful beauty, or with true or false hearts—only one loved her pilgrim soul.

Dylan Thomas, at his father's deathbed, roared his grief: "Do not go gentle into that good night. Rage, rage against the dying of the light."

The opening line of the programmatic long poem of the American Beat Generation reads: "I saw the best minds of my generation destroyed by madness, starving hysterical naked, dragging themselves through the negro streets at dawn looking for an angry fix." Its author, Allen Ginsberg, admitted there was no Beat Generation—only a group of young people who wanted enough to eat and to publish their work.

Behind the sublimation mechanism lies an act of abandonment: when desires are repressed and cannot be satisfied or released, anxiety arises. Intense pain then prompts people to abandon that anxiety and seek higher pursuits aligned with universal values. This is sublimation.

Sublimation helps those trapped in anxiety escape their predicament and carries great positive significance for society. To put it strongly, human history has been driven by people who abandoned personal anxiety to achieve individual sublimation.

#### Revealing Others' Psychological Motivations Through Cognitive Dissonance

**Micro-expression keywords**  
Conflicting cognitions are an original driving force in our psychology. The process in which people, in order to reduce conflicts between cognitions and balance the gap in their hearts, force themselves to accept or seek new concepts, is called the self-balancing of cognitive dissonance.

In the 1950s, Marian Keech, leader of a UFO doomsday cult, prophesied that her followers would be taken away by an alien spaceship on the night of December 20, after which the end of the world would arrive.

Many followers believed her and even quit their jobs to wait at home for the end. At midnight, the followers gathered at the designated spot, awaiting the spaceship.

At midnight exactly, there was no sign of the spaceship; the followers grew slightly tense. By two o'clock it still had not come, and unease spread. After four o'clock, as panic set in, Ms. Keech appeared and told them: "Because of your devotion, the world has been redeemed."

In other words, the followers' faith and waiting had postponed doomsday. This was clearly an absurd lie, yet the waiting followers did not question Keech. Instead, they excitedly ran into the streets to proselytize, telling everyone that the aliens had been moved by their positive efforts and enthusiasm and had spared Earth.

When a person is deceived, the first reaction should be anger.

Yet why did these UFO doomsday cultists become even more devout after being deceived?

To understand this, we must examine the concept of cognitive dissonance proposed by American psychologist Leon Festinger in his book *When Prophecy Fails*.

Cognitive dissonance refers to the uncomfortable feeling triggered when one performs an action inconsistent with one's attitude—that is, when an individual recognizes two conflicting attitudes or a contradiction between attitude and behavior. This contradiction usually produces psychological tension. To overcome it, people employ various methods to reduce the discomfort.

Old Wang had been a heavy smoker for nearly ten years. Recently, after a big argument with his wife, he resolved to quit.

Yet only two days into his resolution, at a class reunion, an old classmate casually offered him a cigarette.

To smoke or not to smoke?

Watching his classmates puffing away, Old Wang felt tempted, but he shook his head and refused: "No thanks, I've quit."

"Come on, if you can quit smoking, I can quit eating," the classmate said, stuffing the cigarette into Old Wang's hand without another word.

Holding the burning cigarette, Old Wang hesitated, then finally lit it with determination.

It seemed he still liked smoking. Even if not for stress relief, there were so many occasions in life that called for it. He could only smoke less. From now on, when offered a cigarette, he would refuse if possible; if not, he would smoke.

Old Wang's psychological shift illustrates cognitive dissonance. His original intention to quit clashed with the behavior of accepting and smoking the cigarette offered by his classmate. To balance the discrepancy, he supplied himself with four justifications—"I still like smoking," "to relieve stress," "there are so many occasions in life that call for it," and "refuse when possible, smoke only when unavoidable"—thereby convincing himself to enjoy the cigarette with a clear conscience.

The UFO doomsday cultists behaved similarly. Their own faith and the subsequent outcome created a psychological gap of "failed expectations." To balance this gap, they had to persuade themselves to believe Ms. Keech's words, resulting in even more fanatical devotion.

Festinger argued that every person's cognitive structure, or psychological space, consists of various cognitive elements. These elements are independent and relative. Once two cognitive elements in a person's mind conflict, cognitive dissonance arises. As dissonance increases, the psychological pressure to reduce or eliminate it grows accordingly.

Cognitive dissonance theory also holds that cognition and behavior are necessarily linked: only after behavior changes does cognition change; cognitive dissonance serves merely as an intermediary. The reason people alter their cognition and balance dissonance is ultimately to provide a rationale for their behavior, rendering it reasonable. Neither Old Wang the smoker nor the fervent cultists escape this pattern.

Therefore, when we notice someone whose words and actions contradict each other or whose attitudes and behaviors differ sharply, we can carefully observe their actions and apply behavioral psychology for analysis. It is then easy to identify the cause of their cognitive dissonance.

Such examples are common in life. Subordinates who privately despise their incompetent superiors—believing they hold their positions only through power—still act obsequious and deferential in front of those superiors. This is a typical case of cognitive dissonance.

#### Eliminating Regretful Emotions, Letting Go of Inner Burdens

Everyone's life has a gap that follows them like a shadow throughout their life. For regrets in life, it is better to accept them with ease and let go of the inner burdens, so that one can cherish everything one has more.

Singaporean singer Xu Meijing has a song called "Regret," which contains these lines: "Stop saying whose fault it is, let everything turn to ash. Unless you let go of the inner burdens, everything will be irretrievable. You always let the past follow you, afraid that the past was in vain..." Regret is actually the feeling of regret when one hopes to do something or is about to do it but ultimately fails to do it, or the feeling of regret when one strives bravely for an ideal but ultimately fails to achieve it.

In life, one inevitably encounters some regrettable things. If we bury regrets in our hearts, over time they accumulate, and we will sink into a quagmire of vanishing willpower from which we cannot extricate ourselves, falling into an abyss of mental lethargy from which we cannot escape. Therefore, we should eliminate regretful emotions so that we can maintain psychological balance.

So how can we eliminate regretful emotions? Here are several methods:

1. **Accept the Facts**  
   William James once said: "To be willing to admit that things are as they are, to be able to accept what has already happened, is the first step in overcoming any misfortune." Missed time is gone forever. Since it has become fact and cannot be changed, what else can one do besides calmly accepting it?

   The TV drama *Half a Lifetime's Fate* introduces a pair of truly loving lovers who, under the tricks of fate, go their separate ways. When they meet again years later, the two are in great pain, full of remorse, left only with regret. Perhaps the greatest regret in the world is that two people in love cannot hold hands for a lifetime, but since it has already happened, one can only accept the facts rather than live in regret and fantasy.

2. **Accept One's Imperfect Self**  
   We always overemphasize shame and guilt while neglecting the importance of acceptance and forgiveness. Admittedly, shame and guilt are very important to the individual, but they must never become shackles that kidnap one's inner self. This is like going to church to confess, unloading one's burdens through confession and, to some extent, gaining forgiveness for oneself.

   No one wants to wallow in self-blame; everyone needs to continue living and pursue happiness. From this perspective, accepting one's imperfect self is necessary, because life has no perfection to speak of. Perfection exists only in ideals. Regrets are everywhere in life; this is real life.

3. **Learn from One's Mistakes**  
   "The tree wants to be still, but the wind does not stop; the child wants to care for parents, but they are no longer there." When children wish to fulfill their filial duties, their parents have already passed away. This must be considered one of life's great regrets.

   Confucius heard someone crying in extreme grief, so he found the person and asked: "Could it be that there has been a death in your family? Otherwise, why are you crying so sorrowfully?"

   The person replied: "I have made three mistakes in my life. When I was young, I traveled the states in pursuit of learning and did not put caring for my family first—that is the first. In pursuit of my ideals, I served the ruler and did not show filial piety to my parents—that is the second. I was close with friends but distant with family—that is the third. The tree wants to be still, but the wind does not stop; the child wants to care for parents, but the parents are no longer in this world. Let me leave this world from now on!" With that, he died.

   Confucius said to his disciples: "You should take this as a warning. I hope this matter will help you understand some truths." As a result, three-tenths of his disciples chose to leave and return home to care for their parents.

   Regarding life's regrets, Bill Gates has a classic metaphor: "Life is like a big fire. The only thing each of us can do is salvage a little more from this fire." So having regrets is not terrible; what is terrible is failing to learn from them and letting them repeat over and over.

4. **Think More About the Positive Meaning of Regret**  
   Regret can also bring us gains. For example, it can increase life experience, broaden horizons, accumulate knowledge, help us recognize our own shortcomings, and prompt us to become better versions of ourselves. For instance, after experiencing the regret of "the child wants to care for parents, but they are no longer there," one will inevitably understand the importance of family ties and value relationships with relatives and friends more.

5. **Do Not Cling to the Past**  
   People with regrets in their hearts often say "If only..." or "Why didn't I back then..." Saying these things is useless and only adds to the sadness. Lost time cannot be recovered; the life one has lived cannot be relived. If one remains immersed in memories, one will lose the good mood of the present and miss more beauty. So for things that have already happened, do not cling to them. Let what is past pass!

#### Taking All Blame: Blindly Assuming Fault Leads to Overwhelming Burden

Taking all blame makes a person feel extreme guilt. Because of a strong sense of responsibility, they shoulder the entire world and ultimately become overwhelmed, unable to breathe.

Do you often feel dissatisfied with yourself and like to say to yourself "I should..." or "If only..."? For example: "If I hadn't said in front of him that this major has good prospects, maybe he wouldn't have chosen the wrong one when filling out his application." "It's all my fault. If I hadn't called him then, he wouldn't have answered while driving and wouldn't have gotten into the accident." Many people fall into the thinking trap of taking all blame because they keep using the "if... then..." way of thinking. The harm of this thinking trap is that it exists only in subjective reasoning and severely undermines a person's confidence.

People who like to take all blame always shoulder the responsibility for things themselves, and their hearts are filled with guilt, self-blame, regret, and other emotions. Psychology calls this phenomenon "guilt." It often arises because we feel responsible for something we did or something we said, thinking we should not have done or said it. The reason guilt is so harmful is that what we criticize is often not only our individual actions but our entire person.

Ms. Guo's younger brother suddenly jumped to his death at home. This caused Ms. Guo great pain, but what pained her even more was that she felt his death was related to her. To prove her guess was correct, she found many irrefutable reasons. Deep guilt tormented her every day, making her wish she were dead. She often blamed herself: "I'm so useless, so stupid! How could I not have stopped this? How could I not have seen that he wanted to commit suicide? I even talked to him yesterday; I shouldn't have said that. I indirectly killed him!"

Ms. Guo is a typical case of taking all blame. Because of distorted thinking, she blindly guessed the cause of her brother's death and felt she was the trigger for his suicide. However, no one has the ability to foresee the future; otherwise, they would certainly find ways to prevent the tragedy. In other words, she should not blame herself for her brother's death; that is illogical. She should not think she should be responsible for her brother's emotions and behavior, because these were not within her control.

Self-blame adds a burden to our minds and subjects us to the torment of guilt and shame. Therefore, we need to strengthen self-awareness and say goodbye to thinking patterns like "I should..." and "I really regret..." When facing things that cause self-blame, we should make objective evaluations, point out our own responsibilities factually, and not blindly exaggerate our responsibility or shoulder responsibilities that are not ours.

If one feels overwhelmed from blindly assuming fault, the following methods can be used to relieve the inner burden.

1. Do Some Things You Want to Do

Shift attention away from things that cause self-blame and do things you want to do, especially ideas hidden deep in your heart, such as traveling somewhere, meeting someone you have always wanted to meet, watching a movie you have really wanted to see, and so on. Make sure you can devote yourself fully without caring about results or achievements, because doing something you are interested in is itself a very meaningful thing.

Psychologists have found that being able to devote oneself fully to something one likes can eliminate people's dissatisfaction. Psychology calls this state "flow." In this state, people forget all their troubles and even forget themselves.

2. Recognize One's Own Limitations

No one is omnipotent; everyone makes various mistakes, so there is no need to blame oneself excessively. A bad outcome may have been caused by you, but more likely it was caused by a combination of various factors, so there is no need to bear full responsibility for one's mistakes.

3. Recognize That Many Outcomes Cannot Be Changed

Recognize that many outcomes cannot be changed. Therefore, guilt is only a negative solution. A more effective solution is to recognize the mistake, analyze the mistake, distinguish one's own responsibilities from others', and not shoulder all the blame oneself.

4. Do Everything Possible to Help Others

The "helping others" mentioned here does not mean only focusing on others' needs and giving unconditionally, but investing one's enthusiasm and doing everything possible to help others. Doing so can give you a sense of satisfaction. A group in the United States surveyed thousands of members of social rescue organizations, asking what they gained from serving others. Their answers were strikingly consistent: "spiritual pleasure and a sense of fulfillment."

#### Overgeneralization: A Single Setback Leads to Complete Collapse

Negative people, even after encountering a single setback, will overgeneralize it as caused by their own lack of ability, thereby completely denying their own abilities and value and falling into despair.

On the road of life, occasional failure is inevitable, but failure is only a moment in our lives; the past and future are not included. If you therefore regard yourself as a worthless person and collapse from then on, you have fallen into the erroneous thinking of overgeneralization. Once your brain is filled with such negative thoughts, more negative emotions will follow, leaving you breathless.

Some people lack confidence because they feel inferior to others in certain areas and never dare to try new things. Some become despondent when a partner leaves and lose faith in love. Some become depressed because of career setbacks and even choose to end their lives to escape this negative emotion.

Severe frustration causes strong psychological reactions and brings enormous pressure. If a person is tormented by this for a long time, physical and mental health will be damaged, and the person will become decadent, depressed, and even collapse completely. At this time, many people become indignant, habitually blame others for mistakes and failures, and even become cold and heartless, treating life and work with a cynical attitude, without knowing how to reflect on themselves. In extreme cases, they may even become mentally deranged and develop psychological disorders.

A young man who had a breakup could not escape the blow of lost love. He gradually became emotionally low, which affected his normal life and made it impossible for him to concentrate on work. He had fallen into an overgeneralization thinking pattern, resenting his ex-girlfriend's heartlessness and regretting having given so much foolishly. Later, he had to seek help from a psychologist.

The psychologist told him that his situation was far less bad than he imagined. To illustrate this, the psychologist asked: "If one day you are sitting on a park bench resting, with a book you like very much on the bench, and suddenly someone walks straight toward you, sits on the book you placed on the chair, and damages your book, how would you feel?"

The young man replied: "I would definitely be very angry and blame him for damaging someone else's things for no reason."

The psychologist continued: "Now let me tell you, if he were blind, how would you feel then?"

The young man scratched his head, thought for a moment, and said: "Then he definitely wouldn't have known there was a book on the chair, so I wouldn't be angry."

The psychologist smiled knowingly and said to him: "The same act of damaging your book produces completely opposite emotions before and after. Do you know why?"

The young man replied: "Maybe because my view of the matter is different!"

Different views of a matter can indeed cause different emotions. Obviously, sometimes what makes us sad and painful is not the matter itself, but incorrect interpretations and evaluations of the matter. If people only evaluate their own behavior and classify it as good or bad, they will hardly experience any emotional distress. Many people are affected by negative emotions because they extend their negative evaluation of their behavior to a judgment of their personal worth. Even if they occasionally make a mistake, they see it as an unforgivable act and even regard themselves as a complete failure.

Psychologists have found that negative thoughts often include unfounded inferences, excessive exaggeration or minimization of problems, and negative associations with oneself. For example, "I didn't do this well, so my career is hopeless," "My partner broke up with me, so no one else will like me," "I was so nervous during the speech that I couldn't speak; I'll definitely be nervous and unable to speak in future speeches too"...

Everyone generates these thoughts to some extent. When facing such ideas, what we need to do is actively question them, because the emergence of negative emotions is actually a warning, reminding us to pay attention to whether our thoughts are reasonable.

#### Mislabeling: Negative Suggestion Leads to Emotional Fluctuations

Labeling oneself means using mistakes to create a completely negative self-image. It is an extreme form of overgeneralization that both creates trouble for oneself and appears absurd and foolish.

In life, many people often say to themselves "I am a very lousy person," "I am worthless," or "I am not good at socializing," thereby affixing a wrong label to themselves. Mislabeling causes one to use inaccurate words when describing things and to be overly emotional. For example, a person who is dieting and eats an ice cream often thinks: "I really am a gluttonous pig; I hate myself!" With this thought, she becomes upset and restless.

After mislabeling, we often use various examples to prove our label. For instance, when doing things we become full of worries, always doubting we will do poorly, and involuntarily prove that we are indeed lousy. This kind of thinking takes deep root in the mind. Every time we do something, these negative contents come to mind, suggesting to ourselves that we will do poorly.

Self-suggestion often has unexpected effects and exerts a tremendous influence on a person's psychological state. When we engage in self-suggestion, we are actually continuously giving ourselves commands. If self-suggestion continues for a long time, it forms a habit. This habit will produce the most direct reaction on a person's attitude and thinking, thereby affecting the person's body and behavior.

Once a person accustomed to negative thinking falls into a fixed thinking pattern, they will evaluate the problems they face negatively. What is even more frightening is that even positive events, once trapped in a negative thinking pattern, will be viewed with a negative attitude. If negativity is allowed to accumulate, it deepens the sense of misfortune, makes one feel disasters more deeply, and leads to greatly reduced self-control.

There was a person who frequently suspected he had cancer. He was scared to death, looked worried every day, fell into a state of anxiety and restlessness, could not eat or sleep well, and every movement showed the behavior of a cancer patient. In just half a month, he lost more than ten pounds. Later, after examinations at multiple hospitals, it was found that he did not have cancer at all. Upon hearing this news, he finally slowly recovered his health.

In contrast, there was a person diagnosed with cancer by the hospital, but he did not take it too seriously. He often engaged in positive self-suggestion: "As long as my spirit does not collapse, I can overcome cancer and gradually get better." When taking medicine, he often muttered: "This medicine must be good; taking it will definitely be effective." When walking, he often suggested to himself: "Life lies in movement; more walking will naturally make the body better." Gradually, this suggestion produced a positive effect on his body and mind. For more than ten years he had no major problems, and he became increasingly confident about his body.

The two people in the cases form a sharp contrast, fully illustrating that negative suggestion and positive suggestion can lead to completely different results. Negative suggestion easily causes emotional fluctuations, produces great errors in judging things, and leads to cognitive deviations from the norm. Such people's thinking is easily led astray; they are often in a state of confusion psychologically, encounter obstacles everywhere in life, and frequently fail at work.

Although the harm of negative suggestion is great, we can use the same principle to cure negative suggestion—that is, to apply positive suggestion more often. French physician Coué, who first proposed autosuggestion therapy in 1920, had a famous saying: "Every day in every way I am getting better and better." He had patients repeat this sentence daily, and many patients recovered as a result. In fact, suggestion therapy gives patients a good mood and the confidence to overcome illness, thereby mobilizing their inner factors and giving play to their subjective initiative. As the ancients said, "When emotions are urgent, a hundred illnesses increase; when emotions are relaxed, a hundred illnesses are removed."

#### Escaping Despair: Resolving Conflict Is Key

Long-term immersion in a state of low mood leaves the inner self extremely fragile, with no hope visible for the present or the future—this is despair. Failure to emerge from despair easily leads to self-abandonment.

“Grief greater than the death of the heart” describes despair as the extreme expression of negative emotion. For a despairing person the heart has died, leaving only a shell; the harm exceeds that of depression.

A despairing person has already sunk into the negative emotion of self-loathing. Watching others succeed and live happily while repeatedly failing and living in pain, such a person falls into self-loathing. Despairing people often mutter “Why am I so useless?” and consequently cannot accept themselves, lose faith in themselves, and stop believing in themselves.

If self-loathing is left unchecked and thoughts of “I am truly useless” flash repeatedly, or if events are exaggerated, self-evaluation drops and the ability to perform calmly declines. Once self-loathing intensifies, the person ultimately abandons all effort.

Despair usually stems from inability to accept the gap between reality and ideals: expectations are too high and fantasies too rosy on one side, while reality is too harsh and life too miserable on the other. High ambition is originally positive, yet setting expectations too high—“I must achieve this,” “I ought to do that”—locks a person inside an ideal cage. Any discrepancy between ideal and reality then triggers self-loathing. Ambition itself is not wrong, but one must also recognize reality, take each step steadily, and gradually approach the goal.

Despair arises from various conflicts in life. Only by handling these conflicts can despair be relieved and released. How, then, is this done?

1. **Resolve conflict with awareness**  
   Research shows that awareness can control the generation of emotion and regulate its intensity. Positive self-suggestion can therefore be used skillfully to resolve conflict—for example, telling oneself “I can…” or “I will…” to indicate what one can and will do, thereby regulating emotion.

2. **Resolve conflict with language**  
   Awareness alone is insufficient; thoughts must be spoken aloud, because voicing them produces an entirely different emotional experience from thinking them silently. Inspirational slogans can also be posted where they are frequently seen, guiding positive emotion from the outside in.

3. **Resolve conflict by shifting attention**  
   When something triggers despair, stop dwelling on it. Shift attention to view or handle it from a fresh angle or in a new way instead of remaining immersed in despair and dejection. Watching mood-regulating films or reading mood-regulating books, or listening to soothing music, can also redirect attention and fill life with positive emotion.

4. **“Out with the old, in with the new”**  
   This means completely abandoning lifestyles that breed despair and adopting those that generate hope—ending a despair-inducing relationship and beginning one that offers hope, or resigning from a suffocating job to find new work. Small changes also help: a new hairstyle, a new fruit, a new outfit. In short, “out with the old, in with the new” frees one from despair.

#### Excessive Expectations: Overly High Demands Lead to Inner Anxiety

Excessive expectations are the root cause of inner anxiety. To escape anxiety and pain, one must discard this mindset and return demands on oneself and others to a rational level.

People differ in their expectations of themselves and therefore in the demands they place on themselves. High personal standards are originally beneficial and can drive excellence. Yet when standards become too high they backfire, imposing invisible pressure that ultimately hinders achievement. Unrealistic goals keep a person in constant tension and high stress, followed by anxiety and pain.

Which mindsets readily produce inner anxiety, and how can they be discarded?

1. **Fast-paced thinking**  
   Many people adopt fast-paced thinking: in pursuit of expected goals they become impatient, demanding an unnaturally rapid work or life rhythm without regard for their own stress limits. When feeling overwhelmed, check whether fast-paced thinking is present. If so, remind yourself that life contains no goals that must be reached. Slow the pace, proceed according to natural rhythms, make goals attainable, enjoy the scenery along the way, and move forward calmly while savoring the process rather than fixating solely on the outcome.

2. **Single-value thinking**  
   People with single-value thinking judge success or failure by only one standard—for instance, that a good life requires a car, a house, and savings. This mindset appears unproblematic in favorable circumstances, yet any gap between reality and the chosen value triggers endless self-conflict. The conflict consumes energy, distances the person from goals and expectations, and creates a vicious cycle.

3. **Absolutist thinking**  
   People with absolutist thinking start from personal wishes and insist that something must or must not happen. They convert “want” or “hope” into “must,” “should,” or “have to.” Typical statements include “I must succeed” or “Others must treat me well.”  
   Such absolutist demands are unreasonable because every phenomenon follows its own developmental laws independent of human will. When events diverge from these absolutist expectations, the person finds them unacceptable and falls into emotional distress.

4. **Idealized thinking**  
   When unrealistic expectations far exceed what reality can satisfy, a person becomes captive to desire and cannot feel relaxed or happy. Desire itself is a neutral primal driving force, yet excessive self-demand equals captivity by desire. As rational beings we should control desire rather than be dominated or consumed by it. Recognizing human smallness in the universe and centering on reality rather than the self removes much pressure.  
   Every phenomenon has its own laws of occurrence, development, and conclusion. One cannot alter these objective laws and can only align with them. Focus attention on actual matters rather than on personal imaginings.

#### Worrying About the Sky Falling: Self-Disturbance Leads to Melancholy

People chronically troubled by sadness tend to view matters pessimistically. They see only the negative side, their mood cannot improve, and sadness easily enters.

Have you ever worried on a rainy day about being struck by lightning, or on a flight about the plane crashing? The ancient Chinese idiom “the man of Qi fears the sky will fall” tells of someone who constantly feared the heavens would collapse. The probability of such events is so low as to be laughable.

Exaggerating a minor matter into a catastrophe or treating it as utterly disastrous generates negative emotions such as anxiety, dejection, despair, and melancholy. These emotions neither improve the situation nor benefit work, life, or health.

Mr. Wu, convinced he had cancer, visited a major hospital hoping for early detection.

The doctor asked, “Do you feel discomfort anywhere?”  
Mr. Wu replied, “Nothing in particular.”  
The doctor asked, “Any sharp pain?”  
Mr. Wu replied, “Everything feels fine.”  
The doctor asked, “Have you lost weight recently?”  
Mr. Wu replied, “No, my weight is normal.”  
The doctor finally asked, “Then why suspect cancer?”  
Mr. Wu answered, “I read a book that said early-stage cancer has no symptoms—and that is exactly my situation!”

Such groundless worry is comical. When a person sinks into wild speculation, others perceive the behavior as absurd. A devoted couple may still hear the wife complain, “Why are you warm to everyone else? You seem indifferent to me but attentive to others.” Even while knowing worry is useless, the person continues to assess how bad things might become and grows agitated through self-disturbance.

When feeling melancholy, first determine whether the worry is real or self-generated; only then can it cease to obstruct growth. Most worries are in fact absurd; examining probabilities reveals them as groundless and eliminates the majority of troubles.

Sadness arises from incorrect ways of viewing problems. Overcoming sadness therefore requires cultivating the habit of seeing matters positively and optimistically. Once formed, this habit changes one’s entire state: problems are met with hope, and hope supplies the strength to surmount difficulties.

Changing perspective belongs to the cognitive approach frequently used in psychology. Cognitive theorists hold that psychological difficulties stem from flawed ways of viewing problems. In therapy they therefore guide clients to examine issues from another, more positive angle; once clients do so, the difficulties are resolved.

#### Compensation Mechanism: The Sweat of Effort Originates from Inferiority

Micro-expression keywords: The compensation mechanism is beneficial and harmless to people. Psychological anxiety is effectively relieved through compensation, and compensatory effort often produces useful outcomes. The behaviors reflecting this mechanism are mostly harmless.

The ancient Greek orator Demosthenes had small lung capacity, difficulty with pronunciation, and a stutter in his youth, yet he resolved to become a successful speaker. He practiced with pebbles in his mouth to improve fluency, rehearsed before a mirror to correct facial distortions, ran uphill each morning to strengthen his lungs, and each evening addressed the roaring sea so his voice would carry. His efforts succeeded; Demosthenes became known as the true “king of orators.”

This inspirational story illustrates a behavioral-psychology principle called the compensation defense mechanism.

The compensation defense mechanism originates in the human sense of inferiority. When a person perceives a personal defect, the resulting feeling of incompetence and distress is called inferiority. Combined with anxiety, inferiority forms an inferiority complex that becomes a powerful inner drive, prompting conscious self-shaping and compensatory effort to overcome the feeling and strive for improvement. This defensive process is the compensation defense mechanism.

Examples surround us. Australian youth of the year Nick Vujicic was born with phocomelia, lacking both arms and legs, yet through extraordinary courage and perseverance he has accomplished what many able-bodied people cannot: riding, playing ball, swimming, earning two university degrees, and serving as a company director.

Vujicic’s achievements rest on effort and courage, yet even this resilient individual attempted suicide three times before age ten. An inferiority complex clearly existed within him; it became the force that drove him beyond the reach of many healthy people.

Everyone possesses an inner “rational ideal,” an uncommon psychological term that may be understood as the self one believes oneself to be and the self one aspires to become.

Physiological or psychological defects often obstruct the path to this ideal self. When the desire for self-realization prompts the rational self to make the more admirable choice of meeting difficulty head-on, compensatory behavior appears.

Ultimately, whether or not the compensation mechanism objectively achieves the desired result, the subjective experience is that one feels considerably lighter after having tried one’s best; anxiety is effectively eased.

#### Jealousy Mechanism: The Malignant Transfer of Those Harboring Resentment

Micro-expression keywords: Unlike the attack mechanism, the jealousy mechanism releases tension more gently and rationality plays a clearer role, making jealousy easier to control. As an effective channel for discharging anxiety, jealousy can be acceptable when properly managed. Only uncontrolled jealousy that produces extreme behavior requires caution.

Forty-three-year-old teacher Liu had lost attraction to her husband, four years her senior, and began transferring her “love” to her students.

Seventeen-year-old Xiao Hua, an average student but handsome, was one of them. One day Liu kept him after class under the pretext of tutoring and initiated a sexual relationship in the empty classroom. The affair lasted nearly three months.

A new transfer student, A Bin, then joined the class. A Bin, a year younger than Xiao Hua, was a sports specialist, 184 cm tall, and already muscular. Liu soon became infatuated with him and used the same methods to win him.

Xiao Hua grew extremely jealous, repeatedly begging Liu to abandon A Bin and stay with him alone. When unsuccessful he turned to threats. Liu was unmoved by a child’s threats and continued the relationship with A Bin while occasionally seeing Xiao Hua as well.

Xiao Hua’s resentment finally erupted. One evening, after failing to persuade Liu and witnessing her intimacy with A Bin, he rushed into the classroom, killed A Bin with an iron clamp, and wounded Liu.

From a police perspective this was a typical crime of passion. Psychology, however, classifies Xiao Hua’s act as an expression of a psychological defense mechanism: jealousy.

“The best husband is always the neighbor’s husband” is a common quip among middle-class circles in certain German regions, usually uttered when men gather to mock their own “tigress” wives for jealousy and complaining.

The jealousy mechanism shares features with the attack mechanism—both manifest through destruction, harm, or conquest—yet the distinction is clear. The attack mechanism arises from blocked self-realization desires that produce violence. Jealous anxiety, by contrast, typically stems from psychological disparity.

What one already possesses, others must not obtain; what others obtain, one must also obtain. This is the typical mindset of the jealous person.

#### Case One: Aunt Zhang and the Vegetable Vendor

Retired Aunt Zhang carried her vegetable basket to the morning market. Passing a stall, she was drawn to the fresh green cucumbers on display and asked the price.

“What! Eight yuan per jin?” Aunt Zhang could hardly believe her ears. “Other stalls sell them for three yuan. Are these golden cucumbers? No wonder you can’t sell them!”

“These are organic cucumbers. Are you buying or not? If not, move along and stop blocking my business.” The vendor was annoyed by her tone.

“Organic? More like a scam!” Aunt Zhang, unfamiliar with the term, grew angry at the vendor’s attitude. “These days people will say anything to make money. They say people full of tricks don’t grow tall—and it’s true.”

The vendor’s short stature was already a sore point. Provoked by Aunt Zhang’s remark, he retorted, “They also say a broad mind makes a plump body. Some old folks are as thin as kindling, yet their minds are narrower than the eye of a needle…”

Aunt Zhang wanted to buy the cucumbers at a reasonable price; saving money was her desire. The vendor’s high price blocked that desire, so she resorted to insults. This is how her aggressive behavior arose.

Such scenes are common in daily life. In a society that moves ever faster, tempers grow shorter. Minor arguments over purchases can escalate to violent outbursts or even fatal revenge after perceived insults. In countless situations, people may harm others out of momentary anger or impulse. In behavioral psychology, such aggressive speech and actions are called the attack defense mechanism.

According to Freud, every person’s mental activity has a dominant tendency: the unconscious strives to reduce or eliminate sudden external stimuli in order to maintain psychological balance. Based on this principle, the attack defense mechanism expresses anxiety and anger caused by displeasure through violence or other destructive, confrontational behavior. This allows the impulse to be discharged and restores inner equilibrium. The targets of attack are those who create conflict or obstruct the discharge.

The quarrel between Aunt Zhang and the vendor escalated from a pricing dispute to personal attacks on each other’s shortcomings precisely because of this mechanism, triggering an all-out confrontation.

#### Resolving Jealousy by Suppressing the Urge to Compare

“Why was there a Zhou Yu if there had to be a Zhuge Liang?” People who envy others constantly compare themselves and, upon discovering their shortcomings, cannot let go. Blind comparison is the root of envy; only by curbing the urge to compare can envy be resolved.

In daily life one often overhears women chatting: “I heard Xiaoman’s husband earns twenty thousand a month plus a two-hundred-thousand bonus. Impressive! But his company is struggling; he might be laid off any time.” “He buys a car and suddenly walks differently.” “Xiaoli’s husband bought her that skirt we saw last time—over ten thousand yuan! The skirt is nice, but it doesn’t look great on her.”

Some people feel admiration—an active emotion—when they meet someone more accomplished; others feel envy—a passive emotion. Envy arises because one covets what another possesses yet lacks the ability to obtain it, resulting in feelings of inferiority, shame, and resentment.

American anthropologist George Foster observed: “In every culture, the tall poppy is treated the same.” Every success provokes envy in those around it, as if others’ gains automatically diminish one’s own.

Envy is a distinctly negative emotion. The envious person suffers at every success of others, even when that success does not harm them. This suffering breeds restlessness and irritability, damaging both mind and body. To escape the pain, the envious heart secretly wishes others would fail. Those consumed by envy may even sabotage others’ success at any cost, including their own interests. As Bacon wrote, “Envy is the worst of devils and ever secretly and quietly ruins the good things of this world.”

How, then, can we resolve envy and curb the urge to compare?

#### Case Three: Mr. Sun and His Wife

Mr. Sun had been married five years. His wife’s family was wealthy; he came from a poor rural background. After arriving in the city he built a career by relying on his wife’s family connections.

Once he had a career, Mr. Sun began to stray. His wife sensed part of it but, for the sake of the family, turned a blind eye. Only when he transferred 500,000 yuan from their joint account did she sense real danger. Investigation revealed he had a steady mistress and planned to buy her an apartment.

The wife realized that once the money was spent she would lose her share of the marital property. She located the other woman’s address and went to confront her.

Unexpectedly, her husband—who should have been at work—arrived for a tryst at the same moment. The three met. Seeing the disheveled pair, the wife screamed at them in fury.

Mr. Sun feared his wife would destroy his career and also dreaded losing the woman in his arms. In this extreme state of mind he struck his wife.

The wife had become an obstacle to his pleasure; under intense anxiety Mr. Sun resorted to violence. Despite his clear moral fault, he could still attack her. Once the attack mechanism takes over, moral judgment at the superego level disappears and reason vanishes. We must therefore stay alert to those who lash out when cornered and also find ways not to be ruled by this mechanism ourselves.

The attack mechanism is perhaps the most direct way to discharge anxiety: it converts anxiety into direct harm inflicted on the immediate party. We have all met people who react emotionally to any frustration by snapping back at whoever crosses them.

Such individuals habitually use the attack mechanism to vent anxiety. We should extend them a measure of understanding: attacking us is not their true intention; they are simply blocked by anxiety.

#### Subjective Assumptions: Bias Easily Introduces Emotional Coloring

When judging an event we often see only one side and automatically ignore other possibilities. In most cases people tend to believe the negative side, plunging themselves into negative emotions.

In daily life we habitually project our own feelings and will onto others, distorting facts and producing mistaken evaluations. Psychology calls this the “self-projection effect.” Many misunderstandings and negative emotions arise in exactly this way.

American psychologist Edward Thorndike termed it the “halo effect”: influenced by mental set, cognition and judgment often start from a single aspect, spread outward, and form an overall impression that overgeneralizes and produces error.

A young man from a poor family discussed his wedding plans with his girlfriend: “Can we keep it simple and skip the gold necklace, ring, and earrings?” She replied, “No, that’s the custom.” Her father insisted the groom buy the three gold items plus a 100,000-yuan bride price. The young man borrowed from everyone he knew and finally gathered the sum.

At the wedding the bride’s father handed the groom a red envelope. Still resentful, the groom threw it on the floor. After much persuasion he picked it up. Someone urged him to open it. Inside was not cash but a passbook showing a 100,000-yuan deposit.

The father-in-law had not intended to extract money; he simply believed local custom required the bride price or the couple would lose face at the wedding.

The young man never inquired into his father-in-law’s real intention; he judged it by his own assumptions, triggering a chain of emotional reactions and impulsive behavior. All of it stemmed from bias.

#### The Blind Self

Next is the window in the upper-right corner of the mind, called the “blind self,” also known as the “back self.” It earns this name because it belongs to the blind-spot area of self-knowledge. The saying “the spectator sees clearly while the participant is lost” refers to the blind self.

The blind self represents unconscious behavioral traits—prominent psychological features, inadvertent gestures, or habits. We usually cannot detect these emotional leaks ourselves; only when others point them out do we become aware, and we typically react with surprise, denial, or doubt, because the trait does not match our self-image.

When her close friend seriously told Xiaohong that she could no longer tolerate her unreliability, Xiaohong felt deeply wronged.

“When have I been unreliable?” she protested. “When did I ever promise something and fail to deliver?”

“Last week you said you would go shopping with me but canceled at the last minute. Last month you said you would introduce me to a boyfriend, yet you’ve probably forgotten completely,” her friend challenged.

Xiaohong was speechless. Until her friend mentioned them, she had almost forgotten these incidents. Still, she muttered, did her friend have to get so angry? Everyone forgets things sometimes.

Xiaohong’s situation illustrates the inability to see one’s own blind self. The trait of making easy promises and then forgetting them was invisible to her until someone else revealed it.

The blind self is the part of the mind that we cannot see but others can. People who habitually reflect on themselves tend to have a smaller blind self; those who never engage in self-reflection have a very large one.

The story of Xi Shi clutching her heart and Dong Shi imitating her carries a similar lesson. Xi Shi did not know how beautiful she looked while clutching her heart, yet others saw it clearly—hence the anecdote of Dong Shi’s clumsy imitation.

#### The Five Things People Regret Most at Life’s End

1. I wish I had had the courage to live the life I truly wanted.
2. I wish I had not spent so much energy on work and had not missed watching my children grow or the warmth of my partner.
3. I wish I had had the courage to express my feelings instead of suppressing anger and negative emotions for so long.
4. I wish I had stayed in touch with good friends instead of letting busy life erode genuine friendships.
5. I wish I had allowed myself to be happier instead of habitually hiding behind a smile in front of others.

A Japanese hospice nurse, Hidekazu Otsu, had a similar experience. After hearing the final regrets of a thousand patients, he wrote the book *25 Things People Regret Before They Die*. The listed regrets include:

1. Not doing what I wanted to do.
2. Not fulfilling my dreams.
3. Doing things against my conscience.
4. Letting emotions rule my life.
5. Not helping others enough.
6. Being overly confident in myself.
7. Not arranging my property properly.
8. Not considering arrangements after death.
9. Not returning to my hometown.
10. Not enjoying fine food.
11. Spending most of my time working.
12. Not traveling to the places I wanted to see.
13. Not meeting the people I wanted to meet.
14. Not experiencing a love worth remembering forever.
15. Never marrying.
16. Not having children.
17. Not seeing my children marry.
18. Not paying attention to my health.
19. Not quitting smoking.
20. Not expressing my true wishes.
21. Not understanding the meaning of life.
22. Not leaving evidence that I existed.
23. Not seeing through life and death.
24. Not having faith.
25. Not saying “thank you” to the people I deeply loved.

#### Manifestations of Regressive Behavior at Different Ages

A six- or seven-year-old child who feels neglected after the birth of a younger sibling may revert to earlier habits such as bed-wetting or thumb-sucking. Scolding or punishment does not reduce the behavior; it may even increase. The cause is not physical but the operation of the regressive defense mechanism.

Adults also exhibit regressive defense mechanisms. A strong man in pain may cry out “Mama!” A capable businesswoman who feels wronged may weep like a child. A woman entering menopause, fearing aging, may become hypersensitive and dress or behave like a teenager.

The reason lies in childhood, when demands were fewer, inner security was greater, and happiness and satisfaction were more abundant. When problems seem insoluble, people therefore adopt regressive defense behaviors—expressing anxiety or anger through actions that are age-inappropriate, regressive, and immature.

Most of these behaviors fail to resolve the anxiety-provoking situation and may even deepen the predicament. Regressive behavior temporarily relieves anxiety, yet childish actions cannot meaningfully address real, uncontrollable circumstances. The relief is therefore short-lived. Once the “impulse” of regression passes and anxiety returns, the psyche suffers an even greater blow. This pattern is even cited as a cause of some psychological disorders.

It is therefore advisable to avoid relying on regressive behavior to relieve stress and instead address problems rationally; doing so better supports long-term well-being.

#### Causes of Regressive Behavior

Regressive behavior usually occurs when anxiety exceeds a certain threshold, causing temporary weakening of rational control and prompting an instinctive, ostrich-like avoidance.

Many martial-arts programs begin by teaching students how to take hits. The goal is not only to build resistance to impact but, more importantly, to counteract the tendency toward regressive behavior during combat.

The threat of violence in sparring arrives with lightning speed and generates intense anxiety. Because the threat is so rapid, reason has no time to suppress the anxiety. When a fist comes toward the face, the instinctive reaction is to close the eyes. We all know closing the eyes solves nothing; the better response is to keep the eyes open and dodge. Yet when anxiety overrides reason, there is no time to think of dodging. The only available action is the most instinctive—and least useful—childhood response: close the eyes, turn the head, hunch the shoulders.

This is why many martial-arts schools have beginners strike each other’s heads (with protective gear or controlled contact). Some traditions call it “training courage.” In Japanese kendo the first lesson is mutual head strikes, known as “courage training.”

As people age they tend to become more rational and mature; childish tantrums or pretending not to see difficulties become rarer. Yet when frustration or stress occurs, the anxiety generated in the unconscious is converted into behavior that abandons maturity and retreats to an earlier stage of life. This defense mechanism—warding off anxiety through anti-mature regression—is the regressive defense mechanism.

#### Controlling Anxiety: Using Release to Escape Torment

Faced with intense competition and rapid change, many people become anxious and suffer greatly, harming both mind and body. Finding ways to overcome anxiety is therefore essential.

Busy work acts like a furnace, heating the mind to a boil; tense living acts like a whip, constantly striking us and leaving us restless. We worry: What if I lose my job? What if I cannot pay the mortgage? Will I receive a pension? Will my partner leave me? Can my child get into a good school? Life is short, yet we harbor worries that span a thousand years. The sources of anxiety are endless, and the negative emotions they produce cling to us—how can we be happy? A German philosopher once said that no emotion torments us more than anxiety; it inflicts enormous psychological pain.

The Tang-dynasty monk Shenxiu wrote a verse: “The body is a bodhi tree, the mind a bright mirror stand. Polish it constantly; let no dust alight.” When Huineng saw it he replied with another verse: “Bodhi has no tree, the mirror no stand. Originally there is not a single thing—where can dust alight?” His verse perfectly captures the sudden-enlightenment spirit of Chan Buddhism. It expresses a transcendent attitude: the world is fundamentally empty; all phenomena are marked by emptiness. The mind is originally empty; there is no need to resist external temptations. Things pass through the mind without leaving a trace. Anxiety is the same. It is not caused by actual threat, and the degree of tension and fear it produces is out of proportion to reality. Anxiety is usually needless worry. To free ourselves completely from its torment we must maintain inner and outer calm.

We can use the following self-regulation methods to free ourselves from anxiety as soon as possible.

#### Common Forms of Bias

1. **Confirmation Bias**  
   Subjectively, if we support a certain viewpoint, we tend to seek out information that supports our original view while unconsciously ignoring information that might overturn it.  
   Confirmation bias acts like a filter in the brain, retaining what it deems correct and discarding the rest into the trash. Whether regarding a person, a movie, or a product, we easily fall into confirmation-bias thinking.  
   Confirmation itself is neither wrong nor unnecessary. The key point is that confirmation represents only part of the picture. If we rely solely on confirmation, comprehensive thinking becomes difficult and erroneous conclusions are likely. Yet when we examine phenomena from the angle of “disconfirmation,” thinking in reverse and raising questions, the final conclusion is often more reliable and closer to reality.

2. **Hindsight Bias**  
   When evaluating an event that has already occurred, we should analyze it based on factors known before the event. Instead, we are often unconsciously influenced by the outcome and assume the event was triggered by factors that could have been predicted. After making a mistake or a decision that was not optimal for us, we frequently feel regret and believe we could have done better; afterward we tend to attribute the result to factors that seem predictable.  
   If we wish to draw lessons from past errors, we should minimize the influence of known outcomes on our thinking and, ideally, forget those outcomes entirely.

3. **Anchoring Bias**  
   Anchoring bias refers to the bias formed when first impressions guide subsequent judgments. Psychologists have found that even when an initial question has no substantive meaning, it can still influence people’s judgments.

#### Psychology Corner

On the surface, perfectionism appears to be an excellent way of life, yet it is in fact a sugar-coated bullet. Many people are deceived by the illusion of meticulousness and responsibility it creates. Perfectionists often insist that if something is worth doing, it must be done perfectly; otherwise they do nothing at all. Once their efforts fail to yield the desired results, they become despondent.

Most feelings of panic, depression, and anger actually stem from people converting hoped-for goals into absolute, unchangeable demands and commands. Everything must unfold exactly as wished; when reality falls short, disappointment and distress arise.

USA Today once conducted a survey showing that being a true perfectionist would require far more than twenty-four hours a day: thirty minutes for fitness training, forty-five minutes for personal hygiene, two to four hours with family, forty-five minutes reading the newspaper, two to four hours watching television, one to two hours commuting, seven to ten hours working, and another one to two hours for meals, plus roughly eight hours of sleep. Additional time would still be needed for reading novels, listening to music, and attending social gatherings. In total, the journalists calculated that forty-two hours a day would be ideal.

A brief calculation therefore reveals that most perfectionist expectations are unrealistic. Their goals and demands are often so idealized that they cannot be realized. Under the perfectionist rule of “do it perfectly or not at all,” most of their time would be spent doing nothing. Hence, somewhat imperfect standards are actually important for us. When outcomes fall short of expectations, we should view them rationally and avoid setting expectations too high.

#### Psychology Corner

When feeling low, the following methods can help lift the mood:

1. Identify your shortcomings  
   When expectations are unmet, avoid complaining or feeling despondent. Instead, reflect on the reasons the expectation fell through and consider which of your abilities may be lacking—whether execution, expression, or interpersonal skills. Once shortcomings are identified, missed opportunities can be faced calmly and a clear direction for improvement emerges.

2. Adjust your work goals  
   After identifying shortcomings, determine whether disappointment stems from goals that were set too high. Immediately revise those goals, setting new ones based on actual circumstances. For example, if the original goal was to start a company within two years, consider extending the timeline to three or four years to allow breathing room.

3. Work steadily toward the goal  
   With more realistic goals in place, pursue them persistently and keep improving your abilities. Daily progress will follow, and emotions will remain stable. Because the goals are reasonable, the pressure they generate stays manageable, and the positive energy accumulated will dispel negative feelings.

4. Experience setbacks  
   Smooth sailing is never conducive to personal growth. Only after weathering storms can one see the rainbow. Setbacks build courage in the face of difficulty. Maintaining the right attitude toward setbacks allows continued maturation and the development of inner strength.

#### Case Two: Zhang Hongli and Professor Gong

Zhang Hongli was an art-major undergraduate studying piano.

Her instructor, Professor Gong, was in his forties, handsome and multitalented. Although married, he frequently engaged in improper sexual relationships with precocious female students.

Zhang Hongli became Professor Gong’s new target; in appearance, figure, and temperament she was the standout among that year’s freshmen. Professor Gong repeatedly took liberties during private lessons.

At first Zhang Hongli could not believe the outwardly respectable professor would actually harass her, but as his advances grew more overt she became increasingly frightened.

Finally, unable to endure it any longer, she fled the piano studio, found the campus police officer on duty, and reported everything in detail. Because of institutional suppression and a settlement reached with Zhang Hongli, the police did not file a case; the matter could have ended there.

Yet the now-disgraced Professor Gong could not let it go. Rumors and irreparable damage to his reputation fueled growing anger. Eventually, whenever he heard the story mentioned, he spread the counter-rumor: “Zhang Hongli seduced me. Every time she asked for private lessons she dressed provocatively and tried to sit on my lap…”

Professor Gong’s attack mechanism did not arise from unsatisfied sexual desire but from the frustration of his wish to “maintain a good reputation.” Zhang Hongli, as the obstacle to that wish, became his target.

Targets of attack mechanisms are usually both specific and arbitrary. The means of attack also vary widely; some involve direct physical violence.

#### Psychology Corner

In daily life one often encounters people who over-interpret ordinary remarks, take jokes as mockery, assume whispered conversations are about them, perceive friendly greetings as insincere, attribute minor setbacks to deliberate sabotage, and suspect even loved ones of disloyalty. They remain hyper-vigilant, treating everyone around them like suspects and sometimes doubting their partners or friends without cause.

Modern psychology indicates that pathological suspicion is a mental disorder belonging to paranoid personality defects. Such individuals often experienced harsh treatment or misfortune in childhood, leading to gradual emotional withdrawal and eventual distrust of everyone. They tend to be hypersensitive, suspicious of everything, narrow-minded, and self-important; they habitually assume the worst and feel that others are deliberately making things difficult. They may even imagine hidden meanings in a cough. Pathological suspicion leaves them trapped in awkward interpersonal situations—unable to get along with family at home or maintain harmonious relations with colleagues at work—resulting in chronically tense relationships. Prolonged anxiety and psychological tension deprive them of genuine love, family affection, and friendship.

#### The Universal Psychological Principle of Jealousy

The ancient saying “A tree that stands out in the forest will be felled by the wind; a bank that protrudes will be eroded by the current; a person of high conduct will be criticized by the many” reflects a widespread psychological principle: people readily feel jealousy toward those who are more successful, more outstanding, or more favored than themselves. This jealousy finds expression through resentment, exclusion, slander, defamation, false accusations, sabotage, conspiracy, or covert harm—indirectly satisfying the emotional impulse of jealousy and temporarily restoring psychological equilibrium.

Although the jealousy defense mechanism can relieve anxiety and restore balance, it often produces serious consequences. Because the satisfaction jealousy itself can generate is limited, those who still cannot regain equilibrium through the defense mechanism may redirect their destructive impulses back onto themselves when external outlets are blocked, potentially leading to mental breakdown or psychological distortion.

One restaurant owner, tormented day and night by jealousy after a new establishment across the street took his business, finally decided to poison the rival’s ingredients with rat poison during the night. His intention was merely to make diners ill and thereby damage the rival’s reputation, but he misjudged the dosage and killed several people. Police investigated, identified him as the perpetrator, and sentenced him to death.

#### Historical Case: Zheng Xiu and the Wei Beauty

During the Spring and Autumn period, King Huai of Chu (Xiong Huai) had a favored consort named Zheng Xiu. She was surpassingly beautiful and enjoyed the king’s exclusive favor.

Yet no flower blooms for a hundred days. After Zheng Xiu had monopolized the king’s affections for only a short time, the state of Wei presented Chu with a beauty whose looks surpassed even Zheng Xiu’s. The king transferred his favor to the Wei beauty and neglected Zheng Xiu.

Although jealousy burned within her, Zheng Xiu was clever. On one hand she repeatedly showed goodwill to the Wei beauty, letting her choose the finest fabrics and jewelry and often accompanying her on walks. On the other hand, she pretended to be helpful and told the Wei beauty, “His Majesty often says he likes you, but your nose is the one flaw. If you cover your nose whenever you see him, he will favor you even longer.”

The newly arrived Wei beauty never suspected a trick and followed the advice, covering her nose each time she met the king.

After some time the king noticed and asked Zheng Xiu the reason. At first she feigned ignorance, but when pressed she replied, “The new beauty has privately said that Your Majesty has a foul odor, so she must cover her nose in your presence.”

The king flew into a rage and ordered his attendants to cut off the Wei beauty’s nose and expel her from the palace.

Zheng Xiu’s methods were ruthless, yet their root lay in only two words: jealousy.

#### Overcoming Suspiciousness and Suppressing Subjective Assumptions

Suspicion and mistrust constitute a psychological disorder and an enemy of happiness; they harm others and trap the suspicious person in endless self-inflicted distress. Therefore it is best to stop suspecting, recognize the causes and harms of suspicion, and thoroughly overcome the habit.

Francis Bacon described suspicion thus: “It is a trap that confuses the mind, leading one to mistake friend for foe and thereby ruin others’ affairs.” Indeed, history abounds with tragedies born of suspicion. King Fuchai of Wu wrongly executed the loyal Wu Zixu because of suspicion; Othello wrongly killed his chaste wife for the same reason. Even the ancient Chinese stratagem of sowing discord exploits humanity’s tendency toward suspicion.

Suspicion and mistrust are psychological disorders that strain relationships, inflict needless emotional harm, and burden the suspicious person’s own mind. Severe suspiciousness can develop into paranoia—the condition seen in those who imagine others are plotting against them.

Feeling suspicious is a normal phenomenon; excessive worry is unnecessary. The important task is to overcome it before it spreads and causes greater damage. How, then, can one dispel suspiciousness in interpersonal interactions?

#### Psychology Corner

A psychologist once conducted an interesting experiment. He asked a group of participants, on the first Sunday of a given month, to write down every worry they anticipated for the coming seven days and drop the lists into a large “worry box.” On the third Sunday he checked each item with the participants. They discovered that 90 percent of the listed worries had never occurred.

The psychologist then asked the participants to place the remaining 10 percent back into the box and return in three weeks to review them. On opening day the participants were surprised to find that the remaining worries were no longer problems; they now possessed sufficient capacity to handle them.

Further research showed that, among the things most people worry about, 40 percent concern the past and 50 percent concern the future; 92 percent of the worries never materialize, and the remaining 8 percent are easily resolved by the worrier.

The experiment illustrates a simple truth: most of our troubles are needless anticipations; the things we worry about usually do not happen. Trouble itself is not frightening; what is truly frightening is remaining trapped in worry without realizing it and wasting precious time on events that will never occur.

#### Psychology Corner

Psychologists define anxiety as a state of intense apprehension and unease arising from the anticipation of a threatening event or situation. It manifests as mental hypersensitivity and high tension; in severe cases it may impair physiological and psychological functioning. Anxiety can be divided into four levels of intensity:

- **The first level is bodily tension.** People at this level feel unable to relax, appear tense, wear serious expressions, furrow their brows, and sigh frequently.
- **The second level involves strong autonomic nervous-system responses.** Because the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems are chronically overloaded, individuals sweat, feel dizzy, breathe rapidly, and experience tachycardia, alternating sensations of heat and cold, cold or hot extremities, stomach discomfort, frequent urination or defecation, and a lump-in-the-throat sensation.
- **The third level is unwarranted worry about the future.** People at this level constantly worry about career, promotion prospects, finances, health, and similar matters.
- **The fourth level is excessive vigilance.** People at this level remain as alert as sentries, reacting to every minor sound or movement.

#### Regression Phenomena in Hospitals

Hospitals frequently observe the following phenomenon:

Elderly patients who have been declared recovered sometimes refuse to leave, preferring to pay high hospitalization fees rather than depart.

Physicians describe such patients as particularly “difficult.” On one hand, continued hospitalization is medically unnecessary and the hospital is reluctant to keep them because beds are already scarce. On the other hand, these elderly individuals inexplicably refuse to leave, ignoring all persuasion from hospital staff and family.

Physicians are puzzled.

A physiological physician may remain puzzled, but a psychologist or psychiatrist would recognize the mindset: staying in the hospital is a classic regressive behavior.

After losing the strength of their prime years, older adults feel especially helpless. This sense of powerlessness makes them simultaneously wish to confront a dangerous world and feel incapable of doing so. The resulting psychological imbalance leads them to revert instinctively to childhood habits and seek refuge in a place that appears safe.

Confronted with the ultimate threats of aging and death, they feel even more powerless and therefore regard the hospital as a vast sanctuary in which they place enormous trust. This is the operating mechanism of the regressive behavior.

#### The Unknown Self

The final window is the “Unknown Self,” also called the “Potential Self.” The Unknown Self is closely linked to what we refer to as the subconscious; one could even say that the Unknown Self is the latent aspect of ourselves we usually discuss.

For any individual the Unknown Self constitutes an undeveloped, virgin territory. Latent abilities or traits, as well as talents that emerge only under specific circumstances, all belong to the Unknown Self.

We must explore and develop the Unknown Self more diligently. Only by better knowing, motivating, and understanding ourselves can we develop and transcend ourselves. Behavioral psychology plays the greatest role in this process, because the Unknown Self is typically expressed through unconscious actions. Mastering behavioral psychology therefore equips one with the skill to discern others’ Unknown Selves.

The four windows of the Johari Window exist within each of us. Recognizing these four windows offers the best method for knowing, analyzing, and improving ourselves. Combined with behavioral psychology, recognizing others’ four windows provides an important and far-reaching means of understanding and relating to them.

#### How to Reduce Cognitive Dissonance

In general, there are four methods that can be applied:

1. **Change a cognition**  
   If two cognitions contradict each other, one of them must be changed to align with the other. For example, if we normally see only white swans, we naturally assume all swans are white. When we encounter a black swan, we must revise our original cognition—that swans can also be black.

2. **Add a new cognition**  
   When two inconsistent cognitions produce dissonance, we can add a new cognition to restore balance. The excuses Old Wang invented for smoking clearly belong to this category.

3. **Alter the importance of a cognition**  
   By comparing the relative importance of two inconsistent cognitions and weighting one accordingly, dissonance can be reduced.

4. **Change behavior**
