   Because cognitive dissonance is closely linked to behavior, changing behavior can also ease the sense of imbalance. For most people, however, changing behavior is more difficult than changing attitude.



#### 1. Think Rationally Instead of Suspecting Without Cause

When you notice yourself suspecting someone or something, pause and ask yourself rationally why the suspicion exists and whether it is justified.

Suspicion is a form of negative self-suggestion: forming baseless conjectures about others in the absence of objective evidence. Under the influence of suspicion, people often trap themselves in closed loops of reasoning, starting from an assumed premise and returning to the same premise. Objectively, conclusions reached this way lack foundation and are frequently absurd.

Suspicion usually stems from a person’s own beliefs and habitual thought patterns. To overcome it, apply reasonable beliefs and thinking styles when interpreting everyday events. For instance, if you meet an acquaintance who does not greet you, do not immediately assume resentment; instead, remind yourself the person may not have seen you or had time to react. Rational thinking prevents or reduces suspicious feelings. The key is refusing to treat minor, non-principle matters as absolute.

#### Opening the Window to the Mind Through the Johari Window

Micro-expression keywords  
Every mind has a four-pane window. Only by opening all four panes can one truly see another person’s inner world; behavioral psychology supplies the key that opens that window.

We often say “know yourself and know your enemy, and you will win every battle.” Yet how many people actually achieve genuine mutual understanding?

Everyone believes they know themselves, but when faced with unexpected events or setbacks, we often react in uncharacteristic ways and realize we do not fully understand who we are.

Understanding oneself is not difficult once the right method and techniques are used.

The Johari Window is the ultimate technique for examining oneself and deeply understanding others.

Psychologists Luft and Ingham introduced the Johari Window model, dividing the mind into a four-pane window: the Open Self, the Blind Self, the Hidden Self, and the Unknown Self.

These four panes together form the window of the mind.



#### Psychology Mini-Lesson

Negative emotions arise from negative self-suggestions. What are some common negative psychological suggestions?

1. “I will definitely mess this up”  
   Some people avoid taking on tasks because they fear failure. They habitually evade opportunities and, even when prepared, retreat at the last moment. They constantly question themselves internally: “Am I really capable? What if I make a mistake?”

2. “I need help”  
   These individuals never trust themselves to complete tasks independently. Their weakness stems from self-distrust; they rely excessively on others and allow others to control situations. Because they repeatedly tell themselves “I can’t,” they end up as dependents of stronger people.

3. “My idea is definitely wrong”  
   These people constantly doubt their own views and hesitate to express their true thoughts, especially when asked for an opinion.



#### Psychology Mini-Lesson

To investigate the origins of self-blame, psychologists surveyed American college students. Participants were asked to recall and record an event that had brought great joy to someone else. The results showed that students’ differing self-views strongly influenced their narratives. Confident students described situations in which their own abilities created happiness for others, whereas less confident students focused on analyzing others’ needs and attending to others’ feelings. Confident individuals emphasized their own capabilities; less confident individuals emphasized altruism.

Thus, people lacking confidence often place others’ needs first while ignoring their own abilities and legitimate needs. When something goes wrong, they assume responsibility and blame themselves for failing to meet others’ expectations. Compared with people who have strong self-awareness, these individuals lack self-awareness and are seen as “nice guys,” yet they pay a high psychological price and are more prone to negative emotions.



#### An Example of Regressive Behavior

A joke circulating online tells of a young preschool teacher who drew an apple on the blackboard and asked the children, “What is this, children?”

“Butt,” the children answered in unison.

The teacher ran to the principal’s office in tears, claiming the children were mocking her.

“How outrageous!” the principal exclaimed and hurried to the classroom. “Why did you make your teacher cry? Who drew that butt on the board?”

The joke is merely amusing, yet the teacher’s reaction illustrates a specific concept in behavioral psychology: the regressive defense mechanism. A key feature of regressive behavior is that it is, to some degree, irrational—both because the behavior itself rejects rationality and because rational analysis struggles to explain its cause.



#### Hidden Self

The third pane is called the “Hidden Self,” also known as the “Private Self.” It consists of information we know about ourselves but others do not—personal secrets, flaws, past events, pain, desires, illnesses, and so on.

No one is entirely without privacy, so everyone possesses a Hidden Self. When the Hidden Self grows too large, the Open Self shrinks, creating a high wall between the mind and the outside world that blocks normal interaction.

People with an excessively large Hidden Self are often withdrawn, repressed, timid, vain, or insecure. They suppress themselves and make those around them feel suppressed as well. Therefore, we should confront the Hidden Self, explore ourselves, and face our true nature.



#### Psychology Mini-Lesson

American psychologists Richard Rahe and Thomas Holmes created a life-events inventory that converts the intensity of emotional change into numerical points to measure the relationship between daily events and emotional stress. Different events receive different point values.

When several events occur simultaneously, the total stress score is the sum of the individual scores. Their research found that 89 percent of people whose annual total exceeded 300 points fell into despair, and most of those individuals developed hypertension, gastric ulcers, migraines, or intestinal colic. Prolonged despair, pessimism, or sorrow also significantly raises the risk of cancer.



#### 4. Stop Comparing Yourself with Others

Frequent comparison with others is another source of anxiety. People often think, “I’m over thirty and still single, while my peers already have children,” or “My neighbor buys designer clothes; I can only afford street-market items—when will this end?” or “My colleagues keep getting promoted while I stay in place—it’s frustrating.” Those who constantly compare themselves become controlled by public opinion and others’ judgments, developing thoughts such as “Everyone else bought one, so I should too” or “They were promoted, so I should be promoted.” Once caught in this mindset, anxiety over perceived gaps is inevitable. Face the differences between yourself and others without constant comparison.



#### Psychology Mini-Lesson

1. **Jealousy is highly domain-specific**  
   Jealousy arises only when two or more people compete within the same domain. Multiple suitors of the same woman, candidates for the same position, classmates in the same class, or athletes in the same event are likely to feel jealous. People feel jealous only toward those in the same domain who outperform them; they do not feel jealous toward people outside their domain or toward those in the same domain who perform worse.

2. **Jealousy is a damaged sense of superiority**



#### 2. Recognize Your Own Strengths and Build Confidence

From a psychological perspective, insecurity often underlies suspicion, and insecurity frequently stems from lack of self-confidence. Everyone wants appreciation and cares about others’ opinions, especially those whose inner state fluctuates easily.

People prone to suspicion tend to harbor strong wariness and hostility toward others and refuse to trust them. The root cause is usually low self-confidence and a tendency toward inferiority. Inferiority breeds sensitivity, and sensitivity breeds suspicion. Therefore, overcoming suspicion requires believing in your own abilities and maintaining sufficient self-confidence.



#### Open Self

The upper-left pane is called the “Open Self,” also known as the “Public Self.” It comprises the parts of ourselves that can be revealed outwardly—appearance, gender, occupation, abilities, hometown, hobbies, achievements, and so on. These publicly shareable facts constitute the mind’s free-action zone and form the basic data for self-understanding and self-evaluation.

The size of each person’s Open Self varies according to the degree of psychological openness, the extent of social interaction, and the strength and breadth of personality expression. A popular actor, for example, has a much larger Open Self than an unknown factory worker.



#### 3. Establish Priorities

Having several tasks to handle at once can also trigger anxiety. In such situations, calmly assess the current state and set clear priorities. Tasks generally fall into four categories: important but not urgent, urgent but not important, neither important nor urgent, and both important and urgent. The recommended order is to handle important-and-urgent items first, then urgent-but-not-important items, then important-but-not-urgent items, and finally neither-important-nor-urgent items. Regardless of the plan, remember to focus on only one task at a time. Once priorities are clear, the mind stops juggling multiple concerns.



#### The Psychological Reaction of Jealousy

Jealousy is the psychological reaction that follows the loss of a sense of superiority. Only when a person possesses superiority and then sees it surpassed does jealousy arise. Without that sense of superiority, the reaction is merely inferiority or envy. A penniless beggar will never feel jealous of an emperor’s status, power, or wealth, because the beggar has never held personal superiority in those areas. Only ministers wielding real power or the emperor’s brothers and uncles who covet the throne possess the necessary sense of superiority and therefore experience jealousy.



#### 3. Use Communication to Overcome Suspicion

Some people are full of suspicion because they rarely communicate with others. Without communication, they cannot know what others are thinking and must rely on guesswork, allowing misunderstandings to enter. Opening up and exchanging views regularly reveals that many doubts are merely misunderstandings; once clarified, suspicion naturally disappears. Regular communication also allows the other person to notice your confused thoughts and help you sort them out.



#### Psychology Mini-Lesson

American psychologist Abraham Luchins tested the primacy effect by writing two descriptions of a boy named Jim. One portrayed him as warm and outgoing; the other portrayed him as cold and introverted.

Luchins combined the passages in different orders and asked four groups of participants to read them and judge what kind of person Jim was. The results demonstrated that the order of information strongly affects social cognition: information presented first exerts greater influence than information presented later.



#### 4. Reduce Horizontal Comparison and Increase Vertical Comparison

Comparison can be either horizontal or vertical. Horizontal comparison means measuring oneself against others. “There are always higher mountains and more talented people.” Even if you compare your strengths with someone else’s, victory is not guaranteed—let alone when you compare your weaknesses with their strengths. Instead of horizontal comparison, practice vertical comparison: measure your present self against your past self, note any progress, and identify long-term development. This growth-oriented mindset provides encouragement.



#### 5. Cultivate a Sense of Achievement

People prone to anxiety often lack a sense of achievement; they underestimate their abilities and exaggerate difficulties. When setbacks occur, anxiety and inferiority surface. Once these weaknesses are identified, address them directly rather than waiting for help. Achievement does not come only from major events; many small daily tasks can generate it. Set modest goals, complete them, and gradually accumulate confidence and the joy of success. Over time, a genuine sense of achievement will develop.



#### 1. Use Self-Suggestion to Strengthen Psychological Resilience

Self-suggestion, also called self-affirmation, is a powerful technique for regulating the mind. It can quickly shift a person’s attitude toward life and increase resilience. Common forms include using encouraging words or actions to motivate oneself. After seeing someone else’s remarkable achievement, for example, silently tell yourself, “I’m not doing badly either” or “With more effort, I could be just as outstanding.” Over time, the habit of blind comparison fades and psychological resilience grows.



#### Five Methods for Resolving Anxiety

Research shows that many anxiety-disorder patients follow a similar developmental path: long-suppressed emotional experiences or past psychological trauma linger in the subconscious, and anxiety symptoms have already manifested in other forms, yet the individual has not paid attention. Once anxiety is noticed, the underlying causes must be brought into conscious awareness so that targeted measures can be taken to reduce it.



#### Chapter 12: Defense Mechanisms—Seeing Through Psychological Weaknesses

Everyone possesses a unique set of defense mechanisms, also called displacement mechanisms. They keep us from losing control when angry, from total despair when depressed, and from becoming carried away when excited—functioning as a remarkable psychological “transformer.” Understanding another person’s defense mechanisms through their behavior helps us quickly grasp their character and weaknesses, enabling us to guard against or make use of them.



#### 2. Maintain a Calm Mindset

Anxiety can stem from time pressure. When tasks pile up because of tight deadlines, the resulting inner tension produces anxiety. In such moments, the worst response is impatience. Close your eyes, breathe deeply, and allow your mind to settle so that attention can focus on the task at hand. A calm mindset is essential for easing anxiety; therefore, approach everything with a lighter perspective.



#### Chapter 9: Emotions Cannot Escape the Prison of Thought

We commonly assume that negative emotions are caused by objective facts and therefore uncontrollable. In reality, negative emotions mainly originate from our thinking patterns. The situations we label as anxiety-provoking, annoying, or worrisome are rarely as severe as we imagine; our perception of their severity arises from flawed thinking. Changing the thinking pattern is often enough to eliminate the negative emotion.



#### 5. Discover Your Own Strengths

Many people feel they have nothing worth comparing with others, yet everyone possesses strengths. Only by identifying those strengths can we leverage advantages, compensate for weaknesses, and achieve greater success. Once strengths are recognized, display them boldly, create conditions to amplify them, and let them become stepping-stones for progress.

#### Chapter 5 Controlling Your Negative Emotions

Many factors around us affect our emotions, and the ability to control emotions determines our lives. People who are good at controlling negative emotions are confident, optimistic, and excellent, while those who are not good at controlling negative emotions are inferior, pessimistic, and mediocre. It can be said that only by controlling one’s negative emotions well can one firmly grasp one’s own life.

#### 3. Appropriate Venting

Jealousy is a very normal negative emotion. There is no need to hide feelings of jealousy or to suppress them in the heart for a long time. One can vent appropriately by telling relatives and friends about one’s dissatisfaction, thereby preventing jealousy from growing increasingly severe.

#### Regression Mechanism: The Older the Age, the Smaller You Live

The biggest drawback of the regression mechanism is that it can only temporarily prevent you from facing anxiety directly. The source of anxiety remains, so your anxiety will return to you shortly afterward. Therefore, do not rely excessively on this mechanism, as it ultimately brings no benefit.

#### 6. Perfecting Yourself

If a person understands that only by perfecting oneself can one gradually improve, they can shift their attention and turn jealousy into motivation for their own efforts. In this way, jealousy acquires positive significance.

#### 2. Objectively Evaluating Yourself

When one realizes that jealous emotions have arisen, one should calmly analyze one’s own strengths and weaknesses and actively adjust one’s awareness and behavior.

#### Attack Mechanism: Violent Catharsis of Self-Anxiety

Micro-expression keywords: The attack mechanism is the most direct method for relieving anxiety. When it does not produce consequences we cannot bear, employing this psychological mechanism to relieve anxiety is not infeasible. The mechanism itself is not frightening; what is frightening is the ultimate impact it produces.

For humans, the most essential source of happiness is the realization of self-desires. When such desires cannot be fulfilled, anxiety arises. When anxiety is generated or pending, people inflict direct violence, soft violence, or cold violence on those or those things that obstruct them. This method of resolving self-anxiety through violence constitutes the essence of aggressive behavior.

### Seeing Through Manipulation Patterns: No One Can Manipulate Me

#### The Liking Principle: Why People Love the House and the Crow

Micro-expression keywords: Liking Principle. This is a simple yet effective principle. People are always more willing to comply with requests from those they know and like, which is sometimes called the “one of us effect.” The key to its application lies in how to gain others’ favor and build friendships. To achieve this, you can enhance your physical attractiveness, identify and strengthen similarities with the other person, and increase contact with them.

Wang Le was a top performer in the sales department of a foreign company and the most popular person in the department. She was exceptionally skilled at dealing with clients. Whether they were old or young, male or female, she could win their favor in a very short time. As a result, her sales performance improved rapidly. In less than two years, she was promoted to assistant to the chief sales representative. Later, when the chief sales representative immigrated to Canada, he handed over most of his business to her. By her third year, her performance far exceeded everyone else in the department, making her the sales champion.

It was not unusual for such an outstanding person to face jealousy and exclusion from colleagues, yet Wang Le successfully avoided these issues and maintained excellent relationships with her coworkers. Everyone was willing to help her whenever she needed it. Once, a friend complained to her about the complexity of interpersonal relationships and the indifference of human feelings, asking, “How do you manage to win so much liking and help from others?” “Because I like them,” Wang Le replied. “I don’t believe you like everyone you deal with,” the friend persisted. “But I show that I like them—that’s enough.”

The once-famous magician Howard Thurston had a famous saying: “I sincerely love my audience!” This remark deeply embodies a psychological technique worth learning: “Liking begets liking.”

People have a strong tendency to like those who like them, even when their values and outlooks on life differ. American social psychologist Elliot Aronson once surveyed his friends: “Why do we like some companions more than others?” The answers varied, but one of the most typical was “Because those people like us in return.”

Think about it: in this world, who do you love most? Most people would probably answer “myself.” This shows that human nature is self-centered and somewhat narcissistic. Therefore, someone who likes you becomes someone you like. They may not be particularly attractive, intelligent, or socially prominent; it is simply because they like you that you like them back. This is what psychology calls the “law of mutual attraction.”

Why do we like those who like us? From a psychological perspective, there are four main reasons:

1. The other person’s liking allows us to experience pleasant emotions. Thinking of them reminds us of the joy we felt in their company, and seeing them puts us in a good mood.
2. The other person’s liking satisfies our need for respect. In human interactions, everyone hopes to be respected. When someone likes us, they usually express respect through their words and actions, which brings us comfort.
3. The other person’s liking gives us confidence. In real life, strictly speaking, no one is completely confident. Most people judge their own worth and adjust their goals by evaluating their achievements and attractiveness. Therefore, most people especially need affirmation from others. Someone’s liking is precisely that affirmation—who would not welcome it?
4. The other person’s liking creates a sense of shared values. We tend to think that if they like us, they accept certain aspects of our behavior, meaning they share similarities with us in some way. It is only natural that we like people who are similar to us.

Because of these four reasons, in social settings we can easily win others’ favor simply by showing that we like them. In daily life and work, to gain others’ goodwill more easily and quickly, we might as well show that we like them.

- If you are a salesperson facing a prospective client you have never met, show that you like them. This will make them like you and, in turn, like the product you are selling.
- If you are a new employee entering a company and meeting colleagues with different personalities, show that you like them. This will help them accept you in the shortest possible time.

Of course, this approach is not universally effective. Sometimes people encounter situations where they like someone who does not like them back, or dislike someone who likes them. In such cases, continue to show goodwill toward the person you like who does not like you, and respond with gratitude to the person you dislike who likes you. Over time, you will find that those who previously liked you like you even more, while those who previously disliked you gradually develop goodwill toward you. By showing that you like others in interpersonal interactions, your circle of friends will grow and your affairs will proceed more smoothly.

People always comply with requests from those they know and like; no one finds this strange. This also reflects the liking principle. However, the principle has at times been exploited by strangers in various ways to get us to comply with their requests. In life, those skilled at using human psychology can always establish common goals with us and work toward them together, creating the feeling that “we are working side by side for a shared objective; we are comrades in the same trench.” This reflects another psychological principle: contact and cooperation.

In May 2001, during a football match held in Accra, the capital of Ghana, after the African champions Hearts of Oak defeated Kotoko 2–1, Kotoko supporters were enraged. They destroyed seats in the stands and clashed with Hearts of Oak fans. When police realized the situation could cause irreversible damage, they fired tear gas at the fans. This triggered panic; people began to flee in all directions, leading to a stampede. The incident ultimately resulted in 150 deaths and nearly 20 injuries.

In intense sports competitions, it is understandable for athletes to become excited, but for sports fans to act so impulsively is somewhat astonishing. Sports activities do possess a magical and irresistible power; the relationship between the sport and its audience is entirely personal. Yet, influenced by the liking principle, fans’ self-image becomes tied to the team or athlete they support. If their favored team loses, they feel they have lost as well, making excitement or dejection understandable. A match is not merely a fixed performance or artistic display for our entertainment; it is something we bet on with our own egos. For this reason, fans feel intense love and gratitude toward their country’s victories and, conversely, develop aversion—even cruel behavior—toward athletes, coaches, or officials they hold responsible for defeat.

From this we can conclude that we always hope the team connected to us wins, thereby proving our own superiority. To whom do we wish to prove this? To ourselves and to others. According to the liking principle, if we succeed, our prestige in the public eye increases significantly. The examples above show that we deliberately manipulate the relationship between ourselves and winners or losers so that this connection becomes obvious, all to appear more prestigious in the eyes of those who can see it. By highlighting positive connections and concealing negative ones, we attempt to make onlookers think more highly of us and feel greater liking toward us.

Abroad, one of the most interesting phenomena is that police interrogators use psychological methods to obtain confessions from suspects. The most commonly employed technique is probably the “good cop, bad cop” approach.

For example, a suspect arrested for robbery is brought to the police station and informed of his right to remain silent before giving a statement. As soon as the suspect sits down, the so-called “bad cop” begins shouting insults. Throughout the interrogation, the “bad cop” continues to berate the suspect, sometimes even kicking the suspect’s chair. His eyes are full of contempt. If the suspect refuses to answer questions, the “bad cop” flies into a rage, angrily declaring that he will make sure the suspect spends the rest of his life in prison. He adds that, if possible, he will urge the prosecutor to seek the harshest charges.

Does the “good cop” simply allow the “bad cop” to do as he pleases? No. At first the “good cop” remains silent. Gradually he intervenes, initially urging the “bad cop” to calm down. The “bad cop” ignores him and continues expressing his displeasure with the suspect. Before long, the “good cop” begins speaking up for the suspect, but the “bad cop” remains unmoved and grows even angrier. At this point, the “good cop” starts addressing the suspect directly.

He calls the suspect by name and points out any details in the case that favor the suspect. If the suspect still refuses to cooperate, the “bad cop” resumes his insults and threats. The “good cop” then intervenes, takes out some money, and sends the “bad cop” out to buy coffee or another beverage.

Once the “bad cop” leaves, the “good cop” begins his real performance. He tells the suspect: “You see, for some reason my colleague simply doesn’t like you. He will do everything he can to find evidence against you—and he has the ability to do so, because we already have sufficient proof. The prosecutor will also punish uncooperative suspects severely. In that case, you could face five years in prison.

“I’m truly sorry. I really don’t want that to happen to you. If you admit to the robbery now, before he returns, I’ll take over the case. I promise to speak well of you to the prosecutor. If you cooperate, your sentence could be reduced from five years to two, or even one. It’s up to you. Tell me what happened. We’ll figure it out together and get through this.”

At this point, the suspect usually confesses all his crimes. The combined “good cop, bad cop” strategy has succeeded completely.

In fact, this is also an effective negotiation tactic. Upon closer examination, we see that the liking principle is at work behind the scenes: once the suspect develops goodwill toward the “good cop,” he becomes willing to follow the “good cop’s” instructions.

The method works for several reasons:

1. The “bad cop’s” threats create fear of imprisonment in the suspect, making the “good cop’s” words and actions seem especially reasonable by comparison.
2. Because the “good cop” speaks up for the suspect and even spends his own money to buy coffee, the principle of reciprocity creates psychological pressure on the suspect to return the favor.
3. The “good cop” always puts himself in the suspect’s position and keeps the suspect’s interests in mind. Even under normal circumstances, such a person would leave a good impression—let alone for a suspect in need of help. This savior figure is undoubtedly trustworthy, so revealing the truth to him feels entirely natural.

Whenever we face two people, we can always create a situation in which we like one and dislike the other. This gives the liked person an opportunity. This involves not only the liking principle but also the contrast principle.

#### The Principle of Reciprocity: You Are Good to Me, I Am Good to You

The principle of reciprocity means that when others treat us well, we treat them well in return and try to repay their favors in kind; otherwise, we feel a sense of indebtedness. Both giving and receiving favors carry a sense of obligation, and repaying or reciprocating is an even stronger duty that cannot be shirked.

“What’s going on? The inspection team arrives tomorrow, and no one told me in advance?” The bureau chief stormed into the office director’s workspace after taking a call from headquarters.

“I, I, I put the notice…” The office director tried to explain, but the chief’s expression cut him off.

“Look at this—how are we supposed to handle it? Nothing’s been prepared!”

“I’m sorry, Chief. It was my oversight. I’ll get everything ready right away.”

In fact, the responsibility did not lie with the office director. As soon as he received the inspection notice from higher authorities, he immediately delivered it to the chief’s office. At the time, the chief was on the phone and signaled with his eyes for the director to leave the notice on the desk.

“Maybe the chief forgot about it as soon as I left,” the office director thought, but he said nothing.

Instead, he rushed back to the chief’s office, retrieved the notice, and worked through the night—making calls and chasing numbers—to prepare all the required materials before the inspection team arrived. The inspection passed smoothly.

The office director breathed a sigh of relief, and so did the chief, who then decided to groom the director for advancement. The chief’s decision was not solely because the director showed responsibility and courage; a more important reason was the “reciprocity mindset” the chief had developed toward him.

The subordinate had taken the blame and endured public criticism on the chief’s behalf. Although the chief preserved his authority and face, he felt psychologically unbalanced and believed he owed his subordinate a favor that needed to be repaid at the first opportunity.

Psychologically, most people experience this reciprocity mindset: after receiving a benefit from someone, they want to return the favor—by helping in return, giving a gift, or treating the person to a meal.

An automobile salesperson once pulled out a pure white handkerchief while showing a car, spread it in front of the customer’s old vehicle that was already slated for replacement, and politely said, “Let me check your car for you.” He then crawled underneath. Moments later, he emerged, patting the now-dirty handkerchief, and said, “Everything looks fine.” Seeing the soiled handkerchief, the customer felt moved and grateful for the salesperson’s attentiveness. Although he had not planned to buy a new car immediately, the salesperson’s service and dedication convinced him the purchase would be worthwhile, so he decided on the spot to trade in his vehicle. This salesperson repeatedly used the technique—letting a handkerchief get dirty for the customer’s sake—to generate gratitude and close sales, significantly boosting his personal performance.

A psychology professor once conducted an experiment: he randomly selected people from a group of strangers and mailed them Christmas cards. Most recipients sent cards back. Those who replied never bothered to find out who the unfamiliar professor was. Their reason for reciprocating was simple: they could not owe anyone a favor, even if that “anyone” was a stranger.

During World War I, certain German special forces units were tasked with capturing prisoners behind enemy lines for interrogation. One soldier had succeeded at this mission many times. On this occasion he slipped through no-man’s-land and entered an enemy trench. A lone soldier was eating, completely unguarded, and was quickly disarmed. Still holding a piece of bread, the soldier instinctively offered some to the German. Startled by the unexpected gesture, the German soldier did not take the man prisoner; instead, he returned alone, knowing his commander would be furious. The reason was that the bread triggered his reciprocity mindset—he felt he had received a favor and must repay it. At that moment, the only repayment he could offer was to leave the enemy soldier free.

Consider this: on a battlefield where life and death hang in the balance, a small piece of bread can save an enemy’s life. In the workplace, can we not use small favors to build good relationships with superiors, colleagues, or subordinates? The answer is yes.

The principle of reciprocity holds that we should repay others in kind for what they have done for us. If someone gives us a birthday gift, we feel obliged to buy one for them on their birthday. Because of this principle, we treat returning a received favor as a duty that will arise at some future time; thus “returning the favor” becomes synonymous with expressing gratitude.

At an airport, a traveler was resting when a fundraiser approached and suddenly pressed a rose into his hand. The traveler instinctively accepted it, then immediately realized what had happened and tried to return the flower. The fundraiser refused and asked for a donation. The traveler tried again to hand the rose back, but the fundraiser again declined. A conflicted expression appeared on the traveler’s face. He could have kept the rose and walked away without donating, yet some force pulled him back as he began to turn. After a moment’s hesitation he turned again, still unable to leave. Finally he donated two yuan. Afterward he felt relieved, but he did not keep the rose; he tossed it into a trash bin.

Many people inwardly reject the rose yet feel compelled to accept it, only to discard it later. As a result, trash bins fill with roses, but the original givers simply collect the “trash” and reuse the flowers until they are no longer usable. This is the essence of the reciprocity principle: even a gift so unwelcome that the recipient discards it at the first opportunity can still exert influence during the reciprocity process.

The power of the principle lies in the fact that even a stranger—whether likable or not—who first offers a small benefit and then makes a request greatly increases the chance that the request will be granted. Some people create a sense of indebtedness simply by doing an unsolicited favor.

Careful consideration shows that the principle only requires us to repay favors we have received; it does not obligate us to repay favors we actively solicited. For example, a disabled-veterans organization found that including a small gift (such as personalized address labels with adhesive backs) in a fundraising letter raised the donation rate from 18 percent to 35 percent. Of course, if we actively request a benefit, the sense of obligation becomes even stronger—even when the benefit was unsolicited.

Why do people develop this mindset? Its social function provides the answer. The principle of reciprocity evolved to facilitate mutual exchange by removing the fear of loss when one party initiates a relationship. Once this function is served, an unsolicited benefit reliably produces indebtedness in the recipient. Most people share the underlying belief that giving is a duty, receiving is a duty, and repaying is an even greater duty.

In daily life, the duty to repay not only weakens our power to choose who gives us favors but transfers that power to others. Because the two parties are rarely equal, the real choice rests with the giver, who decides both the form of the initial favor and the form of repayment. Consequently, even an unsolicited benefit, once accepted, creates a sense of indebtedness.

In fact, even an unwanted gift can produce this feeling. The pressure of reciprocity forces us to repay the giver, regardless of whether we wanted the item. Yet we feel no corresponding pressure to purchase goods we do not actually need.

#### The Principle of Conformity: The Feeling of Being Isolated Is Unpleasant

**Micro-expression Keywords**  
Conformity, also called the herd mentality, is the tendency to change one’s behavior and beliefs to meet the expectations of a group. Many people do what they see others doing, echo what others say, and always try to follow the crowd—this is conformity.

A man walked into a hospital waiting room and was astonished to see everyone sitting in their underwear. Some drank coffee, some smoked, some read newspapers, and some chatted—all in their underwear.

At first he was surprised, but he soon concluded that these people must know something he did not. Twenty seconds later he removed his outer clothes, sat down in his underwear, and waited for the doctor.

The scene comes from American writer Alan Funt’s 1960s television script *Candid Camera*.

Is the story funny? You probably think so. Yet similar laughable situations occur in everyday life.

On a street corner, someone sees a long line and assumes a rare opportunity has appeared, so he hurries to join it. The line grows until it stretches into the street. Only when the line rounds the corner does he realize everyone is waiting for the public toilet.

Most people share this psychological tendency: seeing a line makes them want to join it; seeing a crowd makes them want to approach. In psychology this tendency is called conformity, or the herd mentality—a readiness to alter one’s behavior and beliefs to fit the demands of a group.

Conformity can appear as adopting the dominant behavior in a temporary situation or as long-term acceptance of prevailing ideas and practices. Almost everyone exhibits it.

A young man sees everyone on the street wearing bell-bottom trousers and buys a pair for himself, even though he is slight. A professional woman notices that all her office colleagues have permed hair and decides to get a perm, even though her hair is thick and coarse. A primary-school child sees that every other child has a Snoopy toy and wants one, even though his own toys already fill his room.

We are no exception. When shopping in a commercial district where neighboring stores sell nearly identical goods, some shops are packed while others are empty. Which shop do you usually enter? The one with the crowd, of course.

On television we constantly hear canned laughter—during variety shows, reality programs, crosstalk, skits, even dramas and films. The same holds for radio. If you listen to programs that tell jokes or funny stories, you will notice that laughter or applause follows every punch line, and it always sounds the same. These are recorded laughs.

You may wonder whether this is necessary. Yet the practice persists despite criticism. Humans naturally prefer genuine interaction and authentic responses. People enjoy sincere laughter, so many viewers reject canned laughter in skits and sitcoms, calling it stupid, fake, and shallow.

If audiences dislike it, why do producers continue using it? Because the minority who object does not represent the majority. Producers understand audience preferences and have seen research showing that canned laughter makes viewers laugh more often and longer, increases perceived humor, and makes even weak jokes or unfunny programs more popular.

Adding canned laughter therefore boosts both the apparent humor of a program and the audience’s reaction. The effect is strongest for low-quality content. Producers follow their own logic and interests; if they followed the audience’s logic, that would be surprising. They are not deceiving us—everyone can distinguish recorded laughter from real laughter—yet we are still influenced and may form mistaken judgments.

This reflects the principle of conformity: when judging right and wrong, we usually look first at what others think, especially when deciding on correct behavior. If we see others doing something, we assume it is right. The actions and opinions of those around us shape our own conduct.

The conclusion is reasonable. We tend to regard the majority view as correct because following collective experience reduces mistakes—this is the advantage of social proof. It offers a shortcut for thinking and acting, yet it also makes us vulnerable to manipulation by opportunists. When we automatically respond to social proof, we can be misled by incomplete or false consensus, and problems arise.

Our mistake is not using others’ laughter to judge humor; it is allowing fake laughter to produce an erroneous judgment even though the recording has nothing to do with actual humor.

As ordinary viewers we have grown accustomed to treating others’ reactions as indicators of whether a program is funny, so we can be misled by a sound rather than by facts. Genuine audience laughter can make us laugh along; producers exploit our automatic response to even false consensus.

Merchants of all sizes are perhaps the most skilled at turning this psychology to profit.

In the late 1970s, Japan’s Sony Corporation produced the Walkman, a portable cassette player. To open the market, Sony adopted a novel marketing approach. At the time, English-study fever was sweeping Japanese schools, and every student was required to have a tape recorder. Sony sent ten young employees to walk back and forth in front of school gates carrying Walkmans, playing music at high volume and acting as though they were enjoying themselves.

Students noticed and asked where the devices could be bought. Within days, Sony Walkmans appeared throughout Japanese primary, middle, and high schools. Sony’s advertising campaign was highly efficient: instead of addressing the general public, the company targeted a specific group of students and used their conformity to spark a buying wave.

This psychological tactic is not limited to any one group. Anyone can apply it.

If you plan to open a small shop, invite relatives and friends to mill about inside and outside on opening day, pretending to shop. You need not worry about an empty store; the crowd will attract real customers.

If you are organizing a meeting and fear awkward silence, arrange in advance for several people to ask prepared questions. Once the atmosphere becomes lively, others who would otherwise stay quiet may join in.

If you are chairing a company meeting to discuss a controversial reform and expect most participants to remain silent, speak privately beforehand with a few colleagues and ask them to speak first. Their initiative can prompt others to express opinions as well.

#### Authority Principle: Why People Blindly Follow Others

The powerful psychological pressure formed by social hierarchies has conditioned people who have long obeyed authority to follow orders, suppressing their natural instincts to the point that they would commit murder without hesitation. In daily life, blindly following authority can lead to mistakes.

In 1961, a newspaper in New Haven, Connecticut, ran this advertisement one day:

> "Yale University seeks volunteers for a study on memory and learning methods. Any healthy adult male aged 20–55 who is not a current high school or college student may apply. Participants will receive $4 per hour."

Yale University! Four dollars per hour! Soon, 15 workers, 16 salespeople, and 9 professionals signed up with their own motives.

These 40 applicants had no idea they would become subjects in a psychology experiment designed by 27-year-old Yale psychology assistant professor Stanley Milgram. The recruitment ad was a ruse, a small scheme that leveraged Yale’s prestige and high pay. It was a scheme because Milgram’s experiment proved shocking; in 2005, Britain’s Focus magazine listed it among the ten experiments that shook the world.

The experiment sparked enormous controversy. In response, the United States issued strict guidelines for human psychology experiments in 1975 and, over subsequent decades, blocked all psychologists who attempted to replicate it. Why did this happen? Let us begin with the experiment itself.

The experiment aimed to study whether ordinary people would carry out instructions that violated moral standards. In addition to recruiting the 40 subjects, Milgram hired two qualified “actors.” One played the role of a stern, meticulous authority figure who would issue various experimental commands to the subjects. The other played a student required to perform associative memory tasks and also served as the recipient of electric shocks.

During the experiment, the meticulous “authority figure” instructed participants to administer shocks to the student playing the “recipient” and told them that the higher the shock intensity, the greater the recipient’s pain. The participants began delivering shocks, and screams from the recipient followed—simulated, of course.

The recipient began protesting and demanding that the experiment stop. The participant administering the shocks then asked the “authority figure” whether to continue. The authority figure replied, “Yes, continue.” Through the behavior of these 40 participants, Milgram discovered that two-thirds continued to follow orders without regard for the screams. Most disturbingly, when the recipient fell silent, some participants still carried out the “absurd” commands issued by the authority figure.

You may find this psychological experiment cruel, yet Milgram’s obedience-to-authority experiment revealed an even crueler fact—one that is frightening because it deepens our understanding of human nature. Perhaps you never imagined that a mentally normal person would inflict severe punishment on an innocent individual simply by obeying the orders of a so-called authority figure.

This psychological phenomenon arises because the person administering the shocks shifts responsibility onto the authority figure. This mirrors the defense offered by soldiers who committed atrocities against civilians in World War II concentration camps and massacres when they stood before military tribunals: “We bear no responsibility for those civilian deaths because we were merely following orders from superiors.”

In addition to diffused responsibility, another factor is the inhibitory effect that forms psychologically and morally in individuals at the bottom of the “authority gradient.” In other words, the powerful psychological pressure created by social hierarchies conditions people who have long obeyed authority to follow commands, suppressing their natural instincts to the point that they would commit murder without hesitation.

According to statistics from the aviation industry, in 20 percent of fatal crashes, the co-pilot’s reluctance to point out the captain’s erroneous judgment was a major contributing factor. These co-pilots would rather sacrifice their own lives, those of the passengers, and those of their colleagues than challenge the captain’s authority. This is a startling finding.

On December 1, 1993, a Northwest Airlines flight to Hibbing, Minnesota, suffered a major accident in which no one on board survived. Post-incident analysis of the cockpit voice recorder showed that the co-pilot noticed the aircraft was too high during landing but did not immediately correct the captain. Instead, he cautiously attempted to alert the captain: “Captain, are you planning to maintain this altitude?” Ultimately, the aircraft’s excessive descent angle caused it to miss the runway completely. In the moments before the crash, the co-pilot continued to answer the captain’s questions with deference. It was truly a tragedy.

What is authority? Authority refers to the person or thing with the highest status within a given domain. Authority indicates only status and does not prove absolute correctness; authority and correctness are two separate concepts. Blindly trusting and obeying authority can lead to mistakes. Recognizing the dangers of the psychological tendency to obey authority blindly, we must view every so-called authority figure rationally. We must not blindly follow their instructions. We must maintain our own thinking and never obey without question. Whenever we encounter authority, we should first ask ourselves: Why should I obey you unquestioningly?

#### Commitment Principle: Why People Keep Their Promises

Everyone tends to keep their promises. A person whose words and actions are inconsistent is seen as confused, hypocritical, or even mentally unstable. Conversely, high consistency between words and actions is usually associated with strong character and superior intellect, reflecting a person’s logic, stability, and honesty.

A study by two Canadian psychologists revealed a curious psychological pattern among racetrack bettors: once a bettor places a wager, confidence in the chosen horse immediately rises. The actual probability of that horse winning has not changed at all; it is still the same horse, the same track, and the same venue.

Once we make a decision or take a position, we face pressure from both internal and external sources that forces our words and actions to remain consistent with it. This is called the commitment-consistency principle.

Never underestimate the power of commitment. The vast majority of people, once they have made a statement, will continue to act in accordance with that statement. This results from the combined effect of external and internal pressures: external public opinion discourages becoming a traitor, while the internal constraints of the “self” and “superego” make people attach great importance to their commitments.

In our culture, a high degree of consistency between words and actions is widely praised—and rightly so. Most of the time, persisting consistently in what we do leads to good results. Without consistency, life would be difficult and chaotic.

Having learned the effectiveness of the commitment-consistency principle, we might consider whether this psychological dynamic can be applied in daily life.

I remember living in a compound-like neighborhood as a child, where children from several courtyards played together. When I was ten, my father bought me a soccer ball. This novelty naturally made me the new center of attention among the children, and even kids from distant courtyards came to play with me.

In truth, I preferred the distant courtyards because they had more pretty girls, whereas our courtyards had only boys. My act of “betrayal” naturally caused dissatisfaction. One day, when the children from the distant courtyards were away and I had no one to play with, I went to find playmates in the nearby courtyards, only to be rejected. They declared in unison: “We won’t play with you unless you stop betraying us from now on.”

Not betraying them naturally meant playing only with them. I was unwilling, but with no one else available to kick the ball with, I vaguely agreed. Afterward, whenever I prepared to seek out children from other courtyards, my own courtyard playmates would bring up the matter to pressure me. Out of concern for face, I had to abandon any thought of “betrayal.”

Gradually, I found myself automatically distancing myself from the other children. Even after I started school, I remained closer to these childhood playmates than to my classmates. This, I believe, illustrates an application of the commitment-consistency principle: whether through coercion or inducement, first get the other party to agree to your terms, and then they will gradually and automatically adhere to those terms.

The commitment-consistency principle also offers advantages in retail. The experienced computer assemblers I have met are skilled at managing the rhythm and sequence of their speech. They do not immediately recommend the models that would earn them the highest profit. Instead, they first ask in detail what you intend to use the computer for, appearing genuinely concerned about your purpose.

Next, they describe a configuration that, within their framing, seems tailor-made for you. At the moment you begin to feel this way, they suddenly ask, “How about it? This machine suits you perfectly, doesn’t it?”

At that point, you cannot help but nod. The moment you answer “yes,” you are caught. You will find yourself thinking, “This really is a machine that fits me well.” Thereafter, no matter how many drawbacks the assembler mentions, you may find yourself defending the machine.

Therefore, a wise person must understand that assembling a computer is like betting on a horse race: do not place your bet lightly.

“Foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds.” This is a famous remark by Ralph Waldo Emerson. He meant that while consistency is generally good and even essential, we must also avoid foolish rigidity. We must guard against unthinking, automatic consistency because some people seek to exploit it for gain.

Thus, when we find ourselves maintaining consistency without thinking, we should ask ourselves whether that consistency is truly rational and whether other, more suitable choices exist.

Of course, when we want someone to do something, we can apply the consistency principle: if we can elicit a commitment from the other party, we have set the stage for them to automatically follow through on that prior commitment without further thought.

Written commitments are even better; they serve as an important psychological mechanism to prevent the other party from breaching a contract. They can genuinely change a person, partly because they are easily made public. Public commitments often carry lasting force. Simply having people write down their commitments produces remarkable results: they actually follow through on what they have written.

#### Second, the Desire to Possess Contested Things Is Almost Human Instinct

Shoppers who rush to buy during large-scale clearance sales or major price reductions are almost involuntarily swept along. Infected by the frenzied crowd, they push forward without regard for themselves, joining the scramble and even tossing items they would normally ignore into their shopping bags. This differs little from a herd of animals fighting over food in the wild.

Anglers exploit this psychology. They first cast bait into the water, drawing a school of fish into a frenzied rush. Once the entire area is covered by fish with open mouths competing for food, the anglers throw in hooks without bait. The fish, nearly mad with fear that other fish will snatch their food, bite even the bare metal hooks. In this way, the anglers easily catch large numbers of fish.

Merchants who create an atmosphere of frantic competition to lure customers employ a tactic similar to that of anglers. Merchants holding big sales also publicize heavily, claiming they are conducting tearful clearances, loss-making “jumping off the building” sales, or “crocodile bleeding” discounts. Whatever form the “bait” takes, once it works, it draws a crowd competing for it. Amid the scramble, customers become agitated and anxious under the influence of the scene, completely losing self-control. They forget what they actually need and blindly fight for whatever is being contested, even snatching items from others’ hands. In the end, customers who return home laden with packages often wonder inwardly: What came over me?

When something becomes scarce, not only do we want it more, but when we must compete to obtain it, our desire intensifies. A rational person should determine what they truly need before deciding to purchase. An irrational person may be swayed by advertising campaigns or other information into consuming things they could have done without.

Competition can be a psychological trap set by merchants. Conversely, you can create the illusion of competition to pressure or coerce the other party.

For example, in a newly built residential complex with only one barbershop, the owner may exploit a “sole provider” mentality to raise prices for greater profit rather than improving service quality to attract more customers. In such cases, even if residents repeatedly complain about high prices, the barbershop is unlikely to lower them because it has you cornered—there is no alternative.

If one day a second barbershop opens in the complex, the first now faces competition. If the competitor offers lower prices or better service, the first shop will lose customers. To prevent this, the original barbershop will proactively improve service or reduce prices.

Thus, the best way to make an opposing party yield is to make them believe they are not your only option.

This method is widely applied in real life:

- A young man courts a reserved, aloof young woman. After much effort he grows close to her, yet she remains noncommittal. One day he tells her that someone has introduced him to another girl whose conditions are excellent and that his family insists he meet her; he does not know what to do. Upon hearing this, the woman immediately changes her attitude, and the relationship rapidly warms.
- A project manager develops a project that generates substantial profit for the company. Expecting the boss to proactively raise his salary, he receives no response. He then tells the boss that a larger company is recruiting him for a higher position with greater pay and that he plans to start after the New Year. The boss becomes alarmed, immediately grants a raise, and promises a promotion once an opportunity arises.
- During stalled negotiations, an enterprise’s negotiator has his secretary knock and enter, announcing an urgent phone call. The negotiator appears flustered and leaves “confidential materials” on the table. The other side secretly examines the materials and discovers they are “quotations” from other competitors. When the negotiator returns, the opposing party’s attitude undergoes a 180-degree reversal and makes major concessions. An agreement is soon reached. In reality, the “confidential materials” were carefully fabricated by the negotiator.

#### Manipulation Technique: Traumatic One-Time Learning

When controlling the manipulated party, manipulators frequently employ a fifth technique called traumatic one-time learning.

When Ahua first met Zhang Li, she thought he was a nice, polite man. After several months of contact, the two people of similar background discussed marriage.

Everything proceeded as Ahua had expected until the day they went to buy a wedding bed. Until then, Ahua had made all household decisions, large and small. Although the heavy responsibilities left her somewhat weary, the joy of the approaching wedding made them bearable.

Inside the furniture store, Ahua spotted a stylish round bed priced at 18,000 yuan. Although expensive, she liked its appearance and color, so she habitually took out her bank card to pay without consulting Zhang Li.

“Wait,” Zhang Li’s voice, tinged with anger, came from behind her. “Do you have to buy this bed?”

“What’s wrong?” Ahua had grown accustomed to making decisions alone, and Zhang Li had never voiced an opinion. This situation surprised her.

“I don’t like round beds,” Zhang Li snapped, stiff-necked.

“But don’t you think the beds over there look too plain? Round beds are popular lately,” Ahua replied, not yet sensing anything unusual and assuming he was simply being petulant. She tried to persuade him.

“I said no, so no!”

What followed left Ahua stunned. She had never seen Zhang Li so angry. Even inside the furniture store, he made no effort to control his rage. Eyes wide, he grabbed her arm roughly: “Buy that one!”

“But that one is so ugly…”

Ahua’s protest was drowned out by Zhang Li’s stormy roar: “I said buy that one, so buy that one, or the wedding is off! From beginning to end, everything has to be your way, everything has to be what you like. Where is my opinion? I am the head of the household—where do you put my position…”

This hysterical outburst left Ahua frozen. In tears, she purchased the bed Zhang Li had pointed to. Even the store staff were stunned by the couple’s unusual way of shopping.

From that day on, the dynamic between Ahua and Zhang Li reversed completely. All household matters became Zhang Li’s decisions. Whenever Ahua tried to offer an opinion, Zhang Li needed only to glare, and she would recall the scene in the furniture store. She never dared to speak up again.

The relationship between Ahua and Zhang Li was less that of an engaged couple than that of a manipulated party and a manipulator. The manipulator, Zhang Li, used traumatic one-time learning to intimidate Ahua emotionally, firmly controlling her so that she dared not resist or disobey.

#### Pigeon Experiment

Regarding this point, when conducting experiments, psychologists did not choose white mice again but instead selected two pigeons:

**Pigeon A** was placed in a cage and went an entire day without food. Driven by hunger, Pigeon A pecked around the cage. Whenever it pecked the lever specially placed inside, the psychologists would add a bit of food to the feed trough, and Pigeon A quickly ate it up.

The second time it pecked the lever, it may still have been by chance, but soon afterward Pigeon A discovered that every time it pecked the lever, some delicious food would appear in the feed trough. Before long, Pigeon A formed a habit: as soon as it felt hungry, it would peck the lever.

Next, the psychologists turned their attention to **Pigeon B**, which had been placed in the cage.

Pigeon B’s initial situation was the same as Pigeon A’s. The psychologists trained it through ten lever-pecking sessions. Once Pigeon B had just formed the habit of pecking the lever, the psychologists changed the reward strategy. Not every lever peck by Pigeon B received a reward; rewards became irregular. Sometimes Pigeon B received a reward after two pecks, while at other times it received one only after more than ten pecks.

After both pigeons had formed their habits, the psychologists stopped rewarding them entirely. In other words, no matter how they pecked the lever, they could no longer obtain food.

The psychologists took out a stopwatch and recorded how long each pigeon persisted. Pigeon A continued for only a short time. After a few pecks its rate slowed noticeably, and it soon realized the reward had been completely withdrawn. Within minutes it abandoned the pointless behavior.

Pigeon B, however, kept pecking the lever until it was physically exhausted.

Throughout the process, Pigeon A clearly received more food than Pigeon B, yet it persisted for less time. Why?

In behavioral psychology this phenomenon is called **intermittent reinforcement**, also known as partial reinforcement. Unlike continuous positive or negative reinforcement, this process applies the two types of reinforcement intermittently and irregularly. The intermittency can create an addictive sensation in the subject. Like Pigeon B in the experiment, because its initial rewards were sporadic and unpredictable, it could never determine whether a reward would follow its action. Consequently, even when no reward appeared, it continued to fantasize about one that might come and grew more dependent on the lever. Pigeon A, which had always received consistent positive reinforcement, quickly and decisively abandoned the lever once the reward disappeared.

#### Example of Xiao Jin and Xiao Nan

Xiao Jin and Xiao Nan worked as salespeople at an appliance store. Their daily job was to mind the shop and pitch products whenever customers arrived.

The two were originally equal colleagues, but because Xiao Jin had more seniority and was very familiar with after-sales service and reports, she would occasionally “bully” the newcomer Xiao Nan.

“I want fried rice from the place on the corner.” Every noon Xiao Jin would send Xiao Nan to buy lunch, and most of the time she would claim she had no change and give her no money.

Unable to tolerate it any longer, Xiao Nan finally retorted, “Why is it always me? Can’t you go yourself?”

“Myself?” Xiao Nan’s resistance stunned Xiao Jin. After a long pause she gave a cold laugh. “Fine. From now on I’ll go myself. But without a proper lunch break, I probably won’t have the energy to handle difficult customers in the afternoon. After this, you’ll be responsible for closing any deals you make yourself.”

“Wait… wait a minute.” At the thought of those intimidating customers, Xiao Nan’s resolve collapsed. Because she was unfamiliar with the work, every customer scolded her until she was dizzy and unsure how to respond. In recent days Xiao Jin had indeed solved quite a few problems for her.

If she refused to buy lunch for Xiao Jin, the next time such a situation arose Xiao Jin would certainly refuse to help. The thought made Xiao Nan panic. She hurried after Xiao Jin, grabbed her arm, and said with a forced smile, “Sister Jin, I wasn’t feeling well earlier, so my tone was a bit sharp. Please don’t hold it against me. You want fried rice, right? I’ll go buy it and add two eggs for you, okay?”

Watching Xiao Nan’s retreating figure, Xiao Jin smiled with satisfaction.

The relationship between Xiao Jin and Xiao Nan was clearly one of manipulation. Xiao Jin acted as the manipulator and Xiao Nan as the manipulated. The manipulator controlled Xiao Nan’s obedience by threatening to withhold business assistance if she failed to follow orders.

While punishment may be less effective than positive or negative reinforcement for controlling behavior, its key value lies in its deterrent effect. Under this effect the manipulated party spontaneously performs actions to please the manipulator, making it highly effective for large-scale, widespread manipulation. To achieve better results, punishment is usually combined with other manipulation methods.

#### Story of Xiao Bai and Mike

When Xiao Bai first joined the company, the endless rules and regulations posted on the office wall made his head spin. He had already heard that the CEO of his department was difficult to please, but he had not expected the department’s own rules to far exceed the company’s.

“Good morning. You must be the new hire. I’m your supervisor, Mike Chen. You can call me Mike.” The sharp-looking supervisor extended his hand with a stern expression. Xiao Bai quickly shook it.

“Even though you’re new, you must follow company rules,” Mike said, immediately giving Xiao Bai a warning. “In addition, in our department I don’t want to see subordinates making childish mistakes, so we have more rules than other departments. I’ve already marked the points that require attention, so you’d better memorize them.”

“Understood, understood,” Xiao Bai replied hastily, though inwardly he was unconvinced.

Seeming to read Xiao Bai’s thoughts, Mike’s gaze sharpened. “I’m giving you three days. During those three days you don’t need to do anything else—just memorize the rules on the wall. After three days, come to my office for a test.”

What kind of supervisor had he been assigned? Xiao Bai grumbled inwardly but did not dare disobey.

The three days passed quickly, and Xiao Bai had memorized the wall of rules thoroughly. Afterward he settled into his work routine. What he did not notice, however, was that the three days of memorization were not as useless as he had thought. Whenever he felt like slacking off or cutting corners on a plan, the relevant clause would surface in his mind.

Doing so might save time, but if Mike found out, given his character he would certainly enforce the rules strictly. That would mean trouble.

With this thought, Xiao Bai no longer dared to slack off at work.

Mike’s wall of “rules,” though seemingly cumbersome, proved highly effective for management. Because of their deterrent power, subordinates like Xiao Bai weighed the consequences before slacking off. As a result, Mike’s department consistently ranked at the top of the company; everyone in it worked at 200 percent effort.

#### Real Case

A friend gave up a well-paid position at a large company with an annual salary of several hundred thousand yuan to become CEO of a private enterprise. I once strongly suspected he had been misled, but he said, “These days it’s not easy to find a good job, but it’s even harder to find a good boss.”

The saying “a scholar dies for one who appreciates him” is entirely accurate. After observing for some time, I realized his boss had not won him over with money or generous benefits but with constant praise and approval, making him willing to work devotedly.

Whenever my friend completed a project or closed a deal, his boss never missed an opportunity to offer praise, affirm his ability, and discuss “expanding the present and envisioning the future.” As a result, my friend’s motivation rose further and his loyalty to his boss grew. In contrast, at his previous large company, despite earning several times more, he had never felt valued or received recognition amid the abundance of talent and had remained dispirited and unmotivated.

This boss was truly shrewd. With minimal capital and positive reinforcement he secured a capable subordinate who was willing to serve him wholeheartedly. Praise, encouragement, consideration, smiles, attention, and recognition—do not underestimate these small gestures that cost nothing. Truly skilled manipulators know how to use these minutiae to satisfy the manipulated party’s subconscious vanity, self-confidence, or need for validation through positive reinforcement, thereby making the person willingly obey and regard the manipulator as a “kindred spirit” or “mentor.”

Of course, even more skilled manipulators go beyond verbal praise and set tangible rewards based on the manipulated party’s desires. These rewards feel more desirable and pleasurable than ordinary encouragement, so the manipulated party becomes more inclined to repeat the previously affirmed behavior and applies greater effort.

In the manipulation process, positive reinforcement is the least repellent method. Therefore, if one finds oneself under positive-reinforcement manipulation, there is no need for excessive worry. The only thing to watch is whether the manipulator will actually deliver on promises. In any case, a sustained positive-reinforcement relationship tends to leave both parties satisfied.

#### White Mouse Experiment

After conducting the black-and-white compartment experiment, the psychologists immediately performed another experiment on a different white mouse.

They placed the mouse in the black compartment, which had been wired with electricity. The wires covered the entire black compartment; any slight contact delivered an electric shock. Within seconds the poor mouse kept dodging and jumping, eventually trembling and urinating under the stress. Soon, while trying to hide, it touched the white door and entered the safe zone—the unwired white compartment.

After spending some time in the white compartment, the mouse was returned to the black compartment. This time it took only a short while to run from the black compartment into the white one.

In subsequent trials the time the mouse took to run from the black compartment to the white compartment grew shorter. Eventually, even after the psychologists removed the wires from the black compartment, the mouse would instinctively dash into the white compartment at the first opportunity. In its mind the black compartment had become permanently linked with the pain of electric shock.

Another striking phenomenon occurred during the experiment: the time this mouse took to run from the black compartment to the white compartment was much shorter than that of mice that had received positive reinforcement.

Why did the mouse act faster without any cheese reward? In behavioral psychology this phenomenon is called negative reinforcement. Because the mouse performed the action the scientists wanted—running from the black compartment into the white compartment—it escaped the painful and frightening electric shocks. Thereafter, whenever it was placed back in the black compartment, the danger of shock was immediately imprinted in its mind. Consequently, even after the wires had been removed, the mouse still raced toward what it considered the safe zone.

Negative reinforcement is therefore also known as the “aversive conditioning method.” When the victim yields to the manipulator, the reward is not pleasant praise or a prize but the cessation or avoidance of unpleasant negative stimuli. The manipulator exploits the victim’s fear and aversion to these negative stimuli to bring the victim under control and ensure obedience.

#### Workplace Case

When Xiao Hua first joined the company, her supervisor, Manager Fang, thought highly of her and often praised her intelligence and steady work. With such favor from her superior, Xiao Hua believed her conversion to permanent status would be no problem.

As the end of her probation period approached, however, Manager Fang continued to praise her without giving any indication that she would be retained. Moreover, he kept assigning her various tasks, including work that should have been his, forcing her to work overtime.

Constantly exploited yet receiving no clear answer, Xiao Hua grew uneasy. One day, when Manager Fang seemed in a good mood, she cautiously asked, “Manager Fang, I’ve been working here for almost two months now. Do you think I can be converted to permanent status?”

“Conversion is simple. As long as you work hard, there’s no difficulty,” Manager Fang replied evasively.

“Then… may I take two days off? The overtime has been exhausting, and I’m not familiar with many things. I’m really worn out,” Xiao Hua said hesitantly.

A very important task was due, and Xiao Hua’s request for leave would force Manager Fang to work overtime himself. His expression darkened. “Xiao Hua, I understand your hardship, but isn’t this how all newcomers are? Precisely because you know less, you must put in extra effort to study. If your professional skills aren’t solid, how can I convert you to permanent status?”

“Well…” Compared with conversion, physical and mental exhaustion seemed secondary. Xiao Hua braced herself and nodded reluctantly. “Don’t worry, Manager Fang. I’ll definitely finish the report you gave me today by tomorrow.”

“Good. That’s more like it.” Manager Fang nodded with satisfaction.

The relationship between Xiao Hua and Manager Fang was a typical case of negative-reinforcement control. The manipulator, Manager Fang, firmly controlled Xiao Hua’s behavior by exploiting her fear of losing her job, making her willingly work for him.

Ai Li, a graduate of a prestigious university, was a new force in the company. Diligent and intelligent, she was well liked by her superiors.

During a recent assignment, however, Ai Li was so exhausted that she forgot to make an important phone call. When the client’s contact person called, the project manager summoned Ai Li to his office and scolded her severely.

Perhaps because he was in a bad mood, the manager’s reprimand was harsh and sarcastic; he even pointed at her nose and slammed the desk to express his anger. The tirade left Ai Li terrified. She ran out of the office in tears.

From that day on, whenever Ai Li saw the manager, the image of him losing his temper would flash through her mind. To avoid another outburst, she behaved cautiously in his presence and immediately carried out whatever he said.

No one is immune to mistakes, however. Not long afterward Ai Li was reprimanded again. Although the manager’s anger was milder this time, Ai Li’s fear had reached its peak. She stared at his moving mouth, her ears filled with buzzing, unable to hear clearly what he was saying<|eos|>

#### The Psychological Mechanism of Punishment

Mike’s manipulation technique is called “punishment” in behavioral psychology. As the term literally suggests, punishment means that if the person being manipulated engages in behavior the manipulator does not allow, the manipulated person will directly experience some negative consequence as punishment. Generally, the manipulated person recognizes the connection between their own behavior and the negative experience; out of fear of punishment, they stop the behavior they were about to perform and instead try to do things that please the manipulator in order to reduce their own anxiety about being punished.

Punishment and negative reinforcement share many similarities: both exploit the manipulated person’s aversion and fear of negative events to force compliance. The sole difference lies in timing. In negative reinforcement, the negative experience occurs when the manipulated person fails to follow the manipulator’s wishes; the pressure of that experience forces compliance, and the experience ends only when the manipulated person yields.

In punishment, performing the disallowed action is directly linked to the negative experience. The manipulator sets a rule: “If you do something that displeases me, you will receive this punishment.” In other words, the negative experience has not yet occurred, but the threat already creates a sense of crisis that deters the manipulated person from acting in ways that might anger the manipulator.

The sequence in which the negative experience arises is the clearest distinction between punishment and negative reinforcement.

Punishment is widely applied as discipline or as stipulated clauses. Beyond explicitly stated rules, many common “punishment” phenomena also appear in daily life.

#### The Principle of Positive Reinforcement

The method humans use to manipulate white mice is called positive reinforcement. Positive reinforcement rests on the universal human tendency to seek approval and the persistent desire for others’ praise. When an action receives affirmation or reward and the other party signals a wish for the behavior to continue, that affirmation and reward constitute positive reinforcement. This form of manipulation does not produce aversion or boredom; instead, it generates pleasant experiences, which is why positive reinforcement works.

Positive reinforcement appears frequently in everyday life. When we achieve results at work, a boss may reward us with a promotion. When we earn good grades, parents and teachers offer praise. Even a smile or a word of recognition can motivate further effort. Because this reinforcement brings pleasant experiences and psychological satisfaction, it is the most common and most readily accepted manipulation technique in interpersonal relationships.

In another sense, positive reinforcement is less a one-sided manipulation than a process of mutual influence.
