We unconsciously attend to the actions of those we love, depend on, or respect, and we “approve” of their behavior in various ways; they, in turn, unconsciously strengthen certain behaviors because of the feedback we provide. This interactive pattern is especially common under positive reinforcement.

#### The Essence of Negative Reinforcement

The essence of negative reinforcement is that the manipulator uses behaviors such as intimidation, silent treatment, threats, or shouting to generate fear, inferiority, or guilt in the manipulated person. To end this painful and uneasy feeling, the manipulated person must comply with, acquiesce in, or yield to the manipulator’s unreasonable demands in exchange for temporary peace and stability.

Although negative reinforcement can secure obedience, the negative emotions it produces—irritability, anger, resentment—often accumulate. Excessive buildup may lead to depression, self-abandonment, or even a vicious cycle in which the manipulated person later applies the same technique to others.

Not all negative reinforcement relies on overt intimidation. Some manipulators display pained, pitiful, or injured expressions or engage in constant nagging criticism that induces shame and guilt, prompting willing compliance. This, too, is a form of negative reinforcement.

Compared with positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement is clearly unpleasant. People repeatedly think, “If I don’t do this, he will ignore me again,” “If I don’t work overtime, the boss might fire me,” or “If I report this, he might blame me.” These “what ifs” create the psychological habit of yielding to avoid negative outcomes, allowing the manipulator to succeed repeatedly.

#### Experimental Case

Psychologists once conducted the following experiment. They placed a laboratory white mouse inside a specially constructed cage divided into two compartments—one white, one black—with a white door between them.

The mouse was placed in the black compartment; a large piece of high-quality cheese was placed in the white compartment. Attracted by the scent or the sight of the white door, the mouse pushed the door open, entered the white compartment, and ate the cheese.

In subsequent trials, the psychologists returned the mouse to the black compartment and again placed cheese in the white compartment. Each time, the mouse took less time to move from the black compartment to the white one; it appeared to have grown “smarter.”

The experiment was repeated several times. Each trial showed a further reduction in the time required. Eventually, even when no cheese was placed in the white compartment, the mouse still ran quickly from the black compartment to the white one, as though the behavior had become habitual.

The psychologists intended the experiment to demonstrate positive reinforcement. After completing the task of moving from the black to the white compartment, the mouse promptly received a reward; in its mind, the white compartment became equated with delicious cheese.

#### Post-Traumatic Stress Psychological Disorder

Everyone has experienced traumatic events. Being bitten by a dog in childhood, beaten by parents while growing up, or bullied by stronger classmates—these deepest wounds do not simply fade with time. Most produce serious aftereffects known in behavioral psychology as post-traumatic stress psychological disorder.

Traumatic one-time learning arises from this disorder. The condition appears after a person has undergone an extremely terrifying event—witnessing another’s death or facing one’s own death or serious injury—and exhibits symptoms of psychological debilitation. The victim feels despair and terror not only at the moment of the event; later, any similar situation can re-trigger the memory and the fear.

In the manipulative use of traumatic one-time learning, the manipulator delivers a powerful verbal or physical blow. Under the intense threat, the manipulated person loses control over their own behavior. Thereafter, whenever the manipulator displays a similar expression or action, the manipulated person’s emotions become immediately tense and they strive to prevent the terrifying event from recurring.

#### First, Everyone Has a Competitive Consciousness

Advertisers frequently exploit this psychological tendency. They show in commercials how popular their product is and urge viewers to “buy now before it’s gone.” Television images depict crowds lining up outside stores before opening hours, hands reaching for shelves, and goods disappearing rapidly.

The message conveyed is that the product is in high demand, that many people want it, and that they are competing directly with the viewer for it.

The sensation of competing with others for scarce resources is highly stimulating. An indifferent lover may become ardent when a rival appears; people in relationships often use this tactic by deliberately or inadvertently revealing the existence of admirers. Salespeople also employ the technique. When showing a house to a hesitant buyer, a real-estate agent may mention that many others are interested or have already viewed it. The strategy usually succeeds: fearing they will lose out, the buyer quickly becomes more proactive.

#### Influence on Humans

Intermittent reinforcement affects humans as well as birds. Gamblers seen on television continue to stake their savings despite knowing that “nine out of ten bets lose.” Their behavior resembles that of the hopeful pigeon B: an occasional win functions as a reward and deepens addiction to the game.

Continuous positive reinforcement may lose effectiveness once the connection is broken or the reward no longer satisfies. Continuous negative reinforcement can generate resentment and anger that accumulate and produce unexpected consequences for the manipulator. Intermittent reinforcement, however, deepens addictive behavior because the uncertainty it introduces keeps the manipulated person anxious and unsettled. Throughout the process, the manipulated person remains in suspense, unable to predict whether the next outcome will be a reward or renewed indifference, and therefore complies more cautiously and fearfully.

#### Intermittent Reinforcement: The “Gambling” Style Manipulation That One Cannot Extricate From

Micro-expression Keywords: The most terrifying thing in the world is not gods, demons, or ghosts, but the unknown. Intermittent reinforcement exploits precisely this fact. By using uncertainty to manipulate the other person’s mind, it ensures they can never determine when the next event will occur, leaving them perpetually concerned, anxious, and unsettled, and therefore led by the manipulator.

Both positive and negative reinforcement are uniformly “good” or “bad,” yet in real life no one is consistently good or bad toward another. Manipulators often combine the two techniques and thereby achieve more pronounced results.

#### Trauma: Once Bitten by a Snake, Afraid of Ropes for Ten Years

Micro-expression Keywords: Manipulators typically frighten or threaten the manipulated person through displays of loss of control. As the saying goes, once there is a first time, a second time will follow. After the first successful instance of traumatic one-time learning, the manipulated person’s greatest fear—the second or third occurrence—will eventually arrive.

A Chinese proverb states: once bitten by a snake, one fears ropes for ten years. It describes how a person who has been bitten by a snake remains fearful for a long time afterward, becoming nervous even at the sight of objects resembling a snake. This characteristic closely resembles the manipulation technique discussed below.

#### The Essence of Intermittent Reinforcement

The power of intermittent reinforcement lies in its “gambling”-like quality. The feeling of uncertainty combined with hope dilutes the manipulated person’s attention to their own interests and fosters impulsive behavior contrary to those interests. The reward that may or may not appear prevents the manipulated person from giving up, trapping them in the “game.”

Skilled practitioners of intermittent reinforcement keep the manipulated person in a constant state of anxiety and walking on eggshells while unwilling to abandon hope, thereby shaping both the manipulated person’s perception of the manipulator and their subsequent reactions.

#### Manifestations and Coping in the Family

Traumatic one-time learning appears not only in romantic and workplace settings but also throughout family life. Husbands who beat their wives or abuse their children provide the clearest examples. Tragically, most victims do not anticipate that they are being manipulated; they endure silently until they can no longer tolerate the situation and then erupt in uncontrolled emotion.

Avoiding traumatic one-time learning requires a clear assessment of the situation, a correct understanding of one’s position relative to others, and the overcoming of fear. The manipulated person’s compliance only encourages the manipulator to continue.

#### The Scarcity Principle: The Scarcer the Resources, the More Fierce the Competition

Everyone possesses competitive consciousness. As the saying goes, “the quick hand gets it; the slow hand gets nothing.” People fear losing to rivals, regret missing opportunities, and dislike forgoing something they might obtain by trying. Astute merchants exploit this competitive consciousness to set psychological traps; the unwary easily fall in.

In daily life, merchants frequently hold limited-time flash sales that reliably generate substantial revenue.

What explains this phenomenon?

#### Chapter Thirteen Seeing Through Manipulation Patterns, No One Can Manipulate Me

Living in contemporary society inevitably involves manipulating others and being manipulated. Even if we do not wish to manipulate anyone, living in a world where others manipulate us is always an uncomfortable experience. Therefore, in interpersonal interactions we must learn to read another person’s psychology through their behavior, movements, and expressions, to discern their intentions, and to recognize the manipulation techniques they employ, so that we can break free from being manipulated.

#### Negative Reinforcement: The Psychological Inertia of Compromising with Evil

Micro-expression Keywords: Compared with positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement produces fear, anger, and discomfort. Yet, out of fear that an imagined negative outcome will occur, the person subjected to negative reinforcement consistently yields to the manipulator. Such compliance only encourages the manipulator to continue using negative reinforcement.

#### Punishment: Rules Are an Unsurpassable Mountain

Micro-expression Keywords: The essence of punishment as a manipulation technique is to exploit people’s fear of negative experiences in order to compel obedience. Threats from others, workplace regulations, and even laws and statutes all operate through the mechanism of punishment.

#### Positive Reinforcement: An Affirmation Model Beneficial to Both

Wise parents and effective leaders understand how to apply positive reinforcement to obtain the greatest loyalty and motivation from children or subordinates with the least expenditure of resources. Because the resulting pleasant experience does not generate resentment in the manipulated person, positive reinforcement possesses unique appeal.

### Expanding Psychological Games, Grasping the Key to Victory

#### Cake Division Effect: Bargaining is Also an Art

Micro-expression keywords Regarding the actual situations that may arise from cake division psychology, we can summarize many similar small strategies to help us achieve optimal benefits. But it must be warned that zero-sum games can easily turn into conflicts in some cases, which will result in a "negative sum," and both parties will suffer losses. Therefore, before dividing the cake, one must grasp the other party's acceptable bottom line and try not to touch it.

A cake is given to two children to eat at the same time. Both want to be the one who divides it, fearing the other will cut it unfairly. So they keep arguing about it.

At this point, their father walks over and says: One cuts, the other chooses first. That way it is fair.

Why do the two children keep arguing over dividing the cake? Because if one cuts more, the other eats less. There is only one cake; once eaten, it is gone. If A eats a bit more, B must eat a bit less. Assume that when each eats exactly half, the gain is 0. Then if one eats a little more, the gain is 1, and the other eats a little less, so the gain is -1. The sum of both parties' gains equals zero.

This situation, where one party gains and the other loses in a game, is called a zero-sum game. The psychological state people develop in a zero-sum game is cake division psychology: always fearing the other side will encroach on one's own interests. This leads to the ubiquitous phenomenon of bargaining.

Bargaining is the most common behavior driven by cake division psychology. Both sides hold the view that if you gain an advantage, my returns will decrease. So after calculating costs, the seller sets a price with profit ten times the cost, while the buyer immediately demands a one-third cut.

Theoretically, the ideal outcome of cake division psychology is an even split, producing a relatively fair result where "A cuts the cake and B chooses first." In practice, however, unequal professional knowledge and information between buyer and seller make it difficult for one side to truly maximize its interests. A buyer who haggles a 100-yuan item down to 80 yuan feels triumphant, as if victorious, when the actual cost may be only 30 yuan.

This is the excellent pricing strategy: making consumers believe they have gotten a bargain. The big discounts and clearance sales in shopping malls all align with consumer psychology. In simple terms, it is nothing more than using a black cloth to hide part of the cake during division, causing the other party to misjudge the cake's size.

Consumers cannot know the exact figures for raw material collection costs, factory assembly-line costs, labor costs, energy costs, or marketing costs. We cannot guess how much labor value is embodied in a product. This is the merchant's greatest reliance for active pricing. What consumers can do is merely "shop around." Yet when three merchants reach a consensus to compete on the surface while actually colluding to control the market, consumers can only be deceived.

Returning to the cake, add another assumption: what if it is an ice-cream cake? That is, if the bargaining parties fail to reach consensus within a certain time, both interests are harmed. The time spent bargaining is also a cost; this is called waiting cost. Generally, waiting cost is not applied equally to both sides but often targets one party.

There is a segment in Guo Degang's crosstalk about a man walking on the street who suddenly sees two city inspectors cleaning the area. He runs 500 meters to a lamb skewer stall, orders 100 skewers, and the owner works hard to grill them and hand them over just as the inspectors approach. The owner naturally cannot wait and rolls up his stall to flee.

If the owner had continued waiting, he would have been caught by the inspectors; confiscation and fines would make the waiting cost unbearable, so the customer benefited cheaply.

Of course, in many cases, one party in a game can impose waiting costs on the other. There was a large antique dealer in old Beijing who had three jade bi discs. A wealthy merchant from Yangzhou had reserved them with a 300-yuan silver deposit.

A week later, the Yangzhou merchant arrived at the antique shop to negotiate. The owner quoted 800 yuan for the three discs.

The merchant immediately shook his head: That is an outrageous price. I will buy only two for 500 yuan!

Without a word, the antique dealer picked up one disc from the table and dropped it to the floor. Before the Yangzhou merchant could react, it shattered. The crisp sound reminded him that this jade was a rare treasure.

The merchant stood up at once and questioned the dealer in alarm. The dealer sipped his tea calmly: Since you want only two, the third has no purpose. These two are still 800 yuan.

The merchant grew angrier: Three for 800, two still 800? Are you treating me as a fool?

The dealer picked up another disc and smashed it on the floor. The Yangzhou merchant was stunned. The dealer continued: Now only one remains on the table. I ask 1,000 yuan, take it or leave it.

The merchant protested: One disc more expensive than three? You...

Before he finished, the dealer reached for the last disc. The merchant, forgetting decorum, lunged forward, grabbed the dealer's sleeve, and shouted: 1,000, deal!

After the transaction, the apprentice cleaned the hall and said to the dealer with heartache: Master, you were too ruthless...

The dealer stroked his beard and smiled proudly: The two smashed discs were fakes. I had Master Ye from the east side make them three days ago for less than 100 yuan...

The antique dealer fabricated a waiting cost for the Yangzhou merchant, eliminating any reason to bargain, and at the final moment crushed his psychological defenses, raising the price to a high level and profiting handsomely.

Using waiting costs to bargain is not only the seller's privilege. In my second year studying abroad, two close classmates and I rented a three-person apartment near school. The first year's contract was 1,500 dollars monthly rent. When the lease expired in May of the second year, we prepared to negotiate renewal. The landlord proposed raising it to 2,000 dollars per month.

The landlord said: More and more international students are coming to the university town, and the rental market is heating up. 1,500 dollars was last year's market price; raising you to 2,000 dollars now is also market price and does not take advantage of you. If you have difficulties, you can renew for one month and then look elsewhere. See if 2,000 dollars is worth it.

I understood the landlord was right and roughly grasped his thinking: he saw other landlords raising prices and similar apartments reaching 2,000 dollars, so he was tempted. Yet although he had his reasons, we had ours: three international students already found the apartment tight; such an increase might leave us "sleeping on the street."

My roommates were an ingenuous Indian and a reticent Peruvian. I could not rely on them, so I thought it over and presented the landlord with a calculation: Sir, what you say is reasonable, but you overlook one thing.

The landlord was taken aback: What?

I continued: Let us do the math. If we move out now and new tenants move in at the current market price of 2,000 dollars, compared with last year you would earn an extra 6,000 dollars next year, correct?

The landlord nodded. I went on: But you overlook that it is now May; within half a month all colleges here will begin a three-month summer vacation. This is a university town, so you probably will not rent the place out again at 2,000 dollars a month until at least three months later when school resumes. In other words, if we leave, you lose at least three months' rent, 4,500 dollars, right?

The landlord said: Even so, I would still earn 1,500 dollars.

I replied: Yes, but you must consider many issues: whether new students will smoke, throw parties, or use marijuana in your apartment, or burn the place down. You have seen how carefully we three treat this apartment; the basic furnishings are almost undamaged. We were even twice designated star tenants by the building manager. Frankly, it will be hard to find tenants as good as us. Are you sure you want to take that risk for 1,500 dollars a year?

The landlord sighed; I saw he was moved. I pressed further: But rising rents nearby are an undeniable fact, and we are poor students, sir. You must understand. How about this: we raise the rent symbolically by 100 dollars. According to our earlier calculation, you lose only 300 dollars a year. 300 dollars buys peace of mind, avoids potential trouble from new tenants, and purchases our friendship. Choose, sir.

The landlord laughed heartily: If you were not Chinese I would suggest you run for senator! Deal, as you say!

I often use this incident to teach juniors; it is one of my proudest "bargaining battles." The reason I succeeded was that I seized the landlord's waiting cost, so I should thank the American education system's three-month long summer vacation, which forced him to rent the place before the holiday or lose three months' rent.

Finally, many people feel a certain shame about the "cake division effect" and are reluctant to bargain. More than ten years after graduation, I visited a professor who had taken great care of me during university. The elderly man was nearly seventy and retired at home. When I visited, he was furnishing his son's new apartment and about to buy furniture. I said I had dealt with people in this line and offered to go with him so he would not be cheated.

The teacher gladly took me to the furniture mall. After selecting a set, he prepared to pay. I immediately held his hand and began bargaining with the seller. Eventually the store manager was called and gave an 20 percent discount, saving more than 1,000 yuan.

I was about to claim credit when, on the way back, the teacher sternly scolded me for losing his face. He continued giving me the cold shoulder at dinner. After the teacher's wife learned the reason, she only laughed and told me: Your teacher is like that; do not take it to heart.

I could not be angry with the teacher and could only smile bitterly. After the bitter smile, I understood his temperament. As an old-generation intellectual, his pride made him ashamed of "bargaining." Many people, to varying degrees, share this complex. It is unnecessary, because once a person enters a zero-sum game, avoiding personal loss is natural and justified; it is a person's instinctive psychological reaction.

#### Information Discrimination Effect: Why Billions of Yuan in Ad Slots Are So Sought After

Without control, people's information discrimination is subjective, superficial, and wishful. The process of overcoming this subjective information discrimination is often the shift from emotion-dominated thinking to reason-dominated thinking. This is necessary for a person's maturity and growth. So let us begin with "not judging a person arbitrarily by clothing and appearance."

A few years ago I bought an apartment. When I first moved in, there was inevitable upheaval. Because I had to do dirty and heavy work, I wore very old clothes. After a day of barely getting things in order, my appearance could be described as dust-covered and smoke-stained, temples gray, fingers black.

Feeling thirsty, I went out to buy water. After purchasing a bottle of mineral water at the convenience store, I realized I had left my keys, phone, and wallet behind. I had already drunk from the bottle, so I could not return it. I could only say awkwardly: Sorry, I did not bring money. I live in this neighborhood; can I pay you this evening?

The convenience store owner looked at me suspiciously: There are not many households in this neighborhood; how have I not seen you?

I said I had just moved in, building 16.

Convenience store owner: Building 16 is right across; I can see the unit door. You can go back and get it now.

I said awkwardly again: I did not bring the key.

The owner said somewhat disdainfully: Fine, fine, take the water and go. If you have not eaten I can give you a steamed bun. You have it pretty hard. The neighborhood next door is run by the subdistrict office; they can help unemployed people with reemployment procedures. Let an old man say this: at your age, what can you not do...

Faced with the owner's well-intentioned chatter, I could only smile bitterly. My dark skin from heavy labor and ragged clothes, unable to produce even one yuan for mineral water, being mistaken for a vagrant or beggar was understandable. Later, because I often dealt with this small owner, we became friendly and laughed about the incident. Afterward, however, I realized the event sketched from the side a certain trajectory of human psychology: the information discrimination effect.

The information discrimination effect means that people's cognitive process toward others or things is often achieved through information categorization. For example, when a girl wears a bubble skirt and princess boots, people think she is a cute and petite girl; when she wears a halter dress and high heels, people think she is mature and charming; when she wears a tank top, cropped pants, and canvas shoes, everyone thinks she is energetic, a sporty girl... Yet in reality, this is only the part the girl intends to show outsiders; as for what the girl herself is really like, perhaps even she has not fully grasped.

This method of information discrimination actually stems from human laziness. A person's true character and inner world are extremely complex; when we get to know someone, it is difficult to conduct such deep, all-around recognition. However, we can judge the person through similar labels, saving considerable effort. Zhang San has a hot temper; Li Si is honest and generous. Through such labeling, we treat others as a bundle of information. In this process of information discrimination, people are labeled.

The same applies to objects.

At the end of 2005, the total bid amount for CCTV's 2006 "golden resource" advertising slots reached 5.87 billion yuan. Many large merchants spent hundreds of millions simply to have their products appear on screen for 30 seconds before the evening news.

Statistics show that the combined coverage and viewership of channels airing popular entertainment programs or TV dramas far exceed CCTV's "golden resources." Yet even the total advertising fees for all prime-time slots on these stations do not reach one-fifth of CCTV's same-time rate.

As a promotional method, the strategy of "buying out popular local stations in clusters" is clearly far superior to "CCTV golden resources." Why do so many large manufacturers still flock to CCTV?

The reason is simple: their advertising is not merely to promote products but, more importantly, to tell consumers that the company has the ability to advertise on CCTV, implying abundant capital and substantial resources, so the goods produced cannot be too poor.

In fact, human discrimination effects are also common in nature. In bird populations, female birds often choose males according to this principle: the more splendid the plumage, the more popular.

According to nature's law of survival of the fittest, splendid plumage is actually detrimental to male birds' survival: splendid feathers are often heavy, making males clumsier; moreover, splendid feathers are too conspicuous, making predators and hunters easier to spot.

Yet female birds still flock to males with splendid plumage. Why? Because only strong, healthy males can survive while retaining splendid plumage. In other words, splendid plumage represents a survival cost, and those willing to bear this cost are often the elite among birds. This is analogous to large manufacturers spending enormous advertising fees: hundreds of millions in cost small merchants dare not bear, but I dare, because I have the strength.

Because of the information discrimination effect, people's understanding of things tends to be superficial and labeled. When this simple laziness is exploited, it harms our own interests. Large manufacturers, for instance, do not actually bear the enormous advertising costs; they factor such costs into product pricing, passing them on to consumers.

Therefore, smart people, when choosing goods, do not rely on "reputation" but establish another set of clever, rational discrimination mechanisms: for two similar products with comparable prices, buy the one without reputation, because the famous one necessarily includes advertising costs, so the use value embodied in that product is lower. If concerned about quality, one might as well review it through non-commercial pure quality certification methods: for example, checking whether it has international quality system certification or how the merchants selling it are regarded for reputation...

The same rational discrimination mechanism can be applied to people. A famous story of King Solomon in the Bible offers enlightenment:

Two women and their several-month-old infants lived in one room. One woman accidentally smothered her own child while sleeping and placed the dead infant in the other woman's arms, taking the living infant instead.

At dawn the woman discovered the dead infant in her arms was not her own and brought the matter before King Solomon. In court both women claimed the child as theirs. King Solomon thought for a moment and decided to cut the child in half, giving each woman half.

The false mother agreed to the judgment.

The true mother, upon hearing this, cried out: The child is not mine; give her the child; I do not want it.

King Solomon awarded the child to the true mother.

King Solomon devised a more rational and wise method of information discrimination. In our everyday information discrimination of others, we should likewise draw on King Solomon's wisdom: move beyond traditional, unthinking, intuitive information discrimination and enter deeper information discrimination. Sherlock Holmes represents the extreme of this rational information discrimination; through details of a person's speech, behavior, clothing, and appearance, he could deduce that a beggar had been a noble in his grandfather's generation.

Of course, Holmes's myth-level deductive power appears only in fiction, but this method of information discrimination can be learned by all of us.

#### Stag Hunt Effect: Breaking the Non-Cooperation Misconception, Achieving Common Benefits

Micro-expression keywords: The damage the stag-hunt mentality inflicts on a community is severe; even in small groups it becomes an obstacle to cooperation. Creating a transcendent power is an effective way to overcome that obstacle. Such a power may seem abstract, yet it becomes convincing once you identify a strong guarantor.

In *Discourse on the Origin and Basis of Inequality Among Men*, philosopher Rousseau recounts a story that illustrates a common human habit of mind—

Two hunters are in a forest. Hunting separately with crude bows, each can take three rabbits. Hunting together with a large trap, they can take one stag. Each rabbit feeds one person for three days; the stag feeds each for five days.

Cooperation yields far greater returns than acting alone, yet most hunters still choose not to cooperate, even though the separate hauls are modest.

The episode later became known as the stag hunt effect, describing the irrational aversion to mutually beneficial cooperation. Economics once posited the “rational agent,” whose every action is calculated to maximize self-interest. As consumer-psychology research deepened, the concept grew increasingly theoretical and lost practical force. Today even traditional economists concede that a purely rational agent does not exist in reality, any more than the frictionless plane of classical physics.

The stag hunt effect is one major barrier to perfect rationality. Periodic economic crises in Western societies, when they escalate into financial crises, trigger bank runs. Runs drain liquidity, commercial banks collapse, panic spreads, financial and trust systems disintegrate, currency and commodity exchange freeze, and depression follows. A bank run is the stag hunt effect in action: everyone knows that if no one runs, the bank survives, yet each fears others will withdraw first and therefore rushes to withdraw.

The late-Qing merchant prince Hu Xueyan met his downfall in precisely such a run.

The crisis began when Hu started hoarding raw silk in the 1880s. He accumulated 8,000 bales—two-thirds of Shanghai’s annual turnover—and drove the price to record levels. Still unsatisfied, he continued converting all available cash into silk, believing that once the market was empty he would become the sole supplier and dictate prices.

Then a rumor spread: foreign creditors were demanding repayment and Hu was about to go bankrupt. The rumor was not entirely false. Hu had guaranteed a loan for another merchant; when the borrower defaulted, the foreign lenders turned to him. Hu’s resources and reputation made repayment feasible, yet the public knew none of this. A modest debt of 1,000 silver dollars was magnified into “ten thousand taels of gold.” Depositors stormed his banks; reserves were emptied. Combined with the capital tied up in silk, his commercial empire collapsed overnight.

Hu’s failure was only the prelude. Within a month, runs destroyed hundreds of native banks in Beijing, Yangzhou, Shanghai, Fuzhou, Ningbo, Zhenjiang, and Hankou. A single rumor shattered the Qing empire’s nascent financial-trust system.

Whether in the late Qing or in modern America, people need only pause to realize that if no one runs, a solvent bank remains solvent and everyone continues to enjoy safe, convenient services plus interest. Yet whenever the question is “If everyone refrains, no harm occurs,” each person thinks instead, “If they act and I do not, I lose.” The non-cooperating hunter reasons the same way: what if I help trap the stag and my partner takes it all?

The stag hunt effect inflicts enormous damage on both society and individuals: each person suspects others will harm him, so even when calm cooperation would produce mutual gain, no one cooperates.

Public indifference to communal resources is another manifestation. Outdoor trash bins are battered and filthy while private homes are spotless. People assume household fixtures must be kept clean but treat public property as expendable. Yet the taxes that fund those facilities come from the same citizens. When public property deteriorates, inconvenience rises and government spending increases, leading to higher taxes that fall back on the same people. Everyone knows this, yet the neglect persists—the stag hunt effect at work.

Its harm is not insurmountable. A transcendent regulatory power can restore rationality.

Before Franklin D. Roosevelt took office, the United States followed laissez-faire policies, trusting that market forces would reconcile selfish strategies into an optimal public good. That blind faith produced the financial crisis of the early twentieth century, a worldwide depression that set major economies back decades and left people starving beneath neon lights.

Roosevelt introduced new economic policies: government intervention, large-scale public works, and credit guarantees for banks. The resulting recovery lifted the United States out of the gloom; government had become the economy’s transcendent stabilizer.

In daily life, when you seek win-win cooperation but the other party refuses, you can invoke or create such a transcendent presence to free them from the stag hunt effect. As a hunter preparing to stalk a stag, you might swear on your mother’s name—provided you are known to be filial—that the kill will be divided fairly. Or you might ask the village elder to stand as guarantor.

#### Chicken Game Effect: Appeasement and Compromise—The Heart of Martial Arts Aims to Stop War

Micro-expression keywords: The tendency to avoid harm through compromise lies deep in everyone, rooted in the universal impulse to seek gain and shun loss. In daily life it is useful to recognize both one’s own and others’ chicken-game impulses, distinguishing avoidable conflicts from unavoidable ones. For the former, grasp their nature; for the latter, devise responses.

When two evenly matched people meet on a narrow path, one must yield for the other to pass. Several outcomes are possible:

- Neither yields; they fight to a bloody draw.
- One yields and the other does not; the yielder loses face while the standee wins—or the roles reverse.

The best outcome for either side is the other’s retreat, yet misjudging the situation can produce the worst: mutual injury. The safer course, therefore, is to yield when yielding is appropriate.

In real terms this suggests that a “cowardly” disposition can maximize benefit; Americans therefore call the scenario the “chicken game.” After the term entered Chinese, the slang sense of “chicken” as coward was overlooked and the phrase was rendered “斗鸡效应.”

The chicken game effect highlights the objective advantage of an appeasement mindset in a game-theoretic setting: when interests clash, fighting to the end usually injures both parties, whereas stopping while ahead is the more viable strategy. As the proverb says, “Step back and the sky opens wide.”

George Washington led untrained colonial militias to victory over well-equipped British forces by exploiting Anglo-French rivalry, securing the independence of the thirteen colonies. He understood, however, that Britain had not yet committed its full strength. Once London resolved its conflict with France and redirected its resources to North America, the militias would be overwhelmed. While Britain was still occupied elsewhere, Washington sent his ablest deputy, John Jay, to negotiate the Jay Treaty—an unequal agreement that preserved British trade privileges in North America, restricted American exports, and capped the tonnage of the U.S. Navy.

Thus the newly independent United States remained economically subordinate to Britain and, in effect, acknowledged a residual suzerainty. The terms were unpalatable to a public that had just fought for sovereignty, yet most legislators and informed observers recognized that temporary compromise was the only prudent course. History confirmed that Washington’s restraint spared the young nation premature entanglement in war and granted a century of peace that later underpinned its rise in two world wars.

Although leaders often declare they will never compromise, the human instinct to avoid harm leads people to choose the less damaging path—conciliation with an adversary. The chicken game effect simply measures how much compromise people will in fact tolerate beneath a rhetoric of intransigence.

From the day I entered school my parents urged me to yield and avoid trouble; other children received the same counsel. After a harmonious primary and secondary education, fistfights increased at university. The small plaza outside our dormitory windows became a regular arena for arranged brawls among male students. What began as a dispute over five yuan and eighty cents between two individuals quickly drew in friends and roommates until dozens were involved. Just as the melee seemed inevitable, someone on each side would discover a distant kinship or hometown tie, the fight would be called off, and the original antagonists might even become friends. In practice, the instigators deliberately delayed so that the crowd would grow and the fight would never start.

No one truly wants to fight; the saying “Better a dog at peace than a man at war” captures the universal aversion. Because conflict usually leaves both sides worse off, the chicken game effect is refined to an art in everyday life. Most quarrels of pride reduce to the problem of “providing a face-saving exit.” Once such an exit appears, both parties step back without loss of dignity or goodwill.

The same aversion to harm can produce miscalculation. Neville Chamberlain underestimated Hitler’s ambitions and pursued appeasement, allowing Nazi Germany to overrun half of Europe before turning on France, which fell in weeks.

That is the chicken game effect gone wrong. It is not invincible; objective analysis overcomes its downside. Winston Churchill, who consistently advocated resistance to Nazism, correctly assessed Hitler’s intentions.

When dealing with potential adversaries, therefore, one must analyze objectively to determine which conflicts can be resolved and which cannot.

Bill Gates avoided the chicken game’s distorting influence. Among countless rivals he distinguished those with whom cooperation was possible from those with whom it was not.

He routinely acquired small firms that possessed valuable technology but lacked capital or market presence. When Microsoft’s actions harmed such firms, he preferred settlement to litigation.

Against well-funded competitors he fought for market share yet also sought cooperation. Apple is the classic case. Although Apple computers never adopted Windows, in 2000 Microsoft developed a custom version of Office for the Macintosh platform.

Refusing to be ruled by emotion is essential to neutralizing the chicken game effect; only by objectively identifying the other side’s tolerance threshold can one optimize one’s own interests.

#### The Wise Pig Effect: More Work Does Not Necessarily Yield More Gains, Inaction Is Not Necessarily Laziness

Micro-expression keywords: The psychological cause of the Wise Pig Effect is not laziness. Although inaction caused by laziness and inaction caused by the Wise Pig Effect appear identical, their psychological origins differ greatly. In the former, people cannot overcome their own inertia, yet rationally they should realize that such inaction harms or at least does not benefit them. In the latter, after objective consideration, the individual concludes that inaction is more advantageous than action.

Nobel laureate in economics John Nash once described the following scenario:

Two highly intelligent pigs share a sty—one large pig with a big appetite and one small pig with a moderate appetite.

At one end of the sty is the food trough; at the other is the button that controls it. Pressing the button once releases 10 jin of feed into the trough. Because the distance between trough and button is great, the pig that runs from trough to button expends energy equivalent to 1 jin of feed.

- If the small pig presses the button while the large pig waits at the trough, the feeding ratio is 9:1. After subtracting the small pig’s running cost, the actual ratio becomes 9:0.
- If the large pig presses the button while the small pig waits at the trough, the feeding ratio is 6:4. After subtracting the large pig’s cost, the ratio becomes 5:4.

Because both pigs are intelligent, each selects the strategy that best serves its own interests. The small pig therefore refuses to press the button: if the large pig waits, the small pig’s share barely covers its expenditure and it will eventually starve.

If the small pig remains inactive, the large pig must act or starve. The final outcome is that the small pig waits at the trough while the large pig repeatedly presses the button. The small pig receives less feed than the large pig, yet its net gain exceeds the cost of action. Nash termed this the Wise Pig Effect. The effect objectively explains a group-psychology phenomenon: people assume that more capable individuals should shoulder greater responsibility and perform more labor—i.e., greater ability entails greater responsibility.

The evolution of international relations over the past two centuries illustrates the same group psychology. After the Industrial Revolution, Britain and France rose first, set international rules, reaped benefits, and shouldered mediating responsibilities. In the nineteenth century, Bismarck’s Germany and Metternich’s Austria formed a new powerful alliance, competed more aggressively for overseas colonies, and established a new European order. From the twentieth century onward, Americans have assumed that American values are world values and have promoted their own values more zealously than any previous power.

In China’s Ming dynasty, as East Asia’s strongest state, the court accepted similar duties: during the Yongle reign, Zheng He’s voyages distributed vast treasury wealth as gifts to neighboring states, incorporating them into the Ming sphere. In the mid-to-late Ming, when Japanese daimyo Toyotomi Hideyoshi invaded Korea, the Ming government dispatched troops—an obligation recorded as the “Imjin War.”

The small pig’s gain from inaction largely depends on the large pig’s “large-pig cognition,” which leads the large pig to accept higher costs because inaction would also cause it to starve. The Wise Pig Effect is thus a shared cognition that produces a joint psychological outcome.

In daily life, if you are the large pig, consciously reduce the Wise Pig Effect by weakening the small pigs’ self-perception as “small pigs.” Prevent their self-awakening if possible. Even if they realize they can profit without working, and circumstances force you to expend more labor or cost, perform a remedial favor: make them feel indebted. The simplest method is to act as though the task is difficult or to feign fatigue and hardship.

When the cost burden exceeds the large pig’s capacity, it must find a way to escape the Wise Pig pattern.

I once shared a large house with five others. The others rarely cooked, yet I prepared two meals daily and therefore used the gas stove most. Although my neighbors cooked infrequently, they still used the stove occasionally, resulting in a monthly gas bill of about 50 yuan. At first the bill was split equally. Later they felt this was unfair because I cooked more and proposed a new arrangement. I agreed that I would pay the gas bill alone and stop contributing to the electricity bill. On paper this seemed fair.

I underestimated their ingenuity. Once I assumed the entire gas bill, they began using the stove freely. The next month the bill more than doubled to over 100 yuan. After three months I suggested changing the arrangement again, but they refused unanimously. They knew my dependence on gas was severe: they could endure a shutoff; I could not.

Paying an extra 60–70 yuan monthly was unsustainable. In the third month I stopped paying the gas bill. After the supply was cut, I cheerfully produced a second-hand induction cooker I had bought for a few dozen yuan. The cooker consumed electricity, which, under our agreement, I did not pay for. Within days my neighbors approached me to renegotiate the division of gas and electricity costs.

Actively changing one’s large-pig position is essential for large pigs. Small pigs follow a different maxim: “It is good to rest in the shade of a great tree.” Even without working, a large pig will labor on their behalf. The small pig’s task is simply to bind itself to the large pig’s chariot and make the large pig understand the current reality: the small pig’s inaction causes no immediate harm, yet the large pig’s inaction starves everyone, and the large pig cannot easily discard the small pig.

The sty’s keeper—the manager or rule-maker—should prevent the emergence of Wise Pig Effect mindsets. A rule that permits free-riding frustrates everyone except the small pigs; therefore, rules should reward effort proportionally so that both large and small pigs are motivated to work hard.

#### The Dirty Face Effect: The Operation of Common Knowledge and Unwritten Rules

Micro-expression keywords: According to Gustave Le Bon in *The Crowd*, group psychology is blind and incapable of complex rational thought. When a group possesses certain common knowledge and an individual lacking that knowledge attempts to enter, only two outcomes are possible: the individual is assimilated and acquires the common knowledge, or the individual refuses it and is isolated by the group.

Logician Littlewood once recounted the following story:

Three men with dirty faces sit in a room without mirrors. A beautiful woman enters, sees their faces, and says helplessly, “One of you has a dirty face.”

Each man looks at the other two, sees that both are dirty, assumes his own face is clean, and feels relieved.

When they look up again and notice that everyone else also looks relieved, they immediately understand the situation and all three blush.

Why do they blush together? Because of common knowledge.

Initially they do not know whether their own faces are dirty, but they see the others’ dirty faces and assume their own are clean. The woman has stated that someone’s face is dirty—everyone now knows this information and knows that everyone else knows it. When they observe one another’s relieved expressions a second time, the only explanation is that all three faces are dirty.

This common knowledge changes the situation; Littlewood called the change the Dirty Face Effect. Its core is common knowledge.

The renowned crosstalk performer Liu Baorui once told the following anecdote:

In the late Qing dynasty, a successful tea merchant in Jiangnan decided to purchase an official post. After two years as county magistrate he learned that further promotion required the favor of his superior, the provincial governor. He therefore sent a large bribe and obtained an audience.

Upon arrival he was offered tea. In Qing officialdom, when a subordinate visited a superior, the subordinate was never to drink the tea; its sole purpose was to signal the end of the meeting when the superior lifted the cup.

Unaware of this custom, the magistrate, who knew a great deal about tea, immediately tasted it. Everyone present—the servant, the guards, the governor—was stunned. Even newly admitted scholars knew not to drink a superior’s tea; how could a county magistrate be ignorant of so basic a rule?

The magistrate sensed the awkwardness and said politely, “Your Excellency, in my ten years selling tea I have never tasted anything so fine. Please drink some yourself; don’t let it go cold.”

The governor could only sigh and think: were it not for the generous bribe, he would have been thrown out.

In this incident, “a subordinate must not drink the superior’s tea” and “lifting the cup ends the audience” were two items of common knowledge within the officialdom—shared understandings that everyone in the group knew others also possessed. Historian Wu Si termed such understandings “unwritten rules.”

Entering a group without its common knowledge inevitably incurs extra costs. The magistrate’s “lack of sense” made the governor dislike him; any future promotion would require still more silver.

In the Qing officialdom, the profession of “private secretary” (shiye) existed precisely to sell common knowledge. Although a general set of official rules existed, local variations abounded. A newly arrived magistrate needed to master these local customs, which were never written in books. Private secretaries knew them intimately and therefore became indispensable. Famous private secretaries, such as those from Shaoxing, could amass enough wealth after several years to become large landowners. Many officials borrowed money to hire a good private secretary.

Private secretaries received such generous treatment precisely because officials recognized the importance of common knowledge. Group-psychology founder Gustave Le Bon defined a group as a collection of people who share the same mode of thought and feeling. Common knowledge operates similarly: everyone in the group knows a certain fact and knows that everyone else knows it.

Consequently, anyone who enters a group possessing common knowledge without possessing it will be excluded—that is the force of the Dirty Face Effect. To join a group, one must first acquire its common knowledge.

#### The Gunman Effect: Staying Outside the Conflict, the Commoner’s Victory

Micro-expression keywords: Only the most outstanding individuals win in the end? Wrong. As the saying goes, the tallest tree catches the wind, and when two tigers fight, one is injured. Shelter beneath the excellence of the tall tree; be the fox behind the tigers. Let those who love conflict fight; the rest of us should simply master our skills and do our work well.

American economists fond of Westerns once devised the following game:

Three mutually hostile gunmen in a small town agree to a duel. Each wants to kill the other two. Because they are old enemies, each knows the others’ abilities:

- Gunman A hits eight out of ten shots;
- Gunman B hits six out of ten;
- Gunman C hits four out of ten.

They form an equilateral triangle. Combat is imminent.

An economic psychologist interrupts: which one is most likely to survive?

According to martial-arts novels or Hollywood logic, A should survive because of superior marksmanship. C, the weakest, should be the first to fall.

The economists’ answer is the opposite. A must aim at the greater threat, B; B must aim at A. Consequently, the weakest gunman, C, is targeted by no one. While A and B shoot each other, C can take the first shot at whichever survives. With luck, A and B may eliminate each other.

The psychologist then asks: if C shoots first, whom should he shoot?

He could aim at the greatest threat, A. If he misses, A will not retaliate, because C has demonstrated his poor aim; A would rather eliminate the more dangerous B first.

Yet if C luckily kills A, he becomes B’s only remaining threat and must fight B, who is stronger; C may then die.

Therefore, if C shoots first, the best strategy is to fire harmlessly into the air. As long as the current balance remains, C is the least threatening person present and has the highest survival probability.

The weakest gunman enjoys an advantage so long as he does not upset the balance. Because the strong overlook the weak in combat, this strategic advantage is called the Gunman Effect.

The Three Kingdoms period supplies a vivid illustration. After the Battle of Red Cliff, Sun Quan and Liu Bei defeated Cao Cao, who fled north. Guan Yu released Cao Cao at Huarong Pass, allowing him to return to Xuchang and restore Wei’s power.

The reason is simple: had Cao Cao died on the Yangtze, Sun Wu would have become the dominant power, directly threatening the still-weak Liu Bei. To keep Sun Wu occupied, a unified and formidable Wei had to survive, preserving room for Liu Bei between the two giants.

Several years later the Battle of Yiling destroyed the fragile Sun-Liu accord. Liu Bei led his entire army against Sun Quan but was routed by Lu Xun’s fire attack. Lu Xun pursued the remnants to Yufu. When he prepared to cross the river, he saw stones arranged in an ominous pattern; a sudden gale arose and he withdrew, remarking that Zhuge Liang was truly a sleeping dragon.

Although Lu Xun possessed the strength to continue the pursuit and expand Wu’s territory, he did not. A reasonably strong Shu could threaten Wei more effectively, granting Wu a breathing space of peace.

Events unfolded as Wu expected. Zhuge Liang returned to Shu, spent his remaining years launching northern expeditions (the Six Campaigns on Qishan), while Wu watched from the sidelines and enjoyed years of peaceful development.

The Gunman Effect operates between states and, more commonly, in everyday group life. Whenever interests intersect and conflict arises, avoid direct confrontation. Even when you achieve substantial results, do not draw excessive attention.

When no major stakes are involved, keep your capabilities hidden from rivals. Let your boss alone know your true competence. In the same office, avoid trying to stand out; appear somewhat dull and slow so that seemingly capable colleagues compete with and undermine one another. Simply do your work well and let your superior recognize who is truly capable.

#### Emotional Sunk Cost: The Couple’s Story

When I was studying abroad, a couple lived two doors down from me. Their only child, a six-year-old daughter, was struck and killed by a car while playing in the street. The entire neighborhood witnessed the couple’s grief. The once-helpful pair grew cold and silent; weeds overran their yard—an issue treated in the United States almost as seriously as a credit default. Their relationship also became visibly strained. They used to stroll hand in hand at dusk; at the funeral, observers noted almost no physical contact between them. Everything suggested they had lost their will to live. Left unchecked, the loving couple would likely divorce and spend the rest of their lives in regret.

The neighbors therefore devised a plan.

One night the husband, awakened by a noise he first mistook for a rat, got up to investigate. Suddenly the bedroom door was kicked open. He fell to the floor; his wife woke with a start. Five or six masked men carrying carbines burst into the room. Before the couple could react, gun barrels were pressed to their heads.

The pair did not resist. The husband forced himself to stay calm and said, “Take whatever you want, but please don’t hurt us.”

The men shook their heads. A burly figure spoke in a low voice: “Shut up. You’ve seen our faces.”

The husband replied, “I swear I haven’t. There’s an ATM nearby. My account holds more than three hundred thousand dollars. I’ll withdraw it all—just don’t harm my wife.”

Before the robbers could answer, the wife threw her arms around her husband. “No. If you go, I go. I want to stay with him.”

The burly man snarled, “Quiet. You think we don’t know your game? You want us to take you and leave your wife to call the police so they can catch us at the ATM. Not a chance…”

Suddenly another voice cut in: “Boss, there’s a car outside. Could be the cops.”

The burly man cursed. “Damn it. We have to run—now!”

The intruders fled but did not go far. They crouched beneath the bedroom window, imitating the sound of footsteps receding, then removed their masks. They were the husband’s closest friends in the neighborhood. They listened intently.

Inside, the stunned couple embraced and wept. The husband, still shaken, patted his wife’s back and comforted her. Through tears she said, “Darling, I couldn’t bear to lose both of you.”

The next day, when the husband prepared to report the incident to his best friend—a police officer in the community—the friend stopped him and revealed the truth: he had been the burly robber.

As a witness I was astonished by the Americans’ bold ingenuity, yet I also understood the emotional mechanism that produces the Concorde fallacy. The couple’s grief over their child had blinded them to each other, leaving them without the will to live. In reality they still loved one another. The friends’ extreme intervention forced them, in a moment of terror, to see each other again and to recognize what gave their lives meaning. If you have friends who have withdrawn after losing a loved one, remember that others still love them. Let the past sorrow become sunk cost and live well for those who remain.

#### The Concorde Story

In the 1960s the British and French governments jointly began developing a supersonic airliner meant to astonish the world—fast, high-capacity, safe, comfortable, and versatile.

Vast sums were poured into the project. A single engine component cost hundreds of millions of pounds; the oversized cabin, stability requirements, and aerodynamic challenges turned the aircraft into a financial black hole. France even issued supplementary national debt to keep the program alive.

As work progressed, analysts realized that the passenger volumes of the two national carriers could never generate enough revenue to recover the investment. Yet neither government could afford to abandon the project; doing so would write off billions already spent. They therefore continued pouring money into a venture they knew would never turn a profit.

The supersonic airliner finally flew in 1969 and was named Concorde. Commercial service began on 1 January 1976 on routes between Europe and the Americas. Its high operating costs left it uncompetitive, and it never achieved its commercial targets.

Knowing the plan could not succeed, the governments kept investing because they could not bear to lose the earlier outlays; losses therefore mounted. This irrational pattern, exemplified by the two governments’ actions, became known as the Concorde fallacy. In economics, costs that cannot be recovered once a project is abandoned are called sunk costs. Attachment to sunk costs is what drives the Concorde fallacy. The fallacy lies in mistakenly treating sunk costs as though they were recoverable.

By contrast, Boeing acted more rationally. After learning of the Anglo-French project, Boeing also began work on a supersonic airliner and built two prototypes, the Boeing 2707, by 1971. Market analysis soon showed the investment could not be recouped in the medium term, so the program was cancelled. Britain and France ultimately built twenty Concordes and brought the aircraft into service, but at far greater loss.

Although the Concorde fallacy originated in a “dogfight” between major powers, it is not confined to governments.

#### Personal Case: Guitar and Sunk Cost

My father loved the guitar but, busy with work, could not study it himself. He therefore placed his hopes on me and spent more than three thousand yuan on a classical guitar with a Brazilian rosewood body.

I disliked being constrained. Although I enjoyed music, I resented being forced to practice. My father saw my attitude and realized I was unlikely to study seriously, yet he still felt the three thousand yuan could not be wasted. He therefore spent another six thousand yuan on a youth classical-guitar training course.

Anyone who has studied classical guitar knows how tedious it is for a child. Before long I was leading other pupils in mischief. By the end of the semester I still could not read a full staff. My father later called it his worst investment.

He knew that further spending would only compound the loss, yet he invested the additional six thousand yuan because he over-weighted the original three-thousand-yuan sunk cost. The Concorde fallacy operated in his case as well.

Moreover, anything that can be regarded as a cost—money, time, emotion—can trigger the same error.

#### Film and Time Cost

I once took my girlfriend to a film so poor I will not name it. After fifteen minutes I could not continue and prepared to leave. She insisted we stay, arguing that walking out on a ticket that had cost more than a hundred yuan would be an even greater waste.

Our reasoning differed. She treated the money already spent as a reason to endure the remaining two hours. I viewed the hundred-plus yuan as sunk cost. If the film proved good, the outlay was justified; if merely mediocre, finishing it might still be acceptable. But if it was genuinely bad, the next two hours would be pure waste—two hours added to the original monetary loss.

#### The Story of Lu Xiangxian

Lu Xiangxian, a chancellor in the mid-Tang dynasty, served earlier as prefect of Tongzhou. One of his servants encountered the Tongzhou adjutant in the street but failed to dismount and salute. The adjutant, enraged, ordered his attendants to flog the servant—an act intended to intimidate Lu. Afterward the adjutant went to Lu’s residence to apologize, yet his tone remained arrogant: “I have offended Your Excellency. Please dismiss me from office.”

Lu, holding a book, did not look up. “A servant who fails to dismount before an official may or may not be beaten. An official who beats his superior’s servant may or may not be dismissed.” He then returned to his reading.

The adjutant sat awkwardly for half an hour before taking his leave. Thereafter he behaved with greater restraint.

#### Application in Child-Rearing Strategy

An American friend once compared Chinese and American approaches to raising children. “Punish big mistakes severely, small mistakes lightly, and never let them pass. The harshest punishment is withholding a meal.” After one prank his father ordered him to go twenty-four hours without food, though both knew the real lesson was simply that punishment was possible.

The experience taught him two things:
- He never committed a serious offense under supervision.
- He learned that, in dealing with others, it is enough to make them aware of one’s capacity to punish.

Effective child-rearing does not require frequent punishment; it requires that the child understand both that punishment is possible and that misbehavior will bring it. Constant beating or unchecked indulgence are equally unsuitable.

#### Commitment-Threat Effect in International Relations

During the Cold War the advent of nuclear weapons paradoxically made the world appear safer: each side retained a second-strike capability, so any initiator would also be destroyed. This realization led nations to emphasize “second-strike capability.”

- Indian Navy Admiral Prakash stated that India’s second-strike capability would be especially devastating.
- Russia’s Topol-series missiles gained mobility, and submarine-launched missiles entered service.

Responsible nuclear powers understand that deterrence must be credible: others must believe that using nuclear weapons would produce catastrophic consequences. The commitment-threat effect has allowed the world to survive amid weapons of mass destruction.

#### The Core of the Commitment-Threat Effect

How does one lead, supervise, or simply live among others? Machiavelli wrote in The Prince that people love a ruler of their own free will, but they fear a ruler by the ruler’s will. A prudent ruler therefore grounds authority in his own will.

People respect those who can inflict harm more than those who are unfailingly kind. The proverb “a biting dog does not bark” captures the same idea.

#### Chapter 14 Mastering Psychological Games and Seizing the Winning Edge

Some people always seem to anticipate others’ thoughts and gain the advantage; others can persuade anyone and keep both allies and rivals under control. You may think these abilities are innate and that success is therefore foreordained. I tell you otherwise: if you are less popular or less successful, it is not because you lack luck or talent; it is because you have not yet mastered the psychological tactics of social interaction.

#### Overcoming the Sunk Cost Fallacy

Experienced hunters in the rainforest know that once a crocodile seizes a leg, the only option is to sever the leg with a machete; otherwise the entire body will be lost. This “amputate-the-leg” resolve is the surest way to overcome the sunk cost fallacy. The action looks drastic, yet it minimizes total loss.

Subjective emotions, like objective resources, can also function as sunk costs.

#### Commitment-Threat Effect: The Knife That Is Never Drawn Is Always the Sharpest

Micro-expression keywords: People fear injury and therefore fear threats. A threat that cannot be carried out loses all force. To prevent others from testing your resolve, you must extinguish any hope that you will refrain from acting. The commitment-threat effect therefore has two components: first, make the other party understand that you possess the capacity to harm them; second, make clear that crossing the line will bring that harm.

#### Concorde Fallacy: The Dangerous Trap That Deepens the More One Sinks into It

Micro-expression keywords: The losses caused by the Concorde fallacy are immense yet avoidable. Avoidance requires only a clearer recognition of sunk costs. At any moment the decision to continue investing should rest on future prospects, not on costs already incurred.

#### The Prisoner's Dilemma: Advance to Force Compliance, Retreat to Bluff and Extract Information

##### Unfinished Case: Zhang Bing Verifies Company Crisis

Zhang Bing is a mid-level manager at a logistics company. Recently, the company's logistics network expansion in the southwest region failed, wiping out 70% of its liquid assets. This setback could very well trigger a total collapse. To maintain morale, only the owner and a few senior executives know the details; the information is tightly guarded from mid- and lower-level employees to prevent leaks. Zhang Bing learned the rough outline through a high-level contact at another logistics firm. Although he understands the leadership's fear of widespread panic, he must consider his own future. He needs to confirm the truth so he can plan his next steps.

He devised a method: verify the matter directly with the owner.

The next day, he entered the owner's office carrying an expense reimbursement form.

Although one management layer separates the owner, Sun, from Zhang Bing, Sun recognizes him. On several occasions Zhang Bing handled business with calm competence, leaving a strong impression despite limited direct interaction. Sun asked, "Zhang Bing, what brings you here?"

Holding the reimbursement form, Zhang Bing replied, "Mr. Sun, this is my expense report from the last business trip. Could you please stamp it for me?"

Sun asked in surprise, "According to our policy, the form only needs Manager Song's signature. Why come to me?"

Manager Song is Zhang Bing's direct supervisor and a veteran of the company. At his level and seniority, Song would certainly know any upper-level secrets. Zhang Bing had counted on exactly that point and answered, "Mr. Sun, I already went to Manager Song, but he said the company is tightening cash flow and implementing a liquidity squeeze. From now on, all reimbursements require

**Another Use of the Prisoner's Dilemma**

your personal stamp."

Sun felt a flicker of doubt. The liquidity squeeze was indeed his directive, yet he had also instructed senior managers to treat the matter as a trade secret. How could Song be so careless? This would soon make every employee aware of the cash-flow problem.

Instead of addressing the request, Sun countered, "Did your manager announce this to everyone?"

Zhang Bing said, "No, he didn't make a formal announcement. He just mentioned it casually when I went to him for the signature."

Sun quietly exhaled in relief, then said, "All right, I'll stamp your form. You can go back to work—and while you're at it, ask your manager to come see me… never mind, I'll call him myself now."

Zhang Bing nodded and left. The next day he began searching job sites, found new employment within days, and resigned.

Not long after his departure, signs of insufficient liquid assets began to appear. The collapse was swift, and the company soon declared bankruptcy.

This illustrates another application of the prisoner's dilemma: feed one party the information that "your partner has already confessed." Even if the other side does not fully cooperate, they will reveal usable clues.

##### Historical Case: Li Deyu Investigates the Ganlu Temple Case

Once economists formulated the prisoner's dilemma, law-enforcement practitioners quickly recognized its echoes in countless historical cases.

When the renowned late-Tang chancellor Li Deyu served as military governor of Zhexī, he inherited the famous Ganlu Temple case. Monks accused the previous abbot of diverting temple property for personal gain. Their evidence was the account book: every previous abbot had recorded the exact amount of gold remaining in the temple upon leaving office, yet the accused abbot's final ledger showed no gold, and none remained in the storeroom. Senior monks unanimously testified that the defendant had squandered it.

Although the defendant confessed, the confession gave no details on the gold's whereabouts. Suspecting irregularities, Li Deyu pressed the abbot repeatedly until the old monk admitted the truth: successive abbots had long followed the custom of depleting temple funds; the monks were idle and ignorant of Buddhist doctrine. The ledger had always listed one ingot of gold that had long since been consumed; the recorded figure was fictitious. The defendant, wishing to fulfill his duty, had refused to join the others and therefore prepared a fresh ledger—only to be denounced by the resentful monks.

Li Deyu half-believed the story, but the sheer number of corroborating monks forced him to find a way to test it. He ordered all monks named in the testimony brought together and seated each in a sedan chair facing a wall, isolating them from one another and from the outside. He then had his men prepare lumps of yellow clay roughly the size of the gold ingots the monks had described and instructed each isolated monk to shape his lump into the form of the gold he claimed to have seen.

The perjurers were dumbfounded. Because no gold had ever existed, they had coordinated only on weight and size, not on shape. Unable to match their stories, they confessed to giving false testimony.

Li Deyu's era had no term for the "prisoner's dilemma," yet he instinctively grasped its core: isolate the parties so they cannot exchange information. As the most social of group animals, humans rely heavily on their companions; when they cannot confirm their companions' actions, they grow anxious, and fear and betrayal readily surface.

##### Modern Case: Duke University Professor's Makeup Exam

Many people today skillfully exploit the prisoner's-dilemma mindset.

Two close friends in Duke University's chemical-engineering program, both excellent students, consistently earned B+ or higher on papers and performed well on quizzes. The night before the final exam they stayed out all night at a city bar, confident they could still handle a straightforward test.

They overslept. By the time they drove back to campus the exam had ended. The pair decided to ask the professor for a makeup exam, agreeing beforehand to claim their car had suffered a flat tire on the return trip from the city.

The professor considered the request and agreed. The next day the students arrived for the makeup. He gave each two sheets. The first, worth 40 points, covered standard course material; they finished the twenty-point section in half an hour. The second sheet contained a single question worth 60 points: "Which tire went flat yesterday on your drive back from the city?" The two looked at each other, then at the professor monitoring from the podium, and confessed.

The professor's exam and Li Deyu's clay illustrate a practical point: when using the prisoner's dilemma, block communication between the parties. If they have already coordinated their stories, locate the "blind spot" in that coordination—usually a detail such as the shape of the gold or which tire went flat.

Psychologically, the prisoner's dilemma is a state of mind. One need not create the objective conditions; it suffices to induce the subjective sense of being in a dilemma. This is not difficult: simply present one party with fabricated evidence that the other has "confessed."

##### The Prisoner's Dilemma: Advance to Force Compliance, Retreat to Bluff and Extract Information

Micro-expression Keywords The prisoner's-dilemma mindset has at least two uses: exploit information asymmetry between individuals to compel one or all of them to cooperate; or lead one individual to believe a companion has already "confessed," thereby eliciting useful information. The mindset can be applied regardless of rank—superior to subordinate or subordinate to superior, even achieving "regicide."

Two thieves are arrested, but the police lack sufficient evidence. They separate the suspects and offer each the same deal: if one confesses and the other does not, the confessor receives one year while the silent party receives ten; if both confess, each receives five years.

Under these conditions most thieves confess. Isolated from each other, each fears the other will confess to gain early release, leaving him with a ten-year sentence. Distrust and betrayal therefore prevail, and both confess—giving the police their maximum victory.

When each party can harm the other for personal gain and knows the other possesses the same capacity, each tends to strike first to avoid being harmed. This psychological dynamic is called the prisoner's dilemma. Originally an economic game-theory concept, it also carries implications for international relations, negotiation, criminal investigation, and psychology.

To understand the prisoner's dilemma in its psychological dimension, one must recognize its two necessary preconditions.

##### The Second Premise

The prisoner's dilemma arises only in the final round of a two-player game.

Vendors at train stations often sell expired mineral water, biscuits, or substandard tea eggs, whereas neighborhood supermarkets and cooked-food stalls rarely do. The reason is that transactions at a station are usually one-off; repeat business is unlikely. Each sale is therefore the last round between vendor and customer, so vendors maximize profit by cutting quality. Neighborhood trade, by contrast, is built on repeat customers; every transaction is not the final round. To secure future business, merchants maintain quality so neighbors become regulars and long-term profit is maximized.

Hence the prisoner's-dilemma mindset appears only in the final round of play.

##### The First Premise

The "prisoners" cannot communicate or establish effective trust, thereby creating the dilemma.

If the two prisoners were held together or allowed any effective contact, they would coordinate and the police would obtain nothing. Likewise, if the two criminals were lovers, father and son, or mother and son, the bond would generate sufficient trust to defeat the scheme.

Therefore, the first step in creating a prisoner's dilemma is to sever all channels of information and trust between the "prisoners."
